# Front Binding of the Manuscript

<image-desc>The front cover of this historical volume is made from light-colored **<term>pigskin</term>** <note>a sturdy leather hide frequently used in 16th-century bookbinding for its durability and ability to hold detailed impressions</note>. It features extensive **<term>blind-tooling</term>** <note>a method of decoration where heated metal tools are pressed into the leather to create a design without the use of gold or ink</note>. The layout consists of several rectangular borders within one another, decorated with intricate floral patterns. These were created using **<term>roll stamps</term>** <note>engraved metal rollers used to create continuous decorative borders</note>. In the center, initials and a date are prominently stamped. The spine is reinforced with five **<term>raised bands</term>** <note>the horizontal ridges visible on a book's spine, created by the cords used to sew the pages together</note>.</image-desc>

# THE BIBLE,
## Translated by Sebastian
## Castellio. <note>Sebastian Castellio (1515–1563) was a French theologian and a pioneer of religious tolerance. His translation of the Bible into "Ciceronian" Latin was intended to make the scriptures accessible to scholars who admired classical literature, though it was highly controversial among both Catholics and fellow Protestants like John Calvin.</note>

<insert>From those prohibited in the Index of the 1st Class.</insert> <note>This handwritten note refers to the *Index Librorum Prohibitorum* (Index of Forbidden Books). A "1st Class" prohibition was the most severe, indicating that the author’s entire body of work was banned by the Church.</note>

### TOGETHER WITH HIS OWN

<insert>This belongs to the Vienna Convent of the Order of Discalced Carmelites of Holy Father Augustine.</insert> <note>A handwritten mark of ownership indicating that, despite being a "prohibited" book, it eventually found its way into the library of a Catholic monastery in Vienna.</note>
### Annotations.

->*THE PRINTER TO THE READER.*<-

In this new translation, Reader, you will find the truth of the Hebrew and Greek meaning of the Old and New Testaments faithfully expressed, while the purity and clarity of the Latin language is preserved. You will recognize this most fully by reading it yourself and comparing it with other editions, as well as from the Preface and the Annotations, which contain clear illustrations of the more difficult matters.

->BASEL, BY JO<-
->HANNES OPORINUS.<- <note>Johannes Oporinus (1507–1568) was one of the most famous printers of the 16th century, based in Basel, Switzerland. He was known for his courage in publishing works that were often deemed radical or heretical.</note>

--- Page 7 ---
<meta>Continuity note: This page follows the title page of Sebastian Castellio’s 1551 Latin Bible. It begins the formal dedication of the work to the young King Edward VI of England.</meta>

<page-type>dedication</page-type>
<sig>α 2</sig>
<meta>archival stamp: 039516; catchword: [I might] touch (original: tingerem)</meta>

# Sebastian Castellio to Edward
## the Sixth, most illustrious King of 
### England: Greetings.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'C' depicting two human figures in a dynamic pose, possibly wrestling or an athletic contest, set against a background of foliage and classical architecture.</image-desc>

When I was publishing these books of the Holy Scriptures, which I have translated into the Latin language, most serene King of England, friends urged me to dedicate them to your Majesty. They persuaded me to do so for three reasons. First, because they said the Holy Scriptures could be offered to no one more fittingly than to him whose kingdom was a refuge <term>asylum: a place of sanctuary</term> for those harassed because of their study and defense of the Holy Scriptures. Second, because you recently assigned this same task of translating the sacred books to learned men, but were prevented by the death of one of them. <note>This likely refers to the German reformer Martin Bucer, who died in Cambridge in 1551 before he could complete his work for the English Reformation.</note> Finally, because besides other disciplines and languages, you were also particularly devoted to Latinity—in which we have here taken some care—and you had an erudite master for that purpose. <note>King Edward VI was famously well-educated, tutored by humanists like John Cheke.</note> Led by these reasons, I—a man of the lowest station—dared to offer my labors <term>vigilias: literally "night-watches," a common metaphor for scholarly work done late into the night</term> to you, most illustrious King. I hoped that the higher the peak of dignity upon which God's kindness had placed you, the more mercifully you would receive these humble offerings, for the love of Christ, who, though equal to God, did not hesitate to descend to the lowliest.

If it pleases you, King, and if you do not refuse to read this translation, I will now explain what my purpose was in this undertaking. I have strived for this translation to be faithful, Latin, and clear, as far as possible, so that no one might henceforth be deterred from reading these books by the obscurity of the language, or its harshness, or even the unfaithfulness of the interpretation. But we have given the greatest consideration to clarity and faithfulness. For as far as Latinity <note>original: "latinitatem" - the quality of writing in pure, classical Latin style.</note> is concerned, speech is nothing other than a kind of garment for the subject matter, and we are the tailors. The matter itself remains the same; it is made neither better by elegance of speech nor worse by its plainness. Nor does someone truly love the subject if they are held back from learning it by unpolished language. Furthermore, we see that the secrets of the Gospel were delivered to us in unrefined words, taken from the common people who were unlearned, so that nothing would be attributed to human eloquence.

However, since it was necessary for one engaged in this study to weigh not only the words but also the things themselves (without which the words often cannot be understood), if I noticed anything obscure in the meantime—not only regarding the words but also the subject matter—I attempted to illuminate it briefly. And in explaining the words, I was somewhat bolder. But as for the matter [itself]... <note>The text ends here as the page turns; the final word of the Latin page, "at-", continues as "tingerem" on the next page.</note>

<summary>Sebastian Castellio dedicates his Latin Bible translation to King Edward VI of England, citing England's role as a sanctuary for scholars and the King's own humanist education as primary reasons. He argues that his translation aims for a "classical" Latin style to make the Bible more accessible to educated readers without compromising its sacred truths.</summary>
<keywords>Sebastian Castellio, King Edward VI, Bible translation, Latinity, humanist scholarship, religious refuge, Martin Bucer, Reformation</keywords>

--- Page 8 ---
<meta>Continuity note: This page continues the preface of Sebastian Castellio’s 1551 Latin translation of the Bible, dedicated to King Edward VI. On the previous page, Castellio began explaining his reasons for the dedication.</meta>

<page-type>preface</page-type>
<page-num>2</page-num>
# PREFACE

...I might touch upon these things, the cause was partly the present undertaking of translation, which deals with words; and partly—indeed much more so—my own ignorance. Since these books are written about divine matters, it is necessary that the more human we are, the less understanding we have of them. And indeed, if we wish to admit the truth, our age is still submerged in the deep darkness of ignorance. The clearest testimony of this is found in such grave, persistent, and destructive disagreements; in so many futile gatherings concerning these controversies, and in the great number of books being born daily that disagree with one another as much as heaven and earth <note>original: "toto caelo"; a Latin idiom meaning "by the whole sky," implying they are poles apart</note>. For if there is one spirit of God, and one truth, it is necessary that those in whom the same spirit and truth dwell should be as one and feel the same in spiritual matters. And if the clearest day of truth had dawned for us, we would never light so many dim lamps of books. 

Indeed, as I sought the cause of this ignorance, it seemed difficult to find. It cannot be attributed to a lack of learning or the arts, since nothing could be more erudite than our age. Yet, despite such great studies, such knowledge of languages, and so many arts practiced over so many years, far from making much progress, things grow worse by the day. Therefore, as I considered this matter more attentively, I seemed to have found one and the truest cause of this ignorance: vice and impiety. 

<margin>Daniel 12</margin> Thus the prophecy says to Daniel: *The wicked shall act wickedly, and none of the wicked shall understand.* 
<margin>Psalm 25</margin> And David, on the other hand: *The secret of Jehovah is made clear to those who fear him.* <note>Castellio uses "Ioua" (Jehovah) throughout his translation to approximate the Hebrew Tetragrammaton, rather than the traditional Latin "Dominus" (Lord).</note>
<margin>Isaiah 6</margin> And Isaiah: *Bind up the testimony, seal the teaching among my disciples.* 

Therefore, if we wish to know the secrets of Jehovah hidden in these books, we must fear and worship Jehovah, and obey him as becomes his disciples. This is the true way to the knowledge of divine things; this is the only key to opening this seal of divine secrets. Whoever possesses this key will require no other; whoever does not have it will apply all other keys to this lock in vain. If there were in us a true love and fear of God, and if we put as much study and effort into it as others put into gathering money, or into literature, or into various disciplines, or into seeking honor, then not only would this thick ignorance be absent—allow me to say what I feel—this thick ignorance which holds the world captive; but the earth would be as full of the knowledge of Jehovah, which is to say true piety, as has been promised to us, if we are wise. 

And thus would be born that truly golden age <note>The "Golden Age" is a classical concept of a lost era of peace and harmony, here blended with Christian millennial expectations.</note> in which all would be taught by God, and that which the mighty Lord <term>armipotens Ioua: literally "Jehovah, powerful in arms," a poetic epithet for the Lord of Hosts</term> promised would come to pass in these words: 

<margin>Malachi 4</margin> THEY SHALL BEAT <note>original: "CVDENT EX"</note> their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks; nor shall nation lift up arms against nation, nor shall they learn war anymore; and everyone shall dwell under his own vines and fig trees with no one to make them afraid, for the mouth of the mighty Lord has spoken. 

<margin>Isaiah 11</margin> And this also: THE WOLF SHALL DWELL <note>original: "VERSABITVR"</note> with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and a little child shall lead the calf and the lion and the bull together; the cow and the bear shall graze together while their young lie down together; the lion shall eat straw like the ox; the nursing infant shall play over the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand over the viper's den...

<meta>catchword: ...[will] shake (original: agitabit, from the phrase "manum agitabit")</meta>

<summary>Castellio argues that the religious conflicts and ignorance of his time stem from a lack of true piety and fear of God rather than a lack of scholarship. He envisions a "Golden Age" of peace and divine understanding, quoting biblical prophecies of harmony between enemies.</summary>
<keywords>ignorance, religious dissension, piety, fear of God, Jehovah, Golden Age, prophecy, peace, translation philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>Continuity note: This page continues Sebastian Castellio’s preface to his 1551 Latin translation of the Bible, dedicated to King Edward VI. Having argued that the ignorance and religious conflict of his era are caused by vice, Castellio now quotes biblical prophecies to describe the state of peace and divine knowledge that God has promised to the "Christian commonwealth," contrasting these promises with the violent reality of the 16th century.</meta>

<page-type>preface</page-type>

# PREFACE

α 3

...it will happen. Nowhere will evil or wickedness be done in my holy mountain, for the earth shall be so full of the knowledge of the Lord <note>original: "Iouæ cognitionis"; Castellio uses "Ioua" as a Latinization of the Hebrew name for God, Yahweh, which he felt was more accurate than the traditional "Dominus"</note>, as the waters cover the sea. Likewise, that which was said to Jerusalem—that is, to the Christian commonwealth <note>original: "Christianorum rempub." or Republic of Christians</note>: 

<margin>Isaiah 60</margin>

The men who afflicted you will come humbly to you, and all your detractors will worship the prints of your feet; they will call you the city of the Lord, the Zion of the Illustrious Israelites. Because you were deserted, hated, and inaccessible, I will make you an eternal majesty, a perennial joy, so that you will suck the milk of other nations and the breasts of kings; and you will know that I am the Lord your savior and redeemer, the God of the house of Jacob. Instead of bronze I will bring gold, instead of iron I will bring silver, instead of wood, bronze, instead of stones, iron; and I will make peace your administration and justice your magistrate. No longer shall cruelty be heard in your land, nor devastation or calamity within your borders, and you shall call your walls salvation and your gates praise. No longer shall the sun provide light for you by day, nor the brightness of the moon shine upon you, but the Lord will be your eternal light, and your God your glory. Your sun shall set no more, nor your moon wane: for the Lord shall be your eternal light, the day of your mourning being finished. Your people, all righteous, shall possess the land forever, the branch of my planting, the work of my hands, that I may be honored. The least shall grow into a thousand, and the smallest into a populous nation: which I, the Lord, will hasten in its time. Likewise that:

<margin>Ezekiel 36</margin>

I will fetch you from the nations, and gather you from all lands, and bring you into your own country, and sprinkle you with pure water, so that you may be cleansed from all your filthiness; I will purge you from all your dung-idols <note>original: "stercoreis diuis"; a literal and polemical translation of a Hebrew term for idols, suggesting they are as worthless as refuse</note>, and give you both a new heart and a new spirit in your breasts; and having removed the heart of stone from your bodies, I will give you a heart of flesh: and having put my spirit into your bodies, I will make you obey my statutes and keep my judgments. By doing this, you will remain in the land that I gave to your ancestors: and you shall be my people, and I will be your God, and I will deliver you from all your impurities.

<margin>Revelation 20</margin>

This is the happiness, O King, and the perfect knowledge and obedience of God promised to Christians in these and many other places, and especially in the Book of Revelation. Indeed, the more I consider this by unfolding the sacred books, the less I see it fulfilled thus far, however you understand those oracles. But there arise the lazy voices of those who distrust, who consider it insane if anyone dares to hope for better things than our own times.

<margin>Isaiah 59</margin>

...as if indeed the hand of God were shortened, or his ear dull: or as if one should despair because it has never been so; and not rather hope for it precisely because it has not been, and he promised it who never lies and is even able to restore life to the dead. Truly, one must either confess that these things will be, or that they have already been, or God must be accused of lying. But if anyone says they have been, I will ask him when they were. If he says "in the time of the Apostles," I will ask why the knowledge of God and piety—which were promised to be eternal and more abundant than the waves of the sea—were so meager and faded away so quickly. But if he says "in our time," we will marvel at this "peace," which beats our plowshares and pruning-hooks into swords, and turns household goods and homes into cannons <note>original: "bombardas"; Castellio uses a contemporary term for artillery to highlight the hypocrisy of his age</note> and ramparts. But this peace exists, I believe, among the leaders of letters <note>A sarcastic reference to the "Republic of Letters" or the academic/clerical elite who claim to possess truth while the world is at war</note>.

<summary>Castellio quotes various biblical prophecies of a future age of universal peace and divine knowledge, arguing that since these conditions clearly do not exist in the war-torn 16th century, they must still be in the future.</summary>
<keywords>Sebastian Castellio, biblical prophecy, Isaiah 60, Ezekiel 36, religious peace, Christian Commonwealth, 16th-century warfare, divine knowledge</keywords>

<meta>Continuity note: This page continues Sebastian Castellio’s preface to his 1551 Latin translation of the Bible, dedicated to King Edward VI. In the previous section, he argued that religious knowledge is currently incomplete and that the peace promised in Scripture has not yet arrived. He now addresses the "teachers of the people" regarding the violent religious controversies of the Reformation era.</meta>

# PREFACE

...and the teachers of the people. Whence, then, come the wars of tongues and pens, far more harmful than those of iron? Whence so many and so grave controversies, which for so many centuries and through so many disputes could not be settled, and which almost always break out into the shedding of the blood of the weaker ones, while no one doubts his own judgment, and no one fails to condemn others? We envy, we speak evil, we repay not only evil with evil, but often good with evil: and if anyone disagrees with us on even a single point of religion <term>religionis... puncto: a specific theological detail or doctrine</term>, we condemn him, and through every corner of the earth we hunt him with the spear of tongue and pen. We rage with iron, flame, and water <note>original: "ferro & flamma & undis"; a reference to the execution of heretics by the sword, burning at the stake, or drowning</note>, and we remove the defenseless and the poor from the nature of things. We say it is not permitted for us to kill anyone, yet we hand them over to Pilate <note>Castellio is criticizing the practice where the Church "delivered" heretics to secular authorities—likened here to Pontius Pilate—to carry out the death penalty, while claiming the Church itself did not shed blood</note>, and if he should release the person, we deny that he is a "friend of Caesar." And what is most shameful of all, we cry out that we do all these things out of zeal for Christ, and by his command and in his name, and we hide the ferocity of the wolf under a lamb's skin. O age! Truly, shall we be bloodthirsty out of zeal for Christ, who shed his own blood so that the blood of others would not have to be shed? Shall we uproot the weeds <term>zizania: based on the Parable of the Tares (Matthew 13), where weeds are allowed to grow with the wheat until the harvest</term> out of zeal for Christ, who commanded the weeds to be left until the harvest, lest the wheat be uprooted? Shall we persecute others out of zeal for Christ, who commanded that if our right cheek is struck, we should turn the left? Shall we inflict evil on others out of zeal for Christ, who commanded us to return good for evil?

<margin>1 Corinthians 13</margin>
Where, then, will be that charity <term>charitas: Christian love or "agape," the selfless love for one's neighbor</term> so greatly commended to us, without which, though you hold the tongues of men and of angels, and know all things, and by faith move even mountains, and give away all your possessions, and even hand over your body to be burned, you are nothing? But if anyone boasts of charity, let him consider whether he has the fruits of charity, and performs those things which Paul records as belonging to charity. Charity is kind, he says: charity is not reckless, does not swell with pride, does not behave shamefully, does not seek its own interest, is not easily provoked, thinks no evil, does not rejoice in injustice, but rejoices in the truth: it bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things: charity never fails. Now indeed remain faith, hope, and charity: but the greatest of these three is charity, and in it lies the fulfillment of the law.

<margin>Romans 13</margin>
Finally, charity covers a multitude of sins and heals them. But if today it has grown so cold that hatred reigns in its place—and yet God has promised that pious and just age which I mentioned above—it must be completely admitted that many, and even the greatest, things promised in the oracles <note>original: "oraculis"; referring here to the prophetic books of the Bible</note> have not yet been fulfilled. Ignorance of this fact is the reason why we make God’s gifts quite meager, thin, and lean, and why we interpret most of the prophets’ oracles foolishly, if not ridiculously, while we try to explain, without the Spirit and without the event <note>original: "sine euentu"; meaning before the prophecy has actually been fulfilled in history</note>, those things which are to come and cannot be understood except by those taught either by God or by the outcome of the event, fearing, of course, lest we seem to be ignorant of anything. Since these things are so, O King, and since our age is still blind in such darkness of ignorance, I judge that we must be cautious again and again, lest we commit any act of imprudence.

<margin>1 Maccabees 4</margin>
(as there are many), in these matters I judge that we should follow the action of Judas Maccabeus and his followers, who, when they did not know what to decide regarding the altar of burnt offerings, [kept] its...

He suggests that much of the Bible remains misunderstood and that people should exercise humility and caution rather than violent certainty in theological disputes.</summary>

# PREFACE

...they placed the stones on the mountain of the temple in a suitable place, until a prophet should arrive to give an oracle concerning them <note>This refers to 1 Maccabees 4:46, where the defiled stones of the altar were stored until a prophet could decide their fate; Castellio uses this as an example of holy restraint in the face of uncertainty.</note>. Or rather consider the example of Moses, to whom the command had just been given in express words <margin>Numbers 15</margin> that if anyone committed a sin against the law willfully, he should pay with his life; and yet, he was unwilling to kill the man who had gathered wood on the Sabbath day until an oracle had been returned specifically on that matter. And Moses was a faithful minister of God, and endowed not sparingly with his spirit. To say nothing, meanwhile, of the counsel of Gamaliel, who showed that if this matter is from men, <margin>Acts 5</margin> it will be dissolved; but if it is from God, it cannot be dissolved, lest perhaps one be found to fight against God. 

But if we think these things are better known to us than they were to Moses (since these are times when no one thinks himself to be in error), yet certainly we ought not to be both the accusers and the judges. Rather, we must obey Paul, who thus commands: <margin>Romans 14</margin> "If anyone is weak in faith, help him without doubt in your mind. Who are you to condemn another's servant? He stands or falls to his own master. But he will stand: for God is able to establish him. But you, why do you condemn your brother? Or you, why do you despise your brother? Each of us shall give an account of himself before God." Therefore, let us no longer condemn one another. For if we condemn, we shall be condemned, and it will be repaid to us with the same measure. 

It would be better (in my judgment, at least) to follow the Roman law regarding claims <term>vindicijs: legal assertions of right, specifically regarding a person's status</term>, which was of this kind: If anyone who had hitherto behaved as a free man was called into court by someone asserting him to be a slave, while the case was pending, the claim was granted in favor of liberty <term>secundum libertatem: a legal principle where the person is presumed free until proven otherwise</term>. That is, he whose liberty was put in danger remained in the same condition as free men until it was made clear and pronounced in judgment whether he were free or a slave. And rightly so. For when his condition was in doubt, if he happened to be free, and in the meantime while the lawsuit was pending he had been treated as a slave, a grave injustice would have been done to a free man. 

But how much more equitable is it for this to be done in a capital case: especially in religion, in which the gravest sin is committed. Let us wait for the sentence of the Just Judge, and let us strive not that we ourselves may condemn others, but that we commit nothing for which we should fear condemnation. Let us obey the Just Judge, and allow the tares to remain until the harvest, lest perhaps (while we wish to be wiser than the Master) we root out the wheat. For neither is the end of the world yet here, nor are we the angels <term>genij: here used to refer to the "reapers" or spiritual beings assigned to the final judgment</term> to whom this task has been mandated. 

Add to this that it is absurd for a spiritual war to be waged with earthly weapons. The enemies of Christians are vices, against which we must contend with virtues, and contrary evils must be cured by contrary remedies: so that teaching may drive out ignorance, patience may overcome injury, modesty may resist pride, diligence may be opposed to sloth, clemency may fight against cruelty, and a sincere and religious mind—approving itself to God—may overthrow hypocrisy, along with a pure spirit that seeks to please God alone. These are the true and truly victorious weapons of the Christian religion: not that the office of the teacher be handed over to the executioner <note>original: "carnifici mandetur prouincia doctoris"</note>, and that the outside of the cup be cleansed before the inside. And I wish these things to be said by me concerning religion only. For as pertains to crimes—murders, adulteries, thefts, false witnesses, and such...

<summary>Castellio argues against the execution of heretics, citing biblical examples of restraint (Moses, Gamaliel) and Roman legal principles that favor liberty during disputes. He advocates for "spiritual weapons" like teaching and patience rather than state-sponsored violence to resolve religious differences.</summary>

# PREFACE

...blish. <note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely completing a word from the previous page.</note> As for the rest, which God has both commanded to be punished and prescribed in what manner they should be punished, these things are not called into controversy; nor did God command concerning them obscurely, and they pertain to the defense of good people—unless we wish to be murdered in our own beds, as the times indeed are now. Nor, truly, is there any danger that if a magistrate—appointed by God for the defense of the good—should send a convicted murderer to the cross, he might be killing a good man; nor has anyone ever defended murder, not even a murderer himself. 

But the account of religion and the understanding of the Sacred Scriptures is far different. For since these things have been handed down obscurely, and often through riddles, and have now been disputed for more than a thousand years without the matter being able to be settled—nor can it be settled in the absence of Charity <note>Latin: *charitate*. Castellio emphasizes "Charity" or "Love" as a necessary intellectual and spiritual tool for resolving religious conflict.</note>, which is the resolver of all controversies and the chaser-away of ignorance—and for that reason the earth has been filled with innocent blood: we must certainly (however much we seem to ourselves to know all things) we must, I say, fear lest among the thieves (whom we rightly crucify) we also wrongly crucify Christ. 

And if we not only allow Turks and Jews to live among us (of whom the former have little love for Christ, and the latter even hate him mortally), but we also bear with the slanderous, the proud, the envious, the greedy, the unchaste, the drunkards, and other outrages of men, and we live with them, feast with them, and rejoice with them: we ought at least to grant this common air and breath to those who profess the same name of Christ with us, and who harm no one, and are of such a mind that they would rather die than say or do anything other than what they believe ought to be said or done. 

Meanwhile, I will not even mention that no kind of men is less to be feared. For he who prefers to lose his life rather than speak what he does not feel (for he would sin if he did so, and he who compels him, compels him to sin) is not, I believe, to be feared that he might be corrupted by money or any other thing. 

And indeed, I have persuaded myself of this: that none are more obedient to princes and magistrates than those who simply fear God and show themselves faithful in that which they know. The obedience of others is indeed feigned, nor does it last longer than it is either compelled by fear or enticed by utility. But he who is driven by conscience to obey, and who has learned from God’s teaching that magistrates and powers must be obeyed—even the unjust ones, let alone the just—it is necessary that his obedience be true and eternal, since God (who is the cause of that obedience) remains true and eternal. 

That point indeed (to return to the proposal) is true beyond controversy: *He who judges quickly, hastens to repentance* <note>original: "Ad pœnitendum properat, citò qui iudicat." This is a common Latin proverb urging caution in legal and moral judgment.</note>; and many have repented of having judged, but no one has repented of having suspended judgment. And he who is more inclined toward mercy than toward anger imitates the nature of God, who, although he knows we are guilty <term>sontes: those who are guilty or criminal</term>, nevertheless delays his sentence for a long time and waits until a correction of life occurs. For he who kills immediately leaves no room for repentance. 

But if anyone dares to contradict these things, it will be necessary for him to confess that "blood" is being attacked by him, and defended by us. As for which of the two will have an easier defense of his cause before God the Judge, let him see to it himself. I have this clearly in view: that no one can repent of mercy, patience, kindness, or obedience; but of cruelty and rash judgment, one cannot *not* repent. But if that is the safest path...

<summary>Castellio argues for religious toleration, asserting that while civil crimes are clear, scriptural interpretation is complex and requires charity rather than execution. He maintains that people of conscience make the most loyal subjects and that mercy is the safest path for any judge.</summary>

# PREFACE

...since these times are full of dangers, one must be insane who knowingly and willingly throws himself into danger. Nor indeed do I say these things to you, most illustrious King, because we have heard anything unfavorable about you. Since you are still of that age which is kept under the care of tutors, your own character (especially to us, separated by so great a distance of lands) cannot be sufficiently known. Those who come from there certainly say that such is your disposition and humanity that they hope for all the best from you; to whose hope we so far agree that we hope and even pray for things better (if it were possible) than the best. Since, therefore, we see that our bodies are delivered into your hands by God, but your minds are in the hand of God, we are moved by examples, and we attempt to meet the danger with a manly effort, judging that an evil can never be avoided too soon. Therefore, we pray to God that He may put such a mind into you, that you may be as much more concerned about your own souls (which are in God’s hand) as those are about their bodies who see their lives placed in your hand: as much as the destruction of the soul is more grievous than that of the body. We desire, I say, for you to be such as God commands you to be in these words: <margin>Deuteronomy 17</margin>

> When it shall happen that the king sits on the throne of his kingdom, let him write for himself this law from the Levitical priests in a book, and let him have it with him and read it all the days of his life, so that he may learn to revere the Lord <note>Original: *Iouam*. Castellio used "Ioua" as a Latinization of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton (YHWH/Jehovah), a distinctive feature of his translation.</note> his God, and take care to obey all the words of this law and these institutes, lest his heart be lifted up in pride against his kinsmen, nor let him turn aside from the discipline to the right or to the left, so that he may live long in his kingdom, both he and his sons, among the Israelites.

Likewise Solomon, speaking of a good king, in these words: <margin>Proverbs 16</margin>

> An oracle is upon the lips of the King; his mouth does not commit a crime in judgment. To act wickedly is an abomination to Kings: for the throne is established by justice. Just lips please kings, and they love those who speak uprightly. The king’s wrath is a messenger of death, and a wise man will appease it. In the serenity of the King’s countenance is life, and his favor is like a cloud of the latter rain.

To possess wisdom is far more excellent than gold. Moreover, the head of wisdom is the fear of God, which ought to be before our eyes day and night, both as a bridle against evil and a spur toward the good. These things I had at present, King, about which to warn you—not indeed as a prophet, nor as one sent by divine power, but as one of the many who hate dissension and strife, and who desire that religion be practiced more through charity and piety of heart than through disputes and external matters. Nor indeed does it escape me that nothing is said by me which has not been said by others before me. But those things which are right, being said by many and for so long until they are obeyed, is not useless. Receive therefore, King, this work of ours kindly and humanely: and if there is time (and there ought to be time) and if it pleases you (and it ought to please you), read the Sacred Scriptures with a pious and religious mind: and so prepare yourself to rule your kingdom as one who is mortal and who will give an account to the immortal God. I wish for you the clemency of Moses, the piety of David, and the wisdom of Solomon.
-> Farewell: at Basel, in the month of February. In the year one <-

<meta>Continuity note: On the previous page, the author (Sebastian Castellio) concluded his address to King Edward VI of England, urging him toward religious tolerance and piety. # ADMONITION TO THE READERS.

<image-desc>A square decorative initial 'N' at the beginning of the text, featuring a landscape with classical architecture and figures, surrounded by a border of scrolling foliage.</image-desc>

**W**E HAVE translated the New Covenant <note>original: "Novum foedus," a term Castellio preferred over "Testamentum"</note> from the Greek; the Old from the Hebrew, with the exception of Judith, Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus <note>also known as the Wisdom of Sirach</note>, Baruch, the Maccabees, and parts of Esther and Daniel: which, since they do not exist in Hebrew, we have translated from the Greek. There are also six chapters in Daniel written in Syriac <note>Castellio uses "Syriac" to refer to Aramaic</note>, namely from the second to the seventh; and four in the first book of Ezra <note>Esdras</note>, from the fourth to the seventh: which we, since we have not learned the Syriac language, have interpreted from the translations of others. We translated the Fourth Book of Ezra from Latin into Latin, since we found it in no other language. 

But if we found anything in the Greek or the old Latin translation of any book that exists in Hebrew, which was not in the Hebrew itself, we have inserted it and marked it with the Greek letter **G**, the Latin letter **L**, or both, **G. L.**, up until the letter **H**, by which is signified a return to the Hebrew text. We have done the same in the books translated from the Greek if we found anything additional in the Latin. 

Furthermore, so that you may know to what extent my translation is to be trusted or doubted, it must be known that in these books there is much difficulty, partly in words, partly in the subject matter, and partly in both. The difficulty of words is either in simple or compound words. Simple words are often obscure, pertaining to those things which are either rarely used or merely mentioned without being described: such as most plants and animals; likewise those things whose form changes by nation or by time, such as clothing and vessels. Regarding these, we often have nothing to affirm with certainty: no more than those who interpret Cato <note>Marcus Porcius Cato, author of "De Agricultura"</note> know what he means by a *nassiterna* <note>a water pot with a spout</note>, a *scutriscum* <note>a tray or dish</note>, an *urpex* <note>a heavy rake or harrow</note>, and certain other things; or what Cicero means by the phrase *sessum facere* <note>to take a seat/to sit</note>, which Cicero himself confesses he does not know. 

Therefore, when we translate a "bat," a "diver-bird," or a "heron," and others of that kind, we do not wish our interpretation to be held as certain: we follow only what is probable and ask to be forgiven. But understand that doubts of this sort exist in the Hebrew words. For as far as the Greek is concerned, since that language is more refined and better known, we have less doubt. 

And so much for simple words. The difficulty of compound words, however, usually depends on the difficulty of the subject matter: and unless the matter is known, it cannot be resolved. Such is the case in the twenty-seventh chapter of Isaiah: *Will he strike him with a stroke like that of his striker?* or, *will he be killed with a killing like that of his slain?* For there, due to ignorance of the matter, I do not know whether for "His" and "Their" one should put "Its": since the Hebrew relative is ambiguous, just as in French, if you translate it word-for-word, it sounds like "his killer" <note>original: "son tueur"</note>. 

And difficulties of this kind are sometimes employed by the prophets on purpose. We have occasionally noted this in the margin, lest our interpretation deceive anyone. Some matters are human, others divine. I call "human" those things which can be understood by human intellect even without a prophetic spirit: such as ceremonies, the description of Moses’s tabernacle, the temple of Solomon and Ezekiel, the visions of the Prophets, the parables of Christ, and the entire Apocalypse. For these are narrations of things done, or as if done: even if you do not understand what they signify, that ignorance does not prevent you from being able to translate them into whatever language you wish. Therefore, if any difficulties arose in this category, they were explainable. Although it may happen that in some places a more significant word could be used by one to whom the matter is known. 

I call "divine," however, those things which are covered and outlined by the shadow of human things: such as what Moses teaches, that "hearts must be circumcised"; and David, that the "true sacrifice is a dejected and afflicted spirit"; and Christ, that one "must be born again"; and Paul, that one "must die to the world and cast out the leaven of malice"; and other things of this kind, in which the fruit and end of the sacred books are situated, and without which reading the sacred letters is as useless as the circumcision or washing of the body is if the soul remains uncircumcised and unwashed. But here it is fitting to remember what Peter writes in the first chapter of the second epistle: "We have," he says, "a more certain prophetic word, to which you do well to be attentive, as if to a..."

<meta>Catchword: lucen- (referring to "lucernae" or lamp)</meta>

<meta>Continuity note: On the previous page, Sebastian Castellio detailed the specific Hebrew, Greek, and Latin sources he used for his translation, as well as his method for marking insertions from different manuscripts. Here, he shifts from technical bibliography to the spiritual and intellectual philosophy guiding his work, emphasizing humility and the role of the Holy Spirit.</meta>

## TO THE READERS.

You have a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star <note>original: "lucifer"</note> rises in your hearts: as long as you understand this first, that no prophetic writing <note>original: "fatidicum scriptum"</note> is of private interpretation. For an oracle was never produced by human will, <margin>Note well.</margin> but divine men spoke by the inspiration of the Holy Spirit. From these words of the Apostle, it can be understood that the mind of the sacred scriptures and their divine meaning cannot be perceived by any arts, any sciences, any human industry, memory, or talent. It is a divine matter, which only the Spirit of God—the same who dictated it—knows and teaches. And indeed, the Spirit usually teaches those who are the most unlearned, the weakest, the most despised, the poorest, and the most low-born among men, so that we may not claim any credit for our own erudition, arts, or excellence.

Therefore, I, who do not possess that prophetic spirit, do not generally touch upon those sacred matters, except insofar as it pertains to understanding the flow of the discourse. Or, if I ever step outside these boundaries (which I do so that anyone who wishes may know what we have observed), I follow that reasoning which is the fourth in my discourse <note>referring to his specific method of linguistic analysis</note>, about which we wrote something in our notes on 1 Corinthians 14. Since this is a most dangerous path if one is abandoned by others, we do this only sparingly and when led by many clear reasons; yet we judge that we should not even trust our own reasoning blindly, since we often struggle with ignorance, and what seem to be good reasons to us may not be. Therefore, if anyone has better insights, they may—as far as we are concerned—omit our annotations and use the bare translation.

Furthermore, when I write in some places that I do not understand a certain passage, I do not want it to be taken as if I clearly understand everything else. Rather, I want it known that in other places I have at least some dim light, but in those, none at all; and also, so that my translation is not trusted too much in such places. Yet I do not point out everywhere what I do not understand; for that would be an infinite task. 

Again, when I explain certain oracles in the Prophets <note>original: "Vatibus," literally "Seers" or "Bards"</note>, such as in Isaiah regarding Emmanuel, Cyrus, Sennacherib, and the like, I do not declare them as if nothing more hidden or divine lies buried there. Instead, I set out the human elements shown by the words or the historical events, and I leave the more divine things that are hidden there to those to whom God has granted His Spirit more abundantly. In the meantime, my efforts can (in my own judgment) harm no one, especially since I profess that I am not a Prophet, but a student of the Prophets and of the truth.

It remains for me to beg you, Reader, to take this labor of ours in good part. If I fail to satisfy you in some place, grant me pardon. I have done what I could; and what may displease you will perhaps please another; and again, what you approve, another will condemn. If you find any error of ours (and in such a difficult and long work there will perhaps be not a few), grant us pardon and advise us in a friendly manner, just as we have studied to be of friendly use to you. Or if you are unwilling, or unable, at least advise others whom you see using this translation of our error as soon as possible, especially if there is any danger in it. For we wish to deceive no one, if it can be avoided. Therefore, although we have labored on this work for many years, continuously, with great leisure, good health, and great eagerness, we will hereafter—God willing—take care to correct anything that was erroneous, whether pointed out by others or recognized by ourselves. But if anyone brings a better translation
->to light, we will gladly yield to him.<-

<summary>Castellio humbles himself before the reader, arguing that true understanding of the Bible comes from the Holy Spirit rather than human intellect, and he invites corrections to his translation.</summary>

GENESIS 1

# GENESIS

## CHAPTER I.

<margin>Acts 14:17; Psalms 32, 135; Ecclesiasticus 18</margin>
<margin>The creation of the world.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring a man (possibly a shepherd or biblical figure) in a landscape with a building in the background.</image-desc>**IN THE** beginning God created the heavens and the earth. But when the earth was idle and unformed, and the deep was covered in darkness, and the divine spirit 
<margin>Hebrews 11</margin>
balanced itself over the waters, God commanded that light should exist, and light existed: and when God saw that it was good, he separated the light from the darkness, and he called the light Day, and the darkness Night. Thus, from evening and morning, the first day emerged.

<margin>Psalms 135; Jeremiah 10; Psalms 148; Psalms 32, 88 & 135; Job 38</margin>
Next, God commanded that an expanse <note>original: "liquidum," literally "a fluid thing" or "clear space." Castellio uses this term to describe the atmosphere or firmament.</note> exist among the waters, which would disjoin water from water: and he made the expanse to divide the water which is above the expanse from that which is below it. This being done, he named the expanse Heaven: thus, from evening and morning, the second day emerged.

Next, God commanded that the water which was under the heaven should flow together into one place, so that the dry land might appear. This being done, he named the dry land Earth, and the gathering of the waters the Sea. And noticing that this thing was good, he commanded that the earth bring forth shoots, fruitful herbs, and fruit-bearing trees, each producing fruit according to its kind, and in which their own seed would be within the lands. And so it was done: and the earth brought forth shoots, that is, kinds of fruitful herbs and fruit-bearing trees, in which their own seed was contained. He noticed that this thing also was good: thus, from evening and morning, the third day emerged.

<margin>Psalms 135</margin>
Next, God commanded that lights exist in the expanse of heaven, to distinguish day from night, which would bring about signs, seasons, days, and years, and shining in the expanse of heaven, would illuminate the lands. And so it was done. And God made two great lights, the greater for the governance of the day, the lesser for the governance of the night: then also the stars: and he placed them in the expanse of heaven to illuminate the lands, to govern day and night, and to distinguish light and darkness. And this also he saw was good. Thus, from evening and morning, the fourth day emerged.

Next, God commanded that the water bring forth swimming creatures, and birds that would fly above the earth through the air. And God created great sea monsters <note>original: "cete," referring to whales or massive sea creatures.</note>, and every kind of gliding animal, and winged birds, whichever are moved drawing their origin from the water. When he saw that this thing was good, he made them fruitful with these words: Be fruitful, multiply, fill

<column-break/>

the waters in the sea, and let the birds be multiplied above the lands. Thus, from evening and morning, the fifth day emerged.

Next, God commanded that the earth bring forth kinds of living creatures, namely cattle, and creeping things, and beasts of the earth. And so it was done, and God made diverse kinds of beasts of the earth, and cattle, and all things creeping upon the ground. When he saw that this thing was good, he spoke thus: Let us make man in our image, like ourselves, who may rule over the fish of the waters, the birds of the air, the cattle, and finally the whole earth, and whatever moves upon the earth.

<margin>The creation of man. Ecclesiasticus 3; Below 5, 9; 1 Corinthians 11; Matthew 19; Ecclesiasticus 17; Below 8, 9</margin>
And so God created man in his own, that is, in the divine image; specifically, he created them male and female, to whom he then gave fertility, addressing them thus: Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it: and have dominion over the fish of the waters, the birds of the air, and all the beasts that move upon the lands. Behold, I hand over to you (he said) all herbs which are fruitful on every soil of the earth, and all trees endowed with orchard-fruit, bearing seed, which you may use for nourishment.

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 39</margin>
But to all the beasts of the earth, and the birds of the air, and to whatever moves upon the lands animated by the breath of life, I give all green herbs for food.

<margin>Mark 7</margin>
These things being finished, God noticed all things, whatever he had made, were very good. Thus, from evening and morning, the sixth day emerged.

## CHAPTER II.

<margin>Exodus 20; Hebrews 4</margin>
**THUS** the heavens and the earth were perfected, and all their abundance, and on the seventh day God finished his work which he had made, and on the seventh day, he rested <note>original: "feriatus est," meaning to keep holiday or be at leisure.</note> from all the work he had performed. And therefore he made the seventh day auspicious and sacred, because on it he had rested from all the work which he had created and made.

This is the origin and creation of the heaven and the earth. When the Lord God <note>original: "Ioua Deus." Castellio famously used "Ioua" as a Latinization of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton (YHWH), where the Vulgate used "Dominus."</note> had made the earth and heaven, and no plant of the field was yet on the earth, and no herb had yet sprung up (since the Lord God had not yet rained upon the earth, nor was there a man to till the ground), a vapor exhaled from the earth, which irrigated its entire surface.

<margin>1 Corinthians 15; Paradise.</margin>
But when the Lord God had formed man from the dust of the earth, and had breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, by which man was made a living being, he placed him in an orchard, which he had planted in Eden toward the east. Moreover, the Lord God had produced from the earth every kind of tree, both beautiful to the sight and suitable for eating: also the tree of life in the middle of the orchard, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 24</margin>
A river flowed out of Eden to irrigate the orchard, and from there it divided into four heads: the name of one is Pishon, which river goes around the whole of Havilah, where there is gold (the gold of that region is of the highest quality) and where there is also bdellium and the onyx stone. The second river is called Gihon, which traverses all of Ethiopia. The third is called Tigris: it flows toward the east, where Assyria is. The fourth is the Euphrates. Into this orchard of Eden the Lord God brought the man, and placed him there, so that he might till it, and guard—

Moreover, the Lord <note>original: "Ioua," Castellio's Latinization of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton YHWH, which he uses throughout instead of the traditional "Dominus"</note> God had said: "It is not fitting for Adam to be alone; I will make for him a suitable helper." For when He had brought to him all the beasts of the earth, which He had formed from the ground, and all the birds of the air, to see how he would name them—so that whatever name Adam called each living creature, that should be its name—and when Adam had given names to the cattle, the birds, and all the beasts of the field, <margin>a. While other living creatures each had females of their own kind, Adam alone lacked this assistance.</margin> there was not found for Adam himself a suitable helper. Then Adam said: <margin>1 Cor. 11, Matt. 19, Mark 10, Eph. 5, 1 Cor. 6</margin> "Now at last, this is bone of my bones <note>literally "member of my members"</note> and body of my body. She shall be called 'woman' <note>original: "mulier"</note> because she was taken from man." Therefore a man, leaving his father and mother, shall cleave to his wife, and they shall grow together into one body.

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>The Serpent.</margin>
Furthermore, though Adam and his wife were both naked, yet they felt no shame. Now the serpent, who was the most cunning of all the beasts of the field that the Lord God had made, approached the woman with these words: "Why has God forbidden you to eat from all the trees of the orchard?" The woman replied: "We may eat the fruit of the trees of the orchard; but the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the orchard, God has forbidden us to eat, or even to touch, lest we be struck with death." And the serpent said: <margin>1 Cor. 11</margin> "You shall by no means be punished with death. For God knows that if you eat of it, then your eyes will be opened, and so you will be like gods, knowing good and evil." Here the woman, seeing that the tree was both suitable for food, pleasing to the eyes, and desirable for gaining knowledge, took of its fruit, and ate; and she also gave some to her husband, who <margin>Eccl. 25, 1 Tim. 2</margin> also ate. Then, their eyes being opened, they both realized they were naked; and having woven together fig leaves, they made themselves loincloths. Then, hearing the voice of the Lord God walking in the orchard toward the evening breeze <note>original: "zephyrum," referring to the cool western wind</note>, they both hid themselves from His sight among the trees in the middle of the orchard. But the Lord God called out to Adam: "Where are you?" He replied: "Hearing Your voice through the orchard, I was terrified because I was naked, and I hid myself." And He said: "Who showed you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree from which I commanded you not to eat?" Adam answered: "The woman whom You assigned to me, she gave to me from the tree, and I ate." And the Lord God said to the woman: "Why did you do this?" The woman replied: "I was deceived by the serpent, and I ate." Then the Lord God spoke to the serpent thus: "Because you have done this, you shall be the most cursed of all the beasts of the field, both tame and wild; you shall walk on your belly, and you shall eat dust as long as you live. Furthermore, I will establish such enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers, that he shall strike your head, and you shall strike his heel." Then to the woman He said: "I

<column-break/>

will afflict you with many pains and hardships; you shall bear children in pain, and you shall be dependent upon your husband, <margin>1 Cor. 4</margin> and he shall rule over you." Then to Adam He said: "Because you complied with your wife and ate from the tree which I had forbidden you to eat, the ground shall be ᵃ unhappy <note>In this context, "infelix" means barren, cursed, or unproductive</note> because of you, and you shall seek food from it with labor all through your life; meanwhile it shall produce thorns and thistles for you, and you shall eat the herbs of the field. By the sweat of your brow you shall sustain your life, until you return to the ground from which you were taken. For you are dust, and to dust you shall return." Adam gave his wife the name Eve, because she was the mother of all the living. And the Lord God made for Adam and his wife tunics of skin, and when He had clothed them, He spoke thus: "Since man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil, there is a danger that he might also stretch out his hand to the tree of life, and having plucked and tasted its fruit, live forever." Therefore, He drove him out from the orchard of Eden to cultivate the ground from which he had originated; and having cast out the man, He placed Cherubim at the eastern part of the orchard, and a vibrating flaming sword, to guard the entrance to the tree of life.

### CHAPTER IIII.

<margin>Cain and Abel.</margin>
Now Adam had relations with his wife Eve, and she became pregnant and gave birth to Cain: so named because, having brought him forth, she said, "I have obtained a man from the Lord." She also gave birth to his brother Abel. This Abel was a shepherd, and Cain was a farmer. After some time, when Cain had offered a gift to the Lord from the fruits of the earth, and Abel from the firstborn of his sheep and their fattest parts, the Lord looked upon Abel and his gift; but <margin>Heb. 11</margin> upon Cain and his gift He did not look. Cain took this so bitterly that his face fell. And the Lord said: "Why do you take this so bitterly? Or why does your face fall? Surely if you do well, you will be accepted; if you do not do well, sin lies at the door, and it shall depend on you, and you shall rule over it." But Cain lured his brother Abel with his words into the countryside, and there he attacked and killed him. <margin>Wis. 10, Matt. 3, 1 John 3, Jude 1; a. It moves to punishment in a certain way, as if by a complaint of blood. See margin of Habakkuk 2 at the letter G.</margin> Then the Lord addressed Cain thus: "Where is your brother Abel?" He replied: "I do not know. Am I my brother's keeper?" But the Lord said: "What have you done? ᵃ The very blood of your brother cries out to me from the earth. Therefore you shall be cursed from the ground, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood from your hand; it shall no longer provide its strength to you when you cultivate it, and you shall wander as an exile across the world." Here Cain said: "My guilt is greater than can be forgiven. Look, today I am banished by You from the very soil of the earth; avoiding Your sight, I shall wander as an exile across the world, so that whoever finds me will kill me." But the Lord said: "On the contrary, whoever kills Cain shall suffer a sevenfold punishment." Therefore He placed a mark upon him, so that no one who encountered him would kill him. Thus Cain, departing from the sight of the Lord, dwelt in the land of Nod, which is to the east of Eden. He had a son by his wife named Enoch, and from Enoch's name he called the city he had founded. To this Enoch was born Irad, and Irad fathered...

There follows the enumeration of the progeny of Adam, from the time when God first created him and made man in the divine likeness; that is, He created them male and female, gave them fruitfulness, and called them by the name of "man" on the very day of their creation. Adam was one hundred and thirty years old when he fathered a son in his own likeness and image, whom he named Seth. After he was born, Adam lived eight hundred years and in the meantime fathered other children of both sexes. Thus, reaching the nine hundred and thirtieth year of his life, he died. Seth, in the one hundred and fifth year of his life, fathered Enosh; after he was born, having completed eight hundred and seven years and fathering other children of both sexes in the meantime, he finally died while in his nine hundred and twelfth year. Enosh, when he had lived ninety years, fathered Kenan; then he lived eight hundred and fifteen years, and thus, having fathered other sons and daughters in the interval, he died when he had completed the nine hundred and fifth year of his life. Kenan, in his seventieth year, fathered Mahalalel; after he was born, he lived eight hundred and forty years, and having fathered other sons and daughters in the meantime, he died in the nine hundred and tenth year of his life. Mahalalel, being sixty-two years old, fathered Jared. Then, after fathering others, he died eight hundred and thirty years after the birth of Jared, that is, in the eight hundred and ninety-fifth year of his life. Jared, being one hundred and sixty-two years old, fathered Enoch. Then he lived eight hundred years while fathering others in the meantime, and so he died in the nine hundred and sixty-second year of his life.

### CHAPTER VI.

And when the multitude of men began to increase across the world and daughters were born to them, the most powerful of men, captivated by their beauty, chose wives for themselves from the entire number. Then the Lord said He was unwilling for His spirit to contend with men for so long, seeing as they were carnal, and He determined their lifespan to be one hundred and twenty years. There were 
<margin>Giants.</margin>
Giants in the earth in those times. From the marriages of those powerful men were born the Heroes, men famous from all memory. When the Lord saw that the vices of men were increasing on the earth, and that every effort and thought of their minds was directed toward worse things every single day, He regretted having made men on the 
<margin>Matthew 1</margin>
earth, and He was grieved in His heart. For that reason, He decided within Himself to wipe away the men He had created from the face of the ground; not only men, but also the cattle, the reptiles, and the birds: so much did He regret having made them. Yet He was favorable toward Noah. This is the lineage of Noah: Noah was the most just and upright man of his age, 
<margin>Sirach 44</margin>
and one who conducted himself according to the will of God; he fathered three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. Otherwise, the world was corrupted against God and full of cruelty. ### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>2 Peter 2</margin> When Noah had done all these things that God commanded, the LORD <note>original: "Ioua," Castellio's classical Latin rendering of the Divine Name</note> spoke to him as follows: "Go inside, you and your whole family, into the ark; for indeed I have noticed that of everyone in this age, you are easily the most righteous in my sight. From all the clean four-footed animals, take seven pairs of mixed sex; but from the unclean, take two. Likewise from the birds, take seven pairs, also of mixed kind, so that their offspring may be preserved over the whole earth. For seven days from now, I will cause it to rain upon the lands for forty days and as many nights, and I will wipe out every living thing that I have made from the face of the earth." Noah did all these things according to the LORD's command.

<margin>Matthew 24, Luke 17, 1 Chronicles 3</margin> He was six hundred years old when the earth was flooded with water. For the sake of escaping this flood, he entered the ark together with his sons, his wife, and his sons' wives. Also, from the four-footed animals, both clean and unclean, and from the birds, and from everything that moves upon the ground, pairs came to him into the ark, gathered from males and females, just as God had commanded him. Therefore, when those seven days had passed, a deluge of water flooded the earth.

<margin>The Flood.</margin> In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, on the seventeenth day of the second month, all the springs of the Ocean broke forth, and with the passages of heaven opened, it rained heavily upon the lands for forty days and nights. On that very same day that Noah—along with his sons Shem, Ham, and Japheth, his wife, and his three daughters-in-law—entered the ark, there also entered with them every kind of wild beast and cattle, and things that creep on the ground, and birds, both small and large <margin>a. Both smaller and larger.</margin>, from all bodies endowed with the breath of life; when pairs of all these had entered to Noah into the ark, and indeed all in pairs as God had commanded him, the LORD shut him in. Then for forty days such a flood inundated the lands that the ark was moved from its place by the great mass of water and lifted up from the ground; finally, as the waters grew stronger and stronger over the lands, it was carried along by the waves. These waters increased so greatly that by their overflow all the highest mountains, whichever are under the whole heaven, were not only covered, but were covered to a depth of fifteen cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of measurement based on the length of the forearm, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note>. Thus all living bodies that moved upon the lands were destroyed—birds, cattle, wild beasts, and all things creeping on the ground, as well as humans. Everything, I say, whatever on earth drew the breath of life through its nostrils, died. Thus every living thing was deleted and removed from the world, whether humans, cattle, creeping things, or birds; Noah alone survived, and those who were contained within the ark with him.

### CHAPTER VIII.

After the waters had prevailed upon the lands for one hundred and fifty days, God remembered Noah and all the animals and cattle that were with him in the ark, and he sent a wind over the lands to check the waters. And so, with the springs of the deep and the passages of heaven blocked, the rain from heaven ceased. Then the waters, flowing back here and

there from the land, finally began to decrease after the passage of one hundred and fifty days, and the ark came to rest on the seventeenth day of the seventh month upon the mountains of Ararat. The waters continued to decrease until the tenth month; on the first day of that month, the tops of the mountains became visible. And after forty days, Noah opened the window of the ark which he had made and sent out a raven, which went out and kept returning until the earth was dried of the waters. He also sent out a dove to explore whether the earth was relieved of the waters. Since she found no place to set her foot, because the earth was covered with water everywhere, she returned to Noah in the ark; he reached out his hand and took her, bringing her into the ark to himself. After waiting another seven days, he sent the dove out from the ark again; she flew back to him toward evening, carrying a plucked olive leaf in her beak, from which Noah understood that the earth was uncovered from the waters. He waited yet another seven days and then sent the dove out, and she never returned to him again. In the six hundred and first year, on the first day of the first month, when the waters had flowed away from the earth, Noah removed the covering of the ark and saw that the surface of the earth had emerged from the waters. On the seventeenth day of the second month, the earth being dry, God commanded Noah to go out of the ark, together with his wife, his sons, and their wives. He was also to bring out with him all the animals that were with him—birds, four-footed animals, and finally whatever moved upon the lands—so that they might spread through the lands and produce many offspring. Thus Noah went out along with his sons, his wife, and his daughters-in-law, and with every kind of beast, creeping thing, and bird—briefly, with every kind of creature that moves on the earth.

<margin>Noah leaves</margin> Then he built an altar to the LORD, on which he made a complete sacrifice <note>original: "solidum... sacrificium," implying a whole burnt offering where the entire animal was consumed by fire</note> using victims from every kind of clean cattle and birds. The LORD, delighted by the sweetness of the scent, resolved in his own mind never again to treat the earth with such severity on account of humans (whose efforts and inclinations are wicked even from childhood), so as to never again destroy all mortal things as he had done. "Never again," he said, "as long as the earth exists, shall seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night cease."

<margin>2 Peter 2</margin>

there from the earth, finally decreased after the one hundred and fifty days had passed, and the ark settled upon the mountains of Ararat on the seventeenth day of the seventh month. The waters continued to decrease until the tenth month; on the first day of that month, the tops of the mountains appeared. After forty days, Noah opened the window of the ark which he had made and sent out a raven, which went out and returned until the earth was dried of the waters. Then he sent out a dove to see if the waters had subsided from the face of the earth. When it found no place to set its foot, because the earth was covered with water everywhere, it returned to Noah in the ark; he reached out his hand, caught it, and brought it to himself in the ark. After waiting another seven days, he sent the dove out again from the ark, and it flew back to him toward evening, carrying a plucked olive leaf in its beak; from this, Noah understood that the earth was cleared of the waters. He waited yet another seven days, then sent out the dove, which never returned to him again. In the six hundred and first year, on the first day of the first month, when the waters had flowed off the earth, Noah removed the covering of the ark and saw that the surface of the earth had emerged from the waters. On the seventeenth day of the second month, the earth being dry, God commanded Noah to go out of the ark, together with his wife, his sons, and their wives. He was also to bring out with him all the animals that were with him—birds, four-footed beasts, and finally whatever moved on the lands—so that they might spread through the lands and produce manifold offspring. And so Noah went out together with his sons, <margin>Noah exits.</margin> his wife, and daughters-in-law, and with every kind of beast, serpent, bird—in short, with every kind of thing that moves on the earth. Then he built an altar to Iova, where, using victims from every kind of clean cattle and bird, he offered a whole burnt sacrifice. Delighted by the sweetness of this aroma, Iova determined in his own mind never again to pursue the earth with such severity <margin>Matthew 18</margin> on account of men (whose strivings and inclinations are wicked even from childhood), so as to destroy all mortal things again as he had done. "Never again," he said, "as long as the earth exists, shall sowing and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night cease."

But you, be fruitful and inhabit the earth in abundance by multiplying your kind." Then

Now the whole world used the same speech and the same manner of talking. As people moved from the east, they found a certain plain in the land of Shinar, where they settled and began to encourage one another to make bricks and bake them thoroughly. They used

Abraham stood before Jehovah <note>The text uses "Ioua," a Latin representation of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton, usually rendered as Jehovah or Yahweh in English.</note>, approached him, and said: "Will you truly destroy the good along with the wicked? Then Abraham said: "I will ask this of you one last time, Lord, if I am not a burden to you: What if ten are found?" He replied, "I will not destroy it even for the sake of the ten."

**A**braham then set out from there toward the south and settled between Kadesh and Shur, living as a foreigner in Gerar. Because he said there that Sarah was his sister rather than his wife, Abimelech, the king of the Gerarites, arranged to have her brought to him. But God came to him by night in a dream with these words: "Know that you must die because of the woman you have taken, for she indeed has a husband." Here Abimelech, who had not touched her, said: "Lord, will you kill even the innocent? Did he not say to me himself that she was his sister, and did she not say herself that he was her brother? I did this with a sincere mind and unstained hands." God said to him in the dream: "I also know that you did this with a sincere mind, and therefore I prevented you from committing a crime against me, nor did I permit you to have relations with her. But now, return the woman to her husband, who is a prophet <note>original: "uates" — a term for a seer or diviner, here used for Abraham as an intercessor.</note>, so that by his prayer you may obtain safety. But if you do not return her, know that both you and all who are yours must die." Abimelech rose early in the morning and, having called all his people together, explained the whole matter to them, which caused a great fear to come upon them. Then, calling for Abraham, he spoke to him thus: "What have you done to us? Or what have I committed against you, that you would bring such great guilt upon me and my kingdom? You have certainly acted toward me against your duty. What was in your mind when you did this?" Abraham replied: "I was afraid that if by chance there was no fear of God <note>original: "nulla... religio" — referring to the lack of divine law or moral restraint in the area.</note> in this place, I would be killed because of my wife. Furthermore, she really is my sister on my father’s side, though not on my mother's, and so I took her as my wife. But when God drew me away from my father’s house, I asked this favor of her: that in whatever place we came, she should say I was her brother." Then Abimelech gave sheep, oxen, male servants, and female servants to Abraham, and returned his wife Sarah to him, saying: "My lands lie open to you; you may live wherever it seems best to you." Then speaking to Sarah, he said: "I have given your brother a thousand pieces of silver, which you may use as a defense of your honor <note>original: "pudoris defensione" — literally a covering or protection of her modesty/reputation.</note> before all your people and before strangers." Then, at Abraham's prayer, God healed Abimelech, his wife, and his female servants, and restored to them the power of childbearing. For on account of Sarah, Abraham’s wife, the Lord had closed up all the wombs of Abimelech’s household.

Then Abraham returned to his servants, and they set out from there and came together to Beersheba, and Abraham lived there. After these things happened, it was announced to Abraham that his brother Nahor had fathered children by Milcah: Uz the firstborn, Buz, Kemuel (from whom the Syrians are descended), Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph, and Bethuel, who later fathered Rebekah. Besides these eight born of Milcah, Nahor fathered Teba, Gaham, Tahash, and Maacah by his concubine named Reumah.

### CHAPTER XXIII.

<margin>Sarah dies.</margin>
When Sarah had completed one hundred and twenty-seven years, she died in Kiriath-arba (which is the same as Hebron) in the land of Canaan, where Abraham came to mourn and weep for her. Then, leaving his deceased wife, he addressed the Hittites with these words: "I am a stranger and a foreigner among you: grant me the possession of a burial place among you, where I may bury my dead and remove her from my sight." To this, the Hittites, answering Abraham, said: "Listen to us, Lord. You are a divine prince among us: choose from our burial grounds where you may bury your dead. None of us will deny you his own tomb,

<column-break/>

preventing you from burying [her] there." Here Abraham, when he had stood up and bowed respectfully to the Hittite inhabitants, said: "If it is your heart's desire that I commit my deceased to a tomb, grant me this further favor: intercede for me with Ephron, the son of Zohar, that he may grant me the double cave <note>original: "cauernam duplicem" — referring to the Cave of Machpelah; the name Machpelah is derived from a Hebrew root meaning "double."</note> which he has at the edge of his field. Let him assign it to me in your presence for the full price in silver, for use as a burial place." Now Ephron the Hittite, who was then present among them, answered Abraham in the hearing of all the Hittites as many as had come to the assembly, with these words: "Listen to me instead, my Lord: I give you both the field and the cave of the field, and I do so in the sight of my people, where you may bury your dead." Then Abraham, having offered a humble bow to the inhabitants, replied to Ephron in the hearing of the same: "Rather, you listen to me: I will give you money for the field; accept this from me, and so I will bury my dead there." To him Ephron said: "Lord, listen. This field we are discussing is worth four hundred shekels <note>original: "siclis" — the shekel was a standard unit of weight for silver used in commerce.</note> of silver, if you wish to bury her at such a cost." Having heard this, Abraham weighed out the silver for Ephron according to his appraisal in the presence of the Hittites—specifically, four hundred shekels of commercial-grade silver. Thus Ephron’s field with the double cave, which field is opposite Mamre, along with the cave itself and all the trees that were within its entire boundary, was legally transferred to Abraham as a possession in the presence of all the Hittites who had come to the assembly. Afterward, Abraham buried his wife Sarah in that cave in the land of Canaan. In this manner, the field, together with the cave, was assigned to him by the Hittites for use as a burial place.

### CHAPTER XXIIII.

<margin>Abraham adjures his servant to find a wife for Isaac from among his own people.</margin>
Now when Abraham had grown old and advanced in age, with the Lord prospering him in all things, he spoke to the servant who was the elder of his house and in charge of all he owned, with these words: "Place your hand under my thigh, that I may adjure you by the Lord, the God of heaven and earth, not to take a wife for my son Isaac from the Canaanites among whom I live; but proceed to my own native land, and fetch one for him from there." The servant said to him: "What if the woman is unwilling to follow me to this region? Should I then lead your son back to the region from which you originated?" Abraham said: "Take care that you do not lead my son back there. The Lord God of heaven, who drew me away from my father’s house and my native soil, who spoke with me and swore that he would give this land to my offspring—He, I say, by sending his angel <note>original: "genio"</note> before you, will bring it about that you take a wife for my son from there. But if the woman should be unwilling to follow you, you shall certainly be released from the obligation of this oath, provided that you do not lead my son back there." Then the servant, having placed his hand under the thigh of his master Abraham, swore an oath regarding that matter. Then, taking ten of his master’s camels, he set out, carrying with him some of all his master’s goods, and reached the town of Nahor in Mesopotamia.
