## CHAPTER XXV.

<margin>1 Chronicles 1. Keturah.</margin>
Abraham took another wife named Keturah, by whom he fathered Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. Jokshan fathered Sheba and Dedan. From Dedan came the Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim. <margin>Abraham dies.</margin>
When he had completed one hundred and seventy-five years, having lived a happy life to a ripe old age, he departed from life and was gathered to his people. His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the double cave on the land of Ephron, the son of Zohar the Hittite, which is opposite Mamre. This land was purchased by Abraham from the Hittites, and there he and his wife Sarah were buried. After Abraham died, his son Isaac, with God’s blessing, lived near the well of Lahai-roi.

## CHAPTER XXVI.

<margin>Isaac moves to Gerar because of famine.</margin>
Now there was another famine in the land, besides the earlier one that had occurred in the time of Abraham. So Isaac went to Abimelech, the king of the Philistines, at Gerar. The Lord appeared to him and warned him: "Do not go down to Egypt, but settle in the land I will show you. Stay in this region for a while. I will be with you and bless you; to you and your offspring I will give all these lands. I will multiply your offspring like the stars in the sky—keeping the oath I swore to your father Abraham—and through your offspring all the nations of the earth will consider themselves blessed, because Abraham listened to my voice and kept my statutes, commandments, decrees, and teachings." So Isaac lived in Gerar. When the men of that place asked about his wife, he said she was his sister; he was afraid that if he said she was his wife, the men might kill him because Rebecca was so beautiful. But after they had been there a long time, Abimelech, king of the Philistines, looked through a window and noticed him playing <note>original: "ludentem" — implying affectionate or marital intimacy</note> with his wife Rebecca. He called Isaac over and rebuked him: "But she is your wife! Why then did you say she was your sister?" Isaac replied: "I did it so that I would not be killed because of her." Abimelech said: "Is this how you should have treated us? Someone might easily have slept with your wife, and you would have brought guilt upon us." Then he issued an order to all the people: "Anyone who touches this man or his wife shall be put to death." Isaac sowed crops in that land and in that same year reaped a hundredfold, and with the Lord's favor he grew greater every day until he became extremely wealthy. He possessed many flocks of sheep and goats, herds of cattle, and many servants. Consequently, the Philistines became envious of him and stopped up all the wells that his father Abraham's servants had dug during Abraham's lifetime, filling them with earth. Abimelech himself told Isaac: "Leave us, for you have become far more powerful than we are." So Isaac departed from there, camped in the Valley of Gerar, and made his home there. He reopened the wells that had been dug in the days of his father Abraham and which the Philistines had filled after Abraham’s death, giving them the same names his father had used.

But when Esau noticed that Isaac had prayed for good fortune for Jacob and had sent him into Mesopotamia to take a wife from there, and had forbidden him from taking one from the Canaanites—and that Jacob, obeying both parents, had departed—and when he saw that the Canaanite women did not please his father, he went to Ishmael, the son of Abraham, and took his daughter Mahalath, the sister of Nebajoth, into marriage, in addition to the wives he already had. Jacob, however, hurrying from Beersheba toward Haran, reached a certain place as the sun was setting, where he stayed the night; and using the stones that were in that place as a pillow, he lay down. To him <margin>A ladder reaching from earth to heaven.</margin> in his dreams appeared a ladder, which, resting on the earth, reached its top to heaven; through it, divine spirits <note>original: "genij," referring to angels or celestial messengers</note> were seen ascending and descending. And standing above it, the LORD <note>The text uses "Ioua," a Latinization of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton, Jehovah.</note> spoke thus: "I am the LORD, the God of Abraham your father, and of Isaac: the land upon which you lie, I will give to you and to your offspring. This offspring, increased like the dust, shall be spread toward the sea, to the east, to the north, and to the south; and in you and in your progeny all the nations of the earth shall be blessed. <margin>Deuteronomy 12:19</margin> And I (as you shall know) will be with you and protect you wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land, nor will I ever desert you until I fulfill what I have promised you." Then Jacob, having awakened from sleep, said: "Surely the LORD is in this place, and I did not know it." But how terrifying is this place? (he said, terrified) "It is nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven." Then in the morning when he rose, the stone he had placed under his head he set up as a pillar <note>original: "cippum," a commemorative monument or headstone</note>, and poured oil over the top of that stone, and called the place by the name Bethel <note>Meaning "House of God"</note>, whereas that town was previously called Luz <note>original: "Lusa"</note>. He also pronounced a vow

<margin>Jacob's cunning.</margin> the rods. And as often as the stronger of the flock conceived, he placed the rods in their sight in the troughs, so that they would breed near them. But in the breeding of the less vigorous ones, he did not place them. So it happened that the less vigorous were Laban's, but the stronger were Jacob's. In this way, the man increased his wealth immensely, and acquired a numerous flock of sheep and goats, and servants, and camels, and donkeys.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.

<margin>The abduction of Dinah.</margin>
Now Dinah, the daughter whom Jacob had by Leah, went out to see the women of that region. When Shechem—the son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of that land—saw her, he seized her and violated her. Seized by deep love for the girl, he spoke to her with charming words and pleaded with his father Hamor to take her for him in marriage. When Jacob heard of the defilement of his daughter, he remained silent until the arrival of his sons, who were away in the fields with the livestock. Meanwhile, Hamor went to Jacob to speak with him. By then, Jacob’s sons had returned from the fields upon hearing the news; they were burning with great grief because such a disgraceful crime had been committed against an Israelite, as Jacob’s daughter had been violated contrary to all law. Hamor addressed them with this speech: "My son Shechem is captivated by love for your daughter. Give her to him in marriage, and enter into an alliance with us by giving us your daughters and taking ours in return. Then live with us; settle in our territories as you please, using them as your own possession." Shechem also spoke to the girl's father and brothers: "Grant me this favor, and I will give whatever you impose upon me. Demand as large a dowry and gift as you wish; I will provide whatever you decide, provided you give the girl to me in marriage." To this, the sons of Jacob responded to Shechem and his father Hamor with a deceitful speech (because their sister Dinah had been defiled), saying they could not do what was asked—give their sister to a man who had a foreskin <term>foreskin: the sons of Jacob refer to the lack of circumcision, which was the physical sign of their covenant with God</term>, for that would be a disgrace to them. They said they would only indulge their desire on this condition: if they would conform to them by circumcising every male among them. Only then would they give their daughters to them and take theirs in turn, living together to become one people. But if they did not agree to be circumcised, they would take the girl and depart. This speech pleased Hamor and Shechem, and the young man did not delay in finishing the matter, for he loved Jacob's daughter; furthermore, he was the most powerful in his father’s entire house. Therefore, Hamor and Shechem came to the assembly of the town and informed their citizens that these men were peaceably disposed toward them and could inhabit and use the land, as there was enough territory for them. They urged the citizens to take the Israelites' daughters as wives and give their own in exchange. However, they noted that the men would only consent to live with them and become one people if every male among them was circumcised, just as the Israelites were. By this pact, the Israelites' cattle, wealth, and all their beasts would become theirs, provided they won them over to a common life by complying. Influenced by this speech, all the citizens circumcised every male among them. On the third

<column-break/>

<margin>The destruction of Shechem.</margin>
day, while they were still in pain, two of Jacob’s sons, Simeon and Levi (Dinah’s brothers), took their swords and boldly entered the town. They slew every male and put Hamor and his son Shechem to the sword, then took Dinah from Shechem’s house and departed. The rest of Jacob’s sons arrived at the slaughter and plundered the town where their sister had been defiled. They carried off the sheep, goats, oxen, donkeys, and everything in the town and the fields; they plundered all their wealth, all the children and women, and finally everything in the houses, taking them into captivity. But Jacob, accusing Simeon and Levi, showed that he had been cast into great difficulties by them and brought into the deadly hatred of the Canaanites and Perizzites who lived there; for they were few in number, and the locals would unite against them and destroy him and his family. To this, they replied that it was not right that their sister should be treated like a prostitute.

## CHAPTER XXXV.

<margin>Jacob is commanded to go to Bethel.</margin>
Afterward, Jacob was admonished by God to move to Bethel to live there, and to build an altar there to the God who had appeared to him when he was fleeing from his brother Esau. He commanded his household and all his people that, having removed the foreign gods they held, they should be purified and change their clothes. He told them they would set out for Bethel, and there he would build an altar to God, who had heard him in his most difficult times and helped him on his journey. They gave to Jacob all the foreign gods they possessed, as well as the earrings they wore in their ears; after he hid these under an oak tree near Shechem, they set out. A divine terror was struck into the neighboring cities so that they did not pursue Jacob's family. Thus Jacob arrived at Luz, located in Canaan (which is the same as Bethel), with all his people. "I am God Almighty," He said. "Multiply your descendants greatly, so that a nation, or rather a multitude of nations, may come from you, and kings shall also come from your loins. For the land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac, I will give to you and to your posterity that follows." Having spoken thus, God departed from him from that place. Joseph is bought by Potiphar.

Now Joseph, having been led down into Egypt, was bought by Potiphar—an official <note>original: "eunuchus," often used for high-ranking court officers.</note> of Pharaoh and the captain of the guard <note>original: "magister equitum," literally "master of the horse," but here a title for the head of the palace guard.</note>, an Egyptian man—from the Ishmaelites who had brought him there. Therefore, the master left everything to Joseph, so that he no longer concerned himself with anything except what he ate. Now Joseph was of singular beauty and grace. For that reason, once things were así arranged, his master's wife <margin>Joseph is enticed by his mistress.</margin> cast her eyes upon him and urged him to sleep with her. It happened one day that he entered the house to perform his duties while all the domestic servants were away. She grabbed his cloak and urged him to sleep with her. But he, leaving his cloak in her hand, fled and rushed outside. Then the woman, seeing that his cloak was left in her hand and that he had fled outside, called out to the servants and said: "See how this Hebrew was brought to us to insult us! He came to me to force himself upon me. But when I raised a loud cry, hearing it, he left his cloak with me and fled outside." So she kept the cloak with her until Joseph’s master came home. When he returned, she told him the same story: that the Hebrew servant he brought had come to mock her, and that when she cried out, he had left his cloak with her and fled. Upon hearing his wife’s words accusing his servant of such an injury against her, the master became <margin>Psalm 104.</margin> enraged and threw Joseph into the prison where the king's prisoners were kept in chains. Yet even there the LORD was present with him and showed him kindness; He won him the favor of the chief jailer, so that the jailer committed all the prisoners of that house into Joseph’s power and entrusted him with the administration of everything that was done there. The jailer did not have to supervise anything under Joseph’s care because the LORD was with him and made everything he did prosper.

### CHAPTER XL.

After these things, it happened that two of the King of the Egyptians' officials—one the chief cupbearer <note>original: "praegustatorum," the one who tastes food or drink for the king.</note> and the other the chief baker—were placed in custody by order of the king, who was angry at some offense they had committed against him. This custody was the prison in the house of the captain of the guard, the same place where Joseph was confined. The captain of the guard put Joseph in charge of them to serve them. After they had been in custody for several days, they both had a dream on the same night, each with its own distinct meaning. When Joseph came to them in the morning and noticed they were sad, he asked <margin>The dreams of Pharaoh's officials.</margin> why their faces were so gloomy that day. They replied that they had dreamed and had no one to interpret them. Joseph said: "Does not the interpretation belong to God? Tell them to me now." Then the chief cupbearer explained his dream in this way: "In my dream, a vine appeared before my eyes, and on the vine were three branches. As it budded, it brought forth flowers, and from them clusters of grapes ripened. I was holding Pharaoh’s cup in my hand, and I took the grapes and squeezed them into the cup, and placed it in Pharaoh’s hand." Joseph said: "This is the meaning: The three branches are three days. Within three days, Pharaoh will order you to be brought out and restored to your former position, so that you may serve the cups just as you used to do when you were his cupbearer. Therefore, when it goes well for you, remember me and do me this favor: mention me to Pharaoh to get me out of this house. For I was stolen away from the land of the Hebrews by theft, nor have I done anything here for which I should be shut up in prison." When the chief baker saw that the interpretation was favorable, he said: "I also dreamed that there were three white baskets on my head. In the top basket was every kind of baked food for Pharaoh, but birds were eating them out of the basket on my head." Then Joseph said: "This is the significance: The three baskets are three days. Within three days, by Pharaoh’s command, your head will be taken off <note>The Latin 'securi ferieris' refers to being struck by an axe or executed.</note> and you will be hung on a pole, where the birds will feed on your flesh." On the third day, which was Pharaoh's birthday, he gave a banquet for all his servants. He ordered the chief cupbearer and the chief baker to be brought out before his people; he restored the former to his post of service to handle the cups, but the latter he hanged on a pole, just as Joseph had interpreted to them. Yet the chief cupbearer was unmindful and gave Joseph over to oblivion.

...ears of grain growing on a single stalk, plump and elegant: after which grew up others, thin and scorched by blight, which consumed the choice and full ones. Then Pharaoh, having woken up, saw it was a dream. In the morning, troubled in spirit, he ordered all the soothsayers and wise men of Egypt to be summoned, and told them the dream: when none of them could interpret it, <margin>the chief of the bake<insert>rs</insert></margin> spoke to Pharaoh in this way: "Here I shall recall my sin. When you, Pharaoh, were angry with me and the chief baker, and handed us over into custody in the house of the captain of the guard <note>original: "magistri equitum," literally "master of the horse," but here a title for the head of the palace guard</note>, it happened that we both had a dream of different meaning on the same night. Now, there was a certain Hebrew youth there with us, a servant of the captain of the guard: to whom, when we each told our dream, he interpreted it for both of us, and the outcome proved his interpretation, with me being restored to my place and the other being executed <note>original: "in crucem acto," literally "driven to the cross," used here for execution by hanging</note>. Then Pharaoh ordered Joseph to be summoned: who, immediately released from prison, with his hair shaved and his clothes changed, came to him. And Pharaoh addressed him thus: "I have dreamed something which no one can explain. But I have been advised to bring the interpretation of the dream to you." Joseph replied to him: "Without me, God will give you a favorable answer, Pharaoh." And Pharaoh said: "I seemed to myself to be standing on the bank of the river, when out of it came seven well-fed cows, beautiful in appearance, which grazed in the marsh-grass. Then behold, seven others arose after them, so deformed by thinness and leanness of body that I have never seen anything more foul in Egypt: these lean and ugly ones consumed those seven fat ones from before: yet when they had taken them into their bellies, it was not apparent, for they were still as unsightly as before. I was released from sleep, and being overcome by it again, I seemed to see seven ears of grain growing on the same stalk, full and beautiful, behind which seven others, thin and small and scorched by heat, sprang up and consumed those choice ones. I reported these things to the soothsayers, but there is no one who can explain it." Then Joseph said: "Your dream is one, Pharaoh: God forewarns you of what He is about to do. The seven choice cows are seven years: and likewise, the seven choice ears mean the same: it is one and the same dream. Moreover, the others are as many years in which famine will prevail. God is demonstrating to you (as I said) what He is about to do. Therefore, in the next seven years there will be a great abundance of crops in all Egypt: which will be followed by another seven years plagued by such famine that nothing of that great plenty will remain in Egypt. I say the scarcity of food will be so great that not even a trace of such abundance will be left. For the fact that you dreamed it twice means that God fully intends to do this, and shortly. Therefore, Pharaoh, look for someone knowledgeable and skilled whom you may set over Egypt. Then ensure that, with overseers of the grain-supply appointed, you collect a fifth of the produce in Egypt during the next seven fertile years, so that a great amount of grain may be gathered in your name and stored in the cities...

<column-break/>

...and kept, so that it may suffice for the second seven-year period and defend Egypt from the coming famine and ruin." Pharaoh approved of this plan with all his advisors, and confessed to them that no one existed equal to Joseph in divine spirit. And because you have been taught such great things by God (he then said <margin>Psalm 105; 1 Maccabees 2; Acts 7.</margin> to Joseph), you have no equal in prudence and wisdom; you shall now have the government of my house, so that all my people shall obey your command, and I shall be greater than you only by the throne. "Behold, I hand over to you," he said, "the care of all Egypt," and at the same time he took the ring from his own hand and put it on Joseph's hand, and having adorned him in a fine linen robe, with a gold chain distinguishing his neck, he placed him in the second most prestigious chariot, so that it would be proclaimed before him: "Bow the knee": and he granted him power over all Egypt. "And as I live," he said, "no one in all Egypt shall move a finger against your will." Then he called him Zaphenath-Paneah, <margin>that is, a discoverer of secrets.</margin> and gave him Asenath, daughter of Potipherah, the priest of Heliopolis <note>original: "pontificis Heliopolitani"; Heliopolis was the "City of the Sun" in Egypt</note>, in marriage. Thus Joseph, having departed from Pharaoh at thirty years of age (for he was that old when he stood before Pharaoh), traveled throughout all Egypt, and in those seven years (in which the earth bore most abundantly in Egypt), he gathered the greatest supply of provisions, and brought the food from the fields surrounding each city into the cities themselves, and collected such a quantity of grain that, because it was like the sand of the sea, he eventually stopped counting. Now, two sons were born to him from Asenath before <margin>Joseph's sons.</margin> the scarcity of the grain-supply began: the older of whom he called Manasseh, because God had brought him forgetfulness of all his sorrows and of his father's house. The other he named Ephraim, because God had made him fruitful in the land of his misery. When the seven years of plenty in Egypt were finished, the seven years of famine began to arise, just as Joseph had predicted: and while there was famine in all lands, all Egypt had food available. Then the Egyptians, as the cost of grain increased, appealed to Pharaoh for food: all of whom he sent back to Joseph, ordering them to obey his word. With famine pressing upon the whole land, Joseph opened all the storehouses and began to sell <note>original: "diuendere," to sell or distribute</note> grain to the Egyptians who were suffering from hunger.

### CHAPTER XLIV.

Then, after they had drunk freely with him, he gave orders to his steward to fill their sacks with as much grain as they could carry, and to put each man’s silver in the mouth of his sack; but in the mouth of the youngest brother’s sack, he was to place his silver cup <note>original: "scyphum," a large drinking vessel or goblet</note> in addition to the money for the grain. Having caught up with them, he asked why they had repaid good with evil? <note>original: "G. to commit such a crime. We even brought back to you from the land of the Canaanites the silver we found in the mouths of our sacks; why then would we steal silver or gold from your master’s house? And when he ordered us to return to buy some provisions, we replied that we could not unless our youngest brother accompanied us, for we would not be admitted to your presence otherwise. But our father said that of the two sons his one wife had borne him, one had left him (as we knew) and had been mourned as torn by beasts, and he had never seen him since. If we were to take this one from him as well and some human accident <note>A phrase used to imply death or misfortune</note> should befall him, we would bring his gray hairs down in misery to the grave <note>original: "inferos," the place of the dead</note>. Now, if I come to my father and do not have the boy with me—whose soul is bound up with the boy's—as soon as he sees the boy is not there, he will die. Thus we would lead our father, a grief-stricken old man, down to the grave <note>original: "orcum," the underworld</note>. For I became a surety to my father for the boy’s return, promising that if I did not bring him back, I would bear the blame forever. Therefore, I pray you, let me remain as your slave in place of the boy, and let him depart with his brothers; for I cannot bear to return to my father without him, lest I see the calamity that would befall my father."

### CHAPTER XLV

<margin>Joseph reveals himself to his brothers. Acts 7</margin>
At this, Joseph, who could no longer restrain himself before the many people standing present, cried out with a loud voice that everyone should be sent outside. No one remained with him when he made himself known to his brothers. Then he burst into such loud weeping that the Egyptians and even the house of Pharaoh heard it. Addressing his brothers, he said: "I am Joseph. Is my father still alive?" But his brothers were so terrified by his presence that they could not answer a word. Then he said: "Come closer to me." When they had approached, he said: "I am your brother Joseph, whom you sold into Egypt. But do not be distressed, and do not let it grieve you that you sold me here. For God sent me ahead of you for your preservation. Indeed, besides these two years in which famine has ruled the land, there are still five years remaining in which there will be neither sowing nor harvest. For this reason, God sent me before you so that you might remain as a remnant on the earth, and that you might escape through this miraculous deliverance. Therefore, it was not you who sent me here, but God, who has made me as a father to Pharaoh, lord of his entire household, and ruler over all the land of Egypt. Hurry to my father and tell him this from Joseph his son: he must come down to me without delay—for God has given me dominion over all the Egyptians—and he shall live in the land of Goshen <note>original: "Gossene," a fertile region in the eastern Nile Delta</note>, so that he may be near me, along with his children, grandchildren, flocks, herds, and all his possessions. There I will provide food for him, lest he and his whole family and all he owns perish in misery, since there are still five years of famine to come. Look, you see with your own eyes, and my brother Benjamin sees, that it is my own mouth speaking with you. Having said this, he fell upon Benjamin's neck with tears, and Benjamin likewise wept as he embraced his neck. Then, weeping with them, Joseph kissed each of his brothers one by one; only then did they find the words to speak with him. When the news reached Pharaoh's house that Joseph's brothers had arrived, Pharaoh and his court were pleased. They now begged that he remit this misdeed for the sake of those who worship the same God as their father. At these words, Joseph wept. When the brothers themselves came and threw themselves down before him, offering themselves into his power, Joseph said: "Do not be afraid. Am I in the place of God? Although you intended evil against me, God turned it into good, so that (as the event itself shows) many people might be preserved. Therefore, do not fear; I will provide for you and your families." With this kind speech, Joseph comforted their hearts.

## CHAPTER I.

<margin>Genesis 46</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative letter 'I' showing a man kneeling in a hilly landscape.</image-desc> These are the names of the sons of Israel who came into Egypt with Jacob, each with his own family: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, Benjamin, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher. <margin>Acts 7</margin>
After Joseph died, along with his brothers and that entire generation, the Israelites increased so much in number and multitude, and were so strengthened, that the region was filled with them. Then a new king arose in Egypt who did not know Joseph. He persuaded his people to deal craftily with the Israelite people (who surpassed them in number and strength), lest they grow even further and, should a war arise, join with the enemies and seek to leave the land by force of war.

<margin>The servitude of the Israelites.</margin>
Thus, taskmasters <note>original: "quæstores tributi," literally "collectors of tribute"</note> were set over the Israelite people to oppress them with burdens. They were forced to build store-cities for Pharaoh: Pithom and Ramesses. But the more they were oppressed, the more they grew and multiplied. Consequently, the Egyptians grew weary of the Israelites and began to treat them with greater imperial harshness, making their lives bitter with hard labor in mortar and bricks and every kind of harsh service in the fields. Then the king of Egypt commanded the Hebrew midwives (one named Shiphrah and the other Puah) that when they assisted the Hebrew women in childbirth, if they saw the child was a boy, they should kill him; but if it were a girl, they should let her live.

<margin>Wisdom 18</margin>
But the midwives feared God and did not obey the king's command, but saved the boys. When the king summoned them and asked why they had saved the boys, they replied that there was a great difference between Hebrew and Egyptian women: for the Hebrew women are vigorous and give birth before the midwife arrives.

<margin>2. Offspring</margin>
Therefore, God dealt well with the midwives; the people grew and became very strong, and it happened that God provided families for the midwives because of their piety. Then Pharaoh commanded all his people that every Hebrew male child born should be thrown into the river, but every female child should be saved.

### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>Jehovah addresses Moses.</margin>
On the day Jehovah gave mandates to Moses in Egypt to deliver everything in his name to Pharaoh—at which time Moses replied that Pharaoh would not obey him because he stuttered—Jehovah spoke to him thus: "Behold, I make you as a God to Pharaoh; your brother Aaron shall be your prophet <note>original: "uates"; meaning a spokesperson or one who declares the word</note>. Even if Pharaoh does not obey you, I will lay my hand upon Egypt and bring my hosts—that is, my Israelites—out by great judgments, so the Egyptians may know that I am Jehovah when I have led the Israelites from their midst against their will." Moses and Aaron did as Jehovah commanded; Moses was eighty years old and Aaron eighty-three when they met with Pharaoh. Jehovah had instructed them that if Pharaoh demanded a miracle, Aaron should throw his staff down at Moses' command, and it would become a dragon <note>original: "draco"; often used in Latin translations of the Bible to describe a large serpent or sea-monster</note>. When Moses and Aaron had done as Jehovah commanded, and Aaron had lifted the staff and struck the water of the river before the eyes of Pharaoh and his followers, all the water of the river turned to blood. The fish died, and the stench was so great that the Egyptians could not drink the water; all of Egypt was filled with blood.

### CHAPTER VIII.

Seven days after Jehovah had struck the river, Moses again approached Pharaoh by Jehovah’s command regarding the release of the people to worship Him. When Pharaoh refused, Moses threatened that Jehovah would strike all his borders with frogs. These would swarm from the river in such abundance <margin>Frogs.</margin> that they would enter the houses of Pharaoh, his servants, and his people, penetrating into the inner chambers, bedrooms, ovens, and kneading troughs <note>original: "mactras"; bowls used for preparing bread dough</note>, swarming over Pharaoh himself and all his subjects. By the same command of Jehovah, Moses ordered Aaron to stretch out his hand with the staff over the streams, rivers, and pools, so that frogs would emerge throughout Egypt. When this was done, the ground of Egypt was covered with frogs. The magicians imitated this with their charms and brought frogs up upon Egypt. Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron, urging them to pray to Jehovah to drive the frogs away from him and his people, promising that he would let the people go to offer sacrifices. Moses said to him: "Appoint a time for me when I should pray for you, your servants, and your people, so that the frogs may be driven from you and your houses and remain only in the river." Pharaoh replied: "Tomorrow." Moses said: "It shall be as you say, so that you may understand that Jehovah our God is incomparable. The frogs shall depart from you, your houses, your servants, and your people, yet they shall remain in the river." Thus, after Moses and Aaron left Pharaoh, Moses prayed to Jehovah concerning the frogs He had sent upon Pharaoh. Consequently, they died in the houses, the villages, and the fields, and were gathered into heaps, and the land grew foul with the stench. But when Pharaoh saw that relief had been granted, he hardened his heart and did not grant their request, just as Jehovah had predicted. Then Aaron, at the command of Moses (who had been further instructed by Jehovah), took the staff in his hand and, stretching it out, struck the dust of the earth. By this stroke, <margin>Lice.</margin> all the dust of the entire Egyptian land was turned into lice <note>original: "pediculos"; these may have been lice, gnats, or stinging flies</note>, with which both humans and four-legged animals swarmed. When the magicians tried in vain to imitate this creation of lice with their charms, and as the lice infested both men and beasts, they confessed to Pharaoh: "This is the finger of God." But Pharaoh’s heart was calloused, and he did not listen to them, just as Jehovah had foretold. Early in the morning, as soon as he arose, Moses stood before Pharaoh as he went out to the water by Jehovah's command. He explained Jehovah’s order to let His people go to worship Him. If he would not let them go, Moses declared that Jehovah would send insects <margin>Insects.</margin> upon him, his servants, his people, and his houses, so that the houses of the Egyptians and the very ground they inhabited would be filled with them. But at that time He would exempt Goshen (the land where Jehovah’s people stayed) and make it immune to the insects, so that Pharaoh might understand how great Jehovah was in the land, who placed such a distinction between

<column-break/>

his own people and Pharaoh's people. This sign <margin>Wisdom 16</margin> would occur the following day. And Jehovah did so; a vast force of insects was sent into the house of Pharaoh, his followers, and all of Egypt. While the region was being devastated by them, Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and permitted them to go sacrifice to their God, but only within those borders. Moses replied that this could not conveniently be done, for they would be performing sacrifices to Jehovah their God which the Egyptians detested <note>The Egyptians considered the sacrifice of certain animals, like cattle or rams, to be a religious abomination</note>; if they did this in their presence, they would surely be stoned by them. Instead, they would journey three days into the wilderness to sacrifice to Jehovah their God, as He had commanded them. Pharaoh said: "I will let you go to sacrifice to Jehovah your God in the desert, but on this condition: that you do not go too far. Pray for me." Moses replied: "And I, departing from you, will pray to Jehovah that tomorrow He may drive the insects away from you, your attendants, and your people. But do not deceive us further by not allowing the people to go to the sacrifice of Jehovah." Having departed, Moses obtained by his prayers to Jehovah the removal of the insects from them, so that not even one remained.

### CHAPTER IX.

But as Pharaoh even then stubbornly detained the people, Moses, at Jehovah's command, went to warn him in the name of Jehovah, the God of the Hebrews, to let His people go to worship Him. If he refused to let them go and continued to hold them, he should know that Jehovah would bring a most deadly plague <margin>Plague of Livestock.</margin> upon his livestock in the fields—namely the horses, donkeys, camels, oxen, sheep, and goats—with such a distinction between the Israelite and Egyptian livestock that nothing of the Israelites' would perish. Indeed, Jehovah set the time for this for the following day. On the next day, Jehovah did this, so that all kinds of Egyptian livestock died, while not even one of the Israelite animals perished. When Pharaoh sent messengers and discovered that not a single one of the Israelite animals had died, his heart remained stubborn, and he did not release the people. Then Jehovah commanded Moses and Aaron to take <margin>Boils.</margin> handfuls of soot from a lime kiln, which Moses was to scatter into the air in Pharaoh’s presence. This would turn into dust throughout all Egypt and cause dense, festering boils <note>original: "puſtulæ"; inflammatory sores or blisters</note> on both humans and beasts. When they had done this, the bodies of both men and animals were sprinkled with the sores of the boils, to the point that even the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the sores, which affected them as much as all the Egyptians. But Jehovah hardened Pharaoh's heart so that, just as He had told Moses, Pharaoh would not obey them. Then Jehovah said to Moses: "Rise early tomorrow to stand before Pharaoh and speak to him thus: 'This is what Jehovah, the God of the Hebrews, says to you: Let my people go, so that they may worship me. Otherwise, I will now finally let loose all my blows against your heart, and against your servants and people, so that you may understand there is no one like me in all the earth. Indeed, I could have already wiped you and your people from the earth by my hand with a plague <margin>Romans 9</margin>, were it not that I have spared you to declare my power and that my name might be known in all...'

# EXODUS

<margin>Hail.</margin>
...to be proclaimed throughout the whole world, I have specifically appointed you. But if you even now hinder my people and do not release them, know this: tomorrow I will rain down such a great force of hail as has never been in Egypt since its founding. Therefore, send messengers to gather your cattle and everything you have under the open sky <note>original: "sub dio"; meaning outdoors or in the open air</note>. For all people and livestock found in the open who have not taken shelter will perish, overwhelmed by the hail. Thus spoke Moses. And those of Pharaoh’s household who feared the word of Jehovah <note>original: "Ioua"; a Latinization of the Hebrew name for God, often used in humanist scholarship</note> gathered their servants and livestock into their houses; but those who neglected the warning left them in the fields. Then Jehovah commanded Moses to stretch his hand toward heaven, so that it might hail throughout all Egypt upon people, livestock, and all the herbs. When he stretched his staff <note>original: "uirgam"</note> toward heaven, Jehovah sent forth crashes of thunder and such a force of hail, with lightning flashing down to the earth and gleaming amidst the hail, as had never existed in all Egypt since man was born. This hail battered everything in Egypt that was in the open; it crushed people, beasts, and all the herbs of the field, and shattered the trees. Meanwhile, the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived, was free from hail. Then Pharaoh, having summoned Moses and Aaron, said: "Now I have sinned. Justice is on Jehovah’s side; iniquity is on the side of me and my people. Pray to Jehovah that the thundering and hail may cease, and I will let you go without any delay." Moses replied: "As soon as I have left the city and stretched out my hands to Jehovah, the crashes will stop and the hail will cease, so that you may know that this world belongs to Jehovah’s domain—though I know well enough that you and your servants do not yet revere Jehovah God." In that calamity, the flax and barley were ruined, because the barley was already in the ear and the flax was in the pod <note>original: "siliquabatur"; a botanical term for when the seed vessels have formed</note>. But the wheat and the spelt <note>original: "zea"; a type of hulled wheat common in the ancient world</note> were not ruined, because they grow later. After Moses left Pharaoh and went out of the city, he spread his palms to Jehovah; the thunder and hail subsided, and the flow of rain to the earth was restrained. When Pharaoh saw this, he persisted in his sin, hardening his heart along with his servants, and obstinately held back the Israelites, just as Jehovah had foretold through Moses.

### CHAPTER X.

<margin>Wisdom 16. Locusts.</margin>
Then Jehovah said to Moses: "Go to Pharaoh, for I have hardened his heart and the hearts of his servants, so that I may perform these miracles among them, and so you may tell your children and grandchildren what I have done to the Egyptians and with what wonders I have afflicted them, that you may know I am Jehovah." So Moses and Aaron approached Pharaoh and asked him in the name of Jehovah, the God of the Hebrews, "How long will you refuse to submit to Him? Release His people to worship Him. But if you refuse, know that tomorrow He will send so many locusts into your borders that the ground cannot be seen for their multitude. These locusts shall consume the remnant left by the hail and all the trees growing in the fields; they shall fill your houses and those of all your servants and the Egyptians, such as neither your fathers nor your ancestors have seen since memory began." 

<column-break/>

Having said this, he turned and left Pharaoh. Then Pharaoh’s attendants said: "*To what end will this man be a source of ruin to us? Release the men so they may worship Jehovah their God. Do you not yet realize that Egypt has perished?*" Then Pharaoh, having recalled Moses and Aaron, said: "*Go, worship Jehovah your God. But who specifically are going, and who are not?*" Moses replied: "*We will go with our young and our old; we will go with our sons and daughters, and with our flocks and herds, for we are to celebrate a festival to Jehovah.*" But he said: "*May Jehovah be with you in the same way I let you go with your little ones! Your malice is clear enough. Go instead, you men, for the worship of Jehovah, since that is what you demand.*" Then he drove them from his sight. But Jehovah commanded Moses to stretch his hand over the land of Egypt to stir up the locusts, which would be born throughout Egypt and devour every herb of that region and all the remains left by the hail. When Moses extended his staff over Egypt, Jehovah stirred up an east wind toward that region which, having blown all that day and night, brought in the locusts by early morning. They appeared in such abundance and settled in all the borders of Egypt as had never been seen before nor shall be hereafter. The entire face of the earth was covered by them and darkened; every herb and all the fruit of the trees left by the hail were consumed, so that no greenery of tree or herb remained in all Egypt. Then Pharaoh hastily summoned Moses and Aaron, confessing: "*I have sinned against Jehovah and against you. I ask that this sin be forgiven me, and that you pray to Jehovah your God for me, that he may at last drive this death away from me.*" Moses, departing from Pharaoh, prayed to Jehovah, who turned a very violent sea wind <note>A west wind from the Mediterranean</note>, by which the locusts were lifted and carried away into the Red Sea, so that not even one remained in all the borders of Egypt. But since Pharaoh would not release the Israelites even then (Jehovah hardening his heart), Moses, at Jehovah’s command that there be darkness over Egypt—even darkness that could be felt—stretched his hand toward heaven. This done, such a thick gloom of darkness existed throughout all Egypt for three days that for that entire time no man saw another, nor did anyone move from his place, while meanwhile all the Israelites had light everywhere. Then Pharaoh summoned Moses: "*Go worship Jehovah, even with your little ones; only let your flocks and herds be left behind.*" Moses replied: "*Nay, you must also supply us with victims and those things needed for divine service, which we may offer to Jehovah our God; and we will take our livestock with us, not even a hoof being left behind, from which we may take what is necessary for the divine service. For we do not know with what we shall worship Jehovah until we arrive there.*" But Pharaoh (Jehovah sending him persistence so that he would not release them) said: "*Get away from me! Take care that you do not come into my sight again, for if you do, you shall die.*" And Moses said: "*As you have said, I will not see your face again after this.*"

### CHAPTER XI

<margin>Sirach 45: Moses threatens the death of the firstborn.</margin>
Now, Jehovah <note>original: "Ioua"; a Latinization of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton common in Renaissance scholarship</note> had forewarned Moses that after inflicting just one more blow upon Pharaoh and the Egyptians, he would finally let them go, or rather, drive them out entirely. For this reason, He commanded Moses to instruct the people that every man should ask his neighbor, and every woman her neighbor, for vessels of silver and gold. Jehovah also secured the goodwill of the Egyptians toward the people; moreover, Moses himself was a man of the highest reputation in Egypt, held in great esteem by both Pharaoh’s officials and the common people. Therefore, in his speech, he set forth Jehovah's commands in this manner: that around midnight, Jehovah would go out among the Egyptians, and every firstborn in Egypt would die—from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sits upon his throne <note>original: "folio"; literally a seat or throne</note>, to the firstborn of the female servants who work the millstones, as well as the firstborn of all cattle. There would be a greater outcry in Egypt than there had ever been before or would ever be again. Meanwhile, among all the Israelites, not even a stir would be heard from any creature, whether two-footed or four-footed, so that they might understand how great a distinction Jehovah makes between the Egyptians and the Israelites. "And then," Moses said to Pharaoh, "all these servants of yours shall come down to me and humbly beg that I, along with all the people under my care, should depart. Only then will I leave." With this, he departed from Pharaoh in great anger, for he had learned from Jehovah that Pharaoh would not listen, so that even more of Jehovah's wonders might be performed in Egypt. Despite all the portents he and Aaron had performed in Pharaoh's presence, Pharaoh (his heart being hardened by Jehovah) still would not let the Israelites go from his borders.

### CHAPTER XII

<margin>The law of the Passover</margin>
Then Jehovah spoke to Moses and Aaron in Egypt with this discourse: "This month shall be for you the head of months; that is, let it be the first month of your year. Speak to the entire multitude of Israelites, that on the tenth day of this month every father of a family shall take a lamb for each household. If any family is too small for a whole lamb, the father shall invite his neighbor who is closest to his house, calculating the number of persons and the amount needed to eat the lamb. This lamb must be unblemished, a male, one year old; it does not matter if it is a lamb or a goat. After it has been kept in your care until the fourteenth day of the same month, it shall be slaughtered by the whole gathered community of the Israelites at twilight. Then they shall smear its blood on both doorposts and on the lintels of the houses in which it is eaten. The meat shall be eaten that night, roasted over a fire, with unleavened bread and with chicory <note>original: "cichoreis"; referring to bitter herbs</note>. Do not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but only roasted over the fire, including the head, legs, and entrails. You shall leave nothing remaining until the next day; if anything is left the next morning, you shall burn it with fire. You shall eat it in this manner: with your waists belted <note>original: "succinctis lateribus"; a sign of being ready for travel</note>, sandals on your feet, and staves in your hands, and you shall do so in haste, for it is the Passover of Jehovah. For I will pass through

Egypt that night and strike down all the firstborn of Egypt, both man and beast, and I, Jehovah, will execute judgment upon all the gods of the Egyptians. When I see the blood marking the houses where you are, I will pass over you, and no deadly blow shall touch you when I strike the Egyptians. You shall observe the memory of that day and celebrate it as a feast to Jehovah; you shall hand it down to your descendants to be celebrated as a perpetual religious rite. For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, and on the very first of those days you shall remove leaven from your houses. Whoever eats anything leavened from the first to the seventh day shall be cut off from the number of the Israelites. On the first day, and likewise on the seventh, you shall hold a sacred assembly, and you shall do no work on those days, except for what is necessary for everyone's food—that alone may be done. You shall keep the feast of unleavened bread, because <margin>a. The feast of bread.</margin> <gloss>a</gloss> on that very day I led your ranks out of Egypt; you shall establish this day as a perpetual law for your posterity. From the evening of the fourteenth day of the first month until the evening of the twenty-first day of the same month, you shall eat <margin>Leviticus 23, Numbers 28</margin> unleavened bread, and you shall have no leaven in your houses for those seven days. Whoever tastes leaven shall be cut off from the number of the Israelites, whether he be a foreigner or a native. I say to you, eat nothing leavened; wherever you live, you shall eat unleavened bread." Therefore Moses, having summoned all the elders of the Israelites, spoke to them in this manner: "Set aside and separate for yourselves young sheep for your families, and sacrifice the Passover. Then, dipping a bunch <margin>Hebrews 11</margin> of hyssop into the blood in the basin, smear it upon the lintels and both doorposts; let no one go out the door of their house before morning. For when Jehovah passes through to strike the Egyptians and sees the blood on the lintels and doorposts, he will pass over those doors and will not allow the Destroyer to enter your houses and bring slaughter. Establish this solemn rite for yourselves and your children forever. When you reach the land that Jehovah will give you as he promised, observe this ceremony. And when your children ask you, 'What does this ceremony mean?' you shall answer: 'It is the sacrifice of Jehovah’s Passover, who passed over the Israelites in Egypt when he struck the Egyptians and delivered our houses.'" Then the people bowed down in honor. When the Israelites had departed, they did exactly as Jehovah had commanded Moses <margin>The firstborn die. b. That is, the one reigning. Wisdom 18</margin> and Aaron. At midnight, Jehovah killed all the firstborn in Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh <gloss>b</gloss> sitting on his throne, to the firstborn of the captives in the dungeons, and even all the firstborn of the cattle. Then Pharaoh rose in the night, along with all his attendants and all the Egyptians, and there was a great outcry in Egypt, for there was not a single house without a death. Having summoned Moses and Aaron by night, he said: "Rise up, get out from among my people, both you and the Israelites! Go, worship Jehovah as you have asked! Take your flocks and your herds, as you demanded! Go, and pray for a blessing for me too." The Egyptians also urged the people, hurrying to send them out of their borders,

### CHAPTER XI.

<margin>Ecclesiasticus 45: Moses threatens the death of the firstborn.</margin>
Now, Jehovah <note>original: "Ioua"; a Latinized form of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton, commonly used by Reformation-era scholars to represent the name of God</note> had forewarned Moses that after bringing only one more plague upon Pharaoh and the Egyptians, he would finally let them go from there entirely, or rather, he would cast them out. Therefore, he commanded Moses to warn the people that every man should ask his neighbor, and every woman her neighbor, for vessels of silver and gold. And he secured the goodwill of the Egyptians for the people; moreover, Moses himself was a man of the highest reputation in the land of Egypt, both in the eyes of Pharaoh's servants and the people. Therefore, in that speech, he set forth Jehovah’s commands in this manner: that around midnight Jehovah would go out among the Egyptians, and every firstborn in Egypt would die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh himself, who sat upon the throne, to the firstborn of the slave girls who work at the grinding mills, as well as the firstborn of all livestock. He foretold that there would be a greater outcry in Egypt than there had ever been before or would ever be again. Meanwhile, among all the Israelites, not so much as a dog would bark <note>original: "nihil neq; bipedum omnino, neq; quadrupedum moueretur"; literally "nothing of two-legged or four-legged creatures would move"</note>, so that they might understand how great a distinction Jehovah makes between the Egyptians and the Israelites. "And then," Moses said to Pharaoh, "all these servants of yours shall come down to me and humbly beg that I depart along with all the people entrusted to me. Only then will I go out." And he left Pharaoh's presence in anger, for he had learned from Jehovah that Pharaoh would not listen, so that more of Jehovah’s wonders might be performed in Egypt. Even though Moses and Aaron had performed so many portents in his sight, Pharaoh—because Jehovah hardened his heart <note>original: "comprimente eius animum"; literally "pressing or restraining his mind"</note>—would not let the Israelites go from his borders.

### CHAPTER XII.

<margin>The Law of the Passover</margin>
Then Jehovah spoke to Moses and Aaron in Egypt with this speech: "This month shall be for you the head of months; let it be the first month of the year for you. Speak to the entire multitude of Israelites, so that on the tenth day of this month every father of a household shall take a lamb for each family. If any family is too small for a whole lamb, the father shall take his neighbor who is closest to his house, calculating based on the number of persons and the amount needed to eat the lamb. This lamb must be unblemished, a male of one year; it does not matter if it is a lamb or a young goat. After it has been kept in custody until the fourteenth day of the same month, it shall be slaughtered by the whole multitude of the Israelite community at twilight. Then they shall sprinkle some of its blood on both doorposts and on the lintels of the houses in which it is eaten. The meat shall be eaten that night, roasted over a fire, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs <note>original: "cichoreis"; literally "chicory," a common bitter salad green</note>. You must not eat any of it raw or boiled in water, but only roasted over the fire, together with its head, legs, and inner parts. You shall leave none of it until the following day; and if anything remains the next morning, you shall burn it with fire. You shall eat it in this manner: with your loins girded, your feet shod in sandals, and holding staves in your hands; and you shall do this in haste, for it is Jehovah’s passing over." For I will pass through

<column-break/>

Egypt that night, and I will strike down all the firstborn of Egypt, both man and beast, and I, Jehovah, will execute judgment upon all the gods of the Egyptians. When I see the blood with which the houses where you are stay are marked, I will pass over you, and no deadly plague shall touch you when I strike the Egyptians. You shall observe the memory of that day and celebrate it as a feast to Jehovah, and you shall pass it down to your descendants to be celebrated as a perpetual religious rite. For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, and on the very first of those days you shall remove leaven from your houses. Whoever tastes anything leavened from the first day to the seventh shall be cut off from the number of the Israelites. On the first day, and likewise on the seventh, you shall hold a sacred assembly, and you shall do no work on those days, except for that which is necessary for everyone’s food; that alone shall be permitted. <gloss>a</gloss> You shall keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread, because on that very day I brought your ranks out of Egypt; you shall make this day a perpetual law for your posterity.

<margin>a. The Feast of Bread.</margin>
<margin>Leviticus 23, Numbers 28</margin>
From the evening of the fourteenth day of the first month until the evening of the twenty-first day of the same month, you shall eat unleavened bread. You shall have no leaven in your houses for those seven days; whoever tastes leaven shall be cut off from the number of the Israelites, whether he is a foreigner or a native. You shall never eat anything leavened; wherever you live, you shall eat unleavened bread.

Therefore Moses, having called together all the elders of the Israelites, spoke to them in this manner: "Set aside and separate for yourselves individual bleating lambs according to your families, which you shall sacrifice for the Passover. Then, having dipped a bunch of hyssop into the blood in the basin, stain the lintels and both doorposts; and do not go outside the doors of your houses before tomorrow morning. When Jehovah passes through to strike the Egyptians, he will see the blood on the lintels and the posts, and he will pass over the doors, nor will he allow the destroyer to enter your houses to bring disaster. Establish this solemn thing for yourselves and your children forever. And when you arrive in the land that Jehovah will give you, as he promised, observe this ceremony."

<margin>Hebrews 11</margin>
And when your children ask you, "What does this ceremony mean?" you shall answer, "It is the sacrifice of Jehovah’s passing over, who passed over the Israelites in Egypt when he struck the Egyptians and delivered our houses." Then the people bowed down in honor.

<margin>The firstborn die. b. That is, of the reigning one. Wisdom 18</margin>

Then indeed Pharaoh rose in the night, along with all his attendants and the Egyptians, and there was a great outcry in Egypt, for there was no house without a corpse. Having summoned Moses and Aaron by night, he said: "Go! Depart from my people, both you and the Israelites; go, worship Jehovah as you wish. Take your flocks and herds, just as you asked. Go, and pray for a blessing for me as well." The Egyptians also urged the people, hurrying to send them out of their borders,

When Pharaoh had dismissed the people, God did not lead them toward Palestine <note>original: "Palæstinam"; referring to the land of the Philistines</note>, even though that was the most direct route. Neither the pillar of cloud by day nor the pillar of fire by night ever failed to go before the people.

Therefore, when Moses stretched his hand over the sea, the water returned to its full depth toward morning. As the Egyptians fled against the oncoming water, Jehovah swept them into the middle of the sea. The returning tide overwhelmed the chariots and horsemen of Pharaoh's entire army who had followed them into the sea, such that not even one survived. Meanwhile, the Israelites had walked through the middle of the sea on dry foot, with the water serving as a wall to their right and left. On that day, the Israelites were saved from the harm of the Egyptians by the protection of Jehovah. When they saw the Egyptians dead on the shore and perceived the illustrious deed Jehovah had done against them, they revered Jehovah and placed their faith in Him and in His servant Moses.

<margin>Quails. Manna. Numbers 11, Psalm 78, Wisdom 16, John 6, 1 Corinthians 10</margin>
Therefore, in the evening, so many quails flew up that they covered the camp. In the morning, the ground around the camp was covered with dew. When the dew evaporated, something small, round, and thin was seen on the forest floor, just as if frost had been scattered on the ground. Upon seeing it, the Israelites said to one another: "Man hu?" <note>Hebrew for "What is it?"</note> for they did not know what it was. Moses said to them: "This is the bread which Jehovah gives you for food. <margin>2 Corinthians 8</margin>
They did so, and gathered it, some more and some less. But when they measured it with a gomer, he who had gathered more had nothing left over, and he who had gathered less had no lack; each had gathered exactly as much as was needed for his sustenance. However, Moses had forbidden anyone to leave any of it until the next morning. Some neglected this command and saved some, but it bred worms and began to stink. When Moses became angry with them, they thereafter gathered it every morning, enough for each person's needs; later, as the sun grew hot, it would melt. But on the sixth day, they gathered a double portion of food, namely two gomers for each person. When all the leaders of the community reported this to Moses, he replied that this was exactly what had been announced by Jehovah: that the following day would be the Sabbath, a holy rest to Jehovah. They were to bake and boil what was needed and set aside all the rest to keep for the following day. When they did this according to Moses' instruction, the portion kept for the next day did not stink, nor were there worms in it. days it was to be gathered, but on the seventh day, which was the Sabbath, there would be none. Some of the people, however, went out to gather even on the seventh day, but they found nothing. These were rebuked by Moses at Jehovah’s command, because they refused for so long to keep his precepts and laws. It was clear that because Jehovah had given them the Sabbath, he provided two days' worth of food on the sixth day; they were to remain in their places and no one was to leave his spot on the seventh day. So the people rested on that day. The Israelites named it "Manna" <note>Derived from the question "Man hu?"</note>; it looked like coriander seed, was white, and tasted like wafers made with honey. Moses said that Jehovah had commanded them to set aside a gomer-full of it to be kept for future generations, so they might see the food with which he sustained them in the desert after being led out of Egypt. He commanded Aaron to put a gomer’s measure of Manna into a jar and place it before Jehovah to be kept for future generations. He did as Jehovah had commanded Moses, and placed it before the Testimony <note>original: "oraculum"; referring to the Ark of the Covenant or the place of divine presence.</note> to be preserved. <margin>Nehemiah 9, Judith 5</margin> The Israelites used this Manna for forty years, until they reached the borders of Canaan, a land that was inhabited. A gomer is the tenth part of an ephah <note>An ephah was a larger dry measure, roughly 20-30 liters.</note>.

### CHAPTER XVII.

Therefore, setting out from the Wilderness of Sin, traveling according to Jehovah’s command, they camped in Rephidim. Since there was no water there to drink, they quarreled with Moses, demanding that he give them water to drink. When Moses asked them why they were contending with him or why they were testing Jehovah, they—suffering from thirst and the lack of water—asked him why he had brought them out of Egypt to kill them, their children, and their livestock with thirst. Then Moses called out to Jehovah: "What shall I do with this people? They are almost ready to <margin>Psalm 78, 1 Corinthians 10</margin> stone me." Jehovah said to him: "Go on ahead of the people, taking some of the elders with you, and carrying in your hand the staff with which you struck the river. There, I will stand before you on the rock at Horeb. When you strike that rock, water will flow from it for the people to drink." Moses did this in the sight of the elders, <margin>The place Meribah.</margin> and he named that place Massah <note>meaning "Testing"</note> and Meribah <note>meaning "Quarreling"</note>, because of the Israelites' quarreling and because they tested whether or not Jehovah was among them.

### CHAPTER XVIII

<margin>Jethro comes to Moses.</margin> Now when Jethro, the priest of the Midianites and Moses’s father-in-law, understood what great blessings Jehovah God had bestowed upon Moses and his Israelites—how he had led the Israelites out of Egypt—he brought with him Zipporah, Moses’s wife, whom Moses had previously sent back, and Zipporah’s two sons. The name of one was Gershom, for Moses had said he was a stranger in a foreign land; the name of the other was Eliezer, because the God of his father had been his help and had rescued him from the sword of Pharaoh. With these, Jethro came to Moses in the wilderness, where he was encamped at the mountain of God. He sent word to Moses that he, his father-in-law Jethro, was coming to him along with his wife and her two sons. And Moses went out to meet him and honored him with a kiss. After they had asked each other about their health, they entered the tent. There Moses told his father-in-law in what ways Jehovah had dealt with Pharaoh and the Egyptians for the sake of the Israelites, and how many hardships they had faced on their journey, from which they had been delivered by Jehovah. Jethro was delighted by all these blessings of Jehovah toward the Israelites, because he had rescued them from the Egyptians. *I give thanks to Jehovah,* he said, *who has delivered you from the Egyptians and Pharaoh, and who has rescued the people from the power of the Egyptians. Now at last I understand that Jehovah is the greatest of all gods, and that these things have rightly happened to them because of their pride toward you.* At the same time, he performed a divine service and a sacrifice to God; and Aaron, along with all the Israelite elders, came to feast before God with him. The next day, as Moses sat to administer justice to the people, and the people stood around him from morning until evening, his father-in-law noticed this and said: *What is this thing that you are doing for the people? Why do you sit alone, while all the people stand by you from morning until evening?* Moses replied: *The people come to me to seek an oracle from God. If they have any business, they come to me; I judge their disputes and reveal the divine ordinances and laws.* And his father-in-law said: <margin>Deuteronomy 1. Jethro’s advice.</margin> *You are doing a truly foolish thing; your practice and that of these people is unwise, for the task is too difficult for you to manage alone. But hear my advice, and may God help you. You represent the people before God and bring their cases to Him; instruct them in the ordinances and laws, and teach them the duties they must perform. Then, from among all the people, look for capable and religious men—faithful men who hate greed. Appoint them as captains of thousands, captains of hundreds, captains of fifties, and captains of tens <note>The Latin text uses Roman military terms: "tribunos" (tribunes), "centuriones" (centurions), "semicenturiones," and "decuriones" (decurions) to describe these leaders.</note> to judge the people at all times. If any matter of greater importance arises, let them bring it to you; but let them judge the minor matters themselves, to lighten your burden and share the task with you. In this way, God will command you, you will be able to endure, and all these people will go to their homes in peace.* Moses followed this advice from his father-in-law and did exactly as suggested. He chose capable men from among all the Israelites and

### CHAPTER XXI

<margin>The law of servitude. Deuteronomy 15; Jeremiah 34</margin>
These are the laws you shall set before them. If you buy a Hebrew servant, he shall serve for six years, but in the seventh year he shall be set free without cost. If he came single, he shall be set free single: but if he was a married man, his wife shall be set free with him. If his master gave him a wife from whom he fathered sons or daughters, the woman and the children shall belong to the master: he alone shall be set free. But if the servant, captured by love for his master, his wife, and his children, does not wish to be set free, the master shall bring him to the judges <note>original: "recuperatores," a Roman legal term for judges used here to translate the Hebrew authorities.</note>, and bring him to the door or the doorpost, and pierce his ear with an awl; he shall serve him forever.

If anyone sells his daughter into domestic service, she shall not be set free in the manner of male servants. If she displeases the master and he does not betroth her, he shall let her be redeemed. He shall have no power to sell her to a foreign nation, because he has treated her with dishonor. But if he intends her for his son, he shall treat her according to the same law as he would his own children. If he takes another wife <margin>a. Namely, in addition to her.</margin>, he shall not deprive this one of food, clothing, or <gloss>b</gloss> marital rights <margin>b. Namely, marital intimacy.</margin>. If he does not fulfill these three things for her, she shall be set free for nothing, without payment.

<margin>Penalty for striking. Leviticus 24; Deuteronomy 19</margin>
Whoever strikes a man, if he dies, it shall be a capital offense. But for one who did not lie in wait, but happened upon him by chance <note>original: "fortē fortuna," by a stroke of luck or fate.</note>, I will appoint a place for you where he may flee. But if anyone plots to kill another through deliberate deceit, he shall be dragged even from my altar to his death.

Whoever strikes his father or mother, it shall be a capital offense.
<margin>Jeremiah 20; Proverbs 20; Matthew 15; Mark 7</margin>
Whoever kidnaps a man and sells him, or if the man is found in his possession, it shall be a capital offense.

Whoever curses his father or mother, the penalty shall be death.

If a dispute arises and someone strikes another with a stone or a fist, if he does not die but is confined to bed: if he rises and walks outside leaning on a staff, the striker shall be free from further penalty, provided he pays for his loss of time and for his medical care.

If anyone strikes his male or female servant with a staff, and immediate death follows, he shall be held responsible. However, if the servant survives for one or two days, he shall not be held responsible, since <gloss>c</gloss> he is his money <margin>c. That is, the servant is his property/right.</margin>.

If men fighting wound a pregnant woman and cause a miscarriage, but no further harm <note>original: "pernicies," meaning fatal injury or permanent ruin.</note> follows, a fine shall be paid according to the husband's estimation, and arbitrators shall oversee the matter. But if further harm follows, you shall pay life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, bruise for bruise, wound for wound, stripe for stripe.
<margin>Law of Retaliation. Matthew 5; Leviticus 24; Deuteronomy 19</margin>

If anyone strikes the eye of his male or female servant and destroys it, he shall set them free for the sake of the eye. And if he knocks out the tooth of his male or female servant, he shall set them free for the sake of the tooth.

<margin>If an ox strikes.</margin>
If an ox gores a man or woman with its horn and they die, the ox shall be stoned and its meat shall not be eaten: the owner of the ox shall be unpunished. But if the ox was prone to goring previously and its owner was warned, yet did not keep it contained, if it kills a man or woman, both the ox shall be stoned and its owner shall be put to death...

### CHAPTER XXII.

<margin>The penalty for theft. 2 Samuel 12</margin>
**If** anyone steals <note>original: "clepserit," an archaic Latin term for stealing.</note> an ox or a sheep, and slaughters or sells it, he shall restore five oxen for one ox, and four sheep <note>original: "balantes," literally "bleating ones."</note> for one sheep.

If a thief is caught breaking in and is struck so that he dies, there shall be no penalty for homicide, unless the sun has risen: then there shall be a penalty for homicide. If he has the means to make restitution, let him do so; if he has nothing, let him be sold for his theft.

If the stolen animal is found alive in his possession—whether ox, donkey, sheep, or goat—he shall restore double.

If anyone allows his livestock to graze in another's field or vineyard, he shall make amends for the damage from the best part of his own field or vineyard.

If a fire is started among thorns and catches a stack of grain, or standing grain, or a harvest, the one who started the fire shall pay for the loss.

<margin>The law of deposits. Genesis 31</margin>
If anyone deposits silver or furniture with another, and it is stolen from that person's house, if the thief is caught, let him restore double. But if the thief is not caught, then the master of the house shall be called before the judges <note>original: "recuperatores," a Roman legal term for officials who handled property recovery.</note> to determine if he has misappropriated the other's property. In every case where a crime is alleged—concerning an ox, a donkey, a sheep, a goat, a garment, or any lost thing which is claimed—the case of both parties shall be brought before the judges: whomever the judges condemn shall restore double to the other.

<margin>a. Namely, in the countryside by rustlers or enemies. b. Namely, at home.</margin>
If anyone entrusts a donkey, ox, sheep, goat, or any livestock to another's keeping, and it dies, is injured, or is <insert>a</insert> driven off with no one seeing it, an oath to Jehovah shall be placed between them that he has not diverted the other's property to himself; the owner of the property shall accept this satisfaction, and the trustee shall not have to restore it. But if it was <insert>b</insert> stolen from him, he shall make restitution to the owner of the property. If it was torn by wild beasts, let him bring evidence, and he shall not be liable for what was torn.

If anyone borrows anything from another for use, and it is injured or dies while the owner is absent, he shall make restitution. But if the owner is present, he shall not make restitution, especially if it was hired and covered by a fee.

<margin>Seduction. Deuteronomy 22</margin>
If a man seduces a virgin who is not betrothed and lies with her, he shall pay her dowry to have her as his wife.

If the girl's father refuses to give her to him, he shall pay silver according to the dowry for virgins.

<column-break/>

You shall not allow sorceresses <note>original: "sagas," often implying fortune-tellers or wise-women.</note> to live.

Whoever has sexual relations with an animal shall be put to death.

Whoever sacrifices to gods, except to Jehovah alone, shall be devoted to destruction.

<margin>Duties toward the needy. Leviticus 19; Zechariah 7</margin>
Do not oppress or distress a foreigner: for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.

Do not oppress any widow or orphan <note>original: "pupillum," specifically a fatherless child.</note>. If you do oppress them, when they cry out to me, I will surely hear their complaints; my anger will be kindled, and I will slay you with the sword, and your wives shall become widows and your children orphans.

If you lend money to any of my people who are poor and living among you, do not act as a usurer toward them: do not impose interest upon them.

If you take another's garment as a pledge, return it before sunset: for that is his only covering, the cloak for his skin in which he sleeps. If he cries out to me, I will hear him, for I am merciful.

<margin>Toward elders/authorities. Acts 23</margin>
Do not speak evil of a magistrate.

Do not curse the one who is the leader of your nation.

Do not hold back your harvest or your juices <note>original: "liquorem," referring to the offerings of wine and oil.</note>.

<margin>Toward God. Leviticus 22; Exodus 44</margin>
Give the firstborn of your sons to me. Do the same with your oxen and sheep. Let it stay with its mother for seven days; on the eighth day, give it to me.

You shall be holy men to me; do not eat meat torn by beasts in the field, but throw it to the dogs.

### CHAPTER XXIII.

<margin>Duty toward men. Deuteronomy 22</margin>
**Do** not accept a false report.

Do not join hands with a wicked man to be a malicious witness.

Do not follow a crowd in doing wrong, nor turn aside in a lawsuit from what is right to follow the opinion of the majority. Do not show partiality even to a poor man in his lawsuit.

If you happen upon your enemy's ox or donkey wandering, lead it back to him. If you see the donkey of one who hates you collapsing under its load, do not refuse him help, but assist him.

Do not pervert the justice due to your enemy in a lawsuit.

<margin>Daniel 13; Deuteronomy 16; Ecclesiasticus 20</margin>
Keep away from a false matter. Do not kill the innocent and the just: for I will not acquit the wicked.

Do not accept a bribe: for a bribe blinds even the clear-sighted and perverts the words of good men.

<margin>Genesis 46</margin>
Do not trouble a foreigner: for you know the heart <note>original: "mens," meaning the feelings or state of mind.</note> of foreigners, since you yourselves were foreigners in Egypt.

<margin>The Sabbath.</margin>

For six days do your work: but on the seventh day, rest, so that your ox and your donkey may have relief, and the son of your female servant and the foreigner may be refreshed.

Observe all things that I have said to you.

Do not mention the names of foreign gods, nor let them be heard from your mouth.

<margin>Feast days.</margin>

# CHAPTER XXI.
