If he came single, he shall be manumitted single; but if he was a husband, his wife shall be manumitted with him. If the master gave him a wife, from whom he fathered sons or daughters, the woman and the children shall belong to the master; he alone shall be manumitted. But if the servant, captured by love for his master, his wife, and his children, does not wish to be manumitted, the master shall bring him to the judges <note>original: "recuperatores," a Roman legal term for a board of judges.</note>, and leading him to the door or the doorpost, he shall pierce his ear with an awl, and he shall serve him forever.

<margin>a. Namely, besides her. b. Namely, marital [rights].</margin>
If anyone sells his daughter into service, she shall not be manumitted in the manner of the [male] servants. If she displeases the master, and he does not betroth her, let her be redeemed. He shall have no power to sell her to a foreign nation, because he has treated her with disgrace. But if he has destined her for his son, he shall treat her by the same law as he does his own children. If he takes another [wife], he shall not defraud this one of food, clothing, or $^b$ marital rights. If he does not perform these three things for her, she shall be manumitted for free without a price.

<margin>The penalty for striking. Leviticus 24; Deuteronomy 19</margin>
Whoever strikes a man, if he dies, it shall be a capital offense. But for one who did not lie in wait, but happened upon him by chance, I will establish a place for you where he may flee. But if anyone should devise a another's death through deceit and on purpose, he shall be dragged away even from my altar to be put to death.

Whoever strikes his father or mother, it shall be a capital offense.
Whoever steals a man and sells him, or if the person is found with him, it shall be a capital offense.
Whoever curses his father or mother, let there be a penalty of death.

<margin>Jeremiah 20; Proverbs 20; Matthew 15; Mark 7</margin>
If, when a contention has arisen, anyone strikes another with a stone or a fist, and if the man does not die but lies in bed: if he rises and goes outside leaning on a staff, the striker shall be free from punishment, provided only that he pays for the other's time in bed and for his medical care.
If anyone strikes his male or female servant with a rod, and immediate death follows, he is liable. But if the servant survives for one or two days, he is not liable, because $^c$ he is his money <note>original: "pecunia eius est," meaning the servant is the master's property.</note>.

<margin>c. That is, he is of his right.</margin>
If men while fighting wound a pregnant woman and cause a miscarriage, if no fatal injury follows, let there be a fine according to the husband's estimation of the woman's value, and let there be arbiters for that matter. But if a fatal injury occurs, he shall pay life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, bruise for bruise, wound for wound, welt for welt.

<margin>The law of retaliation. Matthew 5; Leviticus 24; Deuteronomy 19</margin>
If anyone strikes the eye of his male or female servant and destroys it, he shall manumit him for the eye. And if he knocks out the tooth of his male or female servant, he shall manumit him for the tooth.

<margin>If an ox strikes.</margin>
If an ox gores a man or woman with its horn and they die, the ox shall be stoned and its meat shall not be eaten; the owner of the ox shall be unpunished. But if the ox was aggressive before, and its owner was warned but did not keep it under guard, if it kills a man or woman, both the ox shall be stoned and its owner [put to] death.

...shall be punished with death. But if a large fine is imposed on him, he shall give as much as is imposed for the ransom of his life. Whether [the ox] has gored a boy or a girl, the same law shall apply. If the ox has gored a male or female servant, thirty silver shekels <term>shekel: a standard unit of weight for silver used in trade</term> shall be paid to the master, and the ox shall be stoned.

### CHAPTER XXII.

<margin>Punishment for theft. 2 Samuel 12</margin>
If anyone steals an ox or a sheep, and kills or sells it, he shall restore five oxen for one, and four sheep <note>original: "balantes," literally "bleating ones."</note> for one.

If a thief is caught in the act of breaking in and is struck so that he dies, there shall be no penalty for homicide, unless it happened after the sun has risen; then there shall be a penalty for homicide. If he has the means to make restitution, he shall do so; if he has nothing, he shall be sold for his theft.

If the stolen animal is found alive in his possession—whether ox, donkey, sheep, or goat—he shall restore double.

If someone allows his livestock to graze in another's field or vineyard, he shall make amends from the best part of his own field or vineyard.

If a fire is started among thorns and catches a stack of grain, or standing grain, or a harvest, the one who started the fire shall pay for the damage.

<margin>The law of deposits. Genesis 31</margin>
If someone deposits silver or household goods with another for safekeeping, and they are stolen from that person’s house, if the thief is caught, he shall pay double. But if the thief is not caught, then the master of the house shall be brought before the judges <term>recuperatores: officials or arbitrators appointed to settle property claims</term> to determine whether he has embezzled the other person's property. In every case of alleged wrongdoing—whether involving an ox, a donkey, a sheep, a goat, clothing, or any lost item which one claims is theirs—the case of both parties shall be brought before the judges; whomever the judges condemn shall pay double to the other.

<margin>a. That is, in the countryside by rustlers.</margin>
<margin>b. That is, from the home.</margin>
If someone entrusts a donkey, ox, sheep, goat, or any beast to another's care, and it dies, or is injured, or <gloss>a</gloss> is driven off with no one seeing it, an oath by Jehovah shall be placed between them that he has not misappropriated the other's property; the owner shall accept this satisfaction, and the caretaker shall not make restitution. But if it was <gloss>b</gloss> stolen from him, he shall make restitution to the owner. If it was torn by wild beasts, he shall provide evidence, and he shall not have to pay for what was torn.

If someone borrows something from another, and it is injured or dies while the owner is absent, he shall make full restitution. But if the owner was present, he shall not make restitution; especially if it was hired and covered by a fee.

<margin>Seduction. Deuteronomy 22</margin>
If a man deceives a virgin who is not betrothed and lies with her, he shall pay her dowry and take her as his wife.

If the girl's father refuses to give her to him, he shall pay silver according to the customary dowry for virgins.

<column-break/>

You shall not allow sorceresses to live.

Whoever has sexual relations with a beast shall be put to death.

Whoever sacrifices to gods, except to Jehovah alone, shall be devoted to destruction.

<margin>Duties toward the needy. Leviticus 19; Zechariah 7</margin>
You shall not oppress or afflict a stranger <note>original: "peregrinum," a resident alien or sojourner.</note>, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt.

You shall not afflict any widow or orphan. If you do afflict them and they cry out to me, I will surely hear their complaints, and in my anger I will kill you with the sword; your own wives shall become widows and your children orphans.

If you lend money to any of my people who are poor among you, do not act as a usurer toward them; do not impose interest upon them.

If you take another's cloak as a pledge, return it before the sun sets. For that is his only covering, the garment for his skin in which he sleeps; if he cries out to me, I will hear him, for I am merciful.

<margin>Toward elders/superiors. Acts 23</margin>
You shall not speak evil of a magistrate.

You shall not curse a prince of your nation.

Do not withhold your grain and your liquors <note>refers to the offering of firstfruits and wine/oil.</note>.

<margin>Toward God. Leviticus 22; Exodus 44</margin>
Give the firstborn of your sons to me. Do the same with your oxen and sheep. It shall remain with its mother for seven days; on the eighth day, give it to me.

You shall be holy men to me; you shall not eat meat torn by beasts in the field, but you shall throw it to the dogs.

### CHAPTER XXIII.

<margin>Duties toward fellow men.</margin>
You shall not spread a false report.

Do not join hands with the wicked to be a malicious witness.

Do not follow a crowd in doing evil, nor shall you turn aside in a lawsuit from what is right to follow the opinion of the majority. Do not show favoritism to a poor man in his lawsuit.

<margin>Deuteronomy 22</margin>
If you come across your enemy's ox or donkey wandering, you shall lead it back to him. If you see the donkey of one who hates you collapsing under its load, do not refuse your help, but assist him.

Do not pervert the justice due to your enemy in his lawsuit.

<margin>Daniel 13; Deuteronomy 16; Ecclesiastes 20</margin>
Keep away from a false matter. Do not kill the innocent and the righteous, for I will not acquit the wicked.

Do not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds even the clear-sighted and perverts the words of good men.

<margin>Genesis 46</margin>
Do not harass a stranger; for you know the heart of a stranger, since you were strangers in the land of Egypt.

<margin>The Sabbath.</margin>
For six years you shall sow your field and gather its produce. But in the seventh year you shall let it rest and lie fallow, so that the needy of your people may eat, and (if anything is left for them) the wild beasts may eat. You shall do the same with your vineyard and olive grove.

For six days you shall do your work, but on the seventh day you shall rest, so that your ox and your donkey may have relief, and the son of your female servant and the stranger may be refreshed.

Observe all things that I have said to you.

Do not mention the names of foreign gods, nor let them be heard from your mouth.

<margin>Feast days.</margin>
Three times in the year you shall celebrate festivals to me. Observe the Feast of Unleavened Bread, during which you shall eat unleavened bread for seven days (as I commanded you) at the appointed time in the month of spr-

In the Tabernacle of the Testimony, outside the veil which hangs before the Testimony, Aaron and his sons shall set them in order before Jehovah <note>original: "Iouam." The translator uses a Latinized form of the Tetragrammaton, the divine name</note> from evening until morning. This shall be a perpetual rite passed down to their descendants by the Israelites.

->CHAPTER XXVIII.<-

Then set apart for me your brother Aaron and his sons—Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar—from among the other Israelites, so that they may serve me in the priesthood. You shall make sacred garments for your brother Aaron, that he may be splendidly adorned. Speak with all the most skillful men, whom I have endowed with wisdom, and have them make the garments for Aaron for his consecration, so that he may perform the priesthood for me. These shall be the garments: a breastplate, an ephod, a robe, a woven tunic, a turban <term>infula: here referring to the priestly mitre or head-wrap</term>, and a sash. Let them make these sacred garments for your brother Aaron and for his sons, so that they may perform the priesthood for me; for these, they shall use gold, blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine linen. 
<margin>The Ephod.</margin> 
They shall make the ephod of gold, blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine twisted linen, the work of a master weaver <term>phrygionis: literally "of a Phrygian," a term used in antiquity for skilled embroiderers or weavers of patterned cloth</term>. It shall have two shoulder pieces joined at its two edges, so that it is held together. The woven band of the hem, which shall be upon it, shall be of the same workmanship: of gold, blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine twisted linen. Then you shall take two onyx stones and engrave the names of the sons of Israel upon them—six names on each, 
<margin>Wisdom 18.</margin> 
according to their birth. This shall be the work of a stone-cutter, engraved like a seal. See that these names of the Israelites are enclosed in settings of gold. You shall place these two stones on the shoulder pieces of the ephod to be a memorial for the Israelites; Aaron shall bear their names on his two shoulders before Jehovah for the sake of remembrance. You shall make settings of gold, and two small chains of pure gold, finished as cord-work, which you shall insert into the settings. 
<margin>The Breastplate.</margin> 
Likewise, make a breastplate of judgment <term>monile iudiciale: also known as the Rationale of Judgment</term> in the same style of embroidery as the ephod, made of gold, blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine twisted linen. It shall be square and doubled, a span in length and a span in width. Fill it with four rows of set stones. In the first row, there shall be a sardonyx, a topaz, and an emerald. In the second row,

<column-break/>

### EXODUS.

a carbuncle, a sapphire, and a diamond; in the third row, a ligure, an agate, and an amethyst; in the fourth row, a chrysolite, an onyx, and a jasper. These stones shall be enclosed in gold settings and shall correspond to the number of the sons of Israel—that is, twelve. They shall be engraved with twelve names, according to the tribes, just as seals are engraved. Then make for the breastplate braided chains of pure gold. Furthermore, make two golden rings to be fixed to the two ends of the breastplate, and into these you shall insert the two gold chains. The other two ends of the chains shall be attached to the two settings on the front shoulder pieces of the ephod. Then make two more golden rings and attach them to the two inner edges of the breastplate, on the side facing the ephod. Make two other golden rings and place them on the front of the two shoulder pieces of the ephod, below the seam and above the woven band. The breastplate shall then be bound by its rings to the rings of the ephod with a blue ribbon, so that it sits above the woven band of the ephod and is not displaced from it. In this breastplate of judgment, Aaron shall bear the names of the Israelites over his heart when he enters the sanctuary, as a perpetual memorial in the sight of Jehovah. And within this breastplate of judgment, you shall place **CLARITY AND INTEGRITY** <note>original: "CLARITAS ET INTEGRITAS." These are the Latin translations for the Urim and Thummim, sacred lots used by the High Priest to determine the divine will</note>, which Aaron shall have upon his breast whenever he comes into the presence of Jehovah; he shall bear the judgment of the Israelites upon his breast in the 
<margin>The Robe.</margin> 
presence of Jehovah forever. Likewise, make the robe of the ephod entirely of blue. In the middle of the top, there shall be an opening for the head with a woven border around it, like the collar of a coat of mail, so that it does not tear. Around its hem, you shall make pomegranates of blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and fine twisted linen, 
<margin>Ecclesiasticus 45.</margin> 
and place golden bells between them all around. Aaron shall use this in his ministry; the sound shall be heard when he enters the holy place before Jehovah and when he comes out, so that he may be protected from death. Likewise, make a plate of pure gold and engrave upon it, like a seal: SACRED TO JEHOVAH. You shall fasten it to the front of the turban with a blue ribbon, so that Aaron may have it upon his forehead. He shall thus bear any guilt concerning the holy gifts which the Israelites consecrate; he shall have it on his forehead continually to win favor for them before Jehovah. Weave the tunic of fine linen, and make a turban of fine linen, 
<margin>Garments of the Priests.</margin> 
and a sash of embroidered work. Also make tunics, sashes, and caps for Aaron's sons, so they may be decently adorned. With these garments you shall clothe your brother Aaron and his sons; you shall anoint them, ordain them, and consecrate them to the priesthood for me. Then make for them linen undergarments <term>femoralia: breeches or drawers</term> to cover their nakedness, reaching from the loins to the thighs. Both Aaron and his sons shall wear them whenever they enter the Tabernacle of the Testimony or approach the altar to perform the sacred rites, so they do not incur guilt and die. This shall be a perpetual rite for him and for his descendants.

Incense is to be offered to Jehovah <note>original: "Iouam," a Latinized form of the Hebrew divine name Yahweh, commonly written as Jehovah in early modern scholarship</note> for your future generations. On this altar, no foreign incense may be offered, nor shall any burnt sacrifice or grain offering be made, nor shall any wine be poured out as a drink offering. But upon its horns, Aaron shall make atonement with the blood of the sin offering; he shall make this atonement only once a year, a practice to be passed down to your descendants. This shall be most holy to Jehovah.

The Census.
Numbers 1.
Leviticus 7.
Numbers 3.
Exodus 45.

Jehovah also said these things to Moses: When you take a census of the Israelites, each man shall pay a ransom for his life to Jehovah during the census, so that no plague may strike them while they are being counted. Specifically, they shall give half a sacred <term>shekel</term> <note>original: "sicli," a standard weight and currency unit</note>—a shekel being worth twenty <term>obols</term> <note>original: "obolos," a small Greek coin used here to explain the value of a gerah</note>—as an offering to Jehovah. Everyone who is counted, that is, those twenty years of age and older, shall pay this, such that the rich shall not give more and the poor shall not give less than half a shekel, as an offering to Jehovah to make atonement for yourselves. When you have collected this atonement money from the Israelites, assign it to the service of the Tabernacle of the Oracle <note>original: "oracularis tabernaculi," usually translated as the Tent of Meeting</note>, so that it may stand as a memorial before Jehovah to be mindful of the lives of the Israelites.

<margin>
The Basin for washing.
</margin>
Furthermore, he said: make a bronze basin with a bronze stand for washing. Place it between the Tabernacle of the Oracle and the altar, and fill it with water, so that Aaron and his sons may wash their hands and feet with the water. They must do this whenever they enter the Tabernacle of the Oracle or approach the altar to minister and perform the burnt offering to Jehovah, so that they may avoid death through that washing. He and his descendants shall keep this custom forever.

<margin>
The Anointing Oil.
</margin>
In addition, he said: take the finest spices—five hundred sacred shekels of liquid myrrh, half as much of fragrant cinnamon (that is, two hundred and fifty), two hundred and fifty of fragrant cane, five hundred of <term>cassia</term> <note>original: "iris," here used for the fragrant root or cassia</note>, and one <term>hin</term> <note>a Hebrew unit of liquid measure, about 4-6 liters</note> of olive oil. From these, make a sacred anointing oil, blended by the perfumer’s art. Use it to anoint the Tabernacle of the Oracle, the Ark of the Oracle, the table and all its utensils, the lampstand and its utensils, the altar of incense, the altar of burnt offerings with all its utensils, and the basin with its stand. Consecrate them so they may be most holy, so that whatever touches them shall be consecrated. You shall also anoint Aaron and his sons, consecrating them to me for the priestly office. Then instruct the Israelites to consider this oil holy to me for all generations; it must not be poured on the bodies of ordinary men, nor shall you make any other oil with this same formula. It is sacred, and you must treat it as sacred. Whoever mixes anything like it, or puts it on anyone who is not a priest <note>original: "alienū," meaning a stranger or someone unauthorized</note>, shall be cut off from his people.

<margin>The Incense.</margin>
Moreover, he said: take fragrant spices—stacte, saffron <note>original: "crocum," usually identifying onycha in this context</note>, fragrant galbanum, and pure frankincense—all in equal amounts. From these, make a pure, sacred incense, seasoned according to the perfumer’s art. Grind some of it into a fine powder and place it before the Oracle in the Tabernacle of the Oracle, where I will meet with you; you shall regard it as most holy. Do not make any incense for your own use according to this formula, but regard it as holy to Jehovah. Whoever makes anything like it to enjoy its fragrance shall be cut off from his people.

### CHAPTER XXXI.

<margin>Bezalel.</margin>
Behold, he said, I have specifically chosen Bezalel son of Uri, the grandson of Hur, from the tribe of Judah. I have filled him with a divine spirit of skill, intelligence, and knowledge in every kind of craft, so that he may devise ingenious designs and work in gold, silver, and bronze; and that he may skillfully set gemstones and carve wood, and practice every kind of craftsmanship.

<margin>Oholiab.</margin>
To him I have added Oholiab son of Ahisamach, from the tribe of Dan. I have also placed skill into the hearts of all who are gifted, so that they may make everything I have commanded you: the Tabernacle of the Oracle, the Ark of the Oracle and the atonement cover <note>original: "propitiatorium," often called the Mercy Seat</note> to be placed upon it, all the furnishings of the Tabernacle, the table, the pure lampstand (both with their utensils), the altar of incense, the altar of burnt offerings with all its utensils, and the basin with its stand. Also, the ceremonial garments: the sacred garments for Aaron the high priest and the priestly garments for his sons. Finally, the anointing oil and the fragrant incense for the sanctuary. I say again, they shall make all these things exactly as I have commanded you.

<margin>
The Sabbath.
Exodus 20.
</margin>
But you must remind the Israelites, he said, to keep my Sabbaths. For this is a sign placed between me and them for future generations, so it may be understood that they are made holy by me, Jehovah. Therefore, keep the Sabbath and hold it holy. Anyone who violates it shall be put to death; and whoever does any work on that day shall be cut off from the number of his people. Work shall be done for six days, but the seventh day is the Sabbath of rest, sacred to Jehovah. Anyone who performs work on the Sabbath day shall suffer the penalty of death. Therefore the Israelites must see to it that they and their descendants observe the Sabbath as a perpetual covenant. This is a perpetual pledge between me and the Israelites; for in six days Jehovah made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day he rested and was refreshed.

### CHAPTER XXXIII.

<margin>Genesis 12, 3, 23. Joshua 24. Deuteronomy 7.</margin> In the meantime, He said, depart from here, together with the people you led out of the borders of Egypt, to the land which I confirmed by oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, that I would give it to their offspring—a land flowing with milk and honey. I will send an Angel before you to drive out the Canaanites, Amorites, Hittites, Hivites, and Jebusites. For I myself will not go among you—a people of such stiff necks—lest I consume you on the way. After the people heard this harsh word, they turned to mourning, and everyone abstained from their usual grooming and ornaments. For Jehovah, through Moses as intermediary, had reproached them for their stubbornness, saying that if He were to go among them, He might consume them in a moment. For that reason, He commanded them to lay aside their ornaments, so that He might see what He should decide concerning them. So the Israelites stripped themselves of their finery from Mount Horeb onward. <margin>Moses pitches the tabernacle.</margin> Moses, however, pitched the tent outside the camp, far from the camp, and called it the Tabernacle of the Oracle <note>commonly known as the Tent of Meeting</note>. To this Tabernacle of the Oracle, everyone who wished to consult Jehovah went out outside the camp. And as Moses went out to the tent, everyone would rise, and standing generally before their own tents, they watched Moses from behind until he entered the tent. Once he had entered, the pillar of cloud would descend and stand before the tent while He spoke with Moses. The entire people, seeing it standing before the tent, would rise, and as each person stood before their own tent, they would bow down. Jehovah spoke to Moses face to face <note>original: "praesens praesentem," meaning present to one who is present</note>, just as people are accustomed to speak among themselves. Then Moses would return to the camp, while in the meantime his assistant Joshua, the son of Nun, a young man, did not move from the middle of the tent. <margin>Moses prays to Jehovah that He Himself might go with the people.</margin> Moses then spoke these words to Jehovah: Behold, you command me to lead this people, yet you do not show me whom you will send with me, even though you say that I am known to you by name and have found favor in your grace. Therefore, if I have found favor in your grace, teach me your way, that I may know you, so that I may continue to find favor in your grace; and consider also that this nation is your people. Then He said: I myself will go with you in person, and I will give you rest. And Moses said: For unless you yourself go in person, do not lead us away from here. By what means, finally, shall it be known that I and your people have found favor in your grace? <margin>An offering</margin>
Jehovah <note>original: "Ioua," a Latinized form of the Tetragrammaton</note> commands, he says, that you should prepare an offering for Him, according to what each person’s heart is moved to contribute toward this offering for Jehovah of their own accord: namely gold, silver, bronze, blue fabric <note>original: "hyacinthum," referring to a blue or violet dye</note>, purple, double-dyed scarlet, fine linen, goat hair, ram skins dyed red, badger skins <note>original: "pelles melium," likely referring to durable leather, often translated as badger or porpoise skins</note>, cedar wood, oil for the lamps, spices for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense. Furthermore, onyx stones and gemstones suitable for setting, for the ephod <note>a sacred vestment worn by the High Priest</note> and the breastplate. Then, let the most skilled among you come forward to make everything that Jehovah has commanded:

<margin>A summary of the work.</margin>
the tabernacle with its tent, its covering, hooks, boards, bars, columns, and their bases. Likewise the ark, its poles, the mercy seat, and the veil to be hung as a screen. Likewise the table with its poles, all its utensils, and the bread of the presence. Likewise the lampstand for illumination with its equipment, its lamps, and the lamp oil. Likewise the altar of incense and its poles, the anointing oil, the fragrant incense, and the screen for the door of the tabernacle. Likewise the altar of burnt offerings with its bronze grate, its poles, and all its equipment; then the basin with its stand. Likewise the hangings of the court, the pillars with their bases, as well as the screen for the gate of the court, the pegs of the tabernacle and the court, and their cords. Then the extra garments for officiating at the rites, and the sacred garments of Aaron the priest, and the priestly garments of his sons.

<margin>Contributions to the sacred work.</margin>
Therefore, when the whole assembly was dismissed by Moses, the Israelites came voluntarily, just as each person's willing spirit and mind exhorted and urged them. They commonly brought an offering to Jehovah for the work of the tent of meeting <note>original: "oracularis tabernaculi," referring to the place where God spoke</note>, for all its furnishings, and for the sacred garments. Commonly, not only the men but also the women brought of their own accord brooches, earrings, rings, bracelets, and all other such golden ornaments—whoever wished to present gold as a gift to Jehovah. Others brought blue fabric, purple, double-dyed scarlet, fine linen, goat hair, ram skins dyed red, and badger skins, according to what each had in abundance. Others provided silver and bronze for that gift according to their own means. Those who had cedar wood brought it for the work of the whole project. Also, all the most skilled women spun with their own hands blue, purple, and double-dyed scarlet fabric and fine linen, and supplied the spun material. Some (who excelled in the knowledge of such things) spun the goat hair. The leaders, however, provided the onyx stones and other gems suitable for engraving for the ephod and the breastplate, as well as the spices and the oil for both the lamps and the anointing ointment, and for the fragrant incense. Thus the Israelites, not only men but also women, as each person's own will moved them to contribute to any part of the work that Jehovah had commanded to be done through Moses, all performed a voluntary service as a gift to Jehovah.

### CHAPTER XXXVI.

Therefore Bezalel and Oholiab, and all the most gifted men whom Jehovah had gifted with skill, wisdom, and the knowledge of how to act, completed the entire work of the sacred ministry according to Jehovah’s prescription. When they were called forth by Moses to begin the work, as each person’s will was inclined toward it, they took all the collections of the Israelites that had been placed with Moses for that purpose, intending to begin the business and perform the sacred work. But since more was contributed voluntarily day by day, all those craftsmen, leaving the works they were performing, went to Moses and showed him that more was being contributed by the people than what the completion of the work commanded by Jehovah required. Therefore Moses ordered it to be proclaimed throughout the camp that no one, whether man or woman, should henceforth add anything to the sacred offering. Thus the people stopped contributing, because there was already enough and more than enough to finish the whole work.

<margin>The linens.</margin>
Therefore, all those skilled in the work made ten curtains for the tabernacle out of spun fine linen, blue, purple, and double-dyed scarlet fabric, and these were decorated with Cherubim <note>angelic figures</note> in embroidery work. For each curtain of the tabernacle, the length was <note>The number 28 is omitted in the Latin but implied</note> cubits, and the width was four cubits—the same measure for all. These he joined together in two sets of five. Then he made blue loops along the edge of one curtain at the seam, and similarly on the edge of the last curtain at the other seam, fifty on each side, corresponding to each other. Then he made fifty gold hooks, with which he joined the curtains to one another so that it became one tent.

<margin>The coverings.</margin>
He also made eleven curtains of goat hair to cover the tabernacle, thirty cubits in length and four in width, the same measure for all of them. He joined five of these separately and six separately. Then he made fifty loops along the edge of the last curtain at the seam, and the same number along the edge of the other curtain at the seam; and likewise fifty golden hooks to join the covering into one. For this covering, he made an outer layer of ram skins dyed red, and also a covering of badger skins on top of that.

<margin>The boards.</margin>
He also made upright boards for the tabernacle out of cedar, ten cubits in length and one and a half cubits in width, all of which had two tenons fitted to one another. He made twenty of these boards for the southern side of the tabernacle, under which he placed forty silver bases—namely, two for each board, matching the number of tenons. He did the same and in the same manner for the other side, on the northern part. For the western part of the tabernacle, he made six boards, and two in the corners...

### CHAPTER XXXVI.

Bezalel and Oholiab, therefore, along with every talented man whom Jehovah had gifted with skill, wisdom, and the knowledge of how to act, completed the entire work of the sacred ministry according to Jehovah’s prescription. When they were called by Moses to begin the work, according as each man’s will was inclined toward it, they took from Moses all the contributions gathered from the Israelites for that purpose, being ready to enter the business and perform the sacred work. But since more was voluntarily contributed every day, all those craftsmen left the work they were performing and went to Moses, showing that more was being contributed by the people than was required for the completion of the work commanded by Jehovah. Therefore, Moses ordered it to be proclaimed throughout the camp that no man or woman should henceforth add anything to the sacred offering. Thus the people ceased their contributing, for there was already enough and more than enough to finish the entire work. All those skilled craftsmen, therefore, made ten curtains for the tabernacle out of twisted fine linen, blue, purple, and scarlet, with Cherubim worked into them with embroidery. The length of each curtain for the tabernacle was twenty-eight cubits, and the width was four cubits; the measurement was the same for all. He joined five of these curtains to one another. Then he made loops of blue along the edge of one curtain at the seam; likewise on the edge of the last curtain at the other seam, fifty loops on each side, corresponding to one another. Then he made fifty gold hooks, with which he joined the curtains together so that it might become one tent. He also made eleven <margin>Coverings.</margin> curtains of goat hair for a covering over the tabernacle: the length was thirty cubits and the width four cubits, the same measurement for all. He joined five of them by themselves and six by themselves. Then he made fifty loops along the edge of the last curtain at the seam, and fifty along the edge of the curtain at the other seam. He also made fifty bronze <note>The Latin says "aureos" (gold) here, though standard texts often specify bronze for the outer tent hooks</note> hooks to join the covering into one. For this tent, he made a covering of ram skins dyed red, and above that, a covering of fine leather. He also made the frames for the tabernacle out of upright cedar wood, ten cubits in length and a cubit and a half in width, all of which had two tenons fitted to one another. He made twenty of these frames for the south side of the tabernacle, under which he placed forty silver bases, specifically two for each frame, according to the number of tenons. He did the same and in the same manner for the other side, on the north. For the west side of the tabernacle, he made six frames, and two for the corners...

### CHAPTER XXXVII.

<margin>The Ark.</margin> Beseleel <note>often spelled Bezalel in English Bibles</note> also made the ark of cedar wood, two and a half cubits long, and one and a half cubits in both width and height. He overlaid it with pure gold inside and out, and surrounded it with a golden molding. Then he cast four golden rings for its four corners, attaching two rings to each of its sides. Likewise, he made poles of cedar, which he overlaid with gold, and passed them through the rings at the sides of the ark for carrying it. He also made the mercy seat <note>original: "propitiatorium," the golden cover of the Ark</note> of pure gold, two and a half cubits long, and one and a half cubits wide. Then he made two golden cherubim, hammered from a single piece, on both ends of the mercy seat—one at one end and the other at the other end. He made them as part of the mercy seat itself on both sides, so that they covered the mercy seat with their wings spread out above, facing one another across the mercy seat. <margin>The Table.</margin> He also made a table of cedar wood, two cubits long, one cubit wide, and one and a half cubits high. He plated it with pure gold and encircled it with a golden molding, which he fitted to a rim a handbreadth wide <note>original: "margini dodrantali," literally a three-quarter foot or nine-inch margin</note> that surrounded the table. For this table, he cast four golden rings and fastened them to the corners of its four feet, so that they were near the rim to hold the poles for carrying the table. He also made these poles of cedar and plated them with gold. Then he made the vessels to be placed on the table: the dishes, cups, bowls, and pitchers for pouring drink offerings, all of pure gold. <margin>The Lampstand.</margin> He also made the lampstand of pure, solid gold, so that its base, shaft, bowls, knobs, and lilies were all of the same piece. Six branches extended from its sides, three from each side. These six branches had three bowls shaped like almond shells, each with a knob and a lily. On the lampstand itself were four bowls, knobs, and lilies; and under each of the three pairs of branches extending from it was a knob, so that the knobs and the branches were of the piece with the lampstand, all of one solid piece of pure gold. He also made its seven lamps, along with its tongs and trays, of pure gold.

He made this lampstand and all its equipment from a talent of pure gold. <margin>The Altar of Incense.</margin> He also made the incense altar of cedar wood, one cubit square and two cubits high, so that its horns were of one piece with it. He overlaid it with pure gold—namely its top, its sides all around, and its horns—and he surrounded it with a golden molding. Under the molding, he made two golden rings on both of its sides as holders for the cedar poles, which he made and overlaid with gold. He also made the sacred anointing oil and the pure, fragrant incense, according to the art of the perfumer.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII.

<margin>The Altar of Burnt Offering.</margin> He also made the altar of burnt offering of cedar wood, five cubits long and five cubits wide—square—and three cubits high. Its horns were on its four corners and were part of the altar itself, which he covered with bronze. He also made all the bronze equipment: the pots, shovels, basins, meat-forks, and firepans—all of bronze. He made a grate for the altar of bronze mesh work, and placed it under the ledge of the altar, reaching halfway up. Then he cast four bronze rings for the four corners of the grate to hold the poles, which he made of cedar and covered with bronze. He passed the poles through the rings on the sides of the altar for carrying it, having made the altar hollow, out of boards. He also made the bronze basin and its bronze stand from the bronze mirrors of the women who kept watch at the entrance of the Tabernacle of the Oracle <note>original: "oraculi tabernaculo," often translated as the Tent of Meeting</note>. <margin>The Courtyard.</margin> He also made the courtyard: on the south and north sides, there were hangings of fine twisted linen, one hundred cubits long. Their columns were twenty, with twenty bronze bases, but the capitals and bands were of silver. On the western side, the hangings were fifty cubits long, with ten columns and ten bases, and their capitals and bands were of silver. Likewise, on the eastern side, the hangings were fifty cubits long. On each side of the gate, there were hangings of fifteen cubits, with three columns and three bases on each side. All the hangings around the courtyard were of fine twisted linen. The bases of the columns were of bronze, the capitals and bands were of silver, and their tops were overlaid with silver; all the bands of the courtyard columns were silver. <margin>The Screen.</margin> The screen for the entrance of the courtyard was made of multicolored work <note>original: "opere polymito"</note>, of blue, purple, double-dyed scarlet, and fine twisted linen, twenty cubits long and five cubits high (matching the width), following the hangings of the courtyard. <margin>a. Namely, of the hangings that made up the screen.</margin> Their columnsᵃ were four, with four bronze bases; but their capitals were silver, and their heads and bands were plated with silver. All the pegs for the sanctuary and the courtyard all around were of bronze. This is the sum of the expenses for the Tabernacle of the Oracle, as calculated by the command of Moses through the service of the Levites, under the direction of Ithamar, son of Aaron the priest. Beseleel, son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, had made everything that Jehovah <note>original: "Iouæ"</note> had commanded Moses, together with Oholiab, son of Achisamach, of the tribe of Dan, a craftsman, designer, and embroiderer in blue, in purple... <meta>catchword: purple...</meta>

### CHAPTER XXXIX.

<margin>The Ephod.</margin>
From the blue, purple, and double-dyed scarlet fabric, they made the special garments for ministering in the sanctuary, as well as the sacred garments for Aaron, just as Jehovah <note>original: "Ioua," a Latin rendering of the Tetragrammaton</note> had commanded Moses. Therefore, they made the ephod <note>a ceremonial vest-like garment worn by the High Priest</note> of gold, blue, purple, double-dyed scarlet, and fine twisted linen. They beat the gold into thin plates and cut it into threads to weave it into the blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen—the work of a skilled embroiderer. They made two shoulder pieces for it, which were joined together at its two edges. The woven waistband added to it was made of the same material and workmanship: of gold, blue, purple, double-dyed scarlet, and fine twisted linen, just as Jehovah had commanded Moses. They also prepared onyx stones, set in gold enclosures and engraved like seals with the names of the sons of Israel. These were placed on the shoulder pieces of the ephod to serve as stones of remembrance for the Israelites, just as Jehovah had commanded 
<margin>The Breastpiece.</margin>
Moses. They also made the breastpiece <note>original: "monile," referring to the Breastpiece of Judgment</note>, crafted with the same skill as the ephod, of gold, blue, purple, double-dyed scarlet, and fine twisted linen. It was square and folded double, a span <note>about 9 inches</note> in both length and width. They filled it with four rows of gemstones. In the first row were a sardonyx, a topaz, and an emerald. In the second row, a carbuncle, a sapphire, and a diamond. In the third row, a ligure, an agate, and an amethyst. In the fourth row, a chrysolite, an onyx, and a jasper. These gems were enclosed in their gold settings. There were twelve stones, corresponding to the number of the sons of Israel, each engraved with a name according to the twelve tribes. Then they made for the breastpiece two braided chains of pure gold. They also made two gold clasps and two gold rings, which they attached to the two ends of the breastpiece, and they fastened the two gold chains to the ends of the breastpiece.

They inserted the two ends of the chains into the two clasps and fastened them to the front shoulder pieces of the ephod. Then they made two more gold rings and attached them to the other two ends of the breastpiece on the inner edge next to the ephod. They also made two other gold rings and placed them under the two shoulder pieces of the ephod on the front, near the seam above the waistband. They bound the breastpiece by its rings to the rings of the ephod with a blue cord, so that it would sit above the waistband and not come loose, just as Jehovah had commanded Moses. Next, they made the robe <note>original: "prætextam"</note> of the ephod of woven work, 
<margin>The Robe.</margin>

Then they made bells of pure gold, which they interspersed between the pomegranates all around the hem of the robe for use in ministry, just as Jehovah had commanded Moses. Likewise, they made woven linen tunics for Aaron and his sons,

Finally, they made the plate for the holy crown of 
<margin>The Plate.</margin>
pure gold, and inscribed upon it like an engraving on a seal: HOLY TO JEHOVAH <note>original: "IOVÆ SACRVM"</note>. The Israelites did exactly as Jehovah 
<margin>Summary of the work.</margin>

They brought the tabernacle to Moses: the tent and all its furnishings, its hooks, frames, bars, columns, bases, the covering of ram skins dyed red, the covering of badger skins <note>original: "melium pellibus," likely sea-cow or dolphin skins</note>, the screening veil, the ark of the oracle and its poles, the mercy seat, the table and all its utensils, the showbread, the pure lampstand with its lamps set in order and all its utensils, the oil for light, the golden altar, the anointing oil, the fragrant incense, the screen for the entrance of the tabernacle, the bronze altar and its bronze grate, its poles and all its utensils, the basin with its stand, the hangings of the courtyard, the columns with their bases, the screen for the courtyard gate, the cords, the pegs—in short, everything belonging to the tabernacle of the tent of the oracle. Also, the special garments for ministering in the sanctuary, the sacred garments for Aaron the high priest, and those of his sons to serve as priests. In brief, the Israelites did the whole work exactly as Jehovah had commanded Moses. So when Moses saw that they had performed the entire work accurately according to Jehovah’s prescription, he blessed them.

### CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'V' featuring a religious scene with a figure kneeling before a radiant cloud or divine presence in a landscape.</image-desc>
Now Jehovah called Moses, and spoke to him from the tabernacle of the oracle in this manner. Speak to the Israelites in these words: If any of you brings a gift to Jehovah (and you shall do this from the cattle, 

<margin>The law of the whole burnt sacrifice. Exodus 29</margin>
doing so from the ox or the flock), if the gift is a whole burnt sacrifice <note>original: "solidum sacrificium," often called a holocaust</note> from the ox, let him bring a perfect male; let him present him at the door of the tabernacle of the oracle to win favor for himself from Jehovah, and let him lay his hand upon the head of the victim, so that through this supplication favor may be won for him. Then let the offspring of the ox be sacrificed before Jehovah, and let the priests, the sons of Aaron, offer its blood, sprinkling it around the altar placed at the door of the tabernacle of the oracle. Let the victim be flayed and cut into pieces. Then let the sons of Aaron the priest set fire upon the altar, and kindle a pile of wood in the fire: let them arrange the head and the fat from the pieces upon the wood placed on the fire. But let the entrails and the legs be washed with water, and let the priest burn everything on the altar, so that Jehovah may be soothed by the odor of the victim being burned. But if the gift is from the flock—from the sheep or the goats—let him bring a perfect male for a whole burnt sacrifice: and let it be sacrificed on the northern side of the altar before Jehovah: let the priests, the sons of Aaron, sprinkle the blood around the altar: let the victim be cut into pieces. Let the priest set the head and the fat upon the pile of wood placed on the fire on the altar. Let them wash the entrails and the legs with water. Let the priest offer the whole and burn it on the altar, so that the odor of the whole burnt sacrifice may soothe Jehovah. If he makes a whole burnt sacrifice to Jehovah from birds, let him bring it from turtledoves or from young pigeons. Let the priest present it at the altar, wring off its head, and burn it on the altar: let the blood be drained out on the side of the altar: let him remove the crop with its feathers and cast it into the ash-pit on the eastern side of the altar.

Let him tear it by the wings, but not divide it, and burn it on the altar upon the wood-pile, so that Jehovah may be soothed by the odor of that whole burnt sacrifice.

LEVITICUS.

E 3

...you shall make it, let it be made of fine flour in oil. From these things bring the prepared grain offering to Jehovah <note>original: "Iouae," a Latinization of the Hebrew Name of God, YHWH</note>, and present it to the priest; the priest shall then move it toward the altar, take from it a memorial portion <note>original: "monimentum," the part of the offering burnt to represent the whole</note>, and burn it on the altar, that Jehovah may be soothed by the scent of its burning. The remains of the grain offering shall belong to Aaron and his sons, as a most holy portion of the divine sacrifice of Jehovah. Every grain offering that you offer to Jehovah shall be made without leaven: for it is not lawful for you to burn anything of leaven or of honey to Jehovah in a divine sacrifice. You shall offer an offering of the firstfruits to Jehovah: but they shall not be placed upon the altar for a sweet savor. Season every offering of your grain sacrifice with salt: do not deprive your grain offering of the salt of the covenant of your God; indeed, in every one of your offerings you shall offer salt. If, however, you bring a grain offering of the firstfruits to Jehovah, you shall offer the offering of your firstfruits from the earliest fruit toasted by fire, or from crushed grain; add oil and put frankincense upon it: let it be a grain offering of this kind. The priest shall burn the memorial portion from that crushed grain and oil, together with all the frankincense. This shall be a divine sacrifice to Jehovah.

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>Sacrifices for well-being.</margin>
If, however, a person makes a sacrifice for well-being <note>original: "pro salute," often translated as "peace offering"</note>, if he offers from the herd, whether male or female, he shall bring it unblemished into the presence of Jehovah, and shall lay his hand upon the head of his offering, and it shall be sacrificed at the entrance of the tabernacle of the oracle. The priests, the sons of Aaron, shall sprinkle the blood around the altar. He himself shall offer from the sacrifice of well-being as a divine offering to Jehovah the fat that covers the entrails <note>original: "omentum"</note>, all the fat upon the inner parts, and both kidneys with their fat adhering to the loins, and the lobe of the liver, removed with the kidneys. The sons of Aaron shall burn this on the altar, upon the victim placed on the wood of the funeral pile <note>original: "rogali strui," a classical Latin term used here to describe the altar fire</note>, so that Jehovah may be soothed by the scent of its burning. But if he makes a sacrifice for well-being to Jehovah from the flock, whether of sheep or goats, he shall bring a male or female without blemish. If he brings a sheep, he shall present it before Jehovah; he shall lay his hand upon its head and slaughter it before the tabernacle of the oracle. The sons of Aaron shall sprinkle its blood around the altar. He himself shall offer from the sacrifice for well-being as an offering to Jehovah the fat: the entire fat tail, removed close to the spine, the fat covering the entrails, and all the fat upon the inner parts, both kidneys with their fat adhering to the loins, and the lobe of the liver, removed with the kidneys. The priest shall burn this on the altar as the food of the divine sacrifice for Jehovah. If the offering is a goat, he shall present it before Jehovah; he shall lay his hand upon its head and slaughter it before the tabernacle of the oracle. The sons of Aaron shall sprinkle its blood around the altar. He himself shall offer from it as an offering to Jehovah the fat covering the entrails, all the fat upon the inner parts, both kidneys with their fat that is above the loins, and the lobe of the liver, removed with the kidneys. The priest shall burn these on the altar as the food of the divine sacrifice of a pleasant odor, so that all fat may belong to Jehovah. Observe this decree for the future wherever you shall dwell, so that you eat no fat and no blood.

### CHAPTER IIII.

And speak these things to the Israelites, he said: If anyone sins through ignorance <note>original: "per imprudentiam," unintentional sin</note>, and does anything forbidden against any commandment of Jehovah, <margin>Atonement for the priest’s guilt.</margin> if the anointed priest sins to the guilt of the people, he shall offer for the sin he has committed an unblemished young bull to Jehovah as a sin offering <note>original: "piaculum," an offering for atonement</note>.

<column-break/>

He shall present that bull at the door of the tabernacle of the oracle before Jehovah; he shall lay his hand upon its head and slaughter it before Jehovah. The anointed priest shall carry some of the blood into the tabernacle of the oracle, and dipping his finger in that blood, he shall sprinkle it seven times before Jehovah toward the veil of the sanctuary; he shall also smear some on the horns of the altar of fragrant incense before Jehovah, which is in the tabernacle of the oracle; all the rest of the bull’s blood he shall pour out at the base of the altar of sacrifice, which is at the entrance of the tabernacle of the oracle. He shall take away all the fat of the bull of the sin offering: all the fat covering the entrails and the inner parts, both kidneys with the fat adhering to the loins, and the lobe of the liver, removed with the kidneys, just as it is taken from the ox sacrificed for well-being. The priest shall burn these things on the altar of sacrifice. But the hide of the bull and its entire body, with the head, legs, entrails, and dung—in short, the entire bull—he shall carry outside the camp to a clean place where the ashes are poured out, and there he shall burn it with fire upon a pile of wood where the ashes are. <margin>Atonement for public guilt.</margin> But if the entire community of the Israelites acts through ignorance and unknowingly does something forbidden against any commandment of Jehovah and they contract guilt, as soon as the committed sin becomes known, then the city <note>original: "ciuitas," used here to mean the assembly or community</note> shall offer a bull for the sin and bring it before the tabernacle of the oracle. The elders of the city shall lay their hands upon its head before Jehovah. Then the anointed priest shall slaughter it before Jehovah. He shall carry some of the blood into the tabernacle of the oracle, and dipping his finger in that blood, he shall sprinkle it seven times before Jehovah toward the veil; he shall also smear some on the horns of the altar placed before Jehovah in the tabernacle of the oracle. All the rest he shall pour out at the base of the altar of sacrifice, which is at the entrance of the tabernacle of the oracle, and having taken away all its fat, he shall burn it on the altar. He shall do with the bull just as he did with the previous bull of the sin offering, and by supplicating for them, he shall pray for their pardon. He shall carry the bull outside the camp and burn it as he burned the first bull. And this shall be the atonement for the city. <margin>Atonement for the magistrate’s guilt.</margin> If a magistrate sins and unintentionally does something forbidden against any commandment of Jehovah his God so that he is in guilt, as soon as the sin committed by him becomes known to him, he shall bring as his offering a male goat, unblemished. He shall lay his hand upon its head and slaughter it in the place where they are accustomed to slaughter the victim of the burnt offering before Jehovah, for it is a sin offering. Then the priest shall take some of the blood of the sin offering with his finger and smear it on the horns of the altar of sacrifice; the rest he shall pour out at the base of the same altar. ### CHAPTER V.

<margin>Atonement for guilt.</margin>
If anyone has sinned, such as if he is called to take an oath concerning any matter of which he is aware—whether he saw it himself or learned of it elsewhere—yet he does not report it, he has committed a fault: or if someone touches any unclean thing, such as the carcass of an unclean animal, or the carcass of an unclean beast, or the carcass of an unclean reptile, and does so unknowingly, he is defiled and is in a state of guilt: or finally, if he touches any human uncleanness by which one might be defiled, and does so through ignorance, when he realizes it, he is in a state of guilt: or if <margin>a. This means concerning any matter.</margin> <gloss>a</gloss> anyone swears with thoughtless words, whether for evil or for good, regarding anything about which men swear rashly, and does so through ignorance, once he realizes it, he is in a state of guilt because of any of these: if, I say, he has committed a fault in any of these, then having confessed that he has sinned in that matter, he shall bring to Jehovah an expiation for that fault. For the sin he committed, he shall bring a sheep or a female goat as a **sin offering**, and the priest shall pray for his sin. But if his means are not sufficient to obtain a head of livestock, he shall bring for the fault he committed two turtledoves or two young pigeons to Jehovah, one for a sin offering and the other for a **whole burnt sacrifice**. He shall bring them to the priest, who shall offer the one for the sin offering first, and shall wring its head at the neck but not pull it off, and shall sprinkle some of the blood of the sin offering on the side of the altar; the rest of the blood he shall pour out at the bottom of the altar. This shall be the atonement. Then he shall make the second a whole burnt sacrifice, as is the custom, and shall pray for the sin he committed, so that it may be forgiven him. But if his means do not extend to two turtledoves or two young pigeons, he shall bring as an offering for his committed sin a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour, in which he shall use no oil nor add any frankincense, since it is a sin offering. He shall bring it to the priest. The priest shall take his handful of that flour as a memorial, and burn it on the altar for the divine service of Jehovah (this shall be the atonement), and shall pray for the sin committed in any of those matters, so that it may be forgiven him. <margin>He who defrauded consecrated things.</margin> The rest of the offering shall belong to the priest. Furthermore, if anyone, he says, incurs a crime by unknowingly defrauding the sacred things of Jehovah, he shall bring for his fault to Jehovah a ram without blemish from the flock, valued

### CHAPTER VI.

<margin>Atonement for perjury.</margin>
Likewise, if anyone sins, he says, and commits a crime against Jehovah, and denies to another a trust or a deposit, or if he has robbed another, or committed fraud, or has found something lost and denied it, <margin>Numbers 5</margin> and has sworn falsely in any one of these things in which men are prone to sin—if, I say, he has sinned and contracted guilt, he shall restore what was stolen, or <margin>The law of guilt.</margin> what was defrauded, or the trust, or the thing found: in short, whatever he swore falsely about, he shall restore the full amount, adding a fifth part, and give it to the owner of the thing on the day he makes his atonement. And for his fault, he shall lead to Jehovah a ram without blemish from the flock, according to the valuation, as a penalty to the priest, and that priest shall pray for pardon before Jehovah for any one thing in which he committed a penalty. Furthermore, command Aaron and his sons in this way, he says: This shall be the law of the **whole burnt sacrifice**: <margin>The law of the whole burnt sacrifice.</margin> The victim shall remain on the hearth upon the altar all night until morning, with the fire of the altar burning in it. The priest, clothed in a linen tunic and linen breeches over his body, shall take up the ashes reduced from the burning of the victim from the altar and place them beside the altar. Then, having laid aside those garments, he shall put on others and carry the ashes outside the camp to a clean place. But the fire on the altar shall burn unquenched; the priest shall burn wood on it every morning, and arrange the victim on top, and burn the fat of the sacrifices for well-being upon it, with the fire always burning unquenched on the altar. Moreover, this shall be the law <margin>The law of the grain offering.</margin> of the **grain offering** <note>original: "ferti," an offering of grain or flour</note>. Whichever of the sons of Aaron offers it before Jehovah in front of the altar shall take a handful of it—namely, of the fine flour of the offering and the oil, and all the frankincense placed upon it—and shall burn it on the altar for a sweet savor, as a memorial to Jehovah. Aaron and his sons shall eat the remainder of it, and it shall be eaten without leaven in a holy place, namely in the courtyard of the tabernacle of witness: nor shall it be baked with leaven. I assign this portion to them from my divine sacrifice; it shall be most holy, whether it be a sin offering or a guilt offering. All the males born of Aaron shall eat of this, which indeed is a <margin>The offering for the consecration of the high priest. <br/> a. For the son who succeeds him.</margin> perpetual decree to be handed down to your descendants regarding the divine service of Jehovah, so that none but those consecrated may touch them. Concerning the offering of Aaron or <gloss>a</gloss> his sons, he says, which they shall offer to Jehovah on the day they are anointed, understand it thus: A tenth part of an ephah of fine flour shall be a perpetual grain offering, half of which shall be offered in the morning and half in the evening, prepared in a pan with oil; and thus the toasted and crumbled offering, having been cooked, shall be offered to Jehovah for a sweet savor.

Afterward, he brought forward the sons of Aaron, dressed them in tunics, girded them with sashes, and covered them with caps, just as Jehovah <note>original: "Ioua," a Latinized form of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton</note> had commanded him. Then he brought the bull for the **sin offering** <note>original: "piacularem," an offering for atonement</note>. When Aaron and his sons had laid their hands upon its head, he slaughtered it, took the blood, and with his finger smeared it upon the horns of the altar on every side, thus purifying it. The rest of the blood he poured out at the base of the altar and sanctified it, so that atonement could be made upon it. Then he took all the fat of the entrails, the lobe of the liver, and both kidneys with their fat, and burned them upon the altar. But the bull itself, its hide, its flesh, and its dung, he burned with fire outside the camp, just as Jehovah had commanded him. He also brought forward the ram for the **whole burnt offering** <note>original: "solidum sacrificium," where the entire animal is consumed</note>, and when Aaron and his sons had laid their hands upon its head, he slaughtered it. He splashed the blood around the altar and cut the ram into pieces; he burned the head, the pieces, and the suet. He washed the entrails and the legs with water, and burned the entire ram upon the altar. This is a whole burnt offering of a pleasing aroma; this is a divine sacrifice to Jehovah, just as Jehovah had commanded Moses. Then he brought forward the second ram, namely the **ram of initiation** <note>original: "initiatorium," referring to the ordination of the priests</note>. When Aaron and his sons had laid their hands upon its head, Moses slaughtered it and took some of its blood, dipping it upon the tip of Aaron’s right ear, the thumb of his right hand, and the big toe of his right foot. Then he brought forward Aaron’s sons and likewise smeared blood upon the tips of their right ears, the thumbs of their right hands, and the big toes of their right feet; the rest of the blood he splashed around the altar. Then he took the fat, the fat tail, all the fat of the entrails, the lobe of the liver, both kidneys with their fat, and the right shoulder. Then from the basket of unleavened bread placed before Jehovah, he took one unleavened cake, one cake of bread tempered with oil, and one wafer, and placed them upon the fat and the right shoulder. He placed all these things into the palms of Aaron and his sons and waved them before Jehovah. Then, taking them from their hands, he burned them upon the altar for the whole burnt offering. This is the initiation for a soothing aroma; this is a divine sacrifice to Jehovah. Afterward, he took the breast and waved it before Jehovah; this portion Moses himself kept from the ram of initiation, as Jehovah had commanded him. Then he took some of the anointing oil and some of the blood that was upon the altar and sprinkled Aaron and his garments, along with his sons and their garments, and thus consecrated both them and their garments. Then he commanded them in this manner: Cook the flesh at the door of the Tabernacle of the Oracle <note>original: "oracularis tabernaculi," the Tent of Meeting</note>, and eat it there with the bread that is in the basket of initiation, just as I was commanded, saying that Aaron and his sons should eat it. 
<margin>Exodus 29</margin> 
But what remains of the flesh and the bread, you shall burn with fire. You shall not depart from the entrance of the Tabernacle of the Oracle for seven days, until the period of your initiation is completed; for your ordination <note>original: "manus initiabūtur," literally "your hands shall be initiated/filled"</note> shall last seven days. Jehovah commanded that what is done today be done

<column-break/>

to make atonement for you. Remain at the entrance of the Tabernacle of the Oracle day and night for seven days, and keep the charge of Jehovah, lest you die; for so I have been commanded. Therefore Aaron and his sons did all those things which Jehovah had commanded through Moses.

### CHAPTER IX.

<margin>
Nadab and Abihu are struck dead. Numbers 3, 26; 1 Chronicles 24. a. Those who would offer libations to themselves.
</margin>
When the eighth day arrived, Moses called together Aaron, his sons, and the elders of Israel. He commanded Aaron to take a young calf for a sin offering and a ram for a whole burnt offering, 
<margin>Exodus 29</margin> 
both without blemish, to present them before Jehovah. He also told him to command the Israelites to take a he-goat for a sin offering, and a calf and a sheep, both a year old and without blemish, for a whole burnt offering; likewise an ox and a ram for a **peace offering** <note>original: "sacrificium pro salute," a sacrifice for well-being or fellowship</note>, to sacrifice them before Jehovah, along with a **grain offering** <note>original: "fertum," a meal offering</note> mixed with oil. For on that day, Jehovah was to appear to them. Then they brought what Moses had commanded to the front of the Tabernacle of the Oracle, and the whole congregation drew near and stood before Jehovah. Then Moses explained what Jehovah had commanded them to do, for the glory of Jehovah was to appear to them. Next, he told Aaron to approach the altar and perform his sin offering and his whole burnt offering, to make atonement for himself and for the people, and to present the people's offering and make atonement for them, 
<margin>b. That which mourners were accustomed to do.</margin> 
just as Jehovah had commanded. Then Aaron approached the altar 
<margin>Aaron performs the sacred rites.</margin> 
and slaughtered the calf for his own sin offering. When his sons brought the blood to him, he dipped his finger in it and smeared the horns of the altar; the rest he poured at the base of the altar. The fat, the kidneys, and the lobe of the liver from the sin offering he burned on the altar, as Jehovah had commanded Moses. The flesh and the hide he burned with fire outside the camp. Then he slaughtered the victim for the whole burnt offering, and when his sons handed him the blood, he splashed it around the altar. They also handed him the victim, piece by piece, along with the head, and he burned them on the altar. He washed the entrails and the legs and burned them upon the whole burnt offering on the altar. Then he brought forward the people’s gift; he took the goat for the people's sin offering, slaughtered it, and made atonement for the people as before. He presented the whole burnt offering 
<margin>c. Any kind of wine made from something other than grapes.</margin> 
and performed it according to the ritual. Then he presented the grain offering, and taking a handful of it, he burned it on the altar in addition to the morning burnt offering. Then he slaughtered the ox and the ram as a peace offering for the people, and when his sons brought him the blood, he splashed it around the altar. The fat of the ox and the ram—the fat tail, the fat covering the entrails, the kidneys, and the lobe of the liver—I say, he placed these fats upon the breasts and burned them on the altar. But the breasts and the right shoulder Aaron waved as a wave offering before Jehovah, as Moses had commanded. Then, lifting his hand toward the people, he blessed them, and having finished the sin offering, the whole burnt offering, and the peace offering, he stepped down. Then Moses and Aaron entered the Tabernacle of the Oracle, and when they came out, they blessed the people. Then the glory of Jehovah appeared to all the

people, and fire came out from the presence of Jehovah and consumed the 
<margin>2 Maccabees 2</margin> 
burnt offering and the fat upon the altar. When all the people saw this, they shouted for joy and fell upon their faces.

### CHAPTER X.

<margin>a. that through those who approach Him, He would act in the sight of all the people, so that He might appear majestic and glorious.</margin>
Then Aaron's sons, Nadab and Abihu, each took their censer, and having placed fire and incense within, they offered **unauthorized fire** <note>original: "ignem alienum," often translated as "strange fire," referring to fire not taken from the sacred altar</note> before Jehovah, which was against His command. Therefore, fire went out from the presence of Jehovah and consumed them, and they died in the presence of Jehovah. And Moses said to Aaron: "This is what Jehovah had foretold when He said that He, among <margin>a</margin> those who approach Him, would act in the sight of all the people, so that He might appear majestic and glorious." But Aaron remained silent. Then Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan, the sons of Uzziel, the uncle of Aaron, and commanded them to come forward and carry their kinsmen away from the front of the sanctuary to a place outside the camp. This they did according to his command, and they carried them out of the camp still in their tunics. Then Moses warned Aaron and his sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, saying: "Do not <margin>b</margin> shave your heads, nor let your garments be unfastened, lest you pay the penalty of death and wrath be unleashed upon the whole republic <note>original: "rempublicam," here referring to the community or commonwealth of Israel</note>. Instead, let the entire race of your kinsmen, the Israelites, bewail those whom Jehovah has burned."

<margin>b. shave [your heads], nor let your garments be unfastened, lest you pay the penalty of death and wrath be unleashed upon the whole republic: but let the entire race of your kinsmen, the Israelites, bewail those whom Jehovah has burned.</margin>

And they acted according to the instruction of Moses. Then Jehovah commanded Aaron that neither he nor his sons should drink wine or <margin>c</margin> **strong drink** <note>original: "temetum," an archaic Latin term for intoxicating liquor</note> when they were to enter the Tabernacle of the Oracle, so that they would not be punished with death. <margin>c. strong drink, he himself should not drink, nor his sons, when about to enter the Tabernacle of the Oracle, lest they be punished with death; and that this should be an eternal institution handed down to their posterity: both to distinguish the sacred from the profane and the polluted from the clean: and for instructing the Israelites in all the statutes which Jehovah spoke to them through Moses.</margin>
Then Moses said to Aaron and to Eleazar and Ithamar, his remaining sons: "Take what remains of the **grain offering** <note>original: "rediuina," likely referring to the meal or meat offering</note> of Jehovah, and eat it without leaven beside the altar; for it is most holy, and it must be eaten by you in a sacred place. For this has been decreed for you and your sons from the offerings of Jehovah; indeed, so it was commanded to me. But the **waved breast** and the **heaved thigh** <note>original: "pectus porrectitium, armumque excepticium," specific portions of the peace offering given to the priests</note> you and your sons and daughters shall eat in a clean place; for these have been decreed and assigned to you and your children from the sacrifices of the Israelites for their well-being. They shall bring the thigh and the breast along with the fat offerings of the fire, to be waved before Jehovah, which shall be an everlasting statute for you and your sons, just as Jehovah commanded." Then Moses searched for the goat of the **sin offering** <note>original: "piacularem," an atonement sacrifice</note>, and behold, it had been burned up. Therefore, being angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, the remaining sons of Aaron, he said: "Why did you not eat the sin offering in the sacred place, since it is most holy and was assigned to you to bear the guilt of the community, and to make supplication for the republic itself in the presence of Jehovah? See, its blood was not brought into the inner sanctuary; you ought to have eaten it in the sanctuary, as was commanded to me." Aaron replied to him: "Behold, today they offered their sin offering and their **whole burnt offering** <note>original: "solidum sacrificium"</note> before Jehovah, and yet these tragic things have happened to me. If I had eaten the sin offering today, would this have pleased Jehovah?" This response satisfied Moses.

### CHAPTER XI.

<margin>Concerning which animals it is permitted to eat. Deut. 14.</margin>
Then Jehovah spoke these words to Moses and Aaron: "Speak to the Israelites in this manner. These are the animals which it is permitted for you to eat. Of every kind of quadruped that lives upon the earth, whatever has divided hooves and is cloven-footed, if it **chews the cud** <note>original: "ruminant"</note>, you may eat it. But there are some which either chew the cud or have cloven hooves which it is a sin to eat: such as the camel. For though it chews the cud, it is not cloven-footed; let this be unclean to you. And the rock hyrax <note>original: "cuniculus," literally "rabbit" or "coney"</note>: for though it is a cud-chewer, it is not cloven-footed; let this be unclean to you. And the hare: for it chews the cud, but is not cloven-footed; let this be unclean to you. And the pig: for though it has a divided hoof and is cloven-footed, it does not <margin>2 Maccabees 6</margin> chew the cud; let this be unclean to you. You shall not eat their meat, nor touch their carcasses, but hold them as unclean. Likewise, of all aquatic creatures, these are what you shall eat. Whatever among aquatic things has fins and scales, whether <margin>a</margin> living in stagnant water or in rivers, these you are permitted to eat."

<margin>a. Such as those of the sea, lakes, and ponds.</margin>

that thing shall be ritually unclean. And this indeed is the law of beasts, of birds, and of all living creatures that swim in the waters, and of every creature that creeps on the ground, to distinguish between the pure and the impure, and between the animals that may be eaten and those which it is a sin to eat.

### CHAPTER XIII.

<margin>The law of human leprosy.</margin>
Then Jehovah spoke to Moses and Aaron in this manner: "A man who has a swelling in the skin of his body, or a scab, or a bright spot, such that the disease of leprosy <note>The biblical term 'lepra' covered various skin conditions beyond modern Hansen’s disease, including psoriasis or mold.</note> appears to be in the skin of his body, he shall be brought to Aaron the high priest, or to one of his sons the priests. Then the priest shall inspect the affliction in the skin of the body. If the hair in the afflicted area has turned white, and the appearance of the affliction is deeper than the skin of the body, it is the disease of leprosy; having seen it, the priest shall judge him polluted. But if there is a white spot in the skin of the body, and the surface is not deeper than the rest of the skin, and the hair has not turned white, the priest shall shut up the diseased person for seven days. On the seventh day he shall inspect him: if the appearance of the disease remains the same and has not spread over the skin, he shall shut him up for another seven days. On the seventh day he shall inspect him again: if the affliction is somewhat dim and has not increased on the skin, he shall pronounce him pure; it is a scab, and after washing his clothes, he shall be pure. But if the scab spreads further on the skin after he was shown to the priest for cleansing, he must be shown to the priest again. If the priest sees that the scab has grown on the skin, he shall pronounce him unclean; it is leprosy.

If the affliction of leprosy is in a man, he shall be brought to the priest; if the priest observes a white swelling in the skin, and the hair has turned white, and there is living flesh <note>original: "carnem vivam," referring to raw or granulated tissue</note> within the swelling, it is an inveterate leprosy in the skin of the body; he shall judge him impure and shall not shut him up, for he is clearly impure. But if the leprosy breaks out in the skin and covers the whole skin of the diseased person from head to foot, wherever the priest’s eyes can see, when the priest observes that the whole body is covered with leprosy, then he shall judge the diseased person pure; since he has turned entirely white, he is pure. But when living flesh appears in him, he shall be impure; and the priest, having seen the living flesh, shall pronounce him impure; living flesh is impure, it is leprosy. Or if the living flesh returns and is turned white, he shall come to the priest. The priest shall inspect him: if he observes that the affliction has changed to white, he shall pronounce the diseased person pure; he is pure.

If there was an ulcer in the skin of the body and it has healed, and in its place there appears a white swelling or a reddish-white spot, it shall be shown to the priest. If he observes that its surface has settled below the skin and the hairs have turned white, he shall pronounce him polluted; it is the disease of leprosy breaking out in the ulcer. But if he observes that the hairs have not turned white and the affliction is not below the skin but is dim, he shall shut him up for seven days. If it spreads across the skin, he shall judge him polluted; it is a disease. But if the spot remains in the same place and does not grow, it is the scar of the ulcer; he shall judge him clean.
