...[commanded] that they should take up twelve stones, which they were to carry with them and place in the camp for the following night. And Joshua, having called those twelve men whom he had chosen from each of the tribes of the Israelites, assigned the task: that they should go before the Ark of Jehovah <note>original: "iouæ"; a Latinization of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton common in Reformation-era scholarship.</note> their God into the middle of the Jordan and each carry a stone upon his shoulder, according to the number of the tribes of the Israelites. "So that this," he said, "remaining as a sign among you, if ever your children should ask their fathers what these stones mean to you, you may answer: that the waters of the Jordan were divided when the Ark of the Covenant of Jehovah passed through the Jordan at its coming; a memorial of which event these stones shall be for the Israelites forever." Therefore, the Israelites obeyed the command of their leader and took twelve stones from the middle of the Jordan, as Jehovah had commanded Joshua, according to the number of the tribes of the Israelites, which they carried with them to the camp and placed there.

Joshua also erected twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan, in the place where the feet of the priests carrying the Ark of the Covenant had stood; those stones remain there to this day. Now the priests carrying the Ark stood in the middle of the Jordan until all things were completed which Jehovah had commanded Joshua to tell the people, and which Moses had commanded Joshua, according to their prescription. Then, when all the people had quickly crossed over, the Ark of Jehovah and the priests went before the people. The Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh also crossed over armed before the Israelites, just as Moses had exhorted them, into the plains of Jericho before Jehovah, about forty thousand men prepared for war. On that day, Jehovah made Joshua so great in the sight of the Israelites that they feared <note>In this context, "fear" implies a profound religious and civic reverence.</note> him as long as he lived, just as they had previously feared Moses.

Therefore, Joshua, by the command of Jehovah, ordered the priests carrying the Ark of the Testimony to come up out of the Jordan. As soon as those carrying the Ark of the Covenant of Jehovah had come up and pressed their footprints upon the dry ground, the waters of the Jordan returned to their place and flowed over all its banks, just as they were accustomed to do before. The people departed from the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month, and they set up camp in Gilgal, at the easternmost edge of Jericho. Those twelve stones which they had taken from the Jordan, Joshua erected in Gilgal, and he admonished the Israelites that if ever children should ask their parents what those stones meant, they should explain to them that the Israelites crossed this Jordan on dry ground, because Jehovah their God had dried up the waters of the Jordan for their crossing, just as he had done at the Red Sea, which he dried up to lead them across, so that all the nations of the earth might understand how powerful the hand of Jehovah is, and that they might always fear Jehovah their God.

### CHAPTER V.

After all the kings of the Amorites on the west of the Jordan and all the Canaanite kings by the sea heard how Jehovah had dried up the water of the Jordan for the passage of the Israelites, they were breathless with an incredible terror of the Israelites. At that time, Joshua, by the command of Jehovah, having made stone knives, circumcised the Israelites a second time at the Hill of the Foreskins,

<column-break/>

the reason for this circumcision being that all the males who had come out of Egypt, who were able to bear arms (and who had indeed all been circumcised), had died on the journey through the wilderness. For as many as had been born on that journey through the wilderness, after the emigration from Egypt, had not been circumcised. For forty years the Israelites traveled through the wilderness, until the destruction of the entire generation of those fit for military service who had migrated from Egypt; whom Jehovah, because they had not been obedient to his word, had sworn would not possess the land which he had sworn to our ancestors he would give us, a land flowing with milk and honey. Joshua circumcised their sons who were substituted by him in their place. For they were uncircumcised, having not been circumcised on the journey. Therefore, when the circumcision of the whole nation was completed, they stayed in the same place in the camp until they were healed.

<margin>
Gilgal.
</margin>
Then Jehovah said to Joshua that on that day he had stripped them of the reproach of Egypt, for which reason that place is called Gilgal <note>A Hebrew name interpreted here as "rolling away," referring to the removal of the shame of their Egyptian enslavement.</note> to this day. Thus, while the Israelites had their camp in Gilgal, they celebrated the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month, in the evening, in the plain of Jericho. And from the produce of that land on the day after the Passover—on that very day, I say—they ate unleavened bread and parched grain.

The Manna ceases.

Meanwhile, when Joshua was near Jericho, he noticed a man standing opposite him with a drawn sword in his hand, whom he approached and said: "Are you one of ours, or of our enemies?" To which he replied: "Nay, I come now as the commander of the army of Jehovah."

The method for capturing Jericho is prescribed.

Moreover, all you soldiers shall circle the city once in a circuit; do the same for six days, with seven priests carrying seven trumpets of ram's horns before the Ark. But on the seventh day, circle the city seven times, with the priests sounding the trumpets. And when the horn sounds with a long blast, and you hear the sound of the trumpet, let the whole people shout with a great cry; then the walls of the city will fall down in their tracks, and the people shall invade, each one where he stands." Then Joshua the son of Nun, having called the priests, commanded that they take up the Ark, and that seven of them should carry as many trumpets before the Ark of Jehovah. Then he commanded the people to proceed to encircle the city, with the armed men going before the Ark of Jehovah. Therefore, after Joshua addressed the people, the seven priests carrying as many trumpets preceded the Ark of the Covenant of Jehovah and blew the trumpets, with the Ark following them as they played, and the armed men preceding it, while the common crowd followed the Ark, as the trumpets sounded during the march. ### CHAPTER VIII.

Then Jehovah commanded Joshua that, putting aside fear and dread, he should attack Ai <note>original: "Haim"</note> with all his forces. For He would deliver the king of Ai, his people, his town, and his land into Joshua's hand. Joshua was to do to Ai and its king as he had done to Jericho and its king, except that they could seize the plunder and cattle for themselves. He commanded him to set an ambush for Ai behind the city. So, Joshua prepared to attack Ai with all the soldiers. Choosing thirty thousand of the strongest men, he sent them out by night and commanded them: "Pay attention: you shall be in ambush behind the city; stay ready and do not go too far from the town. I and all the troops with me will approach the city. When they come out against us, we will flee just as we did before. Then, when they have come out after us and are drawn away from the city—for they will think we are fleeing as before while we feign retreat—you shall rise from your ambush and occupy the city, for Jehovah will deliver it into your power. Once you have seized it, set it on fire and obey the command of Jehovah. This is what I command you."

Having been dismissed by Joshua, they went to the place of ambush and stationed themselves between Bethel and Ai, to the west of Ai. Joshua, however, spent that night with the army. He rose early in the morning and, after reviewing the soldiers, he approached the city along with the elders of Israel at the head of the army. The entire host followed him and came within sight of the city, making camp to the north, with a valley situated between them and Ai. Now Joshua had placed about five thousand men in ambush between Bethel and Ai to the west of the city. When the soldiers had positioned the main body of the army to the north, with the ambushers to the west of the city, he proceeded that night into the middle of the valley. When the king of Ai noticed this, he and all the townspeople were roused early in the morning and immediately made a sally against the Israelites into the open plain, unaware that an ambush had been set against him behind the city. As Joshua and all the Israelites fled from them toward the wilderness, all the townspeople were called out and lured from the city to pursue them. ## CHAPTER X.

<margin>Adonizedek, King of Jerusalem.</margin>
After Adonizedek, the king of Jerusalem, understood that Joshua had captured Ai and utterly destroyed it—treating it and its king just as he had treated Jericho and its king—and that the Gibeonites had made peace with the Israelites and were living among them, he was struck with great fear. For Gibeon was a town equal in size to the royal cities, larger than Ai, and filled with warlike men. Therefore, he sent word to Hoham of Hebron, Piram of Jarmuth, Japhia of Lachish, and Debir of Eglon, asking them to come to his aid so they might attack the Gibeonites, who had made peace with Joshua and the Israelites.

So Joshua marched from Gilgal with all his military forces; being encouraged by Jehovah not to fear them, for no one would stand against him as He was delivering them into his power, Joshua attacked them suddenly. Having marched all night from Gilgal, and with Jehovah throwing them into confusion at the arrival of the Israelites, Joshua inflicted a great slaughter upon them at Gibeon. ### CHAPTER XI

<margin>Jabin, king of Hazor.</margin>

Since Jehovah delivered them to be conquered by the Israelites, Joshua routed them and pursued them to Greater Sidon, to the burning waters <note>original: "aquarum incendia," likely referring to Misrephoth-maim.</note>, and to the valley of Mizpah to the east, cutting them down until they were exterminated. He did to them exactly as Jehovah had foretold: he hamstrung their horses and burned their chariots with fire. Thus they took everything by force of arms; for it was Jehovah's will that their hearts be hardened so they would meet the Israelites in battle and be destroyed without mercy, just as Jehovah had commanded Moses. During that time, Joshua attacked the Anakim <note>A race of giants mentioned in the Bible.</note> and cut them off from the mountains—from Hebron, Debir, Anab, and all the mountains of Judah and Israel. He destroyed them and their cities so completely that no Anakim were left in the land of the Israelites, except in Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod. Once the entire land was captured (just as Jehovah had commanded Moses), Joshua distributed it as an inheritance to the Israelites, divided according to their tribes, and the land had rest from war.

### CHAPTER XII.

These are the kings of the land whom the Israelites defeated and whose territory they took possession of beyond the Jordan toward the rising sun, from the Arnon Valley to Mount Hermon, including all the eastern plain. First was Sihon, king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon. He ruled from Aroer on the rim of the Arnon Valley—including the middle of the valley—and half of Gilead as far as the Jabbok River, which is the border of the Ammonites. His rule also included the eastern plain toward the Sea of Chinnereth <note>modern: Sea of Galilee</note> and toward the Sea of the Plain, that is, the Salt Sea <note>modern: The Dead Sea</note>, eastward toward Beth-jeshimoth, and southward below the slopes of Pisgah. Next was the territory of Og, king of Bashan, one of the last of the giants, who lived in Ashtaroth and Edrei. He ruled over Mount Hermon, Salecah, and all of Bashan as far as the border of the Geshurites and the Maakathites, and half of Gilead as far as the border of Sihon, king of Heshbon. Moses, the servant of God <note>original: "dei seruus Moses"</note>, and the Israelites defeated them, and Moses gave this land as a possession to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh. The following are the kings of the land whom Joshua and the Israelites defeated on the western side of the Jordan, from Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon to Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir. Joshua gave their land as a possession to the tribes of Israel according to their tribal divisions. This land included the hill country, the lowlands, the plains, the slopes, the wilderness, and the southland—the lands of the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. These were the kings: the king of Jericho, the king of Ai (which is beside Bethel), the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, the king of Eglon, the king of Gezer, the king of Debir, the king of Geder, the king of Hormah, the king of Arad, the king of Libnah, the king of Adullam, the king of Makkedah, the king of Bethel, the king of Tappuah, the king of Hepher, the king of Aphek, the king of Lasharon, the king of Madon, the king of Hazor, the king of Shimron-meron, the king of Achshaph, the king of Taanach, the king of Megiddo, the king of Kedesh, the king of Jokneam in Carmel, the king of Dor in the region of Dor, the king of the nations in Gilgal, and the king of Tirzah—thirty-one kings in total.

<margin>Joshua is commanded by Jehovah to divide the land of Israel.</margin>

### CHAPTER XIII.

When Joshua had grown old and was advanced in years, Jehovah <note>original: "Ioua," a Latinization of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton YHWH, often rendered as "the LORD."</note> said to him: "You are now old and advanced in years, and yet much of the land still remains to be taken over. This includes all the regions of the Philistines and all the Geshurites, from the Shihor River on the border of Egypt to the territory of Ekron in the north (which is considered Canaanite territory), the five Philistine rulers of Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron, as well as the Avvites. To the south, all the land of the Canaanites, and the Sidonian cave from Aphek to the Amorite border, the land of the Gebalites, and all of Lebanon toward the east, from Baal-gad below Mount Hermon to the entrance of Hamath. All the Sidonians who live in the hill country from Lebanon to Misrephoth-maim—I myself will drive them out before the Israelites. You only need to allot this land as an inheritance to Israel, as

<page-num>236</page-num>
<header>JOSHUA</header>

<margin>Numbers 32.</margin>

I have commanded you. Now divide it among the nine tribes and the half-tribe of Manasseh." With the other half-tribe, the Reubenites and Gadites had already received their inheritance, which Moses the servant of Jehovah had given them on the east side of the Jordan, namely: from Aroer on the rim of the Arnon Valley and the city in the middle of the valley, and the entire plateau of Medeba as far as Dibon, and all the cities of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon, out to the border of the Ammonites. Also included were Gilead, the territory of the Geshurites and Maakathites, all of Mount Hermon and all of Bashan as far as Salecah—the entire kingdom of Og in Bashan, who reigned in Ashtaroth and Edrei and was a survivor of the remnant of the giants. Moses defeated these nations and drove them out, though the Israelites did not drive out the Geshurites and Maakathites, for they live among the Israelites to this day.

<margin>Numbers 18.</margin>

However, to the tribe of Levi he gave no inheritance, because the divine service <note>original: "res diuina," referring to the sacrifices and offerings</note> of Jehovah, the God of Israel, is their inheritance, just as he promised them.

<margin>The borders of the Reubenites.</margin>

Moses gave to the tribe of the Reubenites an inheritance according to their clans. Their territory stretched from Aroer on the rim of the Arnon Valley, and the city in the middle of the valley, and the entire plateau of Medeba, Heshbon and all its towns on the plateau, Dibon, Bamoth-baal, Beth-baal-meon, Jahaz, Kedemoth, Mephaath, Kiriathaim, Sibmah, Zereth-shahar on the hill in the valley, Beth-peor, the slopes of Pisgah, and Beth-jeshimoth—all the towns on the plateau and the entire kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon. Moses defeated him and the Midianite leaders—Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba—who were princes subject to Sihon and lived in that land.

<margin>Numbers 31.</margin>

The Israelites also put to the sword Balaam son of Beor, the diviner <note>original: "diuinum," one who practices divination or soothsaying</note>, during the slaughter of the others. The boundary of the Reubenites was the bank of the Jordan. These towns and their villages were the inheritance of the Reubenites, according to their clans.

<margin>The borders of the Gadites.</margin>

Moses also distributed an inheritance to the tribe of Gad according to their clans. Their territory included Jazer, all the towns of Gilead and half the Ammonite country as far as Aroer, near Rabbah; and from Heshbon to Ramath-mizpah and Betonim, and from Mahanaim to the territory of Debir; and in the valley, Beth-haram, Beth-nimrah, Succoth and Zaphon, the rest of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon (the east side of the Jordan, the territory up to the edge of the Sea of Chinnereth). This is the inheritance of the Gadites, according to their clans, with their towns and villages.

<margin>The borders of the half-tribe of Manasseh.</margin>

Moses gave an inheritance to the half-tribe of Manasseh, distributed according to their clans: their territory extended from Mahanaim and included all of Bashan, the entire kingdom of Og king of Bashan—all the settlements of Jair in Bashan, sixty cities. Half of Gilead, and Ashtaroth and Edrei (the royal cities of Og in Bashan), were assigned to the descendants of Makir son of Manasseh—for half of the sons of Makir, according to their clans. These are the inheritances Moses distributed in the plains of Moab across the Jordan east of Jericho.

<margin>Numbers 18.</margin>

But to the tribe of Levi, Moses gave no inheritance; the God of Israel is their inheritance, just as he promised them.

### CHAPTER XIV.

There follows an account of those things which the Israelites received as an inheritance by lot in the land of Canaan, distributed by Eleazar the priest, Joshua the son of Nun, and the heads of the families of the Israelite tribes, just as the Lord <note>original: "Ioua", a Latinization of the Tetragrammaton, often rendered as Jehovah or Yahweh</note> had commanded through Moses for the nine and a half tribes. For Moses had already given an inheritance to the other two and a half tribes beyond the Jordan, though no inheritance was given to the Levites among them. For the descendants of Joseph formed two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim; they gave no portion to the Levites in that region except for cities to dwell in with their surrounding pasturelands <note>original: "pomoeriis", the open space around a city wall</note> for their livestock and possessions. Thus, the Israelites did just as the Lord had commanded Moses in dividing the land. Then the descendants of Judah approached Joshua at Gilgal, and Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite spoke to him: "You know what the Lord commanded Moses, the man of God, concerning me and you at Kadesh-barnea. I was forty years old when I was sent by the Lord’s servant Moses from Kadesh-barnea to explore the region, and I brought back a report to him as I truly felt in my heart. While my kinsmen who went with me made the hearts of the people melt with fear, I nonetheless performed my duty to the Lord my God. On that day, Moses swore an oath, saying: 'The land on which your feet have walked shall be your inheritance and your children’s forever, because you have fulfilled your duty to the Lord your God.' And now, look, the Lord has kept me alive just as he promised for these forty-five years, from the time the Lord first spoke this word to Moses while the Israelites wandered in the wilderness. And know that today I am eighty-five years old, yet I am as strong today as I was on the day Moses sent me; my strength for war or for going out and coming in is the same now as it was then. Therefore, give me this mountain of which the Lord spoke then; for you yourself heard at that time that the Anakites <note>original: "Enaquios", a race of giants</note> were there with great and fortified cities. If the Lord is with me, perhaps I can drive them out, just as the Lord promised." Then Joshua, having followed Caleb the son of Jephunneh with favorable blessings, gave him Hebron as his inheritance. Thus Hebron fell to Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite as an inheritance to this day, because he had performed his duty to the Lord, the God of the Israelites. Now, the name of Hebron was formerly Kiriath-arba, named after the greatest man among the Anakites. And so the region had rest from war.

### CHAPTER XV.

The lot for the tribe of Judah, drawn according to their families, extends to the border of the Edomites in the Wilderness of Zin, to the far south. Its southern border extends from the edge of the Salt Sea <note>original: "falsi lacus", literally "the false lake"</note>, from the bay that faces southward, and stretches south to the Ascent of the Scorpions <note>original: "cliuum Scorpionum", often identified as Akrabbim</note>,

and reaches as far as Zin. From the south it goes up to Kadesh-barnea, then passes on to Hezron, goes up to Addar, circles Karka, and leads to Azmon, ending at the Brook of Egypt, and so terminates at the sea. This shall be their southern border. The eastern border is the Salt Sea as far as the mouth of the Jordan. The northern border starts from the bay at the mouth of the Jordan and goes up to Beth-hoglah, then continues north of Beth-arabah up to the Stone of Bohan, the son of Reuben. From there it rises to Debir from the Valley of Achor, looking north toward Gilgal, which is opposite the Ascent of Adummim on the south side of the river; then it continues to the waters of En-shemesh and ends at En-rogel. Then it goes up through the Valley of the Son of Hinnom on the south side of the Jebusite slope (which is Jerusalem) and rises to the top of the mountain that lies west of the Hinnom Valley, at the northern end of the Valley of the Giants. From the top of that mountain, the border curves to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah and goes out to the cities of Mount Ephron; then it turns toward Baalah (which is Kiriath-jearim). From Baalah it curves westward to Mount Seir, passing along the north side of Mount Jearim (which is Chesalon), descends to Beth-shemesh, and continues to Timnah. From there it goes to the northern slope of Ekron, turns toward Shikkeron, continues to Mount Baalah, ends at Jabneel, and terminates at the sea. The western border is the Great Sea itself. These are the boundaries that surround the descendants of Judah, divided by their families. To Caleb the son of Jephunneh, however, a portion was assigned among the Judeans according to the Lord’s command to Joshua: namely, Kiriath-arba, so called from Arba, the father of Anak, which is now Hebron. From there Caleb drove out the three sons of Anak: Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai, the descendants of Anak.

<margin>Judges 1.</margin>

From Michmethath on the north, it turns eastward toward Taanath-shiloh and passes by it on the east to Janoah. From Janoah it goes down to Ataroth and Naarah, reaches Jericho, and ends at the Jordan. From Tappuah the border goes westward to the Brook Kanah and ends at the sea. This is the inheritance of the tribe of the Ephraimites by their clans. ## CHAPTER XVII.

<margin>The borders of the Manassites. Num. 26.</margin>
Furthermore, from the lot of the tribe of Manasseh (for he was the firstborn of Joseph), Machir the firstborn of Manasseh and father of Gilead, being a man of war, received Gilead and Bashan. The rest of the descendants of Manasseh received their portions according to their clans: the children of Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher, and Shemida. These were the male descendants of Manasseh son of Joseph, the founders of their respective clans.
<margin>The daughters of Zelophehad. Num. 27, 36.</margin>
Now Zelophehad <note>original: "Salphadus"</note> son of Hepher, son of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, had no sons, but only daughters, whose names were Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah. They approached Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and the leaders, pointing out that the Lord <note>original: "Iouam"</note> had commanded Moses to give them an inheritance among their male relatives. Therefore, according to the command of the Lord, an inheritance was given to them among their father’s brothers. Thus, ten portions fell to Manasseh, besides the land of Gilead and Bashan, which are across the Jordan. For the daughters of Manasseh received an inheritance among his sons, while the land of Gilead was assigned to the rest of the descendants of Manasseh. The border of Manasseh ran from Asher to Michmethath, which lies east of Shechem, and the border goes southward to the inhabitants of En-tappuah. (The land of Tappuah belonged to Manasseh, but Tappuah itself on the border of Manasseh belonged to the Ephraimites.) Then the border goes down to the Brook Kanah. South of the brook, these towns belonged to Ephraim though they were among the towns of Manasseh; but the border of Manasseh was on the north side of the brook and ended at the sea. The land to the south belonged to Ephraim and the land to the north to Manasseh, with the sea as their boundary. They reached Asher on the north and Issachar on the east. Within Issachar and Asher, Manasseh also had Beth-shean, Ibleam, and their surrounding towns, as well as the inhabitants of Dor, En-dor, Taanach, and Megiddo—three regions with their respective towns. Yet the Manassites were not able to take possession of these towns, for the Canaanites were determined to live in that land. When the Israelites grew strong, they subjected the Canaanites to forced labor but did not drive them out completely.
<margin>Joshua orders the land to be described for occupation.</margin>
Then the sons of Joseph spoke to Joshua, complaining: "Why have you given us only one lot and one portion as an inheritance, seeing we are a numerous people, whom the Lord has blessed so greatly?" Joshua answered them: "If you are so numerous, go up into the forest and clear a place for yourselves there in the land of the Perizzites and the giants <note>original: "Gigantum", referring to the Rephaites</note>, since the hill country of Ephraim is too narrow for you." They replied: "The hill country is not enough for us, and all the Canaanites who live in the valley have iron chariots, both those in Beth-shean and its towns and those in the Valley of Jezreel." Joshua said to the house of Joseph—to Ephraim and Manasseh: "You are a numerous people and have great power; you shall not have only one lot. The hill country shall be yours; though it is a forest, you shall clear it and possess it to its farthest limits. For you shall drive out the Canaanites, even though they have iron chariots and are strong."

### CHAPTER 18
When the entire assembly of the Israelites had gathered at Shiloh and established the Tabernacle of the Oracle <note>Also known as the Tabernacle of Meeting or the Tent of Presence</note> there—the land having been subdued before them—there remained seven tribes of the Israelites who had not yet received their inheritance. Joshua spoke to the Israelites in this way: "How long will you neglect to take possession of the land given to you by the LORD <note>original: "Ioua", a Latinization of the Hebrew name for God</note>, the God of your ancestors? Choose three men from each tribe, whom I will send to go through the land. When they have described it according to the requirements for inheritance, let them return to me. The land is to be divided into seven parts; meanwhile, the people of Judah <note>original: "Iudæis" (Jews/Judeans), referring here to the tribe of Judah</note> shall keep their borders to the south, and the descendants of Joseph shall keep theirs to the north. You shall therefore describe the land in seven parts and bring the description here to me; I will cast lots for you here before the LORD our God. For the Levites have no portion among you, since the priesthood of the LORD is their heritage. Gad, Reuben, and the half-tribe of Manasseh have already received their inheritance across the Jordan to the east, which was given to them by Moses, the servant of the LORD." Then the men set out. Joshua commanded those who went to survey and describe the land to return to him, so that he might cast lots for them there before the LORD at Shiloh. So the men went and passed through the land, describing it town by town in a scroll <note>original: "scheda" (sheet or leaf of paper/parchment)</note> divided into seven parts. They returned to Joshua at the camp at Shiloh. There Joshua cast lots before the LORD, and he divided the land among the Israelites according to their divisions. And for the tribe of the Benjaminites, the lot was drawn according to their clans. Their borders fell between those of the people of Judah and the Josephites. On the northern side, the border begins at the Jordan and goes up to the northern side of Jericho; from there it goes up through the mountains to the west and ends at the wilderness of Beth-aven. From there it passes toward the southern side of Luz (that is, Bethel) and goes down to Ataroth-addar, to the mountain that lies south of lower Beth-horon. Here the border curves and turns toward the southern side of the sea <note>Likely referring to the direction of the Mediterranean, though here acting as a boundary marker</note>, from the mountain facing Beth-horon on the south, and it ends at Kiriath-baal (that is, Kiriath-jearim), which is a town of Judah. This is the western side. The southern side begins from the edge of Kiriath-jearim and extends to the sea and to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah. From there it goes down to the edge of the mountain facing the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, which is in the Valley of the Giants <note>Latin: "valle gigantū", referring to the Valley of Rephaim</note> to the north; it descends into the Valley of Hinnom to the southern side of the Jebusites and slopes down to En-rogel. From the north it stretches to En-shemesh and goes out to Geliloth, opposite the Ascent of Adummim, and goes down to the Stone of Bohan the son of Reuben. From there it proceeds to the side facing the northern plain and descends into the Arabah. It proceeds to the northern side of Beth-hoglah and ends at the bay of the Salt Sea <note>The Dead Sea</note> at the north, at the southern end of the Jordan. This is the southern boundary. On the east, it is bounded by the Jordan. This is the inheritance of the Benjaminites, according to their clans, circumscribed by its borders on all sides. Now, the towns of the tribe of Benjamin, distributed by their clans, are: Jericho, Beth-hoglah, the Valley of Keziz, Beth-arabah, Zemaraim, Bethel, Avvim, Parah, Ophrah, Kephar-ammoni, Ophni, and Geba—which are twelve towns, besides their villages. Gibeon, Ramah, Beeroth, Mizpah, Kephirah, Mozah, Rekem, Irpeel, Taralah, Zela, Ha-eleph, the Jebusite city (that is, Jerusalem), Gibeath, and Kiriath—which are fourteen towns with their villages. This is the inheritance of the Benjaminites according to their clans.

### CHAPTER 19
<margin>Borders of the Simeonites.</margin> The second lot fell to the tribe of the Simeonites, drawn by their families. ### CHAPTER 20.

<margin>Joshua gives commands regarding the cities of refuge. Num. 35. Deut. 19.</margin>
After the land was divided, the LORD spoke to Joshua, saying: "Tell the Israelites to designate cities of refuge <note>term: "oppida perfugij" (cities of refuge). These were sanctuaries where a person who killed someone accidentally could flee to escape the 'avenger of blood'—a relative of the deceased seeking justice—until a trial could be held.</note>, about which I spoke to you through Moses. This is so that a manslayer who kills a person by mistake or unintentionally may flee there, using these cities to escape the blood avengers. The manslayer shall flee to one of these cities and, standing at the gate of the city, shall state his case to the elders of that city. They shall receive him into the city and give him a place to live among them. If the blood avenger pursues him, they shall not hand him over, because he killed his neighbor unintentionally and had no prior hatred toward him. He must remain in that city until he stands before the assembly for judgment and until the death of the High Priest who is in office at that time. Then the manslayer may return to his own home and to the city from which he fled." Therefore, they consecrated Kedesh in Galilee, in the mountains of Naphtali; Shechem in the mountains of Ephraim; and Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the mountains of Judah. <margin>Deut. 4.</margin> Across the Jordan, east of Jericho, they assigned Bezer in the wilderness on the plain from the tribe of Reuben; Ramoth in Gilead from the tribe of Gad; and Golan in Bashan from the tribe of Manasseh. These are the cities designated for all the Israelites and for the foreigners living among them as a place of refuge, so that anyone who kills a person by mistake might not be slain by the blood avenger before his case is heard.

# JUDGES

### CHAPTER I.

After the death of Joshua, the Israelites consulted the LORD <note>original: "Ioua", a Latinized form of the Hebrew Name of God, often rendered as Yahweh or the LORD</note>, asking which of them should first bring war against the Canaanites. When the LORD answered that the tribe of Judah should go—for he would deliver the land into their hands—Judah asked their brothers, the Simeonites, to join them in the fight against the Canaanites, promising to assist them in their own allotted territory in return. So they set out, and the LORD gave the Canaanites and Perizzites into their hands. They killed ten thousand men at Bezek and encountered Adonibezek <note>The name Adonibezek translates to "Lord of Bezek"</note> there. They fought against him and defeated the Canaanites and Perizzites. As Adonibezek fled, they pursued and captured him, and they cut off his thumbs and big toes. At this, he said that he had once had seventy petty kings, with their thumbs and big toes cut off, gathering scraps under his table; therefore, as he had done, so God had repaid him. They brought him to Jerusalem, and he died there. The men of Judah then attacked Jerusalem and captured it, putting it to the sword and setting the city on fire. Afterward, they went down to fight the Canaanites living in the mountains and the southern plains. They also attacked the Canaanites living in Hebron (which was formerly called Kiriath-arba) and defeated Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai. From there, they marched against the inhabitants of Debir, which was formerly called Kiriath-sepher. There, Caleb promised his daughter Achsah in marriage to whoever could strike and capture Kiriath-sepher. Othniel, the son of Kenaz (Caleb’s younger brother), captured it, and so Caleb gave him his daughter Achsah as a wife. While they were traveling, she persuaded her husband to ask her father for a field. She sighed as she sat on her donkey, and when Caleb asked what she wanted, she requested a blessing: since he had given her dry land, he should also give her springs of water. So Caleb gave her both the upper and lower springs. Furthermore, the descendants of the Kenite, the father-in-law of Moses, went up from the City of Palms <note>Jericho</note> with the men of Judah into the wilderness of Judah, located south of Arad, and lived among the people there. Then Judah went with their brothers, the Simeonites, and killed the Canaanites living in Zephath; they utterly destroyed the town and named it Hormah <note>Hormah means "destruction" or "devotion to God through destruction"</note>. Judah also captured Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron with their territories. With the LORD's help, they took possession of the hill country, but they could not drive out the inhabitants of the plains because they had iron chariots. As Moses had commanded, they gave Hebron to Caleb, who drove out the three sons of Anak from there. However, the Benjamites did not drive out the Jebusites who lived in Jerusalem; therefore, the Jebusites live among the Benjamites in Jerusalem to this day. The descendants of Joseph also attacked Bethel, with the LORD’s favor. The city’s name had formerly been Luz. While scouting it, the guards caught a man coming out of the city and told him that if he showed them the entrance to the city, they would show him mercy. After he showed them the entrance, they put the city

<column-break/>

to the sword, but they let the man and all his relatives go free. He went into the land of the Hittites <note>original: "Mettæoru", likely a transcription error for "Hethæorum"</note>, built a city, and named it Luz, which remains its name to this day. <margin>Which places the Israelites did not occupy.</margin> However, the tribe of Manasseh did not take possession of Beth-shean, Taanach, Dor, Ibleam, or Megiddo, nor their surrounding villages, and the Canaanites persisted in living in those lands. Although the Israelites became stronger and made them pay tribute, they did not drive them out. Likewise, the tribe of Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites living in Gezer; the Canaanites remain among them in Gezer but are subject to tribute. Neither did the tribe of Zebulun drive out the inhabitants of Kitron or Nahalol; the Canaanites remain among them, though under tribute. Neither did the tribe of Asher drive out those living in Acco, Sidon, Ahlab, Achzib, Helbah, Aphek, or Rehob; the Asherites live among the Canaanite inhabitants because they did not expel them. The tribe of Naphtali did not drive out the people of Beth-shemesh or Beth-anath, but lived among the Canaanite inhabitants, though they held the people of Beth-shemesh and Beth-anath as tributaries. The Amorites forced the tribe of Dan into the hill country and would not let them come down into the plains. The Amorites persisted in holding Mount Heres, Aijalon, and Shaalbim, though when the house of Joseph grew strong, they were made to pay tribute. The border of the Amorites ran from the Ascent of Scorpions <note>original: "cliuum scorpionum", likely the Maaleh-akrabbim pass</note> and from Sela <note>the Rock</note> upward.

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>The messenger of the LORD rebukes the Israelites.</margin>
The messenger <note>original: "nuncius", traditionally translated as "Angel"</note> of the LORD went up from Gilgal to Bochim and said: "I brought you out of Egypt and led you into the land I swore to your ancestors. I had determined never to break my covenant with you, provided that you also made no covenant with the inhabitants of this land and tore down their altars. But you have not obeyed me. Therefore, since you have done this, I in turn have decreed that I will not drive them out before you; they shall be a thorn in your sides, and their gods shall be a ruin to you." When the messenger of the LORD spoke these words to all the Israelites, they raised their voices and wept aloud. Because of this, they called that place <margin>Bochos, a place named for weeping.</margin> Bochim <note>meaning "Weeping"</note>, and they offered sacrifices to the LORD there. After Joshua dismissed the Israelites and they each went to take possession of their inheritance, they served the LORD throughout the lifetime of Joshua and the elders who outlived him, who had seen all the great things the LORD had done for Israel. But Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died at the age of one hundred and ten. He was buried within the borders of his inheritance at ᵃ Timnath-heres in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash. After that whole generation had died, another generation arose after them that knew neither the LORD nor the things the LORD had done for Israel.

Wherever they went, the hand of the LORD was against them to bring disaster, just as the LORD had warned and sworn to them. # JUDGES

they did not even obey their judges <note>original: "præsidibus", meaning leaders or governors; in this context, the biblical Judges</note>, but instead prostituted themselves to foreign gods and worshiped them. They quickly turned away from the customs of their ancestors and from following the commands of the LORD <note>original: "Iouæ", a Latinized form of the Hebrew Name of God</note>. Whenever the LORD raised up a judge for them, the LORD assisted that judge and delivered them from the oppression of their enemies throughout the judge's lifetime, for he was moved by their groaning under the cruelty of their tyrants. However, once the judge died, they would again surpass their fathers in wickedness, following and serving foreign gods and refusing to abandon the stubborn ways and practices of their ancestors. Therefore, the LORD grew angry with the Israelites and decreed that because these people had violated the covenant he had made with their ancestors and had not listened to his voice, he would no longer drive out any of the nations that Joshua had left when he died. This was done to test the Israelites, to see whether they would live according to the LORD's commands as their ancestors had, or not. For this reason, the LORD had delayed in driving out those nations and had not subjected them to Joshua.

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>Which nations the Israelites did not drive out.</margin>
These are the nations the LORD left to test the Israelites—specifically those who had not experienced the wars in Canaan. This was done so that the younger generations of Israelites might learn how to wage war, something they had not known before: the five lordships of the Philistines, all the Canaanites, the Sidonians, and the Hivites who lived in the mountains of Lebanon, from Mount Baal-hermon as far as Hamath. These were left to test the Israelites, to see if they would obey the commands the LORD had given their ancestors through Moses. But the Israelites lived among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites; they took their daughters as wives and gave their own daughters in marriage to their sons. They worshiped their gods, and having offended the LORD their God with their crimes and forgotten him, they served the Baals and the Asherahs <note>original: "Astaroth", referring to the Canaanite goddess Ashtoreth or the cult poles associated with her</note>. Because of these things, the LORD was incensed against the Israelites and handed them over to Cushan-rishathaim,

the King of Mesopotamia. After they had served him for eight years, they cried out to the LORD, who raised up a deliverer to help them: Othniel, the son of Caleb’s younger brother, Kenaz.

<margin>Ehud.</margin>
left-handed <note>original: "scæuā", meaning left-handed or ambidextrous</note>. When the Israelites sent him to deliver a gift to Eglon, the King of Moab, he made for himself a double-edged

short dagger, which he fastened under his garment on his right thigh. He presented the gift to Eglon, who was an extremely fat man. After presenting the gift, he dismissed the men who had carried it. When the king commanded silence, and all his attendants had left him, Ehud approached him while he was sitting alone in his cool summer parlor, and announced that he had a divine message for him.

<column-break/>

When the king rose from his throne, Ehud reached with his left hand for the dagger on his right thigh and plunged it into the king's belly with such force that the hilt went in after the blade. The fat closed over the iron, and because Ehud did not pull the dagger out, the king's bowels discharged. Then, having closed and locked the doors of the parlor, Ehud went out. After he had gone, the king's servants arrived. Noticing that the parlor doors were locked, they thought the king was relieving his bowels in the inner room. But when they had waited to the point of embarrassment and he still did not open the door, they took the key and opened it, only to find their lord lying dead on the floor. While they were delaying, Ehud escaped. Passing the idols, he reached Seirah and immediately sounded the trumpet in the mountains of Ephraim. He called the Israelites down from the mountains and, acting as their leader, urged them to follow him, for the LORD had delivered their enemies, the Moabites, into their hands. So they followed him down and seized the fords of the Jordan that lead to Moab, allowing no one to cross. At that time, they killed about ten thousand Moabites, all of whom were robust and powerful men; not one escaped. Thus Moab was brought under the power of Israel that day, and the land had peace for eighty years. After him came Shamgar, the son of Anath, who also defended Israel, killing six hundred Philistines with an
<margin>Shamgar.</margin>
oxgoad <note>original: "baculo, quo boues stimulantur", a long stick used for driving cattle</note>.

## CHAPTER VI.

### JUDGES

<margin>An angel appears to Gideon.</margin>
An angel appeared to Gideon, the son of Joash, while he was threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites <note>The Midianites were nomadic raiders who regularly seized the Israelites' crops; threshing in a winepress—a sunken, hidden pit—was a desperate measure to hide the food.</note>. The messenger spoke to him, saying: "The LORD is with you, most valiant soldier." Gideon replied: "I beg you, my lord, if the LORD is with us, why has all this happened to us? And where are all his miracles, which our ancestors told us about, saying the LORD brought us out of Egypt? For now, the LORD has deserted us and delivered us into the power of the Midianites." Then the LORD turned to him and said: "Go in this strength of yours and defend the Israelites from the
<margin>1 Samuel 12.</margin>
injustice of the Midianites; I am sending you." But he replied: "I beg you, Lord, how can I defend the Israelites? My family is the weakest in the tribe of Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house." The LORD said to him: "With my protection, you shall strike down the Midianites to a man." Gideon then said: "I beg you, if I have found favor with you, show me a sign of who you are, you who speak with me. Do not leave this place until I return to you, bring my gift, and set it before you." The messenger replied: "I will wait for your return." Then Gideon went in and prepared a young goat and an ephah <note>An ephah is an ancient Hebrew unit of dry volume, roughly equivalent to 22 liters or 3/4 of a bushel.</note> of unleavened flour. Placing the meat in a basket and the broth in a pot, he went out to him under the oak tree and offered them. The divine spirit said: "Place the meat and the unleavened bread on this rock, and pour out the broth." When he had done so, the spirit of the LORD reached out the staff he held in his hand and touched the meat and bread with its tip. Fire sprang up from the rock, consuming the meat and bread, and the spirit vanished from his sight. When Gideon realized it was a divine messenger of the LORD, he said: "Woe is me, Lord GOD! For I have seen the messenger of the LORD face to face." But the LORD said: "You are safe; do not be afraid. You shall not die." Then Gideon built an altar to the LORD there and named it *Jehovah-shalom* <note>original: "Iouashalō," meaning "The LORD is Peace."</note>, which stands to this day among the people of Abiezer in the land of Ephraim. That same night, the LORD commanded him to take a bull from his father’s herd, along with a second seven-year-old bull, and pull down his father's altar to Baal. He was to cut down the sacred grove <note>original: "lucum," referring to the Asherah pole or sacred trees associated with the goddess Asherah, often found near Baal's altars.</note> beside it and build an altar to the LORD his God on the top of the same stronghold in the proper manner. He was then to offer the second bull as a burnt
<margin>Gideon cuts down his father's sacred grove.</margin>
sacrifice, using the wood from the grove he had cut down. Gideon took ten of his servants and did as the LORD had commanded; however, because he feared his father’s household and the townspeople, he did it by night rather than during the day. When the townspeople rose in the morning, they noticed Baal’s altar was overturned, his sacred grove cut down, and the second bull sacrificed on the newly built altar. They asked one another and searched for the one who had done it. They discovered that Gideon, the son of Joash, was the author of the deed, and they demanded that Joash hand over his son to be put to death because he had overturned Baal’s altar and cut down his grove. But Joash answered all who stood there: "Will you pursue an injury against Baal, or will you defend him? Whoever fights for him shall surely die before tomorrow morning. If he is a god, let him avenge himself against the one who tore down his altar." From those words, Gideon was then called *Jerubbaal* <note>Meaning "Let Baal plead" or "Let Baal contend."</note>. When the Midianites, the Amalekites, and all the peoples of the East gathered their forces, crossed the river, and camped in the Valley of Jezreel, Gideon was filled with the LORD's

<column-break/>

spirit. He blew a trumpet and, having summoned the men of Abiezer, sent messengers to all the tribe of Manasseh. After they were called, he also sent messengers to the tribes of Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali. When they had come to meet him, he spoke to God: "If it seems right to you to save the Israelites
<margin>Gideon asks for a sign from the LORD.</margin>
by my hand as you promised, look, I will place a fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If there is dew only on the fleece and all the ground is dry, then I will know that you will save the Israelites by my hand as you promised." And so it happened. When he rose the next day and squeezed the fleece, he wrung out enough dew to fill a bowl with water. Then he spoke to God again: "Do not be angry if I speak once more; let me try the fleece one more time. Let the fleece alone be dry, and let there be dew on all the ground." And God did so that night: the fleece was dry, while the whole ground was wet with dew.

Then, when he and his hundred companions reached the edge of the camp at the beginning of the middle watch <note>The "middle watch" was the period from roughly 10:00 PM to 2:00 AM; catching the guards just as they were being woken ensured maximum confusion.</note>, having roused the guards, they blew the trumpets and smashed the jars they were carrying in their hands. Each man stood in his place around the camp. But in the camp, everyone began to run about, screaming and fleeing. ### CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'I' depicting a landscape with figures and buildings.</image-desc>
In the time when the judges <note>original: "præsides"; referring to the biblical Judges of Israel</note> ruled, a certain man from *Bethlehem of Judea*, because a famine had arisen in those borders, set out to live abroad in the *Moabite fields*, together with his wife and two sons. The man’s name was *Elimelech*: the woman's *Naomi*: the two sons *Mahalon* and *Chilion*, *Ephrathites*, from *Bethlehem of Judea*. After they had set out into the *Moabite* field and were living there, *Elimelech* died, with his wife *Naomi* and his two sons surviving him. The sons took *Moabite* wives, of whom one was named *Orpah*, and the other *Ruth*: and having stayed there for about ten years, both *Mahalon* and *Chilion* also died.

<margin>Naomi returns to Judea.</margin>
But the woman, surviving her two sons and her husband, while living among the *Moabites*, heard that *the LORD* <note>original: "Iouam"; a Latinized form of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton</note> had come to the aid of his people and had lightened their harvest. Having departed from that place with her two daughters-in-law, she hurried to return to *Judea*, and on the journey she advised them: "Return, each of you, to your mother’s house: may *the LORD* repay your kindness, which you have shown both toward the dead and toward me. May *the LORD* grant that you each find rest with a husband." When she had spoken these things and kissed them, they broke into tears and declared that they would return with her to her people. <gloss>a</gloss> But *Naomi* urged them: "Return, my little daughters, why would you accompany me? Do I still carry sons in my womb who might become your husbands? Return, my little daughters: Go; for I am too old to be suitable for a husband. Even if I thought there was hope, and were given to a husband even this very night and bore sons, would you wait until they grew up, and remain so long without husbands? Not so, my daughters. Indeed, I grieve greatly for your sake, but the hand of *the LORD* presses upon me." <gloss>b</gloss> Then they began to weep

### CHAPTER III.

Meanwhile, while she remained with her mother-in-law, Naomi spoke to her in this way: "My daughter, I wish to seek a place of rest <note>original: "Requiem"; implying a secure home or marriage</note> for you, so that it may be well with you. Now, is not Boaz our kinsman, with whose young women you worked? Indeed, he is going to winnow barley on the threshing floor tonight. Therefore, wash and anoint yourself, put on your best clothes, and go down to the threshing floor; but do not make yourself known to the man until he has finished eating and drinking. And when he lies down to sleep, take note of the place where he lies; then go, uncover his feet, and lie down. He himself will show you what you must do." And she replied: "Whatever you command me, I will perform." Having said this, she went down to the threshing floor and carried out everything her mother-in-law had commanded. And when Boaz had eaten and drunk and was in good spirits, he went to lie down at the end of a heap of grain. She approached quietly, and having uncovered his feet, she lay down. At midnight the man was startled; he reached out, and noticing a woman lying at his feet, he said: "Who are you?" She replied: "I am Ruth, your servant; I ask that you spread your cloak <note>original: "gremium tuum"; literally "your lap" or "bosom," here referring to the hem of a garment as a symbolic gesture of protection and marriage</note> over me, for you are a near kinsman." And Boaz said: "I pray the LORD <note>original: "iouam"; a Latinized version of the Hebrew name for God</note> may be favorable to you, my daughter. You have made this latter act of kindness greater than the former, in that you did not follow after young men, whether poor or rich. Therefore, be of good courage, daughter: whatever you ask, I will do for you. For the whole city of my people knows that you are a woman of virtue. Nevertheless, although I am a near kinsman, there is yet another closer than I. Stay here tonight. In the morning, if he wishes to take you by right of kinship, well and good, let him do so; but if he is unwilling, I will take you, as the immortal LORD lives. Sleep until morning." So she lay at his feet until morning, but rose before one could recognize another, for he had warned her to be careful lest anyone know a woman had come to the threshing floor. He also told her to bring the cloak she was wearing and hold it out. When she did so, he measured out six measures of barley and placed them on her. Then she went into the town to her mother-in-law, and when asked how she had fared, she explained everything the man had done for her, and how he had given her those six measures of barley, saying she must not return empty-handed to her mother-in-law. Then her mother-in-law said: "Wait, my daughter, until you see how the matter falls. For the man will not rest today until he has finished the business."

### CHAPTER IV.

Now Boaz went to the court <note>original: "curiam"; referring to the city gate where legal matters were settled</note>, and while sitting there, he saw that kinsman of whom he had spoken passing by. Calling him by name, he told him to come over and sit down. After he had done so, Boaz brought ten of the elders of the city and urged them to sit there. When they had sat down, he addressed the kinsman thus: "Naomi, who has returned from the Moabite country, is selling a piece of land that belonged to our kinsman Elimelech. I thought I should advise you of this, so that if you intend to redeem it by right of kinship, you may buy it in the presence of these inhabitants and our elders. But if you will not redeem it, tell me, so that I may know; for there is no one else to redeem it before you, and I am next after you." The man said: "I will redeem it." But Boaz added: "When you buy the field from Naomi, you must also take Ruth the Mo-

<column-break/>

-abitess, the wife of the deceased, so that you may raise up the name of the deceased upon his inheritance." But the kinsman said: "I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I ruin my own inheritance. You redeem my right for yourself, for I cannot do it." Now it was the custom of old among the Israelites, <margin>Deuteronomy 25.</margin> that when someone yielded his right of kinship to another, in order to confirm the whole matter, he would take off his shoe and hand it to the other; this was the form of testimony among the Israelites. Therefore, the kinsman, yielding his right to Boaz, took off his shoe. Then Boaz spoke to all the people and to the elders: "You are witnesses today that I have bought from Naomi all that belonged to Elimelech, and all that belonged to Chilion and Mahalon; furthermore, I have taken Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of Mahalon, as my wife, to raise up the name of the deceased upon his inheritance, so that his name may not be blotted out from among his kinsmen and his native land. You are witnesses today." And all who were present in the court and the elders replied: "We are witnesses. May the LORD make the woman who comes into your house like Rachel and Leah, who both built up the house of Israel. May you do famously in Ephrathah and be renowned in Bethlehem. May your house be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Ju- <margin>Genesis 38.</margin> -dah, through the offspring which the LORD shall give you from this young woman." So Boaz took Ruth <margin>Boaz marries Ruth.</margin> in marriage, and through their union (the LORD granting conception), she bore a son. Then the women said to Naomi: "Thanks be to the LORD, who has not left you today without a kinsman-redeemer; may his name endure in Israel. May he be a restorer of your life and a nourisher of your old age, for your daughter-in-law who loves you has borne him, she who is better to you than seven sons." Naomi took the child and, placing him in her bosom, became his nurse. The neighboring women, celebrating the fact that a son was born to Naomi, gave him the name Obed. He was the father of Jesse, the father of David. This, then, is the lineage of Perez: Perez fathered Hezron; Hezron fathered Ram; Ram fathered Amminadab; Ammina- <margin>Matthew 1.</margin> -dab fathered Nahshon; Nahshon fathered Salmon; Salmon fathered Boaz; Boaz fathered Obed; Obed fathered Jesse; Jesse fathered David.

### CHAPTER V.

<margin>Dagon, god of the Ashdodites, falls before the Ark of Jehovah.</margin>
Now the Philistines carried the captured divine Ark from the "Stone of Help" <note>original: "petra auxilij"; Ebenezer</note> to Ashdod <note>original: "Azotum"</note>, and having brought it into the temple of their god <term>Dagon</term> <note>A Philistine deity, often depicted with the upper body of a man and the tail of a fish</note>, they placed it beside Dagon himself. When they had lifted him up and restored him to his place, they found him again the next day fallen on the ground before the same Ark of Jehovah, with his head and both hands broken off and lying on the threshold; only the trunk of Dagon was left to him. For this reason, the priests of Dagon, or anyone entering Dagon's temple, do not step on the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod to this day, but leap over it. Then Jehovah heavily afflicted and harassed the people of Ashdod, both with a disease <gloss>a</gloss> of the buttocks <margin>Jehovah plagues the people of Ashdod. Psalm 77. a. Therefore, having summoned all the lords of the Philistines, they asked what should be done with the Ark of the God of the Israelites. They replied that it should be moved to Gath. 
<margin>Jehovah plagues Gath and Ekron.</margin>
When they had done this, Jehovah harassed that town with great disturbances, affecting the townspeople from the greatest to the least, so that their buttocks broke out with tumors. Therefore, they sent the divine Ark to Ekron <note>original: "Accaronem"</note>. When it arrived there, the people of Ekron began to cry out that the Ark of the God of the Israelites had been brought to them so that it might kill them and their people. Therefore, having called together all the leaders of the Philistines, they demanded that they take care to return the Ark of the God of the Israelites to its own place, lest it kill the people of Ekron and their kin. For the entire city was oppressed by a deadly plague from God; those who did not die were afflicted with tumors in their seats, and the city’s cries of lamentation rose up.

For his home was there, there he gave judgment, and there he built an altar to Jehovah.

### CHAPTER VIII.

Now when Samuel had grown old, he appointed his sons—the elder named Joel and the other Abijah <note>original: "Abias"</note>—as rulers over Israel in Beersheba. But his sons did not imitate his character; instead, turning aside toward greed, they accepted bribes to pervert justice. All the elders of Israel gathered at Ramah to see Samuel and requested of him that, since he was now old and his sons did not follow their father's ways, he should appoint a king over them to govern them, after the manner of all other nations. Samuel was offended by this demand for a king to govern them, and he called upon Jehovah. Jehovah replied to him in this manner: "Obey the people in everything they ask of you. For they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them. Just as they have always acted toward me since the day I led them out of Egypt, abandoning me to serve foreign gods, so they are doing to you also. Therefore,

<column-break/>

obey them indeed, but only after you have solemnly warned them and shown them the rights of the king who will reign over them." Samuel explained all these commands of Jehovah to the people asking for a king, and spoke thus: "This will be the right of the king who shall reign over you. He will take your sons and appoint them for his 
<margin>
Samuel explains the rights of the king to the people.
</margin>
chariots, and as his horsemen, and as runners before his chariots. He will take your daughters to be his perfumers, cooks, and bakers. He will take the best of your fields, vineyards, and olive groves and distribute them to his attendants. He will take a tenth of your grain and your vintage and give it to his officials and followers. He will take your male and female servants, the choicest of your young men, and your donkeys to use for his own business. He will take a tenth of your flocks. In short, you will be his slaves, and one day you will complain about the king you chose for yourselves, but Jehovah will not hear you then." Refusing to listen to this warning from Samuel, the Israelites insisted that a king be created for them, so they might be like all other nations, with a king to govern them, lead them, and fight their battles. When Samuel reported all the words of the people to Jehovah, Jehovah commanded him to yield to them and create a king. Then Samuel commanded the Israelites to return each to his own city.

### CHAPTER IX.

<margin>Kish, the father of Saul.</margin>

One day, Kish, Saul's father, ordered him to take one of the servants and set out to find Kish's donkeys, which had been lost. When they came to the territory of Zuph <note>original: "Suphios"</note>, he said to the servant who accompanied him: "Come, let us return, lest my father stop worrying about the donkeys and become anxious about us." <margin>a. A Prophet?</margin>

The servant answered again: "I have here a quarter of a silver shekel <note>original: "quadrans sicli argentei"</note>; I will give it to the man of God so that he may direct our way." 
<margin>b. To consult the oracle.</margin>
(In former times among the Israelites, when they went to consult <sup>b</sup> God, they would say: "Come, let us go to the **Seer**" <note>original: "videntem"</note>; for he who is called a prophet today was formerly called a Seer.) ### CHAPTER XI.
Then, according to the Greek <note>original: "G.L." likely referring to the Greek Septuagint</note>, about one month later, according to the Hebrew <note>original: "H."</note>, Nahash the Ammonite launched an expedition and set up camp at Jabesh-Gilead. When all the people of Jabesh begged him to make a peace treaty with them on the condition that they would serve him, he replied that he would make peace on one condition: that he might gouge out all their right eyes, and thereby bring disgrace upon all the Israelites.
<margin>10</margin>
Then the elders of Jabesh asked him to grant them seven days, during which they might send messengers to all parts of Israel. If they could find no defenders, they would surrender to him. So the messengers went to Saul’s town of Gibeah and explained the matter while the people listened; at this, the whole people broke into loud weeping. Saul, who was then coming from the fields driving his oxen, asked what had happened to the people to make them weep. When the story of the men of Jabesh was told to him, and upon hearing the news, he was inspired by God and moved by heavy anger. He took a pair of oxen,
<margin>20</margin>
cut them into pieces, and sent them throughout all the borders of the Israelites by messengers with an edict: that whoever did not set out to follow Saul and Samuel, so should it be done to his oxen. Thus, seized by a fear of Jehovah <note>original: "Ioua"</note>, the men came out as one. He counted them at Bezek; there were three hundred thousand Israelites and thirty thousand men of Judah. Then the messengers who had come were commanded to report to the men of Jabesh-Gilead: "Tomorrow, by the time the sun is hot, you shall have help." When the messengers departed and told this to the people of Jabesh, they were overjoyed and replied to the
<margin>30</margin>
Ammonites that they would surrender the next day and be at their power and mercy. The next day, Saul divided his army into three parts; they entered the middle of the camp during the morning watch and Saul's men slaughtered the Ammonites until the heat of the sun. The survivors were so scattered that no two remained together. Then the people asked Samuel to hand over those men who had rejected Saul as king so they might be killed; but Saul declared that no one would die on that day, for Jehovah had given such a famous victory to the Israelites.
<margin>40</margin>
Then Samuel instructed the people: "Come, let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingdom there." So they all went to Gilgal and there, in the presence of Jehovah, they created Saul king. They made sacrifices for their well-being before Jehovah, and there Saul and all the Israelites rejoiced greatly.

Then the Philistines said: "Look, the Hebrews are coming out of the caves where they hid themselves." Then the garrison soldiers called out to Jonathan and his armor-bearer: "Come up to us, and <margin>a. We will teach you what it means to provoke us; that is, we will kill you.</margin> <gloss>a</gloss> we will show you something." Then Jonathan said to the armor-bearer: "Climb up behind me, for Jehovah has handed them over to the Israelites." Having said this, he climbed up on his hands and feet, with his armor-bearer following him; those men were struck down by Jonathan, and the armor-bearer killed them behind him. In this first slaughter made by Jonathan and his armor-bearer, about twenty men fell within a space of about half an acre of land. This caused such a terror that it spread not only through the camp, the fields, and all the soldiers of the garrison, but even among the raiders; even the earth itself trembled with a divinely inspired terror. When Saul's scouts at Gibeah of the Benjaminites noticed the spreading tumult and that it was increasing more and more, Saul ordered those with him to search and see if anyone had left them. When they had searched, they found that Jonathan and his armor-bearer were missing. Saul then ordered Ahijah to bring the Ark of God, for at that time the Ark was among the Israelites. But while Saul was speaking to the priest, the tumult in the Philistine camp grew greater and greater. Saul told the priest to stop, and gathering all those who were present, he entered the battle. Behold, in the great confusion, the Philistines had turned their swords against each other. Furthermore, the Hebrews who had previously been with the Philistines and had followed their camp went over to the side of Saul and Jonathan. Moreover, all those Israelites who had been hiding in the hill country of Ephraim, hearing that the Philistines were fleeing, joined in the pursuit. And so, on that day, victory was granted.

### CHAPTER XVII.

Now the Philistines, having gathered their forces for war, had assembled at Socoh in Judea; they had set up camp between Socoh and Azekah, in the territory of the Danites. But Saul and the Israelites, having also gathered, had set up camp in the Valley of the Oak <note>Latin: "valle quercus," traditionally the Valley of Elah</note>, and had drawn up their battle line against the Philistines. And with the Philistines standing on a mountain on one side, and the Israelites standing on a mountain on the other, with a valley lying between them, there came out a certain monstrous man from the camp of the Philistines named Goliath, from Gath, six cubits and nine inches <note>original Latin: "sex cubitos & dodrantem," roughly 9 feet 9 inches</note> tall, wearing a bronze helmet on his head and dressed in a coat of scale armor weighing five thousand shekels <note>a shekel is an ancient unit of weight; 5,000 shekels is roughly 125 pounds</note> of bronze. He had bronze leggings on his shins and carried a bronze javelin on his shoulders. The shaft of his spear was like a weaver’s beam, with an iron head weighing six hundred shekels. A shield-bearer walked before him. 

This Goliath, when he took his stand, shouted to the ranks of the Israelites in this manner: "Why is it necessary for you to come out to join battle? Am I not a Philistine, and you the servants of Saul? Choose a man from among you to come down to face me in combat. If he is able to kill me in battle, we shall be your slaves; but if I overcome and kill him, you shall be reduced to slavery and serve us." He said, "This day I bring disgrace upon the ranks of Israel. Give me a man that we may fight hand to hand." When Saul and all the Israelites heard these words of the Philistine, they were struck by no small terror.

Now David was the son of that Ephrathite from Bethlehem in Judea named Jesse, who had eight sons; the man himself was already an old man of advanced age in the time of Saul. His three eldest sons served as soldiers under Saul; the names of these three were: Eliab the firstborn, Abinadab the second, and Shammah the third. While these three eldest were serving under Saul, David, who was the youngest, went back and forth from Saul to Bethlehem to tend his father’s sheep. 

The Philistine came forward every morning and evening, and he continued to do this for forty days. Then Jesse commanded his son David: "Take for your brothers this ephah <note>about 20 quarts</note> of parched grain and these ten loaves of bread, and run to the camp to them. Also carry these ten fresh cheeses to the commander, and see how your brothers are doing, and bring back a token from them." 

So David, while Saul and the brothers and all the Israelites were waging war with the Philistines in the Valley of the Oak, rose early in the morning. Leaving the sheep with a guard, he took those things and set out as Jesse had commanded him. When he arrived within the rampart, the soldiers were going out to the battle line and the war cry was sounding; the ranks of the Israelites and Philistines were drawn up facing each other. David left the things he carried with the keeper of the baggage and ran to the battle line, where he greeted his brothers.

<column-break/>

While he was talking with them, behold, that monstrous Philistine named Goliath, the Gathite, came up from the Philistine ranks and spoke those same words, which David heard. At the sight of that man, all the Israelites fled back in great fear, saying to one another: "Do you see this man who has come up? He comes up to defy Israel. If anyone kills him, the king will enrich him and his house with great wealth, give him his daughter in marriage, and make his father’s house free from taxes among the Israelites." 

David asked those standing by, "What shall be done for the man who strikes down this Philistine and takes away the disgrace of Israel? For who is this uncircumcised Philistine that he should insult the army of the living God?" The people answered him in the common way, telling him what would be done for the one who overcame him. When Eliab, his eldest brother, heard his words to the men, he was offended and rebuked him with these words: "Why have you come down here? And with whom have you left those few little sheep in the wilderness? I know well your arrogance and the wickedness of your heart; you have come down just to watch the battle."

### CHAPTER XVII.
Now the Philistines <note>original: "Palestini," referring to the biblical Philistines.</note>, having gathered their forces for war, met at Sochoh in Judah; they made their camp between Sochoh and Azekah, in the territory of the Danites. But Saul and the Israelites gathered and set up their camp in the Valley of the Oak <note>The Valley of Elah.</note>, and they drew up their battle line against the Philistines. And with the Philistines standing on a mountain on one side, and the Israelites likewise standing on a mountain on the other, with a valley lying between them, there came forth a certain monstrous man from the camp of the Philistines named Goliath, of Gath. He was six cubits and a span tall <note>Approximately 9 feet 9 inches.</note>, wearing a bronze helmet on his head and dressed in a coat of scale armor made of bronze, weighing five thousand shekels; he had bronze greaves on his legs and carried a bronze spear upon his shoulders. The shaft of his spear was like a weaver’s beam, with an iron head weighing six hundred shekels. A shield-bearer walked before him. This Goliath stood and shouted to the ranks of Israel in this manner: "Why is it necessary for you to come out to join battle? Am I not a Philistine, and you the servants of Saul? Choose a man from among you to come down and face me in combat. If he is able to fight and kill me, we will be your servants; but if I overcome and kill him, you shall be reduced to servitude and serve us." He said, "This day I defy the ranks of Israel. Give me a man that we may fight hand to hand." When Saul and all the Israelites heard these words of the Philistine, they were struck with no small amount of terror. Now David was the son of that Ephrathite from Bethlehem in Judah named Jesse, who had eight sons; in the time of Saul, Jesse was already an old man of advanced years. His three eldest sons served in the army under Saul; the names of these three were: Eliab the firstborn, Abinadab the second, and Shammah the third. While these three eldest were serving under Saul, David, who was the youngest, went back and forth from Saul to Bethlehem to feed his father’s flock. The Philistine came forward morning and evening, and he continued to do this for forty days. Then Jesse commanded his son David: "Take for your brothers this ephah of parched grain and these ten loaves of bread, and run to the camp to them. Also, carry these ten fresh cheeses to the commander <note>original: "tribuno," a Latin term for a military officer.</note>, and see how your brothers are faring, and bring back some token from them." So David, while Saul and the brothers and all the Israelites were waging war with the Philistines in the Valley of the Oak, rose early in the morning. Leaving the flock with a keeper, he took the things and set out as Jesse had commanded him. When he reached the rampart, the soldiers were going out to the battle line and the war-cry was already sounding; the ranks of Israel and the Philistines were drawn up facing each other. David left the things he was carrying with the keeper of the baggage and ran to the battle line, where he found his brothers and greeted them.

<column-break/>

While he was talking with them, behold, that monstrous Philistine named Goliath, the Gittite, came up from the Philistine ranks and spoke those same words, and David heard them. At the sight of that man, all the Israelites fled in great fear and said to one another: "Do you see this man who has come up? He comes up to defy Israel. If anyone kills him, the king will enrich him and his house with great riches, give him his daughter in marriage, and grant his father’s house tax-exemption <note>original: "immunitate," a freedom from public burdens or taxes.</note> among the Israelites." David asked the men standing near him what would be given to the man who struck down that Philistine and took away the shame of Israel. "For who," he said, "is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he should insult the army of the living God?" The people answered him with the same words, telling him what would be done for the one who overcame him.
