David, however, having escaped by flight, went to Samuel at Ramah and explained to him all that Saul had done against him; and he and Samuel departed and stayed at Naioth. When it was reported to Saul that David was at Naioth near <gloss>at</gloss> Ramah, he sent messengers to seize David. When these messengers saw the company of prophets in a frenzy, <note>original: "bacchantium," literally 'acting like Bacchants.' The author uses this classical term to describe the ecstatic prophetic state.</note> with Samuel standing among them, they were seized by the divine spirit and began to act in a frenzy themselves. When this was reported to Saul, he sent others, who also fell into a frenzy; likewise he sent a third group, who also fell into a frenzy. Then he himself also set out for Ramath. <margin>Saul falls into an ecstatic frenzy.</margin> When he came to the great well at Secu and asked where Samuel and David were, he heard they were at Naioth in Ramath. He proceeded there, and he too, being seized by the divine spirit, went along in a frenzy until he reached Naioth, which is near Ramah. Stripping off his clothes, he acted in a frenzy before Samuel and lay naked all that day and night; from which arose that saying: "Is Saul also among the prophets?"

# CHAPTER XX.

<margin>David and Jonathan's consultation regarding David's standing in Saul's mind.</margin>
But David fled from Naioth near Ramah and, approaching Jonathan, spoke to him thus: "What have I done? What is my great crime or sin against your father that he seeks my life?" Jonathan said to him: "Far be it from you to die. For since my father does nothing, whether great or small, which he does not share with me, why would he hide this from me? It is not so." But David furthermore <gloss>swore</gloss> and said: "Your father knows well enough that I am dear to you, and therefore he takes care that you do not find this out, lest it grieve you. Believe me, as surely as the Lord lives, and as surely as you live, there is hardly a single step between me and death." Then Jonathan said: "Tell me what you wish me to do for you." And David: "Tomorrow, as you well know, the new moon is observed, on which day I am accustomed to sit with the king at the feast. I, with your knowledge, will hide in the countryside until the evening of the third day from now. If your father asks for me, you shall say that David asked leave of you to run to Bethlehem, to my homeland, for there is an annual sacrifice for the whole kindred. If he approves, I am safe; but if he becomes angry, know that nothing but evil is to be expected from him. But you will grant this favor to me, whom you have joined to yourself in a covenant of the Lord, so that if I have committed a crime, you yourself should kill me rather than hand me over to your parent." But Jonathan said: "Far be it from that. Rather, if I perceive that he is determined to bring about your destruction, I will inform you."

<margin>a. To swear is to solemnly affirm with religious words, which he does in these following words, "As surely as," etc.</margin>
And David said: "Who will report to me whether your father has answered you harshly?" Then Jonathan said: "Come, let us go out <gloss>under the open sky.</gloss>" And when they both had gone out under the open sky, Jonathan spoke thus: "I swear by the Lord God of the Israelites that tomorrow at this time, or the day after, I will sound out my father; and if he is well-disposed toward David, then I will send someone to inform you. But if my father desires to harm you, then may the Lord do so to Jonathan and more, so that I inform you and send you away, that you may go in safety, the Lord being with you, just as he was with my father. And if I am no longer surviving after the Lord has uprooted and avenged every one of David's enemies from the earth, so that you might in turn deliver me from death by the mercy of the Lord, then certainly you shall not keep your mercy closed to my family for the future." And so Jonathan struck a covenant with the posterity of David, and he entreated him again,

<margin>b. That is, looking up to heaven to swear by the Lord.</margin>

### CHAPTER XXI.

<margin>David goes to Ahimelech the priest.</margin>
David came to Nob, to Ahimelech the priest. <note>original: "pontificem," literally "high priest" or "pontiff."</note> Ahimelech was startled by his arrival and asked why he was alone, with no companions. David replied: "The king has entrusted me with a certain matter and commanded that no one should know why I was sent. Therefore, I have assigned my servants <gloss>a</gloss> to a certain place. Now, if you have five loaves of bread, give them to me, or whatever you have at hand." The priest replied: "I have no common bread, but I do have holy bread—provided the young men have kept themselves from women." <gloss>b</gloss>

<margin>a. That is: where they should wait for me, so they do not know where I have gone.</margin>

David said to him: "We have had nothing to do with women for these three days since I set out, and the bodies of the young men are holy. A certain servant of Saul named Doeg, an Edomite and the chief of Saul's shepherds, was there that day, detained before the Lord.

Fearing Achish, the king of Gath, he changed his behavior before them; pretending to be insane in their hands, he drummed on the doors of the gate and let his spit run down into his beard.

### CHAPTER XXIII.

<margin>David consults the Lord about attacking the Philistines.</margin>
When it was reported to David that the Philistines <note>original: "Palestinos"</note> were attacking the town of Keilah and plundering the granaries, he consulted the oracle of the Lord <note>original: "Iouae," a Latinization of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton used frequently in Renaissance texts.</note> about attacking and slaying those Philistines. The Lord replied to him that he should go: for he would conquer the Philistines and defend Keilah. But when his companions said to him that they were afraid even there in Judah, let alone if they should approach the camp of the Philistines at Keilah, he consulted the Lord a second time. The response was that he should set out for Keilah, for He would deliver the Philistines into his hands.

<margin>David strikes the Philistines.</margin>
Then David set out for Keilah with his men and joined battle with the Philistines; having inflicted a great slaughter upon them, he drove away their livestock and saved the inhabitants of Keilah. It happened that when Abiathar, the son of Ahimelech, was fleeing to Keilah to join David, he brought the ephod <term>ephodum: a ceremonial vestment used by the High Priest, often containing the Urim and Thummim used for seeking divine guidance</term> with him. Saul then summoned all his forces for war, so that he might attack Keilah and besiege David and his men.

<margin>David questions the Lord concerning Saul's arrival.</margin>

O Lord, God of the Israelites, reveal this to your servant." To which the Lord replied: "He is coming down." Then David asked: "Will the men of Keilah deliver me and my men to Saul?" The Lord said: "They will." Then David and his companions, about six hundred in number, departed from Keilah to go wherever fortune might lead them. When Saul was told that David had withdrawn from Keilah, he abandoned his expedition. David then occupied the fortified places of the wilderness and held the mountains in the Wilderness of Ziph; and though he was constantly sought by Saul, he was never delivered to him by God. Therefore David, seeing that Saul was plotting his death, remained in the solitude of the forest in Ziph.

<margin>Jonathan goes to comfort David.</margin>
In that forest, Saul's son Jonathan also went to him and encouraged him in the Lord, urging him to be without fear; for not only would he not fall into the power of his father Saul, but he would also obtain the kingship over the Israelites, and Jonathan would be second to him—and Saul his father was not unaware of this matter. And so, having struck a covenant between them before the Lord, David remained in the forest, and Jonathan returned home.

Then David thought to himself that there was a danger that he might one day be destroyed by Saul, and that nothing would be more prudent for him than to withdraw into the borders of the Philistines (so that Saul would cease to seek him any further within the borders of the Israelites), and thus escape his hand. ### CHAPTER XXIX.

Now when the Philistines <note>original: "Palestini," the Latin term used for the Philistines throughout this text</note> had gathered all their forces at Aphek, while the Israelites were encamped by the fountain located in Jezreel, and as the Philistine lords marched past with their army distributed into hundreds and thousands—in which procession David and his companions were marching at the rear with Achish—the Philistine princes asked: "Who are these Hebrews?" To them Achish replied: "This is that David, the servant of Saul the king of the Israelites, who, since he has been with me through these days, or rather years, I have found nothing in him worthy of reproach from the time he fled to us." Here the Philistine princes were offended and said to Achish: "Send the man back to his own province, over which you appointed him, lest if he goes down to battle with us, he should turn against us in the fight. For by what thing could he more easily return to favor with his master than by the heads of these men? Is this not that David of whom they sang in the dances: 'Saul has slain a thousand, but David ten thousand'?" Then Achish called David and spoke to him thus: "I swear by the immortal Jehovah <note>original: "Iouam," a Latinization of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton</note> that you have been upright to me, and your conduct in the camp is pleasing; for I have found no fault in you since you first came to me. But you do not please the lords. Therefore, depart in good peace, so that you do not offend the Philistine lords." David said to him: "But what have I committed? Or what have you found in me to this day, from the time I first came into your sight, that I should not go to battle against the enemies of my Lord the king?" Achish replied: "I know indeed that you please me as much as if you were a divine messenger <note>original: "diuinus genius" — a guardian spirit or angel</note>. But the Philistine lords forbid you to enter the battle with them. Therefore, rise in the morning as soon as it is light, with the servants of your Lord and your companions, and depart." So David rose early with his men to return to the territory of the Philistines; and the Philistines set out for Jezreel.

### CHAPTER XXX.

Meanwhile, when David with his men reached Ziklag on the third day, the Amalekites had made an incursion into the south and into Ziklag, and having captured Ziklag and burned it with fire, they had taken captive all people of all ages, both men and wo-

men; and without killing anyone, they departed, driving them away. Moreover, David's two wives had been captured: Ahinoam of Jezreel, and Abigail, the wife of Nabal of Carmel. David was in great difficulty because the soldiers were preparing to stone him, for all were bitter in spirit on account of their children. When they came to the river Besor, two hundred were left behind this side of the stream, who were unable to cross the river because of exhaustion; David pursued with four hundred. They found an Egyptian man in the fields and brought him to David. After he was given bread to eat and water to drink, and a cake of figs and two clusters of raisins, and had eaten them, his spirit returned (for he had not taken food or drink for three days and as many nights). David asked him who he was and where he was from. The youth said: "I am an Egyptian, the servant of a certain Amalekite, abandoned by my master because I was sick three days ago. Thus David recovered all things that the Amalekites had taken, as well as his two wives, so that nothing at all of any age or sex or spoil taken by them was missing; indeed, he recovered everything. David also took all the sheep and goats and oxen, and they were driven before that flock and called "David’s spoil." Then, when they came to the two hundred who, because of exhaustion, had not been able to follow David and had remained at the river Besor, they came out to meet David and his soldiers; and David approached them and greeted them. But the worst and most wicked of those who had accompanied David said they would not share the recovered spoil with those who had not gone with them, except for their own wives and children.

After these things were done, **David** consulted the Lord <note>original: "Ioua"—the Latin rendering of the Hebrew name for God, often written as Jehovah or Yahweh</note> about departing to one of the towns of **Judah**. <meta>This page continues the narrative of David's reign following his coronation at Hebron. ### BOOK II. <note>original: "LIBER II." – Referring to the Second Book of Kings, known in modern Bibles as 2 Samuel.</note>

[David realized] that he had been created king of the Israelites by the Lord, and that his kingdom had been established by Him for the sake of His people, the Israelites. Furthermore, he took both concubines and lawful wives from Jerusalem after he came from Hebron, from whom he fathered other children of both sexes. The names of those born in Jerusalem are Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon, Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia, Eliada, and Eliphalet. But the Philistines, after they understood that David had been anointed king of the Israelites, made a universal expedition against him. When David heard this, he went down into the stronghold, while they spread out in the Valley of the Giants <note>original: "ualle gigantum" – The Valley of Rephaim.</note>. Then David consulted the Lord, saying: "Shall I attack the Philistines? Will you deliver them into my hand?" The Lord said to him: "Attack, for I will surely deliver the Philistines into your hand." Then David, having set out for Baal-perazim, defeated them there, and said: "The Lord has burst through my enemies before my sight, just as water is poured out." Therefore, that place was named Baal-perazim <note>Literally "The Lord of Breakthroughs."</note>, where David and his men carried away the idols they had left behind. And when the Philistines repeated their expedition and again spread out in the Valley of the Giants, David consulted the Lord, who commanded him not to attack them directly, but to go around them in a long circuit from the rear, approaching where the mulberry trees stood in front, and as soon as he heard the sound of marching in the tops of the mulberry trees, to attack; for then the Lord would go before him to strike down the camp of the Philistines. When David had obeyed these commands of the Lord, he routed the Philistines from Geba <note>original: "Galado"</note> all the way to Gezer.

<margin>2 Samuel 6 <note>original: "4. Reg. 6" – In the Latin tradition, 2 Samuel is often titled 4 Kings.</note></margin>
### CHAPTER VI.

Then, having again gathered thirty thousand of the most elite Israelites, he set out with all his Judean forces to move the divine Ark, in which the name—the name of the Lord of Hosts, who sits above the Cherubim—was invoked. They took this divine Ark from the house of Abinadab in Gibeah, placing it on a new cart, with Uzzah and Ahio, the sons of Abinadab, driving the new cart. Ahio preceded the Ark, while David and the entire Israelite race played music before the Lord with various instruments made of fir wood: harps, lutes, tambourines, flutes, and cymbals. When they came to the threshing floor of Nacon, Uzzah reached out his hand to steady the Ark, which was tilting because the oxen were restless. For this reason, the Lord God was angry and struck him down there for his boldness beside the divine Ark, and he died. David took this slaughter of Uzzah <note>original: "Ozæ stragē" – Often translated as "The Breach of Uzzah" or Perez-uzzah.</note> very poorly, and he called that place "The Slaughter of Uzzah," a name which remains to this day. Then David, fearing the Lord and not daring to admit His Ark to himself, was unwilling to bring it into the City of David, but instead brought it into the house of Obed-edom the Gittite, where it remained for three months; and the Lord blessed Obed-edom and his entire household. After it was reported to King David that the house of Obed-edom and all his possessions had been increased by the Lord because of the divine Ark, he went there and joyfully brought the divine Ark from the house of Obed-edom into the City of David. Indeed, after those who carried the Ark of the Lord had advanced six paces, he sacrificed oxen and fat rams, and he danced with all his might before the Lord, wearing a linen ephod <note>A ceremonial priestly garment.</note>. Thus, while the Ark of the Lord was being led by David and the whole race of Israelites with joyful shouting and the sound of trumpets, as it entered the City of

These things being finished, he blessed the people in the name of the Lord and distributed to the entire multitude, to both men and women, a loaf of bread, a piece of meat, and a flask of wine to each person, and so they all departed to their homes. Then David turned to pray for a blessing upon his own house.

Michal, the daughter of Saul, coming out to meet him, spoke to him thus: "O, how great was the dignity of the king of Israel today! He who stripped himself today in the sight of his servants' handmaids, no differently than the common scoundrels are moved to strip themselves." David replied to her: "It was before the Lord (who chose me over your father and all his line, and commanded me to be the ruler over His Israelite people)—before the Lord, I say, I celebrated. And I will humble myself much more than this, and I will be lowly in my own sight; yet among the handmaids of whom you spoke, among them, I say, I shall be held in honor." Therefore, Michal the daughter of Saul had no children throughout her entire life.

### CHAPTER VIII.

Afterward, David defeated the Philistines, and having subdued them, he took Metheg-ammah <note>A place name meaning "The Bridle of the Mother City."</note> from them. He also defeated the Moabites, whom he measured out by casting them down to the ground; he divided them into three parts, of which he destined two for death and preserved one whole part. The Moabites became subject to him and paid tribute. David likewise defeated Hadadezer the son of Rehob, king of Zobah <note>original: "Sophenæ" – the region of Zobah in Syria.</note>, when he went to extend his empire to the river Euphrates. From him, he took one thousand seven hundred horsemen and twenty thousand footmen; David disabled all the chariot horses except for a hundred, which he left. Furthermore, he slew twenty-two thousand of the Damascene Syrians (who had come to help Hadadezer, king of Zobah). After Syria of Damascus was subdued and made tributary, he stationed guards there, for Jehovah protected him in all his expeditions. ### CHAPTER IX.

<margin>Ziba, servant of Saul.</margin>
David also asked whether anyone of Saul’s family still survived, upon whom he might bestow kindness for the sake of Jonathan. There was a certain household servant of Saul named Ziba; when he was called to him, David asked him if he was Ziba. Upon his confession, the king asked whether anyone from Saul’s line remained, so that he might show him divine kindness. Ziba replied to the king that a son of Jonathan survived, who was lame in his feet. Asked where he was, he replied that he was in the house of Machir, the son of Ammiel, in Lo-debar. Then King David sent messengers to fetch him from the house of Machir at Lo-debar.

<margin>David summons Mephibosheth.</margin>
And when Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan and grandson of Saul, had come and fallen suppliantly at David's feet, David addressed him thus: "Mephibosheth." To which he replied: "Behold, I am your servant." And David said: "Be of good courage, for I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan; I will restore to you all the fields of your grandfather Saul, and I will see to it that you always eat food at my table." But he, bowing down, said: "Who am I, that you should look upon me, who am viler than a dead dog?" Then David, calling Ziba, Saul’s servant, said: "Whatever belonged to Saul and his whole house, I give to your master’s son. You shall till the land for him with your sons and servants, and you shall bring in the produce so that he may have food to use. For Mephibosheth, your master’s son, shall be a perpetual guest at my table." Now Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants. Therefore he replied to the king that he would do whatever he commanded. "So Mephibosheth shall eat at my table," said the king, "as one of the king’s sons." Mephibosheth had a young son named Mica, and the whole family of Ziba served Mephibosheth. So Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem: for he was a constant guest of the king, though he was lame in both feet.

## BOOK II. 326

...Indeed, [Hanon believed] they had been sent not for the sake of honoring his father, but rather for the purpose of spying on, exploring, and over-turning the city. Therefore, Hanon took David’s servants, shaved off half of their beards, and cut their garments in the middle as far as their buttocks, and so dismissed them. When David was informed of this, he sent men to meet them (for they were greatly ashamed) and commanded them to remain in Jericho until their beards had grown, at which point they should return. Then the Ammonites, understanding that they had made themselves a stench to David, hired for wages twenty thousand footmen from the Syrians of Beth-rehob <note>original: "Bethrehobeanorum"</note> and the Syrians of Zobah <note>original: "Sophenorum" – referring to the kingdom of Zobah in modern-day Syria.</note>, as well as King Maakah with a thousand men, and Ish-tob with twelve thousand men. When David learned of this, he sent Joab against them with an army of the most valiant men. Joab—since the Ammonites had come out and drawn up their battle line before the gate, while the Syrians of Zobah, Rehob, Ish-tob, and Maakah were by themselves in the open fields—realizing that he faced a battle both in front and behind him, chose the finest of all the Israelite strength to face the Syrians. The rest he handed over to his brother Abishai <note>original: "Abisæo"</note> to oppose the Ammonites, with these instructions: "If the Syrians are too strong for me, you shall bring me help; but if the Ammonites are too strong for you, I will come to your aid. Be of good courage, and let us fight bravely for our people and for the cities of our God, and Jehovah <note>original: "Ioua"</note> will do what seems good to Him." Having spoken these things, Joab joined battle with his forces against the Syrians, who were put to flight by him. When the Ammonites saw the flight of the Syrians, they also turned their backs to Abishai and retreated to their city. Thus Joab, returning from the Ammonites, came to Jerusalem. When the Syrians saw they were defeated by the Israelites, they gathered together; and Syrians from across the river, summoned by Hadadezer <note>original: "Adarezere"</note>, arrived with their forces, led by Shobach <note>original: "Sobachus"</note>, the commander of Hadadezer’s army. When this was reported to David, he gathered all the Israelites, crossed the Jordan, and came to Helam. There he engaged the Syrians in battle and put them to flight, killing seven hundred of their charioteers and forty thousand horsemen; Shobach, the commander of Hadadezer's army, was also killed there. Then all the kings who were clients of Hadadezer, seeing they were overcome by the Israelites, made peace with Israel and became their subjects, and the Syrians were afraid to help the Ammonites any longer.

### CHAPTER XI.

Then, at the beginning of spring—the time when kings are accustomed to go out on expeditions—David sent Joab and his servants with him, and all the Israelites, who, having routed the Ammonites, besieged Rabbah. David, however, who was then staying in Jerusalem, rose from his bed in the afternoon and was walking on the roof of the royal house when he noticed from the roof a certain woman washing herself, a woman of singular beauty. Then, having sent men to inquire about the woman, he learned she was Bathsheba <note>original: "Bethsabā"</note>, the daughter of Eliam, and the wife of Uriah the Hittite. He arranged for her to be brought by messengers and he lay with her. After she was purified from her uncleanness, she returned to her home. Later, when she found she was pregnant, she sent word to David that she was with child. Then David sent word to Joab to send Uriah the Hittite to him.

As surely as you live, I will not do this thing." Then David commanded him to stay there that day also, saying he would dismiss him the next day. So Uriah remained in Jerusalem that day and the next. The rich man had a great number of flocks and herds. Weakening, drinking from his cup, resting in his bosom: she was, in short, like a daughter to him. A certain guest came to the rich man, and he, intending to receive him, spared to take from his own flocks or larger herds; and having seized the poor man's little ewe lamb, he slaughtered it for his guest. David, incited to great anger against the man, says thus to Nathan:

> By the immortal Jove, the author of that deed is worthy of death, and he shall repay the ewe fourfold, who did not hesitate to commit that deed.

And Nathan said: You are that man, he says. I, says Jove, the God of Israel, anointed you king over the Israelites; I defended you from the injury of Saul; I gave you your master's house, your master's wives to embrace, I gave you the Israelite and Judean stock, and would give you other things besides, if those were not enough. Why have you offended Jove, despising his precepts, with your crime? Since you slew Uriah the Hittite with the sword, and took his wife in marriage, he having been slain by your command by the Ammonite spears. Therefore, war shall never be absent from your house, because you, despising me, have joined the wife of Uriah the Hittite to you in marriage. Know that I (says Jove) will bring evil upon you from your own household, and I will give your wives to another before your eyes, who will lie with them in the sight of this sun. You indeed did it secretly; but I will make this known in the light before all the Israelites.

Then David said: I have sinned against Jove. And Nathan said: Jove also forgives you that sin indeed. Nevertheless, because by this deed you have given occasion to Jove's enemies to speak evil, the son who is born to you shall die. Having said these things, Nathan departed home.

But Jove afflicted the boy, whom Uriah's wife had borne to David, with a hopeless disease. For that boy David prayed to Jove, fasting, and lay on the ground at night. And when his household senators tried to lift him from the earth, he would not, nor did he take food with them. On the seventh day the boy dies; whose death David's servants feared to announce to him, because they conjectured that he, who had not obeyed them when they urged him while the boy was living, would afflict himself much more if they said he was dead. But David, looking at his servants murmuring, understanding that the boy was dead, asked them whether he was dead. And when they had said that he was dead, he arose from the earth, and having washed and anointed himself, changed his garments, and entered Jove's temple and worshiped. Then, entering his house, he asked for food, and when it was set before him, he feasted. When his people asked him what that thing meant that he had done, that he who had fasted and wept for the living boy, had risen up and taken food when he was dead, he replied: While the boy was still alive, I fasted and wept, because it was uncertain whether Jove, having mercy on me, would heal the boy. Now that he is dead, why should I fast? Can I now call him back? I shall go to him, he will not return to me.

Then David consoled his wife Bathsheba, and had intercourse with her, and begat a son by her, whom he called Solomon. Because Jove loved him, he sent Nathan the prophet, who named him ᵃ Jedidiah, on account of Jove. Meanwhile, Joab, besieging Rabbah of the Ammonites, when he had captured the royal part of the city, sent messengers to David, and signified that he had besieged Rabbah, and had captured that part of the city in which was the watering place; he should gather the rest of the army, and attack and capture the city,

<column-break/>

lest, if Joab himself had captured it, that deed should be ascribed to Joab's name. Therefore, David, having gathered all the forces,

attacking Rabbah, conquered it, and having taken the golden crown of their king, which weighed a talent and was adorned with gems, from his head, he placed it on his own, and carried off the city's most copious plunder. He led out the townspeople, and tortured and killed them, and did the same to all the towns of the Moabites, and thus returned to Jerusalem with all his forces.

### CHAPTER XIII.

It happened afterwards, that since Absalom, David's son, had a beautiful sister, named Tamar, Amnon, also David's son, loved her so desperately, that he grew sick because of his love for his sister, because she was a virgin, and it seemed difficult for Amnon to possess her. Now Amnon had a certain familiar friend named Jonadab, the son of David's brother Shimei, a man prudent in the first degree. He asked him why he, who was the king's son, grew thinner day by day? And if your father comes to visit you, you will ask him to have your sister Tamar come, who will prepare food for you, and make a delicacy in your presence, which you may see, and eat from her hand. Therefore Amnon lay down, and feigned sickness. And when the king had visited him, he asked him to have his sister Tamar come to him, who would make two cakes in his sight, which he would eat from her hand. Therefore the king, having summoned Tamar from the house, ordered her to go to Amnon's house, and prepare food for him. Tamar went to the house of her brother Amnon, who was lying down, and took flour, and having kneaded it, she made cakes in his sight, and baked them, and having taken a pan, poured them out before him. And you would be held among the wicked among the Israelites. Therefore speak with the king: for he will not deny me to you.

But he would not obey her, and violently raped her. Then, pursuing her with much greater hatred than he had pursued her with love, he ordered her to depart. In those days, the counsel of Ahithophel was held in such high esteem that whatever he advised was regarded as an oracle, both by David and by Absalom.

When Barzillai had returned home, the king went on to Gilgal and Chimham went with him. He was escorted by half the nation of the Israelites and by all the people of Judah. But the Israelites argued that they, who <margin>b. Ten parts, because there were ten tribes.</margin> held ten parts of the king and had more right to David than the Judeans, should not have been so despised by them as not to have the first word in bringing back their king.

Thus, when the soldiers went out into the field against the Israelites, battle was joined in the forest of the Ephraimites. Meanwhile, as the Israelites had scattered in flight to their homes, talk began to stir throughout all the tribes of Israel. They said that the king, who had defended them from the harm of their enemies and liberated them from the hand of the Philistines, was now a fugitive from his own borders because of Absalom. But Absalom, whom they had anointed as their king, had died in battle: why then did they hesitate to recall the king? 

King David sent a message to the priests Zadok and Abiathar, telling them to urge the elders of Judah <note>original: "Iudæos" — the tribe of Judah</note> not to be the last to bring the king back to his home. Since messengers from all the Israelites had come to his house, he told them that the Judahites, his own kinsmen and blood relations, should not be the last to recall the king. Thus, with the hearts of all the men of Judah leaning as one, they sent word to the king that he should return with all his followers. When he had returned as far as the Jordan, they came to Gilgal to meet the king and escort him across the river. Along with them, Shimei <note>original: "Semeis"</note> son of Gera, a Benjaminite from Bahurim, hurried to meet the king with a thousand Benjaminites, as well as Ziba, the domestic servant of Saul’s house, who was accompanied by his fifteen sons and twenty servants. When they had prepared the passage of the Jordan for the king, they crossed over by boat to bring the king's household across and to do whatever he commanded. 

Shimei, the son of Gera, fell down before the king as he was crossing the Jordan and spoke to him thus: "Do not, my lord king, attribute guilt to me, nor take it into your mind to remember the crime I committed against you when you departed from Jerusalem. But David said: "What is it to you, sons of Zeruiah? Why do you oppose me? Should any man in Israel be put to death today? As if I did not know that only today have I truly become king of the Israelites." The king said to Shimei, "You shall not die," and he swore an oath to him.

### CHAPTER XXI.

<margin>A famine due to Saul’s cruelty toward the Gibeonites.</margin>
Now there was a famine in the time of David for three consecutive years. David consulted the oracle of the Lord <note>original: "Ioue"</note>, who replied that the cause was Saul and his bloodthirsty house, because he had put the Gibeonites to death. The Gibeonites were not Israelites, but a remnant of the Amorites to whom the Israelites had sworn an oath of protection. Saul, however, in his zeal for the people of Israel and Judah, had sought to wipe them out. King David summoned the Gibeonites and asked them what he could do for them, or how he might make amends, so that

<margin>Joab kills Amasa.</margin>
Joab let the sword (which he wore fastened at his side over his garment) fall from its scabbard; then, taking Amasa’s beard with his right hand as if to kiss him, he struck Amasa in the belly with the sword he held in his other hand—which Amasa had not noticed. With that single blow, his entrails spilled to the ground, and he died. Afterward, Joab and his brother Abishai pursued Sheba son of Bichri, while one of Joab’s servants stood by Amasa, proclaiming that whoever favored Joab and stood with David should follow Joab. When this servant saw that everyone who came upon Amasa wallowing in his blood in the middle of the road stopped to stare, he moved him from the road into a field and covered him with a cloth. Once he was moved, everyone proceeded to follow Joab in pursuit of Sheba son of Bichri, who had passed through all the tribes of Israel to Abel-beth-maachah, with all the Berites <note>A clan or group in northern Israel</note> gathered to follow him.
<margin>Joab besieges Abel-beth-maachah.</margin>
<margin>The wisdom of a woman is the salvation of the city.</margin>
They besieged him in Abel-beth-maachah and, having built a siege-mound, began to attack the town. As all of Joab’s soldiers were battering the walls, a certain wise woman cried out from the town in this manner: "Listen, listen! Tell Joab to come here so that I may speak with him." When he approached, the woman asked if he was Joab. He replied, "I am." She said, "Listen to what I say." He replied, "I am listening." Then she spoke: "In the past, the saying was: 'Let them inquire at Abel,' and thus matters were settled. We are peaceful and faithful Israelites; you seek to destroy a town and a mother-city in Israel. Why do you devour the Lord’s <note>original: "Iouæ" — a humanist Latinization of the Divine Name</note> inheritance?" And Joab, answering, said: "Far be it, far be it from me that I should devour or destroy; it is not so. But a certain man from the hill country of Ephraim, named Sheba son of Bichri, has raised his hand against King David. Hand him over alone, and I will depart from the town." Then the woman said: "His head shall be thrown to you over the wall." Having said this, she went to all the citizens and, through her wisdom, ensured that they cut off the head of Sheba and threw it to Joab. Then Joab sounded the retreat, and the soldiers withdrew from the town and went their separate ways home. Joab himself returned to the king in Jerusalem and was placed in command of the entire army of the Israelites.
<margin>David’s officers.</margin>
Benaiah son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and Pelethites. Adoram was in charge of the tribute. Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was the recorder <note>original: "à comentarijs" — keeper of records</note>. Sheva was the scribe; Zadok and Abiathar were the priests. Ira the Jairite was also a priest <note>original: "antistes" — a chief priest or minister</note> to David.

### CHAPTER XXI.

<margin>Famine because of Saul’s cruelty toward the Gibeonites.</margin>
When a famine had prevailed in David's time for three continuous years, David consulted the oracle of the Lord, who replied that the cause was Saul and his bloodstained house, because he had put the Gibeonites to death. The Gibeonites were not Israelites, but of the remnant of the Amorites, to whom the Israelites had bound themselves by an oath. Saul had attempted to kill them out of zeal for the Israelites and Judeans. King David summoned these Gibeonites and asked what should be done for them, or by what means they might be appeased, so that

<margin>Joshua <note>Referring to the original oath in the Book of Joshua</note></margin>
they might bless the Lord’s inheritance. The Gibeonites replied that they sought neither silver nor gold from Saul or his house, nor did they demand the death of any man in Israel. When the king asked what they required of him, they replied that they wished to remove from all the borders of Israel the memory of the man who had consumed and destroyed them. They asked that seven men of his offspring be given to them, so that they might hang them before the Lord at Gibeah of Saul, on the mountain of the Lord. The king promised he would give them, but he spared Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan, son of Saul,

They crucified them on the mountain before the Lord. These seven died together in the first days of the harvest, that is, at the beginning of the barley harvest. Rizpah,

When all these things had been carried out according to the king’s command, God was finally moved to pity for the land. Furthermore, there was war between the Philistines and the Israelites. When David went down with his men to fight the Philistines, he grew faint. # OF THE KINGS

Joab's soldiers followed, along with David’s Cherethites and Pelethites <note>The Cherethites and Pelethites were David’s professional royal bodyguard, likely of foreign origin.</note>, and all the strongest men, to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri. When they reached the great stone at Gibeon, Amasa met them. Then 
<margin>Joab kills Amasa.</margin>
Joab let his sword fall from its sheath (which he had fastened to his side over the garment he wore). He said to Amasa, “Is it well with you, my brother?” and with his right hand he took Amasa by the beard as if to kiss him. With the sword he held in his other hand—which Amasa did not notice—Joab struck him in the stomach. His entrails poured out onto the ground, and he died from that single wound. Then Joab and his brother Abishai pursued Sheba the son of Bichri. One of Joab’s young men stood by Amasa’s body and proclaimed that whoever favored Joab and stood with David should follow Joab. When the servant saw that everyone who came to Amasa, wallowing in blood in the middle of the road, stopped and stood still, he moved the body from the road into a field and covered it with a garment. Once it was moved, everyone proceeded to follow Joab in pursuit of Sheba the son of Bichri, who had passed through all the tribes of Israel to Abel Beth Maacah, having gathered all the Berites <note>A clan or group mentioned in the context of Sheba's flight.</note> to follow him. 
<margin>Joab besieges Abel Beth Maacah.</margin>

a certain wise woman from the town cried out: "Listen, listen! Tell Joab to come here so that I may speak with him." When he approached, the woman asked if he was Joab. He replied, "I am." We are among the peaceful and faithful in Israel; yet you seek to destroy a mother city in Israel. Why would you devour the inheritance of Jehovah?" <note>original: "Iouæ." ### CHAPTER XXI.

<margin>Famine due to Saul's cruelty toward the Gibeonites.</margin>
When a famine had prevailed in David's time for three continuous years, David consulted the oracle of Jehovah, who answered that it was because of Saul and his bloodthirsty house, who had put the Gibeonites to death. The Gibeonites were not of the Israelites but were the remnants of the Amorites, to whom the Israelites had bound themselves by an oath. Saul had attempted to kill these Gibeonites in his zeal for the people of Israel and Judah. King David called these Gibeonites and asked them what should be done for them, or how he might make atonement so that

<column-break/>

they might bless the inheritance of Jehovah. 
<margin>Joshua 9.</margin>
The Gibeonites replied that they sought neither silver nor gold from Saul or his house, nor did they demand the death of any man in Israel. When the King asked what they required of him, they replied that they wished to wipe out the memory of the man who had consumed and destroyed them from all the borders of Israel. They asked that seven men of his offspring be given to them, so they might hang them before Jehovah at Gibeah of Saul, on the mountain of Jehovah. 
<margin>2 Samuel 18. <note>The margin likely intends to cross-reference the previous chapter 18 regarding David's household, or perhaps the later numbering of the books of Kings.</note></margin>
The King promised he would give them. ...praising Him, I call upon the Lord, that He might defend me from my enemies. My God was implored; He heard my voice and my complaint from His palace, and it reached His ears. Then the shaken earth began to tremble, and the foundations of the heavens were shaken and shuddered. For He was angry: smoke rose from His nostrils, and a burning fire erupted from His jaws, glowing with coals. He descended as the heavens bowed, with darkness under His feet. He sat upon the Cherubim <note>Celestial winged beings who serve as God's throne-bearers</note>, and He flew, appearing upon the wings of the wind. Surrounded by darkness, the blackness of waters, and thick clouds as His canopy, the supreme Lord thundered from heaven with a great crash amidst the glow of His presence and burning coals of fire. Hurling arrows and lightning, He scattered those who were joined against me. Then, by His force and the blast of the breath of His nostrils, the depths of the sea were revealed and the foundations of the world were uncovered. He saw to it that I was snatched from on high and drawn out from such a great force of waters. Thus He defended me from my enemies and foes (who were stronger than I), and led me out to safety, strengthened against the dangers they had prepared for me. He delivered me because of His goodwill toward me, and rewarded my virtue and innocence with worthy prizes. For I had kept the standard of the Lord, nor had I been impious toward my God; rather, I kept all His laws before me and did not cast away His statutes, remaining upright before Him and guarding against guilt. Therefore, the Lord repaid me according to my virtue and the sincerity He perceived in me. To the kind, You show Yourself kind; to the upright, You are upright; to the pure, You are pure; but to the perverse, You are difficult. You save the humble, but Your eyes look down upon the proud. You have equipped me with military prowess and subdue my adversaries under me. You make my hostile enemies turn their backs so I may destroy them; they call out, but they are undefended—they call to the Lord, but He does not hear them. I crush them like the dust of the earth; I grind them down and trample them like the mud of the streets. You have delivered me from the rebellions of my people and preserved me for the rule over nations, so that men unknown to me serve me. ### CHAPTER XXIII. <note>In modern Bibles, this is 2 Samuel 24</note>

<margin>David orders the people to be numbered.</margin>
Again the anger of the Lord <note>original: "Ioua," a Latin form of Jehovah</note> was kindled against the Israelites, and King David was moved to command that the Israelites and the men of Judah be numbered. He ordered Joab, the commander of his forces, to travel through all the tribes of the Israelites from Dan to Beer-sheba and count the people, so that he might know their number. Joab replied to him, wishing that his God, the Lord, might multiply the people a hundredfold while the king was still watching; however, he saw no cause for why the king should wish this to be done. But the king's command prevailed over Joab and the leaders of the army, and they departed from him to count the Israelites. Having crossed the Jordan, they camped in Aroer, to the right of the town situated in the middle of the valley of the Gadites. Then they came to Jazer, and into Gilead, and to the borders of lower Hadshi. From there they went to Dan-jaan, and around to Sidon, to the fortress of Tyre, and to all the towns of the Hivites and Canaanites, and finally progressed to Beer-sheba in the southern region of Judah. Having traveled through the whole land, they returned to Jerusalem after nine months and twenty days. Joab reported the number of the census to the king: there were eight hundred thousand men in Israel who could bear arms, and fifty thousand <note>The Latin text says 50,000, though standard biblical versions usually record 500,000 for Judah</note> in Judah. But after this numbering of the people, David was struck in his heart and said to the Lord: <margin>a. Therefore, Lord, forgive my guilt, for I have acted so very foolishly." But in the morning, as soon as he had risen, Gad came to him—David’s seer—to whom a message had been sent by the Lord to propose three things to David in the name of the Lord, that he might choose which one he wished the Lord to do to him. So Gad approached David and proposed whether he wished for seven years of famine in his lands, or to flee from his enemies and be harassed by them for three months, or for his lands

Having bought the floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver, he built an altar to the Lord there and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings. Thus the Lord was appeased toward the land, and the plague on the Israelites was stayed. <margin>The plague is settled.</margin>

### CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'C' showing a king, presumably David, reclining in a bed while a woman, likely Abishag, stands beside him.</image-desc>

When King David had reached old age, he could not keep warm even when covered with clothes. Therefore, his attendants suggested that a young virgin be sought for him to cherish him by her service, and by lying in his embrace, she might keep him warm. Thus, a beautiful girl was sought throughout all the borders of the Israelites, and Abishag the Shunammite was found and brought to the king. She was a girl of supreme beauty who cherished the king and served him, but he did not have sexual relations with her. Meanwhile Adonijah, the son of Haggith, exalted by the hope of the kingdom, prepared for himself chariots, horsemen, and fifty runners to go before him, while his father turned a blind eye so as not to offend him. Now he too was endowed with singular beauty, born of his mother after Absalom. Joab the son of Zeruiah and Abiathar the priest sided with him and supported his cause. However, Zadok the priest, Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, Rei, and the heroes of David did not stand with Adonijah. Therefore, when Adonijah had sacrificed sheep, oxen, and fatlings by the stone of Zoheleth, which is near En-rogel, he invited his brothers

Then all who had been invited by Adonijah were terrified; they rose up and departed, each his own way. Adonijah himself, fearing Solomon, withdrew to the altar and took hold of its horns <note>The "horns" were protrusions at the corners of the altar; grasping them was a traditional plea for sanctuary or mercy</note>. <margin>Adonijah flees to the altar.</margin> When it was reported to Solomon that Adonijah, out of fear of King Solomon, was holding the horns of the altar and asking that King Solomon confirm by an oath that he would not kill him with the sword, Solomon replied that if he proved to be a worthy man, no harm would come to him; but if any wickedness were found in him, he would die. Then he sent men to bring him from the altar. When he had come and humbly greeted King Solomon, the king ordered him to go to his own house.

<margin>Bathsheba asks Solomon for Abishag for Adonijah.</margin> Now Adonijah, the son of Haggith, came to Solomon’s mother, Bathsheba. When she asked if he came in peace, he replied, "In peace. I wish to speak a few words with you." She said, "Speak." He said, "You know that the kingdom was mine, and all the eyes of Israel were turned toward me as the future king; but the kingdom has shifted and been delivered to my brother, for it was destined for him by the Lord. Now I ask one thing of you; do not deny me." She said, "Speak." He said, "Please speak with King Solomon (for he will not refuse you) to give me Abishag the Shunammite in marriage." Bathsheba replied, "Very well; I will speak with the king for you." She then went to King Solomon to speak with him concerning Adonijah. The king rose to meet her and, having honored her, sat upon his throne; a seat was placed for the king's mother, and she sat at his right hand. She said, "I ask one small thing of you; do not deny me." The king said, "Ask, my mother, for I will not deny you." She said, "Let Abishag the Shunammite be given to your brother Adonijah in marriage." But King Solomon answered his mother, "Why do you ask for Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? You might as well ask for the kingdom for him (for he is my elder brother), and for Abiathar the priest and Joab the son of Zeruiah!"

<margin>Adonijah is killed. Solomon removes Abiathar from the priesthood.</margin> <margin>1 Kings 2</margin> "May God not be favorable to me," he said, swearing by the Lord, "if this request does not cost Adonijah his life. Therefore, by the immortal Lord, who has established me and placed me on the throne of my father David, and who has built a house for me as he promised, Adonijah shall die today." Having spoken these things, King Solomon sent Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who struck him down and killed him. To Abiathar the priest, the king commanded that he retire to his estate at Anathoth. "For," he said, "although you deserve death, I will not kill you today because you carried the Ark of the Lord God before my father David, and because you shared in all my father’s hardships." So Solomon removed Abiathar from the priesthood of the Lord, fulfilling what the Lord had threatened against the house of Eli at Shiloh.

But Joab refused, saying he would die there. <margin>2 Samuel 2</margin> <margin>1 Samuel 10</margin> <margin>Joab is killed.</margin> After Benaiah reported Joab’s answer to the king, the king said, "Do as he asks; strike him down and bury him, and so clear me and my father's house of the blood which Joab shed without cause. <margin>Solomon commands Shimei to remain in the city.</margin> Then the king summoned Shimei and commanded him to build a house in Jerusalem and live there, never leaving it. Shimei replied to the king that this pleased him and he would obey the king’s command; so he lived in Jerusalem for a long time. But after three years had passed, two of his servants fled to Achish son of Maacah, king of Gath. When this was told to him, Shimei saddled his donkey and went to Achish at Gath to search for his servants, and he brought them back. When Solomon learned that Shimei had left Jerusalem for Gath and returned, he had Shimei summoned and said to him: "Did I not make you swear by the Lord and warn you that if you ever went anywhere else, you would surely die? You replied that the arrangement pleased you. Why then have you not kept the oath of the Lord and the command I gave you? You know in your own heart," he said, "how much evil you committed against my father David; the Lord now turns your wickedness back upon your own head. Meanwhile, King Solomon shall be blessed, and the throne of David shall be established by the grace of the Lord forever." Then, at the king's command, Benaiah son of Jehoiada went out and struck Shimei down, killing him.

<margin>Solomon's letters to Hiram.</margin>
To which Solomon sent this message: "You know that my father David was unable to build a house to the name of the Lord <note>original: "Iouæ," a Latinization of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton YHWH</note> his God because of the wars that surrounded him on every side, until the Lord placed his enemies under the soles of his feet. But now, know that by the favor of the Lord my God, I have obtained peace on every side, having neither adversary nor any ill-will. Therefore, I intend to build a temple to the name of the Lord my God, just as the Lord told my father David, saying that his son, whom He would place on the throne in his stead, would build a temple to the Lord's name. For this reason, command that cedars from Lebanon be cut for me, and let my servants work alongside yours. I will pay you whatever wages you set for your servants. For you know that among us there are no men skilled in cutting timber like the Sidonians."

<margin>1 Kings 7. 2 Chronicles 2. Hiram's response to Solomon.</margin>
Upon hearing these commands from Solomon, Hiram rejoiced greatly and gave thanks to the Lord, who had given David such a wise son to govern so great a people. He wrote back to Solomon: "I have heard the things you signaled to me. I will comply with all your wishes; my servants shall bring down the cedar and pine logs from Lebanon to the sea. I will bind them into rafts and send them by sea to whatever place you indicate. There, I will have them untied and you shall take them away. In return, you shall satisfy my needs by providing provisions for my household." Thus Hiram supplied Solomon with cedar and pine wood according to his desire, and Solomon provided Hiram with twenty thousand kors of wheat as food for his household, and twenty kors of pressed oil every year. The Lord gave Solomon wisdom, as He had promised him, and there was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and they made a treaty together.

<margin>Solomon's labor force for the temple materials.</margin>
King Solomon drafted a labor force from all Israel of thirty thousand men, whom he sent to Lebanon in shifts of ten thousand a month. They would spend one month in Lebanon and two months at home. Adoniram was in charge of this forced labor. Solomon also had seventy thousand porters and eighty thousand stonecutters in the mountains, besides three thousand three hundred overseers appointed by him to supervise the work. The king commanded that huge, costly stones be quarried to lay the temple’s foundation with squared stones. The builders of Solomon and Hiram, along with the craftsmen, shaped these stones and prepared the timber and stones for the building of the temple.

### CHAPTER VI.

<margin>Solomon builds the temple. 2 Chronicles 3.</margin>
Therefore, in the four hundred and eightieth year after the Israelites came out of Egypt, in the month of Zif <note>The second month of the Hebrew calendar, occurring in Spring</note>, which is the second month, in the fourth year of Solomon’s reign, the king began to build the temple of the Lord. The temple which King Solomon built for the Lord was sixty cubits <note>A cubit is approximately 18 inches or 45 centimeters</note> long, twenty wide, and thirty high. The vestibule in front of the main hall of the temple was twenty cubits long, corresponding to the width of the temple, and ten cubits deep in front of the temple. He made windows for the temple that were framed and latticed. Against the wall of the temple, he built side chambers all around the walls of the main hall and the inner sanctuary, and he made side rooms all around. The lowest of the side chambers

<column-break/>

<margin>a. The stones were squared in the quarries so they would be easier to transport.</margin>
were five cubits wide, the middle ones were six cubits wide, and the third level was seven cubits wide. For he had made offsets in the wall of the temple on the outside all around, so that the beams of the side chambers would not be inserted into the temple walls. ^a The temple was built of finished stones as they were brought from the quarry, so that no hammer, axe, or any iron tool was heard while it was being built. The entrance to the middle story was on the right side of the temple, and one went up by spiral stairs to the middle story, and from the middle to the third. After he had finished building the temple, he covered the ceilings and the walls with cedar. He built the side chambers five cubits high along the whole temple, joining them to the temple with cedar beams. Then the Lord spoke to Solomon, saying: "Regarding this temple you are building, if you walk in my statutes, execute my judgments, and keep all my commandments, I will fulfill the promise I made to your father David concerning you, and I will dwell among the Israelites and will not desert them."

<margin>2 Samuel 7. 1 Chronicles 22.</margin>
So Solomon finished building the temple. He lined the interior walls from the floor to the ceiling with cedar boards, and he covered the floor of the temple with pine boards. He built a space of twenty cubits at the rear of the temple with cedar boards from floor to ceiling, creating an inner sanctuary for the Most Holy Place. The remaining forty cubits of the house formed the main hall in front of the sanctuary. The interior cedar of the temple was carved with gourds <note>original: "cucurbitarum," referring to wild gourds or ornamental carvings</note> and open flowers; everything was cedar, and no stone was visible. He prepared the inner sanctuary within the temple to house the Ark of the Covenant of the Lord. This sanctuary was twenty cubits long, twenty wide, and twenty high, and he overlaid the interior with pure gold <note>original: "auro obrizo," meaning refined or high-quality gold</note>. He also overlaid the cedar altar. He covered the whole interior of the temple with pure gold; he partitioned the sanctuary with gold chains, and he overlaid the entire temple and the sanctuary altar with gold. In the inner sanctuary, he made two Cherubim out of cypress wood, each ten cubits high. Each wing of a Cherub was five cubits long, so that the distance from the tip of one wing to the tip of the other was ten cubits. Both Cherubim were of the same size and shape, both being ten cubits high. He placed them in the innermost part of the temple with their wings spread out, so that the wing of one touched one wall and the wing of the other touched the other wall, while their other wings met in the middle of the room. He overlaid these Cherubim with gold. He carved all the walls of the temple round about with figures of Cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers, both in the inner and outer rooms. He also overlaid the floor of the temple with gold. At the entrance of the sanctuary, he made doors of cypress wood, with five-sided doorposts. On these doors, he carved Cherubim, palms, and open flowers, and overlaid them with gold, spreading the gold over the carvings.

<margin>The House of the Forest of Lebanon. The colonnaded portico. Hiram the metalworker. Two bronze columns. Jeremiah 52.</margin>
Likewise, for the entrance of the main hall, he made four-sided doorposts of cypress wood and two doors of pine, each door having two folding leaves. He carved them with Cherubim, palms, and open flowers, and overlaid them with gold.

### CHAPTER VII.

**B**ut Solomon built his own house over thirteen years, and when it was brought to completion, he constructed the House of the Forest of Lebanon. It was one hundred cubits <note>A cubit is approximately 18 inches or 45 centimeters, based on the length of a forearm.</note> in length, fifty in width, and thirty in height, set upon four rows of cedar columns, upon which cedar beams rested. The ceilings, however, were placed upon forty-five columns—fifteen in each row—and were covered above with cedar. There was a triple row of lights, with windows facing each other in three tiers; all the openings and doors of these windows were square in shape, with the windows aligned across from each other in three rows. He also made a portico of columns fifty cubits long and thirty wide, which, with its own columns and beams placed before them, stood as a front. He also made a judicial portico for the tribunal, where he might administer justice, and he covered it with cedar from the floor to the ceiling. The other courtyard of the houses where he himself lived was of similar workmanship, extending from the houses to the portico; and he built a house according to the plan of this portico for Pharaoh's daughter, whom he had married. All these things were made of choice stones, squared to the rule and trimmed with a saw both inside and out, from the foundation to the coping, and outside toward the great court. The foundation was laid with choice and massive stones, some ten cubits and some eight cubits in size. Above these were choice stones squared to the rule, and cedar. The great court was surrounded by three rows of squared stone and one row of cedar beams, just as was done in the inner court of the temple of Jehovah and in the portico of the temple. King Solomon then arranged for a certain Hiram to be brought from Tyre; he was the son of a widow from the tribe of Naphtali, but his father was a Tyrian, a metalworker of the highest skill, genius, and knowledge in all bronze work. He came to King Solomon and performed all his works. He fashioned two bronze columns eighteen cubits high, the circumference of each being twelve cubits. Then he made two capitals <note>The decorative tops of the columns.</note> to be placed on the heads of the columns, cast from bronze, each five cubits high. These capitals on the heads of the columns each had seven sets of latticework, of intricate design and chain-like texture. Furthermore, he made two rows of pomegranates around each latticework to cover the capitals placed on the heights; he did the same for both capitals. These capitals were decorated with lily-work, occupying four cubits on the columns placed in the vestibule. Upon the capitals, above the rounded projection facing the lattice, were rows of two hundred pomegranates encircling the capital of each column. He erect-

<column-break/>

<margin>The cast sea.</margin>
ed these columns in the vestibule of the sanctuary; the one erect-ed on the right he called Jachin <note>Meaning "He shall establish."</note>, and the one on the left Boaz <note>Meaning "In Him is strength."</note>, and upon the heads of the columns was lily-work. Once the work on the columns was finished, he made a cast sea <note>A massive bronze basin for ritual washing.</note>, circular all around, which measured ten cubits from rim to rim, five cubits in height, and thirty in circumference. Beneath the rim, carvings like wild gourds surrounded the sea on every side, ten to every cubit's space in two rows, cast as one piece with the sea itself. The sea rested upon twelve oxen, three of which looked toward the north, three toward the west, three toward the south, and three toward the east; these were positioned under the sea, with their hindquarters all facing inward. Its thickness was a handbreadth; its rim was shaped like the rim of a cup, like a blossoming lily, and its capacity was two thousand baths <note>An ancient liquid measure; 2,000 baths is roughly 11,000 to 12,000 gallons.</note>.

<margin>Bronze bases.</margin>
He also made ten bronze bases <note>Mobile stands for smaller basins.</note>, each of which was four cubits in length and the same in width, and three cubits in height; the design of these bases was as follows: They had panels set between borders, and on these panels were lions, oxen, and Cherubim. Upon the borders, both above and below the lions and oxen, were added wreaths of hammered work. Each base had four bronze wheels and bronze axles, and at the four corners were supports cast beneath the basin, all facing the wreaths. The opening of the basin at the top was one cubit wide, being a perfectly round opening of one and a half cubits, in which there were also engravings. The panels themselves were square, not round. Beneath the panels were four wheels, whose axles were part of the bases. The wheels were one and a half cubits high, made in the same manner as chariot wheels, with their axles, rims, hubs, and spokes all being cast. The four supports at the four corners of each base were part of the base itself. At the top of the base was a rounded support half a cubit high, and at the top of the base were its stays and panels, which were part of it. He engraved upon the plates of its stays and upon its panels Cherubim in human form, along with lions and palms, with wreaths surrounding them. In this manner he made the ten bases, all of one casting, one measure, and one shape.

<margin>The basins.</margin>
Then he made ten bronze basins, each holding forty baths and measuring four cubits, so that one basin was placed upon each of the ten bases. He placed five bases on the right side of the temple and five on the left; he placed the sea on the right side of the temple toward the east, facing south.

<margin>Summary of the work.</margin>
Then Hiram made the pots, the shovels, and the bowls, and he completed all the work of the temple of Jehovah which he performed for Solomon: namely, the two columns, the rounded capitals atop those two columns, the two sets of latticework to cover these capitals, and the four hundred pomegranates for the two sets of latticework (two rows of pomegranates for each lattice to cover the rounded capitals atop the columns). Also the ten bases and the ten basins to be placed upon the bases, and the one sea with the twelve oxen to be placed under the sea, as well as the basins, shovels, and bowls—briefly, all such vessels which Hiram made for King Solomon for the house of Jehovah were of burnished bronze. ### CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>The Ark is brought into the temple. 2 Chronicles 5.</margin>
<margin>Hebrews 9, Exodus 34.</margin>
<margin>2 Chronicles 6.</margin>
<margin>Solomon’s prayer at the dedication of the temple.</margin>

Then King Solomon summoned the Israelite elders <note>original: "senatores," a classical Latin term used here to describe the tribal leaders</note>, all the princes of the tribes, and the heads of the Israelite families to himself in Jerusalem, to bring up the Ark of the Covenant of the LORD from the City of David, which is Zion. Thus, all the Israelites were assembled before King Solomon at the festival in the month of Ethanim, which is the seventh month. When all the Israelite elders were gathered, the priests lifted the Ark of the LORD, along with the Tabernacle of the Covenant and all the sacred instruments of the Tabernacle. While the priests and Levites carried them, King Solomon and the entire assembly of Israelites gathered before the Ark were present, sacrificing an innumerable and immense multitude of sheep <note>original: "balantū," literally "bleating ones"</note> and oxen. Therefore, the priests brought the Ark of the Covenant of the LORD into its place, into the inner sanctuary of the temple, into the Most Holy Place, beneath the wings of the Cherubim. ### CHAPTER IX.

<margin>The Lord speaks to Solomon again. 2 Chronicles 7.</margin>
**A**fter Solomon finished the temple of the Lord and the royal palace and everything he desired to make, the Lord appeared to him again, as he had appeared at Gibeon, and spoke thus: "I have heard your prayers and supplication made to me; I have consecrated this house built by you so that I may place my name there forever; my eyes and my heart shall be there always. If you, in imitation of your father David, walk before me with a sincere and upright mind, executing all I have commanded you and keeping my statutes and judgments, I will establish the throne of your kingdom over the Israelites forever, just as I promised your father David, saying that <margin>2 Samuel 7. 1 Chronicles 22.</margin> he would never lack a man to sit on the throne of Israel. But if you or your children turn away from me and do not keep my precepts and decrees set before you, and if you go to serve and worship foreign gods, I will uproot the Israelites from the land I gave them, and I will reject the temple I have consecrated to my name. It shall reach such a point that the Israelites will become a proverb and a byproduct of stories among all nations, and this temple will be held up as an example <note>original: "ostentui," an object of spectacle or warning</note>, so that all who pass by will be astonished and hiss, asking for <margin>Deuteronomy 29. Jeremiah 22.</margin> what reason the Lord has so afflicted this land and temple. And the answer will be: because they abandoned the Lord their God, who led their ancestors out of Egypt, and joined themselves to other gods, worshipping and serving them; therefore the Lord brought all this evil upon them."

Hiram had sent the king one hundred and twenty talents of gold.

### CHAPTER X.

<margin>The Queen of Sheba visits Solomon. 2 Chronicles 9. Matthew 12. Luke 11.</margin>
**A**ND when the Queen of Sheba heard of Solomon’s fame, in connection to the name of the Lord, she came to test him with obscure questions <note>or "riddles"</note>. Entering Jerusalem with a very great entourage, with camels carrying a vast amount of spices, gold, and gems, she approached Solomon and proposed to him whatever was on her mind. Solomon answered all her questions, and nothing was hidden from the king that he could not explain to her. When the Queen of Sheba beheld such wisdom in Solomon, the house he had built, the food of his table, the seating of his courtiers, the status and dress of his ministers, his cupbearers, and the sacrifices he made at the house of the Lord, she was astonished and spoke to the king: "Everything I heard in our own lands about your deeds and wisdom is indeed true. I did not believe these things until I came and saw them with my own eyes, and I find that not even half had been told to me; you so far exceed in wisdom and virtue the fame I had heard. Happy are your men, happy these followers of yours, who stand continually before you and hear your wisdom. Thanks be to the Lord your God, who favored you so as to place you on the throne of the Israelites, having always pursued the Israelites with such love that he created you as king to act with justice and equity." Then the Queen of Sheba gave King Solomon one hundred and twenty talents of gold, gems, and such a quantity of spices as had never been seen before. Furthermore, Hiram’s fleet, which brought gold from Ophir, brought from Ophir a vast quantity of pine wood <note>original: "piceæ lignorum," likely referring to the Biblical almug or algum wood</note> and gems. From this pine wood

<column-break/>

<margin>1. The same is shortly called Moloch.</margin>
the king made supports for the house of the Lord and for the palace, as well as lyres and harps <note>original: "citharas & nabla"</note> for the singers. Indeed, such pine timber had never been imported here before, nor seen since. King Solomon also gave the Queen of Sheba whatever she saw fit to ask for, besides those things he gave her of his own accord as was worthy of King Solomon; and so she returned with her people to her own country. The weight of gold that came to Solomon each year was six hundred and sixty-six talents of gold, besides what was paid to him by merchants, spice traders, and all the petty kings of Arabia and the governors of the region. King Solomon also made two hundred shields of hammered gold, spending six hundred <term>shekels</term> <note>A unit of weight and currency</note> of gold on each; and three hundred bucklers also of hammered gold, for each of which three <term>minas</term> <note>A weight roughly equal to 1.25 pounds or 60 shekels</note> of gold were spent. These he stored in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.

<margin>Solomon's ivory throne.</margin>
He also made a massive ivory throne and covered it with the finest gold. The throne had six steps, a rounded top at the back, and armrests on both sides of the seat. Standing by the armrests were two lions, and there twelve lions stood on the six steps, on both sides. No such work had been made in any other kingdom.

<margin>Solomon's riches.</margin>
All King Solomon’s drinking vessels and all the furniture of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were of gold—and indeed the purest gold, without silver, which was held of no value in Solomon's time. For the royal Cilician fleet, together with Hiram’s, crossed the sea every three years, bringing back gold, silver, ivory, peacocks, and apes. Thus King Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth in wealth and wisdom, so that the whole world sought Solomon’s presence to hear the wisdom with which his mind was divinely endowed. Year by year, each brought him silver and gold vessels, garments, weapons, spices, horses, and mules as gifts. He gathered so many chariots and horsemen that he had one thousand four hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen, whom he stationed partly in chariot cities and partly with himself in Jerusalem. The king made gold as plentiful in Jerusalem as stones, and cedars as common as sycamores of the plains. This was Solomon’s method for bringing horses out of Egypt: a company of royal merchants would purchase a multitude of horses at a set price. A chariot was brought out of Egypt for six hundred silver pieces—that is, one hundred and fifty for each horse—and in the same way, they were brought by the merchants to all the kings of the Hittites and of Syria.

Therefore, the Lord raised up an adversary against Solomon: Hadad the Edomite <note>original: "Idumæum"</note>, of the royal line of Edom. This Hadad, when David was in Edom and Joab the commander of the army had gone to bury the slain—after all the males of Edom had been killed by Joab (for Joab stayed there six months with all the Israelites until they had cut off every male of the Edomites)—had fled together with certain Edomite servants of his father to go to Egypt, while he was still a young boy. Setting out from the Midianites, they came to Paran; taking men from Paran with them, they went to Egypt to Pharaoh, the king of the Egyptians. He gave Hadad a house, assigned him food, and granted him land. Hadad found such great favor with Pharaoh that the king gave him the sister of his chief wife, Tahpenes, in marriage. By this sister of Tahpenes he had a son, Genubath, who was raised by Tahpenes in Pharaoh's own house and lived among Pharaoh's family, among Pharaoh's own sons. Now when Hadad heard in Egypt that David had slept with his ancestors and that Joab the commander of the army was dead, he asked Pharaoh for permission to return to his own country. When Pharaoh asked him what he lacked there that he should desire to go to his own land, he replied that he simply wished to be dismissed. Furthermore, God raised up another adversary against Solomon: Rezon, the son of Eliada, who had fled from his master Hadadezer, king of Zobah. Having gathered a band of men, he became a leader of outlaws; and while David was killing the people of Zobah, these men came to Damascus, and having taken up residence there, they occupied the kingdom of Damascus. This Rezon, having gained power over the kingdom of Syria, remained an adversary to the Israelites throughout Solomon's time, harassing them in addition to the trouble brought by Hadad. Moreover, Jeroboam the son of Nebat, an Ephraimite from Zeredah and a servant of Solomon (whose mother was named Zeruah, a widow), conspired against the king. The cause of his conspiracy

was this: while Solomon was building the Millo and repairing the breached part of the city of his father David, Jeroboam was a robust man; and when Solomon saw the young man working diligently, he placed him in charge of the entire labor force of the house of Joseph. On the third day, when everyone had returned to Rehoboam as he had commanded, the king answered them harshly. Neglecting the advice the elders had given and following the counsel of the young men, he spoke thus: "My father pressed you with a heavy yoke, I will increase your yoke; my father punished you with whips, I will punish you with scorpions." The king did not listen to the people, for the Lord <note>original: "Ioua," a Latinized form of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton YHWH, often translated as "the Lord" or "Jehovah"</note> so disposed it to fulfill what He had predicted to Jeroboam son of Nebat through Ahijah the Shilonite. Then all the Israelites, seeing that the king would not listen to them, answered him, saying they no longer had any share <margin>a</margin> in David, nor any inheritance in the son of Jesse. Therefore, the Israelites should return to their homes, and David should look to his own house. And so the Israelites departed for their homes, yet in such a way that the Israelites who inhabited the towns of Judah remained under the reign of Rehoboam. When <margin>b</margin> King Rehoboam sent Adoram, the taskmaster of the tribute, to the Israelites, they all stoned him to death. Therefore, Rehoboam hurried to mount his chariot and flee to Jerusalem. Thus the Israelites have been in revolt against the house of David to this day. When all the Israelites heard that Jeroboam had returned, they summoned him to a meeting of the assembly and created him king over all Israel; only the tribe of Judah followed the house of David. But when Rehoboam arrived in Jerusalem, he gathered the entire house of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, one hundred and eighty thousand chosen and warlike men, to wage war against the house of Israel and recover the kingdom for himself, the son of Solomon. But God commanded Shemaiah, a man of God, to announce to Rehoboam son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to the whole house of Judah and Benjamin and the rest, in the name of the Lord, that they should not set out, nor wage war against their brothers the Israelites, but should return home; for He was the author of this matter. Thus they were obedient to the word of the Lord, and at His command, they abandoned the expedition. Then Jeroboam built up Shechem in the hill country of the Ephraimites and lived there, and departing from there, he rebuilt Penuel. Then he began to think to himself: "Now the kingdom will return to the house of David. If these people go up to Jerusalem to perform divine service in the temple of the Lord, they will turn their hearts toward their lord Rehoboam, the king of Judah, and having killed me, they will return to him." Therefore, having taken counsel,
