When he had approached the altar which he had made at Bethel on the fifteenth day of the eighth month (which month he had devised out of his own desire <note>original: "ad suam libidinem commentus erat," implying he invented the religious holiday for political convenience</note>), and while he was holding a festival for the Israelites and had ascended to the altar to burn incense, there arrived at Bethel from Judah a certain man of God by the command of the Lord. While Jeroboam was standing at the altar to burn incense, the man cried out against the altar by the Lord's command in this manner: "O altar, altar! The Lord commands this to be signaled to you: there shall be born to the house of David a son, Josiah by name, who shall slaughter upon you the priests of the high places who burn incense upon you, and human bones shall be burned upon you." He predicted this sign (giving a sign then): "The altar shall now be split, and the ashes placed upon it shall be poured out." Hearing these words of the man of God which he had pronounced at the altar at Bethel, Jeroboam, stretching out his hand from the altar, ordered him to be seized. But his hand, which he had stretched out against him, withered, so that he could not pull it back to himself. Then the altar was split, and the ashes were poured out from it, just as the man of God had predicted by the command of the Lord. At this, the king addressed the man of God: "Pray, I beg you, to the Lord your God, and petition for me, that my hand may be restored to me." Then the man of God prayed to the Lord, and the king's hand was restored to him and returned to its former state. Then the king addressed him thus: "Come home with me to dine, and I will give you a gift." To which he replied: "Even if you were to give me half your house, I would not accompany you, nor would I take food or drink in this place. For I have a command from the Lord not to take food or drink, nor to return by the same way I came." Having said this, he departed by another way, and did not return by the same way he had come to Bethel. Now there was a certain old prophet in Bethel. His sons came to him and told him everything the man of God had done that day at Bethel, and the words he had spoken to the king. Then the father asked his sons which way he had departed. When they had shown him the way taken by the man of God who had come from Judah, the father commanded his sons to saddle his donkey. When it was saddled, he mounted it and followed after the man of God, and finding him sitting under an oak tree, he questioned—

The man of God replied that it was not permitted for him to return or go with him, nor would he take food or drink in that place, because he had been forbidden by the LORD <note>original: "Ioua," a Latinized form of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton, Yahweh</note> to eat or drink there, or to return by the same way he had come. As they were reclining at the table, the LORD spoke through the old prophet to the man of God from Judea whom he had brought back, crying out to him: "This is the decree of the LORD. Since you were rebellious against the LORD your God and did not carry out the command entrusted to you, but returned and took food and drink in the place where He forbade you to do so, your body shall not come into the tomb of your ancestors." Therefore, when the meal was finished, the prophet who had called him back saddled the donkey for him. As the man of God set out, he encountered a lion on the road and was killed by it. While the lion and the donkey stood by his body cast upon the road, it happened that some men passed by. Seeing the body cast on the road and the lion standing there, they went into the town where that old prophet lived and reported what had happened. Hearing this, the prophet who had brought him back from his journey said that he was the man of God whom the LORD had thrown to the lion because of his rebellion, by which he was mangled and killed, just as the LORD Himself had threatened him. Then he ordered his sons to saddle his donkey. Once it was saddled, he set out and found the man’s body cast on the road, with the donkey and the lion standing by; meanwhile, the lion had neither devoured the body nor torn the donkey to pieces. Then the old prophet lifted the body of the man of God, placed it on the donkey, and brought it back to his town for mourning and burial. He laid him in his own tomb, and they lamented over him as a brother with mournful grief. Once he was buried, he instructed his sons that when he died, they should bury him in the same tomb where the man of God was buried, and place his bones near his bones. For he knew that what the man had proclaimed by the LORD’s command against the altar located at Bethel, and against all the hillside shrines <note>original: "facella," referring to small shrines or chapels often associated with pagan worship or unauthorized rituals</note> located in the towns of Samaria, would surely come to pass. After this event, Jeroboam did not turn away from his evil ways, but again appointed common people as priests of the shrines; whomever he pleased, he consecrated to those priesthoods. This matter caused the house of Jeroboam to suffer loss and to be utterly wiped out from the face of the earth.

### CHAPTER 14.

During that time, while his son Abijah was sick, Jeroboam ordered his wife to change her dress so that she would not be recognized as Jeroboam's wife, and to go to Shiloh. For the prophet Ahijah was there, from whom he had learned that he would be the king of this people. "Therefore," he said, "take ten loaves of bread with you, and some cakes, and a jar of honey, and go to him, so that you may learn from him what will happen to the boy." The wife did as commanded;

and having set out for Shiloh, she sought the house of Ahijah, who was going blind and whose eyes were sluggish with old age. Therefore, when she arrived and was disguising herself, as soon as Ahijah heard the sound of her feet entering through the door, he spoke thus: "Come in, wife of Jeroboam! Why do you disguise yourself? I bring harsh news for you. Go and tell Jeroboam: 'This is the decree of the LORD, the God of the Israelites: Since I chose you from among the common people and made you ruler over my people Israel, and tore the kingdom away from the house of David to give it to you—and yet you have been so far from being like my servant David (who followed my commands and obeyed me with his whole heart, doing only what was pleasing to me), that you have even surpassed all who were before you in wickedness; you have cast me behind your back and gone so far as to make foreign gods and molten images to provoke me; therefore, know this: I am bringing such great evils upon the house of Jeroboam that I will utterly root out everything from Jeroboam's line, whether hidden or prominent among the Israelites. I will sweep away his house just as dung is swept away until it is gone. Those of Jeroboam's house who die in the city shall be devoured by dogs, and those in the country by the birds of the air. ### CHAPTER XV.

<margin>Abijam, King of Judah</margin>
<margin>2 Kings 15.</margin>
<margin>2 Chronicles 13.</margin>
His son Abijam succeeded him in the kingdom, beginning his reign over Judah in the eighteenth year of the reign of Jeroboam, son of Nebat. He reigned in Jerusalem for three years. His mother’s name was Maakah, the daughter of Abishalom. He imitated all the sins committed by his father before him; his heart was not right toward the LORD his God, as the heart of David, the founder of his line, had been. Nevertheless, for David’s sake, the LORD his God granted him a legal successor by appointing his son after him to establish Jerusalem. This was because David had obeyed the LORD and had not turned away from any of His commandments throughout his life, except in the matter of Uriah the Hittite. Now, there was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam throughout his entire life. Regarding all the rest of Abijam’s deeds, they are recorded in the annals of the kings of Judah. This Abijam waged war with Jeroboam, and after he departed to the spirits of his ancestors, he was buried in the City of David.

<margin>Asa, King of Judah.</margin>
<margin>2 Chronicles 14.</margin>
His son Asa succeeded him in the kingdom, entering into the reign of Judah in the twentieth year of Jeroboam, king of the Israelites. He reigned in Jerusalem for forty-one years. His mother was named Maakah, the daughter of Abishalom. This Asa imitated David his forefather and obeyed the LORD: he expelled the shrine prostitutes from the land and removed all the idols made by his ancestors. He even stripped his mother Maakah of her authority because she had made an idol of Pan <note>The text uses the name of the Greek god "Pan" to describe a pagan idol, likely an Asherah pole or similar cult object</note> in a grove; he cut down that idol of Pan and burned it at the Kidron brook. Although the hilltop shrines <note>original: "editorum sacella," referring to the 'high places' used for unauthorized worship</note> were not removed, Asa’s heart remained whole toward the LORD as long as he lived. He brought into the house of the LORD the silver, gold, and vessels dedicated by his father and by himself. There was war between this Asa and Baasha, king of the Israelites, throughout their lives. When Baasha led an expedition into Judah and began to fortify Ramah—to block any exit or entrance for Asa, king of Judah—Asa took all the silver and gold that remained in the treasures of the temple of the LORD and the royal treasures. He sent these, delivered by his servants, to Ben-hadad, son of Tabrimmon, the grandson of Hezion, the king of Syria who lived in Damascus, with a request of this sort: "Let there be a treaty between me and you, as there was between my father and your father. 

<margin>The expedition of Baasha, King of the Israelites, into Judah.</margin>

<column-break/>

I am sending you a gift of silver and gold. Break the treaty you have with Baasha, king of the Israelites, so that he may withdraw from me." Then Ben-hadad, complying with King Asa, sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel. He conquered Ijon, Dan, Abel-maakah, and all of Chinneroth, along with all the territory of Naphtali. When Baasha heard of this, he abandoned the fortification of Ramah and stayed in Tirzah. Then King Asa summoned all the people of Judah, exempting no one, and they carried away the stones and timber of Ramah which Baasha had been using for fortification. With these materials, King Asa fortified Geba of the Benjamites and Mizpah. Regarding all the rest of Asa’s affairs—how great his power was, what he did, and the towns he built—it is recorded in the annals of the kings of Judah. In his old age, however, he suffered from a disease in his feet. After he fell asleep with his ancestors, he was buried with them in the city of his forefather David.

<margin>Nadab, King of the Israelites.</margin>
His son Jehoshaphat succeeded him in the kingdom. Meanwhile, Nadab the son of Jeroboam began his reign over the Israelites in the second year of Asa, king of Judah; he reigned over the Israelites for two years. This Nadab lived against the will of the LORD, imitating the ways and the sins of his father (by which his father had led the Israelites into guilt). Baasha son of Ahijah, of the house of Issachar, formed a conspiracy against him and struck him down at Gibbethon, a city of the Philistines, while Nadab and all the Israelite forces were besieging it. This happened in the third year of Asa, king of Judah. Having killed him, Baasha seized the kingdom. Once he had occupied the throne, he struck down the entire lineage of Jeroboam so thoroughly that he left no one alive, just as the LORD had predicted through his servant Ahijah the Shilonite. This was because of the sins of Jeroboam—not only those he committed himself, but those he caused the Israelites to commit, by which wickedness he provoked the LORD God of Israel. As for all the other acts and deeds of Nadab, they are recorded in the annals of the kings of the Israelites. There was war between Asa and Baasha, king of the Israelites, as long as they lived. In the third year of Asa, king of Judah, Baasha son of Ahijah began to reign over all the Israelites; he reigned in Tirzah for twenty-four years. He acted against the will of the LORD and imitated the deeds and sins of Jeroboam, by which he had bound the Israelites.

### CHAPTER XVIII.

<margin>The Lord commands Elijah to go to Ahab.</margin>
After a long time, in the third year, the Lord commanded Elijah to go and show himself to Ahab, saying that He would send rain upon the lands. Therefore, Elijah set out to show himself to Ahab. Now, since there was a severe famine in Samaria, Ahab called Obadiah, the governor of his house (this Obadiah was a most reverent worshiper of the Lord; for when Jezebel was destroying the prophets of the Lord, he had taken a hundred prophets and hidden them by fifties in underground places, sustaining them for some time with bread and water). Ahab gave him the task of scouting all the springs and rivers of that region to see if they might find grass to keep the horses and mules alive, so they would not be deprived of their beasts of burden. When they had divided the land between them to be surveyed, so that Ahab went one way and Obadiah another by himself, 
<margin>Obadiah meets Elijah.</margin>
Obadiah, having started on his way, met Elijah. Recognizing him, he paid him honor with a bowed face and said: "Is it you, my lord Elijah?" He answered: "It is I. Go, tell your lord that Elijah is here." But he said: "How have I sinned, that you would deliver me into the hand of Ahab to be killed? As the Lord your God lives, there is no nation or kingdom where my lord has not sent people to search for you. And when 
<margin>a. Namely, by God, so they might say whether you were there.</margin>
they denied you were there, he would make those kingdoms and nations <gloss>a</gloss> swear an oath because he could not find you. And now you command me to go and tell my lord that Elijah is here? When I have departed from you, the Spirit of the Lord will carry you away to some place I do not know. Meanwhile, when I go to tell Ahab and he does not find you, I shall be killed by him—I, who have been reverent toward the Lord from my youth. Has it perhaps not been reported to you what I did when Jezebel was killing the prophets of the Lord, how I hid a hundred of them, fifty each in separate caves, and fed them with bread and water? ### CHAPTER XXI.

After these events, since Naboth the Jezreelite had a vineyard in Jezreel near the palace of Ahab, King of Samaria, Ahab contended with him that he should grant him the vineyard so that he might use it for a garden, because it was joined closely to his house. He offered to give him another vineyard better than that one, or (if it seemed better to him) he would pay the price in silver. ### CHAPTER XXIII.

Three years having passed during which there was no war between the Syrians and the Israelites, in the third year, Jehoshaphat <note>original: "Iosaphatus"</note>, the king of Judah, went down to the king of the Israelites. The king of the Israelites pointed out to his followers that Ramoth-Gilead <note>original: "Ramotha Galaaditidis"</note> belonged to them, and therefore they should not hesitate to snatch it from the hand of Syria. Then he asked Jehoshaphat if he would be willing to set out with him to war against Ramoth-Gilead. Jehoshaphat replied to him: "I am as you are; my people and my horses are at your disposal just as <margin>10</margin> your own. But I advise you," he said, "that the oracle of the Lord <note>original: "Iouæ," a Latinized form of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton</note> should be consulted today." Therefore the king of the Israelites, having gathered about four hundred prophets, asked of them whether they should march to attack Ramoth-Gilead in war or not. They replied that he should attack, for the Lord would deliver the city into the king’s hand. But Jehoshaphat said: "Is there not besides another prophet of the Lord whom we might question?" The king of the Israelites said to him: "There is still one man by whom it is permitted to inquire of the Lord's oracle, but I hate him for this reason: he never prophesies <margin>20</margin> anything favorable for me, but only disasters. He is Micaiah <note>original: "Michæas"</note>, son of Imlah." But Jehoshaphat said: "It does not befit a king to speak so." Then the king of the Israelites called a certain eunuch <note>original: "spadoni," an official or chamberlain</note> and commanded that he quickly summon Micaiah, son of Imlah. While the king of the Israelites and Jehoshaphat, the king of the Jews, each sat upon his throne dressed in their robes in an open area at the entrance of the gate of Samaria, with all the prophets prophesying before them, Zedekiah <note>original: "Sedecias"</note>, son of Chenaanah, having made for himself iron horns, <margin>30</margin> spoke thus: "Thus says the Lord: With these you shall gore the Syrians until they are destroyed." And all the prophets prophesied the same: that the king should successfully attack Ramoth-Gilead, for by the Lord's will, he would take it. Meanwhile, the messenger who had gone to call Micaiah urged him that, since the other prophets were predicting favorable things to the king with one voice, he should also follow their example and predict favorable things. But Micaiah swore by the immortal Lord that whatever the Lord commanded him, that alone would he speak. Then when he came to the king, the king questioned him thus: <margin>40</margin> "Micaiah, shall we bring war against Ramoth-Gilead, or not?" He replied: "Go up indeed, may it turn out well, and the Lord will grant you victory." But the king said: "I adjure you again and again by the name of the Lord that you tell me nothing but the truth." Then he said: "I saw all the Israelites wandering on the mountains like sheep without a shepherd, and the Lord saying: 'These have no masters; let each return to his home in safety.'" Here the king of the Israelites, addressing Jehoshaphat, said: "Did I not tell you that he would prophesy nothing prosperous for me, but only adversity?" And Micaiah said: <margin>50</margin> "Therefore hear the judgment of the Lord. I saw the Lord sitting on his throne, with all the heavenly host standing by him on his right and on his left, and he said: 'Who will deceive Ahab, so that he may invade Ramoth-Gilead and fall there?' And while one said one thing and another something else, a certain spirit stepped forward and, standing before the Lord, said, 'I will deceive him.' The Lord asked, 'By what means?' He replied, 'I will go and breathe a lying spirit into the mouths of all his prophets.' The Lord added, 'You shall deceive him, and you shall succeed. Go forth and do so.' Therefore know that the Lord has sent a lying spirit into the mouths of all these prophets—

<column-break/>

—and has intended evil for you." Here Zedekiah, son of Chenaanah, approached and struck Micaiah on the cheek. "When," he asked, "did the spirit of the Lord depart from me to speak with you?" Micaiah replied: "You shall know when you hide yourself in the innermost chamber." Then the king of the Israelites said, <margin>10</margin> "Seize Micaiah and lead him to Amon, the governor of the city, and to Joash, the king's son, and command him to be shut in prison by the king's order, and there let him be fed harshly on bread and water until I return safely." Micaiah said to him: "If indeed you return safely, then the Lord has not spoken through me." And he said, "Hear this, all you people." So when the king of the Israelites and Jehoshaphat, the king of Judah, had come to Ramoth-Gilead, the king of the Israelites advised Jehoshaphat that as they were about to join battle, he should change his appearance and put on the robes of Ahab himself. The king of the Israelites, in turn, having changed <margin>20</margin> his attire, entered the battle. Now the king of Syria had commanded the captains of his chariots—of whom he had thirty-two—not to attack anyone great or small except the king of the Israelites alone. Therefore, when the chariot captains saw Jehoshaphat, thinking he was the king of the Israelites, they turned their weapons toward him. But when Jehoshaphat cried out, they saw he was not the king of the Israelites and ceased pursuing him. <margin>At random</margin> But a certain man shot an arrow at random <note>original: "simpliciter iaculatus," without a specific target</note> and wounded the king of the Israelites between the joints of his armor. Then he <margin>30</margin> commanded his charioteer to turn the reins and lead him out <margin>Death of Ahab.</margin> of the battle line, as he was wounded. He imitated all the ways of his father Asa in obeying the Lord and did not deviate from them. However, the high places <note>original: "sacella," small shrines</note> were not removed, and the Israelites still performed sacrifices and burned incense in them. Jehoshaphat was at peace with the king of Israel. Concerning the rest of Jehoshaphat's deeds and his brave acts and the wars he waged, it is written in the annals of the kings of Judah. The remnant <margin>50</margin> of the male cult prostitutes <note>original: "mollium," literally 'the soft ones'</note> who remained from the time of his father Asa, he removed from the land. At that time, there was no king appointed in Edom <note>original: "Idumæa"</note>. After the death of Ahab, the Moabites revolted from the Israelites. Now Ahaziah <note>original: "Ochozias"</note> fell through the lattice of his upper chamber in Samaria and, as he lay ill, he sent messengers, commanding them to go and consult the oracle of Beelzebub, the god of Ekron <note>original: "Accaronenfis"</note>, to see if he would recover from this disease. But the angel <note>original: "genius"</note> of the Lord gave a command to Elijah the Tishbite <note>original: "Eliæ Thesbitæ"</note> to go and meet the messengers of the King of Samaria and ask them: "Is there no God among the Israelites, that you go to the oracle of Beelzebub, the god of Ekron?" Therefore, the Lord has decreed that he shall not come down from the bed he has climbed into, but shall surely die. When Elijah had delivered this to the messengers, they returned to the king, and when he asked why they had come back, they replied: "A certain man met us and told us to return to the king who sent us, and to ask him, by the Lord’s command: 'Is there no God among the Israelites, that you send to the oracle of Beelzebub, the god of Ekron?' Therefore, from the bed you have climbed into, you shall never descend, but shall surely die."

<margin>
Elijah calls down fire from heaven.

Then the king asked: "What was the appearance of the man who met you and said these things?" They said: "He is a hairy man, with a leather belt wrapped around his waist." And the king said: "It is Elijah the Tishbite." Then he sent to him a captain of fifty <note>original: "semicenturionē"</note> with his fifty men, who, finding him sitting on the top of a hill, addressed him thus: "Man of God, the king commands you to come down." Elijah answered him: "If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty." And fire fell from heaven and consumed him and his fifty men. Again, the king sent another captain of fifty with his fifty men to him, who addressed him: "Man of God, the king commands you to come down quickly." To whom Elijah said: "If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and consume you and your fifty." And the divine fire fell from heaven and consumed him and his fifty men. But the king sent a third captain of fifty with his fifty men. When this third captain reached Elijah, he fell on his knees and begged him, saying: "Man of God, I pray you to spare my life and the lives of these fifty, your servants; since fire falling from heaven consumed the two previous captains and their fifty men, have regard for my safety." Then Elijah, warned by the messenger of the Lord to go down and not be afraid of him, went down with him to the king and spoke to him: "This is the sentence of the Lord: 'Because you sent messengers to consult Beelzebub, the god of Ekron, as if there were no God among the Israelites whose oracle you could consult, therefore you shall not descend from the bed you have climbed into,

but shall surely die.'" And so he died, according to the word of the Lord spoken by Elijah. In his place, Joram <note>original: "Ioramus"</note> obtained the kingdom in the second year of Joram, son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, because Ahaziah had no son. As for the rest of the deeds of Ahaziah, they are written in the annals of the kings of the Israelites.

### CHAPTER III.

Joram <note>also known as Jehoram</note>, the son of Ahab, began his reign over the Israelites in Samaria in the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat, King of Judah; he reigned for twelve years. He was wicked toward the Lord, though not as much as his parents, for he removed the statue of Baal that his father had made. However, he clung to the sins of Jeroboam, son of Nebat, by which he had bound the Israelites in sin, and did not depart from them. 

Now Mesha, King of the Moabites, a man rich in livestock, used to pay the King of the Israelites a tribute of one hundred thousand lambs and as many rams with their wool. After Ahab died, he rebelled against the Israelites. Thus King Joram went out from Samaria and held a census of all the Israelites. He then sent word to Jehoshaphat, King of Judah, to inform him that the King of the Moabites had revolted and to ask him to join the war to pursue the Moabites. He replied that he would be there, and that he, his men, and his horses were at Joram's disposal. He asked which way they should march. Joram replied: "By the way that leads into the desert of Edom <note>original: "Idumææ"</note>." 

Therefore, when the Kings of the Israelites, Judah, and Edom had set out and marched in a circuit for seven days, water was lacking for the soldiers and the pack animals they were leading. And here the King of the Israelites complained: "Alas, the Lord has called these three kings together only to deliver them into the hands of the Moabites!" But Jehoshaphat said: "Is there no prophet of the Lord here, from whom we might seek the Lord’s oracle?" One of the servants of the King of the Israelites replied: "Elisha, the son of Shaphat, is here—the one who used to pour water on the hands of Elijah." And Jehoshaphat said: "He has the oracle of the Lord." 

So the King of the Israelites, Jehoshaphat, and the King of Edom went down to him. Then Elisha spoke to the King of the Israelites: "What business have I with you? Go to the prophets of your father and mother." But the King of the Israelites said: "Rather tell us why the Lord has called these three kings together to hand them over to the Moabites?" Elisha replied: "I swear by the living Lord <gloss>the God whom I serve</gloss> <note>original gloss: "a", likely referencing a marginal cross-reference or clarification of Elisha's standing before God</note>, if it were not for the respect I have for Jehoshaphat, King of Judah, I would not even look at you. Then, while the minstrel was playing, Elisha, moved by the Lord, spoke: "The Lord commands that many trenches be made in this valley, and he promises this: though you shall see neither wind nor rain, this dry bed shall be filled with water, which you and your cattle and pack animals may drink. And this is but a small thing to the Lord; he will also deliver the Moabites into your hands. You shall overthrow every fortified and choice city, cut down every good tree, stop up all the springs of water, and ruin every good field with stones."

### CHAPTER V.

<margin>Concerning Naaman the Syrian healed of leprosy by Elisha.</margin>
Now Naaman was the commander of the army of the King of Syria, a man of great power and authority with his master (for through him the Lord had given victory to the Syrians). He was a very brave man, but he was a leper. Among the household of Naaman's wife was a young girl who had been taken captive by Syrian raiders from the land of Israel. She said to her mistress that she wished her master could meet the prophet living in Samaria, for he would rid him of his leprosy. When Naaman reported these words of the Israelite girl to his master, the King of Syria ordered him to go, saying he would send a letter to the King of Israel. So he set out, taking with him ten talents of silver, six thousand pieces of gold, and ten sets of fine clothing. He brought the letter to the King of Israel, the message of which was this: "As soon as this letter reaches you, know that I have sent my servant Naaman to you, so that you may heal him of his leprosy." When the King of Israel read the letter, he tore his clothes and said: "Am I a god, that I have the power to kill and to heal, that this man sends someone to me to be cured of leprosy? Take note, I pray you, and see how he seeks an occasion for a quarrel against me." When Elisha, the man of God, heard that the King of Israel had torn his garments, he sent word to him, asking why he had torn his clothes; there was no reason for it. Let the man come to him, and he would learn that there was a prophet among the Israelites. So Naaman came with his horses and chariots to the door of Elisha's house. Elisha sent a messenger to him while he stood there, commanding him to go and wash seven times in the Jordan, and thus his body would return to purity. But Naaman was indignant and began to leave. "I thought," he said, "that he would surely come out, stand and call upon the name of the Lord his God, and move his hand over the place to rid me of the leprosy. Are not the Abana and Pharphar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of the Israelites, that I might wash in them and be cleansed?" As he turned to go away in a rage, his servants approached him and urged him: "Father, if the prophet had commanded a great thing, would you not have done it? How much more then, when he simply tells you to wash and be cleansed?" So he went down and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan, as the man of God had commanded; and his body was restored to such purity as that of a little child. Then he returned to the man of God with all his company, and when he came into his presence, he confessed that he knew there was no God in all the world except among the Israelites, and he urged him to accept a gift. But Elisha swore by the immortal Lord whom he served that he would not accept it; even as Naaman pressed him to take it, he refused. Then Naaman said: "I pray you then, let me be given as much earth as two mules can carry; for from now on I will offer burnt offerings and sacrifices to no other gods but the Lord. May the Lord forgive me this one thing: when my master goes into the temple of Rimmon to worship, and I lean on his hand, I must bow down there. May the Lord forgive this bowing of mine in the temple of Rimmon." The prophet said to him: "Go in peace." After they returned to their master, the Syrians ceased making further incursions into the territory of the Israelites.

<margin>The famine in Samaria was so great that mothers ate their own sons.</margin> Later, Ben-hadad, the King of Syria, having gathered all his forces, invaded and besieged Samaria. Because of this siege, such a great famine fell upon Samaria that a donkey’s head cost eighty pieces of silver, and a fourth part of a kab <note>term: "cabi" — a kab was a Hebrew dry measure roughly equal to 1-2 quarts</note> of dove’s dung cost five pieces of silver. As the King of the Israelites was passing along the walls, a woman cried out to him in this manner: "Help, my lord King!" He replied: "If the Lord himself does not help you, from where shall I bring you help? From the threshing floor? Or from the winepress? But regardless, what is the matter?" And she said: "This woman urged me to give up my son so we might eat him that day, and we would eat her son the next day. So we cooked my son and ate him. But the next day, when I asked her to give up her son in turn to be eaten, she hid him." Having heard this woman's speech, the King, passing by the walls, tore his clothes (at which point it was noticed that he wore sackcloth <note>original: "centone", referring to a rough garment of patches worn as a sign of mourning or penance</note> beneath against his skin) and said: "May God destroy me if the head of Elisha, son of Shaphat, remains on him this day." Having spoken this, he sent one of his attendants. Before the messenger arrived, Elisha was sitting in his house with the elders who were present, and he spoke to them thus: "You must know that the son of a murderer has sent someone to cut off my head. See to it that when the messenger comes, you shut the door and hold it fast against him. For I hear the sound of his master's feet following behind him." While he was still speaking with them, behold, the messenger came down to him, followed by the King, who said: "Since this evil is from the Lord, what more should I expect from the Lord?"

Then they began to say among themselves that they were not doing the right thing; for this was a day of good news, yet they remained silent. If they waited until the morning light, they would be found guilty. Therefore, they decided they must go and report this to the royal palace. ### CHAPTER IX.

At that time Elisha the prophet called one of the sons of the prophets and commanded him in this manner: "Gird yourself, and taking this flask of oil with you, set out for Ramoth-Gilead. And the prophet poured the oil upon his head, saying: "Thus says the Lord God of the Israelites: I anoint you king of the people of the Lord, that is, of the Israelites, so that you may destroy the house of Ahab your master, and I may avenge the blood of my servants the prophets, and all the servants of the Lord, upon Jezebel. I shall cause the entire house of Ahab to perish, nor shall there be anything of his lineage among the Israelites, whether hidden or exposed, for I shall utterly overturn everything. I shall reduce the house of Ahab to the state into which the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat and the house of Baasha son of Ahijah <note>original: "Abiae"</note> were reduced. Jehu, however, went out to his fellow servants and was asked how things stood, and why that madman <note>original: "lymphatus"</note> had come to him. In the seventh year, Jehoiada <note>The High Priest</note> arranged for the centurions of the guards and attendants to be summoned. Having brought them into the temple of the Lord and bound them by an oath, he made a pact with them, showed them the king's son, and gave them these instructions: "This is what you must do. A third part of you who come on the Sabbath shall keep watch over the royal palace. Another 
<margin>10</margin>third shall be at the Sur Gate. The final third shall be at the back gate of the guards and shall keep watch over the house of Messa <note>likely referring to the Millo, a rampart or fortification</note>. Two parts of you—that is, all who usually go off duty on the Sabbath—shall keep watch over the king in the temple of the Lord. You shall surround the king on all sides, weapons in hand; and whoever enters within the enclosure must be put to death. You shall stay with the king both when he goes out and when he comes in." The centurions carried out all the commands of Jehoiada the priest, each taking his men—both those who were coming on duty on the Sabbath and those who were going off—
<margin>20</margin>and they went to Jehoiada. The priest gave the centurions the spears and quivers of King David that were kept in the temple of the Lord. The armed guards stood from the right side of the temple to the left, where the temple and the altar were open, so they might surround the king on every side. He then led out the king's son, placed the crown and the testimony <note>original: "oraculum," referring to the book of the Law or the royal statutes</note> upon him; they made him king and anointed him, and clapping their hands, they greeted the king. When Athaliah heard the noise of the people running together, she came to them 
in the temple of the Lord. When she saw the king standing on the 
pulpit <note>a raised platform or dais</note>, as was the custom, and the 
<margin>30</margin>princes and trumpeters beside the king, and all the people of the land rejoicing and blowing trumpets, she tore her clothes and cried out again and again that it was a conspiracy. But Jehoiada the priest commanded the centurions who were in charge of the soldiers to lead her out beyond the temple enclosure, and if anyone followed her, they were to kill him with the sword. For the priest did not want her to die in the temple of the Lord. They seized her and led her out to the road used by horses to enter the palace, and there she was killed. Then Jehoiada made a covenant between the Lord, the king, and the people, that they should be the Lord's people, and also 
<margin>40</margin>between the king and the people. Then the people of the whole region went to the temple of Baal and tore it down; they thoroughly smashed its altars and images, and they killed Mattan, the priest of Baal, before the altars. The priest [Jehoiada] stationed guards at the temple of the Lord, then called together the centurions, the bodyguards, the attendants, and finally all the people. They escorted the king down from the temple of the Lord and brought him into the palace by way of the Gate of the Guards. Once he was seated on the royal throne, everyone rejoiced, and thus the city found peace, Athaliah having been slain by the sword at the palace.

### CHAPTER XII.

**J**oash was seven years old when he began to reign, specifically in the seventh year of the reign of Jehu. He reigned in Jerusalem for forty years. His mother's name was Zibiah, from Beersheba. Joash obeyed Jehoiada as long as he had the priest Jehoiada as his teacher—though the high places <note>local shrines</note> were not removed, and the people still offered sacrifices and incense in them. Joash commanded the priests to take all the money from the sacred things brought into the temple of the Lord—the money from the census according to each person's valuation, and all 

<column-break/>

the money that anyone chose to bring into the temple of the Lord. Each priest was to take it from his own district and use it to repair the damaged parts of the temple wherever ruins were found. But by the twenty-third year of King Joash's reign, since the priests had not repaired the ruins of the temple, King Joash called for Jehoiada the priest and the other priests. He rebuked them for not repairing the damaged areas and forbade them from receiving any more money from their districts unless they spent it on the temple ruins. When the priests had agreed not to receive money from the people nor to be responsible for repairing the temple ruins, Jehoiada the priest took a 
chest, bored a hole in its lid, and placed it by the altar on the right side as one enters the temple of the Lord. The priests who guarded the entrance would put all the money brought into the temple of the Lord into this chest. Whenever it appeared there was enough money in the chest, the royal scribe and the high priest would come, count the money found in the temple of the Lord, and put it into bags. After the account was settled, they would hand it over to the overseers of the work who were in charge of the temple of the Lord. These men would pay the carpenters and builders who were repairing the temple of the Lord, as well as the masons, stonecutters, and for the purchase of timber and quarried stones to mend the ruins of the temple of the Lord—in short, for everything needed for the restoration of the temple. However, from that money collected in the temple of the Lord, no silver basins, musical instruments, bowls, trumpets, or any vessels of gold or silver were made; rather, the money was given to the overseers of the work to repair the temple of the Lord. No accounting was required from the men to whom the money was delivered to pay the workers, because they acted in good faith. However, the money from guilt offerings and sin offerings was not brought into the temple; it belonged to the priests. At that time, Hazael king of Syria attacked Gath in war and captured it. When he turned his path toward Jerusalem, Joash king of Judah took all the things that had been consecrated by his ancestors Jehoshaphat, Joram, and Ahaziah, the kings of Judah, as well as his own dedications, and all the gold found in the 
<margin>40</margin>treasuries of the temple and the palace, and sent them to Hazael king of Syria to persuade him to withdraw from Jerusalem. As for all the other deeds of Joash, they are recorded in the annals of the kings of Judah. This Joash was killed at the house of Millo, which goes down toward Silla, by a conspiracy formed by his own servants, Jozabar the son of Shimeath and Jozabad the son of Shomer. He was buried with his ancestors in the City of David, and his son Amaziah succeeded him as king.

### CHAPTER XIII.

<margin>Jehoahaz, King of the Israelites.</margin>
**I**n the twenty-third year of Joash son of Ahaziah, 
<margin>50</margin>king of Judah, Jehoahaz the son of Jehu began his reign over the Israelites. He reigned in Samaria for seventeen years. Because he offended the Lord and imitated the sin of Jeroboam son of Nebat, which he led the Israelites to commit, and did not turn away from it, the Lord was angry with the Israelites and repeatedly delivered them into the hands of Hazael king of Syria and Ben-hadad the son of Hazael. But when Jehoahaz pleaded with the Lord, the Lord listened to him, seeing the calamities of the Israelites and how they were oppressed by the king of Syria. The Lord provided a deliverer for the Israelites, rescued them from the power of the Syrians, and restored them to their former homes. Nevertheless, they did not turn away from the sins of the house of Jeroboam.

Indeed, of the army of Joahaz, there remained only fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot-men, for the King of Syria had destroyed the rest, grinding them down as if they were dust in a threshing-floor. All the other deeds and the might of Joahaz are written in the annals of the kings of the Israelites.

<margin>Joash, King of the Israelites.</margin>
When Joahaz died and was buried in Samaria, his son Joash succeeded to the kingdom of the Israelites in the thirty-seventh year of Joash, king of Judah; he reigned in Samaria for sixteen years. However, he offended the Lord <note>original: "Iouam," a Latinized form of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton YHWH</note> by not departing from the many sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, into which he had led the Israelites, and by living according to them. All the other deeds and the might of Joash, and how he waged war against Amaziah, king of Judah, are written in the annals of the kings of the Israelites. When Joash died, Jeroboam sat upon his throne. Joash was buried in Samaria with the kings of the Israelites.

<margin>Joash visits Elisha during his illness.</margin>
When Elisha was suffering from the illness of which he would eventually die, Joash, king of the Israelites, visited him and, weeping over him, said: "O my father, my father! The chariot and horsemen of the Israelites!" Then Elisha commanded him to take a bow and arrows. When he had taken the bow and arrows, Elisha told him to place his hand upon the bow. After he had done so, Elisha placed his own hands upon the king’s hands and ordered him to open the eastern window; once opened, he told him to shoot. As he shot the arrow, Elisha said:
> This is the victorious arrow of the Lord, the arrow of victory against the Syrians, whom you shall strike down at Aphek until they are destroyed.

He also spoke to the king:
> Take the arrows.

And when he had taken them:
> Strike the earth.

The king struck the earth three times and then stopped. Whereupon the man of God, becoming angry, said to him:
> If you had struck five or six times, you would then have struck the Syrians down to their utter destruction. Now, you shall defeat the Syrians only three times.

<margin>A dead man returned to life by touching Elisha’s body. Ecclesiasticus 48</margin>
After Elisha had died and been buried, in that same year, Moabite raiders made an incursion into the region. While some men were burying a certain person, they saw the raiders and threw the body into the tomb of Elisha. As soon as the body touched the bones of Elisha, the man returned to life and stood up on his feet. Now Hazael, King of Syria, cruelly harassed the Israelites throughout the time of Joahaz. However, the Lord took pity on them and looked upon them because of the covenant He had made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; He did not wish to destroy them, nor has He cast them off until now. When Hazael, King of Syria, died and his son Ben-hadad reigned in his place, Joash son of Joahaz recaptured the towns from Ben-hadad son of Hazael which he had taken by force from his father Joahaz. Having defeated him three times, Joash recovered the cities of Israel.

### CHAPTER XIV.

<margin>Amaziah, King of Judah. 2 Chronicles 25</margin>
In the second year of Joash son of Joahaz, king of the Israelites, Amaziah son of Joash began his reign over Judah, being twenty-five years old at the time. He reigned in Jerusalem for seventeen years; his mother was Jehoaddan of Jerusalem. He obeyed the Lord, though not quite like David the ancestor of his line, but rather imitating all the deeds of his father Joash; nevertheless, the high places <note>original: "facellis," small shrines or chapels</note> were not removed, and the people still offered sacrifices and incense in them. After his kingdom was firmly established in his hand, he executed his servants who had murdered the king, his father. Yet

<column-break/>

he did not kill the sons of the murderers, as is written in the book of the law of Moses, where the Lord commands that parents shall not die for their children, nor shall children die for their parents, but each shall die for his own sin.

<margin>Deuteronomy 24; Ezekiel 18</margin>
He also slew ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt and captured the rock <note>original: "Petram," referring to the city of Sela or Petra</note> by force of arms, naming it Joktheel, a name which remains to this day.

<margin>Amaziah declares war on Joash.</margin>
Then, having sent messengers to Joash son of Joahaz, grandson of Jehu and king of the Israelites, he challenged him to a confrontation. Joash sent back this reply:
> A thistle of Lebanon sent word to a cedar of Lebanon, asking for the cedar's daughter in marriage for his son. In the meantime, a wild beast of Lebanon trampled the thistle. Because you have defeated the Edomites, your heart is lifted up. Stay at home and enjoy your glory; do not bring disaster upon yourself, lest you fall, and Judah with you.

<margin>Amaziah defeated by Joash.</margin>
When Amaziah would not listen, Joash, king of the Israelites, set out and met Amaziah, king of Judah, at Beth-shemesh, which is in Judah. The Judeans were defeated by the Israelites and fled, each man to his own home. Joash, king of the Israelites, captured Amaziah son of Joash, king of Judah and grandson of Joahaz, at Beth-shemesh. Proceeding to Jerusalem, he tore down four hundred cubits of the wall of Jerusalem, from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate. He took away whatever gold, silver, and vessels were found in the temple of the Lord and in the king’s treasury, and having taken hostages, he returned to Samaria. All the other deeds and power of Joash, and how he waged war with Amaziah, king of Judah, are written in the annals of the kings of the Israelites. When Joash died and was buried in Samaria with the kings of the Israelites, his son Jeroboam succeeded to the kingdom. Amaziah son of Joash, king of Judah, lived fifteen years after the death of Joash son of Joahaz, king of the Israelites. The rest of the deeds of Amaziah are written in the annals of the kings of Judah. A conspiracy was formed against him in Jerusalem; when he fled to Lachish, men were sent there who killed him. He was brought back on a horse and buried in Jerusalem with his ancestors in the City of David.

<margin>2 Chronicles 26</margin>
All the people of Judah then took his son Azariah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in his place. After the king’s death, Azariah rebuilt Elath and restored it to Judah.

<margin>Jeroboam son of Joash, King of the Israelites.</margin>
In the fifteenth year of Amaziah son of Joash, king of Judah, Jeroboam son of Joash began to reign over the Israelites. He reigned in Samaria for forty-one years. He offended the Lord and did not depart from all the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, by which he had bound the Israelites. He restored the borders of the Israelites from Hamath as far as the Sea of the Plain <note>the Dead Sea</note>, according to the oracle of the Lord God of the Israelites which He spoke through His servant Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath-hepher.

<margin>Jonah.</margin>
For the Lord saw the bitterness of the Israelites’ affliction, such that there was no one left, neither bond nor free. Since there was no one to help them, and the Lord did not wish to blot out the name of Israel from the earth, He defended them through Jeroboam son of Joash. All the other deeds of Jeroboam, his might, how he waged war, and how he recovered Damascus and Hamath for Judah <note>the text suggests these were territories formerly held by Judah now within Israel's sphere</note>, are written in the annals of the kings of the Israelites. After Jeroboam went to the spirits of his ancestors <note>original: "manes," a Roman term for the souls of the deceased, used here to mean he died</note> among the Israelites, his son Zechariah obtained the kingdom in his place.

BOOK IV

### CHAPTER XV

In the seventeenth <note>The Latin text says seventeenth, though biblical chronologies usually place this in the twenty-seventh year.</note> year of Jeroboam, king of the Israelites, Azariah, the son of Amaziah, began his reign over the kingdom of Judah, being then seventeen years old. He reigned in Jerusalem for fifty-two years; his mother was a Jerusalemite named Jecoliah. He obeyed the Lord <note>original: "Ioua," a Latinized version of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton YHWH</note> just as his father Amaziah had done, except that he did not remove the high places <note>original: "sacellis," referring to local shrines or altars used for worship outside the central Temple</note>, and the people still offered sacrifices and burned incense there. This king was so afflicted by the Lord that he was a leper until the day of his death; he lived in a separate house while Jotham, his son, managed the palace and administered justice to the people. Regarding the rest of the deeds of Azariah, they are written in the annals of the kings of Judah. When Azariah passed away and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David, his son Jotham reigned in his place.

In the thirty-eighth year of Azariah, king of Judah, Zechariah, the son of Jeroboam, began his reign over the Israelites, which he held in Samaria for six months. Because he lived contrary to the will of the Lord, following the example of his ancestors and not departing from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat—who had led the Israelites into sin—Shallum, the son of Jabesh, formed a conspiracy, killed him publicly, and seized the kingdom. The rest of Zechariah’s deeds are written in the annals of the kings of the Israelites. This fulfilled the oracle of the Lord which had promised Jehu that his descendants to the fourth generation <note>original: "trinepotes"</note> would sit upon the throne of Israel.

Shallum, the son of Jabesh, began his reign in the thirty-ninth year of Azariah, king of Judah. After he had held power in Samaria for the space of one month, Menahem, the son of Gadi, marched from Tirzah to Samaria and killed him there, seizing the kingdom after his death. Regarding the deeds of Shallum and the conspiracy he made, they are recorded in the annals of the kings of the Israelites. Then Menahem laid waste to Tiphsah and everyone in it, and its territories starting from Tirzah, because they had not opened their gates to him; he even brutally ripped open all the pregnant women of Tiphsah.

In the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah <note>The text uses "Oziæ," another name for Azariah</note>, king of Judah, Menahem, the son of Gadi, began his reign over the Israelites, which he held in Samaria for ten years. He lived contrary to the will of the Lord and never departed from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who led the Israelites into sin. When Pul, the king of Assyria, entered the land, Menahem gave him a thousand talents of silver to form an alliance with him and confirm his hold on the kingdom. Menahem exacted this silver from all the wealthy men of Israel—specifically fifty shekels of silver from each man—to give to the king of Assyria. Thus the king of Assyria turned back and did not remain in the land. The rest of the deeds of Menahem are recorded in the annals of the kings of the Israelites.

When Menahem passed away, his son Pekahiah succeeded him to the kingdom of Israel in the fiftieth year of Azariah, king of Judah. He reigned in Samaria for two years. Because he lived contrary to the will of the Lord and did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had bound the Israelites to sin, Pekah, the son of Remaliah—an officer <note>original: "equus trium uir," likely a high-ranking military captain or chariot commander</note>—killed him by conspiracy in Samaria,

<column-break/>

in the citadel of the palace, along with Argob and Arieh, and fifty men of Gilead who accompanied him. After his death, Pekah seized the kingdom. The rest of the deeds of Pekahiah are written in the annals of the kings of the Israelites.

In the fifty-second year of Azariah, king of Judah, Pekah, the son of Remaliah,
<margin>Pekah, King of the Israelites.</margin>
began to reign over the Israelites. He reigned in Samaria for twenty years. He offended the Lord and did not depart from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had led the Israelites into sin. During the time of Pekah, king of the Israelites, Tiglath-Pileser, the king of Assyria, launched an expedition and captured Ijon,

# BOOK IV.

### CHAPTER XV.

In the seventeenth <note>original: "decimoseptimo"</note> year of Jeroboam, king of the Israelites, Azariah, the son of Amaziah, began his reign over Judah, being then seventeen years old. He reigned in Jerusalem for fifty-two years; his mother was a Jerusalemite named Jecoliah. He did what was pleasing to the Lord <note>original: "Iouæ," a Latinized version of the Hebrew Name of God</note> just as his father Amaziah had done; however, he did not fully remove the high places <note>original: "facellis," local shrines where worship was unauthorized by central Law</note>, for the people still offered sacrifices and burnt incense there. This king was afflicted by the Lord and remained a leper until the day of his death; he lived in a separate house, while his son Jotham managed the palace and administered justice for the people. As for all the other deeds of Azariah, they are recorded in the annals of the kings of Judah. When Azariah passed away and was buried with his ancestors in the city of David, his son Jotham succeeded him as king.

In the thirty-eighth year of Azariah’s reign over Judah, Zechariah, the son of Jeroboam, began his reign over the Israelites, which he held in Samaria for six months. Because he lived in opposition to the Lord’s will, following the example of his ancestors, and did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had ensnared the Israelites, Shallum son of Jabesh formed a conspiracy against him; he killed him in public and seized the throne. As for the rest of Zechariah’s deeds, they are recorded in the annals of the kings of the Israelites. This fulfilled the oracle of the Lord, in which He had promised that his descendants to the fourth generation <note>original: "trinepotes," literally great-great-grandchildren</note> would sit upon the throne of Israel; and so it came to pass.

Shallum son of Jabesh began his reign in the thirty-ninth year of Azariah, king of Judah; after he had held power in Samaria for only one month, Menahem son of Gadi set out from Tirzah to Samaria and killed him there, seizing the kingdom for himself. The deeds of Shallum and the conspiracy he organized are recorded in the annals of the kings of the Israelites. Then Menahem utterly laid waste to Tiphsah <note>original: "Thapfam"</note> and everything within it and its borders starting from Tirzah, because they had not opened their gates to him; he even ripped open all the pregnant women of Tiphsah.

In the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah <note>original: "Oziæ," another name for Azariah</note>, king of Judah, Menahem son of Gadi began his reign over the Israelites, which he held in Samaria for ten years. He lived in opposition to the Lord’s will and never turned away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had ensnared the Israelites. When Pul, the king of Assyria, entered the region, Menahem gave him a thousand talents of silver to form an alliance with him and to confirm the kingdom in his own hand. To raise this silver, he taxed all the powerful men of the Israelites, namely fifty shekels of silver per man, to be given to the king of Assyria. Thus the king of Assyria turned back and did not remain in that land. All the other deeds of Menahem are recorded in the annals of the kings of the Israelites.

When Menahem passed away, his son Pekahiah succeeded him to the kingdom of the Israelites in the fiftieth year of Azariah, king of Judah. He reigned in Samaria for two years. Because he lived in opposition to the Lord’s will and did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had bound the Israelites to sin, Pekah son of Remaliah, his captain <note>original: "triumuir," a high military officer</note>, killed him in Samaria through a conspiracy.

<column-break/>

He was killed in the citadel of the palace, along with Argob and Arieh, and fifty men of Gilead who were with him; upon his death, Pekah seized the throne. As for the rest of the deeds of Pekahiah, they are recorded in the annals of the kings of the Israelites.

### CHAPTER XVI.

The Israelites did not turn away from the sins into which Jeroboam had driven them; instead, they continued to follow them, and the sacred grove remained in Samaria. Indeed, Jehoahaz was left with a force of only fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand footmen, for the King of Syria had destroyed the rest, reducing them to something like the dust of a threshing floor. Regarding all the other deeds and strengths of Jehoahaz, they are written in the annals of the kings of the Israelites. When Jehoahaz passed away and was buried in Samaria, his son Joash succeeded him to the kingdom of the Israelites in the thirty-seventh year of Joash, King of Judah; he reigned in Samaria for sixteen years. However, he offended the Lord <note>original: "Iouam," a Latinized form of the Hebrew name for God, Yahweh</note> by not turning away from all the outrages of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had ensnared the Israelites in sin, but rather by living in those same ways. Regarding all the other deeds of Joash and his might, including how he waged war against Amaziah, King of Judah, it is recorded in the annals of the kings of the Israelites. When Joash passed away, Jeroboam sat upon his throne. Joash was buried in Samaria with the kings of the Israelites.

<margin>Joash visits the sick Elisha.</margin>
When Elisha was suffering from the illness that would lead to his death, Joash, King of the Israelites, visited him. Weeping over him, the king said: "O my father, my father! The chariots and horsemen of Israel!" Then Elisha instructed him to take a bow and arrows. When the king had taken the bow and arrows, Elisha told him to place his hand upon the bow. After he had done so, Elisha placed his own hands over the king’s hands and ordered him to open the eastern window and shoot. When he had shot, Elisha said: "This is the Lord’s arrow of victory, the arrow of victory against the Syrians, whom you shall strike down at Aphek until they are destroyed." He spoke again to the king: "Take the arrows." When the king had taken them, Elisha said: "Strike the ground." The king struck the ground three times and then stopped. At this, the man of God <note>original: "diuinus," refers here to the prophet</note> grew angry with him and said: "If you had struck five or six times, you would have struck the Syrians until they were finished. Now, you shall defeat the Syrians only three times."

<margin>A dead man revived by touching Elisha’s body. Ecclesiasticus 48</margin>
After Elisha died and was buried, Moabite raiders began to invade the region that same year. Some people who were burying a man saw the bandits and threw the body into Elisha’s tomb. As soon as the man touched Elisha’s bones, he returned to life and stood up on his feet. Meanwhile, Hazael, King of Syria, cruelly oppressed the Israelites throughout the time of Jehoahaz. Yet, the Lord had mercy on them and looked upon them because of the covenant He had made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; He was unwilling to destroy them or cast them away even until now. When Hazael, King of Syria, died and his son Ben-hadad reigned in his place, Joash son of Jehoahaz took back the towns from Ben-hadad son of Hazael which Hazael had seized by force from his father Jehoahaz. Having defeated him three times, Joash recovered the Israelite cities.

### CHAPTER XIV.

He obeyed the Lord, though not quite like David the founder of his line, but rather imitating all the deeds of his father Joash. However, the high places <note>original: "sacellis," local shrines</note> were not removed, and the people still performed sacrifices there. After his grip on the kingdom was secured, he executed the servants who had murdered the king, his father; yet he

Regarding all the other deeds of Joash, his power, and how he fought against Amaziah King of Judah, it is recorded in the annals of the kings of the Israelites. When Joash passed away and was buried in Samaria with the kings of the Israelites, his son Jeroboam succeeded him. Amaziah son of Joash, King of Judah, lived for fifteen years after the death of Joash son of Jehoahaz, King of the Israelites. The rest of Amaziah’s deeds are recorded in the annals of the kings of Judah. A conspiracy was formed against him in Jerusalem; when he fled to Lachish, they sent men after him who murdered him there. Since there was no one to bring them help, and the Lord was unwilling to blot out the name of Israel from the face of the earth, He defended them through Jeroboam son of Joash. Regarding all the other deeds of Jeroboam, his might in war, and how he recovered Damascus and Hamath for Judah <note>This likely refers to territory previously held by the unified kingdom under David/Solomon</note> among the Israelites, it is written in the annals of the kings of the Israelites. ...to Urijah the high priest; and that priest constructed an altar according to the king's prescription sent from Damascus, completing it by the time of the king's arrival. When the king returned from Damascus and saw the altar, he approached it and performed a divine rite upon it. He burned a whole burnt offering <note>original: "solidam hostiam," a sacrifice entirely consumed by fire</note>, poured out a grain offering and wine, and sprinkled the blood of the peace offering <note>original: "pro salute sua," literally "for his own well-being"</note> upon the altar. The rest of the acts of Ahaz are recorded in the annals of the kings of Judah. When Ahaz passed away and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David, his son Hezekiah succeeded him as king.

### CHAPTER XVII

<margin>Hoshea, King of the Israelites.</margin> In the twelfth year of Ahaz, king of Judah, Hoshea the son of Elah began to reign over the Israelites. He reigned in Samaria for nine years. He indeed offended <margin>30</margin> the Lord, though not to the same extent as the kings of Israel who preceded him. Shalmaneser, the King of Assyria, launched an expedition against him, subdued him, and made him a vassal. Later, however, the king discovered a conspiracy by Hoshea, for he had sent messengers to So, the King of Egypt, and had stopped paying tribute to the King of Assyria as he had done in previous years. Consequently, Shalmaneser seized him and cast him into prison. After invading the entire region, <margin>Shalmaneser transfers the Israelites to Media; the sins of the Israelites.</margin> he attacked Samaria and besieged it for three years. In the ninth year of Hoshea, he captured it and deported the Israelites to Assyria. He settled <margin>40</margin> them in Halah and on the Habor, which are cities in Media situated by the river Gozan. This happened because the Israelites had sinned against the Lord their God, who had brought them out of Egypt and delivered them from the power of Pharaoh, king of Egypt. They had revered foreign gods and followed the customs of those nations whom the Lord had driven out before the Israelites, as well as the practices introduced by the kings of Israel themselves. They performed unlawful deeds against the Lord their God, building local shrines <note>original: "sacella," often translated as "high places"</note> in all their towns, from the watchtower to the fortified city. They set up sacred pillars and groves <margin>50</margin> everywhere on high hills and under <note>A line break in original</note> leafy trees. There, in all those shrines, they burned incense according to the custom of the nations whom the Lord had driven out for their sake. They committed wicked crimes to provoke the Lord, worshipping "dung-gods" <note>original: "stercoreos diuos," a derogatory biblical term for idols</note>, something the Lord had forbidden them to do. Although the Lord had warned both Israel and Judah through all the prophets who foresee the future, <margin>Jeremiah 8:5</margin> telling them to turn from their evil ways and obey his commandments and statutes—as set forth in the law given to their ancestors and the messages sent to them through 

<column-break/>

his servants the prophets—they would not listen. Instead, they remained as stiff-necked as their ancestors, who did not trust in the Lord their God. They rejected his statutes and the covenant he had made with their ancestors, along with the warnings he had given them. They followed worthless idols and became worthless themselves, imitating the surrounding nations whom the Lord had forbidden them to copy. Abandoning all the commandments of the Lord their God, they cast for themselves two idols of calves, made a sacred grove, worshipped all the host of heaven, and served Baal. They even passed their sons and daughters through the fire, and practiced divination and sorcery. They gave themselves over to provoking the Lord with their outrages. Because of this, I say, the Lord was fiercely angry with the Israelites and rejected them from his presence, leaving only the tribe of Judah. Yet even Judah did not keep the commandments of the Lord their God but followed the customs introduced by Israel. So the Lord rejected the entire lineage of Israel; he afflicted them and handed them over to plunderers until he had cast them out of his sight. <margin>1 Kings 11</margin> For when he tore Israel away from the house of David, they made Jeroboam the son of Nebat their king. Jeroboam drew them away from following the Lord and led them into a great sin. The Israelites persisted in all the sins committed by Jeroboam and did not depart from them, until at last the Lord removed Israel from his presence, as he had threatened <margin>Jeremiah 25</margin> through all his prophets. He caused them to be carried away from their own land into Assyria, a captivity that continues to this day. <margin>Origin of the Samaritans</margin> Then the King of Assyria brought people from Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim, and settled them in the towns of Samaria to replace the Israelites. These colonists took possession of Samaria and lived in its towns. However, when these colonists first settled there, they did not worship the Lord. Therefore, the Lord sent lions among them, which began killing them. This was reported to the King of Assyria: "The colonists you relocated to the towns of Samaria do not know the requirements of the God of that land; therefore, he has sent lions among them, and they are being killed." Then the King of Assyria commanded that one of the priests who had been deported be taken back there to live and teach the colonists the requirements of the God of that land. So one of the priests who had been exiled from Samaria came and lived in Bethel, and he taught them how they should worship the Lord. Nevertheless, each group made its own gods and set them up in the shrines that the Samaritans <note>The previous inhabitants of the region</note> had built, each nation in the town where they lived. The people from Babylon made Succoth-benoth; those from Cuthah made Nergal; those from Hamath made Ashima; the Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak; and the Sepharvites burned their children in the fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim. Thus, while they feared the Lord, they also appointed priests for the shrines from among their own people, who performed sacrifices for them. It resulted in them maintaining the religion of the Lord while simultaneously worshipping their own gods according to the customs of the nations from which they had been brought. To this day, they retain their former rituals; they do not truly follow the religion of the Lord, nor do they observe the statutes, ordinances, law, and discipline <margin>Genesis 32</margin> that the Lord gave to the descendants of Jacob (whom he named Israel). When he made a covenant with them, he commanded them: "Do not revere foreign gods, nor bow down to them, nor serve them..."

BOOK 4.

### CHAPTER XV.

In the seventeenth year of Jeroboam, King of the Israelites, Azariah <note>also known as Uzziah</note>, son of Amaziah, began his reign over Judah at the age of seventeen. He reigned in Jerusalem for fifty-two years; his mother was a Jerusalemite named Jecoliah. He did what was right in the sight of the Lord <note>original: "Iouæ," a Latinized form of the Tetragrammaton, Yahweh</note>, just as his father Amaziah had done. However, the small shrines <note>term: "facellis" refers to the "high places" or local altars where traditional worship persisted outside the central Temple</note> were not removed, and the people still offered sacrifices and burned incense there. This king was struck with leprosy by the Lord and remained a leper until the day of his death. He lived in a separate house, while his son Jotham managed the palace and administered justice for the people. As for all the other deeds of Azariah, they are recorded in the annals of the kings of Judah. When Azariah passed away and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David, his son Jotham reigned in his place.

In the thirty-eighth year of Azariah's reign over the Jews, Zechariah son of Jeroboam became king of the Israelites, and he held power in Samaria for six months. He lived in opposition to the will of the Lord, following the example of his ancestor Jeroboam <note>Jeroboam I, the first king of the breakaway northern kingdom</note>. He did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, by which he had ensnared the Israelites. Shallum son of Jabesh formed a conspiracy against him, killed him in public, and seized the kingdom. The rest of Zechariah’s deeds are recorded in the annals of the kings of the Israelites. This fulfilled the oracle of the Lord, in which He had promised Jeroboam that his descendants to the fourth generation <note>original: "trinepotes"</note> would sit on the throne of Israel; and so it came to pass.

Shallum son of Jabesh began his reign in the thirty-ninth year of Azariah, King of Judah. After he had reigned for only one month in Samaria, Menahem son of Gadi went from Tirzah up to Samaria and killed him there. Having slain him, he seized the kingdom. The rest of Shallum’s deeds and the conspiracy he led are recorded in the annals of the kings of the Israelites. Then Menahem utterly devastated the city of Tiphsah <note>original: "Thapsam"</note>, everything in it, and its territories from Tirzah outward, because they had not opened their gates to him. In his rage, he even ripped open all the pregnant women of Tiphsah.

In the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah <note>Azariah</note>, King of Judah, Menahem son of Gadi began his ten-year reign over the Israelites in Samaria. He lived in opposition to the Lord’s will and never turned away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had ensnared the Israelites. When Pul, the King of Assyria, invaded the land, Menahem gave him a thousand talents of silver to secure a treaty and confirm his hold on the kingdom. Menahem exacted this money from all the wealthy men of Israel, requiring each man to pay fifty shekels of silver to be given to the Assyrian king. Thus the King of Assyria turned back and did not remain in the land. All the rest of Menahem's deeds are recorded in the annals of the kings of the Israelites. When Menahem passed away, his son Pekahiah succeeded him in the fiftieth year of Azariah, King of Judah. He reigned in Samaria for two years. He lived in opposition to the Lord’s will and did not turn away from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, by which he had bound the Israelites. Pekah son of Remaliah, one of his chief officers <note>original: "triumuir," likely meaning a high-ranking military commander</note>, conspired against him and killed him in Samaria

<column-break/>

within the citadel of the royal palace, along with Argob and Arieh. He was accompanied by fifty men of Gilead. After the murder, Pekah seized the kingdom. All the other deeds of Pekahiah are written in the annals of the kings of the Israelites.

In the fifty-second year of Azariah, King of Judah, Pekah son of Remaliah began to reign over the Israelites; he reigned in Samaria for twenty years. He offended the Lord and did not turn away from the crimes of Jeroboam son of Nebat, who had ensnared the Israelites. During the time of King Pekah, Tiglath-Pileser, King of Assyria, launched an expedition and captured Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee, and the entire territory of Naphtali, and he deported the people to Assyria. Hoshea son of Elah formed a conspiracy against Pekah, killed him, and seized the kingdom in the twentieth year of Jotham son of Uzziah. All the rest of Pekah’s deeds are recorded in the annals of the kings of the Israelites.

In the second year of Pekah son of Remaliah, King of the Israelites, Jotham son of Uzziah began his reign over Judah at the age of twenty-five. He reigned in Jerusalem for sixteen years. His mother was named Jerusha, daughter of Zadok. He lived according to the will of the Lord, following the example of his father Uzziah, though the small shrines were still not removed, and the people continued to offer sacrifices and incense in them. He rebuilt the Upper Gate of the Temple of the Lord. All the other deeds of Jotham are recorded in the annals of the kings of Judah. During those times, the Lord began to send Rezin, King of Syria, and Pekah son of Remaliah against Judah.

### CHAPTER XVI.

After Jotham passed away and was buried with his ancestors in the City of David, the founder of his line, his son Ahaz took possession of the kingdom of Judah in the seventeenth year of Pekah son of Remaliah. He was twenty years old at the time and reigned in Jerusalem for sixteen years. He was so far from living according to the will of the Lord God of the Israelites—as David the founder of his line had done—that he instead imitated the ways of the Israelite kings. He even passed his own son through fire, following the abominable practices of the pagan nations whom the Lord had driven out before the Israelites.
