But they did not obey; instead, those nations held to their ancient customs. While they followed the religion of the Lord, they also worshipped among their own idols; their children and grandchildren have imitated the customs of their fathers to this day.

### CHAPTER XVIII.

In the third year of Hoshea son of Elah, king of the Israelites, Hezekiah son of Ahaz began his reign over Judah, being then twenty-five years old. He reigned in Jerusalem for twenty-nine years; his mother’s name was Abi, the daughter of Zechariah. He obeyed the Lord, just as his ancestor David had done. He removed the shrines <note>original: "fana," referring to the high places of pagan or unauthorized worship</note>, broke the statues, cut down the sacred grove, and crushed the bronze serpent made by Moses (since up to that time the Israelites were burning incense to it), and he called it Nehushtan <note>A Hebrew term meaning "a piece of brass," used here to mock the idol</note>. He trusted in the Lord, the God of the Israelites. There was no one like him among all the kings of Judah who came after him, nor among those who preceded him. He clung to the Lord without any defection and kept his commandments as they were handed down by Moses. Because the Lord was with him, he acted prudently in all his affairs. He rebelled against the king of Assyria and would not serve him. He subdued the Philistines as far as Gaza and its borders, from the watchtower to the fortified city. In the fourth year of Hezekiah’s reign, which was the seventh year of Hoshea son of Elah, the king of the Israelites <note>Note: This likely refers to the Assyrian king attacking the capital of the Israelites</note> went against Samaria and besieged it. After it was captured three years later—in the sixth year of Hezekiah, which was the ninth year of the king of the Israelites—he led the Israelites away into Assyria and settled them in Halah and Habor (which are cities of the Medes, located by the river Gozan). This happened because they had not listened to the word of the Lord their God, but had violated the covenant and did not obediently perform any of the things commanded by Moses, the servant of the Lord. However, in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib, king of Assyria, launched an expedition against all the fortified towns of Judah and captured them. Then Hezekiah, king of Judah, sent a legation to the king of Assyria at Lachish, confessing his fault and asking him to withdraw, promising he would bear whatever tribute was imposed upon him. When the Assyrian king imposed a tribute of three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold, Hezekiah gave all the silver found in the temple of the Lord and in the royal treasury. At that time, he even gave the king of Assyria the doors of the temple of the Lord and the metal plates with which he himself had overlaid them. But the king of Assyria sent Tartan, Rabsaris, and Rabshakeh <note>These are titles of high Assyrian officials rather than personal names: the commander, the chief eunuch, and the chief cupbearer</note> from Lachish to Jerusalem to King Hezekiah with a great force. When they had reached Jerusalem, they stood by the aqueduct of the upper pool,

<column-break/>

located on the path to the fuller's field, and called for the king. When Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the administrator of the palace, Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph the recorder came out to them, Rabshakeh spoke to them in this manner: "Tell Hezekiah these things in the name of the Great King, the King of Assyria: On what confidence do you rely? Do you think to contend with words, or with counsel, or with strength? In what hope do you trust that you have rebelled against him? Do you perhaps trust in <margin>*The speech of Rabshakeh to the people of Jerusalem.*</margin> that broken staff of a reed—that is, the Egyptians—on which, if a man leans, it pierces his hand? Such is Pharaoh, king of Egypt, to all who trust in him. But if you tell me that you trust in the Lord your God, is it not he whose shrines and altars Hezekiah has removed, commanding the people of Judah and Jerusalem that they should worship God only at a certain altar in Jerusalem? Come now, do you wish to make a wager with my lord the king of Assyria? If I give you two thousand horses, could you even provide enough riders for them? How then do you dare to resist even one single governor, the least of my master’s servants? Do you place your confidence in the chariots and cavalry of the Egyptians? Furthermore, have I come up to lay waste to this place without the Lord? The Lord himself commanded me to make an expedition into this region and depopulate it." At this, Eliakim son of Hilkiah, Shebna, and Joah interrupted Rabshakeh, asking him to speak to them in Aramaic <note>original: "Syriacè"</note> (for they knew it) and not in the Judean language <note>The Hebrew language of the common people</note> while the soldiers on the walls were listening. But Rabshakeh said: "Has my master sent me to speak these things only to your lord or to you? Has he not sent me rather to those who remain on the walls, who will have to eat their own dung and drink their own urine with you?" Then Rabshakeh stood and cried out with a loud voice in the Judean language, saying: "Hear the command of the Great King, the king of Assyria! Thus says the king: Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, for he will not be able to defend you from my hand. Do not let him persuade you to trust in the Lord, as if the Lord will defend you and not allow this city to be given into the hand of the king of Assyria. Do not listen to Hezekiah, for the king of Assyria declares: 'Make peace with me and surrender. Then each of you may live from your own vines, fig trees, and the water of your own wells, until I come to transfer you to a land similar to your own—a land of grain and wine, a land of bread and vineyards, a land fertile with olives, oil, and honey, so that your safety may be provided for.' Do not listen to Hezekiah, who mocks you with the hope of defense from the Lord. Have the gods of other nations defended their own lands from the king of Assyria? Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Have they protected Samaria from my hand? Who is there among all the gods of the lands who has defended his land from my hand, that the Lord should be seen as the defender of Jerusalem?" At these words, the men remained silent and did not answer him a single word. Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the palace administrator, Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph the recorder went to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and reported the words of Rabshakeh to him.

### CHAPTER XXI.

After Hezekiah went to join the spirits of his ancestors, his son Manasseh obtained the kingdom in his place, being then twelve years old. He reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem; his mother’s name was Hephzibah. He offended the Lord, imitating the abominations of the nations which the Lord had driven out for the sake of the Israelites. For he rebuilt the high places <note>original: "sacella," small shrines or chapels</note> which his father Hezekiah had destroyed; he erected altars to Baal; he made a sacred grove <note>original: "lucum," a grove of trees dedicated to a deity, often Asherah</note> following the example of Ahab, King of Israel; he worshiped and served all the host of heaven <note>astral deities or stars</note>; he built altars in the house of the Lord, though the Lord had said that he would place his name in Jerusalem. He built altars for all the host of heaven in both courtyards of the temple of the Lord. He passed his son through the fire; he practiced omens and sorcery; he appointed spiritists <note>original: "uentriloquos," literally "belly-speakers," a term used for those thought to channel spirits</note> and magicians. By committing so many evils, he provoked the Lord. He even placed a carved image of the grove he had made in the temple, concerning which the Lord had said to David and his son Solomon that in this temple, and in Jerusalem—which he had chosen out of all the tribes of the Israelites—he would place his name forever. He promised that he would not make the feet of the Israelites wander anymore from the land he had given to their ancestors, provided they were careful to obey everything he commanded them and the whole law

This King Amon was killed in his own house by a conspiracy of his servants. After the people killed all those conspirators, they made his son Josiah king in his place. The rest of Amon’s deeds are recorded in the annals of the kings of Judah.

### CHAPTER XXII.

<margin>Josiah, King of Judah.</margin>
<margin>2 Chronicles 34.</margin>
After Amon was buried in his tomb in the garden of Uzza, his son Josiah took up the kingdom in his place in the eighth year of his age. He reigned in Jerusalem for thirty-one years; his mother was Jedidiah, daughter of Adaiah, of Bozkath. He obeyed the Lord and followed the whole way of life of his ancestor David, turning aside neither to the right nor to the left. In the twelfth year of his reign <note>note: Biblical accounts usually cite the 18th year for the temple repairs, though this transcription specifies the 12th</note>, Josiah sent Shaphan, son of Azaliah, son of Meshullam, the scribe of the temple of the Lord, to Hilkiah the high priest. He commanded him through Shaphan to calculate the total amount of money brought into the temple of the Lord, which the doorkeepers had collected from the people, so that it might be handed over to the overseers of the work in charge of the temple of the Lord, who were to distribute it to those performing the repairs in the temple of the Lord.

When the king heard the words of the book of the law, he tore his garments and commanded Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam the son of Shaphan, Achbor the son of Micaiah, Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah the royal attendant, to go and inquire of the oracle of the Lord for the king, for the people, and for all the Judeans, concerning the words of this book that had been found. For the great wrath of the Lord had been kindled against them because their fathers had not obeyed the words of this book, nor performed all those things which had been prescribed for them. Therefore Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah went to

Therefore my wrath is kindled against this place so that it shall not be quenched.' But to the king of Judah, who sent you to the oracle of the Lord, you shall report this: 'Thus says the Lord, the God of the Israelites: Concerning the things you have heard, because your heart was tender when you heard what I threatened against this place and its inhabitants—namely, desolation and infamy—and you humbled yourself before the Lord, and having torn your clothes, you wept before me, I also have heard you,' says the Lord. 'Therefore I will gather you to your ancestors, and I will cause you to be buried in peace, nor shall your eyes see such great calamity as I am about to bring upon this place.'"

### CHAPTER XXIII.

<margin>Josiah's piety. 2 Chronicles 34 <note>original: "2. Parā. 24" likely refers to the account in Paralipomenon, though the standard reference is 2 Chronicles 34</note></margin>
After this matter was reported to the king, he took care to summon all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem to himself. With all the Judeans, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the priests, the prophets, and finally the entire population from the greatest to the least, he went up into the temple of the Lord. In their hearing, he read all the words of the book of the covenant found in the temple of the Lord. Standing by the pillar <note>original: "pro fuggestu," referring to a platform or standing place</note>, he made a covenant before the Lord to follow the Lord and to keep his precepts, warnings, and decrees with all his mind and all his soul, by fulfilling all the words of that covenant written in that book. Indeed, the whole people joined in this covenant. Then the king commanded Hilkiah the high priest and the secondary priests

and the keepers of the threshold, to carry out of the sanctuary of the Lord all the vessels made for Baal, for the sacred grove <note>original: "luco," referring to the Asherah pole or grove</note>, and for all the host of heaven. After these were burned outside Jerusalem in the valley of Kidron, he saw to it that their dust was carried to Bethel. He removed the idolatrous priests whom the kings of Judah had appointed to burn incense in the shrines throughout the towns of Judah and the environs of Jerusalem—those who burned incense to Baal, to the sun, the moon, the planets, and finally to all the host of heaven. He carried the sacred grove out from the temple of the Lord to the brook Kidron outside Jerusalem, burned it at the brook, and having ground it into ash, he scattered that ash over the graves of the common people. He also tore down the houses of the male cult prostitutes <note>original: "ganeas," referring to places of ritual prostitution</note> which were located in the temple of the Lord, where the women wove hangings for the sacred grove. Having brought all the priests out from the towns of Judah, he defiled the shrines in which the priests had burned incense, from Geba to Beersheba. He destroyed the shrines of the gates located before the gate of Joshua the governor of the city, which was on the left of the city gate. For the priests of the shrines did not come up to the altar of the Lord in Jerusalem, but they ate unleavened bread among their brothers. He also defiled Topheth, which was in the valley of the son of Hinnom, so that no one might make his son or daughter pass through the fire to Molech. The altars on the roof of the upper chamber of Ahaz, which the kings of Judah had made, and the altars which Manasseh had made in both courts of the temple of the Lord, he destroyed; he cast their dust from there into the brook Kidron.

He broke the statues in pieces, cut down the sacred groves, and filled their places with human bones.

<margin>1 Kings 12</margin>

He reduced the shrine and the sacred grove to ashes by fire. When he looked around and noticed the graves that were there on the mountain, he sent to have the bones taken out of those graves and burned them on the altar, thus defiling the altar, just as the oracle of the Lord had foretold, which that divine man had declared with a clear voice when these very things were happening.

<margin>1 Kings 13</margin>
Then, when he asked what monument it was that he saw, and it was answered by the townsmen that it was the grave of the man of God who had come from Judah and had prophesied these very things which the king had done to the altar of Bethel, he ordered that it be left alone, and that no one should move his bones. So his bones were preserved along with the bones of the prophet who had come from Samaria. Furthermore, Josiah removed all the houses of the high places that were in the towns of Samaria, which the kings of Israel had made to provoke the Lord, and he did to them the same as he had done at Bethel. He slaughtered all the priests of the shrines who were there upon the altars and burned human bones upon them.

# BOOK 4.
<note>Historically known as 2 Kings in modern Bibles; some older Latin traditions labeled the sequence of Samuel and Kings as 1–4 Kings.</note>

to the people, that they should keep the Passover to the Lord <note>original: "Iouae," a Latinized form of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton</note> their God, just as it was written in the book of that covenant. For no such Passover had been held from the times of the judges who had presided over Israel, nor in all the time of the kings of Israel, as this Passover which was held for the Lord in Jerusalem in the eighteenth year of the reign of Josiah. In addition to this, Josiah exterminated the mediums, the diviners, the household gods, the "dung-gods" <note>original: "stercoreos deos," a derogatory term used in Latin translations for idols, reflecting the Hebrew 'gillulim'</note>, and every abomination that existed anywhere in Judah and Jerusalem, so that he might fulfill all the words of the law written in the book which Hilkiah the high priest had found in the temple of the Lord. But although there was no king to be compared to him, neither before him nor after him, who turned to the Lord with his whole mind, his whole soul, and his greatest effort, according to the whole law of Moses, yet the Lord did not calm the great heat of his wrath which burned against the Judeans because of all the outrages with which Manasseh had provoked him. Indeed, he decreed that he would remove the Judeans from his sight, just as he had removed the Israelites, and would reject that city which he had chosen, Jerusalem, and the house in which he had intended to place his name. Concerning all the rest of Josiah's deeds, it stands written in the annals of the kings of Judah. This King Josiah, when he went to meet Pharaoh Necho, King of Egypt, who was marching toward the river Euphrates against the king of Assyria, was killed by him at Megiddo as soon as he engaged with him. After his death, he was carried by his servants from Megiddo to Jerusalem and buried in his own tomb. In his place, the people anointed his son Jehoahaz and made him king instead of his father, in the twenty-third year of his age. He reigned in Jerusalem for three months; his mother was Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah, from Libnah. Imitating his ancestors, he offended the Lord, and Pharaoh Necho threw him into chains at Riblah in the land of Hamath, depriving him of the kingdom of Jerusalem. He fined the nation one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold, and appointed Eliakim, the son of Josiah, as king in place of his father, changing his name to Jehoiakim; but he took Jehoahaz with him to Egypt, where he died. Jehoiakim paid the silver and the gold to Pharaoh, making an assessment of the men and exacting it according to each man's means to pay what Pharaoh demanded. He began his reign at twenty-five years of age; his mother was Zebudah, daughter of Pedaiah, from Rumah. He was impious toward the Lord, just as his ancestors had been.

This happened to the Judeans by the command of the Lord, so that he might remove them from his sight because of the many wicked crimes of Manasseh and the innocent blood he had shed, with which he had filled Jerusalem; nor would the Lord grant them pardon. Concerning all the rest of Jehoiakim's deeds, it stands written in the annals of the kings of Judah.

### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>The progeny of Issachar. Genesis 46</margin>
Issachar had four sons: Tola, Puah, Jashub, and Shimron. Tola's sons: Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jahmai, Ibsam, and Samuel. These were the heads of the Tolaite families, mighty warriors according to their lineages; their number in the time of David was twenty-two thousand six hundred. Uzzi’s son was Izrahiah; all were leaders, and along with them, according to their family lineages, were thirty-six thousand common soldiers, for they had many wives and sons. Their kinsmen throughout all the clans of Issachar were eighty-seven thousand valiant warriors, according to their census.

<margin>The progeny of Benjamin. Genesis 46</margin>

Bilhan’s sons: Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan, Tarshish, and Ahishahar. All these sons of Jediael, heads of families, were recorded as seventeen thousand two hundred soldiers able to bear arms. Iri’s sons were Shuppim and Huppim. Aher’s son was Hushim.

Zabad’s sons were Shuthelah, Ezer, and Elead; they were killed by the natives of Gath <note>This refers to a tragic event where Ephraim's sons were killed while attempting to raid livestock from the Philistines of Gath</note>, when they went down to seize their cattle. Along the borders of the Manassites were Beth-shean, Taanach, Megiddo, and Dor, with their villages. In these lived the descendants of Joseph, the son of Israel.

All these were descendants of Asher, heads of families, choice soldiers, and principal leaders. According to their census, the number of those able to bear arms was twenty-six thousand.

### CHAPTER X.

<margin>
Saul, defeated by the Philistines, kills himself.
1 Samuel 31
</margin>
In the battle of the Philistines against the Israelites, the Israelites fled and were cut down on Mount Gilboa. The Philistines pressed hard after Saul and his sons, and they killed Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchi-shua, the sons of Saul. As the battle intensified against Saul, he was overtaken by the archers and severely wounded. He commanded his armor-bearer to draw his sword and run him through, fearing that those uncircumcised men <note>original: "praeputiati"</note> would come and mock him. But the armor-bearer refused out of great terror, so Saul took a sword and fell upon it. When the armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he also fell upon his sword and died. Thus Saul died, along with his three sons and his entire household. When the Israelites who were in the valley saw that they had fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their towns and fled; the Philistines then came and occupied them. The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the dead, they found Saul and his sons fallen on Mount Gilboa. They stripped Saul, took his armor, and cut off his head, sending them throughout all the land of the Philistines to spread the news of their success in the temple of their idols and among the people. They placed his armor in the temple of their god and hung his skull in the temple of Dagon. But when the men of Jabesh-Gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul, all the strongest men set out and took the bodies of Saul and his sons and brought them to Jabesh. They buried their bones under the oak tree in Jabesh and fasted for seven days. Saul died because of his own guilt which he had committed against the Lord <note>original: "Iouam"</note>, both because he did not keep the Lord's command and because he consulted the oracle of a medium <note>original: "Apollinis" — the translator uses the name of the Greek god Apollo to refer to the spiritist or 'witch' of Endor</note> rather than the Lord. For this reason, the Lord killed him and transferred the kingdom to David, the son of Jesse.

### CHAPTER XI.

<margin>
David is created king at Hebron.
2 Samuel 5
</margin>
Then all the Israelites gathered to David at Hebron and explained that they were his own flesh and blood, and that even previously, when Saul was king, he had been their leader. Now the Lord <note>original: "Iouam"</note> his God had destined for him the governance

<column-break/>

and rule of his people Israel. Then the king made a covenant before the Lord at Hebron with all the elders of Israel who had gathered there, and they anointed him king of the Israelites, just as the Lord had commanded through Samuel. Afterward, David and all the Israelites attacked Jerusalem (which is the same as Jebus). When the Jebusites who lived there claimed he would not break in, he captured the stronghold of Zion, which is now the City of David. David had announced that whoever killed a Jebusite first would become commander and chief; Joab the son of Zeruiah went up first and was made commander. David lived in that fortress, and for that reason it was called the City of David. He built up the city all around it, starting from the Millo <note>term: Millo — a Hebrew word for a rampart or a series of terraces used for fortification</note>. Joab restored the rest of the city, and David's power grew daily, for the Lord of hosts <note>original: "armipotens Ioua" — literally 'the weapon-wielding or powerful-in-arms Lord'</note> was with him. Next, we must speak of the mighty men whom David had, by whom—and by all the Israelites—he was made and confirmed as king, as the Lord had commanded. This is the number of David’s mighty men: Jashobeam, son of Hachmoni, the chief of the thirty, who brandished his spear and killed three hundred in a single encounter. After him was Eleazar son of Dodo, the Ahohite, one of the three mighty men. He was with David at Pas-dammim when the army fled from the Philistines (who had gathered there for battle). They stood their ground in a certain field that was full of lentils and defended it; by striking down the Philistines, they achieved a noble victory by the gift of the Lord. These three from the chief thirty once went down to David at the rock in the cave of Adullam while the Philistines were camped in the Valley of the Giants. David was then in the stronghold, and a Philistine garrison was stationed at Bethlehem. David felt a longing and said he wished someone would give him water to drink from the well of Bethlehem by the gate. Those three broke through the Philistine camp, drew water from the well at the gate of Bethlehem, and brought it to David. However, David refused to drink it, but poured it out as an offering to the Lord. He said, "Far be it from me, by my God, that I should do this—that I should drink water obtained at the risk of men's lives and blood." These things those three heroes did. Abishai, the brother of Joab, was chief of another three; he brandished his spear against three hundred and killed them, winning a name among the second three. He was more famous than the other two and became their captain, though he did not attain the rank of the first three. There was also Benaiah son of Jehoiada, a very brave man from Kabzeel who performed many great deeds. He killed two lion-like men of Moab; he also went down into a pit on a snowy day and killed a lion. He also killed an Egyptian man, a spectacle of five cubits in height <note>about 7.5 feet</note>. Though the Egyptian had a spear like a weaver's beam and Benaiah had only a staff, he closed with him, snatched the spear from the Egyptian’s hand, and killed him with his own spear. These were the deeds of Benaiah son of Jehoiada, who was numbered among the second three heroes and was prominent among the thirty for his valor, though he did not reach the rank of the first three.

### CHAPTER XII.

Following are those who came to David at Ziklag, while he was still keeping away from Saul son of Kish; these were among the bravest auxiliary soldiers, archers who could use both the right and left hand to sling stones and shoot arrows from the bow. They were of Saul’s kinsmen from the tribe of Benjamin: their chief was Ahiezer, and Joash the sons of Shemaah the Gibeathite; Jeziel and Pelet the sons of Azmaveth; Berakah and Jehu the Anathothite; Ishmaiah the Gibeonite (the bravest among the thirty and their leader); Jeremiah, Jahaziel, Johanan, Jozabad the Gederathite, Eluzai, Jerimoth, Bealiah, Shemariah, Shephatiah the Haruphite, Elkanah, Isshiah, Azarel, Joezer, Jashobeam the Korahites, Joelah and Zebadiah the sons of Jeroham from Gedor. From the Gadites, very brave soldiers also went over to David while he was holding the stronghold in the wilderness; they were men trained for war, carrying shields and spears, with faces as fierce as lions and as swift as gazelles running upon the mountains. Their chief was Ezer, the second Obadiah, the third Eliab, the fourth Mashmannah, the fifth Jeremiah, the sixth Attai, the seventh Eliel, the eighth Johanan, the ninth Elzabad, the tenth Jeremiah, and the eleventh Machbannai. These Gadites were captains of the army; the least was a commander of a hundred, and the greatest was a commander of a thousand <note>original: "tribunus... millenarius"</note>. These are the ones who crossed the Jordan in the first month when it had overflowed all its banks, and they put to flight all the inhabitants of the valleys to the east and the west. Some from the Benjaminites and the men of Judah also came to David at the stronghold. David went out to meet them and said: "If you come to me in peace and to help me,

426
<header>BOOK I.</header>

my heart shall be joined with yours; but if you come to betray me to my enemies though I am innocent of any crime, may the God of our fathers look upon it and judge." Then Amasai, the chief of the thirty, was possessed by a divine spirit and said: "We are yours, David, and we are with you, son of Jesse! Peace, peace be to you, and peace to your helpers, for your God helps you." Then David received them and appointed them as captains of his troops. Some from the tribe of Manasseh also defected to David when he went with the Philistines to battle against Saul—though he did not actually help them, because <margin>1 Samuel 29</margin> the lords of the Philistines, after consultation, sent him away, fearing that he might defect to his master Saul at the cost of their own heads. Therefore, as he went back to Ziklag, these men of Manasseh defected to him: Adnah, Jozabad, Jediael, Michael, Jozabad, Elihu, and Zillethai, captains of the thousands of Manasseh. They helped David against the raiding bands, for they were all very brave soldiers and became leaders in the army. Indeed, day by day men came to David to help him, until it was a great and clearly divine army. Now these are the numbers of the divisions of the armed troops who came to David at Hebron to transfer Saul’s kingdom to him, according to the command of the Lord <margin>The number of soldiers who gathered to David at Hebron.</margin>: From the men of Judah carrying shields and spears, six thousand eight hundred, prepared for military service. From the tribe of Simeon, seven thousand one hundred brave soldiers. From the Levites, four thousand six hundred, along with Jehoiada, the leader of the house of Aaron, and with him three thousand seven hundred. Also Zadok, a young and very brave soldier, and twenty-two chiefs from his father’s family. From the Benjaminites, the kinsmen of Saul, three thousand; for until then the majority of them had kept their allegiance to the house of Saul. From the Ephraimites, twenty thousand eight hundred very brave soldiers, famous men in their own families. From the half-tribe of Manasseh, eighteen thousand, who were designated by name to come and make David king. From the tribe of Issachar, men who had an understanding of the times and knew what Israel ought to do, two hundred chiefs, with all their kinsmen at their command. From Zebulun, fifty thousand experienced soldiers, skilled with every kind of weapon of war, ready to help David with undivided loyalty. From Naphtali, one thousand captains, and with them thirty-seven thousand men with shield and spear. From the Danites, twenty-eight thousand six hundred skilled in war. From the Asherites, forty thousand soldiers trained for battle. From across the Jordan—from the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh—one hundred and twenty thousand men skilled with every kind of weapon of war. All these men of war, drawn up in battle formation, came to Hebron with a sincere heart to make David king over all Israel; and all the rest of Israel were of one mind to make David king.

<margin>David speaks with the Israelites about moving the Ark to Jerusalem.</margin>
Moreover, their neighbors, both from the tribe of Issachar, and Zebulun and Naphtali, brought food on donkeys, camels, mules, and oxen—specifically flour, cakes of figs, clusters of raisins, wine, oil, oxen, sheep, and goats in great abundance, for the Israelites were rejoicing. David entered into counsel with the commanders of thousands and hundreds, and with every leader, and then addressed the entire assembly of Israel: "If it seems good to you, and if the Lord <note>original: "Ioua", a Latinization of the Tetragrammaton, here referring to God</note> our God is the author of this matter, let us send word far and wide to our kinsmen remaining in all the territories of Israel, and also to the priests and Levites living in the towns of their suburbs, that they may gather to us, so that we may move the Ark of our God to ourselves (for we did not seek oracles from it in the days of Saul)." When the whole multitude agreed to do this (for the matter pleased all the people), David summoned all the Israelites from
<margin>*2 Samuel 6*</margin>
the Shihor of Egypt as far as Hamath, to seek the divine Ark from Kiriath-jearim. With them, he set out for Kiriath-jearim, which is located in Judah, to bring up from there the Ark of the Lord God, who sits above the Cherubim, where his name was invoked. They carried the Ark of God from the house of Abinadab on a new cart, with Uzzah and Ahio driving the cart. David and all the Israelites were celebrating before God with all their might, with songs, lyres, harps, tambourines, cymbals, and trumpets. When they came to the threshing floor of Chidon, Uzzah reached out his hand to hold the Ark, because the oxen stumbled. And the Lord was angry
<margin>*Numbers 4*</margin>
against him because he had reached out his hand to the Ark, and he struck him dead. Since he died there before God, David was grieved by this slaughter where the Lord had struck down Uzzah; and that place is called "The Breach of Uzzah" <note>original: "Ozæ strages", traditionally Perez-uzzah</note> to this day. Then David, fearing the Lord, did not dare to bring the Ark to himself into the City of David, but instead brought it into the house of Obed-edom the Gittite, where it remained for three months. And the Lord blessed the house of Obed-edom and all his possessions.

### CHAPTER XIV.

<margin>Hiram sends messengers to David.</margin>
<margin>*2 Samuel 5*</margin>

### CHAPTER XVI.

After the divine Ark was brought in and placed inside the tent that David had pitched for it, they offered burnt offerings and peace offerings to God. When David had finished the burnt offerings and peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of the Lord and distributed to all the Israelites—both men and women—a loaf of bread, a piece of meat, and a flagon of wine for each person. Then he appointed some of the Levites as ministers before the Ark of the Lord to commemorate, thank, and praise the Lord, the God of the Israelites. Asaph was the chief, and Zechariah was second to him; then Jehiel, Shemiramoth, Jehiel, Mattithiah, Eliab, Benaiah, Obed-edom, and Jehiel played the instruments, the harps and lyres, while Asaph sounded the cymbals. Benaiah and Jahaziel the priests sounded the trumpets continually before the Ark of the divine covenant. On that day David first appointed Asaph and his kinsmen to give praise to the Lord:

Praise the Lord, call upon his name, make known his nature among the peoples! Sing to him, sing praises to him, meditate on all his wondrous deeds! Glory in his holy name; let the hearts of those who seek the Lord rejoice. Seek the Lord and his power; seek his face forever! Remember his wondrous deeds, his miracles, and the judgments he has pronounced,

<column-break/>

you offspring of Israel his servant, you descendants of Jacob, his chosen ones. He is the Lord our God; his jurisdiction extends over all the earth. Remember his covenant forever—the word he commanded for a thousand generations—the covenant he made with Abraham, and the oath he swore to Isaac. He confirmed it to Jacob as a decree, to Israel as an everlasting covenant, promising: "I will give you the land of Canaan as the portion of your inheritance." When they were few in number and of little account, and strangers in that land, wandering from one nation to another and from one kingdom to another people, he allowed no one to oppress them; for their sake he even rebuked kings.

"Do not touch my anointed ones; do my prophets no harm." Sing to the Lord, all the earth! Proclaim his victory day after day! Declare his glory among the nations, his marvelous deeds among all peoples. For the Lord is great and greatly to be praised; he is to be feared above all gods. For all the gods of other nations are mere idols <note>original: "deastri", literally 'little gods' or 'godlings', a dismissive term for pagan deities</note>, but the Lord made the heavens. Authority and splendor are before him; power and majesty are in his presence. Ascribe to the Lord, O families of nations, ascribe to the Lord glory and power. Ascribe to the Lord the glory due his name; bring an offering and come before him. Worship the Lord in holy splendor; let the whole earth tremble before him! Indeed, the world is established, firm and immovable. Let the heavens be glad, let the earth rejoice, and let it be said among the nations: "The Lord reigns!" Then the trees of the forest will sing for joy at the presence of the Lord, for he comes to judge the earth. Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good; his mercy endures forever! Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, from everlasting to everlasting! Then all the people said "Amen" and praised the Lord.

<margin>David assigns the Levites their duties.</margin>
So David left Asaph and his kinsmen there before the Ark of the Covenant of the Lord to minister regularly before the Ark according to each day's requirements. He also left Obed-edom and his sixty-eight kinsmen (Obed-edom was the son of Jeduthun) and Hosah as gatekeepers. He left Zadok the high priest and his fellow priests before the tabernacle of the Lord at the high place in Gibeon to offer burnt offerings to the Lord on the altar of burnt offering regularly, morning and evening, according to everything written in the Law that the Lord had given to Israel. With them were Heman, Jeduthun, and the rest of those chosen and designated by name to give thanks to the Lord, for "his mercy endures forever." Heman and Jeduthun were responsible for the trumpets, cymbals, and the instruments for sacred song, while the sons of Jeduthun were assigned to the gate. Then all the people departed to their homes, and David returned to bless his own household.

## CHAPTER XVII.

After David settled into his home, he pointed out to Nathan the prophet <note>original: "uati," meaning a seer or diviner</note> that it was not fitting for David to live in a house of cedar while the Ark of the Covenant of the Lord <note>original: "Iouæ," a Latinization of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton YHWH, often rendered as Jehovah or the Lord</note> remained under tent curtains. Nathan replied to him that he should do whatever was in his heart, for God was with him. But that night, God spoke to Nathan in this manner: "Go and announce these things to my servant David."

Thus says the Lord:
> "You shall not build me a house to dwell in; for since the time I led out the Israelites, I have not yet dwelt in a house, but have moved about from tent to tabernacle. As long as I have moved among all the Israelites, did I ever speak a word to any of the tribes of Israel, whom I commanded to govern my people, about building me a house of cedar? Therefore, thus says the Lord of hosts <note>original: "armipotens Ioua," literally 'the Lord powerful in arms'</note> (speaking to my servant David): I took you from the sheepfold, from following the flock, to make you the ruler of my people Israel. I have been with you in all things you have done, and having cut down all your enemies for your sake, I have made your name equal to the names of the greatest on the earth. I have assigned a place for my Israelites, where they may remain firmly planted by me and no longer be disturbed, nor shall they be harassed by the wicked as they were in former times, even from the day I appointed governors over them. Therefore, having subdued all your enemies, I announce this to you: that I, the Lord, will build a house for you. And when you have reached the fullness of your age and depart to join your ancestors, I will raise up your offspring after you, one who shall be from your own sons, whose kingdom I will establish. He shall build a house for me, and I will confirm his throne forever. I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me; nor will I deprive him of my mercy, as I deprived your predecessor. Instead, I will settle him in my house and in my kingdom forever, and his kingdom shall remain firm for eternity."

After Nathan had explained all these words and the entire oracle to David in this manner, David went before the Lord and, standing in his presence, spoke thus:

<margin>David gives thanks to the Lord, who gave him the kingdom and promised it to his descendants forever.</margin>
> "Who am I, Lord God, or what is my lineage, that you have brought me this far? And yet this seemed a small thing to you, O God, unless you also looked toward my lineage in the distant future, and provided for me magnificently in the manner of men, O Lord God? What greater glory can your servant David receive from you? For you have recognized me as your own, O Lord, and for my sake, and because it pleased you, you have acted to bring about all these great things. O Lord, not only is there none like you, but there is no God at all besides you, according to everything we have heard with our own ears. For what nation on the whole earth is to be compared with your Israelites? Whom God went out to redeem for himself and make his own? Thus you gained for yourself a great and terrible name, while for the sake of your Israelites—whom you redeemed from Egypt—you drove out nations, making those Israelites yours forever, and showing yourself, O Lord, to be their God. Therefore, O Lord, what you have promised to me, your servant, and to my

> lineage, let it be established forever, and fulfill your promises. For you, my God, have revealed in my ear that you would build a house for me; that is why I have dared to pray to you. And now, Lord, you are God, and you have promised this blessing to me. Therefore, come now, bless my lineage, so that it may endure through you forever; for with your blessing, it shall be happy for eternity."

## CHAPTER XVIII.

Afterward, David defeated the Philistines <note>original: "Palæstinos"</note> and, having subdued them, took Gath and its villages. He also defeated the Moabites, and having brought them under his power, they became his subjects and paid tribute. He also defeated Hadadezer, king of Zobah, near Hamath, at the time he set out to extend his empire to the river Euphrates. He took from him a thousand chariots, seven thousand horsemen, and twenty thousand footmen. He disabled all the chariots except for a hundred, which he left remaining. Furthermore, from the Syrians of Damascus, who had come to aid Hadadezer, king of Zobah, he slew twenty-two thousand men. Having brought the Syria of the Damascenes under his empire, he held them as tributaries, the Lord serving as his defender in all his expeditions. He also took the golden quivers of Hadadezer’s men and brought them to Jerusalem. Then, from the towns of Tibhath and Cun, which belonged to Hadadezer, he took a vast amount of bronze, from which Solomon later made the bronze sea <note>original: "lacum æreum," a massive ritual basin</note>, the pillars, and the bronze vessels. When Tou, king of Hamath, realized that all the forces of Hadadezer, king of Zobah, had been crushed by David, he sent his son Hadoram to King David to establish a friendship and to congratulate him on the defeat and victory over Hadadezer (for Tou had been at war with Hadadezer). He also sent vessels of all kinds—gold, silver, and bronze—which King David also consecrated to the Lord, along with the silver and gold he had taken from so many nations: namely the Edomites <note>original: "Idumæis"</note>, Moabites, Ammonites, Philistines, and Amalekites. For Abishai, the son of Zeruiah, had defeated the Edomites in the Valley of Salt, slaying eighteen thousand of them. He placed garrisons in Edom, and all Edom was brought under David’s power, the Lord preserving him in all his expeditions. Thus David reigned over all the Israelites, exercising law and justice toward all his people.

<margin>The officers of David.</margin>
He employed Joab, son of Zeruiah, as the leader of the army. Jehoshaphat, son of Ahilud, was in charge of the records <note>original: "A commentarijs"</note>. The high priests were Zadok, son of Ahitub, and Ahimelech, son of Abiathar. Shusha was the scribe. Benaiah, son of Jehoiada, was the prefect of the Cherethites and Pelethites <note>original: "Cerethæorum Phelethæorumq;"—the royal bodyguards</note>. However, David primarily utilized the services of his own sons.

### CHAPTER XIX.

Afterward, upon the death of Nahash, the king of the Ammonites, when his son Hanun had succeeded him in the kingdom, David—wishing to repay the kindnesses that Hanun’s father, Nahash, had shown him—sent ambassadors to console him regarding his father. But after David’s men arrived in the territory of the Ammonites to comfort Hanun, the princes of the Ammonites persuaded Hanun that David had not sent these comforters to honor his father, but rather that they had come to explore, <margin>10</margin> spy upon, and overthrow the land. Therefore, Hanun seized David’s men, shaved them, and cut off their garments in the middle as far as their private parts <note>original: "uerenda," a polite Latin term for the genitals</note>, and sent them away. 

When they had departed and word reached King David, he sent messengers to meet them (for they were greatly ashamed) and commanded them to remain in Jericho until their beards had grown back, and then return. Then the Ammonites, seeing that they had made David their enemy, both they and Hanun sent a thousand talents of silver to hire chariots and horsemen from Mesopotamia, Syria Maachah, and <margin>20</margin> Zobah <note>original: "Sophene," likely referring to the region of Zobah</note>. Having hired thirty-two thousand chariots and the king of Maachah with his forces, they marched and set up camp before Medeba. When David heard this, and that the Ammonites had gathered from their cities for war, he sent Joab with the entire army of his mightiest men. 

The Ammonites marched out and drew up their battle line before the gate of the city, while the kings who had come to help were stationed separately in the open field. When Joab saw that the battle was threatening him from both the front and the rear, he chose the best of all the elite men of Israel to oppose the Syrians. The rest of the troops <margin>30</margin> he entrusted to his brother Abishai, to be drawn up against the Ammonites, saying: "If the Syrians prove too strong for me, you shall come to my aid. But if the Ammonites press you, I will help you. Show yourself brave, and let us fight manfully for our people and for the cities of our God, and may the Lord <note>original: "Ioua," a Latinization of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton YHWH</note> do what seems good to him." 

After these words, Joab and his soldiers joined battle with the Syrians, who were put to flight by him. When the Ammonites saw the Syrians fleeing, they also turned and fled from his brother Abishai and retreated into the city, and Joab returned to Jerusalem. <margin>40</margin> Then the Syrians, seeing they had been overcome by the Israelites, sent messengers and summoned the Syrians who lived across the river <note>The Euphrates</note>, led by Shophach, the commander of Hadadezer’s army. When this was reported to David, he gathered all the Israelites, crossed the Jordan, and advanced against them. He drew up his forces and, once the line was ordered and battle joined, the Syrians turned their backs to the Israelites. David killed seven thousand charioteers and forty thousand infantrymen of the Syrians, and he slew Shophach the commander. Then, seeing <margin>50</margin> that they were inferior to the Israelites, the subjects of Hadadezer made peace with David and served him; nor did the Syrians wish to bring aid to the Ammonites any longer.

### CHAPTER XX.

Then, at the beginning of spring—the time when kings usually go out on expeditions—Joab led out the army and devastated the lands of the Ammonites. He proceeded to besiege Rabbah while David remained in Jerusalem, and having captured it, he destroyed it. And David took the crown of their king <meta>catchword: co-</meta>

### CHAPTER XXI.

But Satan, being an adversary to the Israelites, incited David to count the people of Israel. Therefore David said to Joab and the leaders of the people: "Go, count the Israelites from Beersheba all the way to Dan, and report the number to me so that I may know how many there are." Joab replied: "I pray the Lord makes his people a hundred times more than they are; since they are all under your power, my lord king, why would you bring guilt upon the Israelites by seeking this?" 

But overcome by the king’s command, Joab set out and, having traveled through <margin>20</margin> all the borders of the Israelites, he returned to Jerusalem and reported the number of the surveyed men to David. There were, in total, one million one hundred thousand Israelites who could bear arms. Of the Judeans, there were four hundred seventy thousand who could bear arms. The Levites and Benjaminites were not counted among them, because Joab was revolted by the king’s command. 

God, being offended by this matter, brought a disaster upon the Israelites. David confessed to God that he had sinned gravely in doing this thing, and <margin>30</margin> he asked that the fault he had so imprudently committed be forgiven. But the Lord commanded Gad, David’s seer <note>original: "fatidico," one who tells fates or prophecies</note>, to go to David and offer him three choices from the Lord, of which he should pick one to be carried out against him. 

Therefore Gad approached David and said to him: "Thus says the Lord: Choose whether you prefer three years of famine, or to be defeated by your adversaries for three months and be overtaken by the enemy’s sword, or that for three days the land be infested by the sword of the Lord and pestilence, and all the borders of the Israelites be devastated by the angel <note>original: "genio," here meaning a spirit or divine messenger</note> of the Lord. Therefore, consider what answer I should return to him who sent me." 

And <margin>40</margin> David, speaking to Gad, said: "I am pressed by great anguish; let me fall into the hand of the Lord, for he is endowed with singular mercy, rather than falling into the hands of men." <margin>The Lord rages with a plague against the Israelites.</margin> Then the Lord struck the Israelites with a plague, and seventy thousand men of them fell. And God sent his angel to Jerusalem to destroy it. Then, as the Lord watched, he called back the punishment as it was spreading, and said to the destroying angel: "It is enough; now stay your hand." And so <margin>50</margin> the angel of the Lord stood by the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.

When David beheld this spirit <note>original: "genium," likely referring to the Angel of the Lord</note> standing between the earth and the sky, holding a drawn sword in his hand and pointing it toward Jerusalem, both he and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, threw themselves facedown. O Lord <note>original: "Ioua," a Latin rendering of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton</note> my God, let your hand be against me and my father's house, so that your people may not be afflicted by this plague." Then the messenger of the Lord commanded Gad to instruct David to go and build an altar to the Lord on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. And David went up, just as he had been commanded by Gad in the name of the Lord. Then Ornan, who was then threshing wheat, looked back and noticed the spirit; his four sons, who were with him, hid themselves. When Ornan saw David approaching, he stepped out from the threshing floor and did him honor, bowing with his face to the ground. And David said: "Grant me the site of this threshing floor, so that I may build an altar to the Lord upon it; grant it to me for the full price, so that the slaughter of the people may be restrained." Ornan replied: "Take it, and let my lord the king use it as he sees fit. Behold, I give you the oxen for the offerings, the threshing sledges for the wood, and the wheat for the grain offering; I give it all." But King David said: "No, I will buy it for the fair price, Ornan; for I will not offer what is yours to the Lord, nor will I make a burnt offering for free." So David paid Ornan six hundred shekels of gold by weight for the place. There he built an altar to the Lord and made burnt offerings and peace offerings. He called upon the Lord, and the Lord answered him with fire sent down from heaven upon the altar of sacrifice, and He commanded the spirit to return his sword to its sheath.

<margin>The plague is stayed.</margin>
<margin>1 Chronicles 21</margin>
Then David, seeing that he had been heard by the Lord on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, sacrificed there. For although the Tabernacle of the Lord, which Moses had made in the wilderness, and the altar of sacrifice were at that time in the high place at Gibeon, David was unable to go there to seek an oracle in God's presence, as he was terrified by the sword of the spirit of the Lord.

### CHAPTER XXII.

<margin>David's preparation for the construction of the temple.</margin>
Therefore David, determining that this was to be the temple of the Lord God and the altar of sacrifice for the Israelites, ordered the foreigners who were in the lands of the Israelites to be gathered. He appointed stonecutters to hew squared stones for the construction of the divine temple. Then he prepared a great quantity of iron for the nails for the doors of the gates and for the joints, and an immense weight of bronze, and a countless amount of cedar timber, for the Sidonians and Tyrians had brought a great supply of it to him. For David had decided—since his son Solomon was but a tender youth and the sanctuary of the Lord was to be built so that it might be celebrated in all lands for its greatness, excellence, fame, and magnificence—that he must make the preparations himself. Therefore, he prepared many things before his death.

<margin>David, about to die, gives instructions to Solomon.</margin>

Indeed, according to my limited means, I have prepared for the temple of the Lord one hundred thousand talents of gold, ten hundred thousand talents of silver, and an immense quantity of bronze and iron, as well as timber and stone, to which you shall add more. Therefore, apply your minds and souls to the pursuit of the Lord your God, and arise to build the sanctuary of the Lord God, so that the ark of the covenant of the Lord and the holy vessels of God may be brought into the house built to the name of the Lord."

### CHAPTER XXIII.

So David, now old and full of years, appointed his son Solomon king over Israel. He gathered all the princes of Israel, the priests, and the Levites. David distributed them into divisions named after the sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.

This ministry in the temple of Jehovah was mandated to these leaders of the brave, so that having shared the responsibilities with their brothers, they might take their turns as gatekeepers. Then for his son *Zechariah*, a prudent counselor, lots were cast, and the north fell to him. To *Obed-edom* fell the south, and to his sons fell the courtyard. To *Shuppim* and *Hosah* fell the west, with the gate of the emissary on the ascending path, with guards stationed opposite one another. To the east were six *Levites*; to the north, four per day; to the south, four per day; and at the courtyard, two by two. At the western armory, there were four at the path and two at the armory.

### CHAPTER XXVIII.

<margin>
David speaks to the people about gathering to build the temple for God. 2 Kings 7.
</margin>
King David summoned to Jerusalem all the leaders of Israel: the princes of the tribes, the commanders of the divisions who served the king, the captains of thousands and captains of hundreds, and the overseers of all the property and livestock belonging to the king and his sons, along with the palace officials <note>original: "spadonibus" — literally eunuchs, though often used for high officials</note>, the mighty men, and all the elite soldiers. And when he had risen to his feet, he addressed them thus:

"Hear me, my kinsmen and my people. It was in my heart to build a house of rest for the Ark of the Covenant of the Lord <note>original: "Iouæ"</note> and for the footstool of our God, and I had already made preparations for the building. But God told me that I should not build a house for His name, because I was a man of war and had shed blood. Yet the Lord God of Israel chose me from my father’s entire household

<column-break/>

to be king over Israel forever. For He chose Judah to be the leader, and from the house of Judah He chose my father’s house, and among my father’s sons it pleased Him to make me king over all Israel. And of all my sons—for the Lord has granted me many—He has chosen my son Solomon to sit upon the throne of the Lord’s kingdom over Israel.

<margin>Wisdom 9.</margin>
He said to me: 'Your son Solomon is the one who shall build my temple and my courts, for I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father. I will establish his kingdom forever, provided that he is steadfast in carrying out my commandments and my laws.'

Now therefore, in the sight of all Israel, which is the assembly of the Lord, and in the hearing of our God, take care to seek out all the commandments of the Lord your God, so that you may possess this good land and leave it as an inheritance to your children after you forever.

And you, Solomon my son, know the God of your
<margin>David instructs Solomon.</margin>
father, and serve Him with a sincere mind and a willing soul. For the Lord searches all hearts and perceives every intent of the thoughts. If you seek Him, He will be found by you; but if you forsake Him, He will cast you off forever. See now, for the Lord has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary; be strong and act."

Then David gave to his son Solomon the plan <note>original: "exemplar" — a technical term for a blueprint or architectural model</note> for the porch, its surrounding buildings, its storerooms, its upper rooms, its inner chambers, and the place for the mercy seat <note>original: "propitiatorij"</note>. He also gave him the plan for everything he had in mind for the courts of the temple of the Lord, and for all the surrounding rooms, for the treasuries of the house of God and the treasuries for the dedicated gifts; likewise for the divisions of the priests and the Levites, for all the work of the service in the temple of the Lord, and for all the vessels to be used in that service.

<margin>David’s preparations for the building of the temple.</margin>
He designated a certain weight of gold for all the vessels of every kind of service, and a certain weight of silver for all the vessels of every kind of use. Likewise, a certain weight of gold for the golden lampstands and their golden lamps, and silver for the silver lampstands, according to the specific use of each lampstand. He also designated a certain weight of gold for the tables of the showbread <note>original: "menſas ordinarias"</note>, as was needed for each table, and silver for the silver tables. For the forks, the basins, and the jars, he gave pure gold; and for the golden and silver bowls, he gave a specific weight of gold and silver for each bowl.

Furthermore, for the altar of incense, he gave a certain weight of refined gold, and the plan for the chariot of the golden cherubim, who spread their wings to cover the Ark of the Covenant of the Lord. David said that he had learned the plan for all these works from the description written by the hand of the Lord Himself.

"Be strong and steadfast," he said, addressing his son Solomon, "and show yourself to be fearless and undaunted. For the Lord God, my God, is with you. He will not fail you or forsake you until all the work for the service of the temple of the Lord is finished. The divisions of the priests and the Levites are ready for every service of the temple, and in every task, all those skilled in their craft will offer their services to you willingly, and the leaders and all

### CHAPTER XXIX.

<margin>David in the assembly explains what he has prepared for the temple.</margin>
Then King David, speaking to the entire assembly, said: "God has chosen my son Solomon alone, a youth and tender, though the work is great; for this palace is not for man, but for Jehovah <note>original: "iouæ"</note> God. Indeed, according to my strength, I have prepared for the temple of my God gold for the gold work, silver for the silver, bronze for the bronze, iron for the iron, and wood for the wooden works; onyx stones, gems for settings, colorful and variegated stones, and finally a great abundance of every kind of precious stone and marble. Moreover (as I am well-disposed toward the temple of my God), I have a private treasure of gold and silver which I give to the temple of my God, in addition to all those things which I have prepared for the holy house: three thousand talents <note>A "talent" was a heavy unit of weight, roughly 75 pounds or 34 kilograms.</note> of gold from Ophir <note>A legendary region famous for its high-quality gold.</note>, and seven thousand talents of refined silver for overlaying the walls of the buildings. In short, gold for the gold things, silver for the silver, and for all the works to be made by the hands of craftsmen—now, who else is there today who will offer a gift of his own accord to Jehovah?"

<margin>The wealthy of the Israelites contribute to the construction of the temple.</margin>
Then the heads of the families and the tribes of Israel, the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, as well as the overseers of the royal work, gave spontaneously for the work of the divine temple: five thousand talents of gold, ten thousand drachmas, ten thousand talents of silver, eighteen thousand talents of bronze, and one hundred thousand talents of iron. Furthermore, those who possessed gems gave them to the treasury of the temple of Jehovah, into the hand of Jehiel the Gershonite. This voluntary generosity of theirs—having contributed to Jehovah with such a sincere mind—brought great joy both to the rest of the people and to King David. Therefore, he gave thanks to Jehovah in the sight of the entire assembly.

<margin>David gives thanks to Jehovah, praying that He be present with Solomon in building the temple.</margin>
"I give you immortal thanks, Jehovah God of Israel our father: Yours, O Jehovah, is the greatness, the power, the majesty, the dignity, and the authority; finally, all things in heaven and on earth are yours. Yours, Jehovah, is the kingdom, and a sovereignty excelling above all. With you are both riches and glory: you rule over all. In your hand are strength and power; it is in your power to make great and to strengthen anyone. Therefore we celebrate you, our God, praising your illustrious name. For truly, who am I, or who are my people, that we should expend our strength to offer these things to you voluntarily? For all things are from you, and we return to you what we have received from your hand. For we are strangers before you, and residents, just as all—

<margin>Wisdom 2 <note>This marginal note refers to the Book of Wisdom, chapter 2, regarding the fleeting nature of life.</note></margin>
—all our ancestors were; and our age on earth is like a desperate shadow. O Jehovah our God, all this abundance which we have gathered to build a temple for you and your holy name has come from you; it is all yours. Indeed, since I know, my God, that you search hearts and are delighted by integrity, I have offered all these things with a willing heart; and now I have seen with joy your people, who are present here, offering to you of their own accord. Jehovah God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, our fathers, preserve forever this affection of the will and mind of your people, and direct their hearts toward you.

<margin>3 Kings 3. <note>In the Latin Vulgate, 1 Kings is called 3 Kings.</note> Solomon seeks the tabernacle at Gibeon.</margin>
"Likewise, give to my son Solomon a whole heart, so that he may keep your precepts, warnings, and decrees, and execute all things, and build the temple <note>original: "delubrum"</note> I have prepared." Having said these things, David urged the whole assembly to give thanks to their God, and they all gave thanks to Jehovah, the God of their fathers, and they humbly worshipped Jehovah and the king. They performed a divine service to Jehovah, sacrificing victims to him with solemn sacrifices on the day following: a thousand bulls, a thousand rams, a thousand sheep, with their drink offerings of wine, and besides these a great abundance of victims on behalf of all the Israelites. On that day they feasted before Jehovah with great joy.

They created Solomon the son of David king a second time, and they anointed him for Jehovah as leader, and Zadok as high priest. Thus Solomon sat on the throne, having been made king in place of David his father, and indeed he did so prosperously. All the Israelites obeyed him, and all the princes and soldiers, as well as all the sons of King David, pledged their loyalty <note>original: "manus dederunt," literally "gave their hands."</note> to King Solomon. Jehovah increased Solomon with great dignity in the sight of all the Israelites and granted him such great authority as no king of the Israelites had held before him.

<margin>Solomon asks for wisdom from Jehovah. 1 Chronicles 28. Wisdom 9. 2 Kings 1.</margin>

Therefore David the son of Jesse, who had held the kingdom over all the Israelites, having reigned over the Israelites for forty years—namely, seven in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem—died in a happy old age, full of years, riches, and glory. His son Solomon succeeded him in the kingdom.

As for the rest of the deeds of King David from first to last, they are written in the book of Samuel the seer, in the book of Nathan the prophet, and in the book of Gad the seer, together with all his reign and power, and the times that passed over him, over Israel, and over all the kingdoms of the world.

# THE SUPPLEMENTS
## THE SECOND BOOK.

### CHAPTER I.

Thus Solomon, the son of David, was established in his kingdom, and having Jehovah <note>original: "Ioua", a Latinization of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton, the name of God.</note> his God favorable to him, and being increased by Him in dignity, he commanded all the Israelites—the tribunes, centurions, judges, and finally everyone who held any office of honor among the Israelites as heads of families—to be present. With that entire assembly, he set out for the sanctuary at Gibeon. For the divine Tabernacle of the Oracle <note>Also known as the Tent of Meeting.</note> was there, which Moses the servant of Jehovah had made in the wilderness. Indeed, David had brought the divine Ark from Kiriath-jearim to the place he had prepared for it, for he had pitched a tent for it in Jerusalem. But because the bronze altar made by Bezalel, the son of Uri and grandson of Hur, was there before the Tabernacle of Jehovah, Solomon sought the oracle there together with that assembly. And when he had gone to the bronze altar of Jehovah placed at the Tabernacle of the Oracle, he sacrificed a thousand whole offerings upon it. That night God appeared to him and commanded that he should ask for whatever he wished to be given to him. And Solomon addressed God in this way: "Since You have shown such great favor to my father David as to create me king in his place, I ask of You, Jehovah God, that You fulfill the promises made to my father David, and grant to me—whom You have appointed king over a people more numerous than the sands—such great wisdom and knowledge that I may manage the affairs of this people. Otherwise, who could govern this, Your so vast a nation?" And God answered Solomon thus: "Because you are possessed of such a mind that you do not ask for riches, glory, or even a long life, but seek for yourself wisdom and knowledge so that you may rule My people, over whom I have created you king, not only is wisdom and knowledge given to you, but I will also grant you such riches, wealth, and glory as no king before you has possessed, nor shall any after you possess." Therefore Solomon returned to Jerusalem from the Tabernacle of the Oracle which was in the shrine at Gibeon, and he reigned over Israel. Having increased the number of his chariots and horsemen, he had one thousand four hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen, whom he stationed partly in the chariot cities and partly with himself in Jerusalem. Now the king made silver and gold as common in Jerusalem as stones, and cedars in as great abundance as if they were wild fig trees <note>Likely referring to the sycamore-fig common in the lowlands.</note> of the plains. Moreover, the horses which were brought to Solomon from Egypt were managed in this way: a company of royal merchants purchased the multitude of horses at a set price. A single chariot brought out of Egypt was valued at six hundred silver pieces, and each horse at one hundred and fifty; in the same manner, they were brought by the work of these merchants to all the kings of the Hittites and the Syrians.

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER II.

When Solomon had determined to build both a temple to the name of Jehovah and a palace for himself, he designated seventy thousand men to be carriers and eighty thousand men to cut stones in the mountains, with three thousand six hundred overseers over them. Furthermore, he sent word to Hiram, the King of the Tyrians, in this manner:
<margin>Solomon asks Hiram, King of Tyre, for craftsmen and materials for the temple. 3 Kings 5 <note>In modern Bibles, this is 1 Kings 5.</note>.</margin>
"Since you dealt with my father David by sending him cedars to build the house in which he lived, know that I am about to build a sanctuary to the name of Jehovah my God, where gifts may be consecrated to Him, where fragrant incense may be burned before Him, where the bread of the Presence <note>original: "ordinarij panes", the showbread.</note> may always be, and where whole sacrifices may be made morning and evening on the Sabbaths, the New Moons, and the festivals of Jehovah our God—this being a perpetual duty for the Israelites. This temple I am to build will be vast, for our God is the greatest of gods. Who has enough strength to build a temple for Him? For since the heavens and the heaven of heavens cannot contain Him, who am I to build Him a temple? Rather, I do this for the burning of incense to Him. Therefore, send me a man skilled in working gold, silver, bronze, iron, purple, scarlet, and blue <term>hyacyntbi</term> <note>A deep blue or violet dye often derived from sea snails.</note>, and who knows how to engrave, to work with the skilled men I have with me in Judea and Jerusalem, whom my father David prepared. Send me also cedar, pine, and pitch-wood from Lebanon, so that my men may be with yours; for I know your men are skilled in cutting the timber of Lebanon, so that a great abundance of wood may be prepared for me. For the temple I am about to build will be great and wonderful. I will provide for your stonecutters and woodmen twenty thousand <term>cors</term> <note>A "cor" was a large dry measure, roughly 220 liters or 6 bushels.</note> of ground wheat, an equal amount of barley, twenty thousand <term>baths</term> <note>A "bath" was a liquid measure, roughly 22 liters or 6 gallons.</note> of wine, and an equal amount of oil." To this, Hiram the King of the Tyrians responded in a letter sent to Solomon: "Because of the love Jehovah has for His people, He has appointed you king over them. I give thanks," he said, "to Jehovah the God of the Israelites, the Creator of heaven and earth, who gave to King David a wise son, endowed with prudence and industry, to build both a temple for Jehovah and a palace for himself. Therefore, I am sending you a skilled and clever man, Huram-abi <note>original: "Hyramum Abium".</note>, born of a mother from Dan and a Tyrian father, a man skilled in working gold, silver, bronze, iron, stone, wood, purple, blue, fine linen <term>byssi</term>, and scarlet, and also in every kind of engraving and in handling any ingenious work that might be proposed to him alongside your craftsmen and those of my lord David, your father. Therefore, the wheat, barley, oil, and wine you promised, send to us, my lord; we will carry the timber cut in Lebanon—as much as you shall need—by rafts on the sea to Joppa; you shall then transport it to Jerusalem."
<margin>Hiram's response to Solomon.</margin>
Solomon then numbered all the foreign men who were in the lands of the Israelites, following the census his father David had already taken; and when one hundred fifty-three thousand six hundred were found, he made seventy thousand of them carriers, eighty thousand of them mountain stonecutters, and three thousand six hundred of them overseers to direct the work of the others.

### CHAPTER III.

Solomon therefore began to build the temple of Jehovah in Jerusalem on Mount Moria, the place which had been shown to his father David and designated by him for this purpose, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. He began to build, I say, on the second day of the second month, in the fourth year of his reign. The foundation of this divine temple to be built by Solomon was of such a kind that the length of the first dimension extended sixty cubits, and the width twenty. The length of the Vestibule, matching the width of the temple at the front, extended twenty cubits, and its height was one hundred and twenty; he overlaid it on the inside with pure gold. The larger room of the temple, paneled with pine wood, he encrusted with fine gold, and further adorned it with carvings of palms and chains, covering the temple with precious stones. The gold was from Parvaim <note>original: "Paruaicum", likely referring to a region famous for high-quality gold, possibly in Arabia.</note>, with which he covered the temple, the beams, the posts, the walls, and the doors, carving Cherubim upon the walls. He also made the room of the Holy of Holies, the length of which matched the width of the temple at twenty cubits, and the width was the same; he overlaid it with fine gold, using six hundred talents for this purpose, with fifty shekels of gold for the weight of the nails, and the upper chambers were also covered in gold. In the room of the Holy of Holies, he made two Cherubim, resembling the work of young children <note>original: "opere impuberum simili", perhaps suggesting a specific artistic style or "sculptured work".</note>, and he encrusted them with gold. The length of their wings was twenty cubits—that is, five cubits for each wing; one wing of each Cherub touched the temple wall on either side, while the other wings met in the middle. With these wings of the Cherubim stretched out to twenty cubits, the Cherubim themselves stood on their feet, facing toward the temple. He also made the Veil of violet, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, adorned with cherubim. Likewise, before the temple he set two columns, thirty-five cubits in length, whose capitals were five cubits. He also made chains for the inner sanctuary, which he placed upon the tops of the columns, and made one hundred pomegranates and attached them to the chains. He erected these columns before the main hall of the temple, one on the right and the other on the left: the one on the right he named Jachin, and the one on the left Boaz.

The Altar. The Molten Sea.
1 Kings 7.

### CHAPTER IIII.

He also made a bronze altar twenty cubits long, just as many wide, and ten cubits high. Likewise, he made the Molten Sea <note>original: "lacum fusilem", a massive bronze basin for washing.</note>, round all about, ten cubits from one rim to the other, and five cubits high, with a circumference of thirty cubits. Beneath it, all around, were figures of oxen, ten cubits in diameter, in two rows, cast as one piece with the Sea itself. The Sea rested upon twelve oxen, positioned so that three looked toward the north, three toward the west, three toward the south, and three toward the east, with the hindquarters of all of them facing inward. The Sea was a hand-breadth thick <note>original: "crassitudine dodrantali", literally nine inches or three-quarters of a foot.</note>, its rim blooming like roses, like the rim of a cup, and it held three thousand baths <note>A Hebrew measure of volume.</note>. He also made ten basins, five of which he placed on the right and five on the left, in which they might wash those things used for the sacrifices; for the Sea was intended for the priests to wash in.

<margin>Basins. Lampstands.</margin>
He likewise made ten golden lampstands, according to their design, which he placed five on the right and five on the left in the main hall.

<column-break/>

<margin>Tables, etc.</margin>
Item, he made ten tables, which he also placed in the main hall, five on the right and five on the left, and one hundred golden bowls. He also made the court of the priests and the great courtyard secured with gates, with the doors encrusted in bronze. He placed the Sea on the right side, toward the southeast. Hiram also made the pots, the flesh-hooks, and the bowls, and completed the work which he was doing for King Solomon for the divine temple, namely:

<margin>Two columns.</margin>
the two columns, the globes and the capitals placed on top of the columns, the two networks <note>original: "fascias", bands or wreaths.</note> to cover those globes of the capitals, and four hundred pomegranates for the two networks, specifically two rows of pomegranates for each network to cover the two globes of the capitals attached to the columns. He also made the stands and the basins to be placed upon the stands, and the one Sea, with the twelve oxen to be placed beneath it, and the pots, and the flesh-hooks, and the tridents; Hiram-Abiff <note>original: "Hyramus Abius"</note> made all these instruments for King Solomon for the temple of Jehovah from polished bronze. The king cast all these things in the plain of the Jordan in the clay ground between Succoth and Zeredah; and Solomon made so many vessels that the weight of the bronze was not recorded. Thus Solomon made all the furnishings of the divine temple: the golden altar and the tables upon which the Bread of the Presence was placed; the lampstands of fine gold and their lamps to be lit before the inner sanctuary according to custom; the flowers and the lamps and the tongs were made of gold, and that of the most perfect kind; as well as the musical instruments, the bowls, the spoons, and the censers of the finest gold. Furthermore, the inner doors of the temple for the Holy of Holies and the doors of the main hall of the temple were of gold.
