### CHAPTER V.

Therefore, when all the work that Solomon performed for the temple of Jehovah was finished, he brought in the silver, the gold, and all the vessels dedicated by his father David and stored them in the treasury of the divine temple. Then he summoned the elders of Israel and all the heads of the tribes, the leaders of the Israelite families, to Jerusalem to bring up the Ark of the Covenant of Jehovah from the City of David, which is Zion. When all the Israelites had been summoned to the king for the festival which is in the seventh month, and all the elders of Israel had arrived, the Levites took up the Ark, as well as the Tabernacle of the Oracle and all the sacred furniture of the Tabernacle; as the priests and Levites carried them, King Solomon and the whole assembly of Israel, gathered there before the Ark, sacrificed an innumerable and immense multitude of sheep, goats, and oxen. The priests then brought the Ark of the Covenant of Jehovah to its place in the inner sanctuary of the temple, in the Holy of Holies, beneath the wings of the Cherubim. For the Cherubim stretched out their wings over the place of the Ark, covering it and its poles from above, so that the ends of the poles extended from the Ark toward the sanctuary, yet they could not be seen from the outside. And the Ark is there to this day; there is nothing in it except the two tablets placed there by Moses at Horeb, at the time when Jehovah...

BOOK II.

...established the covenant with the Israelites after they had gone out from Egypt. Then, when the priests had come out of the sanctuary (for all the priests who were present had purified themselves, and did not observe any division of classes), all the Levite singers—Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, along with their sons and relatives—dressed in fine linen <note>original: "bysso", a high-quality white linen often used for priestly or royal garments</note>, stood at the east of the altar with cymbals, harps, and lyres, together with one hundred and twenty priests who were sounding trumpets. And so, when they sounded the trumpets and sang together, creating a single sound by praising and proclaiming Jehovah <note>original: "Iouam", a Latinization of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton (YHWH), the name of God</note>, and by playing loudly with trumpets, cymbals, and musical instruments, celebrating Jehovah—who is good and endowed with eternal mercy—so great a cloud filled the house of Jehovah that the priests could not remain to perform their service because of it, for such was the divine splendor that had filled the temple of God.

## CHAPTER VI.

<margin>1 Kings 8.</margin>
<margin>Solomon gives thanks to Him who fulfilled what was promised to David.</margin>
Then Solomon spoke thus: "I have built for You, Jehovah, who determined to dwell in darkness, a fitting dwelling and a station in which You may live forever." Then the king turned around and, having prayed for the whole assembly of Israelites who were standing there, said: "I give thanks to Jehovah, the God of the Israelites, who has fulfilled in deed what He had promised in words to my father David. For He had said that, after He had led His Israelites out of Egypt, He had not designated any city from any of the tribes of the Israelites for the building of a temple in which His name should be, nor had He chosen any man to be the ruler of His Israelites. But now He has chosen both Jerusalem, where He might place His name, and David, whom He might set over His Israelites. But when it was in the heart of my father David to build a temple to the name of Jehovah, the God of the Israelites, Jehovah showed him that as for what he had in mind—to build a temple to His name—he did well to have such a mind. Nevertheless, not he himself, but the son born from his loins, would be the one to build the temple to His name. Jehovah has fulfilled this promise of His; for I have succeeded my father David and sat upon the Israelite throne, just as Jehovah promised, and I have built the temple to the name of Jehovah, the God of the Israelites, where I have placed the Ark, in which is the covenant of Jehovah struck by Him with the Israelites." After these things were said, Solomon, standing before the altar of Jehovah with his hands spread toward heaven, at a bronze platform <note>original: "lauacrū æneum", likely referring to the bronze scaffold or dais mentioned in 2 Chronicles 6:13</note> which he had made—five cubits long, just as many wide, and three cubits high—and had placed in the middle of the courtyard, knelt down in the presence of the entire multitude of Israelites and spoke thus: "Jehovah,

<margin>Solomon's prayer at the dedication of the temple.</margin>
<margin>2 Chronicles 6:2.</margin>
God of the Israelites, there is no God like You, neither in the heavens nor on the earth, who preserves the covenant and uses mercy toward Your servants who obey You with all their heart; You who indeed have kept the faith given to my father David, and what You promised in words, You have clearly fulfilled in reality. Therefore, Jehovah God of the Israelites, maintain for my father David what You promised him, namely, that You would ensure that from his lineage there should never fail to be one to sit upon the Israelite throne, provided that his descendants so order their lives that they live according to Your law, just as he himself lived according to Your will. Now, Jehovah,

<column-break/>

God of the Israelites, let that which You promised Your servant David be confirmed. But indeed, will God truly dwell among men on earth? Since the heavens themselves, and the heaven of heavens, cannot contain You, how much less this temple built by me! Nevertheless, look upon the prayers and supplication of me, Your worshipper, Jehovah my God; hear the petition and the prayers which I, Your servant, make before You, so that You may have Your eyes open toward this temple night and day (the place which You designated for the placing of Your name), and hear the prayer which I, Your servant, use toward this place; and may You hear from the heavens (which is the place of Your habitation) the supplications of the Israelites (who are Your worshippers and Your people) with which they shall pray toward this place, and having heard them, may You be merciful.

If anyone shall have committed a wrong against another, and shall be called by him to an oath, and that oath is brought before Your altar in this temple, You then hear from heaven, and act so that You may render justice to Your servants, so that both the guilty one is condemned and the innocent is acquitted, and You may repay the latter according to his innocence and the former according to his deeds.

When Your Israelites, having been struck with defeat by enemies because of their sins against You, shall turn themselves back to You, and celebrate Your name, and pray to You suppliantly in this house, hear from heaven and forgive the sin of Your Israelites, and lead them back into the land which You gave to them and to their ancestors.

When the heaven is shut and the desired rain is missing because of their sin against You, and they shall pray toward this place and praise Your name, and—when You afflict them—they turn away from their sins, hear from heaven and forgive the sin of Your servants and of Your Israelite people, directing them into the right way in which they should walk: and irrigate Your land with rain, which You gave to Your people to possess. If famine invades these borders, if plague, if blight, if mildew, if locusts, if devastation approaches, if they are besieged by an enemy in their own country—finally, whatever disaster or disease there may be—every prayer and every supplication which shall be made by any man, or by any of Your Israelites, who, feeling his own wound and grief, shall stretch out his palms toward this house, hear from Your heavenly dwelling and throne, and forgive, and render to each according to his deeds, just as You shall know his mind (for You alone perceive the minds of all mortals), so that fearing You, they may obey You as long as they live in the land given by You to our ancestors.

Furthermore, if a stranger, who is not of Your Israelites, having heard of Your so famous name and Your strong hand and outstretched arm, shall come on account of Your name from remote borders and pray at this house, hear from the heaven of Your dwelling-place and grant all the requests of those strangers, so that all the nations of the earth, having come to know Your name, may revere You just as Your Israelites do, and so that it may be known that this house built by me is called by Your name.

If Your people, having set out for war against enemies wherever You shall have sent them, shall pray to Jehovah toward this city chosen by You, and toward the house built by me to Your name, hear from heaven their prayers and supplications, and take up their cause."

### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>
Solomon offers sacrifice.
2 Maccabees 2.
</margin>
After Solomon had finished his prayer, fire came down from heaven and consumed the <term>burnt offerings</term> <note>original: "solidi sacrificij", literally "whole sacrifices," referring to offerings entirely consumed by fire as a sign of total devotion</note> and the other victims, and such a great splendor of Jehovah filled the temple that the priests could not enter because of that radiance. Seeing this fire descend and the glory of Jehovah in the temple, all the Israelites prostrated themselves with their faces to the ground and worshipped, celebrating Jehovah, who is good and possessed of eternal mercy.

<margin>
1 Kings 8.
</margin>
Then the king and all the people offered sacrifices before Jehovah. King Solomon sacrificed twenty-two thousand oxen and one hundred and twenty thousand sheep and goats; thus the king and all the people dedicated the divine temple. Meanwhile, the priests performed their duties and the Levites used the musical instruments of Jehovah, which King David had made to celebrate Jehovah (who is endowed with eternal mercy) and through which David himself gave praise, while the priests sounded trumpets near them and all the Israelites stood by. Solomon also consecrated the middle of the courtyard located before the temple of Jehovah, because there he offered the burnt offerings and the fat of the <term>peace offerings</term> <note>original: "pro salute," sacrifices offered to celebrate well-being or a restored relationship with God</note>, since the bronze altar he had made could not hold the victims, the grain offerings, and the fat. At that time, Solomon held a seven-day festival along with all the Israelites, a massive multitude who had gathered from the land stretching from Hamath to the River of Egypt. On the eighth day, a solemn assembly was held; for the dedication of the altar lasted seven days, and the festival another seven days. Then, on the twenty-third day of the seventh month, the people went home, rejoicing and glad in heart for the goodness that Jehovah had shown to David, to Solomon, and to His people Israel.

<margin>
1 Kings 9.
Jehovah tells Solomon He has heard his prayers.
</margin>
After Solomon had successfully completed the temple of Jehovah, the royal palace, and everything else he had intended to do both in the temple and in his own house, Jehovah appeared to him at night and said: "I have heard your prayers, and I have chosen this place for myself as a house of sacrifice. If I shut up the heavens so that there is no rain, or command locusts to devour the land, or send a plague among my people—if

---

<page-num>452</page-num>
<header>CHRONICLES</header>

My people, who are called by My name, humble themselves, and correct their wicked ways, and pray to Me and seek My presence, I will hear from heaven and, having forgiven their sin, I will heal their land. Therefore, My eyes will be open and My ears attentive to the prayers of this place; for I have now chosen and consecrated this house, so that My name may be there forever, and there I will always keep My eyes and My heart. If you live according to My decree, following the example of your father David, and carry out everything I have commanded you, observing My statutes and laws, I will establish the throne of your kingdom, just as I promised your father David, saying that there would never fail to be a ruler from his line over the Israelites. But if you turn away and abandon My statutes and commandments which I have set before you, and go to serve and worship other gods, I will uproot the people from the land I gave them, and I will cast out of My sight this temple which I have consecrated to My name. I will make it a proverb and a common joke among all nations, so that this temple, which was once unique, will be an object of horror to everyone passing by. They will ask, 'Why has Jehovah treated this land and this temple in such a way?' And the answer will be, 'Because they abandoned Jehovah, the God of their ancestors, who led them out of Egypt, and joined themselves to other gods, worshipping and serving them; for this reason, He brought all these evils upon them.'"

### CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>
1 Kings 9.
Towns restored by Solomon.
</margin>
At the end of twenty years, during which Solomon built the temple of Jehovah and his own palace, he rebuilt the towns given to him by Hiram <note>King of Tyre</note> and settled colonies of Israelites there. Then he marched to Hamath-zobah and captured it, and built Palmyra in the desert, as well as all the storage towns he constructed near Hamath. He also built Beth-horon, both the Upper and the Lower, towns fortified with walls, gates, and bars; then Baalath, and all the storage towns he owned, as well as the towns for his chariots and horsemen—in short, whatever he desired to build either in Jerusalem, or in Lebanon, or in any part of his dominion.

<margin>
People made tributary to Solomon.
</margin>
As for all the people who remained of the Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, who were not Israelites—that is, the descendants of those whom the Israelites had not been able to destroy and who remained in the land—Solomon imposed a tribute of forced labor upon them, which continues to this day. But from the Israelites, whom he did not use as slaves for his projects, he drew his soldiers, chief officers, and commanders of his chariots and horsemen. Indeed, the chief officials King Solomon had to govern the people numbered two hundred and fifty.

<margin>
Pharaoh's daughter.
</margin>
Solomon moved Pharaoh’s daughter from the City of David to the palace he had built for her, for he said, "I will not allow a woman to live in the house of David, King of the Israelites, because those places where the Ark of Jehovah has entered are holy."

<margin>
Solomon's religious practice.
</margin>
Then Solomon offered burnt offerings to Jehovah on the altar of Jehovah which he had built before the vestibule of the temple. He followed the daily requirement according to the command of Moses, offering burnt sacrifices on the Sabbaths, the New Moons, and the appointed feasts three times a year: namely, the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks <note>original: "Septimanalibus", referring to Pentecost</note>, and...

<margin>-53</margin>
For the Festivals of Weeks and Tabernacles, Solomon established—according to the plan of his father David—the divisions of the priests for their duties and the classes of the Levites for leading praises and serving alongside the priests, as the requirements of each day demanded. He also set the classes of the gatekeepers at every gate, for such was the command of the divine David. No departure was made from what the king had commanded regarding the priests, the Levites, or the management of the treasuries in any matter. All of Solomon’s work was firmly established from the day the foundations of the Temple of Jehovah <note>original: "Iouæ", a Latinized form of the Tetragrammaton YHWH</note> were laid until it was finished. Once the Temple of Jehovah was perfected, Solomon traveled to Ezion-Geber and to Eloth, located on the shore of the Idumean Sea <note>The Red Sea</note>. Hiram sent him a fleet through his own men, along with servants experienced at sea. These men set out for Ophir with Solomon’s sailors and brought back four hundred and fifty talents of gold, which they delivered to King Solomon.

### CHAPTER IX.

<margin>The Queen</margin>
Now when the Queen of Sheba heard of Solomon’s fame, she came to Jerusalem to test him with difficult questions. She arrived with a very large retinue and camels carrying a great quantity of spices, gold, and precious gems. When she approached Solomon, she proposed to him everything she had on her mind. Solomon explained all her questions to her so clearly that nothing remained hidden from him; there was nothing he did not clarify for her. Thus, when the Queen of Sheba observed Solomon’s wisdom, the palace he had built, the food on his table, the seating of his courtiers, the standing and clothing of his attendants, and the sacrifices he offered in the Temple of Jehovah, she was breathless with astonishment and spoke to the king: "The reports I heard in my own country about your affairs and your wisdom are so true that I did not believe the talk of men until I came and saw it with my own eyes. Now I find that not even half of your abundant wisdom was told to me; you far surpass the fame I had heard. Happy are your men, and happy are these followers of yours, who stand before you always and hear your wisdom. Thanks be to Jehovah your God, who favored you so much as to place you on His throne as king for Jehovah your God. Because of the love He has for the Israelites to establish them forever, He has appointed you as king to execute law and justice." Then the Queen of Sheba gave the king one hundred and twenty talents of gold and an immense quantity of gems and spices; no spices could be compared to those given to King Solomon by the Queen of Sheba. The men of Hiram and Solomon, who had brought gold from Ophir, also brought gems and pine <note>original: "piceas", likely referring to Algum or Almug wood</note> trees. From these trees, the king made walkways for the Temple of Jehovah and for the royal palace, as well as lyres and harps <term>nablia</term> <note>ancient stringed instruments similar to a lute or harp</note> for singing. Indeed, such pine trees had never been seen before in Judea. Then King Solomon gave the Queen of Sheba whatever she wished to ask for, in addition to what the king gave her of his own accord; and so she returned to her own country with her followers. The weight of the gold that came to Solomon annually was six hundred and sixty-six talents of gold, besides what was paid to him by merchants and traders, and by all the kings of Arabia and the 

<margin>

<margin>Solomon’s riches.</margin>
<margin>Solomon</margin>
governors of the land, who paid him in gold and silver. King Solomon also made two hundred large shields of hammered gold, each weighing six hundred units, and three hundred small shields of hammered gold weighing three hundred units, which he stored in the House of the Forest of Lebanon. He also made a massive ivory throne and overlaid it with pure gold. This throne had six steps, and the <gloss>from behind</gloss> vault <note>or canopy</note> of the throne had <gloss>on both sides</gloss> armrests at the place of the seat, with two lions standing beside the armrests. Twelve lions stood on the six steps, one at each end of every step. No such work had ever been made in any other kingdom. All of Solomon’s drinking vessels and all the furniture of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were made of the finest gold; for silver was of no value in Solomon’s time. This was because the king’s ships, together with those of Hiram, sailed to Cilicia <note>original: "Cilicium", often identifying the biblical Tarshish</note> every three years, bringing back gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks. Thus King Solomon surpassed all the kings of the earth in riches and wisdom, so that all the kings of the world sought an audience with Solomon to hear the wisdom with which God had endowed his mind. Every year, each visitor brought a gift: vessels of silver and gold, garments, weapons, spices, horses, and mules. Solomon had four thousand stalls for horses and twelve thousand chariots and horsemen, whom he stationed partly in the chariot cities and partly with him in Jerusalem. He ruled over all the kings from the River <note>The Euphrates</note> to the land of the Philistines and the borders of Egypt. He made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones, and cedars as plentiful as the wild fig trees in the lowlands. Solomon obtained horses from all other lands and from Egypt. The rest of the acts of Solomon, from first to last, are written in the book of Nathan the prophet, in the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the visions of Iddo the seer concerning Jeroboam son of Nebat. Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel for forty years.

### CHAPTER X.

<margin>
Rehoboam, following the advice of the young men, loses part of the kingdom.
</margin>
<margin>Rehoboam</margin>
When Solomon died and was buried in the city of his father David, his son Rehoboam succeeded him as king. He went to Shechem (for all Israel had gathered at Shechem to make him king). Jeroboam son of Nebat, who was living in Egypt (where he had fled to escape King Solomon), heard of this and returned after being summoned, together with all the Israelites. They petitioned Rehoboam, saying that since they had been oppressed by his father’s yoke, he should lighten the servitude and the heavy yoke his father had imposed on them; if he did so, they would be under his power. He told them to return to him after three days. After they left, King Rehoboam consulted the elders who had served his father Solomon while he was still alive, asking what they advised as a response to those people. They replied that if he showed himself kind to them and gave them a favorable answer, they would always be under his power. But he rejected the advice the elders gave and sought the counsel of the young men who had grown up with him and were his attendants, asking what they advised him to respon- <meta>catchword: respon-</meta>

he should respond to those petitioning him to relax the yoke imposed by his father. The young men advised him that when they asked him to lighten the heavy yoke of his father, he should reply that his own little finger was thicker than his father's entire waist <note>original: "medium corporis truncū," literally the middle trunk of the body</note>. He should say that if his father had burdened them with a heavy yoke, he would add to that yoke; if his father had punished them with whips, he would punish them with scorpions <note>A "scorpion" was a type of whip or scourge reinforced with jagged metal points or knots</note>.
<margin>10</margin> Therefore, on the third day, when Jeroboam and all the others had returned to King Rehoboam as they had been commanded, the king answered them harshly. Abandoning the counsel of the elders and following the advice of the young men, he spoke thus: "My father burdened you with a heavy yoke, but I shall increase that weight; my father punished you with whips, but I shall punish you with scorpions." Thus the king did not yield to them, for God was so disposing the fates that Jehovah might fulfill what He had foretold through Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam, the son of Nebat. Then all the Israelites, seeing that the king would not comply with them, answered the king that they no longer held any right in David, nor any inheritance in the son of Jesse. "Return to your homes, Israelites! You, house of David, look to your own family!" And so all the Israelites departed for their homes. However, over those Israelites who inhabited the towns of Judah, Rehoboam held kingship. When King Rehoboam sent Adoram, the overseer of the tribute, to the Israelites, he was stoned by them and killed. Thereupon, King Rehoboam hurried to mount his chariot and flee to Jerusalem. Thus the Israelites revolted against the house of David, a defection which lasts to this day.

### CHAPTER XI.

<margin>Rehoboam prepares an expedition against the Israelites. 2 Kings 12.</margin>
When Rehoboam arrived in Jerusalem, he gathered the house of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin—one hundred and eighty thousand chosen warriors—to wage war against the Israelites and recover the kingdom for himself. But the word of Jehovah came to Shemaiah, a man of God, that he should announce in the name of Jehovah to Rehoboam, son of Solomon and king of Judah, and to all the Israelites both of Judah and Benjamin, <margin>40</margin> that they should not set out on the expedition nor bring war against their brothers. Instead, they were to return home, for He Himself was the author of this turn of events. Thus, obeying Jehovah, they desisted from invading Jeroboam. Rehoboam, residing in Jerusalem, restored the fortified towns in Judah for the sake of defense. <margin>Rehoboam fortifies the towns.</margin> He built up Bethlehem, Etam, Tekoa, Beth-zur, Soco, Adullam, Gath, Mareshah, Ziph, Adoraim, Lachish, Azekah, Zorah, Aijalon, and Hebron. These fortified towns were located partly in Judah and <margin>50</margin> partly in the land of Benjamin. Having strengthened these defenses, he appointed commanders and established storehouses for grain, oil, and wine. Then, in each town, he placed shields and spears, fortifying them greatly, and he held Judah and Benjamin. <margin>The Levites gather to Rehoboam.</margin> And the priests and Levites, who were in all the territories of the Israelites, gathered to him from all their borders. For the Levites, leaving behind their pasturelands and 

<column-break/>

possessions, had withdrawn into Judah and Jerusalem because Jeroboam and his sons had rejected them from the priesthood of Jehovah. Jeroboam had appointed his own priests for the high places <note>original: "facellanos," likely referring to priests of the shrines or chapels</note>, and for the satyrs <note>original: "Satyrorum," referring to goat-idols or forest demons</note> and the calves he had made. Those Levites were followed to Jerusalem by people from all the tribes of Israel who had set their hearts on the study of Jehovah, the God of the Israelites, in order to sacrifice to Jehovah, the God of their fathers. Thus they strengthened the kingdom of Judah and <margin>10</margin> established Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, for three years; for during those three years, they followed the way of David and Solomon.

<margin>Rehoboam's children.</margin> Now Rehoboam took as his wife Mahalath, the daughter of Jerimoth and granddaughter of David, and Abihail, the daughter of Eliab and granddaughter of Jesse. By her, he had sons: Jeush, Shemariah, and Zaham. After her, he took Maacah, the daughter of Absalom, who bore him Abijah, Attai, Ziza, and Shelomith. Rehoboam loved Maacah, the daughter of Absalom, more than all his other wives and concubines. (For he took <margin>20</margin> eighteen wives and sixty concubines, and fathered twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters). He appointed Abijah, the son of Maacah, as the chief and leader among his brothers, as he was destined for the kingdom. Regarding the many sons he had by his wives, he distributed them throughout all the borders of Judah and Benjamin and through all the fortified towns, providing them with a great abundance of provisions.

### CHAPTER XII.

<margin>30</margin>
<margin>The expedition of Shishak, King of Egypt, into Judah.</margin>
But when his kingdom was confirmed and established, he himself, along with all the Israelites, abandoned the law of Jehovah. In the fifth year of his reign, Shishak <note>original: "Sefacus," referring to the Pharaoh Shishak I</note>, the King of Egypt, launched an expedition against the people of Jerusalem—who had been unfaithful to Jehovah—with one thousand two hundred chariots, sixty thousand horsemen, and an innumerable multitude of soldiers consisting of Libyans, Troglodytes <note>Cave-dwellers from the Red Sea coast</note>, and Ethiopians who had accompanied him from Egypt. Having captured the fortified towns of Judah, he reached Jerusalem. <margin>40</margin> Then Shemaiah the prophet went to Rehoboam and the leaders of Judah, who had gathered in Jerusalem for fear of Shishak, and said to them: "Thus says Jehovah: You have abandoned me, and I in turn leave you in the hand of Shishak." Then the leaders of Israel and the king humbled themselves, confessing that Jehovah acted justly. When Jehovah saw that they had humbled themselves, he spoke with Shemaiah in this manner: "Since they have humbled themselves, I will not destroy them, nor will my wrath be poured out upon Jerusalem through Shishak to such an extent that they do not escape in some measure. <margin>50</margin> Nevertheless, they shall serve him, so that they may learn the difference between my service and the empire of earthly kingdoms." Therefore, Shishak the King of Egypt, having set out for Jerusalem, took away all the treasures of the Temple of Jehovah and of the royal palace, including the golden shields made by Solomon. In their place, King Rehoboam made bronze ones and entrusted them to the captains of the guards who watched the entrance of the palace. Whenever the king entered the Temple of Jehovah, the guards would come and take the shields, and then return them to the guardroom.

...they were carrying back to the chamber. Therefore, when Rehoboam had humbled himself, not only was the anger of Jehovah <note>original: "Iouæ," a Latinized form of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton, the personal name of God</note> turned away from him so that he was not utterly destroyed, but the state of Judah also fared well. Thus King Rehoboam was strengthened and reigned in Jerusalem; he was forty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem—the city which Jehovah had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel to place His name there. His mother's name was Naamah, an Ammonite <margin>e</margin> <note>The Ammonites were a neighboring nation often in conflict with Israel; Naamah’s presence highlights the foreign influences at court</note>. But he sinned in this: he did not keep his heart devoted to the zeal of Jehovah. The rest of the deeds of Rehoboam, from first to last, are written by name in the books of Shemaiah the prophet and Iddo the seer. There was, moreover, perpetual war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam.

### CHAPTER XIII.

After Rehoboam passed to his ancestors <note>original: "ad manes cōceßit," a classical Latin expression literally meaning "departed to the shades of the dead," here used for the king's death</note> and was buried in the City of David, his son Abijah succeeded him in the kingdom. He began to reign in Judah during the eighteenth year of Jeroboam’s reign <note>The text says "nineteenth year," likely a variation in this specific edition's chronology</note>. He reigned in Jerusalem for three years. His mother’s name was Michaiah, daughter of Uriel of Gibeah. When war broke out between Abijah and Jeroboam, Abijah drew up an army of four hundred thousand <note>original: "quadraginta millibus," literally 40,000, though standard biblical texts often cite 400,000</note> chosen soldiers in battle array, while Jeroboam set against him eight hundred thousand <note>original: "octoginta miliū," literally 80,000</note> equally excellent soldiers. <margin>and</margin> Abijah stood atop Mount Zemaraim, which is in the hill country of the Ephraimites, and delivered a speech in this manner: "Hear me, Jeroboam, and all you Israelites! You ought to know that Jehovah, the God of Israel, gave the kingdom over Israel to David and his descendants forever by a covenant of salt <margin>3.</margin>² <note>A "covenant of salt" refers to an unbreakable, permanent agreement, as salt was a symbol of preservation and incorruptibility</note>. Yet Jeroboam, son of Nebat, the servant of Solomon son of David, rose up and rebelled against his lord. Wicked and abandoned men gathered to him and conspired against Rehoboam, son of Solomon, who, being still young and timid of spirit, could not withstand them. And now you prepare to resist the kingdom of Jehovah, which is in the hands of the descendants of David, and you are indeed a vast multitude, possessing the golden calves which Jeroboam made for you as gods. Indeed, you have rejected the priests of Jehovah, the descendants of Aaron and the Levites, and you have made priests for yourselves after the manner of the other nations of the world; so that anyone who comes to be consecrated <note>original: "manuum suarum initiatum ueniat," literally "to come with full hands," a Hebrew idiom for priestly ordination</note> with a young bull and seven rams becomes a priest of things that are not gods. But as for us, we have Jehovah as our God, whom we have not abandoned; we have the priests as ministers of Jehovah, the descendants of Aaron and the Levites, who perform their work and make whole burnt offerings to Jehovah every morning and evening, with fragrant incense, and the arrangement of bread on the pure table, and the golden lampstand with its lamps to be lit every evening. For we observe the instructions of Jehovah our God, whom you have abandoned. <margin>and</margin> Behold, we have God as our leader, and His priests with the resounding trumpets to sound the alarm against you. O Israelites, do not fight against Jehovah, the God of your ancestors, for you shall not succeed!" Meanwhile, Jeroboam had sent an ambush to come upon them from behind; so the soldiers were in front of the Judeans and the ambush was behind them. Therefore, when they looked back...

<column-break/>

<page-num>458</page-num>

<sig>v</sig>

<margin>The Israelites conquered by the Judeans.</margin>
...the Judeans saw that the battle pressed upon them from both front and rear. They cried out to Jehovah, and the priests sounded the trumpets, and the Judeans raised a battle cry. While the Judean battle cry was sounding, Jeroboam and the Israelites were struck down by divine power before Abijah and the Judeans. They were put to flight and, by the will of God, delivered into their power; Abijah and his forces inflicted a great slaughter upon them, killing fifty thousand <note>original: "quinquaginta millibus," though standard historical sources for this event usually cite 500,000</note> of their chosen soldiers. Thus the Israelites were brought low at that time, and the Judeans prevailed because they relied on Jehovah, the God of their fathers. Abijah pursued Jeroboam and captured some of his towns: Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron, along with their surrounding villages. Jeroboam did not regain his power during the time of Abijah; rather, he was struck down by Jehovah and perished. Abijah, however, grew strong; he took fourteen wives and fathered twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters. The rest of Abijah’s deeds, character, and words are written in the history of the prophet Iddo.

### CHAPTER XIV.

<margin>Asa, King of Judah. 3 Kings 15.</margin>
After Abijah slept with his ancestors and was buried in the City of David, his son Asa reigned in his place. During his time, the land was at peace for ten years. This Asa did what was good and right in the eyes of Jehovah his God: he removed the foreign altars and the high places, smashed the sacred pillars, and cut down the ritual groves. He commanded the Judeans to seek Jehovah, the God of their fathers, and to observe the law and the commandments. He removed the high places and the sun-idols from all the cities of Judah, and his kingdom was quiet. He built fortified cities in Judah because there was peace and no war involved him during those years, for Jehovah gave him rest. For this reason, he commanded the Judeans: "Let us build these cities, surround them with walls and towers, and fortify them with gates and bars while the land is still in our power; since we have sought Jehovah our God, and because of this devotion, He has granted us rest on every side." So they built and prospered. Asa had an army of three hundred thousand shield-bearers and spearmen from Judah, and two hundred and eighty thousand from Benjamin who carried bucklers and bows; all of these were valiant warriors. <margin>The expedition of Zerah the Ethiopian against Asa. 1 Kings 14. Asa prays for God's help against Zerah.</margin> Against these, Zerah the Ethiopian made an expedition with one million <note>original: "decies centenis millibus," literally "ten hundred-thousands"</note> soldiers and three hundred chariots. When he had reached Mareshah, Asa went out to meet him, and they drew up their battle lines in the Valley of Zephathah near Mareshah. Asa called upon Jehovah his God with these words: "Jehovah, to whom there is no difference between the many and the weak when bringing aid, help us, Jehovah our God! For we rely on You and in Your name we come against this multitude. O Jehovah, You are our God; do not let man prevail against You." <margin>The Ethiopians routed by the Judeans.</margin> Therefore, the Ethiopians were defeated by Jehovah before Asa and the Judeans, and they fled. Asa and his soldiers pursued them as far as Gerar. Many of them were slain until they were utterly destroyed, for they were crushed by Jehovah and His army. The Judeans carried away a vast amount of spoil and conquered all the cities surrounding Gerar, for the terror of Jehovah had fallen upon them. They plundered all the towns, in which there was great spoil, and they also destroyed the sheepfolds, driving away a huge multitude of sheep, goats, and camels before returning to Jerusalem.

### CHAPTER XV.

Then Azariah, son of Oded, prompted by the impulse of the divine spirit, went out to meet Asa and addressed him thus: "Listen to me, Asa, and all you people of Judah and Benjamin. Jehovah <note>original: "Ioua," a Latinized form of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton, the personal name of God</note> is with you as long as you are with Him: if you seek Him, He will be found by you; but if you desert Him, He will desert you. For a long time, indeed, the Israelites were without the true God, without a teaching priest, and without law. But when, in their distress, they turned themselves to Jehovah, the God of the Israelites, and sought Him, He was found by them. During those times, there was no peace for those who traveled back and forth, because all the inhabitants were unsettled by many riots, as nation clashed with nation and city with city, for God threw them into disorder with every kind of adversity. You, therefore, be strong, and do not let your hands go weak; for your work shall have its reward."

<margin>
The religious reform of Asa.
2. Two abominations. <note>likely referring to the removal of idols mentioned in the text</note>
</margin>

When he heard this speech and prophecy of Oded the prophet, Asa took courage and removed every abomination from all the territories of Judah and Benjamin, and from all the towns he had captured in the hill country of the Ephraimites. He restored the altar of Jehovah located in front of the vestibule of Jehovah's temple. He gathered all the people of Judah and Benjamin, along with the foreigners living among them from the Ephraimites, Manassites, and Simeonites; for many Israelites had defected to him when they saw that Jehovah his God was with him. They gathered in Jerusalem in the third month of the fifteenth year of Asa’s reign. On that day, they sacrificed to Jehovah from the plunder they had brought: six hundred oxen and seven thousand sheep. Then they entered into a covenant to seek Jehovah, the God of their ancestors, with all their mind and all their soul. Whoever would not seek Jehovah, the God of the Israelites, was to be put to death, whether young or old, man or woman. They swore an oath to Jehovah with a loud voice, with shouting, and with trumpets and horns. All the people of Judah rejoiced in this oath, for they swore with all their heart and sought Jehovah with the greatest desire. He was found by them and gave them rest on every side. King Asa even stripped his mother Maacah of her authority because she had made an image of Pan <note>original: "Pana," referring to the Greek god Pan, used here by the translator to represent a pagan idol or Asherah pole</note> in a grove. The king demolished this image, smashed it to pieces, and burned it at the Brook Kidron. Although the shrines <note>original: "facella," referring to high places or local chapels</note> were not removed from the Israelites, otherwise Asa's heart was blameless throughout his life. He brought into the house of Jehovah the silver, gold, and vessels dedicated by himself and his father. There was no more war until the thirty-fifth year of his reign.

<margin>
Baasha of Israel’s campaign into Judah.
</margin>

### CHAPTER XVI.

In the thirty-sixth year of Asa's reign, Baasha, the king of Israel, launched an expedition into Judah and began to fortify Ramah to block the exit and entrance for Asa, the king of Judah. Then Asa took silver and gold from the treasures of the temple of Jehovah and the royal palace and sent it to Ben-hadad, the king of Syria, who lived in Damascus, with these requests: "As there is a treaty between me and you, and between my father and your father, I am sending you silver and gold. Come, break the treaty you have with Baasha, the king of Israel, so that he may withdraw from me." Ben-hadad complied with King Asa and sent the commanders of his armies to the cities of the Israelites. They conquered Ijon, Dan, Abel-maim, and all the supply centers of the towns of Naphtali.

<column-break/>

When Baasha heard of this, he stopped fortifying Ramah and abandoned his work. Then King Asa summoned all the people of Judah, and they carried away the stones and timber of Ramah with which Baasha had been building the fortification. With these, Asa fortified Geba and Mizpah.

<margin>
The prophet Hanani rebukes Asa.
2. Chronicles 16.
John 9. <note>a marginal cross-reference</note>
</margin>

Meanwhile, Hanani the seer approached Asa, the king of Judah, and spoke to him in these words: "Because you relied on the king of Syria and not on Jehovah your God, the army of the king of Syria has escaped your hand. Were not the forces of the Ethiopians and Libyans huge, with a vast number of chariots and horsemen? And yet, when you leaned upon Jehovah, He gave you victory over them. For the eyes of Jehovah roam over the whole earth in such a way that He may grant strength to those who are possessed of a sincere heart toward Him. Since you have acted foolishly in this matter, from now on you shall be faced with wars." Asa was so indignant at this that, in a fit of rage, he threw the seer into prison; at the same time, he also slaughtered some of the people. As for the deeds of Asa, from beginning to end, they are written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel. In the thirty-ninth year of his reign, Asa became diseased in his feet. Despite the severity of the disease, he did not consult Jehovah, but rather the physicians. He departed this life to the spirits of the dead <note>original: "Concessit ad manes," a classical Latin idiom for dying</note> in the forty-first year of his reign. He was buried in his own tomb, which he had hewn for himself in the City of David. They laid him on a bier filled with spices and ointments prepared by the perfumer’s art, and they burned a very great funeral fire for him.

3. Kings. Ahab’s expedition to Ramoth.
</margin>

### CHAPTER XVII.

<margin>
Jehoshaphat, King of Judah
</margin>

His son Jehoshaphat succeeded him in the kingdom. Having defeated the Israelites, he stationed soldiers in all the fortified towns of Judah and placed garrisons both in Judah and in the Ephraimite towns that his father Asa had captured. Jehovah was with Jehoshaphat because he imitated the ancient ways of his ancestor David. He did not seek the Baals <note>pagan deities</note> but studied his ancestral God and lived according to His precepts, unlike the Israelites. Therefore, Jehovah so established the kingdom in his hand that all of Judah paid him tribute, and having acquired great wealth and glory, he took such courage in the prescriptions of Jehovah that he moreover removed the shrines and groves from Judah. In the third year of his reign, he sent his officials—Ben-hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah—to teach throughout the towns of Judah. With them were the Levites Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah, and Tob-adonijah; and with these Levites were the priests Elishama and Jehoram. They taught throughout Judah, carrying the book of the law of Jehovah with them. They traveled through all the towns of Judah and taught the common people. Consequently, such a terror of Jehovah fell upon all the kingdoms of the lands bordering Judah that they did not wage war against Jehoshaphat. Not only was tribute and silver paid to Jehoshaphat by the Philistines <note>original: "Palæstina"</note>, but even the Arabs paid him livestock: seven thousand seven hundred rams and as many goats. Thus, as Jehoshaphat's power grew so greatly, he built fortresses and store-cities in Judah. He possessed great resources in the towns of Judah, and skilled soldiers of war in Jeru—

### CHAPTER XVIII.

<margin>2 Kings <note>The margin likely references parallel accounts in the Book of Kings.</note></margin> Therefore, having attained great riches and glory, Jehoshaphat formed an alliance by marriage with Ahab, and after some years he went down to visit him in Samaria. Ahab slaughtered a great multitude of sheep and oxen for him and his companions, and while urging him to an expedition against Ramoth-Gilead <note>original: "Ramotha Galaaditarum"</note>, he asked whether he would be willing to accompany him in that campaign. To this, Jehoshaphat replied: "You may use me and my men for war just as your own; but in the meantime, I advise you," he said, "that the oracle of Jehovah should be consulted." Then the king of the Israelites, having gathered four hundred prophets, asked of them whether he should attack Ramoth-Gilead in war, or not. They replied that he should attack, for God would give the victory to the king. But Jehoshaphat spoke with him thus: "Is there not some other prophet of Jehovah here besides these, whom we might question?" "There is still one man," said the king of the Israelites to Jehoshaphat, "from whom we <margin>Zedekiah the prophet.</margin> might seek an oracle of Jehovah, but I hate him for this reason: he never prophesies anything favorable to me, but always unfavorable. He is Micaiah <note>original: "Michæas"</note>, the son of Imla." But Jehoshaphat said, "It does not become the king to speak so." Then the king of the Israelites, calling a certain eunuch, commanded him to quickly fetch Micaiah son of Imla. Now the king of the Israelites and Jehoshaphat king of the Jews each sat on his throne, dressed in their robes, in the threshing floor at the entrance of the gate of Samaria, with all the prophets prophesying before them. And Zedekiah <note>original: "Sedecias"</note> son of Chenaanah, when he had made iron horns for himself, said: "Jehovah promises that with these you shall gore the Syrians even to their destruction." And all the prophets predicted the same: "Attack Ramoth-Gilead successfully; Jehovah will give you victory, O king." Furthermore, the messenger who had gone to call Micaiah warned him that, since the other prophets were predicting favorable things to the king with one voice, he should also follow their example and predict favorable things. But Micaiah swore by the immortal Jehovah that he would speak only what had been commanded to him by Jehovah his God. Then when he came to the king, the king questioned him thus: "Micaiah, shall we bring war against Ramoth-Gilead, or not?" To which he replied, "Indeed, bring it, and may it turn out well; victory over them shall be given to you." But the king said: "I adjure you again and again by the name of Jehovah that you tell me nothing but the truth." Then he said: "I saw all the Israelites wandering on the mountains, like sheep lacking a shepherd, and Jehovah spoke 

<column-break/>

thus: 'These have no masters; let them return home in peace.'" Here the king of the Israelites addressed Jehoshaphat: "Did I not predict to you that he would prophesy nothing prosperous for me, but only adversity?" And Micaiah said: "Therefore hear the judgment of Jehovah: I saw Jehovah sitting on his throne, with all the heavenly host standing on his right and on his left, and he was saying: 'Who shall deceive Ahab king of the Israelites, so that he might attack Ramoth-Gilead and fall there?' And while some said one thing and some another, a certain spirit came forward and, standing before Jehovah, said: 'I will deceive him.' And Jehovah asked: 'By what means?' He replied, 'I will go and breathe a lying spirit into the mouths of all his prophets.' Then Jehovah said: 'You shall deceive him; you shall succeed. Go and do so.' Therefore, know that Jehovah has put a lying spirit into the mouths of these prophets of yours, and he is preparing evil for you." At this, Zedekiah son of Chenaanah approached and struck Micaiah on the cheek: "By what way," he asked, "did the spirit of Jehovah depart from me to speak with you?" "You shall know," said Micaiah, "when you hide yourself in the innermost chamber." But the king of the Israelites said: "Seize Micaiah and lead him to Amon the city governor and to Joash the king's son, and by the king's command, order him to be shut in prison, and there to be fed harshly with bread and water, until I return safe." Micaiah added: "If indeed you return safe, then Jehovah has not spoken through me." And he said, "Listen to this, all you people." So the king of the Israelites and Jehoshaphat king of Judea set out for Ramoth-Gilead, and the king of the Israelites advised Jehoshaphat that, as they were about to enter battle, he should change his appearance and put on the clothing of Ahab himself; and the king of the Israelites also changed his appearance, and so they entered the battle. Now the king of Syria had commanded his chariot commanders that they should seek out no one with their weapons except the king of the Israelites alone. Therefore, when the chariot commanders caught sight of Jehoshaphat, thinking he was the king of the Israelites, they turned their weapons toward him. But when Jehoshaphat cried out, Jehovah God helped him and turned them away from him. For when the chariot commanders saw that it was not the king of the Israelites, they ceased pursuing him. But a certain man drew a bow at random and wounded the king of the Israelites between the joints and the breastplate. Then he commanded his charioteer <margin>The death of Ahab.</margin> to turn the reins and lead him out of the battle line, as he was faint from the wound. And while the fight lasted through that day, the king of the Israelites, having stood in his chariot against the Syrians until evening, died at the setting of the sun. Jehoshaphat, however, the king of Judea, returned home to Jerusalem in safety.

Thus Jehoshaphat, dwelling in Jerusalem, <margin>Jehoshaphat teaches his people piety.</margin> traveled again among the people from Beersheba to the mountain of Ephraim, and led them back to the majesty of Jehovah...

### CHAPTER XX.

<margin>Jehoshaphat, about to fight the Moabites, implores God's help.</margin>
Afterward, the Moabites, Ammonites, and a portion of the Idumaeans <note>original: "Idumæorum", referring to the Edomites</note> waged war against Jehoshaphat. When it was announced to Jehoshaphat that a vast multitude of Syrians <note>The Latin text here uses "Syrorum," though most biblical translations identify these invaders as coming from Edom or across the Dead Sea.</note> who lived across the lake were coming against him, and that they were already at Hazazon-tamar (which is the same as Engedi), he was terrified. Turning his face to consult Jehovah, he proclaimed a fast for all of Judah. When the Jews had gathered from all the towns of Judah to seek an oracle from Jehovah, Jehoshaphat stood in the midst of the assembly of the people of Judah and Jerusalem, in the temple of Jehovah before the new court, and spoke thus: “Jehovah, God of our ancestors, are you not the God of heaven, and do you not rule over all the kingdoms of the nations? In your hand are strength and power, so that no one can resist you. Did you not, our God, drive out the inhabitants of this land for the sake of your people Israel, and give it to the descendants of Abraham your friend forever? Having occupied it, they built a sanctuary for your name in it, with this intention: that if they were afflicted by any evil, such as the sword of vengeance, or plague, or famine, they would present themselves before this temple and before you (for your name is in this temple) and implore you in their adversity, and you would hear and defend them.

<margin>Deuteronomy 1.</margin>
Behold now the Ammonites, and the Moabites, and the inhabitants of Mount Seir, whom you did not allow the Israelites to invade when they came out of Egypt (for they turned away from them and did not destroy them); these people, I say, return this favor to us by coming to drive us out of the possession which you gave to us. Jehovah signifies this to you: do not fear or be terrified by this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God’s. He reigned for twenty-five years in Jerusalem; his mother was named Azubah, the daughter of Shilhi. He imitated the ways of his father Asa and did not deviate from obeying Jehovah. Only the shrines <note>original: "sacella," often translated as "high places," which were unauthorized places of worship</note> were not removed, for the people had not yet set their hearts upon the God of their ancestors. Afterward, Jehoshaphat of Judah entered into a partnership with Ahaziah, the king of Israel, who acted wickedly. In forming this alliance, they agreed to build ships to go to Cilicia <note>original: "Ciliciam." ### CHAPTER XXI.

After Jehoshaphat slept with his ancestors and was buried with them in the City of David, his son Jehoram succeeded him in the kingdom. He had brothers, the sons of Jehoshaphat: Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, Azariah, Michael, and Shephatiah. All these were the sons of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. Their father gave them many gifts of gold, silver, and other precious things, along with fortified cities in Judah; however, he gave the kingdom to Jehoram, as he was the firstborn. But when Jehoram had ascended to his father’s kingdom and established his power, he slaughtered all his brothers with the sword, along with several of the princes of Israel. He was thirty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned in Jerusalem for eight years. He imitated the ways of the kings of Israel, following the example of the house of Ahab (for he had married Ahab’s daughter) and offended Jehovah. Yet, Jehovah did not wish to destroy the line of David because of the covenant He had struck with David, in which He promised to give a perpetual succession to him and his sons. During Jehoram’s time, the Edomites <note>original: "Idumaei"</note> rebelled against the Judeans and set up a king for themselves. Although Jehoram set out with his nobles and all his chariots, rising by night to defeat the Edomites who surrounded him and the commanders of the chariots, the rebellion of the Edomites from the rule of Judah continues to this day. At that same time, Libnah also revolted from his rule, because he had not only abandoned Jehovah, the God of his fathers, but had also built shrines in the mountains of Judah, leading the inhabitants of Jerusalem into unchaste idol worship and causing the Judeans to fall away.

<margin>Elijah</margin>
Therefore, a letter came to him from the prophet Elijah in these words: "Thus says Jehovah, the God of your ancestor David: Because you have not imitated your father Jehoshaphat or Asa the king of Judah, but have followed the example of the kings of Israel, leading the Judeans and the people of Jerusalem into the unchastity of the house of Ahab, and have even killed your own brothers—born of your own father—who were better than you; know that Jehovah will strike your people, your children, your wives, and all your possessions with a great plague. You yourself will suffer from a severe intestinal disease,

<column-break/>

so that because of the sickness, your intestines will fall out day by day." Consequently, Jehovah stirred up against Jehoram the spirit of the Philistines and the Arabs who were neighbors to the Ethiopians. They made an incursion into Judah and, besides carrying off all the wealth found in the king’s house, they also led away his sons and his wives, leaving only Jehoahaz <note>Also known as Ahaziah.</note>, the youngest of his sons. After all these things, Jehovah struck him with such an incurable intestinal disease that as the days passed and a period of two years was completed, his intestines were cast out by the disease, and he died in great agony. His people did not make a funeral pyre for him as they had for his ancestors. He began his reign at the age of thirty-two and reigned in Jerusalem for eight years. He departed with no one regretting his passing, and he was buried in the City of David, but not in the royal burial grounds.

### CHAPTER XXII.

<margin>Ahaziah king of Judah. 4 Kings 8.</margin>
<note>In the older tradition used here, the books of Samuel and Kings were often grouped as 1–4 Kings.</note>
In his place, the inhabitants of Jerusalem appointed his youngest son, Ahaziah, as king; for a band of raiders that had come with the Arabs had killed all the older sons. Thus Ahaziah the son of Jehoram took up the kingdom of Judah in the forty-second year of his age. He reigned in Jerusalem for one year; his mother was Athaliah, the granddaughter of Omri. He also imitated the ways of the house of Ahab (since his mother was his counselor in impiety), offending Jehovah following the example of Ahab’s house, for he used them as advisors to his own destruction after the death of his father. Following their advice, he went with Joram the son of Ahab, king of Israel, to war against Hazael king of Syria at Ramoth-Gilead. When Joram was wounded by the Syrians and returned to Jezreel to heal from the wounds he received in the battle against Hazael, Ahaziah the son of Jehoram, king of Judah, went down to Jezreel to visit the ailing Joram. It happened by divine fate that this visit led to Ahaziah’s ruin. For when he arrived and went out with Joram to meet Jehu the son of Nimshi—whom Jehovah had anointed to cut off the house of Ahab—Jehu, while executing judgment upon the house of Ahab, found the princes of Judah and the sons of Ahaziah's brothers who served Ahaziah and slew them. He then searched for Ahaziah, who was caught hiding in Samaria. He was brought to Jehu and put to death, and he was buried only because he was the grandson of Jehoshaphat, who had applied his whole heart to seeking Jehovah.

<margin>Athaliah destroys the royal line. 4 Kings 21.</margin>
When there was no one left in the family of Ahaziah to claim the kingdom, Athaliah, the mother of Ahaziah, seeing that her son was dead, attempted to destroy the entire royal line of the house of Judah. But Jehoshabeath <note>original: "Iosaba"</note>, the daughter of King Jehoram and wife of Jehoiada the high priest, snatched Joash the son of Ahaziah (whose sister she was) from the midst of the king’s sons who were being killed. She hid him and his nurse in a bedroom chamber, keeping him safe from Athaliah's slaughter.

### CHAPTER XXIII.

<margin>Jehoiada the high priest creates Joash king of Judah.</margin>

When the entire assembly had entered into a covenant with the king in the temple <note>original: "fano," a term for a consecrated space or temple</note>, Jehoiada spoke to them as follows: "Behold the king’s son, to whom the kingdom belongs, just as Jehovah promised to the descendants of David. This, therefore, is what you shall do: A third of you, who come in on the Sabbath to serve as priests and Levites, shall act as gatekeepers of the thresholds; a third shall be at the royal palace; and a third at the Gate of the Foundation. Let no one enter the temple of Jehovah except the priests and the ministering Levites; they may enter because they are holy, but all the rest shall observe the discipline of Jehovah. The Levites shall surround the king on every side, weapons in hand, so that whoever enters the temple shall be put to death; and they shall accompany the king whenever he enters or exits."

The Levites and all the people of Judah executed all the commands of Jehoiada the high priest. Each man took his followers—both those who were coming on duty on the Sabbath and those who were going off duty—for Jehoiada had not dismissed the divisions <note>original: "classes," referring to the rotating shifts of priests and Levites established by King David</note>. Then Jehoiada the high priest handed over to the centurions the spears, shields, and quivers of King David that were kept in the temple. With all the soldiers armed and standing around the king, from the right side of the temple to the left, where the temple and the altar stood open, he brought out the king’s son. Placing the crown and the testimony <note>original: "oraculum," likely referring to the Law of Moses or royal decrees</note> upon him, Jehoiada and his sons proclaimed him king and anointed him, shouting, "Long live the king!"

When Athaliah heard the noise of the people running and praising the king, she came to them in the temple of Jehovah. Seeing the king standing by the pillar at the entrance, with the princes and trumpeters beside him, and all the inhabitants rejoicing, sounding trumpets, singing with musical instruments, and leading the songs of praise, she tore her robes and cried out repeatedly, "Treason! Treason!"

But Jehoiada the high priest led out the centurions who were in command of the troops and ordered them to lead her out beyond the temple precinct, and if anyone followed her, they were to be struck down with the sword; for the priest did not want her to be <margin>Athaliah is killed.</margin> killed in the temple of Jehovah. So they laid hands on her, and when she had been led to the entrance of the Horse Gate of the royal palace, they killed her there. Then Jehoiada made a covenant between himself, all the people, and the king, that they should be Jehovah’s people. Afterward, the whole crowd went to the temple of Baal and tore it down, breaking its altars and images to pieces; they also killed Mattan, the priest of Baal, before the altars.

Jehoiada then entrusted the oversight of Jehovah’s temple to the priests and Levites, whom David had distributed throughout the temple of Jehovah, to offer burnt offerings to Jehovah as written in the Law of Moses, with rejoicing and song, according to the arrangements of David. He also stationed gatekeepers at the gates of Jehovah’s temple, so that no one who was in any way unclean might enter. Then, having summoned the centurions, the nobles, the leaders of the people, and all the inhabitants, he led the king down from the temple of Jehovah. When they reached the middle of the upper gate of the palace, the king was seated upon the royal throne. All the inhabitants rejoiced, and the city was at peace once Athaliah had been put to the sword.

He gathered the priests and Levites and commanded them to go out to the cities of Judah and collect money annually from all the Israelites to restore the temple of their God, and to carry out this matter quickly.

But when the Levites did not hurry, the king summoned Jehoiada the chief priest and complained that he had not required the Levites to bring in from Judah, Jerusalem, and the community of Israel the tax prescribed by Moses, the servant of Jehovah, for the Tabernacle of the Testimony. For the sons of that impious Athaliah had not only wrecked the sanctuary but had even transferred all the sacred objects of Jehovah’s temple to the Baals <note>pagan deities</note>. All the leaders and the common people brought their offerings gladly and cast them into the chest until the task was completed.

Whenever the chest was brought to the Levites (to whom the king had entrusted this duty) and they saw there was a large amount of money, the king’s scribe and the high priest’s representative would come, empty the chest, take the money, and carry the chest back to its place. By doing this daily, they gathered a great sum of money. The king and Jehoiada gave it to those overseeing the work on Jehovah’s temple, who hired stonecutters and carpenters to restore the temple, as well as blacksmiths and bronze-workers to repair it. Thus the overseers labored, and the restoration progressed under their hands until they had restored the sanctuary to its original state and strengthened it. When the work was finished, they brought the remaining money back to the king and Jehoiada, from which he made vessels for the service of Jehovah’s temple, including bowls, flagons, and vessels of gold and silver. Sacrificies were offered continually in the temple of Jehovah as long as Jehoiada lived.

At last, Jehoiada died, being old and full of years, at the age of one hundred and thirty. After the death of Jehoiada, the princes of Judah came to the king and paid him homage; the king listened to them, and they abandoned the temple of Jehovah, the God of their ancestors, to serve sacred poles <note>original: "lucis," referring to Asherah poles</note> and idols. Because of this guilt, wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem. Although prophets were sent to them to bring them back to Jehovah, they would not listen when warned.

But they conspired against him, and by the king's command, they stoned him to death in the court of the temple of Jehovah. ...he said: "May Jehovah see and avenge it." <note>original: "Animaduertet Ioua & ulciſcetur." These were the dying words of Zechariah, the son of the high priest Jehoiada, whom King Joash had ungratefully ordered to be executed.</note> Therefore, at the turn of the year, the Syrians launched an expedition against him. They attacked Judah and Jerusalem, killed all the leaders of the people, and sent all their plunder to the king at Damascus. Although the Syrian soldiers had arrived in small numbers, Jehovah granted them victory over a very large army, because the Judeans had abandoned the God of their ancestors; thus they executed judgment upon Joash. After the Syrians withdrew, leaving him in great pain, his own servants conspired against him to avenge the murder of the son of Jehoiada the high priest. They killed him in his own bed, and he was buried in the City of David, though not in the tombs of the kings. Those who conspired against him were Zabad, the son of Shimeath the Ammonitess, and Jehozabad, the son of Shimrith the Moabitess. ### CHAPTER XXV.

His son Amaziah succeeded him in the kingdom at the age of twenty-five. He reigned in Jerusalem for twenty-nine years; his mother was Jehoaddan of Jerusalem. He did what was right in the eyes of Jehovah, but not with his whole heart. Once the kingdom was firmly in his hand, he executed those of his servants who had killed the king, his father. However, he did not put their children to death, as is required by the writing of the law in the Book of Moses, where Jehovah commands that parents shall not die for their children, nor children for their parents, but each shall die for his own sin. Amaziah then assembled the men of Judah and organized them by their ancestral houses under commanders of thousands and hundreds. He took a census of all the men of Judah and Benjamin who were twenty years old or older, and found three hundred thousand elite men, fit for military service and able to handle spear and shield. Additionally, he hired one hundred thousand soldiers from Israel for one hundred talents of silver. But a certain man of God approached him and warned: "O king, do not let the soldiers of Israel go with you, for Jehovah is not with Israel—that is, with any of the Ephraimites. But if you go, go and act bravely in battle; otherwise, God (who has the power to both help and to overthrow) will let you fall before the enemy." Amaziah said to the man of God: "But what shall be done about the hundred talents I gave to the Israelite soldiers?" And the man of God replied: "It is within Jehovah's power to give you much more than that." So Amaziah dismissed the soldiers who had come to him from Ephraim, sending them back to their own place. They were greatly incensed against Judah and returned home in a rage. Amaziah, however, took courage and led his people to the Valley of Salt, where he killed ten thousand men of Seir <note>The people of Seir are the Edomites.</note>. The Judeans also captured ten thousand men alive, brought them to the top of a cliff, and threw them down from the summit so that they were all dashed to pieces. Meanwhile, the soldiers whom Amaziah had sent back, refusing to let them go to war with him, raided the towns of Judah from Samaria to Beth-horon. They killed three thousand people and took much spoil. After Amaziah returned from the slaughter of the Edomites, he brought the gods of the men of Seir and set them up as his own gods, bowing down to them and burning incense to them. Because of this, Jehovah grew angry with him and sent a prophet, who cautioned him: "Why do you seek after the gods of a people who could not even deliver their own people from your hand?" As he was speaking, Amaziah interrupted him:

<column-break/>
<page-num>470</page-num>

"Have you been appointed as a counselor to the king?" he said. "Stop, lest you be killed." Then the prophet stopped, saying: "I know that God's counsel is to destroy you, because you have done this and have not listened to my advice." Then Amaziah, king of Judah, after consulting his advisors, sent messengers to Joash, the son of Jehoahaz, the grandson of Jehu, king of Israel, challenging him to a confrontation. Joash replied to him with this message: "A thistle in Lebanon sent word to a cedar in Lebanon, saying, 'Give your daughter to my son in marriage.' But <margin>Amaziah declares war on Joash, king of the Israelites.</margin> a wild beast of Lebanon passed by and trampled the thistle. You think to yourself that you have defeated the Edomites, and your heart has become arrogant with glory. Stay home now; why should you provoke trouble to your own hurt, so that you fall, and Judah with you?" But Amaziah would not listen, for it was the will of God to deliver them into the enemy's hand because they had sought the gods of the Edomites. So Joash, king of Israel, marched out. He and Amaziah, king of Judah, met in battle at Beth-shemesh in Judah. The men of Judah were defeated by the Israelites, and every man fled to his home. At Beth-shemesh, Joash, king of Israel, captured Amaziah, king of Judah, the son of Joash and grandson of Jehoahaz. <margin>Joash destroys a part of the walls of Jerusalem.</margin> He brought him to Jerusalem and broke down the wall of Jerusalem from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate—a span of four hundred cubits. He took all the gold, silver, and vessels found in the temple with Obed-edom, along with the treasures of the royal palace and hostages, and then returned to Samaria. Amaziah, son of Joash, king of Judah, lived for fifteen years after the death of Joash, son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel. As for the rest of the acts of Amaziah, from first to last, they are written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel. From the time Amaziah turned away from Jehovah, a conspiracy was formed against him in Jerusalem. He fled to Lachish, but they sent men after him to Lachish and killed him there. He was brought back on horses and buried with his ancestors in the City of Judah.

### CHAP. XXVI.

<margin>Uzziah, King of Judah.</margin> Then all the people of Judah took Uzziah <note>original: "Oziam," also known as Azariah.</note>, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah. After the king went to rest with his ancestors, Uzziah rebuilt Elath and restored it to Judah. He began his reign at the age of sixteen and reigned in Jerusalem for fifty-two years; his mother was Jecoliah of Jerusalem. He did what was right in the eyes of Jehovah, imitating his father Amaziah. He set himself to seek Jehovah during the time of Zechariah, a man skilled in divine visions; and as long as he sought Jehovah, God gave him success. He went on an expedition against the Philistines and broke down the walls of Gath, Jabneh, and Ashdod, and built towns in the territory of Ashdod and elsewhere among the Philistines. God helped him against the Philistines, the Arabs who lived in Gur-baal, and the Ammonites. The Ammonites paid him tribute, and his fame spread as far as the border of Egypt, for he became exceedingly powerful. He built towers in Jerusalem at the Corner Gate, the Valley Gate, and at the Angle, and fortified them. He also built towers in the wilderness and dug many cisterns, for he had much livestock both in the valleys and in the plains. He also had farmers and vinedressers in the mountains and in Carmel, for he was a man who loved agriculture. Uzziah also had an army of soldiers ready for battle, organized by divisions according to the census made by Jeiel the scribe and Maaseiah the official, under the direction of Hananiah, one of the king's commanders. The total number of the heads of the ancestral houses, the brave warriors, was two thousand six hundred. Under their command was an army of three hundred seven thousand five hundred men, who could wage war...
