to support the king against his enemies with military valor. For this entire army, Uzziah prepared shields, spears, helmets, coats of mail, bows, and slings for stones. He also constructed artfully designed engines of war in Jerusalem, which were placed upon the towers and corners to hurl great arrows and large stones. Consequently, his fame spread far and wide, for he had acquired such extraordinary military strength. But once he had obtained this power, his heart became proud to his own destruction, and he sinned against Jehovah his God. For he entered <margin>10</margin> into the sanctuary <note>original: "cellam" — the inner room of the temple</note> of Jehovah to burn incense upon the altar of incense. <margin>King Uzziah is afflicted with leprosy for usurping the priestly office. 2 Kings 15.</margin> Azariah the high priest followed him, and with him eighty priests of Jehovah, men of great courage, who stood before him and warned him: "It is not your place, Uzziah, to burn incense to Jehovah, but rather the duty of the priests, the descendants of Aaron, who are consecrated for this service. Depart from the sanctuary, for you are committing a crime, and this will not be counted to your glory before Jehovah God." At this, Uzziah became enraged; holding the censer in his hand to burn the incense, he grew angry with the priests. But suddenly, leprosy broke out upon his forehead <margin>20</margin> in the presence of the priests in the temple of Jehovah, right by the altar of incense. When Azariah the high priest and all the other priests looked at him and saw the leprosy on his forehead, they hurried him out of that place; indeed, he himself was eager to leave because of the plague sent by Jehovah. Thus King Uzziah remained a leper until the day of his death, and because he was a leper, he lived in a separate house, excluded from the temple of Jehovah. His son Jotham took charge of the royal palace and governed the people of the land. As for the rest of Uzziah's deeds, from beginning to end, they were recorded by the prophet Isaiah, the son of Amoz.

### CHAPTER XXVII.

<margin>Jotham, King of Judah. 2 Kings 15.</margin>
After Uzziah passed away and was buried with his ancestors in the field of the royal burial ground (for they said, "He is a leper"), his son Jotham succeeded him in the kingdom at the age of twenty-five. He reigned in Jerusalem for sixteen years. His mother’s name was Jerushah, the daughter of Zadok. He obeyed Jehovah, imitating his father Uzziah in everything except that he did not enter the sanctuary of Jehovah; however, the practices of the people remained corrupt. He restored the Upper Gate of the temple of Jehovah and performed extensive building on the wall of Ophel <note>a fortified hill in Jerusalem</note>. He built towns in the hill country of Judah, as well as fortresses and towers in the wooded areas. He waged war against the king of the Ammonites and defeated them; in that year, the Ammonites paid him one hundred talents of silver, ten thousand kors <note>a large dry measure, roughly 220 liters</note> of wheat, and the same amount of barley. They paid him this same tribute in the second and third years as well. Thus Jotham grew powerful, because he dedicated his ways to Jehovah his God. As for the rest of Jotham's deeds, all his wars and his achievements, they are recorded in the Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah. He began his reign at the age of twenty-five and reigned in Jerusalem for sixteen years.

### CHAPTER XXVIII.

<margin>Ahaz, King of Judah. 2 Kings 16.</margin>
When Jotham went to join the spirits <note>original: "manes" — a Roman term for the souls of the deceased</note> of his ancestors and was buried in the City of David, his son

<column-break/>

<margin>The impiety of Ahaz.</margin>
Ahaz succeeded him in the kingdom at the age of twenty. He reigned in Jerusalem for sixteen years, but he did not obey Jehovah as his ancestor David had done. Instead, he imitated the actions of the kings of Israel; he not only cast metal idols for the Baals but also burned incense in the Valley of Ben-Hinnom and even burned his own sons in the fire, following the abominations of the nations that Jehovah had driven out for the sake of the Israelites. He performed sacrifices and burned incense at the shrines <note>original: "sacellis"</note>, on the hills, and everywhere <margin>10</margin> under leafy trees. Therefore, Jehovah delivered him into the hand of the King of Syria, who defeated him and took a great number of captives from him, leading them away to Damascus. He was also delivered into the hand of the King of Israel, from whom he suffered a massive slaughter. <margin>Pekah inflicts a slaughter upon the Judeans.</margin> Pekah, the son of Remaliah, killed one hundred and twenty thousand Judeans in a single day—all of them soldiers—because they had abandoned Jehovah, the God of their ancestors. Zichri, an Ephraimite soldier, killed Maaseiah the king’s son, Azrikam the master of the palace, and Elkanah, who was second only to the king. <margin>20</margin> The Israelites took two hundred thousand women, boys, and girls captive from their own kinsmen, and they also seized a vast amount of plunder, which they brought to Samaria. However, a prophet of Jehovah named Oded was there, and he went out to meet the army as it arrived at Samaria, greeting them with these words: "Because Jehovah, the God of your ancestors, was angry with the Judeans, he delivered them into your hand; but you have slaughtered them with such ferocity <margin>The prophet Oded forbids the Judean captives from being brought to Samaria.</margin> that it reaches up to heaven. And now you intend to <margin>30</margin> reduce the people of Judah and Jerusalem to be your male and female slaves? Is this not a crime against Jehovah your God? Therefore, listen to me: return these captives whom you have taken from your brothers, or else you will feel the wrath of Jehovah." Then some of the leaders of the Ephraimites—Azariah son of Johanan, Berechiah son of Meshillemoth, Jehizkiah son of Shallum, and Amasa son of Hadlai—rose up against those coming back from the war and said to them: "You shall not bring the captives here! For by doing so, you would make us guilty before Jehovah, <margin>40</margin> increasing our sin and our crime, as if our guilt were not already great enough, or as if there were too little wrath against Israel." Then the armed soldiers left the captives and the plunder in front of the officials and the whole assembly. The men named above stood up, took the captives, and from the spoils, they clothed all those who were naked. They gave them clothes and sandals, provided them with food and drink, anointed them with oil, and placed all the exhausted ones on donkeys. They brought them to Jericho, the city of palms, to their own kinsmen, and <margin>50</margin> then they returned to Samaria. At that time, King Ahaz sent to the King of Assyria to ask for help. For the Edomites <note>original: "Idumaei"</note> had again attacked and defeated the Judeans and taken captives. Furthermore, the Philistines <note>original: "Palaestini"</note> had made a raid on the towns in the foothills and the south of Judah, capturing Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, Gederoth, Soko, Timnah, and Gimzo, with their villages, and they settled there. For Jehovah was humbling Judah <margin>Hezekiah's speech to the Levites. 2 Kings 18. Tiglath-Pileser.</margin> on account of Ahaz, the king of Judah, who had led the Judeans into wickedness and had acted faithlessly against Jehovah.

### CHAPTER XXIX.

When Ahaz passed away and was buried in the city of Jerusalem (for he was not brought into the tombs of the kings of Israel), his son Hezekiah <note>original: "Ezechias"</note> succeeded him in the kingdom, being twenty-five years old. He reigned in Jerusalem for twenty-nine years; his mother's name was Abijah, the daughter of Zechariah. He did what was right in the eyes of Jehovah, imitating his ancestor David. In the first year of his reign, in the first month, he opened the doors of the temple of Jehovah and repaired them. He brought in the priests and the Levites, assembling them in the eastern square, and addressed them: "Hear me, Levites! Purify yourselves now, and purify the temple of Jehovah, the God of your ancestors, and carry out the filth from the sanctuary. For our fathers committed a great crime; they offended and deserted Jehovah our God, turning their backs on the tabernacle of Jehovah. They even closed the doors of the vestibule and extinguished the lamps; they neither burned incense nor offered burnt offerings <note>original: "solidum sacrificium" — literally a 'solid sacrifice,' referring to a whole burnt offering where the entire animal is consumed by fire.</note> to the God of Israel in his sanctuary. Therefore, the wrath of Jehovah was so great against the people of Judah and Jerusalem that he delivered them over to be an object of dread and hissing, as you see with your own eyes. For this reason, our fathers have fallen by the sword, and our children and wives have gone into captivity. Now, I intend to make a covenant with Jehovah, the God of Israel, so that his fierce anger may turn away from us. My sons, do not be negligent now; for Jehovah has chosen you to stand before him to minister, to be his servants, and to burn incense." Then the Levites rose up: Mahath son of Amasai and Joel son of Azariah, from the Kohathites; from the Merarites, Kish son of Abdi and Azariah son of Jehallelel; from the Gershonites, Joah son of Zimmah and Eden son of Joah; from the sons of Elizaphan, Shimri and Jeiel; from the sons of Asaph, Zechariah and Mattaniah; from the sons of Heman, Jehiel and Shimei; from the sons of Jedu-

From there, the Levites took it and carried it out to the Brook Kidron <note>original: "torrentem Cedronem" — a valley and stream on the eastern side of Jerusalem.</note>. He also stationed the Levites in the temple of Jehovah with cymbals, lutes <note>original: "nablis"</note>, and lyres <note>original: "citharis"</note>, according to the commandment of David and of Gad the king's seer and Nathan the prophet; for this arrangement had come from Jehovah through his prophets. The whole assembly worshiped while the song resounded and the trumpets blasted; all this continued until the sacrifice was finished. When it was over, the king and everyone present bowed down and gave honor to God. Then King Hezekiah and the officials commanded the Levites to praise Jehovah with the words of David and of Asaph the seer. They praised him with joy and bowed their heads in worship. Hezekiah then said, "Now that you have consecrated yourselves <note>original: "manibus suis Iouæ sacratis" — literally 'with your hands consecrated to Jehovah.'</note> to Jehovah, come near and bring sacrifices and thank offerings into the temple of Jehovah." ### CHAPTER XXX.

<margin>Hezekiah arranges for the Passover to be observed.</margin>
Then Hezekiah sent word to all Israel and Judah, and even wrote letters to the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, inviting them to come to the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem to observe the Passover for the Lord, the God of Israel. For the king, his officials, and the whole assembly of Jerusalem had decided to celebrate the Passover in the second month; they could not keep it at the usual time because not enough priests had purified themselves and the people had not yet gathered in Jerusalem. Therefore, it seemed right to the king and the entire assembly to issue a decree throughout all the borders of Israel, from Beersheba to Dan, that everyone should come to Jerusalem to celebrate the Passover for the Lord, the God of Israel; for it had not been performed according to the written law for a long time. So the couriers went throughout all Israel and Judah with letters from the king and his officials, following the king’s command, which said: "Return to the Lord, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, so that he may return to the remnant of you who have escaped the hands of the kings of Assyria. Do not be like your ancestors or your kinsmen, who were unfaithful to the Lord, the God of their fathers, so that he made them an object of horror, as you see. Therefore, do not be stiff-necked as your ancestors were; submit yourselves to the Lord and come to his sanctuary, which he has consecrated forever. Serve the Lord your God, so that his fierce anger may turn away from you. For if you return to the Lord, your kinsmen and your children will find compassion from those who led them away captive and will return to this land. For the Lord your God is gracious and merciful, and he will not turn his face from you if you return to him." But as the couriers traveled from town to town through the territory of Ephraim and Manasseh as far as Zebulun, the people mocked and ridiculed them. Nevertheless, some from Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem. Also in Judah, the hand of God was at work to give them one heart to carry out the command of the king and the officials, according to the word of the Lord. So a very great multitude gathered in Jerusalem to celebrate the Festival of Unleavened Bread <note>original: "Azymalia"</note> in the second month. They began by removing the pagan altars that were in Jerusalem, as well as the incense altars, and throwing them into the Kidron Valley.

<column-break/>

They slaughtered the Passover lamb on the fourteenth day of the second month. The priests and the Levites, being ashamed, purified themselves and brought burnt offerings into the temple of the Lord. They took their accustomed stations as prescribed in the Law of Moses, the man of God; the priests sprinkled the blood which they received from the hands of the Levites. For there were many in the assembly who had not purified themselves; therefore the Levites had to slaughter the Passover lambs for everyone who was not clean, to consecrate them to the Lord. Indeed, a great majority of the people from Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun had not purified themselves, yet they ate the Passover, which was not according to what was written. But Hezekiah prayed for them, saying, "May the good Lord be gracious to everyone who sets his heart to seek God—the Lord, I say, the God of their fathers—even if they are not purified according to the sanctuary's rules." The Lord heard Hezekiah’s prayer and healed the people. So the Israelites who were present in Jerusalem celebrated the Festival of Unleavened Bread for seven days with great joy, while the Levites and priests praised the Lord every day with loud instruments. Hezekiah spoke encouragingly to all the Levites who were well-skilled in the service of the Lord, and they ate the assigned food of the festival for seven days, offering peace sacrifices and giving thanks to the Lord, the God of their ancestors. Then the whole assembly decided to celebrate for another seven days, and they observed those seven days with gladness. For Hezekiah, king of Judah, provided a thousand bulls and ten thousand sheep for the multitude, and the officials provided another thousand bulls and ten thousand sheep, <margin>a. Because there was an abundance for the Levites, who lived on the tithes.</margin> and a great number of priests <gloss>a</gloss> purified themselves. So the whole assembly of Judah rejoiced, along with the priests, the Levites, and the whole assembly that came from Israel, as well as the foreigners who had come from the land of Israel or who lived in Judah. There was great joy in Jerusalem, for since the time of Solomon son of David, king of Israel, there had been nothing like this in Jerusalem. Then the priests and the Levites stood up and blessed the people, and their voice was heard; their prayer reached heaven, God's holy dwelling place.

### CHAPTER XXXII.

After these things and this faithful service, Sennacherib king of Assyria invaded Judah, set up camp against the fortified cities, and resolved to take them by force. Then Hezekiah, seeing that he prepared to attack Jerusalem with war, decided with his nobles and soldiers to block the spring waters that were outside the city. So, with their help, a huge multitude of men was gathered, and all the springs were blocked,

<column-break/>

as well as the stream that flowed through the middle of the region, so that if the kings of Assyria came, they would not find so much water. Then, having strengthened himself, he rebuilt every broken wall, erected towers and another wall outside, repaired Millo <note>original: "Mellonē" — the citadel or defensive terrace of Jerusalem</note> in the City of David, and made a great supply of missiles and shields. He appointed military commanders over the forces and, having called them together in the square of the city gate, spoke kindly to them in this manner: "**Be strong and courageous**, do not be afraid or dismayed by the king of Assyria or the great crowd that accompanies him, for there are more with us than with him. He has the strength of the flesh <note>original: "nerui corporei"</note>, but with us is the Lord our God to help us and to fight our battles." The people were encouraged by this speech of Hezekiah, king of Judah. Later, Sennacherib king of Assyria, who was then at Lachish with all his forces, sent his servants to Jerusalem to Hezekiah king of Judah and to all the Judeans in Jerusalem, saying: "Thus says Sennacherib king of Assyria: On what do you rely, that you remain in Jerusalem under siege?

Does Hezekiah deceive you, to deliver you to death by hunger and thirst, when he promises that your God, the Lord, will rescue you from the hand of the king of Assyria? Do you not know what I and my fathers have done to all the nations of the lands? Were the gods of the nations of other lands able to defend their lands from my hands? Who among all the gods of those nations, which my fathers destroyed, was able to protect his own from my hand, that your God should seem able to defend you from me? Therefore, do not let Hezekiah deceive you or induce you to believe him. For no god of any nation or kingdom was able to defend his people from me and my fathers; how much less shall your gods defend you against me!" The servants of Sennacherib spoke these things and more against the Lord God and against his worshiper Hezekiah, and Sennacherib wrote letters blaspheming and speaking evil of the Lord, the God of the Israelites, affirming that just as the gods of the nations of other lands had not defended their people from him, so Hezekiah’s God would not defend his people from him. Therefore, they cried out with a loud voice in the Judean language to the people of Jerusalem who were on the walls, to terrify and disturb them so they might take the city, speaking against the God of Jerusalem just as they spoke against the gods of the other nations of the world, which were made by human hands. But when King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah, the son of Amoz, prayed and cried out to heaven concerning this matter, the Lord sent a spirit <note>original: "genium" — here referring to an angel or divine messenger</note> who killed all the soldiers, leaders, and princes in the camp of the king of Assyria.

and of their righteous offspring; You who made heaven and earth with all their beauty; who restricted the sea by the word of Your command; who shut up the deep and sealed it with Your terrible and glorious name; at whose powerful presence all things fear and tremble; whose wrathful threat against sinners is unbearable, yet whose promised mercy is immense and unsearchable. Afterward, he built an outer wall for the City of *David* in the valley where the *Gihon* flows to the west, and where one enters by the Fish Gate, and around *Ophel*, and he made the wall very high. He also stationed military commanders in all the fortified towns of Judah. He removed the foreign gods and the idol from the Temple of the Lord, as well as all the altars he had built either on the mountain of the Lord’s Temple or in *Jerusalem*, and he threw them outside the city. He restored the altar of the Lord and offered sacrifices on it for safety and as tokens of gratitude, and he commanded the people of Judah to serve the Lord, the God of the *Israelites*. Although the people still sacrificed at high places, they did so only to the Lord their God. As for the rest of the acts of *Manasseh*, and his prayer to God, and the words of the seers who spoke to him in the name of the Lord, the God of the *Israelites*, they are contained in the history of the kings of *Israel*. Also, concerning his prayer and how it was granted, and his whole sin and crime, and the places in which he built high places or established groves and idols before he humbled himself, these are written in the records of *Hozai* <note>original: "Hozais" — often interpreted as "the Seers" rather than a proper name</note>. When *Manasseh* died, he was buried in his own house, and his son *Amon* succeeded him as king.
<margin>
Amon, King of Judah.
</margin>
*Amon* was twenty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned in *Jerusalem* for two years. He offended the Lord following the example of his father *Manasseh*; *Amon* sacrificed to and served all the idols that *Manasseh* had made. He did not humble himself before the Lord as *Manasseh* had done, but instead he committed many transgressions.

Therefore, his servants killed him through a conspiracy in his own house; however, the inhabitants of the land killed all those conspirators and appointed his son **Josiah** as king in his place.

### CHAPTER XXXIV.

**Josiah** obtained the kingdom at eight years of age and reigned in Jerusalem for thirty-one years. He obeyed the Lord <note>original: "Iouæ" — a Latinized form of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton, used throughout this text for the name of God</note> and, imitating the deeds of David his forefather, he did not turn aside in any direction. In the eighth year of his reign, while he was still a boy, he began to seek the God of his ancestor David. Then, in the twelfth year, he began to purge Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem of the shrines, the sacred groves, and the idols, whether carved or cast. In his presence, the altars of the Baals were destroyed, and he tore down the images placed upon them; he smashed and crushed the groves and the carved and cast idols, scattering the dust upon the graves of those who had sacrificed to them, and he burned the bones of the priests upon their own altars. Also, in the deserted places around the towns of the Manassites, Ephraimites, and Simeonites, even as far as Naphtali, he overturned the altars and groves. He pounded the smaller signs into pieces, and having torn down all the idols of the entire region of the Israelites, he returned to Jerusalem.

In the eighteenth year of his reign, after the land and the temple were purified, he sent Shaphan the son of Azaliah, Maaseiah the governor of the city, and Joah the son of Joahaz the recorder, to repair the temple of the Lord his God. When they came to Hilkiah the high priest, they took the money that had been brought into the temple of the Lord, which the Levites who kept the threshold had collected from the Manassites, the Ephraimites, and all the remnant of the Israelites, as well as from all Judah, Benjamin, and the inhabitants of Jerusalem. They delivered it into the hands of the overseers of the work who were in charge of the temple of the Lord. These overseers, occupied with the work of the temple, spent it on craftsmen and builders to repair and restore the temple, and to purchase squared stones and timber for the couplings and for the roofing of the buildings which the kings of Judah had destroyed.

The men did the work faithfully. Their overseers were Jahath and Obadiah, Levites of the descendants of Merari, and Zechariah and Meshullam of the Kohathites, who urged the work forward; all these Levites were skilled in musical instruments. They were also in charge of the porters and urged on the various tasks of the entire project. Among the Levites, there were also scribes, officials, and gatekeepers. While they were bringing out the money that had been carried into the temple of the Lord, Hilkiah the priest found the book of the law of the Lord given by Moses. He told Shaphan the scribe that he had found the book of the law in the temple of the Lord, and he handed the book to Shaphan. Shaphan brought the book to the king and reported the matter to him, namely, that the king's servants had carried out everything commanded of them: they had melted down the silver found in the temple of the Lord and delivered it to the officials and overseers. Then he further informed the king that a book had been given to him by Hilkiah the priest, and he read it in the presence of the king. When the king heard the words of the law, he tore his clothes and commanded Hilkiah, Ahikam the son of Shaphan, Abdon the son of Micah,

<column-break/>

Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah the king’s attendant, that they should go to inquire of the Lord both for himself and for the remnant of the Israelites and Jews concerning the words of the book that had been found. For he realized that a great wrath of the Lord had been poured out upon them, because their fathers had not taken care to fulfill everything written in that book according to the command of the Lord.

<margin>Huldah the prophetess</margin>
Then Hilkiah and the other royal officials went to Huldah the prophetess, the wife of Shallum (son of Tokhath, grandson of Hasrah), the keeper of the wardrobe. She lived in Jerusalem in the Second District <note>original: "altera urbis parte" — the 'Mishneh' or Second Quarter of the city</note>, and they explained the matter to her. She replied to them: "Thus says the Lord God of the Israelites: Tell the man who sent you to me: 'Thus says the Lord: I am about to bring evil upon this place and its inhabitants, namely all the curses described in the book which was read before the king of Judah. This is because they have abandoned me and burned incense to foreign gods, provoking me with all their deeds. Therefore, my wrath is so kindled against this place that it shall not be extinguished.' But to the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of the Lord, you shall report this: 'Thus says the Lord God of the Israelites: Regarding the words you have heard, because you were of a tender heart and submitted yourself to God when you heard his threats against this place and its inhabitants—because you were humble, tore your clothes, and wept before me—I also have heard you,' says the Lord. 'I will gather you to your ancestors, and you shall be laid in your tomb in peace; your eyes shall not see all the evil that I am about to bring upon this place and its inhabitants.'"

<margin>2 Kings 23</margin>
After this matter was reported to the king, he took care to summon all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem. Together with all the Jews, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the priests, and the Levites—in short, the entire people from the least to the greatest—he went up into the temple of the Lord. In their hearing, he read all the words of the Book of the Covenant found in the temple of the Lord. Standing at his pillar <note>original: "pulpito" — a raised platform or station for the king</note>, he made a covenant before the Lord, that he would follow the Lord and keep His precepts, warnings, and decrees with his whole mind and soul, executing the words of the covenant described in that book. All who were present in Jerusalem and Benjamin stood with him. Thus, the inhabitants of Jerusalem agreed to the divine covenant of the God of their fathers. Josiah removed every abomination from all the lands of the Israelites and directed all the Israelites found there to the worship of the Lord their God, so that throughout his lifetime they did not defect from the Lord, the God of their fathers.

### CHAPTER XXXV.

<margin>Josiah ordains sacred matters. 2 Kings 23; 3 Esdras 1</margin>
**J**osiah also celebrated the Passover to the Lord in Jerusalem; the Passover lamb was sacrificed on the fourteenth day of the first month. He assigned the priests to their duties and encouraged them in the service of the temple of the Lord. To the Levites, who were the teachers of all Israel and were consecrated to the Lord, he commanded that they should place the sacred Ark in the temple built by Solomon, son of David, king of Israel, so that it would no longer be carried on their shoulders. He told them: "Now serve the Lord your God and His people Israel. Prepare yourselves by families and divisions according to the decree of David, king of Israel, and the prescription of his son Solomon. Stand in the sanctuary according to the divisions of the ancestral families of your fellow countrymen..."

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>The altar is restored, and sacrifices are made.</margin>
And now, as the seventh month approached, when the Israelites were living in their towns, the whole people gathered as one man to Jerusalem. Then Jeshua the son of Jozadak and his fellow priests, and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel and his kinsmen, arose to build the altar of the God of the Israelites, to offer burnt offerings <note>original: "solida sacrificia" — literally 'whole' or 'solid' sacrifices, referring to the holocausts or burnt offerings where the entire animal was consumed by fire</note> upon it, as prescribed in the law of Moses, the man of God. Having set the altar upon its foundations—even though terror from the nations of the neighboring regions hung over them—they offered burnt offerings to the Lord upon it, namely the morning and evening sacrifices. They also celebrated the Festival of Booths <note>original: "umbraculorum festum" — also known as Sukkot or the Feast of Tabernacles</note> as prescribed, and the daily burnt offerings according to the ritual and requirement for each day. After that, they offered the continual burnt offering, and the offerings for the new moons and all the consecrated festivals of the Lord, as well as for everyone who made a voluntary offering to the Lord. From the first day of the seventh month, they began to offer burnt offerings to the Lord, though the foundation of the Lord’s shrine had not yet been laid. Therefore, they gave money to the stonecutters and craftsmen, and food, drink, and oil to the Sidonians and Tyrians, to bring cedar timber from Lebanon to the sea at Joppa, as had been granted to them by Cyrus, king of the Persians.

<margin>The restoration of the temple begins.</margin>
In the second year of their arrival at the shrine in Jerusalem, in the second month, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak, along with the rest of their kinsmen, the priests, the Levites, and all who had come to Jerusalem from the captivity, began the work. They appointed the Levites who were twenty years of age and older to oversee the work of the temple of the Lord. Jeshua with his sons and kinsmen, Kadmiel and his sons (the descendants of Judah), stood together to supervise those doing the work in the shrine, along with the sons of Henadad and their sons and kinsmen, the Levites. And when the builders laid the foundations of the Lord's temple, they stationed the priests in their robes with trumpets, and the Levites, the sons of Asaph, with cymbals, to praise the Lord according to the ordinance of David, king of Israel. And they sang, praising and giving thanks for the Lord’s goodness and His eternal mercy toward Israel. As they sang these praises to the Lord while the foundations of the temple of the Lord were being laid, all the people shouted with a great shout. But many of the priests and Levites and heads of families, the old men who had seen the former temple, wept with a loud voice when they saw this temple being founded; yet many others shouted for joy with a loud noise, so that the sound of the people’s joy could not be distinguished from the sound of the weeping, for the people shouted with so great a noise that the sound was heard from far away.

### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>The adversaries want to be admitted into the building partnership.</margin>
After the adversaries of the Jews and Benjamites heard that the shrine of the Lord God of Israel was being restored by the exiles, they approached Zerubbabel and the heads of families and asked to be admitted into the partnership of the building. They claimed that they sought the same God as the Jews and had been sacrificing to Him since the time of Esarhaddon, king of Assyria, who had brought them there. But Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the rest of the heads of the Israelite families replied to them that it was not for them to build the temple of their God together with the Jews; rather, the Jews alone would build it for the Lord God of the Israelites, just as Cyrus, king of the Persians, had commanded them. <margin>The restoration of the temple is hindered.</margin> Thus it happened that the inhabitants of the land hindered the Jews and discouraged them from building, and they hired counselors against them to frustrate their plan all the days of Cyrus, king of the Persians, until the reign of Darius, king of the Persians. <margin>Zerubbabel and Jeshua begin to restore the temple.</margin> And at the beginning of the reign of Ahasuerus <note>original: "Assueri"</note>, they wrote an accusation against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem. ### CHAPTER V.

Now when the prophet Haggai and Zechariah the son of Iddo the prophet were prophesying in the name of the God of the Israelites, which they possessed, to the Jews who were in Judea or Jerusalem, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak were stirred up and began to rebuild the temple of Jerusalem, with those divine prophets present and encouraging them. At that time Tattenai, the governor of Syria, and Shethar-bozenai, and their associates came to them, asking by whose command they were rebuilding that temple and repairing the walls. To which we, responding, indicated the names of the authors of this building. Thus, with God looking upon the Jewish elders, they were not stopped until the matter was reported to Darius and a letter was returned regarding that matter. Now in the copy of the letter which Tattenai, the governor of Syria, and Shethar-bozenai, and their associates the Apharsachites <note>A group of Persian officials or an ethnic group</note> living in Syria sent to King Darius, it was written to this effect: To King Darius, many greetings. Know, O King, that we went into the province of Judea to the temple of the great God, which is being built with massive stones, and the walls are covered with timber; and the work is being done by them both diligently and successfully. We asked those elders by whose command they were building that temple and repairing the walls, and we questioned them for their names, who their leaders are, so that we might write them down and inform you. "We are worshippers of the God of heaven and earth, and we are rebuilding the temple which many centuries ago had been built and completed by a great king of the Israelites. But because our ancestors provoked the God of heaven, he delivered them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, the Chaldean, who destroyed this temple and carried the people captive to Babylon. However, King Cyrus in the first year of his reign in Babylon issued a decree to rebuild this temple, and the gold and silver vessels of the temple, which Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple in Jerusalem and carried into the Babylonian temple, he took from the Babylonian temple and gave them to one named Sheshbazzar (whom he had made governor), and commanded him to go and place them in the temple in Jerusalem, and to take care that the temple be built on its old foundation. Therefore, if it seems good to you, O King, let a search be made in the royal archives which are there in Babylon, to see whether it was decreed by King Cyrus that the temple of Jerusalem should be rebuilt, and signify to us your judgment on this matter.

### CHAPTER VI.

Then King Darius commanded that a search be made in the library where the treasures were stored in Babylon, and a certain book was found at Ecbatana (which is a fortress in the province of Media), in which it was recorded: In the first year of his reign King Cyrus issued a decree that the temple of Jerusalem should be built where sacrifices might be offered, of such a size that the height should be sixty cubits and the width the same, with three rows of polished stones and one row of timber; and the costs should be supplied from the royal treasury. Also the gold and silver vessels of the temple, which Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple in Jerusalem and carried to Babylon, should be returned and brought back to the temple of Jerusalem, each to its place in the house of God.

<margin>Darius commands the temple to be rebuilt.</margin>
Therefore, you, Tattenai, governor of Syria, and Shethar-bozenai, and your associates the Apharsachites living in Syria, keep away from there, and allow that temple to be built and constructed on its site by the governor of Judea and the Jewish elders. Moreover, I command that you act with those elders of Judea for the construction of that temple, so that from the royal treasury—that is, from the taxes paid in Syria—the costs may be diligently supplied to these men, lest the work be interrupted. And whatever is needed—bulls, rams, lambs for sacrifice to the God of heaven, as well as wheat, salt, wine, and oil—let these be provided to them daily without fail according to the judgment of the priests of Jerusalem, so that they may have the means to offer sweet-smelling sacrifices to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and his sons. And I command this, that whoever of men shall change this order, let a beam be pulled from his own house and set up, and let him be hanged on it, and let his house be confiscated and leveled for this reason. May the God who has placed His name there destroy every king or private man who stretches out his hand to change or destroy this temple in Jerusalem. I, Darius, have commanded that this be done diligently.

No one could distinguish the sound of the shouts of joy from the sound of weeping, because the people made so much noise. And the sound was heard far away.

### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>The adversaries wish to be admitted into the partnership of building the temple.</margin>
When the enemies of Judah and Benjamin heard that the exiles were rebuilding the sanctuary for the LORD, the God of Israel, they approached Zerubbabel and the heads of the families and said, "Let us help you build because, like you, we seek your God and have been sacrificing to him since the time of Esarhaddon king of Assyria, who brought us here." But Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the rest of the heads of the families of Israel answered, "You have no part with us in building a temple to our God. We alone will build it for the LORD, the God of Israel, as King Cyrus, the king of Persia, commanded us."

<margin>The restoration of the temple is hindered.</margin>
Then the local residents set out to discourage the people of Judah and make them afraid to go on building. They bribed officials to work against them and frustrate their plans during the entire reign of Cyrus king of Persia and down to the reign of Darius king of Persia. At the beginning of the reign of Xerxes <note>original: "Assueri" — Ahasuerus, often identified as Xerxes I</note>, they filed an accusation against the people of Judah and Jerusalem. And in the days of Artaxerxes king of Persia, Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel and the rest of his associates wrote a letter to Artaxerxes king of Persia. The letter was written in Aramaic script and in the Aramaic language <note>original: "sermone Syriaco" — refers to Aramaic, the lingua franca of the Persian Empire</note>. Rehum the commanding officer and Shimshai the secretary wrote a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king as follows: A copy of the letter they sent to him from Rehum the commanding officer, Shimshai the secretary and the rest of their associates—the judges, officials and administrators over the people from Tripolis, Persia, Erech and Babylon, the Elamites of Susa, and the other people whom the great and honorable Ashurbanipal <note>original: "Asenaphar"</note> deported and settled in the cities of Samaria and elsewhere in Trans-Euphrates. To King Artaxerxes: From your servants, the men of Trans-Euphrates. The king should know that the Jews who came up to us from you have gone to Jerusalem and are rebuilding that rebellious and wicked city. They are restoring the walls and laying the foundations. Furthermore, the king should know that if this city is built and its walls are completed, no more taxes, tribute, or duty will be paid,

As soon as this copy of the letter of King Artaxerxes was read before Rehum the master of accounts, and Shimshai the scribe, and their associates, they hurried to Jerusalem to the Jews and stopped them by force and power. Thus the work of the temple <note>original: "fani" — sanctuary or temple</note> of Jerusalem lay interrupted until the second year of the reign of Darius, King of the Persians.

### CHAPTER V.

However, the prophet Haggai and Zechariah the son of Iddo the prophet, prophesied in the name of the God of the Israelites, which was upon them, to the Jews who were in Judea or Jerusalem. Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel and Jeshua the son of Jozadak arose and began to rebuild the temple of Jerusalem, with the divine prophets present and encouraging them. At that time, Tattenai the governor of Syria, and Shethar-bozenai, and their associates came to them and asked by whose mandate they were rebuilding that temple and repairing the walls. In response to this, we gave the names of the authors of that building project. But because the eye of God was watching over the Jewish elders, they were not forbidden from continuing until the matter could be referred to Darius, and a letter on the subject could be sent back. In the copy of the letter which Tattenai the governor of Syria, and Shethar-bozenai, and their associates the Apharsachites living in Syria, sent to King Darius, it was written to this effect: To King Darius, much health. Know, O king, that we went into the province of Judea to the temple of the great God, which is being built with massive stones and walls covered with timber; the work is being done both diligently and successfully by them. We inquired of those elders by whose mandate they were building that temple and repairing the walls, and we questioned them for their names—who their leaders are—so that we might write them down and signify them to you. They answered us to this effect:

<column-break/>

"We are the worshippers of the God of heaven and earth, and we are rebuilding the temple that was constructed and finished many centuries ago by a very great king of the Israelites. But after our ancestors provoked the God of heaven to anger, he delivered them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar the Chaldean king of Babylon, who destroyed this temple and carried its people captive to Babylon. However, King Cyrus, in the first year of his reign over Babylon, published an edict concerning the rebuilding of this sanctuary; he even took the gold and silver vessels of the sanctuary (which Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple of Jerusalem and carried into the temple of Babylon) out of the Babylonian temple and delivered them to a man named Sheshbazzar <note>original: "Sasbasari"</note>—whom he had appointed as governor—and commanded him to go and place them in the temple of Jerusalem, and to see that the sanctuary was constructed on its same foundation. Then that Sheshbazzar came and laid the foundations of the temple of Jerusalem, and from that time until now it has been under construction, but it is not yet finished." Therefore, if it seems good to you, O king, let a search be made in the royal archives which are there in Babylon, to see if it was indeed decreed by King Cyrus that the temple of Jerusalem should be rebuilt, and signify to us your judgment on this matter.

### CHAPTER VI.

<margin>Darius commands the temple to be rebuilt.</margin>
Then King Darius commanded that a search be made in the library where the treasures were stored in Babylon, and there was found at Ecbatana (which is a fortress in the province of Media) a certain scroll in which it was recorded: In the first year of his reign, King Cyrus issued an edict that the temple of Jerusalem should be built where sacrifices are made, with such dimensions that the height should be sixty cubits and the width sixty cubits, with three rows of massive stones and one row of timber; and the expense should be supplied from the royal treasury. Also, let the gold and silver vessels of the sanctuary, which Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple of Jerusalem and brought to Babylon, be returned and carried back to the temple in Jerusalem, each to its own place in the house of God. Therefore, you, Tattenai the governor of Syria, and Shethar-bozenai, and your associates the Apharsachites dwelling in Syria, keep your distance from there; let the work of that sanctuary proceed, and allow the governor of Judea and the elders of the Jews to build it in its place. I further command that you act with those elders of the Jews regarding the construction of that sanctuary in this way: that from the royal treasury—that is, from the taxes paid in Syria—the expenses be diligently supplied to those men so that the work is not interrupted. And whatever is necessary—bulls, rams, and lambs for sacrifice to the God of heaven, as well as wheat, salt, wine, and oil—let these be provided to them daily without fail, according to the judgment of the priests in Jerusalem, so that they may offer sweet-smelling sacrifices to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and his sons. And I issue this decree: that whoever changes this mandate, a beam shall be pulled from his own house and set up, and he shall be hung upon it, and because of this, his house shall be confiscated and leveled. And may the God who has placed his name there destroy every king or private person who stretches out a hand to change or destroy that temple in Jerusalem. I, Darius, have commanded that this be done diligently.

EZRA

Then Tattenai, the governor of Syria, and Shethar-bozenai, and their associates, diligently executed the command of King Darius. Therefore, the Jewish elders successfully continued building, encouraged by the prophecies of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah the son of Iddo <note>original: "Adonis filio" — while the text says "son of Adonis," this refers to the biblical Zechariah, son of Iddo</note>. They completed the building by the command of the God of Israel and by the decrees of Cyrus, Darius, and Artaxerxes, the kings of Persia. When the temple was finished on the third day of the month of Adar <note>The twelfth month of the Hebrew calendar, roughly February-March</note>, in the sixth year of the reign of King Darius, the Israelites—the priests, the Levites, and the rest of the returned exiles—celebrated the dedication of this temple with joy. For this dedication, they sacrificed one hundred bulls, two hundred rams, and four hundred lambs. As a sin offering for all Israel, they offered twelve male goats, corresponding to the number of the tribes of Israel. They assigned the priests to their divisions and the Levites to their groups for the service of God in Jerusalem, as prescribed in the book of Moses.

<margin>The returning exiles celebrate Passover</margin>
The returned exiles also celebrated the Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month. Once the priests and Levites had purified themselves—and every single one of them was clean—the Levites slaughtered the Passover lamb for all the exiles, for their brothers the priests, and for themselves. Then the Israelites who had returned from exile ate the meal, together with all those who had separated themselves from the impurities of the nations of the land to seek Jehovah <note>original: "Iouæ" — a Latinization of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton, often rendered as Jehovah or Yahweh</note>, the God of Israel. They celebrated the Feast of Unleavened Bread for seven days with joy, because the Lord had filled them with gladness by turning the heart of the king of Assyria <note>Though Artaxerxes was King of Persia, he is here titled after the former empire of the region</note> toward them, so that he helped them in the work of the house of God, the God of Israel.

### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>Ezra sets out from Babylon to Jerusalem.</margin>
After these events, during the reign of Artaxerxes, king of the Persians, Ezra—whose lineage traces back through Seraiah, Azariah, Hilkiah, Shallum, Zadok, Ahitub, Amariah, Azariah, Meraioth, Zerahiah, Uzzi, Bukki, Abishua, Phinehas, and Eleazar, to Aaron the chief priest—departed from Babylon. He was a man highly learned in the Law of Moses and the teachings given by Jehovah, the God of Israel. The king granted him everything he requested because the hand of the Lord his God was upon him. Some of the Israelites, including priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple servants, also went up to Jerusalem in the seventh year of King Artaxerxes. Ezra arrived in Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth month of the king's seventh year, having begun his journey from Babylon on the first day of the first month; he enjoyed the very favorable help of his God. For Ezra had devoted his heart not only to the study and practice of the law of the Lord, but also to teaching the Israelites statutes and justice.

<margin>The letter of Artaxerxes to Ezra.</margin>
King Artaxerxes had given a letter to Ezra the priest and teacher, a man learned in the words of the commandments and statutes given by the Lord to Israel. This is a copy of that letter: "Artaxerxes, king of kings, to Ezra the priest and eminent teacher of the law of the God of heaven, a Canaanite <note>original: "Chananæo" — likely a transcription variant for a greeting or a title of peace</note>. I have decreed that anyone of the people of Israel, their priests, or their Levites in my kingdom who freely chooses to go to Jerusalem may go with you. Since you are sent by the king and his seven counselors to conduct an inquiry regarding Judah and Jerusalem according to the law of your God which is in your hand, you are to carry the silver and gold that the king and his counselors have freely offered to the God of Israel, whose dwelling is in Jerusalem, as well as

<column-break/>

<margin>Ezra summons the priests from Iddo.</margin>
whatever silver and gold you find in the entire province of Babylon, along with the voluntary offerings that the people and priests contribute for the temple of their God in Jerusalem. With this money, you shall diligently buy bulls, rams, and lambs, along with their grain offerings and drink offerings of wine, which you shall offer upon the altar of the temple of your God in Jerusalem. Use the rest of the silver and gold however you and your kinsmen see fit, according to the will of your God. Furthermore, deliver the vessels that have been given to you for the service of the temple of your God before the God of Jerusalem. Any other expenses required for the temple of your God, you may pay from the royal treasury. I, King Artaxerxes, command all the treasurers in Syria <note>Referring to the province of "Beyond the River"</note> that whatever Ezra the priest, the teacher of the law of the God of heaven, requires of you, it must be provided diligently—up to one hundred talents of silver, one hundred cors of wheat, one hundred baths of wine, one hundred baths of oil, and salt without limit. Whoever does not obey the law of your God and the law of the king, let judgment be strictly executed upon him, whether by death, exile, confiscation of goods, or imprisonment."

<margin>Ezra gives thanks to God for the king's benevolence.</margin>
I give thanks to Jehovah, our ancestral God, who put such a thing into the heart of the king to beautify the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem, and who has extended his mercy to me before the king, his counselors, and all the king's mighty officers. I reviewed the group and found none of the Levites <note>The tribe of Israel designated specifically for religious service</note> there, except for Eliezer, Ariel, Shemaiah, Elnathan, Jarib, Elnathan, Nathan, Zechariah, and other men of wisdom. Thus, because the hand of our God was favorable toward us, they brought us a man of great understanding from the descendants of Mahli, the son of Levi and grandson of Israel; they also brought Sherebiah with his sons and brothers, totaling eighteen men; and Hashabiah, and with him Jeshaiah of the descendants of Merari, along with his brothers and their sons, twenty men. Additionally, there were two hundred and twenty temple servants <note>original: "dedititios" — referring to the Nethinim, a group of workers given to the Levites to assist in temple duties</note> whom David and the princes had assigned to help the Levites, all of whom were listed by name. There, at the river Ahava, I proclaimed a fast so that we might humble ourselves before our God and seek from him a safe journey for ourselves, our children, and all our possessions. For I was ashamed to ask the king for soldiers and horsemen to protect us from enemies on the road; for we had told the king that the help of our God is with all who seek him, but his power and wrath are against those who forsake him. Therefore, when we had fasted and obtained what we asked from our God, I chose twelve of the leading priests—namely Sherebiah and Hashabiah, and with them ten of their brothers. To them I weighed out the silver, the gold, the vessels, and the offerings for the temple of our God, which had been contributed by the king, his counselors, his princes, and all the Israelites who were present. I placed into their hands six hundred and fifty talents of silver, silver vessels weighing one hundred talents, one hundred talents of gold, twenty gold bowls worth a thousand drachmas, and two vessels of fine, polished bronze, as elegant as if they were made of gold. Then I said to them: "You are sacred to the LORD <note>original: "Iouæ" — The author uses the Latin name 'Jove' as a humanist convention to refer to Jehovah/YHWH</note>, as are the sacred vessels and the silver and gold freely offered to the LORD, the God of your fathers. Guard them vigilantly until you weigh them out before the leading priests, the Levites, and the heads of the families of Jerusalem in the chambers of the temple of the LORD." When the priests and Levites had received the weight of silver and gold and the vessels to be carried to Jerusalem to the temple of our God, we set out from the river Ahava on the twelfth day of the first month to go to Jerusalem. After we arrived there, having been helped by our God and defended from enemies and ambushes along the way, we remained for three days. On the fourth day, the silver, gold, and vessels were weighed in the temple of our God into the hand of Meremoth the priest, son of Uriah. With him was Eleazar son of Phinehas, and with them were the Levites Jozabad son of Jeshua and Noadiah son of Binnui. Everything was numbered and weighed, and at that very hour the entire weight was recorded. After the king’s mandates were delivered to the royal satraps and the governors of Syria, they gave their support to the people and the sanctuary.

### CHAPTER IX.

<margin>10</margin>
**A**fter these things were completed, the leaders came to me and pointed out that the people of Israel, including the priests and Levites, had not separated themselves from the other nations of the lands, but were instead imitating the abominations of the Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, Ammonites, Moabites, Egyptians, and Amorites. They have taken the daughters of these people for themselves and for their sons, mixing the holy seed with the other nations of the lands; indeed, the leaders and magistrates have been the foremost in this crime. When I heard this, I tore my garments and my cloak, pulled hair from my head and beard, and sat down in mourning. Then everyone who trembled at the words of the God of Israel because of the crime of the exiles gathered around me. After I had sat in mourning until the hour of the evening sacrifice, I rose from my affliction. With my garment and cloak still torn, I fell on my knees and spread out my hands to the LORD my God, and I said: "O my God, I am hardly able

<margin>Shecaniah consoles Ezra.</margin>
Shecaniah the son of Jehiel, a descendant of Elam, spoke to Ezra in this way: "We have indeed committed a sin against our God by taking foreign wives from the local nations. But even so, there is still hope for Israel in this matter. Come now: let us make a covenant with our God to send away all these women and the children born to them, as decreed by the Lord and by those who revere the teaching <note>original: "disciplinam" — referring to the religious instruction or law</note> of our God; and let it be done according to the law. Arise, for this matter concerns you as much as us: take courage and act." Then Ezra rose and compelled the leading priests, the Levites, and all the Israelites to swear an oath that they would do so. And once they had sworn, he left the temple <note>original: "fano"</note> and went to the chamber of Jehohanan the son of Eliashib, where he fasted from food and drink, mourning the crime of those who had returned from exile. Then a proclamation was issued throughout Judah and Jerusalem that all the exiles should assemble at Jerusalem. It was decreed by the leaders and elders that anyone who did not arrive within three days would have all his property confiscated <note>original: "sacrarentur" — meaning dedicated to the temple treasury</note> and he himself would be excluded from the community of the returned exiles. Therefore, all the men of Judah and Benjamin gathered at Jerusalem within those three days, on the twentieth day of the ninth month. The entire assembly sat in the open area of the temple, trembling both because of the matter itself and because of the heavy rain.

<margin>Ezra rebukes the people for taking foreign wives.</margin>
When Ezra the priest stood up, he spoke to them: "You have committed a crime by taking foreign wives, increasing the guilt of Israel. Now, give glory to Jehovah <note>original: "Iouæ" — a Latinization of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton, the name of God</note>, the God of your ancestors, and by obeying His will, separate yourselves both from the local nations and from your foreign wives." To this, the whole assembly responded with a loud voice: "We must do exactly as you have said. However, the people are many, it is the rainy season, and we cannot stay outside; nor is this a task for just one or two days, for we have sinned greatly in this matter. Therefore, let our leaders be appointed for the whole community. Let everyone in our towns who has taken a foreign wife come at appointed times, accompanied by the elders and judges of each town, until the anger of our God is turned away from us concerning this matter." Thus, Jonathan the son of Asahel and Jahzeiah the son of Tikvah were appointed to oversee the business, with Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite assisting them. The returning exiles complied, and Ezra the priest chose men who were heads of their ancestral families, all designated by name. They sat down on the first day of the tenth month to investigate the matter, and they finished dealing with all the men who had married foreign wives by the first day of the first month.

<margin>Those who had married foreign wives.</margin>
Among the families of the priests who had married foreign wives, there were found the sons of Jeshua the son of Jozadak and his brothers: Maaseiah, Eliezer, Jarib, and Gedaliah. # THE SECOND BOOK
## OF EZRA <note>This book is known in most modern Bibles as the Book of Nehemiah</note>

### CHAPTER I.

-> The history of Nehemiah, son of Hacaliah. <-

<margin>a That is, of the reign of Artaxerxes.</margin>
In the twentieth year <gloss>a</gloss>, in the month of Chislev <note>The ninth month of the Hebrew calendar, roughly November/December</note>, while I was in the citadel of Susa, Hanani, one of my kinsmen, arrived with some other men from Judah. When I questioned them about the Jews who had escaped and remained from the captivity, and about Jerusalem, they replied that the survivors in the province were in great trouble and shame: the walls of Jerusalem were broken down and its gates had been consumed by fire. When I heard these things, I sat down and wept and mourned for several days. I fasted and pleaded with the God of heaven with these prayers:

<margin>Nehemiah prays to God to grant him favor with Artaxerxes.</margin>

I confess the sins of the Israelites, which we—both I and my father's house—have committed against you. ## CHAPTER II.

Now, I was the king's cupbearer <note>original: "praegustator" — literally a "pre-taster," an official who tasted wine to ensure it was not poisoned</note>. Therefore, in the month of Nisan, in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes, when I had taken up the wine placed before him and was serving him, and because I appeared unusually sad in his presence, the king spoke to me thus: "Why is it that your face is so sad, though you are not sick? This can be nothing but sadness of heart." At this, I was struck with a great fear and said: "May the king live forever! Can I not have a sad face when the city where the tombs of my ancestors lie is destroyed, and its gates consumed by fire?" Then the king said: "What then do you ask for?" Having prayed to the God of heaven, I said to him: "If it seems right to you, O king, and if I, your servant, please you, I ask that you send me into Judea, to the city containing the tombs of my ancestors, so that I may rebuild it." And the king said, with his wife sitting beside him: "How long will your journey be, and when will you return?" Then, since it seemed good to the king to send me, I set a time for him and replied: "If it pleases you, O king, see that letters are given to me for the governors of Syria <note>Referring to the province "Beyond the River" or Trans-Euphrates</note>, who may escort me until I reach Judea. Also, a letter to Asaph, the keeper of the king's forest, that he may supply me with timber to rebuild the gates of the fortress located near the temple, and for the city walls, and for the house where I shall stay." Then the king, aided by divine help, granted these things to me. I went to the governors of Syria and delivered the royal letters to them, accompanied by captains of the army and horsemen sent by the king. When Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite servant heard of this, they were deeply grieved that a man had come who sought the welfare of the children of Israel. After I came to Jerusalem and had been there for three days, I rose in the night with a few men; I had not told anyone what God had put in my mind to do for Jerusalem, nor did I have any beast with me except the one I rode. So I went out at night by the Valley Gate, passed the Dragon’s Spring, and came to the Dung Gate. I surveyed the demolished walls of Jerusalem and its gates consumed by fire. I proceeded to the Fountain Gate and the King’s Pool, but there was no room for the beast I was riding to pass through. So I went up by the valley stream <note>original: "torrentē" — the Kidron Valley</note> at night, and having inspected the walls, I returned to the Valley Gate and, entering through it, I went back. The magistrates did not know where I had gone or what I was doing; I had not yet revealed it to the Jews, the priests, the nobles, the magistrates, or the rest of those who would do the work. Then I showed them that they themselves saw the trouble we were in: Jerusalem laid waste and its gates burned with fire. Therefore, we must rebuild the walls of Jerusalem so that we are no longer a disgrace. And when I had shown them how much my God had helped me and what the king had said to me, they were greatly encouraged—

## CHAPTER III.

<margin>The walls of Jerusalem are repaired.</margin>

### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>Adversaries mock the restoration of Jerusalem.</margin>
After Sanballat understood that we were restoring the walls, he was incensed with great indignation and began to mock the Jews. "What are these weak Jews doing?" he said among his kinsmen and the Samaritan soldiers. "Will they be allowed to do this? Will they offer sacrifices? Will they ever finish? Will they use these revived stones from the heaps of rubbish, even those that were burned?" And Tobiah the Ammonite, who was with him, said: "Indeed, even if a fox should climb upon their building, it would easily tear down their stone wall." Hear us, our God, for we have become an object of contempt; turn their shame back upon their own heads, and let them be held in contempt as captives in some other land. Do not cover their guilt, nor let their sin be blotted out from your sight, for they have provoked those who build. So we built the wall, and the entire wall was joined together to half its height, for the people had a mind intent on the work. But after Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabs, the Ammonites, and the men of Ashdod heard that the walls of Jerusalem were being repaired and that the gaps were beginning to be closed, they were so grieved that they all conspired together to wage war against Jerusalem and to stir up trouble there. But we prayed to our God and set a guard against them day and night to protect ourselves, although the Jews complained that the strength of the porters was failing, and since there was so much rubble, they were not able to build the wall.

<margin>The walls of Jerusalem are restored despite the enemies.</margin>
Furthermore, our enemies determined to overwhelm us suddenly and unexpectedly, to stop the work by killing us. <margin>a. Frequently.</margin> But when the Jews who lived near them came and told us ten times over from every place where they lived among us, I stationed men by their fa-

<column-break/>

milies in the lower places behind the walls in the trenches, armed with swords, spears, and bows. After surveying the situation, I set out to warn the nobles, the officials, and the rest of the common people not to fear them, but to remember the great and terrible Lord, and to fight for their kinsmen, their children, their wives, and their homes. Thus, after it was heard by our enemies that the matter was known to us, their counsel was broken by God’s will, and we all returned to the walls, each to his own work. From that day forward, half of my young men did the work, while the other half held spears, shields, bows, and coats of mail, with the leaders stationed behind the entire house of Judah who were building on the wall. Those who carried burdens or positioned them did the work with one hand and held a weapon in the other. The builders worked with their swords girded at their sides. The trumpeter remained with me. I had warned the leaders and officials and the rest of the common people that the work was great and widely spread out, and we were scattered on the walls far from one another. Therefore, in whatever place they heard the sound of the trumpet, they were to gather to us there; our God would fight for us. So we did the work, and half of them held spears from the rising of the dawn until the stars appeared. At the same time, I commanded the people that each man and his servant should stay overnight in the middle of Jerusalem, so that we might be on guard by night and work by day. Neither I, nor my kinsmen, nor my servants, nor the guards following me ever took off our clothes; each man held his weapon in his right hand.

### CHAPTER V.

<margin>The complaint of the poor against the moneylenders.</margin>
<margin>Nehemiah’s restraint. I did not take the food allotted to the governor as was customary for previous rulers.</margin>
Meanwhile, there arose a great outcry of the people and their wives against their fellow Jews. There were some who said: "The number of us and our children is great; we must obtain grain so that we may live." Others said: "We must mortgage our fields, vineyards, and houses so that we may obtain grain during the famine." Some said: "We have borrowed money for the king’s tribute <note>A tax paid to the Persian Empire</note> against our fields and vineyards. Now, since our flesh is the same as that of our kinsmen, and our children the same as theirs, yet we have given our children into slavery, and some of our daughters have already been sold, and we have no way to redeem them since others hold our fields and vineyards." When I heard their outcry and these words, and after I had pondered the matter in my heart, I rebuked the nobles and officials who were demanding interest from their own kinsmen. Having called a great assembly because of them, I spoke thus: "We have redeemed our Jewish kinsmen who were sold to foreign nations according to our ability; and will you now sell your own kinsmen, only for them to be bought back by us?" And when they were silent and found nothing to answer, I said: "What you are doing is not right. Should you not live in the fear of our God to avoid the reproach of our foreign enemies? I, too, and my kinsmen and my servants have lent them money and grain; come, let us abandon this debt. Return to them this very day their fields, vineyards, olive groves, and houses, and remit the one-percent interest <note>original: "centesima" — a monthly interest rate of 1% (12% annually)</note> on the money, grain, wine, and oil that you have lent them." Then they promised they would return them and demand nothing more, doing as I had said. And I summoned the priests and made them swear to do so.

# BOOK II.
<note>In the historical context of this manuscript, the "Second Book" refers to the Book of Nehemiah, which was often grouped with Ezra.</note>

Then, shaking out the fold of my garment, I said, "May God so shake out every man from his house and his labor who does not perform this promise; even so may he be shaken out and emptied." And the whole assembly said, "So be it," and they praised God. And the people did according to this word. Furthermore, from the time that the governorship of Judah was committed to me—that is, from the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes until his thirty-second year, for those twelve years—neither I nor my kinsmen lived off the <term>governor’s provisions</term> <note>original: "uictu prætorio" — the official food allowance or tax usually collected to support the local ruler</note>, whereas the previous governors who were before me had burdened the people, taking from them forty silver shekels for bread and wine. Even their servants acted overbearingly toward the common people, but I did not do so, because of the fear of God. Instead, I applied myself to the work of rebuilding these walls, and we did not buy any land; all my servants were gathered there for the work. Moreover, there were at my table one hundred and fifty Jews and officials, besides those who came to us from the surrounding nations. Thus, every day one ox, six choice sheep, and poultry were prepared for me; and every ten days, a great abundance of every kind of wine was provided. Yet, despite this, I did not demand the governor's allowance, because the work weighed heavily enough upon this people. Remember me, my God, for good, according to all that I have done for this people.

### CHAPTER VI.

When it was reported to Sanballat, Tobiah, Geshem the Arab, and the rest of our enemies that I had rebuilt the wall so that no breach remained in it (though at that time I had not yet set the doors in the gates), Sanballat and Geshem sent a message to me, saying: "Come, let us meet together in the villages in the plain of Ono." But they intended to do me harm. I sent messengers to them, saying, "I am doing a great work and I cannot come down; why should the work stop while I leave it to come down to you?" They sent this same message to me four times, and I answered them in the same way. Then, for the fifth time, Sanballat sent his servant to me with an open letter in his hand, written in this manner: "It is reported among the nations, and Geshem says it, that you and the Jews intend to rebel; that is why you are rebuilding the wall, so that you may become their king. It is even said you have appointed prophets to proclaim you king of Judah in Jerusalem. Now, since the king will hear these reports, come now, and let us consult together." Then I sent a reply to him, saying, "Nothing such as you say is happening; you are inventing these things out of your own heart." For they were all trying to frighten us, thinking, "Their hands will grow weak from the work, and it will not be completed." Therefore, I strengthened myself. When I went to the house of Shemaiah son of Delaiah, the grandson of Mehetabel, who was confined to his house, he suggested that we meet in the house of God, within the sanctuary, and close the doors of the temple. He said, "They are coming to kill you; they are coming at night to kill you." But I replied, "Should a man like me flee? Or should someone like me go into the temple to save his life? I will not go in." Then I realized that God had not sent him, but that he had pronounced this prophecy against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him. He was hired for this purpose: that I should be frightened and act in this way and sin, so that they might give me a bad name and reproach me.

<column-break/>

<margin>The wall of Jerusalem is completed.</margin>
Remember, my God, these deeds of Tobiah and Sanballat, and also the prophetess Noadiah and the rest of the prophets who tried to intimidate me. So the wall was finished on the twenty-fifth day of the month Elul, in fifty-two days. When all our enemies heard of it and all the surrounding nations saw it, they lost much of their confidence, for they perceived that this work had been accomplished by our God. Moreover, in those days many letters were sent by the nobles of Judah to Tobiah, and Tobiah’s letters came to them. For many in Judah were bound by oath to him, since he was the son-in-law of Shecaniah son of Arah, and his son Jehohanan had married the daughter of Meshullam son of Berechiah. Also, they spoke of his good deeds in my presence and reported my words to him. And Tobiah sent letters to frighten me.

### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>Nehemiah appoints guards for the walls.</margin>
After the wall had been built and I had set up the doors, and the gatekeepers, the singers, and the Levites had been appointed, I gave charge of Jerusalem to my brother Hanani and to Hananiah the commander of the citadel, for he was a faithful man and feared God more than many. I said to them, "Do not let the gates of Jerusalem be opened until the sun is hot; and while the guards are still standing there, let them shut and bar the doors. Appoint guards from among the inhabitants of Jerusalem, each to his watch, and each in front of his own house." Now the city was wide and large, but there were few people in it and the houses had not yet been rebuilt. Then my God put it into my heart to assemble the nobles, the officials, and the common people to be enrolled by genealogy. I found the <term>register</term> <note>original: "codicē" — a book or ledger</note> of the genealogy of those who had come up at the first, and I found written in it: <margin>Those who returned to Jerusalem from exile.</margin> THESE ARE THE PEOPLE OF THE PROVINCE who came up out of the captivity of those whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried away, and who returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own town. They came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Azariah, Raamiah, Nahamani, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispereth, Bigvai, Nehum, and Baanah. The number of the men of the people of Israel was this: the descendants of Parosh: 2,172; of Shephatiah: 372; of Arah: 652; of Pahath-moab (through the line of Jeshua and Joab): 2,818; of Elam: 1,254; of Zattu: 845; of Zaccai: 760; of Binnui: 648; of Bebai: 628; of Azgad: 2,322; of Adonikam: 667; of Bigvai: 2,067; of Adin: 655; of Hezem: 328; of Bezai: 324; of Hariph: 112; of Gibeon: 95. The men of Bethlehem and Netophah: 188; of Anathoth: 128; of Beth-azmaveth: 42; of Kiriath-jearim, Kephirah, and Beeroth: 743; of Ramah and Geba: 621; of Michmas: 122; of Bethel and Ai: 123; of the other Nebo: 52.

From Pashhur, one thousand two hundred forty-seven. From Harim, one thousand seventeen. The Levites: Jeshua, from the descendants of Kadmiel, from the children of Hodaviah, seventy-four. The <term>Temple Servants</term> <note>original: "Dedititij" — literally "the given ones," referring to the Nethinim who were dedicated to manual labor for the Temple</note>: the descendants of Ziha, Hasupha, Tabbaoth, Keros, Sia, Padon, Lebana, Hagaba, Salmai, Hanan, Giddel, Gahar, Reaiah, Rezin, Nekoda, Gazzam, Uzza, Paseah, Besai, Meunim, Nephusim, Bakbuk, Hakupha, Harhur, Bazlith, Mehida, Harsha, Barkos, Sisera, Temah, Neziah, Hatipha; and also the descendants of Solomon's servants: Sotai, Sophereth, Perida, Jaala, Darkon, Giddel, Shephatiah, Hattil, the people of Pokereth-hazzebaim, and Amon. The total of the Temple servants and the descendants of Solomon’s servants was three hundred ninety-two.
Those who went up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer could not prove their family or lineage, whether they were truly of Israel: the descendants of Delaiah, Tobiah, and Nekoda, six hundred forty-two.
And of the priests: the descendants of <margin>a. He had been made a Gileadite.</margin> Habaiah, Hakkoz, and Barzillai, who had taken a wife from the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite and had <insert>taken on</insert> their name.
