The total sum of the entire multitude was forty-two thousand three hundred sixty, besides their male and female servants, who numbered seven thousand three hundred thirty-seven. Among them were two hundred forty-five male and female singers. There were seven hundred thirty-six horses, two hundred forty-five mules, four hundred thirty-five camels, and six thousand seven hundred twenty donkeys.
Some of the heads of the families contributed to the work: the Governor gave to the treasury one thousand <term>drachmas</term> <note>An ancient unit of currency or weight</note> of gold, fifty bowls, and five hundred thirty priestly garments. Then some of the heads of the families gave to the treasury for the work twenty thousand drachmas of gold and two thousand two hundred silver <term>minas</term> <note>A unit of weight roughly equal to 1.25 pounds</note>. The rest of the people gave twenty thousand drachmas of gold, two thousand minas of silver, and sixty-seven priestly garments.
The priests, the Levites, the gatekeepers, the singers, the common people, the Temple servants, and all the Israelites settled in their towns.

### CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>Ezra reads the law to the people.</margin>
And when the seventh month approached, while the Israelites were living in their towns, all the people gathered as one man in the open square in front of the Water Gate. They told Ezra the <term>scribe</term> <note>original: "professori" — one who teaches or professes the Law</note> to bring the Book of the Law of Moses, which the Lord had given to Israel. Then Ezra the priest, in the presence of the entire multitude of both men and

<column-break/>

<margin>The Levites praise the Lord</margin>
women, and all who were able to understand what was said, brought the Law on the first day of the seventh month. He read it aloud in the square before the Water Gate from daybreak until midday, in the presence of the men and women and those who could understand; and the ears of all the people were attentive to the Book of the Law. He stood upon a wooden platform made for the purpose, and beside him on his right stood Mattithiah, Shema, Anaiah, Uriah, Hilkiah, and Maaseiah; and on his left Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchijah, Hashum, Hashbaddanah, Zechariah, and Meshullam.
So Ezra the scribe opened the book in the sight of all the people (for he stood above all the people). He praised the Lord <note>original: "Iouã" — a Latinization of the Hebrew name for God</note>, the great God, and all the people, lifting up their hands, answered, "Amen, Amen!" Then they bowed their heads and worshiped the Lord with their faces to the ground. Jesua, Bani, Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodiah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, Pelaiah, and the Levites explained the Law to the people while they remained in their places. They read from the Book of the Law of God so clearly and with such explanation that the people understood what was being read.
Then Nehemiah, who is also the Governor, and Ezra the priest and scribe, and the Levites who were teaching the people, instructed all the people: "This day is holy to the Lord your God; do not mourn or weep" (for all the people were weeping as they heard the words of the Law). He said, "Go, feast on choice foods and send portions to those who have nothing prepared, for this day is holy to our Lord. Do not grieve, for the joy of the Lord is your strength." The Levites also quieted all the people, telling them to be still and not to grieve on that holy day. So all the people went away to eat and drink, to send portions and to celebrate with great joy, because they had understood the words that had been declared to them.
<margin>The Festival of Booths is held.</margin>
On the next day, the heads of all the families, the priests, and the Levites gathered around Ezra the scribe to study the words of the Law. They found written in the Law, which the Lord had commanded through Moses, that the Israelites should live in <term>booths</term> <note>original: "umbraculis" — temporary shelters or tabernacles for the festival of Sukkot</note> during the festival of the seventh month, and that they should proclaim in all their towns and in Jerusalem that they should seek branches of olive, cypress, citrus, palm, and myrtle from the mountains to make booths, as it is written.
<margin>a. God had wanted these to be made outside the city. But here enemies were feared.</margin>
So the people went out and brought them and made <insert>for themselves</insert> booths everywhere, <note>original: "apud sua tecta"</note> near their own roofs, in their courtyards, in the courts of the house of God, in the square by the Water Gate, and in the square of the Ephraimites. The whole assembly of those who had returned from captivity lived in these booths they had made. From the days of Joshua son of Nun until that day, the Israelites had not done so, and there was very great rejoicing. Meanwhile, the book of the Law of God was read every day, from the first day to the last. They celebrated the feast for seven days, and on the eighth day there was a solemn assembly, according to the custom.

...of Jehovah <note>original: "Iouæ" — This is a Latinized form of the Tetragrammaton, the four-letter name of God. Then, having ascended the Levites' platform, Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani invoked Jehovah their God with a great voice, and the Levites Jeshua, Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabniah, Sherebiah, Hodiah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah said: "Arise, praise Jehovah your God through all eternity: and let your glorious name, O Jehovah, be so celebrated that it is exalted above every blessing and praise. You alone are Jehovah; you created the heavens, the heaven of heavens, and all their host; the earth and everything that is in it, the waters and whatever is in them: you confer life upon all things, and the heavenly host adores you. You are Jehovah God," said Ezra <note>original: "L. inquit Esdras, H." — These abbreviations likely refer to the Latin (L) and Hebrew (H) sources the translator was consulting.</note>, "who chose Abram, and having led him out from Ur of the Chaldeans, named him Abraham; and finding him possessed of a faithful mind toward you, you made a covenant to give the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Jebusites, and Girgashites to his descendants; a promise which you have indeed fulfilled, for you are just. For you looked upon the misery of our ancestors dwelling in Egypt, and you heard their cry at the Red Sea; and by performing signs and wonders against Pharaoh and all his servants, and against all the people of that land (for you knew they were being proudly oppressed by them), you won a reputation for yourself, as is evident today. Having split the sea before them, and they having crossed through the middle of the sea on dry ground, you cast their pursuers into the depths of the rushing waves, like a stone. Then you led them by day in a pillar of clouds, and by night in a pillar of fire, to illuminate the way by which they should go. Next, you descended upon Mount Sinai and, speaking to them from heaven, you gave them right judgments, true laws, good statutes and precepts; you declared your holy Sabbath to them, and commanded precepts, decrees, and the law through your servant Moses. You supplied bread from heaven for the hungry, drew water from the rock for the thirsty, and ordered them to enter and possess the land which you had promised to give them. But when they and our ancestors acted proudly and stubbornly, they did not obey your commands; rather, refusing to obey and forgetting the miracles you had performed among them, they stubbornly appointed a leader for themselves to return to their former servitude <note>original: "cultum" — literally 'worship' or 'culture', here implying their previous state in Egypt.</note>. Yet you, O God—ready to forgive, gracious, merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in kindness—did not desert them. Even when they had made a molten calf for themselves and proclaimed this to be their god who had led them out of Egypt, committing great and impious acts, you nevertheless, in your singular mercy, did not abandon them in the desert. You did not take away the pillar of cloud by day to lead them on their path, nor the pillar of fire by night to shine before them and show the way they were to go. Instead, you gave your good spirit for the sake of their instruction, nor did you withhold your Manna from their mouths, and you gave water to the thirsty. You sustained them for forty years in the desert so that they lacked nothing; neither did their clothes wear out, nor did their feet swell. Then you gave them kingdoms and nations, so that dispersed here and there, they occupied the lands of Sihon king of Heshbon, and Og king of Bashan. Then, having increased their children like the multitude of the stars in the heaven, you led them into the land...

<column-break/>

...which you had promised their ancestors they would enter to possess. So the children entered and occupied the land. When you had subdued before them the Canaanite inhabitants, their kings, and the peoples of that land to be used at their will, they took fortified cities and a rich land. They occupied houses filled with all good things, hewn cisterns, vineyards, olive groves, and fruit trees in great abundance. Eating these great goods, they were satisfied and grew fat, yet they grew stubborn and rebelled against you. Casting your law behind their backs, they killed your prophets (by whom they were warned to return to you) and committed such impious crimes. Therefore, you gave them into the hands of their enemies, by whom they were oppressed. When they implored you, you heard from heaven, and according to your mercy, you gave them deliverers by whom they were defended from their enemies. But as soon as they obtained rest, they again did what displeased you, and you delivered them into the power of their enemies. When, pressed by that rule, they implored you again, you, hearing from the heavens, protected them for a long time according to your clemency. You warned them to return to your law, but they, in their insolence, did not listen to your precepts and judgments—in the execution of which a man finds life—but sinning against them, they turned a rebellious shoulder and a stiff neck and would not obey. Even though you were patient with them for many years and warned them by your spirit through the work of your prophets, they would not listen. Therefore, you gave them into the hands of the nations of other regions; yet, because of your singular mercy, you did not utterly desert or extinguish them, for you are a gracious and merciful God. Now therefore, O our God, the great, mighty, and terrible God, who keeps covenants and mercy, do not let all the hardship seem small to you that has come upon us, our kings, princes, priests, prophets, ancestors, and all your people, from the times of the kings of Assyria until this day. You are just in everything that has happened to us, for you have acted faithfully while we have acted impiously. Our kings, princes, priests, and ancestors have not followed your law, nor paid attention to your precepts and the warnings by which you cautioned them. In their own kingdom, despite the great goods you bestowed upon them and the wide and rich land you granted them, they did not serve you, nor did they turn from their wicked nature. Behold, we are servants today; in the land you gave to our ancestors to eat its fruit and its good things, behold, we are servants in it. It yields a great harvest to the kings whom you have set over us because of our sins; they rule over our bodies and our cattle at their will, and we are in great distress. And yet, because of all this, we strike and write a firm covenant, to be sealed by our princes, Levites, and priests.

For the Israelites and the Levites must bring the contribution of grain, wine, and oil into the chambers where the vessels of the sanctuary are kept, and where the ministering priests, the gatekeepers, and the singers stay, so that we do not neglect the temple of our God.

### CHAPTER XII.

Now these are the priests and Levites who returned with Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua: Seraiah, Jeremiah, Ezra, Amariah, Malluch, Hattush, Shecaniah, Rehum, Meremoth, Ginnethoi, Abijah, Miniamin, Moadiah, Bilgah, Shemaiah, Joiarib, Jedaiah, Sallu, Amok, Hilkiah, and Jedaiah. These were the leaders of the priests and their brothers in the time of Jeshua. The Levites were Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel, Sherebiah, Judah, and Mattaniah; he and his brothers were in charge of the hymns of thanksgiving. Bakbukiah and Unni, and their brothers, were assigned to stand across from them in the watches. Now Jeshua fathered Joiakim; Joiakim fathered Eliashib; Eliashib fathered Joiada; Joiada fathered Jonathan; and Jonathan fathered Jaddua. In the time of Joiakim, these were the priests who were heads of families: for Seraiah, Maraiah; for Jeremiah, Hananiah; for Ezra, Meshullam; for Amariah, Jehohanan; for Malluch <note>original: "Miliconis"</note>, Jonathan; for Shebaniah, Joseph; for Harim, Adna; for Meraioth, Helkai; for Iddo, Zechariah; for Ginnethon, Meshullam; for Abijah, Zichri; for Miniamin and Moadiah, Piltai; for Bilgah, Shammua; for Shemaiah, Jonathan; for Joiarib, Mattenai; for Jedaiah, Uzzi; for Sallu, Kallai; for Amok, Eber; for Hilkiah, Hashabiah; and for Jedaiah, Nethanel. As for the Levites in the time of Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan, and Jaddua, the heads of families were recorded, as were the priests during the reign of Darius the Persian. The heads of the Levite families were recorded in the Book of the Annals <note>original: "in annalibus"</note> until the time of Johanan, son of Eliashib. Their leaders were Hashabiah, Sherebiah, and Jeshua son of Kadmiel, along with their brothers who were assigned to stand across from them to give praise and thanks according to the command of David, the man of God, watch matching watch. Mattaniah, Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Meshullam, Talmon, and Akkub were gatekeepers guarding the storerooms at the gates. These served in the time of Joiakim son of Jeshua, the grandson of Jozadak, and in the time of Nehemiah the governor and Ezra the priest and teacher <note>original: "professoris," likely referring to his role as a Scribe or Scholar of the Law</note>. At the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, they sought out the Levites from all their places to bring them to Jerusalem to celebrate the dedication with joy, with songs of praise, and with cymbals, harps, and lyres. Thus the guild of singers was gathered together from the plains around Jerusalem, from the villages of the Netophathites, from Beth-gilgal, and from the fields of Geba and Azmaveth (for the singers had built villages for themselves around Jerusalem).

<column-break/>

Then the priests and Levites purified themselves, and they purified the people, the gates, and the wall. And I <note>The first-person voice of Nehemiah</note> ordered the leaders of Judah to go up onto the wall, and I appointed two large processions of those giving thanks. One went to the right upon the wall toward the Dung Gate. Following them was Hoshaiah and half the leaders of Judah: Azariah, Ezra, Meshullam, Judah, Benjamin, Shemaiah, and Jeremiah. From the priestly line with trumpets was Zechariah (who traced his lineage back through Jonathan, Shemaiah, Mattaniah, Micaiah, and Zaccur to Asaph) and his kinsmen: Shemaiah, Azarel, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethanel, Judah, and Hanani, carrying the musical instruments of David, the man of God. Ezra the teacher led them. They went past the Fountain Gate, straight ahead up the steps of the City of David, by the ascent of the wall, past the house of David, as far as the Water Gate on the east. The second procession went to the left, and I followed it with half the people upon the wall, from the Tower of the Ovens to the Broad Wall, and over the Gate of Ephraim, past the Old Gate, the Fish Gate, the Tower of Hananel, and the Tower of the Hundred <note>original: "Meam"</note>, as far as the Sheep Gate <note>original: "portā balanū"</note>; they stopped at the Prison Gate. So the two processions of those giving thanks stood in the temple, as did I and half the officials with me. The priests Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Micaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah, and Hananiah had trumpets. Maaseiah, Shemaiah, Eleazar, Uzzi, Jehohanan, Malchijah, Elam, and Ezer, the singers, sang loudly under the direction of Jezrahiah. On that day they offered great sacrifices and rejoiced, for God had given them great joy; the women and children also rejoiced, so that the joy of Jerusalem was heard from far away. On that same day, men were appointed over the storerooms for the contributions, the firstfruits, and the tithes, to gather into them from the fields of the towns the portions required by the law for the priests and Levites. For Judah rejoiced that the priests and Levites were at their posts, keeping the service of their God and the service of purification, and that the singers and gatekeepers followed the ordinance of David and his son Solomon. For in the days of David and Asaph, long ago, there were directors for the singers and songs of praise and thanksgiving to God. So in the time of Zerubbabel and Nehemiah, all Israel gave the daily portions for the singers and the gatekeepers; they set apart the portion for the Levites, and the Levites set apart the portion for the descendants of Aaron.

Thus, on that day, the matters pertaining to the Lord’s sacrifice were arranged so that the Passover might be held and the victims sacrificed upon the divine altar. By the command of King Josiah, the Israelites who were present at that time kept the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread <note>original: "Azymalia"</note> for seven days. No such Passover had been held among the Israelites since the time of Samuel the prophet <note>original: "uatis"</note>, nor had any of the kings of the Israelites held such a Passover as did Josiah, the priests, the Levites, and all the Jews and Israelites who were present, along with the inhabitants of Jerusalem. And indeed, this Passover was held in the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign. The affairs of Josiah, a man endowed with a mind full of piety, were held in right standing through his Lord. But concerning his deeds, it was written in earlier times where it treats of those who, by so many sins and crimes (by which they surpassed all nations and kingdoms), so offended and provoked the Lord that the things He had threatened against the Israelites came to pass. After this entire affair of Josiah’s, it happened that Pharaoh, the King of Egypt, made an expedition against Carchemish, situated by the Euphrates. When Josiah went out to meet him, the King of Egypt sent a message to him in this manner: "What business have I with you, King of Judah? I am not sent to you by the Lord God; for my war is at the Euphrates. Therefore, since God is with me and urges me on, leave me be, and do not resist the Lord." However, Josiah did not desist from attacking him, but attempted to fight with him. He did not listen to the words spoken by the Lord through Jeremiah the prophet <note>original: "uatis"</note>, and he joined battle with him in the plain of Megiddo <note>original: "Mageddone"</note>. There, after the archers had struck him with arrows, he ordered his servants to lead him out of the battle, for he was greatly weakened. So, having been immediately withdrawn from the battle line by his servants and having boarded his second chariot, he was carried back to Jerusalem. There his life ended, and he was buried in his ancestral tomb. He was mourned in all of Judah, and Jeremiah the prophet lamented for Josiah. Those who are in charge of such matters still lament him today, together with the women; this practice has become a custom throughout the whole race of Israel. These things are written in the book of those matters which have been handed down to memory concerning the kings of Judah. Regarding the individual deeds of Josiah, his glory, and his God-given <note>original: "Dominiceq;"</note> prudence, a record has been handed down briefly—both of these and his other deeds—in the book of the kings of the Israelites and the Jews. In Josiah’s place, his son Jehoahaz <note>original: "Ioachazus"</note>, being twenty-three years old, was chosen for the kingdom by the people. After he had reigned in Jerusalem in Judah for three months, the King of Egypt revoked his kingship over Jerusalem and fined the nation one hundred talents of silver and one talent of gold. He appointed Jehoiakim <note>original: "Ioachum"</note>, his brother, as king of Judah and Jerusalem, and led away the high-ranking men and his brother Jehoahaz in chains to Egypt. This happened so that what the Lord had threatened through the mouth of Jeremiah might come to pass: that is, that the land might enjoy its Sabbaths; for it remained on holiday as long as it was deserted, until seventy years were completed.

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>The edict of Cyrus concerning the restoration of Jerusalem.</margin>
In the first year of his reign, the King of the Persians, having been inspired by the Lord (so that what had been predicted by the voice of Jeremiah from the Lord might happen), issued a decree throughout his entire empire, and did so in writing, in this manner: "Thus says Cyrus, King of the Persians. The Lord of the Israelites, the Most High Lord, has created me king of the world, and He has commanded me to build a temple for Him in Jerusalem, which is in Judah. If there are any of you, therefore, from His nation, let them set out, with their Lord's favor, to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, to build the temple of the Lord of the Israelites, who is the Lord that dwells in Jerusalem. And as for all their fellow countrymen, in whatever place they may dwell, let the people of those places assist them with gold, silver, gifts, horses, and cattle, besides other things that are dedicated as votive offerings for the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem." Then the leaders of the families of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin, the priests, and the Levites, and all those inspired by the Lord, prepared to set out...

In the times of Artaxerxes, King of the Persians, Bishlam <note>original: "Belemus"</note>, Mithridates, Tabeel <note>original: "Tabellius"</note>, Rehum <note>original: "Rathymus"</note>, Shimshai <note>original: "Beeltethmus"</note>, and Shimshai <note>original: "Semellius"</note> the scribe, and the rest of the same order living in Samaria and other places, wrote to him against the inhabitants of Judea and Jerusalem the following letter: To King Artaxerxes our lord, from the men who are under his authority: Rehum the recorder, Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their council, and the governors in Coelesyria and Phoenicia. Be it known, O King, that the Jews who set out from you have come to us in Jerusalem, that rebellious and wicked city, and are restoring it: they are repairing the marketplaces and walls, and laying the foundations of the temple. Now, if this city is restored and its walls finished, they will not only refuse to pay tribute, but will even resist kings. And because the work of the temple is underway, we thought it best not to neglect this matter, but to remind you, our Lord King, so that (if it seems good to you) the books of your ancestors may be searched. You will find in the written records concerning these matters, and you will learn that this city has been rebellious and troublesome to kings and cities, and the Jews inhabiting it have been rebels and authors of revolts since ancient times; for which cause this city was laid waste. Therefore, we show this to you, Lord King, that if this city is restored and its walls repaired, you will hereafter have no access to Coelesyria and Phoenicia.

<margin>Artaxerxes forbids the restoration of Jerusalem.</margin>
Then the king wrote back to Rehum the recorder, and to Shimshai, and to Shimshai the scribe, and the others of the same order dwelling in Samaria, Syria, and Phoenicia, the following reply: I have read the letter which you sent to me. Therefore, I ordered a search to be made, and it was found that this city has from ancient times been contrary to kings, and that men who are authors of revolts and wars dwell in it, and that powerful and fierce kings were in Jerusalem who ruled over Coelesyria and Phoenicia and collected tribute. Therefore, I command that those men be prevented from building the city, and that care be taken that nothing further be done, lest the evil proceed further to the detriment of kings. Then, when what had been written by King Artaxerxes was read, Rehum and Shimshai the scribe, and their associates, set out to Jeru-

<column-break/>

-salem quickly with cavalry and a tumultuous troop and began to hinder the builders; and the construction of the Jerusalem temple lay idle until the second year of the reign of Darius, King of the Persians.

### CHAPTER III.

When this Darius obtained the kingdom, he gave a great banquet for all his subjects, his household slaves, and all the nobles of Media and Persia, and all the satraps, generals, and governors subject to him from India to Ethiopia, in one hundred and twenty-seven provinces <note>original: "satrapijs"</note>. After they had feasted abundantly and departed, King Darius retired to his bedchamber and, overtaken by sleep, fell asleep.

<margin>The dispute of three young men concerning the power of wine, the king, women, and truth.</margin>
Here, three young bodyguards who watched over the king’s person began to encourage one another to each state his own opinion, on the condition that whoever won, and whose statement seemed wiser than the others, King Darius would bestow upon him great gifts and ornaments of victory: such as to be clothed in purple, to drink from gold, to sleep on gold, to have a chariot with gold bridles, a headdress of fine linen, and a chain around his neck; and he should sit second after Darius because of his wisdom, and be called a kinsman of Darius. Therefore, each wrote his own opinion and placed them, sealed, under King Darius’s pillow, with the plan that when the king awoke, they would give him the writing, and to the one whose opinion the king and the nobles of Persia judged the wisest, the prize of victory would be given according to the writing. One wrote: *Wine is strongest.* The second: *The king is strongest.* The third: *Women are strongest, but truth conquers all.* Then, when the king awoke, they handed him the writings. After reading them, he arranged for all the nobles of Persia and Media, the satraps, generals, governors, and counselors to be summoned; and sitting on the tribunal, he ordered the scroll to be read before them. Then he ordered the young men to be called to declare their opinions; and when they had been summoned and entered, he commanded that they themselves give the reasoning for what they had written.

<margin>The power of wine.</margin>
Then the first, who had spoken of the power of wine, began his speech thus: *How powerful is wine, O men! It deceives all men by whom it is drunk; it makes the mind of the king and the orphan, of the slave and the free man, of the poor man and the rich man, the same. It turns all minds to luxury and cheerfulness; it removes the memory of all sorrows and debts. It makes all minds rich; it does not allow one to remember kings or satraps. it makes everything be spoken in talents <note>i.e., in large sums of money</note>, so that when men have drunk, they set aside the memory of friendship and brotherly obligation, and not long after, they draw their swords; nor later, when they have recovered from the wine, do they remember what they have done. Is not wine then very powerful, O men, since it compels these things to happen?*

...men, who hold the lands, the seas, and all things that are within them? And yet the king excels all these and commands them, and he rules in such a way that whatever he orders, they do. If he bids them to wage war among themselves, they do it; if he sends them against enemies, they go, and they demolish mountains, walls, and towers; they kill and are killed, yet they do not exceed the king’s word. But if they conquer, they bring back to the king everything—both what they have plundered and all other things. Likewise, those who, abstaining from military service and war, cultivate the earth; when they have harvested what was sown, they bring it back to the king, and forcing one another, they bring tributes to the king. He alone, if he orders to kill, they kill; if he orders to release, they release; if he orders to strike, they strike; if he orders to devastate, they devastate; to build, they build; to overturn, they overturn; to sow, they sow; and all—both the people and the magistrates—obey him alone. After these words were said, he fell silent. But the third, who had spoken of women and of truth—namely, Zorobabel <note>Also known as Zerubbabel, a leader of the Jewish people</note>—began his speech thus: The king is indeed great, O men, and many men and much wine have great power. But who is it that rules over these? Who is it that commands them? Is it not women? Women gave birth to the king, and every race of men that rules over the sea and the land had its origin from them. These women themselves brought up the planters of the vineyards from which wine is produced. They make the garments of men; they bring glory to men, and men cannot exist without women. But if they have acquired gold, silver, or anything somewhat more elegant, are they not captured by the love of some woman outstanding in form and beauty? Do they not, setting aside all those things, fix their eyes upon her? Do they not gaze upon her with an open mouth? Do they not prefer her to gold, silver, and every beautiful thing? A man leaves his own father, by whom he was brought up, and his country, and clings to his wife; and with his wife, unmindful of father, mother, and country, he ends his life. And so that you may know that women hold power over you, do you not give and bring to women everything that you have prepared with much labor? A man takes up his sword and sets out to commit robbery and theft; he sails across seas and rivers, he endures the sight of lions, and he walks through the darkness; and when he has stolen, plundered, and robbed, he brings it back to his mistress. A man loves his own wife more than his parents, and many have been driven out of their minds because of women; many have been made slaves; many have perished; many have slipped into sin because of women. What? Do you not believe me? Is not the power of the king vast? Do not all nations dread even to touch him? And yet I saw Apame, the daughter of the illustrious Bartacus <note>original: "Bartaci," a reference to a Persian official, sometimes identified as Rabsezaces</note>, the king's concubine, sitting at the king's right hand; she took the diadem from his head and placed it on herself, and then she struck the king's cheek with her left hand, while the king meanwhile gazed at her with an open mouth. If she laughed, he laughed; and if she

<header>III.</header>

was angry, he flattered her so that he might reconcile her to himself. Do not women have much power, O men, who do these things? While the king and the nobles looked at one another, he began to speak of truth in this way. Women are indeed very powerful, O men, and the earth is vast, the heaven is high, and the sun is swift in its course, which circles the heaven in one day and returns again to the place from which it started. 
<margin>The powers of Truth.</margin>
Is he not great who does these things? But Truth is greatest and more powerful than all. The whole world calls upon Truth; heaven itself favors it; all things dread and tremble before it, nor is there anything faulty in it. Wine is faulty, the king is faulty, women are faulty, the whole race of men is faulty, and all their works are of the same faultiness, in which faultiness those who are without truth perish. But Truth is eternally powerful; it lives and flourishes forever and ever. There is in it no respect of persons <note>meaning: partiality or favoritism</note> nor any distinction, but it does what is just, and it abstains from all unjust and wicked things. All people approve of its deeds, and there is nothing unjust in its judgment. Therefore, let the God of Truth be praised for this, and for royal magnificence, and for power, and for the majesty of all ages. When he had finished speaking these things, everyone cried out that Truth is greatest and most powerful. Then the king, addressing him, said: "Ask whatever you wish, even beyond what was written, and we will give it to you, since you have been found the wisest; and you shall sit next to me and be called my kinsman."

<margin>Zorobabel asks Darius that the Jerusalem Temple be restored</margin>
And he said to the king: "Remember the vow by which you promised to restore Jerusalem when you obtained the kingdom, and to send back all the vessels taken from Jerusalem which Cyrus set aside when he vowed to destroy Babylon and swore to send them back there. You also vowed to restore the sanctuary <note>original: "fanum," meaning the Temple</note> which the Edomites burned when Judea was devastated by the Chaldeans. And now, Lord King, this is what I ask and demand from you; this is the magnificence I expect from you. I pray, therefore, that you fulfill what you vowed with your own mouth to the King of Heaven." Then King Darius stood up and, 
<margin>Darius gives letters to Zorobabel regarding the restoration of the temple</margin>
having kissed him, wrote letters for him to all the treasurers, governors, leaders, and satraps <note>term: "satrapas" — Persian provincial governors</note>, so that they might escort him and all his companions who were setting out to restore Jerusalem. Then he commanded all the governors of Coelesyria <note>A region of the Levant</note>, Phoenicia, and Lebanon by letters to transport cedar wood from Lebanon to Jerusalem and to build the city with him. Furthermore, he granted freedom in writing to all the Jews going up from his kingdom to Judea, so that no official, governor, satrap, or ruler should attack their homes, and that all the region they held should be exempt from taxes for them, and that the Edomites should give up the Jewish villages they held. Also, he ordered that twenty talents be given annually for the structure of the temple until it was finished, and likewise for the burnt offerings to be made daily on the altar—seventeen of which they were commanded to sacrifice according to the precept...

# BOOK III.

<margin>
Restore the altar and sacred rites
</margin>
[Zorobabel] the son [of Salathiel], along with his kinsmen, set about restoring the altar of the God of the Israelites, so that burnt offerings <note>original: "solida sacrificia," referring to offerings entirely consumed by fire</note> might be provided upon it, just as is required by those things prescribed in the book of the divine Moses. And although the other neighboring nations—who were at odds with them—conspired against them and all threatened them with violence, they nevertheless set the altar in its proper place. They performed sacrifices at their appointed times, offering morning and evening burnt offerings to the Lord.

<margin>Leviticus 23</margin>
They celebrated the Feast of Tabernacles <note>original: "umbraculorum festum," a harvest festival where participants lived in temporary booths</note>, as prescribed in the law, along with the daily sacrifices as was appropriate. Then they offered the continual libations and the sacrifices for the Sabbaths, the new moons, and all the consecrated festivals, as well as for all who had made voluntary vows to God. Therefore, from the new moon of the seventh month, sacrifices began to be offered to God; and thus the temple of God was being built. Money was given to the stone-cutters and craftsmen, and food, drink, and carts were provided to the Sidonians and Tyrians, so that they might bring cedar timber from Lebanon by sea-floats <note>original: "ratibus"</note> to the port of Joppa, as had been commanded to them in the letters from Cyrus, King of the Persians.

<margin>
The foundations of the temple are laid.
</margin>
Now in the second year, when they had come to the temple of God in Jerusalem, in the second month, Zorobabel son of Salathiel and Jesua son of Josedec, along with their kinsmen and the priests and Levites, and all who had come to Jerusalem from the captivity, set about the business. They laid the foundations of the temple on the new moon of the second month, in the second year after their arrival in Judea and Jerusalem. They appointed Levites twenty years of age and older to oversee the works of the Lord. And so Jesua, his sons and kinsmen, and his brother Cadmiel, and the sons of Madiabun, as well as the sons of Joda, son of Heliadun, along with their sons and kinsmen, were all equally occupied in urging forward the work of the temple.

And while the builders were erecting the temple of the Lord, the priests stood in their vestments with musical instruments and trumpets <note>original: "tibijs," literally pipes or flutes</note>, and the Levites descended from Asaph stood with cymbals, praising the Lord and celebrating together according to the prescription of David, King of the Israelites. Resounding with hymns, they celebrated the Lord, whose goodness and glory toward all Israelites is eternal. Then all the people made a great sound with the blowing of trumpets, praising the Lord at the building of His temple.

But the elders of the priests, the Levites, and the heads of families, who had seen the earlier temple <note>referring to Solomon’s original temple destroyed by the Babylonians</note>, raised a great cry with weeping when they were present at the building of this one. Conversely, many others made a great sound with trumpets in joy, so that the people could not distinguish the sound of the trumpets from the weeping of the men, because the crowd made such a noise with the trumpets that it was heard from far away.

When the adversaries of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin heard this, they approached to learn the reason for the sound of the trumpets. And after they understood that the temple was being built for the Lord God of Israel by those from the captivity, they met with Zorobabel, Jesua, and the heads of families, and offered their assistance for the partnership of building. For they claimed that they obeyed the same Lord as they did, and had sacrificed to Him since the time of Esarhaddon <note>original: "Ascasarethi," the Assyrian king who resettled various peoples in Samaria</note>, the King of the Assyrians, by whom they had been transported there. To them, the leaders replied that the temple for the Lord their God was not to be built by them together, but that they alone would properly build for the Lord of the Israelites, as had been commanded them by Cyrus, King of the Persians.

<column-break/>

Thus the inhabitants hindered those who were in Judea and, by delaying and attacking them, turned them away from the building. By using plots, public speeches, and conspiracies, they impeded the completion of the work during the entire lifetime of King Cyrus. They were prohibited from building for two years, until the reign of Darius.

### CHAPTER VI.

But in the second year of the reign of Darius, when the prophets Haggai and Zechariah <note>original: "Zacharias"</note> son of Iddo <note>original: "Addonis"</note> prophesied to the Jews—both those in Judea and those in Jerusalem—in the name of the Lord of the Israelites, Zorobabel son of Salathiel and Jesua son of Josedec began to build the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem, while the prophets of the Lord were indeed present and helping them. During that time, Sisinnes <note>historically Tattenai</note> the governor <note>original: "prætor"</note> of Syria and Phoenicia, and Sathrabuzanes and his colleagues, came to them and asked by whose command they were building that temple, completing the roof and all other things, and who the builders were who were performing these tasks. But through the Lord's grace toward the Jewish elders and His care for the captives, it was brought about that they were not prohibited from building until a report about them was made to Darius and a response was received from him.

<margin>
The letter from the governors of Syria to Darius, in which he is informed that the temple is being restored.
</margin>
He sent a written letter to Darius, of which this is a copy: "To King Darius, greetings from Sisinnes, governor of Syria and Phoenicia, and Sathrabuzanes and their colleagues, the rulers in Syria and Phoenicia. Let it be known, our Lord King, that we came into the region of Judea and to the city of Jerusalem, and found the elders of the captive Jews in the city of Jerusalem building a huge new temple for the Lord, with polished and costly stones, and with timber placed in the walls. These things are being done diligently, and the work is proceeding for them, and is being completed with the greatest splendor and care.

We inquired of those elders by whose command they were erecting that temple and laying those foundations, asking them so that we might inform you and write about the leaders of that business; for that reason, we requested from them the names of the authors of the work. And they responded to us in this manner: 'We are worshippers of the Lord, who created heaven and earth. This temple was built many ages ago by a great and powerful King of the Israelites and was completed. But because the heavenly Lord of the Israelites was provoked by the sins of our ancestors, He delivered them to Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: "Nabuchodonosori"</note>, the King of the Babylonians and Chaldeans, who both demolished and burned the temple, and led the people away captive to Babylon.

'However, King Cyrus, in the first year in which he obtained the kingship of the Babylonian region, gave a written mandate that this temple should be built. He brought out from the temple of Babylon the sacred gold and silver vessels which Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the sanctuary in Jerusalem and placed in his own temple. These were handed over to Zorobabel and Sanabassarus <note>historically Sheshbazzar</note> the governor, who was commanded to return those vessels to the sanctuary in Jerusalem and replace them, so that the temple of the Lord might be built in its proper place. Then that Sanabassarus arrived and laid the foundations of the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem; since that time until now it has been under construction, but it has not yet been brought to completion.' Therefore, if you so judge, O King, let the records of King Cyrus be inspected. And if it should be found that the building of the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem was done according to the opinion of King Cyrus, and if it seems right to you, our Lord King, respond to..."

Moreover, all the people raised a great shout with the sound of flutes, praising the Lord during the construction of his temple. But the priests, the Levites, and the elders of the families' leaders who had seen the former temple <note>referring to Solomon's Temple, destroyed by the Babylonians in 586 BCE</note>, when they were present at the building of this one, cried out with a great weeping. On the other hand, many made a great sound with flutes and joy, so that the people could not hear the sound of the flutes because of the weeping of the men, as the crowd of people made such a noise with the flutes that it was heard from far away. When the adversaries of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin heard this, they approached to learn the cause of the sound of the flutes. And after they understood that a temple was being built to the Lord God of the Israelites by the captives, they met with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the leaders of the families, and offered their labor to join in the building. For they claimed that they obeyed the same Lord as they did, and had sacrificed to him since the time of Esarhaddon <note>original: "Ascasarethi"</note>, king of the Assyrians, by whom they had been relocated there. To them, the leaders replied that it was not for them to build a temple to the Lord their God together with them, but that they alone would properly build for the Lord of the Israelites, as had been commanded them by Cyrus, king of the Persians.

<column-break/>

Therefore the inhabitants, by delaying and attacking those who were in Judea, turned them away from the building. By making ambushes, speeches, and conspiracies, they hindered the completion of the work during the entire lifetime of King Cyrus; and they were prohibited from building for two years, until the reign of Darius.

### CHAPTER VI.

But in the second year of the reign of Darius, when Haggai and Zechariah <note>original: "Haggaeus et Zacharias"</note> the son of Iddo <note>original: "Addonis"</note>, the prophets, prophesied to the Jews—those who were either in Judea or in Jerusalem—in the name of the Lord of the Israelites with which they were endowed, Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and Jeshua son of Jozadak began to build the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem, while the prophets of the Lord were present and helping them. During that time, Sisinnes, the governor of Syria and Phoenicia, and Sathrabuzanes and his colleagues came to them and asked by whose order they were building that temple, completing the roof and all other things, and who the builders were who were performing these tasks. But by the grace of the Lord toward the elders of the Jews and his care for the captives, it was brought about that they were not prohibited from building until Darius was notified about them and a response was received from him. He then sent a written letter to Darius, of which this is a copy: Sisinnes, the governor of Syria and Phoenicia, and
<margin>Letters of the governors of Syria to Darius, by which he is informed that the temple is being restored.</margin>
Sathrabuzanes and the colleagues, governors in Syria and Phoenicia, to King Darius, greetings. Know, our Lord King, that we have come into the region of Judea and into the city of Jerusalem, and have found the elders of the captive Jews in the city of Jerusalem building a huge new temple to the Lord, with polished stones of great price, and with timber placed in the walls. These things are being done studiously, and the work is proceeding for them, being completed with the greatest splendor and diligence. We inquired of those elders by whose command they were constructing that temple and laying those foundations, questioning them so that we might notify you and write about the leaders of this business; for that reason, we requested from them a list of the names of the authors of the work. And they responded to us in this manner: "We are worshippers of the Lord who created heaven and earth. This temple was built and finished many centuries ago by a certain great and powerful king of the Israelites <note>referring to Solomon</note>. But the heavenly Lord of the Israelites, provoked by the sins of our ancestors, delivered them to Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: "Nabuchodonosori"</note>, king of the Babylonians and Chaldeans, who both demolished and burned the temple, and led the people away captive to Babylon. However, King Cyrus, in the first year in which he obtained the kingdom of the Babylonian region, commanded in writing that this temple should be built. And the sacred vessels of gold and silver, which Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple in Jerusalem and placed in his own temple, he brought out from the temple of Babylon, and they were handed over to Zerubbabel and Sanabassarus the governor, who was commanded to return those vessels to the sanctuary in Jerusalem and replace them, so that the temple of the Lord might be built in its own place." Then that Sanabassarus arrived and laid the foundations of the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem; since then it has been under construction, but it has not yet been brought to perfection. Therefore, if it seems right to you, O King, let the records <note>original: "tablina"</note> of King Cyrus be inspected. And if it is found that the building of the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem was done according to the will of King Cyrus, and it seems so to you, our Lord King, respond to us...

And I pray to the Lord, whose name is invoked there, that He may destroy all—whether kings or private citizens—who shall attempt to either hinder or harm that temple of the Lord in Jerusalem. I, King Darius, have decreed that this be done diligently."

Ezra the priest and teacher <note>original: "professor," meaning a public teacher or expert</note> of the law of the Most High God, shall diligently provide these things: up to one hundred talents of silver, likewise one hundred measures <note>original: "coros," a Hebrew unit of volume</note> of wheat, one hundred measures <note>original: "metretas"</note> of wine, and all other things required by the divine law shall be diligently offered to the Most High God, lest any punishment befall the king, his kingdom, or his sons. With them were Jozabad son of Jeshua and Moeth son of Sabannas, the Levites. Everything was delivered by number and weight, and at that very moment, their entire weight was recorded. Those who had come back from captivity offered sacrifices to the Lord God of Israel: twelve bulls on behalf of all Israel, ninety-six rams, seventy-two lambs, and twelve he-goats for a sin offering <note>original: "pro salute," for well-being/salvation</note>; all these were sacrificed as a burnt offering to the Lord. After the king's orders were delivered to the governors and prefects of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, they honored both the people and the temple of God.
<margin>
It is reported to Ezra that the people have not abstained from foreign marriages.
</margin>
When these things were finished, the leaders approached me, showing that the Israelite people, the princes, the priests, and the Levites had not only failed to separate themselves from the commerce of foreign nations, but were even sharing in the abominations of the Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Jebusites, Moabites, Egyptians, and Edomites. ### CHAPTER IX.

**T**hen Ezra, having gone out from the vestibule of the temple, withdrew into the chamber of Jehohanan <note>original: "Iohannis"</note> the son of Eliashib. While staying there, he neither tasted food nor drank water, mourning the great crimes of the common people. A decree was issued throughout all Judea and Jerusalem to all those returned from captivity that they should assemble at Jerusalem; and whoever did not appear within two or three days, according to the decree of the presiding elders, his goods were to be consecrated <note>original: "sacrarentur," likely meaning confiscated for the temple or destroyed</note>, and he himself would be excluded from the community of those who had returned from captivity. Thus, when all the men of the tribes of Judah and Benjamin had assembled at Jerusalem within three days, on the twentieth day of the ninth month, the entire multitude was present in the temple courtyard, trembling because of the current rain. Standing before them, Ezra spoke these words: "You have committed a crime in marrying foreign wives, thereby increasing the sins of the Israelites.

The Levites likewise exhorted the people, saying this day was holy to the Lord and they should not torment themselves with grief. So everyone departed to feast and rejoice, and to keep a great celebration: for they were still inspired by the words which they had been summoned to learn.

# TOBIAS <note>The Book of Tobit</note>

### PREFACE OF THE
### translator to Tobit.
**T**his book exists in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin. A Hebrew version was recently published; Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the 4th-century scholar who produced the Vulgate</note> testifies that he translated the Latin from the Chaldean language <note>A term often used historically for Aramaic</note>. The core of the history agrees in these three languages, but there is variation in many places. We have translated from the Hebrew text, which seemed more faithful to us. However, those sentences which we found in the Greek or Latin that were relevant but did not exist in the Hebrew, we have marked with the Greek letter L. If in any place, due to a change in person or some other cause, they did not fit well, we have enclosed them in these marks L . J.

### CHAPTER I.
**T**he book of Tobit, tracing his lineage from Nanathiel, then through his father Tobiel, Hananeel, Ariel, Gabeel, and Asael, of the tribe of Naphtali. He was led away from Samaria into captivity with those who were taken in the time of Hoshea, son of Elah, during the reign of Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, having been an inhabitant of a certain Naphtalite town situated in the maritime regions of Galilee. This Tobit, then, speaks in this manner:

I brought the firstfruits and tithes, and the firstborn to the priests, the descendants of Aaron, and I gave grain, wine, oil, figs, pomegranates—in short, produce of the earth of all kinds—to the Levites serving Jehovah in Jerusalem. I also gave the second tithes, and the tithes for the foreigners, orphans, and widows. All these things, I say, I conscientiously performed, seeking out Jerusalem every year by the command of Jehovah and as my paternal grandmother Deborah had instructed me. For I had been left an orphan by both parents. And after I grew up, I took a wife of my own kin named Anna, by whom I had a son whom I named Tobias. L. And from his boyhood, I taught him to be religious and to abstain from all sin. <meta>This page marks the beginning of the Book of Tobit (here titled Tobias). While the previous page concluded the historical account of Ezra and the return from the Babylonian exile, this text shifts to the personal narrative of Tobit, a pious Israelite living in the earlier Assyrian captivity in Nineveh. The text follows his struggle to maintain religious purity and his acts of mercy towards his fellow exiles.</meta>

<page-num>531</page-num>
<page-num>532</page-num>
<header>T O B I T</header>

While all others were eating the food of strangers <note>original: "extraneorum," referring to non-kosher food of the Gentiles</note>, I revered the Lord and would not allow myself to be defiled by even a mouthful of their delicacies. Instead, I kept the memory of the Lord in my whole mind and soul. 
<margin>Tobit deposits money in Media.</margin>
Therefore, God granted me such grace and favor in the sight of Shalmaneser, the King of Assyria, that he entrusted everything he owned to me until the day he died, L. and gave me the freedom to go wherever I wished and to do whatever was necessary. H. Thus, I visited all the captives frequently, giving them helpful advice. H. I also deposited with my kinsman Gabelus—L. whom I saw was in need among my many relatives—H. who lived in Rages, a province of Media, ten talents of silver, L. which the king had given to me. H. 

Later, after Shalmaneser the King of Assyria died and his son Sennacherib reigned in his place, the roads to Media were blocked because of the wars in those borders, and I could no longer go to Media to retrieve my silver. Nevertheless, I performed many acts of kindness for my needy countrymen, as well as for orphans and widows. Whenever I saw the bodies of my slain countrymen thrown out into the streets of Nineveh, I never rested until I had buried them. 

For Sennacherib, the King of Assyria, after he returned shamefully from Judea (because the Lord, the God of the Israelites, had brought a great slaughter upon him in Judea on account of the 
<margin>The reason why Sennacherib raged against the Jews in Nineveh.</margin>
insults and reproaches he had directed at Him), killed many in his rage. But as for me, when I searched for the true reason why such calamity had befallen the tribes of Israel at that time (for I knew for certain that the Lord is a just God toward them, not unjust), I found that the tribes of Israel had shown no concern for the slaughter of their kinsmen, whom Sennacherib the King of Assyria had destroyed by burning their fortifications, slaughtering the young men with the sword, dashing the little ones to pieces, and ripping open the pregnant women. 

Why should they mourn for the calamity that had been raged against their own kinsmen, or why should they submit themselves to the Lord? Instead, they feasted, rejoiced, and played all kinds of songs on harps and lutes, showing no grief for the ruin of the Jews. This ruin happened because of our sins and the sins of our ancestors, just as it is written of the Jews: those who drank wine from bowls and anointed their heads with ointments did not grieve for the ruin of Joseph <note>A reference to the prophet Amos 6:6, criticizing the wealthy for their indifference to the suffering of others</note>. For this reason, the Lord took vengeance on the Jews and those in Jerusalem, casting them out of His sight by sending the King of Babylon against them and carrying the Jews away from their homeland. Therefore, whenever I saw those among the Israelites who were killed and thrown outside the wall, I would often steal their bodies away and commit them to a grave, saying: "O Lord, God of the Israelites, You are just in everything that happens to us; You act rightly, and we have acted wickedly." 

When Sennacherib looked for the bodies of my slain countrymen and could not find them, the people of Nineveh approached him and informed him about Tobit, his servant, to whom he had entrusted all his affairs. The king then sent his men into every street of Nineveh to search for the one who, setting aside his fear of the king, was secretly burying the dead. When I heard of this, I was greatly—

<column-break/>

—afraid, and Sennacherib was exceedingly angry with me. He ordered that I, my wife Anna, and my son Tobias be seized, desiring to kill me in his fury. When I was warned of this, I fled, and he ordered all my property to be plundered. However, I remained hidden from him until—as the widows and orphans of Israel cried out over me with anguish of soul, fasting, and weeping—their cause reached all the way to heaven and moved the heavens. The God of the Israelites then delivered the king into the hands of his two sons, by whom he was killed for the following reason. 

<margin>Why Sennacherib's own sons killed him.</margin>
The king had once asked his counselors and senators why the Lord—that holy and praiseworthy God—was so devoted to the Israelites and those in Jerusalem that His spirit <note>original: "genius"</note> destroyed Pharaoh’s army, all the firstborn of Egypt, and their youth, and why He always gave them victory. His wise men and counselors replied that Abraham, the forefather of the Israelites, had led his own son to be sacrificed to win the favor of his God, the Lord. For this reason, God is protective of his descendants and has avenged your attacks. Then the king said he would sacrifice his two sons to the Lord so that he might obtain His favor and help through them. When this news reached his sons, Adrammelech and Sharezer, they killed him by ambush while he had gone to pray to his false god, Dagon, as it is written: "His sons Adrammelech and Sharezer struck him down with the sword and escaped into Armenia." 

After the death of Sennacherib, King of Assyria, his son Esarhaddon succeeded him. This Esarhaddon appointed Achiacharus <note>original: "Aquicarem," the nephew of Tobit</note>, the son of my brother Anael, over all his affairs and over the entire empire of Assyria. Because of the friendship and kinship between us, Achiacharus spoke well of me to the king so that I was recalled to Nineveh, and my wife Anna and my son Tobias were restored to me—those whom the King of Assyria, in the anger he had felt toward me, had ordered to be seized.

Then Achior, the leader of all the Ammonites, spoke in this manner: "Listen, my lord, to my speech—I who am your servant—and I will tell you the truth about this mountain people living near you; no lie shall fall from my mouth. Because they refused to follow the ancestral gods of the Chaldeans, and having abandoned their ancestral rites, L. which were centered on a multitude of gods, G. they chose for themselves the one God of heaven to worship. Being cast out from the sight of those gods, they fled into Mesopotamia. Having stayed there a long time, they were commanded by their God to migrate from that place of dwelling into Canaan. Thus they migrated, and there they acquired a vast amount of gold, silver, and cattle. But when a famine grew strong in Canaan,

<column-break/>

they went down into Egypt. They stayed there as long as food was supplied, and they grew into such a great multitude that their race became innumerable. Later, when a King of Egypt arose who circumvented them and oppressed them with the labor of making bricks, L. and building cities, G. and used them as slaves, they implored their God. He struck all of Egypt with incurable plagues. Thus the Egyptians cast them out. L. But when, the plague having ceased, they tried to pull them back and reduce them to slavery again, G. God dried the Red Sea for them L. as they fled. G. He did this so that on both sides the water stood congealed as firm as a wall, and they passed through the middle of the sea floor on dry ground. When the Egyptian army followed them into that place, they were so submerged by the water that not even a messenger survived from that innumerable multitude. Having crossed the Red Sea, they came to Mount Sinai, G. and Kadesh-Barnea, L. where no mortal could ever stop or dwell. There they had sweet springs to drink from out of bitter ones, and they received food from heaven for forty years. G. After driving out all the inhabitants of the wilderness, they occupied the borders of the Amorites and destroyed all the Heshbonites by their courage. Having crossed the Jordan, they occupied all the highlands. After driving out all the Canaanites, Perizzites, Jebusites, Shechemites, and Girgashites, they lived there for a long time. L. And wherever they entered, God fought for them; without bow, without arrow, without sword, He defeated their enemies. Never could this nation be resisted, except whenever they turned away from the worship of their God. For as often as they worshiped another God besides their own, they were shamefully exposed to plunder and the sword. But as often as they returned to the worship of their God, God gave them the strength to resist. At last they destroyed the Canaanites, Jebusites, Perizzites, Hittites, Hivites, Amorites, and all the strongest Heshbonites, and occupied their cities and lands. As long as they kept themselves from offending their God, it went well with them, for they enjoyed the favor of their God, who hates wickedness. But in years past, when they turned away from the way of life which God had prescribed for them, they were for a long time destroyed in various wars by different nations, and many were led away into foreign lands as captives, G. and the temple of their God was leveled to the ground, and their cities were captured by adversaries. Now, however, having returned to their God, they have gathered themselves from the places where they were scattered and have regained Jerusalem, where their sanctuary is, and have occupied the highlands which had been deserted. Therefore, my lord, let us inquire if there is any offense among them toward their God. For if they suffer from this disadvantage, let us attack them with arms; L. for their own God will deliver them to you and subject them to your power. But if nothing has been committed by them L. against their God, G. I judge that you must refrain from war, my lord, lest their Lord and God defend them, and we become a disgrace to the whole world."

Their hired and bought servants, their sides wrapped in sackcloth <note>original: *centonibus*; these were rough, patchwork garments worn as a sign of mourning or extreme penance</note>, and everyone—men, women, and little children living in Jerusalem—threw themselves face down before the temple, scattered dust on their heads, spread their sackcloth before the Lord, and girded themselves with sackcloth. They cried out with one mind to the God of Israel, pleading that He not allow their children to be snatched away, their wives to be taken as prey, their cities and possessions to be destroyed, or the holy things to be profanely defiled to the joy of foreign nations.

<margin>
Joachim encourages the Israelites.
</margin>
Then Joachim, the High Priest of the Lord, went around to all the Israelites and encouraged them, saying: <note>The letter "L." refers to the Latin Vulgate tradition.</note> "Know that the Lord will hear your prayers if you persevere in fasts and supplications before Him. Remember Moses, the servant of the Lord, who cast down the Amalekite—who relied on his own strength, power, army, shields, chariots, and horsemen—not by fighting with the sword, but by praying with holy petitions. The same will happen to the enemies of Israel if you persevere in this path." With this exhortation, they continued to call upon the Lord with prayers. And so, God heard their prayers and looked upon their distress. The people fasted for many days, both in all of Judea and in Jerusalem, in the sight of the sanctuary of the Lord Almighty. Moreover, Joachim the priest, and all the priests who stood before the Lord, and the ministers of the Lord, with their sides girded in sackcloth, offered the daily burnt offering, the prayers, and the voluntary gifts of the people. Their priestly headbands <note>original: *infulis*; sacred ribbons or fillets worn by priests</note> were sprinkled with dust, and they cried out to the Lord with all their strength, that He might look kindly upon the entire stock of Israel.

### CHAPTER XIII.

When evening came and his servants had departed in haste, Bagoas closed the tent from the outside and dismissed those who had been present with his lord. They slipped away to their own beds, for they were all exhausted from the lengthy drinking bout. Judith was left alone in the tent, while Holofernes lay on his bed drenched in wine. She commanded her handmaid to stand outside her bedchamber and watch for her exit, just as she was accustomed to do every day; for she had said she would be going out to her prayers, and she had told Bagoas the same. Therefore, when everyone had departed from her and not a single person remained in the chamber, Judith, standing by his bed, spoke thus within her soul: "O Lord, <margin>Judith, about to kill Holofernes, prays</margin> Almighty God of all things, look in this hour upon the works of my hands for the glory of Jerusalem, <term>L.</term> as you have promised. <term>G.</term> For now is the time to aid your inheritance and to fulfill my undertaking, <term>L.</term> which I believed could be done through you, <term>G.</term> for the destruction of the enemies who have risen against us." Having said this, she approached the bedpost that was at Holofernes' head and, drawing down his scimitar <note>original: "acinace" - a short, curved Persian sword</note> which hung there, she drew near the bed. Grabbing him by the hair of his head, she said: "Strengthen me, O Lord God of Israel, this day!" And at the same time, she struck his neck twice with all her might and cut off his head. She rolled his body away from the blankets and, taking the canopy <note>original: "uelo" - the decorative curtain or mosquito net mentioned earlier</note> from the pillars, she went out shortly after and handed the head of Holofernes to her handmaid. <margin>Judith returns to Bethulia, carrying the head of Holofernes.</margin> After it was put into her food bag, they both went out, as was their custom, to pray. ### CHAPTER XVI.

Judith’s song, in which the whole community of Israelites speaks, praising God who destroyed Holofernes through Judith.

Begin the praises of my Lord with timbrels; sing to my Lord with cymbals; compose a new song for him; extol his praises; call upon his name, for he is the God who crushes wars. He is the one who placed his camp in the midst of his people to rescue me from the hand of those who sought to harm me. The Assyrian came from the mountains, he came from the north with thousands of soldiers, so many that their multitude blocked the rivers and their cavalry covered the valleys. He had determined to set fire to my borders, to take my young men by the sword, to strike the nursing infants to the ground, to take the children as prey, and to carry off the young women. But the Lord Almighty struck him down by the hand of a woman. For that powerful man was not brought down by young men, nor did the sons of Titans slay him, nor did massive giants attack him; instead, Judith, the daughter of Merari, subdued him with the beauty of her face. For she took off her mourning clothes <term>L.</term> <note>Latin Vulgate tradition</note> and put on the garments of joy, <term>G.</term> <note>Greek Septuagint tradition</note> to bring relief to the labors of the Israelites. She stole his eyes with her sandals, captured his soul with her beauty, and cut through his neck with a <term>scimitar</term> <note>original: "acinace"; a short, curved sword used in the ancient Near East.</note>. The Persians trembled at her daring, and the Medes were troubled by her confidence. Then my afflicted people <term>L.</term> parched with thirst, <term>G.</term> howled; my weak ones cried out, and at their shout, the enemy was terrified and turned to flight. The sons of young women pierced them through, striking them down like runaway slaves; they perished by the battle-line of the Lord my God, whose praises I will celebrate with a song. O Lord, you are great and glorious, wonderful in power, and invincible. Let all your creation serve you, for it was made at your command; your spirit was sent and it was built, and nothing can resist your word. The very mountains are shaken from their foundations along with the waters; the rocks melt like wax in your sight. But to those who revere you, you show yourself kind. For any sacrifice is too small to delight you with its fragrance, and all the fat is too little for a burnt offering to you; but he who reveres the Lord is always great. Woe to the nations that rise up against my race, for the Lord Almighty will take vengeance on them in the day of judgment, bringing fire and worms to their bodies, so that they shall weep in pain forever. # ESTHER

### CHAPTER I.

<margin>
a. He is called Artaxerxes by the Greeks, the son of Xerxes, according to Josephus. An account of Ahasuerus's banquet.
</margin>
Ahasuerus, who reigned over one hundred and twenty-seven provinces from India even to Ethiopia, after he had attained the throne of his kingdom in Susa, which is the capital of the realm, gave a banquet in the third year of his reign for all his nobles and subjects. Present with him were the most powerful men of the Persians and Medes—namely, the governors and prefects of the provinces—so that he might show off the wealth of his glorious kingdom and the magnificent excellence of his greatness. This banquet lasted a long time, specifically one hundred and eighty days. When that period ended, the king hosted all the people found there in Susa, from the least to the greatest, for a seven-day banquet in the courtyard of the royal gardens. There, hangings of fine white linen, cotton, and blue material were fastened with cords of linen and purple through silver rings hanging from marble columns. There were couches of gold and silver placed on a floor of porphyry, marble, mother-of-pearl, and precious stone. They drank from golden cups that were constantly changed, and royal wine was served in great abundance as befitted the king's wealth. The drinking was conducted according to the law, with no one being forced to drink, for the king had instructed all his stewards to follow the will of each guest. On the seventh day, when the king’s heart was merry with wine, he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcas (the seven <term>eunuchs</term> <note>original: "spadonum"</note> who served him) to bring Queen Vashti before the king—who was herself holding a banquet for the women in the palace of Ahasuerus—wearing the royal crown, so that he might show her beauty to the people and the nobles, for she was remarkably beautiful. <margin>Queen Vashti, ordered to come to the king, does not obey.</margin> But Queen Vashti refused to come at the king’s command brought by the eunuchs. Because of this, the king was incensed with a violent rage. He questioned the wise men who were experts in such matters (for it was the king's custom to propose business to those learned in law and justice, and those closest to him then were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, seven princes of the Persians and Medes who had access to the king and held the highest rank in the kingdom). He asked them what should be done with Queen Vashti, who had not obeyed the command of King Ahasuerus brought by the eunuchs. Then Memucan spoke before the king and the nobles in this manner: "Queen Vashti has not only sinned against the king, but also against all the princes and people who are in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus. For once this news about the queen is spread, all women will look upon their husbands with contempt, saying that the queen..."

### CHAPTER II.

Afterward, when the king's anger was cooled and he remembered Vashti, what she had done, and the decree made against her, his servants and ministers suggested to him that he should arrange for young virgins of outstanding beauty to be sought out for him. They suggested he appoint certain officials in all the regions of his empire to gather all the young virgins of elegant appearance to Susa, the capital of the kingdom, into the house of the women, under the care of Hegai <note>original: "Hegæi"</note>, the royal eunuch <term>eunuch</term> <note>original: "spadonis"; a high-ranking court official, often castrated, who supervised the royal harem</note>, guardian of the women, who would provide them with feminine treatments <note>original: "mundum muliebrem"; the specific perfumes, oils, and ointments used for purification</note>; and whichever girl pleased the king, she should reign instead of Vashti. The king approved this counsel and followed it. 

There was in Susa a certain Jew named Mordecai <note>original: "Mardochæus"</note>, the son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjaminite, who had been deported as a captive from Jerusalem along with those whom Nebuchadnezzar, King of Babylon, had carried away with Jeconiah, King of Judah. He was the guardian of Hadassah, that is, Esther, the daughter of his uncle, who had been orphaned of both parents. She was a girl of elegant form and beautiful face; after her father and mother died, Mordecai had adopted her as his own daughter. 

When the king's mandate and decree were heard and many girls were gathered at Susa under the care of Hegai, this Esther was led into the palace into the custody of Hegai, the guardian of the women. He was delighted by her, and when she had found favor with him, he immediately provided her with treatments and her allotted portions, and assigned seven handmaidens from the palace, as was established. He moved her and her girls into the most luxurious part of the house of the women. Esther did not reveal her people or her homeland; for Mordecai had forbidden it. Every day he would walk in the vestibule of the house of the women to know how Esther was faring and what would happen to her. 

Now, each girl used to be brought in to King Ahasuerus after a certain space of time, as the rule for the women required—specifically, after twelve months were completed. For this was how the time of their preparation was spent: six months assigned to oil of myrrh <note>original: "oleo myrtino"</note> and as many to sweet spices and feminine ointments. Only then was the girl brought from the harem <note>original: "gynæcio"</note> into the palace to the king, so that he might have relations with her; and whatever ornament she asked for was given to her as she went to him. She would go in the evening and return in the morning to a second harem, into the care of Shaashgaz <note>original: "Safagazi"</note>, the royal eunuch and curator of the concubines; nor was she brought in to the king again unless the king took delight in her and she was called by

And while the virgins were being gathered a second time, Mordecai remained at the king's gate. Esther had still not revealed her homeland or her people, just as Mordecai had commanded her; for she followed his mandate no differently than when she was under his direct guardianship. During that time when Mordecai was staying at the king's gate, Bigthan and Teresh <note>original: "Bagathan & Thares"</note>, two of the king's eunuchs from the threshold guards, became angry with King Ahasuerus and attempted to lay hands on him. When Mordecai learned of this, he informed Queen Esther. Esther, in turn, told the king in the name of Mordecai. The matter was investigated and discovered, and both men were raised on a cross <note>referring to execution by hanging or impalement</note>, and the event was recorded in the annals before the king.

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>
Haman.
</margin>
Afterward, the king promoted Haman <note>original: "Amanem"</note>, son of Hammedatha the Agagite, to such a high peak of dignity that he placed his seat above all the nobles he had with him. All the royal servants staying at the king's gate would bow down and venerate Haman, for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai neither bowed nor showed him honor. When he was scolded by the royal servants at the king's gate for acting against the king's mandate, and was warned for several days, he still did not comply. Therefore, they reported it to Haman to see if Mordecai would persist in this; for they understood that he was a Jew. 

When Haman saw that Mordecai did not bow to him or show him honor, he was filled with rage. Thinking it too little to lay hands on Mordecai alone, he attempted to destroy all the Jews (whom he understood to be Mordecai’s people) throughout the entire empire of Ahasuerus.
