### CHAPTER XVI.

Begin the praises for my God with tambourines; sing to the Lord with cymbals; tune a song to him; extol his praises; call upon his name, for he is the God who crushes wars, who has rescued me from the hands of my persecutors, placing his camp in the midst of his people. The Assyrian came from the mountains, he came from the north with thousands of his soldiers, such that their multitude blocked the rivers and their cavalry covered the valleys. He had determined to set fire to my borders, to take my young men with the sword, to dash the nursing infants to the ground, to take the children as prey, and to seize the virgins. But the Almighty Lord struck him down by the hand of a woman. For that powerful one was not cast down by young men, nor did the sons of Titans strike him, nor did massive giants attack him; instead, Judith, daughter of Merari, overcame him with the beauty of her face. For she put off her mourning garments and put on the robes of Gladness <note>original: "Lætitia"; here personified or referring to festive attire</note> to relieve the labors of the Israelites. She anointed her face with ointment; she bound her hair with a headband to deceive him; she snatched his eye with her sandals, stole his soul with her beauty, and pierced through his neck with a scimitar <term>acinaces: a short Persian sword or scimitar</term>. The Persians shuddered at her audacity, and the Medes were troubled by her confidence. Then my afflicted ones groaned <note>original: "ulularunt," literally "howled" or "shouted"</note> because they were parched with thirst, my weak ones cried out, and at their cry, the enemies were terrified and turned to flight. The sons of servant girls <note>original: "filios puellarum"; referring to the Israelite soldiers as humble servants</note> stabbed them; they perished like runaway slaves wounded in battle by the army of the Lord my God, whose praises I will celebrate in song. O Lord, you are great and glorious, wonderful in power, and insuperable. Let every creature of yours serve you, because they were made by your command and constructed by the spirit you sent, and there is nothing that can resist your word; indeed, the very mountains are shaken from their foundations along with the waters, and rocks melt like wax in your sight. But to those who revere you, you show yourself favorable. For any sacrifice is small for a pleasing odor to you, and all fat is the least thing for a burnt offering; but whoever reveres the Lord is always great. Woe to the nations that harass my people, for the Almighty Lord will take vengeance on them in the day of judgment, by applying fire and worms to their bodies, so that they may weep in awareness of their pain forever.

<margin>a. Namely, because of the slaughter.</margin>

Judith dedicated all the household goods of Holofernes given to her by the soldiers, and the canopy which she had taken from his bedroom, as an offering to the Lord. The people remained in sight of the sanctuary celebrating for three months, and Judith stayed with them. After that time, each returned to their own homeland, and Judith returned to Bethulia and remained on her own estates. She was the most celebrated woman in the whole world in her time, and although many desired her, no man knew her <note>euphemism for sexual intimacy</note> for the rest of her life, from the time her husband Manasseh died and was gathered to his people. She became more famous by the day, and she grew old in the house of her husband until she was one hundred and five years old; she also set her handmaid free. # ESTHER

### CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>An ornate initial letter A, featuring a woodcut illustration of a king seated on a throne under a canopy, holding a scepter, and surrounded by attendants in a courtly setting.</image-desc>

<margin>a. Here he is called Artaxerxes in Greek, the son of Xerxes, according to Josephus. The banquet of Ahasuerus.</margin>

Ahasuerus, who held empire over one hundred and twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia, after he obtained the throne of his kingdom at Susa <note>the winter capital of the Persian Empire</note>, which is the capital of the kingdom, in the third year of his reign, he made a feast for all his nobles and subjects. The most powerful men of the Persians and Medes were present with him—namely the governors and prefects of the provinces—so that he might show off the wealth of his glorious kingdom and the exceptional honor of his greatness. This banquet lasted a long time, specifically one hundred and eighty days. When that period had passed, the king hosted all the men found there in Susa, from the least to the greatest, for a seven-day banquet in the courtyard of the royal gardens. There, a multitude of white, green, and blue curtains were fastened with cords of linen and purple, threaded through silver rings and hanging from marble columns. There were couches of gold and silver placed upon a floor of porphyry, marble, mother-of-pearl, and precious stone. They drank from golden cups, which were changed frequently, and there was royal wine in great abundance as befitted the king's wealth. The drinking was conducted according to the law, with no one being forced to drink, for the king had so instructed all his stewards that they should follow each man's own will. On the seventh day, when the king was feeling merry with wine, he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcas (the seven eunuchs who served in his ministry) to bring Queen Vashti—who herself was holding a banquet for the women in Ahasuerus's palace—before the king, wearing the royal crown, so that he might show her beauty to the people and the princes, for she was remarkably beautiful.

<margin>Queen Vashti, ordered to come to the king, does not obey.</margin>

But Queen Vashti refused to come at the king's command delivered by the eunuchs. Therefore the king, incensed with a powerful rage, questioned the wise men who were experts in such matters (for it was the king's custom to propose business to those skilled in law and justice, and those closest to him then were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of the Persians and Medes who resided with the king and held the highest rank of dignity in the kingdom); he asked them, I say, what should be done with Queen Vashti, who had not obeyed the command of King Ahasuerus delivered by the eunuchs. Then Memucan spoke before the king and the nobles to this effect: "Queen Vashti has sinned not only against the king, but also against all the princes and common people who are in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus. ...Queen Vashti, summoned by King Ahasuerus, did not come. And this act of the queen will one day be thrown in the faces of the primary lords of the Persians and Medes by their women, which thing will bring forth great contempt and indignation. This opinion pleased both the King and the lords, and following the counsel of Memucan <note>original: "Mamuchanis," one of the seven counselors to the King</note>, the King sent letters into all his provinces, written in the script of each region and the speech of each people, and explained in the native tongue, by which he decreed that every man should be the ruler in his own home.

### CHAPTER II.

Afterward, when the King’s anger was calmed, and he remembered Vashti and what she had done and the decree against her, his servants and attendants suggested to him that he should arrange for beautiful young virgins to be sought for him. He should appoint certain officials in all the regions of his empire to gather all the elegant young virgins to Susa, the capital of the kingdom, into the house of the women, under the care of Hegai <note>original: "Hegæi"</note>, the royal eunuch <term>spado: a term for a eunuch or a high-ranking court official who guarded the harem</term>, the guardian of the women, who would provide them with feminine finery. And let the girl who pleases the King reign in place of Vashti. Approving this plan, the King followed it. There was in Susa a certain Jew named Mordecai <note>original: "Mardochæus"</note>, son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjaminite, who had been deported from Jerusalem as a captive along with those whom Nebuchadnezzar <note>original: "Nabuchodonoſor"</note>, King of Babylon, had carried away with Jeconiah, King of Judah. He was the guardian of Hadassah <note>original: "Adaſſæ"</note>, that is, Esther, the daughter of his uncle, she being orphaned of both parents—a girl of elegant form and beautiful face, whom he had adopted as a daughter after her father and mother were lost. This Esther, when the King’s mandate and decree were heard and many girls were gathered at Susa under the care of Hegai, was taken into the palace into the custody of Hegai, the guardian of the women. Being delighted with her, and having approved her, he immediately gave her finery and provisions, and assigned seven handmaidens from the palace, as was established. He moved her and her girls into the most luxurious part of the house of the women. Esther did not reveal her people or her homeland, for Mordecai had forbidden it. Every day he would walk in the vestibule of the house of the women to know how Esther was faring and what would happen to her. Now, after a certain space of time, each girl was accustomed to be introduced to King Ahasuerus, according to the rule for women—specifically after twelve months had passed. For thus the period of their preparation was completed: six months assigned to oil of myrrh, and as many for spices and feminine cosmetics. Only then was the girl introduced from the harem <note>original: "gynecæo"</note> into the palace to the King, so that he might have relations with her; and whatever ornament she requested was given to her as she went to him. She would go in the evening and return in the morning to the second harem, under the care of Shaashgaz <note>original: "Saſagazi"</note>, the royal eunuch and curator of the concubines; nor was she introduced to the King again unless, the King being delighted with her, she was called by name.

Therefore, when the time came for Esther, the daughter of Abihail <note>original: "Abichaïlis"</note>, the uncle of Mordecai (who had adopted her as his daughter), to be admitted to the King, she asked for no ornament except what Hegai, the royal eunuch and curator of women, had told her.

And yet, she was pleasing in the eyes of all who saw her. Then he celebrated the nuptials of Esther sumptuously, inviting all his lords and attendants, and he granted immunity <note>This likely refers to a tax exemption or a release of prisoners to mark the celebration</note> to the nations and gave gifts worthy of a king. And when the virgins were being gathered a second time, Mordecai remained at the palace gates. During the time that Mordecai was living at the palace gate, Bigthan <note>original: "Bagathan"</note> and Teresh <note>original: "Thares"</note>, two royal eunuchs from the number of the doorkeepers, being hostile toward King Ahasuerus, attempted to lay hands on him. The matter was investigated and discovered, and both of them were hoisted onto a cross <note>original: "in crucem"; in a Persian context, this often referred to impalement or hanging</note>, and that matter was recorded in the annals in the presence of the King.

<margin>Ahasuerus takes Esther in marriage.</margin>
And when she was led to the king in the palace in the month of Tebeth, which is the tenth month, in the seventh year of his reign, he loved her above all women, and held her as the most pleasing and beloved of all the virgins, so that he placed the royal diadem upon her head and made her queen in place of Vashti. Then he celebrated Esther's wedding lavishly, inviting all his nobles and attendants, and granted tax immunity <note>original: "immunitatem"; likely a release from tribute or a public holiday</note> to the nations and gave gifts worthy of a king. And while the virgins were being gathered a second time, Mordecai remained at the palace gates. Indeed, Esther had not disclosed her fatherland or her people, just as Mordecai had commanded her, whose orders she followed no differently than when she was under his guardianship. During that time when Mordecai was staying at the palace gate, Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king's eunuchs from the number of the doorkeepers, being incensed against King Ahasuerus, attempted to lay hands on him. When Mordecai learned of this matter, he indicated it to Queen Esther. Esther then reported it to the king in the name of Mordecai. The matter was investigated and discovered, and they were both hung on a cross <note>original: "in crucem sublati"; while the Latin suggests crucifixion, in a Persian context it usually referred to impalement or hanging on a gallows</note>, and that matter was recorded in the annals in the presence of the king.

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>Haman.</margin>
Afterward, King Ahasuerus exalted Haman, the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, to such a high point of dignity that he placed his seat above all the nobles he had with him. And everyone dwelling at the king's gate bowed down humbly, because the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai neither bowed down nor showed him honor, and being rebuked by the royal servants who were at the king’s gate for acting against the king's command, and having been warned for several days, he still did not comply. Therefore, they reported this to Haman, to see whether Mordecai would persist in it; for they had understood that he was a Jew. Haman, seeing that Mordecai did not bow to him or show him honor, was full of wrath, and thinking it too little to lay hands on Mordecai alone, he attempted to destroy all the Jews (whom he understood to be Mordecai’s countrymen) as many as were in the whole empire of Ahasuerus. Therefore, in the first month, which is Nisan, in the twelfth year of Ahasuerus's reign, Haman arranged for a lot <note>original: "sortem"; the "Pur" from which the festival of Purim takes its name</note> to be cast in his presence; and having gone through the days and months in order, when the month of Adar, which is the twelfth, happened by lot, he spoke to the king thus: 
<margin>Haman asks Ahasuerus that the Jews be destroyed.</margin>
"There is a certain nation of people dispersed and scattered among the other nations through all the borders of your empire, who have laws alien to the laws of all other peoples, and they do not obey the royal laws; indeed, it is not expedient for you, O King, to tolerate them. If it pleases you, O King, let it be promulgated in writing that they perish: I will weigh out ten thousand talents of silver into the hands of the administrators, to be brought into the treasury." ### CHAPTER V.

<margin>Esther approaches the king.</margin>
Then, on the third day, having finished her prayer, she took off her mourning clothes and put on her splendor. Thus arrayed, and having called upon God, the observer and savior of all, she took two maids, on one of whom she leaned as if for support; the other followed, carrying her train. She was radiant in the flower of her beauty, with a cheerful and lovely expression, though her heart was anxious with fear. Having passed through all the doors, she stood before the King. As he sat on his throne, magnificently adorned, shining with gold and gems and appearing truly terrifying, he raised his head, which glowed with splendor, and looked at the queen so fiercely that she collapsed. Her strength failing and her color fading, she leaned her head against the maid who accompanied her. Then the King—his spirit turned to mildness by divine intervention—leapt anxiously from his throne and took her in his arms. After she regained her senses, he comforted her with gentle words. "What is it, Esther?" he said. "I am your brother <note>A term of royal endearment and shared status</note>; take heart. You shall not die, for our empire is shared; come forward." Then he raised the golden scepter and touched it to her neck, and having kissed her, said, "Speak to me." To which she replied: "When I saw you, you seemed like a divine being, and I was troubled in spirit by the fear of your splendor; for you are wonderful, my lord, and your face is full of grace." While she was speaking, her strength failed and she collapsed again. Then the King was troubled, and his attendants tried to comfort her. And the King said, "What do you wish, Queen Esther? What is your request? For you shall obtain it, even if it be half of the kingdom." Esther replied: "Today is a special day for me; if it pleases you, King, come with Haman today to a banquet that I have prepared for you." Then the king ordered Haman to be summoned immediately so that he might comply with Esther’s wish; and the King and Haman came to the banquet Esther had prepared. And there, over wine, the King spoke to Esther: "What is your petition? For you shall have it. Even if you ask for half the kingdom, it shall be done." Esther answered and said, "My petition and my prayer is this: if I have found favor in your eyes, King, and if it seems good to you to grant my request and do what I ask, let you and Haman return to the banquet which I shall prepare for you, and tomorrow I will do as you command."

...he pulled the ring from his hand and handed it to Haman, son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews, telling him that he both waived the silver payment and placed that nation under Haman's power. Although I rule over many nations and have attained dominion over the whole world, I have wished—not by pridefully abusing the boldness of my power, but by always acting mildly and with kindness—to make the lives of my subjects perpetually tranquil. By providing a quiet and passable kingdom to its furthest borders, I sought to renew for all men that peace which is so desired. When I asked my counselors how this goal might be achieved, Haman—a man among us of exceptional wisdom, most constant in goodwill, proven with firm loyalty, and who has attained the second rank of the kingdom—showed us that one particular people is mixed among all the nations across the globe. They are a people whose laws are contrary to every other race, who perpetually disregard the commands of kings, so that the empire we have established cannot maintain a stable state without offense. Since we have perceived that this one nation is so uniquely structured that it is always contrary to all men, differs in its foreign system of laws, is hostile to our affairs, and is the cause of the worst evils, preventing the kingdom from attaining tranquility, we command that those who shall be pointed out to you in the writings of Haman—the administrator of our affairs and our second father—all of them, along with their wives and children, shall be utterly destroyed by the sword of their enemies without any mercy or pity, 
<margin>a In the Greek it is the fourteenth, but the whole history shows this to be an error.</margin> 
<sup>a</sup> on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month of the current year. ### CHAPTER 4.
When Mordecai learned of all that had been done, he tore his clothes, put on sackcloth <note>original: "centonem," literally a patchwork garment, here signifying mourning rags</note>,

<column-break/>

covered himself with ashes, and went out into the middle of the city, crying out with loud and bitter cries. **G.** He shouted that an innocent nation was being destroyed. **H.** He progressed even to the sight of the royal gate, for it was not permitted for anyone clothed in sackcloth to enter the gate itself. Meanwhile, in every land where the king’s mandate and decree had reached, there was great mourning among the Jews, with fasting, weeping, and lamentation; many lay in sackcloth and ashes. When Queen Esther’s maids and eunuchs told her about Mordecai, she was greatly distressed and sent clothing for Mordecai to wear so he would take off his sackcloth. When he would not accept them, Esther called Hathach <note>original: "Athachum"</note>, one of the king’s eunuchs who had been assigned to her, and ordered him to go to Mordecai to learn what was happening and why he was acting this way. <margin>Esther learns from Hathach why Mordecai is mourning.</margin> Hathach went out to Mordecai in a square of the city in front of the king’s gate. Mordecai explained to him everything that had happened to him and the exact sum of money Haman had promised to pay into the treasury for the destruction of the Jews. He also gave him a copy of the decree posted in Susa for their destruction, to show and explain it to Esther, and to urge her to go to the king and humbly plead with him for her people. Hathach returned and told Esther what Mordecai had said. Then Esther gave Hathach these instructions for Mordecai: "All the king’s servants and the people of the provinces know that there is one law for any man or woman who approaches the king in the inner court without being summoned: they are to be put to death, unless the king holds out the golden scepter <note>original: "uirgam auream"</note> to them so that they may live. As for me, I have not been called to the king for thirty days now." When Esther’s words were reported to Mordecai, he sent back this answer to Esther: "Do not think that because you are in the king’s house you alone of all the Jews will escape. For if you remain silent at this time, relief and deliverance for the Jews will arise from another place, but you and your father’s family will perish. And who knows whether you have attained royalty for such a time as this?" Then Esther sent this reply to Mordecai: "Go, gather all the Jews who are in Susa and fast for me; do not eat or drink for three days, night or day. I and my maids will fast in the same way. After that, I will go to the king, even though it is against the law; and if I perish, I perish." Mordecai went away and did everything Esther had commanded him. **G.** And remembering all the works of the Lord, he prayed in these words: <margin>Mordecai prays for God to be merciful to the Jews.</margin> "Lord, Almighty King, everything is indeed in your power, and there is no one who can oppose you if you wish to save Israel. For you made heaven and earth and everything wonderful under heaven; you are the Lord of all, and no one can resist your majesty. You know all things; you know, O Lord, that it was not out of contempt or pride or desire for glory that I refused to bow down to the arrogant Haman. For I would have been willing even to kiss the prints of his feet for the sake of Israel’s salvation. But I did this so that I might not place the glory of a man above the glory of God, and so that I would not adore anyone except you, my Lord; it was certainly not out of arrogance that I did it. Therefore, O Lord God, King, spare..."

<margin>Esther goes to the King.</margin>

# CHAPTER VI

<margin>Ahasuerus orders the records to be read to him.</margin>
That night, when the king could not sleep, he ordered the records of past deeds <note>the royal chronicles or annals of the kingdom</note> to be brought. While they were being read before him, it was found written how Mordecai had revealed the conspiracy of Bigthan and Teresh <note>original: "Bagathæ & Tharis"</note>, two of the king's eunuchs who guarded the entrance and had attempted to lay hands on King Ahasuerus. The king then asked what honor or dignity Mordecai had received for this deed. When the king's young servants replied that he had received nothing at all, the king asked who was in the court. Now, Haman had come into the inner court of the palace to speak with the king about hanging Mordecai on the gallows <note>original: "patibulo"</note> he had prepared for him. Therefore, the servants answered that Haman was standing in the vestibule. The king ordered him to be brought in, and when he entered, the king said to him: "What should be done for the man whom the king wishes to honor?" Haman, thinking there was no one the king would wish to honor more than himself, replied to the king: "For the man the king wishes to honor, royal robes should be brought which the king himself wears, and a horse on which the king rides, with a royal crown placed upon its head. Let these robes and the horse be delivered to one of the king's most noble princes; then let him lead the man whom the king wishes to honor on the horse through the city square, and let it be proclaimed before him: 'Thus shall it be done for the man whom the king wishes to honor!'" The king said to Haman: "Quickly take the robes and the horse, as you have said, and do exactly this for Mordecai the Jew who stays at the king's gate. Do not omit anything that you have spoken."

<margin>Haman is forced to honor Mordecai.</margin>
So Haman took the robes and the horse, arrayed Mordecai, and led him on the horse through the city square, proclaiming before him: "Thus shall it be done for the man whom the king wishes to honor." Afterward, Mordecai returned to the king’s gate. Haman, however, rushed home mourning and with his head covered, and he told his wife Zeresh and all his friends what had happened to him. His wise advisors and his wife Zeresh said to him: "If Mordecai is of the race of the Jews, and you have begun to fall before him, you will not be able to prevail against him, but you will surely fall." While they were still talking with him, the king's eunuchs arrived to hurry Haman to the banquet Esther had prepared.

I have given, and because he dared to act against the Jews, I have seen to it that he was raised upon a cross <note>original: "in crucem tollēdum"; the Latin specifically refers to crucifixion or being hung on a high pole</note>. You yourselves write to the Jews as you see fit, in the king's name, and seal it with the king's ring. For whatever was written in the king's name and sealed with the king's ring was irrevocable. Therefore, the royal scribes were summoned at that time, on the twenty-third day of the third month, which is Sivan <note>original: "Siuan"</note>. A decree was written according to the will of Mordecai to the Jews, to the satraps, to the governors, and to the rulers of the one hundred and twenty-seven provinces that stretch from India to Ethiopia, to each people in their own language, and also to the Jews in their own script and tongue. These letters were signed in the name of King Ahasuerus <note>original: "Assueri"; identified here as Artaxerxes in the following letter</note> and sealed with his ring. They were sent out by couriers who rode swift horses or the very best mules bred for speed. In these letters, the king permitted the Jews in every city to gather and defend their lives, and to destroy, kill, and annihilate all the armed forces of any people or province that might attack them, including their children and women, and to plunder their goods on a single day throughout all the regions of King Ahasuerus—namely, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is Adar. **G.** The following is a copy of that letter: THE GREAT KING ARTAXERXES <note>The Latin text follows the Greek tradition of identifying the Persian King Ahasuerus as Artaxerxes</note> to the one hundred and twenty-seven satraps who rule the provinces from India to Ethiopia, and to those who stand with us, Greetings. Many, having been frequently honored by the great bounty of their benefactors, have grown proud. They not only attempt to harm our subjects but, unable to handle their own abundance of fortune, they plot evil against those who showed them kindness. Not only do they remove gratitude from among men, but, puffed up by the foolish insolence of wealth, they think they can escape the vengeful judgment of God, who sees all things. Often, the madness of those who have been entrusted with the administration of their friends' affairs has made them accomplices in the shedding of innocent blood, entangling them in incurable calamities. This happens when, through the deceptive cunning of malice, they circumvent the sincere integrity of their rulers. This can be seen both from ancient records and from those things <margin>a</margin> which are right before our eyes—the wicked crimes committed by those who unworthily hold power. Therefore, we must strive hereafter to provide a kingdom of peace and tranquility for all men, no longer paying heed to slanders, but judging those matters that come before our eyes with a more equitable remedy. **L.** You ought not to think that if we issue different orders, it proceeds from a fickleness of mind; rather, we deliver judgment according to the state and necessity of the times, as the utility of the commonwealth demands. And so that you may understand more clearly what we say, **G.** when Haman, son of Hammedatha, a true <margin>b</margin> Macedonian <note>original: "Macedo"; calling Haman a Macedonian in this context frames him as a foreign Greek infiltrator plotting against the Persian Empire, whereas the Hebrew text calls him an Agagite</note> and a stranger to the blood of the Persians—one far removed from our integrity—had gained our favor and experienced the humanity we show toward all mortals, he was even called our father

<column-break/>

and was honored by all as the second person after the king. But, unable to contain his pride, he attempted to deprive us of both our empire and our life. Through many deceitful ways, he demanded the death of our savior and greatest benefactor, Mordecai, and of Esther, the blameless partner of our kingdom, together with their entire nation. By this means, he hoped that once he had oppressed us in our isolation, he might transfer the empire of the Persians to the Macedonians. However, we find that the Jews, who were marked for destruction by that most pestilent man, are not evildoers, but follow the most just laws. They are the children of the most high, most great, and immortal God, who has maintained the kingdom in the best condition for both us and our ancestors. Therefore, you will do well if you do not act upon the letters sent by Haman, son of Hammedatha. For he, the author of those letters, has been crucified at the gates of Susa <note>original: "Susorū"</note> with his entire family, having quickly received the punishment he deserved from God, the ruler of all things. Let a copy of this letter be posted in all places, allowing the Jews to freely use their own laws. Assist them so that they may defend themselves against those who attacked them in their time of trouble, on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is Adar. For God, the ruler of all, has made this a day of joy for the chosen race instead of a day of destruction. Therefore, you also shall keep this day with all gladness as a celebrated feast among your festivals, so that it may be a memorial of safety both now and in the future for us and for those who wish the Persians well, but a monument of destruction for those who harbor malice. Every city or nation that does not follow this shall be laid waste with such wrath by sword and fire that it will be made impassable not only to men, but even to wild beasts and birds forever. Let copies of this be displayed openly throughout the whole kingdom, so that all Jews may be prepared on that day to take vengeance on their enemies. **H.** Thus the couriers, urged by the king’s command, departed in haste, and the decree was published in Susa. Then Mordecai went out from the king’s presence in royal robes of hyacinth <note>original: "hyacintho"; a deep blue or violet color</note> and fine linen, wearing a great golden crown and a cloak of silk and purple. The city of Susa exulted and rejoiced. For the Jews, there was light, gladness, joy, and honor. Throughout every province and city, wherever the king’s command and decree reached, the Jews were filled with joy, holding banquets and holiday celebrations. Furthermore, many of the inhabitants of the land became Jews <note>original: "iudaizabant"; meaning they adopted Jewish customs or formally joined the faith</note>, for the fear of the Jews had fallen upon them.

### CHAPTER IX.

<margin>The Jews take vengeance on their enemies.</margin>
On the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, which is the twelfth month, when the king's command was to be carried out—the very day when the enemies of the Jews had hoped to overpower them—the situation was reversed, and the Jews overpowered their adversaries. The Jews gathered in their cities throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus to lay hands on those who had plotted their ruin. And no one...

Not only did no one resist them—for fear of them had seized all nations—but even all the governors of the provinces, the satraps, the praetors, and the king's administrators assisted the Jews, struck by the dread of Mordecai. For Mordecai was very powerful in the court, and his fame had spread through all the regions, as Mordecai grew greater day by day.

And so the Jews pursued all their enemies with the sword, with slaughter, and with destruction, and they dealt with their adversaries according to their own will. In Susa, they killed and destroyed five hundred men. Additionally, they killed Pharsadatha, Dalphon, Asphatha, Phoratha, Adalia, Aridatha, Pharmasta, Arisai, Aridai, and Jezatha—the ten sons of Haman <note>original: "Amanis"</note>, son of Hammedatha, the adversary of the Jews—but they did not seize any of their goods as plunder. When the number of those killed in Susa was reported to the king that day, he spoke to Queen Esther: "In Susa, the Jews have killed and destroyed five hundred men, besides the ten sons of Haman; what have they done in the other regions of the empire? And yet, whatever you ask for further shall be granted to you, and whatever you request shall be done." Esther replied: "If it pleases you, O king, let the Jews in Susa be allowed to do tomorrow what they did today, and let the ten sons of Haman be hung upon the cross <note>original: "in crucem tollere"; while the Latin suggests a cross, this historically refers to being impaled or hung on a high wooden gallows</note>." Then the king commanded it to be so, and once the edict was proclaimed in Susa, the sons of Haman were hung. The Jews in Susa gathered again on the fourteenth day of the month of Adar and killed three hundred men in Susa, yet they did not seize their goods.

The rest of the Jews in the provinces gathered to defend their lives and to secure rest from their enemies; they slew seventy-five thousand of their adversaries, though they took no plunder from their wealth. Since they did this on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, they dedicated the fourteenth day—the day they achieved rest—to banquets and joy. But the Jews in Susa, who had gathered on the thirteenth and fourteenth days, made the fifteenth day their day of feasting and joy, as it was then they obtained rest. Therefore, the rural Jews celebrate the fourteenth day of the month of Adar with joy, banquets, and merriment, and they send gifts to one another.

Mordecai wrote these things down and sent letters to all the Jews in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, both near and far, in which he established that they should keep the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the month of Adar every year. These were the days on which the Jews secured rest from their enemies, and the month in which their sorrow was turned into joy and their day of mourning into a feast. He instructed them to celebrate those days with invitations and gladness, and to send portions of food to one another and gifts to the poor. Thus the Jews confirmed what they had already begun to do, having been advised by the letters Mordecai had written to them. These letters recounted how Haman, son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the adversary of all the Jews, had plotted their destruction and had cast the lot <note>original: "fortem" / "pur"</note> for their slaughter and ruin, and how the king, approached by the queen, had ordered by letter that his wicked 

<column-break/>

attempt against the Jews should be turned back upon his own head, and that he and his sons should be hung upon the cross. From this, these days were named "Purim" <note>original: "Phuræi"</note>, after the name of the lot. Because of all the words of this letter, and because of what they had seen and what had happened to them, the Jews established and decreed for themselves, their descendants, and all who joined them, that they would observe these two days every year without fail, as they were written and recorded. Therefore, these solemn days of Purim are observed in every nation, family, province, and city, and they are never abolished among the Jews nor forgotten by the memory of their descendants. Queen Esther, daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew also wrote to fully confirm this second letter concerning Purim. Mordecai sent letters to all the Jews in the one hundred and twenty-seven provinces of King Ahasuerus, greeting them with respect and advising them to observe these days of Purim in their proper time, just as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther had decreed, and as they had decreed for themselves and their descendants regarding their fasts and cries of lamentation. And so the observance of these Purim days was confirmed by Esther's authority, by letter, and by command.

<margin>The days of Purim.</margin>
Furthermore, King Ahasuerus made both the lands and the islands of the sea tributary. As for all his acts of power and might, and the great dignity to which the king promoted Mordecai, these are recorded in the annals of the kings of Media and Persia. There it is explained how Mordecai the Jew was second only to King Ahasuerus, the most powerful among the Jews, dear to the multitude of his kinsmen, seeking the welfare of his people, and looking out for the safety of his whole race.

# JOB.

## CHAPTER I.

<margin>a. That region is in Edom, as is shown in Lamentations 4.</margin>
There was a man in the land of <margin>a. Uz</margin> named Job, who was a man of integrity, upright, god-fearing, and turning away from evil. To him were born seven sons and three daughters. His livestock consisted of seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred female donkeys, along with a very large household of servants; indeed, he was the wealthiest man among all the people of the East. Now his sons used to gather and hold feasts in their houses, each on his appointed day, and they would send for their three sisters to eat and drink with them. When the cycle of their feasting days was complete, Job would send for them and purify them, rising early in the morning to offer burnt offerings for each of them, thinking: "It may be that my children have sinned and cursed God in their hearts." Job did this continually. Now it happened on a certain day that the <term>heavenly beings<note>original: "diui." In this classical Latin style, the translator uses a term for "gods" to refer to the angels or sons of God.</note></term> came to present themselves before <term>the Lord<note>original: "Ioua," a Renaissance Latin spelling of Jehovah.</note></term>, and Satan was also among them. Then the Lord said to Satan: "Where do you come from?" Satan answered the Lord: "From wandering through the earth and walking around in it." Then the Lord said to Satan: "Have you noticed my servant Job? There is no one like him on earth—a man of integrity, upright, god-fearing, and turning away from evil." At this, Satan answered the Lord: "Does Job fear God for nothing? Have you not placed a hedge around him, his household, and everything he has? You have blessed the work of his hands, so that his flocks are spread throughout the land. But reach out your hand and strike everything he has, and he will surely curse you to your face." Then the Lord said to Satan: "Behold, everything he has is in your power; only do not lay a hand on the man himself." So Satan went out from the presence of the Lord. Now on a certain day, when Job's sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother’s house, a messenger came to Job and said: "While the oxen were plowing and the donkeys were grazing nearby, the <term>Sabeans<note>A nomadic people from the Arabian Peninsula.</note></term> attacked and carried them off. They put the servants to the sword, and I am the only one who has escaped to tell you!" While he was still speaking, another messenger arrived and said: "The fire of God <margin>b. Lightning</margin> fell from the sky and burned up the sheep and the servants. I am the only one who has escaped to tell you!" While he was still speaking, another arrived and said: "The <term>Chaldeans<note>A people from Mesopotamia, often portrayed as raiders or scholars.</note></term> formed three bands and raided the camels and carried them off. They put the servants to the sword, and I am the only one who has escaped to tell you!" While he was still speaking, yet another arrived and said: "Your sons and daughters were feasting in their oldest brother’s house, when suddenly a mighty wind swept in from the wilderness and struck

<column-break/>

the four corners of the house. It collapsed on the young people and they are dead, and I am the only one who has escaped to tell you!" Then Job got up and tore his robe and shaved his head. He fell to the ground in worship and said: "Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I will return there. The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord." In all this, Job did not sin, nor did he charge God with any wrongdoing.

## CHAPTER II.

On another day the heavenly beings came to present themselves before the Lord, and Satan also came among them to present himself before the Lord. The Lord asked Satan: "Where have you come from?" Satan answered: "From wandering through the earth and walking around in it." And the Lord said: "Have you noticed my servant Job? There is no one on earth like him; a man of integrity, upright, god-fearing, and turning away from evil. He still maintains his integrity, though you incited me against him to ruin him without any reason." But Satan replied: "Skin <margin>a. It is easy to redeem one’s own life with the life of another.</margin> for skin! A man will give all he has for his own life. But reach out your hand and strike his flesh and bones, and he will surely curse you to your face." The Lord said to Satan: "Behold, he is in your hands; but spare his life." So Satan went out from the presence of the Lord and afflicted Job with agonizing sores from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head. Then Job took a piece of broken pottery to scrape himself with as he sat among the ashes. His wife said to him: "Are you still maintaining your integrity? <margin>b. Are you not raving to give thanks to God when he lets you die?</margin> Go ahead, curse God and die!" But he replied to her: "You are talking like a foolish woman. Shall we accept good from God, and not accept trouble?" In all this, Job did not sin in what he said. Now when Job’s three friends heard about all the misfortune that had come upon him, they set out from their homes—Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite—and met together by agreement to go and sympathize with him and comfort him. When they saw him from a distance, they could hardly recognize him; they began to weep aloud, and they tore their robes and sprinkled dust on their heads. Then they sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights. No one said a word to him, because they saw how great his suffering was.

## CHAPTER III.

After this, Job opened his mouth and cursed the day of his birth <margin>Jeremiah 20, d.</margin> with these words: "May the day of my birth perish, and the night that said, 'A boy is conceived!' May that day be darkness; may God above not care for it, nor light shine upon it. May gloom and utter darkness claim it; may a cloud settle over it, and blackness terrify its light. As for that night, may thick darkness seize it; let it not be joined to the days of the year nor entered in the count of the months. Oh, may that night be barren; may no shout of joy be heard in it. May those who curse days curse that night, those who are ready to rouse <term>Leviathan<note>A great sea monster or dragon of chaos.</note></term>. May its morning stars become dark; may it wait for daylight in vain and not see the first rays of dawn, for it <margin>a. Of the womb that carried me, that is, my mother’s.</margin> did not shut the doors of the womb on me to hide trouble from my eyes. Why did I not die at birth? ## CHAPTER VI.

Then Job answered and said: "O that my impatience and my misery were weighed together in the scales! For now it would be heavier than the sand of the sea; therefore my words fail me. For the arrows of the Almighty are within me, the poison of which my spirit drinks up; God’s terrors are marshaled against me. Does the wild donkey bray when he has grass? Or does the ox low over his fodder? Is tasteless food eaten without salt? Or is there any flavor in the white of an egg? My soul refuses to touch them; such things are as loathsome food to me. O that I might have my request, and that God would grant what I long for—that it would please God to crush me, to let loose His hand and cut me off! Then I would still have comfort; I would rejoice in pain, though He does not spare me, for I have not denied the words of the <term>Holy One<note>original: "Augusti," literally "The August One" or "The Venerable One," a title for God.</note></term>. What is my strength, that I should endure? Or what is my end, that I should be patient? Is my strength the strength of stones, or is my flesh bronze? Do I not lack help within myself? And yet I gain nothing. To the afflicted, kindness should be shown by his friends, yet they forsake the fear of the Almighty. My brothers are as deceitful as a brook, like the stream of a torrent that passes away—darkened with ice and hidden under snow—which vanishes when it is warm and disappears from its place in the heat. The travelers who wind along their way go into the void and perish, having looked toward the path to Tema or hoped for the journey to Sheba. They are ashamed because they had been confident; they come there and are confounded. Now you are like this to me: you see my calamity and are afraid. Have I said, 'Give to me,' or 'Offer a bribe for me from your wealth,' or 'Deliver me from the enemy’s hand,' or 'Redeem me from the hand of the ruthless'? Teach me, and I will be silent; make me understand how I have erred."

JOB.

Listen carefully. Provided I may plead my case, I know I will be found innocent: but if he [God] contends with me, I will be breathless and silent. <margin>h</margin> Only do not do two things to me, then I will not hide from your presence. Withdraw your hand from me, and do not terrify me with your dread; then call, and I will answer: or let me speak, and you answer me. How many are my crimes or sins? Show me my offenses and faults. Why do you hide your face, and hold me as an enemy? Will you rage against a wind-blown leaf, and pursue dry stubble? <margin>i</margin> that you write such bitter things against me, and summon the vices of my youth as an accusation, and having fixed my feet in shackles, you observe all my paths, marking the tracks of my feet: when otherwise I waste away like something rotten, or like a garment that a moth eats.

### CHAPTER XIV.

A man born of a woman is of so short a life and so full of misery: who comes forth like a flower and is plucked, and flees like a shadow, and does not endure; and yet <margin>a</margin> you keep your eyes open upon such a one, and bring me into judgment against you? Who can make a pure thing out of the impure? No one. If his age is determined, if the number of his months is with you, if you have set a limit for him which he cannot <margin>b</margin> pass, leave him so that he may <margin>b</margin> depart <note>original: "defungatur"</note>, until he finds pleasure in his day like a hired laborer. For there is hope for a tree, if it is cut down, that it will sprout again, and its branches will not fail. If its root grows old in the earth, and its stump dies in the ground, at the scent of water it buds again, and brings forth shoots like a plant. <margin>c</margin> But man, weakened and extinguished by death, where is he? The water flows out from the lake, and the dried-up river becomes parched: likewise men lie down and will not rise again, until the heavens are no more; they will not wake from their sleep nor be roused. I wish you would hide me away in the Underworld <note>original: "Orco"</note> until your anger subsides, and define a limit for me when you will remember me. If it is so that a dead man rises again, I will certainly wait through the whole space of my time until my transformation comes, when indeed you, longing for the work of your hands, will call, and I will answer you. But now you count my steps, <margin>d</margin> not indeed watching over my sin, but with my offense sealed up in a bundle, ascribing a crime to me. And as mountains fall and are shattered, and rocks are moved from their place, as water wears away stones, and its waves wash away the soil of the earth, you have cut off the hope of man, letting him depart; whether his sons are increased or diminished, he does not know or see. Only the body he possesses feels pain, and his soul mourns.

### CHAPTER XV.

To these things Eliphaz the Temanite replied thus: Does a wise man answer with windy knowledge, and fill his breast with the East Wind, arguing with useless speech, and with words by which nothing is helped? Indeed, you dissolve religion, and drive away concern for God. For with your own mouth you teach your crime, using a crafty tongue. ### CHAPTER XIX.

<margin>a. To punish me more severely than I deserve.</margin>
To this Job responded: "How long will you weary my soul," he said, "and crush me with words? Ten times now you have brought shame upon me, and you are not ashamed to oppress me. The guests in my house and my female servants count me as a stranger; they look at me as an alien. I call my servant, but he does not answer, even when I plead with my own mouth. ### CHAPTER XIX.

Then Job answered: "How long will you weary my soul," he said, "and vex me with words? Now ten times you have reproached me; you are not ashamed to oppress me. To this Job responded, saying: See that you hear my speech, <margin>a</margin> which may serve as your consolation. Bear with me while I speak, and after I have spoken, you may mock. Rivers wander from a strange soil, unknown to feet and uninhabited by men. The earth, from which food arises, is overturned below as if by fire. Men lay their hands upon the flinty rocks; they overturn mountains from the root; they cut out rivers in the cliffs, and their eyes behold every rare thing. They search out the depths of the floods from their weeping <note>original: "ex lachryma," likely referring to the source or "seepage" of water</note>, and bring hidden things forth into the light.

But where shall wisdom be found? And where is the place of understanding? Man does not know its value, nor is it found in the land of the living. The deep says, “It is not in me,” and the sea says, “It is not with me.” It cannot be compared to gold, nor shall silver be weighed for its price. He is the one who gives weight to the wind and sets the water by measure; who prescribes a law for the rain and a path for the lightning and thunder. He saw it then and declared it; He prepared it <margin>verse 1. 4</margin> and searched it out. And He warned and said: The fear of the Lord is wisdom, and to depart from evil is understanding.

### CHAPTER XXXII.

When these three men ceased to dispute with Job, because he seemed innocent to himself, Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the family of Ram, was indignant. He was indignant at Job, who claimed his cause was more just than God's, and at his three friends, because they could not 

<column-break/>

find a way to condemn Job. Elihu, however, had waited while Job was speaking because they were older than he. But when Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite saw those three men had nothing to say in response, he was indignant and spoke these words. I am the youngest, and you are elders; for this reason I hesitated and feared to speak to those of great age, or to exercise the wisdom of so many years. But men are moved by inspiration, and the breath of the Almighty makes them intelligent. It is not <margin>a. You.</margin> the masters who are wise, nor the elders who perceive reason. Therefore I say, hear me, while I also offer my own opinion. Indeed, I waited for your words, listening to your arguments while you searched for speech. But as I watched you, none of you refuted Job, or responded to his words, <margin>b. Nor indeed is there any reason for you to say that you do not contradict him because he is weighed down by evils, lest he be further vexed by your speech. Rather, you are silent because you are unlearned.</margin> lest you should say you have found wisdom—that he must be pursued by God, not by men. He did not direct his speech to me, and I will not respond to him with your words. They are terrified and no longer contradict; they have run out of words. And because they do not speak as I expected, but cease and no longer contradict, I also will speak for my part, and I myself will offer my opinion. For I am full of speech, and the spirit of my breast urges me. Indeed, my breast is like unopened wine; it bursts like new wineskins. I will speak so that I may be refreshed by delivering my discourse and offering a rebuttal. I will not show partiality to anyone, nor will I flatter any man, for I do not know how to flatter; otherwise there would be danger that my Creator would take me away.

### CHAPTER XXXIII.

But hear my speech, Job, and listen to all my words. Behold, I open my mouth; my tongue speaks in my palate. My mind will dictate right words, and my lips will speak a pure opinion. <margin>a. I am a man as you are, so that you may not complain of an unequal contest with God.</margin> The spirit and breath of Almighty God made me and gave me life. If you can, answer me; stand and face me. Behold, I am for God, just as you requested; since I myself am formed from clay, neither my terror shall disturb you, nor shall my authority weigh upon you. You have surely spoken in my ears, and I heard the voice of your speech, saying that you are pure and clean from sin and fault, yet He has found occasions against you and holds you for an enemy, and has put your feet in the stocks and observes all your ways. Then Elihu, proceeding to discourse: "Do you think this is right," he said, "what you said—that your cause is more just than God's—denying that innocence profits or benefits you? Their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers. Job lived after this for one hundred and forty years, and saw his children and grandchildren to the fourth generation; and so Job died, an old man and full of years.

### X.
Why, Jehovah, do you stand far off? Why do you hide yourself in times of adversity?
The wicked proudly pursue the needy, to be caught in their own schemes.
For the wicked man pleases himself in his lust, and the greedy <margin>30</margin> scorner of Jehovah congratulates himself.
The wicked (in his arrogance) not only does not seek God, but indeed all his efforts aim at this: that there seems to be no God.
His deeds are always atrocious: and with your decrees removed from his sight, he scorns all his enemies.
And because he is not in trouble, he never thinks he will be shaken.
<margin>Romans 3.</margin> His mouth is full of perjury, fraud, and <margin>40</margin> treachery: under his tongue are crime and wickedness.
He sits in the ambushes of the crossroads, to kill the innocent from hiding, his eyes fixed on the abandoned.
He lies in wait in secret, like a lion from its lair: he lies in wait to seize the needy; he will seize the needy, having drawn them into his net.
He crouches down humbly, so that the forsaken may fall by his <margin>50</margin> power:
thinking that God is unmindful, and with his face hidden, will never notice.
Rise, Jehovah God, lift up your hand, do not forget the needy.
Why should the wicked man despise God, thinking that you will not notice?
For you see, and you observe such wicked villainy, that you may bring it into your power: you are the guardian of the forsaken and the defender of orphans.

<margin>Hebrews 11.</margin> Since I trust in Jehovah, why do you say to me: "Flee to your mountain like a bird"?
For behold, the wicked bend their bows, their arrows fitted to the string, to shoot secretly at upright men.
<margin>Habakkuk 2, a. If I, who trust in you, nevertheless perish; in whom trusting, does the good man have this foundation of trust shaken? b. Alludes to verse 10.</margin> But <gloss>a</gloss> if the foundations are destroyed, what will the righteous do?

Jehovah, approving the righteous, but pursuing the wicked and lovers of cruelty with the hatred of his soul,
<gloss>b</gloss> will rain down snares, fire, sulfur, and a fierce wind upon the wicked, which is the lot they must endure.
For the righteous Jehovah loves virtues, and gazes upon uprightness with his presence.

### XII.
#### A song of David to be played on the eighth instrument.
Help, Jehovah: for the godly have failed, the faithful have ceased to be among the human race.
They speak wickedly among themselves with flattering lips, they speak with a double mind.
May Jehovah cut off all flattering lips, the tongue that speaks great things,
of those who say: "By our tongues we shall prevail, our lips are our own, who is our lord?"
Because of the calamity of the needy, because of the groaning of the poor, now Jehovah promises he will arise, and will bring them safety against those who despise them.
The promises of Jehovah are pure promises, like silver in a clay furnace of the refiners, purified seven times.
You, Jehovah, preserve them; protect us from this generation forever.
Everywhere the wicked prowl, while wickedness excels among the human race.

### XIII.
#### A song of David to be sung.
<margin>Hebrews 13.</margin> How long at last, Jehovah, will you be unmindful of me? How long will you hide your face from me?
To what end shall I be troubled in spirit and anxious in mind? How long shall my enemy insult me?
Look upon me, hear me, Jehovah my God, enlighten my eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death:
lest my enemy boast that I have been conquered by him: lest, when I am shaken, my adversaries exult.
But I, relying on your mercy, shall exult in my heart in your protection, singing of Jehovah who has dealt so well with me.

OF THE PSALMS

# L.
## A song of Asaph.
Jehovah, the God of gods, speaks, saying that he will summon the whole world, from the rising of the sun to its setting.
Out of Zion, whose beauty is perfect, God shall appear:
Our God shall come without doubt, with a devouring fire before him, surrounded by a mighty tempest.
He shall call to the heavens above and to the earth, to judge his people.
"Let my faithful ones be gathered to me, with whom I have made a covenant through sacrifice."
Then the heavens themselves shall show his justice, for God himself is the judge. <note>original: "Sela" (Selah). This is a Hebrew liturgical or musical direction likely meaning a pause or a lift in volume.</note>
"Hear, my people," he says, "while I speak; O Israelite, while I warn you: I am God, your God.
I will not rebuke you for your sacrifices, nor for your burnt offerings which should be before me continually.
I will not accept bulls from your house, nor goats from your folds.
For all the animals of the forest are mine, and all the beasts on a thousand mountains.
I know all the birds of the mountains, and the creatures of the field are in my power.
If I were hungry, I would not tell it to you, for the world is mine, and whatever is contained within it.
Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?
Sacrifice to God with thanksgiving, and pay your vows to the Most High.
Then call upon me in the time of adversity, and I will defend you so that you may honor me."
But to the wicked man, God speaks thus: "To what end do you recite my statutes, and keep my covenant in your mouth?
Since you hate discipline and cast my words behind your back.
If you saw a thief, you joined with him; and you have fellowship with adulterers.
You let your mouth loose for evil, and your tongue devises frauds.
Sitting down, you speak against your brother, slandering the one with whom you share a common mother.
Doing these things while I remained silent, you thought I would be like you: but I will rebuke you and convict you to your face.
Consider this, I pray, you who are unmindful of God, lest I seize you while you are defenseless.
He who sacrifices with thanksgiving honors me: he who walks in this way, to him I will grant divine salvation."

<margin>2 Samuel 12 <note>Original: "2. Reg. 12." The books of Samuel were often titled as the 1st and 2nd books of Kings in older Bibles.</note></margin>
# LI.
## A song of David to be sung, when Nathan the prophet came to him after he had gone in to Bathsheba.
Have mercy on me, O God, according to your kindness; according to your singular mercy, blot out my offense.
Wash me thoroughly from my fault, and cleanse me from my sin.
For I acknowledge my offense, and my sin is always before my eyes.

<column-break/>

<margin>See 4 Esdras 8 <note>Referring to an apocryphal book often cited by Renaissance scholars regarding human sinfulness.</note></margin>
Against you alone have I sinned, and offended you, so that the equity of your words and the purity of your judgment may be clear.
Indeed, I was born in vice, and in sin did my mother conceive me.
<margin>a. You show that wisdom is to have a pure mind.</margin>
Indeed, you love truth in the heart, and you show me wisdom in secret.
Purge me with hyssop <note>a plant used in ancient rituals for sprinkling and purification</note>, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.
Announce joy and pleasure to me: let the limbs you have crushed exult. <gloss>(delete "tia") <note>This appears to be a printer's or scribe's note regarding a typo in "laetitiam."</note></gloss>
Hide your face from my sins, and blot out all my vices.
Create a clean heart for me, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within my breast.
Do not cast me away from your sight, nor take your holy spirit from me.
Restore to me the joy of your protection, and sustain me with a noble spirit.
I will teach transgressors your ways, so that the guilty may be reconciled to you.
<margin>b. From slaughter and crime.</margin>
Deliver me <gloss>b</gloss> from blood-guiltiness, O God, the God of my salvation: my tongue shall sing of your justice.
O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise.
For you do not delight in sacrifice, that I should offer it; burnt offerings are not accepted by you.
Divine sacrifices are a broken spirit: a broken and afflicted mind, O God, you do not despise.
Do good in your favor to Zion: build the walls of Jerusalem.
Then you will be delighted with just sacrifices, with offerings and whole burnt offerings: then they will offer bulls upon your altar.

# LII.
<margin>1 Samuel 22 <note>Original: "1. Reg. 22."</note></margin>
## An instruction of David to be sung, when Doeg the Edomite went to tell Saul that David had come to Abimelech.
Why do you boast in wicked deeds, O fierce man? Since the kindness of God is daily.
You devise crimes with your tongue, performing frauds like a sharp razor.
You prefer evil to good, and speaking lies rather than what is just.
You love all reckless speech, O deceitful tongue.
God will also destroy you in the end: taken up and torn from your dwelling, he will uproot you from the land of the living.
Seeing this, the good shall be terrified and shall laugh at you: "Behold the man who did not place his strength in God, but relied on the abundance of his riches and leaned upon his own wickedness."
But I shall be like a green olive tree in the house of God, relying on divine kindness for all time.
I will celebrate you, O God, as the author of this thing forever, having hope in your name, which is so near among your faithful ones.

# LIII.
## An instruction of David to be sung to Mahalath.
Fools think in their hearts that there is no God: they are so corrupted by nefarious crimes that there is none who does what is right.
God looks down from heaven upon the human race, to see if there is anyone sane and religious.

<header>BOOK II.</header>

Everyone turns away with equal wickedness, so much so that there is no one who does right, not even one.

<margin>Between this and 14.</margin>
Are the evildoers ignorant—those who consume my people as they would eat bread—that they do not call upon God?

<margin>The same as 14, and also.</margin>
They shall at some time be struck by an incredible fear, even when God shall tear apart the limbs of your <note>original: "b" (referring to a gloss or variant)</note> attackers, while you bring shame upon those whom God loathes.

Oh, that salvation for Israel might be given out of Zion! When God brings back his people from captivity, let the house of Jacob exult, and the Israelites rejoice.

## LIIII.
### An instruction of David to be sung to stringed instruments, when the Ziphites had informed Saul that David was hiding among them.

**O** God, save me by your name, and protect me by your strength.
O God, hear my prayers; give ear to the words of my mouth.
For enemies rise up against me, and cruel men seek my death, not setting God before themselves.
Behold, God helps me: it is the Lord who sustains my life and pays back evil to my adversaries.
Destroy them, O Lord, according to your faithfulness. I will sacrifice to you of my own accord, celebrating your so gentle name, O Lord:
for you have snatched me out of all my troubles, so that my own eyes have seen the punishment of my enemies.

---

## LV.
### An instruction of David to be sung to stringed instruments.

**L**isten, O God, to my prayers, and do not withdraw yourself from my supplication.
Attend to me, and grant what I seek in my complaining and turbulent prayer,
on account of the voices of the enemy and the persistence of the wicked, who devise a charge against me, bitterly opposing me.
My heart trembles in my chest, and the terrors of death assault me:
fear and trembling invade me, and such horror overwhelms me that I say: "Oh, that I had wings like a dove, with which I might fly away to safety."
Indeed, I would go far away to remain in deserted places,
and I would escape more swiftly than the rapid wind or the whirlwind.
Destroy, O Lord, and divide their tongues: for I see cruelty and discord in the city,
which surround it upon the walls day and night; crimes and wicked deeds are within it.
Inhumanity is there, and deceit and treachery do not depart from its streets.
For it was not an enemy who raged against me—for then I could bear it; nor was it my adversary who rose up against me—for then I could avoid him.
But it was you, a man of my own rank, my chief and my familiar friend,
who sweetly shared secrets with me, and with whom I used to go to the temple in company.

<margin>Alludes to the fate of Dathan and Abiram.</margin>
Let death take them away: <note>original: "a"</note> let them go down alive into the depths <note>original: "Tartara" - a classical Greek term for the underworld used here to mean the grave or Sheol</note>, since wickedness dwells among them in their very homes.

<header>BOOK II.</header>

I will call upon God, and the Lord will preserve me.
In the evening, in the morning, and at noon, crying out, I will pray, and he will hear my voice.

<margin>b. God is present for me against many.</margin>
He will protect my life in safety from my attackers, <note>original: "b"</note> for so many are against me.
God will hear and oppress them—he who remains eternal, Selah. <note>original: "Sela" - a liturgical musical pause.</note> Let there be no change in them, for they do not revere God at all.

<margin>c. Against me.</margin>
He stretches out his hands <note>original: "c"</note> against those who were at peace with him, violating his own covenants.
Though he has words in his mouth smoother than butter, he carries war in his heart; using words softer than oil, though they are really darts.

<margin>Matthew 6; Luke 12; 1 Peter 5. d. He speaks to himself.</margin>
<note>original: "d"</note> Cast your burden upon the Lord, who will cherish you, never permitting a good man to be shaken.
But you, O God, shall thrust them down into the pit of destruction: bloodthirsty and deceitful men shall not live out half their days, while I, meanwhile, will trust in you.

## LVI.
### A poem <note>term: segmentum (lit. "a piece/segment") - used here to mean a poetic composition or psalm</note> of David, to be sung <note>original: "a"</note> "Concerning the distant silent dove," when the Philistines had captured him in Gath.

**H**ave mercy on me, O God: for men oppress me, attacking me continually and sharply.
My adversaries oppress me continually, for many fight against me with all their might.
Indeed, in my times of danger, I trust in you.

<margin>b. God will stand by his promises, and I will praise that. See the notes on Psalm 138.</margin>
<note>original: "b"</note> I will praise the promises in God: having confidence in God, I will not fear what mortals may do to me.
Continually they cause trouble for my affairs, turning all their thoughts toward my destruction.
They gather together, they hide, they watch my heels, clearly greedy for my death.
Cast down these angry men, O God, who find refuge in wickedness.

<margin>c. Be mindful of my tears.</margin>
You, who have counted my wanderings, <note>original: "c"</note> put my tears into your bottle—that is, into your record book.
Then my enemies will be driven back when I call upon you, for I know that God stands by me.
I will praise the promises in God: I will praise the promises in the Lord.
Having confidence in God, I will not fear what mortals may do to me.
I owe vows to you, O God; I will pay my thanksgivings to you,
who have defended my life from death—that is, my feet from falling—so that I may walk before God in the light of the living.

## LVII.
### To be sung to the tune "Do Not Destroy," a poem of David, when he fled from Saul in the cave.

**H**ave mercy on me, O God, have mercy on me, for in you I have the confidence of my soul; in the shadow of your wings I take refuge, until this inhumanity passes.
I call upon the Most High God, the God who brings my affairs to an end;
who will act from heaven to defend me from the injury by which I am oppressed, Selah. God will employ his mercy and his faithfulness.

<header>PSALMS</header>

### L.
### A song of Asaph.

Jehovah <note>original: "Ioua"</note>, the God of gods, declares that he will summon the whole world, from the rising of the sun to its setting.
Out of Zion, whose beauty is perfect, God shall appear:
Our God shall come without doubt, with a devouring fire before him, and surrounded by a mighty tempest.
He will call to the heavens above and to the earth, to judge his people.
"Let my faithful ones be gathered to me, with whom I have made a covenant through sacrifice."
Then the heavens themselves shall declare his justice, for God himself is the judge. Selah <note>A liturgical pause or musical direction.</note>.
"Hear, my people," he will say, "while I speak; O Israelite, while I warn you: I am God, your God.
I will not rebuke you for your sacrifices, or for your burnt offerings which are continually before me.
I will not accept bulls from your house, nor goats from your folds.
For all the animals of the forest are mine, and all the beasts upon a thousand mountains.
I know all the birds of the mountains, and the creatures of the field are in my power.
If I were hungry, I would not tell you, for the world is mine, and everything contained within it.
Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?
Sacrifice to God with thanksgiving, and fulfill your vows to the Most High.
Then call upon me in the time of your trouble, and I will so defend you that you shall honor me."
But to the wicked, God will say: "Why do you recite my statutes and have my covenant in your mouth?
Since you hate discipline and cast my words behind your back.
If you see a thief, you join with him; and you keep company with adulterers.
You let your mouth loose for evil, and your tongue frames deceits.
Sitting down, you speak against your brother, slandering the one who shares your own mother.
Because you did these things while I remained silent, you thought I would be like you: but I will rebuke you and convict you to your face.
I pray you, consider this, you who are forgetful of God, lest I seize you when there is no one to protect you.
He who sacrifices with thanksgiving honors me: he who walks in this way, to him I will show divine salvation."

<margin>2 Samuel 12 <note>Latin: 2 Reg. 12.</note></margin>
### LI.
### A song of David to be sung beforehand, when Nathan the prophet visited him after his encounter with Bathsheba.

Have mercy on me, O God, according to your kindness; according to your singular mercy, blot out my offense.
Wash me thoroughly from my fault, and cleanse me from my sin.
For I acknowledge my offense, and my sin is always before my eyes.

<column-break/>

Against you alone have I sinned and offended, so that <margin>See 4 Esdras 8.</margin> the equity of your words and the purity of your judgment may be made manifest.
Truly, I was born in fault, and in sin did my mother conceive me.
<margin>a. You show that it is wisdom to have a pure and religious mind.</margin>
Indeed, you love truth in the inward parts, and you secretly<sup>a</sup> demonstrate wisdom to me.
Purge me with hyssop <term>Hyssop: A plant used in biblical purification rituals for sprinkling.</term>, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow. <margin>...blot out.</margin>
Announce joy and gladness to me: let the members you have crushed exult.
Hide your face from my sins, and blot out all my faults.
Create a clean heart in me, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within my breast.
Do not cast me away from your presence, nor take your holy spirit from me.
Restore to me the joy of your protection, and sustain me with a willing spirit.
I will teach the sinful your ways, so that the guilty may be reconciled to you.
<margin>b. From slaughter and crime.</margin>
Deliver me<sup>b</sup> from blood-guilt, O God, the God of my salvation: and my tongue shall sing of your justice.
O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall declare your praise.
For you do not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it; burnt offerings are not accepted by you.
The divine sacrifices are a broken spirit: a broken and afflicted mind, O God, you do not despise.
Do good to Zion in your favor: build the walls of Jerusalem.
Then you will be delighted with righteous sacrifices, with burnt offerings and whole oblations: then they shall offer bulls upon your altar.

### LII.

<margin>1 Samuel 22 <note>Latin: 1. Reg. 22.</note></margin>
### An instruction of David to be sung beforehand, when Doeg the Edomite had gone to report to Saul that David had come to Ahimelech <note>original: "Abimelechum"</note>.

Why do you boast in wicked deeds, O fierce man? For the mercy of God is daily.
Your tongue meditates on crimes, working deceits like a sharp razor.
You prefer evil to good, and speaking lies rather than what is just.
You love all reckless speech, O deceitful tongue.
God will also destroy you in the end: you shall be removed and uprooted from your tent, and extirpated from the land of the living.
The righteous, terrified by this sight, shall laugh at you: "Behold the man who did not place his strength in God, but trusted in the abundance of his riches and relied on his own wickedness."
But I shall be like a green olive tree in the house of God, trusting in divine mercy for all time.
And I will celebrate you, O God, as the author of this thing forever, having hope in your name, which is so kind among your faithful ones.

### LIII.
### An instruction of David to be sung beforehand to Mahalat <term>Mahalat: Likely a musical instrument or a specific tune for the Psalm.</term>.

The fool <note>original: "infans" - literally "speechless" or "child", here used for one lacking spiritual sense.</note> thinks in his heart that there is no God: they are so corrupted by nefarious crimes that there is no one who does right.
God looks down from heaven upon the human race, to see if there is anyone who is sane and religious.

My life is spent among lions: I lie among a fiery race of men, whose teeth are spears and arrows, and whose tongue is a sharp sword.
Be exalted above the heavens, O God, whose glory is revealed throughout the whole earth.
They set a net for my steps, to cause the ruin of my life: they dig a pit before me, into the middle of which they themselves are about to fall.
My heart is steadfast, O God, my heart is steadfast <note>Latin: *composito sum animo*, literally "I am of a settled mind."</note> for singing in measured melody.
<margin>10</margin>
<margin>John 2 <note>This marginal reference likely points to a New Testament parallel regarding zeal or the temple.</note>.</margin>

->LVIII.<-

->To be sung to the tune of "Do Not Destroy":<-
->A poem <note>original: *fegmentum*, likely translating the Hebrew 'Michtam,' a golden poem or inscription</note> of David.<-

Do you truly speak what is just? Do you judge fairly, O human race?
Rather, in your hearts you devise wickednesses on the earth, and with your hands you weigh out injustice.
The wicked turn aside even from the womb: speakers of lies go astray from their mother's belly.
They possess a poison like the poison of a snake: like that of a deaf asp, which stops up its own ear,
lest it hear the voice of the magician, though he be a skilled master of divine incantations.
O God, shatter their teeth in their very mouths; pull out the lions' fangs, O Jehovah.
Let them flow away like water: let it happen to them as to one who shoots arrows in vain:
like a snail <note>original: *limaci*</note> that dissolves into slime: like a woman's miscarriage, which has never seen the sun.
<margin>a. Let them perish at an immature age, as if meat were pulled from a pot while still half-raw.
b. Fire, which is usually made from thorns.</margin>
And just as if the thorns <gloss>b</gloss> had not yet been felt by one's pot <gloss>a</gloss>, so let them be snatched away in anger while still raw.
The righteous shall rejoice when they see the punishment, and they shall wash their footsteps in the blood of the wicked.
And so men shall confess that there is fruit for the righteous, and that there is a God who governs the earth.

They run and prepare themselves, through no fault of mine.
Arise, then, come to meet me, and look upon these things, O Jehovah, God of hosts <note>original: *armipotens*, "powerful in arms."</note>.
O God of the Israelites, awake to punish all the nations; show no mercy to any of the treacherous and wicked. Selah.
