### LXIII.
### A song of David, when he was in the forests of Judea.

> O God, who are my God, I seek you vigilantly, I thirst for you in my soul: I desire you with my very body, in a squalid, parched, and thirsty land.
> I contemplate you as if in the sanctuary, for the sake of seeing your power and glory.
> Because your gentleness is sweeter than life itself, I commend you with these lips:

<column-break/>

> and so I will praise you as long as I live, lifting my hands in your name.
> Indeed, I seem to be satisfied as if with fatness and richness, while I praise you with my mouth and the melody of my lips,
> whenever I remember you on my bed, and think of you through the night watches.
> For you are a help to me, in the shadow of whose wings I rejoice.
> I cling to you with my soul, you who sustain me with your right hand.
> But those who plot the ruin of my life, they shall descend to the depths of the earth:
> slaughtered by the point of the sword, they shall undergo the same fate as the foxes <note>This refers to being left unburied, food for scavengers.</note>.
> But the king shall rejoice in God, <gloss>a</gloss> and through him, whoever swears shall glory, once the mouths of those speaking lies are blocked.

### LXIV.
### A song of David to be sung.

> Hear, O God, the voice of my prayer: protect my life from the terror of the enemy.
> Withdraw me from the attempt of the wicked, from the assault of evildoers.
> Who sharpen their tongues like swords, darting words like dreadful arrows.
> That they might aim from hiding at the upright, and pierce them unexpectedly, fearing no such thing.
> They strengthen themselves for a wicked matter, consulting about hiding snares, anxious lest anyone notice them.
> They devise iniquities, which once devised they carry out, and indeed by employing the innermost feelings of every mind.
> But God shall pierce them with an arrow, so that they are struck by unexpected blows.
> So much so that, their tongues having failed because of that strike, all who see them shall hesitate.
> Seeing this, all men shall proclaim the work of God and rightly weigh his deed.
> Then the good shall rejoice in Ioua <note>A Latinization of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton, Yahweh.</note>, and all the upright in mind shall trust in him and glory.

### LXV.
### A musical song of David to be sung.

> Praise is destined for you, O God, in Zion, and vows must be paid.
> To you, who hear prayers, all mortals shall come.
> Indeed, the business of vices had overcome me, but you expiate our sins.
> Blessed is he whom you choose and adopt, to dwell in your courts, to be satisfied with the goods of your house, of your holy chamber.
> You indulge us with wonderful equity, O God of our salvation, you who are the confidence of all the ends of the earth and of the remote seas.
> Who establishes the mountains by your power, being girded with strength.
> Who restrains the roaring of the sea, the roaring of its waves, and the tumult of the peoples.
> Those who dwell anywhere fear your wonders, you who make both the rising of the morning and the evening joyful.

# LXIX.
### To be sung to the melody "The Roses of David."

<margin>a. He will suffer punishment undeservedly. <note>original: "Immerito patiet pœnas."</note></margin>
Save me, O God, for the water endangers my life.
I sink into such a whirlpool of swamp that there is no bottom; I have come into such a depth of water that I am overwhelmed by the waves.
My throat is hoarse from the weariness of crying out, and my eyes fail while looking upward for my God.
Those who hate me without cause are more numerous than the hairs of my head; so many enemies attack me wrongly that I must restore what I did not steal.
God, you know if I am at fault, and my crimes are not hidden from you.
Let not those who hope in you be ashamed because of me, Lord Jehovah, Lord of hosts: let not those who seek you be disgraced because of me, O God of the Israelites.
For your sake I endure reproach, having my face covered with shame.
I am considered a stranger and a foreigner by my brothers, born of the same mother.
For I am consumed by zeal for your house, and the insults of those who insult you fall upon me.

<column-break/>

<page-num>66</page-num>

Because I afflict myself tearfully with fasting, this is turned into a reproach for me.
And while I use a rough patchwork cloth instead of a garment, I become a proverb to them.
Those sitting in the court gossip about me, and they sing songs about me over their drinks.
But I strive in prayer to you, Jehovah, at an acceptable time, O God; out of your singular mercy, answer me—which is the faithfulness of your protection.
Rescue me from the mud, lest I be submerged: let me be delivered from those who hate me, and from the depth of the water.
Let not the wave of water overwhelm me: let not the whirlpool swallow me: let not the pit close its mouth upon me.
Hear me, Jehovah, for your mercy is so kind: look upon me according to your excellent kindness.
Do not turn away from your servant, who is in danger: hasten to answer me.
Draw near to redeem my life; ransom me because of my enemies.
You know my reproach, shame, and disgrace; you have all my adversaries in your sight.
My heart is broken by reproach: I anxiously wait for compassion, but there is none; for consolation, but I find none.

Indeed, they give me gall for food, and for my thirst, they offer me vinegar to drink.
Let the table set before them be a snare, and let their very peace be their downfall.
Let their eyes be darkened so they do not see, and make their loins shake continually.
Pour out your wrath upon them, and let your burning anger overtake them.
<margin>a. Acts 1 <note>This refers to the "Field of Blood" and the fate of Judas.</note></margin>
Let their habitation be deserted, with no one dwelling in their homes.
For they persecute the one whom you have wounded, adding to the pain of those you have struck.
<margin>b. Through you they are absolved and justified. <note>original: "Per te absoluantur iustificiantur."</note></margin>
Add fault upon their faults, and let them not come into your righteousness.
Let them be blotted out of the book of the living, and not be written among the righteous.
But as for me, poor and sick, let your protection, O God, shield me.
I will praise the name of God with a song, magnifying him with thanksgiving.
This will be more pleasing to Jehovah than an ox, or a bull with horns and hooves.
The poor will see this and rejoice; those who seek God will live in spirit.
For Jehovah hears the poor and does not despise his prisoners.
Let heaven and earth praise him, the seas and everything that moves in them.
For God will save Zion and build the cities of Judah, so that it may be inhabited and possessed.
The offspring of his servants will hold it, and those who love his name will dwell there.

### LXXI.
->From the Greek: A song of David for the sons of Jonadab, and for those who were first led into captivity.<-

In you, Jehovah, I trust; let me never be frustrated.
In your justice, defend and deliver me: incline your ear to me, so as to preserve me.
Be to me like a firm rock, to which I may always retreat: you who command my preservation, who are to me in the place of a rock and a fortress.
O my God, deliver me from the hand of the impious, from the injury of the unjust and the cruel.
For you are my hope, Lord Jehovah, my trust since my youth.
I have leaned upon you even from the womb: you drew me out from my mother’s belly: in you my praise is made perpetual.
Indeed, to many I am like some kind of omen <note>or "portent," someone whose suffering makes others stare in wonder</note>: but you are my firm confidence.
I keep my mouth full of your praises and honor continually.
Do not cast me away in the time of old age: do not desert me when my strength is exhausted.
For my enemies deliberate against me: and those who lie in wait for my life consult in this manner:
"God has deserted him: he must be pursued and captured, while no one defends him."
O God, do not be far from me; my God, hasten to help me.
Let the adversaries of my life be consumed with shame: let those who seek my harm be covered with infamy and disgrace.
But I, perpetually cherishing hope, will add to all your many praises.
With my mouth, I will continually set forth your justice and victories, the number of which I do not know.
I will walk in the mighty deeds of the Lord Jehovah, remembering your justice alone.
O God, you have taught me from my boyhood, and until now I proclaim your miracles.
Even unto old age and gray hairs, O God, do not desert <margin>a. That is, strength.</margin> me, while I proclaim your ^a^ arm to posterity, and your power to all those to come,
and your lofty justice, O God: you, O God, who do such great things that you are incomparable.
You who, though you showed me many adverse and sad things, having been reconciled, will defend my life: you who, having been reconciled, will draw me out from the depths of the earth:
who will increase my greatness: who, having become more peaceful, will refresh me.
I also will celebrate you with the lute <term>nablo: a ten-stringed Phoenician harp</term>, and your faithfulness, my God; I will sing to you with the lyre, O Holy One of the Israelites.

<column-break/>

I will sing to you with shouting lips, and with my soul, which you have redeemed.
Moreover, my tongue shall meditate on your justice all day long, because those who were plotting evil against me have been shamefully frustrated.

### LXXII.
->Concerning Solomon. From the Greek: a song of David.<-

O God, give your judgments to the king, and your justice to the king's son.
He shall judge your people with equity, and your needy ones with justice.
The mountains shall bring peace to the people, and the hills justice.
He will champion the needy: he will protect the generation of the poor, thinning out the ranks of the cheaters.
And thus, as long as the sun and moon endure, you shall be feared through eternal ages.
He shall be like rain descending upon mown meadows, like a shower watering the earth.
In his time the righteous shall flourish, and there shall be much peace, as long as the moon exists.
And he shall rule from one sea to the other, <margin>a. Namely, the Euphrates.</margin> from the ^a^ river to the ends of the earth.
The dwellers of the woods shall fall down before him, and his enemies shall lick the dust.
The kings of Cilicia <note>original: "Ciliciae," identifying the biblical Tarshish with the region in Asia Minor</note> and the islands shall pay tribute to him: the Arabs and Sabaeans shall bring him tax.
And all kings shall worship him, all nations shall serve him.
For he will deliver the complaining poor, and the needy who lack a defender.
He will have mercy on the frail and the destitute, and will protect the lives of the poor,
vindicating them from fraud and injury, and holding their blood as precious.
He shall live, and there shall be supplied to him the gold of Arabia, and continual prayers shall be made for him, with daily auspicious omens in his favor.
It shall happen that a handful of grain committed to the earth shall rustle its fruit on the mountain top like the cedars of Lebanon, with the citizens flourishing like the grass of the earth.
His name shall be forever: as long as the sun remains, his fame shall be propagated: and in him all nations shall find favor, declaring him blessed.
Praised be Jehovah, the God of the Israelites, the only God who does wonders.
And praised be his glorious name forever, and let the whole circle of the earth be filled with his glory:
Amen and Amen <note>literally: "Again and again"</note>.
Thus far the prayers of David, the son of Jesse.

### LXXIIII.

### PSALM XC.
### The prayer of Moses, the man of God.

Lord, you are our refuge through perpetual ages.
You who, before the mountains were born, before the earth and the world were formed, are God from eternity to eternity,
you turn men back to dust, and command the ^a human race to return.
<margin>a. That is, men [returning] through perpetual offspring.</margin>
For in your sight a thousand years are held as yesterday which has passed, and as a watch in the night.
You scatter them; they are a dream, like grass that grows in the morning.
In the morning it flourishes and grows, and in the evening, cut down, it withers.
For we are consumed by your anger, troubled by your severity.
You place our vices in your sight, our hidden things ^b in the light of your countenance.
<margin>b. That is, you remember and punish, as in Psalm 109.</margin>
For our whole age passes away in your anger: we finish our years swifter than a word.
<margin>Ecclesiastes 18</margin>
The span of our age is limited to seventy years: or (if health be good) eighty: of which, however, the most significant part is labor and hardship, so swift is the cutting off as we fly away.
But if anyone knows the power of your anger, your severity is according to the reverence due to you.
Show us how to measure our age in this way, so that we may apply a wise mind.
Be reconciled, Jehovah, why do you delay? And be appeased toward your own.
Satisfy us in the morning with your mercy, and we shall rejoice exultantly through our whole life.
Gladden us according to the time in which you afflicted us: for the years in which we suffered evil.
Let your work be shown to your servants, and your glory among their children.
And may we obtain the delight of the Lord our God, and complete for us the work of our hands; yes, complete the work of our hands.

### X C I.
### From the Greek: A song of praise of David.

You who dwell in the protection of the Most High, who abide in the shadow of the Almighty,
establish Jehovah to be your confidence, your fortress, and the God in whom you trust.
For he will defend you from the hunter's snare, from the deadly pestilence.
He will protect you with his wing, and under his feathers you shall be safe, with his faithfulness as a shield and buckler.
You shall not fear the terrors of the night, nor the arrows that fly by day.
Not the plague that stalks in the darkness, nor the destruction that ravages at noon.

### A song of David.

I will sing of mercy and justice; I will sing to you, O Lord.

<margin>10</margin> will you come to me? I will conduct myself with a sincere mind within my household.

A perverse mind shall depart from me; I will know nothing of evil.
Those who secretly slander another I will destroy; I will not endure a haughty look or an arrogant heart.
I will keep my eyes upon the most faithful of the land, that 
<margin>20</margin> they may be my companions: those who walk blamelessly shall serve me.

### Lamed.

Forever, O Jehovah, your word remains in the heavens.
You are endowed with eternal truth, you who established the firm earth.
These things indeed stand today according to your purpose: for all things serve you.
If your law were not my delight, I would surely perish in my misery <note>The Latin "inopia" suggests a lack of resources or a state of helplessness.</note>.
I will never forget your commandments: for through them you preserve my life. <gloss>10</gloss>
I am yours, save me, for I study your commandments.
The wicked loom over my destruction, but I weigh your oracles.
I see an end to all perishable things; your
<margin>a. Infinite.</margin>
commandment is exceedingly <gloss>a</gloss> broad.

### Mem.

I love your law so much that it is my daily meditation.
Your discipline makes me wiser than my enemies, for I have it perpetually.
I have more wisdom than all my teachers, because your oracles are my meditation.
I surpass the elders in understanding, because I hold to your commandments. <gloss>20</gloss>
I restrain my feet from every evil way, so that I may obey your words.
I do not turn aside from your judgments, because you instruct me.
Your words are much sweeter to my palate and mouth than honey.
From your commandments I learn, and therefore I hate all false ways. <gloss>30</gloss>

### Nun.

Your words are a lamp to my foot, and a light to my path.
I have sworn (and I will perform it) that I will keep your just laws.
I am greatly tormented, O Jehovah; heal me as your promise brings.
Accept the free-will offering <note>The Latin "liberalitatem" here refers to the voluntary praise or sacrifice of the lips.</note> of my mouth, O Jehovah, and teach me your judgments.
I am in constant danger of my life, yet I do not forget your law.
The wicked spread a snare for me, yet I do not stray from your <gloss>40</gloss> commandments.
I possess your oracles forever; they are the joy of my heart.
I apply my mind to perform your decrees, even unto the end.

### Samech.

I hate those who think wickedly, and I love your law.
You are my hiding place and my bulwark; I hang upon your words.
Depart from me, you wicked ones, so that I may carry out the commands of my God. <gloss>50</gloss>
Sustain me by your word <note>original: "oratione," literally "speech" or "discourse."</note> so that I may live: and do not let my expectation be frustrated.
Support me so that I may be preserved, and I will always delight in your decrees.
You trample all who depart from your decrees, for their cunning is deceitful.
Like dross you destroy all the wicked of the earth; therefore I love your decrees.

My body trembles for fear of you, fearing your judgments.

### Ain.

I do what is just and right; do not leave me to my oppressors.
Secure your servant's well-being; do not let the proud do me injury.
My eyes fail with looking for your protection and your righteous promise. <gloss>10</gloss>
Deal with your servant as your mercy brings, and teach me your decrees.
I am yours; instruct me, so that I may know your oracles.
It is time for you to act, O Jehovah, when your law is violated.
Therefore I love your commands more than gold and <term>refined gold</term> <note>original: "obrizum," referring to pure or tested gold.</note>.
Therefore using all your commandments rightly, I hate every false custom.

### Pe.

Your oracles are wonderful: therefore I keep them in my mind.
The first lessons of your words enlighten and instruct the unlearned. <gloss>20</gloss>
Indeed I draw these in with an open mouth: so greatly do I love your commands.
Look upon me and have mercy on me, according to your justice toward those who love your name.
Steady my steps in your words, so that no wickedness may rule over me.
Deliver me from the wrongs of men, and I will obey your commands.
Shine upon your servant with your countenance, and teach me your decrees. <gloss>30</gloss>
Streams of water flow from my eyes because your law is not kept.

### Zade.

You are just, O Jehovah, and your judgments are right.
You have delivered oracles that are most equitable and most true.
I am consumed with indignation because my enemies have forgotten your words.
Your word is most pure, and I, your servant, love it.
Though I am small and despised, I have not forgotten your commandments. <gloss>40</gloss>
Your justice is an everlasting justice, and your law is true.
Caught in adversity and dangers, I have your commands as my delights.
The equity of your oracles is eternal: instruct me, and I shall live.

### Coph.

I call with my whole heart: hear me, O Jehovah, and I will hold to your decrees. <gloss>50</gloss>
I call to you, save me: and I will obey your oracles.
I anticipate the dawn with my cries, hanging upon your words.
My eyes anticipate the night watches for meditating on your words.
Hear my voice according to your mercy, O Jehovah; according to your justice, preserve my life.
Those who pursue wicked deeds are near, but they are far from your law.
You are near, O Jehovah, and all your commands are true.
I have known long ago concerning your oracles, that you have founded them forever.

### Res.

Look upon my misery and deliver me, for I have not forgotten your law.

### CXXXIX.

-> A song of David to be led by the cantor. In Greek: of Zechariah, when they were dispersed. <-

Jehovah, you have searched and known me.
You know my sitting and my rising, perceiving my thoughts from afar.
You encompass me as I walk and as I lie down: and you have all my paths thoroughly explored:
so much so, that you, Jehovah, know a sentence not even yet uttered by my tongue.
You have formed me both from behind and from the front, and you have placed that hand of yours upon me.
The knowledge of this thing is so difficult and arduous that I cannot attain it.
Where then shall I turn away from your spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence?
<margin>Amos 9</margin> If I climb into heaven, you are there: if I lie down in the underworld <note>original: "orco," the classical Latin term for the realm of the dead, used here for the Hebrew 'Sheol'</note>, you are present.

<column-break/>

even there your hand will hold me, and your right hand will grasp me.
And if I think I should certainly be hidden by the darkness, the night itself is light to me.
The darkness itself is not dark to you: the night shines like the day, with no distinction between darkness and light.
<margin>a. The feelings/affections.</margin> For you possess my <gloss>a</gloss> kidneys <note>The "renes" or kidneys were considered by the ancients to be the seat of the deepest emotions and desires.</note>, you who composed me in my mother's womb.

My limbs were not hidden from you when I was being made in secret, skillfully woven <gloss>b</gloss> in the depths of the earth.

that when I stay awake to count them, they are more numerous than the sand, and <gloss>d</gloss> I am still lingering with you.
<margin>d. Intent on contemplating your nature, I am not yet able to know it fully.</margin> Oh, if only you would overthrow the impious, O God: depart from me, you bloodthirsty men,

Jehovah, I call upon you, hasten to me; listen to the voice with which I call to you.

With my voice I call to Jehovah, with my voice I supplicate Jehovah.

## C X L I I I I.
### Of David.

I give thanks to Jehovah my deity <note>original: "numini," a classical term for a divine power</note>, who teaches my hands for the struggle and my fingers for <margin>30</margin> battle:

Our storehouses are filled high, from one harvest to another: our ewes are increased by thousands and tens of thousands in our streets.
We have oxen bearing burdens: no slaughter, no driving away, no wailing in our streets.

Wine is scurrilous, strong drink is riotous, and whoever is deceived by it is unwise.

### CHAPTER XXI.

<margin>a. The king's mind is a thing close to God, and manageable by Jehovah alone.</margin>

<margin>b. Deadly to life. I read "Ner" [lamp] with the Greek and Latin, not "Nir" [fallow ground].</margin>

### CHAPTER XXV.

->These also are the proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah, king of Judah, compiled.<-

<margin>a. God, like a teacher, conceals a matter to test his students. The king, like a student, searches it out.</margin>

As the heavens are high and the earth deep, so the mind of kings is unsearchable. 
Take away the dross from the silver, and a vessel will come forth for the smith. 
Take away the wicked from the presence of the king, and his throne will be established in justice.

[If] you see [justice] violated in a province, do not be surprised at the license: for a <margin>f</margin> high official is watched by one higher, and others higher still over these, and the highest of all on the earth is the king of the tilled land himself. He who loves money is never satisfied with money: and he who loves riches lacks their fruit, which is also vanity. Where there are many goods, there are many to eat them, nor does their master perceive anything from them other than the sight of them with his eyes. Sweet is the sleep of the laborer, whether he has eaten little <margin>g</margin> or much: but the <margin>h</margin> abundance of the rich man does not let him sleep. <margin>†</margin> There is a wretched vice that I see under the sun: riches which are kept for their master to his own harm, which riches indeed perish most miserably; and when he begets a son, that son will have nothing. And just as he came out from his mother’s womb naked, so shall he return again as he came, nor shall he take anything from his labor to carry away with him. This also is a wretched vice: that just as he came, so he departs, having achieved no benefit, he who has labored for the wind. Add to this that through all his life he eats in darkness, with much weariness, illness, and irritation. Therefore, what I see as good and beautiful is this: that he should feast, and through all his life in all the labor which he endures under the sun, enjoy the goods given to him by God: for these are his lot. And surely, to whatever man God grants riches and wealth, and gives him the power to feast on them, to enjoy this portion of his, and to delight in his labor—this is the gift of God. For he does not much remember <margin>a. His own misery.</margin> the time of his life, since God grants him joy of heart.

### CHAPTER VI.

<margin>
a. A stillborn child.
</margin>
<margin>
b. The good that is seen and is present.
</margin>
<margin>
c. What is hoped for.
</margin>
<margin>
d. To escape death.
</margin>
There is an evil which I see under the sun, and indeed it is frequent among men: namely, that God grants to someone riches and wealth and glory, so that he lacks nothing that his soul could desire, yet God does not give him the power to enjoy them, but a stranger enjoys them; this is vanity and a wretched vice. If a man should beget a hundred children and prolong the years of his life for many years, and yet his soul is not satisfied with good things, and moreover he lacks a burial, I say that a <margin>a</margin> stillborn child is in a better condition than he. For <margin>a</margin> this one comes in vanity and departs into darkness, and its name is covered with darkness; it has neither seen nor known the sun, yet it has more rest than the other. But even if he lived two thousand years, if he has not enjoyed good things, do they not both go to the same place? All the labor of man is for his mouth, yet his appetite is never satisfied. For what does the wise man have more than the fool? What does the humble man have, who knows how to conduct himself among mortals? Better is the <margin>b</margin> sight of the eyes than the <margin>c</margin> wandering of the soul; this also is vanity and a vexation of spirit. Whatever has been, has already been named, and it is known that he was a man, and that he could not <margin>d</margin> contend with one stronger than himself. Since there are many things that increase vanity, what advantage does a man have? For who knows what is good for man in life, during all the time of his frivolous life, which he passes like a shadow? For who can tell a man what will come after him under the sun?

### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>
Prov. 22
a. Joy follows sadness.
b. Gifts that are given so that injury may be done to someone.
c. It is characteristic of fools.
d. To those living.
e. So that he may know that nothing in this life is certain, and thus he becomes prepared for every event.
f. Before the just time of his age.
1 Kings 8
2 Chron. 6
Prov. 20
1 John 1
</margin>
A good name is better than fine ointment, and the day of death than the day of one's birth. It is better to go to a house of mourning than to a house of feasting: for that is the end of all men, and the living will lay it to heart. Sorrow is better than laughter: for <margin>a</margin> by the sadness of the face the mind is made better. The mind of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the mind of fools is in the house of pleasure. It is better to hear the rebuke of the wise than for one to hear the song of fools. For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of a fool. And this also is vanity, that <margin>b</margin> injustice drives a wise man mad, and bribes destroy the mind. Better is the end of a thing than its beginning: better is the patient in spirit than the proud. Do not be quick to be irritable: for irritability <margin>c</margin> rests in the bosom of fools. Do not ask why the former times were better than these: for you do not ask this wisely. Wisdom is as good as an inheritance, and more useful to those <margin>d</margin> who see the sun. For in the protection of wisdom and money, wisdom and knowledge are more excellent, because they grant life to him who possesses them. Consider the work of God: for who can make straight what He has made crooked? In a good time, be in good spirits, and consider the bad time: for God has made the one as well as the other, <margin>e</margin> so that man may find nothing to complain of in Him. I have seen everything in my vain days: there is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness, and there is a wicked man who prolongs his life in his wickedness. Do not be overly righteous, <margin>f</margin> nor overly wise; why should you destroy yourself? Do not be overly wicked, nor be a fool; why should you die before your time? It is good that you take hold of this, and not let go of that: for he who fears God shall escape them all. Wisdom strengthens the wise man more than ten princes in a city. For there is no man on earth so righteous that he does good and never sins. Also, do not pay attention to every word that is spoken, lest you hear your servant cursing you; for you know in your own heart that you yourself have often cursed others. All this I have tested by wisdom, saying, "I will be wise," but it was far from me. That which is far off and exceedingly deep, who can find it? Turning my mind to know, and to search, and to seek out wisdom and the reason of things, and to know the wickedness of folly and the madness of the insane, I find more bitter than death the woman whose heart is snares and nets, and whose hands are chains; he who is pleasing to God escapes her, but the sinner is taken by her. "Behold, this is what I have found," says the Preacher, "weighing things one by one to find the reason, which my soul still seeks but I have not found. <margin>d</margin> One man among a thousand I have found, but a woman among all these I have not found. Moreover, behold, this is what I have found: that God made men upright, but they <margin>e</margin> have sought out many schemes."

Throw$^a$ your sustenance upon the waters <note>Original: "in humorem," literally "into the moisture." This is the famous "cast your bread upon the waters" passage, interpreted here as an act of charity</note>: for after a long time you will find it. Give a portion$^b$ to seven or even to eight people, $^c$ for you do not know what evil may come upon the earth. $^d$ When the clouds are full, they pour rain upon the earth, $^e$ and whether a tree falls toward the South or toward the North, in whatever place it falls, there it remains. $^f$ He who observes the wind does not sow, and he who watches the clouds does not reap. Just as you do not know the path of the wind, or how the bones are formed in a pregnant woman's womb, so you do not know the work of God who makes all things. In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not let your hand rest: for you do not know whether this or that will prosper more, or whether both will be equally good. Indeed, light is sweet, and it is pleasant for the eyes to see the sun: but though a man lives many years, and all of them with pleasure, yet let him remember how long the days of darkness shall be; whatever happens is vanity. Enjoy your youth, young man, and let your mind cheer you in your youthful days, and indulge the inclination of your heart and the sight of your eyes: but know that for all these things, God will bring you to judgment. Therefore, remove ferocity from your mind, and take away wickedness from your body: for youth and ignorance are vanity.

### ->CHAPTER III.<-

In my little bed at night, I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, but I did not find him. I said: "I will rise now and go about the city, through the streets and the squares, seeking him whom my soul loves." I sought him, but found him not. The watchmen who go about the city found me: "Have you seen him whom my soul loves?" Scarcely had I passed them when I found him whom my soul loves; I held him and would not let him go, until I had brought him into my mother's house, and into the chamber of her who conceived me. I adjure you, O women of Jerusalem, by the roes and the hinds of the field, that you do not wake or stir up love, as long as it pleases her. What is this that comes up from the forest like pillars of smoke, perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, and all the powders of the merchant? <note>Original: "seplasiarij," referring to the Seplasia, a famous street of perfumers in ancient Capua.</note> Behold his bed—that is, Solomon's—surrounded by sixty soldiers, the most valiant of Israel, who all hold swords and are expert in war, each with his sword upon his thigh against the terrors of the night. King Solomon made himself a royal litter of the wood of Lebanon; its pillars he made of silver, the bottom of gold, the seat of purple, its middle inlaid with love for the sake of the women of Jerusalem. Go forth and see, O women of Zion, King Solomon wearing the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his wedding, the day of his heart’s delight.

For her company and living with her brings no bitterness or pain, but only delight and joy. As I thought upon these things and weighed them in my heart—that there is immortality in kinship with wisdom, and sweet delight in her friendship, and everlasting riches in the labors of her hands, and prudence in the practice of speaking with her, and renown in sharing her words—I went about seeking how to take her for my own. But understanding that I could not possess her unless God gave her to me (and it was a mark of prudence to know whose gift it was), I called upon the Lord, and praying with all my heart, I spoke thus:

### CHAPTER IX.

> O God of my fathers, and merciful Lord, who made all things by your word and fashioned man by your wisdom to rule over the creatures you have made, and to govern the world in holiness and justice, and to exercise judgment with an upright soul: give me the Wisdom that sits by your throne, and do not reject me from among the number of your servants. For I am your servant, the son of your handmaid, a weak man of short life, and too small to understand judgments and laws. For even if someone among the human race were perfect, if your wisdom were absent, he would be counted as nothing. You have chosen me to be king of your people and a judge of your sons and daughters; you commanded a temple to be built on your holy mountain, and an altar in the city where you dwell, in imitation of your holy tabernacle which you prepared from the beginning. And with you is Wisdom, who knows your works and was present when you founded the world, knowing what is pleasing in your sight and what is right according to your commandments. Send her forth from the holy heavens and from your glorious throne; send her that she may labor with me, that I may understand what is pleasing to you. For she knows and perceives all things, and she shall lead me prudently in my actions and guard me by her glory, so that my works may be acceptable, and I may govern your people justly and be worthy of my father’s throne. For what man can know the counsel of God? Or who can perceive what God wills? For the thoughts of mortals are miserable, and our schemes are dangerous; since the mortal body weighs down the soul, and this earthly vessel <note>Latin: "terrestre uas," referring to the physical body as a container for the mind.</note> overwhelms the mind, so that we can hardly discern the things on earth, and only with great care find those things that are right before us; but who can search out the things in heaven? Who could know your counsel, unless you gave wisdom and sent your holy spirit from on high, so that the ways of those on earth might be corrected, and men might be taught the things that please you, and be saved by wisdom?

seized by a double sorrow, and groaning at the memory of things past. For when they heard that through their own torments others were being benefited, they felt the presence of the Lord. For the one whom they had long ago cast out and rejected with mockery, they came to admire at the end of events, when they suffered a thirst far different from that of the righteous. For the sake of their foolish and wicked thoughts, by which they were deceived into worshipping mindless serpents and vile beasts, you sent a multitude of mindless animals upon them as a punishment, so that they might understand that **by whatever things a man sins, by those same things he is punished.** <note>original: "per quae quis peccat, per eadem puniri." This is the principle of "lex talionis" or poetic justice, often cited in Wisdom 11:16.</note> For your almighty hand, which created the world out of formless matter, was not unable to send upon them a violence of bears, or bold lions, or unknown beasts full of a new kind of rage, breathing out fiery breath, or exhaling a roar of smoke, or flashing horrendous sparks from their eyes; not only could the harm from these things destroy them, but even the sight of them could kill them with terror. Even without these, they could have been cast down by a single breath, pursued by punishment and scattered by the breath of your power. **But you have ordered all things by measure, number, and weight.** <note>original: "omnia modo numeroq; & pondere temperasti." Since the whole world before you is like a speck on a balance, or like a drop of morning dew falling to the earth. But you have mercy on all, because you can do all things, and you overlook the sins of men so that they may repent. For you love all things that exist, and you hate nothing that you have made; for you would not have fashioned anything if you had hated it. How could anything remain unless you willed it? Or be preserved if not called by you? You spare all things, for they are yours, O Lord, the lover of life.

### CHAPTER XII.

For your incorruptible spirit is in all things, through which you rebuke those who go astray little by little, and warning them of the things in which they sin, you punish them, so that they may be freed from vice and put their trust in you, O Lord. For you hated those ancient inhabitants of your holy land because they committed loathsome deeds of sorcery and unholy sacrifices, and you willed to destroy through our ancestors those merciless judges of the innocent, <note>The text refers to the Canaanites.</note> and those who feasted on the bloody entrails of human bodies, and the frenzied priests, and the parents <margin>of those shores. The Canaanites.</margin> who were the murderers of helpless souls, so that the land most honored by you above all others might receive a worthy colony of God’s worshippers. Yet you spared even these as men, and you sent wasps as the precursors of your army to drive them out little by little—not because you were unable to deliver the impious into the hands of the righteous in battle, or to destroy them all at once with fierce beasts or a stern command—but by punishing them little by little, you gave them a place for repentance, not being ignorant that their nature was wicked, and their malice was innate, and that their minds would never be changed, for they were a cursed race from the beginning. Nor was it out of fear of anyone that you granted pardon for their sins. For who shall say to you, "What have you done?" or who shall resist your decree? Who shall accuse you for the destruction of the nations which you made? Or who shall stand against you as an avenger on behalf of unjust men? For <margin>1 Peter 5</margin> there is no other God but you, who cares for all things, that you might show that <note>original: "te non inique puniuisse"</note> you have not punished unjustly. Nor shall any king

<column-break/>

or tyrant dare to look you in the face regarding those whom you have punished. But since you are righteous, you govern all things righteously, and you judge it alien to your power to condemn one who does not deserve punishment. For your strength is the source of justice, and the fact that you are Lord of all makes you spare all. For you show your strength when men do not believe in your perfect power, and you rebuke the audacity of those who do not know you. But you, being master of power, judge with equity and govern us with great indulgence, for the power is yours to use whenever you will. By such deeds you have taught your people that the one who is righteous must be kind, and you have given your children good hope, because you give a place for repentance for sins. For if you punished the enemies of your servants, who deserved death, with such moderation and patience, giving them time and place to turn from their vices, with what great care do you govern your own children, to whose ancestors you gave such good promises through oaths and covenants? Therefore, while you punish us, you scourge our enemies ten thousand times more severely, so that we may carefully weigh your goodness, and when we are judged, we may expect mercy. And so, those who lived a foolish and unjust life, you tormented through their own wicked deeds. For they wandered far astray in the paths of error, regarding as gods even those animals which are held in contempt among enemies, being deceived like foolish infants; therefore, as if to children lacking reason, you imposed a punishment that brought them to shame. But since they were not corrected by that shameful rebuke, they experienced a judgment worthy of God. For <margin>d. By the beasts and other things which are explained in the following chapter.</margin> through those very things which they suffered against their will—when they were tortured by those very creatures they thought were gods—they recognized the true God whom they had formerly refused to know; and for this reason, the ultimate condemnation came upon them.

### CHAPTER XIII.

For all men are vain by nature in whom there is ignorance of God, and who from the good things that are seen are unable to know him who is, nor by considering the works do they recognize the craftsman. Instead, they think that either fire, or wind, or the swift air, or the circle of the stars, or the violent water, or the lights of heaven are the gods that rule the world. If, being delighted by their beauty, they thought them to be gods, let them know how much more excellent is the Lord of these; for the original author of beauty created them. But if they were amazed by their power and influence, let them understand from them how much more powerful is he who fashioned them. For from the <margin>a. Those who seek God sin less than those who worship water or idols.</margin> greatness and beauty of created things, their creator is seen by comparison. Yet in these, there is less cause for blame. For perhaps they go astray while seeking God and desiring to find him; for being conversant with his <margin>Romans 1</margin> works, they search them out and are persuaded by the sight, because the things that are seen are beautiful. Yet even these are not to be forgiven. For if they were able to know so much that they could speculate about the world, how did they not more quickly find its Lord? But miserable are they, and their hopes are set on dead things, who call those things gods which are the works of human hands: gold and silver, fashioned with art, and likenesses of animals, or a useless stone, the work of an ancient hand. <margin>Isaiah 44</margin>

with skill he strips off all the bark from a pliable branch, and with elegant art he fashions a vessel suitable for the needs of life. The leftovers of his work he uses to prepare food to satisfy himself. Then, the refuse of these scraps—which is good for nothing, being crooked and full of knots—he takes this trunk and carves it diligently in his spare time; and, using his skill during his leisure, he forms it and shapes it into the likeness of a man, or makes it like some vile animal. He smears it with vermilion <note>original: "minio," a bright red mineral pigment often used in antiquity.</note> and paint, coloring it red, and covering every blemish upon it. Having made for it a shrine worthy of itself, he sets it in a wall and secures it with iron; he takes care that it does not fall, knowing that it cannot even help itself, for it is only an image and stands in need of help. Yet, he is not ashamed to pray to this inanimate thing concerning his possessions, his marriage, and his children. For his health, he calls upon a weak thing; for life, he entreats a dead thing; for help, he petitions that which is utterly useless; for a journey, he prays to that which cannot even take a step; and finally, for profit, for business, and for the success of his hands, he asks for strength from hands that are completely idle.

### CHAPTER XIV.

Again, when someone prepares to go to sea and is about to pass through the fierce waves, he calls upon a piece of wood more fragile than the vessel that carries him. <margin>a. The art of navigation.</margin> <gloss>a</gloss> For the greed for gain devised that vessel, and a craftsman's wisdom built it, but your providence, O Father, steers it; for you have given a way even in the sea, and a safe path through the waves, showing that you can save a person from everything, even if someone should go to sea without skill. Yet, you do not wish the works of your wisdom to be idle. For this reason, men entrust their lives to a very small piece of wood, and having crossed the waves in a ship, they come safely to shore. Indeed, in the beginning, <margin>b. Namely, the flood.</margin> <gloss>b</gloss> when the proud giants were perishing, the hope of the world took refuge in a ship and left to the ages a seed of life, steered by your hand. For blessed is the wood through which righteousness comes; but the handmade idol is cursed, both it and he who made it: he, because he fashioned it; and it, because, though it is perishable, it is called a god. For the wicked man and his wickedness are equally hateful to God; indeed, the work shall be punished together with the worker. Therefore, there shall be a judgment even upon the idols of the nations, because though they are part of God's creation, they have become an abomination, a snare to the souls of men, and a trap for the feet of the foolish. For the invention of idols was the beginning of fornication <note>In a biblical context, "fornication" often refers to spiritual infidelity or the betrayal of God through the worship of idols.</note>, and the discovery of them was the corruption of life. For they did not exist from the beginning, nor shall they exist forever. Through the vanity of men they entered into the world, and therefore a swift end is destined for them. <margin>The origin of idols.</margin> For a certain father, consumed with excessive grief for a son taken prematurely, made an image of the child who was then a dead man, but now began to honor him as a god, and handed down secret rites and ceremonies to his subjects. Then, as time passed, this impious custom grew strong and was kept as a law, and images were worshipped by the command of tyrants. And when men could not honor them in person because they lived far away, they brought their likeness from afar and made a visible image of the king they wished to honor, so that they might zealously flatter the absent one as if he were present. The ambition of the craftsman also impelled the ignorant to increase this worship. For he, perhaps wishing to please the ruler, used his art to labor at a likeness of greater beauty. And the common people,

allured by the charm of the work, now regarded as a deity the one whom they had honored shortly before as a man. And this became a trap for life: that men, serving either their own calamity or the tyranny of kings, gave to stones and wood the Name that cannot be shared. <note>original: "nulli communicandū nomen," referring to the Tetragrammaton or the unique, incommunicable name of the true God.</note> Moreover, it was not enough for them to err in their knowledge of God; but while living in a great war of ignorance, they call such great evils "peace." For either they sacrifice their own children, or they practice secret rites, or they hold frenzied revels with strange ceremonies; they no longer keep either their lives or their marriages pure, but one man kills another through treachery, or grieves him by adultery. Everything is a confusion of blood, murder, theft, fraud, corruption, unfaithfulness, tumult, perjury, the harassment of the good, forgetfulness of favors, the defiling of souls, the changing of births <note>Likely referring to the passing off of illegitimate children as heirs.</note>, the confusion of marriage, adultery, and lewdness. For the worship of unspeakable idols is the beginning, the cause, and the end of every evil. For they either rejoice to the point of madness, or they prophesy lies, or they live unrighteously, or they quickly commit perjury; for since they trust in lifeless idols, they do not expect to be harmed for swearing falsely. But for both reasons, they shall receive their due: because they thought evilly of God by devoting themselves to idols, and because they swore wickedly in deceit, despising holiness. For it is not the power of those by whom they swear, but the vengeance that follows sinners, which always punishes the offenses of the unrighteous.

### CHAPTER XV.

But you, our God, are kind and true, patient, and ruling all things in mercy. For even if we sin, we are yours, and we know your power; but we will not sin, knowing that we are counted as yours. For to know you is perfect righteousness, and to know your power is the root of immortality. For we have not been deceived by the wicked invention of men, nor by the fruitless labor of painters—figures smeared with various colors, the sight of which stirs up desire in the foolish, so that they long for the lifeless form of a dead image. Lovers of evil things, <gloss>a</gloss> they are worthy of such hopes—both those who make them, those who desire them, and those who worship them. <margin>a. Such gods in whom they have hope. Romans 9.</margin> For a potter, laboriously pressing the soft earth, fashions every vessel for our use; and from the same clay he fashions both the vessels that serve clean purposes and those of the opposite kind, all in like manner. As to what shall be the use of each vessel in either category, the potter is the judge. And then, misusing his labor, he fashions a vain god from the same clay—he who was himself born of the earth only a short time ago, and who after a little while must return to the same earth from which he was taken, when the debt of his soul is demanded of him. But his concern is not that he must labor, nor that his life is short; rather, he competes with goldsmiths and silversmiths, and emulates workers in bronze, accounting it a glory to fashion things of no value. His heart is ashes, his hope is cheaper than dirt, and his life is more worthless than clay; for he is ignorant of the One who fashioned him, who inspired him with an active soul, and breathed into him a living spirit. Instead, they think our life is a game and our existence a profitable fair, saying that one must make a profit from anything, even from evil. For this man knows better than anyone else that he is sinning when, from earthy matter, he fashions fragile vessels and idols. But the enemies of your people, who rule over them, are the most foolish of all and more miserable than the minds of children; for they have judged all the idols of the nations to be gods...

### CHAPTER XIX.

**B**ut as for the ungodly, pitiless anger came upon them to the very end. For God even foreknew what they would do: that though they had allowed the people to depart and had even hurried them on their way, they would change their minds and pursue them. For while they were still mourning and lamenting at the graves of the dead, they adopted another foolish plan: they pursued as fugitives those whom they had begged to leave. For a deserved necessity was drawing them to this end and made them forget what had happened, so that they might fill up the punishment that was lacking from their torments, and that your people might experience an incredible journey, while their enemies found a strange death. For the whole of nature, in its own kind, was fashioned anew from the beginning, obeying your commands, so that your children might be kept unharmed. A cloud overshadowed the camp; where water had stood before, dry land was seen to emerge. A free way appeared out of the Red Sea, and a grassy field rose out of the violent surge. Through this the whole nation passed, protected by your hand, having seen wonderful portents. They were like horses at pasture and they leaped like lambs, praising you, O Lord, their deliverer. For they still remembered the things that had happened during their exile: how the earth instead of producing animals brought forth lice, and how the river vomited up a multitude of frogs instead of fish. Finally, they saw a new kind of bird when, led by desire, they asked for luxurious food. For quails came up from the sea to satisfy them.

# ECCLESIASTICUS,
## OR THE WISDOM OF JOSHUA, SON OF SIRACH.

### Preface.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial C featuring a garden scene with a trellis and foliage.</image-desc>Since many and great things have been handed down to us through the Law and the Prophets, and others who followed them, for which the Israelites deserve praise for the sake of their learning and wisdom; and since it is necessary not only for the readers themselves to become learned, but also for those devoted to study to be useful to those outside <note>referring to people outside the Jewish community or the Hebrew-speaking world</note> both by speaking and writing: my grandfather Joshua, when he had devoted himself much to the reading of the Law and the Prophets and other ancestral books, and had made great progress in them, was himself led to write something of those things which pertain to learning and wisdom, so that those who are studious and have devoted themselves to these things might progress much more toward living according to the Law. I therefore exhort you to read with benevolence and attention, and to grant pardon if in some places we seem, in laboring over the interpretation, not to have attained the full force of certain words. For those things said in Hebrew in their own way do not have the same force when they have been translated into another language. And indeed, not only these, but also other things, such as the Law itself and the Prophets, and the rest of the books, differ not a little when they are spoken in their own tongue. Therefore, in the thirty-eighth year of King Ptolemy Euergetes, when I had come into Egypt and stayed there, and had found a model of no small learning, I thought it especially worthwhile to apply some study and labor to interpreting this book. I applied much vigilance and industry during that span of time, so that when the book was brought to an end, it might be published, so that those who wish to apply themselves to study while in exile might live by conforming their character to the Law.

### CHAPTER I.

All wisdom is from the Lord, and remains with him forever. Who can count the sand of the sea, the drops of rain, and the days of the world? Who can measure the height of heaven, the breadth of the earth, and the depth of the sea? <note>Throughout this text, the markers "L." and "G." denote variations found in Latin and Greek manuscript traditions respectively.</note> Who can search out the wisdom <note>L.</note> of God, which excels all things <note>G.</note>? Wisdom was created first of all things, and prudent understanding from eternity. The source of wisdom is the supreme Word of God <note>L.</note>, and its entrances are eternal precepts. To whom has the root of wisdom been revealed? Who has known her shrewdness? <note>L.</note> To whom has the discipline of wisdom been revealed and made manifest? Or who has known her multi-faceted way? <note>G.</note> There is one who is wise, the supreme creator of all <note>L.</note>, the almighty and powerful King <note>G.</note>, greatly to be feared, the Lord sitting upon his throne <note>L.</note>, and the ruling God. <note>G.</note> He created her <note>L.</note> through the Holy Spirit <note>G.</note>, saw her, numbered her, and measured her. <note>L.</note> He poured her out upon all his works and upon all mortals according to his generosity, and he offered her to those who love him. The fear of the Lord is glory, and boasting, and pleasure, and a crown of joy.

<column-break/>

The fear of the Lord delights the mind, and provides pleasure, joy, and long life. It shall be well at the end for the one who fears the Lord, and he shall be blessed in the hour of his death. The love of God is honorable wisdom <note>L.</note>; those to whom she appears love her at the sight of her, and through the recognition of her majesty. <margin>Proverbs 1:9, Psalm 110</margin> The beginning of wisdom is to fear God <note>G.</note>, and she is created together with the faithful in the womb; she walks with chosen women <note>L.</note>, and is recognized among the just and faithful. The fear of the Lord is the knowledge of religion. Religion guards the mind and makes it righteous, and provides pleasure and joy. <note>G.</note> Among men she delights in an eternal foundation, and is entrusted to their offspring. The fullness of wisdom is to fear the Lord, and she satisfies men with her fruits; she fills every house with her delights and the storehouses with her produce, both of which are gifts of God pertaining to happiness. The crown of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, budding forth peace and healthful safety, whose lovers are abundantly cheered by glory. Wisdom rains down science and the knowledge of prudence, and she extols those who lay hold of her with glory. The root of wisdom is to fear the Lord, and her branches are long life. <note>L.</note> Within the storehouses of wisdom is understanding and the knowledge of religion, but wisdom is hateful to sinners <note>original: "fontibus," likely a typo for "fœneratoribus" or "peccatoribus"</note>. <note>G.</note> [The fear of the Lord drives out sin, and as long as it is present, it wards off anger]. An angry man cannot be justified, for his tendency toward fury is the cause of his ruin. The patient man endures for a time, and afterward joy shall spring up for him. For a time he suppresses his words, and his prudence shall be declared by the speech of many. Understanding is stored in the chambers of wisdom, but piety is hateful to the sinner. If you desire wisdom, keep the precepts, and the Lord will provide her to you. For the fear of the Lord is wisdom and learning, and faith and mildness are acceptable to him. Do not be stubborn against the fear of the Lord, nor approach him with a double heart if you lack anything. <margin>a. Do not praise yourself before others, while crimes lie hidden within you.</margin> Do not be a hypocrite in the sight of men, and take care that you do not extol yourself with your own lips, lest you fall and bring disgrace upon yourself, and the Lord reveal your secrets and cast you down publicly before the crowd, because you did not truly take up the fear of the Lord, but had a heart full of deceit.

### CHAPTER II.

### CHAPTER V.

Do not look upon your riches, nor say that you have enough for your life: L. for they will profit nothing when you are called to punishment. G. Do not delay in returning to the Lord, nor put it off from day to day; for the wrath of the Lord shall come forth suddenly, and in the time of vengeance, you shall perish. Do not look toward unjust riches: for they will profit you nothing 40 when you are sought for punishment. Do not winnow with every wind, nor go into every path, like a wicked double-tongued man. In your certain conviction, L. in the way of the Lord, and in knowledge G. be firm, and let your speech be consistent, L. and let peaceful and just words be familiar to you. Be quick to hear, but slow to return an answer. If you understand the matter, answer your neighbor; if not, press your hand over your mouth, L. lest you be shamefully caught in unlearned speech. G. In speech there is both honor and disgrace, 50 and a man's own tongue is his ruin. Beware, L. if you love your life, G. lest you be called a slanderer, and do not lay traps with your tongue. Stay far away from a man who has the power to kill, and you will not be troubled by the fear of death. But if you approach him, do not commit a fault, lest he take away your life. ### CHAPTER X.

A wise ruler teaches his people, and the sovereignty of a prudent man is well-ordered. As the ruler of the city is, so are his ministers; and as the governor of the city is, such are all its inhabitants. An ignorant king destroys his people, and a city is made populous through the prudence of the powerful. The power of the earth is in the hand of the Lord, and in due time he will set over it one who is useful. In the hand of the Lord is the prosperity of man, and he bestows his glory upon the persons of the learned. Do not be angry with your neighbor for any injury, and do nothing by way of insult. Pride is hateful to both God and men, and both detest unjust deeds. For because of injustices, insults, and wealth gained by fraud, a kingdom is transferred from one nation to another. L. For nothing is more wicked than a greedy man.

### CHAPTER XI.

Wisdom lifts up the head of the humble, and places them among the great. Do not praise a man for his beauty, and do not despise a man for his appearance. Do not answer before you have heard, and do not interrupt in the middle of a discourse. Do not contend in a matter that does not concern you, and do not sit in judgment with sinners. There is one who labors, and toils, and hurries, yet is all the more in need. ### CHAPTER XII.

<margin>a. Hypocrisy is covered, as copper is by rust. b. When the rust of hypocrisy is uncovered.</margin>
If you do good, know to whom you do it, and L. much G. thanks will you receive for your good deeds. Do good to the godly, and L. a great G. reward you shall obtain—if not from them, then from the Most High. There are no good things for him who persists in evils, nor for him who does not give alms to the needy. L. Since the Most High hates the wicked and has mercy on the repentant, G. give to the godly, and do not help the sinner; do good to the humble, and do not give to the ungodly; indeed, withhold his bread and do not give it to him, lest he overpower you by those very means. For you shall receive twice as many evils for whatever good you have bestowed upon him; for the Most High hates sinners and will inflict punishment on the ungodly, whom he reserves for the day of most heavy vengeance. Give to the good, and do not help the wicked. A friend is not known in prosperity, nor is an enemy hidden in adversity. In a man’s prosperity, his enemies are grieved; in adversity, even a friend departs. Never trust your enemy: for like rusted copper, <a> so is his wickedness. Even if he humbles himself and walks bowed down, pay attention and beware of him, and you shall be to him like one who has polished a mirror, and you will eventually know <b> that he is not free of rust. Do not set him next to you, lest he overthrow you and stand in your place. Do not place him at your right hand, lest he try to occupy your seat, and at last you recognize my words and be stung by my warnings. Who will pity a snake charmer bitten by a serpent, or anyone who approaches wild beasts? So it is with him who associates with a wicked man and becomes involved in his sins. For one hour he will stay with you in a right state; but if you turn away, he will not endure. An enemy will use sweet words with his lips, and chatter much, and deal with you with fair speech, and weep with his eyes; but in his mind, he will deliberate about casting you into a pit. If he finds the opportunity, <c> he will not be satisfied with blood. If evils befall you, you will find him there before you; and while pretending to help, he will trip up your heel. <margin>c. He will use unfillable cruelty.</margin> He will shake his head and clap his hands, chatter much, and change his countenance.

### CHAPTER XIX.

A drunken worker does not grow rich: he who disregards small things falls little by little. ### CHAPTER XX.

There is a certain unseemly reproof <note>Latin version</note> in the anger of an insulting man: and there is a judgment which is proved to be wicked: <note>Greek version</note> and there is one who wisely keeps silent. ### CHAPTER XXIV.

->The Praise of Wisdom.<-

Wisdom commends herself, and glories among her own people. In the assembly of the Most High she speaks, and glories in the presence of His power, <note>L.</note> and among her own she is exalted; she is admired in the holy city, and obtains praise in the multitude of the elect, and she proclaims herself blessed among the blessed, saying: <note>G.</note> "I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, <note>L.</note> born before all creation. I caused an undying light to rise in the heavens, <note>G.</note> and I covered the whole earth like a mist. I dwelt in the highest places, and my throne is in a pillar of cloud. Alone I have circled the vault of heaven, and walked in the bottom of the deep. I held sway over the waves of the sea, and all the earth, and all peoples and nations; <note>L.</note> by my power I have trodden upon the hearts of all, both the excellent and the humble. <note>G.</note> After all these things I sought rest, and a place in whose possession I might dwell. Then the Creator of all, who created me, fixed my tabernacle, commanding me to dwell in the house of Jacob, to have my possession in the Israelites, <note>L.</note> and to take root among His elect. <note>G.</note> He created me from the beginning before the ages, and I shall never fail. In the holy tabernacle I served before Him, and so I was established in Zion; in the beloved city I found rest, and my power is in Jerusalem. I took root in a glorious people, in the portion of the Lord's inheritance; I grew tall like a cedar in Lebanon, and like a cypress on the mountains of Hermon. I grew tall like a palm tree on the shores, and like rose plants in Jericho; like a beautiful olive tree in a pleasant field, and I was raised up like a plane tree by the water. Like cinnamon and aromatic balsam <note>original: "aspalathus"</note> I gave off a scent, and like choice myrrh I breathed out a sweet odor: like galbanum, and onycha, and stacte, <note>Spices used in the holy incense of the Temple</note> and like the smoke of frankincense in the tabernacle. Like a terebinth tree I spread out my branches, which are branches of glory and grace. I am like a vine that has sprouted gracefully, and my flowers are the fruit of glory and wealth. [I am the mother of beautiful love, of religion, and of holy hope; to all my children, as God has commanded, I give eternal rewards.] <note>L.</note> In me is all grace of the way and the truth: in me is all hope of life and virtue. ### CHAPTER XXVII.

Many have sinned for the sake of wealth, and he who seeks to be rich turns away his eye <gloss>with an envious eye</gloss>. ### CHAPTER XXVIII.

<margin>Deuteronomy 32.</margin> He who desires vengeance shall find punishment from the Lord, who will surely keep his sins in mind. Remember the commandments and do not be angry with your neighbor; remember the covenant of the Most High, and <gloss>Latin tradition</gloss> overlook the other’s <gloss>Greek tradition</gloss> ignorance. Abstain from strife and you will diminish your sins; for a hot-tempered man kindles a fight. A wicked man troubles his friends and casts slander among those who are at peace. As the fuel is, so the fire burns; as a man's strength is, so is his fury; as a man's wealth is, so his anger swells; and as the quarrel is violent, so the heat increases. A hasty quarrel kindles a fire, and a hasty fight sheds blood. If you blow on a spark, it glows; if you spit on it, it is put out; and yet both come from your mouth. Slanderers and the double-tongued are to be cursed, for they have destroyed many who were at peace. A third tongue <note>The "third tongue" is a Semitic idiom for slander—the tongue that speaks *about* others.</note> has unsettled many, <margin>Against the talkative.</margin> and has driven them from nation to nation, and has pulled down strong cities, and overturned the houses of the great, <gloss>Latin tradition</gloss> and cut off the power of peoples, and destroyed mighty nations. <gloss>Greek tradition</gloss> A third tongue has cast out virtuous women and deprived them of their labors. He who gives heed to it will find no rest, nor will he live in quiet. The stroke of a whip makes a welt, but the stroke of the tongue breaks bones. Many have fallen by the edge of the sword, but not as many as have perished by the tongue. Happy is he who is sheltered from it, who has not fallen into its fury, who has not pulled its yoke, nor been bound by its chains. For its yoke is a yoke of iron, and its chains are chains of bronze. Its death is an evil death, and the Grave <note>original: "Orcus"</note> is more profitable than it. <gloss>Latin tradition</gloss> It does not endure forever, but it holds the habits of the unjust. <gloss>Greek tradition</gloss> It shall by no means hold the pious, nor shall they be burned in its flame. Those who desert the Lord fall into it; it shall burn in them and not be extinguished. It shall be sent upon them like a lion and shall tear them like a leopard. ### CHAPTER XXXI.

WATCHING for riches consumes the flesh, and the worry of them drives away sleep. Wakeful worry prevents slumber, and a heavy illness shakes off sleep. If the rich man labors, it is to gather wealth; if he stops, he is filled with pleasures. If the poor man labors, he lacks food; if he stops, he becomes needy. He who loves gold will not <margin>a. Or done evil and did not do it? Let his righteous deeds be established, and let the <note>Latin: "entire," Greek: "assembly"</note> of saints declare his benefits.

### CHAPTER XXXIII.

No evil shall happen to the one who fears the Lord; on the contrary, he will be defended in times of danger. A wise man
<margin>20</margin> does not hate the law; but he who deals hypocritically with it is like a ship in a storm. A prudent man trusts the law, and the law is faithful to him. As if it were a distinguished inquiry, rehearse what you are going to say: in this way you will find an audience. Prepare your learning and then give your answer. The heart and thoughts of a fool are like a cartwheel or a turning axle. Like a stallion neighing under every rider, so is a mocking friend. Why does one day
<margin>30</margin> excel another, when the light of every day of the year comes from the sun? By the Lord's providence they were distinguished, for He ordained the changes of seasons and festivals. L. And divine wisdom divided them, having made the sun to carry out His commands. G. Therefore He exalted and consecrated some days, and others He placed in the ordinary count of days. Likewise, all men come from the ground, and Adam was created from the earth; but in the fullness of His wisdom the Lord distinguished them and made their ways diverse. Some of them He blessed and exalted, some He consecrated
<margin>40</margin> and took for Himself. Others He cursed and brought low, and overturned from their place. As clay is in the potter's hand, and he fashions it according to his will, so men are in the hand of their Creator, who rewards them as He sees fit. Good is the opposite of evil, and life is the opposite of death: [likewise the sinner is the opposite of the godly, and the godly the opposite of the sinner]. So in all the works of the Most High, you will see them in pairs, one of which is the opposite of the other. I indeed was the last to wake up, like one who gleans after the grape-gatherers; by the Lord’s favor I reached my goal, and like a grape-gatherer I filled the winepress. Consider <margin>Above 24</margin>
<margin>50</margin> that I have not labored for myself alone, but for all those who seek learning. Listen to me, you leaders of the people, and you rulers of the assembly, give ear. To a son or a wife, a brother or a friend, do not give power over yourself while you live; and do not give your property to another, lest you regret it and have to beg for them back. While you still live and have breath in you, do not surrender yourself to any mortal; for it is better that your children should beg from you, than that you should look to the hands of your sons. In all your affairs, remain the master; do not [let a stain touch your glory].

### CHAPTER XXXVII.

Every friend says: "I too am a friend"; but there are some who are friends in name only. Does there not remain a grief unto death when a companion or friend turns into an enemy? O evil mind, from where did you crawl out, to cover the earth with deceit? A companion is delighted by a friend's happy affairs, but in a time of calamity he becomes an adversary. A companion helps a friend for the sake of his belly, and takes up a shield against the enemy. Do not forget a friend in your heart, nor be unmindful of him when you are wealthy. Every counselor extols his own counsel; but there are those who give counsel for their own interest. Guard yourself against a counselor, and first learn what he needs (for he will counsel for himself), lest he cast you into the risk of fortune, and say that your plan is indeed right, but meanwhile stand opposite you to see what will happen to you. Do not consult with one who suspects you; and hide your counsel from those who envy you. L. Do not consult with an irreligious man about holiness, nor with an unjust man about justice, G. nor with a woman about her rival, nor with a coward about war, nor with a merchant about exchange, nor with a buyer about a sale, nor with a stingy man about returning a favor, nor with the unmerciful about humanity, nor with a lazy man about any work,

<column-break/>

nor with a hired hand about the completion of a task, nor with a lazy servant about a great work; I say, do not join in any counsel with these. Instead, frequent a pious man whom you know to be obedient to the Lord's commandments, whose character matches your own, and who, if you should fall, will grieve for your sake. Establish L. the counsel of your own heart G. with yourself, for no one is more faithful to you than it (for a person's own mind sometimes warns him seven times more than seven watchmen sitting on a high tower); and yet, pray to the Most High that He may faithfully direct your path. Let reason be the beginning of every work, and let counsel precede every action. The face is the sign of a change of mind. Four things arise: good and evil, life and death; and the tongue is the perpetual ruler over them. There is a man who is cautious and a teacher of many, and yet he is useless to himself. There is one who claims wisdom for himself in words, but is hated. He should lack all nourishment, for the Lord has not granted him grace, since he lacks all wisdom. There is one who is wise
<margin>a. Otherwise: praiseworthy.</margin>
for himself, whose <sup>a</sup> fruits of prudence are certain in his mouth. A wise man teaches his own people, and the fruits of his prudence are certain. A wise man is filled with all blessings, and everyone who sees him calls him blessed. The life of a man is for a finite time, but the time of the Israelites is infinite. A wise man will obtain glory among his people, and his name will live forever. My son, while you live, test your own soul, and see if there is any vice in it, and do not indulge it: for as not everything is profitable for everyone,
<margin>b. It is possible that some vice exists in your soul.</margin>
so <sup>b</sup> not every soul is satisfied with everything. Do not gorge yourself on any delicacies, nor be gluttonous with food; for sickness accompanies excessive feasting, and greediness leads to bile. Many have died through greediness, while those who are temperate live longer.

Weep bitterly, and raise a passionate lament; perform the mourning as is fitting for one or two days to avoid slander <note>original: "calumniæ uitandæ gratia"; the author suggests social decorum requires a public display of grief to avoid being seen as heartless</note>; then console yourself for your sorrow. In the presence of the mind’s focus, sorrow departs, but the life of the miserable consists of the heart’s affliction. Do not give your heart over to anguish, but push it away from you, mindful of the end. Do not forget that there is no return; you will do him no good, and you will only harm yourself. The learned man.</margin> comes through the opportunity of leisure, and whoever has less business becomes wiser.
