He sets his heart on making furrows, and his sleepless care is for the fodder of the heifers. So it is with every craftsman and master-workman, whether they work by night or by day. Those who engrave signet rings and whose diligence is to offer great variety, they apply their hearts to represent the picture and stay awake to finish the work. Likewise, the blacksmith sitting by the anvil and considering the ironwork; the vapor of the fire parches his flesh, and he struggles with the heat of the furnace; the noise of the hammer deafens his ears, and his eyes are fixed on the pattern of the object; he applies his heart to completing the work and stays awake to polish it perfectly. Similarly, the potter sitting at his work, turning the wheel with his feet, is always anxiously diligent in his work, and doing everything by count; he shapes the clay with his arm, and with his feet he subdues its stiffness; he applies his heart to finishing the glaze and is vigilant in cleaning the furnace. All these trust in their hands, and each is skilled in his own craft. Without them, a city is not built, nor inhabited, nor walked through; [but they are not sought for in the public council,] nor do they shine in the assembly, [nor do they sit on the judge's bench,] nor do they understand the logic of judgments; they do not declare justice and law, nor are they found where parables are spoken. Yet they maintain the fabric of the world, and their prayer is in the practice of their craft.

### CHAPTER XXXIX.

But he who has applied his mind to meditating on the law of the Most High seeks out the wisdom of all the ancients and occupies himself with the prophets. He observes the discourses of famous men and penetrates the subtleties of parables; he seeks out the hidden meanings of proverbs and is conversant with the enigmas of parables. He serves among great men and appears before rulers. He travels through the lands of foreign nations, for he experiences both good and evil among men. He sets his heart to watch for the Lord his creator, and praying to the Most High, he opens his mouth in prayer and makes supplication for his sins. If the great Lord wills it, he will be filled with the spirit of understanding, and he will pour forth words of wisdom and give thanks to the Lord in prayer. He will direct his counsel

<column-break/>

and knowledge aright, and meditate on His secrets. He will show the discipline of His teaching and will glory in the law of the Lord's covenant. Many will praise his understanding, and his memory will never be blotted out or fail, for his name lives through perpetual ages. Nations will proclaim his wisdom, and his praise will be celebrated in the assembly. Whether he dies, he will leave a more celebrated <margin>a. Namely, a name.</margin> <margin>Above 3</margin> <margin>Genesis 7</margin> <margin>Below 4</margin> <margin>Ecclesiastes</margin> name than others, or whether he remains in life and finds rest. I will set forth more things I have reflected upon, for I am as full as the full moon. Listen to me, you pious sons, and bud forth like a rose planted by a stream of water; give off a sweet fragrance like incense, and send forth flowers like a lily. Send out a scent and sing songs of praise, celebrating the Lord for all His works. Ascribe greatness to His name and celebrate Him with His praises, both with songs of the lips and with harps. Thus shall you say in praise: All the works of the Lord are very good, and every <margin>a. As a [violent] noise sounds loudly and then vanishes, so more vainly does the noise of [the world]. b. At His word the water stood like a heap, and at the word of His mouth the waves were solidified. In His command is all favor, and there is none who can diminish His protection. The deeds of all mortals are open before Him, nor can anything be hidden from His eyes. From all eternity to all eternity He sees everything, and nothing is difficult for Him. There is no reason to say: "What is this?" or "Why is this?" for all things were created for their own uses. His favor overflows like a river. And as <margin>Genesis 7</margin> the flood submerged the earth, so the nations will feel His wrath, L. <margin>Exodus 14</margin> who do not care for Him. Just as <margin>b. As good things were created for the good from the beginning, so <margin>Above 29</margin> evil things for the wicked. The sum of all things necessary for human life is water, fire, iron, salt, wheat flour, honey, milk, the blood of grapes <note>gloss: wine</note>, oil, and clothing. All these are good for the pious, but for the wicked they are turned into evil. There are spirits created for vengeance, who strike with severe lashes, and in the time of destruction they pour out their strength and satisfy the wrath of their creator. Fire, hail, famine, and death—all these were <margin>Below 40</margin> created for punishment. The teeth of wild beasts, and scorpions, and serpents, and the sword, punishing the ungodly with capital destruction, rejoice in His command; they are ready on the earth whenever needed, and they do not disobey His orders in their times. For this reason, having investigated and meditated on the matter from the beginning, I have committed it to writing to provide it in its own time: that one thing cannot be said to be worse than another, for all things will be proven good in their time. Therefore, with all your heart and mouth, sing and praise the name of the Lord.

### CHAPTER XL.

<margin>a. Death to all</margin> A huge labor and a heavy yoke are imposed on all men born of Adam, from the day of their departure from their mother’s womb until the day of their return to the mother of all: their thoughts, the fears of their heart, the imagination of things expected, and the day of their death. This applies to him who sits gloriously on a throne as well as to him who is on the ground in filth; to him who wears hyacinth <note>term: "hyacinth" (Latin: hyacinthum) refers to a deep blue or purple fabric, often associated with royalty or the priesthood</note> and a crown, as well as to him who is clothed in coarse linen; I say, fury, jealousy, trouble, commotion, the fear of death, anger, strife, and even at the time of nightly rest in bed, sleep disturbs their minds.

### CHAPTER XL.

<margin>a. Dying to all.</margin>
A great labor and a heavy yoke are imposed upon all men descended from Adam, from the day of their coming out of their mother’s womb until the day of their return to the mother of all: their thoughts, the fears of their hearts, the imagination of things to come, and the day of their death. Little and almost nothing is given to them for rest; then in their sleep, just as if they were on watch, they are disturbed by the visions of their own souls—as if they had escaped from a battle (even though they are out of danger). These things happen to all living creatures, both humans and 9 beasts, but for the wicked there are seven times more: death, bloodshed, strife, swords, oppression, famine, calamities, and ruins. All these things were created for the lawless, and because of them, the Great Flood occurred. 11 Whatever has arisen from the earth returns to the earth, and whatever comes from the water returns to the sea. All bribery and injustice will be wiped away, but faith shall remain forever. The riches of the unjust shall dry up like a river, and <gloss>as</gloss> a great thunder crashes in the rain. While they open their hands, they rejoice; thus, the transgressors shall utterly fail. The offspring of the ungodly will not produce many branches; their roots are like impure plants on the edge of a cliff. 20 Reeds by any moisture or river bank are the first of all plants to be pulled up. Kindness is like a fruitful garden, and acts of mercy endure forever. The life of a worker and of one who is content with what he has is sweet, but he who finds a treasure surpasses both. Children and the building of a city make a name stable, but a blameless wife is to be valued above both. Wine and music delight the heart, but the love of wisdom stands above both. Flutes and the psaltery make sweet songs, but a pleasant tongue conquers both. Though your eyes may long for grace and beauty, the greenness of a field of grain excels both. 30 A friend and a companion meet at the right time, but a wife joined to her husband surpasses both. Brothers and help are for a time of calamity, but acts of mercy protect more than both. Gold and silver provide a firm footing, but good counsel is more commendable than both. Riches and power lift the spirit, but the fear of the Lord does so more than both. In the fear of the Lord, nothing is lacking; you need no other help. The fear of the Lord is like a fruitful orchard, whose beauty surpasses all magnificence. My son, do not lead a beggar's life; 40 it is better to die than to beg. The life of a man who depends on another’s table is not to be considered a life at all; he pollutes himself with another's food—something a skilled and learned man will guard against. In the mouth of the shameless, begging is sweet, but in his belly, a fire burns.

### CHAPTER XLI.

O Death, how bitter is the memory of you to a man who is at peace with his possessions; to a man who is at leisure and still able to take food! O Death, how welcome is your sentence to a man who is in need, whose strength is worn out <margin>at his end</margin> by old age, who is distracted on all sides, who is despairing and 6 stripped of patience! Do not fear the sentence of death; remember <gloss>those who came</gloss> before you and those who come after. Since this is the fate from the Lord for all living things, why do you refuse what pleases the Most High? Whether it be ten, a hundred, or a thousand years, there is no defense of life against the Grave <note>original: "Ditem," referring to Dis Pater or Pluto, the god of the underworld; here used to mean the inescapable power of death.</note>. The children of the wicked are lawless children, and they are those who frequent the dwellings of the ungodly. The inheritance of the children of the wicked perishes, and eternal infamy follows their descendants.

<column-break/>

<page-num>214</page-num>
->ECCLESIASTICUS<-

Children have cause to complain of an ungodly father, because they are disgraced through him. Woe to you, ungodly men, who have forsaken the law of the Most High God! For if you are born, you are born into misery; if you die, your condition is miserable. All things that have arisen from the earth shall return to the earth; likewise, the ungodly go from misery into destruction. The bodies of men are mourned, but the ill-famed name of the wicked is blotted out. Have a care for your name, for that will remain with you longer than a 10 thousand great treasures of gold. The lifespan of a good life is limited, but a good name lasts forever. Children, preserve my teaching in peace: for what is the use of either hidden wisdom or a concealed treasure? Better is the man who hides his own foolishness than the man who hides his own wisdom. Therefore, be ashamed of these things I shall name; for it is not honorable to be held by every kind of shame, and faith is not approved everywhere. Be ashamed of debauchery before your father and mother; of a lie before a prince or a person of power; of a crime before 20 a governor or a judge; of a lawless act before the city and the people; of an injustice before a partner and a friend; of theft before the place where you dwell <margin>b. This is unseemly at the table.</margin> and before the divine <gloss>c</gloss> truth of the covenant. Be ashamed <gloss>d</gloss> to lean your elbow on loaves of bread, and of a crime in giving or receiving a gift; of being silent when greeted; of looking at a harlot; of turning your face away from a kinsman; of snatching away a portion of an inheritance or a gift; of gazing at a married woman; of 30 soliciting her handmaid or approaching her bed; of insulting friends; of upbraiding them after you have given a gift; of repeating a thing you have heard; and of revealing secret words. In this way, you will be truly modest and will gain the goodwill of all men.

### CHAPTER XLII.

<margin>Leviticus 19; Deuteronomy 1:16; Proverbs 24; James 2</margin>
But do not be ashamed of these following things, nor sin by showing favoritism to any person: of the law and covenant of the Most High; of judgment, in deciding according to him who has been wronged; of the accounts of partners and travelers; of the dividing of an inheritance among associates; of the accuracy of scales and 40 weights; of acquiring much or little; of the fair sale of merchandise; of the frequent correction of children; and of making the side of a bad servant bleed <note>original: "mali serui latere cruentando"; a harsh reference to corporal punishment common in the ancient world.</note>. If a wife is wicked, a lock is appropriate; and where there are many hands, lock things up. Whatever you entrust, do it by number and weight; and whatever you either give or receive, record it in a ledger. Correct the senseless and the fool, and also the man of decrepit age who quarrels with young men. Thus you will be truly learned and accepted by all mortals. A daughter is a secret cause of care to a father, and 50 such a great anxiety that she drives away sleep: in her youth, lest she fade away; in marriage, lest she be hated; in her virginity, lest she be defiled and become pregnant in her father's house; when joined to a husband, lest she transgress or be barren after being married off. Keep a very strict watch over a daughter, lest she make you a laughingstock to your enemies, a topic of gossip in the city, infamous among the people, and bring disgrace upon you before the crowd. Do not gaze upon the beauty of any man, nor sit among women; for just as a moth comes from clothing, so 60 wickedness comes from women. <margin>a. Little and almost no rest is given to them: then in their sleep, as if they were on guard duty, they are disturbed by visions of their own minds, as if they had escaped from battle (though they are out of danger). They wake up and marvel at a terror that is non-existent. These things happen to all living creatures, both men and <margin>b</margin> beasts, but for the wicked there are seven times more: murders, killings, strifes, swords, assaults, famine, calamities, and disasters—all of which were created for the sinful, because of whom even the flood happened. <margin>c</margin> Whatever has risen from the earth returns to the earth: and what is from the water returns to the sea. While <margin>d</margin> they open their hands, they rejoice: thus the transgressors shall utterly fail. The offspring of the ungodly will not produce many branches, for they are like impure roots on the top of a crag. Sedge growing in any amount of moisture or on a riverbank is pulled up before all other grass. Kindness is like a garden of blessings, and acts of mercy endure forever. Sweet is the life of the person content with their own and that of the laborer, but he who finds a treasure surpasses both. Children and the building of a city make a name stable: but a blameless wife is to be considered better than both. Wine and music delight the heart: but the love of wisdom is better than both. The flute and the lute make sweet songs: but a sweet tongue surpasses both. Though your eyes may desire grace and beauty, the greenness of a grain field excels both. A friend and a companion meet at the right time: but a wife joined to a husband surpasses both. Brothers and help are for a time of calamity: but acts of mercy protect more than both. Gold and silver make the feet stand firm: but good counsel is more commendable than both. Riches and power lift up the heart: but the fear of the Lord is more than both. Nothing is lacking in the fear of the Lord, nor should you seek help elsewhere in it. The fear of the Lord is like a garden of blessings, whose beauty surpasses all magnificence. My son, do not lead a beggar’s life: it is better to die than to beg. The life of a man hanging on another’s table is not to be considered a life, for he pollutes himself with another's food—a thing which a skillful and learned man will avoid. Begging is sweet in the mouth of the shameless, but in his belly a fire burns.

### CHAPTER XLI.

**O** Death, how bitter is the remembrance of you to a man at peace among his possessions: to a man at leisure, and still able to take his food! O death, how welcome is your sentence to a man in need, whose strength has failed and who is decrepit with age, who is troubled on all sides, despairing, and void of patience! Do not fear the sentence of death: remember those who came before you and those who follow: since this is the decree from the Lord for all living things, why would you reject what pleases the Most High? Whether it be ten, a hundred, or a thousand years, there is no defense of life against the Grave <note>original: "Ditem"; referring to Dis Pater, the Roman god of the underworld, here used to mean the state of death or the grave</note>. The children of sinners are the children of the wicked, and those who frequent the dwellings of the ungodly. The inheritance of the children of the wicked perishes, and eternal

Whatever has risen from the earth shall go back into the earth: likewise the ungodly go from misery into destruction. ...indeed a virtuous woman, but one who is a cause of foul infamy <note>referring to a shameful or unfaithful woman</note>. I will indeed call to mind the works of the Lord, and I will explain those deeds of his that I have learned through his words. The bright sun looks upon all things, and his work is full of his own splendor. Truly, the Lord has not granted even to his holy ones <note>likely referring to the angels</note> the power to describe all his wonders, which the almighty Lord has established so that the universe might stand firm in his glory—he who searches the depths and the hearts of men, and perceives their cleverness. For the Lord knows everything that can be known, and he looks into the signs of the ages; he declares things past and things to come, and reveals the traces of hidden secrets. No thought escapes him, and no word is hidden from him. He has fashioned the greatness of his wisdom in such a way that, as he exists both before the ages and for all ages, he can neither be increased nor diminished, nor does he require anyone’s counsel. Oh, how elegant are all his works! Of which we are permitted to see but a tiny spark. All these things live and endure through the ages, and they obey him for every purpose. All things come in pairs, one opposite the other, and he has made nothing incomplete. Each one confirms the good of the other; and who could ever be satisfied by gazing upon God’s glory?

# CHAPTER XLIII

<margin>
The Sun.
a. Things that happen by fire.
</margin>
The pride of the heights, the purity of the sky, the sight of the heavens is glorious to behold. The sun, appearing at its rising, is a wonderful instrument, the work of the Most High; at noon it parches the fields with heat, and who can endure its burning? They who stoke a furnace work with *a* intense heat, but the sun burns the mountains three times more, breathing out fiery vapors and blinding the eyes with its flashing rays. Great is the Lord who made it, and at whose command it speeds on its journey.

<margin>The Moon.</margin>
He also made the moon to appear in its proper time, a marker of the seasons and a sign for the ages. From the moon comes the sign for feast days—a light that wanes until it disappears. From it the month takes its name, and it changes marvelously in its waxing.

<margin>The Stars.</margin>
High above is an army’s camp <note>a poetic description of the arrangement of stars</note>, the beauty of the heavens shining in the celestial firmament, the splendor of the stars, a glowing ornament in the heights of the Lord, at whose holy command they stand continually, and they do not tire in their watches.

<margin>Genesis 9: The Rainbow.</margin>
See the rainbow and praise its creator; it is most beautiful in its brightness, encircling the sky with a magnificent circle, stretched out by the hands of the Most High.

<margin>Snow, Lightning, Clouds, Hail, Thunder.</margin>
By his command, he drives the snow and hurls the lightnings according to his will. Therefore, the storehouses are opened, and the clouds fly out like birds; as he restrains them by his power, the hailstones are broken small. At his appearance the mountains are shaken, and by his will the south wind blows. The crash of his thunder makes the earth tremble, as do the northern storm and the whirlwind; he scatters the snow like birds flying down, and its falling is like the settling of locusts.

<margin>Frost and Ice.</margin>
The eye marvels at the beauty of its whiteness, and the heart is awed by its falling. He pours out the frost upon the earth like salt, which, when frozen, becomes like pointed thorns. Then the cold north wind blows and turns the water into ice; it settles upon every gathering of water, clothing the water as if with a breastplate. It consumes the mountains, scorches the wilderness, and extinguishes the grass like fire.

<margin>Mist and Dew.</margin>
A mist is a ready remedy for all these things, and the dew appearing after the heat brings refreshment. By his wisdom he calmed the deep, and in it he planted islands. Those who

<column-break/>

<page-num>216</page-num>

<margin>The Sea.</margin>
sail the sea tell of its dangers, and we who hear them with our ears are amazed. For there are incredible and wonderful things, a vast variety of animals, and the nature of sea monsters <note>original: "cetorum," often referring to whales or great sea creatures</note>. Finally, through him his work prospers, and by his word all things hold together. Though we may say much, we shall not reach the end of the matter. The sum of our words is this: He is all. How can we find strength to praise him? For he himself is greater than all his works. The Lord is terrible and very great, and of wonderful power. When you praise the Lord, exalt him as much as you can, for he will still exceed it; in exalting him, exert your full strength and do not grow weary, for you can never say enough. Who has seen him, that he might explain him? Or who can magnify him as he truly is? Many things greater than these are hidden; for we have seen but a few of his works. For the Lord made all things, and to the godly he has given wisdom.

# CHAPTER XLIV

<margin>
Praise of the ancient men of Israel.
</margin>
Let us now praise noble men, the fathers of our race. Through them the Lord has produced great glory, which has been his greatness from all eternity. There were those who ruled in their kingdoms, men renowned for their power; those who were wise in their counsel; those who spoke prophecies; those who led the people by their counsel and their knowledge of the public writings, whose words in their teaching were wise; those who composed musical harmonies; those who set down poems in writing; rich men, excelling in power, who lived at peace in their homes. All these were honored in their generations, and were the glory of their times.

But these were men of mercy, whose righteous deeds have not been forgotten. A good inheritance remains with their descendants; their offspring stand by the covenant; their children endure forever; neither their lineage nor their glory shall ever be blotted out. Their bodies are buried in peace, but their name lives on for all generations. The people declare their wisdom, and the congregation proclaims their praise.

### CHAPTER XLV

<margin>17</margin>
From him <note>referring to the lineage of the ancestors</note> He brought forth a pious man, accepted by all mortals, and dear to both God and men: Moses, whose memory is blessed. He made him equal in glory to the holy ones <note>original: "a sanctis," referring here to the angels</note>, and made him great through the terror of his enemies. At his word, He performed wonders; He honored him in the presence of kings; He gave him commandments for His people and showed him His splendor. He consecrated him in faith and gentleness, and chose him out of all mortals. He allowed His voice to be heard by him, and led him into the dark cloud; He delivered the precepts to him face to face—the law of the knowledge of life—so that he might teach the covenant to the descendants of Jacob and His laws to the Israelites. To him He raised up a peer, the holy Aaron, his brother from the tribe of Levi, with whom He entered into an eternal covenant. He gave him the priesthood of the people, blessed him with ornaments, and clothed him in noble vestments. He arrayed him in perfect beauty and equipped him with magnificent regalia: leggings, a robe, and an ephod <note>a ceremonial priestly garment</note>, and girded him with golden spheres and numerous bells all around, which would tinkle as he walked and resound in the temple, serving as a reminder for the people of his kin. The sacred vestment was worked with gold, blue, purple, and variegated embroidery, featuring the oracle of judgment—**BRIGHTNESS AND PERFECTION** <note>original: "CLARITAS ET INTEGRITAS," translating the Hebrew 'Urim and Thummim,' used for discerning God's will</note>—artfully crafted with scarlet threads and precious stones engraved like seals and set in gold, the work of a jeweler, to serve as a memorial, with an inscription engraved according to the number of the tribes of Israel. Likewise, a gold crown was placed upon his turban, fashioned like a sacred seal—an honorable ornament, an exquisite and elegant work, most beautiful to the eyes, such as had never been made before. No stranger ever wore it, but only his sons and grandsons forever, as the sacrifices were to be consumed twice daily without ceasing.

<margin>.8</margin>

It was assigned to him by an everlasting covenant, and to his posterity as long as the heavens endure: that they should serve God, perform sacred rites, and pray for blessings upon His people in His name. He chose him out of all mortals to offer the burnt offering, the drink offering, and the sweet fragrance to the Lord, as a memorial, so that He might be merciful to His people.

<margin>.16</margin>

When others conspired against him and envied him with furious anger in the wilderness—the followers of Dathan, Abiram, and the faction of Korah—the Lord noticed this and so disapproved that they were consumed by a terrible punishment; the flame of His fire destroyed them in a miraculous way. He added to Aaron’s glory and gave him a possession, <note>b. This was on the condition that they should have no inheritance in the land of the people, nor should they receive a portion among their countrymen, for the Lord Himself was a sufficient portion for their inheritance. ### CHAPTER XLVI

<margin>Joshua.</margin>
Powerful in wars was Joshua, the son of Nun, and the successor of Moses in prophecy. He was of great renown for the salvation of God’s elect, as he took vengeance on hostile enemies so that he might lead the Israelites into their possession. How much glory did he attain, either by <note>a. In prayer, Joshua 10</note> lifting his hands or by brandishing his sword against cities? Who before him stood out as such a man? For he fought the Lord’s battles. Did not the sun stand still because of him, and one day grow into two? When he called upon the supreme and all-powerful One while enemies pressed him from every side, the great Lord heard him and rained down a violent storm of hail upon that nation in the battle. He destroyed the adversaries on the slope, so that the nations might recognize his arms and know that this war was waged against the Lord. For he followed the Powerful One,

<margin>Caleb.</margin>

<margin>Joshua 14.</margin>
Caleb that strength which remained with him even into his old age, so that he climbed the heights of the region, and his descendants obtained the inheritance, so that all the Israelites might understand how good it is to follow the Lord. The memory of all the leaders <note>Presidents, who are usually called Judges.</note> by name—as many as were not of an unchaste mind and did not turn away from the Lord—shall be blessed. May their bones flourish again in their places, and may their name be passed down through successions to the most famous of their descendants. Beloved 
<margin>Samuel.</margin>
by his Lord, the prophet of the Lord, Samuel, established kings and anointed princes over His people. He administered the republic according to the law of the Lord, and through his faithfulness, the Lord came to the aid of the descendants of Jacob. He was proven to be a prophet and recognized as a faithful interpreter of oracles because of his loyalty. When he had prayed to the powerful Lord with a suckling lamb while enemies pressed on every side, the Lord 
<margin>1 Samuel 7 and following.</margin>

Likewise, after he had fallen asleep, he prophesied and showed the king his end; raising his voice from the earth in an oracle, he spoke that the people's wickedness would be blotted out.

### CHAPTER XLVII.

After this man, Nathan arose to prophesy in the time of David. Just as the fat is set apart from the sacrifice for the sake of well-being, so David was set apart from the Israelites. He played with lions as if they were young goats, and with bears as if they were lambs of the flock. Did he not, while still a youth, slay the giant? And did he not take away the shame of the people when his hand moved the stone in the sling and cast down the pride of Goliath? For he called upon the Sovereign Lord, who gave strength to his right hand to strike down a man powerful in war, and to lift up the <term>horn</term> <note>In biblical language, the "horn" symbolizes strength, dignity, and the power of a lineage.</note> of his people. Thus, he brought honor to many legions in his death and celebrated with divine praises, for the crown of glory was granted to him. For he crushed his enemies on every side and overthrew his Philistine adversaries, breaking their power <note>original: "cornu," meaning horn/strength</note> even to this day. In every work he did, he gave thanks to the Sovereign Power with a prayer of honor; with his whole heart, he praised and loved God his Creator, who had given him power against his enemies. He established singers before the altar, composing sweet songs to their melodies. [Who would speak praises daily with their songs.] He added beauty to the feasts and fully adorned the solemn rites, so they might praise the holy name of God and make the sanctuary ring out from early morning. [The Lord wiped away his sins and exalted his horn forever; He made a covenant with him for the kingdom and the throne of majesty among the Israelites.]

<margin>
Solomon.
1 Kings 4 and following.
</margin>

A wise son, Solomon, succeeded him, who flourished greatly because of his father. He reigned in a time of peace and glory, for God had settled everything around him so that he might build a house for His name and prepare a sanctuary to last forever. How wise you were in your youth, Solomon, filled with understanding like a river! Your mind covered the whole earth, and you filled it with the riddles of your proverbs. Your name reached the distant islands, and you were beloved for your peace. The nations admired you for your songs, proverbs, parables, and interpretations, in the name of the Lord God, who is called the God of the Israelites. You gathered gold like tin and amassed silver as if it were lead. But because you leaned your sides against women and were mastered by your body, you brought a stain upon your glory and profaned your lineage. Through this, you brought punishment upon your children and caused your foolishness to grieve them; the empire was divided, and a rebellious kingdom began in Ephraim. But the Lord will never abandon His mercy toward His works, nor let it perish. He would never destroy the descendants of His chosen one, nor take away the offspring of the one who loved Him. Therefore, He gave a remnant to Jacob and a root to David from his own line.

Jeroboam.
</margin>

Therefore, when Solomon rested with his ancestors, he left behind from his seed a man of the people’s foolishness^2: Rehoboam, who lacked wisdom and alienated the people by his counsel. Then there was Jeroboam, son of Nebat, who caused the Israelites to sin and showed the people of Ephraim the way of wickedness. Their sins grew so numerous that they were driven out of their own land; indeed, they sought out every kind of wickedness until a cruel punishment fell upon them, <note>Latin version: "by which they might atone for so many sins." / Greek version: "until the end."</note>

### CHAPTER XLVIII.

Then Elijah arose, a fiery prophet whose word burned like a torch. He brought a heavy famine upon them, and in his zeal, he reduced them to a few, <note>Latin version: "because they could not endure the Lord’s commands."</note> By the Lord’s command, he shut up the heavens and three times brought down fire from the sky. How glorious you became, Elijah, through your miracles! Who can boast of being your equal? By the command of the Sovereign, you raised the dead from the grave and from the underworld. You cast down kings to destruction and brought nobles down from their thrones, <note>Latin version: "and easily broke their power."</note> You heard the Lord’s rebuke at Sinai and the decrees of vengeance at Horeb. You anointed kings for retribution and prophets to succeed you. You were taken up in a whirlwind of fire, in a chariot with horses of fire. You are destined for the rebukes of specific times, to calm the wrath of the Lord's judgment before it turns to fury, and to reconcile the heart of the father to the son, and to restore the tribes of Jacob. Blessed are those who saw you and fell asleep in love; for we shall surely live again.

Elisha.
</margin>

When the whirlwind of Elijah had passed, Elisha was filled with his spirit. In his time, he was not shaken by any ruler, nor was he subject to anyone’s power; he was unconquered in every way. Even when his life was finished, his body prophesied <note>Refers to the biblical account of a dead man coming to life after touching Elisha's bones.</note>; he performed wonders in his life, and even in death, his works were marvelous. But despite all this, the people did not repent, nor did they turn from their sins, until they were driven from their ancestral soil and scattered throughout the whole world. Only a small people and a ruler were left in the house of David; some of these did what was pleasing to God, but others sinned greatly.

<margin>
Hezekiah.
2 Kings 18.
</margin>

Hezekiah fortified his city and brought water into it; he tunneled through the rock with iron and built wells for the sake of water. During his time, Sennacherib made an expedition and sent the Rabshakeh, who raised his hand against Zion and boasted proudly. Then their hearts and hands trembled, and they suffered like women in labor. They called upon the merciful Lord, spreading their hands out toward Him. The Holy One quickly heard them from heaven; <note>Latin version: "He did not hand them over to their enemies because of their sins, but..."</note> <note>Greek version interpreted by the Latin: "He delivered them by the hand of the holy prophet."</note> He struck down the camp of the Assyrians and overthrew them by the hand of His angel. For Hezekiah acted according to the Lord’s will and held fast to the path of his father David, as commanded by Isaiah, that great and faithful prophet of visions. In his time, the sun moved backward, and he lengthened the king’s life. With a great spirit, he saw the end of times and comforted the mourners in Zion; he revealed things to come and hidden matters before they happened.

The memory of Josiah is like a blended incense prepared by the art of the perfumer; in every mouth, it is sweet as honey, or like music at a wine-filled banquet. He acted with skill in reforming the people and removed the abominations of wickedness. His heart was well-disposed toward the Lord, and in a time of lawlessness, he established piety.

### CHAPTER L.

<margin>1.</margin> Simon, son of Onias, the high priest, repaired the house during his life and strengthened the temple in his time. This man took care of his people against adverse events and fortified the city against siege. <margin>5.</margin> How great was his honor when he moved among the people! <margin>6.</margin> As he came out from behind the veil of the temple, he was like the morning star through the midst of a cloud, or like the full moon in its days. <margin>7.</margin> He shone like the sun upon the temple of the Most High, and like a rainbow reflecting in bright clouds; <margin>8.</margin> like the flower of roses in springtime, or lilies by the water brooks; <margin>9.</margin> like a sprig of frankincense in the summer, or fire and incense in the censer; <margin>10.</margin> like a vessel of solid gold adorned with every kind of precious stone; <margin>11.</margin> like a graceful and fruitful olive tree, or a cypress reaching high toward the clouds. <margin>12.</margin> When he put on his noble vestments and clothed himself in perfect glory, <margin>13.</margin> ascending to the holy altar, he brought honor to the sacred court. ...festivals, I do not endure those vain things. Your new moons and your solemnities I hate in my soul; they are burdensome to me: I am weary of bearing them. When you stretch out your hands, I turn my eyes away from you; even though you make many prayers, I do not listen, since your hands are full of blood. Wash yourselves, make yourselves clean, remove the wickedness of your character from my sight: cease to do evil, learn to do good, strive for equity, defend the oppressed, act as protectors for orphans, and plead the causes of widows. Come, let us set ourselves right, says the Lord <note>original: "Iouua," a Renaissance Latin rendering of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton, usually translated as 'the Lord' or 'Jehovah'</note>: even if your sins are like scarlet, they shall be made whiter than snow; if they are like crimson, they shall be made whiter than wool. If you are willing to obey, you shall enjoy the good things of the earth; but if you refuse and remain rebellious, you shall be consumed by the sword, for the mouth of the Lord has spoken. How has the faithful city become so shameless, she who was once full of equity, and in whom justice lived—now murderers are in her! Your silver has turned to dross: your pure wine is mixed with water. Your princes are deserters and companions of thieves; they are all greedy for gifts and chase after bribes. They do not render justice to orphans, nor do they admit the cases of widows. Therefore, thus says the Lord, the God of Hosts <term>armipotens: literally 'powerful in arms,' a humanist translation for the 'Lord of Hosts'</term>, the Power of the Israelites. Alas, I will take vengeance on my adversaries; I will avenge myself on my enemies. And with my hand turned against you, I will purge your dross as purely as possible; I will take away all your lead and restore your judges to you as you once had them, and your counselors as in the beginning. Afterward, you shall be called the City of Justice, the Faithful City. Zion shall be redeemed with equity, and her exiles with justice. But the rebels and the wicked shall be crushed together; those who desert the Lord shall be consumed. For they shall be ashamed of the idols <note>original: "diuorum," referring to false gods or statues</note> that you desired, and you shall repent of the gardens that you chose. For you shall be like an oak whose leaves have fallen, and like a garden lacking water. And that "god" of yours shall become tinder, and its maker a spark; so both shall burn together, with no one to extinguish them.

Then the Lord said: Because the women of Zion are proud, and walk with outstretched necks, with wanton eyes, with a mincing gait and measured steps, the Lord will make the heads of the women of Zion bald, and the Lord will uncover their secret parts. One day, the Lord will take away the finery of their ornaments: their hair-curlers, crescents, pendants, sashes, veils, turbans, bracelets, ribbons, necklaces, earrings, rings, headbands, kerchiefs, linen cloaks, fine robes, purses, mirrors, linen cloths, veils, and delicate garments. Instead of sweet scents, there will be a stench; instead of a belt, a rope; instead of curled hair, baldness; instead of a fine tunic, a garment of sackcloth; and branded skin instead of beauty. Your men shall fall by the sword, and your soldiers in war; and as your gates grieve and mourn, you shall sit destitute on the ground, so much so that seven women will take hold of one man at that time, saying: "We will live on our own food and clothe ourselves; only let us be called by your name, so that you may take away our disgrace."

### CHAPTER IV.

At that time, the sprout of the Lord shall be noble and glorious, and the fruit of the earth shall be excellent and beautiful—namely, for the Israelites who have escaped. And those who are left in Zion and remain in Jerusalem shall be called holy—that is, all who are recorded for life in Jerusalem. This will happen when the Lord has washed away the filth of the women of Zion and has purged the bloodstains of Jerusalem from her midst by a spirit of equity and a spirit of burning. Then the Lord will create over every dwelling place of Mount Zion and over her assemblies a cloud by day and smoke by night, with the glow of a flaming fire by night, so that it may protect all nobility. It shall be a canopy to provide shade by day against the heat, and a refuge and covering against storms and rain.

### CHAPTER VI.

In the year that King Uzziah <note>original: "Ozias"</note> died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and lofty throne, and the edges of His robe filled the temple. Above it stood the Seraphim <term>Seraphim: literally "burning ones," celestial beings who attend the throne of God</term>, each having six wings: with two they covered their faces, with two they covered their feet, and with two they flew. And one cried to another in these words: **H O L Y, H O L Y, H O L Y I S J E H O V A H A L M I G H T Y, W H O S E G L O R Y F I L L S T H E W H O L E E A R T H.** <note>original: "Ioua Armipotens" - translating the Hebrew 'Yahweh Sabaoth' or Lord of Hosts</note> At the sound of this cry, the doorposts of the vestibule were moved, and the entire house was filled with smoke. Then I said: Woe is me, I am undone! For I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell among a people of unclean lips, yet I have seen with my own eyes the King, Jehovah Almighty. Then one of the Seraphim flew to me, holding in his hand a glowing coal which he had taken with tongs from the altar. He touched my mouth with it and said: As soon as this coal has touched your lips, your guilt is gone, and your sin is forgiven. Then I heard the voice of the Lord saying: Whom shall I send? Or who will go for us? And I said: Here am I; send me. And He said: Go, and tell this people in this manner: Listen, but do not understand; see, but do not perceive. Blind the heart of this people, make their ears heavy, and dim their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, and so be converted and healed. And I asked: How long, Lord? And He replied: Until the cities are so wasted that there is no inhabitant, and the houses so that no one is there, and the land is utterly desolate—with men removed so far by Jehovah that there is a vast solitude in the midst of the land. And though there yet be a <margin><sup>a</sup></margin> tenth part in it, it shall be ravaged again, like an oak or a terebinth tree which <margin><sup>b</sup></margin> keep their substance even after shedding their leaves: so the substance of this land shall be the holy seed.

### CHAPTER XXXI.

Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, and rely on horses, and trust in chariots, because they are many; and in horsemen, because they are very strong; but they do not look to the Holy One of Israel <note>original: "Israelitici Augustum," using the Roman title 'Augustus' to denote holiness and majesty</note>, nor do they seek Jehovah. Yet He also is wise, and will bring evil, and will not take back his words, but will arise against the house of the wicked, and against the help of those who work iniquity. Now the Egyptians are men, and not gods; and their horses are flesh <note>original: "corpora," literally bodies</note>, and not spirit. When Jehovah stretches out his hand, both the helper shall fall, and he who is helped shall tumble down, and they all shall perish together. For thus Jehovah has said to me: "As a young lion roars over his prey, even when a multitude of shepherds is called out against him, he is not terrified by their voice, nor does he yield to their noise: so shall Jehovah of hosts <note>original: "armipotens Ioua," literally 'the weapon-powerful Jehovah'</note> come down to fight for Mount Zion, and for its hill." As birds flying, so will Jehovah of hosts protect Jerusalem; protecting, he will deliver it, and passing over, he will defend it. Return to him, from whom you have so deeply revolted, O Israelites. For in that day every man shall cast away his idols of silver and his idols of gold, which your own sinful hands have made for you. Then the Assyrian shall fall by a sword, not of a man; and a sword, not of a human, shall devour him: he shall flee from the sword, and his chosen youths shall be put to forced labor. He shall pass over his stronghold for fear, and his princes shall be afraid of the banner," says Jehovah, whose fire is in Zion, and whose furnace is in Jerusalem.

### CHAPTER XXXII.

<margin>Of the Prince, etc.</margin>
But a king shall reign in justice, and princes shall rule with equity. And a man shall be as a hiding place from the wind, and a shelter from the storm; as rivers of water in a dry place, as the shadow of a great rock in a thirsty land. The eyes of those who see will not be blurred, and the ears of those who hear will listen; and the heart of the rash shall learn to understand, and the tongue of the stammerers shall be ready to speak plainly. No longer shall the fool be called noble, nor the greedy be called generous. For a fool speaks foolishness, and his heart plots wickedness, practicing godliness in a way that wanders from Jehovah, leaving the hungry empty and depriving the thirsty of drink. The greedy man’s methods are evil; he devises wicked schemes to destroy the poor with lying words, even when the needy speak what is right. But the noble man devises noble things, and by his nobility he stands. Rise up, you women who are at ease; hear my voice, you careless daughters, listen to my speech. In a little more than a year, you who are careless will tremble; for the vintage shall fail, and the harvest shall not come. Tremble, you women at ease; be troubled, you careless ones; strip yourselves, make yourselves bare, and gird sackcloth upon your waists and upon your grieving breasts. For the pleasant fields, for the fruitful vine, for the land of my people, thorns and briars shall come up,

yea, in all the houses of joy in the joyous city. For the palace shall be forsaken; the crowded city shall be deserted; the forts and towers shall become dens forever, a joy for wild asses <note>original: "onagrorum"</note>, and a pasture for flocks; until the spirit is poured upon us from on high, and
<margin>See above, Chapter 28</margin>
the wilderness becomes a fruitful field <note>original: "Carmelus," referring to Mount Carmel, which literally means 'fruitful field' or 'orchard'</note>, and the fruitful field is counted as a forest. Then justice shall dwell in the wilderness, and righteousness remain in the fruitful field. The work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of equity, quietness and assurance forever. My people shall dwell in a peaceable habitation, in secure dwellings, and in quiet resting places. But it shall hail when the forest falls, and the city shall be utterly abased. Blessed are you who sow beside all waters, sending out the feet of the ox and the donkey.

### CHAPTER XXXIII.

<margin>a. He addresses Sennacherib.</margin>
<margin>b. Concerning the peace mission sent to Sennacherib.</margin>
<margin>c. Namely, Sennacherib.</margin>
Woe <gloss>a</gloss> to you who plunder, though you were not plundered; and deal treacherously, though they did not deal treacherously with you! When you have finished plundering, you shall be plundered; and when you make an end of your treachery, they shall deal treacherously with you. O Jehovah, be gracious to us; we have waited for you. Be our strength <note>original: "brachium," literally 'arm'</note> every morning, and our salvation in the time of trouble. ### CHAPTER XXXIV.

Draw near, you nations, to hear; and listen, you peoples: let the earth hear, and everything it contains; the world, and all its offspring. For the wrath of Jehovah <note>original: "Ioua"</note> is kindled against all nations and all their armies; he will utterly destroy them and give them over to slaughter, so that the stench shall rise from the corpses of the slain, and the mountains shall flow with their blood. All the heavenly hosts shall waste away, and the heavens shall be rolled up like a scroll; all their stars shall fall, as leaves fall from a vine or shriveled fruit from a fig tree. For my sword has been drenched in the heavens; it shall descend in judgment upon the Idumaeans <note>The people of Edom, traditional enemies of Israel.</note> and upon the people I have devoted to destruction. The sword of Jehovah is full of blood and thick with fat: with the blood of lambs and goats, and the fat of the kidneys of rams. For Jehovah has a sacrifice in Bozrah, and a great slaughter in the land of Edom. The wild oxen shall fall with them, the bullocks with the steers; and so their land shall be drenched with blood, and the soil soaked with fat. For it is the day of Jehovah's vengeance, the year of retribution, for the defense of Zion. Therefore, the rivers of that land <gloss>a</gloss> shall be turned into pitch, and its soil into sulfur; the land, reduced to burning pitch, shall not be quenched night or day; it shall breathe out smoke forever, deserted for all generations, with no one passing through it in any age. But the ibis and the hedgehog shall occupy it, the owl and the raven shall dwell there; <gloss>b</gloss> he has marked it out with the measuring line of ruin and the plumb line of desolation. Its nobles, their kingdom being abolished, shall cry out, and all its princes shall be reduced to nothing. Thorns shall grow in its citadels, and nettles and brambles in its fortresses; it shall be a haunt for dragons <note>Likely referring to jackals or desert serpents.</note> and a station for ostriches. The Sylvan spirits <note>original: "Syluani," Roman forest deities used here to translate desert-dwelling creatures.</note> shall meet with the Fauns, and the Satyrs shall call to one another; even the night-monster <note>original: "lamia," a mythological creature often associated with Lilith in this passage.</note> shall find rest there. There the owl shall nest in safety, and cherish its young in its shadow; there the kites also shall gather together. Seek out and read from the book of Jehovah: not one of these shall be missing; none shall lack its mate. For his mouth has commanded it, and his spirit has gathered them. He himself has cast the lot for them, and his hand has divided the land for them with a measuring line, to possess it forever and to dwell in it throughout all generations.

### CHAPTER XXXVI.

<margin>2 Kings 18</margin>
<margin>2 Chronicles 32</margin>
Now in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria led an expedition against all the fortified cities of Judah and captured them. He sent the Rabshakeh <note>The "Rabshakeh" was a high-ranking Assyrian military title, often acting as a chief messenger or orator.</note> from Lachish to Jerusalem with a great army to King Hezekiah. When the Rabshakeh stood by the aqueduct of the upper pool on the road to the Fuller’s Field, there came out to him Eliakim son of Hilkiah, the palace administrator, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah son of Asaph the recorder. The Rabshakeh spoke to them in this manner: "Tell Hezekiah: Thus says the great king, the king of Assyria: What is this confidence on which you rely? Words of prayer, I suppose, are your counsel and strength for war. But on what hope do you lean that you have rebelled against me? Do you perhaps trust in the support of that broken reed of a staff—Egypt—which pierces the hand of anyone who leans on it? Such is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him. But if you say to me: 'We trust in Jehovah our God,' is it not he whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed, telling the people of Judah and Jerusalem that they must worship at one certain altar? Come now, make a wager with my master the king of Assyria: I will give you two thousand horses, if you are even able to provide as many riders for them! How then can you dare to resist even a single captain, the least of my master’s servants? And yet you put your trust in the chariots and horsemen of Egypt! Moreover, have I come up against this land to destroy it without Jehovah's consent? Jehovah himself told me to go up against this region and depopulate it."
<margin>The Rabshakeh’s speech to the people of Jerusalem.</margin>

Then Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah interrupted the Rabshakeh, asking him to speak to them in Syriac <note>original: "Syriacè," referring to Aramaic, the international language of diplomacy at the time.</note>—since they understood it—and not in the Judean language <note>original: "Iudaicè," referring to Hebrew.</note> within hearing of the soldiers on the walls. But the Rabshakeh replied: "Has my master sent me to speak these things only to your master or to you? Has he not rather sent me to the men who sit on the walls, who will have to eat their own dung and drink their own urine along with you?" Then standing and shouting with a loud voice in the Judean language, he cried: "Hear the command of the great king, the king of Assyria! Thus says the king: Do not let Hezekiah deceive you; for he will not be able to defend you from my hand. Do not let him persuade you to trust in Jehovah, saying that Jehovah will surely defend you and that this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria. Do not listen to Hezekiah; for the king of Assyria says: Make peace with me and surrender. Then every one of you may eat from his own vine and fig tree, and drink the water of his own cistern, until I come and take you away to a land like your own—a land of grain and wine, a land of bread and vineyards—so that your safety may be provided for. Do not let Hezekiah mislead you with the hope of defense from Jehovah. Have the gods of any of the other nations defended their lands from the king of Assyria?"

### CHAPTER XXXVII.

When King Hezekiah heard these things, he tore his garments, clothed himself in sackcloth <note>original: "cetone"</note>, and entered the temple of Jehovah. He sent Eliakim the prefect of the palace, Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests, all wrapped in sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz, that they might say to him: "Thus says Hezekiah: This day is a day of distress, of cruelty, and of disgrace; it is as if the fetus has come to the point of birth, but there is no strength to bring it forth. It would be a wonder if Jehovah your God did not hear the words of the Rabshakeh, whom his master the king of Assyria sent to insult the immortal God with such arrogant words. Since Jehovah your God has heard them, offer up prayers for the remnant that still survives." After Hezekiah’s men reported this to Isaiah, Isaiah answered them in this manner: "You shall say this to your master. Thus says Jehovah: Do not fear the words you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have attacked me. For I will send a spirit upon him so that, upon hearing a certain rumor, he shall return to his own land, and I will cause him to fall by the sword in his own country." The Rabshakeh, having returned, found the king of Assyria—who he had learned had departed from Lachish—attacking Libnah. When the king heard that Tirhakah, king of Ethiopia, was launching an expedition against him, he sent messengers again to Hezekiah with this mandate: "Thus shall you say to Hezekiah, king of Judah: Do not let your God, in whom you trust, deceive you, as if Jerusalem will not fall into the power of the king of Assyria. You yourself have heard what the kings of Assyria have done in devastating so many regions, and will you escape? Did the gods of the nations protect those whom my ancestors overthrew? Where are Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the people of Eden in Telassar? Where is the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, the king of the city of Sepharvaim, of Hena, and of Ivvah?" When Hezekiah received these letters from the messengers and read them, he went up into the temple of Jehovah, and having spread them out before Jehovah, he prayed to him in this manner: "Jehovah, God of the Israelites, who sits above the Cherubim, you alone are God over all the kingdoms of the world, you who made the heaven and the earth. Incline your ear, Jehovah, and hear; open your eyes, Jehovah, and see: hear all the words of Sennacherib, who has sent this man to insult the immortal God. Truly, Jehovah, the kings of Assyria have wiped out all those nations and burned their lands and their gods in the flames; for they were not gods, but the work of human hands, wood and stone; and thus they destroyed them. But you, Jehovah our God, defend us from his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you, Jehovah, are the only one." Then Isaiah son of Amoz sent this message to Hezekiah: "Thus says Jehovah, God of the Israelites. I have dug wells and drunk the waters, and with the soles of my feet I have dried up all <margin>b. That fortified cities should be reduced to heaps of vast solitude, and their inhabitants, like the maimed, should be struck with such shameful fear that they became like wild herbs, like green shoots, and like the grass on the rooftops which withers before it can grow tall. Then the spirit <note>original: "genius"</note> of Jehovah attacked the camp of the Assyrians <margin>4 Kings 19; Tobit 1; Ecclesiasticus 48; 1 Maccabees 7:21</margin> and slew one hundred and eighty-five thousand men. When they arose in the morning, behold, after seeing such a great slaughter, Sennacherib king of Assyria departed from there and returned to Nineveh. After he had settled there, while he was worshipping in the temple of Nisroch his god, his own sons Adrammelech and Sharezer struck him down with the sword and escaped into Armenia; and Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII.

<margin>The illness of Hezekiah. 4 Kings 20; 2 Chronicles 32.</margin>
In those days Hezekiah became terminally ill, and Isaiah the prophet, son of Amoz, came to him and said: "Thus says Jehovah: set your house in order, for you shall die and not recover." But Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to Jehovah: "I beseech you, Jehovah, remember how I have shown myself faithful to you with a sincere heart and have done what was pleasing to you." And Hezekiah wept with a great voice. Then Jehovah spoke to Isaiah, saying: "Go and say to Hezekiah: Thus says Jehovah, the God of your father David: I have heard your prayers and seen your tears; behold, I add fifteen years to your life, and I will protect you and this city from the hand of the king of Assyria, and I will defend it. And this shall be a sign to you from Jehovah, that he will do what he promises: behold, I will cause the shadow of the sundial <note>original: "solarij"</note>, which has gone down on the sundial of Ahaz, to go back ten steps." And the sun returned ten steps, the very steps by which it had gone down.

### The writing of Hezekiah, king of Judah, when he had recovered from the illness by which he had been sick.

<margin>a. In this life.</margin>
<margin>b. As a weaver cuts the thread.</margin>
**I** thought that, my life being cut short, I must go through the gates of the Underworld <note>original: "Orci". The translator uses the Latin term "Orcus" for the Hebrew "Sheol," the place of the dead.</note>, deprived of the rest of my years. I said, I shall no longer see Jehovah <note>original: "Iouā". A Latinized form of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton, the personal name of God.</note>, even Jehovah <margin>a</margin> in the land of the living: I shall not behold mankind any longer among the inhabitants of the world. My dwelling is taken away from me and removed like a shepherd’s tent: my life is cut off <margin>b</margin> in the manner of a weaver. You consume me with wasting disease; from day until night you finish me. I wait until morning: all my bones are crushed as if by a lion; from day until night you finish me. I chirp like a swallow or a crane, moaning like a dove, my eyes failing as I look upward. Lord, I am oppressed; be my security. What shall I say? For he has promised me, and he himself has performed it. Shall I recount my few years in the bitterness of my soul? O Lord, since life is lived longer elsewhere, is the life of my spirit ended in so few years? Or if you put me to sleep, will you call me back to life? Although such a bitter misfortune happened to me while I was safe, do you not wish to rescue this soul from the deadly grave, having cast all my sins behind your back? For the Underworld will not give thanks to you; death will not praise you; those who go down into the pit will not proclaim your faithfulness. The living, the living shall give thanks to you, as I do today: fathers shall make known your faithfulness to their children. Jehovah, attend to my salvation, and we will play my melodies all the days of our life in the house of Jehovah. Now Isaiah had ordered a cake of figs to be taken and applied to the boil as a poultice, so that he might recover. And Hezekiah asked by what sign he would know that he would go up into the temple of Jehovah.

### CHAPTER XXXIX.

<margin>Merodach sends ambassadors to Hezekiah.</margin>
<margin>See 2 Kings 20</margin>
**A**round that time, Merodach-baladan, the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah, for he had heard that he had been sick and had recovered. Hezekiah, delighted by these, showed the ambassadors his storehouse, the silver, the gold, the spices, the precious balsam, his entire armory; in short, there was nothing in his treasures that Hezekiah did not show them, both in his house and in all his dominion. Then Isaiah the prophet approached King Hezekiah with these words: "What did those men say? Or from where did they come to you?" Hezekiah said to him: "They came to me from a far country, from Babylon." Isaiah said: "What have they seen in your house?" He replied: "They have seen everything that is in my house; there was nothing in my treasures that I did not show them." And Isaiah said to Hezekiah: "Hear the word of Jehovah. Know that the time is coming when everything that is in your house, and which your ancestors have stored up to this day, shall be carried away to Babylon; nothing shall be left, says Jehovah. Moreover, some of your own sons, born of you and fathered by you, shall be taken away to be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon." Hezekiah said to Isaiah: "I do not refuse what has been spoken by you at the command of Jehovah," for he thought, "at least there will be peace and stability in my time."

<margin>a. From Jehovah she has received double, that is, heavy punishments. See Jeremiah 16 and 17; Matthew 3; Mark 1; Luke 3; John 1.</margin>

Has it not been told to you from of old? Are you ignorant of the foundations of the earth? He brings the nobles to nothing, and makes the governors of the earth as nothing, so that they are scarcely planted, scarcely sown, their stems having scarcely taken root in the earth, when he blows upon them and they wither, and the whirlwind carries them away like stubble. "To whom then will you compare me, that I should be his equal?" says the Holy One <note>original: "Augustus". In Classical Latin, this meant "majestic" or "venerable." Do you not know, or have you not heard, that the eternal God, Jehovah, the Creator of the ends of the earth, does not faint or grow weary? His prudence is unsearchable; he gives power to the faint, and to those who have no might he increases strength. Even though youths faint and grow weary, and young men stumble and fall, those who hope in Jehovah shall renew their strength; they shall grow wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint.

<summary>This page contains Hezekiah's prayer of thanksgiving after recovering from a terminal illness and Isaiah's subsequent prophecy of the Babylonian exile. It concludes with the opening of the "Book of Consolation," praising God's eternal power and majesty over all earthly nations and idols.</summary>

<keywords>Hezekiah, Isaiah, Babylon, Merodach-baladan, prophecy of exile, comfort, God's majesty, creation, idols, grasshoppers, eagle's wings</keywords>

It contrasts the power of the Creator with the helplessness of idols and introduces the "Servant of the Lord" who will bring justice to the nations.</meta>

->ISAIAH.<-

Who acts and performs, calling the generations from the beginning? I, Jehovah <note>original: "Ioua". This is a Latinized form of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton, the personal name of God.</note>, am the first, and with the last, I am the same. Seeing this, the islands are terrified; the ends of the earth tremble, they draw near and come together. Each helps the other and they encourage one another to be strong. The craftsman encourages the goldsmith, and he who smooths with the hammer encourages him who strikes the anvil, saying of the soldering, "It is good"; and he fastens it with nails so that it cannot be moved. But you, my servant, son of Israel, descendant of Jacob <note>original: "Iacobida". A Latin construction meaning "child of Jacob."</note> whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham my friend; you whom I have taken from the ends of the earth and called from its furthest parts, I have told you: I have chosen you and will not reject you. Do not fear, for I am with you; do not be discouraged, for I am your God. I strengthen you, I help you, I uphold you with my righteous right hand. Indeed, all who are angry with you shall be put to shame and disgrace; the men who strive against you shall be reduced to nothing and perish, so that even if you look for them, you will not find them. The men who contend with you shall be reduced to nothing, and your enemies shall be abolished. For I, Jehovah your God, take hold of your right hand; I, who help you, forbid you to fear. Fear not, O worm of Jacob, O mortal men of Israel; I help you, says Jehovah, your Redeemer, the Holy One <note>original: "Augustus". The Latin translator uses this term, usually associated with Roman Emperors, to translate the Hebrew "Qadosh" (Holy One).</note> of the Israelites. Behold, I will make you into a threshing instrument, a new one with teeth, which shall thresh the mountains and crush them, and make the hills like chaff. You shall winnow them, and the wind shall carry them away, and the whirlwind shall scatter them; while you, meanwhile, shall exult in Jehovah and glory in the Holy One of Israel. When the poor and needy look for water and there is none, and their tongue is parched with thirst, I, Jehovah, will hear them; I, the God of Israel, will not forsake them. I will open rivers on the high hills and springs in the midst of the valleys; I will turn the desert and parched places into pools of water and dry ground into bubbling springs. I will plant in the desert the cedar, the acacia <note>original: "spina," literally "thorn," referring to the thorny acacia tree.</note>, the myrtle, and the cypress; I will set in the wasteland the pine, the elm, and the box tree together, so that it may be seen, understood, noticed, and considered that the hand of Jehovah, the God of Israel, has done and created this. Bring forth your cause, says Jehovah; produce your arguments, says the King of the Jacobites. Let them come forward and 
<margin>
[The text in the margin is fragmented, likely referring to cross-references or theological points regarding the nature of the prophecy.]
</margin>declare to us what is to happen. Tell us the things that are past, and we will consider them and know their outcome; or declare to us the things to come, tell us the future hereafter, so that we may know you are gods. At least do something, good or bad, so that when we see it we may be amazed. But truly, you are nothing, and your work is futile; whoever chooses you is an abomination. I have raised up one from the north, and he shall come; from the rising of the sun he shall call upon my name. He shall trample on princes like mud, as a potter treads the clay. Who declared this from the beginning, that we might know? Who announced it beforehand, that we might say he is right? Indeed, there is no one who tells it; no one who declares it; no one who hears your words. I first show these things to Zion, and I give to Jerusalem a messenger of good news. For among these [the idols] I see no counselor who, when I ask, can give an answer; they are all vanity, their works are nothing, and their images are wind and futility.

justice on the earth, and the islands shall wait for his law. Thus says God Jehovah, who created the heavens and stretched them out, who spread forth the earth and its offspring, giving breath to the people upon it and spirit to those who walk in it: I, Jehovah, have called you in righteousness; I will take you by the hand and keep you. I have destined you for a covenant with the people and a light <margin>Below 49.</margin> for the nations, to open the eyes of the blind, to bring out the prisoners from the dungeon and those who sit in darkness from the prison house. <margin>Below 48.</margin> I am he whose name is Jehovah; I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to carved images. Behold, the former things have come to pass, and new things I now declare; before they spring forth, I tell them to you. Sing to Jehovah a new song, and his praise <margin>Psalm 149.</margin> from the ends of the earth, you who go down to the sea and all that is in it, the islands and their inhabitants. Let the desert and its towns cry out, the villages where the Kedarites dwell; let the inhabitants of Sela <note>original: "Petræ". The city is the capital of Arabia.</margin> glory to Jehovah, and declare his praise in the islands. Jehovah shall go forth like a hero; like a man of war he shall stir up his fury. Crying out and shouting aloud, he shall prevail against his enemies. I have long been silent and held myself back; but now, like a woman in labor, I will cry out, gasping and panting. I will lay waste the mountains and hills and dry up all their herbs; I will turn the rivers into islands and dry up the pools. I will lead the blind by a way they do not know and guide them in paths they have not seen. I will turn darkness into light before them and make the crooked places straight. These things I will do for them and not forsake them. Those who trust in images and say to cast idols, "You are our gods," shall be turned back in utter shame. Hear, you deaf; and look, you blind, that you may see. Who is blind but my servant, or deaf like the messenger I send? Who is as blind as the one who is perfect, as blind as the servant of Jehovah? You see many things, but do not observe them; your ears are open, but you do not hear. Jehovah, favoring him for the sake of his righteousness, will make the law great and honorable. But these are a people robbed and plundered; they are all snared in holes and hidden in prisons. They have become a prey with no one to deliver them, and a spoil with no one to say, "Restore them." Who among you will listen to this? Who will attend and hear for the time to come? Who gave the sons of Jacob for spoil, and Israel to the robbers? Was it not Jehovah, against whom we have sinned? For they would not walk in his ways, nor were they obedient to his law. Therefore he poured out upon them the heat of his anger and the strength of battle; it set them on fire all around, yet they did not understand; it burned them, yet they did not take it to heart.

### CHAPTER XLIII.

But now, thus says Jehovah, your creator, O son of Jacob, and your maker, O Israelite: Do not fear, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by my name. When you pass through the waters, I am with you; through the rivers, they shall not overflow you. When you walk through the fire, you shall not be burned, nor shall the flame consume you. For I am Jehovah your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior. I gave the Egyptians as your ransom, the Ethiopians and Sabeans in your place. Because you are precious in my sight and honored, and I love you, I will give men and peoples in exchange for you and your life. Do not fear, for I am present with you; I will bring your offspring from the east and gather you from the west. I will say to the north, "Give them up," and to the south, "Do not withhold them." Bring my sons from afar and my daughters from the ends of the earth—everyone who is called by my name, whom I created for my glory, whom I formed and made. Lead out the people who are blind, yet have eyes; and the deaf, who have ears. Let all the nations be gathered together; let the peoples assemble.

<summary>This section of Isaiah emphasizes God's sovereignty over history and idols, promising restoration to Israel while introducing the "Servant" who will bring light to the nations. It concludes with an assurance of God's protection through fire and water for his redeemed people.</summary>

Concerning the departure from Egypt.</margin> says Jehovah, who makes a way through the sea and a path through the mighty waters; who brings out the chariot and horse, the army and the power, only for them to lie down together and not rise again—extinguished and quenched like a wick. I will even make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert. The wild beasts of the field will honor me, the dragons and the ostriches, because I give water in the wilderness and rivers in the desert to give drink to my chosen people, the people whom I formed for myself to declare my praise. Yet you have not called upon me, O Jacob; you have not labored for my sake, O Israelite. You have not brought me the sheep of your burnt offerings, nor honored me with your sacrifices. I did not burden you by demanding offerings, nor weary you with incense. You have not bought me sweet cane with your money, nor saturated me with the fat of your sacrifices. On the contrary, you have burdened me with your sins and wearied me with your iniquities. I, even I, am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will remember your sins no more. Put me in remembrance; let us argue together. State your case that you may be justified. Your first father sinned, <margin>c. Moses and Aaron.</margin> and your interpreters <note>The Latin "interpretes" refers to the mediators or spokesmen of the law.</note> have transgressed against me; therefore I have profaned the princes of the sanctuary, and given Jacob to destruction and Israel to reproach.
