### CHAPTER XLIIII.

<margin>Jer. 30, 46.</margin> But now hear, my Jacob, the Israelite whom I have chosen. Thus says Jehovah, your Maker and your Creator, your helper from the womb: Do not fear, my Jacob, you upright one <note>original: "tu probe". This likely translates the Hebrew "Jeshurun," a poetic name for Israel meaning "upright one."</note> whom I have chosen. For I will pour water on the thirsty and streams on the dry ground; I will pour my Spirit on your offspring and my blessing on your descendants, so that they shall spring up like grass, like willows by the flowing water. One will say, "I am Jehovah's"; another will call himself by the name of Jacob; yet another will write on his hand, "To Jehovah," and take the name of Israel. Thus says Jehovah, the King and Redeemer of the Israelites, Jehovah <margin>Above, ch. 41. Below, ch. 48. Rev. 1, 22.</margin> of Hosts <note>original: "armipotens", literally "powerful in arms" or "Lord of Armies."</note>: I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no God. If anyone is my equal, let him cry out, let him declare it and set it forth before me, since I appointed the ancient people. Let them tell the things that are to come and shall happen. Do not tremble or be afraid; have I not told you and declared it long ago? You are my witnesses. Is there any God besides me? There is no other Rock <note>original: "numen", a divine power or deity.</note> unknown to me. All who fashion idols are nothing, and the things they

<column-break/>

treasure are of no use. They themselves are witnesses that these idols see nothing and understand nothing, to their own shame. Who would fashion a god or cast an image that is profitable for nothing? See, all its companions will be put to shame; the craftsmen are but men (all of them gathered together from mankind). Let them tremble and be ashamed together. The blacksmith takes a tool and works it over the coals; he shapes it with hammers <margin>Wisdom 13.</margin> and works it with his strong arm. He becomes hungry and his strength fails; he drinks no water and grows faint. The carpenter stretches out a rule; he marks it out with a line; he fashions it with planes and marks it with a compass. He makes it into the image of a man, according to human beauty, that it may remain in a shrine. He cuts down cedars for himself, or takes a cypress or an oak, and lets it grow strong among the trees of the forest. He plants a pine and the rain nourishes it. Then it serves as fuel for a man to burn; he takes part of it to warm himself, and he starts a fire to bake bread. But from the rest he makes a god and worships it; he makes an idol and bows down to it! Half of it he burns in the fire; over this half he eats meat, he roasts it and is satisfied. He also warms himself and says, "Aha! I am warm, I see the fire!" And from the remainder he makes a god, his idol, and bows down to it in worship and prays to it. He says, "Save me, for you are my god!" They do not know, nor do they consider; for their eyes are smeared over so they cannot see, and their minds so they cannot understand. No one stops to think, nor has the knowledge or insight to say: "Half of this I burned in the fire; I baked bread on its coals and roasted meat to eat. Shall I make the rest into an abomination? Shall I bow down to a block of wood?" <margin>a. The wicked nature of idols. b. He labors in vain.</margin> He feeds on ashes; a deluded heart has led him astray, so that he cannot save himself or say, "Is not this thing in my right hand a lie?" Remember these things, O Jacob, O Israelite who are my servant. I formed you, you are my servant; O Israelite, do not forget me. I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud, and your sins like a mist. Return to me, for I have redeemed you. Sing for joy, O heavens, for Jehovah has done this! Shout, <margin>c. The earth which is the lowest part.</margin> O depths of the earth; break forth into singing, O mountains, O forests and every tree in them! For Jehovah has redeemed Jacob and shows his glory in the Israelites. Thus says Jehovah, your Redeemer and your Creator from the womb: I am Jehovah, the Maker of all things, who alone stretched out the heavens and by myself spread out the earth; who frustrates the signs of the diviners and makes fools <margin>foolish.</margin> of the soothsayers; who turns back the wise and makes their knowledge foolishness; who carries out the word of my servant and fulfills the counsel of my messengers; who says of Jerusalem, "It shall be inhabited," and of the cities of Judah, "They shall be rebuilt, and I will restore their ruins"; who says to the deep, "Be dry, and I will dry up your rivers"; who says of Cyrus, "He is my shepherd," <margin>Cyrus.</note> and he shall fulfill all my purpose; saying of Jerusalem, "Let it be rebuilt," and of the temple, "Let its foundations be laid."

### ISAIAH.

...hope, though you do not know me. I am Jehovah, besides whom there is no other; there is no God except me. I gird you, though you do not know me, so that it may be known from the rising of the sun to its setting that I am the only Jehovah, and there is no one else. I form the light and create darkness <margin>b</margin>; I make peace and create calamity; I, Jehovah, do all these things. Rain down, you heavens from above, and let the skies pour down justice; let the earth open and bring forth salvation, and let justice spring up at the same time; I, Jehovah, <margin>c</margin> am its creator. Woe to him who contends with his Maker, a potsherd among the workers of the earth. Shall the clay say to its potter: "What are you making?" or "Your work has no handles"? <margin>d</margin> Woe to him who asks a father what he begets, or a woman what she brings forth. Thus says the Majestic One <note>original: "Augustus". This title is used here to translate the "Holy One of Israel," emphasizing divine sovereignty.</note> of the Israelites and their Maker, Jehovah: Question me about things to come; concerning my sons and the work of my hands, give me the charge. I am the one who made the earth and created man upon it; I am the one whose hands stretched out the heavens and commanded all their host. I have raised him up in righteousness, directing all his paths; he shall build my city and let my exiles go free, without price or reward, says Jehovah of hosts. Thus says Jehovah: The labor of the Egyptians, the merchandise of the Ethiopians, and the tall Sabeans shall come over to you and be yours; they shall follow you, moving in chains and bowing down to you, making supplication to you: "Surely God is in you, and besides him there is no other God." Truly, you are a God who hides yourself, <margin>e</margin> O God, the Savior of the Israelites. All the makers of idols will be put to shame and disgraced together. But the Israelites shall be saved in Jehovah with an everlasting salvation; they shall not be put to shame or disgraced for all eternity. For thus says the creator of the heavens, Jehovah, the God who fashioned the earth and made it, who established it so that he did not create it in vain but formed it to be inhabited: I am Jehovah, and there is none besides me. <margin>f</margin> I have not spoken in secret, in some dark place of the earth; I did not tell the offspring of Jacob to seek me in vain. I, Jehovah, speak the truth, declaring what is right. Assemble and come, gather together, you who <margin>g</margin> have escaped from the nations! They are so ignorant that they carry the wood of their carved idols and pray to a god who cannot save. Declare and bring forth your case, let them take counsel together. Who signaled this long ago, showing it so far in advance? Was it not I, Jehovah? There is no God besides me; a righteous God and a Savior, there is none except me. Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth! For I am God, and there is no other. I swear by myself, a righteous word has gone out of my mouth that shall not be revoked: to me every knee shall bow and every tongue shall swear, saying that in Jehovah alone are righteousness and strength. People shall come to him, and all who were incensed against him shall be put to shame; in Jehovah all the offspring of Israel shall be justified and shall glory.

### CHAPTER XLVI.

<margin>34 in c. u-</margin> Bel <note>The principal god of Babylon, also known as Marduk.</note> bows down, Nebo <note>The Babylonian god of wisdom and writing.</note> stoops; their statues are placed on beasts and cattle. These things you carry are heavy, a burden for the weary, so that they stoop and bow down, unable to rescue the burden, while they themselves go into captivity. Listen to me, O house of Jacob, and all the remnant of the house of Israel, you who

<column-break/>

have been upheld by me from birth, carried from the womb. Even to old age I am the same, and even to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and I will rescue. To whom will you liken me or make me equal? To whom will you compare me, that we may be alike? Those who pour gold out of their bags and weigh silver on the scales hire a goldsmith to make it into a god, then they fall down and worship it. They lift it to their shoulders and carry it; <margin>Baruch 6.</margin> they set it in its place, and there it stands, unable to move. If one cries out to it, it does not answer, nor does it save him from his trouble. Remember this and take courage; return, you rebels, to your senses. Remember the things of old, for I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like me, declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times things not yet done, saying, "My counsel shall stand, and I will fulfill all my purpose," calling a bird of prey from the east, the man of my counsel from a far country. I have spoken, and I will bring it to pass; I have purposed, and I will do it. Listen to me, you stubborn-hearted, who are far from righteousness. I bring my righteousness near, it is not far off, and my salvation will not tarry; I will put salvation in Zion and give my glory to the Israelites.

### CHAPTER XLVII.

<margin>a. Unconquered.</margin> Come down and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground without a throne, O daughter of the Chaldeans! For you shall no longer be called tender and delicate. Take the millstones and grind flour; take off your veil, strip off your robes, bare your legs, and wade through the rivers. Your nakedness shall be uncovered, and your <margin>Nahum 3. b. With no one resisting me.</margin> shame shall be seen. I will take vengeance, and I will spare no man. Our Redeemer—Jehovah of hosts is his name—is the Majestic One of the Israelites. Sit in silence and go into darkness, O daughter of the Chaldeans; for you shall no longer be called the mistress of kingdoms. I was angry with my people, I profaned my heritage and gave them into your hand; you showed them no mercy; on the aged you made your yoke very heavy. You thought, "I shall be mistress forever," and did not take these things to heart or remember their end. Therefore hear this, you lover of pleasures, who sit securely and say in your heart, "I am, and there is no one else; <margin>Revelation 18. Below 51.</margin> I shall not sit as a widow or know the loss of children." Both these things shall come to you in a moment, in one day: the loss of children and widowhood. They shall come upon you in full measure, despite your many sorceries and the great power of your enchantments. You felt secure in your wickedness and said, "No one sees me." Your wisdom and your knowledge led you astray, and you said in your heart, "I am, and there is no one else." But evil shall come upon you, the dawn of which you will not know; disaster shall fall upon you that you will not be able to ward off; and ruin shall come upon you suddenly, of which you know nothing. Stand fast now with your enchantments and your many sorceries, with which you have labored from your youth; perhaps you may be able to succeed, perhaps you may inspire terror. You are wearied with your many counsels; let those who divide the heavens, who gaze at the stars, who predict at the new moons what will happen to you, stand up and save you! See, they are like stubble; the fire consumes them; they cannot deliver themselves from the power of the flame. There is no coal for warming oneself, no fire to sit before! Such to you are those with whom you have labored, who have trafficked with you from your youth; they wander about, each in his own way; there is no one to save you.

<summary>This portion of Isaiah describes the absolute sovereignty of Jehovah over the idols of Babylon (Bel and Nebo) and prophesies the sudden humiliation and fall of the Babylonian empire. It contrasts the heavy, burdensome nature of man-made idols with the God of Israel, who carries His people from birth to old age.</summary>

### CHAPTER XLVIII.

<margin>a. From the source, the seed.</margin> Hear this, O house of Jacob, you who are called by the name of Israel and have come forth from the $^a$ waters of Judah; you who swear by the name of Jehovah and make mention of the God of the Israelites—though not in truth or in righteousness—inasmuch as you are named after the holy city and lean upon the God of the Israelites, whose name is Jehovah $^b$ of hosts. <margin>b. Namely, concerning the fall of Sennacherib.</margin> The former things I declared long ago; they went out from my mouth and I made them known, and then suddenly I acted and they came to pass. Because I knew that you were stubborn, and that your neck was an iron sinew and your forehead bronze, I told you of these things beforehand; I declared them to you before they happened, so that you could not say, "My idols did them; my carved images and metal gods ordained them." Since you have heard, now witness the whole matter; and surely you will declare it. From this time on I am telling you new things, hidden things that you have not known, which are being created now and not long ago—things you had never heard of before today, so that you cannot say, "I already knew them," for you had neither heard, nor known, nor previously received them by report. For I know how treacherously you deal; <margin>c. This means "to be," as in Matthew 5.</margin> you were called a rebel $^c$ even from the womb. For my name’s sake I will delay my wrath; for the sake of my praise I will restrain it from you, so that I do not cut you off. Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have chosen you in the furnace of affliction. For my own sake, for my own sake I will do it (for otherwise, <margin>See Chapter 42 above.</margin> how great an indignity would it be?) so that I do not yield my glory to another. Listen to me, O Jacobite, and Israelite whom I have called: I am He; I am the first and I am the last. ### CHAPTER L.

Thus says Jehovah: Where, finally, is the bill of divorce of your mother, whom I have sent away? Or who of my <margin>19.</margin> creditors is there to whom I sold you? Or do I lack the strength to set free—I, who by my rebuke dry up the sea and turn rivers <margin>3.</margin> into forests <note>original: "syluas," likely a metaphor for parched, dry land where only scrub grows</note>, so that their fish, killed by thirst, rot for lack of water; I, who clothe the heavens in blackness and cover them with a shroud of sackcloth? He awakens me day by day; he awakens my ear, so that I may listen in the manner of a disciple. The Lord Jehovah opens my ear, and I do not turn back <margin>20</margin> in rebellion. I offer my <margin>5.</margin> back to those who beat me, and my cheeks to those who pluck out my beard; I do not hide my face from insults and spitting. And the Lord Jehovah helps me. For it shall be that they will all wear out like a garment, consumed by moths. ### CHAPTER LI.

Hear me, you seekers of justice, you who are devoted to Jehovah: look to the rock from which you were hewn, to the hollow of the pit from which you were cut. Look to Abraham your father, and to Sarah who gave you birth; for I called him when he was but one, I blessed him, and I multiplied him. For Jehovah will comfort Zion; he will comfort all her ruins, and he will make her wilderness like Eden, and her uncultivated lands like the gardens of Jehovah, so that pleasure, joy, thanksgiving, and the sound of songs may be found in her. Attend to me, my people; listen to me, my nation: for a law shall go forth from me, and I will present my judgment for the enlightenment <margin>1.36.</margin> of the peoples. My justice approaches; my salvation goes forth, and my arms shall judge the peoples; the islands shall hope in me, looking toward my arm. Lift up your eyes to the heavens and look down at the earth: for the heavens shall vanish like smoke, and the earth shall wear out like a garment, and its inhabitants likewise shall die; yet in the meantime my salvation shall endure forever, and my justice shall be unbroken. Hear me, you men who know justice, you who have my law in your minds: do not fear the reproach of men, nor be broken by their insults. For the moth shall eat them like a garment, and the worm shall consume them like wool; but meanwhile my justice shall be forever, and my salvation shall endure through perpetual ages. Awake, awake, put on your power, O arm of Jehovah!

<summary>This portion of Jeremiah contains a scathing rebuke of Israel and Judah for their spiritual infidelity, comparing their idolatry to prostitution and criticizing their political reliance on Egypt and Assyria. It concludes with a promise of restoration and a future where Jerusalem, rather than the Ark of the Covenant, serves as God's throne.</summary>

### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>return-</margin> IF you return, O Israelite (says Jehovah), you shall return to me; and if you remove your abominations from my sight, you shall not be an exile. And you shall swear, "As Jehovah lives," in truth, in judgment, and in justice; and in him the nations shall bless themselves and glory. For thus Jehovah warns the men of Judah <margin>verse 10</margin> and the inhabitants of Jerusalem: Break up your fallow ground for yourselves, and do not sow among thorns. Circumcise yourselves to Jehovah, and take away the foreskins of your hearts, men of Judah <margin>30</margin> and inhabitants of Jerusalem, lest my wrath go forth like fire and burn unquenchably because of the wickedness of your nature. Announce it through Judah, and signal it in Jerusalem; blow the trumpet in the land and cry out fully, speaking in this manner: "Gather together, and let us go into the fortified cities." Raise a standard toward Zion: strengthen yourselves: do not stand still: for I am bringing a great evil and calamity from the north. A lion has come up from his thick forest, a destroyer of nations has set out, departing from his place to reduce your land <margin>40</margin> to such a wasteland that your depopulated cities shall lack inhabitants. For this reason, gird yourselves in mourning clothes <note>original: "centones"; literally patchwork or rags used for mourning.</note> and wail, shrieking, because the bitterness of Jehovah’s anger is not turned away from us. And at that time (says Jehovah), both the king and the princes shall lose heart, the priests shall be stunned, and the prophets shall be struck with consternation. But I said: "Ah, Lord Jehovah, surely you have deceived this people and Jerusalem, promising them peace when there is a deadly war." At that time it shall be said to this people and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem: <margin>50</margin> A scorching wind blows across the heights of the forests toward <margin>Jerusalem... Nebuchadnezzar.</margin> the daughter of my people, not for winnowing or cleansing: a wind too strong for such things comes to me: now I also will execute judgment upon them. Behold, he comes up like clouds, with chariots like a whirlwind, with horses swifter than eagles: woe to us, for we are ruined! Wash your heart from wickedness, O Jerusalem, so that you may be saved: how long will those harmful thoughts remain in your breast?

### CHAPTER V.

<margin>40</margin> Roam through the streets of Jerusalem, and see, and take note, and search through her squares, if you can find anyone who acts justly and seeks the truth, and I will pardon Jerusalem. I will go to the great men and speak to them: for they surely know the way of Jehovah and the judgment of their God." But these, too, have broken the yoke and burst the bonds. For this reason, a forest lion strikes them down, a desert wolf wastes them, a leopard lurks near their towns, so that whoever goes out from them is torn to pieces, because their sins are so many and their rebellions so great. How can I forgive you for this? Your children have forsaken me and swear by those who are not gods. When I had fed them to the full, they committed adultery and trooped to the houses of prostitutes.

## CHAPTER IX.

<margin>Psalm 27</margin> O that my head were waters, and my eyes a fountain of tears, that I might weep day and night for the slain of the daughter of my people! O that I had in the wilderness a traveler’s lodging place, that I might leave my people and depart from them! For they are all adulterers, a company of traitors, who bend their tongues like a bow for lies, and they prevail in the land not by truth, but they proceed from evil to evil, and they do not know me, says Jehovah. Let every man take heed of his neighbor, and do not trust in any brother; for every brother acts as a supplanter, and every neighbor goes about as a slanderer. Everyone deceives his neighbor and they do not speak the truth; they have taught their tongues to speak lies, and they weary themselves with iniquity. Your dwelling is in the midst of deceit; through deceit they refuse to know me, says Jehovah. Therefore, thus says the Almighty Jehovah: Behold, I will refine them and test them; for what else should I do for the daughter of my people? Their tongue is a sharpened arrow that speaks deceitfully; speaking peaceably to others with their mouths, but in their hearts, they lay an ambush. Shall I not punish them for these things? says Jehovah; or shall I not avenge myself on such a nation as this? I will take up a weeping and lamentation for the mountains, and for the dwellings of the wilderness a dirge, because they are so desolated that no one passes through, nor is the lowing of cattle heard; both the birds of the air and the beasts have fled and are gone. I will make Jerusalem a heap of ruins, a lair for dragons <note>original: "draconum"; in this context, it likely refers to jackals or desert serpents that inhabit ruins.</note>, and I will make the cities of Judah so desolate that no one shall inhabit them. ### CHAPTER XVI.

They shall perish by the sword and by famine, and their dead bodies shall be food for the birds of the air and for the beasts of the earth. For thus says Jehovah: Do not enter the house of <margin>a. No one shall break bread in mourning to comfort them for the dead, nor shall anyone give them the cup of consolation to drink for their father or their mother. You shall not go into the house of feasting to sit with them, to eat and drink. This is a copy of the letter which the prophet Jeremiah sent from Jerusalem to the remaining elders in exile, and to the priests and prophets, and to all the people whom Nebuchadnezzar had carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon, after King Jeconiah, the queen, the eunuchs, the princes of Judah and Jerusalem, the craftsmen, and the artisans had departed from Jerusalem. This letter was sent by the hand of Elasah son of Shaphan and Gemariah son of Hilkiah (whom Zedekiah king of Judah sent to Babylon, to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon) with these words: "Thus says the Lord of Hosts, the God of the Israelites, to all the exiles whom I have sent from Jerusalem into exile in Babylon: Build houses to live in, and plant gardens so that you may eat their fruit. Take wives and father children; take wives for your sons and give your daughters in marriage, so that they may bear children; increase there, and do not decrease. Seek the welfare of the city where I have exiled you, and pray to Jehovah for it; for in its welfare, your welfare is placed. For thus says the Lord of Hosts, the God of the Israelites: Do not let your prophets and diviners <note>Latin: "harioli," meaning soothsayers or diviners.</note> who are among you deceive you, nor listen to the dreams which you yourselves dream. For they prophesy falsely to you in my name; I did not send them, says Jehovah. For as soon as seventy years are completed for Babylon," says Jehovah, "I will care for you and fulfill the good things I promised, by calling you back to this place. For I know the thoughts I have toward you," says Jehovah, "thoughts of peace, indeed, and not of enmity, to give you a future and a hope. And when you call upon me and

### CHAPTER XXXI.

"At that time," says Jehovah, "I will be the God of all the families of Israel, and they shall be my people." Thus says Jehovah: "The people who remained from the sword found favor in the wilderness, as the Israelite went to his rest; to whom Jehovah appeared from afar, saying: 'I have pursued you with an eternal love, <note>marginal note "a": refers to the feminine personification of Israel.</note> and therefore I have extended mercy toward you.' In time, with me as the builder, you shall be rebuilt, O maiden Israel; in time, adorned with your tambourines, you shall go out with the choirs of those who play. In time, you shall plant vineyards on the mountains of Samaria, which those who planted them shall also enjoy." <note>marginal note "b": "They shall receive the fruit. An allusion to Deuteronomy 28," where a curse was that one plants but another eats; here the curse is reversed.</note> For there shall be a day when the guards on the mount of the Ephraimites shall cry out: "Arise, let us go up to Zion, to Jehovah our God!" For thus says Jehovah: "Let there be joyful shouting for Jacob, and let it be cried out from the chief of nations, <note>marginal note "c": "In a very high place."</note> speaking words of praise: 'Save, O Jehovah, your people, the remnant of Israel!' Truly, I will lead them from the northern region and gather them from the farthest corners of the earth; they shall return here in a great multitude—the blind and the lame, together with the pregnant and those in labor. Though they departed weeping, I will bring them back with mercy, leading them to rivers of water by a straight path where they shall not stumble; for I am a father to the Israelite, and Ephraim is my firstborn. Hear the words of Jehovah, O nations, and declare it in the islands far away: 'He who scattered the Israelites gathers them and keeps them, as a shepherd keeps his flock.' For Jehovah will redeem the house of Jacob and rescue them from the hand of one stronger than they. They shall come and triumph on the heights of Zion, and they shall flow together to the good things of Jehovah—to the grain, the new wine, the oil, and the young of the sheep, goats, and cattle. Their soul shall be like a watered garden, and they shall sorrow no more. Then the virgins shall rejoice in the dance, along with the young men and the old. I will turn their mourning into joy, comforting them and cheering them after their sorrow. I will drench the appetite of the priests with fatness, <note>marginal note "d": "I will make the land so fertile that the priests shall feast to satisfaction on the first-fruits and firstborn offerings which will be sacrificed."</note> and I will cause my people to be satisfied with my good things," says Jehovah. Thus says Jehovah: "A voice is heard in Ramah, a lamentable voice of bitter wailing: Rachel bewailing her children, refusing to be comforted for them because they are gone." <note>A famous prophecy of mourning, cited in the New Testament (Matthew 2) regarding the Massacre of the Innocents.</note> Thus says Jehovah: "Restrain your voice from wailing and your eyes from tears, for there shall be a reward for your work," says Jehovah, "and they shall return from the land of the enemy. There is hope for your future," says Jehovah, "that your children shall return to their own borders. I hear the Ephraimite grieving for himself: 'You have chastised me, and I was chastised like an untrained calf; bring me back, and I will return, for you are Jehovah my God. For after I turned away, I repented; after I recognized myself, I struck my thigh in grief, blushing with shame because I bear the disgrace of my youth.' Is Ephraim not my precious son? Is he not a delightful child? For as often as I mention him, I still remember him; therefore my heart yearns for him, and I will surely have mercy on him," says Jehovah. "Set up road markers for yourself, place signposts, take note of the highway by which you went. Return, O maiden Israel, return to these cities of yours. How long will you wander, O faithless daughter? For indeed, Jehovah is about to do a new thing in the earth: a woman shall encompass a man." <note>This "new thing" is a cryptic phrase. Historically, it has been interpreted as the reversal of roles, or more famously in Christian tradition, as an allusion to the Virgin Birth.</note>

In those days, it shall no longer be said, "The fathers have eaten unripe grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge." <note>A common proverb of the time suggesting children were punished for their parents' sins.</note> Instead, everyone shall die for his own sin; whichever man eats the unripe grapes, his own <margin>The New Covenant.</margin> teeth shall be set on edge. ### CHAPTER XXXIV.

The word spoken to Jeremiah by the Lord <note>original: "Ioua," a Latin rendering of the Tetragrammaton common in the Renaissance</note> when Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, with all his forces, and the kingdoms and peoples of his empire, was attacking Jerusalem and all its nearby towns. Thus says the Lord, the God of the Israelites: Go and announce to Zedekiah, king of Judah, this message: Thus says the Lord: I am handing this city over to the power of the king of Babylon, who shall burn it with fire. Nor shall you escape his hand, for you will surely be captured and handed over to him; with your own eyes you shall see the eyes of the king of Babylon, and he shall speak to you face to face <note>literally: "with his own mouth"</note>, and you shall go to Babylon. Nevertheless, hear the word of the Lord, O Zedekiah, king of Judah. This the Lord promises you: <margin>10</margin> you shall not die by the sword <note>original: "armis," meaning by weapons or in battle</note>, but shall die in peace. And just as they burned incense for your ancestors, the former kings who preceded you, so shall they burn incense for you, and they shall mourn you, saying, "Alas, Lord!" for I have spoken this word, says the Lord. Then Jeremiah the prophet spoke all these things to Zedekiah, king of Judah, in Jerusalem, while the soldiers of the king of Babylon were attacking Jerusalem and all the remaining towns of Judah—namely Lachish and Azekah—for these <margin>20</margin> were the only fortified towns of Judah that still remained. The word spoken to Jeremiah by the Lord after King Zedekiah had made a pact with all the people in Jerusalem to proclaim liberty to them: that every man should set free his Hebrew slaves and handmaids, so that no one should keep a fellow Jew in servitude. All the princes and <margin>30</margin> commoners who had entered into this covenant obeyed; they complied and set their slaves and handmaids free, no longer using their service. But afterward, they changed their minds and took back the slaves and handmaids they had set free, subjecting them once again to servitude. Therefore, the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah in this manner: Thus says the Lord, the God of the Israelites: I made a covenant with your ancestors when I led them out of Egypt, the house of slavery, saying: At the end of seven <margin>40</margin> <margin>Exodus 22 <note>This refers to the laws of the Sabbath year; specifically Exodus 21 or 22</note></margin> years, every one of you must set free his fellow Hebrew who has been sold to you and has served you for six years; <margin>Deuteronomy 15</margin> you shall, I say, set him free. But your ancestors did not obey me, nor did they incline their ear. Now you, today, had done what was pleasing to me by proclaiming liberty to one another, making a covenant before me in the house called by my name. But then <margin>50</margin> you turned around and profaned my name; each of you took back the slaves and handmaids whom you had set free to be their own masters, and you subjected them to slavery again. Therefore, thus says the Lord: Since you have not obeyed me by proclaiming liberty to one another, I now proclaim a "liberty" for you, says the Lord—to the sword, the plague, and the famine. I will make you a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth, and I will hand over the men who, breaking my covenant, did not stand by the words of the pact...

In the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, the Lord spoke these words to Jeremiah: Take a book-scroll, and write in it all the words that I have spoken to you against the Israelites, the Jews, and all the nations, from the time I first spoke to you in the days of Josiah until this very day. Perhaps if the house of Judah hears how many evils I intend to inflict upon them, each man will depart from his own wicked way of life, and so I may forgive their guilt and their sin. Therefore Jeremiah called Baruch son of Neriah, and Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words which the Lord had spoken to him, onto a book-scroll. Then Jeremiah instructed Baruch, saying: I am shut in <note>Jeremiah may have been barred from the Temple or under some form of arrest</note> and cannot go into the house of the Lord. You shall go, and from the scroll you shall recite the words of the Lord which you have transcribed from my mouth, in the hearing of the people, in the house of the Lord on a day of fasting; and you shall also recite them in the hearing of all the Jews who have come from their cities, so that perhaps, their supplication having been brought before the Lord, they may each depart from their wicked way of life: for great is the anger and the fury which the Lord threatens against this people. So Baruch son of Neriah did everything the prophet Jeremiah had commanded him, reciting the words of the Lord from the book in the house of the Lord. And in the fifth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, in the ninth month, when a fast before the Lord was proclaimed in Jerusalem for all the people of Jerusalem and those who had come from the towns of Judah, Baruch read the words of Jeremiah from the book in the house of the Lord, in the chamber of Gemariah son of Shaphan the scribe, in the upper court, before the new gate of the temple of the Lord, in the hearing of all the people. Then Micaiah son of Gemariah, the grandson of Shaphan, having heard all the words of the Lord from the book, went down into the palace into the scribe’s chamber; there he found all the princes sitting: Elishama the scribe, Delaiah son of Shemaiah, Elnathan son of Achbor, Gemariah son of Shaphan, and Zedekiah

son of Hananiah, and all the leaders; he set forth to them the whole speech which he had heard when Baruch was reading the book in the ears of the people. Therefore Jeremiah took another scroll and gave it to Baruch son of Neriah, the scribe, in which he wrote from Jeremiah’s mouth all the words of the book which Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire, with many other words of that kind added besides.

## CHAPTER XXXVII.

Now King Zedekiah son of Josiah reigned in place of Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, having been appointed king in Judah by Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon; yet neither he, nor his servants, nor the people of the land obeyed the words of the Lord <note>original: "Iouæ," a Renaissance Latin rendering of the Tetragrammaton</note> which He spoke through Jeremiah the prophet. King Zedekiah sent Jucal son of Shelemiah and Zephaniah son of Maaseiah the priest to Jeremiah the prophet with this mandate: "Please pray for us to the Lord our God." Now Jeremiah was moving about freely among the people and had not yet been thrown into prison; and Pharaoh's army had set out from Egypt, and when the Chaldeans <note>The Babylonians</note> who were besieging Jerusalem heard the news of them, they withdrew from Jerusalem. Then the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah the prophet in this manner: "Thus says the Lord, the God of the Israelites. Thus shall you say to the king of Judah, who sent you to consult me: Behold, Pharaoh’s army, which set out to bring you aid, shall return to Egypt, its own land; and the Chaldeans shall return and attack this city, and they shall capture it and burn it with fire. Thus says the Lord: Do not deceive yourselves, thinking that the Chaldeans will surely depart from you; for they shall not depart. Even if you were to strike down the entire army of the Chaldeans waging war against you, so that only the wounded among them remained, those very men would rise up, each from his own tent, and burn this city with fire."

When the army of the Chaldeans had withdrawn from Jerusalem because of Pharaoh’s army, Jeremiah went out from Jerusalem to go into the land of Benjamin, so that he might escape from there among the common people. But when he reached the Benjamin Gate, the man who was in charge of the guard there, named Irijah, son of Shelemiah and grandson of Hananiah, seized Jeremiah the prophet, saying that he was defecting to the Chaldeans. Jeremiah denied it, saying it was false and that he was not defecting to the Chaldeans, but Irijah would not listen to him; he arrested Jeremiah and brought him before the officials, who

viciously beat Jeremiah and threw him into chains in the house of Jonathan the scribe, for they had turned it into a prison. When Jeremiah had descended into the pit <note>original: "barathrum," implying a deep, dark dungeon or hole</note> and the lowest cell of the house, and had remained there for many days, King Zedekiah sent for him to be brought out, and he questioned him secretly in his own house, asking if there was any word from the Lord. "There is," said Jeremiah. "You shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon." Then Jeremiah said, "How have I sinned against you, or your servants, or this people, that you have cast me into prison? And where are your prophets who prophesied to you, saying that the king of Babylon would not attack you or this land? And now hear, I pray, my lord king: let my petition be accepted before you, and do not send me back to the house of Jonathan the scribe, lest I die there." Therefore King Zedekiah ordered Jeremiah to be placed in the court of the guard, and a loaf of bread was given to him daily from the street of the bakers, until all the bread in the city was consumed; and so Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard.

<margin>The capture of Jerusalem. 2 Kings 25, Jeremiah 52.</margin>
When they saw the city was taken (for the city was broken into in the eleventh year of Zedekiah, on the ninth day of the fourth month, though indeed in the ninth year of the same Zedekiah, king of Judah, in the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had come with all his forces and besieged Jerusalem), all the princes of the king of Babylon entered and sat in the middle gate: Nergal-Sharezer, Samgar-Nebo, Sarsechim, the chief officer <note>Latin: Rabfari</note>, Nergal-Sharezer the chief magus <note>Latin: Rabamagus</note>, and all the rest of the princes of the king of Babylon. ### CHAPTER XL.

The word spoken by the LORD to Jeremiah after Nebuzardan, the captain of the guard, had released him from Ramah, where he had found him bound in chains among all the exiles of Jerusalem and Judah who were being deported to Babylon; and he addressed him thus. and done it, because you all sinned against the LORD and did not listen to his voice; therefore this thing has happened to you. ### CHAPTER XLI.

*But in the seventh month, Ishmael son of Nethaniah, <margin>10</margin> grandson of Elishama, of the royal seed, came with the king's nobles and ten men to Mizpah, to Gedaliah son of Ahikam. And there, while they were eating a meal together at Mizpah, Ishmael son of Nethaniah and the ten men his companions rose up and struck Gedaliah son of Ahikam, grandson of Shaphan, with their swords and killed him, whom the king of Babylon had placed in charge of the region. Likewise, Ishmael killed all the Jews who were with Gedaliah at Mizpah, and the Chaldean <note>The Babylonians</note> soldiers who were found there. On the second day after the killing of Gedaliah, while no one yet knew of it, men arrived from Shechem, Shiloh, and <margin>20</margin> <margin>2. Mourners.</margin> Samaria—eighty men in total—with shaved beards and torn clothes, having cut themselves; they were carrying grain offerings and incense with them to bring into the house of the LORD <note>Latin: Iouæ</note>. Ishmael son of Nethaniah went out from Mizpah to meet them, weeping as he went; and when he met them, he invited them to come to Gedaliah son of Ahikam. Then, when they had come into the middle of the town, Ishmael slaughtered them along with his companions and threw them into the middle of a pit. However, ten men were found among them who begged Ishmael not to kill them, saying they had stores of wheat, barley, oil, and honey hidden <margin>30</margin> in the fields; so he refrained from killing them among their kinsmen. Now the pit into which Ishmael threw all the bodies of the men he had killed alongside Gedaliah was the one King Asa had made because of Baasha king of the Israelites; Ishmael son of Nethaniah filled this very pit with the bodies of those he had slain. Then Ishmael took captive the rest of the people who were at Mizpah, including the king's daughters and all the people remaining at Mizpah whom Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, had committed to Gedaliah son of Ahikam; driving them away, Ishmael son of <margin>40</margin> Nethaniah set out to go to the Ammonites. But when Johanan son of Kareah and all the military leaders who were with him heard how great a crime Ishmael son of Nethaniah had committed, they took all their men and set out to make war against him, and they found him at the great pool at Gibeon <note>Latin: Gabaonē</note>. And when all the people who were being led away by Ishmael from Mizpah saw Johanan and all the military leaders with him, they were joyful and returned to Johanan. But Ishmael escaped from Johanan with eight men and went to the Ammonites. Then Johanan <margin>50</margin> and all the military leaders with him took all the remnant of the people whom they had recovered from Ishmael at Gibeon after he had killed Gedaliah—men, soldiers, women, children, and eunuchs <note>Latin: spadones</note>—and they came to Geruth-Chimham <note>Latin: Geruthchamaam</note>, which is near Bethlehem, and stayed there intending to head for Egypt, out of fear of the Chaldeans, because Ishmael had killed Gedaliah, whom the king of Babylon had placed over the province.*

### CHAPTER XLII.

*Then all the military leaders, and Johanan son of Kareah, and Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah, and all the people from the least to the greatest, approached Jeremiah the prophet and spoke to him in this manner: "We pray you, allow us to entreat you to pray for us to the LORD <note>Latin: Iouā</note> your God, for all this remnant—since we are left but a few out of many, as you see us with your own eyes—that the LORD your God may show us the way we should walk and the thing we should do." Jeremiah said to them: "I hear you; <margin>10</margin> as you have requested, I will pray to the LORD your God, and whatever the LORD answers you, I will declare it to you; I will hide nothing from you." And they said to Jeremiah: "Let the LORD be a true and faithful witness between us that we will act according to everything for which the LORD your God sends you to us, whether it be good or evil. We will be obedient to the voice of the LORD our God, to whom we send you, so that it may go well with us when we obey the LORD our God." Therefore, after ten days had passed, the LORD <margin>20</margin> spoke to Jeremiah. He called Johanan son of Kareah and all the military leaders who were with him, and finally all the people from the least to the greatest, and addressed them: "Thus says the LORD, the God of the Israelites, to whom you sent me to present your supplication before him: 'If you remain in this land, I will build you up and not pull you down; I will plant you and not uproot you; for I repent of the evil that I have brought upon you. Do not fear the king of Babylon, whom you fear; do not fear him,' says the LORD, 'for I will be with you to <margin>30</margin> save you and to defend you from his hand; and I will move him to mercy toward you, so that he may return you to your own land. But if you do not obey the LORD your God, and say you will not stay in this region, but will rather go into Egypt, where you think you will see no war, nor hear the sound of the trumpet, nor hunger for bread—then hear the word of the LORD, you remnant of Judah. Thus says the LORD of hosts <note>Latin: armipotens Iouā</note>, the God of the Israelites: If you turn your faces to seek Egypt and go there to dwell, it shall be that the sword which you fear shall <margin>40</margin> overtake you there in Egypt, and the famine of which you are afraid shall follow close behind you there in Egypt, and there you shall die. All the men who turn their faces toward Egypt to go and dwell there shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence; none of them shall remain or escape the evils I will bring upon them. For thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of the Israelites: Just as my anger and my wrath were poured out on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so shall my wrath be poured out on you when you go into Egypt; and you shall be an object of horror, astonishment, cursing, and <margin>50</margin> infamy, and you shall never see this place again.' The LORD has spoken to you, O remnant of Judah, that you should not go into Egypt; know for certain that I have warned you this day. For you have gone astray at the peril of your lives, since you sent me to the LORD your God, asking that I pray to the LORD your God for you, and saying that whatever the LORD your God said, you would do it. Although I have told you this today, you have not obeyed the voice of the LORD your God in anything for which he sent me to you. Now therefore, know for certain that you shall die by the sword, by famine, and by pestilence in the place where you desire to go and dwell."*

# CHAPTER XLV.

<margin>An oracle to Baruch.</margin>
The word that Jeremiah the prophet spoke to Baruch son of Neriah, when he had written these words in a book from the mouth of Jeremiah, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, in these words: "Thus says the LORD, the God of the Israelites, to you, Baruch: You complain miserably that the LORD adds sorrow to your pain, that you are weary with groaning and find no rest. <margin>a. Difficult and hard things, namely finding rest in the midst of everyone’s unrest.</margin> You shall say this to him: 'Thus says the LORD: Behold, what I have built, I will break down; and what I have planted, I will pluck up—namely, this whole land. And do you seek great things for yourself? Do not seek them; for behold, I am bringing disaster upon all mortals,' says the LORD, 'but I will grant you your life as a prize of war in every place you go.'"

### CHAPTER XLVIII.

<margin>Against the Moabites.</margin>

<summary>This portion of Jeremiah 51 describes the violent downfall of Babylon at the hands of the Medes and other northern kingdoms, presented as divine retribution for the destruction of the Temple in Jerusalem. It highlights the futility of Babylonian idols and mentions the historical tactic of the Persians diverting the Euphrates river to capture the city.</summary>

### CHAPTER LII.

<margin>Jerusalem destroyed</margin> Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he began his reign; he reigned in Jerusalem for eleven years. His mother’s name was Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah. He offended Jehovah, just as Jehoiakim had done, because Jehovah was so angry with the people of Jerusalem and Judah that he cast them out from his presence. <margin>Therefore... [highly fragmented note referring to idols and Isaiah 5]</margin> So Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon. Therefore, in the ninth year of his reign, on the tenth day of the tenth month, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came with all his forces against Jerusalem, made camp against it, and built a rampart all around it. When the city had been besieged until the eleventh year of Zedekiah, on the ninth day of the fourth month, a famine gripped the city, and the inhabitants lacked food; the city was breached, and all the sol-

<column-break/>

diers fled, and they went out of the city by night by way of the gate between the two walls near the king's gardens (while the Chaldeans surrounded the city), and they went by the way of the plains. But the Chaldean soldiers pursued King Zedekiah and overtook him in the plain of Jericho; after all his soldiers had scattered, they captured him and brought him to Riblah in the land of Hamath to the king of Babylon, who passed sentence upon him. At Riblah, the king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his very eyes, and also killed all the princes of Judah. Then he blinded the eyes of Zedekiah himself, bound him in chains, took him to Babylon, and put him in prison until the day of his death. On the tenth day of the fifth month, which was the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, Nebuzaradan, the Master of the Horse <note>original: "magister equitum." Usually translated as "Captain of the Guard," a high-ranking military official.</note> and servant of the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem and burned the house of Jehovah, the royal palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem; especially all the greatest houses, he destroyed with fire. All the Chaldean soldiers who were with the Master of the Horse demolished all the walls of Jerusalem on every side. Nebuzaradan carried away into exile the remnants of the people who were left in the city, those who had deserted to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the common people, leaving behind only the poorest of the people to be vinedressers and farmers. The Chaldeans broke the bronze pillars, the bases, and the bronze sea <note>A massive basin used for ritual washing in the Temple.</note> that were in the house of Jehovah, and they carried all their bronze to Babylon. They also took the pots, the shovels, the musical instruments, the bowls, the dishes, and all the bronze vessels used in the service. The Master of the Horse took the basins, the censers <note>original: "acernas." Likely referring to vessels for coals or incense.</note>, the bowls, the kettles, the lampstands, the sacrificial dishes, and the goblets, whether of gold or of silver. As for the two pillars, the one sea, the twelve bronze oxen placed under the bases, which King Solomon had made for the house of Jehovah—the weight of the bronze from all these vessels was immeasurable. One pillar stood eighteen cubits high, with a circumference of twelve cubits; it was four fingers thick and hollow, with a bronze capital five cubits high. It was decorated all around with latticework and pomegranates <note>original: "punicis malis." Literally "Punic apples," the standard Latin name for pomegranates.</note>, all made of bronze; the second pillar was identical in its design and its pomegranates. There were ninety-six pomegranates on each side, the total sum of which made one hundred around the latticework. The Master of the Horse also took Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the second priest, and the three doorkeepers. From the city, he took one eunuch who had been in charge of the soldiers, seven of the king’s advisors who were found in the city, the scribe of the commander who had managed the military affairs of the locals, and sixty local men found in the city. These, I say, having been seized, Nebuzaradan the Master of the Horse led to Riblah to the king of Babylon, who killed them there in the territory of Hamath; and so he carried the Jews away from their homeland. These are the people whom Nebuchadnezzar took into exile: in the seventh year, three thousand and twenty-three Jews. In the eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar, he took eight hundred and thirty-two persons from Jerusalem. In the twenty-third year of Nebuchadnezzar, Nebuzaradan the Master of Horse...

In the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin, king of Judah, on the twenty-fourth day of the twelfth month, Evil-Merodach <note>The son and successor of Nebuchadnezzar II.</note>, king of Babylon, in the year he began his reign, saw to it that Jehoiachin, king of Judah, was released from prison. Speaking to him kindly, he set his throne above the thrones of the other kings he kept in Babylon. He changed his prison garments, and Jehoiachin ate at the king's table for the rest of his life, provided with a daily allowance from the royal storehouse as long as he lived.

Because of the sins you have committed against God, you will be led away as captives to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon. Having entered Babylon, you will remain there for a long time, for many years, even up to seven generations; after that, I will lead you out from there in safety. But now you will see in Babylon gods of silver, gold, and wood being carried on shoulders, striking fear into the nations. Beware that you do not also become like the foreigners and, following their example, stand in awe of those gods when you see the crowd before and behind them worshipping them; but rather think in your minds: "It is right to worship You, Lord." For my spirit <term>genius: a guiding spirit or divine presence</term> is with you; it is he who examines your souls. For indeed, 

<margin>
image
</margin>
the tongues of these gods have been polished by a craftsman, and being gilded and silvered, they are false and cannot speak. And just as one might do for a young girl fond of ornaments, they take gold and fashion crowns for the heads of their gods. Sometimes the priests even take away the gold and silver from their gods and spend it on themselves, or bestow it upon local harlots; they dress them up in clothes like men—these gods of silver, gold, and wood. Yet these gods do not escape rust and rot, even though they are draped in purple clothing, and their faces must be wiped clean of the temple dust that settles thick upon them. Such a god holds a scepter like some governor of a region, yet he cannot kill one who offends him. He holds a dagger or an axe in his right hand, yet he cannot defend himself from war or robbers; from this, it is clear that they are not gods. Therefore, do not fear them. For just as a man's vessel becomes useless once it is broken, so are their gods; when placed in their temples, their eyes are full of the dust stirred up by the feet of those who enter. And just as when someone offends the king,

<column-break/>

the courtyards are closed on all sides to lead him away to his death, so the priests fortify the temples of these gods with doors, locks, and bars, lest they be plundered by robbers. They light lamps for them—and indeed more than for themselves—of which those gods can see none; they are exactly like the beams in the houses. They say that their hearts are licked clean by serpents of the earth, but when they and their clothing are gnawed away, they do not feel it. Their faces are blackened by the smoke of the temple; owls, swallows, and other birds fly over their bodies and heads, and cats do the same. From this, you may understand that they are not gods. Therefore, do not fear them. For although they are covered in gold for the sake of beauty, unless someone wipes off the tarnish, they will not shine; nor did they feel it when they were being cast. Bought at a great price, they are endowed with no breath <term>spiritu: life-force or breath</term>. Having no feet, they are carried on shoulders, displaying their own disgrace to men. They are a cause of shame even to their own worshippers because, if they happen to fall to the ground, they do not rise by themselves, nor if someone sets them upright can they move on their own, nor can they straighten themselves if they lean; but gifts are placed before them as if for the dead, and the priests misuse their sold sacrifices. Likewise, their women preserve the meat from them and share nothing with the poor or the needy. Menstruating women and those in childbirth touch their sacrifices. Therefore, knowing from these things that they are not gods, do not fear them. For why should they be called gods? Since women set food before these gods of silver, gold, and wood, and in their temples the priests sit with torn tunics, with shaved heads and beards, and uncovered, they howl and cry out before their gods just as if they were at a funeral feast. The priests strip the clothing from them to dress their own wives and children. But if these gods are treated poorly or well by anyone, they cannot repay it; they can neither set up a king nor depose one, nor can they give riches or money. If someone does not fulfill a vow made to them, they do not notice it; they rescue no one from death, nor do they defend the weak from the powerful. They do not restore sight to a blind man, nor do they snatch a man out of adversity; they show no mercy to the widow, nor do they do good for the orphan. These deities of wood, gilded and silvered, are like stones from the mountains, and their worshippers will be put to shame. Can they, therefore, be thought of or called gods? When even the Chaldeans <note>The people of Babylonia.</note> themselves dishonor them; for if they see a mute person who is unable to speak, they bring him to Bel <note>Bel-Marduk, the chief god of Babylon.</note> and ask that he speak, as if Bel were able to perceive anything. Yet they themselves, lacking any sense, cannot think to abandon them. Furthermore, the women, girded with cords, sit along the paths burning bran as incense. And if one of them, drawn away by a passerby, has lain with him, she reproaches the other that she was not deemed worthy as she was, and that her cord was not broken. Finally, everything that is done regarding them is false. Can they, therefore, be thought of or called gods? Crafted by carpenters and goldsmiths, they are nothing other than what the craftsmen want them to be; and even the makers themselves do not live long, so how can their handiwork be gods? For they show by the things that happen...

how false and shameful they are. For whenever war or evils befall them, the priests consult among themselves where they might hide away with them. From this, it cannot fail to be understood that they are not gods, who do not deliver themselves from war or evils. Since they are indeed made of wood, and gilded, and silvered, it shall come to pass that all nations recognize them as false, and it will be clear to kings that they are not gods, but the works of human hands, in which there is no divine work. Who does not know they are not gods, who neither create a king for a region, nor give rain to men, nor judge their own cause, nor repel an injury, being as powerless as ravens <note>original: "cornices"</note> hanging between heaven and earth? For if fire falls upon the temple of these wooden or gilded or silvered gods, their priests escape by flight; but the gods themselves, like beams, are burned in the midst, and they resist neither king nor enemies. Can they therefore be thought or called gods? For they escape neither thieves nor robbers—these gods of wood, silver, and gold. The more powerful men take away the gold, silver, and the clothing with which they are surrounded and carry it off, and the gods do not help themselves. Therefore, a king showing his power, or a useful vessel in a house which the master uses, is better than these false gods; a door of a house is better, guarding what is inside, than false gods; and a wooden pillar in a palace is better than false gods. For the sun, and the moon, and the shining stars, which are sent for necessary uses, are obedient. Likewise, the lightning is clear when it flashes. In the same way, the wind blows through every region, and the clouds, commanded by God to pass over the whole world, execute the mandate; fire also, sent from above to consume mountains and woods, does what it is commanded. But these idols are not to be compared with these things in form or strength; wherefore it is neither to be thought nor said that they are gods, since they can neither inflict punishment nor confer benefits upon men. Therefore, understanding that they are not gods, do not fear them. For they neither bless nor curse kings, nor do they show signs to the nations in the sky, nor shine like the moon. The beasts are better than they, for they can flee under a roof and help themselves. Thus, it is in no way clear to us that they are gods. Therefore, do not dread them. For like a scarecrow in a garden of cucumbers that guards nothing, so are their gods of wood, gold, and silver. In the same way, they are like a thorn-bush in a garden, upon which every bird sits. Likewise, their gods of gold and silver are like a dead man lying in the dark. <margin>c. Plastering.</margin> Finally, from the purple and the marble-work <note>The Latin "marmorato" refers here to a polished or plastered surface that imitates marble, which is now decaying.</note> rotting upon them, you shall know they are not gods, and they themselves shall at last be consumed to the disgrace of men. Therefore, the just man who has no images is better, for he shall be far from disgrace.

### CHAPTER II.

Therefore the Lord has fulfilled what he threatened against us and our leaders who ruled the Israelites, and against our kings, our magistrates, and the people of Israel and Judah, by bringing upon us such great evils that nothing like what happened in Jerusalem has ever occurred under the whole heaven, just as it is written in the Law of Moses <margin>Deuteronomy 28.</margin>, even to the point that there were those among us who ate the flesh of their own sons and daughters. Indeed, he has brought them under the power of all the kingdoms neighboring us, and exposed them to disgrace and desolation among all the surrounding peoples where the Lord has scattered them, so that they are beneath and not above. For we have sinned against the Lord our God by not obeying his words <margin>previously in chapter 1.</margin>. Righteousness belongs to the Lord our God, but to us and our ancestors belongs shame and disgrace, a fact that is clearer than the light of this day. All these many evils which the Lord threatened against us have befallen us, yet we did not entreat him, though each of us turned away from the inclinations of our own evil minds. For this reason, the Lord has kept watch to bring these evils upon us, and indeed the Lord has done all things justly, since we did not obey his command to follow the Lord's precepts which he set before us. Now, O Lord God of the Israelites <margin>Daniel 9.</margin>, who brought your people out of the land of Egypt with a strong hand, an outstretched arm, with signs and wonders and great power, and gained a name for yourself that is famous to this day: we have sinned, we have acted impiously and wickedly, O Lord our God, against all your laws. But let your anger be turned away from us, for we are but a few left among the nations where you have scattered us. For the dead in the underworld <note>original: "inferos"</note>, whose spirit has been taken from their breasts, will not give glory and righteousness to the Lord; rather, the soul that is tormented by the magnitude of its decline and failing, <margin>of the Israelites.</margin> and the failing eyes and the hungry soul, will give you glory and righteousness, O Lord. For we do not make our humble appeal before you, O Lord our God, relying on the virtues of our ancestors or our kings, you who have vented your anger against us, just as you threatened through your servants the prophets in this manner: "Thus says the Lord: Bend your shoulders to serve the king of Babylon, and you shall inhabit the land which I gave to your ancestors. But if you do not listen to my voice and serve the king of Babylon, I will cause the voices of joy and gladness, and the voices of the bridegroom and the bride, to cease in the cities of Judah and in Jerusalem, and the whole region will become desolate and uncultivated." serve the king of Babylon. Yet you have dealt with us, O Lord our God, according to your great kindness and singular mercy, just as you foretold through your servant Moses, when you commanded him to write the law in the presence of the Israelites to this effect: "If you do not listen to my word, surely this great and numerous multitude will be reduced to a tiny few among the nations where I will scatter them. Then I will lead them back into the land which I swore to their ancestors Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and they shall possess it; and I will multiply them, and they shall not be diminished. I will make an eternal covenant with them, so that I will be their God and they shall be my people, and I will never again remove my people Israel from the land I have given them."

## CHAPTER I.

<margin>
The glory.
</margin>
<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'A' featuring architectural structures, columns, and decorative flourishes.</image-desc>
In the thirtieth year, on the fifth day of the fourth month, when I was among the exiles by the river Chebar <note>original: "Chobar"</note>, the heavens were opened and I saw divine visions. On the fifth of the month, in the fifth year of King Jehoiachin's <note>original: "Ioachinus"</note> exile, the word of the Lord <note>original: "Iouæ," a Latinization of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton</note> came to Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi, in the land of the Chaldeans by the river Chebar. There, moved by the hand of the Lord, I perceived a stormy wind coming from the north, a great cloud, and a gathered fire surrounded by splendor. From the midst of that fire there appeared something like electrum <note>original: "electri," a glowing alloy of gold and silver, or perhaps amber</note>, and in it the form of four living creatures, whose faces had the likeness of a human being. Each of them had four faces and four wings; their feet were straight, with the soles of their feet resembling those of calves, sparkling like polished bronze. Human hands were under their wings on the four sides of their square forms, and those four had their faces and wings arranged so that their wings were joined to one another. They did not turn as they went, but each one moved straight ahead toward wherever its face looked. As for the appearance of their faces, the four had the face of a man and a lion on the right side, and the face of an ox and an eagle on the left. Their faces and wings were separated above, so that two wings of each were joined together, and the other two covered their bodies. Each moved straight forward; wherever the spirit led, they went, and they did not turn as they moved. The form of the living creatures was like burning coals of fire, in the manner of torches; this fire moved among the creatures, possessing a brilliance, and lightning flashed from the fire. The creatures ran and returned with the appearance of a flash of lightning. As I looked at these creatures, I noticed wheels on the ground beside them, one for each of their four faces. The appearance and workmanship of the wheels was like the color of chrysolite <note>original: "chrysolithi," a yellowish-green gemstone</note>, and the four of them had the same form and workmanship, as if a wheel were set within a wheel. When they moved, they went toward their four sides and did not turn as they went. The wheels themselves had rims that were high and formidable, full of eyes all around. When the creatures moved, the wheels moved beside them; and when the creatures were lifted up from the earth, the wheels were also lifted up. Wherever the spirit went, they went, driven by the spirit, and the wheels were lifted up along with them. For the spirit of the creatures was in the wheels: when the creatures went, they went; when they stood, they stood; and when they were lifted from the ground, the wheels were also lifted up along with them, for they were endowed with the spirit of the living creatures. Over the heads of the creatures was the likeness of the firmament <note>original: "ætheris"</note>, like awesome crystal, stretched out over their heads from above. Under this firmament their wings were stretched out, one toward another; two wings of each covered their bodies. And I heard the sound of their wings, like the sound of many waters, like the voice of the Almighty. As they went, the sound—

<meta>catchword: sound</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>354</page-num>

—was tumultuous, like the sound of an army. But when they stood still and let down their wings, a voice came from the firmament hanging over their heads. Above the firmament over their heads was the likeness of a throne, appearing like a sapphire stone, and upon the likeness of the throne was a figure like a human being, placed high above it. And I saw something that resembled electrum in appearance, looking like fire enclosed all around, above what appeared to be his waist; and below his waist, I saw something like the appearance of fire surrounded by brilliance. This surrounding splendor was like the appearance of a bow that is in the clouds when it rains. This was the vision of the likeness of the glory of the Lord.

## CHAPTER II.

When I saw this, I fell on my face, and I heard the voice of one speaking, saying to me: O man <note>original: "Homo," often translated in bibles as "Son of man"</note>, stand upon your feet, and I will speak to you. Then as soon as he spoke to me, the spirit entered into me and set me on my feet, and I heard him speaking to me in these words: O man, I am sending you to the Israelites, a rebellious race of men, who have rebelled against me—both they and their ancestors—and have revolted from me even to this very day. I am sending you to children with stubborn faces and hard hearts, to whom you shall say: "Thus says the Lord God." Whether they listen or—as they are a defiant race—whether they refuse to listen, they shall certainly know that a prophet <note>original: "vatem"</note> has been among them. But you, O man, do not fear them, nor fear their words, even though you live among the refractory and the intractable, and dwell among scorpions. Do not fear their words or be terrified by their looks, even though they are a defiant nation. Speak my words to them, whether they listen or not, for they are defiant. You therefore, O man, hear what I say to you: do not be defiant like that defiant nation. Open your mouth, and eat what I give you. Then I noticed a hand stretched out toward me, in which was a written scroll; he unrolled it before me, and it was written on both the front and the back, inscribed with dirges, laments, and mourning.

In the thirtieth year, on the fifth day of the fourth month, while I was among the exiles by the river Chebar, the heavens were opened and I saw divine visions. On the fifth of the month, in the fifth year of the exile of King Jehoiachin, the word of the Lord <note>original: "Iouæ," a Latin rendering of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton YHWH, often translated as Jehovah or the Lord.</note> came to Ezekiel the priest, son of Buzi, in the land of the Chaldeans, by the river Chebar. There, prompted by the hand of the Lord, I perceived a stormy wind coming from the north, a great cloud, and a gathering fire surrounded by radiance; from the midst of this fire there appeared something like the likeness of electrum, <note>original: "electri," a precious alloy of gold and silver, or perhaps amber, known for its brilliant shine.</note> and within it the form of four living creatures, whose faces had the appearance of human form. Each one had four faces and four wings: their legs were straight, with the soles of their feet like those of calves, sparkling with the appearance of polished bronze. Human hands were beneath their wings on the four sides of their square frames, and those four had their faces and wings arranged such that their wings were joined to one another; they did not turn as they went, but each one moved straight ahead, in the direction its face was looking. As for the appearance of their faces, those four had a human face and a lion’s face on the right side; on the left, they had the face of an ox and the face of an eagle. Their faces and wings were divided above, so that two wings of each were joined together, and the other two covered their bodies. Each one moved straight forward: wherever the spirit drove them, they went, and they did not turn as they moved. The form of the living creatures was such that their appearance resembled burning coals of fire in the manner of torches; this fire moved among the living creatures, possessing a radiance, with lightning flashing out from the fire. And the living creatures ran and returned, appearing like a flash of lightning. While looking at these creatures, I noticed certain wheels on the ground beside the creatures, at their four faces; their appearance and workmanship were like the color of chrysolite, <note>original: "chrysolithū," a yellow or green precious stone, likely beryl.</note> and the four of them had the same shape, their form and work being as if a wheel were set within a wheel. When they moved, they went in any of their four directions without turning as they went. The four wheels also had rims, and they were high and formidable, full of eyes all around. When the living creatures moved, the wheels moved beside them; and when the living creatures were lifted up from the earth, the wheels were also lifted up. Wherever the spirit moved, they went, driven by the spirit, and the wheels were lifted up along with them. For the wheels were endowed with the spirit of the living creatures; when those moved, these moved; when those stood still, these stood still; and when those were lifted from the ground, the wheels were also lifted along with them, being endowed with the spirit of the creatures. Over the heads of the living creatures was the likeness of an expanse, <note>original: "ætheris," referring to the firmament or sky.</note> like terrifying crystal, stretched out over their heads from above. Beneath this expanse their wings were stretched out, one toward another; each creature had two wings covering their bodies. I heard the sound of their wings, like the sound of many waters, like a mighty sound as they moved, a

<column-break/>

tumultuous sound, like that of an army. But when they stood still and let down their wings, a sound came from the expanse hanging over their heads. And I saw something that resembled electrum in appearance, like the sight of fire enclosed all around, above what looked like his waist; and below what looked like his waist, I saw something like the appearance of fire surrounded by radiance. This surrounding radiance had the appearance of the bow that is in the clouds on a rainy day. This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the Lord.

## CHAPTER II.

When I saw this, I fell on my face, and I heard the voice of one speaking, saying to me: "Son of man, <note>original: "Homo," literally "Man," the standard Latin translation for the prophetic address "Ben-Adam."</note> stand on your feet, and I will speak to you." Then, as soon as he spoke to me, the spirit entered into me and set me on my feet, and I heard him speaking to me in these words: "Son of man, I am sending you to the Israelites, a rebellious race of men, who have rebelled against me—both they and their ancestors—and who have revolted from me even to this very day. To children of a hard and stubborn heart, to these I send you, to whom you shall say: 'Thus says the Lord God.' <note>original: "dominus Iouæ."</note> And whether they listen, or (since they are a defiant race) do not listen, they will certainly know that a prophet has been among them. But you, Son of man, do not fear them, nor fear their words, even though you live among the rebellious and intractable, and dwell with scorpions. Do not fear their words or be terrified by their look, though they are a defiant nation. But speak my words to them, whether they listen or not, for they are defiant. You therefore, Son of man, hear what I speak to you; do not be defiant like that defiant nation. Open your mouth and eat what I give you." Then I noticed a hand stretched out to me, in which was a scroll of a book, which he unrolled before me; it was written on both the front and the back, and inscribed upon it were dirges, complaints, and lamentations.
