### CHAPTER II.

I call upon you, O Jehovah, in my distress, and you answer my prayer, hearing my voice from the belly of the underworld <note>original: "orci uentre," referring to the depths of the grave or Sheol</note> as I pray. Indeed, when you cast me into the heart of the deep sea, when I was overwhelmed by the floods and oppressed by all the swirling depths of your waves, I seemed to myself to be driven far from your sight. Surely (I said) I shall yet look again upon your holy sanctuary, even though I am surrounded by lethal waters, covered by the deep, my head wrapped in seaweed as I am carried down beneath the roots of the mountains, and barred forever by the gates of the earth: and will you, O Jehovah my God, truly pull my life out from destruction? Therefore, when my soul was despairing, you, Jehovah, came into my mind, and my prayer reached you in your holy sanctuary.
<margin>a. That is, the God who would otherwise be merciful toward them.</margin>
Those who hold fast to the vanity of wickedness, they abandon their own source of mercy <margin>a</margin>. But I, with a voice of thanksgiving, will sacrifice to you and will perform what I have vowed. Salvation is from Jehovah.

### CHAPTER III.

Then the fish, at the command of Jehovah, vomited Jonah out onto the dry land, and Jehovah gave a command to Jonah a second time, that he should set out for Nineveh, that great city, and proclaim in it that which He Himself commanded him. Therefore Jonah set out for Nineveh according to the command of Jehovah. Now Nineveh was a city of divine proportions <note>original: "diuinæ magnitudinis," a Hebrew idiom for "an exceedingly great city"</note>, a journey of three days across. When Jonah had proceeded into this city a journey of one day, he proclaimed that after forty days Nineveh would be overturned.
<margin>Matthew 12. Luke 11.</margin>
But the people of Nineveh, having faith in God, proclaimed a fast and put on sackcloth <note>original: "centones," literally patchwork garments or rags</note>, from the greatest among them to the least. When this news reached the King of Nineveh, he rose from his throne, and laying aside his royal robes, he covered himself in sackcloth and sat upon the ground. He ordered it to be preached and announced throughout Nineveh by a decree of the king and his nobles, that neither men nor cattle, whether greater or lesser, should taste anything, nor should they graze or drink water. Then they—
<margin>Jeremiah 18.</margin>
humans and beasts alike—clothed in sackcloth, were to implore God vehemently and turn themselves back from their depraved ways and the injustice they had practiced, in the hope that
<margin>Joel 2.</margin>
perchance God might be reconciled, restrain Himself, and pull back from the heat of His anger, so that they might not perish. And so God, seeing their deeds, that they had turned themselves away from the depravity of their ways, restrained Himself and abstained from the punishment He had decided to inflict upon them.

### CHAPTER IIII.

This outcome displeased Jonah so much that he became angry and prayed to Jehovah with these words: "O Jehovah, was this not exactly what I said when I was still in my own country? For this reason I was preoccupied with fleeing to Cilicia <note>The translator identifies the biblical "Tarshish" with Cilicia in Asia Minor</note>, for I knew that you are a God who is easy to entreat and merciful, slow to anger, of great clemency, and one who withholds punishment.
<margin>Psalm 85. Joel 2.</margin>
Therefore, Jehovah, I beg you, take this life from me: for it is better for me to die than to live." But Jehovah asked him if he was right to be angry. So Jonah, having left the city, sat down to the east of the city, making a shelter for himself there, under which he might remain in the shade until he saw what would happen to the city. Now Jehovah God had prepared a gourd <note>original: "cucurbitam," a reference to the famous translation debate between St. Jerome and St. Augustine over whether the plant was a gourd or ivy</note>, which rose up

<column-break/>

<page-num>456</page-num>

over Jonah to provide shade for his head and defend him from discomfort; and Jonah rejoiced greatly because of this gourd. But God also prepared a worm at the dawn of the next day, by which the gourd was struck and withered. Then when the sun rose, a piercing East wind was brought in by divine power, and it struck Jonah's head so that he, burning with heat, prayed for death, saying that death was preferable for him over life. Then God said: "Are you right to be so angry because of a gourd?" He replied: "I am right to be angry, even unto death." And Jehovah said: "You are moved to pity for a gourd for which you neither labored nor made grow, which rose in one night and perished in one night. Should I not be moved by Nineveh, such a great city, in which there are more than one hundred and twenty thousand people who do not know how to distinguish their right hand from their left, and also so many cattle?"

### CHAPTER II.

10 Woe to those who devise iniquity and work evil upon their beds! When the morning is light, they practice it, because it is in the power of their hand. They covet fields and seize them, and houses, and take them away; they oppress a man and his house, even a man and his inheritance. Therefore, thus says Jehovah: Behold, against this family I am planning a disaster, from which you shall not remove your necks, nor shall you walk haughtily; for it will be a time of misery. In that day, they shall take up a proverb against you and lament with a doleful lamentation, saying: "We are utterly ruined; He has changed the portion of my people; how He has removed it from me! Instead of restoring our fields, He divides them." Therefore you shall have no one to stretch out a measuring line by lot in the assembly of Jehovah. "Do not prophesy," they say; yet if they do prophesy, let them not prophesy of such things, lest they be overtaken by disgrace. But of late my people have risen up as an enemy; you strip the robe from the garment of those who pass by securely, like men returning from war. The women of my people you have cast out from their pleasant houses; from their children you have taken away my glory forever. Arise and depart, for this is not your resting place; because it is polluted, it shall be destroyed, even with a grievous destruction. If a man walking in a false spirit should lie, saying, "I will prophesy to you of wine and strong drink," he would be the prophet for this people. I will surely assemble all of you, O Jacob, and gather the remnant of Israel; I will put them together like the sheep of Bozrah <note>original: "Bosranae," a city in Edom famous for its flocks</note>, like a flock in the midst of their fold; they shall make a great noise because of the multitude of men. The one who breaks open <note>original: "irruptor," the breaker or liberator</note> shall go up before them; they shall break through, pass the gate, and go out by it; and their king shall pass before them, with Jehovah at their head.

### CHAPTER IV.

20 <margin>Isaiah 2.</margin> Now it shall come to pass in the latter days that the mountain of the house of Jehovah shall be established on the top of the mountains, and shall be exalted above the hills; and peoples shall flow to it. How long, Jehovah, shall I cry out and you will not hear? Though I complain to you of cruelty, will you not bring aid? Why do you make me see iniquity, <margin>a</margin> why do you look upon crimes? I have destruction and injustice before my eyes, and strife and contention flourish. Therefore the law is slackened, and justice never reaches its end, because the wicked man outwits the innocent; for this reason, jurisdiction is perverted. Look among the nations and see with wonder, for a work shall be done in your time which would seem incredible to you if it were told. For I am about to raise up the Chaldeans <note>The Neo-Babylonian Empire, known for their swift military conquests</note>, a bitter and hasty nation, marching across the breadth of the earth to occupy dwellings that are not their own. That nation is horrible and terrible; its sense of justice and dignity arises only from itself. Their horses are swifter <margin>b</margin> than leopards <note>original: "tigribus" (tigers), though often translated as leopards in this biblical context</note> and keener than evening wolves; their horsemen spread out and come from afar, flying like an eagle hastening to devour. All of them come for violence, their faces set like the east wind, gathering captives <margin>b</margin> as numerous as the sand. This nation mocks kings and treats tyrants as a joke; it laughs at every fortress and captures it by heaping up earth. But eventually, his spirit swelling, he shall cross the limit and commit a crime, attributing his strength to his own god. Surely you are from of old, O Jehovah my holy God, we shall not die. I stood at my guard post and kept myself on the rampart, watching to see what he would say to me, and what I should answer to my critic. Then Jehovah answered me with these words: Write the oracle and make it plain upon tablets, so that even those who run may read it. For the oracle still refers to a future time; it speaks of the end and does not lie. If it seems slow, wait for it; for it will surely come. But as for the stubborn man, his mind is not right; yet the righteous shall live by his faith. Moreover, wine deceives the arrogant man, and he shall not endure—he who opens his throat wide like the Underworld <note>original: "Orcus"; the Roman god/realm of the dead</note> and, like insatiable death, gathers and collects all nations and peoples to himself. Surely all these shall take up a proverb against him and use a dark saying, saying: "Woe to him who piles up many things that are not his own! <margin>a</margin> How long? You are only loading yourself with a great weight of thick clay." Indeed, those who will tear you with their bites shall suddenly rise up and awaken, and you shall be their prey. Because you have plundered many nations, all the rest of the peoples shall plunder you, because of human blood and the cruelty shown to the land, to the city, and to all its inhabitants. Woe to him who gains evil profit for his house, setting his nest on high to escape misfortune. You have planned shame for your house by cutting off so many peoples, and you sin against yourself; for the stone shall cry out from the wall, and the wooden beam shall answer it from the timber. Woe to him who builds a city with blood and founds a town upon iniquity. Surely it is from Jehovah of Hosts that <margin>b</margin> the peoples labor for the fire, and the nations weary themselves for nothing. For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of Jehovah, as the waters cover the sea. Woe to him who gives his neighbors drink, adding your fury to it so that they become drunk, that you may look upon their nakedness. You are filled with disgrace rather than glory; you also drink and be exposed! The cup in Jehovah's right hand will come around to you, and shameful vomit will cover your glory. For the violence done to Lebanon shall overwhelm you, and the destruction of the terrified beasts, because of human blood and the cruelty shown to the land, to the city, and to all its inhabitants. What profit is a carved image once its maker has shaped it—a molten image and a teacher of lies—that the maker trusts in his own creation, making dumb idols? Woe to him who says to wood and to the silent stone, "Awaken and rise up!" Can it teach? Behold, it is overlaid with gold and silver, yet there is no breath within it. But Jehovah is in his holy temple; let all the earth be silent before him.

When the Holy God came from *Teman <margin>a.</margin> and from Mount Paran, Selah <note>A liturgical or musical pause</note>, his majesty covered the heavens, and the earth was filled with his praise. You marched through the land in indignation, threshing the nations in anger. With his own weapons, you pierced the head of his villages as they rushed out like a whirlwind to scatter us, with a fervor as if to secretly devour the poor. You walked through the sea with your horses, through the great mass of waters. When I heard this, my heart trembled; my lips quivered at the report; rottenness entered my bones and I trembled in my tracks, yet I will rest in the day of trouble, when he comes up against the people who will invade them. For though the fig tree shall not blossom, and there be no fruit on the vines; though the labor of the olive fails, and the fields yield no food; though the flock be cut off from the fold, and there be no cattle in the stalls: yet I will rejoice in Jehovah, I will exult in the God of my salvation. Jehovah the Lord is my strength; he will make my feet like those of a deer, and he will lead me upon my high places, to sing to my stringed instruments.

# ZEPHANIAH ►

### CHAPTER I.
#### The word of Jehovah spoken to Zephaniah the son of Cushi, the son of Gedaliah, the son of Amariah, the son of Hezekiah, in the time of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah.

Howl, you inhabitants of the <sup>d</sup> Mortar <note>original: "Molaris"; likely a marketplace or hollow district in Jerusalem</note>, for the entire merchant class is destroyed; all those burdened with money are cut off. At that time, I will search Jerusalem with <sup>e</sup> lamps and punish the men who are <sup>f</sup> settled on their dregs <note>original: "concretos foecibus"; a metaphor for spiritual stagnation, like wine left too long on its sediment</note>, who say in their hearts, "Jehovah will do neither good nor evil." Therefore, their wealth shall become a spoil and their houses a desolation; they shall build houses but not inhabit them, and they shall plant vineyards but not drink their wine. The great day of Jehovah is near, it is near and hastens greatly! The sound of the day of Jehovah is bitter; even the <sup>g</sup> warrior cries out there. That day is a day of wrath, a day of trouble and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and thick darkness, a day of the trumpet and battle cry against the fortified cities and against the <sup>h</sup> high towers. I will bring such distress upon men that they shall walk like the blind because they have sinned against Jehovah; their blood shall be poured out like dust and their flesh like dung. Neither their silver nor their gold shall be able to deliver them in the day of Jehovah's wrath; but the whole land shall be consumed by the fire of his jealousy, for he will make a swift and total end of all the inhabitants of the land.

### CHAPTER II.
Gather together and assemble, O nation not desired, before the decree is issued and the day passes like chaff, before the burning anger of Jehovah comes upon you, before the day of Jehovah's anger comes upon you. Seek Jehovah, all you humble of the earth who carry out his judgment; seek righteousness, seek humility, if perhaps you may be hidden in the day of Jehovah's anger. For <margin>a. Into captivity.</margin> <sup>a</sup> Gaza shall be forsaken and Ashkelon shall be a desolation. Ashdod shall be driven out at noon, and Ekron shall be uprooted. Woe to the inhabitants of the seacoast, the nation of the Cherethites! The word of Jehovah is against you, O merchants of the land of the Canaanites <note>original: "Palestinae"</note>; I will destroy you so that no inhabitant remains. The seacoast shall be dwellings for shepherds' huts and folds for sheep, which the remnant of the house of Judah shall possess; they shall pasture there and lie down in the houses of Ashkelon in the evening, when Jehovah their God visits them and restores them from captivity. I have heard the reproach of the Moabites and the insults of the Ammonites, with which they have taunted my people and boasted against their borders. Therefore, as I live, says

All-powerful Jehovah <note>original: "Ioua"; a Latin rendering of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton (YHWH)</note>, the God of the Israelites, declares that Moab shall be like Sodom, and the Ammonites like Gomorrah: a place of nettles, salt pits, and eternal desolation. The remnants and survivors of my people and nation shall plunder them and take possession of them. This shall happen to them because of their insolence, for they have ignominiously acted with pride against the people of all-powerful Jehovah. Jehovah will be terrible against them, for he will wipe out all the gods of the earth and ensure that everyone worships him in their own place—even all the inhabitants of the islands of the nations. You Ethiopians also shall be slain by his sword. 10 
And stretching out his hand toward the north, he will destroy Assyria <margin>Isaiah 34</margin> and reduce Nineveh to an uncultivated and deserted wasteland, so that all the wild animals of the nations shall lie down in it. Both the pelican <note>original: "onocrotali"</note> and the hedgehog shall dwell in its door-posts; their voices shall resound through the windows of those who are in <margin>d. Buildings of cedar.</margin> the light, for the <gloss>d</gloss> cedar-work shall be uncovered. Is this, then, that carefree city that lived in security, saying in her heart that she was the only one, and there was none besides her? Has she been reduced to a wasteland? A stable for wild beasts? So much so that whoever passes by her shall hiss and wave their hand. 20

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>a. Leaving no prey behind, that is, they are voracious.</margin> Woe to the rebellious and defiled, that dreadful city, which does not listen to the word, does not accept discipline, does not trust in Jehovah, and does not draw near to her God. Her princes within her are roaring lions; her judges are evening wolves <gloss>a</gloss>, leaving no bones <note>original: "exossantes"; literally "de-boning"</note> for the following day. Her prophets are reckless and treacherous men; her priests profane what is holy and violate the law. Jehovah is indeed just within her; he does no iniquity. 30 
Day by day he does not fail to bring his judgment to light; but the unjust know no shame. <margin>b. The walls.</margin> I have destroyed nations and laid waste to their <gloss>b</gloss> battlements; I made their streets desolate so that no one passes through. Their cities are so utterly seized that no inhabitant remains. I thought: surely she will fear me and accept discipline, and so her dwelling place would not be cut off, despite all the many ways I punished her. But they, instead, were eager to corrupt all their ways. Therefore, wait for me, says Jehovah, until the day when I finally rise up. 40 
For my judgment is to gather the nations and assemble the kingdoms, to pour out my fury and all the heat of my anger upon them; indeed, the whole earth shall be consumed by the fire of my zeal. # ->HAGGAI ‣<-

### CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'A' showing a seated scholar or prophet at a desk with books, surrounded by a square border of floral and architectural patterns.</image-desc>
In the second year of King Darius, on the sixth day of the first month, the word of Jehovah was delivered through the prophet Haggai to Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, the governor of Judea, and to Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, in these words. Thus says all-powerful Jehovah: This people says that the time has not yet come to rebuild the house of Jehovah. Therefore, through the work of the prophet Haggai, Jehovah speaks these words: Is it time for you to live in your paneled houses <note>original: "laqueatis ædibus"; referring to luxurious, ceiled houses</note> while this house lies in ruins? For this reason, thus says all-powerful Jehovah: Give careful thought to your ways. You sow much, but <margin>Deut. 28</margin> <margin>1 Mac. 6</margin> harvest little; you eat, but are never satisfied; you drink, but your thirst is not quenched; you clothe yourselves, but do not get warm; and he who earns wages puts them into a bag with holes. Thus says all-powerful Jehovah: give careful thought to your ways. Go up into the mountain, bring timber, and build the house; and I will take pleasure in it and be honored, says Jehovah. You looked for much, but there is little; and when you brought it home, I blew it away. Why? says all-powerful Jehovah: because of my house, which lies in ruins, while each of you runs to his own house. Therefore, the heavens have withheld the dew from you, and the earth has withheld its produce. I have called for a drought upon the land and the mountains, upon the grain, the new wine, the oil, and upon everything the ground produces, upon men, upon livestock, and upon all the labor of your hands. Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, with all the rest of the people, obeyed the voice of Jehovah their God and the words of the prophet Haggai, because Jehovah their God had sent him; and the people feared Jehovah. Then Haggai, the messenger of Jehovah, as he carried the mandate of Jehovah, spoke to the people: I am with you, says Jehovah. So Jehovah stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, the governor of Judea, and the spirit of Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest,

## CHAPTER II.

On the twenty-first day of the seventh month, Jehovah spoke through Haggai the prophet <note>original: "uatem"</note> in these words: Speak to Zerubbabel <note>original: "Zorobabelem"</note> son of Shealtiel, governor of Judea, and to Joshua <note>original: "Iosuam"</note> son of Jehozadak, the high priest <note>original: "pontificem"</note>, and to the rest of the people, saying: Who among you survivors saw this house in its former glory? As you see it now, does it not seem like nothing to you? Yet now be strong, O Zerubbabel, says Jehovah; be strong, O Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest; be strong, all you people of the land, says Jehovah, and act. For I am with you, says all-powerful Jehovah, just as I covenanted with you when you came out of Egypt, and my spirit remains among you: do not fear.

<margin>12</margin>
For thus says all-powerful Jehovah: Shortly it shall be that I will shake the heaven, the earth, the sea, and the dry land; and I will shake all nations, so that all nations shall come eagerly, and I will fill this house with glory, says all-powerful Jehovah. The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, says all-powerful Jehovah. The glory of this latter house shall be greater than the former, says all-powerful Jehovah, and in this place I will give peace, says all-powerful Jehovah.

On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, in the second year of Darius, Jehovah spoke with Haggai the prophet in this manner. Thus says all-powerful Jehovah: Ask the priests concerning the law: If someone carries holy meat in the fold of his garment, and touches with that fold bread, or stew, or wine, or oil, or any food, shall it be consecrated? No, the priests answered and said. Then Haggai said: If one who is defiled by a corpse <note>original: "exequijs"</note> touches any of these, will it be defiled? It will be defiled, the priests answered and said. Then Haggai replied: So it is with this people, and so it is with this nation before me, says Jehovah; and so is every work of their hands, so that whatever they offer there is impure. Therefore, consider from this day onward—before a stone was placed upon a stone in the temple of Jehovah—how things were: when one came to a heap of twenty measures, there were but ten; when one came to the wine vat to draw fifty vessels, there were but twenty. I struck you, even all the works of your hands, with scorching heat, mildew, and hail, yet you did not turn to me, says Jehovah. Consider from this day forward, from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month, the day the foundation of Jehovah’s temple was laid: while the seed is still in the granary <note>original: "uaginis"</note>, and the vines, the fig trees, the pomegranates, and the olive trees have not yet yielded fruit, from this day I will give fertility.

Again the word of Jehovah came to Haggai on the twenty-fourth day of the month, saying: Speak to Zerubbabel, governor of Judea, in this manner: I will shake the heavens and the earth, and I will overthrow the throne of kingdoms; I will destroy the strength of foreign kingdoms, and I will overthrow the chariots and those who ride in them, and I will cause...

## CHAPTER I.

In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius, the word of Jehovah came to Zechariah son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo, the prophet, in this manner. Jehovah was very angry with your fathers. Therefore say to them: Thus says all-powerful Jehovah: Return to me (says all-powerful Jehovah) and I will return to you, says all-powerful Jehovah. Do not be like your ancestors, to whom the former prophets cried out by the command of all-powerful Jehovah, saying that they should turn from their evil ways and intentions; but they did not listen, nor did they attend to me, says Jehovah. Your ancestors, where are they? and the prophets, do they live forever? But my words and my decrees, which I commanded my servants the prophets, did they not overtake your fathers? So that they turned and confessed: "Just as all-powerful Jehovah decreed to deal with us according to our ways and intentions, so has he dealt with us."

On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, which is the month of Shebat <note>original: "Sabat"</note>, in the second year of Darius, the word of Jehovah came to Zechariah son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo, the prophet, in this manner. I saw by night a man sitting upon a red horse, and he stood among the myrtle trees that were in the hollow <note>original: "profundo"</note>; and behind him were horses—red, speckled <note>original: "uarij"</note>, and white. "What are these, my lord?" I asked. Then the spirit <note>original: "genius"</note> who talked with me said: "I will show you what these are." And the man standing among the myrtle trees answered and said: "These are those whom Jehovah has sent to patrol the earth." And they spoke to the spirit of Jehovah standing among the myrtles, saying: "We have patrolled the earth, and behold, the whole earth is at rest." Then the spirit of Jehovah spoke: "All-powerful Jehovah, how long will you not have mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, with which you have been angry these seventy years?" And Jehovah answered the spirit who talked with me with kind and comforting words. So the spirit who talked with me said to me: Cry out these words: Thus says all-powerful Jehovah: I am moved with great zeal for Jerusalem and for Zion, and I am likewise greatly <gloss>a</gloss> angry with the complacent nations; for while I was only <gloss>b</gloss> slightly angry, <gloss>c</gloss> they helped forward the calamity.

Cry out again, saying: Thus says all-powerful Jehovah: My cities shall again overflow with prosperity, and Jehovah shall yet comfort...

When I had lifted my eyes, I noticed four horns; I said to the angel <note>original: "genio"; the guiding spirit or angel common in Zechariah’s visions</note> who was speaking with me: "What are these?" And he said to me: "These are the horns that have scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem." And when Jehovah had shown me four blacksmiths, I said: "What are these men coming to do?" And he said: "These are the horns that scattered the Jews, so much so that no one could lift his head. But these blacksmiths have come to terrify <margin>10</margin> them, to cast down the horns of the nations that lifted their horn against the land of Judah to scatter it."

### CHAPTER II.
**Likewise**, lifting my eyes, I noticed a man who had a measuring line <note>original: "amussim"; a tool for leveling or measuring</note> in his hand, and I said: "Where are you going?" And he said to me: "To measure Jerusalem, so that I may see how great its width and length shall be." And behold, the angel who was speaking with me went out; and another angel came out to meet him and said: "Run, speak with that young man in these words: 'Jerusalem shall be inhabited without walls, <margin>20</margin> because of the multitude of men and livestock that shall be in her; and I will be to her (says Jehovah) a wall of fire all around, and I will be the glory within her.' Ho, ho! Flee from the land of the north, says Jehovah; for I have scattered you through the four regions of heaven, says Jehovah. Ho, Zion! Escape, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon." For thus says the all-powerful <margin>a. To bring forth glory in punishing them. However, it is Christ speaking.</margin> Jehovah: ᵃ For the sake of glory, he has sent me to the nations that plundered you; for whoever touches you, touches the pupil of his eye. Indeed, I will shake my hand <margin>30</margin> against them, so that they become plunder for their own servants, and you shall know that I have been sent by the all-powerful Jehovah. Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion: for I will come and dwell in you, says Jehovah. And many nations shall be joined with Jehovah at that time, and they shall be my people while I dwell in you; and you shall know that I have been sent to you by the all-powerful Jehovah. And Jehovah will possess Judah as his portion in the holy land, and he will choose Jerusalem once again. Let all mortals be silent at the coming of Jehovah: for he is roused from his holy dwelling.

### CHAPTER III.
**He showed** me Joshua the high priest <note>original: "pontificem maximum"</note> standing before the angel of Jehovah, with Satan standing at his right hand to oppose him. And Jehovah said to Satan: "Jehovah rebuke you, Satan! Jehovah, who has chosen Jerusalem, rebuke you! Is this man not a brand plucked from the fire?" Now Joshua was dressed in filthy clothes as he stood before the angel, and the angel addressed those who stood before him with these words: "Take the filthy garments off him." And he said to him: "Behold, I take away your guilt from you, and I clothe you in splendid robes. Let a pure turban <note>original: "infula"; a ritual headband or miter</note> be placed upon his head," he said. So they placed the pure turban upon his head and clothed him in garments, while the angel of Jehovah stood by. The angel of Jehovah then warned Joshua with these words: "Thus says the all-powerful Jehovah: 'If you walk in my ways, and if you keep my requirements, you also shall rule my house and guard my courts, and I will give you access among these standing here.' Listen now, Joshua the high priest, you and your companions who live with you—for they

<column-break/>

are indeed ᵃ men of omen <note>original: "portentosi"; men who serve as a sign of things to come</note>: for I am about to bring <margin>a. Who portend something. See Chapter 6.</margin> my servant, the Branch <note>original: "Germen"; a Messianic title</note>. For behold the stone I have set before Joshua: upon this single stone are seven eyes; I will engrave its inscription, says the all-powerful Jehovah, and I will remove the guilt of this land in a single day. On that day (says the all-powerful Jehovah), you will invite one another to sit under the vine and under the fig tree."

### CHAPTER IV.
**Again** the angel who was speaking with me waked me, just as if someone were being waked from sleep, and he said to me: "What do you see?" I said: "I see a lampstand <note>original: "candelabrum"</note> all of gold, with a bowl <note>original: "lenticula"</note> at its top, and upon it are seven lamps, and there are seven pipes to the seven lamps on its top; and near it are two olive trees, one to the right of the bowl and the other to its left." And I questioned the angel who was speaking to me: "What are these, my lord?" And the angel answered me: "Do you not know what these are?" I said, "No, my lord." Then he answered me: "This is the command of Jehovah to Zerubbabel <note>original: "Zorobabelem"</note> in these words: 'Not by might, nor by strength, but by my spirit,' says the all-powerful Jehovah. 'Who are you, O great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you shall become a plain; and he shall bring forth the capstone <note>original: "lapidem primarium"</note> with shouts of "Grace! Grace!" to it.'" Likewise, Jehovah spoke to me thus: "The hands of Zerubbabel have founded this house, and his hands shall finish it; and you shall know that I have been sent to you by the all-powerful Jehovah. For those who despised the day of small things shall rejoice and see the plumb line <note>original: "stanneum lapidem"; literally, the tin stone</note> in the hand of Zerubbabel. These seven are the eyes of Jehovah, which range through the whole earth." Then I spoke to him: "What are these two olive trees on the right and left of the lampstand?" And questioning him again: "What are these <margin>40</margin> two olive branches, which are beside the two golden pipes that pour gold out of themselves?" And he said to me: "Do you not know what these are?" I said, "I do not know, my lord." He said: "These are the two sons of oil <note>meaning the "anointed ones"</note> who stand before the Lord of the whole earth."

### CHAPTER V.
**I lifted** my eyes again and saw a flying scroll. And he said to me: "What do you see?" I said: "I see a flying scroll, twenty cubits long and ten cubits wide." And he said to me: "This is the curse <note>original: "diritas"</note> going out over the face of the whole land. <margin>a. This passage is translated as best as it can be, for I do not understand it.

### CHAPTER VII.

In the fourth year of King Darius, the word of the Lord came to Zechariah on the fourth day of the ninth month, which is Kislev <note>original: "Casleu"; the Hebrew month roughly corresponding to December</note>. For the people of Bethel sent Sharezer and Regem-melech and their men to pray to the Lord, and to ask the priests and prophets of the house of the all-powerful Jehovah: "Should we weep in the fifth month and fast, as we have done for these many years?" Then the all-powerful Jehovah spoke to me in these words: "Say to all the people of the land and to the priests: 'When you fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh months for these seventy years, was it really for me that you fasted? Or when you ate and drank everywhere, was it not for yourselves that you ate and drank?'"

"Indeed, it is just as the Lord proclaimed through the ancient prophets, when Jerusalem was inhabited and prosperous, along with its surrounding towns, and the south and the plains were inhabited." Thus says the all-powerful Jehovah, speaking to Zechariah: "Judge with true judgment, and show mercy and kindness to one another. Do not wrong the widow, the orphan, the stranger, or the humble; and do not devise evil against one another in your hearts." But they refused to listen; they turned a stubborn shoulder and stopped their ears so as not to hear. They made their hearts as hard as adamant <note>the hardest legendary stone, often used to mean diamond</note>, so as not to hear the law and the words which the all-powerful Jehovah sent by his spirit through the work of the ancient prophets. Therefore, great wrath came from the all-powerful Jehovah. "And so, just as they did not listen when I called, I will not listen when they call," says the all-powerful Jehovah. "I will scatter them among all the nations unknown to them; the land was left desolate behind them, with no one passing through it. Thus the pleasant land was reduced to a wasteland."

### CHAPTER VIII.

Then the all-powerful Jehovah spoke in this manner. Thus says the all-powerful Jehovah: "I who pursued Zion with great force and great heat, am now reconciled to Zion," says Jehovah. "I will dwell in the middle of Jerusalem, and Jerusalem shall be called the City of Truth, and the mountain of the all-powerful Jehovah shall be the Holy Mountain." Thus says the all-powerful Jehovah: "Old men and old women shall once again stay in the streets of Jerusalem, and men shall have staves in their hands because of their great age. The streets of the city shall be filled with boys and girls playing in the streets." Thus says the all-powerful Jehovah: "If it seems difficult to the remnant of this people in that time, will it also seem difficult to me?" says the all-powerful Jehovah. Thus says the all-powerful Jehovah: "I will save my people from the land of the East and the land of the setting sun. I will lead them to inhabit Jerusalem; they shall be my people, and I will be their God, in truth and justice." Thus says the all-powerful Jehovah: "Let your hands be strong, you who hear in this time these words spoken by the mouth of the prophets, who were there when the foundations of the house of the all-powerful Jehovah were laid for the building of the temple. For before that time, there was no wage for man or beast, nor was there peace for those coming or going because of adversity, for I set all men against one another. But now I will not deal with the remnant of this people as in former times," says the all-powerful Jehovah. "For there shall be a seed of peace; the vine shall give its fruit, the earth its produce, and the heavens their dew, and I will give all these things to the remnant of this people to possess. And just as you were a curse among the nations, O descendants of Judah and Israel, so I will save you that you may be fortunate. Do not fear; let your hands be strong." For thus says the all-powerful Jehovah: "Just as I determined to bring disaster upon you when your ancestors provoked my wrath," says the all-powerful Jehovah, "and I did not relent, so now that I am reconciled, I have determined in these times..."

# THE SECOND BOOK OF ESDRAS.

#### A Note to the Reader.
> This book exists only in Latin, but in such a style that I suspect it was first made into Greek from Hebrew, and then into Latin from Greek—or at least written first in Greek by someone who thought in Hebrew, as we see happening in the New Testament. We have rendered it from the partial Latin into a more classical Latin (lest the difference in speech here should offend anyone, and simultaneously to make it clearer in some places) and have joined it with the others as various <margin>30</margin> prophecies, so that all might be held in one volume. The author himself calls this book "the second." But lest there be any trouble in citing it, since it is usually called the "fourth," let it indeed be called the fourth.

I, Ezra, saw upon Mount Zion a great multitude that I could not number, all of whom praised the Lord with songs. In their midst was a young man of tall stature, standing above them all, who placed crowns upon the heads of each of them; he himself was higher than the rest. He answered me, saying, "These are they who have put off the mortal clothing and put on the immortal, and have confessed the name of God. Now they are crowned and receive palms." Then I asked the angel, "Who is that young man who places crowns upon them and gives palms into their hands?" He answered me, "He is the Son of God, whom they confessed in their mortal life." Then I began to praise those who had stood so bravely for the name of the Lord. Then the angel said, "Go, and tell my people what kind of wonders of the Lord God you have seen, and how great they are."

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>Ezra’s complaint to God concerning the affliction of the Israelites.</margin>
In the thirtieth year after the destruction of the city, while I was in Babylonia, I was troubled as I lay upon my bed. Thoughts began to well up in my mind because I saw the desolation of Zion and the abundance of those living in Babylon. My soul was deeply vexed, and I began to address the Most High with religious words in this manner: "O Sovereign Lord, in the beginning, you alone gave the command when you founded the earth. You commanded the people—for you gave an inanimate body to Adam, which was itself the handiwork of your hands, and you breathed into him the spirit of life. When he attained life before you, you led him into the garden <note>literally "pomarium," an orchard or garden; referring to Eden</note> which your right hand had planted before the earth even existed. You commanded him to love the way of life prescribed by you, but when he neglected it, you immediately imposed death upon him and his descendants. From him were born nations, tribes, peoples, and innumerable kindreds. When each nation followed its own lusts and committed horrific acts against you, despising your precepts, you again brought a flood upon the inhabitants of the world and destroyed them. What happened to Adam in death happened to all of them by the deluge. Although...

<meta>catchword: Although</meta>

<column-break/>

486

->III. IIII.<-

...you left one of them remaining, Noah with his family, from whom all good men have sprung. But when the inhabitants of the earth began to multiply, and they had fathered many children, peoples, and nations, they began again to surpass their predecessors in impiety. Offended by their vices, you chose for yourself a man from among them named Abraham. You loved him so much that you showed your will to him alone, and establishing an eternal covenant with him, you promised that you would never desert his seed. To him you gave Isaac, and to Isaac you gave Jacob and Esau. You rejected Esau and claimed Jacob for yourself. When he had grown into a numerous offspring, you brought his progeny out of Egypt and led them to Mount Sinai. You lowered the heavens, fixed the earth, moved the world, shook the depths, and troubled the universe. Your splendor passed through the four gates of fire with earthquake, wind, and frost, so that you might give the Law to the seed of Jacob and the posterity of Israel, to be kept with diligence. Yet you did not take away their evil heart <note>The "evil heart" or "root of evil" is a central theological concept in this book, explaining why humans struggle to follow God's law.</note> so that your law might bear fruit in them. For just as the first Adam, burdened with an evil heart, transgressed and was overcome, so also were all who were born of him. This infirmity became permanent, as did the law in the souls of men, along with the wickedness of the root; and so, while the good was removed, the evil remained. Then, after a certain interval of time had passed, you raised up for yourself a servant named David, whom you commanded to build a city in your name, in which incense and offerings might be sacrificed to you. After this had been done for a long time, the inhabitants of the city went astray, imitating the deeds of Adam and all his descendants, for they too were possessed of an evil heart. Therefore, you delivered your city into the hands of your enemies. Do the Babylonians truly do better, that they should therefore rule over Zion? Indeed, when I came here and saw such innumerable crimes (for I have observed many wicked people here now for thirty years), my soul was astonished. For I saw how you endure these sinners, and spare those who act impiously, and have destroyed your own people while preserving your enemies. You have not explained why these things happen, nor does it come to my mind how this state of affairs ought to be resolved. Does Babylon do better than Zion? Or does any other nation acknowledge you besides the Israelites? Or what nations have believed your oracles as the descendants of Jacob have? Their reward does not appear, nor has their labor produced fruit. For as I travel through the nations, I see them in abundance, yet they are unmindful of your commandments. If you were to weigh our vices in a balance against those of the rest of the world’s inhabitants, your name would be found nowhere but among the Israelites. When have the inhabitants of the earth not sinned against you? Or what nation has kept your commandments so well? You will find some individuals among these who have followed your commands, but among the foreigners, you will find none."

### CHAPTER IIII.

Then the angel named Uriel, who had been sent to me, answered in this manner: "Your mind fails you in this life while you attempt to comprehend the reasoning of the Most High." I said, "It is so, my Lord." And he said, "I have been sent to show you three ways and to set before you three parables. If you can explain one of these to me, I will demonstrate to you the reasoning you desire to see, and I will teach you the source of the evil heart." And I said, "Speak, my Lord." <summary>In this passage, the angel Uriel uses parables and metaphors, such as a forest fighting the sea and a pregnant womb, to explain to the prophet Ezra that human understanding is limited to earthly matters. The text concludes with a series of apocalyptic signs—including celestial disturbances and nature turning against itself—that will herald the end of the current age of injustice.</summary>

<summary>In this passage from 4 Ezra, the prophet Ezra witnesses a grieving woman transform into a magnificent city, which the angel Uriel explains is a vision of the fallen and future glory of Zion (Jerusalem). Uriel interprets the woman's 30-year barrenness and the death of her son as historical metaphors for the time before Solomon's Temple and the eventual destruction of the city.</summary>

# BOOK IV.

<margin>A vision [of the eagle]</margin>
### CHAPTER XI.
I seemed to see in my dreams an eagle ascending from the sea, which had twelve feathered wings and three heads. I saw her spread her wings over the entire world, and all the winds of heaven blew toward her and gathered together. Then I saw contrary wings growing out of her feathers, which turned into tiny and small winglets. Her heads were resting; the middle head was larger than the others, yet it also rested with them. I saw the eagle fly with her wings and reign over the earth and its inhabitants, and everything under heaven was so subject to her that no one—none of those created on earth—opposed her. Then, while I watched, the eagle stood up on her talons and sent out a voice from her wings, saying: "Do not all wake at once; sleep each in your own place, and wake at a fixed time; but let the heads be preserved for the end." I noticed that the voice did not come from her heads, but from the middle of her body. I counted her contrary wings, and I found eight of them. Then I saw one wing rise on the right side, which ruled over the whole world. And while it was ruling, its end came, so that its place appeared no more. Then the next one stood up and ruled, and it held power for a long time. While it was ruling, its end also came, so that it vanished like the first one. Then a voice was sent to it, saying: "Listen, you who have held the world for so long: I announce this to you before you begin to vanish. No one after you shall hold your position for your length of time, nor even for half of it." <note>This refers to Augustus Caesar, whose long reign (the Pax Romana) was never matched in duration by his immediate successors.</note> Then the third appeared, and after it held the leadership as the others had, it also vanished. And the same happened to all the others one by one, as they took leadership and then faded away. Then, as I watched in the intervals of time, the following wings were raised on the right side to hold the leadership themselves, and among these were some that held power but immediately vanished; some of them were raised but did not obtain the leadership. After this, I noticed that the twelve wings and two winglets were no longer there, and nothing remained of the eagle’s body except the two resting heads and six winglets. Then I saw two of the six winglets separate and remain under the head that was on the right side, while four remained in their place. Then I saw the under-wings rise up and attempt to seize the leadership; one was raised, but immediately vanished; and the following ones vanished even more quickly than the first. Then I saw the two that remained attempting to reign between themselves, and while they were attempting this, the larger of the two heads woke up. Then I noticed the two heads joined together, and the head turned with its companions and devoured the two under-wings that were striving for the kingdom. This head terrified the whole world and governed the inhabitants of the earth with much oppression; it held power over the inhabitants of the world in the last times. And so I slept that night and the following one, just as he had commanded me.

<column-break/>

above all the wings that had been before. Afterward, I saw the middle head also suddenly vanish, just as the wings had, with the two heads remaining, which themselves likewise held the kingdom over the world and its inhabitants. Then I noticed the head on the right side devour the one on the left, and I heard a voice saying to me: "Look in front of you, and consider what you see." And I saw something like a lion, roused and roaring out of the forest, who spoke to the eagle with a human voice. <note>The lion is a traditional symbol for the Messiah, the "Lion of Judah," who comes to judge the corrupt worldly powers.</note> "Listen," he said, "while I speak to you by the command of the Most High. You are surely the one remaining of the four animals <note>original: "quatuor animalibus"; a reference to the four beasts in Daniel chapter 7.</note> to whom I gave rule over my world, so that through them the end of those times might come. You, the fourth to arise, have overcome all the animals that came before, and you have held the world's age in your power with great terror, and the whole world with the heaviest oppression. For so long a time you have inhabited the world with fraud, and you have not ruled men with justice. For you have harassed the peaceful, injured the quiet, loved liars, destroyed the dwellings of the honest, and torn down the walls of those who did you no harm. Therefore, your insult and pride have reached the Most High, and the Most High has looked upon these proud times—and behold, they are finished, and your crimes are fulfilled. Therefore, perish, you eagle, with your horrible wings, your wicked little feathers, your evil heads, your most cruel talons, and finally with all that worthless body of yours, so that the whole world may be refreshed and, free from your violence, may hope for the justice and mercy of its Creator."

### CHAPTER XII.
Meanwhile, as the lion was speaking these words to the eagle, I noticed the remaining head vanish, as well as the four wings that had moved to it and risen to reign, whose kingdom had been meager and full of turmoil. I saw them perish, I say, and the whole body of the eagle catch fire, while the world trembled violently. At this, because of the disturbance, the loss of my senses, and heavy fear, I woke up and spoke thus within my heart: "Behold, you are the cause of this for me, you who search out the ways of the Most High. Since I am so weary in spirit and weak in mind that there is not even a little strength in me due to the great fear with which I have been struck this night, I will pray to the Most High that he may strengthen me to the end."

<margin>Ezra asks God for the interpretation of the vision.</margin>

Then he said: "This is the interpretation of this vision. The eagle you saw ascending from the sea is the kingdom that was shown to your brother Daniel in a vision, but was not then explained; therefore, I will now interpret it for you. It shall come to pass that a kingdom will exist in the world whose terror will be sharper than all the kingdoms that went before it. In it,

As for the three resting heads you saw, this is the meaning: In its last days, the Most High shall raise up three kingdoms, and he shall bring back many things into them, and they shall rule over the earth and its inhabitants with greater oppression than any who came before them. Afterward, I saw that all who had gathered to fight him were greatly afraid, yet they dared to fight. All of these were mixed together—the blast of fire, the flaming breath, and the great storm—and they fell with violence upon the multitude that was prepared to fight, and burned them all up. Suddenly, of the innumerable multitude, nothing remained except the dust of ashes and the smell of smoke. When I saw this, I was terrified.

Unhappy one, you shall travel through the seas and suffer evils again. In passing, they shall crush the slaughtered city and destroy some portion of your land and abolish part of your glory, when they return from the overthrown Babylon. And you, being destroyed, shall be like straw for them, and they shall be as fire to you. They shall consume you, your cities, your land, your mountains, all your forests, and your fruitful trees; they shall burn them with fire. They shall lead your children away as captives, take your wealth as plunder, and destroy the glory of your face.

### CHAPTER XVI.

**W**oe to you, Babylon and Asia! Woe to you, Egypt and Syria! Gird yourselves with sackcloth <note>original: "centonibus & cilicijs" - traditional garments of mourning and repentance</note> and hair-shirts; lament your children and grieve, for your destruction is at hand. The sword is sent against you—who may turn it back? Fire is sent against you—who may extinguish it? Evils are sent against you—who may drive them away?

<meta>catchword: shirts</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>510</page-num>

Who can drive away a hungry lion in the forest? Or who can extinguish a fire in the straw once it has begun to burn? Who can turn back an arrow shot by a strong archer? When the mighty Lord sends evils, who shall drive them away? Who can quench the fire when it breaks out from His anger? Who shall not fear when He lightens? Who shall not tremble when He thunders? When the Lord threatens, who shall not be utterly crushed at His sight? The earth trembles from its foundations; the sea stirs up waves from its depths. Both its waves and its fish are disturbed at the sight of the Lord and the glory of His power. For His right hand, which bends the bow, is strong; the sharp arrows He shoots shall not fail when they begin to be sent to the ends of the earth. Behold, evils are sent forth and shall not be recalled, but shall invade the earth. The fire is kindled and shall not be extinguished until it consumes the foundations of the earth. Just as an arrow shot by a mighty archer does not return, so the evils sent upon the earth shall not be recalled. Woe is me! Woe is me! Who will defend me in those times? Many sorrows and groans are coming; much famine and destruction are coming; wars are coming that shall terrify the powers; evils are coming at which everyone shall tremble. What shall I do in those evils when they arrive? Famine, slaughter, calamity, and distress shall be sent as scourges for the correction of life, yet for all these things people will not turn away from their crimes, nor will they ever be mindful of the scourges. Behold, there shall be such cheapness of provisions <note>original: "annonae uilitas" - a deceptive period of plenty that precedes a final collapse</note> on the earth that men will think peace is prepared for them. Then evils shall sprout upon the earth: the sword, famine, and great confusion, so that many of the inhabitants of the earth shall perish from hunger, and the sword shall destroy the rest who survive the famine. The dead shall be cast out like dung, and there shall be no one to comfort them. For the earth shall be left desolate, and its cities shall be overthrown, with no one left to till the earth or sow it. The trees shall give fruit which no one shall gather; the grapes shall become ripe which no one shall tread. There shall be such a solitude in those places that <margin>a. Therefore the earth shall be left desolate; its fields shall grow wild, and all its ways and paths shall bring forth thorns, because no men shall travel through them. Bridegrooms shall mourn for lack of brides; women shall mourn for lack of husbands; their daughters shall mourn because they have no help, for their bridegrooms have been consumed in war and their husbands destroyed by famine. ### CHAPTER I.

<margin>Alexander the Great.</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'A' depicting a landscape with a building and figures, including a seated person and someone approaching them.</image-desc> **A**lexander, son of Philip the Macedonian, coming from the land of Kittim <note>original: "Chethim" - an ancient term referring to the islands or coastlines of the Mediterranean, particularly Cyprus or Greece.</note>, was the first king of Greece. After he defeated Darius, king of the Persians, and occupied his kingdom, he waged many wars, captured fortified places, and slaughtered the kings of the earth. He advanced to the ends of the earth and plundered many nations. When the world became quiet and subject to him, he became arrogant and his heart was puffed up. Having gathered a very strong army, he ruled over regions, nations, and tyrants, and imposed tribute upon them. Afterward, he fell ill, and realizing that death was near, he summoned his noble attendants, who had been brought up with him from childhood, and divided his kingdom among them while he was still alive. After he had reigned twelve years, he died. When he was dead, his successors each took control of his own place and all put on crowns, as did their descendants for many years. From them—while evils abounded in the world—arose a wicked root, Antiochus Epiphanes <note>Antiochus IV Epiphanes, a Seleucid king known for his brutal persecution of the Jews.</note>, 
<margin>Antiochus Epiphanes</margin>
son of King Antiochus, who had been a hostage at Rome. He began to reign in the one hundred and thirty-seventh year of the kingdom of the Greeks.

On the twenty-fifth day of the month, they sacrificed upon the altar which was set upon the altar of God. According to the edict, they put to death the women who had caused their children to be circumcised, hanging the infants around their necks, and they plundered their houses and killed those who had circumcised them. Howbeit many in Israel were fully resolved and confirmed in themselves not to eat any unclean thing. They chose rather to die, that they might not be defiled with meats and that they might not profane the holy covenant; and so they died.

And behold, our sanctuary, even our beauty and our glory, is laid waste, and the Gentiles have profaned it. To what end should we live any longer?" Seeing this, Mattathias was filled with indignation, and his heart trembled. Driven by a spirit of vengeance, he ran forward and slaughtered the man upon the altar. At that same moment, he killed the king's officer who was forcing them to sacrifice, and he tore down the altar. He was inspired by a zeal for the Law, just as Phinehas <note>A biblical figure from the Book of Numbers who killed an Israelite for idolatry</note> had done to Zimri the son of Salu. Then he cried out through the town with a great voice, saying: "Let everyone who is zealous for the Law and maintains the covenant follow me!" He then fled with his sons into the mountains, leaving behind all his possessions in the town. At that time, many who sought virtue and righteousness went into the wilderness so they could live there with their children, wives, and cattle, since they were weighed down by so many evils.

<margin>
The Jews, refusing to fight on the Sabbath, are killed.
</margin>
When it was reported to the king's men and the soldiers who were in the City of David at Jerusalem that men who had violated the king's command had withdrawn into hiding places in the wilderness, many pursued them. Having caught up with them, they besieged them and prepared for battle on the Sabbath day. They urged them to stop their resistance and come out to obey the king's orders so that they might live. But they refused to come out, saying they would not obey the king nor profane the Sabbath day. And though they were pressed in battle, they neither answered their adversaries, nor threw stones at them, nor blocked up their hiding places. Instead, they encouraged one another to die in their innocence, calling heaven and earth to witness that they were being killed unjustly. Thus, attacked by arms on the Sabbath, they perished along with their wives, children, and cattle, numbering about a thousand people.

The followers of Mattathias resolve to fight even on the Sabbath.

After Mattathias and his friends learned of this, they mourned for them greatly. They began to say to one another: "If we all do as our brothers have done, and do not fight against the foreign nations for our lives and our laws, they will soon wipe us off the face of the earth." Therefore, they decided on that day that whoever

The company of the Hasideans.

Then the company of the Hasideans <note>original: "Asidæorum" — a group of "pious ones" dedicated to strict observance of the Law</note> joined them. These were the mightiest of the Israelites, as many as were devoted to the Law. All those who were fleeing from the many evils joined them as well. Strengthened by these people, they formed an army and, inflamed by anger, they struck down the wicked and lawless men. While the survivors fled to foreign lands to seek safety, Mattathias and his friends went around tearing down altars. They forcibly circumcised any uncircumcised boys they found within the borders of Israel. They hunted down the arrogant men, and as the work prospered in their hands, they rescued the Law from the hands of the Gentiles and the kings; they did not allow the sinner to triumph.

<margin>
Mattathias encourages his sons to defend the Law.
</margin>
Finally, as the day of his death drew near, Mattathias spoke to his sons in this way: "Now pride, punishment, the time of destruction, and fierce anger prevail. Therefore, my sons, defend the Law and give up your lives for the covenant of our ancestors. Remember the deeds our ancestors did in their generations, and you will achieve great glory and an everlasting name. Was not Abraham found faithful in temptation, and it was credited to him as righteousness? Joseph, in his time of trouble, kept the commandment and became lord of Egypt. Phinehas, our forefather, through his great zeal, obtained the covenant of an everlasting priesthood. Joshua, by fulfilling his office, became a leader in Israel. Caleb, for the testimony he gave before the assembly, received a possession of land. David, for his mercy, inherited the throne of the kingdom forever. Elijah, for his great zeal for the Law, was taken up into heaven. Ananias, Azarias, and Misael <note>The three youths in the book of Daniel who survived the fiery furnace</note>, by having faith, were delivered from the flame. Daniel, by his integrity, was defended from the mouths of lions. Finally, consider this: in no generation has anyone who trusted in God been defeated. Do not fear the words of a wicked man, for his glory shall turn to dung and worms. Today he is exalted, but tomorrow he will not be found; he returns to his dust, and his schemes come to nothing. But you, my sons, be strong in the Law and act like men, for through it you will achieve glory. Behold, your brother Simeon—I know him to be a man of counsel; always listen to him. He shall be a father to you. And Judas Maccabeus, a man of excellent strength from his youth, shall be the leader of your army in conducting the people's war. Gather to yourselves all who obey the Law, avenge the wrongs of your people, repay the foreigners in kind, and pay heed to the precepts of the Law." Having said these things, he blessed them and was gathered to his ancestors. He died in the one hundred and forty-sixth year <note>Approximately 166 BCE</note> and was buried by his sons in Modein in the tomb of his fathers. All Israel mourned him with great lamentation.

When the survivors fled to foreign nations for safety, Mattathias and his friends went around and tore down the altars. They forcibly circumcised the uncircumcised boys they found within the borders of Israel. They hunted down the arrogant men, and the work prospered in their hands. Thus they rescued the law from the hands of the Gentiles and the kings, and they did not let the 

<margin>Mattathias encourages his sons to defend the Law.</margin>
sinner triumph. Now when the time drew near for Mattathias to die, he spoke to his sons in this way: "Now pride, oppression, the time of destruction, and fierce anger have grown strong. Therefore, my sons, be zealous for the law, and give your lives for the covenant of our ancestors. Remember the deeds our ancestors did in their generations, and you shall receive great honor and an everlasting name. Was not Abraham found faithful in temptation, and it was credited to him as righteousness? Joseph, in his time of distress, kept the commandment and became lord of Egypt. Phinehas our father, through his great zeal, received the covenant of an everlasting priesthood. Joshua, by fulfilling his mission, became a leader in Israel. Caleb, for the testimony he gave before the assembly, received an inheritance in the land. David, for his mercy, inherited the throne of the kingdom forever. Elijah, because of his great zeal for the law, was taken up into heaven. Ananias, Azarias, and Misael <note>Better known by their Babylonian names: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.</note>, by having faith, were saved from the flame. Daniel, in his integrity, was delivered from the mouths of the lions. And so, consider throughout all generations that none who trust in God shall be overcome. Do not fear the words of a sinful man, for his glory shall turn to dung and worms; today he is exalted, and tomorrow he is nowhere to be found, for he has returned to the dust and his scheme has come to nothing. But you, my sons, be strong and show yourselves men in behalf of the law, for by it you shall gain glory. Behold your brother Simon, whom I know to be a man of counsel; always listen to him; he shall be a father to you. But Judas Maccabaeus, a man of great strength from his youth, shall be your commander in war and lead the people in battle. Gather to yourselves all who obey the law, and avenge the wrongs done to your people. Pay back the Gentiles in full, and heed the precepts of the law." After he had blessed them, he was gathered to his ancestors. He died in the one hundred and forty-sixth year <note>Approximately 166 BCE.</note>, and was buried by his sons

## CHAPTER III.

Then his son Judas, called Maccabeus <note>The nickname "Maccabeus" likely comes from the Aramaic word for "hammer," reflecting his role as a military striker.</note>, rose up in his place. All of his kinsmen and everyone who had joined his father supported him, and they carried on the war for Israel with great spirit. He increased the glory of his people, Judas, putting on his breastplate like a giant. Girded in his battle armor, he fought many engagements, protecting his camp with his sword. In his deeds, he was like a lion, or like a young lion roaring as it hunts its prey. He hunted down the lawless, searching them out, and those who troubled his people he burned with fire. The wicked shrunk back for fear of him, and all evildoers were thrown into confusion as success followed his victories. He provoked many kings to anger, but he brought joy to the people of Jacob <note>original: "Iacobeos" — referring to the descendants of the patriarch Jacob, i.e., the Israelites</note> by his deeds, and he has left behind a memory blessed forever. He traveled through the cities of Judea, destroying the ungodly there and turning away the wrath of God from the Israelites. His name became known even to the ends of the earth.

<margin><unclear>Judas</unclear> defeats Apollonius.</margin>
When Apollonius <note>The Seleucid governor of Samaria</note> gathered a massive army from both foreign nations and from Samaria to wage war against the Israelites, Judas learned of it and went out to meet him. Judas defeated and killed him; many others fell, and the rest fled. He took their spoils, including the sword of Apollonius, which he used in battle for the rest of his life. Then Seron, the commander of the Syrian army, heard that Judas had gathered a loyal band of faithful men to go to war. He decided to win fame and glory for himself in the kingdom by defeating Judas and his followers, who treated the king’s command with contempt. He set out with a powerful army of godless men to assist him in taking revenge on the Israelites. When he approached the ascent of Beth-horon, Judas went out to meet him with only a few men. But when those with Judas saw the army marching against them, they said to Judas, "How can we, so few and exhausted by fasting today, fight against such a powerful multitude?" Judas replied to them in this manner:

<margin>Judas encourages his men.</margin>
> It is easy for many to be overcome by a few. In the eyes of the God of Heaven, there is no difference between saving by many or by few. For victory in battle does not depend on the size of the army, but strength comes from Heaven. They come against us with a shameful and wicked multitude to destroy us, our wives, and our children, and to plunder us. But we fight for our lives and our laws. God himself will crush them before us; do not be afraid of them.

<margin>Seron is defeated by Judas</margin>
When he had finished speaking, he suddenly charged the enemy. Seron and his army were defeated, and Judas pursued them down the slopes of Beth-horon into the plain. About eight hundred of their men fell; the rest fled into the land of the Philistines <note>original: "Palaestinam" — referring here to the coastal plains held by the Philistines</note>. Then a great fear and terror of Judas and his brothers began to seize the surrounding nations, so that his name reached the ears of the king, and all the nations spoke of Judas's victories. When King Antiochus heard these things, he was enraged and sent orders to assemble all the forces of his kingdom—a truly massive army. He opened his treasury and paid his soldiers a year's wages in advance, ordering them to be ready for any

The king himself, taking the other half of the army, set out from Antioch, the capital of his kingdom, in the one hundred and forty-seventh year <note>Approximately 165 BCE in the Seleucid calendar</note>. After crossing the Euphrates, he traveled through the upper provinces. They set out with their entire force and made camp near Emmaus in the plains. They were joined by soldiers from Syria and the lands of the foreigners. But Judas and his brothers saw that the evil was increasing and that armies were camped within their borders. Knowing the king's command to utterly destroy the people, they encouraged one another to push back the ruin of their people and to fight for them and for the sanctuary. So a great multitude gathered to be ready for war and to beg for grace and mercy from God.

Joy had been taken away from the people of Jacob, and the flute and the harp were silent. Therefore, they gathered at Maspha <note>Mizpah, a traditional place of prayer near Jerusalem</note>, a place opposite Jerusalem that had formerly been a place of prayer for Israel. There they fasted that day, put on sackcloth, sprinkled ashes on their heads, and tore their clothes. They opened the Book of the Law—those books which the foreigners searched so they could paint the likenesses of their idols in them <note>A reference to the Seleucids attempting to "paganize" Jewish scriptures with images</note>. They brought out the priestly vestments, the first-fruits, and the tithes, and they brought forward certain Nazarites <note>People who had taken a vow of separation to God, whose hair was left uncut</note> who had completed their period of consecration. # CHAPTER III.

<margin>On the deeds of Maccabeus.</margin>
And Judas, who was surnamed Maccabeus <note>The name "Maccabeus" is often thought to mean "The Hammer" (Aramaic: *maqqaba*).</note>, succeeded him. He was Mattathias’s son, and all his kinsmen and those who had remained loyal to his father supported him; thus they carried on the war for the Israelites with great spirit. He increased the glory of the people of Judah, putting on his breastplate like a giant. Girded with his weapons of war, he fought battles, protecting the camp with his sword. In his deeds, he was like a lion, or like a lion's cub roaring for its prey. He hunted down and tracked the wicked, and those who troubled his people he burned with fire. The wicked shrunk back for fear of him, and all the evildoers were thrown into confusion. Because victory was achieved through him, he provoked many kings, but delighted the house of Jacob <note>original: "Iacobeos" — referring to the descendants of the patriarch Jacob, i.e., the Israelites</note> with his deeds, leaving behind a noble memory of himself forever. Furthermore, by traveling through the cities of Judea and destroying the ungodly there, he turned away the wrath of God from the Israelites. His name became known even to the ends of the earth.

<margin>Judas defeats Apollonius.</margin>
When Apollonius <note>The Seleucid governor of Samaria</note> gathered a large army from both the foreign nations and from Samaria to wage war against the Israelites, Judas learned of it and went out to meet him. He defeated and killed him; many were slain, while the rest fled, and Judas took their spoils. Among the loot was the sword of Apollonius, which Judas used in battle for the rest of his life.

<margin>Seron attacks Judas.</margin>
Then Seron, the commander of the Syrian army, heard that Judas had gathered a band of faithful men to go to war with him. He decided to win fame and glory for himself in the kingdom by defeating Judas and those with him, who held the king’s command in contempt. Therefore, he set out with a powerful army of the ungodly to help him take vengeance on the Israelites. When he approached the ascent of Beth-horon <note>A strategic mountain pass on the road from the coast to Jerusalem</note>, Judas went out to meet him with only a few men. But when those with Judas saw the army marching against them, they said to him: "How can we, being so few and exhausted by fasting today, fight against such a powerful multitude?"

<margin>Judas encourages his men.</margin>
Judas answered them with this sentiment: "It is easy for many to be overcome by a few. In the eyes of the God of Heaven, there is no difference between saving by many or by few. For victory in war does not reside in the size of an army, but rather strength comes from Heaven. They come against us with a lawless and arrogant multitude to destroy us, our wives, and our children, and to plunder us. But we fight for our lives and our laws. God himself will crush them before us; therefore, do not fear them."

<margin>Seron is slain by Judas.</margin>
When he had finished this speech, he suddenly rushed upon the enemy. Seron and his army were defeated, and Judas pursued them down the slope of Beth-horon into the plain. About eight hundred of their men fell; the rest fled into the land of the Philistines <note>original: "Palæstinam"</note>. Then a great fear and terror of Judas and his brothers began to fall upon the neighboring nations, so that his name reached the ears of the king, and all the nations spoke of Judas’s victories. When King Antiochus heard these things, he was furious. He sent out orders to assemble all the forces of his kingdom, which was an immense army. Opening his treasury, he paid the soldiers'

<column-break/>

wages for a year and commanded them to be ready for any need throughout that year. However, he saw that the money in his treasury was failing and that the tribute from the provinces was small because of the rebellion and the disaster he had caused in the land by abolishing the ancient laws. He feared that he would not have enough (as he had once or twice before) for his expenses and the gifts he used to give with a lavish hand—for he had surpassed previous kings in his generosity. He was greatly troubled in his mind.

<margin>Antiochus Epiphanes sets out for Persia, leaving Lysias to take vengeance on the Jews.</margin>

He handed over to Lysias half of his forces and the elephants. He gave him instructions concerning everything he wanted done, especially regarding the inhabitants of Judea and Jerusalem: that he should send an army against them to crush and destroy the strength of Israel and the remnant of Jerusalem, to blot out their memory from that place, and to settle colonies of foreigners in all their territories, distributing the land to them by lot. The king himself, taking the remaining half of the forces, departed from Antioch, the capital of his kingdom, in the one hundred and forty-seventh year <note>165 BCE by the Seleucid calendar</note>. After crossing the Euphrates, he traveled through the upper provinces. Meanwhile, Lysias chose Ptolemy the son of Dorymenes, Nicanor, and Gorgias—mighty men among the "Friends of the King"—and sent them with forty thousand infantry and seven thousand cavalry into Judea to lay it waste, as the king had commanded. They set out with all their forces and camped near Emmaus in the plain. When the local merchants heard the news of them, they took a vast amount of silver and gold, along with servants, and came to the camp to buy the Israelites as slaves. They were joined by forces from Syria and the land of the foreigners. But Judas and his brothers saw that the evil was increasing and that armies were camped within their borders. Knowing the king’s command to destroy the people utterly, they encouraged one another to restore the ruins of their people and to fight for them and for the sanctuary. So a great multitude gathered to be ready for battle and to ask for grace and mercy from God.

The sanctuary was trampled down, the citadel was a dwelling for foreigners and Gentiles, joy was taken away from the house of Jacob, and the flute and the harp were silent. Therefore, they gathered at Mizpah <note>original: "Maspha" — a place of traditional religious assembly near Jerusalem</note>, which is a place opposite Jerusalem where the Israelites had formerly gone for prayer. There they fasted that day, put on sackcloth <note>original: "centonibus" — rough garments signifying mourning</note>, sprinkled dust on their heads, and tore their clothes. They opened the Book of the Law (which the foreigners used to search so they could paint the likenesses of their idols in them). They brought out the priestly garments, the firstfruits, and the tithes, and summoned certain Nazirites <note>Consecrated people who had taken a vow of separation to God</note> who had completed their days of dedication.
