OF THE MACCABEES

<margin>a. Namely, for the Nazirites. <note>Nazirites were Israelites who took a vow of consecration to God, abstaining from wine and letting their hair grow. During the occupation, they were unable to complete their rituals at the Temple.</note></margin>
<gloss>a</gloss> What shall we do with these? Or where shall we lead them? Since our sanctuary has been trampled and profaned, and your priests live in mourning and misery; and moreover, foreign nations have gathered together to destroy us. You know well what they plot against us; how will we be able to withstand them unless you help us? Then they sounded the trumpets and let out a great cry.

<margin>Judas organizes his military affairs.</margin>
Afterward, Judas appointed leaders of the army: tribunes <note>commanders of a thousand</note>, centurions <note>commanders of a hundred</note>, leaders of fifty, and leaders of ten. Then he proclaimed to those who were fearful that they should return home, as the Law required. <note>According to Deuteronomy 20:5-8, those who were afraid or had new domestic obligations were exempt from military service.</note> Then, having moved the camp and positioned it to the south of Emmaus, he encouraged his men in this way: "Gird yourselves and show yourselves to be brave; be ready in the morning to fight against these nations that have gathered to destroy us and our sanctuary. For it is better for us to die in battle than to see the ruin of our nation and our holy things. However, as it seems fit to Him who is in heaven, so let Him do."

### CHAPTER IV.

But Gorgias, taking five thousand infantry and a thousand chosen cavalry, departed from the camp by night so that, by attacking the camp of the Jews unexpectedly, he might cut them down, using those who were in the citadel as his guides. When Judas learned of this, he set out with his soldiers to crush the king’s forces stationed at Emmaus while a portion of the enemy soldiers was away from their camp. After Gorgias reached the camp of the Jews at night and found no one, he began to search for them in the mountains, suspecting that they had fled.

<margin>Judas, about to engage with the enemy, strengthens his men.</margin>
But at daybreak, Judas appeared in the plain with three thousand men; they were not as well protected with armor and swords as they wished, and they noticed the column of the foreigners was strongly armored, surrounded by cavalry, and experienced in war. Judas spoke to his men thus: "Do not fear their multitude, nor be terrified by their assault. Remember in what manner our ancestors escaped from the Red Sea when Pharaoh pursued them with his forces. Therefore, let us call upon the God of heaven; if perhaps He will have mercy on us and remember the covenant of our fathers, He will crush that army before us today, and He will make it so all the nations know that there is one who redeems and defends Israel." Then the foreigners, seeing them coming against them, came out from the camp to battle. The Jews, giving the signal with the trumpet, engaged in conflict. The foreigners were routed and turned to flight through the fields; those at the rear were cut down by the sword, and they pursued them as far as Azotus and the plains of Idumea, Ashdod, and Jamnia. Then returning from pursuing them, Judas with his forces—having killed about three thousand of the adversaries—spoke to his men thus: "Do not covet the plunder. For war stands against us, and Gorgias with his army is in the mountain near us; but stand now against our enemies and defeat them, so that afterward you may gather the spoils in safety." While Judas was still speaking these things,

<column-break/>

a part of Lysias's force was seen appearing from the mountain. When they noticed their own men turned to flight and the camp set on fire by the Jews (for the smoke that was seen indicated what had happened), they were greatly terrified. Then, seeing Judas's column in the plain ready for conflict, they all fled into foreign regions. Judas then returned to the plundering of the camp, in which they obtained much gold, silver, turquoise, and sea-purple <note>original: "purpuræ marinæ"—Tyrian purple, a precious dye extracted from sea snails</note>, and great riches. Returning, they praised the God of heaven and gave thanks to Him, because He is good and His mercy is forever. And the victory of that day was a glorious one for the Israelites. Those of the foreigners who had escaped went to Lysias and reported to him what had happened. When he heard this matter, he was confused and angry, because things had not turned out for the Israelites as he wished, nor as the king had commanded him.

<margin>Judas, about to fight with the inferior army of Lysias, implores God.</margin>
Therefore, in the following year, Lysias gathered sixty thousand chosen men and five thousand cavalry to invade Jerusalem in war; he came into Idumea and made camp at Beth-zur. Judas went to meet them with ten thousand men, and having noticed the strength of their forces, he prayed with these words: "Thanks be to you, Savior of Israel, who broke the assault of that powerful man by the hand of your servant David, and delivered the camp of the foreigners into the hands of Jonathan son of Saul and his armor-bearer. Hand over this army also to your people Israel, that they may be ashamed of their strength and their cavalry. Strike them with fear, and melt the boldness of their strength, so that they may be shaken by their own slaughter. Cast them down by the swords of those who love you, so that everyone who knows your name may praise you with songs." So the battle was joined, and about five thousand men of Lysias's army fell. Then Lysias, seeing his battle line turned and seeing how great the boldness of the Jews was—that they were prepared either to live or to die nobly—departed to Antioch. There he held a recruitment of mercenaries, and having increased the army, he planned to march into Judea again with those reinforcements.

<margin>Judas goes to purify the temple.</margin>
But Judas and his brothers decided, after the enemies had been routed, to go to purify and dedicate the sanctuary. Having gathered the whole army, they went up to Mount Zion, where they saw the sanctuary deserted, the altar profaned, the gates burned, and bushes growing in the courtyards as in a forest or on some mountain, and the chambers destroyed. Tearing their clothes, they let out a great lamentation, and having sprinkled their heads with dust, they fell prostrate on the ground. At the sounding of the signal trumpets, they cried out to heaven. Then Judas assigned certain men the task of fighting those who were in the citadel <note>original: "arce" — referring to the Acra, a Seleucid fortress overlooking the Temple</note> until he had purified the sanctuary. He chose blameless priests, devoted to the Law, who cleansed the holy place and carried away the polluted stones to an unclean place. While they were deliberating what they should do with the altar of burnt offerings which had been profaned, the thought conveniently came to them to tear it down, lest perhaps it become a reproach to them because the foreigners had contaminated it. Therefore, they tore down the altar and put the stones on the temple mount in a convenient...

at a suitable time, they put [the defiled stones] aside until a prophet should come who might give an oracle concerning them. Having taken whole stones, as the law required, they built a new altar similar to the previous one. They restored the sanctuary, the inner parts of the temple, the courtyards, and everything else. They fashioned new holy vessels: they brought the lampstand <note>the Menorah</note>, the altar for burnt offerings, the incense altar, and the table into the temple. They burned incense at the altar, lit the lamps on the lampstand, and illuminated the temple. They placed the bread on the table and hung the curtains. When all these things were finished, as soon as they rose in the morning on the twenty-fifth day of the month of Kislev <note>original: "Casleu," the ninth month of the Hebrew calendar, roughly December</note>, in the one hundred and forty-eighth year <note>This refers to the Seleucid era, corresponding to 164 BCE</note>, they performed the sacrifice according to the law upon the new altar of burnt offerings they had made. This occurred at the same time and on the same day on which it had been profaned by foreigners. On that same day, it was dedicated with songs, harps, lutes, and cymbals. All the people fell prostrate and reverently gave thanks to the God of heaven, who had been favorable to them. They celebrated the dedication of the altar for eight days, joyfully offering burnt sacrifices and sacrifices for deliverance and praise. Then they adorned the front of the temple with golden crowns and small shields; they restored the gates and the side chambers and replaced their doors. There was great joy among the people because the disgrace brought by the foreigners had been removed. Therefore, Judas and his brothers, and the entire assembly of Israel, decreed that the days of the dedication of the altar should be observed every year at their proper time for eight days, starting from the twenty-fifth day of the month of Kislev, with joy and gladness. At that same time, they fortified Mount Zion with a high wall and strong towers on all sides, lest the foreigners should come and devastate it as they had done before. They stationed a garrison of soldiers there and fortified the mountain to defend Beth-zur, so they might have a defense against Idumea.

### CHAPTER V.

<margin>Judas takes vengeance on the Idumeans, the Baeanites, and the Ammonites.</margin>
When the neighboring nations heard that the altar had been rebuilt and the sanctuary restored to its former state, they were so deeply angered that they decided to destroy the race of Jacob living among them. They began to kill and destroy them, but Judas waged war against the descendants of Esau, the Acrabattenes in Idumea <note>a region south of Judea</note>, because they were besieging the Israelites. He restrained them by inflicting a great slaughter and plundered them. Next, remembering the injury caused by the Baeanites—who would lie in wait along the roads to cause loss and harm to the Israelites—he drove them into their towers. Having brought his army against them, he devoted them to destruction and burned the towers with everyone who was inside them. From there, he marched against the Ammonites and encountered a strong force and a numerous army led by Timothy. He engaged in many battles with them, and after they were routed and defeated, he occupied Jazer and its surrounding villages. Later, after he returned to Judea, the people of Gilead gathered to destroy the Israelites living in their territories. The Israelites fled into the fortress of Dathema and sent a letter to Judas and his brothers to this effect:

<column-break/>

<margin>The Jews from Bozrah seek help by letter.</margin>
"Our neighbors have gathered against us to destroy us, and they are preparing to come and seize the fortress into which we have fled, with Timothy leading the army. Therefore, come to defend us from their injury, for many of our people have fallen. All our kinsmen who were in the land of Tob <note>original: "Tubini"</note> have been killed; their wives, children, and property have been taken into captivity, and about a thousand men have died there." While the letters were still being read, behold, other messengers arrived from Galilee with their clothes torn, reporting similar news: that the people of Ptolemais, Tyre, Sidon, and all the foreigners of Galilee had gathered to wipe them out. When Judas and the rest heard this, a great assembly was called to consult on what should be done for their kinsmen who were in such distress and were being attacked. Then Judas ordered his brother Simon to take chosen men and go to defend his brothers in Galilee; he and his brother Jonathan would set out for Gilead. However, he left Joseph, son of Zechariah, and Azariah, leaders of the people, with the rest of the army in Judea for protection, with the command that they should lead those people but not engage in battle with foreigners until their return. Three thousand men were assigned to Simon to set out for Galilee, and eight thousand men to Judas for Gilead.

<margin>Simon defeats the enemies in Galilee.</margin>
Simon, having set out for Galilee, fought many battles with the foreigners. After routing them, he pursued them all the way to the gates of Ptolemais. Having killed about three thousand of them, he took their spoils. He brought the Jews from Galilee and Arbatta, along with their wives, children, and all their possessions, back to Judea with great joy. Meanwhile, Judas Maccabeus and his brother Jonathan crossed the Jordan and, after a three-day journey through the wilderness, they encountered the Nabateans. Having been received by them in a friendly manner, they learned everything that had happened to their brothers in Gilead: that many of them had been forced into <margin>a. Badé is now called Bozrah. Josephus calls it Beth-zur. <note>The translator is noting a geographical discrepancy between the source text and the historian Josephus.</note></margin> Bozrah, Bosor, Alema, Casphor, Maked, and Carnaim—all of which were strong and large cities—and that they were surrounded in other towns of Gilead. They also learned that the enemy intended to move their army against the fortifications the next day, and once captured, to destroy everyone in a single day.

<margin>Judas overwhelms the city of Bozrah.</margin>
Then Judas and his army turned their march through the wilderness toward Bozrah. Having taken the city by surprise, he put all the males to the sword, and after plundering everything, he burned the city with fire. Setting out from there by night, he hurried toward the fortress. When it was already becoming light, they noticed an innumerable multitude of men carrying ladders and engines of war to capture the fortress and attacking those within. Here, Judas, seeing that the battle had begun and that the cry of the townspeople, along with a great sound of trumpets, was rising to heaven, exhorted his soldiers to fight that day for their brothers. He attacked the enemy from the rear in three divisions with the sound of trumpets and the cries of those praying. But when the men of Timothy realized it was Maccabeus, they took to flight, and he inflicted a great slaughter upon them.

<margin>Judas inflicts a defeat on the followers of Timotheus.</margin>
After this, having slain about eight thousand of their men on that day, he turned aside to Mizpah <note>original: "Maapham"</note>; having captured it, he killed all the males within, plundered it, and set it on fire. From there he set out and took the towns of Caspin, Maked, Bosor, and the rest of the towns in the region of Gilead <note>original: "Galaaditidis"</note>. After these things were done, Timotheus gathered another army and made camp opposite Raphon, across the river. When Judas had sent spies to observe this camp, it was reported back to him that all the neighboring nations had gathered against the Jews—a massive force—and they had even hired Arabs as mercenaries to assist them. These forces were camped across the river, prepared to attack him in war. Then Judas went out to meet them. As he approached the river with his army, Timotheus warned the leaders of his forces: "If he crosses over to us first, we will not be able to withstand him, but will be defeated by him; but if he is terrified and camps across the river, we shall cross over to him and be victorious." But when Judas approached the river, he stationed the scribes of the people by the water and commanded them not to allow anyone to set up camp, but that everyone should go into battle.

<margin>Judas routs the followers of Timotheus.</margin>
He himself was the first to cross toward the enemy, with all his men following him, and he so thoroughly routed all the foreigners that they threw down their arms and fled into the temple at Karnaim <note>original: "Carnai"</note>. Once the town was captured, Judas burned that temple along with everyone who was inside it. Thus Karnaim was overturned. Since the enemy could no longer withstand him, Judas gathered all the Israelites of Gilead, from the least to the greatest, together with their wives, children, and possessions—which was truly a massive multitude—to head for Judea.

<margin>Judas destroys the city of Ephron.</margin>
When they came to Ephron, a large and very well-fortified city situated on the road, it was impossible to turn away from it to the right or the left; they had to pass through it. However, the townspeople had closed the gates against them and blocked them with stones. Judas sent messengers to them to ask peaceably for permission to pass through their territory to reach his own, promising that no one would harm them and they would only pass through on foot. But when the townspeople refused to open the gates, he ordered it to be proclaimed throughout the army that everyone should attack the city from the position they were in. And so the soldiers attacked the city all that day and night. Having gained control of it, he put all the males to the sword, razed the city, plundered it, and marched through it over the bodies of the slain. After crossing the Jordan, they came into a wide plain situated in sight of Bethshan <note>original: "Bethsanis"</note>. Meanwhile, Judas gathered the stragglers and encouraged the people throughout the entire journey until they arrived in Judea. Then they ascended Mount Zion with gladness and joy and offered whole burnt offerings because they had returned safely without losing a single one of their men.

<margin>Joseph and Azarias fight unsuccessfully against the followers of Gorgias.</margin>
In the meantime, while Judas and Jonathan were in Gilead and their brother Simon was in Galilee against Ptolemais, Joseph the son of Zechariah and Azarias, the commanders of the forces, heard of their distinguished deeds in war and decided that they too should win fame and attack the neighboring peoples with arms. Therefore, having ordered an expedition for their soldiers, they set out for Jamnia. But as they came out from

This great disaster befell the Israelites because they did not obey Judas and his brothers, thinking they would perform great deeds themselves, though they were not of the lineage of those men to whom the defense of Israel had been entrusted. ## CHAPTER VI.

<margin>Antiochus Epiphanes repulsed from Elymais.</margin>
Meanwhile, King Antiochus, as he was traveling through the upper provinces, heard that there was a city in Persia called Elymais, renowned for its wealth of gold and silver. In it was a very opulent temple where there were golden coverings, breastplates, and weapons left there by Alexander, son of Philip, the king of the Macedonians, who first reigned in Greece. Therefore, he went there, desiring to occupy and plunder the city. But he was not able to, because the citizens, having learned of his plan, resisted him with arms. He was turned to flight and hurried to return to Babylon with great sorrow. In the meantime, someone arrived in Persia to announce to him that the forces sent into Judea had been defeated, and that Lysias, who had set out first with a great hand, had been routed by them. He learned that the Jews had grown strong in arms, power, and much plunder, which they had taken from the armies they cut down; and that they had demolished that "abomination" <note>original: "nefas illud," referring to the pagan altar</note> which he had erected on the altar in Jerusalem, and had surrounded the sanctuary with a high wall as it was before, as well as his town of Beth-zur. When he received these reports, the king was vehemently astonished and struck down; he took to his bed and fell into a sickness born of grief, because things had not turned out according to his wishes. He remained there for many days, his sorrow growing ever more bitter. Realizing that he must die, he summoned all his friends and spoke to them thus:

<margin>The dying Antiochus Epiphanes addresses his friends.</margin>
"Sleep has left my eyes, and my heart fails because of my sorrow. Now, as I reflect on the misery and the storm into which I have fallen, I remember the evils I perpetrated in Jerusalem, how I took all the vessels of gold and silver from there, and how I sent orders to destroy the inhabitants of Judea without cause..."

Only a few men remained in the sanctuary because they were overcome by hunger, and others had scattered here and there.

<margin>Lysias persuades Antiochus to make terms with the Jews.</margin>
Then Lysias heard that Philip—whom King Antiochus, while still alive, had appointed to raise his son Antiochus for the kingship—had returned from Persia and Media with the forces the king had taken with him, and that he was seeking to take the kingdom and the administration of affairs. Immediately leaving the citadel, Lysias went to the king and spoke to him and the leaders of the army and the rest: "We are failing daily, our food is scarce, the place we are besieging is strong, and the care of the kingdom falls upon us. Therefore, let us give these men our right hand and make peace with them and their whole nation, on the condition that they be allowed to use their own laws as before. For it is because of their laws, which we abolished, that they have become angry and done all these things." The speech pleased the king and the leaders; the king sent messengers to them concerning peace, which they accepted. The king and the leaders swore an oath to them, and so they came out from the fortification.

<margin>Antiochus violates the oath he gave.</margin>
But when the king entered Mount Zion and saw the strength of the place, he violated the oath he had given and ordered the wall to be torn down all around. Then, departing in haste, he returned to Antioch, where he found Philip ruling the city. He attacked him and took the city by force.

In the one hundred and fifty-first year <note>Approximately 161 BCE.</note>, Demetrius the son of Seleucus departed from Rome and came with a few men to a <sup>a</sup> coastal city, and there he seized the kingdom. It happened that as he was entering the palace of his ancestors, the soldiers seized Antiochus and Lysias to bring them to him. When he learned of this, he forbade them to be brought into his sight; and so they were killed by the soldiers. After Demetrius occupied the throne of the kingdom, the most impious men—led by Alcimus, who was seeking the high priesthood—accused their own people before the king in this manner: "Judas and his brothers have destroyed all your friends, and they have driven us out of our fatherland. Therefore, send someone whom you trust so that, having gone there, he may see how much calamity they have brought upon us and the royal region, and let him take vengeance on them and all their helpers." Then the king entrusted this task to Bacchides, a friend of the king and <sup>b</sup> governor across the river <note>original: "trans fluuium"; referring to the region west of the Euphrates.</note>, a man of great authority in the kingdom and faithful to the king. He sent him along with that impious Alcimus, whom he appointed high priest, and commanded him to take vengeance on the Israelites. They set out for Judea with a large force and sent messengers to Judas and his brothers with deceitful words of peace. However, Judas and his men ignored their words, for they saw that they had come with a great army. A group of scribes gathered before Alcimus and Bacchides to seek justice, and the first among the Israelites to seek peace from them were the Hasideans <note>original: "Asidei"; a group of pious Jews who initially trusted Alcimus because of his priestly lineage.</note>, thinking that they would not be harmed by a man who was a priest of the line of Aaron coming with soldiers. But he spoke to them in a friendly manner and, having offered an oath, promised that he would bring no harm to them or their kinsmen. When they believed him, he seized sixty men from among them and slaughtered them in a single day, in which event that which was written happened: "The bodies of your saints and their blood they have poured out around Jerusalem, and there is no one to bury them." After this was done, fear and terror of them pervaded everyone, for they thought there was no faith or justice in men who had broken a pact and the oath they had given. Then Bacchides, departing from Jerusalem, set up camp at Bezeth; he sent for and captured many of the deserters from his own side and some of the Jews, whom he slaughtered and threw into a vast pit. Having delegated the province to Alcimus and left soldiers with him to assist him, Bacchides himself returned to the king. Alcimus then struggled for the high priesthood, and all the troublers of their own people having gathered to him, he took control of Judea and afflicted the Israelites with a great slaughter. But Judas, seeing that Alcimus and his followers were doing as much harm to the Israelites as the foreigners had never done, went about all the borders of Judea on every side and took vengeance on the deserters, prohibiting them from further raids. Alcimus, seeing that Judas and his men were superior and realizing he was unequal to them, returned to the king and bitterly accused them. Then the king sent Ni-

Therefore, the battle being joined by the armies on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, Nicanor’s forces were defeated, and Nicanor himself was the first to fall in the fight. When his soldiers saw that he was dead, they threw down their arms and took to flight; the Jews pursued them for a day's journey from Adasa as far as Gazara, and having given the signal with trumpets behind them, men came out from all the neighboring villages of Judea on every side. These attacked them and turned them back toward those who were pursuing, and so all were slaughtered by the sword to a man. The Jews took the spoils and cut off Nicanor’s head and his right hand, which he had so proudly stretched out, and they carried them and hung them up in Jerusalem. The people were filled with great joy and decreed that this day, the thirteenth of the month of Adar, should be observed every year; and so Judea was quiet for a while.

...they were dear to their allies, and established friendship with all who approached them. <margin>Macedonia.</margin>
Furthermore, they had crushed in battle and subdued Philip and Perseus, the kings of the <gloss>a</gloss> Kittim <note>original: "Citiorum"; here referring to the Macedonians</note>, and others who dared to resist them. In addition, they had defeated Antiochus the Great, the King of Asia, who had launched an expedition against them with one hundred and twenty elephants and a massive force of cavalry, chariots, and soldiers. They took him alive and imposed a heavy tribute upon him and his successors in the kingdom, and 

<margin><gloss>b</gloss> In both the Greek and Latin texts it reads "Media," but the text is otherwise corrupted; see also Livy’s accounts of these events.</margin>
they took from him Lycaonia, Myliada, and <gloss>b</gloss> Lydia, along with other very beautiful regions, and gave them to King Eumenes. Likewise, when the Greeks attempted to attack and destroy them, the Romans learned of the matter and sent a commander to wage war against them. Many Greeks were slain, and many were taken captive along with their wives and children; the Romans seized their land, destroyed their fortifications, and took them as plunder, reducing them to a servitude that lasts to this day. They also devastated and brought under their power all other kingdoms and islands that resisted them. Yet they maintained friendship with their own friends and those who sought peace. Having taken possession of kingdoms both near and far, they became a terror to all who heard their name. They could establish or depose kings at their will. Though they were so highly exalted, none of them wore a crown or dressed in luxurious purple robes. Instead, in their Senate, three hundred and twenty men met daily in council, always consulting on how to properly administer the republic. They would entrust the annual administration of their republic and the governance of their entire empire to a single man <note>referring to the Roman Consul</note>, and everyone obeyed that one man, and there was no envy or jealousy among them. 

When Judas understood these things, he chose Eupolemus, son of John, and Jason, son of Eleazar, and sent them to Rome to enter into a friendship and alliance with them, so as to lift the yoke of the Greeks from the Israelites, who were being reduced to slavery. They set out for Rome on a very long journey, and having entered the Senate chamber, they spoke as follows: they were sent by Judas Maccabeus, his brothers, and the Jewish community to the Romans to make a peace treaty and alliance with them, so that they might be enrolled as allies and friends. This proposal pleased the Romans, and they wrote a decree of the Senate, a copy of which they engraved on bronze and sent to Jerusalem to remain with the Jews as a monument of peace and alliance.

<margin>Judas sends men to secure a treaty of friendship with the Romans.</margin>
<margin>The Roman Senate's decree regarding the alliance with the Jews.</margin>
MAY IT BE FAVORABLE TO THE ROMANS and the Jewish nation by land and sea forever: may war and enemies be far from them. However, if war breaks out against the Romans first, or any of their allies throughout their entire empire, the Jewish nation shall provide aid in good faith as the circumstances permit. They shall not give or supply the enemies with food, weapons, money, or ships, as the Romans see fit; and they shall keep these conditions without compensation. Similarly, if war happens to the Jewish nation first, the Romans shall provide aid in good faith as the circumstances permit, and shall not help the enemies with food, weapons, silver, or ships, as the Romans see fit; and they shall keep these conditions without deceit. On these terms, the Romans made a pact with the Jewish people. If hereafter both parties wish to add or remove anything, they shall do so by mutual consent, and whatever they add or remove shall be valid. Regarding the wrongs done to them by King Demetrius, we have written to him that he must not harass our friends and allies the Jews; and if they complain about him again, we shall pursue their injuries and wage war against him by land and sea.

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER IX.

<margin>Demetrius sends Bacchides and Alcimus into Judea.</margin>
Furthermore, when Demetrius heard the outcome of the battle involving Nicanor and his forces, he sent Bacchides and Alcimus into Judea a second time with the right wing of the army. They marched toward Galgala and set up camp at Masaloth (which is a town in Arbela), and having captured it, they killed many people. Then, in the first month of the one hundred and fifty-second year, having moved their camp toward Jerusalem, they set out for Berea with twenty thousand infantry and two thousand cavalry. Now Judas had his camp at Eleasa with three thousand chosen men. When they saw the great multitude of the enemy host, they were so terrified that many slipped away from the camp, until only eight hundred of them remained. When Judas saw his soldiers drifting away and himself pressed by war, he was broken in spirit and weakened, because he did not have time to gather them back. He encouraged those who remained to attack their adversaries to see if they could defeat them. But they tried to discourage him.

> "We cannot," they said, "but for now let us retreat and save our lives. For since our men have slipped away, we are too few to fight the enemy."

But Judas said:

> "Far be it from me to commit such a crime as to flee from them. If our fatal hour has come, let us die bravely for our brothers, and let us not leave a stain upon our glory."

Meanwhile, the enemy army emerged from their camp and stood opposite them, arranged so that the cavalry was divided into two parts. The slingers and archers went before the main body, and all the strongest men were in the front line, with Bacchides on the right wing. The phalanx advanced from both sides at the sound of the trumpets, and the Jews also sounded their trumpets and rushed forward. The battle began and lasted from morning until evening. When Judas noticed that Bacchides and the strength of the army were on the right side, he took all the most courageous men and made an assault there. Having routed the right wing, he pursued the enemy as far as <margin>c. Josephus calls this Mount Ashdod.</margin> Mount Azotus.

The rest of the acts of Judas, his battles, and the brave and great deeds he performed were not all written down. There was such great distress in Israel as had not been seen since the time a prophet had last appeared among them.

<margin>Jonathan succeeds his brother Judas.</margin>
Then all the friends of Judas gathered to Jonathan and told him: "Since your brother Judas died, there is no one like him to lead us against our enemies and Bacchides, and against those of our nation who are hostile to us. Therefore, we choose you today to be our leader and commander in his place, to wage our war." So Jonathan accepted the leadership and succeeded his brother Judas. When Bacchides heard of this, he attempted to kill him. Upon learning this, Jonathan, his brother Simon, and all their companions fled into the wilderness of Tekoa and camped by the waters of the pool of Asphar. When Bacchides found out, he crossed the Jordan with his entire army on the Sabbath day. Jonathan then sent his brother John, who was in charge of the multitude, to his friends the Nabateans <note>An Arab people who were often allies of the Maccabees</note>, to ask if they might store their heavy baggage, of which they had much, with them.

Later, it was reported to Jonathan and his brother Simon that the sons of Jambri were celebrating a prominent wedding and were bringing the bride from Nadabatha with great ceremony—she was the daughter of one of the primary Canaanite nobles.

<margin>Jonathan and Simon ambush the wedding party.</margin>
Remembering the blood of their brother John, they went up and hid under the cover of the mountain. When they saw a great, noisy crowd and much baggage, and the bridegroom coming out with his friends and kinsmen to meet them with tambourines, musicians, and many weapons, they rose up against them from their ambush and slaughtered them. Many were killed, and the rest fled into the mountains while the brothers seized all their spoils. Thus the wedding was turned into mourning and the sound of music into lamentation. Having avenged the blood of their brother, they returned to the marshes of the Jordan.

<margin>Jonathan, about to clash with Bacchides, encourages his men.</margin>
When Bacchides heard of this, he came on the Sabbath day to the banks of the Jordan with a massive force. Then Jonathan exhorted his men, saying: "Come now, let us fight for our lives! For

<column-break/>

the situation today is not as it was in days past. Behold, the enemy is in front of us, and the water of the Jordan is behind us; on this side and that are marshes and woods, and there is no place to turn aside. Therefore, cry out to heaven that you may be delivered from the hands of your enemies." Then the battle was joined, and Jonathan stretched out his hand to strike Bacchides, but Bacchides drew back. Then Jonathan and his soldiers leaped into the Jordan and swam across to the other side, and the enemy did not follow them.

<margin>Bacchides establishes garrisons throughout Judea.</margin>
On that day, Bacchides lost about a thousand men. He then returned to Jerusalem and rebuilt fortified towns in Judea: the fortifications of Jericho, Emmaus, Beth-horon, Bethel, Timnath, Pirathon, and Tephon, strengthening them with high walls, gates, and bars. He placed garrisons in them to harass Israel. Furthermore, he fortified the town of Beth-zur, Gazara, and the citadel, placing soldiers and provisions in them. He also took the sons of the leading men of the region as hostages and put them under guard in the citadel at Jerusalem.

<margin>The death of Alcimus.</margin>
In the one hundred and fifty-third year <note>referring to the Seleucid era, roughly 159 BCE</note>, in the second month, Alcimus <note>The Hellenizing High Priest</note> ordered the wall of the inner court of the sanctuary to be torn down, destroying the work of the prophets. But as soon as he began the demolition, he was struck by a disease that hindered his purpose. His mouth was stopped and he was paralyzed, so that he could no longer speak or even make a will. Thus he died in great agony. When Bacchides saw that Alcimus was dead, he returned to the king, and Judea was at peace for two years.

<margin>Traitors summon Bacchides to kill Jonathan.</margin>
Then all the lawless men plotted together, saying: "Behold, Jonathan and his followers are living in quiet and security; let us bring Bacchides here, and he will capture them all in a single night." So they went and persuaded him. Bacchides set out to come with a large force, and he sent secret letters to all his supporters in Judea to seize Jonathan and his companions. But they were unable to do so because their plan became known. Instead, Jonathan's men seized about fifty of the local men who were the leaders of this conspiracy and put them to death.

Then Jonathan, Simon, and their followers withdrew to the town of Bethbasim in the wilderness; they rebuilt it and fortified it. When Bacchides learned of this, he gathered his entire army and called up the soldiers from Judea, and he came to attack Bethbasim. He besieged it for many days and used siege engines. But Jonathan left his brother Simon in the town and went out into the countryside with a small band of men. He struck down Odomera and his brothers, and the sons of Pharison in their tents. As he began to strike them and advance with force, Simon and his men made a sally from the town and burned the siege engines. They fought against Bacchides and defeated him so soundly that he was greatly distressed because his plan and expedition had failed. He was enraged at the wicked men who had advised him to undertake the campaign, and he killed many of them, deciding then to return to his own land.

## CHAPTER X.

<margin>Demetrius attempts to reconcile with Jonathan.</margin>
In the one hundred and sixtieth year, Alexander, the son of Antiochus Epiphanes, set out for Ptolemais and occupied it; being welcomed by the inhabitants, he held the kingdom there. When King Demetrius heard this, he gathered a very large army and set out to pursue him in war. However, he also sent a friendly letter to Jonathan, in which he praised him. He did this with the intention of securing Jonathan's friendship before Jonathan could form an alliance with Alexander against him, for Demetrius remembered the many injuries that Jonathan, his brothers, and their whole nation had suffered at his hands. Therefore, he granted Jonathan the authority to recruit an army and prepare weapons, so that he might be his ally; he also ordered that the hostages held in the citadel <note>The Akra, the fortress in Jerusalem held by the king's forces</note> be handed over to him. After Jonathan arrived in Jerusalem, he read this letter in the hearing of everyone, including those who held the citadel. They were greatly terrified when they heard that the king had given him the power to raise an army. Those in the citadel surrendered the hostages to him, whom he returned to their parents. Living in Jerusalem, he began to build and restore the city, commanding the overseers to reconstruct the walls and to fortify Mount Zion all around with squared stones, which they did. Consequently, the foreigners who were in the fortifications built by Bacchides fled, and leaving the places they held, each departed to his own country. However, some who had abandoned the Law and the commandments remained in Beth-zur, as it served as their refuge.

<margin>What Alexander heard regarding the letter Demetrius sent to Jonathan.</margin>
But King Alexander, when he heard what Demetrius had offered Jonathan in his letter, and when Jonathan’s battles, noble deeds, and the hardships he and his brothers had endured were described to him, he realized he would find no other man like him. He decided to make him a friend and ally, and sent him a letter written in these words: "KING ALEXANDER TO JONATHAN his brother, greetings. We have heard that you are a man of outstanding virtue and worthy of being our friend. For this reason, we appoint you today as the High Priest of your nation and desire that you maintain friendship with us." Along with this, he sent him a purple robe and a golden crown. Therefore, Jonathan put on the sacred vestments in the seventh month of the one hundred and sixtieth year, during the Festival of Tabernacles <note>An important Jewish pilgrimage festival also known as Sukkot</note>. He also recruited an army and prepared many weapons. When Demetrius heard of these things, he was grieved, complaining that he had achieved nothing because Alexander had forestalled him in winning the friendship of the Jews for...

<margin>Demetrius tries in vain to win over the Jews by letter.</margin>
"KING DEMETRIUS TO THE JEWISH NATION, GREETINGS. We have heard and rejoiced that you have kept your treaties with us, remained in our friendship, and have not defected to our enemies. Therefore, continue to keep faith with us, and we will repay this service to us with benefits. We will grant you many exemptions and give you gifts. Even now, I free you and remit for all Jews the taxes on salt and the crown levies <note>A tax originally paid in the form of golden crowns, later a monetary tax</note>. Furthermore, I remit from this day forward the third part of the grain and half of the fruit of the trees which are due to me from Judea, as well as from the three districts belonging to Judea—namely, Samaria, Galilee, and Transjordan—and<gloss>a</gloss> indeed I remit these forever.

<margin>a. This word has been added from the works of Josephus.</margin>

Moreover, I grant free manumission to all Jewish persons who were taken captive from Judea into any part of my kingdom, and let them all be free from taxes, along with their livestock. In addition, all festivals, Sabbaths, New Moons, solemn days, and the three days preceding a festival and the three days following a festival shall be days of immunity and freedom for all Jews living in my kingdom; no one shall have the right to disturb any of them or trouble them regarding any matter. Let there also be enrolled in the king's army about thirty thousand Jews, to whom pay shall be given, as is done for all the king's soldiers. Some of these shall be stationed in the king's greatest fortresses, and others shall be assigned to other needs of the kingdom where trust is required. Their officers and leaders shall be from among themselves, and they shall live by their own laws, just as the king commands to be done in Judea. Likewise, let the three districts that were added to Judea from Samaria be joined to Judea, so that they may be considered under one authority and obey no other power than that of the High Priest. I give Ptolemais and its territory as a gift to the sanctuary at Jerusalem for the expenses necessary for the holy rites. Furthermore, the five thousand shekels of silver which I used to receive annually from the sanctuary's taxes are also remitted, so that they may be paid to the priests who perform the divine service. And whoever flees to the sanctuary in Jerusalem or within its entire precincts, whether because they have offended the king or for any other crime, shall be acquitted, along with everything they possess in my kingdom. <margin>Demetrius is killed by Alexander.</margin>
King Alexander, having gathered a huge army, set up camp against Demetrius. When the two kings met in battle, the troops of Demetrius fled. Alexander pursued them, overcame them, and continued the battle very fiercely until sunset; and on that day, Demetrius fell in battle. Afterward, Alexander sent ambassadors to Ptolemy, the King of Egypt, 

<margin>Alexander seeks the daughter of Ptolemy in marriage.</margin>
with a message of this kind: "Now that I have returned to the land of my kingdom, gained power, and occupied the throne of my ancestors—having routed Demetrius and secured our region, and having joined battle with him and defeated him and his army so that we might sit upon the throne of his kingdom—come now, let us enter into friendship with one another, and give me your daughter in marriage. I shall be your son-in-law, and I will give you and her gifts worthy of you." To this, King Ptolemy responded in this manner: "Fortunate is the day in which you returned to the land of your ancestors and obtained the throne of their kingdom. Therefore, I will do as you write. But meet me at Ptolemais <note>Modern-day Acre, Israel</note>, so that we may meet, and I shall make you my son-in-law as you request." Thus Ptolemy set out from Egypt with his daughter Cleopatra and came to Ptolemais in the one hundred and sixty-second year <note>c. 150 BCE according to the Seleucid era</note>. He gave his daughter Cleopatra in marriage to King Alexander, who had come to him, and he celebrated the wedding at Ptolemais magnificently, as was fitting for kings. King Alexander also wrote to Jonathan, asking him to come to him.

<margin>Jonathan comes to Ptolemais for the wedding of Alexander.</margin>
So, Jonathan set out for Ptolemais with great splendor and met the two kings. He presented them with silver and gold, and gave gifts to their friends, thereby securing their goodwill. Even when certain wicked and villainous Israelites came together to bring accusations against him, King Alexander not only rejected their charges but also ordered Jonathan to be stripped of his own garments and clothed in purple <note>Purple was the color of royalty and high-ranking "Friends of the King"</note>. Once this was done, the king sat him beside him and commanded his nobles to lead him into the center of the city and proclaim that no one should accuse him of any crime, nor should anyone trouble him for any reason. When his accusers saw this honor, the proclamation, and the purple robe, they all fled. The king held him in such high honor that he recorded him as the first among his Friends, and made him a general and a partner in the government. Thus, Jonathan returned to Jerusalem safe and joyful.

<margin>Apollonius, the governor under Demetrius, challenges Jonathan to battle.</margin>
In the one hundred and sixty-fifth year <note>c. 147 BCE</note>, Demetrius <note>Demetrius II Nicator</note>, the son of Demetrius, came from Crete to his father's land. When King Alexander heard this, he was moved by great grief and returned to Antioch. But Demetrius appointed Apollonius, the governor of Coelesyria <note>The region between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon mountains</note>, as his general. Apollonius gathered a great army, camped at Jamnia, and sent this message to Jonathan the high priest: "You alone exalt yourself against us, and I have become

<column-break/>

a laughingstock and a target of mockery because of you. But do not think you can overcome us in the mountains; come now, if you trust in your strength, descend to us in the plain where we may contend. Indeed, the strength of the cities is with me. Inquire and learn who I and my allies are, and you will hear that you cannot resist us, since your ancestors were twice routed in their own land. Much less will you be able to withstand such cavalry and such great forces, especially in the plain, where there are neither rocks nor pebbles, nor any place for refuge." When Jonathan heard these words of Apollonius, his spirit was stirred. He chose ten thousand men and set out from Jerusalem, with his brother Simon coming to his aid. He brought his army to Joppa <note>Modern Jaffa</note>, but the gates of the town were closed against him because a garrison of Apollonius was there. He attacked it, and when the townspeople opened the gates out of fear, Jonathan took possession of Joppa. When Apollonius heard this, he set out with three thousand cavalry and a great multitude of infantry, as if he were heading for Azotus <note>Ashdod</note>, but at the same time he advanced into the plain, relying on his cavalry, of which he had a great force. Jonathan pursued him toward Azotus and began to provoke him to a fresh battle. Apollonius had left a thousand cavalry hidden behind them, an ambush of which Jonathan was not ignorant. Thus, when they surrounded his troop and hurled spears at the soldiers from morning until evening, the soldiers stood their ground, just as Jonathan had commanded. Then, when the enemy's horses were exhausted, Simon brought forward his line and engaged the phalanx. Since the horses were worn out and scattered through the fields, the enemies were routed by him. They fled to Azotus and entered the temple of Dagon <note>A Philistine deity</note>, their god, for safety. But Jonathan

<margin>Jonathan burns Azotus and other places.</margin>
set fire to Azotus and the neighboring towns, taking them as plunder. He burned the temple of Dagon and those who had fled there. The number of those who perished by either sword or flame was about eight thousand men. Moving on from there, Jonathan moved his army toward Ascalon <note>Ashkelon</note>, and the townspeople came out to meet him with great honor. Thus Jonathan returned to Jerusalem with his men and a great deal of plunder. When King Alexander heard of these things, he increased the honors given to Jonathan, sending him a golden buckle <note>original: "monile... aureum"</note>, such as is customary to be given to the kinsmen of kings, and gave him Ekron <note>Accaron</note> with its borders to possess.

<margin>Antiochus, son of Alexander, having defeated Demetrius, wins Jonathan to his side.</margin>
The young Antiochus <note>Antiochus VI Dionysus, the child-king supported by the general Tryphon against Demetrius II</note> sent word to Jonathan, confirming him in the high priesthood and appointing him over the four districts, and naming him among the "Friends of the King." He sent him golden cups and a set of table service, and gave him the right to drink from gold, to wear purple, and to wear a golden buckle <note>The golden buckle was a specific mark of high status in the Seleucid court</note>. He also appointed Jonathan's brother, Simon, as commander from the Ladder of Tyre to the borders of Egypt. Thus Jonathan set out and traveled across the river, visiting the cities; all the soldiers of Syria gathered to him as allies. He came to Ascalon and was received honorably by the townsmen. From there he went to Gaza, but the people of Gaza shut him out; so he besieged it and burned the surrounding suburbs and plundered them. Then, when they pleaded for peace, he gave it to them; he took the sons of their leaders as hostages and sent them to Jerusalem. He then traveled through the region as far as Damascus. When he heard that the generals of Demetrius were present at Kadesh in Galilee with a great army, intending to remove him from those borders, he went out to meet them, leaving his brother Simon in the country.

<margin>Simon takes possession of Bethsura.</margin>
Simon moved his camp against Bethsura <note>A strategic hilltop fortress south of Jerusalem</note> and attacked it for many days. When the besieged people requested a truce, he granted it, and after they were removed from there, he took the town and reinforced it with a garrison. Meanwhile, Jonathan and his soldiers camped by Lake Gennesaret <note>The Sea of Galilee</note>. Early the next morning, the enemy army was seen marching through the plain of Hazor toward him. The enemy had set an ambush for him in the mountains, while they themselves met him head-on. Thus, when the battle began and those in the ambush broke from their positions and attacked Jonathan’s men, all of Jonathan’s troops fled to a man, except for Mattathias the son of Absalom and Judas the son of Chalphi, the captains of the army.

<margin>Jonathan’s battle and victory.</margin>
At this, Jonathan tore his clothes, sprinkled dust on his head, and prayed to God. Then, renewing the battle against the enemy, he turned them to flight. Seeing this, his soldiers who had fled turned back toward the enemy and pursued them all the way to their camp at Kadesh, where they made their own camp. About three thousand of the enemy were killed that day, and Jonathan returned to Jerusalem.

### CHAPTER XII.

When the legates arrived in Rome, they entered the Senate and said they had been sent by Jonathan the High Priest and the Jewish nation to renew their former friendship and alliance. The Romans then gave them letters addressed to the people of each region, so that they might lead them safely back to Judea. the alliance and friendship were discussed. Therefore, at all times, on our feast days and other appropriate days, we remember you in the sacrifices we offer and in our prayers, as it is right and fitting to remember brothers, and we rejoice in your glory. We ourselves have been surrounded by many hardships and wars, harassed by the kings around us, but we did not wish to be a burden to you or our other allies and friends in these wars. Meanwhile, Tryphon, seeking to seize the kingdom and crown of Asia and fearing that Jonathan might hinder him and attack him with arms, sought a way to seize and kill Jonathan; he then set out for Beth-shan <note>An ancient city at the junction of the Jezreel and Jordan valleys</note>. But when Jonathan came to meet him with forty thousand elite men prepared for battle, Tryphon, seeing him arrive with such a large army, did not dare to use force against him. Jonathan, believing him, did as he was told and sent his soldiers back to Judea, keeping only three thousand men; of these, he sent two thousand to Galilee and took one thousand with him. <margin>This is announced to Simon: Jonathan is dead.</margin>

When those pursuing them saw that they were fighting for their lives, they turned back; and so they all arrived safely in Judea. They mourned Jonathan and his companions, and all Israel, filled with great fear, lamented bitterly. All the neighboring nations then attempted to destroy them, saying: "They have no leader or defender; now is the time to defeat them and wipe their memory from among mankind."

### CHAPTER XIII.

<margin>Simon consoles the people.</margin>
Then Simon, hearing that Tryphon had gathered a great army to invade and devastate Judea, and seeing that the people were in terror and fear, went to Jerusalem. He called an assembly and consoled the people with these words: "You yourselves know what I, my brothers, and my father’s house have done for the laws and the sanctuary—the wars and hardships we have endured—to the point that all my brothers have perished for Israel's sake, and I alone am left. Therefore, far be it from me to spare my own life in any time of trouble, for I am no better than my brothers. Rather, I will avenge my nation, the sanctuary, and our wives and children, against whom all the nations have conspired in their hatred to destroy us." Upon hearing this

### CHAPTER XIV.

<margin>Demetrius is captured by Arsaces.</margin>
<margin>The noble deeds of Simon.</margin>
In the one hundred and seventy-second year, King Demetrius gathered all his forces and set out for Media to obtain help so he could fight Tryphon. When Arsaces, the King of Persia and Media, heard that he had entered his borders, he sent one of his generals to capture him alive. The general attacked Demetrius, defeated his army, and led him to Arsaces, who put him in prison. Judea was at peace during all the days of Simon. He sought the good of his people, and they were pleased with his rule and his glory. He captured Joppa with great renown and made it a harbor, opening an entrance to the islands of the sea. He expanded the borders of his nation and ruled the land.

<column-break/>

He brought back many captives and took control of Gazara, Beth-zur, and the citadel, removing all defilements from them; no one could resist him. The fields were cultivated in peace, the earth yielded its crops, and the trees their fruit. The elders sat in the streets, discussing their prosperity, while the young men dressed in splendid military attire. He supplied the towns with provisions and fortified them with weapons and defenses, so that his fame reached the ends of the earth. <margin>Peace in Judea under Simon.</margin> He established such peace in Judea that the Israelites enjoyed great pleasure, each man sitting under his own vine and fig tree <note>a biblical metaphor for total security and prosperity</note>, with no one to terrify them. War vanished from the land, and the kings of that time were defeated. He comforted the afflicted among his people, was devoted to the law, and removed every lawless and wicked person. He beautified the sanctuary and increased the number of sacred vessels. When the Romans and Spartans heard that Jonathan had died, they were deeply grieved. But when they heard that his brother Simon had succeeded him as High Priest and was ruling the region and its wars, they wrote to him on bronze tablets to renew the friendship and alliance they had established with his brothers Judas and Jonathan. These tablets were read before the assembly in Jerusalem. <meta>This page continues the account of Simon Maccabeus’s leadership. Following the capture of his brother Jonathan, Simon has taken the mantle of High Priest and Commander. The previous page detailed the liberation of the Jews from the Seleucid yoke in the year 142 BCE. This page records the formalization of Simon's authority by the Jewish people and the shifting diplomatic relations with King Antiochus VII and the Roman Republic.</meta>

Simon succeeded him, and he waged war on behalf of his people. He spent much of his own wealth, providing weapons for the soldiers of his nation and giving them wages. He fortified the towns of Judea, including Beth-zur on the borders of Judea, where the enemy's weapons had previously been kept, and there he stationed Jewish men as a garrison. He fortified Joppa, located by the sea, and Gezer <note>original: "Gaza," but historically referring to Gazara/Gezer</note> situated in the territory of Ashdod, which the enemy had previously inhabited. He established a colony of Jews there and equipped it with everything necessary for proper administration. Having seen Simon's loyalty and the zeal with which he worked to bring glory to his nation, the people appointed him as their governor and high priest. This was due to his many deeds, his justice, and the faith he kept with his people; he sought to honor them in every way. In his time, he enjoyed such great success that the foreigners were removed both from other places and from the City of David in Jerusalem (who had built themselves a citadel from which they went out to undermine the sanctuary <note>original: "sanum"</note> on every side and brought great calamity to the holy worship). He settled Jewish men in that citadel and fortified it for the protection of both the religion and the city, and he rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem. Therefore, King Demetrius confirmed him in the high priesthood, counted him among his friends, and treated him with great glory, because he had heard that the Jews were called friends and allies by the Romans, and that Simon’s ambassadors had been received by them with honor. Furthermore, the Jews and their priests decided that Simon should be their governor and perpetual high priest—until a true prophet should arise—and that he should be their commander in war, assign duties to each, oversee the provinces, the military, and the fortifications, and take care of the sanctuary and command all people. It was also decreed that everything done anywhere should be written in his name, and that he should wear purple and gold. It was not permitted for any person, whether private citizen or priest, to rescind any of these things, to contradict his orders, to form a faction without him, or to wear purple or a gold chain <note>original: "aureum torquem"</note>. Whoever acted against these decrees or rescinded any of them would be subject to punishment. All the people agreed that these terms should be presented to Simon, and Simon accepted them, consenting to become the high priest, the commander of the military, and the governor of the Jews and the priests, and to preside over all. It was ordered that this decree be inscribed on bronze tablets and posted in a prominent place within the temple precinct, and that a copy of it be placed in the treasury so that Simon and his sons might have it.

### CHAPTER XV.

<margin>Antiochus sent letters to Simon the high priest.</margin>
Now Antiochus, the son of King Demetrius, sent letters from the islands of the sea to Simon, the high priest and governor of the Jews, and to the entire nation, to this effect: KING ANTIOCHUS to Simon, the High Priest and Governor, and to the Jewish nation: Greetings. Since certain wicked men <note>original: "pestilentes homines"</note> have seized the kingdom of my ancestors, I wish to reclaim it so that I may restore it to its former state. I have gathered a great force of soldiers and prepared a fleet for war, intending to land in our region to attack those who have devastated it and plundered many towns in the kingdom. Therefore, I confirm to you whatever immunities my royal ancestors granted you, and whatever gifts they bestowed. I permit you to strike your own coinage with the unique mark of your homeland, and I decree that Jerusalem and the sanctuary shall be free. Whatever weapons you have prepared and whatever fortified places you hold, keep them. Furthermore, whatever is owed to the king, or would be paid to him, let it be remitted to you from this time forth and forever. Once we have restored our kingdom, we will bestow such great glory upon you, your nation, and the temple, that it shall be known throughout the whole world. Therefore, in the one hundred and seventy-fourth year <note>roughly 138 BCE</note>, King Antiochus entered the land of his ancestors; and when all the soldiers had gathered to him, he pursued Trypho, with whom only a few remained.

<margin>Antiochus besieges Trypho.</margin>
Trypho, seeing that his destruction was certain and that he had been deserted by the soldiers, retreated in flight to the town of Dor, located by the sea. Antiochus moved his army toward that town, having one hundred and twenty thousand infantry and eight thousand cavalry. With these forces surrounding the town, and the fleet moved in by land and sea, he besieged it so fiercely that he allowed no one to enter or leave. Meanwhile, Numenius and his companions returned from Rome with letters addressed to kings and peoples, in which the following was written:

<margin>The letters of the Romans to kings and peoples, in favor of the Jews.</margin>
> LUCIUS, CONSUL OF THE ROMANS, to King Ptolemy: Greetings. The ambassadors of the Jews, our friends and allies, have come to us to renew our long-standing friendship and alliance, having been sent by Simon the high priest and the Jewish people. They brought a golden shield weighing one thousand minas <note>a "mina" was a unit of weight; a thousand minas would be nearly 1,000 pounds of gold</note>. It has pleased us, therefore, to write to kings and nations, that they should not harm them, their towns, or their region, nor wage war against them, nor bring aid to those who do wage war. It also seemed good to us to accept the shield sent by them. Therefore, if any wicked men have fled from their borders to you, hand them over to Simon the high priest, so that he may punish them according to their own law. These same things were written to King Demetrius, Attalus, Arathes, Arsaces, and to all the nations: Sampsacus, the Spartans, and to Delos, Myndus, Sicyon, Caria, Samos, Pamphylia, Lycia, Halicarnassus, Rhodes, Phaselis, Cos, Side, Gortyna, Cnidus, Cyprus, and Cyrene. A copy of these was also written to Simon the high priest.

<margin>Antiochus demands back what Simon occupied, through Athenobius.</margin>
However, King Antiochus attacked Dor again, and by the constant use of assaults and siege engines, he reduced Trypho to such straits that he blocked every entrance and exit. Although Simon sent two thousand elite men to help him, along with silver, gold, and many vessels, Antiochus refused to accept them. Instead, he broke all the agreements he had previously made with him and became estranged from him. He sent to him a certain Athenobius, one of his friends, for a conference with mandates of this kind: "You hold Joppa, Gezer, and the citadel of Jerusalem, which are cities of my kingdom, and you have brought destruction and seized many places of my kingdom into your power. Therefore, return the towns you have captured and the tributes of the places you have occupied outside the borders of Judea. Or certainly, give five hundred talents of silver for them, and for the damage you have caused and for the taxes of the places, another five hundred. Otherwise, we will wage war against you." Therefore, Athenobius, the king's friend, went to Jerusalem, and seeing the splendor of Simon, the golden cup, the gold and silver furniture, and such great preparation, he was amazed; and he delivered the king's commands to him. Simon answered him in this manner: "We have neither taken foreign land, nor subjected foreign things, but rather our own inheritance, which was for some time unjustly held by our enemies. We, having found the opportunity, [reclaimed it]."

While Tryphon was fleeing by ship to Orthosia, the king appointed Cendebaeus as commander of the seacoast, assigning him both infantry and cavalry. ### CHAPTER XVI.

<margin>Simon sends his sons against Cendebaeus.</margin>
When John set out from Gezer and reported these deeds of Cendebaeus to his father Simon, Simon called his two oldest sons and spoke to them thus: "I, my brothers, and my father’s house have waged war against the enemies of Israel from our youth until this very day, and so successfully that we have many times delivered Israel. Now that I am old, you—who by both God's favor <note>original: "pietatem," meaning religious duty or devotion</note> and your age are able to succeed me and my brother—go forth and fight for our nation. I pray for help from heaven for you." So they chose twenty thousand soldiers from the nation, along with cavalry, and marched against Cendebaeus. After spending the night at Modein, they moved into the plain early in the morning and saw a great force of infantry and cavalry against them. However, a river lay between them. Having set up camp, John noticed his soldiers were hesitant to cross the river, so he crossed first. When the soldiers saw him, they crossed after him. Then he drew up the battle line, placing the cavalry among the infantry, for the enemy’s cavalry was very numerous. When the trumpets sounded, Cendebaeus and his men were put to flight; many of them were killed, and the rest fled into the fortress. Then John pursued them—though his brother Judas was wounded—all the way to Kedron, the city Cendebaeus had rebuilt. The enemy fled to the towers in the fields of Ashdod <note>original: "Azotij," referring to the Philistine city of Azotus/Ashdod</note>, and John burned them with fire. About two thousand of the adversaries were killed, and he returned safely to Judea. Now Ptolemy, son of Abubus, had been appointed governor over the plain of Jericho. Since he had much silver and gold (for he was the son-in-law of the high priest), he became arrogant and decided to seize the region and to eliminate Simon and his sons through treachery.
<margin>Ptolemy son of Abubus kills Simon and his sons.</margin>
Therefore, while Simon was visiting the towns of the region and overseeing their administration, he went down to Jericho with his sons Mattathias and Judas in the one hundred and seventy-seventh year, in the month of Shebat <note>The eleventh month of the Hebrew calendar, roughly February</note>. That son of Abubus received them deceitfully into a small fortress called Dok, which he had built. He prepared a great banquet for them, but had hidden men there. After Simon and his sons had drunk freely, Ptolemy and his men rose up, took their weapons, and entered the dining hall. He killed Simon,

-> OF THE MACCABEES <-

his two sons, and some of their servants. After he committed this great crime and repaid good with evil, Ptolemy sent word to the king asking for an army to be sent to help him, promising to deliver the region and the cities of the Jews to him. Furthermore, he sent others to Gezer to eliminate John, and sent letters to the military tribunes inviting them to come to him so he could give them silver, gold, and gifts. He also sent others to seize Jerusalem and the Temple Mount <note>original: "sanum montem," the holy mountain</note>. But someone ran ahead and informed John of the murder of his father and brothers, and that men had been sent to kill him. Utterly shocked by this news, John seized the men who had come to destroy him and killed them, for he knew they were plotting his death. As for the rest of the acts of John, his wars, his brave deeds, the walls he built, and his achievements, they are written in the chronicles <note>original: "commentarijs"</note> of his high priesthood, from the time he became high priest after his father.

<meta>This page continues the transition from the author's preface—where he explains his method of abridging the five books of Jason of Cyrene—into the historical narrative of the Second Book of Maccabees, specifically the story of Heliodorus and the temple treasury.</meta>

->OF THE MACCABEES<-

Considering how much boasting there is in lengthiness, and how much difficulty arises from the abundance of material for one who wishes to engage in the narration of historical deeds, we have taken care to provide pleasure for those who wish to read, ease for those students who wish to commit these things to memory, and utility for all our readers. And for us indeed, who have undertaken the labor of this abridgment <note>original: "compendij"; the author is explaining that his book is a "shorter version" of a much longer work</note>, it is not a simple task, but one of great toil and sleepless nights; just as preparing a banquet and serving the comfort of others is not easy. However, for the sake of many we will gladly undergo this, and while leaving the detailed execution of every point to the original writer, we will work hard to follow the plan of the proposed summary. For just as the builder of a new house must take responsibility for the entire construction, while the one who attempts to carve or paint must seek out what serves to decorate it, so I believe it is for us: to tell everything consistently and to dwell on every detail belongs to the original author, but to pursue brevity of speech and to avoid a detailed account of every event must be granted to the one who gathers the matter into a few words. Therefore, let us now begin the narration, bringing the preface to an end here. For it is absurd to be wordy before the history begins, yet to shorten the history itself.

## CHAPTER III.

<margin>A certain man named Simon informs Apollonius about the money in Jerusalem.</margin>
When the holy city was inhabited in total peace and the laws were observed as well as possible because of the piety of Onias the high priest and his hatred of wickedness, it happened that even the kings themselves held the place in honor and adorned the sanctuary with the most excellent gifts, so much so that Seleucus <note>Seleucus IV Philopator, king of the Seleucid Empire</note>, the king of Asia, provided all the expenses necessary for the administration of the sacrifices from his own revenues. However, a certain Simon from the tribe of Benjamin, who had been appointed overseer of the temple, had a disagreement with the high priest Onias concerning the administration of the city market; and when he could not overcome him, he went to Apollonius, the son of Thraseas, who at that time was the governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia. He reported to him that the treasury in Jerusalem was full of an unspeakable amount of money, so much so that the sum of the funds was beyond counting, and that since these funds did not belong to the account of the sacrifices, they could be brought under the king's power. When Apollonius met with the king, he revealed to him the information about this money; and the king appointed Heliodorus, his chancellor, to this business and sent him with orders to see to the removal of the aforementioned money. Heliodorus immediately began the journey, ostensibly to visit the cities of Coelesyria, but in reality to carry out the king's will. When he arrived in Jerusalem and was kindly received by the high priest of the city, he explained the report and declared the reason he was there, and asked if these things were truly so. Then the high priest showed him that these were deposits for widows and orphans, and some also belonged to Hyrcanus, the son of Tobias, a man of very great standing—not as the wicked Simon had falsely claimed—and that the total sum was four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold <note>A talent was a massive unit of weight; this represents a fortune worth millions in modern currency</note>. He stated that it was an utter sin to defraud those who had put their trust in the holiness of the place and the majesty of the sanctuary, which is revered throughout the whole world for its right of asylum. But Helio-

<column-break/>

dorus, because of the orders he had from the king, judged that this money must entirely be surrendered to the royal treasury; therefore, on the appointed day, he entered to oversee the inspection. Then indeed there was no small trembling throughout the whole city: the priests threw themselves down before the altar in their priestly vestments and called out to heaven to Him who had given the law concerning deposits, asking that He keep the funds safe for those who had deposited them. Now, whoever looked upon the face of the high priest was wounded in his soul. For his appearance and the change in his color revealed the inward heat of his mind; for the man was surrounded by a certain fear and a horror of the body, from which it became clear to those watching what pain was in his soul. Then people rushed out from their houses in crowds for public supplication, because the holy place was about to be brought into contempt. Women, with hair disheveled and wearing sackcloth <note>original: "centones"; literally rags or patchwork garments used in mourning</note> beneath their breasts, filled the streets; and the young women who were usually kept indoors ran out, some to the gates, some to the walls, while others looked out through the windows. All of them, with hands stretched out toward heaven, made their prayers, so that the expectation of the crowd—mixed from every kind of person—and the high priest in his great agony, was a miserable sight. Therefore, they pleaded with the Almighty Lord that the things entrusted to them might be kept safe and sound for those who had entrusted them. Meanwhile, Heliodorus began to carry out what had been decided. But <margin>Heliodorus is divinely repelled from plundering the money.</margin> as he was already standing with his guards at the treasury, the Lord of our fathers and the Ruler of all things showed such a great vision that all who had dared to come there were struck by the power of God and were nearly drained of life by fear. For there appeared to them a certain horse carrying a terrible rider, adorned with a most beautiful covering, which, rushing forward with force, struck Heliodorus with its front hooves. And the one who sat upon the horse was seen to have golden armor; likewise, two other young men appeared before him, excellent in strength, most beautiful in appearance, and dressed in noble clothing. They stood on either side of Apollonius <note>The text here refers to Heliodorus; "Apollonium" is likely a scribal error in the Latin source for Heliodorus</note> and scourged him continually, raining many blows upon him. Suddenly he collapsed to the ground and was surrounded by great darkness; his men snatched him up and placed him on a litter—the man who had just entered that aforementioned treasury with such a great crowd and his entire bodyguard—and they carried him out, his own weapons helping him not at all, as they openly acknowledged the power of God. And he indeed lay there, mute by divine action and destitute of all hope of safety. But the people gave thanks to the Lord, who had graced His own place with such honor; and the temple, which a little while before had been full of fear and confusion, now overflowed with joy and gladness at the presence of the Almighty Lord. Then immediately some of Heliodorus’s close friends asked Onias to pray to the Most High God to grant life to him, as he was at his very last breath. The high priest, fearing that perhaps the king might suspect the Jews had committed some crime against Heliodorus, offered a sacrifice for the man's health. And while he was performing the atonement, the same young men appeared again to Heliodorus, dressed in the same clothes, and standing by him, they said: "Give great thanks to Onias..."
