### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>Simon slanders Onias.</margin>
But that man Simon, mentioned earlier, who was the betrayer of the money and of his country, began to slander Onias, as if Onias himself had incited Heliodorus and had been the author of these evils. He dared to call this man—who had deserved well of the city, was a lover of his own people, and a guardian of the laws—a seeker of rebellion. These enmities proceeded so far that murders were even committed by some of Simon’s close associates. Onias, seeing the danger of the strife and the madness of Apollonius (who, as governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, was fueling Simon’s wickedness), went to the king—not as an accuser of his fellow citizens, but as one looking out for the public and private welfare. For he saw that without the king’s oversight, it was impossible for affairs to remain peaceful, and that Simon would not end his madness. Later, when Seleucus had died and Antiochus, who was surnamed Epiphanes <note>original: "Epiphanes"; the name means "The Illustrious" or "God Manifest"</note>, had obtained the kingdom, 

<margin>Jason usurps the high priesthood.</margin>
Jason, the brother of Onias, usurped the high priesthood by approaching the king and promising him three hundred and sixty talents of silver, and eighty talents from another revenue. Furthermore, he promised he would sign for another hundred and fifty if he were granted the power to establish a gymnasium and an *ephebium* <term>ephebiam: a Greek educational institution for training young men in athletics and citizenship</term> for him, and to enroll the people of Jerusalem as citizens of Antioch <note>original: "Antiochenos transcribendi"; this allowed the Jewish elite to gain the social and economic privileges of Greek citizenship</note>. 

<margin>Jason turns the Jews toward Greek customs.</margin>
Thus, having obtained the leadership with the king’s consent, he immediately began to lead his countrymen toward Greek customs. He abolished the privileges granted to the Jews by previous kings—which had been obtained through John, the father of Eupolemus (the man who had conducted the embassy to the Romans regarding friendship and alliance)—and, destroying the lawful institutions of the republic, he introduced illegal practices. For he deliberately built a gymnasium right under the citadel itself, and he forced the most noble of the youths to serve under the broad-brimmed hat <note>original: "sub uelarium"; likely referring to the *petasos*, a Greek hat associated with the god Hermes and worn by those in the gymnasium, which traditional Jews saw as a sign of pagan influence</note>. And so, through the wicked and unpriestly crime of this ungodly Jason, the Greek fashion and the adoption of foreign customs flourished to such a degree that the priests were no longer dedicated to the duties of the altar. Instead, despising the temple and neglecting the sacrifices, they hurried to take part in the unlawful displays of the wrestling arena and the competition of the discus, holding their ancestral honors as nothing and considering Greek glories to be the finest of all.

<column-break/>

<page-num>354</page-num>

Because of these things, they suffered a heavy calamity; those very people whose customs they envied and whom they sought to resemble in every way became their enemies and executioners. For to sin against the divine laws is no light matter, as the following time will declare. Now, when the five-year games were being held at Tyre in the presence of the king, the wicked Jason sent spectators from Jerusalem as "Antiochians," carrying three hundred drachmas of silver for the sacrifice to Hercules. However, those who carried the money requested that it not be spent on a sacrifice (for they felt it was not appropriate) but that it be applied to some other expense. Thus, the money was sent by the sender for the sacrifice to Hercules, but because of those who carried it, it was used for the construction of triremes <term>triremes: ancient warships with three banks of oars</term>. Later, when Apollonius, the son of Mnestheus, was sent to Egypt for the day when King Ptolemy Philometor was to be greeted, Antiochus, having learned that the king had become alienated from his affairs, began to think about the security of his own realm. Therefore, he set out for Joppa and came to Jerusalem, where he was magnificently received by Jason and the city, and admitted with torches and acclamations; from there he returned to Phoenicia.

After a three-year period, Jason sent Menelaus, the brother of the Simon mentioned before, to carry money to the king and to deliver reports on necessary matters. 

<margin>Menelaus transfers the high priesthood to himself.</margin>
But Menelaus, having been recommended to the king and having flattered him, transferred the high priesthood to himself under the appearance of authority, outbidding Jason by three hundred talents of silver. Having received the king’s mandates, he returned; he brought nothing worthy of the high priesthood, but rather the spirit of a cruel tyrant and the rages of a savage beast. And so Jason, who had cheated his own brother, was himself cheated by another and driven as a fugitive into the region of the Ammonites. But Menelaus, having obtained the leadership, performed none of the things he had promised the king, even though Sostratus, the governor of the citadel, demanded the money, for the collection of the taxes was under his care. For this reason, both were summoned by the king and removed from their offices; they left successors: Menelaus left his brother Lysimachus for his priesthood, and Sostratus left Crates, the governor of the Cyprians. 

While things were in this state, it happened that the people of Tarsus and Mallus stirred up a revolt because they had been given as a gift to Antiochus’s concubine, Antiochida. Therefore, the king set out in haste to settle the matter, leaving behind Andronicus, a man of high dignity, as his deputy. Then Menelaus, thinking he had found a convenient opportunity, stole some golden vessels from the temple and gave them to Andronicus as a gift, and he had already sold others to various people in the neighboring cities and in Tyre. When Onias became certain of this, he rebuked him, after having withdrawn himself into a place of sanctuary at Daphne, which is located near Antioch. Therefore, Menelaus privately urged Andronicus to kill Onias. Andronicus came to Onias and, having deceived him with a pledge of safety and his right hand given with an oath, persuaded him to come out of the sanctuary (even though he was suspected). Immediately, with no regard for justice, he murdered him. 

<margin>The murder of Onias.</margin>
For this reason, many people of other nations, as well as the Jews, were indignant at the wicked murder of such a man.

In this way, they wounded many of them, struck some down, put them all to flight, and killed the sacrilegious man himself beside the treasury. Afterward, an indictment concerning these matters was drawn up against Menelaus. When the king came to Tyre, three men sent by the senate <note>The Gerousia, or council of elders in Jerusalem.</note> argued the case before him. But Menelaus, being already convicted, promised many things to Ptolemy, son of Dorymenes, to persuade the king to change his mind. Therefore, Menelaus took the king aside into a certain peristyle <note>A courtyard surrounded by columns.</note>, as if for the sake of cooling off, and so altered his mind that he acquitted Menelaus, the author of all the evil, of the charges; but those miserable men (who, if they had spoken even before Scythians <note>The Scythians were famously regarded by Greeks and Romans as the most barbaric and merciless of peoples.</note>, would have been found innocent) he condemned to death. Thus, those who had pleaded the cause of the city, the people, and the sacred vessels quickly suffered an undeserved penalty. For this reason, even the Tyrians, out of hatred for the crime, provided magnificently for everything pertaining to their burial. But Menelaus, through the greed of those in power, remained in his high office, increasing in malice and becoming the greatest betrayer of his fellow citizens.

### CHAPTER V.

<margin>Portents.</margin>
About that time, when Antiochus had undertaken his second expedition into Egypt, it happened that throughout the entire city, for nearly forty days, there were seen in the air horsemen racing in golden clothing, armed cohorts with spears, and organized troops of cavalry. Conflicts and charges were seen on both sides, with the clashing of shields, thickets of spears, drawn swords, the hurling of missiles, the flashing of golden armor, and every kind of breastplate. Everyone prayed that these omens <note>original: "ostentū"</note> might turn out for good. However, when a false rumor arose that Antiochus had died, Jason gathered no fewer than a thousand men and made a sudden attack on the city. Although those on the walls resisted, when the city was finally being taken, Menelaus fled to the citadel. But Jason 
<margin>Jason’s cruelty toward his own people.</margin>
committed a slaughter of his own citizens, sparing no one, not considering that success against one's own kin is the greatest misfortune—acting as if he were taking tro- <column-break/> phies from enemies rather than from his own people. Yet he did not obtain the high priesthood; 
<margin>The flight of Jason.</margin>
instead, finding a shameful end to his plot, he fled again as a fugitive into the land of the Ammonites, and reached an end worthy of his wicked life. For, being accused before Aretas, the tyrant of the Arabs, he fled from city to city, hunted by all and pursued with hatred as a deserter of the laws, and detested as an executioner of his country and citizens. He was eventually driven into Egypt. He who had deprived many of their homeland perished as an exile, having set out for the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans; there was a contemporary legend that the Jews and Spartans were related.</note>, as if they would provide him protection because of their kinship. He who had left many unburied was himself unmourned by any, lacked all funeral honors, and was denied the tomb of his ancestors. When these things were reported, the 
<margin>Antiochus devastates Jerusalem.</margin>
king suspected that Judea was revolting. Therefore, departing from Egypt with a feral mind, he took the city by force and commanded his soldiers to slaughter without mercy anyone they met and to kill those who took refuge in their houses. Thus, there was a slaughter of young and old, a killing of men, women, and children, and a massacre of virgins and infants, so that in no more than three days, eighty thousand people perished. Forty thousand were taken captive, and no fewer were sold into slavery than were killed. Not content with this, Antiochus dared to enter the most holy temple in all the world, with Menelaus—the traitor to the laws and the fatherland—as his guide. Taking the sacred vessels with his wicked hands, and handling the gifts of other kings that had been brought for the ornament, glory, and honor of the place, he profanely plundered and distributed them. Meanwhile, he became puffed up in spirit, not seeing that because of the sins of the city's inhabitants, the Lord was angry for a little while, and for that reason, 
<margin>See above, Chapter 3.</margin>
this place was held in contempt. If it had not happened that they were entangled in many sins—just as Heliodorus, who was sent by King Seleucus to take the money, had been suddenly repulsed from his audacity by a scourging—the same would have happened to this man. But God did not choose the people for the sake of the place, but the place for the sake of the people. Therefore, the place itself, which shared in the calamities that befell the nation, was later made a partner in the benefits bestowed by the Lord; and that which was abandoned in the anger of the Almighty was restored with all glory when the supreme Lord was reconciled again. So Antiochus, having carried away eighteen hundred talents from the temple, went quickly to Antioch, thinking in his pride that he could make the land navigable and the sea passable by foot: such was the arrogance of his mind. He left behind governors to harass the Jewish race: at Jerusalem, Philip, a Phrygian by nation, more cruel in character than the one who appointed him; at Mount Gerizim, Andronicus; and besides these, Menelaus, who was more bitter toward his own people than all the rest, and possessed a hostile mind toward the Jewish citizens. The king also sent that infamous leader Apollonius with an army of twenty-two thousand men, commanding him to kill all the adults and to sell the women and youths. When he reached Jerusalem, pretending peace, he waited until the holy day of the Sabbath. Finding the Jews resting, he ordered his men to take up arms, and he slaughtered all who had gone out to the spectacle; then, rushing through the city with armed men, he laid low a vast multitude. ### CHAPTER VI.

<margin>King Antiochus sends an Athenian to compel the Jews to depart from their ancestral laws.</margin>
Not long after that time, the king sent an Athenian senator to compel the Jews to depart from the laws of their fathers, to cease using the divine laws, and to pollute the temple in Jerusalem, renaming it after Jupiter Olympus; and to rename the temple at Gerizim "Jupiter the Hospitable," as those who lived in that place requested. The state of such great evil was heavy and grim for the common people. For the temple was filled with the luxury and gluttony of foreigners, who dallied with harlots in wickedness, and had relations with women within the sacred walls, and moreover brought in illicit things. The altar was full of abominable things forbidden by the law; it was not permitted to keep the Sabbath, nor to observe the ancestral feasts, nor for anyone to even confess himself to be a Jew. By bitter force, the Jews were led every month on the king's birthday to sacrifice, and during the *Bacchanalia* <note>The festival of the god Bacchus or Dionysus</note>, they were compelled to wear ivy and celebrate the Orgies in honor of Liber <note>original: "Libero"; another name for Bacchus, the god of wine and theater</note>. Furthermore, an edict was published at the suggestion of Ptolemy in the neighboring Greek cities, that they should follow the same practice and drive the Jews to sacrifice; and those who refused to cross over to the Greek customs were to be slaughtered. Therefore, one could see the present calamity. For two women were brought forward who had circumcised their sons; after their infants were hung from their breasts, they were led publicly through the city and then thrown headlong from the wall. Others, who had fled into nearby caves to keep the seventh day in secret, were betrayed to Philip and burned in the flames, because they feared to defend themselves out of respect for so religious a day. Therefore, I urge the readers of this book not to lose heart because of these adverse events, but to consider that these punishments are not for our destruction, but for the correction of our race; and that the fact that the wicked are not left unpunished for long, but immediately face penalties, is proof of a great benefit. For the Lord does not patiently wait, as He does with other nations, until he punishes them when they have reached the height of their crimes; but He decided to act thus with us so that He would not have to take vengeance on us after we had reached the extreme of sins. Therefore, He never withdraws His mercy from us, and though He disciplines His people with adverse events, He does not forsake them. But let these few words be said by way of a reminder. Now we must come to the narrative.

<margin>Eleazar, persevering in Judaism, is put to death.</margin>
Eleazar, one of the primary scribes, a man already advanced in age and of a very beautiful countenance, was being forced to eat swine’s flesh by having his mouth pried open. But he, preferring a glorious death to an infamous life, went forward of his own accord to the *tympanum* <note>a drum-like rack or instrument of torture</note>, spitting it out, as was proper for those to do who preferred to undergo torture rather than taste forbidden things out of a desire for living. But those who presided over the wicked sacrifice, because of their long acquaintance with the man, took him aside privately and urged him to bring meat prepared by himself which was lawful for him to use, and to pretend that he was eating the meat of the sacrifices commanded by the king. They suggested this so that by this reason he might avoid death, and because of the old friendship he had with them, he might be treated humanely. But he, following an honorable 

<column-break/>

358
BOOK II.
cc 2

reasoning, worthy of his age and the excellence of his seniority and his distinguished gray hair, and his excellent education from childhood—or rather, in accordance with the holy and divinely given law—replied immediately, saying he would rather be sent to the underworld. "For it is not worthy of our age," he said, "to pretend, lest many young people, thinking that Eleazar, a ninety-year-old man, had gone over to foreign rites, might themselves also err because of my deception and fault for the sake of a brief and fleeting life, and thus I would bring infamy and a stain upon my old age. For even if in the present I avoid the punishment of men, I shall not escape the hand of the Almighty, neither living nor dead. Therefore, if I now courageously end my life, I shall show myself worthy of my old age, and I shall leave an excellent example to the young for meeting death eagerly and nobly for the sake of such venerable and holy laws." Having spoken these words, he immediately went to the *tympanum*. And those who were leading him, having changed the goodwill they had shown a moment before into malice because of his speech (which they interpreted as madness), as he was about to end his life under the blows, he groaned and said: "It is clear to the Lord, who has holy knowledge, that although I could have escaped death, I endure hard pains of the body being beaten; but in my soul I suffer these things gladly because of my reverence for Him." In this manner he departed from life, leaving his death as an example of greatness of soul and a monument of virtue, not only to the young, but also to the majority of his nation.

### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>Concerning the seven brothers and their mother, put to death for Judaism.</margin>
<margin>The First.</margin>
It also happened that seven brothers with their mother were arrested and were being tortured with whips and thongs by the king to compel them to taste swine’s flesh against the law. One of them, who spoke first, said: "Why do you hesitate to ask and learn from us? For we are ready to die rather than violate the laws of our fathers." At this, the king, seized with fury, ordered pans and cauldrons to be heated; when these were glowing with fire, he immediately ordered the tongue of the one who had spoken first to be cut out, the skin of his head to be pulled off, and his hands and feet to be amputated, while the rest of the brothers and the mother looked on. And when he was thus completely mutilated, the king ordered him, while still breathing, to be brought to the fire and fried. As the vapor from the pan spread widely, the brothers and the mother exhorted each other to meet death nobly, saying: "The Lord God sees these things, and in truth He has compassion on us, just as Moses declared in his song, which openly bears witness against the Israelites, saying: 'And He will have compassion on His servants.'"

<margin>The Second.</margin>
When the first had died in this manner, they led the second to the same torture; and having torn the skin of his head with the hair, they asked him if he would eat before his body was torn limb from limb. But he replied in his father's tongue that he would not do it. Therefore, he also underwent the following sequence of torture, just as the first had. When he was at his last breath, he spoke thus: "You, indeed, O furious man, release us from this life; but the King of the world will raise us up, who have died for His laws, into an eternal restoration of life."

<margin>The Third.</margin>
After him, the third was mocked; and being ordered to put out his tongue, he immediately did so, and boldly stretched out his hands, speaking nobly: "I have these from heaven, and for the sake of His laws I [count] these..."

<margin>The Mother.</margin>
But the mother was beyond measure wonderful and worthy of happy memory, who, seeing seven sons perish in the space of a single day, bore it with a steady mind because of the hope she placed in the Lord. She encouraged each of them in her native language <note>original: "patrio sermone"; referring to Hebrew or Aramaic</note>, full of a noble spirit; stirring up her womanly nature with a manly courage, she spoke to them thus:

<margin>a. He suspects from the mother's pronunciation (for he himself did not know Hebrew) that she was cursing him, etc.</margin>
But Antiochus, thinking himself despised and suspecting the <gloss>a</gloss> reproachful voice, while the youngest was still alive, not only used words of encouragement but even confirmed with an oath that he would make him rich and happy if he would turn away from his ancestral customs, and that he would count him among his friends and entrust him with honors. When the youth was not moved at all, the king called the mother and urged her to give the boy saving counsel. But she, after being much urged by him, promised she would persuade her son. Leaning toward him and mocking the cruel tyrant, she said thus in her native language:
> "My son, have pity on me, who carried you in my womb for nine months, who nursed you for three years, who educated you and brought you to this age. I ask you, son, to look at the heaven and the earth and all that is in them, and recognize that God made these things from nothing, and so the human race was created. Do not fear this executioner, but prove worthy of your brothers and accept death, so that by God's mercy I may receive you back with your brothers."

<margin>The Seventh.</margin>
While she was still saying these things, the youth spoke thus: "Whom are you waiting for? I do not obey the king's command, but I listen to the command of the law given to our ancestors through Moses. But you, the inventor of every wickedness against the Hebrews, shall not escape the hand of God. We indeed suffer these things for our own sins; but if for the sake of correction and discipline our immortal Lord is angry for a little while, He will again be reconciled to His servants. But you, impious man and most wicked of all humans, do not be puffed up with uncertain hope while you lift your hands against the children of heaven."

"For you have not yet escaped the judgment of the almighty and all-seeing God. For our brothers, having now suffered a brief pain, have entered into the divine covenant of eternal life. But you, by the judgment of God, shall pay the just penalties for your pride. I, following the example of my brothers, surrender both body and soul for the laws of our fathers, praying to God that He may soon be merciful to our nation, and that you, amidst tortures and lashes, may confess Him to be the only God; and that in me and my brothers the wrath of the Almighty may be stayed, which has justly raged against our entire race." At this, the king, moved with rage, treated him more cruelly than all the others, taking the mockery bitterly. And so this one ended his life purely, trusting entirely in the Lord; and last of all, after her sons, the mother died. And concerning the ritual sacrifices <note>original: "uiscerationibus"; literally the eating of sacrificial meats, here referring to the forced eating of swine's flesh</note> and the tortures at their hands, let this much be said.

## CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>Judas gathers forces.</margin>
But Judas Maccabeus and his companions, creeping secretly into the villages, called their kinsmen together; and taking with them those who had remained faithful to Judaism, they gathered about six thousand men. They prayed to the Lord to look upon His people, who were being harassed by all, to have mercy on the temple profaned by impious men, to pity the city which was being laid waste and was about to be leveled to the ground, to hear the blood crying out to Him, to remember the wicked slaughter of innocent infants, and to avenge the insults directed against His name. Therefore, once his band was formed, Maccabeus became unstoppable to the nations, for the wrath of the Lord was turned into mercy. Attacking towns and cities unexpectedly, he set them on fire; and by seizing strategic locations, he put many of the enemy to flight, using the cover of night as his greatest aid for such ambushes. As the fame of his valor spread everywhere, Philip <note>The Seleucid governor of Jerusalem</note>, noticing the man gaining ground little by little and frequently succeeding in his affairs, wrote to Ptolemy, the governor of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia, to come to the aid of the king's business. He immediately sent Nicanor, son of Patroclus, one of the primary friends, assigning to him no fewer than twenty thousand men of various nations to wipe out the entire race of the Jews. To him he also joined Gorgias, a man experienced in command and military matters. Nicanor, moreover, determined to raise the tribute of two thousand <term>talents</term> <note>A talent was a massive unit of weight/currency; 2,000 talents would be several dozen tons of silver</note> which the king owed to the Romans by selling Jewish captives. He immediately sent word to the coastal cities inviting people to buy Jewish slaves, promising to sell ninety bodies for one talent, not expecting the punishment from the Almighty that was hanging over him.

<margin>Nicanor's expedition into Judea.</margin>
When this expedition of Nicanor was announced to Judas, and he had informed his men of the army's arrival, those who were fearful and distrustful of God's vengeance fled and slipped away. Others sold all their remaining possessions and together prayed to the Lord to protect those who had been sold by the impious Nicanor even before they were captured—if not for their own sake, then for the sake of the covenants He had made with their ancestors, and because His venerable and majestic name was called upon them.

Therefore Maccabeus, having gathered his men, who were six thousand in number, exhorted them not to fear the enemies, nor...

# BOOK II.

...[they should not] fear the multitude of foreigners attacking them with injustice, but fight spiritedly. They should keep before their eyes the wicked insult those men offered to the holy place, the vexation of the shamefully wasted city, and furthermore, the overturning of their ancient institutions. "They indeed," he said, "rely on their weapons and their boldness; but we trust in the Almighty God, who is able with a single nod to strike down both those who attack us and the entire world." He likewise reminded them of the help brought to their ancestors from heaven, such as the event against Sennacherib <note>A reference to the Assyrian king whose army was destroyed by an angel; see 2 Kings 19</note>, in which one hundred and eighty-five thousand men perished. He also mentioned the battle fought in Babylonia against the Galatians, where, although only eight thousand had come to perform the deed along with four thousand Macedonians, and the Macedonians hesitated, those eight thousand—through the intervention of celestial aid—overcame one hundred and twenty thousand of the enemy and gained incredible advantages.

<margin>4 Kings 19; Tobit 1; Ecclesiasticus 48; Isaiah 37</margin>

When he had increased the courage of his men with these examples and made them ready to die for their laws and their country, he divided the army into four parts. He placed his brothers Simon, Joseph, and Jonathan each in charge of their own division, assigning fifteen hundred soldiers to each. Furthermore, he appointed Eleazar to lead the reading of the Holy Book. Having given the watchword "Divine Help," he himself led the first division and joined battle with Nicanor. With the aid of Almighty God, they killed over nine thousand of Nicanor’s men; they wounded and physically disabled the vast majority, and drove them all into flight. 

<margin>The Nicanorians defeated by the Jews.</margin>

They took the money of those who had come to buy them as slaves, and after pursuing them for a time, they retreated, being limited by the hour because it was the day before the Sabbath; for this reason, they did not press the pursuit for long. After gathering the enemies' weapons and stripping the spoils, they observed the Sabbath, giving great thanks and praise to the Lord, who had preserved them until that day and had shown them a sign of His mercy. After the Sabbath, they shared the prey with the afflicted, the widows, and the orphans; the remainder they divided among themselves and their servants. These things being finished, they made a public supplication, praying the merciful Lord to finally be reconciled with His servants.

They then attacked Timotheus and Bacchides, killing over twenty thousand of them. Having nobly gained possession of high fortifications, they divided very great spoils, which they shared equally among themselves and those who had suffered loss: the orphans, the widows, and even the elders. Having captured the enemies' weapons, they carefully stored everything in suitable places, and the rest of the booty they brought to Jerusalem. They also killed the commander of Timotheus’s forces, a most wicked man who had brought much loss upon the Jews. Then, celebrating the victory in their homeland, they burned Callisthenes, who had set fire to the sacred gates, after he had fled into a certain hut. Thus he received the worthy reward for his impiety.

<margin>Nicanor’s flight.</margin>

But that criminal Nicanor, who had brought a thousand merchants for the sale of the Jews, was humbled by the Lord’s help by those whom he judged

<column-break/>

to be most worthless. Casting off his splendid clothing, he fled across the sea like a fugitive, acting as his own guide through the wilderness, and arrived at Antioch with his business most unhappily managed and his army destroyed. He, who had undertaken to pay the tribute to the Romans from the captives of Jerusalem, now announced that the Jews had a Protector, and for this reason they could not be harmed, because they followed the laws established by Him.

## CHAPTER IX.

<margin>Antiochus Epiphanes repulsed from the city of Persepolis.</margin>

Around that time, Antiochus had retreated in disgrace from the regions of Persia. For he had entered the city called Persepolis and attempted to rob the temple and occupy the city. Therefore, the common people were stirred up to take up arms, and it happened that Antiochus, being repulsed by the inhabitants, made a shameful retreat. While he was at Ecbatana, he received news of what had happened to Nicanor and Timotheus. Swelling with anger, he thought to take out on the Jews the injury he had received from those who had put him to flight. Therefore, he ordered his charioteer to drive without stopping to finish the journey, while celestial punishments were clearly pressing upon him. For he had spoken thus proudly: "I will make Jerusalem a graveyard for the Jews when I arrive there."

<margin>2 Chronicles 16</margin>

But the Almighty Lord, the God of the Israelites, struck him with an incurable and unseen disease. For as soon as he uttered that word, 

<margin>Antiochus Epiphanes is afflicted with torments from God.</margin>

he was seized with an irremediable pain in his bowels and bitter torments of the intestines—and most justly so, for he had tortured the bowels of others with so many and such unheard-of punishments. Yet he was so far from ending his ferocity that, filled with even more pride, he breathed fire in his mind against the Jews and ordered the journey to be accelerated. It happened, however, that as he was being carried rapidly along, he fell from his chariot; being injured by the heavy fall, all the members of his body were racked with pain. He who just a moment ago, with arrogance exceeding human measure, thought he could command the waves of the sea and weigh the heights of mountains in a balance, was now cast down to the ground and carried in a litter, showing the manifest power of God to everyone. Worms swarmed out of the impious man's body, and while he was still living, his flesh fell away in pain and torments. The stench was so great that it was offensive to the whole army; he who a little while before seemed to touch the stars of heaven, no one could now carry because of the intolerable poisonous smell.

Here, therefore, being shaken, he began to abandon his excessive pride and come to a knowledge of himself, as his pains increased more and more under the divine scourge. Not even he could bear his own smell, and so he spoke: "It is right to be subject to God, and not, since you are mortal, to arrogantly equal yourself to God." The criminal then prayed to the Lord (who would no longer have mercy on him), saying that he would make the holy city free (toward which he was hastening with such speed to level it to the ground and turn it into a graveyard); and that he would make all the Jews equal to the Athenians <note>To be made "equal to the Athenians" meant granting the Jews the highest possible civic status and rights within the Greek political world of the time.</note> (whom he had previously judged not even worthy of burial, but to be thrown out with their little ones to be devoured by birds and beasts). He also promised to adorn the sacred temple, which he had previously plundered, with the most beautiful gifts...

But when his pains did not cease at all (for the just judgment of God had come upon him), despairing of his condition, he wrote to the Jews the letter written below, composed in the manner of a petition, containing these things:

<margin>
The flattering letter of Antiochus Epiphanes to the Jews.

TO THE GOOD JEWISH CITIZENS, King and Governor Antiochus sends much greeting, wishing them health and prosperity. If you and your children are well, and if your affairs are as you wish them, I give the greatest thanks to God, having my hope in heaven. For my part, I am in weak health. Returning from the region of Persia and having fallen into a difficult illness, I remembered with affection your honor and goodwill, and thought it necessary to take care for the common security of all. I do not indeed despair of myself, for I have great hope that I shall escape this sickness. But considering that my father also, at the time he made an expedition into the upper regions, appointed a successor, so that if anything unexpected should happen, or any ill news be reported, the inhabitants, knowing to whom the administration of affairs had been left, would not be disturbed; furthermore, observing that the neighboring dynasts and nearby kingdoms are watching for the right moment and waiting for the outcome, I have designated my son Antiochus as king, whom I often commended and entrusted to many of you when I was hurrying back to the upper satrapies <note>Satrapies were provinces in the Persian and Seleucid empires governed by satraps.</note>. Therefore, I exhort and ask you that, being mindful of the benefits I have provided both publicly and privately, you maintain toward me and my son the same goodwill that each of you has. For I am confident that he, following my principles, will deal with you with moderation and humanity. Thus that murderer and blasphemer, having suffered terrible things just as he had treated others, ended his life by a most miserable fate in the mountains in a foreign land. When Philip, who had been brought up with him, took away his body, he feared the son of Antiochus and withdrew himself to Ptolemy Philometor in Egypt.

### CHAPTER X.

<margin>
Maccabeus purifies the temple and restores the city.
</margin>
But Maccabeus and his companions, under the Lord’s guidance, recovered the temple and the city. They pulled down the altars which the foreigners had built in the marketplace, as well as the shrines, and having purified the temple, they made another altar. Striking fire from flints, they offered sacrifice after a lapse of two years and six months, and they attended to the incense, the lamps, and the bread of the Presence. When these things were done, they fell prostrate and entreated the Lord that they might not fall into such evils again, but if they should ever sin, they might be chastened by Him with gentleness, and not be handed over to blasphemous and barbaric nations. Now on the same day that the temple had been profaned by foreigners, it happened that the purification of the temple took place on that very day, which was the twenty-fifth day of the same month, namely Chislev <note>The ninth month of the Hebrew calendar, roughly December.</note>. They celebrated it with joy for eight days, in the manner of the Feast of Tabernacle-

Therefore, carrying thyrsi <note>Wands or branches wrapped in ivy or vine leaves used in processions.</note>, green boughs, and also palms, they offered hymns of praise to Him who had granted them the favor of purifying His own holy place. They ordained by a public decree and a vote of the people that the entire nation of the Jews should observe these days every year. Such was the end of Antiochus, who was called Epiphanes.

<margin>
Antiochus Eupator.

Having obtained the kingdom, he committed the administration of affairs to a certain Lysias, the chief governor of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia.

Ptolemy Macron dies.

For Ptolemy, who was called Macron, being determined to maintain justice toward the Jews (because of the great injury that had been done to them), endeavored to conduct business with them peacefully. For this reason, he was accused by his friends before Eupator and was repeatedly called a traitor because he had abandoned Cyprus, which Philometor had entrusted to him, and had gone over to Antiochus Epiphanes. Seeing that he held no honorable position of power, he ended his life with poison because of his mental anguish.

<margin>
Gorgias.

But Gorgias, having become the governor of those places, hired soldiers and nurtured constant war against the Jews. Added to this, the Idumeans, who held well-placed fortifications, harassed the Jews and, receiving those who had been driven out of Jerusalem, attempted to keep the war alive.

The Maccabees’ excursion and battle against the Idumean fortifications.

But those with Maccabeus, having made supplication and prayed to God that He would be their helper, made an assault upon the strongholds of the Idumeans. Having fiercely attacked those places, they took possession of them; and having overcome all who fought from the walls, they slaughtered those who fell in their way, killing no fewer than twenty thousand. When no fewer than nine thousand had fled into two very strong towers, which had everything necessary to endure a siege, Maccabeus left Simon and Joseph, and also Zacchaeus with his men, to besiege them, while he himself departed to places where he was more urgently needed. But those with Simon, led by greed, were bribed with money by some of those in the towers; having accepted seventy thousand drachmas, they allowed some to slip away. When this was reported to Maccabeus, he called the leaders of the army together and accused those men of having sold their brothers for money by letting their enemies go against them. He executed those who had been traitors and immediately captured the two towers. Using arms successfully in everything he did, he destroyed more than twenty thousand men in those two fortifications.

But Timotheus, who had previously been defeated by the Jews, having gathered a huge army of foreigners and no small number of Asian cavalry, arrived as if to subdue Judea by force of arms. But as he approached, the Maccabeans turned to pray to God, sprinkling earth upon their heads and girding their loins with sackcloth. Prostrate at the foot of the altar, they prayed that He would be merciful to them, but be an enemy to their enemies and an adversary to their adversaries, as the law declares. Then, having finished their prayer, they took up their arms and advanced a good distance from the city; and when they had come near the enemy—

Then, as soon as day broke, both sides joined in battle; the one side holding a pledge of success and victory joined with virtue, having their refuge in the Lord; the other side using fury as their leader in the struggle. Therefore, once the sharp battle was joined, there appeared to the adversaries from heaven five magnificent men on horses with golden bridles, leading the Jews. ### CHAPTER XI.

<margin>
Lysias enters Judea.
</margin>
A very short time later, Lysias, the king’s guardian and kinsman, who was the administrator of affairs, took these events very badly. Having gathered about eight thousand <note>The text reads 'eight thousand' (octo millia), though historical editions usually record eighty thousand (octoginta millia), which is more consistent with the mention of eighty elephants.</note> infantry and all his cavalry, he marched against the Jews. He intended to make the city a dwelling for Greeks, to make the temple a source of profit (like the other shrines of the Gentiles), and to have the high priesthood for sale every year, thinking nothing of the power of God. Thus, fierce with his great cavalry and even greater infantry forces, and eighty elephants, he entered Judea. He approached Beth-zur, a naturally fortified place about five stadiums <note>original: "quinque stadia". Note: Five stadiums is roughly 1 kilometer. Historical accounts usually place Beth-zur much further from Jerusalem—about 30 kilometers.</note> distant from Jerusalem, and began to besiege it.

When the Maccabeans understood that he was besieging the fortifications, they, along with the common crowd of people, besought the Lord with wailing and tears to send a good spirit <note>original: "bonum genium". In this context, a guardian angel or divine protector.</note> of Israel for their safety. Maccabeus himself was the first to take up arms, and he exhorted the others to undergo the danger with him to help their kinsmen. So, as they set out together eagerly and were not yet far from Jerusalem,

<margin>
a prodigy
</margin>
a rider appeared preceding them in a white garment, shaking golden weapons. Then they all together gave thanks to the merciful God, and were so strengthened in their spirits that they were ready to pierce through not only men, but even the fiercest beasts,

<column-break/>

and iron walls. Thus they moved forward in battle array, having a heavenly helper through the mercy of the Lord. Charging into the enemy like lions, they overthrew eleven thousand infantry and sixteen hundred horsemen, and put all the rest to flight; most of whom escaped wounded and naked. Lysias himself escaped by a shameful flight. Being a man of some sense, and considering within himself the loss he had sustained, and reflecting that the Hebrews were invincible because the Almighty God fought for them,

<margin>
Lysias is put to flight and sends envoys to the Jews for peace.
</margin>
he sent envoys to them to discuss a settlement on whatever terms were just, promising that he would persuade the king to become their friend. Maccabeus, consulting the people's welfare, granted all the requests of Lysias. Indeed, whatever Maccabeus set forth in writing to Lysias concerning the Jews, the king conceded. For the letter written to the Jews by Lysias was in this manner:

LYSIAS TO THE JEWISH PEOPLE, GREETINGS. John and Absalom, sent by you, after they delivered your written requests to us, asked for a response concerning the things signified therein. Therefore, I have laid before the king the things that had to be referred to him, and he has granted what was allowable. If you maintain your goodwill in these affairs, I will endeavor in the future to be a cause of good things for you. But concerning these matters in detail, I have instructed both your men and mine to confer with you. Farewell. In the year one hundred and forty-eight, on the twenty-fourth of Dioscorus <note>A month in the Seleucid calendar, roughly corresponding to spring.</note>.

The king’s letter contained this: KING ANTIOCHUS to his brother Lysias, greetings. Since our father has been translated to the gods <note>A polite way of saying he has died and been deified.</note>,

<margin>
The letter of Antiochus Eupator to Lysias, in which he grants liberty to the Jews.
</margin>
and wishing that those who are subject to the kingdom should conduct their own affairs without disturbance, we hear that the Jews do not consent to the change to Greek customs made by my father, but prefer to cling to their own institutions, and request that their own laws be granted to them. Desiring, therefore, that this nation also be without trouble, we decree that the temple be restored to them, and that they may live according to the customs of their ancestors. You will do well, therefore, if you send messengers and give them your word, so that knowing our will, they may be of good cheer and gladly resume the administration of their own affairs.

The king’s letter to the nation was as follows:

<margin>
The king’s letter to the Jews.
</margin>
KING ANTIOCHUS to the Senate of the Jews and to the other Jews, greetings. If you are well, it is as we wish; we also are well. Menelaus has shown us that you wish to return to your own homes and stay there. Therefore, to those who return by the thirtieth day of the month Xanthicus <note>Roughly April.</note>, we grant protection and the right to use their own food and laws as before, and no one shall be molested in any way for errors committed. I have also sent Menelaus to reassure you. Farewell. In the year one hundred and forty-eight, the twenty-fifth of Xanthicus.

Quintus Memmius and Titus Manlius, legates of the Romans, to the Jewish people, greetings. What Lysias the king’s kinsman has granted you, we also approve. But concerning the things he judged should be referred to the king, deliberate upon them and send someone as soon as possible, so that we may settle the matter as is best for you.

### CHAPTER XII.

<margin>The people of Joppa drown the Jews.</margin>
Therefore, in the one hundred and forty-eighth year <note>Approximately 164 BCE</note>, on the twenty-fifth of Xanthicus <note>A month in the Macedonian calendar roughly corresponding to April</note>, once these agreements were made, Lysias departed to the king. The Jews turned themselves to farming. But the governors of the regions—Timotheus and Apollonius, the son of Gennaeus, as well as Hieronymus and Demophon, and besides them Nicanor the governor of Cyprus—would not allow them to live in a quiet and peaceful state. The people of Joppa also committed a crime of this sort: they urged the Jews living among them to board small boats which they themselves provided, along with their wives and children, as if no ill-will existed between them. But since the city had made this a public decree, and because the Jews consented—as they desired peace and had no suspicion—the people of Joppa led them out into the deep water and drowned them, no fewer than two hundred. Then, because the town was closed against him, he departed, intending to return and uproot the entire city of the people of Joppa. ...he demanded that he might carry away the bodies of the fallen, and that they might be committed to their ancestral 
<margin>...for the tombs ... Deuteronomy 7</margin> tombs along with their brothers. However, they found under the tunics of all the dead men votive offerings <note>original: "donaria"</note> consecrated to the idols of Jamnia, which the law forbids to the Jews. From this, it became clear to everyone that they had fallen for this very reason. Therefore, they all praised the Lord, the just judge, who makes hidden things manifest, and turning to prayer, they begged that the sin committed because of this might be entirely blotted out. Then the noble Judas exhorted the multitude to keep themselves blameless, seeing before their eyes what had happened because of the sin of the slain. Then, having collected a contribution and gathered two thousand drachmas of silver, he sent them to Jerusalem to provide a sacrifice for sin—acting rightly and honorably, as he was mindful of the resurrection. For if he did not hope that those who had fallen would rise again, it would have been superfluous and foolish to pray for the dead. Furthermore, because he considered that a very great grace is laid up for those who have fallen asleep in godliness, it was a holy and pious thought. For this reason, he provided an expiation for the dead, so that they might be released from their sin.

### CHAPTER XIII.

In the one hundred and forty-ninth year <note>Approximately 163 BCE</note>, word was brought to Judas that Antiochus Eupator was coming with a great force into Judea, and with him Lysias, the procurator and administrator of affairs, both of them leading Greek forces consisting of one hundred and ten thousand infantry, five thousand three hundred cavalry, twenty-two elephants, and three hundred scythed chariots. Menelaus also joined himself to them, and with much deceit exhorted Antiochus—not for the safety of his country, but in the hope of attaining 
<margin>Antiochus Eupator punishes Menelaus with death.</margin> leadership. But the King of kings <note>A title for God</note> stirred up the mind of Antiochus against that criminal. Thus, when Lysias showed that he was the cause of all the evils, Antiochus ordered him to be led to Beroea and to be killed in that place according to the custom. There was in that place a tower fifty cubits high, full of ash, which had a circular machine that precipitated into the ash from all sides. There, they would thrust down to their death those convicted of sacrilege or those bound by any other exceptional crime. By such a fate, it happened that the wicked Menelaus died, not even obtaining a burial. And quite rightly so, for he who had committed many crimes against the altar, where the fire and ash were holy, met his death in the ash. But the king, savage in spirit, proceeded to perpetrate the most foul things against the Jews, such as had been done under his father. When Judas learned of this, he commanded the multitude to beseech the Lord day and night that if ever he had helped them, he would do so now especially for those who were in danger concerning the law, the country, and the sacred temple; and that he would not allow the people, who had just recently been restored, to fall into the power of blasphemous nations. When they had all done this together, beseeching the merciful Lord with weeping and fasting, lying on the ground for three consecutive days, Judas consoled them and ordered them to be ready. He himself held a council apart with the elders, so that before the king's army could invade Judea and take possession of the city, they would go out and decide the outcome of the matter by the help of the Lord. Therefore, having committed the business to the Ruler of the world, and having exhorted his men to fight bravely for the laws, the sacred rites, 

<column-break/>

the city, the country, and the commonwealth even unto death, he made camp near Modin. Having given his men the watchword, "The Victory of God," he attacked the king's tent by night with the most excellent of the chosen young men. He slew about four thousand 
<margin>Judas invades Antiochus's camp at night. a. Lucinus fourteen.</margin> men in the camp and dispatched the chief elephant with the crowd of his household. Thus, having filled the camp with terror and confusion, he departed after the business was successfully conducted. This was done as day was now breaking, with the protection of the Lord helping him. Then the king, having taken a taste of this Jewish audacity, attempted the locations with skill, and moved his army toward Bethsura, which was a strong fortification of the Jews. But he was repulsed, he met with failure, and was inferior, while in the meantime Judas sent necessary supplies to those who were inside. However, Rhodocus, from the Jewish army, revealed the secret to the enemies; he was sought out, captured, and cast into chains. The king again spoke with the people of Bethsura, gave and received a pledge of faith, and departed. He engaged with Judas and was defeated. Afterward, when he learned that Philip, who had been left at Antioch to manage affairs, had revolted, he was troubled and 
<margin>Antiochus makes peace with the Jews.</margin> pleaded with the Jews. He submitted and swore to all their conditions. Peace being settled, he performed a sacrifice, showed honor to the temple, and behaved with humanity toward the place. He returned to favor with Maccabeus and, having left Hegemonides as governor from Ptolemais as far as the Gerrenes, he came to Ptolemais. And when the people of Ptolemais took the agreement poorly, being indignant because they wished to violate the conditions, Lysias went up to the platform and defended the cause so persuasively that he persuaded them and pacified them. Thus, their goodwill being reconciled, he withdrew to Antioch. In this manner did the king's expedition and retreat happen.

### CHAPTER XIV.

After three years had passed, it was reported to Judas that Demetrius, the son of Seleucus, had sailed into the port of Tripolis with a strong force and a fleet, and had taken possession of the region, having removed Antiochus and his procurator Lysias. Now a certain Alcimus, who had previously been high priest but who, during those times 
<margin>Alcimus approaches Antiochus to accuse Judas.</margin> when everything was in turmoil, had been voluntarily polluted, thinking that no way was now open to him either for safety or for the sacred altar, approached King Demetrius in the one hundred and fifty-first year <note>Approximately 161 BCE</note>. He brought him a golden crown and a palm, and also some of those branches which were usually used in the temple. On that day, he kept himself quiet. Then, having found a time suitable for his madness, being called into council by Demetrius and asked in what state the Jews were or what they were attempting, he responded in this manner: "Those of the Jews who are called Assideans <note>Hasideans; a sect of Jews devoted to the strict observance of the Law</note>, whose leader is Judas Maccabeus, foster war and sedition, not allowing the kingdom to enjoy tranquility. Therefore, I, being deprived of my ancestral dignity (I mean the high priesthood), have come here now—first, being sincerely devoted to the king's interests, and secondly, having regard for my own citizens. For our entire race is being harmed in no small way by the impudence of those whom I have mentioned. All these things being looked into, you, O King, should provide for both the region and our surrounded race, according to the ease of your humanity toward all. For as long as Judas survives, it is impossible for affairs to enjoy peace." When such things were said by him, the rest of the friends, who were ill-disposed toward Judas, immediately...

They set a day for a conference, on which day they would meet together privately. When that day arrived and separate chairs were placed for each, Judas stationed armed men in strategic locations, ready in case any treachery should suddenly arise from the enemy; they held the conference properly. After this, Nicanor remained in Jerusalem and committed nothing out of order; having dismissed the throngs of common soldiers, he kept Judas always in his sight, and treating him with human kindness, he encouraged him to take a wife and have children.

<margin>The pious Razis.</margin>
Now a certain Razis, a senator of Jerusalem, was reported to Nicanor. He was a man who loved the republic and had an excellent reputation, who because of his goodwill was called the father of the Jews. For in former times, when the Jews abstained from commerce with other nations, he had defended the cause of Judaism and had risked both body and soul for Judaism with the greatest constancy. Therefore Nicanor, wishing to make clear the hatred he bore toward the Jews, sent over five hundred soldiers to arrest him, for he judged that if he were captured, it would be a great calamity for the Jews. When the multitude of soldiers was just about to capture the tower, and was forcing the entrance gate, and he ordered fire to be brought and the doors set ablaze, Razis, being cornered, fell upon his sword. He preferred to die nobly rather than fall into the hands of wicked men and suffer an indignity unworthy of his noble birth. But because the wound was not properly inflicted in the heat of his trepidation, and the crowd was now bursting through the doors, he ran with great courage to the wall and bravely threw himself down into the crowd. When they quickly scattered and gave way, he fell into the middle of his belly; and while still breathing and inflamed with spirit, he sprang up, and with a fountain of blood flowing and being afflicted with heavy wounds, he ran through the crowd. Standing on a steep rock, now utterly drained of blood, he pulled out his intestines and, grasping them with both hands, threw them at the crowd, praying to the Lord of life and spirit that He would restore them to him again; in this manner, he ended his life.

those who approach your holy people with impious insults.” With this, he made an end of his prayer. But Nicanor’s men were advancing with trumpets and war-songs. The Jews, however, joined battle with the enemy by calling upon God and with prayers. Fighting with their hands but praying to God in their hearts, they laid low no fewer than thirty-five thousand men; they were greatly cheered by the presence of God. Then, when the work was done and they were withdrawing with joy, they learned that Nicanor had fallen in his armor. 
<margin>The death of Nicanor.</margin>
When a shout and a tumult arose, they gave thanks to the Almighty God in their ancestral language <note>Hebrew or Aramaic.</note>. Then Judas, who was in every way—both in body and spirit—the chief protector of his citizens and had preserved his goodwill toward his countrymen throughout his whole life, ordered that Nicanor’s head and his hand, cut off along with the shoulder, be carried to Jerusalem. When he arrived there, having called his countrymen together and positioned the priests before the altar, he ordered those who were in the fortress <note>The Acra, the Syrian-held citadel in Jerusalem.</note> to be summoned. Having shown them the head of the wicked Nicanor and the hand of that blasphemer—which he had stretched out against the holy house of the Almighty, boasting with proud words—he cut out the tongue of the impious Nicanor and said he would give it piece by piece to the birds, and would hang the hand of the madman in front of the temple. Then they all gave thanks toward heaven to the noble Lord and proclaimed His praises, He who had kept His place undefiled. He fixed Nicanor’s head to the fortress as a clear and manifest sign of the Lord’s help to everyone. They all decreed by common vote never to let that day pass without notice, but to hold it as a distinguished day: the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is called Adar in the Syrian tongue, one day before the Day of Mordecai <note>The festival of Purim.</note>. Since these things regarding Nicanor turned out this way, and from those times the Hebrews have held the city, I also will end my book here. And if I have written well and fittingly to the story, this is what I desired; but if poorly and weakly, it is what I was able to do. For just as it is unpleasant to drink wine alone, or again water, but just as wine tempered with water is sweet and brings a pleasing delight, so the arrangement of the discourse delights the ears of the readers by its construction. And here shall be the end.

<meta>This page marks the beginning of Book III. While the previous page concluded a historical narrative regarding the Maccabean revolt in Book II, the author now shifts to a theological meditation on the nature of divine glory, the limitations of human reason, and the ultimate destiny of the soul.</meta>

# BOOK III.

Rr
<meta>catchword: Hence</meta>

<margin>
Here, the discussion is not about human glory, but divine.
</margin>
...conclusions are not so firm, nor so well-founded in their principles, as are those which we draw here from the Holy Scriptures and derive from them. Certainly, we who have spent much time among these sacred pages—exercising our minds (inspired by the breath of the divine Spirit) upon these great and sublime matters—have seen many and remarkable things, at least according to our capacity, which are not easily found in human literature. Nor indeed are we concerned here with any glory or empty titles, but with that eternal and immortal kingdom of glory, and with that eternal happiness, which we have attempted to pursue and investigate from the sacred pages. For here the discourse is not of human glory, which like a "flower of the grass" <note>original: *flos fœni*; a biblical allusion to Isaiah 40:6-8, suggesting the fragility of life</note> is seen today and withers tomorrow, but of that glory which "no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man," which God has prepared for those who love Him.

<margin>
Our goal.
</margin>
Toward this goal <note>original: *metam*; literally the turning post in a race, signifying a final destination</note> we have directed all our studies and all our efforts, so that through these subtle divine and heavenly matters we might be able to reach it.

<margin>
Wisdom not in words but in power.
</margin>
This is that wisdom which is not in words, but in power <note>original: *virtute*; in this context, it refers to spiritual efficacy or moral strength rather than just "virtue"</note>: which has dwelt not here on earth, but in the heavens, from whence it descended to us, most poor "little men" <note>original: *homunculos*; a diminutive used by early modern authors to express human insignificance before God</note>, whose place and dwelling are here on earth.

<margin>
God’s goodness toward mankind.
</margin>
Oh, the inestimable goodness of God, who did not hesitate to pursue us, vile creatures, with such great gifts and graces! For He not only created this world of lands which we inhabit for our delights and conveniences, but He also opened an entrance for us to those heavenly and eternal things. Nor was this even enough: He even bestowed such honor upon us that He willed us to be heirs of His kingdom and co-heirs with Christ.

<margin>
Human dignity.
</margin>
Oh, how great is the dignity of the human race here! How great the glory! It seems to surpass all human minds. Certainly, there is nothing here that does not seem to ring with something divine. And although we have discussed these matters in this manner and explained them according to our small measure, it must not be thought that we have explained everything fully here. For who can fully explain those things which not even an angelic mind can attain?

<margin>
In a riddle.
</margin>
Here we see only as if "through a mirror and in a riddle" <note>original: *per speculum & in ænigmate*; a famous reference to 1 Corinthians 13:12 regarding the obscured nature of divine knowledge in this life</note>, things which we shall then see face to face, when we have been received into that choir of the blessed.

<margin>
The ardor of the Spirit.
</margin>
Hence it can be understood how great the ardor of the divine Spirit is here, which glides into our breasts and carries us away into such high thoughts that we see certain things as if through dreams and visions. Nor indeed should it be thought that we are speaking here of just any matters, but of those which pertain to divine worship and to our salvation. For who would lead us into error here, when Truth itself guides us?

<summary>In this opening of Book III, the author argues that knowledge derived from Scripture is far superior to human philosophy, emphasizing that humanity's true dignity lies in being co-heirs with Christ to an eternal, heavenly glory.</summary>
<keywords>divine glory, Holy Scripture, human dignity, wisdom, Holy Spirit, salvation, beatitude</keywords>

### CHAPTER ONE.

<margin>The lineage of Christ.</margin>
The account of the lineage of JESUS CHRIST, descended from David, descended from Abraham. Abraham fathered Isaac. Isaac fathered Jacob. <margin>10</margin> Jacob fathered Judah and his brothers. Judah fathered Perez and Zerah by Tamar. Perez fathered Hezron. Hezron fathered Ram. Ram fathered Amminadab. Amminadab fathered Nahshon. Nahshon fathered Salmon. Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab. Boaz fathered Obed by Ruth. Obed fathered Jesse. Jesse fathered David the king. David the king fathered Solomon, <margin>20</margin> by her who had been the wife of Uriah. <note>original: "ex ea quæ fuerat Vriæ" — referring to Bathsheba, who is not named directly here.</note> Solomon fathered Rehoboam. Rehoboam fathered Abijah. Abijah fathered Asa. Asa fathered Jehoshaphat. Jehoshaphat fathered Joram. Joram fathered Uzziah. Uzziah fathered Jotham. Jotham fathered Ahaz. Ahaz fathered Hezekiah. Hezekiah fathered Manasseh. Manasseh fathered Amon. Amon fathered Josiah. Josiah fathered Jehoiakim. Jehoiakim fathered Jeconiah and his <margin>30</margin> <margin>1 Chronicles 4:3</margin> brothers at the time of the Babylonian exile. After the Babylonian exile, Jeconiah fathered Shealtiel. Shealtiel fathered Zerubbabel. Zerubbabel fathered Abiud. Abiud fathered Eliakim. Eliakim fathered Azor. Azor fathered Zadok. Zadok fathered Achim. Achim fathered Eliud. Eliud fathered Eleazar. Eleazar fathered Matthan. Matthan fathered Jacob. Jacob fathered Joseph, the husband of Mary, from whom was born JESUS, called Christ. <margin>2. Degrees of the lineage.</margin> Therefore, in total, from Abraham to David there are fourteen generations. Likewise, from David to the Babylonian exile, fourteen. From the Babylonian exile to Christ, fourteen. <margin>The birth of Christ. Luke 1</margin> Now the birth of Jesus Christ happened in this way. When his mother Mary was betrothed to Joseph, before they came together, she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit. But Joseph her husband, being a just man and not wishing to make a public example of her, decided to divorce her secretly. While he was considering these things, behold, an Angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream and spoke thus: "Joseph, descendant of David, do not fear to take Mary as your wife; for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Spirit. She will bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus; for he will deliver his people from their sins." Now all this

<column-break/>

<margin>Isaiah 7</margin> was done so that what had been spoken by the Lord through the prophet <term>vates</term> <note>The Latin 'vates' implies a divinely inspired poet or prophet.</note> might be fulfilled, saying: "A virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and he shall be named Emmanuel," which is the same as saying: "God with us." Therefore, having awakened from sleep, Joseph did as the Angel of the Lord had commanded him, and took his wife; but he did not know her until she had brought forth her firstborn son, whom he called by the name Jesus.

### CHAPTER TWO.

<margin>The Magi.</margin> Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judea, in the time of King Herod, wise men <note>original: "magi" — historically, these were members of a priestly caste from Persia, often associated with astronomy and dream interpretation.</note> came from the east to Jerusalem, asking where the born King of the Jews might be. For they said they had seen his star in the east and had come to worship him. When King Herod heard these things, he was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him; and having gathered all the chief priests and scribes of the people, he inquired of them where the Christ was to be born. They answered him, "In Bethlehem of Judea; for so it is written by the prophet: <margin>Micah 5</margin> 'And you, Bethlehem in the land of Judah, are by no means the least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come forth a leader for me, who shall rule my people Israel.'" Then Herod, having secretly called the wise men, inquired of them the time when the star had appeared, and sent them to Bethlehem, saying: "Go, and search diligently for the child; and when you have found him, bring me word, so that I also may go to <margin>40</margin> worship him." So, having heard the king, they set out; and then the star, which they had seen in the east, went before them, until it stood over the place where the child was. When they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceeding great joy, and entering the house, they found the child with Mary his mother, and fell down and worshiped him; and opening their treasure chests, they offered him gifts: gold, frankincense, and myrrh. Then, having been warned <margin>Psalm 71, Isaiah 60</margin> in a dream by an oracle not to return to Herod, they withdrew into their own country by another way. After they had departed, an Angel of the Lord <margin>50</margin> appeared to Joseph in a dream, saying: "Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and stay there until I tell you. For Herod is going to search for the child to kill him." ### CHAPTER XXI.

Even when you saw this, you did not finally change your mind and believe him. <margin>Concerning the master of the house who leased the vineyard. Mark 11.</margin> Listen to another example. There was a certain master of a house who planted a vineyard, put a fence around it, dug a winepress in it, built a tower, and leased it to tenant farmers, then went abroad. When the time for fruit drew near, he sent his servants to the farmers to receive his fruit. But the farmers seized his servants; they beat one, killed another, and stoned another. Again, he sent other servants, more than the first, and they did the same to them. Finally, he sent his son to them, thinking: 'They will respect my son.' But when the farmers saw the son, they said among themselves: 'This is the heir; come, let us kill him and seize his inheritance.' So they took him, threw him out of the vineyard, and killed him. Therefore, when the lord of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those farmers?" They said to him: "He will bring those wretches to a wretched end and lease the vineyard to other farmers who will pay him the fruit in its season." Jesus said to them: "Have you never read <margin>The stone which the builders rejected, etc. Psalm 118.</margin> in the scriptures? The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner; this was the Lord's doing, and it is marvelous in your eyes. Therefore know that the kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits. And whoever falls on that stone will be broken to pieces; but on whomever the stone falls, it will <margin>Mark 11.</margin> crush him." When the chief priests and Pharisees heard his parables, they understood that he was speaking about them; but though they wanted to arrest him, they feared the crowd, because they held him to be a prophet.

Then after six days, Jesus took Peter, James, and John, and led them separately up a high mountain by themselves; there he was **transfigured** before them. His garments became radiant and as white as snow, such as no launderer <note>Original: "fullo," a person who treats and whitens cloth.</note> on earth could bleach them. But even so, their testimonies were not consistent. Then the high priest stood up in their midst and questioned Jesus: "Do you answer nothing? What is it that these men testify against you?" But Jesus remained silent and answered nothing. Again the high priest questioned him with these words: "Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed God?" And Jesus said: "I am; and you shall see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of power, and coming with the clouds of heaven." Then the high priest tore his garments and said: "What further need have we of witnesses? You have heard the blasphemous word; what do you think?" And they all condemned him as worthy of death. And some began to spit on him, to cover his face, to strike him with their fists, and to say: "Prophesy!" And the attendants struck him with the palms of their hands. While Peter was below in the courtyard, one of the high priest's maidservants came, and seeing Peter warming himself, she looked at him and said: "You also were with Jesus of Nazareth." But he denied it, saying: "I do not know, nor do I understand what you are saying." Then he went out into the vestibule, and the cock crowed. And the maidservant, seeing him, began again to say to those standing by that he was one of them. But he denied it again. A little later, those standing by said to Peter again: "Surely you are one of them, for you are a Galilean, and your speech matches." But he began to curse and to swear that he did not know that man of whom they spoke; and the cock crowed a second time. Then Peter remembered the word that Jesus had spoken to him, that before the cock crowed twice, he would deny him three times; and he began to weep.

## BY THE AUTHOR LUKE.

### PREFACE.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial V featuring floral motifs and a face.</image-desc>
<margin>2. Carefully, namely from those who from the beginning etc.</margin>
Inasmuch as many have undertaken to compile a narrative of the things accomplished among us, just as those who from the beginning were both eyewitnesses and ministers of the matter handed them down to us, it seemed good also to me, who have followed all things diligently <gloss>2</gloss> from the source, to write to you in an orderly way, most excellent Theophilus, so that you may know with certainty the things which you have received by word of mouth.

### CHAPTER I.

<margin>1. Chronicles 24.</margin>
<margin>Zechariah.</margin>
<margin>Elizabeth.</margin>
There was in the times of Herod, king of Judea, a certain priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah, whose wife was descended from Aaron and named Elizabeth. Now they were both righteous before God, conducting themselves blamelessly in all the commandments and institutes of the Lord. But they had no children, because Elizabeth was sterile and
<margin>20</margin>
both were advanced in age. It happened that while he was performing the priest’s office before God in the order of his division, according to the custom of the priesthood, it fell to him by lot to burn incense. And so he entered into the temple of the Lord, while the whole multitude of the people was praying outside at the hour of incense. Then there appeared to him a spirit <note>original: "genius," used here to mean a divine messenger or angel</note> of the Lord, standing at the right side of the altar of incense. Seeing him, Zechariah was troubled and struck with fear. But the spirit <note>original: "geniº"</note> addressed him thus: "Do not fear, Zechariah; for your prayers have been heard, and your wife Elizabeth shall bear you a son, whom you shall call by the name John. He shall be a joy and a delight to you, and many shall rejoice at his birth; for he shall be great in the sight of the Lord; he shall drink neither wine nor strong drink <note>original: "temetum," an archaic Latin word for intoxicating liquor</note>, and he shall be filled with the holy spirit even from his mother's womb. He shall reconcile many of the Israelites to the Lord their God, and he himself shall go before him, endowed with the spirit and power of Elijah, to reconcile the hearts of fathers to their children, and the disobedient to the prudence of the righteous, to prepare for the Lord

a well-ordered people." But Zechariah said to the spirit: "How shall I know this for certain? For I am an old man, and my wife is now advanced in years." And the spirit, answering, said to him: "I am Gabriel, who appears <gloss>2</gloss> before God, and I have been sent to speak to you and to announce these joyful things to you. And behold, you shall be mute and unable to speak until these things have come to pass, because you did not believe my words, which shall be fulfilled in their own time." Meanwhile, the people were waiting for Zechariah and wondering why he stayed so long in the temple. He himself gestured to them and remained mute; and when the time of his service was completed, he went home. After that time, his wife Elizabeth conceived and hid herself for five months, because the Lord had done this for her while he cared to take away her disgrace among men. In the sixth month, the spirit Gabriel was sent by God to a town in Galilee named Nazareth, to a virgin betrothed to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the name of the virgin was Mary.

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>1 Kings 2</margin>
<margin>20</margin>
In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea, Herod tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Iturea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas, the word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness. He went through all the region of the Jordan, proclaiming a washing <note>original: "lotionem." This is the word used for baptism, emphasizing the ritual cleansing aspect.</note> of life-amendment for the forgiveness of sins, as it is written in the book of the words of the prophet Isaiah, saying: <margin>John the Baptist begins to teach. Matthew 3, Isaiah 40, Mark 1.</margin> <margin>30</margin> "The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight. Every valley shall be filled, and every mountain and hill shall be brought low; the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough ways shall be made smooth; and all mortals shall see the divine salvation." He said therefore to the crowds who came out to be washed by him: "You brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath? Therefore produce fruits worthy of a corrected life, and do not think to say among yourselves: 'We have Abraham as our father.' For I tell you that God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones. Even now the axe is laid to the root of the <margin>40</margin> trees. Therefore, every tree not producing good fruit is to be cut down and thrown into the fire." And the crowd asked him, "What then shall we do?" He answered them in this way: "He who has two tunics, let him share with him who has none; and he who has food, let him do likewise."
