### CHAPTER VIII.

Afterward, he went through the towns and villages preaching and announcing the kingdom of God, with the twelve accompanying him, and certain women who had been cured of evil spirits and infirmities: 
<margin>Luke 14</margin>
Mary, called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out, and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod’s steward, and Susanna, and many others, who provided for him from their own resources. Moreover, as a huge multitude was gathering, and people from the towns everywhere were coming to him, he spoke by a parable. 
<margin>The Sower. Matthew 13, Mark 4</margin>
"A sower went out to sow his seed; and as he sowed, some fell by the wayside, and it was trampled down, and the birds of the air ate it. Other seed fell upon rock, and when it sprang up, it withered because it had no moisture. Likewise, other seed fell among thorns, and the thorns growing up with it choked it. Other seed fell into good ground, and having grown, produced fruit a hundredfold." Saying these things, he cried out: "He who has ears with which he can hear, let him hear." But his disciples asked him what that comparison meant. 
<margin>Matthew 13, Mark 4, John 12, Isaiah 6, Acts 28, Matthew 13, Mark 4</margin>
To whom he said: "To you it is given to know the secrets of the divine kingdom; but with the others it is done through comparisons, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand. Now this is the comparison: The seed is the divine word. Those by the wayside are those who hear; then the Devil comes, who carries away the word from their hearts, lest they believe and so be saved. Those on the rock are those who, when they hear, receive the word indeed with joy, but they have no root; therefore they believe for a time, and in a time of danger they fall away. That which fell among thorns are those who, when they have heard, go out so that they are choked by the cares and riches and pleasures of life, and do not bring fruit to maturity. But that which is in the good ground are those who, with a worthy and good heart, retain the word they have heard, and bear fruit with patience. 
<margin>Matthew 5, Mark 4, Luke 11</margin>
No one, however, covers a candle he has lit with a vessel, or puts it under a bed, but puts it on a lampstand, so that those entering may see the light."

So it happens to him who stores up for himself, and is not rich toward God. For this reason I say to you (he said to his disciples): do not be anxious about your life, what you may eat, nor about your body, what you may wear. Life is more than food, and the body than clothing. Consider the ravens, which neither sow nor reap, which have neither cellar nor granary, yet God feeds them: how much more do you excel over the birds? But which of you by his own care can add a single cubit <note>A cubit was an ancient unit of measurement, roughly the length of a forearm.</note> to his stature? If you cannot do even the smallest thing, why are you anxious about the rest?

<margin>Matthew 6</margin>
Consider the lilies, how they grow, though they neither labor nor spin. But know that not even Solomon in all his splendor was usually clothed like any one of these. But if God so clothes the grass, which is in the field today and tomorrow is thrown into the furnace, how much more will he clothe you, O you of little faith? Therefore, do not seek what you shall eat or what you shall drink, nor be in suspense. For the nations of the world seek all these things, which your father knows you have need of. But seek the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you. Do not fear, O little flock: for it has pleased your father to give you the kingdom.

<margin>Luke 12. In the same place. Matthew 6</margin>
Sell your possessions and give to the needy. Make for yourselves purses that do not grow old, an inexhaustible treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys. For where your treasure is, there also is your heart. Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning, and be like men waiting for their master when he returns from the wedding, so that as soon as he comes and knocks, they may open to him. Blessed are those servants whom the master finds watching when he comes. Believe me, he will gird himself and bid them sit down to eat, and he will come to serve them. And if he comes in the second or third watch <note>The Roman "watches" of the night were periods of guard duty; the second and third watches were the middle of the night.</note> and finds them so, blessed are those servants. But know this: if the master of the house knew at what hour the thief was coming, he would watch and not allow his house to be broken into.

<margin>Ephesians 1, 2. Peter 1. Matthew 24</margin>
You therefore be ready: for at an hour you do not expect, the one born of man <note>original: "homine natus," a literal translation of the title "Son of Man."</note> will come. Then Peter said to him: "Lord, do you say this parable to us, or also to everyone?" And the Lord said: "If there is a faithful and wise steward whom the master has set over his household to provide the measured portion <note>original: "demensum," a ration of food given to slaves or soldiers.</note> at the proper time, blessed is that servant whom his master finds doing his duty when he comes. Believe me for certain: he will set him over all his possessions."

<margin>Matthew 24. Mark 13.</margin>
<margin>A good steward. Matthew 24.</margin>
But if that servant thinks in his heart that his master will be a long time in coming, and begins to strike the menservants and maidservants, and to feast, and to drink and be drunk, the master of that servant will come on a day he does not expect and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in pieces and assign him a place with the unfaithful.

<margin>A wicked servant.</margin>
But that servant who knew his master’s will and did not carry out his commands, nor obey his will, shall be beaten more severely. But he who did not know it, yet did things worthy of blows, shall be beaten less. From everyone to whom much has been given, much will be required; and to whom more has been entrusted, so much more will be demanded of him.

<margin>I desire nothing so much as that it should burn.</margin>
I have come to cast fire onto the earth, and if it is already kindled, what more do I want?

<margin>Matthew 10. Micah 7.</margin>
I have a washing <note>original: "lotione," usually translated as baptism, but here emphasizing the ritual cleansing or immersion.</note> to be washed with, and how I am greatly distressed until it is finished! Do you think I have come to bring peace on earth? Not at all, I tell you, but rather discord. For from now on there will be five in one house divided, three against two and two against three. Father will be divided against son, and son against father; mother against daughter, and daughter against mother; mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law, and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law.

<margin>Matthew 16. Future things are to be predicted from present ones.</margin>
Then to the crowd he said: "When you see a cloud rising from the west, you immediately say rain is coming, and so it happens. And when the south wind blows, you say there will be heat, and it happens. Hypocrites <note>original: "Ficti homines," literally "feigned men."</note>, you know how to discern the face of the earth and the sky; how is it you do not discern this time? Or why do you not judge what is right from yourselves?"

<margin>Matthew 5. In the same place.</margin>

Believe me, you will not get out of there until you have paid even the last penny <note>original: "teruncium," a small Roman coin worth three-twelfths of an as.</note>.

### CHAPTER XIII.

<margin>The guilty will perish. Acts 5.</margin>
There were some present at that time who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices. Jesus responded to them with these words: "Do you think those Galileans were the worst of all Galileans because they suffered such things? Not at all, I tell you. But unless you return to a right way of life <note>original: "ad frugem redieritis," a Latin idiom meaning to reform or return to virtue.</note>, you will all perish in the same way."

<margin>Ezekiel 18. Ecclesiasticus 17.</margin>
"Likewise those eighteen whom the falling tower in Siloam killed—do you think they were the most guilty of all the inhabitants of Jerusalem? Not at all, I tell you: but unless you reform, you will all perish in the same way."

<margin>Matthew 21. The unfruitful tree must be cut down.</margin>
He also spoke this parable: "A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came seeking fruit from it but found none. So he said to the vinedresser, 'Look, for three years now I have come seeking fruit from this fig tree and find none; cut it down, why should it take up the ground uselessly?' But he answering said to him, 'Lord, let it alone this year also, while I dig around it and apply manure, to see if perhaps it might bear fruit. But if not, you shall cut it down afterward.'"

<margin>A weak woman is healed.</margin>
Now he was teaching at one time in a certain synagogue <note>original: "collegio," literally an assembly or college.</note> on the Sabbaths, and a woman was there who had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years, and she was so bent over that she could not straighten herself at all. When Jesus saw her, he called her and said to her: "Woman, you are released from your infirmity." And he laid his hands on her, and immediately she was made straight and gave thanks to God. But the ruler of the synagogue, indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, spoke to the people with these words: "There are six days in which work ought to be done; come on those days to be healed, and not on the Sabbath day."

<margin>Luke 14.</margin>
But the Lord spoke back to him: "O hypocrite <note>original: "personate," literally one wearing a mask, an actor.</note>, does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the stall and lead it to water? And should not this woman, being a daughter of Abraham, whom Satan has bound for eighteen years, be released from this bond on the Sabbath day?" When he said these things, all his adversaries were ashamed: but the whole crowd rejoiced at all the glorious things being done by him.

He was saying also: "To what is the divine kingdom like? Or to what shall we compare it? It is like a grain of mustard, which a man takes and puts into his garden..."

<margin>On the prodigal son.</margin> Likewise, he said this: A certain man had two sons, the younger of whom said to the father: "Father, give me my rightful share of the goods." And so he divided his resources between them, and not many days later, the younger son, having gathered everything together, set out on a journey into a distant region, and there he squandered his resources by living luxuriously. After he had consumed everything, a severe famine arose in that region and he began to be in need. And so he went to one of the citizens of that region and attached himself to him, and that man sent him to his farm to feed pigs. He desired to fill his belly with the pods that the pigs were eating, but no one gave him anything. Therefore, returning to himself, he thought: "How many of my father's hired hands overflow with bread? And I perish with hunger. I will take myself back to my father, and I will say to him: 'Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you, so that I am no longer worthy to be called your son: treat me just as one of your hired hands.'" 

So he set out and came to his father. While he was still far off, his father saw him, and moved with pity, he ran to him, fell upon his neck, and kissed him tenderly. And the son spoke to him thus: "Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you, so that I am no longer worthy to be called your son." But the father said to his servants: "Bring out the finest robe and put it on him, and place a ring on his hand and shoes on his feet, and lead out the fattened calf and slaughter it, and let us feast joyfully: for this son of mine, who was dead, has lived again; and he who was lost has been found." And so they began to rejoice. 

But his older son was in the field. As he was coming and drew near the house, hearing the music and dancing, he called one of his servants and asked what these things meant. To him the servant said: "Your brother has come; and so your father has slaughtered the fattened calf, because he has received him back safe and sound." But he was angry and did not want to go in. When his father came out and urged him, he answered his father in this manner: "Behold, I have served you so many years, and never have I gone against your command, and you never even gave me a young goat so that I might rejoice with my friends. But when this son of yours came, who devoured his resources with harlots, you slaughtered the fattened calf for him." But he said to him: "Son, you are always with me, and all my things are yours. Indeed, it was necessary to be joyful and glad, because this brother of yours was dead and has lived again; he was lost and has been found."

### CHAPTER XVI.

<margin>On prudent stewardship.</margin> **H**e also said to his disciples: A certain rich man had a manager, who was reported to him as one who was squandering his goods. He called him and spoke thus: "What is this I hear about you? Give an account of your management: for you will no longer be allowed to be manager." Then the manager thought to 

<column-break/>

himself: "What shall I do? Since my master is taking away my management from me. I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg. I know what I shall do so that, when I have been removed from the management, there will be those who receive me into their homes." And so, having called each of his master's debtors, he said to the first: "How much do you owe my master?" "A hundred baths <note>A Hebrew liquid measure equal to about 8 or 9 gallons.</note> of oil," he said. <margin>a. The bond, which I have here.</margin> And he said to him: "Take your <gloss>a</gloss> writing, sit down quickly, and write fifty." Then he said to another: "And you, how much do you owe?" "A hundred cors <note>A dry measure equivalent to about 10-12 bushels.</note> of grain." He said: "Take your writing and write eighty." And so the master praised the dishonest manager, because he had acted prudently. For the people of this age are more prudent in their own generation than the people of light. 

And I say this to you: Make friends for yourselves from false money <note>Traditionally "unrighteous mammon"; wealth of the world.</note>, so that when you have died, they may admit you into eternal dwellings. He who is faithful in a very small thing is also faithful in a great thing: and he who is unjust in a very small thing is also unjust in a great thing. If you have not been faithful with false money, who will trust you with true wealth? <margin>Matthew 6. b. The resources of this life which are given to you for a time. c. No servant can serve two masters: for either he will hate one and love the other, or he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money. 

The Pharisees, who were lovers of money, also heard all these things, and they mocked him. There was a certain rich man, who was clothed in purple and fine linen, daily indulging luxuriously in pleasures. And there was a certain poor man named Lazarus, who lay at his gate covered in sores, and desiring to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man's table. Even the dogs came and licked his sores. It happened that the poor man died and was carried by the Spirits <note>Angels.</note> into Abraham's bosom. The rich man also died and was buried. And in the Underworld <note>original: "Orcus", the Roman name for the realm of the dead.</note>, lifting his eyes while he was in torments, he saw Abraham far off, and Lazarus in his bosom, and crying out he said: "Father Abraham, have mercy on me, and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water to cool my tongue: for I am tormented in this flame." 

But Abraham said: "Son, remember that you received your good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise received evil things. Now he is here in comfort, and you are in pain. Besides all this, a vast chasm is fixed between us and you, so that those who want to cross from here to you cannot, nor can those from there cross to us." Then he said: "I beg you then, father, to send him to my father's house, so that he may warn my brothers (for I have five), lest they also come into this place of torment." But Abraham said to him: "They have Moses and the prophets: let them hear them." And he said: "No, father Abraham, but if someone from the dead goes to them, they will change their ways." Abraham said to him: "If they do not hear Moses and the prophets, they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead."

# CHAPTER 20

<margin>Matthew 21. Mark 11. By what authority you do these things.</margin>
On one of those days, while he was teaching the people in the temple and instructing them, the chief priests and the scribes came together with the elders, and they spoke to him in this way: "Tell us, by what authority do you do these things, or who is it that gave you this authority?" Responding to them, he said: "I will also ask you one question; tell me: Was the washing <note>original: "lotio", referring to the baptism</note> of John from heaven, or from men?" But they reasoned among themselves, saying: "If we say 'from heaven,' he will say, 'Why then did you not believe him?' But if we say 'from men,' all the people will stone us, for they are persuaded that John was a prophet <note>original: "vaté", a seer or inspired poet</note>." And so they answered that they did not know where it was from. And Jesus said to them: "Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things."

<margin>The example of him who leased out a vineyard. Matthew 21. Mark 12.</margin>
Then he began to tell the people this example <note>original: "exemplum", a parable</note>: "A certain man planted a vineyard, and after leasing it to tenants, he was away from home for a long time. Then at the proper time, he sent a servant to the tenants so that they might give him some of the fruit of the vineyard. But the tenants beat him and sent him away empty-handed. He then sent another servant, and they beat him too, treated him with contempt, and sent him away empty-handed. When he sent a third, they wounded him as well and drove him out. Then the lord of the vineyard said: 'What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps they will show him reverence when they see him.' But the tenants, seeing him, spoke among themselves, saying: 'This is the heir; come, let us kill him, so that the inheritance may become ours.' And so they threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. What, then, will the lord of the vineyard do to them? He will come and destroy those tenants, and lease the vineyard to others." Having heard this, they said: <margin>a This deed is unheard of.</margin> "May it not be!" But he looked at them and said: "What then is this that is written: <margin>Psalm 117. Matthew 21. Mark 12. Acts 4. 1 Peter 2. Matthew 21. Mark 12.</margin> 'The stone which the builders rejected, the same has been placed at the head of the corner'? Whoever falls on that stone will be broken to pieces; and on whomever it falls, it will crush him." Therefore the chief priests and scribes tried to lay hands on him at that same hour, for they understood that he had spoken that example against them; but they feared the people. So they kept watch, sending out spies who would pretend to be good men, so that they might catch him in his words and thus deliver him to the magistrate and the power of the governor. And they questioned him thus: "Teacher, we know that you speak and teach rightly, and that you do not favor any person, but truly teach the divine way of life.

<margin>Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar? Matthew 22. Mark 12. Acts 23. The question regarding the seven brothers who had the same wife. Deuteronomy 25. b Answer: those out of the seven.</margin>
Is it lawful for us to pay tribute to Caesar, or not?" But he, perceiving their craftiness, said to them: "Why do you test me? Show me a denarius. Whose image and inscription does it have?" "Caesar’s," they replied. And he said to them: "Pay therefore to Caesar the things of Caesar, and to God the things of God." Thus they were unable to criticize any word of his before the people, and wondering at his answer, they were silent. Then some of the Sadducees, who deny that there is a resurrection, approached and questioned him: "Teacher, Moses wrote for us that if a man’s brother dies having a wife, and he dies without children, his brother should take the wife and raise up offspring for his brother. Now there were seven brothers; the first took a wife and died without children. The second took the wife, and he also died without children. Then the third took her, and likewise the <margin>b</margin> seven, and they left no children. After them, the woman died too.

<column-break/>

<margin>c That is, they imply.</margin>
Finally, of all of them, the woman died as well. Therefore, in the resurrection, whose wife will she be? Since seven of them had her in marriage." And Jesus answered them: "The people of this life both take wives and are given in marriage. But those who happen to attain that life and rise from the dead neither take wives nor are given in marriage, since they can no longer die; for they are like the spirits <note>original: "geniorum", often referring to angels or celestial beings</note>, and they are the sons of God, being people of the resurrection.

<margin>That the dead rise. Exodus 3. Matthew 21.</margin>
But that the dead rise, even Moses indicated at the bush, where he calls the Lord 'the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.' Now he is not the God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him." Then some of the scribes spoke to him: "Teacher, you have spoken well." And they did not dare to ask him anything further.

<margin>Matthew 22. Mark 12. The Lord said to my lord. Psalm 109. Matthew 23. 12. Luke 13. Mark 12. d While they make long prayers, they appear religious to the skilled; equally they draw out gifts, and that on account of much contact with them.</margin>
And he said: "How is it that they say Christ is the descendant of David? Since David himself says in the book of Psalms: 'The Lord said to my lord, sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool <note>original: "subfellum"</note> for your feet.' If David calls him 'Lord,' how then is he his descendant?" Then, with all the people listening, he said to his disciples: "Beware of the Pharisees, who like to walk in long robes and love greetings in the marketplaces, the first seats in the gatherings <note>original: "collegijs"</note>, and the first places at feasts; who devour the houses of widows <margin>d</margin> under the appearance of long prayers; they will receive a heavier judgment."

# CHAPTER 21

<margin>Mark 12. The poor widow contributed the most in hope with God.</margin>

On the third day, a wedding took place at Cana in Galilee, where the mother of Jesus was; and Jesus and his disciples were also invited to the wedding. When the wine ran out, the mother of Jesus spoke to him thus: "They have no wine." Jesus said to her: "What is that to me? <note>original: "Quid tum postea?" literally "What then afterwards?"</note> Woman, my time has not yet come." His mother warned the servants to do whatever he commanded them. Six stone jars were placed there, according to the purification rites of the Jews, each capable of holding two or three measures. Jesus ordered them to fill those jars with water. When they had filled them to the brim, he ordered them to draw some out now and carry it to the master of the feast. And they carried it. But when the master of the feast tasted the wine made from water, not knowing where it came from (though the servants who had drawn the water knew), he called the bridegroom and spoke to him thus: "While all men first set out the good wine, and then the worse after the guests have drunk, you have kept the good wine until now." Jesus provided this beginning of miracles at Cana in Galilee, and showed his glory, and his disciples had faith in him. Afterwards, he went down to Capernaum along with his mother, his brothers, and his disciples, and they stayed there not many days. And as the Passover of the Jews was approaching, <margin>Matt. 4.</margin> <margin>Luke 4.</margin> Jesus went up to Jerusalem; and having found in the temple those selling oxen, sheep, and doves, and the money-changers sitting there, he made a whip out of leather thongs <note>original: "scutica," a Roman-style whip.</note> and drove them all out of the temple, along with the sheep and oxen, and poured out the money of the money-changers and overturned the tables. were performed by the Apostles. All the believers lived together and held all things in common; they sold their

### CHAPTER III.

Now Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer, namely the ninth. And a certain man, who was lame from his mother’s womb, was being carried, who was placed daily at the gate of the temple which is called "Beautiful," so that he might ask for alms from those entering the temple. When he saw Peter and John about to enter the temple, he asked them to show him kindness. But Peter, with John 
<margin>A lame man healed by Peter.</margin> by his side, looked intently at him and said, "Look at us." And as the man fixed his attention on them, hoping he would receive something from them, Peter spoke thus: "I have neither silver nor gold, but what I have, I give to you. In the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, rise up and walk." And taking him by the right hand, he lifted him up. And immediately, his feet and ankles being made strong, he leaped up, stood, and walked; and he entered with them into the temple, walking and leaping and praising God. When all the people saw him walking and praising God, they recognized him as the one who used to sit for alms at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, and they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him. And so, while the healed lame man held onto Peter and John, all the people ran together to them in the portico which is called Solomon’s, being utterly astonished. Seeing this, Peter spoke to the people: "Men of Israel, why do you wonder at this, or why do you stare at us, as if by our own private 
<margin>Peter’s speech concerning the healed lame man.</margin> power or piety we had made this man walk? The God of Abraham, and of Isaac, and of Jacob, the God of our ancestors, has glorified his son Jesus, whom you delivered up and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had judged that he should be released. But you rejected the holy and innocent one, and asked that a murderer be granted to you; but you killed the author of life, whom 
<margin>Matthew 27, Mark 15</margin> God raised from the dead, of which we are witnesses. And by faith in his name—the name, I say, of this man whom you see and know—he has been made strong; and the confidence 
<margin>Luke 23</margin> placed in him has achieved this wholeness in the sight of you all. And now, brothers, I know that you did this through ignorance, as did also your rulers. But 
<margin>Ecclesiastes 17, Matthew 4, Mark 1, Ezekiel 18, Luke 13, Revelation 2, Below 4:7, Deuteronomy 18</margin> God has in this way fulfilled those things which he had foretold by the mouth of all his prophets <note>original: "vatum," meaning seers or prophets.</note>, that Christ should suffer. Therefore, return to a sound mind <note>original: "ad sanitatem revertimini," Castellio’s classical rendering of "repent."</note> and correct yourselves, so that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the Lord, and he shall send the Jesus Christ foretold to you, whom heaven must receive until the times of the restoration of all things, which times God spoke of long ago by the mouth of all his holy prophets. For Moses said to the ancestors: 'The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your kin, like 

<column-break/>

me; you shall obey him in all things whatever he shall say to you. And every person who will not obey that prophet shall be removed from the number of the people.' Likewise, all the prophets from Samuel onwards, who have spoken, also foretold and announced these times. You are the descendants of the prophets, and included in the covenant which God made with our 
<margin>Genesis 12:u</margin> ancestors, when he said to Abraham, 'Through your seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed.' To you first, God sent his son <note>original: "puerum," literally 'boy' or 'servant,' here referring to Jesus.</note>, having raised him up, to bless you, if each of you turns away from his vices."

### CHAPTER IIII.

While they were speaking to the people, the priests, and the overseer of the temple, and the Sadducees came upon them, being annoyed that they were teaching the people and announcing the resurrection from the dead through Jesus. Therefore 
<margin>The Apostles are cast into prison.</margin> they laid hands on them and put them in custody until the next day, because it was already evening. Many 
<margin>Above 2</margin> of those, however, who had heard that speech believed, and the number of the men was about five thousand. The next day, their rulers, elders, and scribes gathered in Jerusalem, along with Annas the high priest, and Caiaphas, and John, and Alexander, and as many as were of the high-priestly lineage. And having placed them in the middle, they inquired by what power or in what name they had done this. Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, spoke to them thus: "Rulers of the people and senators of the Israelites, if we are questioned today concerning the 
<margin>Matthew 21, Mark 12, Luke 20, 1 Peter 2, Philippians 2, Hebrews 1</margin> benefit bestowed upon a sick man, by what means he was healed, let it be known to you and to all the people of the Israelites, that by the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead—by him, I say, this man stands here before you healthy. This is the stone rejected by you builders, which has been made the head of the corner; nor is there salvation in any other, nor is there any other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved." Now when they saw the confidence of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlettered and untrained men, they wondered, and they 
<margin>1 Corinthians 1</margin> recognized that they had been companions of Jesus. But seeing the man who had been cured standing there with them, they had nothing to say in contradiction. Therefore, having 
<margin>Below 4:a</margin> ordered them to withdraw from the council, they conferred among themselves with these words: "What shall we do to these men? For that a conspicuous miracle has been done by them is manifest to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so much so that we cannot deny it. But lest this spread further among the common people, let us threaten them that they should no longer speak 
<margin>Below 4:b</margin> to any mortal in this name." And having called them, they commanded them not to speak at all, nor to teach in the name of Jesus. But Peter and John answered them thus: "Whether it is right in the sight of God to obey you rather than God, you judge. For we cannot help but speak of the things we have both seen and heard." But they, having further threatened them, let them go, finding no way to punish them because of the 
<margin>Above 2</margin> people, because everyone was giving thanks to God for what had happened. For the man on whom this miracle of healing had occurred was more than 40 years old. Being released, they went to their own people and reported what the high priests and elders had said to them. When they heard this, they all lifted up their voice to God with one accord, and said:

->**OF THE APOSTLES.**<-

<margin>Psalm 2:1</margin>Lord, you are the God who made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are in them, who by the mouth of your servant David said: Why do the nations rage? and the peoples plot in vain? <margin>Acts 4:23</margin>The kings of the earth conspire, and the rulers gather together, against the Lord and against his Anointed <note>original: "Unctū," a Latin translation of the Greek "Christos," meaning the one anointed with holy oil.</note>: For indeed Herod and Pontius Pilate, with the Gentiles and the people of Israel, gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, to do whatever your hand and your counsel had <margin>Gen. 3:17, 16</margin>predestined to be done. And now, Lord, behold their threats, and grant to your servants to speak your word with all liberty, by stretching out your hand to heal, and that signs and wonders may be done through the name of your holy servant Jesus. When they had prayed, the place where they were gathered was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and they spoke the divine word with freedom. Now the multitude of those who believed were of one mind and one heart, nor did anyone say that any of his possessions was his own, but they held all things in common. With great power the apostles gave testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all. Nor was there anyone needy among them, for as many as possessed lands or houses sold them, and brought the price of the things sold and <margin>Matt. 15:1; Tobit 1; above, 4</margin>placed them at the feet of the apostles. Distribution was made to each as any had need. And Joses, who was surnamed Barnabas by the apostles (which is translated "son of consolation"), a Levite of the country of Cyprus, sold a field which he had, and brought the money and placed it at the apostles' feet.

Paul was to be kept in custody, but given some liberty, and none of his people were to be forbidden from serving him or visiting him. ### CHAPTER XXV.

When Festus had entered the province, after three days he went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem. "Therefore," he said, "let those of you who are able go down with me; and if there is any crime in this man, let them accuse him." Then, after he had stayed among them for more than ten days, he went down to Caesarea; and the next day, sitting on the judgment seat, he ordered Paul to be brought in. When he arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many serious charges against Paul which they could not prove, while he defended himself, saying that he had committed no offense against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar. ### CHAPTER XXVII.

<margin>Paul’s voyage to Italy. 2 Corinthians 11. Colossians 4. See below ch. 28.</margin>
Now when it was decided that we should sail for Italy, Paul and certain other prisoners were handed over to a centurion named Julius, of the Augustan cohort. Boarding a ship of Adramyttium, about to sail to places along the coast of Asia, we put to sea, accompanied by Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica. The next day we put in at Sidon; and Julius, treating Paul humanely, permitted him to go to his friends to receive their care. When we put out from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus because the winds were against us. After sailing across the sea of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we arrived at Myra in Lycia. There the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy and put us on board. After sailing slowly for many days and arriving with difficulty off Cnidus, the wind preventing us, we sailed under the lee of Crete off Salmone. Passing it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea.

<margin>2 Corinthians 11.</margin>
Now since much time had passed and sailing was already dangerous because the Fast <note>original: "tranquillitas"; likely referring to the Day of Atonement or the end of the safe sailing season</note> had already passed, Paul warned them with these words:

> Men, I see that this voyage will be with injury and great loss, not only of the cargo and the ship

<column-break/>

but also of our lives.

But the centurion gave more heed to the pilot and the captain than to what Paul said. And because the harbor was not well-suited for wintering, the majority decided to set sail from there as well, hoping they might reach Phoenix to winter, a harbor of Crete facing toward both the southwest and the northwest.

<margin>The Storm.</margin>
So when a gentle south wind blew, thinking they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed past Assos, along Crete. But not long afterward, a whirlwind <term>Euro-Aquilo (the Northeaster)</term> <note>original: "Euroaquilo"; a violent Mediterranean wind</note> struck against it. When the ship was caught and could not face the wind, we gave way and were driven along. Running under the lee of a small island called Clauda, we were scarcely able to secure the ship’s boat. When it was hoisted up, they used cables to undergird the ship; and fearing they might run aground on the Syrtis sands, they lowered the gear and so were driven along. But because we were violently tossed by the storm, the next day they began to throw the cargo overboard. On the third day, we threw the ship’s tackle overboard with our own hands. When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and a great storm continued to press upon us, all hope of our being saved was finally abandoned.

<margin>2 Corinthians 11. Paul speaks to the sailors.</margin>
After they had gone a long time without food, Paul stood in their midst and spoke thus:

> Men, you should have listened to me and not set sail from Crete, and so have avoided this injury and loss. Now I urge you to take heart, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship.

<margin>See above ch. 11, 23. See above ch. 25.</margin>
> For this night an angel <note>original: "genius"; here used for a divine messenger or angel</note> of the God to whom I belong and whom I worship stood by me and said: "Do not fear, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you." Therefore, men, take heart. For I trust God that it will be exactly as I was told. However, we must be cast upon some island.

Then, when the fourteenth night came, as we were being driven about in the Adriatic Sea, toward midnight the sailors suspected they were approaching some land. Dropping the lead line, they found twenty fathoms. Then, moving a little further and sounding again, they found fifteen fathoms. Fearing that we might run aground on rocky places, they dropped four anchors from the stern and prayed for daybreak. But as the sailors were trying to escape from the ship and had lowered the boat into the sea under the pretense of laying out anchors from the bow, Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers:

> Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved.

Then the soldiers cut the ropes of the boat and let it fall away. While they waited for daybreak, Paul urged them all to take some food:

> This is the fourteenth day, he said, that you have been in suspense and gone without food, having taken nothing. Therefore I urge you to take some food; for this is for your survival. For not a hair shall fall from the head of any of you.

<margin>Matthew 10. Luke 12. "Not even a tiny bit shall be harmed." Matthew 15. John 6.</margin>
Having said this, he took bread, gave thanks to God in the presence of all, broke it, and began to eat. Then they all took courage and took food themselves. There were in all two hundred and seventy-six souls on the ship.

Then, satisfied with food, they lightened the ship by throwing the wheat into the sea. When day broke, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a certain bay with a beach, where they intended, if possible, to beach the ship. So, having cast off the anchors, they left them in the sea; at the same time, loosening the lashings of the rudders and hoisting the foresail to the breeze, they headed for the shore. But falling into a place where two seas met <note>original: "bimarem"; likely a sandbar or a point where opposing currents converged</note>, they ran the ship aground. Thus, the prow remained fixed and immovable, while the stern was broken by the force of the winds. Now the soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners, so that no one might escape by swimming. But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, prevented them from this plan and ordered those who could swim to throw themselves overboard first and get to land; the rest followed, some on planks and others on various things from the ship. And so it happened that everyone escaped safely to land.

### CHAPTER XXVIII.

Once they had escaped, they finally learned that the island was called Malta <note>original: "Melita"</note>. The locals <note>original: "Barbari"; in this context, the term refers to non-Greek speakers, not necessarily "uncivilized" people</note> showed us unusual kindness. For having lit a fire, they welcomed us all because of the looming rain <margin>2 Corinthians 11.</margin> and the cold. When Paul had gathered a large bundle of brushwood and placed it on the fire, a viper <margin>Paul bitten by a viper, but not harmed.</margin> came out because of the heat and fastened onto his hand. When the locals saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said to one another: "This man is certainly a murderer; though he was saved from the sea, Justice <note>original: "fas"; refers to the personification of divine or natural Law</note> does not allow him to live." But he shook the creature off into the fire and suffered no harm, while they expected that he would swell up or suddenly fall down dead. But after waiting a long time and seeing nothing bad happen to him, they changed their minds and said he was a god. Now in those places were the estates of the chief man of the island, named Publius, who received us and treated us kindly with hospitality for three days. It happened, however, that the father of Publius lay sick with fevers and dysentery <note>original: "torminibus"; intestinal distress</note>; Paul went in to him, and after praying and laying his hands on him, he healed him. When this was done, the rest who had diseases on the island also came and were cured; they also honored us with many marks of respect, and when we set sail, they supplied the things we needed. After three months, we set sail in an Alexandrian ship that had wintered at the island, marked with the sign of the Twin Brothers <note>original: "Castoribus"; referring to the gods Castor and Pollux</note>; and having arrived at Syracuse, we stayed there three days. From there, making a circuit, we reached Rhegium; and after one day, a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli, where we found brothers and were urged to stay with them for seven days, and so <margin>See above ch. 15.</margin> we came to Rome. From there the brothers, when they had heard about us, came out to meet us as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns. When he saw them, Paul <margin>Paul arrives in Rome.</margin> thanked God and took courage. After <margin>See above ch. 27.</margin> we arrived in Rome, the centurion handed the prisoners over to the commander of the infantry. But Paul was permitted to live by himself with a soldier to guard him. After three days, Paul called together the leaders of the Jews, and after they had assembled, he spoke to them thus: "Brothers, although <margin>See above ch. 24, 25, 26.</margin> I had done nothing against the people or the customs of our fathers, I was delivered as a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans, who, after examining me, wanted

<page-num>174</page-num>
<header>TO THE ROMANS.</header>

to release me, because there was no capital crime in me. But because the Jews opposed it, I was forced to appeal to Caesar—not that I had any accusation to bring against my own nation. For this reason, therefore, I have called for you, to see you and speak with you. For it is because of the hope of Israel that I am bound with this chain." And they said: "We have neither received letters about you from Judea, nor has any of the brothers arrived who reported or spoke anything evil about you. However, we desire to hear from you what you think. For concerning this sect, it is known to us that it is spoken against everywhere." And when they had set a day for him, many came <margin>Luke 21.</margin> to him at his lodging, to whom he explained, testifying to the kingdom of God and trying to persuade them about Jesus, from the law of Moses and the prophets, from morning until evening. Psalm 66. Isaiah 11, 40, 60. Jeremiah 16, 31. Joel 3. Maccabees 1. ## TO THE ROMANS.

For I do not want you to be unaware, brothers, that I have often intended to come to you (though I have been hindered until now) so that I might gather some fruit among you as well, just as I have among the other nations. I am a debtor both to Greeks and to <term>barbarians</term> <note>In the Roman world, "barbarian" referred to anyone who did not speak Greek or Latin, rather than being a comment on their character.</note>, to the wise and to the ignorant. For I am not ashamed of the gospel of Christ, because it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, <gloss>c</gloss> to the Greek and to the Jew alike. For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men who suppress the truth in unrighteousness. For what can be known about God is plain to them, because God has made it clear to them. For his invisible attributes—such as his eternal power and divinity—have been clearly seen since the creation of the world, being understood through the things he has made. So they are without excuse, because although they knew God, they did not give him the glory or thanks worthy of God, but turned to vain reasonings, and their senseless minds were darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools: <gloss>d</gloss> they exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man, and birds, and four-footed animals, and serpents.

<margin>Romans 9.</margin>
Therefore God gave them over to the lusts of their hearts, to such impurity that they degraded their own bodies among themselves, because they exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshipped and served created things rather than the Creator, who is to be praised forever. For this reason, God gave them over to shameful passions; for their women exchanged natural relations for those that are against nature. Similarly, the men, giving up natural relations with women, were consumed with lust for one another, men committing shameless acts with men, and receiving in themselves the penalty worthy of their error.

<margin>d. Although they knew God, they did not honor him as was worthy.</margin>
And just as <gloss>d</gloss> they did not see fit to acknowledge God, so God gave them over to a depraved mind, to do what ought not to be done. They are filled with all unrighteousness, sexual immorality, strife, deceit, and malice. They are gossips, slanderers, haters of God, insolent, haughty, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, senseless, faithless, heartless, and ruthless. Although they know God’s righteous decree—that those who do such things deserve death—they not only do them but also give approval to those who practice them.

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>Matthew 7.</margin>
Therefore you are without excuse, O man, whoever you are who passes judgment. For in that very act of judging another, you condemn

yourself, since you who judge practice the same things. But we know that the judgment of God will be severe against those who do such things. Do you suppose, O man (you who judge those who do such things and yet do them yourself), that you will escape the judgment of God? Or do you despise the riches of his kindness, tolerance, and patience, not knowing that God’s kindness is meant to lead you to repentance?

<margin>Matthew 15.</margin>
But because of your stubbornness and unrepentant heart, you are storing up punishment for yourself for the day of punishment and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God, who will repay each person according to their deeds: that is, to those who, by persevering in good works, seek glory, honor, and immortality, he will give eternal life.

But for those who are contentious and disobedient to the truth, yet obedient to unrighteousness, there will be wrath and punishment, calamity and distress for every human soul who does evil, for the Greek and the Jew alike. But glory, honor, and peace for everyone who does good, for the Greek and the Jew alike.

<margin>Ephesians 6. Galatians 3. Colossians 3. Acts 10. James 2. 1 Peter 1. Matthew 7. James 1.</margin>
For there is no partiality with God. For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law; and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law. For it is not the hearers of the law who are innocent before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified.

<margin>a. That they both praise virtues and blame vices, which the same Law of Moses teaches.</margin>
<margin>b. As my teaching will show.</margin>
For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, by nature <gloss>a</gloss> do what the law requires, they are a law to themselves, even though they do not have the law. They show that the work of the law is written on their hearts, as their conscience also bears witness, and their thoughts will either accuse or defend them on the day when God judges the secrets of men <gloss>b</gloss> according to my gospel, through Jesus Christ.

Indeed, you are called a Jew, and you rely on the law and boast in God; you know his will and approve what is superior because you are instructed by the law. You are convinced that you are a guide to the blind, a light to those in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, and a teacher of the simple, because you have the embodiment of knowledge and truth in the law. You, then, who teach others, do you not teach yourself? You who preach against stealing, do you steal? You who say one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege? You who boast in the law, do you dishonor God by breaking the law? For as it is written: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.”
<margin>Ezekiel 36.</margin>

For circumcision is indeed of value if you obey the law. But if you break the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision. So, if an uncircumcised man keeps the requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision be regarded as circumcision? Then the one who is physically uncircumcised but keeps the law will condemn you, who have the written code and circumcision but break the law.

<margin>Deuteronomy 10, 30.</margin>
For a person is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is true circumcision something outward and physical. But a person is a Jew who is one inwardly; and true circumcision is a matter of the heart, by the Spirit, not by the letter. Such a person’s praise is not from men, but from God.

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>John 3:8.</margin>
**W**hat then is the advantage of the Jew? Or what is the benefit of circumcision? Much in every way. First, because the divine oracles <note>original: "oracula diuina" — the promises and scriptures of the Old Testament.</note> were entrusted to them. For what if some did not believe? Shall their lack of faith nullify the faithfulness of God? By no means. Let God be true, though every man be a liar; as it is recorded in the scriptures: *So that you may be shown to be just in your words, and prevail in your case.*
<margin>Psalm 51:4 (referenced as Psalm 15, 56 in the original text).</margin>
<margin>b. <unclear>unconquered</unclear> righteousness.</margin>
But if our injustice commends the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Is God unjust for inflicting punishment? I am speaking in human terms. By no means. Otherwise, how could God judge the world? But if the truth of God is increased to his glory by my falsehood, why then am I still condemned as a sinner? Why not rather say: let us do evil, that good may come? For this is how we are slandered, and how some claim we speak—whose condemnation is well-deserved. What then? Do we excel them? Not at all. For we have already charged that both Jews and Greeks are all under the power of sin, just as it is in the scriptures:
<margin>Psalm 14 (referenced as Psalm 13).</margin>
> There is no one righteous, not even one; there is no one who understands; there is no one who seeks God. All have turned aside together, they have become useless; there is no one who does right, not even one.

> Their throat is an open grave, they use their tongues for deceit; the venom of asps is under their lips. Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness, their feet are swift to shed blood, ruin and misery are in their paths, and the way of peace they do not know. There is no fear of God before their eyes.

Now we know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be silenced, and the whole world may become accountable to God, because by the works of the law no mortal will be made righteous in his sight. For through the law comes the knowledge of sin.
<margin>Galatians 2. b. Which is granted to man by God.</margin>

For there is no distinction. For all have sinned and fall short of the divine glory, being justified freely by his favor through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,
<margin>1 John 1.</margin>
<margin>1 Timothy 2.</margin>
whom God set forth as a <term>means of atonement</term> <note>original: "placamentum" — a sacrifice or offering intended to bring reconciliation.</note> to be received through faith in his blood, to demonstrate the righteousness of God, who in his forbearance grants pardon for past sins, so that he might demonstrate his righteousness at this present time, being himself just and the one who justifies those who have faith in Jesus. Where then is the boasting? It is excluded. By what law? That of works? No, but by the law of faith.
<margin>Galatians 2.</margin>
For we conclude that a person is justified by faith apart from the works of the law. Is God the God of the Jews only? Is he not also the God of the <term>foreigners</term> <note>original: "extraneorum" — usually translated as Gentiles, or non-Jewish people.</note>? Yes, of the foreigners also, since there is one God who justifies the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through faith. Do we then abolish the law through faith? By no means; rather, we uphold the law.

</margin>
...died, he died to sin once; but in that he lives, he lives to God. So you also must consider yourselves to be dead indeed to sin, but alive to God through Christ Jesus our Lord. Therefore, do not let sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey sin in the desires of the body; nor present your members to sin as weapons of injustice, but present yourselves to God as those living from the dead, and your members as weapons of righteousness to God. For sin shall not rule over you, because you are not under the law, but under grace. What then? Shall we sin because we are not under the law but under grace? Far from it. Do you not know that to whomever you present yourselves as servants for obedience, you are the servants of the one you obey? Either of sin leading to death, or of obedience leading to righteousness. But thanks be to God, that though you were servants of sin, you have obeyed from the heart that form of teaching which was delivered to you; and having been set free from sin, you became enslaved to righteousness.

<margin>
e. Because of which it leads to death.
f. While I call you servants of yourselves, that is finally true liberty.
</margin>
I speak in a human way because of the weakness of your human nature. For just as you presented your members as servants to impurity and to wickedness leading to more wickedness, so now present your members as servants to righteousness leading to holiness. For when you were servants of sin, you were free from righteousness. But what fruit did you then gather from those things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. But now, having been set free from sin and enslaved to God, you gather your fruit unto holiness, and in the end, you shall obtain eternal life. For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord.

## CHAPTER VII.

<margin>
1 Corinthians 7.
Matthew 5.
</margin>
Do you not know, brothers (for I speak to those who know the law), that the law has power over a man only as long as he lives? For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives. But if the husband dies, she is released from the law of the husband. Therefore, if she belongs to another man while her husband is living, she shall be called an adulteress. But if the husband dies, she is free from the law, so that she is not an adulteress if she belongs to another man. In the same way, my brothers, you also have been put to death to the law through the body of Christ, so that you might pass into the right of another—of him who was raised from the dead, so that we might bear fruit for God. For when we were in the body, the disturbances of sins arising from the law were at work in our members, so that we bore fruit for death. But now we are released from the law, having died to that by which we were held, so that we may serve in a new spirit, and not in the old letter.

<margin>
Galatians 3.
Exodus 20.
Deuteronomy 5.
</margin>
What shall we say then? Is the Law sin? Not at all: but I would not have known sin except through the Law. For I would not have known desire unless the Law said: *Thou shalt not covet.* But sin, taking the opportunity through the commandment, worked in me every kind of desire. For without the Law, sin is dead. Indeed, I once lived without the Law. But when the commandment came, sin revived and I died; and so the commandment, which was intended for life, was found by me to be deadly. For sin, taking the opportunity through the commandment, deceived me, and through the commandment, killed me. Therefore the Law indeed is holy, and the commandment is holy...

<margin>
1 Timothy 1.
</margin>

<margin>a. The author [speaks] as if he were another, and [as if] I am being forced in your [regard].</margin>...holy, and just, and good. Therefore, was that which is good made to be death for me? By no means; rather, it was sin. So that it might be revealed as sin, it produced death in me through that which is good, so that sin might become exceedingly sinful through the commandment. For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am merely human, sold into the slavery of sin. For I do not recognize <note>In this context, "recognize" or "acknowledge" suggests the inner conflict where one's actions feel alien to their own values.</note> what I am doing. For I do not do what I want to do; instead, I do the very thing I hate. But if I do what I do not want to do, I agree that the law is good. Now, it is no longer I who do it, but the sinfulness inhabiting me. For I know that no good thing dwells in me—that is, in my human nature. For the will to do good is present in me, but I do not find the way to perform it. I do not do the good I want to do, but I practice the evil I do not want. But if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but the sinfulness inhabiting me. Thus, I find this rule through the law: that for me, wanting to do good, evil is present within. For I delight in the law of God according to the inner man: but I see another law in my limbs, fighting against the law of my mind, which makes me a captive to the law of sinfulness that exists in my limbs. <margin>b. That this is certain for me through death by our authority.</margin> Wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from the body of this death? I give thanks to God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Therefore, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my body, the law of sin.

### CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>a. Made Christians.</margin> Therefore, there is now no condemnation for those who, being in Christ Jesus, obey not the will of the body, but of the spirit. For the law of the life-giving spirit in Jesus Christ has freed me from the law of sin and death. For what the law could not do, because it was weak in that regard <margin>a. Through the Son, who was like those who sin, advancing man.</margin> due to the body, God performed by sending his own Son in a body like that of the guilty; and because of sin, he condemned sin in the body, so that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us, who do not obey the body. For those who live according to the will of the body care for bodily things; but those who live according to the spirit care for spiritual things. For the pursuit of the body is death, but the pursuit of the spirit is life and peace. Indeed, the pursuit of the body is enmity against God, because it does not obey God’s law; nor, in fact, can it. Those who are in the body cannot please God. But you are not in the body, but in the spirit, since the spirit of God dwells in you. But if anyone does not have the spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Christ. But if Christ is in you, the body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is alive because of righteousness. But if the spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also call your mortal bodies back to life, through his spirit dwelling in you. Therefore, brothers, we are debtors not to the body, to live according to the lusts of the body. For if you live according to the will of the body, you shall die. But if by the spirit you kill the <margin>a. 1 Timothy 1. Galatians 4.</margin> actions of the body, you shall live. For as many as are led by the spirit of God, these are the children of God. For you have not received the spirit of slavery again unto fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption, by which we cry out,

<column-break/>

Abba, Father. <note>Abba is an Aramaic word for "Father," used here to show an intimate, familial relationship with God.</note> This spirit testifies to our souls that we are the children of God. And if children, then heirs—heirs, I say, of God, and co-heirs with Christ, if <margin>1 Corinthians 12.</margin> only we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified together. <margin>Hebrews 4.</margin> For I consider that the sufferings we must endure at this time are by no means equal to the glory that is to be bestowed upon us. For the expectation of the nature of things <note>The "nature of things" (rerum natura) refers to all of creation.</note> waits for the revealing of the sons of God. For nature was subjected to vanity, not of its own will, but through him who subjected it in hope, so that the nature of things itself might also be set free from the slavery of destruction into the glorious liberty of the children of God. For we know that all of nature groans and suffers together until now. And not only it, but we also, who have the firstfruits of the spirit, groan within ourselves, waiting for adoption, the liberation of our body. For we are saved by hope. But hope for those things which are seen is not hope. For why should someone hope for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience. Add to this that the spirit also helps our infirmities. For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought; but the spirit itself supplicates for us with inexpressible groans. But the searcher <margin>Psalm 17.</margin> of souls <margin>Jeremiah 17.</margin> knows what the pursuit of the spirit is, which indeed prays for the saints just as God requires. We know, moreover, that for those who love God, all things work together for good—for those who are called according to his divine decree. For those whom he foreknew, he also destined to be shaped in the likeness of the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. Likewise, those whom he destined, he also calls; and those whom he calls, he also justifies; and those whom he justifies, he also makes glorious. What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare <margin>John 3.</margin> his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, <margin>Isaiah 53.</margin> can he not also grant us all things along with him? Who shall accuse God’s chosen? It is God who acquits; who is it that condemns? It is Christ who died, or rather who rose again, who is even at the right hand of God and supplicates for us. Who shall tear us away from the love of God? Shall calamity? Or distress? Or <margin>a. Namely toward us, as in chapter 5.</margin> persecution? Or hunger? Or nakedness? Or danger? Or <margin>Psalm 43.</margin> the sword? As it is written: *For your sake we are killed all day long, we are led like sheep to the slaughter.* And yet in all these things we prevail through him who loved us. For (as I am persuaded) neither death, nor life, nor <margin>2 Corinthians 12.</margin> spirits, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come, nor heights, nor depths, nor any other thing in nature shall be able to tear us away from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

### CHAPTER IX.

<margin>Galatians 4.</margin> I speak the truth through Christ, I do not lie; my conscience is a witness to me through the Holy Spirit, that I am affected by great sorrow of heart and unceasing torment. For I could wish that I myself were unhappily alienated from Christ—

to be estranged <note>original: "alienatum esse." This refers to Paul’s willingness to be "accursed" or separated from Christ if it could save his kin.</note> for the sake of my brothers: mine, as far as human nature is concerned: my kinsmen, who are Israelites, to whom belong the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the worship, and the promises: to whom belong the fathers, and from whom is Christ, as far as humanity is concerned, who is God over all, to be praised forever. Amen <note>original: "Etiam," a Latin affirmation used here like the Hebrew "Amen."</note>.

<margin>a. I do not grant this to the Israelites only because I am unaware that God did not declare the true Israelites to be those born of Abraham, but etc.</margin>
Nor do I say this as if the word of God has failed. For not all those who are descended from Israel are Israelites: nor because they are Abraham’s offspring are they all his children. But, "Your offspring shall be named through Isaac" <margin>Galatians 4</margin>: that is, it is not the children of human nature who are God’s <margin>Genesis 21</margin> children: but the children of the promise are counted as the offspring. <margin>Genesis 18</margin> For this is what the promise said: "When I return at this time, Sarah shall have a son." And not only she, but also Rebecca, when she had conceived by one man, our ancestor Isaac <margin>Genesis 25</margin>, though the children were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—so that God’s purpose according to election might stand, not because of works but because of him who calls—it was said to Rebecca: "The elder shall serve the younger." <margin>Malachi 1</margin> Just as it is written: "Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated." What shall we say then? Is there injustice in God? By no means. For he says to Moses <margin>Exodus 33</margin>: "I grant grace and I bestow mercy on whomever I please." Therefore it does not depend on the one who wills, nor on the one who runs, but on God who shows grace. For so it is said in the scriptures <margin>Exodus 9</margin> to Pharaoh: "I have raised you up for this very purpose, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed throughout the whole world." Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills. You will say to me: "Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?" But indeed, O man, who are you to argue with God? <margin>Isaiah 45</margin> Shall the thing formed say to the former: "Why did you make me like this?" <margin>Ecclesiastes 38</margin> As if indeed the potter does not have the right <margin>Jeremiah 18</margin> to make from the same lump of clay one vessel for honorable use and another for dishonorable use. What if God, <margin>b. Destined for punishments.</margin> wishing to exercise his wrath and make his power known, endured with much patience the **b** vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, so that he might also make known the riches of his glory upon the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory—that is, upon us, whom he called not only from the Jews but also from the other nations? Just as <margin>Hosea 2, 1 Peter 2</margin> he says in Hosea: "I will call those who were not my people, 'my people': and her who was not loved, 'loved': and in the place where it was said to them, 'You are not my people,' there they shall be called children of the living God." But Isaiah cries out concerning the <margin>Isaiah 10, c. Few.</margin> Israelites: "Even if the Israelites are as numerous as the sand of the sea, only a **c** remnant shall be saved. For the Lord will execute his word on the earth, strictly and once for all, and that with justice." And as <margin>Isaiah 1</margin> Isaiah had already said: "Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah." What shall we say then? That the other nations, who did not pursue righteousness, have attained righteousness—that is, the righteousness that comes from faith. But the Israelites, pursuing the law of righteousness, did not arrive at the law of righteousness. Why? Because they did so not by faith, but as if by the works of the law; for they stumbled over the stumbling stone, as it is written: "Behold, I am placing in <margin>Isaiah 28</margin> Zion a stumbling stone and a rock of offense,

<column-break/>

and whoever trusts in him will not be put to shame."

### CHAPTER X.

<margin>Leviticus 18, Galatians 3, Deuteronomy 30. a. Do not doubt, as if he cannot be saved. b. To deny that he ascended. Isaiah 28.</margin>
Brothers, my heart’s desire and my prayer to God is for the salvation of the Israelites. For I testify concerning them that they have a zeal for God, but they do so ignorantly. For being ignorant of divine righteousness, and seeking to establish their own righteousness, they have not submitted to divine righteousness. For Christ is the end of the law, for righteousness to everyone who believes. For Moses writes concerning the righteousness that is situated in the law, that the person who performs its commands shall live by them. But the righteousness that comes from faith says this: **a** "Do not say in your heart: 'Who will ascend into heaven?'" That is, to bring Christ **b** down. "Or who will descend into the abyss <note>original: "Tartara." Castellio uses this classical term for the underworld to describe the "deep" or the place of the dead.</note>?" That is, to bring Christ up from the dead. But what does the scripture say? "The word is near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart." This is the word concerning faith that we proclaim: that if you confess with your mouth the Lord Jesus, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation. For so the scripture says: "Everyone who trusts in him will not be put to shame." There is indeed no distinction between Jew and Greek, since the same Lord is Lord of all, rich to all who call upon him. <margin>2 Corinthians 8, Joel 2, Acts 2</margin> For "everyone who calls on the name of the Lord shall be saved." But how can they call on him in whom they do not trust? Or how can they trust in him of whom they have not heard? Or how can they hear without a preacher? Or how can they preach unless they are sent? <margin>Isaiah 52, Nahum 1, Isaiah 53, John 12</margin> As it stands in the scriptures: "How beautiful are the feet of those who bring news of peace, who bring news of good things!" But not all have obeyed the gospel. For Isaiah says: "Lord, who has believed our message?" Therefore faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the divine word. But I ask, have they not heard? Certainly, <margin>Psalm 18</margin> since "their sound has gone out into all lands, and their words to the ends of the world." But I ask, did the Israelites not know? First Moses says: "I will make you jealous by <margin>Deuteronomy 32</margin> those who are not a nation: I will make you angry by an ignorant nation." And Isaiah even dares to say: "I was <margin>Isaiah 65</margin> found by those who did not seek me: I made myself manifest to those who did not care for me." But concerning the Israelites he says: "All day long I have stretched out my hands to a stubborn and contrary people."

### CHAPTER XI.

<margin>1 Kings 19</margin>
I ask then, has God rejected his people? By no means. For I myself am an Israelite, of the offspring of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people, whom he foreknew. Or do you not know what the scriptures say about Elijah: how he appeals to God against the Israelites? "Lord," he says, "they have killed your prophets and overturned your altars; I alone am left, and they are seeking my life." But what does the divine response say to him? "I have left for myself seven thousand men who have not bowed their knees to Baal." So too at this present time there is a remnant remaining through a gracious election. But if it is by grace, then it is not by works: otherwise grace would no longer be grace. But if it is by works, it is no longer grace: otherwise work would no longer be work.

<margin>Isaiah 6. Matthew 13. Mark 4. Luke 8. John 12. Acts 28. Psalm 69 <note>original: "Ps. 68." The numbering follows the Vulgate system.</note>.</margin>
What then? That which the Israelites are searching for, they have not attained: but the chosen have attained it, while the rest were blinded, just as it is recorded in the scriptures: God gave them a spirit of stupor: eyes, so that they might not see: and ears, so that they might not hear. This continues to this very day. Likewise David says: Let their own table be a snare, and a trap, and a stumbling block and a punishment for them. Let their eyes be darkened, so that they might not see: and keep their backs bent forever. I ask therefore, did they stumble so that they might fall? Not at all. But by their fall, salvation has come to the other nations, so that they themselves might be provoked to jealousy. Now if their lapse is the wealth of the world, and if their lack is the riches of the remaining nations, how much more will their full abundance be? For I say to you <term>foreigners</term> <note>original: "extraneis," usually translated as "Gentiles."</note>: insofar as I am indeed an apostle to the foreigners, I bring honor to my ministry, if by any means I might entice my own kinsmen, and save some of them. For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance be, if not life from the dead? Now if the <margin>a. Abraham</margin> firstfruits<sup>a</sup> are holy, so then is the whole batch: and if the root is holy, so then are the branches. But if some of the branches <margin>b. Grafted into the trunk of the olives.</margin> were torn away, and you, being a wild olive<sup>b</sup>, were grafted in among them, and became a sharer in the root and the richness of the olive tree, do not boast against the branches. But if you do boast, remember that you do not support the root, but the root supports you. You will say: The branches were torn away so that I might be grafted in. Correct. They were torn away because of their lack of trust: you stand by faith. Do not be arrogant, but be afraid. For if God did not spare the natural branches, what if he does not spare you either? See therefore the kindness and the severity of God: toward those who fell, severity: toward you, kindness, provided you remain in that kindness. Otherwise, you too will be cut off: and they, unless they persist in their lack of trust, will be grafted in. For God is able to graft them in again. For if you were cut out of a natural wild olive tree, and were grafted contrary to nature into a good olive tree: how much more will these, according to nature, be grafted into their own olive tree? For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this secret, lest you be conceited: that a blindness has happened in part to the Israelites, until the full number of the other nations has entered, and so all Israelites may be saved, just <margin>Isaiah 59.</margin> as it is recorded in memory: The deliverer will come out of Zion, who shall turn away wickedness from the descendants of Jacob. And this is the covenant which I make with them, namely, that I will take away their sins. As far as the gospel is concerned, they are enemies for your sake: but as for the election, they are beloved for the sake of their ancestors. For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable. For just as you who once did not obey God have now obtained mercy through their defiance, so these now, through the mercy shown to you, do not obey, so that they too may be granted mercy. For God has confined <margin>Jews and foreigners</margin> all in defiance, so that he may have mercy on all. O the deep wealth of the wisdom and knowledge of God: how profoundly hidden are his judgments, <margin>Wisdom 7, 9. Isaiah 40. 1 Corinthians 2.</margin> how inscrutable are his ways? For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, that he should be repaid? For from him, and through him, and because of him are all things: to him be glory <margin>Romans 15.</margin> forever. Amen <note>original: "Etiam," a Latin affirmation.</note>.
