# THE SECOND [EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY]

<sig>LLL 2</sig>

[Remember Jesus Christ] raised from the dead, descended from the seed of David, according to my gospel, for which I suffer hardship even to the point of chains, like a criminal; but the word of God is not chained. Therefore I endure all things for the sake of the elect, so that they also may obtain the salvation which is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory. It is a certain thing: if we have died with him, we shall also live with him. If we endure, we shall also reign with him. If we deny him, he also will deny us; if we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself. Remind them of these things, solemnly charging them in the sight of the Lord not to engage in battles over words, a thing that is of no benefit and even ruins the listeners. Strive to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who does not need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth. <margin>1 Timothy 4</margin> Avoid profane and empty chatter, for it leads to more and more impiety, and their talk will spread like a gangrene; among whom are Hymenaeus and Philetus <note>Hymenaeus and Philetus were early Christian teachers whose views on the resurrection were considered heretical by Paul.</note>, who have wandered from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already taken place, and they upset the faith of some. Nevertheless, the firm foundation of God stands, bearing this seal: "The Lord knows those who are his," and "Let everyone who names the name of Christ depart from iniquity." Now in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay, some for honorable uses and some for dishonorable. Therefore, if anyone purifies himself from <margin>a. That is, up until what he said</margin> these things <gloss>a</gloss>, he will be a vessel set apart for honor, useful to the master, prepared for every good work. Flee youthful passions; pursue righteousness, faith, charity, and peace, together with those who call on the Lord with a pure heart. Avoid foolish and ignorant disputes, knowing (as you do) that they breed quarrels, and a servant of the Lord must not be quarrelsome, but must be kind to everyone, an apt teacher, patient under injury, correcting opponents with gentleness; perhaps God will grant them a change of heart so they may come to the knowledge of the truth, return to their senses, and escape the snare of the devil, by whom they have been captured to do his will.

### CHAPTER III.

<margin>2 Timothy 4, 2 Peter 3, Jude 1</margin>
Know this also: that in the last days difficult times will come. For people will be lovers of themselves, greedy, arrogant, proud, abusive, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, irreligious, heartless, oath-breakers, slanderers, without self-control, brutal, enemies of virtue, traitors, reckless, conceited, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God, having a form of godliness but denying its power. Turn away from such people. For among them are those who slip into houses and captivate weak women who are overwhelmed by sins and led away by various passions, always learning and never able to reach the knowledge of the truth. <margin>Exodus 7</margin> And just as Jannes and Jambres <note>According to Jewish tradition, Jannes and Jambres were the names of the Egyptian magicians who opposed Moses in the court of Pharaoh.</note> resisted Moses, so these men resist the truth—men of corrupt minds, disqualified regarding the faith. But they will not get very far, for their folly will be plain to everyone, as was that of those men. You, however, have followed my teaching, my way of life, my purpose, faith, gentleness, charity, patience, persecutions, and sufferings—the kind of things that happened to me at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra; the persecutions I endured, and from

<column-break/>

all of them the Lord rescued me. Indeed, all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted; while evil people and impostors will go from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived. But as for you, continue in what you have learned and have become convinced of, knowing from whom you learned it, and how from childhood you have known the sacred writings, which are able to instruct you for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. <margin>2 Peter 1 a. Namely the sacred [writings], of which he spoke. b. A Christian</margin> Every scripture is inspired by God <gloss>a</gloss> and is useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, so that the <gloss>b</gloss> man of God may be complete, well-equipped for every good work.

### CHAPTER IV.

Therefore I solemnly charge you in the sight of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, who is to judge the living and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom: preach the word; be ready in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and exhort with the utmost patience and teaching. For the time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears, they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions, and will turn away from listening to the truth and wander into myths. As for you, always be sober; endure suffering; do the work of an evangelist; fulfill your ministry. For I am already being poured out as a sacrifice, and the time of my departure has come. I have fought the good fight; I have finished the race; I have kept the faith. From now on there is reserved for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me on that day—and not only to me, but also to all who have loved his appearing. Do your best to come to me soon. For Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica; Crescens has gone to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia. Only Luke is with me. <margin>Colossians 4</margin> Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for ministry. I have sent Tychicus to Ephesus. When you come, bring the cloak that I left with Carpus at Troas, and also the books, especially the parchments. Alexander the coppersmith <note>original: "faber ferrarius," literally a worker in iron or a blacksmith.</note> did me much harm; the Lord will repay him according to his deeds. You also should beware of him, for he strongly opposed our words. At my first defense no one came to my support, but all deserted me; may it not be counted against them. But the Lord stood by me and gave me strength, so that through me the message might be fully proclaimed and all the Gentiles might hear it; and so I was rescued from the lion's mouth. The Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen. Greet Prisca and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus. Erastus remained at Corinth, and I left Trophimus ill at Miletus. Do your best to come before winter. Eubulus sends greetings to you, as do Pudens and Linus and Claudia and all the brothers. The Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Grace be with you. Amen.

TO TITUS

# THE EPISTLE OF PAUL THE APOSTLE
## TO TITUS.

### CHAPTER I.

<margin>
2 Timothy 3.
</margin>
PAUL, a servant of God and an Apostle of Jesus Christ, according to the faith of the elect of God and the knowledge of the truth which is set within religion together with the hope of eternal life, which God, who never lies, had promised before the eternal ages, and has revealed in his own time—namely, his word to be made known through preaching. This preaching was committed to me by the command of God our Savior; to Titus, my true son <note>original: "germano... filio," implying a legitimate or spiritual kinship</note> according to our common faith: grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ our Savior. I left you in Crete for this reason: so that you might set in order the things that remain and appoint elders <term>seniores: the Greek term is 'presbyteros,' referring to leaders of the local church</term> in every town, as I directed you. If anyone is blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children who are not accused of luxury or rebellion. For it is necessary for a bishop <term>episcopum: an overseer or guardian of the community</term> to be blameless, as God's steward; not arrogant, not quick-tempered, not given to wine, not violent, not greedy for money, but hospitable, a lover of virtue, sensible, just, holy, temperate, a defender of the faithful word used in teaching, so that he may be able both to exhort with sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict it. For there are many who are rebellious, empty talkers, and crafty—especially those of the circumcision—who must be refuted, for they subvert entire households by teaching illicit things for the sake of shameful gain. <margin>a. Epimenides, who was himself a Cretan.</margin> One of them, their own prophet, said: "Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies." This testimony is true; therefore rebuke them severely so that they may be sound in the faith, <margin>Romans 4.</margin> not giving heed to Jewish fables and the commandments of men who turn away from the truth. To the pure, all things are pure; but to the defiled and unfaithful, nothing is pure; indeed, both their minds and their consciences are defiled. They profess to know God, but they deny him by their deeds, being abominable, disobedient, and useless for every good work.

### CHAPTER II.

BUT you, speak the things that befit sound doctrine: That the older men be sober, grave, sensible, and sound in faith, charity, and patience. Likewise, that the older women be reverent in behavior, not slanderers, not enslaved to much wine, well-instructed, so that they may teach the young women to be lovers of their husbands and children, sensible, chaste, stay-at-homes, good, and obedient to their husbands, so that the divine doctrine is not spoken of poorly. Likewise, exhort the younger men to be sensible, showing yourself in all things an example of good works; <margin>a. Namely, outstanding.</margin> in your teaching ª showing integrity, gravity, and sound speech that cannot be condemned, so that opponents may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say of you. <margin>Ephesians 6. Colossians 3. 1 Peter 2.</margin> Let servants be obedient to their own masters, pleasing in all things, not talkers-back, not thieves, but demonstrating the highest good faith, so that they may honor the doctrine of God our Savior in all things. For the divine kindness has appeared, bringing salvation to all men, which trains

<column-break/>

us to say farewell to impiety and worldly desires, and to live sensibly, justly, and piously in this age, awaiting the hoped-for blessedness and the glorious coming of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us to redeem us from all wickedness and to purify for himself a special people, eager for good works. Speak these things, and exhort, and rebuke with all authority, so that no one may despise you.

### CHAPTER III.

REmind them to be subject to magistrates and powers and to obey their commands: to be ready for every good work, to speak evil of no one, not to be contentious but equitable, showing the greatest kindness toward all men. For we ourselves were also once foolish, disobedient, led astray, serving various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another. <margin>a. 2 Timothy 1.</margin> But after the goodness and humanity of God our Savior appeared—not because of works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy—he saved us <margin>a. As far as we know, and as we may hold it from the Holy Spirit.</margin> by the washing ª of rebirth and the renewal of the Holy Spirit, which he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that having been made righteous by his grace, we might become heirs of the eternal life that is hoped for. This is a certain thing. I want you to insist on these things, so that those who trust in God may be careful to practice good works. These things are excellent and <margin>b. 2 Timothy 1.</margin> useful to men. But avoid foolish questions, genealogies <note>original: "antiquitatibus," referring to the tracing of ancient lineages or myths</note>, disputes, and legal battles; <margin>b. Let him be so corrupted that he perishes himself, because he sins out of error.</margin> for they are useless and futile. Avoid a stubborn man after a first and second admonition, knowing that such a person is perverse and sins in such a way that ᵇ he is condemned by himself. TO PHILEMON.
<sig>LLL 3</sig>

...which you possess both toward the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints, so that the sharing of your faith, placed in Christ Jesus, may become effective through the recognition of all the good that is in you. For we have great joy and comfort in your charity, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed by you, brother. Therefore, although I have great authority in Christ to command you regarding your duty, I prefer to appeal to you for the sake of charity—being such a one as I am, Paul the aged, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ. I appeal to you, I say, for my son Onesimus <note>The name Onesimus in Greek means "useful." Paul is making a wordplay here on his former status as a runaway slave.</note>, whom I have fathered in my chains, who was once useless to you, but now is useful to both you and me, and whom I have sent back. You, therefore, receive him—that is, my very heart—whom I wanted to keep with me, so that he might serve me in your place while I am in chains for the Gospel. But I did not want to do anything without your consent, so that your good deed might not be by compulsion, but voluntary. For perhaps he departed for a time for this reason: so that you might receive him forever, no longer as a slave, but more than a slave—as a brother most dear to me, and even more so to you, both in the flesh and in the religion of the Lord. Therefore, if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would me. And if he has wronged you in any way, or owes you anything, charge it to me. I, Paul, have written this with my own hand; I will repay it—not to mention that you owe me your very self. Yes, brother, let me have this benefit from you in the Lord; refresh my heart in the Lord. Confident in your obedience, I have written to you, knowing that you will do even more than I ask. Moreover, prepare a guest room for me, for I hope that through your prayers I shall be restored to you. Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you, as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers. May the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirits. Amen.

My brothers, do not hold the faith of our glorious Lord Jesus Christ with partiality toward persons. Listen, my most dear brothers: has not God chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom which He has promised to those who love Him? ### CHAPTER III.

This is now the second letter I am writing to you, beloved, in which I stir up your sincere mind by way of a reminder, so that you may remember the words spoken long ago by the holy 
<margin>1 Timothy 4. 2 Timothy 3. Jude 1.</margin>
prophets and the commandment of us, the apostles of the Lord and Savior. Know this first: that in the last days mockers will come,

<column-break/>

following their own lusts, saying, "Where is the promise of his coming? For since the fathers fell asleep, all things remain in the same state they have been since the beginning of creation." For they deliberately ignore this: that by the word of God the heavens existed long ago and the earth was formed out of water and through water. 
<margin>Ezekiel</margin>
By these things the world of that time was flooded with water and perished. But by the same word, the heavens and earth that now exist are being reserved for fire, kept for the day of judgment and the destruction of ungodly men. But do not let this one thing escape your notice, beloved: that with the Lord one day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like one day. The Lord is not slow 
<margin>1 Thessalonians. Revelation.</margin>
concerning his promise, as some count slowness, but is patient toward us, not wishing for anyone to perish but for all to come to repentance. But the day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night, in which the heavens will pass away with a roar, the burning elements will be dissolved, and the earth and the things in it will be burned up. Since all these things are to be dissolved in this way, what kind of people ought you to be in holy conduct and godliness, as you look for and hasten the coming of the day of God? Because of that day, the heavens will be destroyed by fire 
<margin>Revelation.</margin>
and the burning elements will melt. But according to his promise, we look for new heavens and a new earth, in which righteousness dwells. Therefore, beloved, since you are looking for these things, make every effort to be found by him in peace, without spot or blemish. Regard the patience of our Lord as salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote to you according to the wisdom given to him. He speaks of these things in all his letters, though there are some things in them that are difficult to understand, which the ignorant and unstable twist to their own destruction, as they do the other Scriptures. You, therefore, beloved, knowing this beforehand, be on your guard so that you are not led away by the error of the wicked and fall from your own stability. But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.

# CHAPTER III.

See with what great love the father has pursued us, that we should be called children of God. For this reason the world does not know us, because it did not know him. Beloved, we are now children of God, although it is not yet clear what we shall be. And everyone who has this hope in him purifies himself, just as he is pure. Whoever commits sin commits a crime <note>Latin: *crimen*; here used for the Greek *anomia*, implying lawlessness or a violation of divine law</note>, for sin is crime. You know that he appeared for this purpose: to take away our sins; and in him there was no sin. Whoever remains in him does not sin; whoever sins has not learned of him nor known him. Little children, let no one deceive you. He who does what is right is righteous, just as he is righteous. He who commits sin is of the devil, <margin>Revelation 22. John 8.</margin> since the devil has been sinning from the beginning. For this reason the son of God appeared: to destroy the works of the devil. Whoever is born of God does not commit sin, because <margin>Genesis 4.</margin> God's seed remains in him; therefore he is unable to sin, because he is born of God. In this the children of God and the children of the devil are made manifest: whoever does not do what is right is not of God, nor is the one who does not love his brother. Whoever confesses that Jesus is the son of God, God remains in him and he in God. And we have known and believed the love with which God pursues us. God is love, and he who remains in love remains in God, and God in him. In this we are endowed with perfect love, f so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment, c because as he is, so are we in this world. In love there is no fear; rather, perfect love drives out fear, because fear involves torment, and he who fears is not perfect in love. We love him because he first loved us. If someone says that God is loved by him, and yet...

<column-break/>

<margin>
Luke 19.
John 10, 13.
Matthew 22.
</margin>
...hates his brother, he is a liar. For he who does not love his brother, whom he has seen, how can he love God, whom he has not seen? And we have this command from him: that he who loves God must also love his brother.

### CHAPTER V.

<margin>
1 Corinthians 15.
[*] These <insert>verses</insert> do not exist in certain manuscripts.
a The testimony of these three is the same. John 10, 3.
b In the Holy Spirit.
c By the Devil.
</margin>
Whoever believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God; and whoever loves the parent also loves the one born of him. By this we understand that we love the children of God: if we love God and obey his commands. For this is the love of God: that we obey his commands, and his commands are surely not heavy. For whatever is born of God overcomes the world, and this is the victory that has overcome the world: our faith. Who is it that overcomes the world except the one who believes that Jesus is the son of God? This is he who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ; not in water only, but in water and blood. And it is the spirit who testifies, since the spirit is truth. For there are three who testify in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; a and these three are one. Likewise there are three who testify on earth: the spirit, the water, and the blood, and these three are one. <note>This section (verses 7-8) is known as the *Comma Johanneum*. The marginal note [*] correctly identifies that it was missing from many early Greek manuscripts.</note> If we accept the testimony of men, the testimony of God is greater. And this is the testimony that God spoke concerning his son: He who has faith in the son of God has the testimony of God in himself. He who does not believe God makes him a liar, because he does not have faith in the testimony that God spoke concerning his son. And this is the testimony: that God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his son. He who has the son of God has life; he who does not have the son of God does not have life. I have written these things to you who have faith in the name of the son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life, and so that you may add faith to the name of the son of God. And this is the confidence we have toward him: that if we ask anything according to his will, he hears us. And if we know that we are heard by him in whatever we ask, we know that we have obtained those things which we requested from him. If anyone sees his brother committing a sin that is not lethal, if he asks God, God will give him life—namely, to those sinning non-lethally. There is b a lethal sin for which I do not teach that one should pray. All injustice is sin. There is also a sin that is not lethal. We know that whoever is born of God does not sin, for the one born of God preserves himself, nor does c the Evil One touch him. We know that we are from God, and the whole world lies in the Evil One. We know also that the son of God has come and has given us this understanding so that we may know the true God; and we are in the true one, in his son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life. Little children, beware of false gods <note>original: *deastros*; a term for idols or "little gods" contrasted with the true God</note>.

->Amen.<-

# THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS.

## CHAPTER I.

<margin>Wisdom 7</margin>
In many parts and in various ways, God spoke to our ancestors long ago through the prophets <note>original: *uates*, a classical term for divinely inspired poets or seers</note>. In these last days, he has spoken to us through his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, and through whom he also created the world. Since the Son is the radiance of his glory and the exact image of his essence, and sustains all things by his powerful command, after he had by himself achieved the purification of our sins, he sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high. He was made so much superior to the angels <note>original: *geniis*, a classical term for spirits</note> as the name he has inherited is more excellent than theirs. For to which of the angels did God ever say: *You are my Son, today I have begotten you*? And again: *I will be a Father to him, and he shall be a Son to me*? And again, when he brings the firstborn into the world, he says: *And let all the divine angels worship him.* Regarding the angels he indeed says: *He who uses spirits as his messengers, and a flame of fire as his ministers.* But concerning the Son he says: *Your throne, O God, remains for all eternity; the scepter of justice is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions.* And: *In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They indeed shall perish, but you remain; they all shall grow old like a garment, and as*
<margin>Ps. 2, Acts 13, 2 Sam. 7, Ps. 96, Ps. 103, Ps. 44, Ps. 45, Ps. 101, Ps. 109.</margin>

<column-break/>

*as a cloak you will fold them up, and they shall be changed. But you are the same, and your years shall have no end.* Furthermore, to which of the angels<sup>b</sup> did he ever say: *Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet*? Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out to serve for the sake of those who are to obtain salvation?
<margin>b In the plural number.</margin>

## CHAPTER II.

<margin>b We forget.</margin>
Therefore, we must pay much closer attention to what we have heard, so that we do not perhaps drift away<sup>b</sup>. For if the message spoken through angels was binding, and every transgression and disobedience received a just penalty, how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation? This salvation, which was first announced by the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard him, while God also bore witness by signs, wonders, various miracles, and gifts of the Holy Spirit, distributed according to his own will. For he did not subject the world to come, of which we speak, to angels. But someone has testified somewhere, saying: *What is man, that you are mindful of him? Or the son of man, that you care for him? You made him a little lower than the angels; you crowned him with glory and honor, and set him over the works of your hands. You put all things in subjection under his feet.* For in subjecting all things to him, he left nothing that is not subject to him. But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him, but we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone. For it was fitting that he, for whom and through whom all things exist, in bringing many sons to glory, should make the author of their salvation perfect through sufferings. For both he who makes people holy and those who are made holy are all from one. For this reason, he is not ashamed to call them brothers, saying: *I will declare your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will praise you.* And again: *I will put my trust in him.* And again: *Behold, I and the children whom God has given me.* Since the children have flesh and blood, he himself likewise shared in the same, so that through death he might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who, through fear of death, were subject to lifelong slavery. For he does not give help to angels, but he helps the descendants of Abraham. Therefore, he had to be made like his brothers in every way, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest <note>original: *pontifex*</note> in divine matters, to make atonement for the sins of the people. For because he himself suffered when he was tested, he is able to help those who are being tested.
<margin>Ps. 8, 1 Cor. 15, Phil. 2, Ps. 21, Isa. 8, 1 Cor. 15.</margin>

## CHAPTER III.

Therefore, holy brothers, partners in a heavenly calling, consider the ambassador and high priest of our profession, Christ Jesus, who was faithful to him who appointed him, just as Moses was faithful in all his house. For this man was counted worthy of so much more glory than Moses, as the builder of the house has more honor than the house itself. For every house is built by someone, but the builder of all things is God. And Moses indeed was faithful in all his house as a servant, to testify to the things that were to be spoken. But Christ is faithful as a Son over his own house; and we are his house, if only we hold onto our confidence and the glory of our hope—
<margin>Num. 12.</margin>

->CHAPTER V<-

For every high priest chosen from among men is appointed on behalf of men in matters pertaining to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins. He is able to deal gently with the ignorant and the erring, since he himself is surrounded by weakness, and because of this, he must offer sacrifices for his own sins just as he does for the people. And no one takes this honor for himself, but only he who is called by God, just as Aaron was. So also Christ did not claim the honor for himself to become high priest, but was appointed by him who said to him: "You are my son, today I have begotten you." As he says in another place:

"You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek." While Christ was living his mortal life, having offered up prayers and supplications with loud cries and tears to him who was able to save him from death, and having been heard because of his piety, though he was a son, he nevertheless learned obedience from the things he suffered. And having been made perfect, he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him, having been called by God a high priest according to the order of Melchizedek. We have much to say about him,
<margin>a Listeners.</margin>
which is difficult to explain, since you^a^ have become dull of hearing. For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to teach you again the first elements of the divine oracles; you are those who have need of milk, not solid food. For anyone who lives on milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, being a mere infant. But solid food is for the mature, who by reason of use have their senses trained to distinguish between good and evil.

->CHAPTER VI<-

Therefore, leaving behind the talk of the elementary teachings of Christ, let us press on toward perfection, not laying again a foundation of repentance from dead works, of faith in God, of the doctrine of washings, of the laying on of hands, of the resurrection of the dead, and of eternal punishment. And we will do this if God permits. For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened and have tasted the heavenly gift, and were made partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the excellent words of God and the powers of the age to come, and yet fall away, to be renewed again to repentance
<margin>Below, 10.</margin>
since they crucify the Son of God again for themselves and make a public example of him. For the land which drinks in the rain that often falls on it, and brings forth a crop useful to those for whom it is cultivated, receives a blessing from God. But that which produces thorns and thistles is worthless and close to being cursed, and in the end, it is to be burned. Though we speak in this way, friends, we are persuaded of better things regarding you, things that accompany salvation. Nor...

<meta>catchword: Nor</meta>

<summary>This section of the Epistle to the Hebrews warns against the "defiance" shown by the Israelites in the wilderness and exhorts believers to enter God’s promised rest. It establishes Jesus as a superior High Priest in the order of Melchizedek, contrasting his perfection and suffering with the temporary nature of the Levitical priesthood.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the Epistle to the Hebrews, picking up at Chapter 6, verse 11. <header>TO THE HEBREWS.</header>

But we desire that each of you show the same zeal, toward the fullness of faith, even to the end, so that you are not sluggish, but rather imitators of those who, through faith and patience, obtain what was promised. For when God made a promise to Abraham, <margin>Gen. 22</margin> since he could swear by no one greater, he swore by himself, saying: "Surely I will bless you and multiply you." And so, after he had been patient, he obtained the promise. For men swear by one greater than themselves, and for them, an oath is the end of all controversy for the purpose of confirming a matter. Therefore, wishing to <margin>a. of the promised happiness.</margin> demonstrate more vehemently the unchangeability of his counsel to the ^a^heirs of the promise, God interposed an oath, so that through two unchangeable things (in which it is impossible for God to lie), we might have a strong consolation—we who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us. We hold this hope as an anchor of the soul, safe and firm, entering even within the veil <note>original: *siparium*; a theatrical term for a curtain or veil, used here for the sanctuary curtain</note>, where Jesus has entered as a forerunner for us, having become a high priest forever according to the order <note>original: *rationem*; can mean reckoning, order, or manner</note> of Melchizedek.

### CHAPTER VII.

<margin>Gen. 14</margin> For this Melchizedek, king of Salem <note>original: *Solymæ*; a classical name for Jerusalem</note>, priest of the most high God, met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him with favorable omens. To him Abraham also gave a tenth of everything. First, his name signifies "King of Justice"; then he is "King of Salem," which means "King of Peace." Without father, without mother, without ancestors, having neither beginning of days nor end of life, but made like the Son of God, he remains a priest forever. Now consider how great this man was, to whom even Abraham, that great patriarch, gave tenths from the spoils. And indeed, those from the lineage of Levi who enter the priesthood have a mandate to take tithes from the people according to the law—that is, from their own kinsmen, even though they have descended from the loins of Abraham. But this man, who is not traced to the same descent as them, took tithes from Abraham and blessed him who held the promises. Now, without any controversy, the lesser is blessed by the greater. And here, mortal men receive tithes; but there, he receives them of whom it is witnessed that he lives. And, so to speak, even Levi, who receives tithes, paid tithes through Abraham. For he was still in his father's loins when Melchizedek met him. If, therefore, perfection were found in the Levitical priesthood (for under that priesthood the law was given to the people), what further need was there for another priest to be said to arise according to the order of Melchizedek, and not <margin>Galat. 4</margin> according to the order of Aaron? For when the priesthood is transferred, it is necessary that a transfer of the law also takes place. For he of whom <margin>a. should perform the priestly office.</margin> these things are said belongs to another tribe, from which no one ^a^stands at the altar. For it is evident that our Lord arose from Judah, a tribe for which Moses spoke nothing concerning the priesthood. And this is even more manifest if another priest arises according to the likeness of Melchizedek, who is made not according to the law of a human commandment, but from the power of an indestructible life. For he testifies: "You are a priest forever, according to the order <margin>Ps. 109</margin> of Melchizedek." For there is an abrogation of the former commandment because of its weakness and uselessness (since the law perfected nothing), but it was the introduction of a better hope, through which we draw near to God; a better hope,

<column-break/>

<page-num>272</page-num>
I say, insofar as it is not without an oath. For those were made priests without an oath; but this one with an oath, by him who says of him: "The Lord has sworn and will not change his mind: you are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek." By so much has Jesus become the guarantor of a better testament <note>original: *testamenti*; refers to a covenant or legal will</note>. And those priests indeed were many, because they were prevented by death from continuing. But this one, because he endures forever, <margin>1 John 2.</margin> has a priesthood that shall never pass away. Therefore, he is able to fully save those who approach God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them. For such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, free from vice, undefiled, separate from foreign sources <note>original: *a fontibus alienis*; likely meaning separate from sinners or worldly corruption</note>, and made higher than the heavens. He does not have the daily necessity, like other high priests, to first offer sacrifices for his own sins, and then for the people's. For he did this once and for all when he offered up himself. For the law appoints men as high priests who are endowed with weakness; but the word of the oath, which followed the law, appoints the Son, who is perfected for eternity.

### CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>Above, 4.</margin> Now the summary of this discourse is that we have such a high priest, who has sat down at the right hand of the throne of Majesty in the heavens, a minister of the sanctuary and of the true tabernacle which the Lord set up, and not man. For every high priest is appointed to offer gifts and sacrifices; therefore, it is necessary that this one also have something to offer. For if he were on earth, he would not even be a priest, since there are priests who offer gifts according to the law, who serve <margin>a. That the form of it is an example and shadow of heavenly things.</margin> as an ^a^example and shadow of heavenly things, just as Moses was warned by an oracle when he <margin>Exod. 25, Acts 7.</margin> was about to complete the tabernacle. "See," he said, "that you make all things according to the pattern shown to you on the mountain." But now he has obtained a ministry as much more excellent as he is the mediator <note>original: *sequester*; a legal term for a mediator or trustee</note> of a better testament, which is established upon better promises. For if that first one had been faultless, no <margin>Jer. 31.</margin> place would have been sought for a second. But accusing them, he says: "The time is coming (says the Lord) when I will make a new testament with the house of Israel and the house of Judah; not like the testament I made with their ancestors on the day I took them by the hand to lead them out of Egypt. For they did not remain in my testament, and I neglected them, <margin>Rev. 21.</margin> says the Lord. But this is the testament I will make with the house of Israel after that time, says the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds, and I will write them upon their hearts; and I will be their God, and they <margin>Jer. 31.</margin> shall be my people. And no longer shall they teach one another or their neighbors to know the Lord, for all shall know me, from the least of them to the greatest. For I will grant pardon for their vices, and I will remember their sins and crimes no more." By saying "new," he has made the first one old. Now, what is made old and grows aged is near to vanishing away.

### CHAPTER IX.

<margin>a. Hesychius and the older version. Exodus 25.</margin>
Now the former covenant <note>original: *testamentum*; refers both to a legal will and a solemn agreement between God and humanity</note> had regulations for ceremonies and a worldly sanctuary. For the first tent was prepared, in which were the lampstand, the table, and the setting of the loaves, which is called the Holy Place.
<margin>Exodus 26.</margin>
Behind the second curtain was the tent which is called the Most Holy Sanctuary, having a golden altar for incense and the ark of the covenant, covered on all sides with gold, in which was the golden jar containing manna, and Aaron’s rod that had budded, and the tablets of the covenant. Above it were the glorious Cherubim, overshadowing the mercy seat; of these things we cannot now speak in detail. When these things were thus arranged, the priests always enter the first tent to perform the ceremonies: but into the second, only the high priest <note>original: *pontifex*; the author uses the Roman term for a high priest to bridge the gap between Jewish and Classical traditions</note> enters once a year, not without blood, which he offers <note>original: *libat*; literally "pours out as a drink offering," but here meaning to offer a sacrifice</note> for himself and for the sins of the people committed in ignorance. By this the Holy Spirit declares that the way into the sanctuary was not yet made open while the former tent was still standing: which was a symbol for the present time, in which gifts and sacrifices were offered that could not make the worshiper perfect as far as the conscience is concerned, being based only on foods and drinks, and various washings, and human regulations, until the time of correction. But Christ has arrived, the high priest of future good things, who through a greater and more perfect tent, not made with hands (that is, not of this structure), nor through the blood of goats and calves, but through his own blood, entered once into the sanctuary, having obtained eternal deliverance.
<margin>Romans 5. 1 Peter 1. 1 John 1. Revelation 1.</margin>
For if the blood of bulls and goats, and the ashes of a heifer, sprinkling the defiled, purifies the body, how much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal spirit offered himself most innocent to God, purge our conscience from dead works, so that we may worship the living God? And for this reason he is the mediator <note>original: *sequester*; a legal term for a neutral third party or trustee</note> of the new covenant, so that by means of death for the expiation of the offenses under the first covenant, those who are called might receive the promised eternal inheritance. For where there is a testament, the death of the testator must follow.
<margin>Galatians 3.</margin>
For a testament is valid after death, since it has no force while the testator is living. Thus, not even the first was sanctioned without blood. For when every commandment of the law had been spoken by Moses to all the people, he took the blood of calves and goats, with water and scarlet wool and hyssop, and sprinkled the book itself and all the
<margin>Exodus 24.</margin>
people, saying: *This is the blood of the covenant, which God has commanded to you.* Likewise he sprinkled with blood the tent and all the vessels of the ceremonies. And almost everything is purged with blood according to the law, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness.
<margin>b. Remission, or forgiveness is given. Hebrews 9.</margin>
It is necessary therefore that the copies <note>original: *exempla*; patterns or models</note> <sup>b</sup> of heavenly things be purged with these, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these. For Jesus did not enter into a sanctuary made with hands, which would be a copy of the true sanctuary: but into heaven itself, so that he now appears before the face of God for us. Nor that he should offer himself often, as the high priest enters the sanct-

<column-break/>

-uary every year with the blood of another: otherwise he would have had to suffer punishment often since the foundation of the world. Now once at the end of the ages, he has appeared to blot out sin by his sacrifice. And just as it is appointed for men to die once, and after that to undergo judgment, so Christ was offered once to take away the sins of many; he will be seen a second time without sin by those who wait for him for salvation.
<margin>Romans 5. 1 Peter 3.</margin>

### CHAPTER X.

For the law, having a shadow of the good things to come, and not the very representation of the things, can never make those who approach perfect by the same annual sacrifices which are offered continually. Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered, because the worshipers, once cleansed, would no longer be conscious of any sin? But in those sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year. For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins. Therefore, entering into the world, he says: *Sacrifice and offering do not please you, but you have perfected a body for me: you are not delighted with burnt offerings and sin offerings: Then I said: Behold, I am here: in the head of the book it is written of me that I should perform, O God, your will.* When he had said above: *Sacrifice, and offering, and burnt offerings, and sin offerings did not please him, nor were they accepted, which are done according to the law*, then he says: *Behold, I am here, to perform, O God, your will.* He takes away the first, to establish the second: in which will we have been cleansed once through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ. And while every priest stands daily performing ceremonies and often making the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins, he, having performed one sacrifice for sins forever, sat down at the right hand of God, waiting from then on until his enemies are made a footstool for his feet. For by one offering he has perfected forever those to be cleansed, that which the Holy Spirit also witnesses to us, who had predicted: *This is the covenant, which I will make with them after that time, says the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds, and I will write them on their hearts, and I will no longer remember their sins and crimes.* But where there is forgiveness of sins, there remains no more offering for sin. Therefore, brothers, since we have free access to the sanctuary through the blood of Jesus, which way he has cleansed for us, new and living, through the veil, that is, through his body: and since we have a high priest set over the house of God, let us approach with a true heart and full faith, with hearts washed from an evil conscience, and bodies washed with pure water, <sup>a</sup> let us hold the profession of our hope unmoving (for he who promised is faithful) and let us see that we provoke one another to charity and good deeds, nor let us desert our assembly, as some are accustomed to do: but let us encourage, and all the more so, because you see the day approaching. For if after we have received the knowledge of the truth, we sin deliberately, there no longer remains any sacrifice for sins, but a certain fearful expectation of judgment, and a fury of fire about to consume the adversaries. If anyone has committed an offense against the Mosaic law, he dies without any mercy, on the testimony of two or three

## CHAPTER XI.

<margin>Genesis 1, 4.</margin> Now faith is the foundation <note>original: *subiectio*; here meaning the underlying substance or reality</note> of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen; and by it the men of old were approved. By faith we understand that the world was fashioned by the command of God, so that from things which did not exist, those things which are seen were made. By faith Abel offered to God a more excellent sacrifice than Cain, through which it was witnessed that he was just, with God giving testimony <gloss>a</gloss> to his gifts: and through faith, though dead, he still speaks. <margin>Genesis 5. Wisdom 4. Ecclesiasticus 44.</margin> By faith Enoch was translated so that he did not experience death, and because God translated him, he was found nowhere. <margin>a. Since his blood [cries out] to God and is returned to it, Genesis 4. See below, chapter 12.</margin> For before his translation, it was witnessed that he pleased God, and without faith it is impossible to please him. For he who approaches God must believe that God exists and that he rewards those who seek him. By faith Noah, being <margin>Genesis 6. Ecclesiasticus 44. Genesis 12, 13.</margin> warned by a divine oracle about things not yet seen, feared God and built an ark for the salvation of his family, through which he condemned the world and obtained the righteousness that is based on faith. By faith Abraham, when called, obeyed by setting out for a place which he was to receive as an inheritance; and he set out not knowing where he was going. By faith he migrated to the promised land as if it were a foreign country, and lived in tents with Isaac and Jacob, co-heirs with him of the same promise. For he was waiting for a city that has foundations, whose architect and builder is God. By faith Sarah herself also received the power <margin>Genesis 21.</margin> to conceive seed, and she gave birth past the proper age, since she considered him faithful who had promised. Therefore, from one man, and he as good as dead, there were born as many as the stars of heaven in number, or the sand of the seashore, which is innumerable. All these died endowed with faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them from afar, they believed and embraced

<column-break/>

And all these, though approved through faith, did not obtain the promise, for God provided something better for us, so that they should not be made perfect without us.

## CHAPTER XII.

<margin>Ephesians 4. For consider him who endured such great insults from wicked men against himself, so that you do not grow weary and lose heart.

### CHAPTER XV.

<margin>The sea of glass.</margin>
**I** saw another great and marvelous sign in heaven: seven divine spirits <note>original: "genios," a classical term used here by the translator to mean angels</note> who held the seven final plagues, in which the severity <note>original: "seuitia," meaning the harshness or wrath</note> of God is reached its end. And I saw what looked like a sea of glass mixed with fire, and those who had been victorious over the beast, its image, its mark, and the number of its name, standing upon the sea of glass, holding divine lyres <note>original: "citharas"</note> and singing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, as follows:
<margin>Hebrews 10</margin>
Great and marvelous are your works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are your decrees, King of the Saints. Who would not fear you, Lord, and celebrate your name? For you alone are holy; for all nations shall come to worship before you, because your righteous laws have been revealed.
<margin>The seven spirits of the seven final plagues.</margin>
Afterward I saw the shrine <note>original: "fanum," a classical term for a temple or sanctuary</note> of the tabernacle of testimony open in heaven, and from the shrine came the seven spirits holding the seven final plagues, dressed in pure and shining linen, and their chests bound with golden sashes. To these seven spirits, one of the four living creatures gave seven golden bowls <note>original: "phialas"</note> full of the severity of the living God throughout the succession of all ages. And the shrine was filled with so much smoke from the splendor and power of God that no one could enter the shrine until the seven plagues of the seven spirits were completed.

### CHAPTER XVI.

### CHAPTER XVII.

### CHAPTER XVIII.

<margin>The punishment of Babylon</margin> **A**fterward I saw another spirit <note>original: "genium," a classical term for a guardian spirit, used here by the translator to mean an angel</note> descending from heaven, endowed with great power, and the earth was illuminated by his splendor. And I heard another voice from heaven saying: Depart from her, my people, so that you are not participants in her sins, and that you do not suffer from her disasters; for her sins have reached even to heaven, and God remembers her crimes. Treat her as she herself has treated you, and repay her double for her deeds; in the same cup in which she mixed, mix a double portion for her. To the same degree that she glorified herself and lived in luxury, give her that much torment and grief, for she thinks thus in her heart: I sit as a queen, and I <margin>Isaiah 47</margin> shall not be a widow, nor shall I be touched by grief. Therefore, her disasters shall come in a single day—death, grief, and famine—and she shall be burned with fire, for the Lord God, who will take vengeance upon her, is mighty. The kings of the earth, who committed lewdness and lived in luxury with her, shall weep for her and lament when they see the smoke of her burning, standing <margin>Jeremiah 51</margin> far off for fear of her torment, saying: Alas, alas, that great city Babylon, that mighty city, whose punishment has come in a single hour! # THE REVELATION.

...as many angels <note>original: "genios"</note>, and names inscribed upon them, namely those of the twelve tribes of the Israelites. From the east there were three gates; from the north three; from the south three; and from the west three. The wall of the city had twelve foundations, and upon them the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb. Now he who was speaking with me held a golden reed to measure the city, its gates, and its wall; the layout of this city was such that it was square, as long as it was wide. He measured this city with the reed to twelve thousand stadia <note>A stadium was a Greek unit of distance; 12,000 stadia is roughly 1,400 miles</note>, equal in length, width, and height. He measured its wall at one hundred and forty-four cubits, by the measure of a man—that is, of an angel <note>original: "genij"</note>. The structure of its wall was of jasper; the city itself was of pure gold, like clear glass. The foundations of the city wall were adorned with every kind of gemstone. The first foundation was jasper, the second sapphire, the third chalcedony, the fourth emerald, the fifth sardonyx, the sixth sardius, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh hyacinth, and the twelfth amethyst. The twelve gates were twelve pearls <note>original: "uniones," a term for large, high-quality pearls</note>, each individual gate consisting of a single pearl. The open square of the city was pure gold, transparent as glass. I saw no temple <note>original: "fanum"</note> within it, for the Lord God Almighty <margin>Isaiah 60</margin> is its temple, along with the Lamb. The city has no need for the sun or the moon to shine upon it, for the glory of God illuminates it, and the Lamb is its lamp. And the nations of those who are saved shall walk in the light of that city, and the kings of the earth shall bring their glory and honor into it. Its gates shall never be closed by day (for indeed, there shall be no night there), and the glory and honor of the nations shall be brought into it. Nothing profane shall enter it, nor anyone who commits an atrocity or a lie, but only those written in the Lamb's book of life.

# ANNOTATIONS.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'H' featuring a landscape with a building on the left and a figure in the foreground.</image-desc>
HERE it is my purpose to give an account of my translation (if it should seem necessary in any place) and then to briefly open up the meaning of certain more difficult passages.
<margin>10</margin>
Let the readers remember, however, that I am not accustomed to repeat the same things I have noted once if they should occur again; nor do I note things that are common knowledge and admitted by everyone, or things that can easily be understood by a person of moderate learning. I do not refute anyone’s error (unless the matter compels it), nor am I so bound to the words that I do not often put pronouns in place of names, and have more regard for the sense than for the words, just as the custom of
<margin>20</margin>
the <term>Latin language<note>original: "Romanae sermonis"</note></term> requires. Yet, I do this in such a way that I never knowingly deviate from the author's meaning. Above all, let them remember that I often change <term>direct speech<note>original: "directam orationem"</note></term> into <term>indirect speech<note>original: "obliquam"</note></term>. I call "direct" that which the Greeks call **mimetic** <note>original: "μιμητικὴν" - imitative or quoted speech</note>, and "indirect" that which they call **diegetic** <note>original: "διηγητικὴν" - narrative or reported speech</note>. If it were direct, this example from Deuteronomy 18 would be used: "Just as you requested from the Lord your God in Horeb, saying: Let us no longer hear the voice of the Lord our God, or see that great fire anymore, lest we
<margin>30</margin>
die." This is how it reads word-for-word. But if you look at the words, the Israelites had not spoken this way in Exodus 20, but rather: "Speak you with us, and we will hear; let not God speak with us, lest we die." You see here the same meaning, but different words. Therefore, it is permitted to turn the following sentence into the indirect style according to Latin custom: "Just as you requested, when you asked that you might no longer hear the voice of the Lord your God, or see that massive fire, lest you
<margin>40</margin>
die." Likewise, in Exodus 32, it reads word-for-word: "Remember your servants, Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, to whom you swore by yourself and promised thus: I will make your offspring equal to the stars of heaven, etc." But God never spoke to those three, or two of them, at the same time so as to use the plural number. Therefore, that speech must necessarily be changed into the indirect form. This same thing happens in many other places in both <term>Testaments<note>original: "foedere" - literally "covenant," referring to the Old and New Testaments</note></term>. This causes many passages to appear obscure, which fair readers might tolerate if they follow our custom. Just as those who wrote in Hebrew spoke in the Hebrew manner,
<margin>50</margin>
so we also, writing in Latin, serve Latin ears. Regarding proper names, in these I have generally followed the <term>old translator<note>Referring to the Vulgate/St. Jerome</note></term>, who softened them somewhat to fit Latin custom. I do this partly because they are now so commonly used that changing them would cause obscurity and offense, and partly because it is fitting for one writing in Latin to imitate the Latins.
<margin>60</margin>
If it was permitted for them to make *Hercules* from *Heracles*, and *Aesculapius* from *Asclepius*, surely it will be permitted for us to make

<column-break/>

*Sephora* from *Zeppora*, and *Zabulon* from *Zebulun*. And in this matter, as in many others, the old translator seems to me to have been not a bad translator. For why should one say *Sedom* rather than *Sodom*? *Amora* rather than *Gomorra*? *Jehudaean* rather than *Judean*? For if someone is ignorant of the Hebrew language, they do not know what a *Jehudaean* is any more than a *Judean*; if they do know Hebrew, they will have learned these things in Hebrew books, not Latin ones. Thus, this foreignness of Hebrew words, besides being harsh and unusual to Latin ears, is also useless. Add to this that those who "Hebraize" in this way do not even imitate the Hebrews. For the Hebrews turn the word for *Romans* into *Romijim*—that is, they adapt foreign words to their own language. It was fitting for those imitating us, in turn, to make *Palestinians* from *Philistim*, and when speaking Latin, to have regard for Latin ears. I do not say these things to find fault with them, but so that, if we endure them, they in turn might endure us. But I do not follow the old translator where the names in his work degenerate too much from the Hebrew (especially if they are the kind that are rarely used), or if they are phrased too harshly; in those cases, I return them to the original or make them a little softer, and sometimes I imitate Josephus, who made them Greek when writing in Greek. Furthermore, since the old translator does not <term>decline<note>i.e., change the endings of nouns to show their grammatical role (case)</note></term> many names, I decline almost all of them: either because the Latin language requires it, or because it avoids many ambiguous statements. Ambiguity occurs in the Latin language (which lacks articles to show the case) when it is often unknown to which verb a noun should refer if all the cases end in the same syllable. Otherwise, as far as the matter is concerned, it does not matter whether you decline these names or not, since we see that not only are some declined by the Apostles, though all are indeclinable to the Hebrews, but even in Matthew the name of *Mary* is declined, while in Luke it is not.

### ON GENESIS.
#### FROM CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>A decorative initial 'E' depicting a seated figure, possibly a scholar or a representation of God the Father, in an architectural setting.</image-desc>
**The first day came forth from evening and morning.**) That is, the first day existed, consisting of night and day. For here a <term>part is put for the whole<note>A rhetorical device called synecdoche</note></term>, as in Daniel "evening-morning" is used for days, and among the poets "four autumns" are said for "four years." The day begins from the evening because darkness existed before light was created. The Hebrews begin it thus, which Julius Caesar records the Gauls used to do in the past, and Cornelius Tacitus says the same of the Germans.

**An expanse among the waters.**) <note>original Hebrew: רקיע (*Raqia*)</note> Named from "spreading out": it signifies a liquid-like expanse, which differs as much from the air or heaven as light does from day, water from the sea, or dry land from the earth. For since this divides the upper water from the lower, and it is established that the lower water is the sea, it is necessary that this expanse...

<meta>catchword: ...is</meta>

<meta>Continuity note: The catchword "tione" from the previous page likely completed the word "perfectione" or a similar noun ending in -tion, following the translator's discussion on the nature of language and interpretation.</meta>

### ON GENESIS

<column-break/>

...while it may be air, which is also called **liquid** <note>original: "liquidum"</note> by Latin poets following the Hebrew custom, because that element is joined to the sea. For whatever either separates or joins two extremes must touch both. Moreover, the **upper water** is rain; although it is not above the entire "liquid" (that is, above the whole heaven), it is enough to be called "above the liquid" if it has liquid below it. Indeed, it is not likely that Moses, while speaking specifically here about waters, would make no mention of rain, which is a matter of no small importance, and which the **Sibyl** <note>The Sibylline Oracles, a collection of Greek oracular utterances attributed to the Sibyls, often cited by early Christian scholars to bridge pagan and biblical thought.</note> mentioned when speaking of the creation of the world. Likewise, **Josephus** <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Jewish-Roman historian.</note>, interpreting Moses, says that the heaven was made to be "rainy." To say "rain above the liquid" is nothing other than what the Latins call **celestial water**. 

Therefore **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist and author of "Natural History."</note>, at the beginning of Book II, speaks of waters thus: *They climb into the heights and claim the sky for themselves as well; by the cover of clouds, they stifle the vital spirit. This cause draws out lightning as the world itself stands in discord. What can be more marvelous than waters standing in the sky?* These are Pliny’s words. In the same way, in **2 Samuel 21** <note>original: "2. Reg. 21" - in older Latin Bibles, the books of Samuel were often called 1 and 2 Kings.</note>, water is said to "distill from heaven," which refers to rain.

It should also be noted that what is called **air**, **ether**, and **moisture** <note>original: "ὑγρόν" - hygron</note> in Greek is encompassed by the Hebrews under the single name of **liquid** or **heaven**. The Latins also encompass all this under the name of **heaven**. But if anyone stubbornly denies that what Moses speaks of here is what is called "air" in Greek and "heaven" in Latin, let him show what it is that divides the sea from the upper water, and what the Hebrews call the air. There is nothing else that divides the waters. Today, the Hebrews call air by a Greek name; but what did they call it before the Greek language existed—that is, before the Tower of Babel, when only Hebrew was spoken? Did they have no name for such a common thing? Or if they had one, why does it not appear in the Sacred Scriptures? But it certainly does exist; for **firmament** <note>original: "רקיע" - rakia</note> and **water** <note>original: "מים" - mayim</note> (that is, liquid, or air, or heaven) are just as much the same as "dry land" and "earth." Nor is the name for **heaven** <note>original: "שמים" - shamayim</note> derived from water for any other reason than that it is the seat of the rains. Thus Moses writes that during the flood, the "floodgates of heaven" were opened. Hence we have the **birds of heaven**, meaning those of the air. 

Moses shows that heaven was created on the second day when he says God commanded the **liquid** to exist on the second day. The same is taught in **4 Ezra 6** in these words: *On the second day you created the breeze of the air.* As for Moses placing heaven before earth in his opening statement, he does so for the sake of **dignity**, not because of the order of creation. For in Chapter 2, he says: *When the Lord made the earth and the heaven,* where he places the earth before the heaven. From this it is clear that the order of words is not always the same as the order of time. Indeed, it is fitting that the earth, acting as a foundation, was made first. Nor is it necessary that heaven, because it is more excellent, should therefore be created first; for even the beasts and plants, which are lowlier than man, were nonetheless created before man.

**Let the dry land appear.**) What the Latins express through the **neuter** gender, the Hebrews (who have no neuter gender) sometimes express through the **feminine**. For this reason, the ancient translator <note>Jerome, the author of the Vulgate.</note> translated it as **the dry** <note>original: "arida" (feminine)</note> and the Greek as **the dry** <note>original: "ξηρά" - xēra (feminine)</note>.

**Let the earth bring forth plants.**) In Hebrew it is **greenery/sprouts** <note>original: "דשא" - deshe</note>

<column-break/>

which, if one may coin a word, means **to plant-ify** <note>original: "stirpāre"</note>, that is, to create plants. It is as if you said, "Let the earth **plant plants**," just as **Aristotle** said in Book 3 of *On the Generation of Animals*: *They lay a perfect egg* <note>original: "ωοτοκοῦσι τέλειον ᾠόν"</note>, or as we say "to live a life." Such are these French terms: **to give birth** <note>original: "enfanter"</note>, **to calve** <note>original: "ueler"</note>, **to farrow** <note>original: "cochonner"</note>; which in Latin would be rendered as "to bring forth a child, a calf, a piglet." There are many such examples in Sacred Scripture, like "to swear an oath" or "to sin a sin," which should be spoken in the Latin manner. Having noted this once, let it suffice. 

There are three kinds of plants: trees, shrubs, and herbs; but Moses includes shrubs under trees. He calls them **fruit-bearing trees** and **grain-bearing herbs**, not because they are all fruitful (though they all have seeds), but because it is their nature to bear fruit. Similarly, poets call fish **scale-bearers**, because scales are characteristic of fish, even though not all of them have them. Furthermore, in these words, a **specific power** is given to the plants at the very moment they are created—a power that was given separately to the animals.

**Swimming living things.**) The Greeks translated this as **creeping things** <note>original: "ἑρπετά" - herpeta</note> and the Latins as **reptiles**. But they use the same word for those things that arose from the earth on the fourth day, making it seem as if reptiles arose from both water and earth, which is absurd. The Hebrew word is **swarming/creeping thing** <note>original: "שרץ" - sheretz</note>, which in Leviticus 11 is used for fish, many-legged winged insects, and serpents. We do not have a word with such a broad meaning. Yet these terms, like the nature of the things themselves, are closely related in the words used by the Latins. For birds are said poetically "to swim through the air," and **Daedalus**, *by the rowing of his wings, sailed forth on an unaccustomed path to the cold North.* Therefore, fish and birds (both two-legged and many-legged) arose from the water; but from the earth came cattle, land beasts, and serpents. These serpents are signified by the word **creeping thing** <note>original: "רמש" - remes</note>, which elsewhere means "to be moved," and in Psalm 104, "to swim."

**Let us make man.**) He seems to be speaking with his son, about which the **Sibyl** says in Book 8:
> For having formerly used his counsel first,
> The Almighty spoke thus: Let us, from our own seed,
> Both make mortals in the image of the Son.
> Now I will take care with my hands; you, then,
> Shape our likeness with words, so we may build a common work.

**Let him have dominion.**) In Hebrew, this is in the plural: **Let them have dominion**. But since he is speaking of the whole race, it makes no difference which number you use, as long as you account for the custom of speaking.

**For if she should eat of it.**) **On the day** <note>original: "ביומ" - biyom</note> is put for **on the day** <note>original: "ביום" - hayom</note>, as often elsewhere, as in Ruth 4 and 2 Kings 2.

**He had created and made.**) Literally, **he had created by making** (for the letter *lamed* often forms a gerund, as in 2 Kings 19, **by loving** <note>original: "לאהבה" - le'ahavah</note>), where two words of the same meaning are placed together. It is like in 1 Corinthians 12, **the holy ones will announce** <note>original: "ἁγίοις ἀπαγγελῶσι"</note>, instead of **to the holy ones and those announcing**. It is similar to that line of **Cicero**: *The fallen weapons dropped from the hands of the most audacious citizens,* which means, "they fell and dropped."

-># ANNOTATIONS.<-

...[perfec]tion <note>original: "tione"</note> might be interrupted, He briefly touched upon the creation of man on the sixth day, which He then approaches again with a grander beginning after the mention of the Sabbath. For it is not that what is recounted after the Sabbath actually happened after the Sabbath, since all things were made within the six days.

<margin>Ioua God.)</margin>
Ioua <note>Jehovah</note> is the most holy name of God, derived from the verb that means "to be" (as He Himself declares to Moses in the bush). It is a name of such great majesty that the Jews, whenever it occurs to be read, read *Adonai*, which means **Lord**. From this, I believe it happened that the **Septuagint** <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> interpreted it as <term>kyrios</term> <note>original: "κύριος", Greek for "Lord"</note>, whose interpretation the Apostles followed. For they were teaching religion, not language. We, however—who (because life is short) strive to join language with religion—do not think it is forbidden for us to follow those who are eloquent in speech while agreeing with them in life, and to use the proper Hebrew name of God (so that nothing of His majesty is lost). Since this is customary with other proper names in any language, it seems unjust to deny this to us in this case. As for those who deny that this sacred name is permitted to be read, let us leave that to Jewish superstition. For if it was permitted for Moses to write it, it is permitted for us to read it. Surely he did not write things that were not to be read. Moreover, those who say that these vowel points by which it is marked are not its own are easily refuted by the words derived from it: **Jehoshaphat**, **Jehoram**, **Hallelujah**, **Isaiah**, etc. Though this matters little. For the power of the word does not reside in the Latin speech, however you may pronounce it, nor in the vowel points of the Hebrew speech, but in the etymology, which remains the same however you pronounce it. But if anyone shrinks from this name, they may, as far as I am concerned, imitate the Jews, and where they find "Ioua," let them read "Lord," just as they read *Adonai*. This will at least provide a convenience in our translation: the reader will have no doubt where "Ioua" or "Adonai" is written in the Hebrew, which would happen if we had translated "Ioua" as "Lord."

<margin>But a vapor rose from the earth.)</margin>
Namely on the third day, when God commanded the plants to spring forth.

<margin>And He commanded that they should eat.)</margin>
He addresses both of them. For in Chapter 1, where the same matter is briefly touched upon, God is said to have permitted the eating of plants to **them**, not just to **him**; and in Chapter 3, Eve speaks in the plural, saying: "God forbade **us** to taste." In the same way, Lot is forbidden from looking back, even though it is clear from the punishment that this applied to his wife as well. The order of the narrative is this: God formed Adam; then, having brought the beasts to him, He formed Eve; afterwards He introduced them into the orchard, where He permitted the eating of the fruits. All of these things were done on the sixth day.

<margin>Member of members, and body of body.)</margin>
<note>original Hebrew: "עצם" (etsem - bone) and "בשר" (basar - flesh)</note> These do not always signify "bone" and "flesh," but often signify "member" <note>limb</note> and "body," as in **Psalm 6** and **Psalm 38**, where the prophet says he is sick in his "bones" and soul. For bones, which have no nerves, do not feel and are not "sick." And in **Leviticus**, God often commands a man to wash his "flesh," that is, his body. What of that which they translated: *My bones*

<column-break/>

*have withered like firewood?* <note>Psalm 102:3</note> For members are said to wither from disease, not bones. Likewise: *And the humbled bones shall rejoice:* <note>Psalm 51:8</note> that is, I shall rejoice in my members and body. Now, a woman is rightly called a "member" of a man, and a "body" taken from a man, who is both a complete body and has the man as her head. Thus **Paul** in **1 Corinthians 6** interprets it so: for he calls them <term>mele</term> <note>original: "μέλη", Greek for "members" or "limbs"</note>, which are here declared by the word <note>Hebrew: "עצם" (etsem)</note>. And he calls the same thing <term>soma</term> <note>original: "σῶμα", body</note> and <term>sarxa</term> <note>original: "σάρκα", flesh</note>. *He who is joined to a prostitute is one body; for it says, the two shall be in one flesh.* <note>original Greek: "ὁ κολλώμενος τῇ πόρνῃ ἓν σῶμά ἐστιν, ἔσονται γάρ, φησιν, οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν."</note> Which sounds like this word-for-word: "He who is coupled with a harlot is one body. For they shall be, he says, two in one flesh."

<margin>She shall be called woman.)</margin>
The reasoning for the Hebrew word is as if you were to say **virago** from **vir** <note>man</note>. And a little later, what we translate as "wife" is the same word. But because in Latin "woman" <note>mulier</note> is not usually said for "wife" <note>uxor</note>, while the Hebrew word is common to both, we had to use another.

<margin>To the west wind.)</margin>
In the Hebrew it is <note>Hebrew: "לרוח היום", 'to the spirit/wind of the day'</note>. The Septuagint seem to have read <note>Hebrew: "לים", 'to the sea'</note>, that is, the western wind, which is the **Zephyrus**; for they translated it <term>to deilinon</term> <note>original: "τὸ δειλινὸν", the evening</note>, that is, in the evening; as if it were "evening-like" instead of "western."

<margin>By hardships.)</margin>
<note>Hebrew: "עצב" (etsev)</note> is the pain of childbirth, which in Greek is called <term>odin</term> <note>original: "ὠδίν", birth-pangs</note>; we do not have a specific name for it.

<margin>Mother of all living.)</margin>
By the Hebrews, men are sometimes named from "life" <note>living ones</note>; the Latins call them **mortals**. But here, because of the reasoning of the name, it was not permitted to say "mortals."

<margin>There is a danger lest.)</margin>
Word-for-word: "And now lest," which is a **reticence** <note>a figure of speech where a sentence is left unfinished</note>. The French speak this way sometimes. Such is that in **Matthew 25**: <note>original Greek: "μήποτε οὐκ ἀρκέσῃ ἡμῖν καὶ ὑμῖν", 'lest there not be enough for us and you'</note>. And that in **Romans 9**: <note>original Greek: "μήπως οὐδέ σου φείσηται", 'lest He also not spare you'</note>. And **Aristotle** in the **Nicomachean Ethics**: <note>original Greek references regarding various cautionary 'lest' statements</note>.

---
### FROM CHAPTER IV.
---

<margin>Surely if you do well, you will be accepted.)</margin>
In Hebrew: "If you do well, an uplifting"; namely, there will be one, that is, an obtaining of favor. Which Hebrew expression the French express when they say *to be exalted* <note>original: "exaltari"</note> for **litare** <note>to offer an acceptable sacrifice</note>, that is, to obtain by sacrificing or supplicating, *to be heard* <note>original French: "estre exaucé"</note>. Moreover, this is the meaning: "Surely (for this is what <note>Hebrew: "הלא"</note> means, and it is not always a question) if you do well, like your brother, I will look upon you just as I do him. If not, guilt—that is, the punishment for sin, and even sin itself—lies in wait for you, crouching like one at the doors; which guilt will depend on your command. For by doing right you will overcome it, like your brother who is not harmed by it; but by doing poorly, you will be overcome. Therefore, if you wish to be a companion of brotherly happiness, be a companion of virtue as well. For as he who sins is a slave to sin, so he who lives rightly is a master of sin." This kind of speech is in **Numbers 32**: "Unless you do so, know that you sin against Ioua, and it will be that your sin finds you out," that is, that you will pay the penalty. Moreover, that <note>Hebrew: "חטאת" (sin)</note> is of the masculine gender is clear from the adjective <note>Hebrew: "רבץ" (crouching)</note>, lest anyone perhaps deny that it can agree with the relative pronoun.

<margin>Who first lived in tents.)</margin>
In the beginning, shepherds lived in tents and frequently changed their location, because of which they were called **Scenites** <note>tent-dwellers</note>, as is found in **Pliny**,
