-># ON GENESIS<-

Pliny. Moses record here the author of this matter.

**If I have killed a man with my wounds.** In recording the descendants of Cain, Moses notes their notable deeds or sayings in passing. Therefore, he recounts this famous lesson of Lamech. Murder is considered so wicked by God that He decreed if anyone killed even Cain—a man who was a fratricide—that person would be worthy of such punishment that if he could die seven times, he should be killed seven times. What, then, is just to happen in the killing of a man who was not a murderer? "If I should kill a man with blows, if I should kill any mortal with wounds" (the sentence is doubled, as is common in proverbs); that is, if anyone should kill any man (for he uses the first person "I" to represent anyone, just as Paul does when he says: "If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels," etc.). Since killing Cain, a wicked man, is so detestable that a sevenfold punishment is enacted, certainly—for so I interpret the letter <term>waw</term> <note>The Hebrew letter ו, often used as a conjunction or to introduce a conclusion.</note>, which often serves a concluding role, as in Ezekiel 33—in the case of Lamech (that is, in the case of one who kills a man who is not a murderer), the penalty would be much heavier. 

However, as for my translation "If I should kill," though it is the past tense in Hebrew, it must be known that the Hebrews use the past tense for the subjunctive, as occurs elsewhere in Job 3, Psalm 44, Judges 8, and Jeremiah 17. Likewise, what I translate as "mortal," is in Hebrew <term>yeled</term> <note>original: "ילד"</note>, named from the act of being born. Although this almost always signifies a "youth," here no account is taken of age, but rather of the condition of being born. In the same way, in chapter 16, all the "children" <note>original: "ילדי", yeled</note> of Abraham's house are said to be circumcised—meaning all those born in the house, of whatever age they might be. Also in Numbers 13, "the children of Anak" <note>original: "ילדי הענק"</note> means the Anakites, being the same as "sons of Anak" as they are called shortly after. And in Isaiah 2, "children of foreigners" <note>original: "ילדי נכרים"</note> means "strangers." Nor is it absurd to say "all those born" instead of "all mortals," especially here where the same thought is repeated with different words; since the meaningful verb was occupied in the first part, it was sufficient in the latter part to place something related—a common occurrence in the Psalms. In the fourth book of Ezra, chapter 4, we likewise read: "Who can make one about to be born so that you may question me about these things?"—that is: "who among mortals?" which seems to be translated from the Hebrew.

**The most powerful of men.** In Hebrew it is "Sons of the Gods." But the Hebrew language often uses nouns in place of adjectives, which they lack: thus "Sons of the Gods" stands for "divine ones," that is, "excellent ones." In Psalm 82, judges and governors of others are called "gods" or "divine ones." And in Job 41, "the powerful." Just as the French <note>original: "Galli"</note> name things from "God" that excel in their kind, such as "fire of God" for a bright fire, or a "man of God" for a divine and religious man—just as the Latins speak of the "divine Plato." Furthermore, the word "Son" is often the same as "man": as in "Sons of Israel," meaning the men or males of Israel; "Sons of man," meaning men. The French say "child of Lyon" <note>original: "enfant de Lyon"</note> for a citizen of Lyon; "child of the city" <note>original: "enfant de ville"</note> for a citizen; "lost child" <note>original: "enfant perdu"</note> for a reckless or desperate man. The Greeks also say "sons of the Achaeans" <note>original: "υἷες ἀχαιῶν"</note> for Achaeans, and "children of doctors" <note>original: "ἰατρῶν παῖδες"</note> for physicians.

**He denied He would remain with men.** God judged it unworthy for Himself, who was Spirit and God, to quarrel for so long with men, who were corporeal and mortal. Therefore He decided to shorten the life of men. God is said to contend and fight 

<column-break/>

with men when He is provoked by their crimes (against which nothing is more repugnant to divinity). Since they were men who turned their very long lives, their immense strength, and their great numbers toward every kind of disgrace, becoming worse by the day, God decided to meet this evil by pre-defining a shorter span of living. Thus, by living for less time, they might commit fewer disgraces—just as certain cities are accustomed to hinder the tyranny of their magistrates by the brevity or weakness of their power. But first He tried the remedy of the Flood, with life immediately cut down by almost half: for those born after the Flood died before their five hundredth year, whereas before they had surpassed nine hundred. Then He caused the division of languages. Finally, when those were not enough, He did what He had threatened. Thus Abraham is an old man at sixty, while his great-great-great-grandfather Eber lived 464 years. You see here the brevity of life. Nor is it an obstacle that some even after Abraham exceeded one hundred and twenty years; for many in the time of Moses surpassed eighty years, even though he set that limit for human life in Psalm 90. For it is enough that this is the just and common way of living; years are not to be counted so strictly, any more than the grains of sand on the shore. Josephus interprets this passage in the same way. Add to this that the age of one man seems to secretly indicate the age of the whole human race, if calculated in Jubilee years.

**From terebinth wood.** They say that the terebinth <note>The turpentine tree, common in the Mediterranean.</note> is a tough material and faithful against decay; it is tall in Syria and notable near Damascus. It is the only wood that welcomes being oiled and becomes better with oil. Its berries are sulfurous, which pertains to the reasoning behind its name: for this tree is called <term>gopher</term>, while sulfur is called <term>gophrith</term>. Led by these things, I translated it as "terebinth." For the pine (which some think it is) has another name. Yet I do not affirm the terebinth with absolute certainty, but I have nothing more certain.

---

### FROM CHAPTER VI.

**The length shall extend to three hundred cubits, etc.** The proportion of the dimensions of this Ark is the same as that of a man lying on his back, as a certain Italian taught me. For that Ark was a kind of image of a dead man lying down, and yet one who would see life again and be resurrected. Regarding this matter, see 1 Peter 3 toward the end, and also what was written by Paul concerning baptism.

---

### FROM CHAPTER VII.

**Upon the mountains of Ararat.** The Sibyl <note>Prophetic priestesses in the ancient world; the author refers to the Sibylline Oracles.</note> records that this mountain is in Phrygia <note>An ancient kingdom in west-central Anatolia (modern Turkey).</note>, in these words:

> From here, when the fatal beam swam to and fro,
> Tossed by the hoarse murmur of the sea’s flowing,
> It reached a small patch of land, and at last rested.
> A certain mountain rises in the borders of dark Phrygia,
> Steep, seeking the heights, which they call by the name Ararat, etc.

**Of your blood indeed, etc.** The sense is: I will avenge the killing of a man against both men themselves and against beasts (which He does through the magistrate, when He orders even a beast to be killed if it has killed a man); however, the killing of beasts by men shall not be avenged in the same way.

### FROM CHAPTER IX.

**He sent out a raven, which having gone out, returned.** In the Greek and Latin versions, it is denied that it returned. From this was born the French proverb... <note>The text cuts off here at the word "prouer-" (proverb).</note>

<page-num>9</page-num>
...the proverb, **The crow's messenger**: which marks one who is sent but does not return. <note>original: "Corui nuncius." This likely refers to the raven sent by Noah from the ark, which did not return (Genesis 8:7).</note> Which reading is truer, I do not affirm. The Sibyl indeed denies that it returned.

### FROM CHAPTER XV.

**Do not pass me by.**) In the Hebrew it is, *Do not pass by your servant.* But the Latin language rejects this Hebrew idiom <term>Hebraism</term>; the French retains it: *your servant* <note>original: "uostre feruiteur"</note>. As for why he salutes one person, he does so because the Hebrew language is accustomed to saluting a master in the singular number, even if there are several present: which same thing Lot does later.

### FROM CHAPTER XVII.

**Would that you might only cause Ishmael to be propagated.**) Literally thus: *Would that Ishmael might live before you.* Moreover, to be "before" or "in the sight" of someone is said of that which is in one’s power, and is brought about—or can be brought about—by someone. Just as above in chapter 13, Abraham said to Lot: *The whole land is in your sight.* This means: it is exposed to you, it lies open to you, use it at your judgment. Likewise in 2 Chronicles 6: *There shall not fail you a man from my sight to sit upon the throne of the Israelites*: that is, I will bring it about that there shall never be a lack of your descendants, etc. That the verb for "living" is used in this place regarding the propagation of the lineage becomes clear from those things which God responds immediately to these words of Abraham.

### FROM CHAPTER XVIII.

**Who should hasten to make it.**) To *make* a calf is used instead of *to slaughter* or prepare it: a type of speaking that is frequent in the works of Cato and Varro. <note>The author is noting that "making" food often meant the entire process of preparation from the field to the table in classical Latin.</note>

**As the year turns.**) In the Hebrew it is, *At the time of life*, or *at the vital time*, which (as I judge) signifies "in the next year": since life, that is, an age, is numbered by years, not by days or months. For in the previous chapter he had also said, *At this time of the next year.*

**Then the Lord to Abraham.**) It should be noticed that here there are three spirits <term>genii</term>, or angels, two of whom are sent to Sodom, while one speaks with Abraham and is called the **Lord** <note>original: "Ioua"</note>, and does not go to Sodom: who this person might be, we shall say in Exodus chapter 3, God willing. Moreover, they are called **men** because they had taken on human figures. As for the fact that they eat and drink here, even though spirits do not have flesh and bones that might be fed by bodily nourishment, the nature of this will be clear from Tobit 12, where Raphael speaks thus: *For as long as I was with you, you saw me eat and drink, though in reality I neither ate nor drank.*

**I beg you, Lord, do not take it poorly.**) In the Hebrew it is, *Let not my lord take it poorly.* But I turned this into the vocative <note>Addressing the person directly</note> so that I might speak in the Latin manner: which same thing I often do.

### FROM CHAPTER XX.

**Will you even kill the innocent?**) In the Hebrew it is, *Will you even kill a righteous nation?* Virgil spoke in the same way: *Are you awake, nation of Aeneas, born of the gods?* <note>original: "Vigilás ne deūm gens Aenea?" from the Aeneid.</note> though he was speaking of one person. And in French thus, *Must you put the good people to death?* <note>original: "Dois tu faire mourir les gens de bien?"</note> even if one speaks of a single individual.

**She is my sister from my father.**) That is, a blood relative (for so the Hebrews speak) begotten by Terah my father: but not by my mother. For Abraham and Sarah’s fa-

<column-break/>

<page-num>10</page-num>
-ther, Haran, were not born of the same mother. Truly there is an ambiguity in the Hebrew speech which would not be in the Latin if she were called a "blood-relation" <term>consanguinea</term>.

**But when God drew me away from my father’s house.**) In the Hebrew it is, *When the gods drew me away.* Because the name of God, **Elohim** <note>original: "אלהים"</note>, is plural in number, the verb is also placed in the same number, as also below in chapter 35 and 1 Samuel 28, where the soothsayer <term>saga</term> speaks thus literally: *I see gods ascending from the earth.* That she speaks of one is clear from the narrative itself, because she is said to have seen Samuel, and Saul asks what his appearance is. The Latins also speak this way regarding nouns lacking a singular form, which must sometimes be translated into a foreign language in the singular number: such as if you translate **nuptials** <note>Latin: "nuptias"</note> as **wedding** <note>Greek: "γάμους", German: "hochzeyt"</note>.

**Flocks and herds.**) The term <term>tson</term> <note>original: "צאן"</note> is a general word for sheep and goats, like the Greek **sheep** <note>original: "μῆλον"</note> and the Latin **bleaters** <note>original: "balantes"</note>, named from their voice. But because it would be rather harsh, I prefer to say either "flocks," as Pliny does, or to put down both. Although in some places I will call them "bleaters" so that I may interpret more expressively.

**By which defense of your modesty.**) In the Hebrew it is: *This indeed shall be to you for a covering of the eyes among all who are with you, and among all, and for a cleansing, or defense.* Moreover, it is called a **covering of the eyes** as a defense of modesty: since modest women are accustomed to be veiled because of their shyness before men, as when Rebecca met Isaac: whereas immodest women fear nothing from the gaze of men. Therefore, this is the sense: I have given the money, not to you, lest I seem to have paid a price for your modesty: but to your husband, an honorable man, who certainly would not have accepted it if he thought you had been corrupted by me, lest he be thought to have sold his wife’s modesty. By this money I wish it to be testified that you are untouched by me: and this shall be a defense for you, if anyone should perchance disparage you. As for what I translate as **among strangers**: in the Hebrew it is, *among all.* But since he had already said *your own people*, it must be understood here as "strangers": a thing which often happens. Just as when Balaam says that the Israelite people shall not be reckoned *among the nations*: this is to be understood as "among the other nations." And when Christ commands that we do to *men* those things which we wish to be done to us: it is understood as "to other men."

### FROM CHAPTER XXIIII.

**Let her be the one whom you have destined for your Isaac.**) "My," "your," "his," "our," "your" cannot be said in Hebrew except by words that signify these things joined with substantive nouns, and specifically common nouns. Hence it happens that if they are to be joined with proper names, some common substantive noun is added which is capable of taking the pronoun. Therefore, if one must say "your Isaac" (as in this place), since that cannot be said in Hebrew, "servant" or "worshiper" is added; for one cannot say **your Isaac** <note>original: "יצחקך"</note>. The same happens in "People." For when one must say "your Israelites," since it cannot be said, one says *your people.* Nor yet do I deny that Isaac is God's servant, and the Israelites are a people and are rightly called so. But I am attempting to show this: that these things can sometimes be accommodated to Latin custom.

<page-num>11</page-num>

->ON GENESIS<-

For just as, if what was said in Latin were "your Isaac," it would be turned into Hebrew as "your servant Isaac," or "friend"; so too, what is said in this way in Hebrew, if it were turned into Latin, ought to be spoken according to the custom of the Latins. And just as he who rendered Latin into Hebrew in such a way would not be blamed, so I, while I translate both this and other <term>Hebraisms</term> <note>A Hebrew idiom or grammatical structure preserved in another language.</note>, think it fair that I be granted some indulgence. One may see these kinds of ways of speaking in our own languages as well. For what is said in Latin as "greet our Peter" is rendered in French as: *Recommend me to our friend Peter* <note>original: "Recommande moy à nostre amy Pierre"</note>. Likewise, "he visits his own" is: *He has gone to see his people* <note>original: "Il est alle uoir ses gens"</note>; and in German: *he has gone to his little folk* <note>original: "er ist zu sinem uœlcklin gangẽ"</note>. Nor is it dissimilar to what we say, "To drink the blood of the poor" <note>original: "Sanguinem pauperum bibere"</note>, which is *to drink the blood of poor people* <note>original: "boire le sang des pauvres gens"</note>. For it would not be correctly said in Latin to "drink the blood of poor nations."

**If you have it in mind to deserve well of my lord by this benefit and duty.**) What I have translated as "duty" <note>original: "officio"</note> is, in the Hebrew, **אמת** (*emet*), which properly signifies "faith" or "truth." Now, just as in Latin "it is true" <note>original: "uerum est"</note> is said in place of "it is fair" <note>original: "æquum est"</note>, so it is also in the Hebrew **אמת**. And yet equity is justice, which consists in giving to each his own: in which there is "duty" <note>original: "officium"</note>, from which those who are beneficial and who do what they ought to do are called dutiful. He speaks in the same way below in chapter 32.

### FROM CHAPTER XXV.

**When he had stood firm against all his brothers even until his death.**) Literally, *he fell against all his brothers*; this means he persevered and stood even until his fall and death, as if you were to say, "I shall die in this opinion," that is, I will persevere even unto death. For he alludes to what the angel <note>original: "genius"</note> of Hagar had said in chapter 26: that Ishmael would endure in brotherly animosity.

### FROM CHAPTER XXVII.

**That you may pray well for me.**) In the Hebrew it is, *that your soul may pray well for me.* Now "soul" is often used for "person": as when 70 "souls" are said to have descended into Egypt, which the Latins call "heads" <note>original: "Capita"</note>. The French retain the Hebraism here. For they say, *there is not a soul* <note>original: "il ny a ame"</note> for "no one is present," and *my person* <note>original: "ma persone"</note> for "myself."

**Those born to you from the same mother.**) That is, brothers, who are named from the mother for the reason that offspring from a mother are more certain than from a father. Although elsewhere they are named from the father. This is, however, a more sublime kind of speaking than common speech. Therefore the sentiments are doubled, and that speech is employed which among us is either poetic or certainly not common.

**He shall be away from the fatness of the earth.**) Others translate it, *he shall be in the fatness.* But since the father [Isaac] could not give to Esau what he had given to Jacob, and Esau wept over that very thing and afterwards threatened his brother with death because of it, it is necessary that we understand this passage differently. Now, the father had already furnished Jacob with grain and wine; if he then furnishes Esau with the fertility of the soil and the dew of heaven, he confers the same things. But if he can confer the same things, why does Esau grieve? Why should I grieve that another enjoys the sun, when nothing is taken away from me? For as to what is written in the Epistle to the Hebrews, that Isaac...

<column-break/>

<page-num>12</page-num>

...blessed both: I confess it is a matter of a favorable prayer that Esau is said to be destined at some time to shake off the yoke of Jacob in turn. Which fact is read in 2 Kings 8 <note>Today known as 2 Kings 8:20-22</note>, where the Edomites, who had previously served the Jews, revolted from them. Now, to show that the words are from us, it is read as **משמני** (*mishmande*), that is, "from the fatness," or "without fatness." In which way it is read literally in the 109th Psalm: *My knees fail for lack of food, and my body wastes away* **משמן** (*mishaman*), "from fatness," that is, from a lack of fatness and because of thinness. And in Jeremiah 48: **מירעת** (*miyeraat*), that is, "through ignorance," "without knowledge," "without end." And in Lamentations 4: **מניבת שרו** (*minibat saro*) "for lack of fruits." In Latin also, "a" or "ab" signifies "without" and "to be away from," as when we say "away from the matter" <note>original: "Ab re"</note>, and in Greek *to die away* <note>original: "$\dot{\alpha}\pi\grave{o} \text{ }\tau\epsilon\theta\epsilon\tilde{\iota}\nu$"</note>, *away from the forms* <note>original: "$\dot{\alpha}\pi\grave{o} \text{ }\tau\tilde{\omega}\nu \text{ }\epsilon\text{i}\delta\tilde{\omega}\nu$"</note>, and *a misanthrope [away from] humanity* <note>original: "$\mu\iota\sigma\alpha\nu\theta\rho\omega\pi\grave{o}\varsigma \text{ }\dot{\alpha}\pi\grave{o} \text{ }\dot{\upsilon}\pi\grave{\epsilon}\rho$"</note>: and in compound words, "mindless" <note>original: "amens"</note>, "to be away" <note>original: "abesse"</note>, and "to give up hope" <note>original: "$\dot{\alpha}\pi o\gamma\iota\nu\dot{\omega}\sigma\kappa\omega$"</note>.

**Lest perhaps I be bereaved of both of you at once.**) That is, lest he kill you, and then either flee or pay the penalty with his head; by which deed, I would be deprived of both. Moreover, that I translate **עות** (*ma*) as "lest" <note>original: "ne"</note>, this must often be done; for it is not always the word of one asking a question, no more than **חלות** (*halot*), as is evident in many other places, and in 1 Samuel 20. Likewise, what I translate as "at once" <note>literally "some time"</note>, is in the Hebrew "in one day": a Hebraism which the French also possess.

### FROM CHAPTER XXIX.

**Because the space of time seemed very short to him, so much did he love her.**) And yet the night is long for those whose mistress is false; and the day
> Seems long for those owing labor; and the year is slow
> For wards, whom the long guardianship of mothers oppresses.
<note>The author quotes Horace's *Epistles* (1.1.20-22) to contrast Jacob's experience with the common feeling that time drags when one is unhappy.</note>

But this is the sense: Jacob valued Rachel so highly out of love that he thought a seven-year service was short, by which he might obtain so great a reward. For nothing is hard that is done willingly.

### FROM CHAPTER XXX.

**But Jacob from the poplars, etc.**) The sense of this whole passage is: He placed rods partly stripped of their bark, and therefore variegated in color, in the watering troughs, so that by looking at them the flocks would be stimulated while breeding, and thus would bring forth variegated offspring. Then he placed those offspring before the flocks to be bred, for the same reason. But lest nothing be left for Laban if every birth were variegated, he made "fringes," that is, separate flocks for himself from the born variegated cattle, and segregated them from the single-colored cattle, which were Laban's cattle; and for that reason they were less noble, because Jacob did not set down the rods for the breeding of the less noble ones, and therefore those produced offspring similar to themselves in both color and kind.

### FROM CHAPTER XXXI.

**Which was before this.**) In the Hebrew it is, *As yesterday and the day before*: a Hebraism which even Herodotus used, *yesterday and the day before* <note>original Greek: "$\chi\theta\grave{\epsilon}\varsigma \kappa\alpha\grave{\iota} \pi\rho\acute{\omega}\eta\nu$"</note>, unless my memory fails me; and Cato, in *On Agriculture*, spoke in that sense as "the day before."

**No one is present with us.**) Pacts are confirmed by the testimony of men; the same, if no witness was present, can be denied. Therefore Laban makes a pact with a condition, to this effect: If you [Jacob] treat my daughters harshly...

->ANNOTATIONS<-

...you will find mine more harshly, I call God to witness, these agreements then would be just as if no one were present here: that is, they will be void. Not dissimilar to that saying: "what you know, you do not know": that is, act just as if you do not know. <note>The author is finishing a thought from the previous page regarding legal or social "voiding" of knowledge.</note>

### FROM CHAPTER XXXII.

<margin>10</margin> **He touched the hollow of his thigh.** <term>Kaf</term> <note>original: "בכף"</note> signifies a hollow: in the hand it is the palm, in the foot the sole, and in the leg it is the hollow of the knee or the ham.
**By the shrinking nerve.** Certain nerves draw the limbs toward the body and contract them, such as those in the back part of the thigh which pull the lower leg up via the ham. If these are affected by some condition so that they contract and cannot be extended, they prevent the limbs from being stretched out. This is the cause of Jacob's limping: because the nerve had become shorter, he was unable to extend his leg.

### FROM CHAPTER XXXIII.

**He bought it for a hundred pieces of money.** I believe the <term>quesita</term> <note>A Latinization of the Hebrew "Kesitah," an ancient unit of weight or currency.</note> was a coin of significant value. I gather this both from this passage and from the final chapter of Job, where it is written that Job’s friends each gave him a *quesita*.

### FROM CHAPTER XXXVII.

**Later Reuben returned to the pit.** Reuben (as the historian Josephus relates) had departed after Joseph was lowered into the pit and was not present for the sale. Later, returning at night to secretly rescue his brother and not finding him, he lamented to his brothers, from whom he learned what had happened.
**To Pharaoh’s eunuch, the master of the horse.** <margin>30</margin> Kings used to place eunuchs in charge of queens—men who had been castrated so they would not violate them. But gradually the custom took hold (as I suspect) that officials were called "eunuchs" even if they were not actually eunuchs; just as among the Latins men are called "Senators" <note>From the Latin "senex," meaning old man.</note> even if they are not old. For if Potiphar was castrated, why did he have a wife? Or what need did Pharaoh have of a castrated man who did not serve the queen? As for my translating "master of the horse" <note>original: "magistrum equitum"</note> rather than "master of the slaughterers" or "cooks," as others and Josephus do (who uses the Greek word <term>archimageiron</term> <note>original: "ἀρχιμάγειρον", meaning chief cook or head of the guard.</note>), <margin>40</margin> the reason is that in the Second Book of Kings, chapter 24, Nabuzardan is called by this same name when he was ordered to burn Jerusalem. Such a task is certainly not the duty of a master of cooks or slaughterers. Therefore, in that passage, the same Josephus more correctly translates it as <term>slaughterers</term> <note>original: "σφαγέων"</note>. Among the Hebrews, the term is derived from "slaughtering," <term>Tabachin</term> <note>original: "טבחים"</note> and <term>Sar Tabachin</term> <note>original: "שר טבחים"</note>, perhaps because he carried out punishments upon the guilty. He is much like the official who today in French is called "the provost of the marshal" <note>original: "le preuost du mareschal"; a military police official.</note>.

### FROM CHAPTER XLI.

**God, not I, shall give you a favorable answer, Pharaoh.** Literally it reads: "Without me, God will answer the peace of Pharaoh." But the name <term>Shalom</term> <note>original: "שלום"</note> declares not only peace, but also health and welfare. This is seen in Daniel, in the letter of Nebuchadnezzar: "Nebuchadnezzar to the nations, may peace be multiplied to you" (for so they translate it); that is, he wishes them "much health." But of this, more elsewhere. The meaning here is: "I shall give you a favorable answer, but God will be the author of this response."
<margin>60</margin> **He shall not lift a finger against your will.** That is, he shall not dare anything. In the Hebrew it is: "He shall not move hand or foot." But Hebraisms of this kind must be changed into our own custom of speaking, such as that in chapter 14: "I will not take so much as a thread or a shoe-latch from you." In Latin, this is said as "Not even a hair." Likewise, "Neither good nor evil" stands for "not a word" or "nothing at all." And that phrase, "Neither to the right nor to the left," means "in no direction." I mention these many examples here so that I do not have to repeat the same explanations later.

<column-break/>

### FROM CHAPTER XLII.

<margin>10</margin> **And he held them as spies.** Literally it reads: "And he placed us for spies." Thus in 1 Kings chapter 1: "Do not place me among the wicked women," which means "do not consider me a wicked woman." The Latins also use "to place" <note>original: "ponere"</note> in the sense of "to judge" or "to consider," as in "to place pleasure among the good things," or "Suppose [Place] it to be so."

### FROM CHAPTER XLIII.

**They drank liberally with him.** In the Hebrew it is: <margin>20</margin> "they were intoxicated." But that word does not always signify being drunk; it is used in the sense of "drinking one's fill" just as "satiated" is used for eating. And at the end of Isaiah 49, those who drink blood are said to be "intoxicated" with blood.

### FROM CHAPTER XLVIII.

**Through you let the Israelite pray well.** In the Hebrew it is: "through thee" (singular). But since the blessing is said to both [sons], and the Greek reads <term>among you</term> <note>original: "ἐν ὑμῖν"</note> (plural), I preferred to translate using the plural. <margin>30</margin> The sense is this: "I wish you such great happiness that hereafter, whoever wishes to pray well for another will use your names in their prayer."

### FROM CHAPTER XLIX.

**You shall not excel.** It was Reuben's right, as the eldest, to surpass his brothers in age and all other matters. But because he defiled his father's concubine, he lost that right. I understand this not only regarding the prerogative of age, but also regarding the number of men, in which the tribe of Reuben was surpassed by others. <margin>40</margin> Moses predicts the same in Deuteronomy 33 with these words: "Let Reuben live and not die, but let his men be few in number."
**I would not wish my life to come into their trust, nor my honor to be committed to their company.** What I translate as "trust," in the Hebrew is "secret." The meaning is this: "I would not wish to commit my life to their secret (that is, to their trust; for we do not hesitate to enter into the secrets and private places of those we trust)." For they would do to me as they did to the Shechemites, whom they slew despite given trust. Likewise, I would not wish to entrust my honor to their company. For they are treacherous, failing to keep their promises; it would be a disgrace to me if I were their associate. <margin>50</margin> He speaks in the first person on behalf of anyone, as in the proverb: "It is not safe to trust them with one's life or honor." This is how Vergil speaks: "Let it not then please me to pluck soft slumbers under the open sky, nor to lie upon the grass on the ridge of the grove"; that is, "it is dangerous to sleep or lie in the open at that time." When he says, **They undermined a wall**, he signifies their wicked raid on Shechem. Then what follows, **I will distribute them among the Jacobs**, signifies this: "They must be scattered among others, so they are less able to unite for harm." This is a way of speaking where someone is said to have done, or is about to do, what he declares is done or will be done. As Vergil says of Silenus:

->ON EXODUS<-

"Then he encircles the daughters of Phaethon with the moss of bitter bark, and raises the tall alders from the soil." <note>This is a quotation from Virgil’s *Eclogues* (6.62-63), describing the mythological transformation of Phaethon's sisters into trees.</note> For Silenus <note>A figure from Greek mythology</note> did not perform these things himself, but rather sang of their being done. You will find a similar figure of speech in Ezekiel, at the beginning of chapter 43.

Regarding **Judah**, because he compares him to a **lion's cub** and a **lion**, he is prophesying the military courage of his tribe. When he says that a ruler shall not be lacking from his **inner thighs** <note>original: "interfeminio"</note>: this is a roundabout way of saying "from his loins," referring to that which is emitted from between the thighs. The Hebrew words are quite descriptive: <note>original: "מבין רגליו"</note> "from between his feet" (to use such language for the sake of teaching), for "foot" often signifies the entire leg. Thus, I believe I have not translated it poorly as "inner thighs." The same way of speaking is found in Deuteronomy 28, where it speaks of menstrual flow "between the feet." The meaning, therefore, is that there will never be a lack of offspring from his seed who shall rule and hold power. For this is what **lawgiver** signifies <note>original: "מחוקק"</note>, derived from the root "to decree" <note>original: "חקק"</note>. What follows next, **Until the bringer of safety comes**, is in the Hebrew <note>original: "שילה"</note> **Shiloh**, which, derived from a root meaning "to send," signifies one who is hospitable and the author of happiness: that is, **JESUS CHRIST** our Lord, born from the seed of Judah. Upon his arrival, the kingdom passed to **Herod**, a man of foreign birth (an Idumaean), whereas before then the tribe of Judah had always held either the power or certainly the right of rule. Herod, understanding this, attempted to utterly destroy the Davidic line.

What he says regarding the **vine** or the **palm** (which is the same thing, for the sentiment is doubled) signifies an immense abundance of wine, which makes the eyes of the Judeans red (as usually happens from drinking wine), and also of milk, which makes the teeth white from drinking. This does not mean the teeth are made permanently white by milk as the eyes are by wine, but rather that at the moment the milk is drunk, the teeth appear white because of it.

**Issachar is a strong-boned donkey.** Just as a slow and stubborn donkey, having found pasture, prefers to be burdened by loads and sink down while feeding rather than move on, so the people of Issachar would rather be subjects of tribute than abandon the good land they have found.

**Dan shall avenge his people.** This is understood to refer to **Samson**, who was like a serpent in that he struck the Philistines with great slaughter by surprise. It is added, **I wait for your salvation, O Yahweh**: where Jacob, in the name of all Israelites, says he expects help from that Samson. For "Salvation" often signifies this kind of help. And regarding Samson, it is written in Judges 13: "He shall begin to save the Israelites from the Philistines," meaning he will defend or avenge them. Just as in Matthew 1 it says Christ will save his people from their sins: that is, he will defend and liberate them.

**Gad shall be scattered by a troop.** "Gad" signifies a troop, which is a battle line drawn up in the shape of a wedge. This signifies that the Gadites would be conquered at first, but would eventually overcome.

**Joseph is a fruitful son.** In the Hebrew it is "fruitful son." But "son" is often used for what we express in English with an adjective: such as "son of wrath" for someone to be punished, or "son of perdition" for one who is lost. This term is also used for plants, as it is here. For it alludes to a tree planted by a spring, so that the

<column-break/>

<page-num>16</page-num>

meaning is: Joseph is like a tree planted by a spring, and therefore fruitful; so beautiful that in their eagerness to see him, girls climb upon the walls, as happens when the streets are full of spectators. Nor is he only beautiful, but also strong and self-controlled; he resisted the arrows of both his brothers and of Potiphar's wife as if with a most robust bow and strong arms—not by his own strength (for he could not have escaped otherwise), but by the power, that is, the protection of the Divine <note>I translate the word "Abir" <note>original: "אביר"</note>, which declares one to be strong and invincible, this way</note> of Jacob. From that source—that is, from that Divinity—comes the shepherd and the stone of Israel, namely **JESUS CHRIST**, the shepherd and the most firm foundation of the Israelites. Then he declares more openly who that Divinity is. He says: "The muscles of your arms, Joseph, were strengthened by the God of your father (that is, my God), who helped you in your adversity; by the Almighty, who will enrich you with everything produced by the climate of the heavens and the goodness of the earth (neither of which is sufficient without the other); and also with the offspring of both women and cattle, and with milk." These are the riches of your father, which indeed surpass the "mountains of abundance" (as we say in Latin, "mountains of gold") and the "delight of the everlasting hills" (meaning the longest-lasting). That is, these most abundant blessings shall overflow upon your head; they will fall upon you in heaps, you who are the most excellent of your brothers (for this was the privilege of his age, as noted in 1 Chronicles 5). For it is right that you, who surpass others in virtue, should also precede them in happiness. For the word **Nazir** <note>original: "נזיר"</note>, derived from a word meaning "to cut off" or "to set apart," signifies one who is eminent and separated from others because of excellence; as it is used in Nahum 3, and of the **Nazirites** (a word derived from this), who were men devoted to God and set apart from the number of others as singular individuals.

**Benjamin shall raven as a wolf.** This signifies that the tribe would be fond of hunting and warlike.

# ON EXODUS.
### FROM CHAPTER III.

<image-desc>Historiated ornamental drop cap 'V' depicting a figure (Moses) kneeling before the burning bush in a hilly landscape.</image-desc>

The same **spirit** <note>original: "genius"</note> or messenger who appears here to Moses is called both **Yahweh** <note>original: "Ioua"</note> and **God** in this chapter. The same one is called Yahweh in Genesis 18 when he appears to Abraham. He also speaks to Hagar, wandering in the desert, as both a spirit and as God. The same one is called a spirit when he meets Balaam riding on his donkey; and yet he says that Balaam's journey was set against him—a statement belonging to God, not to a mere speaking spirit. Jacob also calls the same being both God and a spirit in Genesis 48. Not to pursue every single instance too lengthily, the scriptures are full of such examples. Therefore, we must examine this matter a little more deeply. In the first place, the one who speaks to Moses here does not seem to be the Supreme Prince and Father of Christ, God himself; for he could not be called a messenger <note>original: "nuncius"</note> since he has no one by whom he could be sent. Nor, likewise, is he merely a spirit; for he would not be called Yahweh, since that is the proper name of God, and because he commands with greater authority than is fitting for a spirit. Who, then,

...is indeed the one: specifically, the one whom Paul says in 1 Corinthians 10 was tempted by the Jews, and because of this, they were destroyed by serpents. This is clearly Christ, through whom God both made and rules the world. The Sibyl <note>The Sibylline Oracles were a collection of Greek prophetic verses often cited by early Christians to find pagan "proofs" for Christ.</note> calls him the Son of God in those verses which I placed in the first chapter of Genesis. He is the one who led the Israelites out of Egypt, the one with whom Moses and Elijah spoke on Mount Tabor, and who is called in this passage the "messenger of God" because he was sent by the Father—since mortals cannot endure the direct presence of the Father himself. He is likewise called **Ioua** <note>A Latinized form of the Tetragrammaton, Yahweh or Jehovah.</note> from the Hebrew name <note>original: "יהוה"</note>, which signifies "to be," because he always was, always is, and always will be. This is just as it is said in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation 1:4.</note>: <note>original: "ὁ ὤν, ὁ ἦν, ὁ ἐρχόμενος"</note> "The one who is, who was, and who is to come." For he is one with the Father and co-eternal with him, upon whom the nature of all things depends. Isaiah also calls him **Ioua** in chapter 40 when he speaks of John the Baptist in these words: "The voice of one crying in the wilderness: prepare the way for **Ioua**." And a little later: "Behold, the Lord **Ioua** coming with strength," etc. And David, in Psalm 68, if one reads him carefully, uses the same name for God. Thus Thomas, being truly overcome, confesses: "My Lord and my God." And Paul in Romans 9 professes: "From whom," he says, "Christ was born according to the flesh, who is God over all things, to be praised forever." Furthermore, the angel in Luke 1 calls him the God of the Israelites. The Sibyl also calls him God in these words from Book 8:

"The King now described for you in our verses in the highest order,
this is our God, the eternal Creator of our salvation,
who suffered on our behalf."

->And in the same book, Gabriel addressing Mary:<-
> "Receive, O Virgin, the undefiled one in your modest womb."

### FROM CHAPTER 4.

**When Ioua sought him to kill him.** Moses, seemingly deferring to his wife <note>Zipporah</note> (for she, not being Judean, was repulsed by circumcision), had not circumcised his son. For that reason, God sought to kill him, as one who was more obedient to his wife than to God. But Zipporah, understanding the cause, circumcised the son and cast the foreskin at her husband's feet, calling him a "bloody husband" because she had redeemed his life with the blood of their son.

**The finger of God.** This means the hand (using a part to represent the whole), that is, his work. Thus in the eighth Psalm, the heavens are called the "work of God's fingers," meaning his hands.

### FROM CHAPTER 9.

**The death of livestock of every kind.** Literally, it is read that "all livestock died," meaning livestock of every category, yet not every individual animal, as appears later during the plague of hail and regarding the chariot horses. In this same way, in Genesis 24, Abraham's steward is said to carry "all his master's goods" into Mesopotamia; and in Acts 10, it is said that in that vessel (which Peter seemed to see) were "all the four-footed creatures of the earth."

### FROM CHAPTER 11.

**From the firstborn of Pharaoh himself, who sat upon the throne, to the servant girl.** In the Hebrew language, it is uncertain whether Pharaoh or the son is said to be "sitting on the throne"—that is, reigning or (if referring to the son) about to reign. But since the author contrasts Pharaoh with the servant girls (the highest with the lowest), there is no doubt that he contrasts Pharaoh’s task (which is to sit on a throne) with the servant girls’ task (which is to push a millstone). Furthermore, the present participle, which

<column-break/>

<page-num>18</page-num>

sounds like "sitting," would not be very aptly placed if it meant "about to sit."

### FROM CHAPTER 12.

**Let them take lambs by households.** Regarding the word we translate as "lambs," the Hebrew term is common to both lambs and kids; but here we suffer from a lack of a specific word in our language.

**With chicory.** This is a herb named by the Hebrews for its bitterness, as it is by the Greeks, who translated it as <note>original: "πικρίδα"</note> "bitter herbs." The Latins call it endive or chicory.

**And I will take punishment from all the gods of the Egyptians.** In the Hebrew, it says "I will perform judgments." But the judgments of men are often separated from their effect; whereas with God's judgment and decree, the outcome of the matter is joined. Thus it happens that "judgment" is often put for the "vengeance" that follows judgment. In the same way, the word <note>original: "ברך" (barak)</note> when said of men, signifies "to wish well" or "to pray for"; but when said of God, it signifies "to make fortunate" and "to make fruitful," because the reality itself is joined to God's will. God took punishment from the gods of the Egyptians when he killed the Egyptians who were under their protection, even against those gods' wills. Yet they were not truly gods, since there is only one; but he calls them gods according to human custom—whatever it was that they held to be a god.

### FROM CHAPTER 15.

**I sing to Ioua.** That is, "we sing": the singular for the plural, which often happens even in the first person, not only among the Hebrews but also among the Greeks, especially in the choruses of tragedies; and among the Latins, as in Livy at the beginning of Book 9 of the first decade.

**Ioua, a man of war.** In the Hebrew it is <note>original: "מלחמה"</note>, that is, "a man of war." But it must be understood that the Hebrews do not have adjectives derived from substantives in the same way the Latins do. Thus, they call an "iron bolt" a "bolt of iron," and a "wooden house" a "house of wood," just as the French say <note>original: "Maison de bois"</note> "House of wood." So, instead of "warlike man," they say "man of war." Furthermore, calling him a "man" shows that **Ioua** is Jesus Christ, who is both God and man; he is also called "man" in Deuteronomy 33. We shall write more on this in Matthew 1, God willing.

### FROM CHAPTER 16.

**Man hu: what is this?** The Hebrews interpret *Man hu* as "it is a gift," but in my opinion, they do not do so correctly. First, this word is never used for "gift" anywhere else, unless they want to claim it is a mutilated form of <note>original: "מנה" or "מנת"</note>. But this is to play around, or rather, to hallucinate. For by this logic, it would be possible to derive any word from any other, provided they share even a single letter. Furthermore, the Hebrews would not say "it is a gift," but "it is food," and certainly with an article. For God had not promised them a gift, but food. To this, since Moses says, "For they did not know what it was," there must be doubt and ignorance in the term. There would be no ignorance if they were saying "it is a gift." But the Greeks and Jerome translated it well as: "What is this?" The reason for this question is added immediately: "For they did not know what it was." Nor does it hinder the meaning that it reads *man* rather than *mah*. For Moses recorded the actual speech of the common people, who often pronounce things incorrectly. Additionally, *man* in the Chaldean language signifies "what?"—a word that is also placed in Psalm 61. Josephus interprets it in the same way: <note>original: "τί τοῦτ' ἔστι;"</note> "What is this?" I will mention in passing that the ancient Latins called a "good thing" *manum*, according to Varro; which word seems to be derived from *manna*.

<header>ON EXODUS</header>

### FROM CHAPTER XVII.

**Because the hand of Jehovah was moved to the sign.** <note>original Latin: "Quia Iouæ manus signo admota est."</note>) Literally, it reads: "Because the hand is toward the sign of Jehovah; there is a war of Jehovah with the Amalekites forever." This provides the reasoning for the name of the altar, which he called **Jehovah-Nissi** <note>original Hebrew: "יהוה נסי"</note>, from the word **Nes** <note>original: "נס"</note>, which means "sign" or "banner." For where the Hebrew text reads **Kes** <note>original: "כס"</note>, it is an error. First, because the reasoning for the name would not be provided, as the name *Iouanissi* is not derived from *Kes*, but from *Nes*. Second, because *Kes* means nothing, although some want it to stand for **Kisse** <note>original: "כסא"</note>, meaning "throne." <margin>10</margin> However, they change the vowel points, mutilate the word, and pervert both the etymology and the meaning. Furthermore, there is no other place where the word is used this way, and since this passage is disputed, it cannot serve as evidence. Now, how easily a **Nun** <note>The Hebrew letter נ</note> might degenerate into a **Kaph** <note>The Hebrew letter כ</note> can be understood from the similarity of their shapes. Josephus indeed agrees with me, saying that God was named by Moses as "the Victorious One" <note>original Greek: "νικαίῳ"</note>, certainly from "victory," which is marked by a standard-bearer. Unless perhaps he derived "Victorious" from *Nes*, with the 'N' changing to a 'P' sound, just as **Pascha** <note>Passover</note> comes from **Pesach** <note>original: "פסח"</note> <margin>20</margin> by the same letter change, but aspirated. This reasoning agrees with my reading. The sense is this: Jehovah moved his hand to destroy the Amalekites forever.

### FROM CHAPTER XIX.

**We established certain boundaries for it.**) Literally, it reads: "You warned us with these words: Set bounds for the mountain and sanctify it." And yet, God had not ordered the mountain to be bounded and sanctified a little earlier, but rather the people. Therefore, it seems we should read **the people** <note>original Hebrew: "העם" (ha-am)</note> instead of **the mountain** <note>original: "ההר" (ha-har)</note>. <margin>30</margin>

### FROM CHAPTER XX.

**An image of anything that exists.**) In the Hebrew, it literally reads: "Do not make for yourself a carved image, and any likeness that is in heaven." But this lacks sense: for one does not "make" a likeness that is in heaven, but rather an image of the likeness—that is, of a visible thing that is in heaven. Therefore, it is read more correctly in Deuteronomy 5, where it is written without the conjunction "and" <note>original Hebrew: "ו" (vav)</note>: "Do not make <margin>40</margin> for yourself a carved image of any likeness," or of any visible thing. We have expressed the force of this word with the verb "Exists." Pliny speaks in a similar way in Book 1, Chapter 3: "Since from there (namely, from heaven) seeds of all things fall, innumerable monstrous forms are born, especially in the sea, and mostly from confused shapes." Thus Pliny calls the animals themselves "images" because they possess distinct forms. As for the word "To you" <note>original Hebrew: "לך" (lekha)</note> in the Hebrew, it is superfluous, as it often is. For example, when it is frequently said "Go, go to you" <note>original: "לך לך" (lekh lekha)</note>, it just means "Go." The French say this well: <margin>50</margin> **"va ten"** <note>Modern French: "va-t-en," meaning "go away," where "en" acts as a reflexive or directional particle.</note>. The Latins have a similar Hebraism, but in the first person, as in Horace: "What does Celsus do for me?" <note>original: "Quid mihi Celsus agit," where "mihi" adds a personal flavor rather than literal possession.</note> Sometimes it appears in the second person, as in Cicero's *For Sextus Roscius*: "The other one goes down from the palace for you, and from his own house." Therefore, "Do not make an image for me" could be said in French as: **"Ne me fay point d'image."** <note>Old French for "Do not make me an image."</note>

<column-break/>

<page-num>20</page-num>
<header>ON EXODUS</header>

### FROM CHAPTER XXI.

**If chance should happen upon him.**) In the Hebrew it is: "God threw him into his hand." But "God" is used for "chance" in Hebrew because those things which men think happen by accident—since they did not foresee them—actually happen by God's providence, to whom nothing can be accidental. The Greeks also use **daimona** <note>original Greek: "δαίμονα"</note> for fortune; hence **eudaimona** <note>original: "εὐδαίμονα"</note> means happy (fortunate), and **kakodaimona** <note>original: "κακοδαίμονα"</note> means unhappy. Cicero also testifies that "God" is called "Fortune." <margin>10</margin>

### FROM CHAPTER XXII.

**Do not turn away your produce and your liquor.**) In the Hebrew it is: "Your fullness and your tear." That is, dry and liquid fruits, such as oil and wine, whose tithes he forbids to be withheld.

### FROM CHAPTER XXIII.

**The son of your handmaid.**) That is, your servant. Just as "born of a dove" means a dove, and "sons of men" means men.
**Keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread.** <note>The author coins a Latin term *Azymalia*.</note>) Just as the ancient Latins said **Agonalia, Floralia, Liberalia**, and so on <note>Names of Roman religious festivals.</note>, I thought it right for me to call the feast of unleavened bread **Azymalia**, the harvest feast **Messalia**, and the feast of storage **Conditalia**.

### FROM CHAPTER XXV.

**Cedar wood.**) Some record that **shittim wood** <note>original Hebrew: "עצי שטים"</note> is cedar wood, and rightly so, in my judgment. For since cedar is sweet-smelling, eternal in duration, and never suffers decay, I do not see what better wood these things could have been made from. The Greeks also translated it as **incorruptible wood** <note>original Greek: "ξύλα ἄσηπτα"</note>, which Josephus also followed; a quality that fits no nature better than cedar. But since there are two kinds, I think it refers here to the "great cedar," which is called **cedrelate**. For the other is simply called **kedros**.
**Place in that ark the oracle which I will deliver to you.**) The word **Od** <note>original Hebrew: "עוד"</note> does not only mean "to testify" or "to bear witness," but also "to warn," as it was used above in Chapter 19. Hence **to testify thoroughly** <note>original Greek: "διαμαρτύρεσθαι"</note> is used for "to warn," as in <margin>40</margin> 2 Timothy 2. When it is said of God, it means "to deliver an oracle," which is God's warning and response, as it is used here and in Chapters 29 and 30. From this comes **Devir** <note>original Hebrew: "דביר"</note>, which we translate as "oracle"—that is, the commandments of God which were stored in the ark. From this also comes "the Tabernacle of the Oracle," or the "Oracular Tabernacle."
**The bread of presence.** <note>original Latin: "Panem appositiuum," literally "the set-forth bread."</note>) **Panim** <note>original Hebrew: "פנים"</note> sometimes signifies "presence," as in 2 Kings 17 and Exodus 32. <margin>50</margin> Moses urges God that "His face"—that is, his presence itself—should go with the Israelites. Hence "the set-forth bread," which was always present and ready, and set before Jehovah. For when it was removed due to age, another was immediately put in its place.
**And their tongs.**) I call "tongs" the tools with which the lamps are trimmed, and "fire-pans" those into which the trimmings are thrown. But because there are many difficulties in the Tabernacle, we will add diagrams <note>original: "figuras"</note> by which we may teach as if by hand, and at the same time we will explain all the most difficult points.

### FROM CHAPTER 17

**Because Ioua's hand was moved to the sign.** <note>original: "Quia Iouæ manus signo admota est." Referring to Exodus 17:15-16 regarding the altar Moses built.</note> Literally, it is read: "Because there is a hand upon the sign of Ioua; Ioua has a war with the Amalekites forever." This provides the reason for the name of the altar, which he called <note>original: "יהוה נסי"</note> **Ioua-nissi**, from the word <note>original: "נס" (*nes*)</note>, which means a sign, that is, a banner. For what is read in the Hebrew as <note>original: "כס" (*kes*)</note> is an error. This is because the reason for the name would not be given, as the name *Iouanisi* is not derived from *kes*, but from *nes*. Furthermore, *kes* means nothing, although some want it to stand for <note>original: "כסא" (*kisse*)</note>, meaning a throne. But they change the vowel points, mutilate the word, and pervert both the etymology and the sense; nor do they have any other place where it is positioned this way except here, which, being controversial, cannot serve as evidence. How easily a **נ** <note>The Hebrew letter *Nun*.</note> might degenerate into a **כ** <note>The Hebrew letter *Kaph*.</note> can be understood from the similarity of their shapes. Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Jewish historian.</note> certainly agrees with me, saying that God was named <term>victorious</term> <note>original: "νικαῖον" (*nikaion*)</note> by Moses, undoubtedly from the "victory" which confirms the battle-standards. Unless perhaps he said *nikaion* from the word *nes*, with the *N* changed to an *M*—just as from the Hebrew <note>original: "פסח" (*pesach*)</note> comes the Greek <term>Pascha</term> <note>original: "πάσχα" (Passover)</note>, by the same letter change, though aspirated. This reasoning agrees with my reading. The sense is this: He moved Ioua's hand to the sign to destroy the Amalekites forever.

### FROM CHAPTER 19

**We established certain boundaries for it.** Literally, it is read: "You warned us with these words: Set a boundary for the mountain, and sanctify it." Yet, God had not ordered the mountain to be bounded and sanctified a little while before, but the people. Therefore, it seems it should be read not as <note>original: "הָהָר" (*ha-har*), "the mountain"</note> but as <note>original: "הָעָם" (*ha-am*), "the people"</note>.

### FROM CHAPTER 20

**The likeness of anything that exists.** <note>Exodus 20:4, the prohibition of graven images.</note> Literally in the Hebrew it reads: "Do not make for yourself an idol, and any figure that is in heaven." But this lacks sense: for a figure that is in heaven is not "made," but rather an image of that figure is made—that is, an image of a visible thing that is in heaven. Therefore, it is read more correctly in Deuteronomy 5, where it appears without the conjunction "and": <note>original: "לא תעשה לך פסל כל תמונה"</note> "Do not make for yourself an idol of any figure, or visible thing." We have expressed the force of this word with the verb **Exists**. Pliny speaks in the same way in Book 1, Chapter 3: "Since from there (namely from heaven) from the falling seeds of all things, innumerable and mostly confused monstrous shapes are born in the sea." Pliny says this, calling the animals themselves "shapes." Furthermore, the word "to you" in the Hebrew is superfluous, as is common, such as when it is often said "go to you," meaning simply "go." The French say this well: *va-t'en* <note>original: "ua ten"</note>. The Latins have a similar Hebraism, but in the first person, as in Horace: "What does Celsus do for me?" <note>original: "Quid mihi Celsus agit"</note>. Sometimes also in the second person, as in Cicero's *In Defense of Sextus Roscius*: "The other man descends for you from the palace and his own house." Therefore, "Do not make an image for me" could be said in French as *Ne me fay point d'image* <note>Do not make me any image.</note>.

<column-break/>

### FROM CHAPTER 21

**He happens upon him by chance.** <note>Exodus 21:13, regarding accidental killing.</note> In the Hebrew it is: "God threw it into his hand." But "God" is used for "fortune" in Hebrew because those things which men think happen by chance—inasmuch as they did not foresee them—actually happen by the providence of God, for whom nothing can be accidental. The Greeks also use the word <term>daimon</term> <note>original: "δαίμονα"</note> for fortune; hence <term>adaimonon</term> <note>original: "ἀδαιμόνων"</note> means lucky or divinely favored, and <term>kakodaimonon</term> <note>original: "κακοδαιμόνων"</note> means unlucky. Cicero also testifies that God is called "Fortune."

### FROM CHAPTER 22

**Do not turn away your crops and your liquor.** <note>Exodus 22:29.</note> In the Hebrew it is: "Your fullness and your tear." That is, dry and liquid fruits, such as oil and wine, whose tithes he forbids from being withheld.

### FROM CHAPTER 23

**The son of your handmaid.** That is, your servant. Just as "born of a dove" means a dove, and "sons of men" means men.

**Keep the festivals of Unleavened Bread.** Just as the ancient Latins spoke of the *Agonalia*, *Floralia*, and *Liberalia*, I have thought it right to call the feast of unleavened bread the **Azymalia**, the harvest feast the **Messalia**, and the feast of the collection the **Conditalia**.

### FROM CHAPTER 25

**Cedar wood.** <note>Exodus 25:5.</note> Some translate <note>original: "עֲצֵי שִׁטִּים" (*atzei shittim*)</note> as cedar wood, and rightly so, in my judgment. Since cedar is sweet in scent, eternal in duration, and never suffers from rot, I do not see what better wood these things could have been made from. The Greeks also translated it as <term>decay-resistant wood</term> <note>original: "ξύλα ἄσηπτα" (*xyla asepta*)</note>; Josephus followed the same, a quality that fits no nature better than cedar. But since there are two kinds, I think this refers to the great cedar, which is called *cedrelate*. The other is called <term>arkenthos</term> <note>original: "ἀρκενθος" (juniper).</note>.

**In that ark place the oracle which I shall give you.** <note>original: "עֵדֻת" (*eduth*)</note> does not only mean to testify or witness, but also to warn, as was set down above in Chapter 19. Hence the Greek word <term>to solemnly charge</term> <note>original: "διαμαρτύρεσθαι"</note> is used for "to warn," as in 2 Timothy 2. When it is said of God, it signifies to deliver an **oracle**, which is God's warning and response, as it is used both here and in Chapters 29 and 30. Hence *eduth*, which we translate as **oracle**, refers to God's precepts which were stored in the ark; hence the "Tabernacle of the Oracle."

**The appositive bread.** <note>Exodus 25:30. Usually called Showbread.</note> <note>original: "פָנִים" (*panim*)</note> sometimes signifies "presence," as in 2 Kings 17 and Exodus 32. God exhorts Moses that His "face"—that is, that He Himself being present—should go with the Israelites. Hence "appositive bread" <note>From the Latin *appositivus*, meaning placed before or set out.</note>, which was always present and ready, set before Ioua. For when it was removed due to age, another was immediately put in its place.

**And their tongs.** I call "tongs" those things with which the lamps are trimmed; and "fire-pans" <note>original: "foculos"</note> those into which the trimmings are cast. But because there are many difficulties in the Tabernacle, we shall add diagrams to teach as if by hand, and at the same time we will explain the most difficult parts.

<header>ANNOTATIONS. THE ARK OF THE ORACLE.</header>

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of the Ark of the Covenant (Arca Oraculi). It depicts a rectangular chest with two long carrying poles inserted through rings on its sides. On the top cover (Propitiatorium), two winged cherubim are positioned at opposite ends, facing each other with their wings extended. The chest is situated on a tiled floor against a background of a stone block wall.</image-desc>

The Mercy Seat <term>Latin: *propitiatorium*</term> is the cover of the ark, from which God gave responses and showed himself to be merciful <note>or "propitious"</note>; hence it is called the *propitiatorium*. The historian Josephus interpreted this word as a "covering" <note>original Greek: ἐπίθημα (*epithema*)</note>, and following him, we had at first translated it as "cover." But later, having been advised by a certain learned man, and simultaneously realizing ourselves the specific theological weight inherent in this word, we restored the term *propitiatorium*. Although this word is less commonly used among classical Latin authors, it nonetheless must be accepted,
<column-break/>
since it is both necessary and follows a standard linguistic form, just as *repositorium* <note>a storage case or stand</note> and many other things are named among the Latins. Furthermore, at each end of this cover were individual Cherubim, fashioned from the cover itself. A crown also surrounded the cover; this should be understood as being crafted on the rim which extended beyond the dimensions of the ark, so that the crown could encircle the cover, which was of equal length and width to the ark.

# ANNOTATIONS.

## THE ARK OF THE ORACLE.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of the Ark of the Covenant (Arca Oraculi). It is a rectangular chest with decorative paneled sides. The lid, identified in the text as the propitiatory, features two winged cherubim facing each other with their wings extended. Two long carrying poles (staves) pass through rings attached to the sides. The ark is positioned on a tiled floor against a background of a stone block wall.</image-desc>

The **Propitiatory** <note>original Latin: "Propitiatorium," often referred to in English Bibles as the "Mercy Seat."</note> is the lid of the ark, from which God gave His answers and showed Himself to be favorable <note>or "propitious."</note>; hence, it is called the "propitiatory." The historian Josephus interpreted this word as *hilasterion* <note>original Greek: ἱλαστήριον, meaning an offering or place of atonement.</note>, and following his lead, we had at first translated it simply as "lid" <note>original: "operculum."</note>. However, having later been advised by a certain learned friend, and simultaneously realizing ourselves that there is a specific theological power in this word, we restored the term **propitiatory**. Although this word is less frequently used among Latin authors, it nevertheless ought to be accepted,

<column-break/>

since it is both necessary and formed in the same manner as the Latin word for "repository" <note>original: "repositorium," a place where things are stored.</note> and many other such terms. Furthermore, there were individual **Cherubim** <note>winged celestial beings</note> at each end of this lid, crafted from the lid itself. A **crown** <note>original: "corona," referring here to a decorative molding or rim.</note> also surrounded the lid; it should be understood that this was fashioned as a border which extended beyond the main body of the ark, so that the crown could encircle the lid, which was of equal length and width to the ark.

# ON EXODUS: THE LAMPSTAND.

<image-desc>A detailed woodcut illustration of the Menorah, the seven-branched golden lampstand from the biblical Tabernacle. The lampstand features a central shaft with three branches curving upwards on each side, all ending in decorative bowls or lamps. The stem is ornate with spherical and bowl-like ornaments. It sits on a multi-tiered circular base, which is placed atop a decorative pedestal featuring elaborate scroll-work or ribbon-like elements.</image-desc>

The things that follow concerning the tabernacle are somewhat obscure. We will teach them in this way: first concerning the planks, then the curtains, and the rest in a different order than Moses wrote; for otherwise, the matter would be more obscure. Therefore, *Mishkan* <note>original Hebrew: מִשְׁכָּן</note>, derived from the word for "dwelling," sometimes signifies the whole tabernacle described here together with its courtyard; sometimes it signifies that part which contains the chamber <term>Latin: *cella*</term> and the inner sanctuary <term>Latin: *penetrale*</term>. This is just as in Ezekiel, where *Bayit* <note>original Hebrew: בַּיִת</note> sometimes denotes the whole temple with its courts, and sometimes only the sanctuary building. We translate this as "tabernacle." It was surrounded by forty-eight planks: twenty on the right side, just as many on the left, and eight on the west. Toward the east, in place of planks, there were five columns. Since these planks were each a cubit and a half in width, the result was that the length of the tabernacle was thirty cubits; the historian Josephus records the width as twelve cubits. But let us see what sort of arrangement this might be. For if the eight planks of the width are placed so that they are within the length of the tabernacle, they will take away as much from its length as they are themselves 

<column-break/>

wide. Thus it would happen that the length of the tabernacle—excluding the thickness of the planks that make up the width—would not be thirty cubits, and yet the width would be twelve. Furthermore, if you then divide the tabernacle and assign ten of its cubits to the inner sanctuary, neither will the sanctuary itself be a perfect square, nor will the proportions of the curtains (which are described later) match. Nor will the length of the remaining part (which we call the "chamber" <term>Latin: *cella*</term>) be double the width. Yet both of these proportions are found in Solomon’s Temple (3 Kings 6 <note>In modern Bibles, this is 1 Kings 6</note>) and in Ezekiel 41, for both of those temples were constructed according to the proportions of this tabernacle. Therefore, the planks that create the length must be positioned so that the northern ones are ten cubits distant from the southern ones, and the western ones thirty cubits from the eastern columns. In this way, their two outermost cubits are consumed in the thickness of the corners, placed outside their length, as you see in the figure below, in which the foundations of the planks are 
delineated.

# THE GROUND PLAN OF THE TABERNACLE.

<image-desc>
A rectangular floor plan diagram of the Tabernacle's layout, oriented with "Oriens" (East) at the top, "Occidens" (West) at the bottom, "Septentrio" (North) on the left, and "Meridies" (South) on the right. The plan is divided into two interior sections: the larger "CELLA" at the top and the smaller "PENETRALE" below it. The walls are composed of boards, with those along the sides labeled "a" and those along the bottom (western) end labeled "b". Corner boards are labeled "c" and "d". Five columns, labeled "r", stand at the entrance at the top. Various letters (e, f, g, h, i, k, l, m, n, o, p, q, s, t, u) designate specific points, dimensions, and structural elements discussed in the text.
</image-desc>

**a** the planks of the length. **b** the planks of the width. **c** and **d** are the two corner planks <term>Latin: *asseres*</term>, whose two outer ends **e–f** and **g–h** are set against the thickness of the length-planks. This thickness is one cubit <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of measurement, roughly the length of a forearm (18 inches).</note>, leaving ten cubits to form the width **i–k**. If you add those two ends, **e–f** and **g–h**, the width becomes twelve cubits **l–m**, just as Josephus records. But by this reasoning, the length is thirty-two cubits **n–o**, even though Josephus assigns only thirty to it—specifically by excluding the two cubits which the planks and columns of the width occupy. Therefore, by this calculation, the width within the walls is ten cubits **i–k** and the length is thirty cubits **p–q**. If you assign ten cubits of this length to the inner sanctuary <term>Latin: *penetrale*</term>, it is likewise a square, and the width of the main chamber <term>Latin: *cella*</term> is half of its length. This same proportion is found in the temples of both Solomon and Ezekiel. As for why I attribute a thickness of one cubit to the planks, when Josephus assigns only four fingers

<column-break/>

to them, the reason is that ratio of width to length which I mentioned. Josephus also indicates this, albeit obscurely, when speaking of the corner planks in these words: "They make two other columns divided from one cubit, which they placed as corners" <note>original Latin: "Duas alias colūnas faciunt ex uno cubito diuisas, quas angulares posuerunt"</note>. By these words, he seems to mean that for those two columns **c** and **d** (for he calls "columns" what we call "planks"), one cubit each is joined to the length-planks. The half-cubits **g–r** and **e–s** are added to the nine cubits of the six planks, ensuring the interior width is ten cubits **g–e**. Furthermore, when Moses writes that the corner planks are to be coupled together at the bottom and the top by a single ring, he means the outermost planks of the width are joined with the outermost planks of the length—**d** with **t**, and **c** with **u**—so that they might hold together more firmly. **r** marks the five columns. Inside this tabernacle were placed the items Moses records, as can be seen in the following figure.

# ANNOTATIONS.

From the front part of the chest, these were drawn over the fabric of the ephod and under the armpits, where they were tied to the rings located under the armpits at the joining of the shoulder-pieces.
