This binding of ribbons ensured that the breastplate clung to the ephod; <margin>10</margin> otherwise, it would shift or hang loose whenever the High Priest leaned his body forward, as it was only fastened at the top and would otherwise hang straight down toward the ground. **N** is the outer robe <note>original: *praetexta*</note>. **Q** represents the pomegranates interspersed with bells. **R** is the fine linen tunic. **Q** is the golden plate <note>on the miter</note>. **S** is the headband <note>original: *infula*</note>. **T** is the girdle.

### FROM CHAPTER XXIX.

**So that Jova <note>A Latinized form of the Tetragrammaton, Yahweh</note> may be delighted by that odor of the divine rite.**) What I interpret as "divine rite," the Hebrew text gives as *nihoach* <note>original: ניחוח</note>. This word, derived from a root associated with fire, signifies a divine matter <margin>20</margin> or a sacrifice to which fire is applied. However, we do not have a word that carries the exact same weight; nor is it necessary to mention fire by name, since it is understood in the description of the sacrifice itself. Elsewhere, I translate this as "fragrance."

### FROM CHAPTER XXX.

**Let it be done with a new sacrifice of grain, or a cake: nor let wine be poured as a libation.**) An *olah* <note>original: עולה</note> is a "holocaust," so named in Greek because the entire victim was burned. Therefore, we generally interpret it as a "solid sacrifice," though it is often used for any host or victim. Thus, we have interpreted it according to the sense of the <margin>30</margin> sentence. However, *zebach* <note>original: זבח</note> signifies a sacrifice in which the victim was "pollucated," that is, eaten <note>Referring to fellowship offerings where the worshipers shared the meal</note>. A *mincha* <note>original: מנחה</note> was a "meal gift," named from "leading" or "bringing," just as in Latin a *fertum* <note>a sacrificial cake</note> comes from "bringing" (*ferendo*), a term used by the poet Persius and by Cato in *On Agriculture*. From this comes the phrases "to make a cake-offering," "to perform a feast," or "to present a cake." Sometimes it signifies a gift, whether made to God (as in Genesis 4) or to a man (as in Genesis 33). We have translated it as the context requires.
**Five hundred of iris.**) They interpret *kiddah* <note>original: קדה</note> as <margin>40</margin> cassia. But the Hebrews call cassia by the same name as the Latins <note>original: *casia*</note>, as seen in Psalm 45. Therefore, I preferred to follow the historian Josephus here.
**As an honorary gift.**) *Terumah* <note>original: תרומה</note> properly means "to lift up," but sometimes "to receive and set aside," much like the French term *lever* <note>to raise or collect</note>, as used in Ezekiel 45 and 48, where the portion of land set apart for God is called the *terumah* of Jova. This is <margin>50</margin> an "honorary gift," lest anyone argue too stubbornly that this word must be translated more superstitiously as "lifting up" or "carrying out." It is used in the same way in Proverbs 29. From this we get the "breast of the wave offering" <note>original: *pectusculum exceptitium*</note>; hence things destined for God and set apart were called "Excepted Things" <note>original: *Exceptitia*</note>.

### FROM CHAPTER XXXIII.

**I myself will go in person.**) It has already been noted above that "faces" <note>original: פנים - *panim*</note> signifies "presence." Hence God says His face will go with them, meaning Himself. For this reason, He speaks to Moses "face to face" <note>original: פנים אל פנים</note>, that is, openly, and person to person.

### FROM CHAPTER XXXIIII.

**Inclined toward help.**) *Emet* <note>original: אמת</note> signifies "faith" or "truth." Even in Latin, "faith" (*fides*) is used to mean help and protection; as when we say "to implore someone's faith," 

<column-break/>

or "I beseech your faith," or "to be in someone’s faith," meaning to be under their protection.

# ON LEVITICUS.

### FROM CHAPTER IIII.

**If the anointed priest shall sin to the guilt of the people.**) That is, an act by whose fault the people are also held liable. Just as a disease of the head or any member pertains to the whole body; and just as the sin of Achan or David harmed the entire people.
**But if the whole republic of the Israelites.**) *Edah* <note>original: עדה</note> and *kahal* <note>original: קהל</note>, which are interpreted as "multitude" and "assembly," have almost the same meaning. They signify the "republic" and the "city-state," which the Greeks call a *polis* <term>πόλιν</term>, and which is (as Cicero defines it) a gathering of men associated by law. Josephus interprets it this way in *Antiquities* Book 3, where he records that Moses drove the lepers out of the *polis* <term>πόλεως</term>, that is, out of the assembly of others and the city.

### FROM CHAPTER V.

**Two offspring of a dove.**) That is, young pigeons. "Sons of the dove" <note>original: בני היונה</note> for the bird. Similarly, Varro in Book 1 of *On Agriculture* says: "A farmer in a nursery-field should not let the offspring of a goat graze"—that is, a goat. He cites this from a local law so that you may understand that the ancient speech of the Latins approached closer to the Hebrew idiom.

### FROM CHAPTER XI.

**Whatever have divided hooves and are cloven-footed.**) *Miphreset parsah* <note>original: מפרסת פרסה</note>, that is, what has feet divided into two slits, or more. *Shosa'at shesa* <note>original: שסעת שסע</note>, however, means that which is "two-forked" or "cloven." Therefore, those that are cloven-footed and chew the cud are permitted for eating. As for why the hare and the rabbit are denied to be *miphreset parsah* in this place, this must be understood <margin>40</margin> by joining it to what was stated in the proposition *shosa'at shesa*. The sense is: "The hare does not have divided hooves," meaning it does not have what I set forth in the proposition—feet that are split, and split into two. This was the reason I translated it thus. Anyone who diligently examines this whole chapter and Deuteronomy 14 will easily understand this to be the case. You will find something similar in Isaiah 58 and Ezekiel 21.

### FROM CHAPTER XIII.

**But if the leprosy shall have blossomed out.**) He calls it "leprosy" <margin>50</margin> while there is still a suspicion of leprosy, for as long as it is doubted; even though it may not be leprosy, as appears shortly after. He often speaks in this manner.
**Whether in the outer part or the inner part.**) They translate *sheti* <note>original: שתי</note> and *erev* <note>original: ערב</note> as "warp" and "woof." I cannot understand how a spot could be in only one of the two, since those two are so mixed together that it seems one cannot be infected by leprosy without the other. I believe what is signified here is the outer "face" <margin>60</margin> of the cloth, which is exposed to the eyes, and the "inner" face, which is usually shaggier and less elegant, as we commonly see in woolen cloths and linens. But I do not affirm this for certain.

**He-goats of the goats.**) It is customary in the Hebrew language to...

### FROM CHAPTER XX.

<margin>10</margin> *And one shall have possessed the private parts of the other.*) that is, they shall have had intercourse between themselves. It is in the Hebrew, "they shall have seen the private parts" <note>original: *Verenda uiderint*</note>. But "to see" is often put for "to attain" or "to perceive": as "to see corruption," or "to see the land promised by God."

### FROM CHAPTER XXI.

*Not even in the leader's.*) A single letter seems transposed in the Hebrew; it should be read as *be-Baal Ammi* <note>original Hebrew: בבעל עמי</note> not *be-Baal Peor* <note>original Hebrew: בבעל פעור</note>; for Jerome also translates it thus, and the sense requires it, since here the precepts are given not <margin>20</margin> to the leader, but to the priests.

### FROM CHAPTER XXIII.

*The warning Sabbath.*) I derived this adjective from "warning" <note>original: *monendo*</note>, in the same way the Latins called Juno "Moneta" <note>The Roman goddess Juno Moneta was the "Advisor" or "Warner"; the Roman mint was located in her temple, which is where the word "money" originates.</note>.

*The fruit of the peach-tree, of palms, the spadices, etc.*) In this place I have followed Josephus, who had often even seen these things with his own eyes. He, therefore, in the *Antiquities* Book 3, Chapter 10, writes of them thus: "carrying in their hands branches of myrtle and willow, along with a frond of palm <margin>30</margin> prepared with a basket, and apples of those things which are on the plant" <note>original Greek: φθέντας ἐν ταῖς χερσὶν ἀιφνιδίως μυρσίνης, καὶ ἰτέας σὺν λάρνακι φοίνικος πεποιημένης, καὶ μήλων ὧν τῇ ποίᾳ προσόντων</note>. He says: "Bearing in their hands a branch of myrtle and willow, with a prepared palm frond, with the fruit of the peach-tree adhering." In Hebrew, a "noble tree" is called for the citron, but the myrtle "leafy": because this one has eternal leaves, and the other, besides, has fruits, with others always growing beneath. Although the same Josephus also records the use of citrons <note>original: *citrijs*</note> in *Antiquities* Book 13, Chapter 21, which he perhaps took from 2 Esdras 8 <note>Commonly known as Nehemiah 8</note> where this place is cited: in which place of Esdras, *Hadas* seems to be the citron, and mention is made there of <margin>40</margin> olive and cypress, which are not commemorated here.

# ON NUMBERS.

### FROM CHAPTER XIII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial "A" featuring floral scrolls and a bird/animal figure within a square border.</image-desc>
**A**t the river Eshcol.) [The word used] does not always signify a torrent, but often a perennial river. Therefore Moses uses this name elsewhere when speaking of the Arnon, which Josephus calls a *potamon* <note>original Greek: ποταμὸν</note>, that is, a river, in *Antiquities* Book 4, Chapter 4. And in 1 Maccabees 5, the same is called both a *cheimarrhos* <note>original Greek: χείμαῤῥος, a winter-torrent</note> and a *potamos* <note>river</note>.

### FROM CHAPTER XXI.

<margin>50</margin> *For Ar is the boundary of the Ammonites.*) In the Hebrew it is read *Ar* <note>original Hebrew: ער</note>, but erroneously, as I conjecture: both because it is read here in the Greek as *Asyr* <note>original Greek: ἄσυρ</note>, which ends in *r*; and because in Deuteronomy 2, the same place is called Ar, placed between the Moabites and Ammonites, in these words: "Today you are to pass the boundary of the Moabites, namely Ar."

*To the rivers of Arnon.*) that is, to the Arnon river: as in Virgil, "To the rivers of Thermodon" (*Aeneid* 11). Just as in Psalm 74, the Jordan is <margin>60</margin> called "rivers": in the way poets often say "mouths" and "necks" for "mouth" and "neck."

<column-break/>

*You have perished, people of Chemosh, whose males are also scattered.*) In the Hebrew it is literally: "You have perished, people of Chemosh, he gave his sons, etc." But there is a switching of persons, such as in Genesis 49, where Jacob addresses Joseph now in the second, now in the third person. Furthermore, regarding "He gave his sons": the singular number is used for the plural, "they gave": which is to be interpreted through the passive, "they were given": a thing which the Latins do through the plural <margin>10</margin> only, saying *perhibent* (they maintain), *aiunt* (they say), *ferunt* (they report), instead of *perhibetur* (it is maintained), *fertur* (it is reported). Moses spoke in the same way often elsewhere, and below in Chapter 23, and Numbers 35, which same thing occurs in 2 Kings 11. But as for what follows, "Yet their light is Heshbon": it is said poetically, standing for the capital of the kingdom and the strongest city.

### FROM CHAPTER XXII.

*On which journey of his, God being angry.*) God's mind was that Balaam should bless the Hebrews; therefore he had ordered him to go with this intention. But Balaam hoped that he would curse them, as he later <margin>20</margin> showed enough. The journey undertaken with this intention was displeasing to God.

*Have I ever been accustomed to do such a thing to you?*) [The donkey speaks:] "Since I do this contrary to my custom, you ought to think that some graver cause underlies it, and search for that, rather than strike me unjustly." (That journey was undertaken against my [God's] will.) So Josephus interprets it: "the ways having happened contrary to the mind of God" <note>original Greek: τῶν ὁδῶν παρὰ γνώμην θεοῦ γενομένων</note>.

### FROM CHAPTER XXIII.

*Behold a people that shall dwell apart.*) that is, the most <margin>30</margin> excellent of all, and therefore to be separated from all others, and singular. "Who [can count] the dust of the Jacobites?" that is, of the innumerable multitude.

### FROM CHAPTER XXIV.

*He who saw the things pre-signified by the Almighty.*) *Mnachash* <note>original Hebrew: מנחש</note> when said of a man, signifies a vision, and a fore-feeling of a thing, and fore-knowledge: but when said of God, it signifies a prediction and a pre-signification (if I may speak so). And in this way it is often put in the prophets for prophecy, by the same reasoning that *Mnachash* <note>Hebrew root for divination or omen</note> in a man is to pray well, but in God <margin>40</margin> is to make fruitful and to prosper.

*From whose pipe.*) <note>A reference to Numbers 24:7, often translated as "water shall flow from his buckets."</note> that is, from whom offspring shall arise, which shall increase vehemently, like trees in moist earth. And whose king shall overcome Agag, that is the kings of the Amalekites: for they say they were so called, as the Pharaohs of Egypt.

*When a fleet [comes] from the borders of the Kittim.*) Who the Kittim are, Josephus declares in *Antiquities* Book 1, Chapter 7, with these words: "Chethimus held the island of Chethima; it is now called Cyprus, from which both all islands <margin>50</margin> and a good part of the maritime regions are named Chethim by the Hebrews." One of the cities of Cyprus supports my speech, which was able to retain the name. For it is called *Cetios* by those who made its name Greek, not even thus avoiding the name of Chethim. Thus says Josephus. In Isaiah <margin>59</margin> chapter 23, Alexander [the Great], the conqueror of Tyre, is also said to come from the Kittim. And the same Alexander in 1 Maccabees 1 is said to have risen from the land of Chetim, though he was a Macedonian. And in Chapter 8 of the same book, one reads "Perseus king of the Kittians," that is, Perseus the king of the Ceteans: which is written concerning Perseus, the king of the Macedonians.

# ANNOTATIONS.

From these things it is clear that the Kittim <note>original: "Cittimos"</note> are called Greeks or Macedonians. I also recall having read somewhere that the name of the Macedonians was derived from "Cethim," with a syllable added at the beginning and the letter *t* changed to *d* due to their similarity.

### FROM CHAPTER XXVII.

*In their eyes, command him.*) <note>Numbers 27:19</note> That is, give him precepts and teach him. Cicero spoke in this manner in *On Duties*, Book 1, with these words: "So that a mind well-formed by nature is unwilling to obey anyone, except one who instructs, or one who, for the sake of utility, commands justly and lawfully."

### FROM CHAPTER XXX.

*All her vows shall be void.*) <note>Numbers 30:5</note> If a father can dissolve a vow made to God by his daughter, then surely those today do not judge well who deny that betrothals made without the knowledge of parents can be voided by the parents—unless, perhaps, a promise made to a human being binds more strictly than one made to God.

### FROM CHAPTER XXXIII.

*For the western boundary you shall have the sea.*) <note>Numbers 33:5</note> In the Hebrew it is "the great sea," <note>original: *mare magnum*</note> because the Hebrews call both the sea and a lake by the same name; this was specified so it would not be understood as a lake. For us, who call a lake by its own proper name, it is not necessary to say "great sea," but "sea" is enough. The same occurs elsewhere, and in Joshua 1.

# ON DEUTERONOMY.

### FROM CHAPTER II.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'V' depicting a figure seated in a landscape with trees.</image-desc>
*Where he had provided you a safe journey.*) In the Hebrew it is, "Who knew your journey." But I have rendered the sense, not the words. For God is said to "know" those whom He preserves as His own, just as He is said to "ignore" those whom He allows to perish as strangers. Thus, in Psalm 1, He is said to "know" the way—that is, the character and deeds—of the good; the opposite of which is said of the wicked: that their way shall perish. Likewise, in 1 Samuel 2 <note>original: "1. Reg. 2." refers to 1 Kings in the Vulgate, which is 1 Samuel in modern Bibles.</note>, the sons of Eli are said "not to know Jehovah," meaning they despised and did not care for Him.

### FROM CHAPTER III.

*We took the land on this side of the Jordan from the two kings of the Amorites.*) The word *be-eber* <note>original Hebrew: בעבר</note> signifies "across" or "beyond." But since Moses is in that very land of which he speaks, there is no doubt that he calls it "this side of the Jordan" <note>original: *cis-iordaniana*</note>. In the same way, if we speak of that part of Gaul which the Romans call "Transalpine" (across the Alps), we would undoubtedly call it "Cisalpine" (this side of the Alps) according to our own custom, not "Transalpine" according to the custom of the Romans—unless we were speaking from their books. Thus Moses cannot call Bashan "across the Jordan" unless he speaks as if he were already in Canaan, which is absurd since he is speaking here in his own person. Otherwise, he would call Lebanon "this side of the Jordan," yet a little after this passage he says it is "across the Jordan," using the same word as here. Therefore, it is necessary either that the same word signifies both, or that there is a scribal error, *l* <note>ל</note> for *m-eber* <note>מעבר</note>, which means "on this side"—unless *ve-halah* <note>והלאה</note> is added, for then it signifies "beyond." This same word is often

<meta>catchword: pe (often)</meta>

<column-break/>

# ANNOTATIONS.

often ambiguous in Joshua and Deuteronomy 5. I follow the sense.

### FROM CHAPTER VI.

*And you shall swear by His name.*) To swear is to religiously summon the witness of truth. He who swears by another besides God fashions another god for himself—one who would be the truth and who would know all things. This is wicked, since God alone knows those things which we affirm by swearing. Therefore, one must swear by God alone. <margin>10</margin> Nor is God more offended by a holy oath than a good man is when he is summoned as a witness; rather, He is pleased. But this must not be done "in vain"—that is, not in a false matter, for that would be to make God a liar; nor in a trivial matter, for that would be to despise God; nor if you are believed without an oath, or if the matter does not require it, for that would be superfluous; nor if the matter can be proven by human means, for that would be to reject the method of testimony given by God.

### FROM CHAPTER VII.

<margin>20</margin>
*And without doubt repaying them in person rewards worthy of their deeds.*) This passage is translated by others to say that God avenges the wicked "immediately," without delay. But that is foreign to the nature of God, who is "slow to anger," and the reality itself cries out that the wicked are not punished immediately—a fact which many others, including Jeremiah, complain about. Furthermore, the word *ya-achar* <note>original Hebrew: יאחר</note> does not properly signify "to delay," but rather what can be called *hysterein* in Greek <note>meaning to fall short or be lacking</note>. In Latin, it is expressed by two <margin>30</margin> negatives in this way: "If you make a vow, do not *not* pay it," that is, pay it without fail. As it is in Deuteronomy 23. and in Habakkuk 2, it is read: "If he tarries, wait for him, for he will come and will not *ya-achar*" <note>original Hebrew: לא יאחר</note>—that is, without doubt. In French it is well expressed: *Et n'y faudra point* <note>"And he will not fail/miss in this."</note>. For if it were rendered "He will come, he will not delay," it would be contrary to what was placed before: "If he tarries, wait for him."

### FROM CHAPTER VIII.

*That man does not live by bread alone, etc.*) <margin>40</margin> Although God naturally nourishes men with bread, He is not so beholden to bread that He cannot feed them without it if there is a need. For what He has promised, He provides even when nature resists. Thus He sustained them with manna; thus Moses by His presence; thus Elijah by the raven; thus that poor woman by the multiplied oil—so that we may understand that our life is not placed in bread, but in the promise of God and the fulfillment of that promise.
*A land abounding with rivers of water, springs, and lakes.*) <margin>50</margin> What I translate as "lakes," in the Hebrew is "depths" <note>original: *profundis*</note>. However, he calls the "depths" quiet waters, such as ponds and lakes, which we see called "seas" in the Gospel after the Hebrew custom.

### FROM CHAPTER X.

*And His name is to be celebrated.*) The word *ul'obdo* <note>original Hebrew: ולעבדו</note> signifies both "to pray well" and "to celebrate." But if it signified "to pray well" here, the speech would first of all be cut short. Secondly, since the chief part of the Levitical office is to praise God (as found in 1 Chronicles 16), it is not <margin>60</margin> consistent that in this place—in which the office of the Levites is specifically discussed—no mention would be made of this matter. This was the reason I translated it thus. And others also translate it with the same meaning in 1 Chronicles 23.

*A prophet from the midst of you.*) Since my presence...

...you cannot bear my presence, henceforth I will no longer speak to you myself, except through prophets, as I do now through Moses.

### FROM CHAPTER XVIII.

<margin>*Except if he has anything.*</margin> ) If that Levite, having sold his paternal goods, has acquired money from them, he may enjoy that money as his own property; and in addition, he may enjoy in common the portions owed to him from his ministry. For it is not fair that, as far as he serves, he should live off his paternal goods. For he who serves in sacred things ought to live from sacred things. <term>ממכר <note>original: mimkar</note></term> moreover signifies a thing sold, as in Ezekiel 7, and it is used for the price of a thing sold, just as <term>מקנה <note>original: miqnah</note></term> is used for a thing purchased: Leviticus 25.

### FROM CHAPTER XXI.

<margin>*As if the trees of the countryside were men.*</margin> ) The law of war is: *To spare the subjected, and to war down the proud.* <note>The author quotes Virgil's Aeneid 6.853, a famous Roman principle of governance and warfare.</note> Trees are subjected; they do not fight back against you in a siege as men do. You ought, therefore, to spare them.

<margin>*To the court of that place.*</margin> ) In the Hebrew it is: "to the gate." But because the courts were located in the gates of cities, "gate" is used to mean "court." Just as today they call the court of the King of the Turks "the Porte" <note>original: "Portam"; a reference to the Sublime Porte, the central government of the Ottoman Empire.</note>.

### FROM CHAPTER XXII.

<margin>*Protect its roof with a parapet.*</margin> ) In Palestine, roofs are flat. He commands them to be surrounded by a certain enclosure and fence (which I translate as *lorica* or "parapet") so that no one falls from there. For men often spend time on them, which is understood even from the saying of Christ, who commands the Apostles that what they are taught in darkness, they should preach from the rooftops; this is also evident in Joshua, concerning Rahab.

<margin>*Lest both the yield of the seeds you sowed and the fruit of the vineyard be consecrated.*</margin> ) They used to consecrate fruits by pouring out the firstfruits to God. But if the same field were planted with both vines and grain, its yield would be neither a harvest nor a vintage; therefore, it could be consecrated to God under the name of neither, but as a mixture. This is like the mule among animals; such confusion displeases God, who loves simplicity.

### FROM CHAPTER XXIII.

<margin>*Or the price for the admission of a dog.*</margin> ) I have followed the interpretation of Josephus, who translates it as <term>by those very people</term> <note>original Greek: ὑπ' ἐκείνων αὐτῶν</note>. Otherwise, it is read literally as "the price of a dog." <note>This refers to the prohibition against bringing the earnings of prostitution—metaphorically called "dog's pay"—into the sanctuary.</note>

### FROM CHAPTER XXIX.

<margin>*The hidden things belong to Jehovah our God.*</margin> ) We must obey without hesitation those things which God has declared to us. If the reasons for them are obscure, or if something deeper lies hidden in them, or if they seem absurd to us (being dull like smoke), we must nevertheless grant so much to God that we do it because he commanded it. Nor should we seek his will from anywhere else than from his law. For if there are more hidden things (I believe Moses here hints at the secrets of the Gospel and other things which lie hidden even in the law, which God indeed declared to Moses but commanded him to hide, as is found in 4 Esdras 8), God keeps those in his own power, to be brought forth when it pleases him.

### FROM CHAPTER XXXII.

<margin>*And indeed I had determined to so scatter them.*</margin> ) I would utterly abolish the race of Israelites on account of their crimes, were I not afraid that their enemies, through whom I would destroy them, would claim the glory of this deed not for me, but for themselves. For the enemies do not have so much reason and prudence as to think it could not happen 

<column-break/>

that so many Israelites could be overcome by so few enemies (which is nonetheless what will happen when I punish the Israelites) unless they had been not only abandoned by me, their God, but even subjected and broken. Especially since not even the enemies themselves could say that our God—that is, me (for there is a change of person here, as if the people themselves are speaking, not God)—is so weak that it could seem that the Israelites were destroyed by the gods of the enemies while I was unconquered. For they know that I led my people away against the will of the Egyptian gods (if they were gods at all) and did those unheard-of things despite everyone's opposition. For their gods are such as appears from the morals and institutions of the men themselves—morals which are no less wicked than those of the Sodomites of old. Someone might say: How does it happen then, that while your people are so afflicted, you allow the enemies to go unpunished? Truly, I know what, and why, and for how long I shall act. What is now known to me alone will then be understood by others as well, when I again favor the Israelites as they perform penance, and when I take vengeance on the enemies who have grown insolent with success. These are the words of Moses, which will be more easily understood if they are compared with the previous chapter, in which he threatens the same future events in the same order.

### FROM CHAPTER XXXIII.

If we remember here that he who is called "Jehovah" is Christ the Son of God—as we showed in Deuteronomy 3—we will understand this passage more easily. This is the meaning: Jehovah, that is, the Son of God sent by God, who is one with God the Father, came from Sinai; for he appeared there and gave the law. <margin>*He rose from Seir,*</margin> where he also spoke to Moses and commanded the bronze serpent to be made. <margin>*He shone forth from Mount Paran,*</margin> where he promised the quails to Moses; <margin>*and he came on account of the holy legions,*</margin> that is, on account of the holy people of the Israelites. He held for those legions the "fire of discipline," that is, a fiery discipline at his right hand, meaning he brought the law to them with much fire. <margin>*Truly a lover of men.*</margin> For his love must be wondrous, he who being God did not disdain to dwell among men. <margin>*All his holy ones,*</margin> namely the Israelites who are in his faith and protection, <margin>*are in your hand,*</margin> O God his Father. <margin>*And indeed they prostrate themselves at your feet, they are suppliants to you, and*</margin> they hang upon you, receiving through him, your Son, your words; for whatever law he delivered to Moses, he received from you. Moses, furthermore, was not the author of the law, but its instructor and master, who delivered the law received from Jehovah to the republic of the Jacobites <note>The descendants of Jacob/Israel</note> to be kept. This Moses was king among the upright—that is, among the Israelites approved by God—while he gathered their heads, organized the republic, and punished the guilty, which are the works of a king. As for my translation <term>On account of the legions</term>, in the Hebrew it is <term>מרבבה <note>original: meribebah</note></term>, a word which properly signifies myriads, that is, tens of thousands; but it is used for any great number and multitude, just as in Latin we say "a thousand times" for "very often." Moreover, I interpret <term>מרבבה</term> as <term>On account of</term>, so that it signifies the cause and utility, in the same way the Latin *ex* is used when we say "it is for your benefit" <note>original: "Ex re tua est"</note> or "to act for the republic" <note>original: "Ex republica facere"</note>, meaning for the utility of the republic. Ezekiel spoke in this manner in chapter 45 with these words: <term>וכן תעשה בשבעה בחדש מאיש שגה ומפתי וכפרתם את הבית <note>original: "And so you shall do on the seventh day of the month for every one that erreth, and for him that is simple: so shall ye reconcile the house."</note></term> that is: And so you shall do on the seventh day of the month...

## ANNOTATIONS.

...on the day of the month for the man who has sinned through imprudence or through error, you shall pray for the house. That is, you will do this when you offer a sacrifice on account of a person's lapse through imprudence. And in **Deuteronomy 17** <margin>Deut. 17</margin> <term>משמרו את השבע <note>original: mishmaro eth ha-shavuah</note></term> that is, "on account of keeping the oath." Likewise in Isaiah 7 and Psalm 59. <margin>Psalm 59 & Latin</margin> In Latin, as found in Cicero: "to weep *about* <note>Latin: *de*</note> the death of a son." And in Varro’s *On Agriculture*, book 3: "Going *about* <note>Latin: *de*</note> the controversies," meaning "on account of the controversies." 

However, where I translate, *He taking from your words*, although the Hebrew uses a future verb rather than a participle, it should be known that Hebrew verbs are often used in place of participles, especially the future tense when they are placed without a conjunction, because that language lacks a future participle. This happens often elsewhere, as in Genesis 49 where Jacob blesses Joseph, and in Numbers 23. John imitated this in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> when he said <term>ὁ ὢν, καὶ ὁ ἦν <note>original Greek: "the one who is and the one who was"</note></term>, where the article *ho* <note>the</note> is used with the verb in place of a participle. 

Where I translate *the upright*, the Hebrew has <term>ישרון <note>original: Jeshurun</note></term>, a singular used for a plural—a Hebrew idiom—which signifies the straight, the just, and (as I said) the upright: that is, the Israelites, as they are also called in Isaiah 44. Regarding what is said here of Reuben, it was explained in the Testament of Jacob. Regarding Judah, this is the meaning: *The tribe of Judah will be warlike, and it alone will dare to bring war to its enemies, if it hopes that it will return safely to its own people through God's protection.* Thus, let "bring back" stand for "return," just as in Hebrew "to go" is not infrequently used for "to return." 

Regarding Levi, he speaks thus: *Your integrity and clarity* (he alludes to these words, which were inscribed on the High Priest's breastpiece <note>The Urim and Thummim, often translated as "Lights and Perfections" or "Clarity and Integrity."</note>), that is, the uprightness of your character and the excellence of your teaching, by both of which you ought to shine before men, is situated in your merciful man, that is, in Jehovah, who especially favors you through his mercy by granting the priesthood. You provoked Him at Massah, and you quarreled with Him at the Waters of Strife <note>Referring to the events at Meribah where Moses struck the rock.</note> (for Moses and Aaron, who were Levites, did not keep faith with God when they brought water out of the rock; for since they ought to have given the glory for that matter to God, they sinned in that they said: *Listen, you rebels, shall we bring water out of this rock for you?* For they ought to have spoken like Paul, who says: *Not I, but Christ in me*). This "merciful man" of yours, who is Jehovah-Christ, values obedience more than kinship; and He regards those as kinsmen who obey your words, O God (for there is a change of person here). Just as Christ himself teaches in **Matthew 12** <margin>Mat. 12</margin>: *Whoever does the will of my Father, he is my brother and sister and mother.* 

But concerning the clarity and integrity of the priests situated in Christ, it is worthwhile to consider something written by Josephus in *Antiquities*, Book 4, to this effect: Of the gems which I said above the High Priest wears on his shoulders (they were sardonyxes), one of them, whenever God was present at the divine service, used to shine—specifically the one that adorned the right shoulder—with a brilliance breaking forth and appearing from a great distance, even though that luster was not previously in the gem. This is truly a wonder to those who have not used their wisdom to hold divine matters in contempt. But I will say something even more marvelous: for through the twelve gems which the High Priest wears sewn to his breast <note>The "Essen" or Breastplate of Judgment.</note>, God would signify victory to those about to engage in 

<column-break/>

battle. For such a great splendor flashed from them, even before the army moved, that it was known to the whole multitude that God was present to help. Whence the Greeks, who hold our customs in high esteem because they have nothing to say against them, call the "Essen" the *Rationale* <note>A term for the breastplate emphasizing its role in revealing God's reason or judgment.</note>. However, both the "Essen" and the sardonyx ceased to shine two hundred years before I composed this work, because God was indignant at the violation of the laws. Thus says Josephus. From this, it can be understood that that splendor ceased around the time of Christ (who is the true light of the Levites). For Josephus wrote in the thirteenth year of the reign of Domitian Caesar. 

What follows is clear; for it teaches that the duty of the Levites is to teach and to perform sacred rites. Regarding what is said of Benjamin, that God will dwell between his shoulders, it signifies that God's dwelling and Temple would be within the borders of the Benjaminites, which indeed happened. 

Of Joseph, he thus prophesies: *Blessed by the gift of Jehovah be his land.* In the Hebrew it is: *fortunate by Jehovah be his land*, that is, it has Jehovah's favor. Just as we say in Latin, "happy in her offspring is the woman who has given birth," meaning one who has such offspring; or "happy are you with such a patron." Then he shows wherein that happiness of the land is situated: namely, in the climate of the sky, in the dew, and the rain; in the goodness of the soil; in the sun, in which is a fruit-bearing power; and in the moon, which aids the ripening of fruits, while with a softer and "imperfect" power (to use Pliny’s words) it releases so much moisture and even increases it, which the rays of the sun then consume. And the moon, illuminated by the sun (as Cicero says), brings about the heavy cycles of birth and the maturity of procreation. *In the head of the ancient mountains*, that is, the immovable ones (spoken in a poetic manner); *in the produce of the hills*, that is, in those things which are born on the mountains and hills; *in the favor of the dweller in the bush*, that is, Jehovah, whom the dying Jacob called the shepherd and the stone of Israel. I interpret "favor" as <term>חנני <note>original: chen/chanani</note></term>, which in the New Testament is usually called <term>χάρις <note>original Greek: charis, meaning grace</note></term>. 

Furthermore, because he calls his firstborn a "comely ox," it signifies that the Ephraimites will be warlike, the metaphor being drawn from the ox and the "monoceros" <note>A one-horned animal, often translated as a unicorn or wild ox/re'em.</note>. Then, when he mentions the "legions of Ephraim" and the "cohortes of Manasseh," he speaks significantly, placing Ephraim before Manasseh in number, just as Jacob had done. I have expressed the matter in the Latin fashion, which in Greek could be expressed word-for-word by "myriads" and "thousands." Nor does it matter that the word "legion" does not signify precisely ten thousand, or "cohort" exactly one thousand. For a fixed number is not set here, but words are used where one signifies many and the other fewer. 

The Zebulunites shall be famous abroad, as they are inhabitants of the sea and practitioners of seafaring, while the Issacharites remain at home. They shall invite the peoples to the mountain: for they will be a maritime people and will abound in maritime riches (for this is what he calls "maritime abundance" and "treasures hidden in the sand," that is, on the shore). Invited by these riches, men of foreign nations will have commerce with them and, by custom, will be drawn to the mountain, that is, Jerusalem, where Sion the mountain of God is, so that they may perform there the rightful sacrifices, as those handed down by God, since all others are...

...lest they be impious and polluted, and therefore unjust. Thanks are to be given to the one who expands Gad, that is, to God, by whose protection the Gadites repel their neighbors with military force and enlarge their borders. 

As for why I translate the word as *Grates* <note>meaning "thanks" or "blessings"</note>, in the Hebrew it is <term>ברוך <note>original: baruch</note></term>, which others translate as *blessed*, following the Greeks who use <term>εὐλογητός <note>original: eulogetos</note></term>. But this word often signifies the act of giving thanks: which happens when someone is praised and blessed because of some benefit received. This is clear from the Gospel of Luke; where Mark uses the word <term>εὐλογήσας <note>original Greek: "having blessed"</note></term> regarding what Christ said at the Last Supper, Luke uses <term>εὐχαριστήσας <note>original Greek: "having given thanks"</note></term>. 

As soon as these people noticed that the lands of Og and Sihon were suitable for them—for those who would live in peace and command—they went to Moses and the leaders of the people so that they might obtain those lands. They fulfilled their promise once the Israelites had been brought into their own possessions. Dan (that is, the tribe of Dan) shall be more noble than a lion. Naphtali is dear to the Lord <note>The original Latin uses "Iovæ," a common early modern Latinization for the Hebrew name of God, Yahweh</note>. Asher is rich in progeny, dear to his brothers, and abounds in oil, iron, and bronze: his strength shall be in proportion to his age, so that just as Asher held a certain place in age among his brothers, his descendants may hold that same position of strength among the tribes. 

What follows pertains to all the tribes collectively. None is to be compared with the God of the Israelites: who, although He dwells in the heavens, does not look down on earthly things in such a way that He does not always reach down His arms to His land. That is, He is present with the Israelites, and once their enemies are driven out, He places them in safety. He ensures that Jacob casts his eye toward a fertile land—that is, that he sees a fertile land and takes possession of it (for as we have noted before, "to see" is often used for "to possess"). Happy are the people of the Israelites, and clearly incomparable, you who have such a defender in the Lord, who is the sword of your highness: that is, He who by His protection raised you to that height and dignity, so that your enemies are subjected to you. The Hebrew word is <term>נחשׁ <note>original: nakhash</note></term>, which can be well explained in Greek as <term>σφάλλονται <note>original: sphallontai</note></term>, meaning "they shall succumb unwillingly."

## ON JOSHUA.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'H' with floral flourishes and a grotesque mask at the base.</image-desc>
THAT THIS book was not written by Joshua can be proved by a single argument: that in the tenth chapter, the *Book of the Upright* <note>The "Book of Jashar," a lost collection of ancient Hebrew poetry and history</note> is cited to prove the history of the sun being ordered to stand still. Certainly, that book could not have been cited by Joshua, since it was written after the time of David. For in the first chapter of the first book of Kings <note>modern 2 Samuel 1:18</note>, the history of David is cited from the *Book of the Upright*. 

Another argument is that in chapter 15, things are written about Achsah, the daughter of Caleb, which took place after the death of Joshua, as is recorded in the first chapter of Judges. From these points, it should be clear that neither this book was written by Joshua, nor the *Book of the Upright* by Moses, but later—or certainly not before the time of David.

### FROM CHAPTER VI.

*Seven trumpets of rams' horns.*) <term>יובל <note>original: yobel</note></term> is an adjective by which the sound of the trumpet is marked. From this, "Jubilee" is named, because in that year liberty was proclaimed by the blast of the trumpet. From this, the Latin verb *Iubilare* <note>to jubilate or shout for joy</note> seems to be derived. Since I did not have a better word, I used "trumpets" as an adjective. For if I had said "clanging"

<column-break/>

instead of "clangorous" (to speak thus), the speech would not have lacked ambiguity.

### FROM CHAPTER XX.

*Until he has pleaded his case in the council.*) After he has first explained his case alone to the elders at the gate, he shall indeed be received, but on the condition that if a redeemer of blood <note>an "avenger of blood," a relative seeking legal retribution for a killing</note> should come, he shall present himself for judgment, and before that judgment, he shall be safe in the city. But if either the accuser does not come, or does not prevail in the case, the slayer may live there until the death of the high priest.

## ON THE BOOK
## OF JUDGES.

### FROM CHAPTER V.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'I' depicting a figure in a robe, possibly a biblical judge, seated and holding an object.</image-desc>
IN the valley you were the last, Benjamin. (The text reads <term>במעמלק <note>original: be-Amalek</note></term>, that is, "among the Amalekites," but the meaning cannot stand. The Greek interpreter seems to have read it differently, as he translates it as <term>ἐν κοιλάδι <note>original: en koiladi</note></term>, "in the valley," which fits the sense of the passage. For a little later, Barak is said to have been sent into the valley where the battle was fought. Therefore, this is the meaning of this passage: the Benjamites were not present in this battle, but their fellow tribesmen the Ephraimites and Manassites were, who arose from Machir, the son of Manasseh, and were worthy to rule thereafter; likewise the learned leaders of Zebulun, and the men of Issachar under the leadership of Barak.

### FROM CHAPTER VIII.

*He assigned hunters to them.*) In the Hebrew it reads <term>ירע <note>original: yara</note></term>, which makes no sense, or at least a forced one. A little earlier, <term>ורשע <note>original: ve-rasha</note></term> had been placed, meaning "and I will crush." Therefore, since the other words are repeated here in the same way, I think it should be read as <term>וירעשׁ <note>original: vayar'ash</note></term> <note>meaning "he caused a thundering or shaking sound"</note>.

### FROM CHAPTER XI.

*You are the one who disturbs me.*) In the Hebrew it is, "You are among my disturbers," that is, you disturb me. On this manner of speaking, see the notes on Psalm 54.

### FROM CHAPTER XII.

*He was buried in the towns of Gilead.*) Because he does not specify the town by name, he speaks using the plural number. Thus in Genesis 19, Lot is called an "inhabitant of the cities," although he was in one. And Cicero said, "I was in these places."

### FROM CHAPTER XIV.

*He encountered a lion.*) I interpret <term>כפיר אריות <note>original: kephir arioth</note></term> as "a lion," just as <term>שׂעיר העזים <note>original: se'ir ha-izim</note></term> is "a male goat," of which there are many examples in the Hebrew language. For a little later, the lion is called by a single name.

*He had been the arranger of that very alliance.*) I have followed Josephus, who translates this as <term>νυμφοστόλον <note>original: nymphostolon</note></term>; and the old translator, who uses "bridal attendant"; and the Greek, who uses <term>νυμφαγωγόν <note>original: nymphagogon</note></term> <note>meaning a "best man" or wedding-leader</note>.

### FROM CHAPTER XV.

*With a heavy and great slaughter in a certain tract.*) Literally it reads: "He struck them hip upon thigh." Since I could elicit no fitting meaning from this, I followed Josephus, who translates it as: <term>πολλοὺς ἐν τῷ πεδίῳ τῶν παλαιστίνων ἀποκτείνας <note>original Greek: "having killed many in the plain of the Palestinians"</note></term>. For <term>שׁוק <note>original: shok</note></term> signifies not only a thigh, but also a region.

<header>ANNOTATIONS.</header>

**The jawbone of an ass, a donkey-like ass.**) <note>original Hebrew: חמור חמרתים</note>: A "donkey-like ass" is spoken of in the same way we noted that one might say a "goaty goat" or a "bully bull." It is similar to Judges 5: <note>original Hebrew: רחם רחמתים</note> "a girl-like girl," that is, a young maiden. This is an elegant form of repetition, especially common in proverbs or poetic sentences. I do not find it pleasing to follow the clever Jewish interpreters here who interpret the word as "a heap." If we did, the sentence would be both incomplete and less elegant. Furthermore, that word is not written with the same vowels when it signifies "a heap," except in this specific passage—if we are to believe their traditions. <margin>10</margin> But since the meaning is ambiguous, it cannot be used as evidence; nor should a forced interpretation push aside the literal one.

### FROM CHAPTER XVII.

The events that follow from here to the end of the entire book actually took place before there were governors in Israel whom they call "judges." This is evident from the history itself: in chapter 18, the Danites are seeking <margin>20</margin> their inheritance; and in the same chapter, the priest is Jonathan, the grandson of Moses, who could not have lived so long after the period of the Judges; and in chapter 20, we see Phinehas, the son of Eleazar. Furthermore, in chapter 19, it is said that the Israelites do not dwell in Jerusalem, even though they are said to have occupied and inhabited it in the first chapter. Add to this that Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian</note> narrates the events written in chapter 19 before the events written earlier in the book.

### FROM CHAPTER XVIII.

**The most contemptible of their soldiers.**) <note>original Hebrew: בני חיל</note> This does not always mean "brave men," but simply soldiers, as is clear from <margin>30</margin> many places in the Book of Numbers and 2 Samuel 17. The most "contemptible" (or low-ranking) were sent so that they might more easily deceive the enemy.

**Because they were far from the Sidonians.**) From this, it appears they were either clients or certainly allies of the Sidonians, by whom they could not be defended because of the great distance between their locations.

# ON RUTH.

### FROM CHAPTER I.

**The KINDNESS you have shown to the dead.**) To use kindness toward <margin>40</margin> the dead means to do good to the relatives or friends of the deceased for their sake.

### FROM CHAPTER III.

**He came into the town to the hearth.**) In the Hebrew, the word "came" is masculine <note>suggesting "he" rather than "she"</note>, but I suspect this is an error, both based on the context and from the ancient version <note>the Vulgate</note>, just as <margin>50</margin> in the following chapter, "the redeemer" is erroneously read instead of "the redemption." <note>original: הגאל pro הגאל—likely a note on vowel points or spelling variants in the Hebrew</note>

# ON THE BOOKS OF KINGS.

The first two books of Kings are called "Samuel" among the Hebrews; the latter two are called "Kings." I have decided to keep the <margin>60</margin> Latin title. For it is absurd to ascribe a book to Samuel that records events that happened after Samuel’s death.

<column-break/>

<page-num>50</page-num>
<header>FROM CHAPTER I.</header>

**To the Lord mighty in battle.**) In the Hebrew it is, "The Lord of Hosts." They are called "hosts" (armies) not only because of soldiers, but because everything in existence is an instrument which God may use, just as commanders use soldiers. God uses all things according to His will. Therefore, "the Lord mighty in battle," or "powerful in arms," is He who commands all things. The nature of this authority is illustrated by that Centurion in the Gospel who demonstrated to Christ that he held authority over his soldiers; whatever he commanded them, <margin>10</margin> they carried out.

### FROM CHAPTER VI.

**Golden [images]; the likenesses which they, etc.**) In the Hebrew it is <note>original: כלי</note>, which signifies "vessels" or "tools," but it has a broader meaning, like the Greek word <note>original: σκεῦος—skeuos</note>. Therefore, since he is speaking here of likenesses (statues), I did not dare to translate it as "vessels" or "utensils," because it does not seem that statues can be signified by those specific words.

**And at that great stone.**) The text reads <note>original: אבל—abel, meaning mourning</note>. But since mention of a stone was made previously, and I do not understand how the Ark could be placed upon "mourning," <margin>20</margin> and the Seventy <note>the Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament</note> translated it as "stone" <note>original: λίθον—lithon</note>, I think the reading should be <note>original: אבן—eben, meaning stone</note>.

### FROM CHAPTER VIII.

**These tribunes, these centurions.**) In the Hebrew it is "leaders of thousands" and "leaders of fifties." However, a fixed number is not necessarily prescribed here; and one must speak to Latins in the Latin manner. Wherever a specific number must be defined, one may call them "half-centurions." For one must be bold when <margin>30</margin> necessity demands it.

### FROM CHAPTER XII.

**It is the wheat harvest; I will call upon the Lord, and it shall thunder.**) That thunder at the time of the harvest was beyond the course of nature, and therefore a miracle, because thunder usually happens only in the spring and autumn. The reason for this is that thunder is stirred up by the conflict of hot and cold, which conflict can happen neither in winter (when cold dominates) nor in summer (when heat dominates), <margin>40</margin> especially in sweltering lands such as Syria. For among us [in Europe], thunder in the summer is not rare.

### FROM CHAPTER XIII.

**Saul entered upon his kingdom, etc.**) Among the Hebrews, it reads literally: "Saul, the son of a year when he began to reign, and he reigned two years." Some interpret this to mean: "Saul had been king for one year, and when he had reigned two years, etc.," so that the first number refers to the duration of his reign, not Saul's age. But in this way, the Hebrew words are twisted, <margin>50</margin> and the meaning remains unclear. For one does not say "acting a year" or "born a year" in reigning to mean "when he had already reigned a year"; such a way of speaking—"born so many years"—is never used among the Hebrews, nor among the Latins, except regarding a person's age, counting from birth. Furthermore, it wouldn't say "Born a year," but "Born one year." For the Hebrews are accustomed to expressing the number even <margin>60</margin> when speaking of "one." Additionally, several things would have to be supplied [to the text], which makes the passage suspect. Usually, in these books, the age of the Kings and the time of their reign are placed at the beginning of the narrative of their deeds, as in the second chapter of the second book...

<header>ON THE SECOND BOOK OF KINGS <note>Now known as 1 Samuel</note></header>

where it is written: "Ishbosheth, the son of Saul, was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned two years." The same thing occurs regarding other kings. Therefore, I believe it was written in this place how many years old Saul was when he began his reign, and how many years he reigned, but the passage has been damaged <note>The author suspects a "lacuna" or missing text in the Hebrew scroll</note>. For he did not reign only two years, but forty, as is held in Acts 13 and in Josephus <margin>10</margin> at the end of the sixth book, where it is said that Saul reigned for eighteen years while Samuel was alive, and for twenty-two years after his death.

->FROM CHAPTER XIV.<-

**And he should destroy them until the morning light.**) In the Hebrew it is "they should strip" <note>original Hebrew: *diriperent*</note>, but it is used in place of "to kill," just as the word *enarizein* <note>original Greek: *ἐναρίζειν*, meaning to strip a fallen foe of their armor</note> is often used in Homer.

->FROM CHAPTER XVII.<-

<margin>20</margin> **A certain man of immense size.**) "A man of the spaces between" <note>original Hebrew: *ben binayim* (גלית), often translated as 'champion' or 'intermediary'</note> is derived from "between," so that it means a "man of sons," which is to say, of men (for "son" is used for "man"), meaning an excellent man. Similarly, the Latins speak of a "man of the few" <note>original Latin: *hominem paucorum*, meaning an exclusive or superior person</note>.
**Now an old man and advanced in age.**) In the Hebrew it is read as "He had entered into days" <note>original Hebrew: *ba bayamim*</note>. If it were read as "Advanced in years" <note>original Latin/Hebrew: *ba bashanim*</note>, the sense would be beautifully clear: "advanced in years." And the sacred authors are accustomed to speak in this manner.

->FROM CHAPTER XX.<-

<margin>30</margin> **But you shall descend a third time.**) It is helpful to remember what was said a little before: "tomorrow or the day after." Therefore, the meaning is this: "If I am able, I will be at that place tomorrow. But if I cannot know tomorrow how my father is disposed, I will take care to know it at least by the day after tomorrow. Therefore, you shall descend tomorrow. But if I do not come tomorrow, assume I have not yet been able to find out; so descend also the day after, or even on the third day from now, if perhaps I do not come on the day after: so that on whichever of these three days I come, you will be present." Regarding my translation, "You shall descend three times," the Hebrew says "you shall third your descending" (if I may speak so), just as elsewhere one reads "you shall right your doing" (to coin a word for the sake of teaching) instead of "you shall do rightly." And in Jeremiah 49: "deepen your staying" instead of "stay deeply," that is: hide yourselves away thoroughly. In French, they say "to make a triumph" for "triumphal things" or "he does things worthy of a triumph," meaning magnificent things. Of this kind is that passage in Horace:
> Whose age has trembled
> To close its eighth lustrum <note>A lustrum is a five-year period; the person is forty years old</note>.
that is, "it closed tremulously."
And another from the same author:
> You neglect to commit a crime that will harm
> Your descendants born after you.
that is, "you commit it negligently."

->FROM CHAPTER XXV.<-

**With his men descending toward her.**) Since both David and Abigail are said here to be "descending" when they meet each other, it must be understood that there was a valley lying between them.
**Those who accompany you.**) Literally: "Those who are at the feet of my Lord." To be "at the feet" or "to go at the feet" means to be in someone's power and to serve them. Such is that phrase in Homer: "It lies upon the knees of the gods" <note>original Greek: *θεῶν ἐπὶ γούνασι κεῖται*</note>, which means it is in their power and judgment.

<page-num>53</page-num>

->FROM CHAPTER XXVIII.<-

**He passes over to him.**) Regarding what is read as "he has become your enemy" <note>original Hebrew: *vayehi arecha*</note>, the Greek translator seems to have read it as "he has become with your neighbor" <note>original Greek: *γέγονε μετὰ τοῦ πλησίον σου*</note>. And Jerome translates it: "And he has passed over to your rival." I have followed their reading, as also a little later: "the Lord will do for you." I preferred "from your friend" <note>original Hebrew: *merea’cha*</note>, which is in the margin—the way they translated it—rather than "your enemy."

->FROM CHAPTER XXX.<-

**All people of all ages, both men and women.**)
<margin>10</margin> In the Hebrew, it reads literally: "All the women from the small to the great." But since this is a solecism <note>a grammatical error</note>—for it should have said "from the small woman to the great woman"—and since they carried away not only the women but also the men, I followed the Greek, where it is read: "the women, and everyone who was with her, from the small even to the great."

# ON THE SECOND BOOK
<margin>20</margin> ## OF KINGS <note>Now known as 2 Samuel</note>

->FROM CHAPTER V.<-

**The lame and the blind, hateful to David.**) It is clear that this passage is mutilated, both because in the eleventh chapter of Chronicles <note>referred to as *Paralipomenis*</note> there is added what <margin>30</margin> is missing here. However, as to who these "blind and lame" are, there is great controversy. I think it refers to those whom the Greeks call *Atlantes* and the Latins call *Telamones* <note>Architectural supports carved in the shape of men, often used to hold up roofs or cornices</note>, which are statues in the shape of men that support blocks or crowns in buildings. And I believe this is the meaning of the passage: the height of the citadel was so great that the Jebusites denied it could be overcome; therefore, they said to David when he attacked that he would only break into the citadel when he had removed those *Telamones* who, representing the figures of the blind <margin>40</margin> and the lame, were at the top of the fortress. This was the same as saying it was impossible for him to break in. Then David, understanding that men are moved to virtue by rewards and honors, announced that he who first overcame the Jebusites and ascended to the gutters of the roof of the citadel (where those lame and blind *Telamones* were) and removed those statues, would be the commander. David hated them because they were mockingly opposed to him by the enemies, as if <margin>50</margin> he could not even overcome the lame and the blind—the speech passing jokingly from the statues to the men. From this, a proverb was born.

->FROM CHAPTER VII.<-

**Which you have done on earth for the sake of your people.**) The ancient Latin translator correctly reads "for them" <note>original Hebrew: *lahem*</note> and "for the land" <note>original Hebrew: *la'aretz*</note>.

->FROM CHAPTER XII.<-

**When he had captured the royal part of the city.**) In the Hebrew it is "the city of the kingdom." And a little later, what I translate as "the part of the <margin>60</margin> city where the watering place was," in the Hebrew it is "the city of waters." Just as one says "Greater and Lesser Basel" for the greater and lesser parts of the city of Basel, and "the rest of the body" for the remaining part of the body.

ANNOTATIONS.

### FROM CHAPTER 14. <note>From 2 Samuel 14, concerning the woman of Tekoa</note>

***Why then [have you planned] such a thing against the people of God?***) Why do you not grant Absalom to the people who desire him, since you grant my son to me for the sake of my having no one else to provide for my posterity? For who shall succeed you, if not Absalom? You might say you will have others. But what if you should die first? For we are mortals, which is why we must take greater care to propagate our lineage. You might say that Absalom is a murderer, and that murderers must be killed according to God’s command. But what about you, David? Does Uriah not come to your mind? By killing him, you offended God no less than Absalom did by killing his brother. If God had been as severe with you as you are with your son, you would have perished. But God gave you pardon; for He prefers to spare the suppliant rather than punish the guilty. Therefore, He considers again and again how this might be achieved. And so that you might understand my reasoning: when I wished to pray to you for the recall of your son, I feared that what the people could not obtain, I would achieve even less. I decided to pretend that my own affairs were at stake, so that once you had made a concession to me regarding my son, you could not deny your own in a similar matter. The woman says these things, but briefly and obscurely; for she is a skilled woman speaking to a skilled man, and furthermore, she reminds the king of the memory of Uriah only timidly and in a veiled manner.

### FROM CHAPTER 15.

***After four years had passed.***) In the Hebrew it reads "forty" <note>original: *ארבעים* (arba'im)</note>; but it was an easy slip from *four* <note>original: *ארבע* (arba)</note> to *forty*, and Josephus interprets it as four.

### FROM CHAPTER 18.

***For you are worth ten thousand.***) It appears from the sense of the passage, and from both the Greek and Latin translators, that the reading should not be *now you* <note>original: *עתה אתה* (atah atah)</note>. You will find the same error in the third book <note>1 Kings</note>, chapter one, in Bathsheba's speech to the king.

***Scattered by flight to their homes.***) In the Hebrew it is: "they fled each man to his own tent." However, "tent" is used for "house," the reason being that the use of tents existed before houses. Later, when huts and cottages, and eventually houses, were built, the same word remained. This is just as in Latin we use the word *libros* <note>books</note> for things that are not literally books <note>in the sense of bark</note>, yet the word remains because in the beginning, writing used to be done on a *liber*, which is to say, on the bark of trees.

### FROM CHAPTER 21.

***On the mountain of Jove.*** <note>The author uses "Jove" as a Latinate synonym for God/the Lord</note>) It seems the reading should be *chosen* <note>original: *בחר* (bachar)</note> rather than *on the mountain* <note>original: *בהר* (be-har)</note>, as the same word is repeated shortly after. Otherwise, the meaning is nonsensical.

### FROM CHAPTER 23.

***A religious ruler.***) In the Hebrew it is: "a ruler of the fear of God"—that is, one endowed with the fear of God. For they do not signify "religion" with a single word, much like the French, who say *crainte de Dieu* <note>fear of God</note>. Nor is it out of place that he attributes the fear of God to God <note>in the person of the Messiah</note>; for he speaks of Christ, who received the human race from the Father to be ruled, as is found in the second Psalm. What follows is a comparison, such as appears in the first Psalm. Just as the sun and rain nourish the plants and ensure their kind never perishes, so the favor and zeal of God will cherish my 

<column-break/>

posterity, whereas the wicked (like Saul) are torn out by the root like thorns. For I interpret the phrase *not with* <note>original: *בלי לא* (beli lo)</note> as an affirmation rather than a negation; it is used in the same way in Genesis 18, where *not* <note>original: *לא* (lo)</note> is the same as "on the contrary." For "not" is not always used by one who denies, as in Ezekiel 3, where *with not* <note>original: *עם לא* (im lo)</note> is used for "but if." This is also commonly used in swearing and affirming, standing for what the Greeks call "truly" <note>original: *ἢ μὴν* (e men)</note> or "by [God]" <note>original: *μὰ μὰ* (ma ma)</note>. Likewise in 2 Kings 13, 4 Kings 5, and Ezekiel 15, "not" is used for confirmation, and often elsewhere, just as in Ecclesiasticus 29 "not even" <note>original: *ἀν' οὗ μὴ* (an' hou me)</note> signifies "furthermore"; and in Matthew 6 and Mark 2 it means "otherwise"; and in 2 Timothy 2 "lest perhaps" <note>original: *μήποτε* (mepote)</note> means "if by chance." Just as with the Greeks, "how" <note>original: *ὅπως* (hopos)</note> as a single word can be used for affirmation. If the "not" here were a negation, the contrast would be absurd and contrary to the nature and the comparison established by the same David in the first Psalm.

***Jashobeam, son of Hachmoni.***) I have translated this passage partly from the Books of Chronicles <note>original: *Paralipomena*</note>. For the text here is so corrupted that no meaning can be discerned. In the other place it is written that he overcame three hundred, while here it says eight hundred. There he is called the leader of the thirty, while here the leader of the three. However, both can be said correctly: that he was the leader of the three principal men among the thirty. Josephus calls him Jessimus, son of Achemaeus, and writes that eight hundred were cast down by him; this is more probable than three hundred, since he is called the strongest of all, yet Abishai is written to have slain the same number [three hundred] shortly after this passage.

# ON THE THIRD BOOK OF KINGS. <note>Now known as 1 Kings</note>

### FROM CHAPTER 5.

***Cedar and pine timber.***) I interpret the word *berosh* <note>original: *ברוש*</note> as "pine" rather than "fir," since in 2 Kings 6 it is written that musical instruments were made from that tree.

***Cypress wood.***) In the Hebrew it is: "From the tree of oil," which some wish to be the olive. But in 2 Nehemiah 8, the olive (which is *shemen* <note>original: *שמן*</note> without controversy) is clearly distinguished from the "tree of oil." For this reason, I have translated it here as "cypress," following the Greek. For Pliny also teaches that oil is made from cypress. Add to this that Josephus, in describing the materials brought for the temple, names the cypress; there would be no mention of it in these books if it were not this tree.

### FROM CHAPTER 6.

***The length of which temple was sixty cubits, the width twenty, the height thirty.***) What he says regarding the length and width must be understood not as the whole temple, but of the main hall and the inner sanctuary. For the main hall was forty cubits long, and the sanctuary twenty; both were twenty wide, as will appear later. Regarding the height, there is a controversy. For here it is recorded as thirty cubits; in the Greek as twenty-five; and in Chronicles and Josephus as one hundred and twenty—a truly great difference. But if we say the hall and the shrine were thirty cubits in height, but the rest of the building placed upon them had the remaining height—

### ON THE FOURTH BOOK OF KINGS
<note>In the older Latin tradition, the books of 1 and 2 Samuel and 1 and 2 Kings were grouped together as 1, 2, 3, and 4 Kings. This text discusses 1 Kings 6.</note>

...height, I do not see how the remaining ninety cubits could be assigned to the rest, since it is recorded here that the small room placed atop the entire building was only five cubits high. Therefore, it seems there is an error <note>original: "mendum"</note> either here or in Chronicles <note>original: "Paralipomenis"</note>. But I find this passage suspicious. For a height of thirty cubits seems too low for the excellence of this temple, especially since after the Babylonian captivity it was restored to a height of sixty cubits, as stated in Ezra 6, even though that temple was by no means comparable to Solomon’s. Therefore, I believe that in this place "sixty" <note>Hebrew: ששים, *sheshim*</note> was turned into "thirty" <note>Hebrew: שלשים, *shloshim*</note> by the insertion of a single letter, so that the height of the inner chamber <note>original: "cellae"</note> would be sixty cubits—equal to the height of the three levels of side-chambers that surrounded it, each of which was twenty cubits high, as Josephus teaches. Furthermore, a small upper room was placed upon the inner chamber, also sixty cubits high (for there also seems to be an error in the description of its height); thus the total height became one hundred and twenty cubits, so that this matches Chronicles and Josephus. The vestibule was of the same size as that in Ezekiel 40; but while that one is positioned to the north, as we shall show there, this one is to the east. This is clear from the fact that he says it is at the front of the width of the temple: for "width" runs from north to south, and "length" from east to west. The vestibule and the entrance to the temple were in the eastern part, as is apparent from Moses’s Tabernacle—in imitation of which this temple was built—and likewise from Ezekiel chapter 8. Add to this that Josephus records the same. I say this so that no one may be deceived by the custom of modern churches, which all have their entrance from the west—a practice which Vitruvius <note>A famous Roman architect whose works influenced the Renaissance</note> also records should be followed, evidently according to Roman custom, which our people have imitated.

***He illuminated the temple with windows that were "openable and closable."***) This means windows that could be opened and shut: that is, they had shutters <note>original: "fores," literally "doors"</note>, to distinguish them from those that only have "lights"—that is, holes to admit light but which lack shutters. For those are not "closable," since they are never shut.

<column-break/>

**56**

***Against the wall of the temple, he built side-chambers, etc.***) This is an obscure passage that can hardly be understood without the description of the temple found in Ezekiel, where these side-chambers, surrounding the inner chamber and the most holy place <note>original: "penetrale"</note>, are called "stories" <note>original: "tabulata"</note>, as they are here. The only difference is that those in Ezekiel are four cubits wide from the foundations, while these are five. As for the fact that in Josephus the width of these is written as "twenty-five" <note>Greek: *εἰκοσι πέντε*, eikosi pente</note> cubits, this is a manifest error. The chambers would then be wider than the temple itself, even though he calls them "small houses." Therefore, "twenty" should be deleted. In both accounts, however, they increase by two-cubit extensions, and in both there are thirty of them, arranged in three stories. For Ezekiel records that many there, and Josephus does so here. But since in Ezekiel their length only covers the length of the inner chamber and the shrine <note>original: "adyti"</note>, as we shall teach there, the length of these extends even behind the most holy place; indeed, these are longer than those by as many cubits as they themselves are—namely, thirty. If indeed thirty-five cubits make one hundred and fifty, and you occupy sixty of those for the length of the inner chamber and shrine to the south and sixty to the north, thirty cubits remain. This equals six side-chambers, four of which, placed behind the most holy place, will occupy the width of the most holy place itself, while two will be in the corners opposite the two rows of sixty cubits. The middle stories of these cells—that is, the middle cells placed upon the lowest ones (for "cell" and "story" are the same thing in this passage)—had doors on the right side of the temple, namely the right-hand stories; and the left-hand ones on the left, in the vacant space that surrounded them. Furthermore, a temple wall surrounded this vacant space, receding in contractions by the same amount that the stories projected in their extensions. But regarding this entire matter, see our diagrams for Ezekiel’s temple; without understanding that building, this temple can hardly be understood. For the present, we will provide the floor plan <note>original: "areae"</note> of this shrine and the outlines of the foundations, from which you may understand the entire structure of the temple.

**A** is the courtyard. **B** represents three rows of stones. **C** is one row of cedar beams, specifically upright ones <note>original: "arrectariarū"</note>. **D** is the thickness of the wall, to which I assign six cubits—namely, one and a half cubits for each row—since that is the thickness of the courtyards in the Book of Ezekiel. But why it is called "inner," and how the courtyards were arranged, will be made clear in the discussion of Ezekiel. This is not because there are as many courtyards here as there are there; for there are eight in Ezekiel's vision, while here there seem to be only two, as appears in 2 Kings 23 <note>original: "4. ### FROM CHAPTER VII.

*The House of the Forest of Lebanon.*) This house was in Jerusalem; it was so named because it was situated in a grove called by the name of Lebanon. Josephus calls this <term>Armana Libanon<gloss>original: "Αρμανα Λιβανον" — A Greek transliteration likely referring to "the forest of Lebanon"</gloss></term>, that is, an oak-grove or wood of Lebanon. Of this house, as well as its portico, we provide the following floor plan.

<image-desc>A schematic diagram showing rows of small squares, representing a forest of columns. The rows are labeled A, B, C, and D on the left. Between the rows are letters F, G, H. To the right are letters B, D. Below the main grid are further squares labeled with K, L, M, and I.</image-desc>

**ABCD** represent the four rows of columns. **AE** is the length of one hundred cubits. **AD** is the width of fifty cubits. Upon these columns, crossbeams <note>original: "transtra"</note> were placed, specifically running transversely from **A** to **B**, from **B** to **C**, and from **C** to **D**, and so on for the others. Upon these crossbeams the flooring was placed—that is, the building itself. That part of the building which rested upon forty-five columns (the three rows **ABC**) was covered with cedar. The remaining part was not, namely the section placed along the portico and resting on the column rows **CD**. For the middle rows of columns served two sets of flooring, so that there were three rows of floor-spaces, **F**, **G**, and **H**, of which **H** was not covered in cedar. **I** is the columned portico, positioned in front of those columns, fifty cubits long (**KL**) and thirty cubits wide (**KM**). Regarding what is recorded about the windows: they were square, corresponding to one another in a triple row, so that if you were to drop a line from the center of any window in the highest row, it would cut through the two 

<column-break/>

windows of the lower rows exactly through the middle. As for the <term>capitals<gloss>The ornamental "heads" or tops of the columns</gloss></term> of the columns (for the other details are clear), they were round and adorned with flowers. They were surrounded by seven interwoven nets <note>original: "plagis perplexis" — likely referring to the bronze latticework described in the Bible</note>, which did not run from top to bottom but encircled the capitals from right to left, in the manner that nets are usually spread. The "warp and woof" of the nets—that is, the cords from which the nets were made—were linked together, meaning they were twisted with multiple strands as is common. And indeed, through the six meshes of the nets, the floral decorations of the capitals were visible. But the "bellies" of the capitals—that is, the middle part where the capitals swell the most—were surrounded by two rows of pomegranates. Each of these rows contained one hundred pomegranates, so that each individual capital had two hundred pomegranates, projecting through the middle nets where they faced the swelling "belly."

# ON THE THIRD BOOK OF KINGS
<note>In older Christian Bibles, such as the Latin Vulgate, 1 and 2 Samuel were called 1 and 2 Kings, making our modern 1 Kings the "Third Book of Kings."</note>

A B C D E F G represent the seven rows, of which D is the center where the pomegranates are located. H is the head of the column. I is the shaft. K and L represent the circumference of the shaft, measuring twelve <term>cubits|An ancient unit of measure based on the length of the forearm, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters</term>. In Greek, this is called the <note>original: "θριγκὸς" (thrigkos)</note> **cornice** or **coping**, whose <note>original: "διάμετρος" (diametros)</note> **diameter** is one-third of the circumference—that is, four cubits. This is what the author indicated when he said the columns occupied four cubits.

->**He made a molten lake.** <note>The Latin text uses "lake" (lacum), though most English Bibles translate the Hebrew "yam" as "sea."</note> It is called a "sea" in the Hebrew, but "sea" is used to mean a lake or large basin, as can be seen in the Gospels; the Latins also call vessels of this type "lakes." <image-desc>A detailed woodcut illustration of the Biblical 'Molten Sea' (the large laver in the Temple of Solomon).
