Now let us explain the author’s words. Each of the bases (he says) extended four cubits in length (marked A B) and the same in width (A C). The height was three cubits (B D). The panels had frames placed between them (marked E). Although what we translate as "panels" <note>original: "areolas"</note> refers to the "border" in the description of the table in Exodus, in that instance the name comes from "closing in" (because it encloses something), whereas here it is named because it "is closed in." This becomes clear from the fact that the panels are said to be "placed between the frames." The frames are the bands themselves that surround the square panels, which are decorated with lions, oxen, Cherubim, and palms in human likeness. He adds this last part specifically to be understood regarding the Cherubim, whose form was like that of a human. Indeed, this decorated part was similar to what architects call the <term>Zoophorus|A "life-bearing" frieze, a continuous band of relief sculpture featuring animals or people</term> on the uppermost part of an entablature, where the panels take the place of the <term>metopes|The square spaces between triglyphs in a Doric frieze</term> and the frames take the place of the <term>triglyphs|The vertically channeled blocks between metopes</term>.

**Mouldings added above the frames (marked F).** Whether the Hebrew word <note>original Hebrew: "לויות" (luyot)</note> **wreaths** signifies <term>tori|Large, convex mouldings, usually at the base of a column</term>, or <term>cymatia|Wave-like architectural mouldings</term>, or <term>scotias|Deep concave mouldings</term>, or <term>simas|The upturned edge of a roof or cornice</term>, is not yet clear to me, and I would not want anyone to be misled. For now, I shall call them "mouldings." If they are indeed tori, he calls them "flattened," meaning they do not have a perfect roundness but are somewhat curved by the compass. **And bronze planks.** He uses "planks" to refer to the bronze material itself from which the bases were made, even though we use the word "plank" loosely here, as planks are properly made of wood.

<column-break/>

**And "shoulders" at the four corners.** The bases had four corners, not level with the rest of the surface but bulging out in the manner of "shoulders." These were positioned opposite and above the mouldings that surrounded the bases to support the bellies of the wash-basins; these shoulders are marked with the letter F. G represents the wash-basin itself.

**The mouth of the wash-basin within, etc.** In the middle of the head of the base, a small round cap rose up half a cubit. This was inserted into a hollow which the wash-basin had protruding inward at its bottom. Thus it happened that while the "mouth" of the basin (from the very bottom to the top rim) was one and a half cubits deep, it only appeared to be one cubit deep from the top of the cap to the rim, because the cap took up half a cubit of that depth. Because this is somewhat obscure and could not be clearly shown in the illustration we provided due to the perspective, I will explain it more plainly <note>original: "crassiore minerua" - a Latin idiom meaning "with a thicker Minerva," or more simply/plainly</note>.

Let **A** be the head <note>original: "capitulum" — the crowning top part of the stand</note> of the base. **B** is the recess <note>original: "sinus" — a hollow or indentation</note> of the basin <note>original: "lauacri" — a ceremonial wash-vessel or laver</note>. **C** to **D** is the height of the mouth of the basin, measuring one and a half <term>cubits|An ancient measurement of approximately 18 inches (45 cm), based on the length of the forearm</term>. If you place the basin upon the head of the stand so that the head is hidden within the recess of the basin, the mouth of the basin will extend above the head—that is, from the part where it curves to receive the head—by a height of one cubit (**E D**). This is because, while it otherwise extends one and a half cubits (**C D**), the recess itself accounts for half a cubit (**C E**).

Furthermore, when the text says the mouth of the basin was round on all sides, it is indicating its width. For if its height was one and a half cubits, its width was double that—that is, three cubits—since the mouth of the basin was round in every direction, forming the shape of a hemisphere <note>original: "dimidij globi figura" — literally, the figure of half a globe</note>. ->FROM CHAPTER 10<-

<margin>Pine wood.</margin> I have followed the Greek, which translates it as *pine wood* <note>original Greek: "ξύλα πεύκινα"</note>; and Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Jewish historian</note>, who translates it as *pine* <note>original Greek: "πεύκην"</note>, and records that it is a true pine, not like the common sort, but similar to the fig tree, though whiter and more brilliant. In 2 Chronicles 2, the same wood is called *Algumim*, with the word slightly changed, for here it is called *Almugim*.

->FROM CHAPTER 15<-

<margin>She had made a Pan in the grove.</margin> The reason I do not think this should be translated as *Priapus* <note>A minor Greek fertility god often depicted with a permanent erection, sometimes associated with garden statues</note> is that it is hardly credible that a woman would have made a Priapus. Furthermore, this was placed in a grove, which is more suitable for Pan <note>The Greek god of the wild, shepherds, and flocks</note>, whereas Priapus was usually placed in gardens. Moreover, the Hebrew name *Miphletseth* <note>Hebrew: מפלצת</note> is derived from "striking terror," which fits Pan: from which the term "Panic fear" is derived.

For these reasons, I have followed the Greek copy in this place, where it reads: "and put on my clothing" <note>original Greek: "καὶ ἐνδυσαι τὸν ἱματισμόν μου"</note>.

### FROM CHAPTER 20

<margin>10</margin>*With which Hezekiah was delighted.*) <term>Ishmael|original: ישמעאל</term> is incorrectly read instead of <term>Shemaiah|original: ישמעיה</term>, as the history, the old translation, and the book of Chronicles show.

# ON THE BOOKS OF CHRONICLES
<note>Paralipomenon is the traditional Latin title for the Books of Chronicles, derived from Greek, meaning "things passed over" or "omitted."</note>

### FROM CHAPTER 2

<margin>20</margin><image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'U' featuring a small landscape scene with a tree and a structure.</image-desc>He took as wives Azubah and Jerioth.) Literally the text reads, "He begat Azubah his wife, and Jerioth." But it is absurd for a wife to be said to have been "begotten" by her husband. Moreover, it is soon clear that Azubah was his wife: for when Azubah died, he is said to have married Ephrath. Additionally, the Greek <note>The Septuagint</note> and the old Latin translation <note>The Vulgate</note> agree with our interpretation. The cause of the error seems to have been that the verb "to beget" is repeated so many times in this chapter.

<margin>30</margin>*Caleb took Ephrath.*) Here also I have followed the same translators.

*The sons of Salma: Bethlehem and the Netophathites.*) This passage is of such a kind that I can note nothing, except that I understand nothing in it.

*From Bathsheba.*) In the Hebrew it is, "From Bathshua." But both the Greeks and Jerome translate it as Bathsheba: and in the books of Kings she is called Bathsheba, never Bathshua.

### FROM CHAPTER 3

<margin>40</margin>*Six sons were born to Iegal.*) This passage is also mutilated; for although they are said to be six, only five are named.

### FROM CHAPTER 4

*The families of the linen factory.*) This whole passage is so corrupted that it can be corrected neither from the Greek nor the Latin.

### FROM CHAPTER 11

Eleazar.) What is attributed here to Eleazar—and not to him alone—is ascribed in 2 Samuel 23 to Shammah, of whom no mention is made here, even though three are said to be the chief men. This passage appears to be mutilated, as are many others in these two books.

### FROM CHAPTER 23

<margin>60</margin>*So that two families were assigned to Eleazar, and one to Ithamar.*) I believe this passage in the Hebrew is also corrupted. For since, a little before, twice as many families were attributed to Eleazar as to Ithamar, here the opposite occurs. Therefore, I suspect that in the first part we should read "to Ithamar," and in the latter part, in which <term>house of the father|original: לבית אב</term> is placed twice, "to Eleazar." For this word does not always signify possession, but a number, or (as the Latins say) a "head" <note>A unit of counting</note>, especially when it is said of animals: in which sense it is used in Numbers 31, where it is used 

<column-break/>

<page-num>70</page-num>
instead of what was said shortly before, <term>lamb|original: שה</term>. This is therefore the meaning: when the families came to Ithamar <term>one by one|original: אחד אחד</term>, that is, individually, they fell to Eleazar <term>one by one|original: אחד אחד</term>, that is, in pairs. For this is what the doubled word signifies.

### FROM CHAPTER 25

<margin>10</margin>*Of those prophesying with harps.*) He calls "prophesying" the handling of divine matters or the writings of the prophets, and the speaking of God’s praises; just as the word <term>propheteuein|original: προφητεύειν</term> is used by Paul. This is because the interpreters of the prophets seem to come closest to the divination of those whom they interpret. The Athenians also called certain divine priests <term>mantes|diviners or seers</term> (as Cicero writes), which is to say, prophets.

### FROM CHAPTER 26

<margin>20</margin>*The father of the family of Tebiel was born.*) In the Hebrew, this name is placed in the plural number, even though it is said of one person. This often happens, as above in the twenty-third chapter, where the "sons of Eliezer" are mentioned, of whom Rehabiah was the first, even though it is denied in the same place that Eliezer had others. The Latins also speak in this way when they call offspring "children" in the plural number, even when speaking of only one.

# ON THE SECOND BOOK OF CHRONICLES

### FROM CHAPTER 9

<margin>30</margin><image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'S' featuring dense foliage and a stylized animal form.</image-desc>Shields of beaten gold, six hundred each.) Literally thus: "Six hundred of beaten gold went into one shield." This is to be understood as <term>shekels|The standard weight and currency of the ancient Hebrews</term>, because the Hebrews weigh in shekels. Just as in Latin, if you say a stone is a "hundred-weight," it will be understood as being of a hundred pounds, because the Latins use pounds. Likewise, if you call a man a "sixty-year-old," you speak of years, because age is counted by years. And in the same way for the rest. Now, because <margin>40</margin> here shields of "three hundred" are mentioned, while in the first book of Kings chapter 10 it is written that three <term>minae|An ancient unit of weight; one mina was roughly 1.25 pounds or 600 grams</term> were spent on each, it appears that a mina is worth one hundred shekels.

*From behind.*) It seems we should read <term>from behind him|original: מאחריו</term>, as in 1 Kings 10. Otherwise, if you read <term>from behind them|original: מאחריהם</term>, the meaning will not be consistent.

### FROM CHAPTER 13

*Forty thousand choice soldiers.*) In the Hebrew it is four hundred thousand, and likewise soon after eight hundred thousand, and in the victory five hundred thousand. But since <margin>50</margin> this number is incredible, I preferred to follow the Greek and Latin translator, and Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian</note>, who all agree on this point.

### FROM CHAPTER 20

*The Ammonites and part of the Edomites.*) In the Hebrew it is, "And part of the Ammonites." But it would be absurd to say "the Ammonites, and part of the Ammonites": and the history shows that the Edomites, inhabitants of Mount Seir, were present. It is unlikely that mention of them would be <margin>60</margin> omitted here.

### FROM CHAPTER 21

*The sons of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah.*) In the Hebrew it is, "King of Israel." But the old and Greek translators read "of Judah," and the history requires it so.

### FROM CHAPTER 22
<note>This refers to 2 Chronicles 22.</note>

**He went down to visit Ahaziah who was sick in Jezreel.**) In the Hebrew, the name is Azariah, but in the ancient Latin and Greek translations it is read as Ahaziah <note>original: Ochozias</note>, and so it is in 2 Kings 9, which is how the history stands.

### FROM CHAPTER 28
<note>This refers to 2 Chronicles 28.</note>

**To the king of Assyria to seek help.**) In the Hebrew it says, "To the *kings* of Assyria," but the ancient Greek and Latin versions say "king" in the singular, and so the history records it. Likewise, a little later, Ahaz is incorrectly called the King of Israel, which contradicts both the history and the two versions I mentioned <note>Ahaz was King of Judah, though the Hebrew text sometimes uses "Israel" in a broader sense</note>.

### FROM CHAPTER 29
<note>This refers to 2 Chronicles 29.</note>

**He had defiled it by his crime.**) The Hebrew word <term>וַיְטַמְּאוּ|original: vay-tam'u</term> should be read such that the last letter is *He* (<term>ה</term>). For the sense of the sentence requires it, and the Greek translates it as **they defiled** <note>original: ἐμίαναν</note>, while the Latin says **he had defiled**.

### FROM CHAPTER 36
<note>This refers to 2 Chronicles 36.</note>

**With what character he was endowed.**) Word for word, this reads: *What was found in him.* In this context, "to be found" is used for "to be," "to exist," or "to stand out." This is because nothing can be "found" that does not already exist. As in Philippians 2: **He was found in appearance as a man**, which means: *He existed as a man.* And in Latin, we say: *This one man was found who could do it*, meaning: *one man stood out.* Also in 2 Chronicles 19: **Good things are found in you**, meaning: *certain praiseworthy qualities exist within you.*

# ON EZRA

### FROM CHAPTER 6

**It was found in Ecbatana.**) In the Chaldean <note>Aramaic</note> text, it is **Amatha**, but both the ancient translation and Josephus translated it as **Ecbatana**. It seems this place was called one thing in Chaldean and another in other languages, as often happens in many other cases.

### FROM CHAPTER 7

**Sharply learned.**) In the Hebrew, it is **a swift scribe** <note>original: literatus celer</note>. However, "swiftness" is used here to mean "sharpness of mind," just as in Latin we speak of "swiftness of genius." Likewise, the term **scribe** <term>סוֹפֵר|original: sopher</term> (which in Greek is called <term>γραμματεὺς|original: grammateus</term> from the word for "letters") sometimes means a person who is taught and learned. This is used either in combination, as a little after this passage <term>סוֹפֵר וְעָנָה|original: sopher ve-anah</term>, which is the same as a **teacher of the law** <note>original: νομοδιδάσκαλος</note>, a legal expert or professor—whom Plato in the sixth book of *Laws* calls an **interpreter** <note>original: ἐξηγητὴν</note>—or it is used on its own, as in Isaiah 33, where we would call such a person **lettered** or **learned**. Sometimes it refers to a **royal scribe**, or to the Jewish sect of the **Scribes**; in those cases, we translate it as "scribe."

# ON NEHEMIAH

### FROM CHAPTER 4

**In which they lived near us.**) In the Hebrew, this is in the second person, but both the meaning and the ancient translation force us to admit that it ought to be in the third person. Furthermore, this book is corrupted in many places; for example, in the third chapter, where instead of 

<column-break/>

**after him** or **following him**, it often reads "after them." And conversely, in Ezra chapter 10, in the place we translate as **All the women, and those born of them**, the pronoun "them" in Hebrew is masculine, though it ought to be feminine. Likewise in Nehemiah chapter 7, where the same material from Ezra chapter 2 is repeated, the numbers and names of the men often disagree. I say this so that no one, upon coming across such passages, thinks I have failed to see them. I do not consider it necessary to write down every tiny detail, as these can easily be understood by anyone willing to compare the texts.

**Each holding his weapon in his right hand.**) Here, too, where the Hebrew reads <term>הַשֶׁלַח|original: ha-shelach</term>, it seems it should be read as <term>הַשָּׁלֹוחַ|original: ha-shaloach</term>; otherwise, no matter how you turn it, the sentence remains absurd.

# ON THE THIRD BOOK OF EZRA
<note>Known today as 1 Esdras in many English bibles, this is an apocryphal Greek version of the history of Ezra.</note>

### FROM CHAPTER 3

**He was called an intimate of Darius.**) The Greek word is <term>συγγενὴς|original: syngenes</term>, which means "kinsman" or "relative." However, it seems to be translated from the Hebrew word <term>רֵעַ|original: rea</term> (for I judge this book to have been made into Greek from a Hebrew original, even though the Hebrew has since been lost). That word also signifies an **intimate** or a **friend**. It is more appropriate to call him the king's "intimate" here than his "kinsman," for wisdom cannot make someone a blood relative, and anyone can be a relative, but only those who are held in high esteem are called "intimates."

# ON TOBIT

### FROM CHAPTER 4

**And so pour out bread and wine upon the graves of the righteous.**) Since he has already commanded that whatever is left over should be given in charity, how can he then command that it be "poured upon graves"? For charity is practiced toward the living, not the dead. The meaning, therefore, is this: **The true pouring upon graves is generosity toward the living**, which is more pleasing to the dead than if you were to drench their actual tombs with wine. In this same way, in Ruth chapter 1, those young women are said to have "dealt kindly with the dead"—that is, they were pious toward the living in memory of the dead. This is also how David speaks in Psalm 51, when he says that a "true sacrifice" is a broken and contrite heart. And the Sibyl, in her eighth book, teaches the same thing as Tobit with these words:

> Man is my image, a child of right reason:
> To him, set a table willingly, without blood,
> And fill it with good things: give bread and drink
> To the hungry and thirsty: cover the naked body with a garment.
> From your own labor, give with pure hands:
> Refresh the oppressed: comfort the weary in their toils.
> Let this be the living victim given by you to the living:
> Sow the seed piously, so the Lord may grant these things to you.

## ON JOB.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' containing a scene of a figure (possibly a scholar or a saint) seated at a desk or in prayer, surrounded by floral and architectural scrollwork within a square border.</image-desc>THOSE WHO THINK this narrative and discussion of Job is fictional <note>original: "fictam esse putant"</note> seem to me to do so for no good reason. For nothing can exist in a true history that is not also in this one; thus, he who denies this history could deny all histories. But if they think it is absurd that God speaks with a man in this book, He also spoke with Noah, Abraham, and others. Unless, perhaps, they object that those men were from a divinely chosen race of people, while Job was an Idumean <note>An inhabitant of Edom, a region south of Judea; the author is arguing that God's grace extends beyond Israel</note>—as if there were any race of men that God has rejected, <margin>10</margin> or as if He does not love all who live rightly, just as He hates all who live unjustly, regardless of their nation. And these are the reasons by which those people may be refuted, if by chance they are little moved by the authority of Ezekiel and James <note>referring to Ezekiel 14:14 and James 5:11</note>, who certainly would never have made such honorable mention of Job if the matter were a fable. <margin>20</margin> However, it is uncertain at what time Job lived. That he lived a long time after Moses becomes clear from chapter 15, where mention is made of the Israelites being led into Canaan as a thing that happened long ago. Likewise, from the twenty-eighth chapter, where it is said that God once declared to man that wisdom is the fear of the Lord; this sentiment is surely taken from Deuteronomy 4 or from Psalm 111. <margin>30</margin> Just as in chapter 12 there is this sentiment: **He pours contempt upon princes**, translated almost word-for-word from Psalm 107. Unless, perhaps, they will say it was not translated from the Psalm, but the other way around; even if that is left in doubt, what I said before certainly cannot be doubted: that Job lived long after Moses. Now, the argument of the dispute is this: the friends assert that Job was wicked because he fell into such calamity, for God <margin>40</margin> afflicts none with evil except the wicked. Job, on the contrary, fights back, saying that even the good are afflicted with evils by God—such as himself, who was innocent. And when the friends say that he indeed *seemed* innocent, but that his innocence was not true, and that this is judged by the outcome (since he is paying the penalty for sin, for misery is the punishment for sin), Job shows that it even goes well for the wicked, and that this is apparent in reality. <margin>50</margin> Since this is the case, it is no more absurd to say that someone good is in the midst of evils than it is to say someone evil is in the midst of goods. But God, the judge of the controversy, first reproves Job, who complains that he is being treated unjustly by God because he does not see the reason why he is afflicted with such great evil. God shows that His works are so arduous that men must confess that whatever is done by God is not done without cause or reason. If they are ignorant of the cause, they should attribute it to their own ignorance, not accuse God of injustice. It is as if He says: "Although I have inflicted calamity upon you, an innocent man, you ought nevertheless to think so highly of Me, who am so great, as to believe there is some just though unknown cause why I, the judge and creator of the world, act thus with you." <margin>60</margin> However, He does not add the cause of why He did it; for He wishes His will to be held as the reason, which

<column-break/>

while it might be unfair in a man (since he can both err and act unjustly), is most just in God. And that cause is clear to us from the beginning of the book: for He did it to test Job’s integrity, and that at the instigation of Satan. Nor indeed was the Lord <note>original: "Ioua," a Latinization of the Tetragrammaton (Yahweh)</note> defeated by Satan in this contest; for the Lord <margin>10</margin> contended that Job would remain in his integrity. Satan, however, asserted that Job was upright only because his affairs were prosperous; but if he fell into calamity, that uprightness would be so nonexistent that he would even curse God in the manner of the impious. This did not happen. For Job remained whole, and was not so changed by adverse things that he wished to imitate the wicked. And yet, he was to be reproved in this: that he said he was being treated unjustly by God. But that fault <margin>20</margin> is not one of wickedness, but of ignorance. For since his friends argued that all calamity is the punishment for sins, and Job was not conscious of any crime, he thought he was being treated unjustly. Therefore, God chastises that error of Job with words, as has been said, but does not punish him. However, He argues more severely against Job’s friends, who did not speak as rightly about God as Job did. For in that which Job asserted—that even upon the innocent, evils are brought by God—he spoke rightly; when they denied this, they did not speak truly about God. Add to this that <margin>30</margin> Job saw that God’s justice is not to be judged from this life, but from the future one, in which it will be well for the good and ill for the wicked; this can be understood from chapter 19, in which he speaks of the resurrection. Therefore, the Lord teaches that Job spoke rightly; nor does He think those voices of impatience—faulty indeed, but squeezed out by the magnitude of his grief—ought to be punished.

### FROM CHAPTER III.

> *Let those curse it who detest the day, who are prepared to rouse Leviathan.*) Leviathan is a whale, Job 40 <margin>40</margin> and Psalm 104. Since the whale is the greatest of all animals, it seems to be placed for the greatest of furies and demons, Isaiah 27 and 4 Esdras 6. In the same way, dragons and sea monsters <note>original: "cetae"</note> are used for the Egyptians, and Leviathan or the whale is used for Pharaoh in Psalm 74. This, therefore, is Job's meaning: Let that night be cursed by those who detest days infamous for some calamity, and who establish them as grim and ill-omened <note>original: "nefastos"</note>, as the Romans did for the battles of Allia and Cannae <note>Reference to the "Dies Alliensis" and the aftermath of Cannae, dates considered unlucky on the Roman calendar due to military disasters</note>. These people indeed attempt to rouse Leviathan, that <margin>50</margin> is, they stir up curses, using dreadful imprecations, which happens in sad and atrocious matters.

### FROM CHAPTER V.

> *Call now, if there be any, etc.*) Call upon God, and if indeed you are holy, He will hear you and deliver you from that evil. For if you consider holy men, their condition is such that God always defends them. But if God does not hear you, but destroys you, it appears that you are wicked; for God does not destroy any but the wicked. And this is the argument of this whole chapter, which, briefly encompassed in the first two <margin>60</margin> verses, is thereafter treated more explicitly. It can be formed in this way: Those who are pious and holy, God defends against evils; but He does not defend you, therefore you are not pious. Likewise, those who are killed by the severity of God...

# ON JOB

they are called fools; yet you are being killed by God’s severity, therefore you are a fool.

### FROM CHAPTER VI.

*Would that my impatience, etc.* <note>Job 6:2</note>) I seem to you to bear my pain too immoderately. But if the magnitude of the pain by which I am weighed down were compared with my complaints, the pain would be found so much heavier than my lamentation that I could not express it in words. For God presses upon me most sharply, which may be understood in this way: When a wild donkey brays, it is certainly understood that he lacks fodder; I say the same of the ox. For animals of this kind are not such that they complain without cause. Likewise, since I complain now, do not think I do so without great evil. Furthermore, when you see me desire death, you ought to consider that there is some great cause which makes such a bitter thing (as death is) pleasing to me. For if tasteless foods, such as the white of an egg, do not please without salt even though they are food, how much less do those things taste good to the palate which are bitter by nature? But if you were to see someone eager for bitter food, you would certainly judge there to be some cause which softens and seasons the bitterness of the food with a kind of salt, as it were. Yet I seek death, than which nothing seems sadder, and which I previously dreaded; and I seek it as those who hunger are accustomed to seek food. Since this is so, there is no doubt that my pain is so great that the bitterness of death is overcome by it, and, as if seasoned by a kind of salt, it seems to be sweet; whence it happens that I seek to end my pains by death. But if God were to rage in killing me, this would be most pleasing to me; and so far am I from rejecting or dreading the words of the Majestic One <note>original Latin: "Augusti"</note>—that is, of God—that I desire Him to vent His rage on me not with words, but with lashes and death. As for what I have interpreted as, "It would be enough for my sustenance," it is read as <term>the slime of the yolk</term> <note>original Hebrew: 'ḥeleq ḥalamut,' a difficult phrase often translated as the white of an egg or the juice of mallows</note>; otherwise the sentence would be insipid. Nor indeed (says Job) is there reason for you to think, when I pray for death, that I am too soft and weak: this is not to be ascribed to my weakness, but to the weight of the pain by which I am so pressed that, although I do what is in me to do, I am nevertheless forced to succumb. Therefore it would not be strange if, in such great evil, I were not religious enough, since those who are tortured by some great evil are accustomed to do the same, even though friends are present and help them—pain, clearly, overcoming patience. But for me, not even this is present, that friends should console me; for you, who are my brothers and friends, do not relieve me, but deceive me: just as if a torrent were darkened and covered with ice, then covered with snow, which snow results in its being encrusted with less dense ice, so that it can be dissolved by even a slight heat and keep its original course. For if travelers come to that torrent and touch the ice (as usually happens) and test it with sticks or feet, they will find it too fragile to carry them. Therefore they will have come in vain, which will go badly for them (for that is what he means when he says "they perish"); nor will they be able to cross to where they were heading, namely to Tema, or anywhere else. Just as the torrent deceives them, so you deceive me; nor are you true friends, who, having seen my misfortune,

<column-break/>

are afraid and are inconstant. And yet there is nothing for you to fear, for I demand nothing from you.
*Is it not for the sake of arguing?* <note>Job 6:25-26</note>) That you rebuke me with contrived words is more than a mere rebuke; nor do those wicked and unjust words vanish into the wind—that is, they are not empty or harmless—but they press upon and undermine me, an orphan, that is, a destitute and miserable man. As if <margin>10</margin> he were to say: What you dispute against me, you do not do for the sake of proving a point, but for the sake of hurting me, or certainly in doing so, you hurt me.

### FROM CHAPTER XIIII.

*And as the mountains fall and are undermined, etc.* <note>Job 14:18</note>) There is nothing that cannot happen in the space of time: mountains fall, rocks are moved away, etc. But man can hope for nothing better in any age after this life, if indeed he is never to live again. Nor indeed does Job say this as if he hoped for no resurrection; for in chapter 19, he clearly demonstrates that he <margin>20</margin> hopes for it. But here he disputes from the opinion of his adversaries and refutes them thus: If only this life is considered (as your disputes consider it, in which no account is taken of a future life), surely nothing is more miserable than man, who not only becomes calamitous in this life, but also lacks all hope for the future.

### FROM CHAPTER XVII.

*Lay down a pledge, make a wager with me, etc.* <note>Job 17:3</note>) He addresses God. If we must contend by a legal pledge <note>original Latin: "sponsio," a Roman legal term for a mutual wager to settle a dispute</note> as to whether <margin>30</margin> You do me an injustice or not: I will win, if only I have suitable sponsors who will give me their hand—that is, who will pledge on Your behalf in Your absence. But where shall I find such sponsors? Will You give these friends of mine as sponsors? I think not. For You have taken away the wit from their minds; that is, they have no intelligence, they are stupid and ignorant of things. And therefore they are hardly fit for this pledge, if I may speak freely and without flattery. He says, moreover, that God "took away" their wit, <margin>40</margin> meaning He did not give it: just as in chapter 39, God is said to have deprived the ostrich of wisdom—that is, He did not impart wisdom to it—as is clear from the doubled phrasing in that same place.

### FROM CHAPTER XXI.

*Is my dispute with men? etc.* <note>Job 21:4</note>) You, with whom I dispute, are unworthy to be called men. For if you were truly men—that is, if you were sensible and prudent—my speech would be shorter; that is, you would agree with my speech, <margin>50</margin> which is true. Thus it would happen that, with you not contradicting at all, I would have been silent long ago, nor would I make so many words in refuting you. Moreover, he says "men" meaning "truly men" (for there are some who are men in name only), just as Solomon in Proverbs 28, and likewise in Proverbs 16, calls kings "good kings"; and in Ecclesiastes 7, he speaks of "man" and "woman" in the same way. It is like when we say "Latin speech" to mean "elegant speech."
*If they do not have their good in their hand, the counsel of the* <margin>60</margin> *wicked is far from me.* <note>Job 21:16</note>) All things seek the good and direct their actions toward it. If this is so, what the wicked do, they do for the sake of obtaining some good. And yet, if they saw that they obtained no good, nothing could be more stupid than they, who, knowing they are frustrated...

# ANNOTATIONS

they would act as they do. Therefore, I do not see by what reasoning they live in such a way, except that they see themselves gaining good things by living thus. For they do not do what they do without a reason. Consequently, it is necessary that you admit to me that the wicked are happy in this life.

### FROM CHAPTER XXIV.

*Why are times not hidden from the Almighty, etc.* <note>Job 24:1</note>) He calls "God's times and days" those things which God does at each time and day, and he speaks to this effect: The <margin>10</margin> ungodly are fortunate in life, and in death they are not tortured for long. While the righteous see this (for it is more manifest than can be denied), they are tortured, as is held in Psalm 73. Therefore, it would have been better (so it seems) for these things to be hidden from the righteous.

*They are swift upon the waters.* <note>Job 24:18</note>) They are like stalks growing in moisture and marshy ground, which perish quickly, such as the rush; nor do they regard the nature of vineyards—that is, they are not like the vine, which lives even without moisture in a dry place. And I say this is a part of their happiness: to die quickly, and not to languish long as the good are accustomed to do. The ungodly perish quickly, as snow-water is consumed by heat; and they perish in such a way that the womb forgets them, that is, as if they had never come forth from the womb or been born. This is pleasant to them: to be extinguished after they have lived happily and delighted themselves in wicked deeds—by destroying the fetuses in the wombs of women they have defiled <note>A reference to induced abortion or infanticide to cover up adultery</note> so that the disgrace might not be exposed, and by doing harm to widows (this notes adulterers and violent men) and by attacking, killing, betrayingly, and waylaying even high-born men. After they have flourished in this way for some time, they do not pay a penalty, but die like everyone else, and perish quickly. And these things are too clear to be refuted.

### FROM CHAPTER XXVII.

*For what hope will the hypocrite have, etc.* <note>Job 27:8</note>) If I were a hypocrite and impure, my hope would have perished along with my substance; for God would not hear me when I called upon Him. But now I am religious, and therefore I hope for better things. For this is the difference between the upright and the wicked: that the wicked finally perish utterly, and no hope remains for them; but for the upright, it remains. You do not look at this hope, in which you are surely foolish, though you wish to seem to speak like oracles. For you urge this again and again: that unless I had been wicked, I would not have been in such evils. I say that even the upright are afflicted, and indeed often more grievously than the ungodly, but they are not forsaken by hope.

### FROM CHAPTER XXVIII.

Moreover, that hope is placed in religion (as I said), which religion is true wisdom—the most precious of all things that are sought, and the most to be desired. But it is not to be sought where those things are sought which mortals usually desire, who with the greatest labor and diligence search for gems and gold deep in the bowels of the earth. Wisdom is to be sought in each person's own soul. This is the argument of the entire chapter: if you wish to understand it clearly, read Pliny, Book 33, Chapter 4; there will be nothing more you require for the explanation of this passage of Job. We shall, however, explain it in a few words. Men find (he says) metals: silver, gold, iron dug from the ground, and copper from stone. Pliny

<column-break/>

teaches this in Book 34, Chapter 1. *An end is set to darkness* <note>Job 28:3</note>; he penetrates under the earth where there is darkness, and they bring light there, and by the light of lamps they examine gems hidden in the dark. *Rivers are diverted from a foreign soil*, namely, to irrigate the excavated earth in which gold is sought; these rivers they call <term>corruges</term> <note>From the Latin 'corrivatio', a technical term for artificial channels used in hydraulic mining</note>, from the word for "collecting waters." *And unknown to the foot, and which lacked men, they wander*, namely the rivers: that is, the water that flowed under the earth, which no people lived near, is drawn out by human labor and taught to hold another course; as is found in Pliny, Book 33, Chapter 6. *The earth is overturned as if by fire.* <note>Job 28:5</note> They drive tunnels through great spaces and go under the earth, not otherwise than fire does, as in Etna and Vesuvius. Nay, even the flint-stones they encounter under the earth they break with fire and vinegar <note>A classical mining technique attributed to Hannibal and described by Pliny</note>, while men seek gems and gold there, where never any beasts, however wild or fierce, had penetrated, nor had even the most sharp-sighted <margin>20</margin> ever looked. *From the tear they search the rivers:* Where they see "tears" <note>Seepage or moisture on the rock face</note> in the cliffs, they hollow them out to draw out the channels.

### FROM CHAPTER XXIX.

*As I was in the time of my spring.* <note>Job 29:4</note>) In the Hebrew it is read as "winter" <note>original: "choref"</note>. But since the Hebrews divide the year into winter and summer, it happens that the first part of spring is attributed to winter, just as the later part is to summer, as is seen in Matthew 24. For the beginning of spring is the end of winter. That he is speaking of his "spring," however—that is, of his youth—is <margin>30</margin> clear from the whole sentiment.

### FROM CHAPTER XXX.

*Whom no one helps.* <note>Job 30:13</note>) <gloss>belo ya'azor</gloss> <note>Hebrew: "without he helps"</note> just as in Genesis 9 it is put for <gloss>belo 'ezer</gloss> <note>Hebrew: "without help"</note>, with the letter <term>vav</term> <note>The Hebrew letter 'ו'</note> interposed; just as we taught regarding the letter <term>vav</term> inserted in <gloss>ammindab</gloss> in Hosea 12. Otherwise, the meaning would be cold.

### FROM CHAPTER XXXI.

*It is indeed my desire.* <note>Job 31:35</note>) <gloss>ta'awati sepher haddin</gloss> <note>Hebrew: "my desire is the book of judgment"</note> is placed as a contracted word, just as in Isaiah 43 <margin>40</margin> <gloss>gadi</gloss> is for <gloss>bigdi</gloss> <note>Hebrew: "my garment"</note>. For the meaning forces this admission, which is otherwise unsuitable. Add that the old translator <note>The Vulgate</note> renders it "desire."

### FROM CHAPTER XXXIII.

*If God is greater than man.* <note>Job 33:12</note>) You act foolishly when you wish to dispute with God as if you were His equal. For it belongs to those who are equals to dispute among themselves and to hear each other's reasons in turn. But God is so much greater than man that it is unworthy for Him to give man an account of all that He does. For to give an account belongs to one <margin>50</margin> whose deed can be doubted as to whether it be right or not. God is He of whom it must be said, "He Himself has spoken": and His authority is to be held as the reason. Therefore, what He has once pronounced, He does not repeat. Meanwhile, He warns men through dreams and concludes their punishment; that is, He shows that one must not dispute why they are so afflicted with evils, but that the punishment is certain and fixed, and from its Author no account is to be demanded. While He does this, He withdraws man from his deeds—that is, He shows him to be guilty, <margin>60</margin> and that he has done those things and sinned, on account of which he should not be proud, but must pray for pardon. Thus it happens that man, noticing the greatness of God, submits himself, and so obtains pardon and salvation. See nearly the same things in Chapter 36.

ON THE PSALMS

### FROM CHAPTER XXXIV.

*Is it possible that he who [hates justice should govern?]* <note>Job 34:17</note>) This I interpret as: He correctly cares for what he does. In Hebrew, that word means <term>to wrap a wound in bandages <note>original: "uulnus falcijs inuoluere"</note></term> and to heal. And because it is the physician’s role not only to drive away diseases but also to ward them off, it happens that this word, when applied to other things, signifies not only healing a present evil but also acting in such a way that evil is absent and good is present. In Greek, this can be expressed by the single word <term>to set right <note>original: κατωρθοῦν</note></term>. This is the meaning: If God were not just, He could not rightly perform what He cares for and does. For it cannot be said that He sins out of fear. Let this be a trait of men—that they fail through fear of those more powerful—but no one is more powerful than God, so much so that He considers even kings as nothing. Yet He administers the world rightly; therefore, He is just.

### FROM CHAPTER XXXVI.

*In which indeed spreading out His light, He covers the roots of the sea.* <note>Job 36:30</note>) When the sky is cloudy, the light, caught and hindered by the clouds, cannot penetrate to the lower regions. Thus, "the roots of the sea are covered"; that is, the light is blocked by the covering of the clouds from penetrating to the bottom of the sea. For so he calls the deepest part "the roots." Furthermore, through the clouds, God both avenges peoples—when He ruins crops with excessive rain—and grants food abundantly—when He nourishes the fruits of the earth with moderate rain. *He covers the light with His palms*, that is, with the clouds, which are like the palms of God’s hands as He sits in the heavens. And He ensures that the light is met—that is, that the clouds block it. When God "announces the clouds to the light"—that is, rouses them against the light—the light grows angry against the rising clouds that stand in its way. See Chapter 38 regarding the sea.

### FROM CHAPTER XXXVIII.

*And let the wicked be deprived of it, etc.* <note>Job 38:15</note>) Adulterers, thieves, robbers, traitors, and the others whom he calls "wicked" here, stay awake at night for their crimes; likewise, when day arrives, these <term>shunners of light <note>original: "lucifugi"</note></term> flee. And, as if "the seal of red wax has been changed"—that is, once the night that covers and encloses them is scattered (just as a seal of red wax or any other thing covers what is marked by it)—they become like a garment: they contract themselves, fold up like clothes, and cast themselves into hiding places. The wicked are deprived of their light; just as Job said in Chapter 24, that the morning is to the wicked like the shadow of death. For while other men go out to work in the morning, they retire then; so here, God calls the night the "light" of the wicked, because they act at night, and like owls, they treat the day as night and the night as day. *And the uplifted arms are broken*: the wicked lose their strength and boldness when the light rises, and they retreat in fear, though they are otherwise fierce at night.

### FROM CHAPTER XL.

*With the branchy sinews of the top of its tail.* <note>Job 40:17, describing Behemoth</note>) Here he calls the <term>trunk <note>original: "promuscidem"</note></term> the "tail." Furthermore, <term>taqar <note>original: תָּקָר</note></term> is the upper part of the tail, attached to the spine, which is so called from "fear," because animals usually contract it when they are afraid. And in the same way, in Greek it is called <term>to shrink back <note>original: ἐῤῥύω</note></term>, from which comes the word for "fearful." That God is speaking of the tail here is clear from the fact that He previously compared the tail to a cedar; and when He wished to repeat that sentiment (as is His custom), He no longer calls it a cedar, but (what is closest) "branchy sinews."

<sig>X 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: FROM</meta>

<column-break/>

### FROM CHAPTER XLI.

*And so let your hope be false.* <note>Job 41:9</note>) In the Hebrew it is "his hope." But since He had previously used the second person to refer to anyone—namely, "clash your hand with it" for "if anyone should join battle with it"—I wanted to avoid the ambiguity that would have existed in the third person. This is the meaning: In vain would you hope that it [the Leviathan] can be conquered; you could not even endure the sight of it.

### FROM CHAPTER XLII.

*He had also seven sons and three daughters.* <note>Job 42:13</note>) Yet a little earlier, it is said that God doubled everything for him; while this happens with the livestock, it does not happen with the children, for he had the same number as before. But here it must be understood that a mystery of the immortality of souls lies hidden. For though Job’s livestock had perished, the children who had departed from this life had not perished; for all live to God. If a double number of children had been returned to him, he would have had a triple number in total. A certain Italian man taught me this matter.

# ON THE PSALMS.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' containing an illustration of a seated King David playing a harp in a landscape.</image-desc>
Before we come to the explanation of individual passages, a few things must be said in general. Among the Hebrews, this book is called the <term>Book of Praises <note>original: "Liber laudationum," translating "Sefer Tehillim"</note></term>, and in it the praises of God are contained. In Greek, it could be called the *Book of Hymns*; but because they are "psalmed"—that is, these songs are sung to strings—and most are inscribed as <term>Mizmor <note>original: "Mizmor," Hebrew for a melody set to instruments</note></term>, that is, a <term>Psalm <note>original: ψαλμὸν</note></term>, they called them "Psalms" or the "Psalter," a name common among the Latins which we have retained. Some have titles, others do not. Those that do not, I consider to be by David. But those that have titles exist in the Greek only, or even in the Hebrew—and in the Greek indeed in two ways: for either the whole title is Greek, or a part of the title is. And this is sometimes indicated in the Greek with these words: <term>untitled among the Hebrews <note>original: ἀνεπíγραφος παρ' ἑβραíοις</note></term>; sometimes it is not indicated. Therefore, if the whole title is Greek, I have indicated that by placing these two letters at the head of the title: <term>Gr.</term>, something I explained more fully in the first Psalm. If part of the title is Greek, I placed the same letters before that part. Moreover, what I say about the Greek, I want said of the Latin as well; for the common Latin translation of the Psalms, in my judgment at least, is derived from the Greek, not the Hebrew.

Titles indicate either the event that gave occasion for the song, or the author, or the subject matter, or the type of song, or the musical instrument on which the song should be sung, or the singer by whom it should be sung—or sometimes several of these, sometimes fewer. As for the events, these are clear from sacred histories. The chief of the authors is David; but there are others, such as Moses, Asaph, and the rest. Regarding those inscribed <term>for the sons of Korah <note>original: לִבְנֵי קֹרַח</note></term>, I do not think they belong to the sons of Korah for the reason that they are also ascribed to David. But it should be noted that the letter <term>Lamed <note>The Hebrew letter ל used as a prefix meaning 'to' or 'for'</note></term> prefixed to a proper name can cause that name to be used as an adjective, since the Hebrews lack adjectives of this sort. I gather that this occurs in titles of this kind both from other instances and from the inscription of Psalm 117, which among the Greeks...

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the Book of Psalms, specifically examining the inscriptions of the psalms and difficult linguistic passages in Psalms 7 through 18 on the first column, and Psalms 22 through 49 on the second. It builds on the previous discussion of how Hebrew idioms are rendered in Greek and Latin.</meta>

-># ANNOTATIONS.<-

In those psalms numbered 156 <note>this refers to a numbering system in certain Greek manuscripts</note> the inscription reads: <note>original: "τῷ Δαυῒδ διὰ ἱερεμίου"</note> "To David through Jeremiah." But the phrase "to David" is used in place of "of David" (as is seen in other places), which is a translation of the Hebrew <note>original: "לדוד"</note> *le-David*, which ought to be translated as "Davidic." Thus, it would be "a Davidic song of Jeremiah"—meaning it belongs to that genre which David was accustomed to use. This same pattern occurs in the two following psalms. I believe the same is true for the "sons of Korah," where the name is used as a <term>patronymic <note>a name derived from an ancestor</note></term>—the "Koranides"—and the song is called a "Koranidean song," just as a song from Asclepiades is called "Asclepiadean." If you wished to make the inscription of an "Asclepiadean poem of Horace" into Hebrew, you would say: "A poem of Horace, son (or sons, if there were many) of Asclepius." As for the genres of songs and musical instruments, they are so unknown today that nothing can be easily affirmed. This is less surprising in Hebrew when even in the French language there are certain types of poems whose name's origin can scarcely be explained, such as the one called a *Balade* <note>Ballade</note>. Therefore, I have interpreted what I could; others I have left in the Hebrew, such as *Githith* or *Almuth Labben*, until I find something more certain. I have done the same with the word *Sela*, which occurs often in the psalms; it seems to pertain to the musical arrangement, but is unknown today.

### FROM PSALM VII.

**He shall bring forth wickedness.**) In the Hebrew it is, "He shall bring forth a lie." But just as "truth" is used for what is fair and just among both the Hebrews and the Latins, so "falsehood" is used among the Hebrews for "injustice." This occurs frequently in the Psalms and in Isaiah 44. It also happens among the Latins with the adverb *fallò* <note>falsely</note>, used in place of "undeservedly" or "unjustly."

### FROM PSALM XI.

**What lot they must endure.**) Literally, it reads: "The portion of their cup." But that word is used for "lot" and "condition," as in Psalm 63: "They shall be a portion for foxes"—meaning they will undergo the same condition as foxes. In the New Testament, this word is sometimes called <note>original: "μερὶς"</note> *meris* and sometimes <note>original: "κλῆρος"</note> *kleros*, as in Luke 10: <note>original: "Μαρία τὴν ἀγαθὴν μερίδα ἐξελέξατο"</note> "Mary chose the good portion." And in Matthew 24: <note>original: "καὶ τὸ μέρος αὐτοῦ μετὰ τῶν ὑποκριτῶν θήσει"</note> "He will make his lot the same as that of the hypocrites"—that is, he will count him in the same number or place as deceitful and impure men. In French, too, a "condition" is called a *party*, a word derived from "part" <note>original: "partie"</note>. The "cup" is mentioned to represent a thing that must be experienced, whether joyful (as in Psalm 16) or sad (as here). This latter translation is expressed in Latin by the verb *exantlare* <note>to drain or suffer to the end</note>, which means to exhaust, and being related to the drinking of a cup, is used for "to fulfill" or "to suffer."

### FROM PSALM XV.

**And that which he swore to another, he does not revoke.**) In the Hebrew it is: "And that which he swore to his own hurt <note>original: "ad malum"</note>." But the sense is not quite right. For "to swear to evil," if you look at the Hebrew idiom, would mean to swear that one will do evil or harm someone, as can be seen in Psalm 37. Among the Hebrews, the same word signifies both "evil" and "neighbor" if the vowel points are changed—a mistake that is easily made. Therefore, the Greek translates it as <note>original: "τῷ πλησίον αὐτοῦ"</note> "to his neighbor," and the Latin as "to his neighbor"; this sense seems more appropriate to me. "Neighbor," moreover, is used for "another" not only in Hebrew but also in Greek as <note>original: "ὁ πέλας"</note> *ho pelas*.

### FROM PSALM XVIII.

**Like a bow of iron.**) In the Hebrew it is "bronze." But bows are not made of bronze; the word is used for "metal," and further for "iron" if an iron object is being discussed, just as <note>original: "χαλκός"</note> *chalkos* <note>bronze/copper</note> is used in Homer.

<column-break/>

### FROM PSALM XXII.

**Upon the hind of the morning.**) He calls Christ a "hind," whom the Jews hunted like dogs hunt a hind. He calls it "of the morning" because of the Resurrection soon to follow, which in Psalm 49 is also called "the morning," because that is the beginning of light—that is, of the blessed life.

**From you comes my praise.**) That is, you will be the author of my praise, and I will praise you. In the same way Virgil said:
> From Jove is the beginning, O Muses.
And that other line,
> From you is the beginning, in you it shall end.

### FROM PSALM XXIII.

**Who does not use his soul for wickedness.**) That is, who does not swear falsely and maliciously, as follows immediately after. For in swearing we testify to what we have in our souls, as can be seen in Jeremiah 38 where Zedekiah swears. But if we swear falsely, we abuse our soul.

### FROM PSALM XXXVII.

**Do good, and inhabit the land.**) In Hebrew, the word "inhabit" is in the imperative mood, but here it is used for the future tense. As in this same Psalm: "Depart from evil, and do good, and endure forever." For so it is read literally, in place of "you shall endure"; for he does not command one to endure forever, since that is not in the power of the man to whom he gives the command. Isaiah speaks this way too in chapter 5. The Latins do as well, like Virgil:
> Now we have made you of marble for the time; but you,
> If the offspring shall fill the flock, be of gold. <note>He uses "be" (imperative) to mean "you shall be" (future).</note>

**Better is the small portion of the righteous than the abundance of the wicked.**) In the Hebrew it is: "Better is the small portion of the righteous than the abundance of many wicked." This is the same type of Hebrew idiom found in those words of Christ: "Are you not of more value than many sparrows?" in place of "Are you not of much more value than sparrows?"

**But the wicked shall pay the penalty.**) This half-verse is missing in the Hebrew, but it must be added; for all the other verses of this poem consist of two members. It would be absurd for this not to happen here. Furthermore, since this poem is written according to the order of the letters <note>an acrostic poem</note>, the letter *Ayin* is missing here. From this it is clear that the passage is mutilated. It was not mutilated when it was translated into Greek, where it reads: <note>original: "ἄδικοι δὲ ἐκδιωχθήσονται"</note> "But the unjust shall be driven out." And in the Latin, "The unjust shall be punished." From this, the conjecture is that they read <note>original: "עַוִּילִים"</note> *awilim* <note>the unrighteous</note>.

### FROM PSALM XLIII.

**And you sent them in against the other nations with ill intent.**) "To be sent in" <note>original: "immitti"</note> or "to be layered" is said of <term>cuttings</term>—that is, the shoots which are left when others are pruned away so that they may bear fruit. Thus in this place, God, having cut away the Canaanites, is said to have "sent in" and propagated the Hebrews. Ezekiel used this same word <note>original: "שָׁלַח"</note> *shalach* in chapter 31 to mean to spread out foliage or to grow luxuriantly.

### FROM PSALM XLV.

**Your children shall succeed your parents.**) In the Hebrew, the pronouns are of the masculine gender, but they should be referred to the queen. This kind of transition of pronouns often happens, as we explain in Jeremiah 11. You will find such things also in Numbers 27 and 36. For if you refer this to the king here, the meaning will be cold; but it is most fitting for the queen, and consistent with what he had said—that she must forget her father’s house.

### FROM PSALM XLVI.

**God helping her early.**) In the Hebrew it is: "At the rising of the morning." That is, in the morning, which is often used for "early," just as in French *matin* <note>morning</note>, "You did not come early enough" <note>original: "Tu’ nes pas uenũ proú matin"</note>. And in German *frů* <note>early</note>. And in Latin *serò* <note>late</note> for "tardily."

### FROM PSALM XLIX.

**The punishment of my heels surrounding me.**) That is, imminent...

...that death is imminent for me, the cause of which is Adam’s sin; for this reason, death is less to be feared, since it only bruises the heel and does not utterly extinguish the man, as he is to be recalled to life by Christ. He alludes, moreover, to that passage in Genesis 3: "That it [the seed of the woman] shall crush your head, and you shall crush his heel." For the Devil, who was the serpent, did not wound man lethally, because Christ was the healer. Nor should this interpretation seem too far-fetched, for riddles are usually like this, and the author calls this song a "riddle." The word *yeshimennu* <note>original: "יְשִׁימֶנּוּ"</note>, however, is used for "punishment" (as we have translated it) both here and in 1 Samuel 28.

### FROM PSALM 54.

**For enemies rise up against me.** In the Hebrew, it says "strangers" <note>original: "peregrini"</note>: but "stranger" is used for "enemy," as in Isaiah 1; just as in Latin the word *hostis* <term>enemy <note>Originally, in Latin, *hostis* meant a foreigner or guest, but it evolved to mean a public enemy.</note></term> is used for a traitor, even though *hostis* once meant the same thing as a foreigner.

**The Lord is he who sustains this soul.** In the Hebrew, it says: "The Lord is among those sustaining my soul," even though it speaks of only one person. For it is a repeated sentiment, signifying the same thing as the previous one: "God succors me." Not dissimilar to this way of speaking is what the Greeks say: <term>those around Plato <note>original: "οἱ περὶ τὸν Πλάτωνα"</note></term>, which means simply "Plato." It is the same in John 11: <term>those around Martha and Mary <note>original: "τὰς περὶ Μάρθαν καὶ Μαρίαν"</note></term>. Likewise, you will find the same noted in the margin of Psalm 55, and in Psalm 69: "They persecute him whom thou hast smitten, increasing the pain of your wounded ones." Also in Judges 11: "You are among those troubling me," which is to say, "You trouble me." And in Isaiah 41: "With the last, I am he," meaning, "the last." And in Hosea 11: "To them I was as those lifting up," meaning, "as one who lifted up." In French we also say, "I am not of the richest" <note>original: "Ie ne suis pas des plus riches"</note>, meaning, "I am not very wealthy." In the same way the Greeks say, <term>lifting the boat <note>original: "ἄρας τὸ πλοῖον"</note></term> instead of "lifting a boat."

### FROM PSALM 59.

**To thee I attribute my strength.** *Uzi* <note>original: "עָזִי"</note>—"My strength." In the Hebrew it is read as "His strength" <note>original: "עָזֹו"</note>: but this contradicts the sense, as well as the Greek and the Old Latin translation. From these, it appears one should read *uzi* (my strength) rather than *uzo* (his strength), as it is also read in the final verse.

### FROM PSALM 60.

**To escape from the bows.** There <note>original: "שָׁם"</note> it is incorrectly read as "a lie" <note>original: "שֶׁקֶר"</note>, whereas <unclear>40</unclear> suggests it should be read as "truth" <note>original: "שָׁת" with a final Tau</note>, as the context and the ancient Greek and Latin translators demonstrate.

### FROM PSALM 62.

**How long will you be injurious toward me?** In Latin, one says "I know the man" instead of "I know him." In Hebrew, this also happens in the first person; in this way, Christ often says "the Son of Man" for "man," speaking of himself. Therefore, what we translate here as "against me," in the Hebrew is "against a man." Because this Hebraism would bring obscurity to this passage, we have translated the place according to Latin custom. That he is speaking of himself is apparent from what comes before and after, where he says he rests in God and leans upon Him, so that he cannot be shaken by their attempts. As for what I interpret as "those attempting to kill," in Hebrew there is one word that signifies "to kill," although the vowel markers indicate it is passive. However, both the ancient translator and the context show it to be active. In the same way, the word *yeshimennu* is placed in Proverbs 11. It must be noted, however, that the meanings of Hebrew words are broad, so that the same word can be primary, frequentative <note>expressing repeated action</note>, or desiderative <note>expressing desire or intent</note>, since the Hebrews lack these specific forms. Therefore, "to kill" is used here for "wanting to kill" (if I may speak thus), which is to say, "to wish to kill." A similar Hebraism is found in Acts 7 with these words: <term>who were driving them together into peace <note>original: "οἳ συνήλαυνον αὐτοὺς εἰς εἰρήνην"</note></term>. For Moses did not actually restore the quarreling men to favor,

<column-break/>

<page-num>84</page-num>
<header>ON THE PSALMS</header>

<margin>23. it says <term>do not wish <note>original: "μὴ θελήσητε"</note></term> instead of "do not grant your will."</margin>
but he attempted to do so. And it is the same in Matthew 23. In the same way, I say in passing regarding compound words among the Latins: because the Hebrews lack these, they signify many things with one word. For example, *sham* <note>original: "שָׁם"</note> can mean to fight, to defend, to attack, to resist, and to conquer. And so it is in many other cases.

### FROM PSALM 68.

Because this song is obscure, we shall explain it at greater length—yet in such a way that we affirm nothing, leaving the judgment to others. When the Ark of the Covenant set out, Moses used to say this preface: "Arise, O Jehovah, and let thy enemies be scattered," etc. Since David begins this song with these words, it must be understood that a declaration of that event is contained within it. But this cannot be understood unless we know that he who is called there and here "Jehovah," and "Genius" <note>a guiding spirit or divine messenger</note>, and "God," and "Lord," is Christ, as we declared in the second chapter of Exodus. Certainly, if this is ignored, one must necessarily wander in the dark regarding the chief points of Christian teaching. Therefore, we shall declare this song thus: "Arise, O God,"—that is, Christ, the same who in the time of Moses led the Israelites. When he comes into the lands, having conquered his enemies (the Devil and his wicked servants) by his life, teaching, and resurrection, he will lead the good to happiness. This is the argument of the whole song. Then, he commands that the glory of this matter be referred to God, the Father of Christ, by whose mandate the Son shall do these things—the Father who has granted his own name, "Jehovah," and furthermore his power, to his Son. For this is what he says: "whose name is in Jehovah"; that is, Christ is endowed with the name of that God, as it says in Exodus 23, where God speaks thus to the people:

> Behold, I am going to send a spirit <note>original: "genium"</note> before you to protect you on the way, and to lead you into the place I have prepared. Take heed of him: obey him: do not provoke him. For he will not forgive your crimes, because he will be endowed with my name.

You see that this guiding spirit is Christ, who has the same name as Jehovah; to whom God gave a name which is above every name. Thus, he who showed that the name of Jesus is derived from Jehovah seems to have spoken well. Therefore, he attributes the praise of this salvation, won for us through Christ, to God, who, dwelling in his holy heavenly home, looks after the humble and casts down the proud. Presently he repeats the whole argument more fully, in this manner: Just as you, O God, placed the Israelites, led out of Egypt, in the promised land after their enemies were overcome; so Christ is to introduce the true Israelites into the heavenly kingdom—of which that land of Canaan was a certain shadow. Christ, I say, the Lord, will provide the theme for the women, the messengers of a great army: that is, having conquered death, he will return to life and show himself to the women, who will announce his resurrection to the disciples (who are called a "great army"). This news will be most joyful; for since death, the devil, the world, and man's corrupt nature have been conquered like certain military leaders, the disciples of Christ, though staying at home and being unwarlike, may triumph over them through Christ. Therefore, even if you have lain among the black cooking pots, O disciples of Christ—even if you have been disfigured by filth and sorrow while Christ was dead—henceforth, now that he lives, you shall shine. And the land—that is, the Church—will henceforth be whiter than snow. Moreover, he calls the Church the mountain of God, in which Jehovah-Christ shall always dwell, having many troops (for this is what he means by "Not once ten thousand," that is, many ten thousands; just as in Latin we say "not once" to mean "often," and as in Psalm 62 "twice" is used for "once," that is, to mean "frequently"). Among these troops is he himself in his holy place,

...in his own place, he who had likewise given the law on Mount Sinai. Then he turns his discourse to Christ: "You," he says, "having conquered death, ascend into heaven; you will lead away those who were captives (for many returned to life with Christ), and from there you will exercise your gifts; namely, you will send the Apostles and the other teachers of the church: even among those men who resist this matter, by the labor of these teachers it shall come to pass that Christ is recognized and God is worshiped." Therefore, let the Lord, the Father of Christ and author of our salvation, be praised, for the Lord Jehovah is God even unto the exit of death: that is, while he recalls Christ, Jehovah, and the Lord back to life. However, we read here <note>original: למות תוצאות (le-mavet totsa'ot)</note> "the escapes from death," just as in Isaiah 68 <note>Likely a reference to Isaiah 26:19 or similar, as Isaiah only has 66 chapters; the author may be citing a specific edition's numbering.</note>, and <note>original: ועל (ve-al)</note> in Amos 6, and <note>original: מעשות השבת (me-asot ha-shabbat)</note> "from doing on the Sabbath" instead of "he shall put," and <note>original: למספר יודעי נהי (le-mispar yode'ei nehi)</note> "to the number of those who know lamentation" instead of <note>original: אל ידעי נהי (el yode'ei nehi)</note> "to those who know lamentation."

Truly, God will strike off the head of his enemies, namely Christ’s enemies: that is, he will subdue the wicked. For he promises thus: "I will bring back and deliver the Lord, namely Christ, from death and capital danger," such as might come from Og the king of Bashan, or in the Red Sea, "so that you may wash your feet (there is a change of person here) in the blood of the enemies, O Christ: and your dogs may lick it," that is, so that you may achieve a full victory, and thus triumph with a great display of songs and praises. Praise God from the fountain of Israel, that is, you Israelites. This can be expressed more significantly in Greek as <term>those from the fountains <note>original: οἱ ἐκ τῶν πηγῶν</note></term>, and in French as <term>those of the fountain <note>original: ceux de la fontaine</note></term> (just as in Psalm 148, "Praise Jehovah from the heavens" means "heavenly beings"), especially the Benjamites, the Zebulunites, and those of Naphtali, among whom, being excellent in knowledge, Christ first became known—concerning which matter more is said in Isaiah 9.

God has established your power, O Christ, which I desire him to confirm for us, so that other nations may come to Christ: for this is what it means to "bring gifts to Jerusalem." Destroy the republic of those who disturb other nations like bulls do calves, a nation submerged in segments of silver: that is, a greedy nation, waging war out of a desire for possession. That is, destroy, O Christ, the kingdom of the Romans, so that you may be recognized both by other nations and by the Egyptians and Ethiopians. For the kingdom of Christ succeeds the Roman Empire, as may be seen in that statue seen by Nebuchadnezzar in his dreams in the book of Daniel, which the falling stone shatters. What is said here, "Ethiopia shall run her hands to God," means she will offer them swiftly, as in that line of Virgil:

-> "Run, spindles, run; such ages the Fates have decreed." <- 
<note>original: "Talia secla suis dixerunt currite fusis." From Virgil's Eclogue IV, often interpreted by Christians as a prophecy of Christ.</note>

This means: "Hasten such ages," or "bring them forth quickly." Therefore, sing to God, who, although he is in heaven, nevertheless has such care for the earth that he is about to send the most effective voice of the Gospel to men, by which they may be called to salvation—both others and, most especially, the Jews.

### FROM PSALM LXIII.

**Fearing no such thing.**) In the Hebrew, the preceding word is in the singular number, but it is used for the plural. Therefore, a plural verb follows, which often happens; and conversely, as in Psalms 62, 63, and 68.

### FROM PSALM LXIX.

**Heap their vices upon vices.**) Christ (about whom this song was written) does not call down these curses upon everyone by whom he is treated unjustly; for while dying, he prayed for pardon for those by whom he was driven to the cross. But he added a reason, saying, "because they know not what they do." From this, it is proper to understand that in this song, he calls down curses upon the perverse and those who sin out of a depravity of nature, such as the scribes and Pharisees were.

<column-break/>

**Heap their vices upon vices.**) Let them indeed continue to sin, since they are so wicked, lest they enjoy your equity: that is, lest you have mercy on them. On this matter, see more in Isaiah 6 and Matthew 12.

### FROM PSALM LXXII.

**As long as the sun and moon shall endure.**) In the Hebrew, it is: "With the sun, and in the presence of the moon," or "before the moon": that is, as long as the sun and moon shall be present.
**Thus far the prayers of David.**) To be sure, in these first two books there are songs by others besides David. But because David is their principal author, they are ascribed to him; just as we call them "Cicero’s epistles," even though there are letters from others among them. Moreover, although there are also psalms of David in the three following books, yet the prayers of David are said to be finished here, either because the following ones are by many authors, or because, having already concluded the earlier books, he composed the rest later.

### FROM PSALM LXXVIII.

**Men ate such noble bread.**) Word for word, it is: "The bread of nobles." As in Judges 8, "the bowl of nobles" is said instead of a "noble bowl"; and in Zechariah 9, a donkey is called "the son of she-asses": that is, a beast of burden, or one born of a she-ass.

### FROM PSALM LXXXI.

**I withdrew your shoulders from the burden.**) In the Hebrew, there is a silent change of both person and number. We have served clarity here, as in many other places.

### FROM PSALM LXXXIIII.

**Who, if they pass through the valley of weeping, shall make it a place of springs.**) That is, wherever they go, God supplies them with necessities, so much so that if nature denies them, he would rather act against nature: as once in that parched wilderness where he brought forth a spring for his people from the rock. When he speaks of a "valley of weeping," he means a thirsty place. For if you cannot find water in the valleys, which by nature are usually abundant with springs, what remains but to weep? Regarding what he says about the fish <note>The author likely reads a variation of the word for "pools" or "blessings" as related to fish or water storage.</note>, this is the meaning: if they have pools or cisterns, as is common in mountainous places, God will so fill them with rain that they are covered and clothed with grass, so that they lack nothing either in the valley or on the mountain. Nor does it matter that they do not rouse the good springs themselves, as is said here: that is, they do not provide for themselves, but God supplies what is necessary. For they are said to do, in a poetic manner, that which is done for their sake.

### FROM PSALM LXXXVI.

**This man was born there.**) That is, a few; and what follows, "One and then another": that is, many, which are signified by the repetition, as is also the case among the Latins. Not unlike this is what is said in Isaiah 61, "double shame" for "great shame," and in Psalm 8, "tears of <note>original: שלשים (shalishim)</note>," meaning "threefold" or "triple," so to speak, for "large tears"; and in Proverbs 22, <note>original: שלשים (shalishim)</note> "triply," for "greatly" or "again and again."

### FROM PSALM XC.

**For if anyone should know the power of your wrath, etc.**) If anyone should understand what the cause and power of that wrath is, by which you make our life so short, he will understand that you rage according to how much you are feared: and that you make life so much shorter the less men revere you. But if we were to rightly weigh how short our life is, and understood the cause of this brevity to be our sins and contempt for you, we would apply a wise mind—that is, we would revere you (for the beginning of wisdom is the fear of you)—and...

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the Psalms. The previous page concluded a discussion on Psalm 68 and the victory of God over his enemies. This page begins with the conclusion of a prayer for the restoration of life through the Messiah, then moves into specific linguistic and natural-philosophical annotations for Psalms 107, 110, 111, 117, 137, and 138.
