# ON THE PSALMS

...anger, we might follow a life both long and happy through obedience, which sin and stubbornness have rendered short and miserable. But our own guilt prevents us from attaining the strength for this; it remains for you to effect this in us, and to teach us this right way of living. This you will not do unless you are appeased; nor can you be appeased except through the Messiah, the restorer of our life. Send, therefore, the Messiah quickly, through whose work you may, according to your mercy, grant us full and perpetual <margin>10</margin> happiness. And may you do this "in the morning," that is, when we shall live again. For this life is night, wrapped in the shadows of so many evils. That life will be day, full of light and joys. Therefore, just as we are afflicted by perpetual evils in this life, bring us that other life in which we may enjoy eternal goods. Show this, your most excellent work, to us and to our children, so that we may obtain that divine happiness. And complete the work of our hands for us; that is, perfect that which we attempt in vain. We attempt to arrive at life (for this <margin>20</margin> is innate in all, that they desire the good; and God is the Good, living a blessed life, for the sake of attaining which we labor, and in whose likeness we were created), but because we achieve nothing, we expect this from you. Compare this passage with Isaiah 26.

->FROM PSALM 107<-

*They that go down to the sea in ships.)* The Latins say "to climb up" <note>original: "conscendere"</note>, namely into a ship. Virgil puts it thus: *With twice ten ships I climbed the Phrygian sea* <note>original: "Bis denis Phrygium conscendi nauibus æquor"</note>. But here our author says "to descend into the sea": that is, to <margin>30</margin> sail on the sea, where one descends from the land, just as Jonah is written to have "descended" into the ship: for so it is read literally in Jonah 1. For it is evident that the sea is lower than this land of ours which is inhabited, from the fact that everywhere through the lands rivers run down into the sea; nor could you come from the land into the sea without descending. Hence it is that in Psalm 24, God is said to have founded the earth upon the sea. For as to what the Latins call the "high" sea <note>original: "altum"</note>, understand that "high" is used here to mean "deep." However, as to why the sea appears high to those looking from the shore, that happens because of the roundness <margin>40</margin> of the water; since the sight of the eyes is not curved according to the ratio of the globe, but stretching out straight, it hits upon the swelling of the globe. For if the sea were truly high, ships would hang in a tranquil sea as if in a steep place, which one would have to climb from the shore; and from the sea to the shore they would descend of their own accord without wind (as if to a lower place) like a following river; and they would be carried from the shore to the deep with more difficulty than from the deep to the shore. Finally, if the water of the sea were higher than the land, it would flow down onto the land. Unless perhaps one wishes <margin>50</margin> to invert the nature of water, so that it does not flow down of its own accord.

->FROM PSALM 110<-

*From the womb of the morning you shall have the dew of your youth.)* He calls the "dew of youth" the innumerability of young men, just as in Numbers 23, Balaam speaks of the "dust of the people of Jacob" to represent an infinite number. He calls the "womb of the morning" the dawn, because dew falls in the morning and is given birth by the dawn.

->FROM PSALM 111<-

*The head of wisdom.)* That is, the highest and first wisdom. And this is also declared by the Greeks as *arche* <note>original: ἀρχὴ - meaning beginning or first principle</note>, by which word they are accustomed to translate the Hebrew *reshit* <note>original: רֵאשִׁית - the first or beginning</note>, just as Isocrates <margin>60</margin> in *Nicocles* calls the "highest honors" *tas archas tōn timōn* <note>original: τὰς ἀρχὰς τῶν τιμῶν</note>. And the Latins call those things "first" which are highest and most excellent.

->FROM PSALM 117<-

*Who dwelling on high, sees the humble; dwelling in the heavens, he sees*

<column-break/>

the lands.) So it is read literally: "He who dwells high, sees lowly, in heaven and on earth": so that "in heaven" refers back to the word "Dwells," and "on earth" to the word "Sees." There is a similar way of speaking in Deuteronomy 32, where it is read literally: "I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall eat flesh: with the blood of the slain and the captives, by the head of the leaders of the enemy." So that "with the blood of the slain" refers back to "I will make my arrows drunk," and "by the head of the leaders" refers to the "sword." Likewise in Matthew 7, it is read: "Give not that which is holy to the dogs, neither cast your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you." This speech, if the order were changed, would become clear thus: "Give not that which is holy to the dogs, lest they turn and rend you; neither cast your pearls before swine, lest they trample them." Or by repetition, which the Latins use, thus: "Give not that which is holy to the dogs, nor cast pearls to the swine: to the swine, lest they trample them; to the dogs, lest they rend you." You will find such a figure also in Micah 1. Such is also that line from Virgil: *Pastor, arator, eques, paui, colui, superaui: Capras, rus, hostes, fronde, ligone, manu.* <note>The author quotes a mnemonic verse: "Shepherd, plowman, knight; I fed, I tilled, I overcame: The goats, the fields, the enemies; with leaf, with hoe, with hand." This illustrates how the first three nouns correspond to the next three verbs and the final three objects/means.</note> I have used this kind of repetition in this passage of the Psalm for the sake of clarity.

->FROM PSALM 137<-

*When we have forgotten you.)* They give the reason why they do not know how to sing: after we lost Jerusalem, we lost all skill both of plucking the strings and of singing with the mouth, and our tongue sticks to the roof of our mouth; that is, we are mute (for this is a mode of speaking also in Job 29), nor can we sing any more than if our tongue stuck to our palate; because Jerusalem is the "head of our joy": deprived of which, we lack joy; just as birds deprived of liberty do not know how to sing. As for the phrase "We have forgotten," the verb in this place signifies "to lose," as in Genesis 41, where it is read literally: "There shall arise seven years of famine after them, and all the plenty shall be given to oblivion." For there is no "oblivion" of plenty while famine is raging, but rather memory and longing. From which it appears that the word here signifies "to be lost" and "to be wiped out," as it is also placed in Deuteronomy 31, and Job 28, and Lamentations 3, where in another word of the same meaning, the commonwealth of Jerusalem says she has "forgotten good": that is, she no longer knows good and has lost it. For she had not "forgotten" the thing which she was longing for. And in the same way Virgil spoke: *And the apples degenerate, having forgotten their former juices.* That is, having lost their former flavor. And Juvenal: *To not know wine for the whole of December*; that is, not to use it. This was the reason that in this passage of the Psalm we translated the verb which signifies "to remember" as "to be in possession of," following the logic of opposites.

->FROM PSALM 138<-

*Who make your promises greater than is your name alone.)* That is, you who perform greater things than your reputation suggests, which is nevertheless great. It must be understood that, just as the judgment of God is often put for the action—since whatever he judges should be done, he does, seeing that he can be hindered by nothing—so also the "word" or "promise" in this passage of the Psalm is put for the fulfillment of the promise: because he promises nothing that he does not fulfill. Just as in Psalm 56, where he says he "praises the promises in God": for promises are only praised if they are fulfilled. Of the same kind is also that in Isaiah 44: "Who says to Jerusalem, You shall be inhabited, and to the cities..."

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the scriptures. The previous page discussed the restoration of life through the Messiah and began annotations on the Psalms. I command Judea to be rebuilt, etc. For here "to command" is used for taking care that something is done, and thus doing it. Such is also that saying of Christ: *Which is easier to say, "Thy sins are forgiven thee," or to say, "Take up thy bed and walk"?* <note>original: "Vtrum facilius est dicere..." from Luke 5:23</note> For there "to say" is used for effecting through a command; otherwise anyone could command, but one could not command confidently, and therefore effectively. Juvenal spoke in the same way in his 6th Satire: *Therefore the mushroom of Agrippina will be less harmful, since it pressed the heart of only one old man, and commanded his trembling head to descend into heaven.* <note>Juvenal, Satire 6.620. This is a sarcastic reference to the Empress Agrippina poisoning Emperor Claudius, "ordering" his death and subsequent deification (the "descent" into heaven).</note> This is to say, it forced Claudius to die. And Virgil: *At Hector’s tomb under the high walls of Troy... commanded to die;* <note>Virgil, Aeneid 3.321.</note> that is, killed by command.

# ON ECCLESIASTES

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'H' within a square frame, decorated with classical foliate patterns.</image-desc>

<margin>20</margin>
This book is written about the ends of goods, or about the vanity of life. In it, we are taught that this life is entirely vain and miserable, and no part of it is truly blessed. This is placed both in the proposition of the whole book and in its conclusion. If anyone asks what is good in this life, Solomon responds: nothing, for all things are vain and miserable. Yet if you ask what might be "good" (that is, the least evil) within this misery itself, he responds that it is pleasure. While all other things are troublesome and evil, in pleasure <margin>30</margin> there is at least some seasoning of life granted to humans by divine providence. Someone might say: "Shall I then indulge in pleasure?" Truly, says Solomon, if you wish to enjoy the fleeting good of this life. But one must take care that in pursuing an empty good, you do not lose the true good. For although in this life all things seem to happen at random, I know nevertheless that it shall be well for the religious and not well for the impious, and the works of all, however hidden, shall be judged. Since this does not happen in this life—for as <margin>40</margin> it appears, it goes badly for the good and well for the wicked—another life must be expected, in which it will be well for the good and badly for the wicked. Therefore, if you take no account of the other life, then feast and drink while there is life, for after death there is no pleasure. But if you seek the happiness of the other life, conduct yourself so that you may be worthy of 그 good: that is, fear God, who will repay each with rewards worthy of their deeds. This is the argument of this book, which I wished to touch upon lest anyone be deceived here. For there are some (would that they were few!) who do not look <margin>50</margin> to the end and goal of books, but having found one passage that seems to favor their own lust, they seize upon it and use it to patronize their own license—as if they were going to have God as a judge who is just like they are when they judge themselves.

## FROM CHAPTER III.

*To every thing there is a season.*) Since all things happen in their own time, and the question here is what is good, one must take care not to seek it at the wrong time. For just as there is one time for sowing and another for reaping, etc., so there is one time for unhappiness and another for happiness. In this life, it is the time of misery. If anyone seeks the "good" in it, he acts just as if he wished to reap at the time of

<column-break/>

<page-num>90</page-num>
<header>90</header>

sowing. The harvest must be waited for: that is, the future life, in which (unlike in this one) injury shall not reign as if by right, but justice and truth alone shall dominate once errors have been removed. But if you do not care for that life, then indulge in pleasure.

*He hath so set life in their hearts.*) For the heart is the fountain of life. As for my translating it as "life," in the Hebrew it is "the world" or "the age" <note>original: "seculum, siue æuum"</note>, which is used for "life." For in chapter 7, the noun <margin>10</margin> signifying "life" is used for the same thing.

# ON ECCLESIASTICUS

## FROM CHAPTER XV.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'A' inside a square border with floral decorations.</image-desc>

*The truthful shall attain through it alone,* etc.) This sentence in the Latin translation (for this verse does not exist in the Greek) reads: *And truthful men shall be found in her, and shall have success even unto the inspection of God.* I think this sentence was written as <term>αγαθωσυνην εν αυτω</term> <note>original Greek: agathosynen en auto, "goodness/virtue in him/it"</note>, because this verb also in Greek means "to reach" or "attain," just as the Hebrew word <term>נמצא</term> <note>Hebrew: nimtsa, "to be found" or "to reach"</note> does; and it is used in this way in Philippians 3.

# ON ISAIAH

## FROM CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'V' featuring detailed floral scrolls within a square frame.</image-desc>

*The vision of Isaiah.*) The Hebrew word <term>חזון</term> <note>Hebrew: Chazon</note> means not only to see, but also to foresee, and when applied to the mind, it means to perceive beforehand. Just as other Hebrew words are often used as simple forms for compound ones, as we have <margin>40</margin> explained elsewhere. Hence <term>חזון</term> denotes not only a vision discerned by the eyes, but also that which is perceived by the mind, which in Latin can be called *praesensio* (fore-feeling). But because prophets use this word to declare that they predict to men the things they perceive through divine inspiration, I sometimes translate it as "oracle" or "prediction," and sometimes even as "fate," as in Daniel 8, where it reads literally: *How long shall the vision of the perpetual unexpiated calamity last?* That is, how long would that which was in the fates be signified by that prediction and oracle—namely, that the perpetual sacred thing would lie wasted.

*Wash yourselves.*) In the Hebrew it is "Wash" (active), but the active verb is often used for the passive or neuter, as in Latin with the verbs *to move*, *to wash*, *to cast down*, <margin>50</margin> *to turn*, and many others.

*Come, let us correct ourselves.*) That is, "Correct yourselves." For the first person plural is elegantly used for the second person of either number. This also occurs in the second chapter in these words: *Come, O house of Jacob, let us walk in the light of the Lord.* We often speak this way in French. In Latin, too, Cicero said in the third action against Verres: *But if it is necessary for the cause to be known, is it too little known? We are pretending, Hortensius, what we have often experienced in speaking.* This means: "Are you not pretending, Hortensius?" <margin>60</margin>

## FROM CHAPTER IV.

*Namely the escaped of Israel.*) In Hebrew, the letter *lamed* serves as a nominative article, as also in 1 Chronicles 22 and 2 Chronicles 1.

### FROM CHAPTER VI.

*Hear, and do not understand.* <note>original: "Audite, & ne intelligite"</note>) The imperative mood is used here instead of the indicative, which usually happens when the speech is vehement and agitated. It is like that phrase: *Fill up the measure of your fathers* <note>Matthew 23:32</note>: that is, "you will fill it up," or "it is necessary that you fill it up." And in Ezekiel 20: *Go, serve everyone his filthy idols.* <note>Ezekiel 20:39</note> Thus, what is said here, *Make the minds of these people dull*, is just as if he were saying, "their minds are dull and sluggish." Therefore, the Greeks <note>The Septuagint translators</note> translated this speech of Isaiah using the indicative mood. The Romans also speak in this manner, as in Livy’s 10th book of the 4th decade, where King Philip addresses his sons: *Come now, you wicked ears of a father, decide by accusations, you who are soon to decide by the sword; say openly whatever truth you can, or whatever you please to invent.*

### FROM CHAPTER VII.

*But if you do not believe (as you are unbelieving), ask for yourself a sign, he said, etc.*) To the word, it is read thus: *But if you do not believe, as you are unbelieving, Jehovah goes on to speak thus to Ahaz: Ask, etc.* This speech becomes clearer in English through a parenthesis, similar to that in Mark 2: *But that you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins, he says to the paralytic: I say to you, arise.* <note>Mark 2:10-11</note> This would be clearer as: *I command you to rise, he says to the paralytic.*

*Is it a small thing for you to weary men.*) Not only do you cause trouble for me, who am a man, while I am forced to warn you because of your wickedness; but you even weary God, whom you drive by your lack of faith to provide you some sign by which he may give you faith in this promise. Therefore, receive this sign. There is a certain young woman <note>original: "puella", a translation of the Hebrew 'almah'</note> now pregnant, who will bear a son, and she shall call him Emmanuel, from the help of God, who will be present with us at the birth of that boy. That boy shall eat butter and honey *by learning* (for thus I translate the infinitive joined to the letter *Lamed* by a gerund, as often happens, as in 2 Kings 19 and Daniel 9); that is, at that age when one learns what the difference is between good and evil, namely, infancy. This means that before this boy can discern good from evil by age, this city will be freed from siege, and Samaria and Syria (whose kings are besieging you) will be reduced to such a wilderness by the Assyrians that even cultivated places will be filled with briars and thickets due to the devastation. As a result, livestock will graze freely everywhere and thus grow fat, and yield so much milk that if anyone has one heifer or two sheep, he will abound in milk. So it will happen that butter made from that milk, and in the same way honey (for there is also an abundance of honey when there is forage, because of the plentiful flowers), will be brought into this city (which the siege now prevents), and with these things that boy, who is still in the womb, can be nourished, so that you may understand how shortly your salvation will be present. Moreover, regarding my translation of *pregnant young woman* in the present tense, there is a similar way of speaking elsewhere, and in Genesis 16, where the spirit addresses the pregnant Hagar. But why Matthew cited this place concerning Christ, we shall discuss in Chapter 9.

### FROM CHAPTER VIII.

*Taking faithful witnesses.*) Namely, those who would be present at

<column-break/>

<page-num>92</page-num>
<header>ON ISAIAH</header>

the birth, so that no one could falsely claim that a girl had been born and a male child secretly substituted in her place.

*For thus Jehovah spoke to me, as if grasping me by the hand.*) Jehovah, he says, spoke to me as if I were grasped by the hand: that is, he spoke secrets to me separately and directly, as if he were saying: Because I promise you safety against the Assyrians through the birth of Emmanuel, understand that I am not speaking only of that Emmanuel, or of Sennacherib; <margin>10</margin> for there is to be another, true Emmanuel: that is, the Messiah, the Savior and God who is to dwell among you, who will defend you from far more serious dangers. If you ask how he can be recognized when he comes, I will tell you, but obscurely. He will be of such a kind that this people will call him seditious and think he should be avoided. But you, do not side with the people, nor fear that Messiah; rather fear lest, by rejecting the Messiah, you offend Jehovah, who sent the Messiah. That Messiah will indeed be holy and <margin>20</margin> a source of salvation to those by whom he is recognized; but many, not recognizing him, will take offense, and will perish through him by their own fault. What I say is an oracle, certainly obscure and closed, since it is to be understood only by my own people. Therefore I (says Isaiah, and any of the godly) will wait for the Messiah of Jehovah, who is to come in such a way that he remains hidden from the Israelites. But how will his disciples recognize him? In this way, he says: *Behold, I and the children, etc.* <note>Isaiah 8:18</note> That is, there will be someone who will have young disciples, assigned to him by Jehovah, with whom he will perform signs <margin>30</margin> and miracles among the Israelites. Recognize him as the Savior, and obey him. If any should persuade you that magicians or Apollo should be consulted, respond that everyone ought to consult his own God: that Jehovah is your God, and so you will seek counsel from him. For it is absurd to consult the dead on behalf of the living, which is what magicians do. One must go to the Law: that is, to the books of Moses, in which there are oracles concerning Christ, at whose coming Apollo will fall silent, <margin>40</margin> Pan will become mute, and errors will vanish. Therefore those magicians and soothsayers accustomed to consulting such gods, when they see there is a famine of oracles—that Delphi, Dodona, and all are silent, and that there is nothing certain anywhere for them to answer—will speak uncertainties. Angered by that difficulty, they will curse both their gods and their kings, in whom there is no protection for them. See Micah 3. Therefore, doctrine must be sought from Christ, after it can be found nowhere else. <margin>50</margin>

### FROM CHAPTER IX.

Although I say there will be distress—namely, once the magicians and false gods have been conquered by Christ—that distress will indeed be ruinous for idol-worshipers and the wicked, who are blinded by the light of Christ; but it will be a source of salvation for the elect and those who receive Christ. For doctrine will be brighter in those lands in which Christ will teach than it was before his coming among the Zebulunites and <margin>60</margin> Naphtalites, which two tribes were famous for doctrine, as appears from the final words of Jacob and Moses in Genesis 49 and Deuteronomy 33, and from the song of Deborah in Judges 5. But their doctrine was light and obscure compared to what the future...

<header>ANNOTATIONS.</header>

<margin>95</margin> That light of Christ, by which he will one day so enlighten Galilee and the other unlearned nations that a great number of them will become Christian; this event will give birth to joy, like the winning of spoils. For Christ will triumph over his enemies and claim his own for liberty, just as was done long ago by Gideon against the Midianites <note>A reference to the story in Judges 7, where Gideon's small force miraculously defeated a vast army.</note>. But the battles of Gideon and others are waged with the sword. Yet the battle of Christ will be waged with the fire of the Gospel, by which the whole world will be set ablaze. For *a child is born to us* <note>original: "puer nobis natus est"</note>; Christ, the Son of God, is known to have been sent for our sake, who carries the sovereignty upon his shoulder—that is, by his own power and authority. He is called—that is, he truly is—the **Wonderful Counselor**, and therefore he is the one to be consulted, not magicians or soothsayers, or the people of Zebulun and the rest, even if any are considered learned. He is **God**, so that he may be the true Emmanuel—that is, "God with us." For that boy who was born during the siege of Jerusalem <note>Referring to the immediate historical child mentioned in Isaiah 7</note> is not God, but a sign of this Christ-God. He is **Mighty**, so that it may be understood that the enemies will be easily overcome by him, just as the Midianites were by Gideon. **Father of eternity**, so that his kingdom may be hoped for as perpetual. **Prince of peace**, so that under his reign no wars may be feared. He shall reign forever on the throne of David, but in a divine kingdom, as he himself will be God.

You see, reader, that Isaiah prophesies about Emmanuel in such a way that he gradually leads us to the true Emmanuel, Christ. He does the same thing later from chapter 45 regarding Cyrus, just as in Ezekiel chapter 16 a transition is made from the Sodomites to nations similar to the Sodomites; and in chapter 20 from the idol-worshipping Israelites to the true Israelites; and in Ezekiel 31 and Daniel 4 from a tree to a man. Unless we understand these types of transitions, we must necessarily fall into great errors. 

But this must be greatly noted, which Isaiah says: *A child is born to us.* For if he is a child, he is a man; if he is born, he is born of a woman, since a man cannot be born except from a woman. Again, what he says—**Mighty, Father of eternity**—shows that he was not begotten by a man. For a mortal man cannot beget an immortal God, as the Sibyl <note>The Sibylline Oracles: ancient texts of prophecies used by early Christians to show that even pagans predicted Christ.</note> teaches in these words:

<margin>(by a male</margin>
> For if he is begotten, he utterly perishes, and
> God cannot be created from a female limb.

But if he was not begotten by a man, and yet was born, it is necessary that he was born of a virgin, just as the Sibyl says:
> Receive, O Virgin, God in your chaste and pure womb.

If this is so, it appears here that Isaiah prophesies about Christ being born of a virgin. Therefore, when Matthew described the origin of Christ, he rightly brought forward the beginning of this prophecy concerning Christ: *Behold, a young woman is pregnant* <note>original: "Ecce puella pragnans"; Matthew 1:23, citing Isaiah 7:14.</note>. For while we consider the beginning of the prophecy in relation to the whole prophecy—for Matthew does not mean that Isaiah, by those words *a young woman is pregnant*, only meant the beginning of the virgin—it does not matter that in Matthew she is called a "virgin" <note>Greek: *parthenos*</note> rather than a "young woman" <note>Hebrew: *almah*</note>. For whether he wrote in Hebrew (as Sophronius reports in his *Life of Matthew*) and used Isaiah’s own words, or in Greek (for I can affirm neither), he followed the Greek translator in this word, where it is "virgin." And he did this not ineptly, since he was speaking of the true Emmanuel, whose birth from a virgin Isaiah had predicted not just by a word, but in reality and meaning. As for what I translated above as *and affecting such great joy*, I understand 
<margin>nasa</margin>
was put for
<margin>hal</margin>
<note>Grammatical note on Hebrew verbal roots *nasa* (to carry/lift) and *halal* (to praise/shine).</note>
as is found to have happened elsewhere, such as below in chapter 49.

### FROM CHAPTER XV.

*Through its streets they are dressed in sackcloth.* <note>original: "saxtis induti sunt," likely a variant or error for "saccis"</note>) In the Hebrew, the relative pronoun "Its" is of the masculine gender, for it refers to Moab, that is, the Moabite man. But other feminine relatives follow: for they refer to Moab, that is, the Moabite land. This change must be noticed, for the same thing happens elsewhere, as in Jeremiah 11, Ezekiel 32, and above at the beginning of chapter 9.

### FROM CHAPTER XVI.

*The shout of your summer and of your harvest has fallen.*) In the Hebrew, it is literally: *Upon your summer and your harvest, a shout has fallen.* That is, the jubilee and joyful song which those who reap or gather grapes are accustomed to use has perished for you, the fields being laid waste. Thus "shout for the summer" stands for the adjective "summery," and the noun "shout" is joined with "summer"; this can be better expressed in Greek by the article: *the shout over the summer fruits* <note>original Greek: "τὸ ἐπὶ τῶν θερείων κέλευσμα"</note>. And the verb "Fallen" is used (as often happens) for "perished," as the following words declare. Compare this with Jeremiah 48.

### FROM CHAPTER XVII.

*At that time he shall be made thin.*) So that you may understand this and the following chapter, read Ezekiel 38, 37, 38, and 39 carefully. You will find the same course of meaning, which here is as follows: "I will so diminish the Damascenes and Syrians," says Jehovah, "as I will the nobility of the Jacobites"—that is, the noble Jacobites <note>The people of Israel</note>. "These Jacobites I will diminish so much that few remain, just as when the harvest is done, a few ears of grain are left for gleaning," etc. But let the Syrians or others not think this will be perpetual. "For I will recall the Israelites, who will afterwards be in their own fatherland, and there they will truly worship me." 

But before that happens, their cities will be destroyed, so that upon their arrival, scarcely thin remnants of them will remain: just as when a forest is cut down, certain shrubs remain to testify that a forest was once there. "And this calamity will happen to you, O Israelite people, because you have not worshipped your God. Therefore, when you seem to yourself to be restored, when you are recalled by Cyrus and gathered in your fatherland, and you hope to be there forever—nevertheless, because even then you will not worship me, calamities will press upon you one after another. Nor will you gain anything, but finally (which will be the heaviest grief) you will be destroyed by the Romans, and so you will remain deserted for a long time. Then, after that calamity, you will be recalled, and only then will you truly worship me." Compare this passage with what we wrote in chapter 31. 

What follows, *Oh, the roar of many nations*: seems to be an oracle concerning **Gog and Magog** <note>Symbolic enemies of God's people in apocalyptic literature</note>, concerning whom I seem to have noticed five oracles, besides the Sibylline ones: the first is this one, the second is Isaiah 56, the third Ezekiel 38, the fourth Micah 5, the fifth Revelation 20. And the last of these is the most clear, as usually happens in other oracles. But let us explain what follows concerning the same Gog.

### FROM CHAPTER XVIII.

*O land shadowing with wings.*) The "wings of the land" refer to the extremities and borders. A land "shadowing with wings" is a spacious one: as if you were to call a bird "shadowing with wings," you would mean it was large.

and vast. He addresses a nation situated beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, namely beyond the Nile, which wanders through immense stretches of land before it flows down into Egypt. Its inhabitants, as Pliny the Elder <note>A Roman author and naturalist who wrote the *Natural History*</note> teaches, use boats made of papyrus and reeds. After crying out to this nation, he addresses the messengers of that people. "Go," he says, "you messengers of that nation, who are accustomed to announce new things; carry this message to your nation, to a people most formidable of all who dwell further off, to a scattered and plundered nation"—that is, a nation dwelling near great rivers, which wear away its land and lay it waste, and by floods, overflows, and diversions, scatter and divide it, and thus often change its boundaries and produce one after another. Then he declares why he calls upon that nation, as if to say: "Because I call upon the most remote of nations, I wish to signify that I am about to do something that must be announced to the most remote people—that is, to the whole world: a very great thing." For those things announced to the distant are both great, and are announced even more so to those nearby. Therefore, behold, all you mortals, the signal raised on the mountain, and hear the trumpet. This means: I announce war to you, which will take place in the mountains of the Israelites, in which war "I will watch quietly, and I will most gently cherish and protect my Israelites against the enemies, like heat after rain, and like a dewy cloud in the heat" <note>original: "ego quietus spectabo, & meos Israëlitas aduersus hostes mollissimè fouebo ac tuebor, tanquam æstus post pluuiam, & tanquam roscida nubes in calore"</note>; that is, I will refresh them sweetly and protect them against all violence. But the enemies, when they thought themselves nearly in possession of victory, shall perish; and it shall happen to them just as if crops were devastated before the harvest, or vineyards before the vintage, frustrating the hope of the farmers. And so they shall lie slain on the ground, to be devoured by beasts. The fame of this victory will be so bright, and the name of Jehovah so formidable, that the furthest of the nations shall humbly bring gifts to Zion.

### FROM CHAPTER XXIX.

*And the needy shall gain joy in Jehovah, and the poor shall exult in the Holy One.* <note>The Latin text uses "Augusto" (The August/Holy One) here to refer to God.</note>) "In Jehovah," that is, in "Jehovah-ness," so to speak, because they will be of Jehovah. This mode of speaking is very frequent in the Sacred Scriptures: as in Paul, "to glory in Christ," "to die in Christ"—that is, to glory as a Christian, to die as a Christian. Nor is it the case that the Latins do not speak this way. As Horace says, *You shall learn of Penelope and glass-green Circe laboring in one* <note>original: "Disces laborantes in uno Penelopen uitreãque Circen"</note>. "In one," namely in Ulysses: that is, in "Ulysses-ness." And Terence says: *Let him make an end in that woman.* Also in Pliny, in the second book at the end of chapter 25: Augustus interpreted that he was born in that star (which was seen after the death of Julius Caesar). These words are not to be understood as if he thought he was born in the very body of the star, but in the "star-quality" itself, so to speak.

### FROM CHAPTER XXXI.

*He shall betake himself to flight, not because of the sword.*) I read <term>לא</term> <note>Hebrew: "lo," meaning "not"</note> instead of <term>לו</term> <note>Hebrew: "lo," meaning "to him"</note>, following the old Latin and Greek interpreters.

### FROM CHAPTER XXXII.

*Until we are drenched by the spirit.*) He speaks of the devastation of the Jewish nation to be begun by Sennacherib <note>King of Assyria who besieged Jerusalem</note>, and to be completed toward the time of Christ. Although Sennacherib did not take the city, he

<column-break/>

<page-num>96</page-num>

laid waste to Judea and began that calamity, which other calamities followed one after another, until finally through the times of Christ the race of the Jews was destroyed. For the Babylonian captivity followed Sennacherib, and continual evils infested those who returned, so that the city was captured and laid waste by Antiochus, then by Pompey, then by Herod and Sosius, and finally it was utterly overturned and leveled to the ground by Titus <note>A chronological list of the conquerors of Jerusalem ending with the Roman destruction in 70 AD</note>. And in the meantime came
<margin>10</margin> Christ, who breathed upon his own with the Holy Spirit from above, and reduced the uncultivated place into a Carmel <note>A mountain in Israel known for its fertility; here used to mean "cultivated land"</note>: and on the other hand, those outsiders who were uncultivated and alien to the true religion, he cultivated with the Gospel. But the Jews, who were a Carmel—that is, cultivated by the discipline of the Law and the oracles (for Carmel was a cultivated place)—he reduced to a forest, while he transferred the kingdom from them to a nation that would produce fruit. And so justice remains, both in the uncultivated and the cultivated place: that is, whether someone be a barbarian or a Jew,
<margin>20</margin> the way to Christ lies open to him, so that through faith he may become just and innocent, and furthermore, happy. Moreover, this Carmel—that is, the city of Christians—will not have to fear the hail of evils: for the city shall lie in a humble and flat place: Christians will be humble, modest, and safe by the protection of Christ. But whatever evils happen, they will happen in the falling of the forest—that is, to the outsiders and those not leveled by the cultivation of the Gospel.
*Happy are you who sow upon every water.*) For so I interpret <term>שׁדי</term> <note>Hebrew: "shedi," often translated as "fields" but here linked to "watered land"</note>, which here signifies that water
<margin>30</margin> which, soaking the earth, nourishes the stalks, as it is placed in Numbers 24 and Jeremiah 51. That is, happy are you who publish the Gospel in the whole world, wherever there is "moisture"—that is, where there is hope that it will grow and be nourished, just as stalks are by moisture. And this you do "sending in the foot of the ox and the donkey"—that is, with no distinction between Jews or outsiders. For he alludes to the precept of Moses, in which he forbids plowing with an ox and a donkey together. This is to say, if you consider the force of the precept more deeply, it forbids the Jews to have commerce with the rest of the
<margin>40</margin> nations, as if with a dissimilar race: just as Paul refers that precept about "not muzzling the mouth of the ox while it treads the grain" to a more divine matter, namely to the nourishment of those who teach the Gospel. Therefore, that distinction was removed by the Gospel, and happy are the teachers of the Gospel, who teach all people, with no distinction of race either of those teaching or those to be taught.

### FROM CHAPTER XXXIII.

*Be their arm early in the morning.*) The relative
<margin>50</margin> "whose" <note>original: "quorum"</note>, in the Hebrew is a third-person pronoun, "of them," which often refers to any person, as among the Latins "who" <note>original: "qui"</note> does. Just as a little later what we interpret as "you whose treasure, etc.," in the Hebrew is "of him," which is frequently placed for a relative pronoun, as in Psalm 15, where it reads thus literally: "Let Israel trust in Jehovah, he is their helper and defender"—that is, "O Israelites, trust in Jehovah, of whom (namely of you) he is the helper." You will find such things also at the beginning of chapter 54 and elsewhere often.
<margin>60</margin> ### FROM CHAPTER XXXVIII.

*Those who are buried shall not proclaim your faithfulness.*) <term>ישברו</term> <note>Hebrew: "yishberu" - they shall hope</note> seems to be written for <term>יבשֹרו</term> <note>Hebrew: "yebasseru" - they shall proclaim</note> with a transposed letter, so that there are here three words of the same notion: to give thanks, to praise, and to proclaim faithfulness, which correspond

...correspond to the three names placed for the same thing: Orcus <note>The Roman name for the underworld or the god of the dead</note>, the dead, and the buried.

### FROM CHAPTER XLI.

*Be silent before me, islands.* <note>Isaiah 41:1</note>) In the previous chapter, he promised the coming of Christ, having attacked the false gods. Now he confirms the Israelites’ expectation of Christ with these arguments: "Do not doubt what I promise concerning the Messiah, for I will fulfill it, as I am the first and the last God." This means he is the only God, just as we say "head and tail," "prow and stern," and similar phrases to signify the whole or everything. So too Livy <note>Titus Livius, a Roman historian</note> in the first book of his first Decade: *As those first and last things were read out from those tablets as certain* <note>original: "Vt illa palàm prima postrema ex illis tabulis, certá ue recitata sunt"</note>; that is, everything. Someone might ask: "What then, are there no other gods?" Let us see what kind they are. It is the nature of God to do great things, let alone to predict them. But these idols not only do nothing, they cannot even predict. Can they predict the coming of Cyrus, king of the Persians? They cannot. But I not only predict him, I also lead him, and I subject the nations to him in such a way that even the islands and Greece dread him. Go now, and question those gods of the nations made by hand and artifice about this future event. If they can neither predict, nor harm, nor help, do not worship them, but worship me; and hope for Christ the Savior, whom I promise. And when this man arrives of whom I speak—Cyrus, king of the Persians, who will recall you to your fatherland—hope that He will also come who inhabits the deserts: that is, Christ, who shall teach the foreigners. Moreover, he calls Cyrus "justice," meaning "the just one" (just as in Latin we use "wickedness" to mean "a wicked man") <note>This is a figure of speech called metonymy, where an abstract quality represents a person</note>, because he was to liberate the Jews, and he signified Christ the Savior not only in deed but also in name. For Cyrus signifies "the sun" in the Persian language, as Plutarch teaches in his life of *Artaxerxes* <note>A Greek biographer and philosopher</note>; and Christ is the light of the world. Thus far the argument. Regarding the phrase *And with the last I am the same*, it is as if he were saying, "I am the last." On this way of speaking, see the notes on Psalm 58.

*The first to Zion...* <note>Isaiah 41:27</note>) He alludes to what he had said above: *I, Jehovah, am the first, and with the last I am the same*. It is as if he says: "I, Jehovah, who called myself above the first and the last—that is, the only one—foretell these things."

### FROM CHAPTER XLIII.

*I will send to Babylon, and bring down the bars.* <note>Isaiah 43:14</note>) In the Hebrew it is: *I will send and I will demolish*. This is like the passage in Matthew 14: *sending, he beheaded* <note>original Greek: "πέμψας ἀπεκεφάλισε"</note>: that is, he sent someone to behead him. The meaning is this: I will send Cyrus and the Persians to Babylon to demolish its bolts and bars; that is, those who will capture it and sell the Chaldeans as captives, to be carried in ships to various lands, and thus they shall wail in their ships.

*Nor indeed because you had called upon me.* <note>Isaiah 43:22</note>) The conjunction *because* is in the latter part of the verse in Hebrew, yet it must be understood in the first part. He argues here like Paul <note>The Apostle Paul, likely referring to the Epistle to the Romans</note>, who shows that Abraham did not obtain righteousness because of circumcision or the Law, since the Law had not yet been given when he was considered righteous. Likewise here God teaches: "I led you out of Egypt, O Israelites" (for he had spoken of this shortly before)

<column-break/>

"and I led you safely through the deserts as my own. Why, then, did I do this? Was it because of your prayers and sacrifices? But you had not yet sacrificed, for I had not yet handed down the laws for sacred rites. Was it because of your virtue? But you were rebellious and wicked. Why then did I do good to you? For my own sake, freely. If I did so then, expect the same in the future regarding the salvation I am to bring you through Christ, so that you may attribute it not to your own merit, but to my kindness, and praise me for it."

### FROM CHAPTER XLIV.

*Let him declare things to come.* <note>Isaiah 44:7</note>) In the Hebrew it is *let them declare for themselves*, in the plural number; such a change in number frequently occurs in the Hebrew language. Furthermore, the word "for themselves" is superfluous even in the plural, just as we taught it occurs in the singular in the books of Moses. It is placed the same way in Psalm 80, which reads literally: *You have made us a source of contention to our neighbors, and our enemies laugh for themselves*; that is, they laugh or mock. In French, this is expressed as *s'en moquent* <note>they mock/laugh at it</note>.

*To act falsely.* <note>Isaiah 44:20</note>) In the Hebrew it is *to have a lie in his right hand*. Since men act with their hands, especially the right hand, the hand or "right hand" is often used to signify an action. Among the Hebrews, "false" is used for "unjust," just as "true" is used for "just." On this, see Psalm 7.

### FROM CHAPTER XLVI.

*Nor can they carry the burden.* <note>Isaiah 46:2</note>) The word I translate as "carry," the Hebrew word signifies "to deliver" and "to cause to escape." But sometimes it means "to bring to completion," as in Isaiah 34, where it reads literally: *There the owl shall nest and deliver*; that is, she shall nest safely, and bring her young to completion, and nourish them thoroughly. Micah spoke in the same way in chapter 6. In this way of speaking, we say in French that the chicks *have escaped* <note>original French: "evasiffe pullos"</note>, meaning they no longer fear anything, since they have been nourished to the point that they no longer fear the harm to which tender age is subject. We say the same of grapes and the other fruits of the earth. Therefore, here, to protect or deliver a "burden" is to carry it to where you intended. The same is to be understood in the words that follow shortly after: *The same I will bear and carry through.*

### FROM CHAPTER XLVII.

*Nor shall any man meet me.* <note>Isaiah 47:3</note>) In Hebrew it is: *Nor shall I meet any man*; which is the same thing, though more obscure. This is like the passage in Mark 14: *a man carrying a pitcher of water will meet you* <note>original Greek: "ἀπαντήσει ὑμῖν ἄνθρωπος κεράμιον ὕδατος βαστάζων"</note>. This means: *you will meet the man*, or you will run into or happen upon the man.

*Indeed they are like stubble, they shall be burned in the fire.* <note>Isaiah 47:14</note>) He speaks of the Chaldeans, whom the King of Babylon, Belshazzar, ordered to be burned because they could not divine what the writing on the wall signified, as found in Daniel 5. Therefore, they shall be burned like stubble, which is consumed so completely that no coals remain; that is, they shall be utterly burned. It does not matter that they were not actually burned (due to Daniel's intervention). For it was not because of their ignorance—which is attacked here—that they escaped the flame.

-> ON EZEKIEL <-

Isaiah is carried along this same line of reasoning. And in this way, it is said that Abraham, in the second chapter of James <note>James 2:21</note> and the eleventh of Hebrews <note>Hebrews 11:17</note>, sacrificed his son—whom he was *going* to sacrifice, had he not been hindered. I say the same regarding the overturning of Babylon, which the prophets in many places predicted would be utterly overturned by Cyrus: a thing which Cyrus, however, did not actually do. For this signifies that Babylon was to be deprived of its empire, so that it would no longer be that ancient mistress Babylon, any more than if
<margin>10</margin> it had been utterly overturned. Although in that Babylon, another far more hidden Babylon is to be understood <note>The author likely refers to the spiritual or "mystic" Babylon mentioned in later scripture</note>.

## FROM CHAPTER XLVIII.

*Which if you had heard, prophesy.*) If the "if" is not in the Hebrew, it is often understood or left silent, as in the works of Pliny the Younger: *Had you given this mind a matching body, he would have done what he desired* <note>original: "Dediffes huic animo par corpus, feciffet quod optabat"</note>; that is, *if* you had given it. Likewise, the word *and he shall call* <note>original Hebrew: וקרא</note> is not rarely used for "to predict" and "to prophesy." You will find examples of both elsewhere often, and in Isaiah. Otherwise, this sentence is most obscure because of the brevity of the speech, and at first glance, it seems poorly suited and disconnected; yet if you attend to it diligently, you will find it most appropriate. For we must consider what was said before, in this manner: "I predict to you (says God to the Israelites) the coming of Cyrus: and I predict it so that when it happens, you may attribute the praise for that event to me, and not to your statues and false gods." These gods are so far from being able to do such
<margin>30</margin> a thing that they cannot even predict it. "For if they predict, they predict to you who worship them: and if they predict to you, then you—at their prompting—predict those things which you have heard from them, which are now being signaled to you by me concerning Cyrus." But you cannot: for these things are unknown to you. From this, it is clear that their glory is not to be attributed to your gods, who do not even predict to you, though you are their worshippers; but to me, who signals these things even to the stubborn, so that
<margin>40</margin> when they happen, you may attribute them to the one who predicted them, which is me. The reason why I signal these things is because I know that you—such is your perpetual wickedness—would attribute the praise for this matter to those gods of yours unless you were forewarned by me. If you were to do that, I would rage against you unto total destruction because of such an ungrateful spirit and perfidy. But I do not wish to root you out entirely: rather, I wish to preserve your race for the sake of my name—that is, so that this matter may bring me praise and I may keep my promise. For this
<margin>50</margin> reason, I will shut you out from my praise <note>Meaning God will prevent them from taking the credit themselves</note>; that is, I signal these things to you so that when they happen, you do not praise yourselves or your gods for them, since you did not even foreknow them through your gods, let alone let them seem to be the authors of these events. Rather, understanding that such praise does not fall to you, you should ascribe it to me; and so it shall happen that I, being praised by you, may restrain my anger and not overturn you. And we see that this actually happened. For after the Babylonian captivity, the Jews
<margin>60</margin> abstained from idols. "I will not cut you off," I say, "but I will test you, and having exercised you with adversity and proven you like metal in a furnace, I will choose you." Not indeed for the sake of money, as those who test metals with fire are accustomed to do; but I will do it freely, and

<column-break/>

<margin>180</margin> for my own sake, lest anyone be able to claim the praise of this matter for themselves, which would be most unworthy.
*I have not spoken in secret from the beginning.*) This means: I predicted the fall of Sennacherib <note>The Assyrian King who besieged Jerusalem</note> not obscurely, and now after it has happened, I do not hide (which I would do out of shame if what I predicted had not occurred), but I present myself as present to show that I have predicted true things, and thus I deserve trust concerning the future things I signal. That is, concerning Cyrus, whom I shall send endowed with my spirit. But understand this concerning the *true* Cyrus, which is Christ, who will be endowed with the divine spirit, as it says in chapter 42.

## FROM CHAPTER XLIX.

*And that Israel might be gathered to him.*) In the Hebrew it is read *he shall not be gathered* <note>original Hebrew: לא יאסף</note>, as elsewhere, and as the ancient version <note>The Vulgate</note> shows, as well as those things which precede and follow soon after. For it is a twin sentiment: that it is the same to lead the descendants of Jacob back to him and to gather the Israelites to him. As for what he said a little before—that he labored in vain—it does not mean that no Israelite becomes a Christian, but rather, very few: so many that such a tiny profit does not seem worthy of Christ's labor, unless the rest of the
nations are added.

*Shall the captive of the fierce escape?*) The ancient version reads *the righteous* <note>original Hebrew: צדיק</note> and not *the fierce* <note>original Hebrew: עריץ</note>, translating it as "the robust one," and correctly so, it seems. For it is a twin sentiment, and it is repeated in the same words; nor is it unusual in repetition for the same or at least a related word to be placed. Add to this that, as it is usually read, the meaning is not fitting: for justice does nothing to retain prey, but ferocity does. The meaning is this: "Will you be able, O Jehovah, to snatch us from the power of the Babylonians—men so powerful and so fierce?"

## FROM CHAPTER LVI.

*Also, I will gather others to those already gathered to him, the beasts of the field.*) This means: when I have gathered the Israelites to the holy mountain through Christ, they will be attacked by Gog and Magog <note>Names used in prophecy to represent the enemies of God's people</note>. I will defeat them and hand their bodies over to be eaten by beasts. See Ezekiel 38 and 39, and Isaiah 18. The sentence is brief, in which the preceding things must be understood from the following ones.

## FROM CHAPTER LVII.

*For I will not contend forever.*) These things are to be joined with the preceding ones in this way: I said I would lead my people back to my holy mountain,
<margin>50</margin> Jerusalem. The Israelites will say, as in Ezekiel 37: "How will you lead us back to Zion, when our bones are dried up and no hope remains?" Such is your severity toward us. I answer: This severity will not be eternal; for a breath of spirit is brought in from me, and I will make them living beings. That is, having been appeased toward my people through Christ, I will animate their bodies with the spirit, and I will recall them into life, and lead them into the happiness promised by me. For now, indeed, I am angry at them for their fault, and I allow them to be carried headlong into
<margin>60</margin> their own lusts. But I will eventually heal their evils, and I will send a messenger by whom peace may be announced to all, wherever they may be. But lest they think that all who are Israelites by human nature shall obtain this peace, I announce this:

### FROM CHAPTER 57.

**You satisfy your lust.)** In the Hebrew it reads, "you find lust," but "to find" is used here in the sense of "to achieve and obtain," or "to indulge and obey." This is seen at the end of this same chapter, where it says "to perform lust," and shortly after in the same sense, "to find lust." Paul speaks in this same manner <margin>10</margin> in Philippians 3: *that I may gain Christ, and be found in him* <note>original Greek: "ἵνα χριστὸν κερδήσω, καὶ εὑρεθῶ ἐν αὐτῷ"</note>; that is, that I might gain Christ, and find satisfaction in him, or be satisfied by him.

**In this way you shall fast.)** In the Hebrew, it is "according to the day." For what we translated just before as "Then, when you fast," is read literally as "On the day you fast," and the same word is repeated here: "Do not fast according to the day," which means "in the manner I have described." It is not unlike what we translated a little <margin>20</margin> later as "speaking in this way," namely, the way I mentioned above. He had said, *and you shall remove the wicked speech*.

# ON JEREMIAH.

## FROM CHAPTER 2.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter Q. Inside the letter, a seated figure—likely a prophet—is depicted in a natural landscape with trees, suggesting a scholar in contemplation or a prophet in the wilderness.</image-desc>
<margin>30</margin> **Why do you arrange your reasoning to catch love?)** Why do you prepare yourself for the worship of foreign gods? And why do you teach other cities your own abandonment of faith, thus becoming the cause of their worship of foreign gods, which is destructive to them? This is the same as if you were to kill the innocent and stain your clothes with their blood. Nor do you do this secretly, as thieves are accustomed to do, but openly, worshipping your gods under shady trees. As for what I translate elsewhere, and shortly after, as "oaks," the vowel points <term>vowel points: the small marks added to Hebrew letters to indicate pronunciation</term> in the Hebrew <margin>40</margin> are slightly different, but these are sometimes changed, as we have shown elsewhere. Certainly, the meaning supports my view, which otherwise is inconsistent. In the latter word, the Greek translator, who renders it as *oak* <note>original Greek: δρύϊ</note>, suggests that in the former we should read *reoth* ("neighbors"), meaning "others"—just as the Greeks say *hetairas* for "another." In the latter case, however, it is *elah* or *allah*, which is written with the same letters as *elleh*.

## FROM CHAPTER 3.

<margin>50</margin> **Seeing as I.)** I believe this verb should be read in the third person, as the ancient translator <note>referring to the Vulgate or a similar early Latin version</note> reads it.

## FROM CHAPTER 9.

**Against all who are of uncircumcised foreskin.)** All these nations mentioned here practiced circumcision. Some, being ignorant of this, have corrupted this passage—which the ancient translator had rendered well (as he did many others). They did not follow the author but were led astray, namely by following <margin>60</margin> their Jewish teachers, like the blind leading the blind. These teachers think that only Jews were circumcised, whereas not only the Egyptians were circumcised, but also the Ethiopians, Colchians, Macrones, and Syrians, as Herodotus teaches in *Euterpe* <note>the second book of Herodotus's *Histories*</note>.

<header>NOTES.</header>

### FROM CHAPTER 10.

**Thus you shall say to them.)** <note>original: "Cosi gli direte," in Italian</note> Jeremiah, while writing in Hebrew, wrote this specific verse in Chaldean <term>Chaldean: the Aramaic language, which was the vernacular in Babylon</term> so that he might address the Chaldeans in their own language. Attempting to imitate this, I have written the same in Italian. The meaning of those words is this: "The gods who did not make heaven and earth shall perish from the earth and from the places under heaven."

### FROM CHAPTER 11.

**What has my beloved to do in my temple, when she commits so many atrocities?)** In the Hebrew, the verb "commits" and those following are feminine, even though the noun "Beloved" is masculine. For he calls the Jewish man "beloved," then addresses the Jewish woman in the feminine gender, which is the same thing; both are called by the same name in Hebrew. We noted a similar change in Isaiah 15. There are many such shifts in this sentence in the Hebrew: "So many" <margin>20</margin> is plural, while "atrocities" is singular; "let them do" is plural, and "flesh" is singular. And shortly after, "whose leaves" is masculine, and "whose branches" is feminine. I have noticed this often elsewhere, but it is not necessary to point it out every time.

**Let holy meats depart from you, you who exult in doing evil.)** That is, you sacrifice victims in vain. For they do not please me when they are sacrificed by the wicked. See Isaiah 1.

### FROM CHAPTER 15.

**Your wealth and resources.)** In the Hebrew, the singular number is used for the plural. It is clear these things are not said of Jeremiah, because it speaks of "borders," as if Jeremiah had many borders in which his sins were exposed. This is said not of Jeremiah, but of the Jews, who had as many gods as they had towns, as Jeremiah himself says. Furthermore, the plural is used at the end of the sentence. Additionally, in Chapter 17, <margin>40</margin> the same sentiment is placed where it is clear these things are said against the Jews. Therefore, I have compared these two passages, and helped one by the other, since both seem somewhat corrupted. For what is read here as *ve-ha'avarti*, seems more correctly read there as *le-ha'avirakha*, through the easy change of the letter *daleth* into *resh* because of the similarity of their shape <note>In the Hebrew alphabet, daleth (ד) and resh (ר) are very similar and frequently confused by scribes</note>. It is the same meaning found in Chapter 16 in these words: *I will cast you out of this land into a land unknown to you and your ancestors.* Let <margin>50</margin> these two passages be carefully compared.

### FROM CHAPTER 16.

**Neither shall bread be distributed in mourning.)** I read "bread" <note>Hebrew: לחם, lechem</note>, as both the ancient and Greek translators read, and as the meaning suggests. This agrees with what follows shortly after: "for the sake of taking food and drink."

### FROM CHAPTER 17.

**But I, following you, do not attempt to trouble you.)** <margin>60</margin> *Mere’eh*, derived from *ra’a’*, means to trouble, and is taken to mean "to announce evil." Just as in Chapter 1, Jeremiah is said to be sent "to destroy," etc.—that is, to announce ruin. Likewise, in Leviticus, "to cleanse" or "to pollute" is often used for...

to pronounce the pure as polluted or vice versa. There is, however, a double meaning, as it happens that one might try to cause harm while also desiring a cruel day.

### FROM CHAPTER 18.

**For example.)** The Hebrew word *tsiyah* <note>original: צִיָּה, meaning dry land or drought</note> is rendered literally in Greek as *auchmos* <note>original: αὐχμὸς</note>, or "drought."

**Shall the snow of the open-air rock of Lebanon be left behind?)** He who wants snow, let him seek Lebanon, which is perpetually snowy; he who wants water, let him seek a perpetual spring, from which cold water flows—that is, rising from the depths—fearing <margin>10</margin> nothing from the heat. Likewise, he who wishes to be well, let him seek me, the living fountain of all good things. But my Israelites, having abandoned me, burn incense to false gods: which is just as if someone, having abandoned a perpetual spring, should go to broken and dry cisterns.

**Neither shall the law perish from the priest.)** Just as the law is never lacking to the priest, nor counsel to the wise: so to Jeremiah, who is a prophet, there is never a lack of something to say. Therefore, his talkativeness must be restrained. The comparison is arranged just like that of Virgil: <margin>20</margin>
> Neither is cruel love satisfied with tears, nor the grass with streams,
> Nor are bees satisfied with clover, nor goats with leaves.
<note>Virgil, Eclogues 10.29-30</note>

That is, just as the grass is not satisfied by streams, etc., so love is not satisfied by tears.

### FROM CHAPTER 22.

**You are Gilead to me, O head of Lebanon.)** He alludes to the meaning of the name Gilead, which is found in Genesis 31, where Gilead is called a "heap of witness." This, therefore, is the meaning: O head of Lebanon, that is, O house of the king of Judah: for Jerusalem is the head of Judah, as if of a forest (for <margin>30</margin> he also calls the Jewish nation a forest at the end of the upper head). You are Gilead to me, that is, a heap of witness: that is, I call you to witness, just as Laban called the Gilead heap to witness in the presence of Moses. Thus, he uses the name of Gilead in affirming and swearing an oath, because of that famous Gileadite oath: in the same way the Romans in marriages used to use the name of *Thalassius*, by which the bridegroom was indicated. <note>Thalassius was a traditional Roman wedding shout, the origin of which was linked to the Rape of the Sabine Women.</note>

### FROM CHAPTER 28.

**War or evil.)** Consider whether for "evil" <note>Hebrew: רָעָה, ra'ah</note> <margin>40</margin> it should be read as "famine" <note>Hebrew: רָעָב, ra'av</note>.

### FROM CHAPTER 31.

**To whom your [fame] appeared from afar.)** In the Hebrew, instead of "to them" <note>Hebrew: לָהֶן, lahen</note> it seems it should be read "to her" <note>Hebrew: לָהּ, lah</note>, as both the meaning shows and the Greek translator reads, who turns it as "it shall be seen by him" <note>original Greek: ὀφθήσεται αὐτῷ</note>. For God is speaking, not the people: unless perhaps there is a change of person, such as in Psalm <margin>50</margin> 91. And in this way also, my translation will be consistent with the matter.

**A voice was heard in Ramah, a lamentation.)** Ramah was a town in the territory of the Benjaminites, as held in Joshua 18. Rachel weeps, that is, the Benjaminite women descended from Rachel, the mother of Benjamin. Therefore, it could also be translated thus: "The voice of the daughters of Rachel mourning their children." For "Rachel" is said for "the daughters of Rachel": just as a little later <margin>60</margin> "Ephraim" is used for the "Ephraimites," which mode of speaking is very frequent among the Hebrews, and also exists among the Latins, who sometimes say "Romulus" for "a Roman," as Persius says, *Are you fawning, Romulus?* <note>Persius, Satires 1.87</note>. Regarding the fact that Matthew cites this passage in

<column-break/>

the second chapter, concerning the infants killed by Herod, it should be known that the sayings of the prophets often look further than they may seem. When Isaiah speaks of Emmanuel and of Cyrus, he comes to Christ, a matter about which we wrote in his 7th, 8th, and 9th chapters. Likewise, when he writes about the calamity to be brought by Sennacherib, he <margin>10</margin> extends it to Titus, the son of Vespasian. Concerning this, see what we wrote on Isaiah chapter 32. In the same way, what Jeremiah writes here about the calamity of the Ephraimites should be extended even to the times of Christ: which is evident from the fact that both what is said a little after this passage and what is said in the previous chapter about recalling the captives are clearly to be referred to Christ. From this it is clear, since he encompasses under one name of "calamity" those things which the Jews were to suffer until they were recalled: and since they were to be recalled through Christ, Matthew rightly applied this passage to the infants, who were the first to be killed because of Christ. <margin>20</margin>

**A woman shall encompass a man.)** It is new and unusual for a woman to "encompass" or seek a man in marriage, when the opposite is usually done. But (says Yahweh) I will kill so many Israelites that, because of the scarcity of men, women will seek out men, and yet from such a great scarcity there will be those who escape. See Isaiah 4, and you will find the same sentiment.

### FROM CHAPTER 33.

**I will open the ornament of the covenant and of faith.)** It seems it should be read *atarah* <note>Hebrew: עֲטָרָה</note>, with the letter *teth* second, so that it signifies a crown and ornament: such as <margin>30</margin> the translation found in Psalm 5. Otherwise, the meaning is cold and forced.

### FROM CHAPTER 37.

**And there was given to him daily one loaf of bread.)** The old translator <note>Jerome/The Vulgate</note> renders the word *kikkar* as "loaf": he did so truly indeed, but with little Latinity. For the Hebrew word signifies a thing shaped in the way loaves usually are. Therefore, if it is money, it is called a "talent"; if it is another thing, it is <margin>40</margin> called a "mass" <note>original: massa</note>. As in Virgil,
> —He brings back a mass of pitch from the city.
<note>Virgil, Georgics 1.275</note>

Or a "lump" <note>original: gleba</note>, as Caesar calls them "lumps of pitch." But I would hardly dare to say a "mass" or "lump" of bread. Therefore, I preferred to say "one loaf," which is the same thing: for it signifies an entire bread, which was, it seems, of such a size as to be enough for a man for a day. The French express this well literally, <margin>50</margin> for they say in other matters *pain* [bread/loaf]: such as, *ung pain de miel ou de cire* <note>a loaf of honey or wax</note>. In the case of bread, they say *une miche de pain* <note>a loaf of bread</note>, which cannot be said quite the same way in Latin.

### FROM CHAPTER 46.

**Which destruction shall invade from the north.)** Jerome seems to have read "it comes upon her" <note>Hebrew: בָּא בָהּ</note>, who translates it "it shall come to her": as does the Greek translator, who says "from there upon it" <note>original Greek: ἔνθεν ἐπ᾿ αὐτήν</note>, which reading seems truer to me.

### FROM CHAPTER 51.

**I [will stir up] against Babylon and the inhabitants of Leb-Qamai.)** This word signifies "the heart of those who rise up against me": by which <margin>60</margin> word he hints at the land of Chaldea, both by the meaning of the word (for it was contrary and hostile to God) and by the word itself: for these letters, *L-B-Q-M-Y* <note>Hebrew: לִבְּ קָמָי</note>, if you count the alphabet backwards, are in the same number...

<meta>The catchword "numero," (number) at the bottom indicates the explanation of the Atbash cipher—where 'Leb-Qamai' is a code for 'Kasdim' (Chaldeans)—continues on the next page.</meta>

Therefore the Greeks translated it as **Chaldeans**. # ON LAMENTATIONS.

### FROM CHAPTER 3.
#### In the section "Beth."

<margin>20</margin> Encompassing with gall and weariness.) "Weariness" does not join well with "gall." See whether it should instead be read as **wormwood** <note>original Hebrew: ולענה, *la'anah*</note>, so that gall might be joined with wormwood—two most bitter things—as occurs a little after this place in the section "Zain," and in Deuteronomy 29.

#### In the section "Zain."

<margin>30</margin> Of misery and bitterness.) It seems it should be read as **misery** <note>original Hebrew: מרודי, *merudhi*</note>; the second-to-last letter being a *daleth* <note>the Hebrew letter "d"</note>, which is an easy slip of the pen given the almost indistinguishable similarity of the letters <note>In Hebrew, the letters Daleth (ד) and Resh (ר) look very similar; a scribe could easily mistake "rebellion" (marudhi) for "misery" (merudhi)</note>. For it is a twin sentiment, elegantly composed. Otherwise, how would it sound: "Remember my misery and my rebellion"? For it is rather the rebellion that God ought to forget so that He may have mercy.

#### From Lamentations 4 in the section "Mem."

It is on account of the sins of her prophets.) False prophets and priests were the authors of such great calamity; those who in Jerusalem poured out the blood of the innocent— <margin>40</margin> that is, they prophesied false things, and the people who followed them fell into these evils. For they went like blind men (since they were not inspired by God) through the men of the city, so contaminated by that blood I mentioned that their garments could not be touched, because they were so

<column-break/>

<page-num>106</page-num>

soaked in blood that nothing but blood could be touched on them. That is, they were the cause of a great slaughter. Furthermore, they repelled others from themselves, as if the holy were repelling the profane (see Isaiah 65), and they quarreled everywhere while prophesying.

# ON EZECHI-
->EL.<-

### FROM CHAPTER 1.

The form of four living creatures, whose faces were such that they had the form of a man.) And yet he says that each of them had four faces. But it must be understood that their bodies were human, but their faces were those which he describes. It must also be understood that in this chapter there is much variation of grammatical gender <margin>20</margin> among the Hebrews. For in what we translate as, "Whose face was such," the relative pronoun there is feminine, as the noun for "living creature" <note>Hebrew: *chayot*</note> requires. In the following parts, it is masculine, and then feminine again. The same applies to number: for in what we translate regarding the wheels, "Certain wheels on the ground near the living creatures at their four faces," the relative pronoun "their" in Hebrew is singular, even though the preceding noun is plural. Literally, it reads: "Near the living creatures at **its** four <margin>30</margin> faces," meaning the face of the creature—that is, the collective group of creatures. Furthermore, this relative pronoun in Hebrew is masculine, even though "living creature" is feminine. And a little later, where we translate, "The wheels were lifted up according to **them**," the "them" in Hebrew is masculine, even though it refers back to the living creatures. And what are called "living creatures" here are called "living creature" in the singular in chapter 10. I say the same of the "wheel," which he calls "one" here, by which name he signifies one team <margin>40</margin> of wheels, as appears immediately after. Therefore, we have interpreted it in the plural. We have explained changes of this kind also in Jeremiah 11. But so that this chariot <note>term: *quadriga*, a four-horse chariot, used here to describe Ezekiel's vision of the divine throne-chariot or *Merkabah*</note> can be more easily understood, we will place before your eyes the vision depicted in some way, in this manner:

- Top Right (labeled '3'): Letters A (top), L (right), H (bottom), B (left). To its right is written "South."

->West.<-

<columns>2</columns>
**H** is the face of the man. **L** of the lion. **B** of the ox. **A** of the eagle. The first animal, the second, and so on; although in reality none is truly "first," I arrange them this way for the sake of teaching. Now let us explain the more difficult words. *The appearance of their faces was such that those four had the face of a man and a lion on the right side, and the face of an ox and an eagle on the left.* <note>Ezechiel 1:10</note> By these words, "right" or "left" side should be understood not as belonging to each individual animal, but to the whole group, as you see in the diagram. For if this were done in each individual—for example, if the first animal had the face of a man and a lion to the south (which is the right side), and the ox and eagle to the north—it would follow that it had no face to the east or west, and the same would happen to the others. Yet the wheels moved alongside those animals; and the wheels moved toward the four directions of their square structure, as seen in chapter 10, where the same matter appears: that is, toward the east, west, south, and north. But if the animals had no faces toward the east and west, it would follow that when the chariot <term>quadriga|A four-horse chariot; here referring to the four living creatures carrying God's throne</term> moved in those directions, there would be no faces looking forward. This is clearly false from these words of the first chapter: *each of them went straight forward.* That is, toward the front part, with the face turned that way, so that in whatever direction it moved, every animal would always have one face looking there. For instance, if they moved toward the east, the facing side would be the ox in the first, the eagle in the second, the ox in the third, and the eagle in the fourth. Thus it happened that whichever way they moved, there were always four faces looking forward, and just as many looking back; just as many to the right, and just as many to the left. As for what it says, *they did not turn as they went,* and yet a little later follows, *they ran and returned:* this means that this chariot does not turn around as others usually do (where the pole always leads), but is moved in such a way that the faces which were previously in front become the rear when it returns. If it proceeds toward the east, the faces of the ox and eagle are in front, while those of the man and lion are behind. But if it returns toward the west, it does not do so by turning around so that the ox and eagle always lead;

<column-break/>

rather, it moves backward, with the man and lion leading and the others following. It is as if the stern and prow of a ship were made with the same shape, and the ship was driven without turning, so that the part which was the prow when going out becomes the stern when returning. And the logic of the wheels is the same: they are carried similarly in all directions, so that the part of them which was in front when going east is the same part that is behind when going west. I understand the same regarding the north and south. As for what pertains to "electrum" <note>original: "electrum"; a brilliant alloy of gold and silver, or amber</note>, in Hebrew it is *Hashmal*. Because the ancients translated this as "electrum," we have followed them, since we have nothing more certain about it. In the Hebrew language, that word signifies nothing known, unless perhaps you arrange the letters in reverse order (for there are certain such enigmas in the Holy Scriptures, as we showed regarding Jeremiah 51). For it would then be "for the Messiah" <note>original Hebrew: למשיח (L-M-Sh-Y-Ch)</note>, who in Greek is called *Christos* and in Hebrew *Messias*. The letter *Lamed* [L] would be placed in the same way as in Jeremiah 51 and John 13: *hina*, where "that it might be fulfilled" <note>original Greek: ἵνα πληρωθῇ</note> is said instead of "must be fulfilled" <note>original Greek: πληρωτέον</note> or "it is necessary to be fulfilled" <note>original Greek: πληρωθῆναι δεῖ</note>. On this matter, read what we wrote in 2 Corinthians 8. Thus *Hashmal* would be "the one to be anointed," just as if in Latin you said *sudnegnu* for *ungendus* [to be anointed], or *Susei* for *Iesus*. Now another secret occurs. Just as *Hashmal* signifies nothing if you read it in the Hebrew manner, but signifies "Messiah" if read in the Greek or Latin manner—that is, in reverse letter order (since we write from left to right, while the Hebrews write from right to left)—so too if you understand what is written about Christ in the Hebrew oracles as the Jews do, you will crucify Christ and be far from knowing Him. But if you understand as the Greeks do—that is, the Christians, who were mostly brought in from foreign nations—you will learn Christ, and from Saul you will become Paul. Likewise, though this name *Hashmal* is written by a Hebrew author, namely Ezechiel, it is nonetheless not to be read in the Hebrew fashion if you wish to draw out the meaning. So it is with the oracles about Christ delivered by the Hebrews: if you examine them in the Hebrew manner, you will have mere letters and sound without meaning. For they have a veiled face when they read these things. But...
