111 112

### ON EZEKIEL

These things concerning the *Hashmal* <note>original: "Haſmal"; a mysterious substance or color mentioned in Ezekiel 1:4, often translated as "amber" or "electrum"</note> I wish to offer as proposals, yet I do not affirm them as absolute, lest we mistake the uncertain for the certain.

### FROM CHAPTER III.

*And you shall prepare them with these entrails.*) The Hebrew word signifies to perfect or to complete, which is used here in place of the word for "digesting": just as in the writings of Pliny, food is often said to be "perfected" instead of "prepared" or "digested."

### FROM CHAPTER XIV.

*Yet there are some left in her who, having escaped, shall be led out.*) Indeed, I punish all the sources of other nations, sparing only the innocent. But I am more merciful toward the Israelites: this can be understood from the fact that, although all Israelites are guilty and therefore all ought to be put to death if I wished to exercise the full extent of the law, nevertheless some shall escape, preserved by my mercy. When these survivors reach you, you will receive consolation from them, and you will understand that I acted justly in treating Jerusalem as I did. Moreover, you will see that in leaving a remnant, I acted mercifully, even though their crimes deserved a destruction similar to that of Sodom. See Amos 9 and Obadiah.

### FROM CHAPTER XV.

*What shall become of the wood of the vine among all the branching trees?*) He calls them "branching trees," using a redundant adjective which is actually a noun in Hebrew, though placed in the position of an adjective. This is similar to how we often say "aerial birds" or "marine or aquatic fish," adding a word that is not strictly necessary. Likewise, what I translate as "in the forest of trees" is in Hebrew "in the trees of the forest," but "forest" signifies a multitude of trees, whether wild or domestic: just as in Genesis chapter 3, "herb of the field" is used for terrestrial fields, whether they be wild or cultivated. It does not matter that the vine is more a shrub than a tree, for among the Hebrews, even shrubs are called "trees," omitting that more subtle classification which places shrubs as a middle ground between herbs and trees. This is the Prophet's meaning: just as nothing is more useless than a vine (otherwise a most useful plant) if it is sterile, so too nothing is more empty than the Israelites if they lack the fruit of good deeds. Christ said the same when comparing his followers to salt.

### FROM CHAPTER XVI.

*And in these also your own.*) The possessives "mine," "yours," "his," "ours," and "yours [plural]" cannot be expressed in Hebrew except by joining them to other words, as we wrote regarding Genesis 24. For instance, if you wish to translate into Hebrew what is said in Latin as "my father and yours," you are forced to say "my father and your father." For this reason, since the noun for "captivity" is often repeated in this passage in the Hebrew tongue due to the nature of the language, I have placed that noun only once in the Latin—where such necessity does not exist—and in the following parts, I found it sufficient to use pronouns. I wish this to be noted here as well as elsewhere, for it occurs often. Furthermore, regarding what he says about restoring the captives of Sodom: it should be known that the word used here indicates not only "captivity" but also "misery." This is seen in Job 24, and also in the French language, where a word derived from

<column-break/>

captivity denotes misery: *chétiveté* <note>Original: "chétiueté"; an Old French term meaning wretchedness or misery, derived from the Latin "captivitas"</note>. Now, because Ezekiel speaks of the captives of Samaria and Jerusalem, he uses the same word even for Sodom, which he joins with them, although the people of Sodom were not actually taken captive. But what does it mean when he says he will restore them to their former state? For if Sodom and Samaria are restored to their former state, they will be restored to an evil state. <margin>10</margin> For they always abounded in vices, especially Samaria, whose beginning and progress were both evil. Thus, if they are returned to their former state, there would be a perpetual cycle of sinning and being punished. Therefore, it must be understood that in this passage, a transition is made from that historical Sodom to another "Sodom"—that is, to the Gentiles who are like the Sodomites. This is similar to how, in chapter 20, a transition is made from the idol-worshiping Israelites to the true Israelites. Thus the meaning is: Sodom and Sa-<margin>20</margin>maria—that is, the nations like them—shall be restored to their former state. This means they will eventually stand through Christ, though they now lie under the tyranny of Satan, just as Sodom and Samaria once stood but now lie in ruins. (He speaks here of Sodom’s change from a fallen state to a restored state.) The same shall happen to you among them: when you see yourself restored, you will be ashamed of your crimes, which were so foul that by committing them, you "comforted" those nations. This means you made them <margin>30</margin> appear less guilty when compared to you; such a comparison often brings a kind of consolation. But what manner of restoration that shall be will be known in its own time.

### FROM CHAPTER XVII.

*It grew into a luxuriant vine, low in stature.*) These two things are not in conflict: for a vine can be luxuriant in the fertility of the soil and yet remain low, especially if it is recently planted and not yet full-grown. It is the same as what is said a little later: *It put forth <margin>40</margin> branches.*

### FROM CHAPTER XIX.

*When he grew up into a lion.*) *Kephir* <note>original: כפיר</note> and *Aryeh* <note>original: אריה</note> differ just as *Adam* <note>original: אדם</note> and *Ish* <note>original: איש</note> do—that is, as "human" and "man." And just as the same person can be called both "human" and "man," so both of those Hebrew words are said of the same lion in Judges 14, concerning which matter see our notes on that passage. However, the Latin language has fewer words for "lion" than the He-<margin>50</margin>brew. Therefore, understand "growing up into a lion" as if you were saying "a calf grows into a bull."

*And he ravaged their citadels.*) The text reads *vayedah* <note>original: וידע</note>, which means "and he knew." But what does "he knew the citadels" mean? Others translate it as "he knew the widows," but it is not correctly said that a lion "knew widows," since the metaphor must be maintained, and lions do not "know" the widows of men. Furthermore, he would not use the word for "knowing," which is too gentle, but rather a word for ravishing or violating. I suspect the reading should be <margin>60</margin> *vayera* <note>original: וירע</note>, a word most suitable for leonine violence <note>The author is noting a likely scribal error between the Hebrew letters Dalet (ד) and Resh (ר), which look very similar</note>. For the Greeks also translated it as *elymenato* <note>original: ἐλυμήνατο</note>, which means "to depopulate" or "to ravage." This same error creeps in also in Judges 8, where there is a mistake involving the same letter, with a *Resh* placed for a *Dalet*. Concerning which...

wherefore read what we have written there.
*Your mother like a vine.*) In this allegory there is a general confusion of number and gender in the Hebrew language, such as we indicated in the first chapter and have often noticed elsewhere, so that it need not be explained everywhere. However, the meaning is the same as the prior allegory. Your mother, Jerusalem, blood-stained by the blood shed among you, is like a vine flourishing due to an abundance of moisture. She had 
<margin>10</margin> rods, that is, men who held scepters—namely, kings. When these had grown so tall that they stood out among the others like "arrows" <note>original: "sagittæ"; likely referring to the shoots or prominent branches</note> among the vine-shoots, Jerusalem herself was destroyed: and if anything in her was excellent, it perished, and the kings were slain. Now she lies deserted; her kings were the cause and beginning of this calamity, and they no longer remain within her.

### FROM CHAPTER XX.
<margin>20</margin> *And I promised to the offspring of the house of Jacob.*) In the Hebrew it is, *I had lifted my hand*: because that was the custom in affirming and promising. This figure of speech is not inconsistent with the word "promise" [**promittere**]: for to promise is to send forth [**mittere**] or to send upward [**altè**]. And because men used to pledge themselves with outstretched hands, as it seems, the usage prevailed that they said "to promise the hands," and then, with the noun dropped, they simply said "to promise" instead of "to pledge." We see certain words are habitually dropped in other cases as well: as when we say "ten times" [**decies**] to mean "ten hundred thousand sesterces" <note>A common Roman shorthand for large sums of money</note>; and how in the sacred scriptures "the Name" is sometimes said for "the Name of Jehovah"; and "to pass over" for "to pass through the fire." I say these things so that the natures of languages may be observed, and so no one is offended if, speaking in Latin, I translate many foreign customs into the Latin habit.

<margin>30</margin> *What then was the shrine to which they went?*) He gives the reason for the name. For since he asked them what that <term>Bamah</term> <note>original: "במה"; a "high place" used for worship, often associated with idolatry in the Old Testament</note> was to which they were going, the name later stuck, so that the shrines built there were called by that word. Now *Bamah* is as if you were to say "lofty" or "elevated": which in Latin can be called a temple [**templum**], since shrines began to be built in higher places. But later they were also made in other places; 
<margin>40</margin> thus in chapter 16 they are said to be made in every street, where they are called by another word, though of the same meaning.

### FROM CHAPTER XXI.
<margin>50</margin> *Shall we then rejoice?*) This entire passage is extremely obscure until the end of the chapter. A little before, the Prophet was ordered to groan and to give the reason for his groaning. It would be a wonder if we should rejoice. Do you ask, O Israelites, why I groan? As if we truly had cause for joy and not for grief, when the scepter of my son rejects every wood: that is, 
<margin>60</margin> finds no wood from which it can be made: that is, when the scepter and command are taken away from my son, as will be declared later. Now, he calls the Israelite "his son": not because the Prophet himself is the father of the Israelites, but it is an imitation of 

<column-break/>

God speaking, who calls the Israelites His sons. Such a way of speaking is found also in the Song <note>The Song of Solomon</note> in the seventh chapter; and in the French tongue, and in the Italian, when they say *monsieur* and *monseigneur*, *misser* and *monsignor*, that is, "my lord," even though they are speaking of the lords of others: just as we commonly call teachers "our masters," though they are in no way ours. Moreover, the scepter shall be taken from the Israelites by the sharp sword of God, which He will hand over to the slayer: that is, God will take it away through the King of Babylon, to whom He will grant power over that matter. This is a thing worthy of wailing and the striking of thighs. This was also customarily done among the Greeks in sad circumstances, as in Homer when Achilles sees the burning of the ship:
> With a smiting of his thighs, he speaks such things to Patroclus. <note>original Latin: "Cum femorum planctu Patroclo talia fatur." A translation of a line from the Iliad.</note>
It is asked from what wood a scepter can be made: for it is an inquiry into who can be the king of the Israelites. No one is found; the kingdom is taken from the Israelites. Even if the scepter did not "reject every wood"—that is, if some king remained—it would nevertheless profit nothing, nor could he avoid the impending evil.

*But you, O king condemned to death.*) You, Zedekiah [**Sedecia**], who have committed a capital crime, the day of whose punishment has come now that you have completed your crime (for I am not accustomed to punish before the crime is finished): take off the miter <note>original: "cidarim"; a royal or priestly head-covering</note>, that is, you shall be deprived of the kingdom: and that which is, shall not be: and that which is not, shall be. So great a change of things shall occur that the humble shall be exalted, and vice versa. Those who now reign shall be deprived of the kingdom; but he who shall be humble, he shall reign: namely, Christ. For as pertains to that crown, I will reduce it utterly to nothing (for this is what the three-fold word signifies <note>Ezekiel 21:27: "A ruin, ruin, ruin, I will make it"</note>, and the meaning is the same as declared above, *the scepter rejects every wood*), but that shall not happen yet. For although the King of Babylon oppresses you in slavery, the kingdom shall nevertheless return after the captivity, so that it may seem not abolished, but interrupted: lest you think that I, in placing the same word three times, am speaking of this interruption. But it shall happen when he comes to whom the judgment belongs, namely Christ, about whom the dying Jacob prophesied, that the scepter would not be lacking to the Jews until the Savior [**Sospitator**] <note>original: "Sospitator"; a Latin title for a deliverer or savior, here referring to the Messiah/Shiloh</note> comes.

### FROM CHAPTER XXIV.
*For her blood is in her.*) In the Hebrew it is, *In her middle*: but that is put for "in," as often elsewhere, and in the twenty-sixth chapter, where it reads literally that Tyre would be *for the spreading of nets in the middle of the sea*, when Tyre was very far distant from the middle of the sea.

### FROM CHAPTER XXVI.
*Now the ships tremble at the day of your ruin.*) Some want *athi* [**אתי**] to be for *iyyim* [**איים**], "islands." But I prefer the old translation, in which it is "ships." For the sense fits better, and it could have been formed from *oni* [**אֹנִי**] as much as from *ayin* [**אין**].

*I will thus reduce you to nothing.*) And here I say the same: the old translator rendered it better, *Who will reduce you to nothing*.

<header>ON EZEKIEL</header>

...as well as you: and the Greek, which renders it as *dissolved* <note>original: "ἀναλελυμένον"</note> or *a net* <note>original: "δίκτυον"</note>: as our own translators, who render it *terrors*. For it is derived from the Hebrew word *balah* <note>בלה</note>, which means to wear out or grow old; the meaning of which is most fitting for this passage.

## FROM CHAPTER XXIX.

*You shall pierce their whole sides.*) The Latin translator renders this as *you have dissolved*. The Greek as *you have crushed* <note>original: "συνέθλασας"</note>. From this, I gather that they did not read the Hebrew as *he’emdah* <note>העמדה</note>, which does not fit the context, but rather *he’emqat* <note>העמקת</note>, which means to hollow out or pierce, and fits this passage most appropriately.

## FROM CHAPTER XXXI.

*So that its top is among the clouds.*) The Greek translates this passage well. For it is the same sentiment found in Daniel chapter 4, where this tree is said to touch the sky with its head, so that here *abotim* <note>עבתים - thick boughs</note> is the same as *abim* <note>עבים - clouds</note>.

*I will deliver him into the hand of the God of the nations.*) He calls Cyrus, the king of the Persians and the overthrower of the Assyrian kingdom, the "God of the nations," just as in Psalm 45 Solomon is called a god, or a divine being. Similarly, people call Cicero the "god of orators," and the Romans called their emperors *divi* <note>divine/deified ones</note>, such as the Divine Julius or the Divine Trajan. However, in what follows—*as his impiety demands*—the prophet speaks of a man. Then, in naming the branches, he speaks of a tree, mixing the thing being compared with the thing it is compared to; for at the beginning of the allegory, he set down both the Assyrian king and the cedar tree. But in the Hebrew language, both are of the masculine gender. Since the Latin language does not allow this <note>tree names are often feminine in Latin</note>, I have changed the gender: where the discourse is about the tree, I have used the feminine, but where it is about the man, the masculine.

## FROM CHAPTER XXXII.

*Cast them down with those who descend into the depths of hell.*) The Prophet is said to "act" in a poetic manner when he announces what has been done, or what will be, as we explained in Genesis 48. Furthermore, in this speech toward the end of the chapter, there is a frequent change of gender and number, of the kind I explained in Jeremiah 11 and Isaiah 15.

## FROM CHAPTER XXXIII.

*They make songs with their mouth.*) They speak well with their mouth, and as it says in Isaiah, *they honor me with their lips*, but their words are merely "songs"—that is, they do not feel what they say. Just as those who sing songs often say one thing while thinking another, so these people, while speaking well with their mouths, follow greed in their hearts. They treat you and your words exactly as if you were singing some elegant and rhythmic poem, which delights them but does not move them to action.

## FROM CHAPTER XXXVII.

*I will put spirit into you, that you may come back to life.*) I have explained elsewhere that simple Hebrew words must often be translated into Latin using compound verbs, because the Hebrews lack compound forms. Thus, here *hayah* <note>חיה</note> means "to come back to life" <note>original: "reuiuiscere"</note>, as the ancient interpreter translated it. Similarly, the Greek word *to live* <note>original: "ζῆν"</note> is placed in Matthew 9 and John 5 and 11 in place of *to come back to life* <note>original: "ἀναζῆν"</note>, following the Hebrew custom, just as *banah* <note>בנה - to build</note> is used for "to repair" or "to restore." The meaning of words of this kind is perceived from the flow of the sentence.

## FROM CHAPTER XXXVIII.

*Set your face toward Gog, of the land of Magog.*) Josephus, in the first book of the *Antiquities*, chapter 7, records that the Magogites were founded by Magog, whom the Greeks

<column-break/>

116

call Scythians. From Meschus came the Meschinians, who are called Cappadocians; from Thobel, the Thobelites, who are the Iberians <note>referring to Caucasian Iberia, modern Georgia, not Spain</note>; from Phut, the Phutites, who are the Libyans; from Gomar, the Gomarenes, who are the Galatians; from Thygramma, the Thygrammanes, whom the Greeks call Phrygians. He adds others, but I list only those who pertain to this passage and about whom there might be doubt. Now, the names he provides are adapted to the Greek language. In Hebrew, they are read as: Magog, Mesech, Thubal, Phut, Gomer, Thogorma. In the others I follow the common names, except for the name Magog, where I use the Hebrew form because of the fame of this prophecy. However, I interpret "Mesech" differently. For since the Cappadocians are called *Caphthorim* in Genesis 10, and because the Greek and Latin interpreters call what is read here as Mesech "Mosoch," it is more probable that the *Moschi* are meant. The name fits, and they are joined with the Iberians both here and in chapter twenty-seven—both nations being in the region of Themicyra. For they wish it to be understood that these are the Iberians of the east, not the Spanish, as there are other Iberians in Spain. But as for the nature of this prophecy concerning Gog and Magog, I do not know. I suspect these things have not yet happened. On this matter, read carefully Isaiah 17, 26, 56, and 57, Ezekiel 37, etc., and Revelation 20. Add, if you please, the third book of the Sibyl, in which all these things are treated in abundance.

## FROM CHAPTER XL.

*And a wall surrounded the temple.*) There follows a description of the temple. Because it is very obscure, we shall explain it not only with words but also with figures <note>illustrations</note>, without which these things can hardly be understood. Therefore, this temple was enclosed by a square wall that extended five hundred cubits in every direction; this entire space was sacred. The temple was situated on a mountain, so that from whichever side it was approached, one had to ascend.

Its parts are nine, and all of them are square, one hundred cubits long and just as many wide: namely, the house itself, and around it eight courts, two from each quarter of the heavens. Those joined to the house are called "inner" courts; the remaining four are "outer." Through the outer ones there is access to the inner ones, and further on to the house. These nine members are further divided into other members, as can be seen in the drawing. These are described piece by piece by Ezekiel in the order they were shown to him by the spirit <note>original: "genio"</note>, which makes the description more obscure. For the sake of clarity, we will sketch each part. I shall use an <term>ichnography</term> <note>a floor plan or ground-level drawing</note>—that is, a drawing of the area, the ground, and the foundation—so that all the spaces can be seen clearly. This could not be done in an <term>orthography</term> <note>an elevation or facade drawing</note>, which is a picture of the upright front of a building.

*The man having a measuring rod in his hand.*) In the Hebrew it is "a measurer's reed," that is, a pole. He describes its length as six cubits—specifically sacred cubits. He clarifies this by saying these cubits are larger than others by one handbreadth <note>original: "palmo"</note>. I did not call it a "measuring reed" because the name <term>decempeda</term> <note>a ten-foot measuring pole used by Roman surveyors</note> is the proper term for this thing. There is also at Carcassonne in Aquitaine...

### ON EZEKIEL
119, 120

<image-desc>A simple architectural diagram showing a floor plan. At the top, a small rectangle contains the letters C and D. Below it, a larger rectangular section is flanked by the letters A on the left and B on the right. This represents the connection between the gate walls and the chamber roofs.</image-desc>

But those same spaces of five cubits must also be understood to exist between the chambers and the wall of the gate, from point **o** to **p**, as will become clear in the measurement of the gate's length. The **vestibule** <note>original: "uestibulum" — the entrance hall or porch of the gateway</note> is eight cubits wide from **r** to **f**; this vestibule is six cubits away from the threshold of the gate (that is, from the outer line of the threshold), marked **e f**. For the thickness of the threshold is not attributed to the vestibule itself. This vestibule had **appendages** <term>appendages: in this context, these are architectural projections like pilasters or pillars supporting the structure</term> of two cubits; that is, their projection extended one cubit into each doorway, running inward from **f** to **t**. If we were to interpret this as giving two cubits to each, the result would be that the vestibule's appendages would have double the projection of the chamber appendages. Furthermore, the vestibule appendages would then be closer to the chamber appendages than the chamber appendages are to one another; both of these inequalities would result in a deformed appearance.

The appendages, however, were sixty cubits <note>The author is likely referring to the total height or the cumulative length of these structural supports throughout the gate complex.</note>; this must be understood as the total space of the appendages. Individually, they extended eight cubits, from **u** to **x** (we state this for one appendage, but intend it to apply to all of them). These, multiplied by eight, make forty-eight. The appendages of the doors were six cubits long, from **y** to **z**: thus the number becomes sixty cubits in total. As for why these were shorter than the others, the reason is that their length was not increased by the addition of the side-sections, as was the case in the chambers. For if there were no side appendages in the chambers, the appendage at the front would be the same size as the door’s, namely seven cubits, from **A** to **B**.

Therefore, the width of this gate building on the inside, excluding the wall, is twenty-five cubits, from **C** (where the roof of the chambers ends) to **D** (the roof of the gate, which is the wall surrounding the gate). For the vestibule extends eight cubits, and the chambers on either side extend eight each, which totals twenty-four. One cubit is missing—half a cubit on each side—which is occupied by the roofs of the upper chambers extending to the back, and by the roofs of the wall rising half a cubit on each side, joining there with the roof of the wall where the letters **C** and **D** are placed. The width of the gate is measured from these junctions of the roofs. The length, however, from the beginning of the outer door's threshold to the furthest line of the inner door's threshold (that is, from **e** to the other **e**), was fifty cubits, which is twice the width. The length of the chambers was eighteen cubits from the foundations: six cubits for each, with spaces between the chambers, and between the chambers and the wall. In the width of the gate, there were four spaces of five cubits each, which, when joined with that number, makes thirty-eight; if you add the twelve cubits for the two thresholds, it makes fifty. And the doors themselves correspond to one another: for from **b** to the other **b** is a straight line.

<column-break/>

This eastern gate was ascended by seven steps, and it was surrounded by an **atrium** <term>atrium: the open courtyard or court area surrounding the sacred buildings</term>. The "atrium" refers to the remaining space of this entire square, an area extending one hundred cubits in length and width. It is called the "outer" atrium because between it and the temple there was another inner atrium. Therefore, in this outer atrium, there was a **pavement** <note>original: "pauimentum" — a stone-floored area within the court</note> along the side of the gates. He uses the plural "gates" because he wants the same thing to be understood for the north gate as he records here for the east gate, as will appear shortly. That pavement was on lower ground than the gate, following the length of the gate from **E** to **F**. Along this pavement were thirty **chambers** <note>original: "cœnacula" — literally 'dining rooms' or 'upper rooms', used here for the administrative or storage cells lining the court</note>. How these were arranged cannot be understood from this passage alone, but must be sought from Chapter 42, where we will explain the logic of this arrangement using this same figure.

*He measured the width from the front of the lower gate before the inner court on the outside as one hundred cubits.*) He calls the "lower gate" the first gate of the inner court. For from that gate, one ascended by steps into the inner atrium, which is why it is called "inner." From this it appears—as is taught later regarding the steps—that they are not outside the thickness of their own wall. Otherwise, the door could not be called "lower" if it were placed above the steps. Furthermore, the steps of the inner courts themselves would occupy part of the length of the outer courts. Nor should we fail to notice that the same wall placed between two atria does not serve the atrium everywhere; rather, there are two walls there, one for each atrium. For if there were only one, the length and width of the one-hundred-cubit courts would not be consistent, nor would the five-hundred-cubit length of the entire sacred space. Therefore, he measured the width from the front of the lower gate, which is before the inner court, where the letter **G** is, for one hundred cubits, on the outside, from **H** to **I**. For on the inside, from **K** to **L**, it would only be eighty-eight, as the thickness of the wall occupies six cubits on each side. He did this both toward the east and toward the north: that is, in both the eastern and northern atria, so that we may understand that two atria of the same kind are being described here.

<margin>Likewise, observe the gate which was toward the north at the outer atrium, etc.</margin>
That is, he measured the gate of the northern inner atrium, which looked outward toward the northern outer atrium, by the same logic as the gate of the eastern outer atrium which he just described—and also the northern one, which he mentioned at the same time. And that inner gate of the northern atrium was ascended by seven steps, in front of which were the appendages of the gate. Since the steps extend ten cubits at the threshold (which is the width of the gate, **c d**, so that the figure placed above may serve both, since the logic of the gates is the same), and the fronts of the appendages are eight cubits apart (which is the width of the vestibule, **r s**), it follows that the projections of the appendages—which are one cubit each—correspond on both sides to the final cubit of the steps. Since from **C** to **M** and from **d** to **N** are straight regions, these appendages are displayed internally before the ends of the steps. Now, the interior gate...

# ON EZEKIEL

...and rows. The individual rows of stories <note>original: "tabulatorum" — likely referring to the side chambers or galleries surrounding the main building</note> surrounded the main hall and the sanctuary on the right and left, with a width of four cubits. These stories were further surrounded on both sides by an empty space five cubits wide, which was enclosed by a wall six cubits thick. Thus, this width became fifty cubits. On the northern side was the vestibule of the temple, twenty cubits in length; this <margin>10</margin> length of the vestibule matched the width of the temple building. Thus the width of the building, when increased by the length of the vestibule, became seventy cubits—which would not be possible unless the vestibule was situated to the north. To the south, in place of a vestibule, there was an empty space as wide as the vestibule was long, namely twenty cubits. If you add to these the thickness of the wall on both sides (which is five cubits at the upper part of the wall itself), the width of the entire temple becomes one hundred cubits. The length <margin>20</margin> was arranged so that the main hall was forty cubits long and the sanctuary was twenty cubits. On the west and the east there was a space of four cubits; in the east was the gate, and after that space was an empty area of five cubits. Add to each side the building wall of six cubits thick, then the temple wall of five cubits (specifically at the top, due to the tapering <note>original: "contracturam" — the narrowing of the wall as it rises</note>, for what is taken from the wall is added to the temple space). Thus the length becomes one hundred cubits. Now let us come to the Prophet’s interpretation.

<margin>30</margin> *He measured the vestibule at five cubits.*)
This means each threshold of the vestibule was five cubits thick, from **i** to **k**, and from **l** to **m**. Since the wall of the temple and the wall of the building were six cubits thick at the foundation, one cubit is taken from the thresholds and assigned to the transverse additions; the space for these additions is not assigned to the vestibule, otherwise the vestibule would be twenty-two cubits long. <margin>40</margin> *The door on each side—that is, both the interior and exterior—was three cubits wide, n o, and p q.* The vestibule was twenty cubits in length, **k l**, and ten cubits in width, **r f**; although in the Hebrew text it reads "eleven." However, the width would then not be half of the length, which is the case in all the other vestibules. Furthermore, this odd number would not quite correspond with the other dimensions. For these reasons, I have followed the Greek version in this place, which says "ten" <note>original: "δέκα" (deka)</note>. *To which one ascended by ten steps: these are <margin>50</margin> within the thickness of the outer threshold.* I read here not <term>thickness</term> <note>original: עבי (‘obî)</note>, but <term>post</term> <note>original: איל (’ayil)</note>, for the Greek reads it this way, and the meaning is not consistent otherwise; although the Latin translates it as "eight." Regarding the additions: The additions on the right and left were projections of one cubit each. This is understood from what was said about the threshold: that the additions of length should be of equal projection with those of width—that is, with the transverse additions—as we showed happening in the first figure. From here, on one side and <margin>60</margin> the other, was a column. Whether these columns were at the beginning or at the end of the vestibule, he does not add; therefore, we have not marked their location. For in 1 Kings 7 <note>original: "3. & 4. Reg. 7" — in older Bibles, 1 & 2 Kings were called 3 & 4 Kings</note>, where there are columns of this kind, they are said to be in the porch, or temple vestibule;

<column-break/>

but in what exact spot is not expressed. However, Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, the 1st-century Jewish historian</note> says they were placed at the pilasters <term>antae: square posts at the end of a wall</term>, which seems to be the case. Just as in Moses' tabernacle, the two corner columns at the entrance correspond to the planks, from which the logic of the pilasters seems to have originated. As for the thickness of the vestibule wall, Ezekiel makes no mention of it, but since all other walls of this structure are six cubits thick, we <margin>10</margin> attribute the same to this one.

### FROM CHAPTER 41.

*He measured the additions on each side to a width of six cubits.*) He calls the "additions" of the main hall the "stories" <note>or galleries</note>, about which we will debate shortly. The lowest of these were four cubits wide, and the highest were six. Insofar as they are the highest, they are called additions. Moreover, I want "additions" to be understood in this place not only as that part of the structure which projects <margin>20</margin> outside the space of the foundation (as the term is usually used), for by that logic these additions would only be one cubit on each side, but as the entire upper room itself which possesses the addition. This is why he says the additions were six cubits wide, as if to say this must be understood regarding the uppermost part. Therefore he adds: *Which was the width of the covering—that is, of the highest part which covered the rest.* For the Hebrew word <term>the covering</term> <note>original: הַמְּכַסֶּה (ha-mekasseh)</note> signifies not only the tabernacle, but also a covering, as seen in Exodus 26 and Psalm 132. <margin>30</margin> *The width of the entrance was ten cubits.*) From the vestibule, one comes through the empty space to the entrance of the main hall on the east, from **m** to **t u**. The reason the entrance is not directly aligned with the vestibule is due to the arrangement of the stories, which will be explained later. The width of the entrance was ten cubits, **x y**. The "shoulders"—that is, the sides of the gate which remained from the width of the hall on the right and left—were five cubits each, **y z**, and **x A**. The length of the main hall was forty cubits, **B C**; the width was twenty, **D E**. *Then he entered <margin>40</margin> into the inner room—that is, into the sanctuary—and measured the addition of the entrance—that is, the projection of the addition:* two cubits, **C F**. The entrance was six cubits in width, **G H**. The width of the "shoulders" was seven, **H I**, and **G K**. He determined the length of the inner sanctuary to be twenty cubits, and the width just as many. As for the partition itself which divides the sanctuary from the hall, he does not add its measurement; but it must be understood that this partition is counted within the length of the sanctuary, as is done in Moses' tabernacle. Otherwise, the length of the hall and <margin>50</margin> the sanctuary would be more than sixty cubits, which is contradicted both by this entire description of the temple and by Solomon’s, for which the same length and width are recorded in 1 Kings 6. The wall of the building was also measured at six cubits, namely in thickness. *As for the stories:* He calls "stories" the rooms of the three levels of flooring, which in Solomon’s temple are called "side chambers." They were all around the circuit of the building: that is, on this side and that, for they could not be all the way around, otherwise there would be no place for the gate. And there were <margin>60</margin> three levels, one placed upon the others, and this thirty times: that is, thirty rooms (so to speak) of three-story construction. Since each one occupies four cubits, and the length of the hall and sanctuary is sixty cubits, it results in fifteen on each side.

# A N N O T A T I O N S

...and in this way they fulfill this length. For fifteen times four makes sixty. *Which projected toward the wall of the temple, surrounded on all sides by the floorings themselves: that is, they had projections by which they were extended toward the wall of the temple, namely the middle story by half a cubit, and the uppermost by just as much. Thus they were continuous among themselves, as appears from the number: for they fill the entire length. Nor did they actually touch the wall of the temple: for a vacant space came between them. Moreover, the higher the stories were, the wider they were: specifically toward the south and toward the north. For toward the east and west they could not grow with additions, since they touched each other at the lowest part. And of a greater circuit: for the wider anything is, the wider an enclosure it has. Because the circuit of the temple, the higher it was, the wider it lay open: that is, the wall of the temple was so contracted on the inside that, while it was six cubits at the foundation, it was five at the roof; this retraction caused the temple at its highest part to be as much wider as the progression of the stories was.* <note>The author is explaining a "stepped" wall design where the wall gets thinner as it goes up, allowing the rooms attached to the outside to become wider at each higher level.</note> *Let **a** be the story, **b** the wall, **c** the vacant space, **d** and **e** the projections of the story, **f** and **g** the retractions of the wall opposite the projections.*

[A schematic architectural cross-section diagram showing stepped walls and floors labeled with letters. The diagram illustrates how rooms (stories) widen in higher levels as the main structure's wall recedes. Labels 'a' through 'i' mark specific points of intersection and dimension.]

*As much as there is between **h** and **i**, which are the foundations, there is just as much between **d** and **f**, and likewise between **e** and **g**, because **g** recedes outward from **i** by just as much (which makes the temple wider) as **e** proceeds beyond **h** to the perpendicular, which progression makes a larger circuit for the story.*

And so they had the lowest to the highest by way of the middle. This is clear from 3 Kings 6 <note>Modern Bibles refer to this as 1 Kings 6:8.</note>, where it is said there are spiral stairs <note>original: "cochleæ"</note> from the bottom, which lead to the middle stories, and by which one ascends to the top.

**And when the height of the house, etc.** This means that from the bottom the stories were indeed four cubits wide: but when I contemplated their top, I noticed that if a plumb line were dropped from the outermost additions, and the space between the bottom of the plumb line and the lowest stories were assigned to the foundation of the stories, that space would be one cubit on each side: thus the foundations of the stories are six cubits each.

For let **a b** be the foundation of the story, lying open four cubits. **c d** the top of six cubits. If you drop a line from **c** to **e**, and from **d** to **f**, and assign what is between **e** and **f** to the foundation (since it lies beneath the building) as much as is from **c** to **d**, so much will be from **e** to **f**: be-

-cause from **e** to **a** is one cubit, and from **b** to **f** likewise one, which, added to those four, make six.

The thickness of the wall, however, which was outside the stories—that is, the wall of the temple—was five cubits, namely at the top: for from the ground it was six cubits. From this it appears that the projection of the stories is partly on the inside. For if it were entirely on the outside, since it is two cubits, the projection would proceed further than the temple wall recedes. **Which space of the temple was vacant between the stories.** Here we read *berit* <note>Hebrew: ברית, usually "covenant"</note> instead of *bein* <note>Hebrew: בין, "between"</note>, as both the matter and the Greek translator show: just as in Proverbs 8 and Job 8, where the old version also translates it as "there." The space between the stories is the cell <note>inner room</note> and the sanctuary. That space is twenty cubits, by which space the stories are distant, namely the southern ones from the northern ones. This gap must be understood from the lowest stories: for the highest ones are less distant because of the forward movement of the additions.

The doors of the stories were in the vacant place, which was between the stories and the temple wall. Some facing north, namely the northern ones, at letter **L**: others south, at letter **M**.

The space vacant round about was five cubits in width. Whether this place also surrounded the inner shrine from the west, he does not add: but this is to be understood from the entire description. Whether, however, there were also stories in that part, he does not teach. But if you look at the number of the stories, since there were only thirty, none of them remained beyond the length of the sides. But because these stories are made according to the logic of the boards of the Tabernacle, which Moses constructed (for they surround the temple, as those also did), and there were also boards there from the west, it seems that in this temple also there were stories from the west, although they are not counted among the thirty: though I would not dare to affirm this. **"Thus the building itself."** He calls the temple the building, the construction of which he shows. **"Placed at the front of the enclosure."** To the south there was a space twenty cubits wide, ninety long, occupied by no building: which the Prophet names in Hebrew from the word for "separating," because it was separated from the whole body of the building. We interpret it as the **enclosure**. Next to that enclosure was the building, that is, the temple, lying open in width on the western part seventy cubits, from **N** to **O**. For the length of the vestibule is placed in the width of the building. In length it was ninety, from **P** to **Q**. ### FROM CHAPTER 42.

A very confused and highly difficult passage follows, in which the author repeats what he had said briefly in chapter 40 about the dining chambers <note>original: "cœnaculis"</note> of the courts, and explains the position and logic of the dining chambers in more detail. You must remember, however, that the description of all the courts is the same: but here the inner parts are described, since mention was made of the outer parts in chapter 40. Therefore, the second figure <note>referring to an architectural diagram elsewhere in the volume</note> which we placed there is to be applied here, and adapted to the east, north, west, and south. *He led me out into the outer court, by the way that led north, and led me to the dining chambers that were over against the enclosure, and over against the building.* By "this enclosure," I understand the two parts of the place which were vacant to the north within the temple wall to the right and left of the vestibule, where the letter **S** is in the temple area: the "building," however, is the temple itself. Opposite that place, the inner court lay open for a length of one hundred cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length based on the forearm, roughly 18 to 21 inches.</note>, **O P**: and a width of fifty **Q** on the inside, and **S**, since the remaining fifty were occupied by the construction of the gate. *Over against the twenty of the inner court, and over against the pavement of the outer court.* The chambers were in the inner court, between the space of twenty cubits of the inner court itself, **R S**: (for let us imagine this figure to be the inner court, which was previously the outer; so that everything may appear in the same figure: since the logic of all the courts is the same) and the pavement of the outer court, on which pavement were the dining chambers, namely thirty, as was said in chapter 40: which are marked with the letter **T**. Indeed, these dining chambers had projections <note>original: "processus"</note> facing the projections of one another. # NOTES.

...completing one hundred cubits, so that each of the rows of dining chambers <note>original: "cœnaculorum"</note> has a width of six cubits; in this way, 96 is produced. Four are missing, which are assigned to the barriers of as many paths: these barriers are marked with the letter **h**. But there are two reasons why I have placed longer rows at the gates rather than shorter ones: one is that in that second passage, which I cited above from chapter 40, the additions to the gate are said to be 50 cubits in surrounding length, which would not happen if this row were shorter. The other reason is that in the same chapter, two dining chambers are said to be outside the inner gate **y**, <margin>10</margin> of which the northern one faces south, and the southern one faces north, **h**. But if these chambers are outside the inner gate, it is necessary for the row here to be larger. However, these things are to be understood as referring to the dining chambers of the eastern court: otherwise the description would not fit. Therefore, I have corrected this passage in chapter 40, which is corrupted in the Hebrew, by using the Greek. For where the text has *two* <note>original: "שתים" (shtayim), feminine "two"</note>, the Greek correctly reads *two* <note>original: "שנים" (shenayim), masculine "two"</note>, more rightly, as I <margin>20</margin> think: as is clear from the use of the dining chambers, which are shortly assigned not to singers, but to priests. And for the word *which* <note>original: "אשר" (asher)</note>, it reads *one* <note>original: "אחד" (echad)</note>; and for *before them* <note>original: "בפניהם" (bifneihem)</note>, it reads *their faces* <note>original: "פניהם" (pneihem)</note>; and *from its structure* <note>original: "מבניה" (mibneiah)</note>, using a feminine singular relative, even though the former is masculine and disagrees in gender with the noun *chamber* <note>original: "לשכה" (lishkah)</note>. And for *eastward* <note>original: "הקדים" (ha-kadim)</note>, it reads *southward* <note>original: "הדרום" (ha-darom)</note>, so that it may be opposed to the north: as the logic of the placement soon declares. But if you wish these chambers <margin>30</margin> to be understood as being in the northern court, it will be necessary for what is said here about the southern and northern parts to be said about the eastern and western parts. 

As for the barrier that was outside, that is, outside the dining chambers: it was alongside the chambers, namely in length: toward the outer court, toward **Y**. It was fifty cubits in length, **K s**. On both sides: for it proceeded outside the gate by as much as the thickness of the wall at the outer court. For the length of the dining chambers of the outer court was fifty <margin>40</margin> cubits. From this it is clear that he is speaking of the inner court, and comparing it with the outer one, which follows the same logic. Since there were one hundred cubits along the face of the cell, **hi**. He calls the temple itself the *cell* <note>term: "cella" refers to the inner sanctuary or main body of the temple building</note> here. Truly, below those dining chambers was the entrance from the east. Now he speaks of the dining chambers of the eastern inner court, to which there was an entrance through which they might be approached from the outer court, at letter **Y**, so that this figure is now the eastern one. Moreover, he says, "below the dining chambers": since that entrance was in the <margin>50</margin> wall of the outer court. This he declares when he says, "In the width of the barrier of the court," calling the wall the barrier, **YE**. The entrance was on lower ground than the dining chambers themselves, inasmuch as it was approached from the outer court, which was lower than the inner one: as is clear in the gates, where he teaches that one ascends from the outer court

<column-break/>

to the inner one by steps. These dining rooms faced the building, the front. For the length of those on the left stretched toward the view: but those on the right toward the building, that is, toward the vestibule of the temple, which is part of the building. And before them was a path of the same form as the dining chambers that were toward the north. From this it appears that he is now speaking of the eastern ones, which he compares with the northern ones. Moreover, he calls that a *path* <note>original: "iter"</note> here which he had previously called a *walkway* <note>original: "ambulationē"</note>. And with doors which were then similar to those, namely the northern ones: and also to the doors of the dining chambers which were toward the south: from this it appears that the same things were also in the southern court. So that the door was at the head of the path, in **YE**: for there is the head of the path. And the path was before the fitted barrier, **EF**. Toward the east. In the eastern court, this path turns from the west toward the east, from **F** to **E**. He measured the eastern region with a ten-foot rod <note>term: "decempeda" - a measuring rod ten feet long</note> by five hundred ten-foot-rod cubits. Literally it is read, "by five hundred of the ten-foot rods," namely cubits. For it must not be translated as "five hundred ten-foot rods": for the entire space of the temple contradicts this, and the Greek translator, though otherwise not good, nevertheless rendered this passage well: *five hundred cubits* <note>original: "πηχεις πεντακοσίους" (pēcheis pentakosious)</note>. For it is a phrase in which the name of "cubit" is omitted, since it is the sum of the whole upper dimension; and since everything there was measured in cubits, it is omitted here: and it is added that the cubits are "ten-foot-rod" cubits, that is, of that measure which was set down above. And that the name of the measure is thus omitted is also apparent from the end of this chapter, where the length and width are said to be "of five hundred," and "cubits" is not added. Nevertheless, the old Latin translator correctly added it there. Moreover, regarding what is said—that he measured that region in a circuit—it is not to be understood as if that one region encircles everything: but that it is part of the enclosure of the temple, which he measures here in a circuit. To distinguish the sacred from the profane. And yet a little earlier he said that the inner courts in which the priests moved were sacred, as if the rest were not sacred. But it must be known that the entire place, enclosed by a wall of five hundred cubits, is indeed sacred: but in such a way that the innermost parts are the most sacred: whereby it happens that when the outer parts are compared with them, they are called "profane," since the inner parts are accessible only to consecrated priests. Therefore, this place extended five hundred cubits in length and as many in width, with the temple so placed that it had two courts in order from the four regions of heaven: since these were of equal measure with the temple itself, namely one hundred cubits, it results that if you place two from the east and as many from the west, with the temple itself placed between them, there are

# ANNOTATIONS. FROM CHAPTER 43.

**A** is the cubit-deep base: <note>original: "sinus cubitalis"</note> that is, one cubit in height. This manner of speaking was used above regarding the height of the washing basins, and will be used shortly regarding the height of the **Ariel** <note>The "Ariel" refers to the altar hearth or the "Lion of God."</note>. This base is of the same width as it is height. **B** is a nine-inch space <note>original: "spaciō dodrantale." A 'dodrans' is three-quarters of a Roman foot.</note> which surrounds the base at its rim: that is, at the ledge of the base itself. And this is indeed the descent of the Altar: that is, the base at the lowest part of the altar. From this base to the lower ledge: that is, from **A** to **C**, there are two cubits. Moreover, he calls the "ledge" a retraction or step of the altar, with a width of one cubit **C D**. From this ledge to the upper one, there are four cubits **D E**. However, he calls the lower ledge "smaller," not in length (for it is two cubits longer than the upper one), but in its total area, since it is only one cubit wide, whereas the upper ledge—that is, the roof of the altar, so to speak—extends twelve cubits in length and width. Furthermore, he names the upper part of the altar—that is, whatever is above the lower ledge—the **Ariel**, a word which in 2 Kings 23 and 1 Chronicles 11 signifies a "huge lion." It sounds like "Lion of God" or "Divine Lion," by which name that part of the altar is called because the victims are burned upon it, and are consumed as if by a lion. Therefore, we have translated it as **God-lion** <note>original: "leodeum"</note>. The **God-lion** extends in height

<column-break/>

<margin>10</margin>
<margin>20</margin>

four cubits **D E**; in width twelve cubits **E F**, and in length just as many **G H**. It is squared on its four sides: that is, on its flanks and ribs, so to speak, and has four horns at its summit. The ledge is two cubits longer than the **God-lion**, specifically as much as the retraction (which is its width), so that it is fourteen cubits long and wide **I K** and **I L**, surrounded by a space of half a cubit, which is the nine-inch span mentioned above. For this space, marked with the letter **A**, surrounds the entire body of the lower altar, which reaches down to the ground. And this altar is ascended by steps facing the east, marked with the letter **M**, since the temple is also turned toward the east.

### FROM CHAPTER 46.

*There were single small courts in each corner of the courts.)* <note>original: "Erant in singulis atriorum angulis singula atriola."</note> That which I translate as "small courts" <note>original: "atriola"</note> is in the singular number in Hebrew, but is used for the plural; just as in the first chapter "wheel" is said for four joined wheels. And in Exodus 27, "lamp" is used for "lamps." For among the Hebrews, derivatives are often used for primitives: so that "small court" is placed here for a "court-structure," so to speak; because this cannot be said in Latin, the plural must be used. He speaks of the four corner small courts, which in the figure of the temple are located...

...marked with the letter **N** you will find, whose length indeed I have made from east to west, which is the length of the temple. They were moreover *shomrot* <note>original Hebrew: שמרות</note>, which word is derived from "to smoke," meaning smoky—that is, blackened by smoke—because the kitchens were located in them. As for what I translate as "mansions," in Hebrew it is *tirot* <note>original Hebrew: טירות</note>, which elsewhere signifies an order or a row; but a little later the same thing is called *shirot* <note>original Hebrew: שירות</note>, which word seems to signify mansions, or chambers placed above the kitchens. The Greeks translated it as *exedras* <note>original: "exedras," referring to the Greek ἐξέδραι, meaning outdoor seats or covered porticos.</note>.

### FROM CHAPTER 48.

In this chapter is the distribution of the whole region, which we shall explain with the figure placed below.
The whole region is divided into thirteen parts, all of which are of equal length and width, namely twenty-five thousand cubits, square. Moreover, the length of each individual part is from east to west. But the length of the whole region is from north to south, three hundred and twenty-five thousand, while the width is only twenty-five thousand, as much as the length of the individual parts. The whole middle part is called the **exceptitium** <term>exceptitium: a "reserved portion" or "sacred contribution," land set apart from common use for God and his ministers</term>, because it is excepted [taken out] from the others. Furthermore, it is divided into three parts, of which one, placed next to the tribe of Judah, extends twenty-five thousand in length **A B**, and ten thousand in width **A C** and **B D**. In its middle is the temple **E**. And this entire part is assigned to the Zadokite priests. **F**, the other part, is of the same size, assigned to the Levites as attendants, for the possession of twenty chambers, as is written in chapter 45; that is, what would be the possession of the Levites, who dwell in twenty chambers. There remains a space five thousand wide **G H**, and twenty-five thousand long **H I**; this place is the "profane" <note>In biblical architectural terms, "profane" does not mean unholy, but rather "common" or intended for public, non-sacred use.</note> part of the city. In its middle is the square city **K**, measuring four thousand five hundred cubits, from which five hundred remain out of the five thousand width, which are assigned for the **pomerium** <term>pomerium: the open, unbuilt space immediately inside or outside a city wall</term>, two hundred and fifty on each side, and the same to the east and west. There remain ten thousand in length to the east **L M**, and just as many to the west **N O**, which are assigned to the city's inhabitants. And this whole area is called the reserved portion, whose part assigned to the city is profane, the rest sacred. In both, the prince has a possession: in the sacred part along the side of Judah, in the part of the Levites and Zadokites twenty-five thousand long **A B**. However, in the profane part in the possession of the city, along the side of the Benjamites, **H I**: which is the principal possession between the borders of Judah and Benjamin. But how great the width of that principal possession is, the author does not add. Moreover, it should be noted that the Lord's reserved portion is not in the center of the whole region. For from the north there are seven tribes, while from the south there are only five.

### FROM CHAPTER 3.

<header>ANNOTATIONS.</header>

**The fourth of whom has a form like one born of God.**) "One born of God" <note>original Latin: "Deo natus"</note> is used here to mean God, or a divine being, just as "one born of man" <note>original Latin: "homine natus"</note> is used for a man—a point I have discussed elsewhere. Thus, the meaning is that the form was like one born of God: a form more majestic than a human form, of a divine race, or similar to a divine being. This is similar to 1 Samuel 28 (referred to here as 2 Kings 28), where the witch said to Saul that she saw "gods ascending from the earth"—that is, a person of a certain majestic and divine appearance.

### FROM CHAPTER 4.

<margin>10</margin> **This matter is by the decree of the watchers, etc.**) Word for word, it reads: "The matter is by the decree of the watchers, the request is by the proclamation of the holy ones." This sentence is a parallel. For "watcher" <note>original Latin: "uigil"</note> and "holy one" are the same thing; as stated above, "a watcher and a holy one" refers to the same individual. Likewise, "decree" and "proclamation" are the same, as are "matter" and "request." He calls the law that is to be passed a "request" <note>original Latin: "rogatio"</note>, just as the Romans do. Before a law was passed, those whose job it was to sanction it were "asked" <note>original Latin: "rogabantur"</note> whether they wished to accept it. <margin>20</margin> The formula for such a request was of this sort: "Is it your will and command that Marcus Tullius Cicero be interdicted from fire and water?" A request of this kind was brought among the spirits <note>original Latin: "genios"</note> deliberating over Nebuchadnezzar: "Is it your will and command that Nebuchadnezzar, etc." I do not mean to suggest that I wish to transfer this exact formula to divine matters, but rather that it should be understood that when mention is made here of a "decree" and "request" of the spirits, it signifies that there was a deliberation among them concerning Nebuchadnezzar. You will see a similar deliberation in 1 Kings 22 (referred to as 3 Kings 22), <margin>30</margin> where there is a consultation between the Lord <note>original Latin: "Iouam," likely using the humanist 'Iova' for 'Jehovah'</note> and the Spirits about luring Ahab into a deception; however, these things are described in a human manner.

### FROM CHAPTER 11.

**And he shall cause that a woman, etc.**) Antiochus the Great will give his daughter Cleopatra in marriage to Ptolemy Epiphanes, so that, having corrupted her, he might win the kingdom of Egypt for himself (the father). But she will not perform this; she will favor her husband rather than her father. Then that Antiochus, having conquered many, will besiege Ptolemy at Alexandria. But the ruler—that is, the Roman people—will restrain Antiochus <margin>40</margin> from the siege. Thus, they will curb Antiochus’s insult against the Romans (for it was a disgrace to the Romans that Ptolemy, who had sought help from them, should be besieged), so that Antiochus would not do the same thereafter. Seleucus Philopator will succeed Antiochus. After Seleucus comes Antiochus Epiphanes. What follows, I do not understand. For there seems to be a transition from Antiochus to some kind of "spiritual" Antiochus; we have written in our commentary on Isaiah 9 that such transitions are common. <margin>50</margin> Therefore, we omit both these things, the seventh chapter of Daniel, and countless other things in the Prophets, lest the blind lead the blind.

-># ON HOSEA.<-

### FROM CHAPTER 2.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter 'O'. It depicts a classical landscape with a prominent building featuring a tower and a smaller structure beside it, possibly a farmhouse or a shrine, under a clear sky.</image-desc> **When I show whether there is faithfulness among the Israelites.**) <margin>55</margin> Word for word it reads: "In the tribes of the Israelites, when I show faithfulness." For that verb must be rendered as a participle, which often happens when a verb is not joined to the preceding verb by any conjunction. An example occurs just before this passage, where we translated it as: "They shall go to seek the Lord, but they shall not find Him, for He is turning away from them." If you translate it word for word, it reads: "They shall not find Him, He turned away from them"—that is,

<column-break/>

<page-num>138</page-num>
<header>ANNOTATIONS.</header>

with Him turning away from them. However, the sense of this passage is: "I will show that there is no faithfulness in the tribes of the Israelites when I take vengeance on them as faithless people." This way of speaking is also found in Psalm 69, where it reads word for word: "God, you know my madness (or fault)." This means: "You know whether I am at fault; you know that I am without fault," for in that psalm David defends his innocence.

### FROM CHAPTER 6.

**You also, O Judah, prepare a harvest for yourself, etc.**) This means: you Jews are also going to sin, and thus you will bring upon yourselves a punishment which is the "harvest" and "fruit" of your sin. I will impose this punishment on you at the time when I recall my captives—namely, the good ones. For you who are wicked shall not obtain my peace, but only my own people—that is, the good. Regarding this matter, see what we have written on Isaiah 57. As for his saying, "Prepare for yourself a harvest," he uses the imperative command in place of the future tense, just as Christ did when He said, "Fill up the measure of your fathers," as we have taught elsewhere. Regarding the harvest signifying punishment, see chapters 8 and 10.

### FROM CHAPTER 7.

**The Ephraimite is bread baked on the hearth, not turned over.**) This is bread <note>original Latin: "depstitius panis"</note> that is usually cooked quickly on a hearth; unless it is turned over, it burns on the side touching the fire. It is not cooked evenly, as in an oven. So the Ephraimites are burned and worn down by their enemies.

### FROM CHAPTER 8.

**I might have written for him.**) I have indeed written about the altars in the Law, but they do not obey any more than if I had not written to them. **Sacrifices for me to taste.**) Their sacrifices are not pleasing to the Lord because they do not obey Him.

### FROM CHAPTER 9.

**The feast of the good.**) They shall not be in Judea so that they might make a feast for the Lord in Jerusalem for the sake of their well-being. **What will you do on the solemn day?**) You will be exiles and will not be able to celebrate the solemnities of the Lord at Jerusalem. **A prophet with my God.**) One who professes to be a prophet and to have commerce with my God. **To the slayer.**) Into Egypt, where he may be killed.

### FROM CHAPTER 10.

**Where those who were not to be touched stood, etc.**) That is, where the Israelites were present with the intention of punishing the Benjaminites, without themselves receiving any disaster in the war, since they relied on the justice of their cause and were waging war against the wicked. And indeed, I punished the Benjaminites as I wished, but I punished them in such a way that the rest of the Israelite people suffered the same, very many of whom fell in that same war. I did this because both were guilty and both were bound by their own crime. For the Israelites, who were so eager to punish the others, were not innocent themselves. **Riding upon the Ephraimite.**) I will thoroughly subdue both the Israelites and the Jews.

### FROM CHAPTER 12.

**Judah still ruling with God.**) Since the Jews still worship God, they therefore retain their power. <margin>60</margin> **It is carried.**) Namely, by the Ephraimites, seeking help from the Egyptians. **And there he spoke with him.**) The Hebrew word *immanu* <note>original Hebrew: עמנו, meaning 'with us'</note> is placed here for *immo* <note>original Hebrew: עמו, meaning 'with him'</note>, with the letter *nun* inserted, as happens in the word *mimmenu* <note>original Hebrew: ממנו</note> and at the end of Psalm 5, *taateri* <note>original Hebrew: תעטרי</note> for *taaterenu* <note>original Hebrew: תעטרנו</note>, for so the grammar requires.

ON MICAH <note>Though the header says Micah, the initial sections appear to conclude the commentary on Hosea from the preceding pages.</note>

this history requires it, and the Greeks translated it as "toward them" <note>original Greek: "πρὸς αὐτοὺς"</note>, using the plural instead of the singular, but referring to the same person.

**Jehovah was God, mighty in arms.**) He held Jehovah in memory and worshipped him; you also ought to imitate his religion if you wish to attain the same happiness as he did.

**I will place you in tabernacles.**) <note>A reference to Hosea 12:9.</note> The preceding events must be understood from the later ones. I will make you a captive; then I will call you back and lead you home, joyful, as is customary on feast days.

## FROM CHAPTER 13.

**Who have sacrificed a man.**) They attribute so much to their forged calves that they only admit those who sacrifice their own sons to kiss them.

**In the narrowness of children.**) In pain, such as that of a woman in labor when the offspring is at the mouth of the womb.

## FROM CHAPTER 14.

**Accept that which is good.**) Good and pleasing victims: that is, the offering of thanks, which we will pour out to you instead of bulls. But I do not dare to affirm this. For the word is ambiguous and can be rendered as **to join benefits**. Now, he who gives gifts, receives and distributes them. The same word is placed in the same way in Psalm 68. Moreover, this "beneficence" required by God is the forgiveness of all crimes, which he had just requested.

# ON JOEL.

## FROM CHAPTER 1.

**A powerful and innumerable nation.**) He calls the locusts a "nation," just as in Proverbs 30 the ants and rock hyraxes are called "peoples." Maro <note>The Roman poet Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro).</note> speaks in this same manner concerning bees in the fourth book of his *Georgics*:
"I shall tell of these great-hearted leaders, and the customs,
pursuits, peoples, and battles of the whole race in order." <note>original Latin: "Magnanimo hęc duces, totiusq́; ex ordine gẽtis / Mores, & studia, & populos, & pręlia dicam."</note>

# ON AMOS.

## FROM CHAPTER 3.

**Prepare yourself to meet your God.**) After you have not become better through punishments, you seem to want to contend with God. See to it, therefore, that you prepare yourself to engage with him who is, etc.

## FROM CHAPTER 5.

**Did you offer victims to me?**) The fact that I defended you for forty years was not because of your sacrifices—since you were not yet making any—so do not think they will be of use now, when they were of no use then.

## FROM CHAPTER 6.

**They put away the evil day.**) They indulge in pleasure and are unjust.

**Does one plow on rocks, etc.**) You act as absurdly as if someone were to plow rocks with oxen, etc.

# ON OBADIAH.

**For as you have drunk upon my holy mountain, etc.**) Just as you strangers, after Jerusalem was destroyed, rejoiced and feasted in Zion because of your joy, so the nations in turn shall be "drunk"—that is, they shall be destroyed—so that it may be "drunk" concerning them just as it was concerning Jerusalem. And they shall be so swallowed up that not even a trace remains, nor shall any of them escape. 

<column-break/>

But from Zion there shall be those who escape. Moreover, this signifies that he will destroy the rest of the nations on account of their sins, but he will only punish the Israelites, not destroy them. You will find this sentiment declared in Amos chapter 9. However, it is read here word-for-word: "They shall drink all the nations," which is to be interpreted through the passive voice, as often happens. Examples of this are found in the words of Christ: "Do they light a lamp?" <note>original Latin: "Nunquid accendunt lucernam?"</note> etc., instead of "Is a lamp lit?" And "They do not put new wine into old wineskins," instead of "it is not put."

# ON MICAH.

## FROM CHAPTER 2.

**We are ruined (says the people, or anyone from among the people); God takes away from us, who are the people, our field and possessions.** Not only does he not return them to us, but he even divides them among the enemies, as if they were alienated from us, so that we might not hope to recover them. Therefore, you shall not have (says the prophet to the people) anyone who might divide the land for you by lot in the community of the Israelites, as Joshua once divided it. This means you will lose your homeland. You will say this oracle is gloomy, by which I foretell calamity to you—or that one should not prophesy, or at least not prophesy in such a way that we are threatened with gloomy and shameful things. What then? Do you want me to announce joyful things to you? I cannot, unless I wish to lie. For God threatens gloomy things; yet he does not threaten them as if he were either unable or unwilling to promise and provide joyful and favorable things. For why should he be less able to be good to you than to Jacob, from whom you draw your lineage? For his spirit is not contracted or weakened so that he cannot bestow upon you what he could on him; nor, on the other hand, has his goodness changed so that he now refuses what he then willed, and thus be both weak and inconstant. What then stands in the way, you ask, of him promising joyful things? He indeed promises joyful things, but to the upright, as will be said shortly. But your wickedness makes him promise you less joyful things—you who, though you were formerly his people, have now become his enemies (for this is what it means "to rise up as an enemy" <note>original Latin: "surgere in hostẽ"</note>, just as if you were to say a bush "rises into a tree," that is, it becomes tree-like). For you rob travelers and strip them of their honorable garments, though they fear no such thing but are returning securely from war. For those who have escaped the enemy fear nothing further; yet you are enemies to them. And you are such not only abroad, but even at home toward that sex which ought most to be spared—namely, women, whom you violently eject from their dear homes, oppressed by usury and other inequities. Furthermore, you rob their children and deprive them of the clothing with which they were gifted and adorned by me, so that, oppressed by this cruelty, they can never emerge from misery and want. These crimes, by which the land is polluted, are the reason why I denounce exile and dire calamity upon you. I know these things do not please you, as you are those who demand joyful things. Therefore, if there were some windy and vain man who would lie and promise you much wine, you would believe him, despite his lying, rather than one speaking the truth, for no other reason than that he predicted joyful things.

->ANNOTATIONS.<-

...I too preach good things, but for those who are to be good. For you will remember what I said above, that my words are good for those walking rightly, lest by chance the wicked hope for this happiness which I am now about to describe. I do not preach about wine, but about the greatest of all matters, which is of this kind: After I have sent you away into exile (as I threatened above), I will bring back those of you who remain, and I will gather you together like noble sheep in Jerusalem, as if in a sheepfold, in such numbers that the account can scarcely be reckoned because of the multitude of men. Moreover, your leader will be the Messiah, your king, who will break through and conquer the enemies, and thus open the way for you to the blessed kingdom. There you shall hereafter live freely, with the Messiah as your protector, king, and head; in which head shall be Jehovah his Father, since the Father is in the Son, and the Son is in the Father. And these things I promise to the good and upright.

->FROM CHAPTER 3.<-

For I denounce calamity to the wicked, and to false prophets, I denounce blindness and an absence of oracles.

->FROM CHAPTER 5.<-

**Now you shall make an assault on the enemy, you daughter of Zion, against whom an assault is now being made.**) This means that the Israelites (who are Christians) <note>The author uses a "typological" interpretation, where the promises to Israel are fulfilled by the Christian Church.</note> will conquer Gog and Magog (concerning whom see Ezekiel and Revelation), who will besiege us Israelites. Among these Israelites, Christ, the judge of the Israelites, was beaten and nailed to a cross, yet under his leadership, they will conquer. He shall be born in Bethlehem, but his origin shall be from eternal times. In this place, Micah signifies that the Messiah, regarding his humanity, was to be born in Bethlehem; regarding his divinity, however, he was not "born" in the same sense, as he is everlasting. **Therefore he will give them up.**) He gives the reason for what was said before regarding the beaten Christ. Since the Jews rejected and killed Christ, he says, he will desert them until the mother church (for so she is called in Revelation 12) brings forth Christ: that is, until Christ is preached to the remaining nations. And so, the time of the Gentiles being completed, the rest of Christ's brothers—that is, the Jews—shall return to the Israelites—that is, to the Christians, who are the true Israelites: which is to say, they shall become Christians. This will happen when Christ has grown to the ends of the earth: that is, when the discipline of Christ has been made known throughout the whole world. This is the same sentiment found in Luke 21 in these words: "And Jerusalem shall be trodden down by the Gentiles, until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled"; Paul teaches the same in Romans 11. **And he shall be.**) Namely, the Messiah: our peace. That is, he will protect us if the enemy invades us. For he calls any enemy "the Assyrian." As in that line of Maro <note>The poet Virgil (Publius Virgilius Maro), from Eclogue 4.</note>: "There will then be another Tiphys, and another Argo to carry chosen heroes." <note>original: "Alter erit tum Typhis, & altera quę uehat Argo Delectos heroas." The author argues that just as Virgil uses names from old myths to describe future events, the prophet uses "Assyrian" to represent any future oppressor.</note>

->FROM CHAPTER 2.<-

**He remembers his nobles.**) The king of Nineveh, hearing of the arrival of the enemy, commands his nobles to hasten to the walls for defense: though they do this as swiftly as possible, they nevertheless find the siege engines already prepared by the enemy, and the city is immediately captured as the enemy enters through the mouths of the rivers.
