**Go through the mud.**) You shall go away into exile, and there you shall serve in the brick-kilns <note>literally "the place of pottery."</note>.
**The locusts shall spread themselves out.**) Your people will depart, just as locusts are accustomed to fly away.

### ->ON HABAKKUK.<-

->FROM CHAPTER 1.<-

**For from itself is its judgment.**) It has claimed imperial power for itself, and does not depend on the authority of another.
**Having a face.**) Scorching all things by their arrival.
**With earth heaped up.**) Surrounded by a siege mound.
**Swelling in spirit.**) Being prideful.
**Strength to his god.**) Namely, attributing his power to his own god.
**You have established him for punishing.**) For this reason you have supported the Assyrian with such great power: so that you may gloriously destroy him.
**Therefore will he not empty.**) Will he forever capture the nations?

->FROM CHAPTER 2.<-

**Against your very self, great... etc.**) The things you gather will profit you no more than mud; indeed, they will only harm you.
**The stone shall cry out from the wall.**) It will stir God to take punishment on you for the injury you do to those from whom you extort their goods to build your own edifices.
**Infamous vomit.**) You will be forced to vomit shamefully and lose what you have snatched away; you will pay the penalty for the cruelty you used against Lebanon—that is, against the Israelites. The men whom you terrified will be your ruin: that is, you will pay the penalty because of them. He calls the men "beasts" to continue the metaphor, because he had called the homeland of the Israelites "Lebanon," referring to "Lebanese cruelty."

### ->ON ZECHARIAH.<-

->FROM CHAPTER 14.<-

**With the saints accompanying him.**) In the Hebrew it is, "accompanying *you*." But the old version <note>The Latin Vulgate.</note> seems to have read it better.
**It will not be a bright day or a concretion.**) There will be no alternation of day and night, which usually makes the day more dear after the night.
**At evening time there shall be light.**) That is, when it is now evening and night. See the book of the Sibyl... toward the end of the first part, concerning the rewards of the good.
**But they shall be struck with a plague.**) He does not threaten the Egyptians with a lack of rain as he does others, since they could not be pressed by that, as they use the Nile and not rain.

### ->ON MALACHI.<-

->FROM CHAPTER 2.<-

**But if one did.**) Abraham, who is your one parent as was said above, did indeed take a foreigner into marriage—Hagar the Egyptian—but he did it by the instinct of God, and was not for that reason unfaithful to his first wife.

# ON THE SECOND BOOK OF ESDRAS <note>original: "IN ESDRÆ LIBRVM IIII." In the older numbering used here, the Fourth Book of Esdras refers to what is now commonly called 2 Esdras in the Apocrypha.</note>

### BOOK 4.

->FROM CHAPTER 4.<-

<note>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' with floral flourishes.</note>
**But if you, O Lord, are to be present there.** <note>original: "AD si tu Domine, ijv adfuturus es." The OCR "ijv" is likely a misreading of "vis" or "si."</note>) If you will save those who are there when the day of the last judgment comes, you do not seem likely to save those who died before.

->FROM CHAPTER 8.<-

<margin>10</margin> **Drink up then, O my soul.**) If few are to be saved, I will not be among those few, since I am not righteous. Therefore, I must learn in this life. For regarding the future life, the matter is already decided.

**Unless you permit me.**) Unless you make us good, not one of mankind can be saved, since all are fountains <note>original: "fontes." This likely refers to the "fountains" or "sources" of sin or human nature, or it could be a variant spelling of "sons" (guilty).</note>.

**You are likened to him.**) You compare yourself with a farmer; you "sow" men just as a farmer sows seed.

<margin>20</margin> **Other things must be done for the present.**) I will indeed have mercy, as you ask: but it is not yet time. And each thing must be done in its own proper time.

->FROM CHAPTER 9.<-

**For then everyone.**) This seems to mean, "Then all things were obedient," so that the masculine "everyone" stands for the neuter "everything," following the Hebrew word *Chol* <note>The Hebrew word "Kol" (all/everything) is often used in a way that can be translated as either "everyone" or "all things."</note>.

->FROM CHAPTER 11.<-

<margin>a</margin> <margin>30</margin> **Which however rested with them.**) It reads, "But also she." This error seems to stem from the fact that in the Greek language, the word for "head" (*kephalē*) is of the feminine gender.

->FROM CHAPTER 16.<-

**How she is stirred.**) Thus it reads in the Latin: *The harlot envies a virtuous woman.* But it seems it should read: *A virtuous woman envies a harlot*, so that the vice which adorns itself is compared with a painted harlot. Or, if the current reading is correct, the translator was deceived by either the Greek or Latin from the Hebrew speech, in which there is no distinction of grammatical cases.

## ON THE BOOK OF WISDOM.

->FROM CHAPTER 17.<-

<margin>50</margin> <note>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' with floral flourishes.</note>
**But when there is less expectation within, it imagines more things, etc.**) That is, when something unexpected happens, the mind, which is within, cannot suddenly collect itself; instead, struck by the sudden event, it fears things are worse than they are because it is ignorant of the cause of that evil. For example, if someone suddenly hears the sound of a cannon <note>original: "sonitū bōbardicum." An early reference to "bombards" or artillery used as a metaphor for a sudden, terrifying noise.</note>, he is terrified because his mind cannot reason quickly enough that there is no danger, and thus meet the fear. But if he hears the same thing anticipated, he is not terrified, since reason comes to his aid and shows that danger is absent. Furthermore, it should be read here "through ignorance" <note>original: "διὰ τὴν ἄγνοιαν" (dia tēn agnoian)</note>; so that the meaning is the same as that placed above: "they thought those things were rejoicing which were not seen" <note>original: "ἡγοῦντο χαίροντα τὰ μὴ βλεπόμενα" (hēgounto chaironta ta mē blepomena)</note>. For both the sense and the old Latin translator teach that it should be read thus. Likewise that which follows shortly after: "that an unexpected fear came upon them" <note>original: "ἀπροσδόκητον φόβον ἐπελθεῖν" (aprosdokēton phobon epelthein)</note>.

ON MATTHEW 144

### ON THE NEW TESTAMENT.

<note>Woodcut illustration of an Evangelist (likely St. Matthew) writing at a desk, set within a circular floral border. This serves as a historiated initial 'S'.</note>
**IT SHOULD BE KNOWN** that the New Covenant was written in Greek in such a way that the phrasing is Hebrew. This results in many things—which in the Hebrew language would be very easy—being not only obscure in Greek to those who have not learned Hebrew, but sometimes even seeming to mean something other than what the author intends. Hence it happens that many sentences must be explained with many words, whereas (if they were said in the Latin way in Latin) no interpretation would be needed. I add that just as every nation is delighted by its own customs, so every language is delighted by its own habit of speaking: it flees the strangeness of foreign expressions. These two causes seemed great enough to me—as I worked toward both clarity and proper Latinity—to justify why I should translate this work in a way that avoids "Hebraisms" <note>An "Hebraism" is a Hebrew idiom or grammatical structure translated literally into another language, often making it sound awkward or unclear.</note>.

### ON MATTHEW.

->FROM CHAPTER 1.<-

<margin>30</margin> <note>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring a figure and foliage.</note>
**Enumeration of the lineage.** <note>original: "ENumeratio generis."</note>) At first glance, some will judge this unusual; they will cry out that they prefer "The Book of the Generation," since they are accustomed to it. But if someone learned in Latin should read these words for the first time now, he would indeed recognize the words as Latin, but he would either not understand the subject or would understand it wrongly. For under those words, the meaning would be: "In this book is written how Jesus was begotten," which is not Matthew's meaning. Furthermore, if you want the speech to be meaningful and clear, "Book" does not accurately express an enumeration, or a list of names, or a register, which the Hebrews call *Sepher* <note>Hebrew: ספר (Sefer)</note>, which the author here translates as *Biblos* <note>Greek: Βίβλος</note>. Nor is "generation" the same as a series of ancestors or a lineage; to the Latins, it refers to the act of begetting, which Matthew does not signify by the word *genesis* <note>Greek: γένεσις</note>, for he is declaring that which the Greeks call *genealogy* <note>Greek: γενεαλογίαν</note>. You see here that it makes a significant difference which words you use to describe a thing, even if the word count is the same. Likewise, what follows soon after, "of David" <note>original: "τοῦ Δαυίδ" (tou Dauid)</note>, they translate as "son of David." But the word *Ben* <note>Hebrew: בן</note>, from which it is drawn, is used for both immediate sons and distant descendants, just as the Hebrews often signify with one simple word what we do with many compound words: from which it happens that in translating, one must consider the reason for the meaning. Furthermore, "son" is not usually said in Latin for someone who has arisen from an ancestor through many degrees of lineage. Likewise, the phrase repeated so often, "who begat" <note>original: "ὁ ἐγέννησε" (ho egennēse)</note>, is a Hebrew custom which is not necessary for us to retain in the Latin language (since it adds nothing to the point). Likewise, the phrase "at the time of the deportation" <note>original: "ἐπὶ τῆς μετοικεσίας" (epi tēs metoikesias)</note> is put for "captivity" <note>original: "αἰχμαλωσίας" (aichmalōsias)</note>, as often happens in the Old Testament, from the word *Galut* <note>Hebrew: גלות</note>, which means exile. And that phrase "all the generations" <note>original: "πᾶσαι αἱ γενεαί" (pasai hai geneai)</note>... and "for having been betrothed" <note>original: "μνηστεuθείσης γὰρ" (mnēsteutheisēs gar)</note>, the "for" is superfluous in the Latin language. Likewise that...

<meta>This page continues the linguistic and theological commentary on the New Testament, specifically the Gospel of Matthew. # ANNOTATIONS

that phrase, *and do not fear his name* <note>original: "καὶ μὴ φοβεῖσθε τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ"</note>, *his name shall not cease* <note>original: "οὐ μὴ παύσεται τὸ ὄνομα"</note>, likewise *his people* <note>original: "τὸν λαὸν αὐτοῦ"</note>, meaning his own. Finally, there are countless places of this kind, some of which I have briefly touched upon here, not so that I should do the same everywhere hereafter (for that would be infinite), but so that when such instances occur here and there in the future, it may be understood that I could have done the same there as I did here to explain the reasoning for all of them. However, I have partially declined to do so because of the length it would require, and partially because I judged it less necessary.

<margin>10</margin> **Nor did he wish to make an example of her.**) This means to take public punishment, which the law commanded to be done to adulteresses. But if he had divorced her secretly, she would be thought to be a disgraced single woman. For betrothals (which are usually done within private walls) could be hidden. In this way, Joseph would have saved Mary, not from infamy (for the divorce would be accompanied by the infamy of unchastity), but from death. This merciful man preferred that she seem a disgraced single woman rather than be <margin>20</margin> put to death as an adulteress. Concerning the passage from Isaiah which is cited here, see what we have written on Isaiah 7 and 9.

Regarding the name of **Jesus**, I hold the same view as Andreas Osiander <note>A prominent 16th-century German Lutheran theologian and scholar</note>: namely, that it is derived from the name **Ioua** <note>original: "Ioua," a Latinized form of the Hebrew Tetragrammaton YHWH, often rendered as Jehovah or the LORD</note>, with the letter *shin* <note>the Hebrew letter ש</note> placed in between. Since no one should have to write more on this matter, see Osiander's annotations on the *Gospel Harmony*. But when I considered long and hard why the letter *shin* should be placed in this name, and did not see why this letter would be inserted here, especially since <margin>30</margin> it is not "servile" <note>In older grammar, "servile" letters are those added to a root word to change its form, rather than being part of the core root itself</note>—that is, of that class of letters which are usually added to original words in derivatives—I began to think that this word must be a composite. Finally, by the grace of God, I seem to have discovered that just as Jesus is both God and man, so his name is fused from the name of God and the name of man. I learned this from <margin>40</margin> Exodus chapter 15, where it is said: *Ioua is a man of war* <note>original: "יהוה איש מלחמה / Ioua istch milehamah"</note>. Here he is called a warlike man because the discourse is about Christ, who was to be a man. Therefore, the name of **Jesus** is a composite of *Ish* <note>Hebrew for "man"</note> and *Ioua*, with the letter *shin* <note>ש</note> inserted from the name *Ioua*, while the other two letters are rejected because they are servile and are often added or removed, resulting in **Yehoshua** <note>original: "יהושוע"</note> or **Jesus**. This is the same as "Ioua-man" or "human" (for *Ish* also signifies a human being), so that we understand Jesus to be not *Ioua* (for this is said of his father), but *Ioua-man*: that is, <margin>50</margin> the embodied Ioua, made man. This is what those words in Exodus 3 seem to predict: *I will be who I will be*. Also, *I Will Be sent me to you*. It is as if he said this: "Indeed, he who is, is indeed that one, but he is not yet what he will be." For he is God, but he is also going to be man. And this is what the same Jesus, not yet made man, seems to indicate to Jacob in Genesis 32 when he forbids him to ask his name, because it is wonderful. For this point about its "wonderfulness" stands in the Greek and Latin texts, not without reason, although <margin>60</margin> that force is missing in the Hebrew. But the same is also in the Hebrew in Judges 13. For what is more wonderful than that the same person is both Ioua and man? Moreover, because in this name, the part that signifies "man" is placed in the middle of the word—though this is not usually done in other composites—in this there seems to be

<column-break/>

a hidden secret. For it signifies that man was made from Ioua, and conversely, Ioua was made from man: just as you see the name **Yehoshua** <note>original: "יהושוע"</note> begin with the name of Ioua and end in the same, with the name for "man" placed in between. And since this name of Jesus is specific to our Savior and not common to any mortal, we have preferred to call those who are called "Jesus" in Greek by the name **Joshua** <note>original: "Iosuas"</note>. For they are not called *Yehoshua* <note>with the mystical spelling</note>, but *Yehoshua* <note>standard spelling</note>.

### FROM CHAPTER 2.

**As many as were under two years old.** <note>original: "Quotquot erant infra bimitatum."</note>) Literally, it reads "from two years and under," which is a Hebraism, such as is read in 2 Kings 20 in these words: "If I say to the boy, the arrows are from you and this way, take them and come," etc. And shortly after: "but if I say thus to the youth, the arrows are from you and beyond," etc. where "from you and this way" is nothing other than "on this side of you," and "from you and beyond" is "beyond you." Likewise in Leviticus 22: "From the eighth day and beyond he shall sacrifice," that is, when he has passed the eighth day.

### FROM CHAPTER 3.

**John the Baptist.** <note>original: "Iohannes Baptista."</note>) The reason I aspirate the second syllable in the name of John <note>adding the 'h' sound</note> is because it is aspirated in the Hebrew name. This is not done in Greek because the Greeks do not have aspiration except at the beginning of words, with the exception of the letter *rho*. Think the same of *Gehenna*, *Abraham*, and many others, though in these matters let everyone use their own judgment as far as I am concerned. For I see these things are changed everywhere in the sacred writings, so that the first syllable of *Jerusalem* is aspirated in Greek, but not so in Hebrew; whereas the opposite happens with the name *Anna*.

### FROM CHAPTER 4.

**To be tempted by the devil.** <note>original: "Ut tentaretur à diabolo."</note>) The devil is a slanderer and an accuser. For the word *diabolos* <note>original: "διάβολος"</note> denotes not only to slander but also to accuse. Therefore, in Revelation 12, he is called the "accuser" <note>original: "κατήγορος"</note>, because he accuses the saints before God day and night. Regarding my translation of "the Tempter" <note>original: "Tentatorem"</note>, it is the participle *the one tempting* <note>original: "ὁ πειράζων"</note>; but the Hebrews use participles in place of nouns derived from verbs, just as in Mark 6, "John the one baptizing" <note>original: "ἰωάννης ὁ βαπτίζων"</note> is said, who is elsewhere called "the Baptist" <note>original: "βαπτιστής"</note>.

**Having set out for Capharnaum.** <note>original: "Capharnaum profectus."</note>) Certain words not aspirated by the Greeks are aspirated by the Latins, such as *Ioseph* and *Iosephios*, which the Latins call *Joseph* and *Calphurnius*, and *tropaion* becomes *trophaeum*. Of this kind are *Capernaum* and *Elisabeth*, which the ancient translator correctly called *Capharnaum* and *Cleophas*.

### FROM CHAPTER 5.

**Men will revile you.** <note>original: "Vobis conuiciabuntur homines."</note>) In Latin, it happens in a few verbs that active personal forms are used for impersonals—"they say," "they report," "they assert" (meaning "men" do these things) instead of "it is reported" or "it is asserted." This happens among the Hebrews in all sorts of verbs; although they are active, they must be interpreted as passive or impersonal, or something must be added. Such is the case with the phrase placed shortly after this passage: *neither do they light a lamp* <note>original: "οὐδὲ καίουσι λύχνον"</note>. If you translate this literally, you must add "men": "Men do not light a lamp." Or through the passive thus: "Neither is a lamp lighted," or "it is not customary for a lamp to be lit." Such is also this expression, "They will revile you"; for "men" must be added, as Latin speech requires, and the ancient translator correctly added it. Or the passive should be used: "Revilements shall be made against you."

<meta>This page continues a scholarly commentary on the Gospel of Matthew, specifically focusing on Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount. The author uses linguistic analysis to bridge the gap between Hebrew idioms, Greek New Testament phrasing, and classical Latin usage to explain the deeper moral meaning of Christ's teachings.</meta>

### ON MATTHEW

(*He shall be counted as least.*) In Latin, you might say "not at all" <note>original: "nullus"</note> instead of "you shall not speak." Likewise here, *he shall be counted as least*, or shall be called least, is placed instead of saying "he shall not be called at all." Furthermore, "to be called" is often used to mean "to be," as when Isaiah says the Messiah will be called—or named—Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, etc. <note>Isaiah 9:6</note>. This signifies that he is not only to be called these things, but will be them in actual fact. Similarly, when the angel in Luke says Jesus will be called the Son of God <note>Luke 1:35</note>, <margin>10</margin> he speaks not only of a name but of the reality. Therefore, the meaning of this sentence is: He shall be held in no place, or shall have no place, in the heavenly kingdom. Cicero speaks in much the same way when he says "to be numbered among the living" instead of "to be alive" in his speech *In Defense of Sextus Roscius*.

(*Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the Scribes and Pharisees.*) Reader, attend carefully to this sentence so that you may understand those that follow. In this place, Jesus teaches where true virtue and righteousness are situated: namely, in <margin>20</margin> obeying the law. But he shows what it means to *truly* obey the law. The law forbade killing and adultery, etc. The Scribes and Pharisees did not kill and did not commit adultery, and so they seemed to be righteous, since righteousness is obeying the law. But Christ denies that they obey the law. For it is not enough to refrain from the act of killing unless you have a mind free from the intent of murder. Since the mind is so much more excellent than the body—so much so that men are named for their minds (indeed, the **HEBREWS** use a term for "man" that implies this, and the **LATINI** use <margin>30</margin> "souls" <note>original: "animas"</note> for people)—it is like that saying: *Happy are the souls whose first care was to know these things and to climb into the dwellings of the gods above.* <note>A quote from Ovid’s Fasti, praising early astronomers/philosophers.</note> He is truly a murderer who has a murderous mind. And yet, he who is angry with another without cause, or who hurls insults, has the mind of a murderer. For he who can be angry without cause or reason can likewise, without cause, speak evil, strike, and kill. For a curse is no further from anger, nor a blow from a curse, nor a killing from a blow, than unjust anger <margin>40</margin> is from reason. He who allows anger to overwhelm reason is easily driven to insults and slaughter. For once you have crossed the limits of reason, there is no limit to sinning. Someone might say: "But the law is not so severe; it does not decree the death penalty for anger or insults." I believe it. For the law committed the imposition of punishment to magistrates, who, being human, punish deeds, not will, and actual damages, not thoughts. They cannot prove the intent of men's minds without the <margin>50</margin> testimony of two or three people, without which it is not permitted to punish anyone. Therefore, to be safe from the magistrate, it is enough not to kill a man, even if your mind is murderous. By this standard, the Pharisees are indeed righteous. But if Christ’s kingdom were an earthly one, he would have nothing else to teach; but since his kingdom is heavenly, the judge will be heavenly, the witnesses heavenly, and the judgment heavenly, in which there will be no place for ignorance. There, not only the physical murderer (as is the case among men, <margin>60</margin> where the kingdom is physical) but also the murderous mind will be punished. Therefore, if you wish to avoid eternal punishment, you must obey the law not just in appearance, but truly and from the heart, with God as your witness and confidant, who considers the desire for a crime as the crime

<column-break/>

itself and punishes it. This is Christ’s meaning, from which it becomes clear that he is not saying that one who is angry without cause should be punished by a civil magistrate. For he would be commanding something that could not be done. Rather, he teaches that he who is angry without cause is a murderer in his mind, and will be condemned by the heavenly judgment of Christ and the assembly of the saints, and will suffer the eternal punishments of the fire of Gehenna. And what we have said here regarding murder, <margin>10</margin> understand the same regarding adultery and the rest. Furthermore, when he says *To his brother*, he calls every human being "brother," since we are all born from the same parent of the human race, Adam. And although "brother" is not usually used in Latin for "another person" among the ancient authors, I think it is permissible now and should be adopted into custom, just like certain other words; otherwise, while we are more scrupulous in our speech, we might be less scrupulous in our religious practice. *Gehenna* signifies the Valley of Hinnom, mentioned in Jeremiah <margin>20</margin> 7. It is also used to represent eternal punishment by the Sibyl <note>The Sibylline Oracles, a collection of Greek oracular verses</note> in these words: 
->*And the just shall endure the punishment of the unquenchable fire of Gehenna.*<-
*Raca*, which we translate as "scoundrel" <note>original: "balatronem"</note>, is a word of insult derived from *reyka* <note>original: "רֵיקָא"</note>, which properly signifies "empty," and when applied to people, signifies "worthless." The Greeks call it by the same name, *rhacha*; the Latins call it *balatronem* <note>a jester or buffoon</note> or *nebulonem* <note>a worthless fellow</note>; the French say *belistre* <note>beggar</note>, *coquin* <note>rascal</note>, or *babouin* <note>baboon/fool</note>.
<margin>30</margin> *Settle with your adversary.*) Since Christ is teaching the way to the heavenly kingdom, and before this passage spoke of offering gifts to God, not to man, he is not here instructing his followers on how they should behave in human legal disputes. Rather, he teaches that what people prudently do in human disputes should also be done in divine matters. Just as prudent men prefer to settle with an opponent rather than <margin>40</margin> come before a judge—because the opponent might act more mildly, whereas the judge is most severe and acts according to the strict letter of the law—so it is better, if you have offended someone or if you are at odds due to hatred, to settle with them and lay aside enmities quickly while it is possible in the course of this life, rather than incur the severe judgment of God, in which repentance will be too late. In using the imperative command, he makes the analogy shorter and more elegant, like that one: *Either make the tree good and its fruit good, etc.* <margin>50</margin> For he is not commanding that a tree be made good, but he teaches that just as a good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor a bad tree good fruit, so a virtuous man cannot act wickedly, nor a wicked man virtuously. Likewise that phrase: *First clean the inside of the cup.* Also the one about sitting in the lower part of the table at banquets. The Latins speak no differently when they say, *Do not stir up the hornets.* For they are not giving instructions about hornets, but it is as if they were saying: "Just as it is dangerous to irritate hornets, so it is to provoke that man," or something similar. Of this same kind is: <margin>60</margin> *Do not give what is holy to dogs.* "What is more than this is from the Evil One": he calls the devil "the Evil One" <note>original: "Malo"</note>, as in 1 John 3, where he said, "He who commits sin is of the devil." Shortly after, bringing an example of this matter, he says: "Not as Cain, who was of the Evil One and killed his brother."

The author clarifies terms like Gehenna and Raca, emphasizing that spiritual reconciliation must happen before facing God's final, absolute judgment.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s linguistic and theological commentary on the Gospel of Matthew. Having previously discussed the nature of the "Kingdom of Heaven" and the true meaning of fulfilling the Law, he now moves into specific interpretations of the Sermon on the Mount (Chapters 5 and 6), focusing on how Hebrew idioms were translated into Greek and how they should be understood in Latin and English.</meta>

-># ANNOTATIONS.<-

<margin>We must not resist injury.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 5.</margin>
(We must not resist injury.) The Hebrew word <term>עַיִן</term> <note>original: "Ayin," literally "eye," but used in idioms for "evil" or "malice"</note>, which the Greek text here calls "the evil one" <note>original: "ponērō"</note>, often signifies "injury" among the Hebrews. This is similar to the Greek word for "evil" <note>original: "kakon"</note>, which appears in the word "to remember an injury" <note>original: "mnēsikakein"</note>. I have preferred to translate this as "injury" rather than "evil," so there is no room for ambiguity. For many things are "evil"—the plague, hunger, cold, war, and sin—and Jesus does not forbid us from resisting those. Rather, he forbids us from resisting the specific injuries he goes on to list. If you wish to understand this passage better, read 1 Corinthians 13.

<margin>To love one's neighbor.</margin>
(Love your neighbor.) The Hebrew term <term>רֵעֲךָ</term> <note>original: "re'aka"</note> sometimes means a neighbor or a friend, and sometimes simply "anyone else." Therefore, when the command is given to love your "neighbor," the Hebrew phrasing is ambiguous: does it mean we are commanded to love only our friends, or everyone? This ambiguity disappears if you translate it into Latin using a word that only means one or the other. However, to preserve the possibility of both meanings, I have used the word "neighbor" <note>original: "proximum"</note> here, as it is also used in Luke 10. Thus, while in God’s commandment the word signifies "the other"—that is, any person—there were those who chose the other meaning, interpreting it as a command to love only their friends. From this, they wrongly concluded that it was acceptable to hate their enemies. Therefore, the Teacher <note>Jesus</note> acts in this passage to remove that error; he teaches that this commandment requires us to love everyone, even our own enemies. He wants us to understand that "neighbor" <note>original: "re'aka"</note> here does not mean "friend," but "the other person," whoever they may be.

### FROM CHAPTER VI.

<margin>Chapter 6.</margin>
<margin>On hypocrites.</margin>
(They love to be in the assemblies.) The Greek word is "standing" <note>original: "hestōtes"</note>. This word does not always mean the physical act of standing; sometimes it simply means "to be" or "to be present." This is just like the Hebrew word <term>עָמַד</term> <note>original: "amad," to stand or remain</note>, as seen in Matthew 16 and John 12. It is used the same way in Luke 19 regarding the whole crowd at the village; it does not describe their physical posture. This is how we should understand the hypocrites praying here. Jesus is not teaching us what physical posture they used; indeed, it is more likely they were praying on their knees rather than standing, as seen in Acts 20. I say the same regarding the word "to sit," which does not always mean sitting, but sometimes "to remain," as in the final chapter of Luke.

<margin>On the Gentiles.</margin>
(Do not babble like the outsiders.) The Hebrews call all non-Hebrews "the nations" <note>original: "gentes"</note>: that is, foreign nations or aliens. The Latins and Greeks call them "barbarians." Therefore, what the Hebrew calls <term>גּוֹיִם</term> <note>original: "goyim"</note> can be expressed in Latin as "foreign nations." An example of this usage is the phrase "to be seen by men," meaning "by other people." From this comes the Greek word for "heathen" or "Gentile," meaning an outsider or a barbarian.

<margin>The will of God.</margin>
(Thy will be done.) This means: let what you desire happen. This way of speaking is common among Latin authors as well. Quintilian spoke of "doing the will," and Cicero spoke of "preserving the will," both meaning to do what someone wanted. Cicero also spoke of "attaining the promises of the Chaldeans," meaning the things promised, or "attaining a purpose," meaning that which you set out for yourself. It is just like the line from Virgil <note>original: "Maronis"</note>:

> His own promises are now demanded.

Thus, "the scriptures" is often used for "the things written," "hope" for "the thing hoped for," and "word" or "speech" for "the thing being said."

<margin>Daily bread.</margin>
(Our nourishing food.) For the word "daily" <note>original: "epiousion"</note>, some testify that they read <term>מָחָר</term> <note>original: "machar"</note> in Hebrew, meaning "of tomorrow"; others read <term>הַתָּמִיד</term> <note>original: "hatamid"</note>, meaning "continual" or "perpetual." This variation seems to indicate that the Hebrews did not have a single reading in their own language (for if they did, the reading would be consistent). Instead, it seems they translated the Greek word back into Hebrew in different ways. This shows that they, like us, were uncertain about the meaning of this word.

<column-break/>

The word "daily" <note>original: "epiousion"</note> cannot be derived from the phrase "of the coming day," as neither the rules of grammar nor the logic of the passage allow it. Nouns of this sort are not derived from feminine participles. Furthermore, if Christ were teaching us to ask for "tomorrow's food" here, he would be contradicting himself, since a little later he forbids us from being anxious about tomorrow. Therefore, "daily" <note>original: "epiousion"</note> is derived from "substance" or "existence" <note>original: "ousia"</note>. It does not matter that the "i" is not dropped, as it is in some other compound words; the "i" is often retained in Greek compounds, as seen in words for "perjurer" or "overseer." In the Holy Scriptures, "substance" <note>original: "ousia"</note> is the same as "possessions" or "livelihood," as seen in Luke 15. Therefore, "daily bread" <note>original: "epiousios"</note> is that which pertains to our sustenance. The old translator <note>the Vulgate</note> translated this as "daily" in Matthew, but as "supersubstantial" in Luke. If he had translated it as "substantial"—for the prefix "super" <note>original: "epi"</note> does not always mean "above" in these words; it can simply emphasize the root—he would have captured the sense truly and clearly, even if the Latin was a bit awkward. This is because "substance" should be understood as "livelihood" or "essential means."

<margin>On temptation.</margin>
(Lead us not into temptation.) The word "temptation" <note>original: "peirasmos"</note> sometimes means "danger," as in Luke 22 and 1 Timothy 6. Other times it means "trial" or a "solicitation to evil," as it does in this place and many others. Anyone who considers it carefully will find that "temptation" is a fitting Latin term; Cicero uses "temptations of diseases" to describe when a sickness tries or attacks us. From this, the devil is called "the tempter," and in this passage, he is called "the Evil One."

<margin>On fasting.</margin>
(Who disfigure their faces.) The Hebrew word <term>שָׁחַת</term> <note>original: "shachat"</note> used here often has a relative meaning. The Greek word <note>original: "aphanizein"</note>, which I translate as "to disfigure," means to reduce something to nothing or to corrupt it so that it no longer appears as it should. From this comes the word for "to perish" in Acts 13 and "to vanish" in James 4. Thus, "to disfigure the face" means to mar the countenance with neglect and filth. This is expressively captured in French when they say a person has "a drawn face" <note>original: "le uisaige deffait"</note>; that is, a face that is neglected, stained, or deformed by thinness.

### FROM CHAPTER VIII.

<margin>Chapter 8.</margin>
<margin>Sons of the kingdom.</margin>
(While meanwhile the royals...) In the Greek, it is "sons of the kingdom." Similarly, in Chapter 9, "sons of the wedding chamber" is used for those who attend a wedding. Regarding this Hebrew idiom, see what we wrote on Genesis 49 concerning Joseph. It is not unlike how Christ shortly after calls himself "the one born of man" (as the Latins would say), meaning "the Son of Man." Ezekiel is often addressed in the same way. But because Christ is specifically called by this name, and the Latin language permits it, and many might be offended by a change, I did not wish to alter it.

### FROM CHAPTER IX.

(Neither does anyone put a patch of unshrunk cloth...)

<meta>This page continues Erasmus’s linguistic and theological commentary on the Gospel of Matthew. The previous page discussed the Sermon on the Mount in chapters 5 and 6; here, the text transitions to chapter 9 and the beginning of chapter 10, focusing on Jesus's metaphors for the new ministry and his instructions to the twelve disciples.</meta>

# ON MATTHEW

(If you sew a piece of raw and not yet worn cloth, etc.) If you sew a small piece of new, unshrunk cloth onto an old and worn garment to repair a torn section, that piece you added will be stiffer than the garment itself. Thus, once sewn on, it will not hold for long: moved by use, it will be pulled away and take with it that part of the garment to which it was attached by the seam. Thus, though you wish to close a tear, through lack of skill you make it larger. Regarding his use of the phrase "its fullness" <note>original: "τὸ πλήρωμα αὐτοῦ" (to plērōma autou)</note>, the word "fullness" is in the nominative case, meaning the same as the word "patch" <note>original: "ἐπίβλημα" (epiblēma)</note> used earlier. It refers to the supplement of the garment—the small piece used to fill and repair what has been consumed by age. He calls the old garment "worn out," just as in Luke 5 he calls the other "new" and "not worn," which is how we commonly speak. Regarding what he says about the wineskins, he speaks according to the custom of Syria, where wine is stored in skins. In our own lands, it is not absurd to put new wine into old barrels, and it is commonly done. By these two metaphors of the clothing and the wine, he signifies nothing other than what he had previously taught regarding those at a wedding: namely, that it is just as inappropriate for the disciples to fast while he is still present (which is a matter of sadness, when they ought rather to rejoice) as it would be if someone repaired a garment as described, or stored new wine in old skins. As we say in the proverb, "Ointment in the lentils" <note>original: "In lente unguentum"—a Latin proverb describing something precious wasted on something common or a mismatch of quality</note>, by which we signify an absurd thing.

*Have mercy on us, Son of David.*) I know this patronymic <note>a name derived from a father or ancestor</note> "Davidid" <note>original: "Dauidide"</note> will seem harsh. But certainly, it is the proper way to express one who is called "born of David" in the Hebrew manner. On this matter, see what we wrote at the beginning of our observations on the Psalms. Nevertheless, I do not consider myself forbidden from translating it sometimes as "Davidid" and sometimes as "descended or sprung from David." For we ought to be flexible with words, provided the meaning itself is understood. Indeed, at the very start of Matthew, I would have called Jesus "the Davidid" and "the Abrahamid" <note>the son of David and son of Abraham</note> had I not feared that the novelty of the words would offend the reader at the very threshold.

*That he might send out laborers into his harvest.*) The word "to cast out" <note>original: "ἐκβάλλειν" (ekballein)</note> does not always mean to eject or push out by force, but also to send forth or bring out, as in John 10: "when he brings out his own sheep" <note>original: "ὅτ’ ἂν τὰ ἴδια πρόβατα ἐκβάλῃ"</note>, and Matthew 12: "from the good treasure of the heart he brings forth good things" <note>original: "ἐκ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ θησαυροῦ τῆς καρδίας ἐκβάλλει τὰ ἀγαθά"</note>. For neither does that man push the sheep out of the fold, nor does this one push good things out of the storehouse of his heart, but rather sends them forth and produces them: that is, "he brings them forward" <note>original: "προφέρει" (propherei)</note>, as it is written in Luke.

### FROM CHAPTER 10.

*Jesus sent them out, instructing them thus.*) This was well translated by the ancient interpreter. Nor does it matter that "instructing" <note>original: "παραγγείλας" (parangeilas)</note> is in a past tense. For past participles of this kind are often to be rendered as present: such as the phrase "answering he said" <note>original: "ἀποκριθεὶς εἶπεν" (apokritheis eipen)</note>, or "he answered and said." For he did not answer before he spoke; rather, that answer is the speech itself, so that "having answered" stands for "answering." Similarly, what is said here, "he sent, having instructed," is the same as "he sent, instructing," or "he sent and instructed." For that sending is the instruction itself, since he orders them to go to the lost sheep of Israel. For with the same words he both sends

<column-break/>

and instructs. I mention this so no one wonders why the tense of the verb does not always correspond. Often one tense is put for another, such as "he comes" and "he has come" for "he is about to come"; and "that disciple is not dying" for "that disciple is not going to die." And "What are we doing?" for "What shall we do?" Likewise, "I do not dine at home" for "I am not going to dine." I give the same warning regarding the proper meaning of words, if anywhere we seem to translate less literally, such as when "sufficient" <note>original: "ἱκανὸς" (hikanos)</note> is put for "worthy" <note>original: "ἄξιος" (axios)</note>, and "that" <note>original: "ὅτι" (hoti)</note> for "for" <note>original: "γὰρ" (gar)</note>, and many other such things.

*Nor into any city of the Samaritans.*) "Into a city do not enter" for "into no city enter" is a Hebraism. Such is also that in John 19: "a bone you shall not break of him," meaning you shall break no bone of his. The French speak in the same way: "there is not a soul" <note>original: "il n'y a ame"</note> for "there is no soul"—that is, "no man." "Do not enter into city of Samaria" for "into any city."

*Let this house be greeted.*) "Peace" <note>original: "שלום" (Shalom)</note>, which is spoken here, is the word of one greeting, which the Turks even now retain. For when greeting, they say "Schalamalech" <note>Erasmus's transcription of the Arabic/Syriac 'As-salamu alaykum'</note>, which is "Peace be to you" <note>original: "שלום לך" (Shalom leka)</note>, that is, "Greetings." And truly the words for peace and health are related in meaning. For he who is at peace is healthy and safe; and he who is not healthy lacks peace. For I do not call "war" only that which is commonly known by this name; but he who is sick, in pain, or hungry—he is at war with disease, pain, and hunger, and cannot be said to enjoy peace (even if human enemies are absent) while he must struggle with such troublesome foes. Thus, in Livy, those who ask the gods for health and prosperity in all things are often said to "entreat the peace of the gods." But in greetings, "to be well" and "health" are more fitting and clear words, from which the verb "to greet" <note>original: "salutandi," from "salus" (health/safety)</note> is derived. Therefore, Gabriel, greeting Mary—which in Hebrew is "Peace to you" (for it can be nothing else)—said "Greetings" <note>original: "χαῖρε" (chaire), literally 'rejoice'</note>, that is, "Health to you" or "Hail." Furthermore, when he says: "If indeed the house be worthy, let your peace come upon it," he uses the imperative for the future tense, meaning: if they are worthy of health, your peace will come upon them—that is, the happiness you wish for them by greeting them. Otherwise, your greeting will benefit them no more than if you had not greeted them.

*He who finds his life will lose it.*) To "find" <note>original: "εὑρίσκειν" (heuriskein)</note> means both to discover and to produce, or to seek and acquire. But here "to produce" or "to acquire" one's life cannot be correctly said (for one would have to say "to save one's soul" or "to take care of one's life"), and because of the verb "to lose," it was necessary to use a verb of the opposite concept. In French, this can be beautifully expressed with the words "to gain" <note>original: "gaigner"</note> and "to lose" <note>original: "perdre"</note>.

*He who receives a prophet in the name of a prophet.*) This is the same as what he said before: He who receives one who is sent deserves as much as if he received the sender. He who receives any prophet in the name of another prophet—that is, because he was sent by a prophet—will obtain the reward of a prophet: that is, he will have the same prize...

<summary>This page contains Erasmus's linguistic commentary on Matthew 9 and 10, explaining the metaphors of the wineskins and cloth, the nuances of the Greek verb "ekballein," and the Hebrew roots of greetings involving "peace" and "health." Erasmus emphasizes how translation must account for idioms, such as the Hebrew use of double negatives and the functional equivalence of "peace" and "safety."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on the Gospel of Matthew, moving from the instructions to the disciples in chapter 10 to the criticisms of the Jewish leadership and the nature of the "sin against the Holy Spirit" in chapters 11 and 12. The author focuses heavily on the specific Greek and Hebrew vocabulary used in the scriptures.</meta>

<page-num>151</page-num>
<header>ANNOTATIONS.</header>

<column-break/>

will have: that which he would have had, if he had received that prophet by whom he was sent. For example, he who receives the prophet Elisha in the name of the prophet Elijah will have the same reward as if he had received Elijah the prophet himself. However, he speaks of "the reward of a prophet" <note>original: "mercedem uatis"</note> more briefly, and therefore more obscurely, for "the reward on account of having received a prophet." Just as in the twelfth chapter, "blasphemy of the spirit" <note>original: "βλασφημία πνεύματος" (blasphemia pneumatos)</note> stands for "against the spirit."

### FROM CHAPTER XI.

<margin>10</margin> *Blessed is he who shall not be offended in me.)* "To be offended" <note>original: "σκανδαλίζεσθαι" (skandalizesthai)</note> is sometimes to be harmed, as in Romans 14: "your brother is tripped up or offended," for there "to trip up" <note>original: "προσκόπτειν" (proskoptein)</note> and "to be offended" are almost the same thing—that is, to be harmed and to suffer loss, which the Latins call "to strike against" <note>original: "offendere"</note>. Therefore, this is the meaning of Jesus: I am the stone against which one strikes; blessed is he who conducts himself so that I am useful to him, not harmful.

<margin>20</margin> *It is just like children staying in the marketplaces.)* "It is like little children" <note>original: "ὁμοία ἐστὶ παιδαρίοις" (homoia esti paidariois)</note>, namely, those who are shouting. And yet the Jewish nation was not like the shouting children, but like those refusing to listen. Christ and John the Baptist, however, were like the shouting children. Therefore, this passage must be understood and interpreted so that we understand a similar thing happens among the Jews as happens in what the children sing in a common nursery rhyme: that is, the Jews are moved neither by the gentleness of Christ nor the severity of the Baptist, just as those children sing to their playmates who are stirred neither by a happy song to dance, <margin>30</margin> nor by a dirge to mourn. I say the same about many other places, as when in Matthew 13 the kingdom of heaven is said to be "like a man sowing." For it is not like the sower, but like the sowing. Thus the whole matter, not a single word, is being compared.

<margin>40</margin> *And wisdom is justified by her children [as if alien].)* This is a concluding remark <term>epiphonema: a striking concluding sentence or summary</term> to what was said before. The Israelites, to whom the gospel properly belonged, reject it. He set forth the same sentiment above, when he said that the royal heirs were to be thrust down into the deepest darkness—calling the Jews "royal," for theirs was the kingdom. Furthermore, "to be justified" <note>original: "δικαιοῦσθαι" (dikaiousthai)</note> means to be free, and to have nothing to do with someone, as in Romans 6: "for he who has died has been justified from sin," meaning he who has died is set free from sin. This is what he had said before: "so that the body of sin might be destroyed, that we should no longer serve sin." Thus "justified from sin" <note>original: "δικαιοῦται ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας"</note> is the same as "no longer serving sin" and "sin being destroyed for him," or "having been set free from sin." <margin>50</margin> Just so in Romans 7 regarding a wife: "if her husband dies, she is set free from the law of the husband," that is, "she is justified." If the man is dead, she is liberated from the law of the husband; that is, "the law of the husband is idle for her," and nothing of it pertains to her. Therefore, "wisdom is justified"—that is, "set free"—"from her children." That is, she is idle to them, she pertains nothing to them, she is rejected by them as if alien. Moreover, what Luke adds when speaking of this same matter, "by all" <note>original: "πάντων"</note>, is not to be understood as if all <margin>60</margin> Jews rejected Christ, but almost all. Just as when Christ says John neither eats nor drinks, he does not mean he eats nothing at all, but almost nothing; that is, he ate very little food.

<column-break/>

<page-num>152</page-num>
<header>ANNOTATIONS.</header>

Nor does it escape me that others explain this passage differently, saying that wisdom is "justified" <note>original: "δικαιοῦσθαι"</note> by her own—that is, approved and admitted—but neither is an adversative conjunction placed before it, nor is the Greek word "by" <note>original: "ὑπὸ" (hypo)</note> used, but rather "from" <note>original: "ἀπὸ" (apo)</note> the children.

### FROM CHAPTER XII.

<margin>10</margin> *I prefer mercy to sacrifice.)* The word "mercy" <note>original: "חֶסֶד" (chesed)</note> in Hosea is more than the word used here, "pity" <note>original: "ἔλεος" (eleos)</note>. Next, what is here "and not" <note>original: "καὶ οὐ"</note>, is indeed "not" <note>original: "לֹא" (lo)</note> there, but it is put in place of "not." For the word "mercy" is placed in the other half of the sentence, which nevertheless means the same thing. For so it is read word-for-word in Hosea: "I want mercy, and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings," where "I want" is put for "I prefer," as in Homer:
> I prefer the people to be safe, rather than to perish <note>original: "βούλομ’ ἐγὼ λαὸν σόον ἔμμεναι, ἢ ἀπολέσθαι" (Iliad 1.117)</note>.

Secular authors also use "and not" <note>original: "καὶ οὐ"</note>, just like "and not" <note>original: "καὶ μή"</note>, in place of "rather than" <note>original: "μᾶλλον ἤ"</note>, as Isocrates says to Nicocles: <margin>20</margin> "choose to be lacking, and not to take too much"; that is, prefer to have too little than too much. For the Latins speak this way too, as Cicero: "You would prefer to be healthy, than to be rich" <note>original: "Valere malis, quàm diues esse"</note>.

*Every sin and curse, etc.)* What the sin against the Holy Spirit is appears clearly enough from this passage. For he who contradicts divine works made by the power of the Holy Spirit—which are so clear and plain that they cannot be spoken against—and yet still resists and does not allow himself to be persuaded of that which <margin>30</margin> cannot be refuted: he is stubborn, hard, and unteachable, one who can never be persuaded by anything. He always remains in stubbornness and never becomes better; therefore, pardon is never given to him. Such were the Scribes and Pharisees. This is what it means to sin against the Holy Spirit. However, they are said to sin against "the man"—that is, against Christ as a man—who do not yet see the spiritual works in him. Such a one was Paul when he was not yet a Christian; he sinned against the man Jesus. But if he had persecuted him after he was recognized, <margin>40</margin> pardon would never have been given to him. Here someone might object: "As often as the guilty one groans, I will remember his sins no more." This is true. But those who are such as described in Hebrews 6 and 10 never groan; there, this is called a "lethal sin." This can best be understood if you carefully consider that oracle from Isaiah 6: "Dull the hearts of these people, stop their ears, and dim their eyes, lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their hearts, and so be converted and healed." As <margin>50</margin> if he were saying this: "Because they are so stubborn and wicked, I want to punish them. But my mercy is so great that although they are most villainous, yet if they corrected their ways and sought pardon, I would give it. Therefore, lest they pray for pardon, I want them to remain in their stubbornness, so that I may punish them." As for what he says, "Neither in this age, nor in the one to come," I know some explain it so that they think it is nothing other than what is written in Mark about the same thing: "Never." But Matthew should not be explained by Mark in this <margin>60</margin> matter; rather, Mark—who wrote more briefly—should be explained by Matthew, who wrote more copiously. Thus, what is "never" in Mark signifies "neither in this age nor in the one to come." But what that "future age" is, I do not know.

<summary>This page analyzes the linguistic nuances of Matthew chapters 11 and 12, arguing that 'justified' can imply rejection by the Jews and defining the sin against the Holy Spirit as persistent, willful rejection of clear divine truth.</summary>

--- Page 820 ---
<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on the Gospel of Matthew, specifically focusing on chapters 12 through 23. The author continues to analyze the Greek and Hebrew origins of the text to clarify difficult passages for a Latin-speaking audience, frequently comparing biblical idioms to French customs or classical Latin literature.</meta>

<page-num>153, 154</page-num>
<header>ON MATTHEW</header>

<column-break/>

*Either make the tree good.*) <note>Matthew 12:33</note> Here, "to make" is used in place of "to affirm," just as in John 8: "Whom do you make yourself out to be?" Therefore, the meaning is this: Hold this as certain, that it is necessary that where a tree is good, its fruit is good; and whatever fruit is bad, that fruit belongs to a bad tree. But these words of yours are bad fruit: from which it follows that you yourselves are of a bad root.

->FROM CHAPTER XIII.<-

*Immediately it fell away.*) <term><note>original: "ἀπανθισθῆναι" (apanthisthēnai)</note> This Greek verb means to shed blossoms, to depart, to fail, or to faint.</term> Therefore, it is used in place of the word found in Luke chapter 9, "they fall away" <note>original: "ἀφίστανται" (aphistantai)</note>.

->FROM CHAPTER XV.<-

*If anyone shall say to his father or mother.*) <note>Matthew 15:5</note> The Jewish priests were enticing men to contribute gifts to the temple, and they did this not for God's sake, but for their own, since those gifts returned to them. And lest any son should contribute less because he wished to spend his resources on his parents' maintenance (as was commanded), those priests would wash away that religious obligation through a perverse interpretation of the law: "Show your father that what you are contributing to the temple will benefit him before God; it is not necessary that you spend that money on him, since you already honor him by making an offering for yourself and for him, more so than if you were otherwise to spend it on his physical needs." Even if you do not honor your parents in another way, you have still not acted against the law.

->FROM CHAPTER XVIII.<-

*But whoever shall trouble even the least of these who have faith in me.*) <note>Matthew 18:6</note> Literally: "One of these little ones," which is a <term>Hebraism</term> <note>an idiom derived from the Hebrew language</note> for which I wish to provide examples here. In Matthew chapter five, there is a similar Hebraism involving the superlative degree: "Whoever shall act against one of these least commandments," that is, against "even the minimum of these." For those were not truly "least" commandments, not even in appearance. And in Proverbs 26, using the positive degree: "The sluggard seems wiser to himself than seven men who respond prudently," that is, he seems to himself "seven times" or "far wiser." And in Matthew chapter ten: "You are better than many sparrows," which means "you are much better than sparrows." And a little later in the same chapter: "Whoever shall give a drink to one of these little ones," that is, "to even the least of these." Likewise in chapter 25. As for the phrase "the level surface of the sea," two words of the same meaning are used, as in Genesis 14 where "the liquid of heaven" is put for "heaven," so "the level surface of the sea" <note>original: "maris æquor"</note> is put for "the sea." I preferred to say "the level surface of the sea" according to Latin custom, rather than using the term "the sea's depth" <note>original: "maris pelagus"</note>, which is foreign to the Latin way of speaking, though it is found in the Greek.

->FROM CHAPTER XIX.<-

*That it is easier for a cable.*) <note>Matthew 19:24</note> The Greek word <term><note>original: "κάμιλος" (kamilos)</note> means both a "camel" (the animal) and a "nautical rope," which is called a cable.</term> This Greek name, slightly changed as usually happens, remains even now in the French language, in which it is called a *cable*. However, <note>the scholar</note> Favorinus maintains that it should be written with the letter *iota* in the second syllable. But whether it should be written as *kamilos* or whether that word signifies both, there is no doubt that it ought to be understood in the sense that is more suitable to the sentence. We should not force Christ to use a most unfitting comparison here, when it can be most apt and very similar to the others he is accustomed to using. Nor is there any reason for anyone to say that Jesus elsewhere 

<column-break/>

<margin>10</margin> uses absurd comparisons, such as the one about the man who has a beam in his eye. For whoever says that is absurd says so absurdly; he does not understand that absurdity is one thing, and an immense exaggeration—which the Greeks call <term>hyperbole</term>—is another. Neither Christ nor anyone speaking well has ever spoken absurdly. But others use hyperboles, and Christ used one there most aptly. For if a piece of straw were to grow, it would become a beam. But a thread (for a thread is usually drawn through the eye of a needle), no matter how much it grows, will never become a camel, not even in a camel's judgment; but it *can* become a rope or cable.

->FROM CHAPTER XX.<-

<margin>20</margin> *It is not mine to give, except to those for whom it has been prepared by my father.*) <note>Matthew 20:23</note> The Greek says "but to those for whom it has been prepared" <note>original: "ἀλλ' οἷς ἡτοίμασται"</note>, just as in Mark chapter nine: "they now saw no one, except Jesus alone" <note>original: "οὐκέτι εώρων οὐδένα, ἀλλὰ τὸν ἰησοῦν μόνον"</note>. It is used in the same way in 2 Corinthians 2, even with the old translator rendering it thus. This is the meaning: "As for sitting at my right or left, it is indeed mine to give, but not to give to just anyone; rather, only to those whom my father has destined." Therefore, even though you drink from my cup, and even though you endure death for me, you will not necessarily obtain it for that reason. For that dignity does not depend on the bearing of the cross or your merits, but on my father's eternal will and counsel.

->FROM CHAPTER XXI.<-

<margin>30</margin> *Hosanna to the Son of David.*) <note>Matthew 21:9</note> *Hosanna* means "save, I pray." It is a type of song that was usually sung during the Feast of Tabernacles, in which "Hosanna" was repeatedly echoed, just as in France around the birth of Christ songs are commonly sung about the birth of Christ in which "Noel" is repeatedly echoed. But concerning *Hosanna*, see the work of Andreas Osiander in his *Harmony*.

->FROM CHAPTER XXII.<-

<margin>40</margin> *Which is the greatest commandment in the law?*) <note>Matthew 22:36</note> The Greek says "great" <note>original: "μεγάλη" (megale)</note> instead of "greatest" <note>original: "μεγίστῃ" (megistē)</note>, as in Hebrews 4, "a great high priest" <note>original: "ἀρχιερέα μέγαν"</note> means "the highest priest"; and in Luke 9: "He who is the least among you all, he is great." For the same is said in Matthew 23 as "greater" <note>original: "μείζων"</note>, that is, "greatest." So in this place, this commandment is said to be "great," namely above the others: that is, the greatest of all, as the old Latin translator also renders it a little later. Otherwise, it would be absurd to call this "great" as if the others were small. It is, however, a Hebraism, such as often occurs elsewhere, and in Genesis 6, where it reads literally: "Noah was a just man, perfect in his generation," that is, the most perfect of his generation.

->FROM CHAPTER XXIII.<-

<margin>50</margin> *But they use wide [phylacteries].*) <note>Matthew 23:5</note> In Greek it is "they widen," similar to Leviticus 11, where beasts are said to "divide the hoofs," that is, to have them divided. And in Latin, one says "he broke his leg" instead of "his leg was broken."

<margin>60</margin> *But if there is any faithful servant.*) <note>Matthew 24:45</note> The Greek word "who" <note>original: "τίς" (tis)</note> is not always that of someone asking a question, as in James 1: "If anyone among you is wise and understanding, let him show it," etc. Just as the Hebrew word is often placed without a question, as at the end of the 107th Psalm, where it is literally:
<meta>The text breaks off here at the bottom of the page; "Quis" (Who/If anyone) is the catchword for the next page.</meta>

The author also clarifies several Hebrew idioms (Hebraisms) regarding superlatives and the meaning of "Hosanna."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary on the Gospel of Matthew (specifically chapters 24-27) before transitioning into the Gospel of Mark. The author, likely a Renaissance humanist scholar, compares Latin, Greek, Hebrew, and French idioms to clarify the meaning of the biblical text.</meta>

<page-num>155</page-num>
<header>ON MARK <note>Though the header says "On Mark," the text here concludes the commentary on Matthew.</note></header>

"Who is wise will observe these things." This should be understood without a question mark: just as in the French language, where "Who is wise" <note>original: "Qui est sage"</note> can be used both by one who asks a question and one who does not.

*He will find him doing his duty.*) Just as in Latin "fair and equal" <note>original: "æquum & par"</note> are used for that which is just and ought to be done, so in Hebrew the adverb "so" <note>original: "כֵּן" (ken)</note>—that is, *thus*—sometimes signifies "duty." As in 4 Kings 17 <note>original: "4 Reg. 17," modern 2 Kings 17</note>: the Israelites designated things "which were not so" <note>original: "אֲשֶׁר לֹא כֵן" (asher lo ken)</note>, meaning wicked things that ought not to have been done. In this sense, Matthew used the word "thus" <note>original: "οὕτως" (houtōs)</note> in this place, as did Paul in the fourth chapter of Philippians: "stand fast thus in the Lord," meaning, persist in the Lord as is right and proper.

## FROM CHAPTER XXVI.

*That they should go into the city to a certain man.*) In the Greek, "to so-and-so" <note>original: "πρός τὸν δεῖνα" (pros ton deina)</note>; that is, the speech is direct: *Go into the city to a certain man.* In Latin, this is "indefinite," meaning it must be interpreted indirectly and from the persona of the author. For Christ did not actually say, "go to a certain man"; rather, he named him. In the French language, indeed, it would be permitted to speak directly: "Go to such a one" <note>original: "Allez uous en a un tel"</note>; but Latin custom does not allow the same. And from this place, as from many others, it is clear that the sacred authors do not always report the sayings of those about whom they narrate in the exact same number of words; instead, they narrate as we are accustomed to do when we report the same thing a second or third time—we often use different ways of speaking, yet we do not speak falsely. I will bring forward a few examples from among many. In Exodus chapter 20, the commandments of God are written, engraved by the finger of God himself; and yet those same commandments are repeated in Deuteronomy 5 in such a way that some things are said slightly differently in words, though not in substance. Yet the matter is of the greatest importance, spoken once by God, written twice by the same God in Hebrew words, and reported by the same Moses in the same language. Another example occurs a little after this passage of Matthew which we have in hand, where it is read: *For this is my blood of the new covenant, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.* But the same is said a little differently in Luke 22: *This cup is the new covenant in my blood, which is shed for you.* Yet Christ did not pronounce these things in different ways, but only once and in one way. I say the same regarding the Lord's Prayer. From these things, it is plain that words are not always to be called to account too strictly.

*And in three days rebuild it.*) "Building" <note>original: "οἰκοδομῶν" (oikodomōn)</note> is put in place of "rebuilding" <note>original: "ἀνοικοδομῶν" (anoikodomōn)</note>, as is often done with the Hebrew word "to build" <note>original: "בָּנָה" (banah)</note>. For this verb is of that kind where simple forms are often used for compound forms, since the Hebrews lack compound verbs; a matter we wrote about regarding Psalm 62.

## FROM CHAPTER XXVII.

*Then Judas, seeing that he was condemned.*) That is, judged by the high priests to be worthy of death, and destined for death. For the verb "to condemn" is used this way in Mark 10: "The Son of Man," he says, "shall be delivered to the high priests and scribes, who shall condemn him to death, and deliver him to the outsiders." Likewise in Mark 14. And in this manner, Cicero is called the "condemner of Verres" by Tacitus—not because he himself condemned him, but because he accused him and pronounced that he ought to be condemned.

<column-break/>

<page-num>156</page-num>
<header>ON MARK</header>

*If he favors him.*) "He wants him" <note>original: "θέλει αὐτòν" (thelei auton)</note> from Psalm 22, which signifies to favor, or to be supportive and desirous of someone.

# ON MARK.

## FROM CHAPTER VI.

<image-desc>Decorative historiated woodcut initial 'D' depicting a scholar or evangelist seated at a desk or lectern, writing in a book.</image-desc> *To sit down in groups.*) "Banquet by banquet" <note>original: "συμπόσια συμπόσια" (symposia symposia)</note> is a Hebraism for "distributed into individual banquets," but in such a way that "banquet" signifies a "company" or a class of guests; just as in Latin "the city" is used for the citizens, and "youth" for the young men. Since it cannot be said meaningfully in Latin "banquet-wise" or "distributed into banquets" (for it would seem to mean something else), I preferred to translate it as "in groups" <note>original: "cateruatim"</note>. Although that word does not fully express the sense (for people can be placed in groups for something other than eating), nevertheless, since the verb for "sitting down" is used here—by which reclining at a feast is signified—the meaning cannot be doubted, and I thought I might translate it thus. I say the same regarding "plots by plots" <note>original: "πρασιαὶ πρασιαὶ" (prasiae prasiae)</note>; for *prasiae* are the beds or plots of gardens. Since these words cannot be aptly placed here in Latin, I preferred to say "ranks" <note>original: "classes"</note>, using a word of broader meaning.

## FROM CHAPTER XII.

*She contributed two mites.*) What is called here and in Luke 12 a "thin coin" <note>original: "λεπτόν" (lepton)</note>, is called a "farthing" <note>original: "quadrans"</note> in Matthew 5. Moreover, Budé <note>Guillaume Budé, a famous French humanist scholar</note> teaches that the *quadrans* is the same as the *teruncius* <note>a small Roman bronze coin</note>.

## FROM CHAPTER XIII.

*Spiked nard.*) As for what Erasmus writes—that it is possible Mark, speaking in a common manner, used a Latin word corruptly, calling it "pistic" <note>original: "pisticam"</note> instead of "spiked" <note>original: "spicata"</note>—this seems likely to me, and it agrees with the old translator who (as found in several copies) translated it "spiked nard." And I say the same regarding the same word in John 12. We see the same thing happen with the "pound," which John (as do other Greeks) calls a *litra*, with a similar mutation of the word, whether *litra* comes from *libra* or vice versa; and in the "cloak" <note>original: "penula"</note> which Paul calls a *phailone* <note>original: "φαιλόνην"</note> in 2 Timothy 4. Other things said regarding "pistic" <note>original: "πιστικῆς"</note> seem absurd to me, whether you think it is named from a place or from "faith." For no place, as far as we know, made famous by nard, is called that; and from "faith" it would be called *pistos* <note>faithful</note>, not *pistike*. I will say in passing that the old translator turned what Mark said in the feminine gender into the neuter "spiked" <note>original: "spicati"</note>; he did this on purpose, I believe, so that he might retain the same ambiguity of words in the Latin language (in which nard is also used in the neuter gender) that exists in the Greek, in which the word for "costly" <note>original: "πολυτελοῦς" (polytelous)</note> can refer both to the nard and to the ointment. I have deliberately avoided the ambiguity, because I think the price definitely refers to the ointment, not the nard. If the word "spiked" were not added, one could translate it thus: "An alabaster jar of precious nard ointment"; thus there would be no ambiguity.
