<meta>This page continues the philological commentary on the New Testament, transitioning from the Gospel of Matthew (concluded on the previous page) into a detailed analysis of the Gospel of Luke. The translator focuses on how Hebrew idioms influence the Greek of the Evangelists and how these should be rendered in Latin and vernacular languages.</meta>

### FROM CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated woodcut initial 'E' depicting a scholar or evangelist seated in a study with an open book and a terrestrial globe; a window in the background reveals a landscape with a tree and a small building.</image-desc>

*He shall drink neither wine nor strong drink.* <note>original Latin: "nec uinum, nec temetum bibet"</note>)
*Sicera* <note>A Latinized form of the Hebrew 'shekar,' meaning fermented liquor</note> is every artificial wine: such as that which is made from grains, pears, pomegranates, cornel cherries, medlars, rowan berries, blackberries, pine nuts, and so on. Likewise from herbs, asparagus, savory, oregano, and many others. We, not having a specific word of our own, translate it as *temetum* <note>An archaic Latin term for intoxicating drink</note>, from which the word 'intoxicated' <note>Latin: *temulenti*</note> is derived; just as *sicera* was deduced by the Hebrews from a verb that signifies 'to become intoxicated.' But if *temetum* signifies the same thing as wine, then all those other drinks are also called 'wines' by the Latins. And *sicera* in Psalm 69 is used for any wine whatsoever, so that there seems to be almost no difference between this word and the Hebrew.

*He will reconcile them to the Lord their God.* <note>Latin: "Domino ipsorum Deo reconciliabit"</note>) He calls the Lord 'Jehovah' <note>original: "Iouam"</note>, that is, Jesus (concerning whose name see the notes on Matthew, chapter 1). For that this is said of him appears from what follows: *And he will go before Him.* For whom will John go before? Surely the one of whom the Angel <note>original Latin: "Genius," a classical term for a spirit or messenger</note> spoke earlier: namely the God of the Israelites, who is Christ; for he did not precede God the Father.

*Hail, accepted one.* <note>Latin: "Salue accepta"</note>) Namely by God: for it is the same as what is declared a little later, *you have found favor with God* <note>Greek: "εὑρες χάριν παρὰ τῷ θεῷ"</note>; that is, you are accepted and pleasing to God, and you have him as favorable. This Hebraism <note>A Greek or Latin idiom that mimics Hebrew grammar or thought</note> frequently occurs in the Old Covenant.

*Immediately his mouth was opened and his tongue loosed.* <note>Latin: "Aperto protinus eius ore, solutaq; lingua"</note>) In the Greek, 'loosed' is not present; but it is easily understood. For the tongue is not 'opened'; rather, what is meant by the mouth being opened for speaking is that the tongue is loosed. If anyone denies that the tongue was tied, I would also deny that the mouth was closed; otherwise, he could not have taken food. But it is called 'closed' because he spoke no more than if it had been closed. The same must be said of the tongue.

*Let us serve Him before him piously and justly.* <note>Latin: "Eum coràm piè iustèq; colamus"</note>) In the Greek it is *with holiness and justice* <note>Greek: "μετὰ ὁσιότητος καὶ δικαιοσύνης"</note>, after the manner of the Hebrews, who, lacking adverbs of this kind, use nouns. Furthermore, our translators are accustomed to interpret *holiness* <note>Greek: "ὁσιότητα"</note> and *righteousness* <note>Greek: "δικαιοσύνην"</note> or *sanctity* <note>Greek: "ἁγιωσύνην"</note> with the same word, 'holiness,' even though they are not the same. For *holiness* <note>Greek: "ὁσιότης"</note> is that which in Hebrew is called <insert>piety/loving-kindness</insert> <note>Hebrew: "חסידות" (chasidut)</note>: which, if attributed to a man, is piety; if to God, it is clemency—though in Latin it can be called 'piety' even in God, as in the poet Virgil:
> O Gods, if there is any piety in heaven that cares for such things. <note>Aeneid, 2.536</note>
This is usually called by another word, *godliness* <note>Greek: "εὐσέβεια"</note>, in both God and man. Therefore, we, in this place and many others, interpreting not so much the nature of the Greek word as the Hebrew, render it as 'piety.' But *sanctity* <note>Greek: "ἁγιωσύνη"</note> is in Hebrew <insert>holiness/sacredness</insert> <note>Hebrew: "קדש" (qodesh)</note>: a word which signifies sometimes 'holy,' sometimes 'sacred.'

### FROM CHAPTER II.

*And on earth peace, toward men goodwill.* <note>Latin: "Et in terra pax, erga homines beneuolentia"</note>) Peace, as we have declared elsewhere, encompasses all the counts of happiness. But *goodwill* <note>Greek: "εὐδοκία"</note> (which we interpret as benevolence) is that which in Hebrew is called <insert>favor/will</insert> <note>Hebrew: "רצון" (ratzon)</note>, and signifies zeal, favor, desire, or goodwill, which elsewhere is usually

<column-break/>

called *grace* <note>Greek: "χάρις"</note>, from the verb *to be well-pleased* <note>Greek: "εὐδοκεῖν"</note>, meaning to wish well, or to hold as accepted and pleasing, and to be desirous and studious of someone, and to favor them. Moreover, when he says, *goodwill among men* <note>Greek: "ἐν ἀνθρώποις εὐδοκία"</note>, it is the same as *toward men* <note>Greek: "εἰς ἀνθρώπους"</note>. For the sacred authors often write 'in' <note>Greek: "ἐν"</note> for 'unto' <note>Greek: "εἰς"</note>. And 'to be well-pleased' <note>Greek: "εὐδοκεῖν"</note> is used in both ways: for both *in whom my soul is well pleased* <note>Greek: "εἰς ὃν εὐδόκησεν ἡ ψυχή μου"</note> and *in whom I am well pleased* <note>Greek: "ἐν ᾧ εὐδόκησα"</note>, the former in Matthew 12, the latter in Matthew 3 and 17. Therefore, one can say *goodwill in men* <note>Greek: "εὐδοκία ἐν ἀνθρώποις"</note>, attributing the same things to the noun as to the verb, <margin>10</margin> just as in Latin one says 'a returning home' <note>Latin: "domum redditio"</note> as one says 'to return home.' Therefore, this is the meaning of this passage: Let there be peace on earth, which peace is God’s love, zeal, and favor toward men: that is, the happiness which comes from God’s gift and liberality. Read carefully the 1st chapter of Ephesians, and you will find this whole sentiment most copiously explained.

*They brought him to Jerusalem.* <note>Latin: "Tulerunt cum Hierosolymam"</note>) *Goodwill* <note>Greek: "εὐδοκίαν"</note> is here used for *good cheer* <note>Greek: "εὐθυμίαν"</note>. Just as, conversely, 'to be of good cheer' <note>Greek: "εὐθυμεῖν"</note> or 'to speak well' <note>Greek: "εὐφημεῖν"</note> is often put for 'to love' <note>Greek: "ἀγαπᾶν"</note> in the sacred scriptures. Thus <margin>20</margin> the old translator rendered this place well. For we indeed use the verb 'to be well-pleased' <note>Greek: "εὐδοκεῖν"</note> for one who goes on foot: something that cannot be said of Christ at that age.

*He was then.* <note>Latin: "Erat tum"</note>) *Behold* <note>Greek: "ἰδοὺ" and "ἰδὲ"</note> does not always signify 'lo' or 'see,' but is often a marker of time: as in Mark 4, *behold, a sower went out* <note>Greek: "ἰδοὺ ἐξῆλθεν ὁ σπείρων"</note>, that is, 'once upon a time a sower set out.' Sometimes it is demonstrative, such that it means the same as 'know' or 'know ye': as in Luke 1, *and behold, you shall conceive* <note>Greek: "καὶ ἰδοὺ συλλήψῃ"</note>, meaning 'know that you will be silent.' <note>The author uses this to explain the sense of "Behold, you will conceive" as an announcement of fact.</note> Sometimes it is the same as 'I am about to,' signifying a future time: as in Matthew <margin>30</margin> 11, *Behold, I send my messenger* <note>Greek: "ἰδοὺ ἐγὼ ἀποστέλλω τὸν ἄγγελόν μου"</note>, meaning 'I am about to send my messenger' <note>original: "genium"</note>. It also means 'since,' as in Luke 15, *Behold, I have served you these many years* <note>Greek: "ἰδοὺ τοσαῦτα ἔty δουλεύω σοι"</note>, etc., meaning 'since I have served you for so many years.' Likewise it means 'and yet,' as in 2 Corinthians 6, *as dying, and behold we live* <note>Greek: "ὡς ἀποθνήσκοντες, καὶ ἰδοὺ ζῶμεν"</note>, just as if dying, 'and yet we live.' And all these many notions of this word are not proper to the Greek word *idou*, but to the Hebrew <insert>behold/look</insert> <note>Hebrew: "הנה" (hinneh)</note>, for <margin>40</margin> besides those things we have said, it signifies 'quickly indeed,' or 'imagine/suppose it to be so' in Psalm 78 and Exodus 3; 'namely' in Isaiah 58; 'meanwhile' in Ezekiel 9; 'if' or 'what if' in Ezekiel 15; and 'now' in Luke 13.

*Know that this one is for the fall of many, etc.* <note>Latin: "Scito hunc multorum uel casui"</note>) Christ is ruinous to the wicked, but salvific to the upright. He is likewise a kind of standard or banner set out for the peoples, to which they flee if they wish to be safe. But many will attack that banner and deny it is true. You also, Mary, will endure heavy sorrows while he is driven to the cross: while this happens, the mindset of each person will appear. For in favorable times he will have many followers; <margin>50</margin> but in times of adversity, few. From this it will appear that the sincerity of the mind belongs to the few; for adversity reveals friends.

*It goes excellently with him also.* <note>Latin: "Præclarè cum quoq; agitur"</note>) *Established* <note>Greek: "ἐπεστηρίχθη"</note> signifies both 'seasoned' and 'well-composed,' so that nothing is lacking to it. In this place it signifies the same as what was said in the same sense in Matthew 10, *it is enough for the disciple* <note>Greek: "ἀρκετὸν τῷ μαθητῇ"</note>; he ought to be content with good and demand nothing more, but think that it goes well with him. However, the Greek sentence is shortened, <margin>60</margin> which would be full if *it would be* <note>Greek: "ἦν ἂν"</note> were interposed in this way: *everyone would be established as...* <note>Greek: "ἐπεστηρίχθη ἂν ὁ πᾶς ὡς..."</note>. And the old translator seems to have read it thus, who rendered it: *Everyone will be perfect, if he is like his teacher.* Nor was it difficult for the second 'was' to drop out. But even if it was not so...

The author emphasizes how Greek biblical expressions often mask underlying Hebrew concepts of piety, holiness, and divine favor.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological annotations on the Gospel of Luke, moving from the earlier chapters into a discussion of specific Greek and Hebrew idioms found in Chapters 7 through 18. The translator continues to reference classical authors like Plato and Demosthenes alongside contemporary scholars like Budé and Osiander to clarify the nuances of the biblical text.</meta>

# ANNOTATIONS.

Even if one does not read it this way, the meaning remains the same.

### FROM CHAPTER VII.

**It happened the next day.** <note>original Latin: "Accidit postridie"</note>) I believe it is more correctly read as *in the following* <note>original Greek: ἐν τῇ ἑξῆς</note> rather than simply *the following* <note>original Greek: τῇ ἑξῆς</note>, as it is found in some copies. For in chapter 9, it is written in full: *on the following day* <note>original Greek: ἐν τῇ ἑξῆς ἡμέρᾳ</note>.

### FROM CHAPTER IX.

**The days of his assumption.** <note>original Latin: "Eius assumptionis dies"</note>) "Day," when it signifies a span of time, is spoken in the singular in Latin, but in the plural in Hebrew. For this reason, because Luke spoke here in the plural, *the days* <note>original Greek: τὰς ἡμέρας</note>, I have rendered it in the singular, as I have also done elsewhere.

### FROM CHAPTER X.

**That the kingdom of God has come to them.** <note>original Latin: "Ad eos diuinum regnum uenisse"</note>) The word *has come* <note>original Greek: ἤγγικεν</note> in the <margin>10</margin> perfect tense sometimes signifies "has arrived," as in Lamentations 4: **Our end has drawn near** <note>original Hebrew: קרב (qarav)</note>. Therefore, what is written here as *has come* <note>Greek: ἤγγικεν</note> is the same as in chapter 11: *the kingdom of God has come upon you* <note>original Greek: ἔφθασεν ἐφ’ ὑμᾶς ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεוῦ</note>, and in chapter 12, *to draw near* <note>Greek: ἐγγίζειν</note> means to approach.

### FROM CHAPTER XII.

**Whatever you have said in the darkness.** <note>original Latin: "Quicquid in tenebris dixeritis"</note>) The phrase *whatever [things] in the darkness* <note>original Greek: ὅσα ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ</note> <margin>20</margin> uses the indicative for the future subjunctive, following the custom of the Hebrews, who lack a subjunctive and use the indicative in its place, as we pointed out in Genesis 4.

**The things you have prepared, whose will they be?** <note>original Latin: "Quæ uerò parasti, cuius erunt?"</note>) The Greek *to whom will they be* <note>τίνι ἔσται</note> is a Hebraism for *whose will they be*, corresponding to the Hebrew: **to whom shall it be?** <note>original Hebrew: למה יהיה (le-mi yihyeh)</note>. For among the Hebrews, the letter **L** <note>The Hebrew prefix Lamed (ל)</note> serves as a marker not only for the dative case but also for the genitive.

**Neither be of doubtful mind.** <note>original Latin: "Néue pendete"</note>) To be *meterorized* <note>original Greek: μετεωρίζεσθαι</note> is to be "on high," like clouds and flying birds; now, things that are on high, resting on no firm soil or foundation, waver and are tossed about. From this, it follows that this word <margin>30</margin> signifies to doubt and to be uncertain and anxious. In this sense, the Latins properly use the word *pendere* <note>To hang or be in suspense</note>. Demosthenes used this same notion in his speech *On the Crown* regarding those who have received [bribes].

**I am greatly distressed.** <note>original Latin: "Vehementer angor"</note>) The phrase *how I am constrained* <note>original Greek: πῶς συνέχομαι</note> does not always indicate a question (as we have taught elsewhere regarding the Hebrew particles **Is it not?** <note>הלא</note> and **How much better?** <note>ממה טוב</note>), but is also used for emphasis without a question, like the Latin *quam* (how much). As in Proverbs 16: **How much better** <note>ממה טוב</note> it is to get wisdom. And often elsewhere. Even secular <margin>40</margin> authors use "how" <note>Greek: πῶς</note> in this same way.

**Why do you not judge what is right from yourselves?** <note>original Latin: "Cur ex uobismetipsis nō iudicatis ex æquo?"</note>) Why do you not imitate your own behavior, and use the same prudence in divine matters that you employ in human disputes? You are accustomed to settle with an adversary rather than come before a judge who might judge more severely. Since, therefore, you see from these signs that God’s judgment is pressing, why do you not return to a better way of life while you can? For when you come before the judge, repentance will be too late. However, when he says, "Give effort" <note>to settle</note>, he is not prescribing how one must act in lawsuits, for men are wise enough in that matter already. Just as in Matthew 23 when he says: "Blind Pharisee, first cleanse the inside of the cup and the dish, that the outside may also be clean," he is not teaching how to wash cups—for they knew that well enough—but it is as if he were saying: "Just as he who cleans the outside of a cup but not the inside acts foolishly, so you act preposterously, being religious in small things but dissolute in great things." Thus, in this place, Christ teaches that what is done <margin>60</margin> in lawsuits ought to be done in the business of the heavenly kingdom. But he teaches this more briefly through the imperative.

### FROM CHAPTER XIII.

**If perhaps it bears fruit; but if not.** <note>original Latin: "Si fortè fructum ædat. sin minus"</note>) In Greek, it is word for

<column-break/>

word: *And if indeed it should bear fruit; but if not.* It is exactly the same, but a shortened sentence; yet it is such that one can easily understand something left silent. It is "well," or (as Cato says) "it is best." There is a similar passage in Plato, in the ninth book of *The Laws*: *And if indeed to you doing these things, the disease is somewhat mitigated; but if not, choosing a better death, depart from life.* <note>original Greek/Latin: καὶ ἐὰν μὲν οἷσι δρῶντι ταῦτα, λωφᾷ τι τὸ νόσημα· εἰ δὲ μή, καλλίω θάνατον σκηψάμενοι, ἀπαλλάττου τοῦ βίου</note> But regarding this manner of speaking, Budé <note>Guillaume Budé, a famous French humanist</note> wrote more <margin>10</margin> in his *Annotations on the Pandects*.

**After the master of the house has entered.** <note>original Latin: "Postquam intrauerit paterfamilias"</note>) In the Greek it is *arisen* <note>original Greek: εἰσήλθεν</note> <note>Note: The translator notes a discrepancy between the Greek 'egerthe' (arisen) and 'eiselthe' (entered)</note>; but this fits poorly. For he is not speaking of a master of the house who is lying down or sleeping, but of one who enters from outside. Furthermore, one who has arisen does not close the doors, but rather opens them, since they are usually closed before going to bed. For these reasons, I have followed the old translator, who rendered it as *entered*, from which he seems to have read *entered* <note>Greek: εἰσήλθεν</note>. <margin>20</margin>

**That he would perform healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day depart.** <note>original Latin: "Sanationes q; peracturum esse hodie & cras, perendie autem disceffurum"</note>) He speaks obscurely of a "day" in place of a "year" (as Osiander <note>Andreas Osiander, a Reformation theologian</note> taught), signifying that he still had two years of labor, and then must die in the third year, and that in Jerusalem.

### FROM CHAPTER XIV.

**For it shall be repaid to you in the resurrection of the just.** <note>original Latin: "Reddetur enim tibi in resurrectione iustorum"</note>) Just as "a walk," "a dinner," or "a carriage-ride" do not always signify the action itself, but the place where one walks or dines, etc.; so in this place (as elsewhere), "resurrection" does not declare the action of rising again, but that <margin>30</margin> state of life which will exist when the good have risen.

### FROM CHAPTER XV.

**Bring forth the first robe.** <note>original Latin: "Proferte priorem stolam"</note>) *the robe the first* <note>original Greek: τὴν στολὴν τὴν πρώτην</note>. The article shows that he is not speaking of just any robe, but of a specific one: just as a little later, *the calf the fatted* <note>original Greek: τὸν μόσχον τὸν σיτευτόν</note>, he speaks of a specific calf. But the force of that article cannot be expressed in Latin, yet it is understood, as when we say, "The poet says" <note>original Greek: φηסὶν ὁ ποιητής</note>: we do not speak of any poet, but of a specific and most famous one, namely Maro <note>Virgil</note>. And yet it is not necessary <margin>40</margin> to say, "That poet says," for that would be less effective and could be understood as someone else. Likewise, when the ancients said "The City" <note>original Greek: τὴν πόλιν</note>, they meant Rome; yet they did not add "That one," for that would be something else entirely. But languages that have articles express this better.

### FROM CHAPTER XVI.

**Men of light.** <note>original Latin: "Homines lucis"</note>) This will perhaps seem harsh, as are those phrases: "Spirit of weakness," "spirit of consolation." But even the Latins speak this way, as when <margin>50</margin> they call Love "the god of peace." Likewise when they say "a man of three letters" <note>A Latin idiom for a thief, *FUR*</note>, and "a man of few [words]." However, we have taught elsewhere that "sons" <note>Greek: υἱοὺς</note> is said in place of "men."

### FROM CHAPTER XVIII.

**Lest by her constant coming she weary me.** <note>original Latin: "Ne me assiduè uenitians obtundat"</note>) *Unto the end* <note>original Greek: εἰς τέλος</note> is a translation of the Hebrew **weary** <note>יגעה</note>. The Greek word <note>ὑπωπιάζῃ - literally "to give a black eye"</note> means to strike under the eye or bruise; but it does not refer to reputation or ignominy (since that judge <margin>60</margin> did not respect men and therefore had no regard for reputation, which is signified by the word *weary*), but to this: "Lest she create trouble for me, lest by her persistence and impudence she, as it were, strike and stun me."

# ON JOHN

this is what the French mean when they say "to break the head" <note>An idiom for being persistent or annoying.</note>.
And he will be so difficult toward them. ) *being patient* <note>original Greek: μακροθυμῶν</note> is the reading: *Chrysostom* reads it as *being patient*: the ancient translator seems to have read it as *being patient*, as he rendered it "he will have patience." And this reading is more suitable with the verb *he will do*, so that the conjunction *and* might connect a future verb with a future verb. However, whichever way you read it, the meaning remains the same. Now, *being patient* <note>original Greek: μακροθυμῶν</note> means to be enduring and tolerant. So the sense is: Will God be so patient, so hard and inexorable, that he would rather allow himself to be worn down by the prayers of his people than to avenge them quickly?
Often doubled. ) *many times more* <note>original Greek: πολλαπλασίονα</note>, or "multiple," so to speak. Therefore, if you translate it as "much more," you do not sufficiently express the force of the word. For he who receives one hundred and seventy in place of one hundred receives "much more," yet not "many times more" <note>original Greek: πολλαπλασίονα</note>. Thus Matthew said *a hundredfold* <note>original Greek: ἑκατονταπλασίονα</note>.

### FROM CHAPTER XIX.

A certain man, called by the name Zacchaeus. )
<margin>20</margin>
What I am about to say, I would have thought too well-known to be worth mentioning, had I not seen certain people stumble over it, thinking that Zacchaeus was not an Israelite. I suppose this is because he was a tax collector, as if Matthew were not also a tax collector. Certainly, there are many things that force one to admit Zacchaeus was a Jew: first, because his name is Hebrew. Second, because the Jews do not rage against Jesus for visiting a Roman or a foreigner, but because he visited a "notorious man" <margin>30</margin>; they certainly would not have omitted the point if Zacchaeus had not been a Jew. Third, because Zacchaeus says he will restore fourfold: something he had learned from Moses, although a Roman could also have learned the same in Judea; but the former is more likely. Fourth, because Jesus calls him a "descendant of Abraham," or one born of Abraham. For that is what *son of Abraham* <note>original Greek: υἱὸς ἀβραάμ</note> signifies; this is said of Zacchaeus himself, not of his household. For that would be harsh and contrary to the custom of speaking. It does not matter that there is a change of person <margin>40</margin>; for the speech must be rendered indirectly, as indicated by the word *that* <note>original Greek: ὅτι</note>. Even if that word were absent, it would not be absurd for the person to change, since Christ is addressing not only Zacchaeus but also the others who were present, as appears from what follows: "While they were hearing these things." Moreover, a change of person often occurs. Nor do I agree with those who think he is called a "descendant of Abraham" simply because he had faith in Christ; for that would be a more unusual and obscure way of speaking than could have <margin>50</margin> been understood at that time. Rather, he calls the man a "descendant of Abraham" because he is a Jew: to whom salvation was brought because he was a descendant of Abraham (to whom salvation had been promised). Just as in Luke 13, Christ says that the bent woman ought to be healed because she was a daughter of Abraham. Therefore, the ancient translator rendered this passage well.

### FROM CHAPTER XXII.

And those who command them are called "Benefactors." )
<margin>60</margin>
*Nobles* <note>original Hebrew: נדיבים (nadivim)</note>, who in the sacred scriptures are usually called *benefactors* <note>original Greek: εὐεργέται</note>, are leaders, governors, and princes. Therefore, "those who exercise authority over them are called benefactors" <note>original Greek: οἱ ἐξουσιάζοντες αὐτῶν εὐεργέται καλοῦνται</note> is the same as if he had used the words of the first part in the same way: "those who rule over the nations are called kings" <note>original Greek: οἱ κυριεύοντες τῶν ἐθνῶν, βασιλεῖς καλοῦνται</note>. Now, this is the

<column-break/>

meaning: among the nations, as each man prevails most in resources, so he is most truly a king, and the most powerful man most easily obtains the title of prince.
Let him become like the youngest. ) He opposes *younger* <note>original Greek: νεώτερος</note> to *greater* <note>original Greek: μείζονι</note>, from the word *small* <note>original Hebrew: צעיר (tsa'ir)</note>, which refers not to age, but to status; and yet it can refer to age because age adds to one's stature.
But now, let him who has a purse take it. ) By these words, he shows nothing else than that misfortunes and dangers are <margin>10</margin> imminent, for which purses and swords are usually employed. Jeremiah speaks in this manner in chapter 9: "See that you take care to call for the mourning women, and send for the wise women, that they may come quickly to perform a dirge for us." For the Prophet does not literally command the mourning women to be summoned; rather, he teaches that mourning is imminent, for which mourning women are usually employed. When Christ says that "two swords are enough," he speaks as if a father were to say a house must be bought, and an ignorant son <margin>20</margin> says he has two farthings <note>original Latin: teruncios — a very small Roman coin</note> for that purpose; then the father replies, "It is enough"—meaning, "Of course, a house can be bought with two farthings!" <note>The author interprets Jesus' response as ironic rather than literal.</note>

### FROM CHAPTER XXIII.

It was their day of preparation, and the Sabbath began to dawn. )
On what it means for the Sabbath to "dawn," as well as many other things in this and the following chapter, see Osiander <note>Andreas Osiander, a German Lutheran theologian known for his work on Gospel harmonies.</note>.

## ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN.
### FROM CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'G' featuring a seated bearded figure in classical robes writing in a book, set within an architectural frame with floral scrollwork.</image-desc>
<margin>30</margin>
Full of grace and truth. ) I have moved this here from the end of the sentence for the sake of clarity, something I have found must often be done in both the Old and New Testaments. For example, in John 17: "Father, glorify me with the glory which I had with you before the world was." For it reads this way word-for-word, and "with you" seems to refer to "the world," when it should be joined with "I had" <margin>40</margin> and moved there: "the glory which I had with you." Likewise in Revelation 13: "Whose names are not written in the book of life of the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world." Here, "from the foundation of the world" should refer to "not written," not to "slain." You will find a similar figure of speech in Genesis 25 regarding the death of Ishmael.
And his splendor. ) *Glory* <note>original Greek: δόξα</note> is called *kavod* <note>original Hebrew: כבוד</note> in Hebrew, a word that declares not only "glory" but also "splendor." And so the word *glory* <note>original Greek: δόξα</note> is used both elsewhere and in Luke 2 and Acts 22. It is permissible to say "splendor" in Latin <margin>50</margin> (since this word indicates both things to the Romans), and in this and similar places, it is necessary. For he is speaking of that splendor of Christ which the author of this book himself, along with others, saw in the Transfiguration of Christ.
As the splendor of the only-begotten of the Father. ) "As" is not always a mark of similarity. For instance, if you say, "I rebuked my son, as a father," it means: "as becomes me, and according to my authority, since I am a father." So in this place, it says "splendor as of the only-begotten," which means splendor worthy of the unique Son of God.
<margin>60</margin>
And grace for grace. ) This means one grace in place of another, like that phrase in Job 1: "Skin for skin," meaning one for his own. And "a nail for a nail," meaning one for another. And "man for man," etc. Now, he calls a benefit "grace," as it is also called in Latin.

# ANNOTATIONS.

<margin>10</margin>
...and this is the meaning: That the law was brought by Moses was a divine benefit. In place of that benefit (since it could not be of use within us), another benefit and grace is bestowed upon us through Christ, and indeed that grace which is named "true grace." For this is what he says: *Grace and truth.* <note>John 1:17</note> It is not that Moses did not deliver the truth. But John in this passage calls the "truth" the reality of the thing itself: so that it is grace and truth—grace which is grace in actual fact and truly. Thus Cicero, in his speech *For Quintus Roscius*, says: *What is false in truth:* <note>original Latin: "Quod est ueritate falsum"</note> that is, in the reality of the matter. Jesus speaks in this same way later in chapter 6, when he denies that manna was given to the Israelites by Moses: that is, he denies that that manna was the *true* manna.

> Are you Elijah? I am not. Are you the Prophet? No.

<margin>20</margin>
What had been predicted by the oracles—that Elijah would come before the Messiah arrived—was to be understood in this way: that a prophet would come similar to Elijah and endowed with the spirit of Elijah. Just as those things said in the Revelation <note>The Book of Revelation/Apocalypse</note> concerning Babylon are not to be understood as being about that literal Babylon of the Chaldeans. For this reason, there is that line from Maro <note>The poet Virgil</note>:
*And once more a great Achilles shall be sent to Troy:* <note>A reference to the idea that history repeats itself with similar figures.</note>
That is, there will still be wars and heroes like the Trojan war and Achilles. But the Jews thought that Elijah himself would come; therefore, John rightly denies that he is him. However, as for his denial that he is "the prophet," there are those who think this should be understood as the prophet promised by God through Moses—that is, Christ—and this is because of the article <note>The grammatical word "the"</note>, because he is not called "a prophet" <note>original Greek: προφήτης</note> but "the prophet" <note>original Greek: ὁ προφήτης</note>. But since they had already asked about Christ, that would be redundant, unless perhaps they thought that "the prophet" would be someone other than the Messiah. But if they thought so, they would surely add another question: "If you are not that prophet, nor another prophet," which they do not do. Instead, they conclude: *Why then do you baptize, if you are neither Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet?* They gather this from his responses, having nothing else to name. Therefore, in this later passage, the article is not added, although it is added in some copies. But it seems those who add it followed the authority of Theophylact <note>A prominent Byzantine biblical exegete</note>, who testifies that he added it. I think nothing should be taken away from the former nor added to the latter; rather, "the prophet" there is the same as "prophet" here, because the sacred authors in the Greek language often add a redundant article, as in Revelation 3: *you do not know that you are the wretched one* <note>original Greek: ὁ ταλαίπωρος</note>, etc. The reason for this is that the Hebrews have two articles: one of which, which is the letter "He" <note>original Hebrew: ה</note>, is often joined with others, yet cannot be expressed in Greek. For example: *God created the heavens and the earth* <note>original Hebrew: את השמים ואת הארץ</note>. Here you see two articles, the first of which <note>original Hebrew: את (et)</note> is expressed in Greek as the heavens and the earth <note>original Greek: ἢ οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν</note>, but the other cannot be expressed. Yet these authors, who often "Hebraize" <note>Adopt Hebrew grammar patterns</note> in the Greek language, attempt to express it. Therefore, what is said in Hebrew as *the prophet* <note>original Hebrew: הנביא (ha-navi)</note>, John calls *the prophet* <note>original Greek: ὁ προφήτης</note> so that he might express the article. Although the Hebrew "He" <note>ה</note> can sometimes be expressed by the Greek "He" <note>η</note>. But when that should be done must be judged from the context. In this place, however, in German, French, and Italian, the article can either be omitted or expressed as:

<column-break/>

"a prophet," "un prophete," "uno profeta," <note>German, French, and Italian for "a prophet."</note> if you omit the Greek article. But if you add it and speak properly, "the prophet" <note>original Greek: ὁ προφήτης</note> will be "der prophet," "le prophete," "el propheta" <note>German, French, and Italian for "the prophet."</note>. Regarding this matter, we have written a fair amount on Matthew 11 and Luke 15. And so much for the word. As far as the meaning is concerned, John does not deny that he is a prophet, for he was a prophet. But he speaks in such a way that if you were to ask the King of the Persians, "Are you a king?" he might say, "I am not." "What then?" "The King of kings." He would not be denying that he is a king. And in this manner God speaks in Numbers 11: *The Lord will give you meat,* he says, *which you shall eat, and you shall eat not for one day, nor two, nor five, nor ten, nor twenty, but for a whole month.* He does not deny that they will eat for one or two days, etc., but he says more. It is like when we say, "Not once," meaning "more than once." Thus in this place John shows that he is not just a prophet, but the greatest prophet, and (as Jesus says of him) "more than a prophet." And that this is so appears from what he says: *I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Make straight the way of the Lord.* For that this is the duty of a prophet appears from the song of his father Zechariah, where it is read: *And you, child, shall be called the prophet of the Most High.* Then the reason is added: *For you shall go before the Lord to prepare his ways,* etc.

Indeed, I did not know him.) John knew that the Messiah was born and that he had been sent before him; otherwise, he would be ignorant of his own duty and the song of his father Zechariah. He even knew that he was his relative, born of Mary, since he had already recognized him in his mother's womb. Even if he had not recognized him in the womb, or had later forgotten as he grew up, he certainly had learned it from his parents or others; nor could he be ignorant of so great, so recent, and so closely related a matter. But since he had not lived together with Jesus, he did not know him by face. However, as soon as he saw him coming, he recognized him—evidently by divine inspiration, just as his mother Elizabeth had understood that Mary was pregnant with the Lord upon her arrival. This is evident from the fact that he says he ought to be baptized by him. Then, to this divinely inspired knowledge was added the Spirit descending upon Jesus in the form of a dove, by which things John recognized Jesus. Therefore, when he says that he was not known to him, it must be understood as being "by face," and that was before he had come to him to be baptized.

## FROM CHAPTER II.

> What then?

Literally, *What to me and to you?* <note>The phrase "Quid mihi & tibi?" is a literal translation of the Greek "Ti emoi kai soi," often rendered as "Woman, what does this have to do with me?"</note> which way of speaking should sometimes be translated as: *What business do I have with you?* Sometimes, as we have interpreted it, as in 2 Kings 16, where it is read literally: *What is it to me and to you, sons of Zeruiah, if he curses?* etc., where the meaning will be foolish if you translate it as: *What business do I have with you if he curses?* But if you translate it: *What then, if he curses?* it will be most fitting. Sometimes it means, *What is that?* as in 4 Kings 17.

## FROM CHAPTER III.

Nicodemus, a leader of the Jews.) This whole conversation between Nicodemus and Jesus is obscure and abrupt. Because I have explained it more fully in the *Sacred Dialogues*, I will pass over it here.

        *   Text: *χαρᾷ χαίρει* (charā chairei) -> "with joy he rejoices."
        *   Note: Plautus' style. Hebrewisms (morte mori - dying to die/surely die).
        *   Translation: He takes pleasure from the voice of the bridegroom. He rejoices with joy (literally). Like Plautus. It means "he greatly rejoices." Examples: "living a life," "serving a servitude." Explaining Hebrewisms like "dying the death" (surely die/long for death).

        *   Translation: He who is of the earth speaks. "From the earth" instead of "the things of the earth." Hebrewism found in Psalm 68.

        *   Text: "Sic apud fontem resedit."
        *   Reference: Virgil's "Sic uertice cœli Constitit."
        *   Translation: "Thus he sat by the spring." "Thus" (Sic) is used here as Virgil uses it: "Thus he stood on the summit of heaven," where "Thus" is almost redundant.

    *   *Section 4 (John 4:36):* "Et messor mercedem accipit..."
        *   Text: Lack of "sator" (sower) in Greek.
        *   Translation: "And the reaper receives a reward, and the [sower] gathers fruit." The word "sower" is missing in Greek but should be understood. The sower rejoices in gathering fruit, the reaper in his wage. Mention of 1 Tim 4.

    *   *Section 5 (John 5:2):* "->EX CAP. V.<-" (From Chapter 5)
        *   Text: "Apud ouiaricam piscinam." *Bethesda* (House of Mercy/Kindness). *Beth* and *Hesed*. *ἀγωγεδοχείον* (hostel/infirmary).
        *   Translation: "At the sheep pool." Reading *kolymbēthra* (pool) in the dative case. Bethesda means "House of Kindness/Mercy" (*Beth* + *Hesed*), a place for the poor (infirmary/hostel).

    *   *Section 6 (John 6:62-63):* "->EX CAP. VI.<-" (From Chapter 6)
        *   Text: "Quid si uideritis homine natum eò ascendentem..." (What if you see the Son of Man ascending...).
        *   Content: Dealing with the "Eat my flesh" difficulty. Flesh profits nothing; the words are spirit and life.
        *   Translation: "What if you see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before?" Explaining that eating flesh seems absurd, but the sacrifice on the cross provides life. The words are spiritual. Bread of life.

    *   *Section 7 (John 8:44):* "->EX CAP. VIII.<-" (From Chapter 8)
        *   Text: "Vt qui fit mendax, mendaciýq; pater." (He who is a liar and the father of lies).
        *   Linguistic point: The Greek phrasing "He who is a liar and the father of it/him." Ezekiel 33 reference. Pliny ref on goat milk.
        *   Translation: "As one who is a liar and the father of lies." The Greek reads "He who is a liar and his father," which must be interpreted like Ezekiel 33. The devil has lying in him and is the father of it. French comparison (le pere vs pere). Pliny example: "Goat's milk is best for the stomach because they [the goats, implied in 'goat-ish'] eat leaves."

    *   *Section 8 (John 8:58):* "->Antequam Abrahamus esset, ego sum.<-"
        *   Text: "Before Abraham was, I am."
        *   Grammar: Use of the present tense implies continuation (was and is).
        *   Translation: "Before Abraham was, I am." The present tense signifies continuity, as in John 14: "I am with you so long," meaning "I have been and am." Latin example: "He is sick for four days already" (meaning he started being sick and still is).

    *   *Section 9 (John 9:39):* "->EX CAP. IX.<-" (From Chapter 9)
        *   Text: *κρίμα* (krima). Discrimination/Judgment.
        *   Translation: "For such a distinction I [have come]..." *Krima* sometimes means to discern with reason, as in "to speak with judgment." Since "judgment" doesn't fit well here, I translated it as "distinction/discrimination."

    *   *Section 10 (John 13:31):* "->EX CAP. XIII.<-" (From Chapter 13)
        *   Text: *ἐδοξάσθη* (edoxasthē - was glorified). Hebrew style using past for present.
        *   Translation: "Now the Son of Man is glorified." The past tense is used for the present, a common Hebrew idiom. Also seen in Latin (memini, noui).

    *   *Section 11 (John 18:1):* "->EX CAP. XVIII.<-" (From Chapter 18)
        *   Text: "Trans torrentem Cedronem." *τῶν κέδρων* vs *τοῦ κέδρων*.
        *   Philology: Cedron is a Hebrew name (singular). Some Greek scribe thought it meant "of the cedars" (*kedrōn*) and changed the article to plural (*tōn*).
        *   Translation: "Across the brook Cedron." Since Cedron is a Hebrew singular noun, the plural article "of the" (*tōn*) is either redundant or should be singular (*tou*). A Greek scribe likely mistook it for the Greek word for "cedars" and "corrected" the grammar.

# ON JOHN

He takes pleasure from the voice of the bridegroom) <note>John 3:29</note> *He rejoices with joy* <note>original Greek: χαρᾷ χαίρει; a literal translation would be "with joy he joys."</note> if you were to translate it word-for-word, in the manner that the Roman playwright Plautus spoke. However, that seemed a bit too "Plautine" to me. It simply means "he greatly rejoices," just as "to live a life" or "to serve a servitude" means nothing other than to live or to serve. But one may explain these types of Hebrew-isms <term>Hebraism: A Hebrew idiom or grammatical structure preserved in a translation.</term> so that where the text says "to die by death," we might say "to be destined for death"; or "to desire with desire" might be "to be led or held by desire." Or, <margin>10</margin> if the situation allows, we may render in a single word what was said in two.

->He who is of the earth speaks.) <note>John 3:31</note> *From the earth* <note>original Greek: ἐκ τῆς γῆς</note> instead of *the things of the earth*; we pointed out this Hebrew-ism in our notes on Psalm 68.<-

->FROM CHAPTER 4<-

Thus he sat by the spring.) <note>John 4:6</note> *Thus* <note>original Latin: sic</note> is placed in this location in the same way it is used by the poet Virgil: *Thus he stood on the summit of heaven,* where "Thus" is almost redundant or used for emphasis.

And the reaper receives a reward, and the [sower] gathers fruit.) <note>John 4:36</note> In the Greek text, the word for "sower" is missing; it should be supplied because <margin>20</margin> it is the role of the sower, not the reaper, to perceive the start of the fruit's growth. Note that what follows—*So that the sower and the reaper may rejoice together*—means the sower rejoices in the gathering of the fruit, while the reaper rejoices in his wage. This cannot be understood unless you understand the name of the "sower" from the conclusion of the sentence to also be present in the opening premise. These types of shortened sentences also appear in secular literature, as we shall demonstrate in 1 Timothy 4, God willing.

->FROM CHAPTER 5<-

<margin>30</margin> At the sheep pool.) <note>John 5:2</note> I read the word *pool* <note>original Greek: κολυμβήθρα (kolymbēthra)</note> in the dative case for two reasons: first, because the adjective *sheep* <note>original Greek: προβατικῇ (probatikē)</note> would not be well-placed without a noun; second, because the pool was called Bethesda. That word does not mean "pool," but "house." It is a word derived from *Beth* and *Hesed*, meaning "House of Kindness" or "Mercy," where the poor are treated kindly; such a place is called an *infirmary* <note>original Greek: ἀγωγεδοχείον (agōgedocheion), a place for receiving the sick or poor.</note>.

->FROM CHAPTER 6<-

What if you see the Son of Man ascending to where <margin>40</margin> he was before?) <note>John 6:62</note> It seems absurd to you, he says, that I said my flesh must be eaten and my blood drunk by anyone who wishes to be saved. But it will seem much more absurd when I ascend into heaven (which I shall do while you are watching). For then it will be possible to say: "Christ ordered his body to be eaten, and yet he has ascended into heaven." How shall we now eat on earth that which is in heaven? O, you are slow to understand; it is this slowness that makes my words seem absurd, though <margin>50</margin> they are not. For the flesh indeed profits nothing—it will not be eaten in a literal sense—but it will be offered on the cross for your sake, and having died, it will rise and ascend into heaven. But because it will be crucified for your sake, and by this means life will be granted to you, I said that it must be eaten by you. My words are spirit and life: that is, my discourse about obtaining life through my flesh is a spiritual one. For though <margin>60</margin> I address mortal men and speak in a human manner, when I wish to indicate that I will give you life, I say my flesh must be eaten and my blood drunk, because my flesh and blood will pay the penalty to grant

<column-break/>

life to you. Thus, "eating me" is consistent with what I said above: *I am the bread of life; he who comes to me shall never hunger, and he who believes in me shall never thirst.*

->FROM CHAPTER 8<-

As one who is a liar and the father of lies.) <note>John 8:44</note> The literal word-for-word reading is: *As one who is a liar and his father.* This phrasing must be untangled in the same way as the passage in Ezekiel chapter 33, where it reads literally: *And the righteous man <margin>10</margin> shall not be able to live through her, if he sins.* "Her" refers to the *righteousness* implied in the name "righteous man." For a righteous man is one in whom righteousness exists; thus we untangle the sentence to mean: "He in whom righteousness exists shall not be able to live through it." And in Proverbs 14: *In the fear of Yahweh <note>original Latin: Iouæ (Jehovah/Yahweh)</note> there is safe strength, and there will be a refuge for his children*—meaning the children of the one who fears Yahweh. In this way, we untangle this current sentence: "In the devil there is a lie, and he is the father of the lie." It is no obstacle <margin>20</margin> that the definite article <note>original Greek: ὁ (ho)</note> is added to the word "father." For we have shown elsewhere that the article is sometimes redundant; in this place, it can be either used or omitted without change in meaning. This is just as in French, where one can say both *Il est le pere* (He is the father) or *il est pere de mensonge* (he is father of lies). This way of speaking is not unlike what Pliny says in Book 28, chapter 9, concerning milk: *Goat's milk,* he says, *is most suitable for the stomach, since they eat leaves more than grass.* He means "the goats," <margin>30</margin> who are implied in the word "goat-ish." So "goat's milk" is "the milk of goats, which goats," etc.

->Before Abraham was, I am.) <note>John 8:58</note> By using the verb in the present tense, he signifies a continuation, as in chapter 14: *I am with you for so long,* which means, "I have been and I am." Both meanings would not be expressed by the past tense alone. This is seen in Latin: "He is sick for four days already" <note>meaning he began being sick four days ago and remains so.</note>.<-

->FROM CHAPTER 9<-

For such a distinction I [have come]...) <note>John 9:39</note> The word *judgment* <note>original Greek: κρίμα (krima)</note> sometimes means to distinguish with reason and choice, as <margin>40</margin> above in chapter 8: *I have many things to say and to judge concerning you* <note>original Greek: λαλείν καὶ κρίνειν (lalein kai krinein)</note>, which is to say, *to speak with judgment and reason.* We speak this way in Latin when we say something was done with "no judgment," meaning imprudently and without choice or reason. But in this passage, because the word "judgment" would not fit well, I have rendered it "distinction."

->FROM CHAPTER 13<-

Now the Son of Man is glorified.) <note>John 13:31</note> The word *was glorified* <note>original Greek: ἐδοξάσθη (edoxasthē)</note> is in the past tense, which in the Hebrew manner is frequently put <margin>50</margin> for the present tense. Since examples of this are infinite, there is no need to list them. We see this also happening among the Latins in certain words like *memini* (I remember) and *noui* (I know). Likewise in others, "it was profitable to do that" instead of "it is profitable" or "it is usually profitable." And let me advise this once: using one tense for another is very common in these books.

->FROM CHAPTER 18<-

Across the brook Cedron.) <note>John 18:1</note> Since Cedron is a Hebrew name in the singular number, either the plural article *of the* <note>original Greek: τῶν (tōn)</note> <margin>60</margin> is redundant, or it should read *of the [singular]* <note>original Greek: τοῦ (tou)</note>. This could easily have been corrupted by some minor Greek scribe who, thinking that *kedrōn* meant "of the cedars" (as it would be if the word were Greek), wanted to avoid a grammatical error and changed *of the [singular] Cedron* into *of the [plural] cedars.* For I see certain... <note>The text cuts off, likely continuing on the next page.</note>

ANNOTATIONS.

...certain things of this kind occur through an ignorance of the Hebrew language, such as in *Jerusalem* and *Jerubbaal*. The Greeks, thinking these were Greek words, rendered them as *Hierosolyma* <gloss>Holy Solyma</gloss> and *Hierobaal* <gloss>Holy Baal</gloss>, as if they were derived from *the sacred things* <gloss>original: para ta hiera</gloss>. From this it happened that, although these words are not aspirated <note>pronounced with an 'h' sound</note> among the Hebrews, they are aspirated among the Greeks, and subsequently among the Latins. I say these things not for the sake of changing them, but for the sake of pointing them out; for whether you aspirate names of this sort or not, I judge it to matter very little.

### FROM CHAPTER 21.

**Young men, do you have any food?** etc.) He calls them *young men* <gloss>neaniskous</gloss>, whom the Hebrews call *na’arim* <note>original: נערים</note>, a word common to both boys and youths; just like the French *enfans* <note>original: "children"</note>.

**Dragging the net of fish.**) This means the net in which the fish were; it is phrased in the same way Cicero spoke of a "bowl of sweet drink" and a "cup of honey-wine."

# ON THE ACTS
## OF THE APOSTLES.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'V' featuring a man standing in a landscape with trees and distant buildings.</image-desc>
**S**ince "acts" is also sometimes used in Latin for "deeds," and this book is commonly cited by this name, I did not wish to change the title.

### FROM CHAPTER 2.

**Something like tongues of fire.**) It would be smoother to say "Fiery tongues"; but because the following verb, which refers to the fire, is in the singular, if I had said "fiery," I would have had to say either "they sat upon" <note>plural</note> or "it sat upon" to refer to the noun "fire" which would be implicitly contained in the word "fiery"—much as in John the devil is called a "liar and the father of it," namely, of lying. So in this place, it would have been said "fiery tongues which sat upon," namely the fire. But that would be more obscure.

**And they began to speak in diverse tongues.**) In this place, I cannot restrain myself from refuting those who think the disciples spoke in their own language, but that a miracle occurred so that everyone understood, just as if each heard his own language. As if a disciple said, for example, *God* <note>original Hebrew: אלהים, Elohim</note>, and one heard *God* <gloss>theos</gloss>, another *God* <gloss>thios</gloss>, another *Gott* <note>German</note>, another *deus* <note>Latin</note>, another *dieu* <note>French</note>, another *diô* <note>Italian dialect</note>. Those who speak thus, I ask, what else are they saying but that Luke lied? For he says in express words that they spoke in "diverse tongues"—the very thing Christ had promised. But that would not be speaking in "tongues" <note>plural</note>, but in "a tongue" <note>singular</note>; and yet it follows, *As the Spirit gave them utterance.* What is *to speak* <note>original: fari</note>? Is it the same as "to be heard"? Furthermore, the miracle would not be in the speakers, but in the listeners. Thus they would not have been accused of drunkenness. Moreover, Paul would have lied in 1 Corinthians 14, where he says: "He who speaks in a tongue (meaning a foreign one) speaks not to men, but to God; for no one hears," that is, understands. To this one could respond that everyone hears their own native speech and there is no need for any interpretation (which he nevertheless orders to be provided), for a divinely inspired tongue (the kind he speaks of) would be understood by everyone. Additionally, this gift bestowed upon the disciples would be imperfect and incomplete, and less

<column-break/>

would be given to them than to the listeners. For they didn't just have to speak, but also to hear anyone who wanted to ask questions or converse. For if Peter (for example) were conversing with some Parthian, the Parthian would understand Peter. But what of Peter—would he not understand the Parthian? How then would he respond to the Parthian’s question? It would be necessary either for the Parthian to speak Hebrew (and so <margin>10</margin> the Parthian, not Peter, would have learned a language on the spot) or for Peter to understand the one speaking Parthian. Thus it would happen that Peter both knew Parthian and, because he was able, ought to speak it; or that the Parthian speaking Parthian would be thought to be speaking Hebrew—and so there would be nothing more in Peter than in the Parthian. Or an interpreter would have to be employed, and thus the gift of tongues would be useless. I do not see what thing produced this error, except that they do not think the same man can speak in different tongues at the same time; nor do they see that while they flee one monster <note>a logical absurdity</note>, <margin>20</margin> they fall into another. For it is no less monstrous that when I say *shamayim* <note>original Hebrew: שמים, heavens</note>, you hear "heaven" or *the sky* <gloss>ouranon</gloss>, than that I should sound both at the same moment. But it is not necessary to introduce either of these monsters. Luke does not write that anyone spoke in so many tongues at one time (which is impossible), but that they spoke in diverse tongues so that whatever nation of men they encountered, they could address them in their own speech: so that here Peter, having found Asians, might speak in an Asiatic tongue; there John, having found Egyptians, in Egyptian; or <margin>30</margin> the same man might speak to anyone in any speech, as he happened upon them. Thus, that the disciples speak in diverse tongues is not against nature; but that they learned these tongues on the spot, that is divine and against nature. Just as it is not a wonder that Lazarus, having been restored to life, should live; but to be restored to life was the wonder. Unless we interpret these things this way, we make deceptive tricks out of divine works, so that the thing is not actually done, but only appears to be done—as if some street-performer appears to swallow a <margin>40</margin> sword when he does not swallow it. Certainly it would be no different if the disciples were said and seen to speak in foreign tongues when it was not so. Some person (to whom this passage seemed very clear at first glance) will dwell on this place and wonder why I spend so much paper explaining such a transparent matter; and indeed I would have passed over it entirely untouched, had I not feared that the authority of someone might deceive the unlearned.

**Concerning the highest father David.**) Just as *high priest* <gloss>archiereus</gloss> is so called, and <margin>50</margin> *chief physician* <gloss>archiatros</gloss>, and other words composed with *chief* <gloss>archē</gloss>, so *patriarch* <gloss>patriarchēs</gloss> can be called in Latin "highest father," and it is a title of dignity.

### FROM CHAPTER 5.

**The high priest and the overseer of the temple.**) He calls him *the priest* <gloss>ton hierea</gloss> whom he called *high priest* <gloss>archierea</gloss> shortly before; just as among the Hebrews, *the High Priest* <note>original: כהן הגדול, Kohen ha-Gadol</note> is often called the same thing as *the Priest* <note>original: הכהן, ha-Kohen</note>. For the Hebrews do not have a single name by which they distinguish the high priest from a priest. <margin>60</margin> Thus they call the pontiff "highest priest," and sometimes just "priest"; just as the Latins call a "great poet" simply "a poet."

**To announce Jesus Christ.**) To be sure, *to evangelize* <gloss>euangelizesthai</gloss> is properly to announce a joyful thing; but sometimes

<sig>hhhh</sig>
<meta>catchword: for</meta>

is said to announce, just like *basar* <note>original: בשׂר; a Hebrew verb for bringing news, often good news</note>, which, although it expresses the same thing, is sometimes used even for a sad matter, as in 1 Samuel 4.

### FROM CHAPTER VIII.

**For I see that bitter gall hangs over you.**) In the Greek it is *cholēn pikrias* <note>original: χολὴν πικρίας</note>, that is, "gall of bitterness." This Hebraism <note>a Greek or Latin phrase that mimics Hebrew grammar</note> may be rendered into Latin just as we have rendered it, or by inversion one might say "the bitterness of gall," in the same way the Latins say "the height of the mountains" instead of "the high mountains."
<margin>10</margin>
In the Hebrew manner, this would be expressed as "mountains of height." Regarding my interpretation "hangs over" <gloss>original: imminere</gloss>, it should be noted that the preposition *eis* <note>original: εἰς; usually meaning "into"</note> sometimes indicates something in the future, as in Luke 2: "This child is destined for the fall and rising of many" <note>original: οὗτος κεῖται εἰς πτῶσιν καὶ ἀνάστασιν πολλῶν</note>. This means: He is to be the cause of either the fall or resurrection for many. That is, for many, a fall hangs over them or a resurrection is to come from him. And as I interpret a little later, "that you are bound by wickedness," since it is the same preposition in "being in the bond of iniquity" <note>original: εἰς συνδεσμὸν ἀδικίας ὄντα</note>, yet the use of the preposition is different.
<margin>20</margin>
As in the same passage from Luke I just cited, where it follows: "for a sign that will be spoken against" <note>original: εἰς σημεῖον ἀντιλεγόμενον</note>, which can no longer be translated using a verb of "hanging over." However, this is Peter’s meaning: "I see that bitter gall, that is, heavy punishments from God, hang over you because of your crime," as is clear from the following response of Simon <note>Simon Magus</note>, who prays for those threats to be averted. It is very well known from the sacred scriptures that "gall," or "wrath," is used to mean the punishments and God's vengeance upon men.

### FROM CHAPTER X.

**Those of the circumcision who believed.**) To be "of the circumcision" means to be from among the circumcised, just as Cicero said, "Those who are of that discipline." Furthermore, *pistoi* <note>original: πιστοὶ</note> means "the faithful," for the word *pistos* <note>original: πιστὸς</note> is used in both senses; for instance, "God is faithful" <note>original: πιστὸς ὁ θεὸς</note> is rightly said to mean "faithful" or "trustworthy." But when *pistos* is said of a Christian, it signifies "one who trusts" <gloss>original: fidentem</gloss>—not one to whom trust should be given (who in Latin is called *fidelis*, "faithful"), but one who *has* faith, namely, in Christ. I want "Believer" <gloss>original: Fidens</gloss> to be a noun here, just as "called" <note>original: κλητὸν</note> is used in Paul, who can be called "the called one" or "the summoned one" so that it is a noun, not a participle—as if you were to say, a "vocationary." The Latins use nouns of this kind when they speak of "attendants" <gloss>accensos</gloss>, "reservists" <gloss>euocatos</gloss>, and "ambassadors" <gloss>legatos</gloss>; let us not think it a sin for us to do the same when necessity presses.

### FROM CHAPTER XIII.

**I will give to you the faithful mercies of David.**) This passage is from Isaiah 55, where *chasidim* <note>original: חסדים; meaning "loving-kindnesses" or "mercies"</note> (as also frequently elsewhere) refers to benefits or acts of beneficence. Here they are less appropriately called "holy things" <note>original: ὅσια; hosia</note>, because that same word among the Hebrews signifies "piety," which in these books is called "holiness" <note>original: ὁσιότης; hosiotēs</note>. The passage in Isaiah reads: "I will make an everlasting covenant with you, the faithful mercy (or beneficence) of David, whom I will give as a witness to the people, a leader and commander for the people." Paul correctly cites this passage regarding the resurrection of Christ. For since Christ is here called "David," it is necessary that he be a man, and further, that he should die; for it is necessary for all born of Adam to die. And yet, his "mercy" is promised here to be "faithful," that is, ratified, firm, certain, and lasting. For the word "faithful" or "trustworthy" expresses this even among the Latins, when they speak of a "faithful

<column-break/>

<page-num>170</page-num>
<header>IN ACTA APOSTOLORVM</header>

peace" or "material that is faithful for eternity." But if the mercy and covenant of our David is to be lasting and eternal, it is necessary that he himself be eternal; for if he himself were to cease, his covenant would also have an end. But if he is eternal, and yet a man (that is, mortal), it is necessary that he should die and then return to infinite life, and thus bestow eternal benefits upon his Israelites.

### FROM CHAPTER XVII.

**Finally, may he bestow all things.**) The text is correctly read as *kai ta* <note>original: καὶ τὰ; "and the"</note>, not *kata* <note>original: κατὰ; "according to"</note>.

### FROM CHAPTER XVIII.

**And with him Priscilla and Aquila, since he had shaved his head.**) Whether Paul or Aquila shaved his head cannot be determined with certainty from the Greek speech. However, it seems more likely that this is said of Aquila, because Luke placed the wife before the husband—I see no reason for this order (since he does not usually do so) unless it was so that the participle "having shaved" <note>original: κειράμενος; keiramenos</note> would be understood to refer to the name of Aquila, to which it is immediately joined. This would not happen if he had placed Aquila first.

### FROM CHAPTER XIX.

**Or rather lest hers.**) It should be read *mallon de* <note>original: μᾶλλον δὲ; "but rather"</note>, not *mellon te* <note>original: μέλλων τε; "being about to"</note>.

### FROM CHAPTER XXVII.

**Because the tranquility had passed.**) "Because even the fast was already over" <note>original: διὰ τὸ καὶ τὴν νηστείαν ἤδη παρεληλυθέναι</note>. But what does a "fast" have to do with the danger of sailing?
<margin>30</margin>
For if you call the "fast" a "lack of food," how could that be the case? They were in a port, and a very large island could supply provisions; a little later they are said to be lightening the ship of grain. Add to this that *nēsteia* <note>original: νηστεία</note> is not used for "starvation" <note>original: ἀσιτία; asitia</note>, nor does it fit with the verb "to have passed" <note>original: παραλελυθέναι</note>; for the lack of food ought not to have passed, but to be pressing upon them. Nor should it be called "starvation," but a "scarcity of provisions." If you say the "fast" means the "time of fasting," that neither fits nautical matters nor
<margin>40</margin>
does it contribute anything to the point. For my part, while I consider this narrative more diligently, I suspect we should read not *nēsteian* <gloss>the fast</gloss> but *eunēsian* <note>original: εὐνησίαν</note>, which is "tranquility from the winds." For that both fits the narrative and could easily have been corrupted by a moderately learned person who was ignorant of the meaning of the word *eunēsia*.

# ON THE EPISTLE OF PAUL
## TO THE ROMANS.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'Q' containing a grotesque face or mask within the letterform.</image-desc>

<margin>50</margin> **AS FAR AS concerns the flesh.**) We have declared in Genesis that *sarka* <note>original: σάρκα; flesh</note> in the sacred scriptures is sometimes the "body." Sometimes it signifies a "corporeal thing," hence "all flesh" means all humans, or even all mortal things. Thus in John 8, "to judge according to the flesh" <note>original: κατὰ σάρκα κρίνειν</note> is what Paul usually calls judging "according to man" <note>original: κατ᾽ ἄνθρωπον</note>. Therefore, you might call this word in Latin "humanity," or "the human condition," or "nature," or even "the body." For in the 7th
<margin>60</margin>
chapter of this epistle, Paul said "the sufferings of the bodies" <note>original: τὰ παθήματα τ. σωμάτων</note> instead of "of the flesh" <note>original: τ. σαρκὸς</note>. Hence "fleshly" <note>original: σαρκικός; sarkikos</note> is the same as "human," "earthly," or "corporeal," to which is opposed "spiritual" <note>original: πνευματικός; pneumatikos</note>, which in Latin can rightly be called "divine," from the divine spirit. But since it is permitted in all arts [for each to have] its own...

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological annotations on the New Testament, specifically focusing on the Epistle to the Romans. The author (likely Erasmus of Rotterdam, given the style and references to Budé) is defending his choice of Latin vocabulary by comparing it to Greek and Hebrew originals and classical Latin usage.</meta>

-># NOTES.<-

their own terms, it must be permitted to us, that at least in the translation we may call it "flesh" and "spirit," wherever it seems appropriate, so as not to offend anyone: yet in such a way that we do this without superstition. For since Paul himself does not always use the same word for the same thing, we also should not be forced into specific words, provided the matter is clear.
*To all who are in Rome, grace and peace.*) Literally it reads, *Grace to you and peace*: which is a Hebraism <note>original: "Hebraismus"; a phrase structure borrowed from Hebrew grammar</note> that should be changed into the accusative case according to Latin custom. I have shown elsewhere that the word for "peace" <note>original: "pax"; translating the Hebrew "Shalom"</note> is used in greetings among the Hebrews, and can be called "salvation" or "health" <note>original: "salutem"</note> in Latin. But it is not always necessary for this to be done, especially where it is joined with other things.
*That I might have some progress among you also.*) He calls "progress" <note>original: "profectum"</note> *fruit* <note>original: "καρπὸν" (karpon)</note>, specifically of the Gospel: as in Philippians chapter 1, where both terms are used for the same thing. From this, the Gospel is said *to bear fruit* <note>original: "καρποφορεῖσθαι" (karpophoreisthai)</note>, that is, to make progress, in Colossians 1.
*I am a debtor to the learned and the unlearned.*) To the Greeks, "the wise" <note>original: "σοφοῖς" (sophois)</note>, just as "the wise" <note>original: "חכמים" (hakhamim)</note> to the Hebrews, declares not only a wise man, but also a learned one. And among the Latins formerly, according to the testimony of Cicero, the "learned" were the same as the "wise."

### FROM CHAPTER III.

*That he might justify those having faith.*) This verb <note>original: "iustificet"; to justify</note> seems tolerable even to the followers of Cicero: for it is no harsher than "to make base" <note>original: "turpificare"</note>. I say the same regarding "atonement seat" <note>original: "propitiatorio"</note> and "the uncircumcised" <note>original: "præputiato"</note>; I do not see why these could be said any less than "decisive," "grown into a head," "armed with a spear," or "shield-bearing," especially since words of this kind both occur frequently and pertain to expressing the matter more significantly. Now, the word "faith" <note>original: "fides"</note>, as we use it in this argument, was shown by Budé <note>Guillaume Budé (1467–1540), a famous French humanist scholar</note> to be used even in Latin, citing examples from antiquity. For if it is correctly said "to have faith in Christ," there is no reason why that thing cannot be called "faith": let us not obey the superstition of those who want it to be called "persuasion": since that word neither fits everywhere, nor declares exactly the same thing. For "persuasion" <note>original: "persuasio"</note> is not plainly the same as "faith" or "trust" <note>original: "fiducia"</note>: nor can you say, "I have persuasion in Christ" in the way you say "I have faith in Christ," or "I have trust placed in Christ." Nor is "Great is your persuasion" the same as "Great is your trust," or "faith." Finally, in few places could you correctly say "persuasion" for "faith," and it is called by its own name *peismonē* <note>original: "πεισμονὴ"</note> by the Greeks, and is joined with faith in Ephesians 3. Now indeed, if authority must be used, I do not see why Jacopo Sannazaro <note>1458–1530; an Italian poet famous for his refined Latin style</note> should be rejected in this matter, a poet to be compared with even a few of the ancients, and likewise diligent even to the point of superstition in the choice of words, in whose work Mary addresses the departing Gabriel thus:
> Now, now let faith conquer, let the obedient will conquer.
*He who [justifies] the circumcision from faith, and the uncircumcision through faith, etc.*) That is, the circumcised and the uncircumcised: just as "the academy" and "the youth" are often said instead of "academics" and "young men." However, the reason we translated differently in chapter 2 was the condition of the sentence. For there it reads literally: *But if the uncircumcision keeps the requirements of the law, surely his uncircumcision will be counted as circumcision.* where the relative pronoun "his" is masculine in the Greek language, while "uncircumcision"

<column-break/>

*akrobystia* <note>original: ἀκροβυστία</note> is feminine: from which it appears that "uncircumcision" was said for "an uncircumcised man," so that it might agree with the relative pronoun. This was done according to the custom of the Hebrews, who rarely have adjectives of this kind derived from substantives <note>nouns</note>: and so they use substantives in place of them. The same thing often happens with the noun *ethnos* <note>original: ἔθνος</note>, which signifies a "nation," being put for men of a foreign nation, as in Acts 15: *And all the nations who are called by my name.* where in Greek "nations" <note>original: ἔθνη</note> is neuter, while the relative is masculine.

### FROM CHAPTER IIII.

*Who justifies the guilty.*) The word *ha-rasha* <note>original: הרשע</note> sometimes declares the "guilty" and "one who does injury to another": as in Exodus 2. In that sense, the word *asebēs* <note>original: ἀσεβὴς; ungodly</note> is placed in this spot, as also in chapter 5, where *asebēs* and *hamartōlos* <note>original: ἁμαρτωλὸς; sinner</note> are the same.
*Not to those only who are of the circumcision.*) It was said *tois ouk ek peritomēs monon* <note>original: τοῖς οὐκ ἐκ περιτομῆς μόνον</note>, instead of *ou monon tois ek peritomēs*, as the old translator correctly rendered it. Just as in 1 Thessalonians: *For from you the word of God sounded forth, not only in Macedonia, but also in every place your faith has gone out* <note>original: ἀφ’ ὑμῶν γὰρ ἐξήχητ’ ὁ λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ, οὐ μόνον ἐν τῇ μακεδονίᾳ, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν παντὶ τόπῳ ἡ πίστις ὑμῶν ἐξελήλυθεν</note>, instead of "For not only from you," etc. But in Paul's writing, the sentence is a little more disturbed, which can be clarified thus: Abraham is the father of all who believe. Now there are two kinds of believers: the uncircumcised, and the circumcised. He is the father not only of the circumcised believers, but also of the uncircumcised believers. The same sentiment follows a little later: Not only that which is from the law, but also that which is from the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all. But how is he a father (someone will say) since he is dead? Do we have a dead father? Or can he be called a father, who does not exist? For these things are contradictory: that the same person exists and does not exist. To have perished is to not exist: to be a father is to exist. Therefore, he who has perished cannot be a father. To these things Paul responds: He is our father not among us, for whom he does not live: but before God, to whom he lives (for all live to Him) and by whom he is to be called back into life. Therefore, God already calls him "Father of Many" <note>original: "Multiparentē"; a Latinization of the meaning of the name Abraham</note> (for this is what the name Abraham declares) just as if he were already a father of many, although he is not yet so to us, but is going to be: for he will be called back into life by God. Now he already is so to God, to whom all things are present. Similar is that saying of Christ in Luke 20: *He is the God of the living, not of the dead: since all live to him.* concerning which I wrote nothing there because I did not yet understand it: for it seemed to show the immortality of souls when he was disputing about the resurrection. Although I will not affirm it even now: I will only say what has come into my mind. Since God is called the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, it is necessary that either they live, or God is the God of the dead. But to be the God of the dead is to be the God of nothing, since the dead do not exist. It is necessary, therefore, that they live. But they do not live. I confess, they do not live to men: to whom only the present life is present: but they live to God, who will recall them into life, which life is future to us, but present to God. Therefore, there will be a resurrection of the dead. With these points, Christ refutes the Sadducees <note>a Jewish sect that denied the resurrection</note>. But what it means for "all to live to God," and for "all things to be present to Him," still remains somewhat obscure. We will try to explain it thus. To an ant, the earth is present in the length of a palm, because with its lowly body, it does not see further. To a man, there is present (for the sake of example)...
