<meta>This page continues a series of philological and theological annotations on the Epistle to the Romans. It concludes a discussion on God's perspective of time (eternity) before moving into specific verse-by-verse commentary on chapters 5 through 12. The author uses analogies from nature and geography to explain how God views all moments as present simultaneously.</meta>

grace) in the length of ten palms <note>A "palm" is an old unit of measurement based on the width of a human hand</note>. Thus, whatever is within one palm is present to the ant; nine palms are absent. But to a human, both that one palm and the remaining nine are present. Thus it happens that the same thing is absent to the ant and present to the human. I will bring another similarity. The water of the Rhine flows. A small portion of it is now present to me, which a little before was present to the people of Schaffhausen, and the same will a little later be present to the people of Strasbourg. But the Sun holds this entire space as present, and Strasbourg is as present to it as Basel. Thus time flows like water: that part of time in which we exist is present to us; but to God, who is greatest and eternal, all of time—what was, what is, and what will be—is present. Thus, the fact that Abraham will one day live again and live is absent and future to us. But to God, that time, and therefore that event, is already present. See 2 Esdras 5, where God's judgment is said to be like a circle.

### FROM CHAPTER 5

*For perhaps for a good man someone might dare to die.*) He gives the reason why he said "scarcely" <note>Referring to the previous verse: "scarcely for a righteous man will one die"</note>. It is as if he says: The reason I say scarcely anyone dies for an innocent person is that I do not entirely deny it can happen that someone (though rarely) might dare to die for the sake of an innocent and good man. For this can happen. But for a guilty person, no one dares to die: this is unique to Christ, and a thing of unheard-of love. Moreover, he calls the "righteous man" <note>original: "δίκαιον" (dikaion)</note> the same person he calls the "good man" <note>original: "ἀγαθὸν" (agathon)</note>. For "righteous" is derived from "justice," from which good men are named; and he opposes him to the "unjust" <note>original: "ἀδίκῳ" (adiko)</note> or "sinner" <note>original: "ἁμαρτωλῷ" (hamartolo)</note>.

### FROM CHAPTER 6

*As many as were washed in the name of Christ Jesus.*) He said *into Christ* <note>original: "εἰς χριστὸν" (eis Christon)</note>, in the way it is usually said elsewhere *into the name* <note>original: "εἰς τὸ ὄνομα" (eis to onoma)</note> or *in the name of Christ* <note>original: "ἐν τῶ ὀνόματι χριστοῦ" (en to onomati christou)</note>. But he spoke more harshly, I believe, so that it would fit with what follows: *into his death* <note>original: "εἰς τὸν θάνατον αὐτοῦ" (eis ton thanaton autou)</note>. To me, there seemed to be no reason to say "to be washed into Christ" in Latin.

*That the body of sin might be destroyed.*) That is, that sin might be destroyed, which is the "body"—meaning that which has the likeness of a body. Just as a body is destroyed by death, so sin is destroyed by the renewal of life. See the observations on Colossians 1.

*He rose in the glory of the Father.*) That is, glorious. He said *through glory* <note>original: "διὰ τῆς δόξης" (dia tes doxes)</note> instead of *in glory* <note>original: "ἐν τῆ δόξη" (en te doxe)</note>, just as in chapter 4, verse 11: *believing through uncircumcision* <note>original: "πιστεύοντι δι᾿ ἀκροβυστίας" (pisteuonti di' akrobystias)</note> instead of *in uncircumcision* <note>original: "ἐν ἀκροβυστίᾳ" (en akrobystia)</note>, just as "through" <note>original: "διὰ" (dia)</note> is said twice regarding life. And just as "throughout all life" is the same as "in all life," so in this place "through glory" is the same as "in glory." But in Latin, "through glory" cannot be used with the same meaning as "through life."

*To whom you present yourselves as slaves by obeying.*) *Whom you obey* <note>original: "οἷς ὑπακούετε" (hois hypakouete)</note> is spoken in the Hebrew manner, where the letter *Lamed* <note>A Hebrew letter used as a prefix to indicate "to" or "for"</note> has the force of a gerund.

*To that pattern of doctrine which was delivered to you.*) *Into which pattern you were delivered* <note>original: "εἰς ὃν παρεδόθητε τύπον" (eis hon paredothete typon)</note> instead of *into the pattern which was delivered to you* <note>original: "εἰς τύπον ὃς ὑμῖν παρεδόθη" (eis typon hos hymin paredothe)</note>. Just as in Galatians 2: *I have been entrusted with the gospel* <note>original: "πεπίστευμαι τὸ εὐαγγέλιον" (pepisteumai to euangelion)</note> instead of *the gospel was entrusted to me* <note>original: "τὸ εὐαγγέλιον μοί πεπίστευται" (to euangelion moi pepisteutai)</note>. And the Greeks speak this way with this verb and others: *I am handed the book by you* <note>original: "ἐγχειρίζομαι ὑπό σου τὴν βίβλον" (egcheirizomai hypo sou ten biblon)</note> instead of *you hand the book to me* <note>original: "σὺ ἐγχειρίζεις μοί τὴν βίβλον" (sy egcheirizeis moi ten biblon)</note>. We will explain something similar in 2 Corinthians 11.

### FROM CHAPTER 7

*You also have been killed to the law.*) Since he compared the law to a husband and people to a wife, it seems it <column-break/> should have been said here: "The law was killed to you," so that the comparison would fit in this way: "Just as a woman is free when her husband is dead, so you, the law being dead, are free from the law." But it must be understood that these are interchangeable, so it is the same thing: "You are dead to the law" and "the law is dead to you," so that you have nothing to do with the law, and the law has nothing to do with you, no more than the living have with the dead, or vice versa.

### FROM CHAPTER 8

<margin>10</margin> *By him who subjected it in hope.*) *Because of him who subjected it* <note>original: "διὰ τὸν ὑποτάξαντα" (dia ton hypotaxanta)</note> is said instead of *through him who subjected it* <note>The author is discussing a nuance of Greek grammar where the word for "through" takes on different meanings depending on the case of the following word</note>, as was said a little before *because of sin* <note>original: "διὰ ἁμαρτίαν" (dia hamartian)</note>, as is clear from the meaning. For he explains what he said: "Not of its own will." That is, by another. If he said "on account of another," it could happen both of its own will and yet on account of another. I see that "through/because of" <note>original: "διὰ" (dia)</note> with the accusative case is used in this sense even among secular authors, as in the Panegyric of Isocrates, where "they were benefited *because of* us" <note>original: "δι᾿ ἡμᾶς ὠνήσαντο" (di' hemas onesanto)</note> is said instead of "they were benefited *through* us" <note>original: "δι᾿ ἡμῶν ὠνήσαντο" (di' hemon onesanto)</note>, as Hieronymus <margin>20</margin> Wolf, his translator, noted. And he showed me that Demosthenes spoke in the same way twice at the end of his oration *For the Megalopolitans*.

### FROM CHAPTER 11

*And you, a wild olive, were grafted into them.*) And yet, a wild olive is not usually grafted into a cultivated olive, but a cultivated olive into a wild one. But since Paul compares the root with the stock of the Jewish race, and the grafted branch with a foreign person, if he had drawn the comparison from the usual <margin>30</margin> custom of grafting, there would be this inconvenience: that the Jews would have to be compared with the wild olive, and the foreigners with the cultivated olive. Since this would be absurd (for the Jewish race is superior), he preferred to draw the comparison from a type of grafting that is indeed unusual, but no less possible. For if you graft a wild olive cutting into a cultivated olive, the wild olive cutting will live and be nourished by the moisture of the cultivated olive. It does not matter that it will not bear domestic fruit, but wild fruit (for the fruit is always of the same nature <margin>40</margin> as the grafted branch); for Paul is not speaking about the fruit, but about the method of grafting and the nourishment of the branch. And thus far the comparison fits, which should not be followed further than as it pertains to the subject at hand.

### FROM CHAPTER 12

*By the mercy of God.*) "Mercies" <note>original: "οἰκτιρμῶν" (oiktirmon)</note> is in the plural number. But it must be understood that words which among us declare a state of being, among the Hebrews are spoken both of the state and of the action: but of the state through the <margin>50</margin> plural number, and of the action through either one, depending on whether there is one or many. For example, if they wish to say "a kindness," they say *Chesed* <note>original: "חסד" (chesed)</note>; but if they mean "kindness" as a character trait, they use the same word but in the plural number; and they do the same if they want to signify many "kindnesses." You will find as many examples as you wish by reading the sacred books. Therefore, "mercy" <note>original: "οἰκτιρμοῖς" (oiktirmois)</note> is an act of pity. But in the plural number, it is "mercy" as a quality, in the Hebrew manner, as the ancient translator correctly interpreted in this place.
<margin>60</margin> *Do not present yourselves as similar to this age.*) That is, to the people of this life. I did not want to depart from this way of speaking because it is both meaningful and the Latin language allows it. For Lucretius <note>A Roman poet and philosopher</note> often said "the ages of beasts" <note>original: "secla ferarum"</note> for "the kind of beasts"—

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary on the Epistles of the New Testament. The previous page discussed the nature of time and God's eternal perspective regarding the book of Romans. This page concludes the notes on Romans (Chapters 11, 13, and 15) and begins the commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, focusing on the concepts of worldly wisdom versus divine "foolishness."</meta>

<page-num>175, 176</page-num>
->**ANNOTATIONS**<-

Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), a Roman poet and philosopher</note> wrote: and some of the ancients said that greed or ambition now rules the world.

*And because of him, all things.*) <note>original Latin: "Et propter eum omnia"</note> The Greek phrase *unto him* <note>original: εἰς αὐτὸν</note> is used instead of *through him* <note>original: δι' αὐτὸν</note>. As in 2 Corinthians 2: *those who were in Greece for the Gospel*. And Colossians 1: *all things were created through him and for him* <note>original: πάντα δι' αὐτοῦ, καὶ εἰς αὐτὸν ἔκτιςαι</note>. Latin writers also speak this way: such as Cicero, who wrote "to mark something for memory" <note>original: Ad memoriam aliquid notare</note>, meaning "because of memory." And Columella <note>A Roman writer on agriculture</note> used "it was done into this" <note>original: In hoc factum est</note> for "on account of this very thing" <note>original: εἰς αὐτὸ τοῦτο</note>. However, in Latin, using the accusative case for a person would be harsher and more obscure if we said all things are "toward Christ." Therefore, I preferred to say, "because of Christ."

### FROM CHAPTER 13

*The night has passed, the day is at hand.*) <note>original Latin: "Discessit nox, dies adest"; Romans 13:12</note> I know that *to know* <note>original Greek: γινώσκειν; the author may be discussing a variant or misreading of the text which usually uses "proekopsen" (has advanced)</note> means to progress, and *to draw near* <note>original: ἐγγίζειν</note> means to approach. But Paul did not say, "the day is approaching" <note>original: ἡμέρα ἐγγίζει</note>; rather, he said, "it has arrived" <note>original: ἤγγικεν</note>. That which has arrived is no longer merely approaching, but is present. And in this way, this word is often used elsewhere, as in Luke 10. Nor does it escape my notice that "approaching him" is often said. But how that is to be interpreted must be learned from the context. In this specific place, it is clear that Paul is not speaking of a future light, but of the present light, because he urges them to behave honestly as if in the day—that is, as is fitting to do now, since it is day. If he called this "day" the future resurrection of humanity, he would be urging them in vain to behave honestly after death. Instead, he speaks of the light of the Gospel, which having dawned, the darkness of ignorance has retreated.

### FROM CHAPTER 15

*Therefore I have reason to boast in Christ Jesus.*) <note>original Latin: "Itaq; habeo quod in Christo Iesu glorier"; Romans 15:17</note> This means: in the business of Christ Jesus, or in Christianity, or in the Christian cause. This way of speaking occurs often above in chapter 8 and below in the final chapter. I did not always want to retain this way of speaking, but I have done so occasionally because even Latin authors do not shrink from it, as we explained in Isaiah 29.

# ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

### FROM CHAPTER 1</u>

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'N' featuring a figure seated amidst dense foliage and vines.</image-desc>
**N**OT many wise men indeed.) <note>1 Corinthians 1:26</note> From these words, it cannot be known for certain whether he speaks of those who called and taught, or of those who were called. But the entire argument shows that he is speaking of the Apostles and the teachers of the Gospel. For what he said a little before—"What is foolish of God is wiser than men"—he certainly said regarding the Gospel doctrine, which becomes foolishness to those who are perishing, as he had taught previously. What he adds next—"For you see how you were called"—gives the reason for what he had said about foolishness, as shown by the conjunction "For." It is as if he says: "The reason I say the foolishness of God (so to speak) is wiser than men is that you yourselves see this in those by whom you were called to the Gospel, who are generally unlearned, poor, and of low birth; yet through them, the learned, the powerful, and the noble are refuted." Therefore, what Paul says in this place—"God chose the most foolish things of the world to put the wise to shame"—is what he had said before: "It pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe." For the wise are not refuted by those who are taught, but by those who teach. Consider, reader, the whole course of Paul's speech and the second chapter, where he repeats in the conclusion the same thing he had said (as is usually done) in the proposition: you will find the matter to be so. Furthermore, regarding "the most foolish things of the world" <note>original: τὰ μωρὰ τοῦ κόσμου</note>, we have translated this according to the Hebrew custom; they often use positive adjectives in place of superlatives, which they lack. For example: "blessed are you among women" <note>original: εὐλογημένη σὺ ἐν γυναιξὶν</note> instead of "most blessed of women" <note>original: εὐλογητάτη τῶν γυναικῶν</note>. And in 1 Corinthians 12: "our unpresented parts have more abundant presentation" <note>original: τὰ ἀσχήμονα ἡμῶν, εὐσχημοσύνην περισσοτέραν ἔχει</note>, meaning our "most unseemly" parts receive the greatest honor. Such things are also found in poetic expressions like "divine among goddesses" <note>original: δῖα θεῶν</note> and "under all."

<column-break/>

### FROM CHAPTER 2</u>

*But we speak wisdom among the mature.*) <note>original Latin: "Sapientiam autem loquimur apud perfectos"; 1 Corinthians 2:6</note> He calls "wisdom" the more hidden doctrine regarding more difficult matters. By "the mature" <note>original: perfectos</note>, he means Christians who are more advanced in doctrine and capable of understanding secrets. It is as if he says: "The fact that I taught you simply about Christ, and him crucified, I did not do because I lacked more perfect and far greater things to teach. But since you were infants in the doctrine of Christ and not capable of greater things, I taught the fundamentals, and fed you with milk (so to speak), as he says in the following chapter." This meaning is so clear from Paul's words that nothing could be clearer; nor would I have spoken a word about it, unless I saw some people so deluded in this matter that they seem to close their eyes and the eyes of others in broad daylight. They think "the mature" <note>original: perfectos</note> in this place refers to any Christians for whom the Gospel is wisdom. But Paul's words resist this. For he does not say, "we speak wisdom in all the mature" <note>original: σοφίαν λαλοῦμεν ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς τελείοις</note>, as if "all the mature" referred to "wisdom." Rather, it refers to the verb "we speak": "we speak wisdom among the mature" <note>original: σοφίαν λαλοῦμεν ἐν τοῖς τελείοις</note>. Someone will ask: "What? Does he not speak wisdom among the imperfect and unrefined Christians?" He does not. For he calls "wisdom" the more perfect, more lofty, and difficult doctrine. Just as in Revelation 13, "wisdom" <note>original: σοφία</note> refers to a sharp question and a riddle concerning the number of the beast. And Demosthenes, in his letter concerning the children of Lycurgus, says: "these things are too wise for you" <note>original: ταῦτα μὲν σοφώτερα ἢ καθ' ὑμᾶς εἶναι</note>, meaning these things are too sharp for you to follow. Therefore, this more hidden doctrine of Paul cannot be delivered among the fundamentals. Speaking of this a little later, Paul says: "But things which eye has not seen, etc.," which speech refers back to the verb "we speak." We speak things that are not human, nor common, but things which eye has not seen, etc.—namely, when we are among the mature and those capable of these secrets. Therefore, the article "the" <note>original: ὁ</note> is placed twice there, meaning "the things which": the first refers to "we speak," the second to "he prepared." This speech cannot be understood or fit together otherwise. Thus, those who interpret it differently either omit the second article or think it is superfluous; this should not be done unless the meaning cannot stand any other way. But even if the words could be stretched to their opinion, they should not...

The previous pages examined the distinction between human wisdom and the hidden wisdom of God, specifically looking at Paul's rhetoric in the opening chapters. This page delves into the definitions of "perfection," the nature of the spirit, and specific linguistic choices regarding legal and moral conduct within the Corinthian church.</meta>

<page-num>177</page-num>
<page-num>178</page-num>
->**ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS**<-

if they were allowed to be drawn along, the meaning would still be absurd. For Paul cannot call the Corinthians "perfect" <note>original Latin: perfectos</note>, since in the following chapter he calls them "carnal" <note>original Greek: σάρκινοι; sarkinoi</note>: that is, worldly and unrefined; and "infants" <note>original: νηπίους; nepious</note>, that is, babies and imperfect. He gives this as the reason why he could not teach them wisdom—that is, the more perfect things. If whoever was a Christian were called "perfect," then those who are not Christians could be called "imperfect." Yet one cannot be called "imperfect" unless he has at least begun, and in whom something has already been done; this cannot apply to non-Christians, nor will you ever find it said of them, as far as I know. Nor is there any reason to shrink from this opinion of Paul's, as if he were not accustomed to speak of anything greater or more recondite among the perfect than what is found in his writings. For if God showed greater things to Paul (who was perfect), what forbids Paul from declaring them to the perfect? Were they less worthy to hear them than Paul was to see them? Why then did he not commit them to letters? Because most people who read letters are imperfect, and they can no more grasp such arduous things than a child learning the alphabet can understand the most difficult points of logic. Read 4 Esdras 14 <note>An apocryphal book where the prophet Ezra is told to reveal some things openly but hide others for the wise</note>.

*Except the spirit of man, which is in him.*) The word "spirit" <note>original Greek: πνεῦμα; pneuma</note> declares both the mind and the spirit, after the manner of the Hebrews, among whom it is *ruach* <note>original Hebrew: רוח</note>. Since I did not dare to say "the mind of God" in this sentence—especially since it would not fit in the following parts, and yet the same name had to be placed in both members of the sentence—I said "the spirit of man" instead of "the mind."

### FROM CHAPTER 4

*For who is to judge you?*) He says "judging" <note>original Greek: διακρίνων; diakrinon</note>, which he had previously called "to examine" <note>original: ἀνακρίνειν; anakrinein</note>, to judge and pass sentence. He uses the present tense for the future, as is his usual custom, such as above: *the one who judges me is the Lord* <note>original: ὁ ἀνακρίνων με κύριός ἐστιν</note>. It is the same thought: Who is going to bring judgment on you, as to whether you are more excellent than the others? The Lord Christ. Why then do you prefer yourself to others, as if you were the judge yourself? And why do you do this before the time, when the judgment of the Lord is to be expected?

*You reign without us.*) "You reign" <note>original Greek: βασιλεύετε; basileuete</note> is used just as the Hebrew *malak* <note>original: מלך</note> can mean both "to reign" and "to obtain a kingdom." Now, he who has obtained a kingdom, reigns. Therefore, the old translator correctly rendered the past tense "you have reigned" <note>original: ἐβασιλεύσατε</note> by the present "you reign," just as he did with "you have become rich" <note>original: ἐπλουτήσατε</note>.

### FROM CHAPTER 5

*Since it is for you to judge those of your own.*) "To judge" <note>original Greek: κρίνειν; krinein</note> is in the indicative mood, which must often be explained as we have rendered it. It is like that passage in Matthew 11: *Are you the one who is to come, or should we look for another?* <note>original: σὺ εἶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος, ἢ ἕτερον προσδοκῶμεν;</note>. Or: Must we wait for another? Latin speakers talk this way too: "What are we doing?" instead of "What ought we to do?"

### FROM CHAPTER 6

*And that under the untrusting*) If the word "unbelievers" <note>original Greek: ἀπίστων; apiston</note> is said of a Christian man, he can be called "dissenting" in Latin. But in this place, since it is used for a man alienated from the religion of Christ, "dissenting" cannot be said properly enough. For he is one who is void of faith, that is, of the Christian religion. For this reason, I thought I should be bold and use a new word for a new matter. If it was lawful for Cicero to coin the word "indolence" <note>original Latin: indolentiam</note> and to fashion certain other terms for things

<column-break/>

not previously treated in Latin, what forbids us from relieving our own poverty of speech?

<margin>10</margin>
*Anything is permitted to me, etc.*) He proceeds to discourage them from sexual immorality through a comparison of opposites, in this manner: There is not the same freedom in practicing any kind of lust as there is in eating any kind of food. For it is permitted to use any food, provided it does not harm anyone—which would happen if someone still weak in faith were offended by my eating. For where there is danger from this, I would not wish to be so subject to anything—for example, my stomach or my lust—that I would not rather abstain from meat than hurt anyone. Otherwise, as far as food is concerned, it is permitted to eat any food: for there is no use for foods unless they are eaten, and no use for the stomach unless it eats. Thus, one was created for the sake of the other. Why then is it not permitted to practice any kind of lust, just as one uses any
<margin>20</margin>
food? Because while the stomach serves food, the body ought not to serve lust, but Christ. For the stomach will be so abolished that in the other life, for which the Gospel prepares us, there will be no use for the stomach. Thus it happens that the stomach is only to be considered for living this life, and therefore it does not matter by what kind of food it is nourished. But the body is to be called back to life by Christ, and will be with him in eternal life; hence it follows that it ought to be kept pure for that life. Therefore, just as
<margin>30</margin>
food serves the stomach and the stomach serves food, because one belongs to the other, so the body ought to serve Christ, even as Christ served our bodies when he died and rose again for their sake, so that our bodies might be members of Christ, not of a prostitute.

*Every sin is outside the body; but he who commits sexual immorality sins within his own body.*) What he calls "outside the body" <note>original Greek: ἐκτὸς τοῦ σώματος; ektos tou somatos</note>, he opposes with "into the body" <note>original: εἰς τὸ σῶμα; eis to soma</note>. From this it appears that "into the body" is said for "inside the body" <note>original: ἐντὸς τοῦ σώματος or ἐν τῷ σώματι</note>, just as in Luke 11: *my children are with me into bed* <note>original: τὰ παιδία μου μετ' ἐμοῦ εἰς τὴν κοίτην εἰσίν</note>, for "in bed." Just as Plautus <note>Titus Maccius Plautus, Roman playwright</note> said: "It was into my mind" <note>original Latin: Mihi in mentem fuit</note> for "in my mind." Moreover, this is the meaning: Other sins have their seat in the soul: the soul is the murderer, the soul is the slanderer, the false witness, the envious, etc. In these sins, the body is the servant of the dictating soul. But lust has its seat deep within the body itself, and although it arises from the soul (as all other things do), it is nevertheless committed inside the body, while others are committed outside the body. From which it follows,
<margin>50</margin>
not that sexual immorality becomes the greatest of all sins (for murder and certain others are greater), but that it is most intimate to the body. Therefore, it defiles the body more than others, than which nothing can be more foul or unworthy: that the same body should be the home and temple of both the filthiest lust and the purest divine spirit.

### FROM CHAPTER 7

*For the untrusting husband is made holy, etc.*) It happens sometimes that an untrusting husband is made a Christian by his wife
<margin>60</margin>
(for he calls Christians "holy"), and vice versa. He repeats this same thought a little later in other words: *How do you know, woman, etc.* Otherwise, if a divorce should occur between a Christian wife and a non-Christian husband, he will lead away the children...

it will be done so that they are born impure, that is, like the father, who will teach them not to be Christians. But if they remain together, the mother will teach them Christ, and so they will become Christians.

**And so he is divided.** Likewise the unmarried woman or virgin.) I have followed the edition of Colines <note>original: "Colinæi exemplar"; referring to the 1534 Greek New Testament published by Simon de Colines</note>, in which it is read thus: <gloss>and he is divided, and the unmarried woman and the virgin are anxious for the things, etc.</gloss> <note>original Greek: καὶ μεμέρισται, καὶ ἡ γυνὴ ἡ ἄγαμος καὶ ἡ παρθένος μέριμνα τὰ, &c.</note> He says the man is "divided" <margin>10</margin> because he must serve both God and his wife. He calls a widow an "unmarried woman," or even one who may have been a prostitute (for nothing forbids these also from serving God), to whom he joins the virgin: for their condition is the same as far as the worship of God is concerned, because both, lacking a husband, are free to devote all their effort to the cult of God. It appears the old translator followed this reading. There is another reading: <gloss>the wife and the virgin are divided; the unmarried woman is anxious for the things, etc.</gloss> <note>original Greek: μεμέρισται ἡ γυνὴ καὶ ἡ παρθένος, ἡ ἄγαμος μέριμνα τὰ, &c.</note> In which this fault exists: that <gloss>is divided</gloss> <note>original Greek: μεμέρισται</note> is poorly placed instead of <gloss>differs</gloss> <note>original Greek: διαφέρει</note>. <margin>20</margin> Secondly, because this division would more suitably be placed before the prior part, thus: <gloss>the unmarried man and the virgin are divided</gloss> <note>original Greek: μεμέρισται ὁ ἄγαμος καὶ ἡ παρθένος</note>. Thirdly, "woman" <note>original Greek: γυνὴ</note> would be less aptly used for "a married woman" <note>original Greek: γαμήσασα</note>, and "the unmarried" <note>original Greek: ὁ ἄγαμος</note> for "one who has been separated" <note>original Greek: ὁ χωρισθείς</note>, which does not fit, since both a widow is "unmarried" and a repudiated woman was called by the same name shortly before. Add to this that this would be denied to widows, the repudiated, and former prostitutes, even though they are no less free from a husband than virgins.

## FROM CHAPTER VIII.

**Now concerning those things which are sacrificed to godlings.**) <margin>30 1 Cor. 8.</margin> see <unclear>☌</unclear> they are called what the Hebrews call <term>Elim <note>original Hebrew: אלים; meaning "gods" or "mighty ones"</note></term>, and the Latins call "divine ones" <note>original: "divos"</note>, such as Jupiter, Neptune, etc. But since that would be ambiguous (for "divine" is usually used as praise), we have fashioned the word <term>deastros <note>translated here as "godlings"; a diminutive or pejorative form of "deus"</note></term>, by which true gods would not be signified—following the form by which "philosophaster," "oleaster," and other such things are said by the Latins. Nonetheless, their images are also commonly called idols. But it is clear that Paul is not speaking of images here, because a little later he calls them <gloss>gods</gloss> <note>original Greek: θεὸς</note>, that is, gods, so that you may understand that those he calls <gloss>idols</gloss> <note>original Greek: εἴδωλα</note> <margin>40</margin> are those things which are addressed by the name of gods. Add to this that those who sacrificed to Jupiter were not said to sacrifice to the image of Jupiter, but to Jupiter himself.

**Charity benefits others.**) He says <gloss>builds up</gloss> <note>original Greek: οἰκοδομεῖ</note>, which in chapters 6 and 10 is <gloss>is profitable</gloss> <note>original Greek: συμφέρει</note>, <gloss>but not all things are profitable</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἀλλ᾽ οὐ πάντα συμφέρει</note>, to which is opposed <gloss>to cause to stumble</gloss> <note>original Greek: σκανδαλίζειν</note>, to harm, to stand in the way, to hurt, to inconvenience, which is placed a little after this passage. But these refer to others, so that <gloss>to build up</gloss> means to be useful to others. <margin>50</margin>

## FROM CHAPTER X.

**Through Moses in the cloud and the sea.**) He said <gloss>into Moses</gloss> <note>original Greek: εἰς τὸν μωσῆν</note> instead of <gloss>in Moses</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἐν τῶ μωσῆ</note>, just as in chapter 6 he said <gloss>into the body</gloss> <note>original Greek: εἰς τὸ σῶμα</note> for <gloss>in the body</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἐν τῶ σώματι</note>, as we wrote there. However, <gloss>in Moses</gloss> will mean <gloss>through Moses</gloss> <note>original Greek: διὰ τοῦ μωσέως</note>, for he often uses the preposition <gloss>in</gloss> for <gloss>through</gloss> in this way, after the manner of the Hebrews, among whom the letter *beth*, which is a preposition, indicates both. And in the same way he spoke in chapter 15: <gloss>death has died in something</gloss> <gloss>unto victory</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἐν τινὶ τέθνηκεν ὁ θάνατος ἀνὰ νίκος</note>, for <gloss>through victory</gloss> <note>original Greek: διὰ τοῦ νίκου</note>, or victoriously.

**That they used spiritual food, etc.**) And yet both the manna <margin>60</margin> and the water flowing from the rock were human things, since the manna was eaten and nourished the body of a man, and was ejected through the waste of food, nor did it deliver men from death, no

<column-break/>

more than other foods: I say the same of the water. But he calls it spiritual or divine food because, although it was human, it signified something else: so that in this place "spiritual food" is nothing other than <term>typical <note>original Greek: τυπικός; meaning symbolic or acting as a "type" or foreshadowing</note></term>, and indicating something else, as Paul declares a little later, as in Revelation chapter eleven. Understand the same regarding the rock from which the spring flowed, which rock is here called Christ because it indicated Christ, the perennial spring of life. Paul says these things so that what he will soon say about the bread (which is Christ) may be understood, so that like may be compared with like. And by these few words of Paul (if anyone considers them diligently), that question which so greatly vexes learned men today is explained. <note>Likely a reference to the Reformation-era debates over the Real Presence of Christ in the Eucharist.</note>

**Asking nothing for conscience' sake.**) You will find the declaration of this passage in the eighth chapter, and this is the meaning: if you ask about food that has been bought or set before you, the answer will be that it is a victim or an offering for the godlings. Then if you eat, he who pointed it out to you—who is indeed a Christian, but as yet little confirmed in doctrine—will be driven to eat the same food you eat: and because he will do so doubting whether he eats rightly, he will sin, because he will act with uncertainty, and thus you will have wounded his conscience. That is, you will have been the cause for him to do something contrary to what he thinks he ought to do. Therefore, when I forbid you to eat for conscience' sake, I speak of the conscience of the other, as I have said. For as far as your own conscience is concerned—you who understand the matter—it cannot be wounded in this, nor condemned, since you know that whatever is born of the earth was created by divine power for the use of men, and therefore it is permitted for a man to eat them as his own. Nor can your liberty in this be condemned by another who is weaker, since you think it right for you to eat any food, provided you do not show yourself ungrateful to God. Therefore, you do not sin in that you eat, but that you are the cause for another to eat with doubt, and thus to sin. For the sake of the other, therefore, you ought to abstain, lest you harm anyone. From this doctrine of Paul, it is clear that those people sin who compel men by fines, or threats, or any other means to work on feast days, or to eat any food on any day, or to swear into some form of religion, or to do anything else against what they think is lawful for them. This is to compel miserable and ignorant men to sin.

## FROM CHAPTER XI.

**Every man praying with his head covered.**) Shameful and faulty things ought to be covered: honest things, on the contrary, and those lacking fault, should be uncovered and shown. If a man performs prayers with his head covered, he shows that his head is faulty, and therefore must be covered. But the head of the man is Christ, who is without fault. Therefore, the man's head ought to be uncovered, by which it is indicated that Christ (who is the man's head) is without fault. But the woman's head is the man, who since he is guilty and faulty, the woman ought to cover her head, so that she may confess her head—that is, the man—to be the source <note>original: "fontem"; likely meaning the source of the fault</note>. An Italian man once told me that this was Paul’s meaning.

**But if any man seems to be contentious.**) Since he had said that long hair is a disgrace to a man, but a decoration for a woman...

<page-num>182</page-num>
->ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS<-
<note>Despite the header, the commentary is actually discussing 1 Corinthians 11–14.</note>

[that long hair] is fitting, someone could contend that this does not happen by nature. For nature gave hair equally to men and women. To this Paul responds in such a way that he almost admits it is so, but he denies it is a matter of custom; and custom is to be maintained in matters of this kind, which are indifferent <note>The term "indifferent" (Latin: *indifferentes*) refers to *adiaphora*—actions that are neither commanded nor forbidden by God, but governed by social decorum.</note>.

### FROM CHAPTER 12.

**You know that when you were foreigners, etc.**) Word for word it is read thus: *You know how when you were foreigners, you were led away to mute little gods.* <note>original Greek: οἴδατε ὅτι ὅτε ἔθνη ἦτε, πρὸς τὰ εἴδωλα τὰ ἄφωνα ὡς ἂν ἤγεσθε ἀπαγόμενοι</note>. In this passage, "when" <note>original Greek: ὅτε</note> and "as" <note>original Greek: ὡς</note> <margin>10</margin> have the same value. Therefore, both could be expressed in Latin thus: *You know how when you were foreigners, how I say to the mute, etc.* But because the Latins are not accustomed to repeat particles of this kind with the word "I say" (*inquam*), unless after many intervening words—lest the word already placed, and still pending, should fall from the memory unless it were repeated—since, I say, this is usually done for the sake of memory, I did not think that particle should be repeated in this place where there was no danger to the memory, <margin>20</margin> as only a few words had been interjected. However, "but" is superfluous in this place, as are several things in Paul’s writing. *Once led away* <note>original Greek: ἅπαξ ἀπαγόμενοι</note> is used for *you were led and you were led away*, which is the same thing we wrote about in Genesis chapter 1. <margin>30</margin>

**That no one speaking by divine inspiration, etc.**) Just as whoever curses Jesus with words and does not acknowledge him as Lord is devoid of the divine spirit, so whoever acknowledges the Lord is endowed with the Holy Spirit. This is so you may understand that not only those who speak in foreign tongues and do other miraculous things are divinely inspired. This is the argument: *Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.* If the soul is evil, the mouth speaks evilly; likewise if good, it speaks well. And conversely, if the mouth speaks evilly, the soul is evil; but if well, it is good and divinely impelled. From this it appears that Paul is speaking of that speech which comes from the soul, when what is felt is spoken—not that which is feigned and differs from the soul. <margin>40</margin> However, because he speaks of divine and spiritual things, a distinction must be applied. Whatever humans do excellently, they do divinely, as appears in Moses regarding Bezalel <note>The craftsman of the Tabernacle in Exodus 31</note>, the builder of the tabernacle, whom God says he filled with his spirit for that craftsmanship. Likewise in Isaiah 28, where God is said to teach the farmer. Thus, if someone builds a house well, cultivates a field exceptionally, or does anything else prudently, he has it divinely. But in this place Paul is not speaking of these <margin>50</margin> gifts of the Holy Spirit; for these are not called "divine" in this specific sense, since they are acquired by human industry and labor, and were common even before the Spirit was poured out by Christ upon Christians. Therefore, if someone speaks in a foreign language which he learned through long labor, I will not call his knowledge of speaking divine and **spiritual** <note>original Greek: πνευματικὴν</note>, no more than that of King Mithridates, or Cleopatra, or others who had learned many languages. But Paul calls "divine" those things of which Christ speaks in <margin>60</margin> John 7, where John says: *The Holy Spirit was not yet given*; that is, he had not yet inspired men to do those things which Paul recounts here. Because the Spirit teaches these according to the

<column-break/>

occasion, and they happen divinely and against nature, they are called divine. Therefore, if a physician cures a disease with herbs or some other natural method, you would call that human knowledge—though its giver is God, who is indeed the author of all good things. But if Peter or Paul cures a sick person by naming Jesus, call that "against nature" and "divine." Likewise, if Cicero speaks in the Greek tongue, in which he labored much in learning, it is human; but if Peter, a fisherman and a man of little learning, speaks in Latin or German when he has never learned them, that is divine.

**We were washed into one body.**) That is, so that we might be made one body. He calls the "Christian commonwealth" one body, whose head is Christ; just as a state is called one body whose head is the magistrate, or a people's head is the king, or a couple's head is the husband. Therefore, a little later he says, *But you are, to some extent, the body of Christ*, so that it may be understood that the speech is figurative.

### FROM CHAPTER 13.
<note>This section actually discusses 1 Corinthians 14.</note>

**But especially that you may prophesy.**) **To prophesy** <note>original Greek: προφητεύειν</note>, if you look at the force of the word, is to predict; but it is used for that which is in Hebrew <margin>30</margin> **nava** <note>original Hebrew: נבא</note>, and in Greek **to divine** <note>original Greek: μαντεύεσθαι</note>; that is, to speak secrets, unknown things, great things, divine things, and finally oracles, whether it be something past or present (which is called **under-knowledge** <note>original Greek: ὑπόγνωσις</note>) or future (which is properly called **prophecy** <note>original Greek: προφητεία</note>). Thus, in 1 Timothy, Paul calls Epimenides a "prophet" <note>original Greek: προφήτην</note> of the Cretans, not because he spoke of the future, but because he spoke certain and true things, such as oracles are. Hence that verse: *He who guesses well, him I think the best seer.* Therefore, seers were once called "Viewers" among the Hebrews, because they saw those things which were unknown to others. <margin>40</margin>

**He who speaks in a foreign tongue.**) <note>original Greek: ὁ λαλῶν γλώσσῃ</note>, that is, he who is a little later called "he who speaks in tongues" <note>original Greek: ὁ λαλῶν γλώσσαις</note>, and also a little later "with other tongues" <note>original Greek: τὸ ἑτερογλώσσοις</note> and "in other lips" <note>original Greek: καὶ ἐν χείλεσιν ἑτέροις</note>, as we have sometimes shown that "men" is used for "other men," and "nations" for "foreign nations."

**But let him speak mysteries in his mind.**) That is, let him speak so that he understands himself, but is not likewise understood by others. For since the use of speech is to declare the feelings of the mind to others, he who speaks so that others do not understand speaks more with his mind than with his mouth, since there is no difference whether he speaks thus or thinks silently. Moreover, "to speak mysteries" is the same as "to prophesy." But since Paul opposes the prophesier to him who uses a foreign tongue in this place, it must be understood that a prophesier <margin>50</margin> is what he calls one who does it in a language known to the listeners, just as "to speak in a tongue" means to speak in a foreign tongue, and "to prophesy" means to prophesy in one's own tongue.

**Unless there be in my speech a revelation, etc.**) That is, unless I address you so that you learn something which has been revealed to me, or known, etc. He calls it a "revelation" <note>original Latin: patefactionem, literally 'an opening'</note> when God declares and lays open something to a human, as to John those things which are contained in that book whose title is **Apocalypse**, that is, **Revelation**. <margin>60</margin> If to this there is added a stirring and incitement of the mind, it is called "prophecy" <note>original Latin: uaticinatio</note>, such as we see in the seventy elders under Moses, and also in Saul and others; which is sometimes so great that the men rave as if snatched outside themselves. He calls "knowledge" that which [is perceived] from having seen or heard...

<meta>catchword: repros</meta>

<meta>This page continues the philological and theological commentary on the First Epistle to the Corinthians (Chapter 14 and 15) and transitions into the Second Epistle to the Corinthians (Chapter 1). The author continues to use classical references, such as Pliny the Elder and Roman legal history, to clarify Paul's terminology.</meta>

<page-num>184</page-num>
<header>ANNOTATIONS.</header>

<column-break/>

proceeds from the fact, as is the case with the histories of John and Luke: who narrate, the latter what he heard and learned from others, the former what he saw and in some part performed. However, he calls "doctrine" that which is acquired through letters and reason, such as Paul’s disputation regarding the faith of Abraham; for what he teaches, he confirms by the authority of the sacred scriptures and by reasons. And this latter method, if it be destitute of the former two, is extremely dangerous, because <margin>10</margin> men do not serve the sacred scriptures, but compel them to serve their own affections and lusts. From this is born that discord among modern teachers, which surely would not exist if all possessed what they ought to possess.

**Let him pray that he may interpret.**) He said "to pray" for praying to God, just as the Latins say "saluting" for those who go in the morning to salute princes and wealthy men; or "to disturb" for disturbing one's fortunes, and "to make" for making poems. Therefore, it matters nothing whether <margin>20</margin> you say "to pray to God" or just "to pray," in the same way that Livy also spoke in Latin. Just as we taught a little while ago, "to speak with a tongue" and "to speak with a foreign tongue" are the same thing. Furthermore, it appears from this passage that those who spoke in tongues did not all speak in every tongue (for God did not give everything to one person) but gave different ones to different people; otherwise, God would not need to be prayed to for the sake of interpretation.

**As for what pertains to the meaning.**) *Nous* <note>original Greek: νοῦς</note> is the mind, and it is used for the "meaning of the mind" also in 2 Thessalonians 2 and <margin>30</margin> Revelation 17. So also among the Latins, it is customary to speak of the "mind" <note>Latin: *mens*</note> of a certain writer. Hence, "to pray with the mind" <note>original Greek: νοῑ</note> is to pray significantly, and as he spoke before, "to give a clear word" <note>original Greek: λογον εὔσημον διδοναι</note>, to bring it about so that the hearer can see the mind and understand what is being said.

**I would rather speak five words thus.**) He said "five" for "a few," and "speech" <note>original Greek: λογος</note> for "words" <note>original Greek: ῥήματα</note>: a thing which is accustomed to happen in the plural number. As in Chapter 2 of this epistle: "with learned words" <note>original Greek: διδακτοῖς λογοις</note>, with learned words or a learned oration. Indeed, in this <margin>40</margin> passage, it is not permitted by Latin custom to say "speeches" <note>Latin: *sermones*</note>. For the Latins do not say, "I will finish in three speeches" (for that would have a different meaning), but "I will finish in three words."

### FROM CHAPTER 15.

**Then to the twelve.**) Since twelve Apostles had been chosen, they retain the name of "the Twelve" even after Judas was removed, though there were only eleven: just as if someone has ten thousand soldiers, and then after some battle, with several thousand having been lost, he nevertheless continues to call them "the ten thousand," because <margin>50</margin> so great a reduction has not been made that the former and famous name ought to be lost. Or if one of the *Decemviri* <note>The *Decemviri* were a ten-man commission in ancient Rome.</note> at Rome should die, the rest are nevertheless called not the *Novemviri* [the Nine], but the *Decemviri*.

**He appeared also to me, as if to one born out of time.**) "Abortion" <note>Latin: *abortus*</note> refers not only to a dead birth, but also to a small fetus, not of the proper size, even if it lives. And thus my fellow countrymen speak commonly, calling it an *auorton*. So Pliny speaks in Book 12, Chapter 2: "For even dwarf-planes <note>Latin: *chamæplatani*</note> are so called because of their forced <margin>60</margin> shortness, since we find 'abortions' even among trees." This unhappiness, therefore, will also be said of the race of dwarfs. Thus says Pliny. Hence Paul calls himself an "abortion" as the least of the Apostles, and a "pumilio" <note>Latin: *pumilio* means a dwarf or pygmy.</note>, and as if a dwarf.

<column-break/>

**Otherwise, what will those do who are washed for the dead?**) "They will waste their labor," someone will say. And yet by this very act they show that they hope for the resurrection of the dead. "They hope in vain" (says he who denies that there is a resurrection), "for if they are acting deliriously in being washed for the dead (for what can be so foolish as for a living person to be washed for a dead one?), it is not absurd to say that they also act foolishly in hoping for the <margin>10</margin> resurrection." You see how this argument of Paul's has no weight against those who deny there is a resurrection, if indeed you understand these words as they are commonly interpreted, saying that at that time there were those who were washed for other dead people: which did not happen, as I think; and if it did happen, it ought to have been rebuked by Paul, not brought forward as an example. Therefore, so that you may understand this passage of Paul, consider the reason and nature of washing <note>The author is discussing baptism (Greek: *baptisma*), which literally means washing.</note>: which is described in the Epistle to the Romans, Chapter 6, in these words: *As many of us as were washed into the Lord Jesus,* <margin>20</margin> *were washed into his death, etc.* and a little later: *For if we have been planted in the likeness of his death, we shall be also in the likeness of his resurrection.* This, therefore, is Paul's argument: Christians, while they are washed, are washed for this purpose, that they may die with Christ, and then rise again. This is "to be washed for the dead": that is, for themselves in the hope of the thing which they are to attain after death, namely, the resurrection, which would be foolish if there were to be no future resurrection. A certain Italian taught me this opinion.

# ON THE SECOND
## TO THE CORINTHIANS
### Epistle.

### FROM CHAPTER 1.

<margin>30</margin> <image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'V' (used as 'U') containing a seated figure with a book, set within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>**That by many persons.**) "From" <note>original Greek: ἐκ</note> is put for "by" <note>original Greek: ὑπὸ</note>. Just as in the following chapter, "he who is grieved by you" <note>original Greek: ὁ λυπούμενος ἐξ ὑμῶν</note> for "by you" <note>original Greek: ὑπ' ὑμῶν</note>. However, "for you" <note>original Greek: ὑπὲρ ὑμῶν</note> in the second person <margin>40</margin> should be read in the second place, as some copies have it, so that it may correspond to the word "working together" <note>original Greek: συνεργούντων</note>, so that the benefit may be conferred by your labor and for your sake.

**When I therefore deliberated this, did I use lightness? etc.**) It is a mark of "lightness" <note>fickleness or inconstancy</note> to promise something certainly which perhaps you are not going to perform. If I had promised that I would certainly come to you, I would be "light," since I have not come. Now, I did not promise certainly, for I said that I would come if God willed (for so I wrote in the <margin>50</margin> previous epistle, Chapter 4 and at the end); which exception vindicates me from the charge of lightness and inconstancy. For I do not deliberate as men are accustomed to do, unmindful of their own fragility, so that "Yes" should be "Yes" with me, and "No," "No": that is, so that when I say I will do something, I affirm it certainly, as if I were absolutely going to do it; or when I deny it, I deny it certainly, as if I were absolutely not going to do it. For with me it sometimes happens that "Yes" becomes "No," and "No" becomes "Yes," as when I said I would come to you, that was a "Yes"; but <margin>60</margin> the same thing has now become a "No," because I have not come: for God did not permit it, in whose power are our actions, so that we can affirm or deny nothing certainly concerning ourselves. For our promises are not certain, in the manner of God's,

<meta>catchword: us men [nos ho-]</meta>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, specifically clarifying Paul’s defense of his character and his theological explanations of the resurrection body and Christian charity. The catchword from the previous page "tur" likely completed a verb such as "videntur" (they seem) or "impediuntur" (they are hindered), leading into the discussion of human limitations versus divine certainty.</meta>

<page-num>185, 186</page-num>
<header>ON THE EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS</header>

<column-break/>

We little men <note>original: "homunciones"</note> are hindered; God, however, cannot be hindered, but what he has once promised, he faithfully performs. Therefore, what we have taught you concerning Christ, we did not teach in such a way that we affirmed it at one moment and denied it at another; rather, we always and constantly affirmed it concerning Christ. For these were not our promises, but the promises of God, who promised the things concerning Christ with certainty, and with no condition or exception. And it is no wonder: for he is God, who cannot be hindered, and so his promises are certain to us, confirmed by the pledge of his inspiration. But I am a man: if I did not come to you, I had not promised it with absolute certainty, and there was a just cause for not coming. For I did this in order to spare you. For if I had come, I would have come with a rod (as I threatened in the first epistle)—that is, I would have punished you more severely because of that shameful act of incest. Someone might say: "Do you then think us to be of such little faith and constancy that we cannot bear your present correction?" I certainly do not think so. For I know that you are constant in faith, nor do I take that away from you, but I have regard for your joy. For if I, being present, had punished you, that matter (to say nothing of myself) would have caused you grief, which grief will now be absent. Now, "to lord over" <note>original Greek: "κυριεύειν"</note>, which we translate as "to take away," means not only to be a master, but also to become a master and to gain possession, just as we wrote before concerning the word "to reign" <note>original Greek: "βασιλεύειν"</note>. Thus, "to lord over the faith" <note>original Greek: "κυριεύειν τῆς πίστεως"</note> means to make oneself the master of another's faith—that is, to drag down another's confidence and strength, and to deny its existence.

### FROM CHAPTER II.
*It has not grieved me except to some extent, lest I should overcharge you all.*) That is, it caused grief not only to me, but also to you. But if I were to say that I alone grieved over that shameful act, I would overcharge and weigh you all down with a crime, as if you yourselves did not also grieve at his disgrace, which would have been a fault in you.

*I did this for your sakes in the person of Christ.*) That is, as one bearing the person of Christ, and as his vicar, who taught that whatever we loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven. But if we did this in our own person—that is, by our own authority and name—Satan would circumvent us and cast us into sin; for we would be sinning if we were to usurp for ourselves what belongs to God (namely, forgiving the sins of another). Moreover, if anyone doubts that "face" <note>original Greek: "πρόσωπον"</note> is used for "person," he will find it elsewhere, and also in Galatians chapter 2.

*For we are not like many, etc.*) Since he had said that his office was of such a kind that no one could be fit for it, someone might object in this way: "As if it were difficult to do what you do—that is, to teach Christ!" I confess (says Paul) that to prattle about Christ, and to teach him in a perfunctory way for the sake of profit, is not difficult; and many do that. But to do it sincerely and by divine inspiration, and to have one's service approved by God (which is what we do)—this is indeed the most difficult thing of all, and greater than human strength.

### FROM CHAPTER V.
*Desiring to be clothed over with our heavenly dwelling, etc.*) That is, the heavenly body which we are to have in the next life. We desire to be clothed over with that body, if only, being clothed, we shall not be found naked: that is, if at Christ's coming we are still in this life,

<column-break/>

and not yet naked or stripped of this body. For we would not wish to be stripped of this body if it were possible; that is, we would not wish to die, but would wish at Christ's coming to be suddenly changed, our mortality being swallowed up, and to be clothed over with immortality. Paul is speaking here of all Christians, who, while they desire immortality, naturally shrink from death, and would wish, if it were possible, to be among those of whom it was said in the previous epistle that "we shall not all sleep."

*We are not occupied in the thing itself.*) He used the word "indeed" <note>original Greek: "τὸ δὴ"</note> to mean "the true and present," just as Latin legal experts use the term "species" <note>This refers to the specific form or actual instance of a legal case.</note> for the thing itself which happened. Isocrates, in his *Praise of Helen*, calls it "appearance/form" <note>original Greek: "ἰδέαν"</note> when speaking of beauty in these words: *But we shall find that nothing of those things which lack beauty is loved, but all are despised, unless they have shared in this form* <note>original Greek: "τῶν δὲ κάλλους ἀντιποιουμένων οὐδεὶς ᾠήθημεν ἀγαπώμενον, ἀλλὰ πάντα καταφρονεῖσθαι, πλὴν ὅσα τῆς ἰδέας ταύτης κεκοινώνηκε"</note>, that is, in this reality. He used the word in the same way a little later. In the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 10, it is called "true." Not dissimilar is what is written in Mark chapter 10: "those who seem to rule" <note>original Greek: "οἱ δοκοῦντες ἄρχειν"</note>, that is, those whom we see ruling, who actually rule.

### FROM CHAPTER VI.
*You are not restricted toward us, but toward the man to whom you are intimate, you are restricted.*) I open my soul to you generously and perform my duty. But if you perform your duty in a narrow and stingy way, you do this not to me (that is, not to Paul), but to one who loves you most, and clearly to your father. Therefore, see to it that you obey me, your father, dutifully and liberally, just as I dutifully and liberally give you precepts as if to my children. What we translate as "Toward the man to whom you are intimate," reads literally as "Toward your own bowels." This Hebraism <note>A phrase reflecting Hebrew idiom, where the internal organs represent deep emotion or mercy.</note> is to be explained and interpreted thus: "Toward us, since you are our bowels"—that is, you who are most dear to us, and who are in our hearts, as he says in chapter 7, alluding to this place.

### FROM CHAPTER VIII.
*As we encouraged Titus.*) Namely, that he should advise and urge you, so that God, in his kindness, might give you such a mind that you may complete what you have already begun to do—specifically, regarding generosity toward the needy. Moreover, he calls that inclination of the mind toward acting kindly a "benefit of God" upon the Corinthians, just as he spoke a little earlier regarding the Macedonians. For that will to do good is a result of divine gift and grace.

*Not only to do, but also to will.*) He is not comparing the magnitude of the things between themselves; otherwise he would say, "not only to will, but also to do," since doing is more than willing. But he joins the things together, so that "Not only to do, but also to will" is the same as "Both to do and to will," so that both began from the previous year. He spoke in the same way in Romans chapter 1: *Not only do they do them, but they also consent to those who do them.* That is, they both do them and consent.

*For there ought not to be ease for others and restriction for you.*) The word "that" <note>original Greek: "ἵνα"</note> is sometimes put for "because" <note>original Greek: "ὅτι"</note>, as in John chapter 13: *I know whom I have chosen; but that the scripture might be fulfilled*—that is, "but it shall indeed be fulfilled." And the same in the first epistle chapter 2: *but that they might be made manifest*, which is said in the Hebrew manner.

<meta>This page continues the philological annotations on the Epistles of the New Testament. The previous page concluded a discussion on the certainty of God's promises in 2 Corinthians, contrasting human fallibility with divine constancy. This page moves into the specific Greek and Hebrew linguistic nuances of chapters 11 and 12, then begins the commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians.</meta>

<page-num>187</page-num>

...is sought, as in Jeremiah 1: <note>original Hebrew: לאמר</note> "to say." This is used <note>original Greek: ἵνα λέγηται</note> "so that it might be said," in place of <note>original Greek: λέγειν</note> "to say," which means it is being asked or answered.

### FROM CHAPTER 11

**I wish you would bear with a little of my foolishness.**) <note>original Greek: μικρόν τι ἀφροσύνης</note> "A little something of foolishness" is correctly read in some manuscripts, and the old translator reads it this way. He calls his boasting "foolishness," which he hopes they will endure; then, what is more, he asks that they actually bear it. Therefore, the word <note>original Greek: ἀνέχεσθε</note> "bear with" is in the imperative mood <note>a command or direct request</note>. Then the reason is given why they ought to bear it: *for I am jealous over you* (he says) *with a godly jealousy*: for I have betrothed you to Christ. For this is how <note>original Greek: ἡρμοσάμην</note> "I have joined/betrothed" is correctly translated by the old translator, as both the sense requires (for this concerns the marriage of Christ and the church) and the nature of the verb <term>harmózesthai<gloss>to fit together or betroth</gloss></term> allows. For Plutarch <note>a famous Greek historian and essayist</note> used the word in this way.

**Lest they be corrupted from simplicity.**) <note>original Greek: φθαρῇ ἀπὸ τῆς ἁπλότητος</note> "Corrupted from simplicity" is a brief and obscure phrase, in which the word "corrupted" must be explained by two words, as we have done. I have noticed this happens sometimes in the Holy Scriptures, as in Genesis 45: "I am Joseph your brother, whom you sold into Egypt"; and in Acts 7: <note>original Greek: τὸν ἰωσὴφ ὃν ἀπέδοντο εἰς αἴγυπτον</note> "Joseph whom they sold into Egypt." This means: they sold him, and being sold by them, he was led into Egypt.

**That an occasion may be found for them in what they boast, etc.**) These pretenders, he says, seek an opportunity for boasting, just as we boast. But if we did not teach the gospel for free, they could boast that they do the same as us. Now, since we teach for free, they do not have that opportunity; for they cannot endure to teach for free, since they serve their own bellies. The word <note>original Greek: ἀφορμὴν</note> "occasion/opportunity" is used here as the Hebrew word <note>original Hebrew: מצא</note> "matsa," which in the passive often means "to exist" or "to be available," and in the causative <note>the Hiphil stem</note> means "to supply" or "to suggest." For here, the phrase "that they may be found in that which they are reproved" is said instead of "that they may find for themselves that in which they boast." Just as in Philippians 3: "that I may win Christ, and be found in him," meaning that in him I may have enough supplied to me. Likewise in Ecclesiasticus chapter 15, in the Latin (for this verse does not exist in the Greek), it is read:
> Lying men shall not be mindful of her, but men that speak truth shall be found in her, and shall have success even unto the inspection of God.

This means that wisdom will confer so much upon the truthful that, etc. A similar case is what we explained in Romans 6 regarding the "form of teaching into which you were delivered." And it does not differ much from that line of Horace <note>the Roman poet</note>, "Bellerophon burdened by his horse": that is, the horse was a burden to Bellerophon. And that in Matthew 13: "He who was sown by the wayside": that is, he who received the seed.

**I speak indecorously.**) Just as <note>original Greek: κατ' ἄνθρωπον</note> "according to man" and <note>original Greek: κατὰ σάρκα</note> "according to the flesh" mean "humanly," so here <note>original Greek: κατ' ἀτιμίαν</note> means "indecorously" or "disgracefully." That is, I shall speak contrary to how it would befit me to speak. For it is unbefitting for me to boast, but I will boast like a fool. As if we were unable: namely, to boast the same things about ourselves that they do about themselves. However, the word <note>original Greek: ἠσθενήκαμεν</note> "we have been weak" is an indicative used for a subjunctive, as is often placed by Paul in the Hebrew manner, whose language lacks a subjunctive mood.

### FROM CHAPTER 12

**There was given to me a thorn in the flesh.**) That is, *for* the flesh: in the way Cato <note>Cato the Elder</note> is accustomed to speak in his book *On Agriculture*: "trappings for oxen, cloths for donkeys, lids for jars, patchwork quilts for boys," and many such things.

<column-break/>

<page-num>188</page-num>

**My strength is made perfect in weakness.**) This means: a Christian man, who takes his name from me, Christ, cannot turn out to be most brave except by struggling with the enemy. In this struggle, he should feel that he is unequal to the task unless my favor is present; and so, by trusting in me, he may become perfectly brave and worthy of me.

**And I may mourn many who have sinned before.**) <note>original Greek: μὴ πάλιν ἐλθὼν πολλοὺς τῶν προημαρτηκότων</note>: that is, "many who had previously sinned," as in chapter 10: "to compare themselves with some of those who commend themselves": that is, "with certain ones who commend themselves." For it is not a division, as if he dared to compare himself with some but not with others. We explained something similar regarding Psalm 54.

# ON THE EPISTLE
->TO THE GALATIANS.<-

## FROM CHAPTER 2

<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial E featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or saint, within a landscape.</image-desc>
**Lest perhaps I should run, or had run, in vain.**) This means "lest I should seem or be said to run or have run." It is like what is said in 1 Corinthians 1, that God chose the most foolish things of the world, and "things which are not": that is, those which *seem* to be most foolish and even non-existent. And that line of Lucan <note>a Roman poet</note>: "Right is where the greatest reward is." And Ovid's: "The harvest is always more fertile in another's field."

**Because he was to be blamed.**) <note>original Greek: κατεγνωσμένος</note> The participle is used for a noun, just as <note>original Greek: εὐλογημένος</note> "blessed" is used for "the blessed one," and <note>original Greek: ὁ πειράζων</note> "the tempter" for "the one who tempts."

**If you, being a Jew, live after the manner of Gentiles, etc.**) If you freely eat any kind of food, as foreigners are accustomed to do, and you feel that it is permitted for you to do so, why do you now abstain? By this pretense, you are the cause for not only the Jews refusing to eat certain foods, but even foreigners imitating you and abstaining from foods, thus "Judaizing." Why did I and you, and the rest of the Jews, become Christians? Surely so that we might become righteous. But if we could achieve that through the Law, there was no reason for us to turn to Christ, since we would have had in the Law what we seek in Christ. But because the Law could not provide that for us, we fled to Christ, who could. From this it follows that we who are now Christians are innocent. But if we obey the Mosaic Law (which you are now doing) because we obey it in order to obtain righteousness, it follows that we are guilty, since we are not satisfied with Christ. Thus it would happen that we obtain sin from Christ, not righteousness—which is absurd. But if anyone rebuilds the same thing he destroyed—that is, if he returns to the Law (which he had rejected and said goodbye to when passing over to Christ) and seeks protection from it again—he confesses himself to be a guilty person who seeks innocence from the Law. For he who has turned to Christ has said goodbye to the Law and has no more business with it; rather, he lives, and is righteous and innocent through trust in Christ, which is a gift of God. But if he returns to the Law, he rejects this gift, because he does not want to be made innocent by Christ, but by the Law. Thus it happens that for him, Christ's death (which he underwent to destroy their sins...)

<meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence at the end of the page. The final word "oppetijt" (he underwent/met) refers to Christ's death for the sake of blotting out sins.</meta>

<page-num>189</page-num>
<header>ON THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS <note>The header in the original text is mislabeled; the content below actually discusses the Epistle to the Galatians.</note></header>

...it profits nothing. Thus far Paul has rebuked Peter. Regarding the translation of <note>original Greek: ὁ γὰρ διὰ νόμου</note> "for he who is through the law," or "but if," etc., it should be known that <note>original Greek: γὰρ</note> "for" is sometimes adversative <note>meaning it shows contrast</note>, just as the Romans use "But indeed," as in Romans 3: <note>original Greek: εἰ γὰρ ἡ ἀλήθεια τοῦ θεοῦ</note> "But indeed if the truth of God," etc. He said <note>original Greek: παραβάσεωv χάριv</note> "because of transgressions" instead of "for sinners," as is clear from the word "to distinguish," placed immediately before concerning the same matter.

### FROM CHAPTER III.

<margin>10</margin>**The cause of sins was added, etc.**) The Law was enacted so that sins might be recognized (for *I would not have known lust, unless the law forbade it*, Romans 7). It was meant to last until the seed of Abraham should come—that is, Christ—to whom it was promised that all nations would be blessed through him. The Law was established through angels <note>original Latin: genios, referring to the "disposition of angels" mentioned in the New Testament</note> so that it might be understood to be divine; it was brought forth, administered, and proclaimed through a <term>sequester<gloss>a mediator or middleman</gloss></term>, namely Moses. Now, a mediator is a go-between for two parties who are making an agreement between themselves. But God <margin>20</margin>is one, not two; therefore, it is necessary that Moses was the mediator between God and the Israelites. For he could not have been a mediator between God and God, since there are not two gods. If this is the case, it is necessary that in making that covenant, something was promised by both sides; for that is the nature of covenants. What did God promise? Life. For he says, *he who does these things shall live*. What did the Israelites promise? Obedience. For when it was proclaimed that those who were defiant would be accursed, they answered "Amen," and they pledged <margin>30</margin>that they would do all that Jehovah commanded. Now, because they are unable to obey the law, they are liable to punishment. Thus it happens that the law makes their sins plain and shows them to be worthy of punishment. But if this is so, the law seems to be contrary to the promises of God, since God's promises confer righteousness and happiness, while the law confers sin and punishment, than which nothing can be more contrary. In truth, the law is so far from being contrary to the promises that it attempts to achieve the same thing as the promises. For the law promises life and righteousness to the obedient. But if <margin>40</margin>men do not obey, it is not the fault of the law, but the weakness of men who are unable to obey. For if they did obey, they would attain life through that obedience, and thus they would become righteous through the law. But because (as it is recorded in scripture) all sin, all stand in need of the righteousness of Christ. He, being obedient to the law, was righteous, and he imparts his righteousness to us—which in him is the righteousness of the law (so that it appears righteousness is situated in the law, since Christ is righteous by the righteousness of the law, having indeed obeyed the law). <margin>50</margin>This same righteousness is in us the righteousness of faith, because by trusting in Christ, we share in his righteousness.

### FROM CHAPTER IV.

**For these are the two covenants, etc.**) Hagar and Sarah, he says, are—that is, they signify (mark this word carefully, reader)—two covenants. Hagar signifies one covenant, which was struck on Mount Sinai, namely the law; this covenant of the law gives birth into slavery—that is, those who are from the law are slaves, just as the children of Hagar are slaves. For Hagar <margin>60</margin>is Sinai—that is, she signifies Sinai, the mountain of Arabia, on which mountain the law was given. For just as Hagar was a slave, so Mount Sinai, which is signified by Hagar, is in slavery, namely to the Romans; in 

<column-break/>

<page-num>190</page-num>
which respect it certainly agrees with this earthly Jerusalem, which itself, along with its citizens, is subject to the Roman Empire. Therefore Hagar, the slave, represents Sinai, and further the earthly Jerusalem, which is a slave. But Sarah, the free woman, represents the heavenly Jerusalem, which is free, of whom we are children. If this is so, we are free like our mother; we are children of the promise, like Isaac. Therefore we ought not to serve the law as if we were slaves. He used the phrase <note>original Greek: τὸ γὰρ ἄγαρ</note> "for the Hagar" <term>technically<gloss>grammatically, using the neuter gender for the name</gloss></term>. The phrase <note>original Greek: συvστοιχεῖ δὲ</note> "but it corresponds to" means it marks and signifies. The phrase <note>original Greek: δουλεύει γὰρ</note> "for she is in slavery" is used while the law exists, as it appears in the Colinaeus edition <note>a famous 16th-century printed edition of the Greek New Testament</note>, not "but she is in slavery"; for it gives the reason why Sinai is similar to Jerusalem, specifically in that Jerusalem serves just as Sinai does. For "she is in slavery" is said of Jerusalem, as is clear from the pronoun <note>original Greek: αὐτῆϛ</note> "of her," which cannot refer back to Hagar.

### FROM CHAPTER VI.

**But let each man examine his own work, etc.**) He rebukes those who are pleased with themselves because they are better than others. There is no one who, if he compares himself with others, will not find people worse, or certainly just as bad. Miserable is the boasting that depends on the wickedness of others! Therefore, if others were not wicked, would you be unable to boast of yourself? "I am not a usurer <note>someone who lends money at high interest</note>." Therefore, if usurers did not exist, you could not be pleased with yourself. It is a fine thing indeed to be the kind of person who only looks good because someone else is found to be worse! But God will not judge us in that way; he will not make a comparison of men. You are black, you will be condemned. "But there are others who are also black." And others will be condemned, but their blackness will not make you white. Therefore, look not at whether you are better than others, but whether you are good and whether you obey God. Thus it will be that your boasting is your own, and does not depend on others. Moreover, the phrase "unto himself" <note>original Greek: εἰϛ ἑαυτὸv</note> is said for "towards himself" <note>original Greek: πρὸϛ ἑαυτὸv</note>, just as we wrote regarding 1 Corinthians 6.

## ON THE EPISTLE
->TO THE EPHESIANS.<-

### FROM CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'I' featuring floral and scrollwork designs within a rectangular woodcut frame.</image-desc>
**In the heavenly things of Christ.**) He said <note>original Greek: ἐv τοῖϛ ἐπουραvίοιϛ χριστῷ</note>, just as in 2 Corinthians 10 he calls his weapons <note>original Greek: δυvατὰ τῷ θεῷ</note> "powerful to God," that is, by the power of divinity, or "God-power" if I may speak so—that is, having divine virtue. So here he calls "in the heavenlies" the "Christ-heavenly things," that is, things which are heavenly and belong to Christ. Now, this epistle is obscure and stretched out into immense complexities of words, which we have cut where possible, and as far as could be done, we have aimed for clarity.

### FROM CHAPTER III.

**I act as an ambassador.**) The word <note>original Greek: πρεσβεύω</note> "I am an ambassador" is added in the Colinaeus edition, and rightly so, as the following words show. Otherwise, the verb is missing. But if you say that in the phrase "in which also," the verb "I am" is understood, first, he would not have added the article <note>original Greek: ὁ</note>. Furthermore, the following words explain the nature of the embassy, not the nature of the chains. Add to this that at the beginning of the next chapter he joins the phrase "the prisoner" <note>original Greek: τὸ ὁ δέσμιοϛ</note> with the verb "I beseech," and in chapter 6, "I am an ambassador in a chain."
