The author continues to use philological methods—comparing Greek syntax with classical authors like Isocrates and Latin poets like Juvenal—to clarify the Apostle Paul's intended meaning.</meta>

<page-num>191</page-num>
<header>ANNOTATIONS.</header>

<margin>5</margin>**In your hearts, and being rooted in charity.**) <note>original Greek: ἵνα ἐν ταῖς ὁραῖς ὑμῶν, ἐν ἀγάπῃ ἐρριζωμένοις</note> "that in your hearts, being rooted in love," occurs with a change of grammatical case, which is frequent in Paul's writing and occasionally appears in secular authors, such as in Isocrates’ *Panathenaicus*, as noted by Hieronymus Wolf <note>a 16th-century German humanist known for his editions of Isocrates</note>: <note>original Greek: ἀσεβὲς γάρ μοι ἦν μὲν, ἐν αἰτίαις ὄντα διὰ τὸν βίον, τόν τε σωτῆρας</note> "For it would have been impious for me, being under accusation because of my life, [to neglect] the saviors." Truly, it cannot be said that Isocrates did this out of ignorance, since it is recorded that he spent twelve years composing that work.

<margin>10</margin>->FROM CHAPTER V.<-

**Once dark, now full of light.**) He said <note>original Greek: σκότος</note> "darkness" and <note>original Greek: φῶς</note> "light" instead of <note>original Greek: σκοτεινοὶ & φωτεινοὶ</note> "darkened" and "enlightened," using a noun in place of an adjective. He does this often, as when he said "uncircumcision" for "the uncircumcised," and in 2 Corinthians 3, <note>original Greek: δόξα</note> "glory" for "that which was glorified," and in chapter 5, <margin>15</margin><note>original Greek: ἁμαρτίαν</note> "sin" for "sinner." There are infinite other examples, such as among the Latin authors using "wickedness" for "the wicked man" or "ruin" for "the ruinous man"; and in Juvenal, "At what price do you hire darkness?" instead of "a dark house."
<margin>20</margin>**But it is of light.**) <note>original Greek: φωτὸς</note> "of light" is the correct reading in the Colinaeus edition <note>referring to the Greek New Testament printed by Simon de Colines in 1534</note>, and the sense of the passage demands it, rather than <note>original Greek: πνεύματος</note> "of the spirit."

**By divine words.**) <note>original Greek: ἐν ῥήματι</note> "In the word" is said by <term>antonomasia<gloss>a figure of speech where a title or epithet is used instead of a proper name</gloss></term> to mean "in the word of God," as is written in the following chapter. However, he says <note>original Greek: ῥῆμα</note> "utterance/word," where elsewhere he more <margin>24</margin>properly calls it <note>original Greek: λόγον</note> "the Word." In the same way, it was said a little earlier, "full of the spirit," for "full of the Holy Spirit," just as the old translator <note>the Vulgate</note> rendered it there without error. So in Leviticus 24, it says someone "reviled the Name," meaning the Name of God. The Romans <margin>30</margin>also used to say "the Good" for the "Good Goddess" <note>Bona Dea</note>, and "the straight" for a "proper dinner" <note>recta cœna</note>, and "the Flaminian" for the "Flaminian Way." They do this so freely that sometimes they use both words, and sometimes only one. I think the same should be permitted to us, provided that logic and clarity are maintained.

->FROM CHAPTER VI.<-

**Spiritual wickedness.**) He said <note>original Greek: τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας</note> "the spiritual things of wickedness," just as the Latins say "the flats of the fields" or "the heights of the mountains" instead of "flat fields" and "high <margin>40</margin>mountains." By "in heavenly things," I understand him to mean in the business of the Gospel and religion, which in the Gospel is often called "heaven."

# ON THE EPISTLE
## TO THE PHILIPPIANS.

->FROM CHAPTER I.<-

<margin>50</margin><image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'N' in a square frame</image-desc>**For to me to live is Christ.**)
He soon declares what this means when
he says: "But if my fruit of work is
situated in this, if I live in the
body." <note>original Greek: καρπὸν ἔργου</note> "Fruit of work,"
or what he calls the progress of the
work, is clear a little later where he says, <note>original Greek: εἰς τὴν ὑμῶν προκοπήν</note> "for your progress," so that "fruit" is the same as "progress," as also in Romans 1. That is, the progress of the Gospel, which depends on him living in the body. For if he were dead, he could not <margin>60</margin>advance the Gospel. Therefore, "for me to live is Christ" means: if I live, I will teach Christ, and so Christianity will be advanced.

**And I indeed desire to depart.**) The word <note>original Greek: ἀναλῦαι</note> "to depart/loose" is used in this way in Luke 13, Judith 13, and Wisdom 2.

<column-break/>

<page-num>192</page-num>
<header>FROM CHAPTER II.</header>

**Who, being in the form of God, etc.**) Since Christ, before he was made man, was God and equal to God, leading the same life as God, he did not tenaciously hold onto that equality with God as <margin>5</margin>greedy men do who allow nothing to be taken from them. Instead, he made himself lesser than God by his own will and took the slavish form of a man—that is, he became human, etc. To be "in the form of God" means to be like God, which is to be God. Likewise, to be "like men" means <margin>10</margin>to be a man like others, except for sin. Also, to be "found as a man" means to be found to be and actually be a man. He uses <note>original Greek: μορφὴν, ὁμοίωμα & σχῆμα</note>—that is, "form," "likeness," and "figure"—to mean the same thing. He says "to have as robbery" or "to regard as a thing to <margin>15</margin>be seized" to mean "to use and retain greedily." Just as the Romans say, "to hold in the number of enemies" instead of "to kill as an enemy." For the word <note>original Greek: ἡγεῖσθαι</note> "to consider/lead" is usually placed such that it refers not only to a thought, but to a reality. As in the following chapter, <note>original Greek: ἀναγκαῖον ἡγησάμην Ἐπαφροδίτον πέμψαι</note>: "I have considered it necessary to send Epaphroditus"—that is, I sent him, because I thought it necessary and worthwhile. And in Genesis 31: "We are counted as strangers"—that is, treated as strangers.

**By wicked thoughts.**) The word <note>original Greek: διαλογισμὸς</note> "thought/reasoning" is neutral. But if it is blamed or forbidden, it is <margin>25</margin>understood as a "wicked thought." Just as in Latin the word *valetudo* <note>meaning "state of health"</note> is used. If you say, "I could not come because of my *valetudo*," an adverse state of health is understood. But if you say, "May grace, fame, and *valetudo* happen in abundance," good health is understood.
<margin>30</margin>->FROM CHAPTER III.<-

**Look out for the mutilated.**) He alludes to the name of circumcision. And he calls the "mutilated" <note>original Latin: concisos, a pun on the Greek 'katatome' vs 'peritome'</note> those who were not truly circumcised—that is, those Jews who, although they boasted of circumcision and Judaism, were not truly Jews, <margin>35</margin>since true Judaism is placed within the Christian religion.

->FROM CHAPTER IIII.<-

**True companion.**) He calls someone who was his partner in the work of the Gospel a "true and sincere companion." <margin>40</margin>Nor am I unaware that there are some who think <note>original Greek: σύζυγε γνήσιε</note> "true yoke-fellow" are Attic feminine forms, and that he is addressing his wife. But since the words are plainly in the masculine gender, and the meaning contains no ambiguity, to twist them and make Paul an "Atticizer" <margin>45</margin>at the expense of clarity is nothing other than "looking for a knot in a bulrush" <note>a Latin idiom for finding difficulty where there is none</note>. Not to mention that the facts themselves resist this. For when Paul, speaking to the Corinthians about celibacy, <margin>50</margin>says he desires them to be like himself—that is, celibate, so they might be more ready for the worship of God—it is not believable that he later did the very thing he discouraged others from doing. Unless, perhaps, someone says that he was later overcome by the stings of lust and married, <margin>55</margin>entangling himself in the greatest hindrance to the business of the Gospel. But he could not be overcome by lust, he to whom God responded: "My favor is enough for you." (For he whom God favors is invincible). And if he had been overcome, he ought to have <margin>60</margin>taken his wife along with him; if he was not going to take her along, it was foolish to marry. Yet he did not take one along, as he himself declares.

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary on the Epistles, transitioning from the end of the notes on Ephesians (on the previous page) to a detailed analysis of the Epistle to the Colossians, specifically chapters 2 and 4. The author remains focused on clarifying Paul's Greek by comparing it to Hebrew idioms and classical Latin and Greek literature.</meta>

ON THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS.

# ON THE EPISTLE
## TO THE COLOSSIANS.

### FROM CHAPTER II.

**Having stripped off the body of human sins.** This means having stripped off sins, which are the body: that is, they are signified by the body in circumcision, as in chapter 3: "the stripping off of the sins of the flesh," <note>original Greek: τὴν ἀπέκδυσιν τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν τῆς σαρκός</note> that <margin>10</margin> is, "the inheritance, which is the recompense." <note>original Greek: τὴν κληρονομίαν, ἤ τις ἐστὶν αὐταποδοσίς</note> Secular authors speak in the same way, such as Pliny in Book 1, Chapter 5: "The earth is balanced in the middle space, suspended by the force of this (namely the air) with the fourth element of the waters." He calls the "element of the water-carrier" simply the waters, because that is the element.

**Having blotted out the handwriting of ordinances.** "Having carried away the handwritings in the decrees" <note>original Greek: Βαστάξας τὰ χειρόγραφα τοῖς δόγμασι</note>; here he uses the dative case, so that it can be rendered by the genitive, similar to that in 2 Corinthians 2: <margin>20</margin> "A thorn was added to me for the flesh," <note>original Latin: Appositus est mihi stimulus carni</note> that is, of the flesh and the body; or, "for the stimulating of the body," which amounts to the same thing. As in Revelation 3: "the smoke of the incenses for the prayers," <note>original Greek: καπνὸς θυμιαμάτων ταῖς προσευχαῖς</note> instead of "of the prayers." For this is a <term>Hebraism</term> <note>an idiom derived from the Hebrew language</note>, which we explained in the titles of the Psalms regarding the word "to" <note>original Hebrew: תהל</note> for David. Such are also those phrases of Cato which we cited in 2 Corinthians 2: "Ornaments for the oxen, covers for the jars"; which could be said as "Ornaments of the oxen, covers of the jars." So here, "handwriting for the decrees" <note>original Greek: χειρόγραφα τοῖς δόγμασι</note> is the <margin>30</margin> handwriting of the ordinances, that is, the very decrees and statutes of the divine law by which we were held bound, as if by a signed document. Indeed, it was pronounced that whoever did not obey the law was accursed, and this was sanctioned by our own—that is, the people's—acclamation, when everyone responded, "Amen": Deuteronomy 27. By that "handwriting" we were forced to obey the law; because we were unable to do so, Christ obeyed for us and paid the penalty, and thus he deleted the handwriting as if by <term>acceptilation</term> <note>a legal term for the formal verbal discharge of a debt without payment, or here, Christ’s payment counting as our discharge</note>.

<margin>40</margin> **Of which things the body is Christ.** Christ is the reality foreshadowed by those shadows. In the Greek it is, "Of which the body is of Christ"; which is the same as in Latin, "The height of misery is of civil war" and "The height of misery is civil war." But I have favored clarity here.

**Let no one supplant you, etc.** He used "to cheat of a prize" <note>original Greek: καταβραβεύειν</note> in the same way one says "to out-wrestle" or "to trip up" <note>original Greek: καταπαλαίειν</note>, and thus to hinder you from reaching the prize and the palm of victory. This is what they do who lead Christians <margin>50</margin> away from the true path of doctrine. He calls "modesty" that which only *appears* to be modesty. Such is that line of Terence: "Looking at the ground modestly," that is, with the appearance of modesty. And Juvenal: "When now the roof walks in a dizzy circle, and the table rises up with twin lamps." For he is speaking of drunkards, to whom these things seem to happen. And the same author, a little later in that same sixth Satire, calls Clodius a "female lutanist" because he wore the dress of a lutanist. So therefore Paul in this place calls it "modesty" when a man humbles himself <margin>60</margin> so that he modestly abstains from certain foods, as he will soon declare. Where he translates "pleasing himself," the Greek is "willing" <note>original Greek: θέλων</note>, translated from the Hebrew word <note>original Hebrew: חפץ - chaphets</note>, which at other times is usually said as "being well pleased" <note>original Greek: εὐδοκῶν</note>, as in Matthew 27: "let him deliver him now, if he

<column-break/>

wills him," that is, "if he is well pleased in him." For it is in the Hebrew, in Psalm 22, from which that place is translated: <unclear>for he delighted in him</unclear> <note>original Hebrew: בי חפץ בו - ki chaphets bo</note>. Likewise Psalm 115: "all things whatsoever he willed, he did," <note>original Greek: πάντα ὅσα ἠθέλησεν ἐποίησεν</note> using the same Hebrew root. "Worship of angels" <note>or "genii"</note>, he calls the practice of those who were worshipping angels <note>original Greek: σέβων</note>: instead of "imitations." As in John 8: "the things which you have heard from your father, you do." <margin>10</margin>

**And not holding the Head, from whom.** In the Greek, "head" is of the feminine gender, but "from whom" is masculine: for it refers to the reality, not the grammatical word, so that the "head" is Christ, "from which" Christ, etc.

**Dead as far as the rudimentary things of the world are concerned.** That is, you now have nothing to do with the first institution of the world, which are "rudiments" or "elements" necessary for children but useless for adults (and Christians are adults). He said "departed from the elements" <note>original Greek: ἀπελθόντι ἀπὸ στοιχείων</note>, just as the Latins say, "Prepared in terms of money," that is, as far as money is concerned.

<margin>20</margin> **Do not handle.** namely, unclean things. **Do not taste.** that is, do not eat: just as Caesar records that the Britons do not "taste" hare. **Do not touch.** Not only must it not be tasted, but not even touched. This is an imitation of the speech of those who were forbidding these things. Paul's words follow: "All of which things," he says, "are such that they perish with the use." For I translate it thus: "which are all for corruption in the using" <note>original Greek: ἅ ἐστι πάντα εἰς φθορὰν τῇ ἀποχρήσει</note>. As in Acts 8: "I see that thou art in the gall of bitterness": that is, I see him to be one whom bile threatens, and who is destined for punishment. So here: "All these things" (says Paul) that <margin>30</margin> is, all foods (which those people forbid tasting) are destined to perish by being used; otherwise there would be no use for them, and they would perish without purpose, and thus God would have made something useless. He placed the same sentiment in the letter to the Corinthians: "The belly for meats, and meats for the belly." He used "consuming" <note>original Greek: ἀποχρήσει</note> instead of "using" <note>original Greek: χρήσει</note>: just as Cato is accustomed to say "misuse" <note>original Latin: abuti</note> to mean to consume by using. And Isocrates in the *Panegyric* said "having used up" <note>original Greek: καταχρησάμενοι</note> with the same notion.

**And they pertain to the satisfying of the body, not that they are in any honor.** These words from the end of the chapter I have moved to this place for the sake of clarity, just as I <margin>40</margin> did in John 1 regarding "full of grace and truth." For that which he said about foods is an addition: they were prepared to be consumed by use and to fill the body and the belly, not so that they should be "in honor"—that is, not so that so much honor should be paid to them that it becomes a sin to touch them.

**These are indeed decrees.** To the word, it is "Which are" <note>original Greek: ἅ ἐστιν</note>: which I wanted to explain more clearly, otherwise it would be more obscure because of the words placed in between.

**That they may have a reputation for wisdom.** So that a "reason" <note>or "account"</note> can be given for them as if they were wisely done, <margin>50</margin> because they seem to be done modestly and religiously, and because in that continence the body is treated severely and harshly. Moreover, he used "in" <note>original Greek: ἐν</note> for "because of," as above: "let no one judge you in food," and in Ephesians 3: "I ask that you do not lose heart in my tribulations."

### FROM CHAPTER IV.

**Redeeming the time.** Things that are bought are dear <note>expensive</note>; and therefore we take care to keep them diligently, so as not to misuse them. To "redeem the time" is therefore to value time highly, and to take care <margin>60</margin> lest it be lost or badly spent. That is, to use the whole time well, and not to let any opportunity for doing right pass by.

<summary>This page provides a philological commentary on Colossians 2 and 4, explaining Paul's warnings against legalistic "ordinances" by analyzing Greek grammar, Hebrew idioms, and classical references. The author emphasizes that Christ has canceled the legal debt ("handwriting") and that external rituals like food prohibitions are merely "shadows" compared to the reality of Christ.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the philological commentary on the Epistles, moving from 1 Thessalonians and 2 Thessalonians into the first chapters of 1 Timothy. The translator continues to resolve grammatical difficulties by appealing to Hebrew idioms (Hebraisms) and classical precedents in authors like Pliny and Cicero.</meta>

ANNOTATIONS. FROM CHAPTER II. 196

# ON THE FIRST EPISTLE
## TO THE THESSALO-
### nians.

#### FROM CHAPTER IV.

**We who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord.** That is, the Christians who will remain. For he does not speak as if he himself were going to remain. Such is that speech of Moses to the Israelites in Deuteronomy 1: "At that time I set before you that I alone could not lead you," etc. This means: "I set before your fathers." For when Moses said those things to the people, those to whom he had set them were already dead.

# ON THE SECOND EPISTLE
## TO THE THESSALO-
### nians.

#### FROM CHAPTER I.

**They will suffer punishment from the Lord.** "From the face" <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ προσώπου</note> is a <term>Hebraism</term> <note>an idiom derived from Hebrew grammar</note> from the word *mipne* <note>original Hebrew: מפני</note>, which is often put in place of "from" <note>original Hebrew: מן</note>, just as in Greek *apo tinos* is used for *hypo tinos* or simply *hypo*, etc. That is, they will be punished by the Lord, or they will pay the penalty to the Lord. Thus "to pay the penalty" <note>original Greek: δίκην τίνειν</note> is used in a passive sense, just as in Latin it is said "he perished by a stronger man," which means "he was killed."

#### FROM CHAPTER II.

**That day will not come unless the falling away comes first, etc.** What he calls the "falling away," he soon declares when he says: "It only remains that he who now restrains be taken out of the way." This means: that the nations should fall away from the Roman who now reigns. For just as it was necessary for the kingdom to be snatched from the Jews before Christ came to earth, so it was necessary for the Romans to be deprived of their empire before the arrival of the Antichrist. However, be careful not to think Paul is speaking of a falling away from the faith of Christ. For that falling away is the very reign of the Antichrist. But Paul speaks of two things, one of which will precede the other: that the political falling away precedes the state of being Antichristian.

**And he shall appear, the man...** "To be revealed" <note>original Greek: ἀποκαλυφθῆναι</note> is said in the sense of "to exist" or "to arrive," as elsewhere and in Luke 17.

**Whose wicked coming, etc.** That is, he who, being wicked when he arrives, will perform false wonders, etc. He calls them "false wonders" because they only seem to be wonders, when they are actually tricks and lies—as if someone persuaded another to pretend to be lame, and then "healed" him. Such are the miracles of the Antichrist; let no one think they will be true miracles, since Paul calls them false.

# ON THE FIRST EPISTLE
## TO TIMOTHY.

#### FROM CHAPTER I.

**Endless genealogies.** "Generations" <note>original Greek: γενεὰς</note>, like the Hebrew *toldot* <note>original Hebrew: תלדות</note>, is not only a lineage but also an age or era. From this comes Paul’s "genealogy," which Josephus and others call "archaeology" <note>ancient history</note>. Pliny, in his preface, calls it "antiquity."

<column-break/>

#### FROM CHAPTER II.

**But the woman will be saved.** That is, women will be saved (for it makes no difference which number you use when speaking of the whole group) through the procreation of children. That is: since she pays the penalty for her sin in this life while she gives birth to children in pain, so that this "childbearing" <note>original Greek: τεκνογονία</note> refers to the whole class of women, not to a single woman. For it would go badly for women if sterile or unmarried ones could not be saved. Women will be saved, therefore, but only if they remain in their duty. For "if they remain" <note>original Greek: μείνωσι</note> is said of "women" with a change in number <note>from singular to plural</note>, which is common among the Hebrews; as in chapter 5 of this epistle: "If any widow has children or descendants, let them learn" <note>original Greek: μανθανέτωσαν</note>, meaning the widows. Therefore, the ancient translator correctly rendered it in both places using the singular number.

#### FROM CHAPTER III.

**The husband of one wife.** In the East, individual men sometimes had several wives at the same time, which is still done today by the Turks and the Jews. Therefore, Paul requires greater temperance in a bishop than in others; thus he forbids him to have two at once.

**Vindicated by the spirit.** "He was justified" <note>original Greek: ἐδικαιώθη</note> is used here as it is in Luke 7: "they justified God" <note>original Greek: ἐδικαίωσαν τὸν θεὸν</note>, meaning the tax collectors commended and praised God. Moreover, Christ was commended and approved through the spirit when the Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove at his washing <note>baptism</note>. Likewise, he was seen by the spirits <note>angels</note> who announced him to the shepherds.

#### FROM CHAPTER IV.

**Through the hypocrisy of lying men.** I have added "men," lest the "liars" and the following words be referred back to the "demons."

**Forbidding to marry, [commanding] to abstain from foods.** This sentence is shortened, and should be expanded so that you say "commanding not to" instead of just "forbidding," in this way: "Commanding that marriages not be contracted, and commanding that one abstain from foods." I have added nothing because authors also speak this way in Latin. For example, Pliny in Book 25, Chapter 5, concerning hellebore: "They forbid it to be given to old men and children, likewise to those of a soft or feminine body or mind, to the slender or tender, and to women less than men." This is from Pliny, where the word "forbid" is not to be joined with the words "to women less than men," but expanded thus: "They command that it not be given to the old, and they command that less be given to women than to men." Likewise Cicero in *On the Ends of Good and Evil*, Book 2: "Rightly therefore he denies that Gallonius ever dined well; rightly [he calls him] miserable," etc. This should be expanded: "Rightly he says Gallonius never dined well; rightly he says he was miserable." For Laelius did not deny that he was miserable, but affirmed it, as the poems placed a little before show, in which Laelius speaks thus in the work of Lucilius:
"O Publius, O glutton Gallonius, you are a miserable man;
You have never dined well in your life," etc.

#### FROM CHAPTER V.

**Let them first teach their own family.** The word "let them learn" <note>original Greek: μανθανέτωσαν</note> is plural, even though "widow" is singular, which is a <term>Hebraism</term> as we indicated in chapter 2. Moreover, "let them learn" is used here for "let them teach" <note>original Greek: διδασκέτωσαν</note>, somewhat loosely, as Paul is sometimes accustomed to speak; just as in French *apprendre* <note>to learn/to teach</note> and in German *lehren* <note>to teach</note> can mean both to teach and to learn.

and to learn. Therefore, it is the same thing whether it says, "let them learn to rule their own house" <note>original Greek: μανθανέτωσαν τὸν ἴδιον οἶκον</note>, or whether children or descendants (which is the same) should "show piety" <note>original Greek: εὐσεβεῖν</note>. This is the same as "let them support their children" <note>original Greek: τεκνοτροφησάτωσαν</note>, a word he uses a little later, and "showing piety" is the same as "returning recompense to their ancestors" <note>original Greek: ἀμοιβὰς ἀποδιδόναι τοῖς προγόνοις</note>.
And this is the meaning: Those who are truly widows should not
marry (as he taught in 1 Corinthians 7) but, remaining single,
should teach their own family, not a foreign one through marriage, and
bring up their children. But if any widow does not take care of
her own, she has denied the faith, as Paul says a little
<margin>10</margin> later, where he calls "their own and their household" <note>original Greek: τοὺς ἰδίους & οἰκείους</note> the same ones he here calls "their own house" <note>original Greek: ἰδίῳ οἴκῳ</note>. But if you refer "let them learn" <note>original Greek: μανθανέτωσαν</note> to the children
or grandchildren, Paul would seem to be giving instructions
not to the widows, but to the children, even though in this place he is giving precepts to widows—unless you say it is the same thing whether the children learn or the
mother teaches. But "showing piety" <note>original Greek: εὐσεβεῖν</note> would then be said of the parents, whereas it is never (as far as I know) referred to ancestors,
but is always said of the family or descendants,
just as in Latin *domus* (house) or *familia* (family).

**After they began to grow wanton, rejecting Christ.** <note>original Latin: Postquam Christum repudiantes lasciuire coeperunt</note>)
<margin>20</margin> "They grew wanton against Christ" <note>original Greek: ἐστρηνίασαν κατὰ τοῦ χριστοῦ</note>. It is, 
however, used in contrast, so that "to grow wanton against Christ" <note>original Greek: καταστρηνιάσαι τοῦ χριστοῦ</note> means to reject Christ, to whom she had devoted herself, to 
break faith with him, and to seek another suitor. Moreover, "to grow wanton" <note>original Greek: καταστρηνιάσειν</note>
in this place means to act luxuriously, so to speak: just as "to be king" <note>original Greek: βασιλεύειν</note>
is not only to reign, but also to become king, as
we have explained elsewhere.

**That you do these things without any discrimination.** <note>original Latin: Vt haec sine ullo discrimine exequare</note>) It is "prejudgment" <note>original Greek: πρόκριμα</note>,
when one is "preferred" <note>original Greek: προκρίνεται</note> over another: that is, when the
person is looked upon, not the facts, which elsewhere is called "respect of persons" <note>original term: προσωποληψία, or partiality</note>.
<margin>30</margin> And that same "respect of persons" occurs here when
we are more inclined toward someone. I have translated it "without any
discrimination," in the way Maro <note>The poet Virgil</note> speaks:
*Whether he be Trojan or Italian, I shall hold them with no distinction.*

**The sins of some men are evident, etc.** <note>original Latin: Nonnullorum hominum peccata perspicua sunt</note>)
He brings forward a reason why he forbade that hands be 
immediately laid upon anyone, and that they be 
co-opted into the office of teaching. The men who are being 
considered for admission to that office are either wicked or upright. Of the
wicked, some are openly wicked, and their
<margin>40</margin> wickedness "goes before them to judgment" <note>original Latin: iudiciū anteuenit</note>, that is, it is 
evident before their admission is deliberated 
upon. And these indeed must be rejected. The 
wickedness of others is hidden, and they seem to be good men. These 
must not be admitted immediately, but one must delay 
and wait until whatever hidden wickedness there is 
becomes clear. For just as their right actions are evident,
so also if anything is otherwise—that is, if there is some 
hidden vice in them—it too will eventually be 
revealed if one waits. For nothing is so 
<margin>50</margin> hidden that it will not be made manifest. Thus it follows that to 
delay is safest: since if they continue to be 
good, they will be admitted soon enough; but if they are evil, they 
ought not to be admitted.

#### FROM CHAPTER III.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial E featuring a figure in a landscape with trees and classical architecture.</image-desc>
**And by which you have been made faithful.** <note>original Latin: Et per que fidens factus es</note>) That
is, a Christian. Note, <margin>60</margin>
however, that it is not written "you believed" <note>original Greek: ἐπιστεύθης</note>,
but "you were assured" <note>original Greek: ἐπιστώθης</note>, that is, "you became faithful" <note>original Greek: πιστὸς ἐγένου</note>,
a form used like "to be justified" <note>original Greek: δικαιωθῆναι</note>,
"lying" <note>original Greek: ψεύδοντα</note>, etc.

<column-break/>

<page-num>198</page-num>
<header>ON THE EPISTLE OF JAMES.</header>

### ON THE EPISTLE OF JAMES.
#### FROM CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial C featuring figures in a classical landscape setting.</image-desc>
**With his riches.** <note>original Latin: Cum suis copijs</note>) It seems that "the rich man" <note>original Greek: πλουσίῳ</note>, should be read, not "riches" <note>original Greek: πλούτῳ</note>, so that the 
rich man's resources are 
compared to the flower of the grass, 
not his journeys.

#### FROM CHAPTER II.

**Whoever fails in one point is guilty of all.** <note>original Latin: Qui in uno delinquit, is omniũ tenetur</note>) That is, he is equally condemned as if he 
had failed in all, nor does it profit him to have been obedient in others, 
so as to avoid the punishment for that sin; nor can 
his virtues abolish that sin. Just as if someone 
serves a king faithfully, yet commits a capital offense, 
he pays the penalty to a severe king, no less than if he 
had committed many sins. See Ezekiel 3 and 33.

**Show me your faith without your works.** <note>original Latin: Ostende mihi tuam fidem sine tuis operibus</note>) "Without works" <note>original Greek: χωρὶς τῶν ἔργων</note> 
is correctly read in some manuscripts, and so the 
ancient version reads. Let the meaning be: You have faith, as you 
say; I have works. I confess that if I, lacking faith, 
should have works, I would not have enough. But I say that I, since 
I have works, also have faith. For since 
works proceed from faith, it is necessary that where 
these works are, faith is in the same place; otherwise from where 
would they proceed? But you who boast of faith, and lack works, 
do not even have faith. For since 
faith produces works, and without them is dead, it is 
necessary that you, who lack works, also lack faith. 
Otherwise, show it without works. You 
cannot. Therefore, it is nothing, unless works are present.

#### FROM CHAPTER III.

**And setting on fire the course.** <note>original Latin: Et cursum inflammans</note>) "The wheel of nature/birth" <note>original Greek: τροχὸς τῆς γενέσεως</note>, from the 
verb "to run" <note>original Greek: τρέχειν</note>. This is the orb and course of life, which 
properly is nativity or origin. But 
as the Hebrews call men "sons" <note>original Hebrew: בנים, banim</note>, or "children" <note>original Hebrew: ילדים, yeladim</note>, that is, the born 
ones or sons, so in this place "birth/nature" <note>original Greek: γένεσις</note> is said for the 
age of a man: whereas in the first chapter 
it is used for the figure and stature of the body, which 
in Matthew 6 is called "age/stature" <note>original Greek: ἡλικία</note>.

#### FROM CHAPTER IV.

**Degenerate men and women.** <note>original Latin: Degeneres & uiri & fœminæ</note>) He said "adulterers and adulteresses" <note>original Greek: μοιχοὶ καὶ μοιχαλίδες</note>, 
just as Christ called them an "adulterous generation." Because 
you indulge in vices, he says, you are friends of the world, which 
is submerged in vices, and thus you fall away from 
God, and are his enemies. But that indeed does not 
proceed from the Holy Spirit, who is accustomed to confer 
a greater benefit than to be prone toward envy, and the rest 
of the vices I have mentioned, or to 
lead men to them. You fall away from him when you 
envy, and cannot bear for others to excel you: 
that which is a matter not only of envy, but also of pride. 
But God opposes the proud: therefore 
submit yourselves, so that he may favor you. Here you see, 
reader, that this passage is "difficult to understand" <note>original Greek: δυσνόητον</note>, etc. 
not without reason it has been added in some 
Greek texts and in the ancient Latin. For it pertains to what follows: "he yearns."

**We will go into that city, etc.** <note>original Latin: Proficiscemur in illam urbem</note>) And here "let us go" <note>original Greek: πορευσώμεθα</note>, and the other verbs with "o" <note>subjunctive forms</note> are incorrectly read by the ancient version. 
For it is not to be rebuked if someone says, "Let us go." But 
if someone says, "We will go," he is to be rebuked, since 
it is uncertain to him what will be. Therefore, one must add 
"if God permits" <note>original Greek: ἐὰν ὁ θεὸς ἐπιτρέπῃ</note>, as Paul speaks to the 
Corinthians, "if God permits," "God willing," and such things.

Following the previous page's focus on the Epistles of Timothy and James, this section provides detailed linguistic and structural analysis of the First and Second Epistles of Peter, the First Epistle of John, and the Epistle to the Hebrews. The commentator continues to reference the editions of Erasmus and the printer Simon de Colines (Colinaeus) to resolve textual discrepancies.</meta>

<page-num>199 200</page-num>
<header>ANNOTATIONS.</header>

# ON THE FIRST EPISTLE
## OF PETER.
### FROM CHAPTER III.

*As of manifold benefit and life*.) <note>original Greek: ποικίλης χάριτος & καὶ ζωῆς</note> This is how it is read in the edition by Colinaeus <note>Simon de Colines, a prominent 16th-century Parisian printer known for his accurate Greek editions</note>, and correctly so, in my judgment. This is also the case in several subsequent passages where his edition is more corrected than others. I mention this so that his edition may be consulted whenever I appear to differ from other versions; for in many places, it contains readings that were not present in any of the manuscripts used by Erasmus.

# ON THE SECOND EPISTLE
## OF PETER.
### FROM CHAPTER II.

*For if God [spared not] the spirits, etc*.) This is an incomplete sentence <note>In rhetoric, this is called an "anacoluthon," where the author begins a "since" or "if" statement but never provides the concluding clause</note>. Nothing follows to answer the word *if*, as if the author forgot his point after listing so many examples. However, this causes no trouble, because the meaning is easily understood: If God did not spare those ancient spirits, he certainly will not spare these people either.
<margin>30</margin>*Of the perishing degenerate, full of sin*.) He calls the sin of degenerate men "degenerate." Furthermore, the word "ceaseless" <note>original Greek: ἀκαταπαύστου</note> is correctly read in the genitive case, and it is found this way in the Colinaeus edition.
*Of the lustful body*.) <note>original Greek: σαρκὸς ἀσελγείας</note> I believe it should be read as "of the body of lust." Otherwise, it hardly fits if you read "lusts" in the dative plural. This is similar to what is read in the Epistle of Jude, "other flesh" <note>original Greek: σαρκὸς ἑτέρας</note>, in place of "their own."
*They had almost escaped*.) The Colinaeus edition has "almost" <note>original Greek: ὀλίγως</note>, though others read "truly" <note>original Greek: ὄντως</note>. But if you prefer "truly" (as it is in other versions), interpret it thus: Those who would have truly escaped.

### FROM CHAPTER III.

*That the heavens and the earth existed of old, consisting out of water and in water*.) This means that the flooding of water was so great that both heaven—that is, the air—and earth were nothing other than water; that is, they were submerged in water, so that only water remained. The Sibyl <note>An ancient prophetess whose verses were often cited by early Christians to support biblical accounts</note> described it thus:
> The ground shall swim, the mountains swim, the air itself shall float,
> All shall be drink, and the sea shall ruin all.
<margin>50</margin>He used "through water" <note>original Greek: δι’ ὕδωρ</note> instead of "in water" <note>original Greek: ἐν ὕδατι</note>, just as we have written elsewhere regarding the Lord. In Latin, "through the mountains" is the same as "in the mountains." The participle "consisting" <note>original Greek: συνεστῶσα</note> must be repeated, so that there are "consisting heavens" <note>original Greek: οὐρανοὶ συνεστῶτες</note> and a "consisting earth" <note>original Greek: γῆ συνεστῶσα</note>. Here, this word is used to mean "to exist," just as in Cicero’s *On Friendship*, the word "to consist" <note>original Latin: constare</note> is placed this way: "Those things which consist in the whole nature of things and the entire world, these things friendship brings together, and discord scatters." "Through which things" <note>original Greek: δι’ ὧν</note>, that is, by which flood. The world of that time, meaning the people and other animals. This is Peter's argument: Wicked men will think that this state of affairs will last forever, just as it seems to have always been the same. But it was not always the same, nor will it always remain the same: for once the world perished by water, and likewise it will perish by fire.

<column-break/>

# ON THE FIRST EPISTLE
## OF JOHN.
### FROM CHAPTER II.

*What he promised us, that is eternal life*.) The phrase "eternal life" <note>original Greek: τὴν ζωὴν τὴν αἰώνιον</note> is in the accusative case because of the verb "he promised" <note>original Greek: ἐπηγγείλατο</note>; however, since it refers back to the noun "promise" <note>original Greek: ἐπαγγελία</note>, it should be rendered in the nominative case in Latin. <margin>10</margin>The author of Revelation speaks in the same way in Chapter 1: "The mystery of the seven stars, which you saw in my right hand, and the seven lampstands" <note>original Greek: τὸ μυστήριον τ’ ἑπτὰ ἀστέρων... καὶ τὰς ἑπτὰ λυχνίας</note> instead of "and the seven lampstands" in the nominative case. He uses the accusative because of the verb "you saw."

# ON THE EPISTLE
## TO THE HEBREWS.
### FROM CHAPTER IV.

*Lest perhaps the promise should cease, etc*.) <margin>20</margin>The promise will cease when one has already entered into His rest. Therefore, effort must be made to obey while we may, lest if we are too slow in the matter, we be overtaken unexpectedly and thus "seem to have been slow"—that is, we actually were slow. For "to seem" <note>Greek: δοκεῖν, Latin: uideri</note> is sometimes joined to the reality itself in Greek and Latin. For instance, Aristotle says, "all things seem to seek the good" <note>original Greek: πάντα τ’ ἀγαθοῦ ἐφίεσθαι δοκεῖ</note>, which means it is apparent that all things seek the good, or we see that all things seek the good. You will find many such examples in Isocrates, and also in Cicero, such as in *Offices*, Book 1: "We must never, by fleeing danger, allow it to happen that we seem cowardly and fearful"—that is, that we *are* so.
*Not joined with the faith of those who had heard*.) <note>original Greek: μὴ συγκεκραμένους τῇ πίστει τοῖς ἀκούσασι</note> used instead of "the faith of the hearers." Regarding this manner of speaking, see what we wrote on Colossians 2.
*For we who have faith enter into rest*.) <margin>40</margin>This means that only those who have faith enter into rest. The argument is as follows: When David speaks of the Lord's rest, he must be speaking either of the Sabbath, in which God rested, or of the rest which the Israelites obtained when they entered Canaan, or of another rest that is still to come. But he cannot be speaking of the first two, since one of them existed from the very beginning of the world's creation, and the other existed many centuries before David. It is necessary, therefore, that he is speaking of a future rest.

### FROM CHAPTER VI.

*Who through faith and patience*.) The word for "patience" <note>original Greek: μακροθυμία</note> is sometimes derived from the Hebrew "long of nostrils" <note>original Hebrew: ארך אפים</note>, literally "long-tempered" <note>original Greek: μακρὸς θυμῷ</note>, or slow to anger. In Latin, such a person is called "slow" <note>original Latin: lentus</note>; hence this "slowness" is the patience that can sometimes be called mercy or gentleness. Paul usually uses the word in this way. I am not unaware that "slowness" is sometimes considered a vice, but it can also be spoken of as a virtue when you praise that which others might criticize. Sometimes this word for patience is used for "endurance" <note>original Greek: ὑπομονῇ</note>; thus the Evangelists and this author speak, as the context shows when it is joined with hope, such as in 1 Thessalonians 1: "the endurance of hope."

### FROM CHAPTER IX.

*Where there is a testament, it is necessary for the death of the testator to follow*.) The word used here is "covenant" <note>original Hebrew: ברית</note>, which is a treaty or an agreement...

<summary>This page provides philological commentary on the Epistles of Peter, John, and Hebrews, focusing on grammatical cases, textual variants in the Colinaeus edition, and the philosophical definition of "rest" and "patience." It highlights how biblical authors used specific Greek and Hebrew idioms to describe divine judgment, creation, and the virtues of faith.</summary>

--- Page 844 ---
<meta>This page concludes the annotations on the Epistle to the Hebrews and provides the complete commentary on the Book of Revelation (the Apocalypse). It maintains the scholarly focus on Greek and Hebrew philology seen in the previous sections on the Epistles of Peter and John.</meta>

<page-num>202</page-num>
<header>202 ANNOTATIONS ON THE APOCALYPSE 203</header>

In Greek it could be called a *syntheke* <note>original: συνθήκη; a general word for a treaty or pact</note>. However, the sacred authors use *diatheke* <note>original: διαθήκην</note> instead of *syntheke*, a word which properly sounds like "testament" <note>a legal will</note>. This is why we usually call the sacred books the "Old and New Testaments," even though, if you wished to speak in proper Latin, they should be called the "Old and New Covenants" <note>original: fœdus</note>. But the author of this letter, not weighing the force of the Hebrew word, wrote in Greek (for it can be proven from this very passage that this epistle was written in Greek; indeed, no one could argue this way in Hebrew, to turn a pact into a testament and thereby introduce the death of a testator) and drew his argument from the Greek word *diatheke*. He did something similar in Chapter 2, where he used "spirits" <note>original: genios</note> in place of "God." This circumstance was the reason why, in this epistle, we translated *diatheke* as "testament," contrary to our usual practice. Otherwise, if we had translated it as "covenant," this discussion by the author would have no place.

### FROM CHAPTER XI.

**Now faith is the substance of things hoped for.** *Hypostasis* <note>original: ὑπόστασις</note> is substance, the very thing and matter itself, as in Chapter 1 of this epistle. It is transferred to other meanings, as in 2 Corinthians 11: *in this matter of boasting* <note>original Greek: ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ ὑποστάσει τῆς καυχήσεως</note>, meaning in this material or argument for boasting. Nor does it deviate from that notion when it is placed in Chapter 3 of this epistle for the subject of a dispute, or the place of an author which he has proposed for himself to treat, so that it is a *hypostasis* when a thing "subsists" <note>original: ὑφίσταται</note>, is proposed, placed under consideration, and established as present. Therefore, here it is called the "subjection" <note>bringing to presence</note> of those things which are hoped for, because it places under us and proposes things that are absent, and makes them seem to be present. In this passage, *hypostasis* is the same as *elenchos* <note>original: ἔλεγχος; proof or evidence</note>, and "things hoped for" is the same as "from the promise," a doubled sentiment, as appears from the fact that these are joined by no conjunction. Thus, one might join them like this: Faith is the subjection and demonstration of things that are not seen, but hoped for.

**So that from things which were not visible.** <note>original Greek: εἰς τὸ μὴ ἐκ φαινομένων</note> used instead of <note>original Greek: εἰς τὸ ἐκ τῶν μὴ φαινομένων</note> <note>A grammatical note on the Greek word order regarding the negation of things appearing</note>.

**From whence he seems to have received him back in a certain way.** *Parabole* <note>original: παραβολὴ</note> is a comparison and a likeness. Abraham received his son back from the dead "in a figure" <note>original Greek: ἐν παραβολῇ</note>, just as he is said to have sacrificed him a little before. For he neither sacrificed him, nor did he receive him back from death. But since he was about to do it, it is just as if he had sacrificed him, and received him back restored to life. This is what he means by "in a figure," that the thing itself was not actually done, but appeared to have been done.

### FROM CHAPTER XIII.

**By the giving of thanks.** He said *chariti* <note>original: χάριτι; by grace/gratitude</note> instead of *eucharistia* <note>original: εὐχαριστίᾳ</note>, which he soon calls the sacrifice of praise.

**Let us assist constantly.** Written as *adialeiptos* <note>original: ἀδιαλείπτως</note> with a capital <note>likely referring to a large letter in the manuscript</note>, the old version reads correctly. For it is an exhortation, as the tenor of the speech indicates.

## ON THE APOCALYPSE.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'D' depicting a seated figure, possibly a scholar or saint, surrounded by classical architectural motifs and foliage.</image-desc>

There is doubt concerning the author of this book. He calls himself John the Theologian. Who he was, or when he lived, I am no more concerned about than I am about a wine barrel or its age, provided the wine is good. That the author of this book was a true prophet and a disciple of God,

<column-break/>

a disciple of God, I am firmly persuaded; nor do I doubt him any more than I doubt the Gospel of John. And yet, I understand scarcely a thousandth part of this book.

### FROM CHAPTER I.

<margin>10</margin> **From him who is, and who was.** <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ ὁ τοῦ ὁ ὤν καὶ ὁ ἦν</note> instead of <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ ὄντος</note>, etc. But because no participle is derived from the imperfect *en* <note>original: ἦν; "was"</note> (which is usually placed for the past tense), he used the verb itself as a participle—a thing that is sometimes done by the Hebrews. As far as the solecism <note>a grammatical error</note> is concerned (such as follows a little later, "from Jesus Christ the witness" <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ ὁ μάρτυς</note> instead of "of the witness" <note>using the nominative case instead of the genitive</note>), do not be disturbed. Such things often occur even in Paul. You should learn your character from good men, but your speech from the eloquent.

### FROM CHAPTER III.

**I will compel some.** "I give" <note>original: δίδωμι</note> is said in the Hebrew manner, which he says the same way a little later as "I will make them so that," etc.

<margin>20</margin> **The head of the creation of God.** That is, the most excellent and first of all God's works. *Arche* <note>original: ἀρχὴ; beginning/origin</note> is a Hebraism from *reshit* <note>original Hebrew: ראשׁית</note>, as it is said of the elephant in Job 40: *He is the beginning of the ways of God* <note>original Hebrew: הוא ראשית דרכי אל</note>. That is, the most principal of the works of God; or as the French say, *un chef d'oeuvre*, the "head of the work"—that is, the highest and most outstanding work.

### FROM CHAPTER IIII.

<margin>30</margin> **Twenty-four seats.** *Thronoi* <note>original: θρόνοι</note> is both a throne, a judgment seat, and a chair; therefore, he interprets the same word differently at different times, as the meaning requires.

### FROM CHAPTER V.

**Whose number was distributed into millions of hundreds of thousands.** *Myrias myriadon* <note>original: μυριάς μυριάδων</note> are ten hundred thousand <note>one million</note>. *Myriades myriadon* (as it is written here) is this number in the plural. If, for the sake of example, it were "all the myriads of myriads," I would have translated it "three thousand times a hundred thousand." But because it is not written exactly how many times this number should be placed, I <margin>40</margin> translated it thus, lest it be thought this number should be placed only once; but rather that it be understood that those praisers of God were distributed into classes, some of which consisted individually of thousands of hundreds of thousands, others of tens of hundreds of thousands. How many those classes were, however, is not added. And understand this same reasoning in Daniel, Chapter 7.

### FROM CHAPTER VIII.

**That [he might give] the prayers of all saints, etc.** <note>original Greek: ἵνα δώσῃ ταῖς προσευχαῖς</note> I think it should read "the prayers" <note>original Greek: τὰς προσευχὰς</note> in the accusative, and the cause of this error was what follows immediately, "to the prayers" <note>original Greek: ταῖς προσευχαῖς</note> in the dative, the scribe thinking the same thing should be read in both places.

**Of the incense of the prayers of the saints.** "To the prayers" <note>original Greek: ταῖς προσευχαῖς</note> is said in the Hebrew manner instead of "of the prayers." Concerning this, see the observations on the Epistle to the Colossians, Chapter 2.

You have here, Reader, what we were able to provide for the present. If anything has been well said, praise ought to be attributed to God, the giver of all good things; but <margin>60</margin> if any error has been made, forgive us, as you yourself would wish to be forgiven. Hereafter, if God wills that we learn more and better things, we shall give more and better things, God willing.

->THE END.<-

# AN OFFERING TO CHRIST
# FROM XYSTUS. <note>Xystus is the Latinized name of the author, Sixtus Birck.</note>

O Christ, my God, to you I bring these things in awe; receive these gifts from my heart,
Accept these pure and well-intentioned offerings <note>original Greek: "thyēpolias," a term often used for sacred sacrifices or priestly rites.</note>.
I reach out to you, O Christ, with the fruits of my labors in my hands,
And in your goodwill, receive these gifts of the mind <note>The author distinguishes between the physical labor of printing/arranging the book and the intellectual labor of the "mind" (noou).</note>.
Grant me your grace, so that I may lead a blessed life
And a life of purity; to you, O God, be glory and renown.

# TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS AND PRUDENT
# MEN, MESSRS. JOHANN WELSER,
## and Jakob Herbrot, Consuls of the Republic of Augsburg,
### who have served with the highest merit, his lords,
->*SIXTUS BIRCK SENDS GREETINGS.*<- <note>original: "XYSTVS BETVLEIVS S." Sixtus Birck (1501–1554) was a German scholar and rector of the St. Anna School in Augsburg. The "S." stands for "Salutem," a standard Latin greeting meaning "Health" or "Greetings."</note>

<image-desc>Woodcut initial 'V' depicting a standing male figure, likely an apostle or saint (possibly St. Paul), holding a sword in his right hand and a closed book in his left. The figure is framed within an ornate square border filled with scrollwork and foliage.</image-desc>

VARIOUS ARE THE GIFTS, MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MEN, given to mortals from heaven; yet they are given to no one for his own private use, but rather so that each person might contribute his own portion for the praise of God, or for the benefit of his neighbor, and even for the fellowship of human life. To some, the most kind Giver of things has granted the wisdom to rule His people, whom every good person looks up to with due veneration and recognizes as the deputies and stewards <note>original: "œconomos," a term derived from Greek meaning managers of a household or estate</note> of God. Others He has appointed as interpreters of His divine will, to feed His people with the most wholesome nourishment of the life-giving Word. To others He has commanded other duties of Christian charity according to each person’s portion. To me, certainly, the most kind God has delegated a duty in our Republic <note>The Free Imperial City of Augsburg</note>, one which is laborious enough, yet most honorable, and very close to the office of a bishop. I do not judge it by the opinion of the common people, for I easily recognize how much effort a man brings to the Christian Republic when he shapes the minds of the growing citizenry toward piety and skill. In His goodness, God has given me the spirit to do this willingly and to take delight in that which seems to most people a burden heavier than Mount Etna; He has granted, I say, that I might find satisfaction in the progress of boys.

He has given so much support for the administration of this province <note>Birck uses "prouinciam" here in the classical sense of a sphere of duty or specific responsibility—his role as an educator</note> that I easily keep myself within my own modest limits. And truly, I think things have gone splendidly for me when I see some fruit arising from my labors for the use of the Christian Republic. Therefore, when I saw that I was born to endure these labors, literary tasks began to grow sweet to me through habit, so much so that I thought every moment was lost which I did not spend on advancing the study of divine wisdom. Meanwhile, although I easily understood my own insignificance, my plan was—after invoking the favor of the divine power—to undertake a labor on my shoulders which was (as I thought) not unequal to them, and so joined with my school duty that I saw it could be done not only without harming the youth to whom I owe my effort, but that it would even bring a great deal of benefit to our school work. Now, the work I was laboring upon was one which I understood, through my own experience, that students of sacred scripture could only lack with great difficulty and not without the greatest longing. Yet, until now, the difficulty of the labor—which seemed insurmountable—has deterred many from it; though they otherwise easily recognized that they could help their theological studies in no better way. Not a few others, who were otherwise very tolerant of labor, were not deterred by the sheer size of such a praiseworthy undertaking, but were failed by the method of completing the work. When it seemed to me that I possessed this method properly, I shared this plan of mine...

<meta>This page continues Sixtus Birck’s dedication to the leaders of Augsburg. In the previous section, he established that God grants different gifts to different people for the common good. Here, he recounts the specific advice and encouragement he received from his colleagues to begin the arduous task of compiling a Greek concordance of the New Testament.</meta>

# XYSTUS BETULEIUS 
<note>The Latinized name of Sixtus Birck (1501–1554), the author of this work and rector of the St. Anna School in Augsburg.</note>

...with that man, without whose approval—owing to the proven faithfulness I saw in him—I was accustomed to undertake nothing rashly; I speak of Boniface Lycosthenes <note>Bonifacius Lycosthenes (also known as Wolfhart), a prominent Reformer and pastor in Augsburg</note>, at that time the most skillful leader of our church. I told him that if my effort were approved by him, I had resolved to arrange what they call Concordances <note>A reference work that lists every word in a text and where to find it</note> for the Greek New Testament. When he had kindly praised these holy efforts of mine and had embraced them warmly, he implored me by Christ, the common redeemer of mortals, not to withdraw my foot from such a laudable and pious plan. He kept stating that this task uniquely belonged to his own profession; and he affirmed that regarding sacred studies, so far as it concerned the reconciling of passages of divine scripture, they were otherwise well-provided for. However, he said the convenience of such studies would only be complete if this one work of mine were added. 

He noted that Latin Concordances for the whole Bible did indeed exist, and while they brought very many and great fruits to the study of Theology, they could not be solid and mature because of the variety of interpretations. For not only does Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus (1466–1536), whose new Latin translation of the New Testament often challenged the traditional church version</note> himself often vary from the old interpreter <note>The "old interpreter" refers to the Vulgate, the standard Latin translation of the Bible used for centuries</note>, but both of them often interpret the same words in different ways. For this reason, he said I would find no less favor from scholars than the compiler of the Hebrew Concordances had found, whose work he praised to the skies. This example pleased me, though I am ignorant of that most holy language <note>Birck admits here that he does not know Hebrew, though he is an expert in Greek</note>. For we cannot all do everything; and various gifts have been granted to mortals by the most kind God, as I have said before.

He added, moreover, firm reasons by which he might strengthen my plan and inflame my mind—otherwise already eager—to undertake this laudable work. He said—what all truly learned men confess—that it is established that without knowledge of the Greek language, no less than that holy one <note>Hebrew</note>, a professor of Theology cannot skillfully perform his duty. And for that reason, there is a need for Greek Concordances for the New Testament, no less than for the Hebrew for the Old. For in those original languages, there is not only clear perspicuity but also a solid foundation and a ready method of explanation when, as usually happens, discussions lead to "logomachies" <note>original: "logomachias," meaning arguments or battles over the specific meaning of words</note>. 

Why say more? The reasons for this sacred and honorable task were established; its necessary utility was established. There remained the difficulty of the task. Since he could not diminish this while remaining truthful, he preferred to soothe it rather than take it upon himself. He pointed out that this work was very closely joined to my school labors. He noted that the task of reading the New Testament had been assigned to me, and at other times, themes had to be dictated to the boys; therefore, in the task of sorting—which would be the most tedious drudgery of all—I could use the labor of my students. 

Why say more? He persuaded me all the more easily because piety had already commanded the same. Thus, with Christ as my guide, I took up the burden, which right from the start appeared far heavier than I had thought. He encouraged me diligently so that I would not fail. When I had already made some progress, Ambrose Blaurer <note>Ambrosius Blaurer (1492–1564), an influential German Reformer</note> came to us (you know what kind of man he is). While he was staying with our Boniface, performing an apostolic function among us for some time, I became more familiar with him due to the domestic intimacy I shared with them. Having understood...

# PREFACE

...He began to embrace me with even greater love for these labors of mine than before, and diligently encouraged me to proceed; nor, in the meantime, while I was completing the work, did he cease to urge me through letters. Furthermore, **Simon Grynaeus** <note>Simon Grynaeus (1493–1541) was a famous German scholar and theologian who helped reform the University of Tübingen</note>, a man as holy as he was absolutely learned in every branch of knowledge, when he understood from me that I had undertaken this Work, begged me with the greatest effort—and even commanded me by his own right over me—that I should undertake no other labors until I had first put an end to these. While he was alive, the authority of this one man alone carried as much weight with me as the most extensive influence; his authority alone could have authorized me to undergo such a great burden. 

But what shall I say of our **Wolfgang Musculus** <note>Wolfgang Musculus (1497–1563) was a prominent Reformer and influential theologian in Augsburg and later Bern</note>? When he realized that this Work would be useful for his own studies, he insisted I proceed almost shamelessly, often with what seemed like reproaches, acting like a <term>taskmaster</term> <note>original Greek: "ergodioctes," meaning one who drives or oversees laborers</note>. The entire order of Preachers here among us approved of my undertaking and praised my indefatigable endurance for labor quite kindly—though they were all more ready to encourage than to take up the burden themselves. 

**Wolfgang Weissenburg** <note>Wolfgang Weissenburg (1496–1575) was a theologian, geographer, and professor at Basel</note>, professor of sacred Theology at the renowned Basel and my teacher (to say the least), a man to be especially honored by me, also added his own goad. Furthermore, many friends urged me on. As equity itself dictated that I should comply with them, even though I was often exhausted to the extreme, I was loath for so much labor as had already been spent to have perished for me in vain. 

I saw, meanwhile, how much of my time was slipping away—time which I felt I could have spent on more useful studies. For my mocking reason was flattering those more "profane" Muses <note>A reference to classical Greek and Latin literature, which Birck also loved and edited</note>, as if all these efforts were being made to their detriment. The love of possession and the desire for honor supported this clever reasoning; for consultants, as you know, can be corrupted. No hope of reward appeared from that immense mass of labor, and no opportunity for the display of my own wit was left. 

But against these thoughts, the Spirit of Christ said: "Well done! <note>original: "Macte virtute"</note> Do not succumb to these labors. You do not know that this talent of yours has been entrusted to you by divine providence." Therefore, having often gathered my strength from exhaustion in this way, I renewed my labors and repeatedly recalled the work I had set aside. And indeed, that work which I spent five years in writing brought with it some degree of utility and delight; however, the remaining three years given to the distribution and organization of the text contained nothing at all besides troubles and boredom—except for this one thing: I knew I was serving a most powerful and magnificent Lord. 

My students lightened this burden for me in great part, for they performed excellent work in this matter, and they must not be cheated of their praise. This work, I say, will rightly be called the work of the **Augsburg School** everywhere among nations and in every age. It will have this monument, which shall not perish until that great day of the Lord arrives. I hope that I have contributed my portion to the religion of Christ in such a way that neither the **Roman Pontiff** <note>The Pope</note> nor the **Council of Trent** <note>The major Catholic ecumenical council (1545–1563) held to counter the Reformation</note> with the whole clergy will have reason to proscribe it; nor will the inquisitors of "heretical depravity" (if it pleases the gods) find anything to attack; nor will the proponents of vain opinions find anything in these pages to rebuke. But if they themselves were as ready to undertake such labors...

<meta>catchword: ready,</meta>

He dedicates the work to the Augsburg School and asserts its theological neutrality against potential Catholic censorship.</summary>

# PREFACE

...[if they were as] ready [to support] as they are inclined to pursue the truth of Christ, things would certainly be better for the Christian world than they are. Books of this kind reconcile dissenting opinions and offer a genuine interpretation of the Divine Scripture. I especially wished to share this great convenience for explaining heavenly doctrine with the Christian and Catholic Church under your name, most distinguished men, because I see you striving with the greatest zeal so that the glory of Christ may flourish as much as possible in our Republic. I acknowledge that I owe this to you out of duty. Nor do I think I could appoint any more upright guardians for my labors than you, who are the most skillful guardians of our Christian Republic. Therefore, take this gift along with its author into your patronage, so that the author may understand he is placing his work at the service of the Christian community, if you continue (as you are doing) to promote literature—indeed, the business of the School, as the foundation of the Christian Republic—according to your wisdom. Farewell.

->To Your Excellencies<-
->most devotedly<-
->**Xystus Betuleius.**<- <note>Xystus Betuleius is the Latinized name of Sixtus Birck (1501–1554), a noted humanist, schoolmaster, and dramatist in Augsburg.</note>

->TO THE KIND READER<-
->Xystus Betuleius sends greetings.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' depicting a scene with two figures in a landscape; one figure is seated on the ground on the left, while the other stands or walks on the right, perhaps representing a teacher and a student or a biblical encounter.</image-desc>

*I explained the reasons for undertaking this labor in the dedication itself. Now I believe I will do something worthwhile if I teach the pious reader in what ways this "Symphony" <note>original: "Symphonia." Birck uses this term rather than "concordance" to emphasize the "sounding together" or harmony of the biblical texts.</note> of ours differs from the Latin Concordances, which I had nevertheless set before myself as a model from the beginning. But as usually happens in the construction of buildings, the progress itself taught me many things. If these reflections had entered my mind from the start, the work could have risen much more splendidly. A certain theologian had begun this work before me, quite laudably; but when he did not grasp the method for completing it, he asked me to prescribe for him some brief plan for finishing this work. When he saw that the difficulty was greater than expected, he was deterred by it; failing in his labor at the very threshold, he shamefully abandoned this most holy work (not yet properly begun) just as laudably as he had started it. When I realized this, I thought I could not better invest my small talent <note>A reference to the Parable of the Talents in Matthew 25:14–30; Birck uses "talentulum" to humbly describe his own skill.</note> than by bringing this little portion of mine to the common use of students. This could have been, as I said, more polished if I had organized it differently from the start than the Latin Concordances are. But progress warned me about many things which I thought would not be unwelcome to a student of theology—though most of them came quite late. The compilers of the Latin Concordances first placed the <term>declinable parts</term> <note>original: "partes declinabiles." These are words that change form, such as nouns, adjectives, and verbs.</note> first, as if the substance of things were located primarily in them; but in the course of time, it was understood how much power, and how much energy or emphasis, often lies in the indeclinable parts <note>Words that do not change form, such as adverbs, conjunctions, and prepositions.</note>...*

<meta>This page continues the technical introduction to the Greek concordance. The author, Sixtus Birck, is explaining the linguistic difficulties of translating Greek into Latin and how he has organized this reference work to be more precise than existing Latin concordances.</meta>

### TO THE READER

α 4 <note>Signature mark indicating the fourth leaf of the first gathering.</note>

<meta>catchword: since</meta>

...[if they] were with them, some added those as well, but separately. Truly, how often the variation of interpreters occurs in both languages is more easily understood by those learned in Hebrew and Greek than I can signify in a few words. I will provide one example of uninflected words <note>original: "τῶν ἀκλίτων"; these are particles or adverbs that do not change their form</note> from which the rest can easily be gathered. Interpreters translate the Greek words *choris*, *ektos*, *para*, and *plen* <note>original: "χωρίς, ἐκτὸς, παρὰ, πλὴν"</note> all as the Latin *praeter* <note>meaning: "except" or "besides"</note>. But they sometimes translate *plen* <note>original: "τὸ πλὴν"</note> as *praeter*; at other times as *quin* <note>but</note>, or *quinimo* <note>nay rather</note>; and frequently even as *attamen* <note>nevertheless</note>. There is not much danger in these instances even if the interpreters vary among themselves, but they nonetheless serve as proof that no one can correctly rely on **Latin Concordances**, since this discrepancy often happens even in words that are highly significant and most emphatic <note>original: "ἐμφατικωτάτοις"</note>. What of the fact that words frequently occur which no Latin interpreter could translate without a long explanation to express the nature of the thing? What of the fact that Latin Concordances serve only the old and common translation <note>referring to the Vulgate Bible</note>, being almost useless for others? *Plerophoria* and *plerophoreo* <note>original: "πληροφορία & πληροφορέω"; meaning "full assurance" and "to fully satisfy/fulfill"</note> are apostolic words; but if you look in the Latin Concordances, you will find hardly anything other than *plenitudinem* <note>fullness</note>; yet this is something far different from either *pleroma* or *plerosis* <note>original: "πλήρωμα, πλήρωσις"; different nuances of "fullness" or "completion"</note> or anything else of that sort.

In the Latin works, so that the infinite forest of a single naming might be organized, they are distinguished only by the difference of numbers, while the variety of meanings remains; this lightens the trouble of searching in some way. We, consulting your needs better, have distinguished between **homonyms** <note>terms that are spelled the same but have different meanings</note>, and as far as the correction was completed, we have observed the modes of speaking derived from the same verb. We have arranged **passive** and **middle** voices separately from **active** ones, but we have placed the participles of both under the roots of their own verbs. We have, however, given specific headings to words acting as participles.

The Latin concordances have one convenience which we were by no means able to attain. For throughout the entire Bible, individual chapters are distinguished by certain letter characters <note>A system of dividing chapters into sections A, B, C, D, etc., used before standard verse numbering was universal</note>, to which the letters in the Concordances correspond. Because the editions of the **Greek Bibles** for the most part lack these, we were unable to achieve what we wished. I said "for the most part" because in that larger **Froben edition of the New Testament** <note>The landmark Greek New Testament printed by Hieronymus Froben in Basel, famously edited by Erasmus</note>, especially in the Gospels and in Paul’s epistles to the **Romans** and **Corinthians**, certain letters are assigned between the chapter headings from an ancient Greek codex, if I am not mistaken. Because these had been neglected from the beginning, it would have been a labor of infinite effort to correct the neglect. And I certainly would have corrected it, had not a certain most learned man, very close to me and long-engaged in the study of sacred letters, drawn me back from this useless labor; saying what was true: that I would disadvantage the student of **Theology** more with this work than I would benefit him, since no small editions have those markers. Furthermore, there is something that the student will perhaps wonder at: why we have often prefixed a Latin interpretation to the same word, right at the root or the title of the naming, without a distinction of meanings. This was done especially when...

<summary>Birck explains the technical superiority of his Greek concordance over Latin ones, noting that Latin often collapses nuanced Greek theological terms into single, imprecise words. He also discusses his editorial decisions regarding verb voices and the lack of standardized chapter markers in Greek manuscripts compared to the Latin Vulgate.</summary>
<keywords>Greek language, Latin Concordances, biblical translation, linguistics, Froben edition, New Testament, homonyms, theology, Sixtus Birck</keywords>

### TO THE READER

...since every opportunity for amending the original plan was closed off. Furthermore, because diverse interpretations of a single word are often nearly synonymous, and seeing that Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus (c. 1466–1536), whose Latin translation of the New Testament was a major humanist milestone</note> himself was not overly scrupulous about these small details, I did not wish to appear more superstitious than him in these matters. Additionally, at the start, I had no intention of adding word interpretations, as I was not committed to any single translation; but eventually, in the final arrangement of the work, when the subject matter seemed to require it, and the desire to avoid ambiguity <note>original: "homonymiæ"</note> demanded it, reason persuaded me—not without a doubling of my labors—to observe these things more studiously, to the point that I even wished at times to indicate the Erasmian version. Meanwhile, however, as I said, setting translations aside, I assigned the meanings that came to mind <note>original Latin idiom: "quae in buccam ueniebant," literally "whatever came into the mouth"</note>. We wished to advise you of this, pious Reader, so that you might have some understanding of the reasoning behind this work. If I have satisfied you, I am glad; if not, remember that the opportunity for doing better has been left to you. **Farewell.**

---

# ON THE HARMONY OF THE NEW TESTA-
## ment by Sixtus Birck, a poem by Sebastian
### Castellio <note>Sebastian Castellio (1515–1563) was a French theologian and a leading figure in the early proponents of religious toleration</note>.

In the sacred letters there are not a few words
That are obscure; yet if you compare them from many places,
They become clear, and in place of commentaries
They often reveal the matter, not to mention the speech itself.
But in order to compare them, it is necessary to hold
The locations in mind: and so that the locations might be at your hand,
In the Greek books of the New Covenant <note>original: "fœderis noui"</note>
Sixtus Birck has achieved this with the greatest labor,
With the words brought back into alphabetical order,
And with the Latin meaning rendered for each one.

### ON THE CONCORDANCE OF SIXTUS BIRCK,
### extemporaneous trimeters <note>A poetic meter consisting of three pairs of iambic feet, common in Greek drama and verse</note> by Conrad Gessner <note>Conrad Gessner (1516–1565) was a monumental Swiss scholar, physician, and "father of bibliography," who likely shared Birck's passion for organizing vast amounts of information</note>.

For a mortal to help fellow transitory mortals, 
And to bring a shared vision to life for all— 
Not leaning only toward oneself or one's own profit, 
Nor looking away from others— 
This is a divine and venerable way of thinking, 
Surpassing the ordinary nature of man. 
But he is even more to be envied if he should well educate 
Minds, which are superior to the body, 
Through wisdom, speech, and every kind of virtue. 
Most supreme of all, and by nature 
Closest to being an equal and likeness of God, 
Is he who shares his skill and art with mortals, 
Providing them at once with an instrument of great joy. 
Such is the Harmony <note>original: "Συμφωνίαν" (*Symphonian*). In the context of 16th-century biblical study, this refers to a Concordance, which "harmonizes" the text by linking every occurrence of a word</note> of the New Testament 
That Sixtus Birck <note>original: "Ξύστος Σημύδας" (*Xystos Semydas*). *Semyda* is the Greek word for "Birch," mirroring his German name *Birck* and Latin name *Betuleius*</note> has produced in his writing, 
Desiring to be a benefactor to all. 
From this work, the seeker of Divine Scripture 
Will draw varied use. For this is no hateful 
Mortal invention, nor a mere story; 
Rather, Scripture explains itself, 
Through the gathering of many similar passages. 
Indeed, the Gospel is best understood 
From the Greek tongue, in which it was first written— 
Just as the Old Testament was written in Hebrew. 
Often, a great light shines forth 
From the original words. 
Therefore, you who are living now and those in time to come, 
All you who are God-fearing and lovers of Greek <note>original: "φιλέλληνες" (*philellēnes*)</note> 
Who diligently seek the sacred books, 
Praise this most beautiful Harmony greatly, 
Make use of it, and speak well of the craftsman, 
Owing him your gratitude.
